The city itself is the hero, speaking through its streets, flats, and lunch counters. O. Henry's humour is warm and his endings are neat, though never merely clever. The book is a fine sample of his New York manner at its most humane, and a good companion to his earlier city tales.
14478-the-story-of-the-american-legion-t:
George Seay Wheat wrote this 1919 history of the American Legion's birth, the first of a series planned after each national convention. Putnam published it with illustrations of the St. Louis caucus.

Wheat follows veterans from latter war days in France through the Paris caucus of March 1919, the advance committee, and the St. Louis meeting in May, then covers Bolshevism, conscientious objectors, and jobs for returning soldiers. The book prints the constitution and resolutions. It captures the Legion's founding hopes and quarrels from inside. Wheat wrote as a participant observer close to the organizers.
1449-the-valley-of-the-moon:
Jack London's novel follows Saxon Brown and Billy Roberts, a young Oakland couple of working people, from dance halls and prizefights to the road. After strikes, hardship, and a bitter city life, they set out on foot and by wagon to find a valley of their own in the California hills.

Their search becomes a story of labour, love, and the land, as they learn farming, meet country folk, and dream of a small holding where work can be free. London's sympathy for working people runs warm throughout. The book is a long, earnest romance of California and the hope of a fresh start.
14495-de-carmine-pastorali-prefixed-to-t:
René Rapin's treatise On Pastoral Poetry, prefixed to Thomas Creech's 1684 translation of Theocritus, is reprinted here by the Augustan Reprint Society in 1947, with an introduction by J. E. Congleton. Rapin wrote as a French critic of the classical tradition.

The treatise divides bucolic matter into low, middle, and high, citing Virgil's fourth eclogue and its bushes, shrubs, and woods as emblems of rising subjects. Rapin argues for decorum in shepherd poetry. The reprint gives students a key text of neoclassical criticism, short, learned, and influential in its day. Creech's Theocritus translation carried Rapin to English readers.
14518-handbook-of-home-rule-being-articl:
James Bryce edited this 1887 handbook of articles on Irish Home Rule, with a preface by Earl Spencer and pieces by Gladstone, John Morley, Lord Thring, Canon MacColl, E. L. Godkin, and R. Barry O'Brien. The second edition gathered new and reprinted essays.

The articles argue the case for an Irish legislature, answer lawyers' objections, and spell out reserved imperial powers, from foreign money to copyright. The handbook was a campaign document for Gladstone's Home Rule cause, written for voters and MPs. It remains a clear statement of the constitutional argument as it stood before the bill's defeat.
14525-prefaces-to-fiction:
This Augustan Reprint Society volume of 1952, with an introduction by Benjamin Boyce, gathers prefaces to fiction from 1674 to 1754. The pieces show how novelists defended a new form.

Scudéry prefaces Ibrahim, and Mary Manley prefaces The Secret History of Queen Zarah. D'Argens contributes a letter from The Jewish Spy, Warburton prefaces Richardson's Clarissa, and Derrick prefaces a memoir of Count Du Beauval. Together they argue for romance, history, and moral purpose. The collection is a short, useful source for students of the early novel. Boyce's introduction places each preface in its moment.
14535-a-christmas-sermon:
Robert Louis Stevenson wrote this short Christmas sermon, published in New York in 1900, as a valedictory piece after a year of magazine writing. Stevenson opens with Charles II's dying wit.

He urges readers to be honest and kind, to earn a little and spend a little less, to make a family happier, and to keep friends without surrender. The heroism he praises is patience, not grand gesture. The sermon is brief, humane, and personal, and it remains a favorite Stevenson piece for the Christmas season. Readers still quote its counsel on kindness at Christmas.
1455-the-hated-son:
Balzac's historical tale opens in a sixteenth-century bedroom, where the Comtesse d'Herouville bears a child she comes to hate, believing it the fruit of a crime. The boy grows up scorned by his mother and protected only by a loyal servant, while court intrigue and family honour swirl around him.

Through two parts, How the Mother Lived and its sequel, the story traces a mother's cruelty and a son's struggle for a place in a house that rejects him. Balzac's tone is stern and pitying by turns. It is a dark, little-known study of maternal hatred and a child's endurance.
14640-mcguffey-s-first-eclectic-reader-r:
McGuffey's First Eclectic Reader, in its revised edition, taught beginners to read in the schoolroom of 1900. The Eclectic Educational Series issued it, and John Wiley and Sons later held the McGuffey trademarks.

Each lesson opens with vocabulary words, then a picture description and a short reading exercise, sometimes with script for copying. Lesson numbers run in Roman numerals, and the moral tone stays plain: a boy runs to fetch grandma a drink, and Lucy listens to what lives in a flower. The book still suits a teacher starting a child in reading and writing.
14642-mcguffey-s-eclectic-primer-revised:
McGuffey's Eclectic Primer, in its revised edition, is the simplest book of the Eclectic series, meant for a child's first lessons. Copyrights run from 1881 through 1909, and the primer opens with the alphabet in capitals and small letters.

Lessons stay to a few short sentences each. Cows feed in the shade of a big tree and come home at night. The sun sets as one old cow with a bell leads the way, and brave men row through a storm to save five men from a wrecked ship. Pictures sit beside nearly every lesson. The primer is plain, moral, and built for the very first reader.
1472-in-a-german-pension:
Katherine Mansfield's first book gathers sharp sketches of life in a German pension, or boarding house, where English guests meet German manners at table. Germans at Meat, The Baron, Frau Fischer, and The Child-Who-Was-Tired each catch a moment of social friction, snobbery, or quiet cruelty in a few pages.

Mansfield's eye is cool and her humour is dry, and she lets a phrase or a meal expose a whole character. The stories show her early gift for the telling detail. Together they form a witty, sometimes biting portrait of pre-war Europe seen from a boarding-house dining room.
14730-the-redemption-of-david-corson:
Charles Frederic Goss's 1900 novel traces David Corson from an Eden of innocence through temptation, fall and slow return. Chapter titles chart the descent: Satan comes also, Egyptians and a woman appear, light lies, a serpent trails, a broken reed snaps and paths converge.

Found wanting, turned tempter, snared and derelict, David becomes a fugitive and vagabond under the shadow of death. Alienation and an inevitable hour follow, then a signal in the night, heart hunger and a search for the one who might save him. Goss writes a moral romance in biblical colours, where redemption is earned through suffering, confession and a safe haven at last.
14757-the-war-poems-of-siegfried-sassoon:
Siegfried Sassoon's 1919 volume gathers 64 poems of the First World War, twelve of them printed here for the first time and the rest chosen from two earlier books. An epigraph from Henri Barbusse sets the mood: war as hideous in moral terms as in physical ones.

Short lyrics follow troops on the march, on trench duty, wiring parties and working parties, and at stand-to on Good Friday morning. Dreamers, a redeemer, a hero and men before battle appear in turn. Sassoon's anger at waste and false glory is plain, but so is pity for ordinary soldiers. The poems stay spare, direct and bitter, and they remain a central English record of the trenches.
14758-mary-anderson:
J. M. Farrar's 1885 book tells the story of Mary Anderson, opening at Long Branch, a famous American watering place in midsummer. Wooded hills, white frame villas and the purple Atlantic set the scene, after a summer storm has left waves tipped with foam and the sun sinking in rose, violet and gold.

A rambling country house stands a mile back from the shore, ringed by Rose of Sharon in full bloom, with perfume rising from rain-laden earth and birds making the air musical. Anderson, the young actress whose career Farrar follows, grows up in this bright, cultivated world. The book blends biography with atmosphere, tracing a stage life from its American beginnings.
1482-modeste-mignon:
Balzac's novel follows Modeste Mignon, a young woman in a Normandy chalet who dreams of love through letters. She writes, under a false name, to a famous poet. When the poet's secretary answers in his place, a comedy of mistaken identity grows into a serious romance with money, pride, and family honour at stake.

Through letters, visits, and a father's return from abroad, Modeste must choose between a poet's fame and a plain man's truth. Balzac treats her dreams with sympathy and irony. The novel is a warm, clever study of a girl's imagination meeting the real world.
14836-a-voyage-in-the-sunbeam-our-home-o:
Mrs. Brassey calls the yacht Sunbeam her home on the ocean for eleven months, and this long voyage narrative follows her family around the world. Farewell to old England leads to Madeira, Tenerife and the Cape Verde Islands, then Palma to Rio de Janeiro and life on the pampas.

River Plate to Sandy Point in the Straits of Magellan, Chile, Santiago and Valparaiso, Tahiti and the South Sea Islands, Hawaii and Kilauea by day and night follow. Brassey writes as a mother, hostess and observer, noting ports, people and daily shipboard life. The book remains a classic Victorian travel account, leisurely, curious and full of sea air.
14849-leaves-of-life-for-daily-inspirati:
Margaret Bird Steinmetz gathers leaves of life for daily inspiration, with Bible text from the American Standard Revised Bible of 1901, used by permission. Dedicated to those who helped gather the leaves and to those who may gather something from them, the book gives a reading for each day of the year.

January opens with Longfellow's Janus, god of avenues and gates, counting years through his portals, blocking roads, drifting fields with snow and lighting hearths and hearts. January first notes Murillo baptised in 1618, Paul Revere born in 1735 and Betsy Ross. Poems, birthdays and short reflections follow through the months, making a devotional calendar for home use.
1485-the-use-and-need-of-the-life-of-car:
Carry A. Nation, the Kansas temperance crusader famous for smashing saloons with a hatchet, writes on the use and need of her own life story. She presents her crusade as a calling, not a stunt. Nation, born in Kentucky in 1846, smashed her first saloon in Kansas in 1900.

Nation tells of drink, prayer, jail, and public scorn, urging readers to join the fight against alcohol. The short book gives her voice directly, fierce, pious, and unforgettable, and it documents a key figure of American reform. Her hatchet, nicknamed her weapon, became a symbol of temperance across America.
14952-selections-from-wordsworth-and-ten:
Pelham Edgar, professor of English at Victoria College, Toronto, edits selections from Wordsworth and Tennyson with introduction and notes, published in Toronto in 1917. Wordsworth's Michael, a pastoral poem, opens, with To the Daisy, To the Cuckoo, Nutting and the influence of natural objects.

Elegiac stanzas, London poems of 1802 and sonnets on twilight and age follow, before Tennyson's Oenone, the Epic, Morte d'Arthur, The Brook and In Memoriam. Biographical sketches, chronological tables, appreciations and notes close each section. The volume suits students who want the two poets side by side, with guidance but not a full collected works.
15030-the-unity-of-western-civilization:
A volume on the unity of Western civilization argues that Europe shares more than it divides, from prehistoric times through Greece and Rome to the Middle Ages. Unity and diversity in law, common elements in literature and art, and science and philosophy as unifying forces follow.

Unity of education, commerce and finance as world forces follows. Industrial legislation, common ideals of social reform and political bases of a world state complete the argument. Religion as a unifying force and the growth of humanity close the book. The book, written in the shadow of war, seeks grounds for cooperation: shared law, learning, trade and ideals across national borders.
15033-tell-england-a-study-in-a-generati:
Ernest Raymond's 1922 novel Tell England, a study in a generation, divides into five gay years of school and the rest, war. Its epigraph speaks for all emotions tense and strong, and for utmost knowledge. Hills, lakes and trees would give a thousand years to sing of life and man's high feelings.

A young man who has lived deep can sing into the face of death, poor and disappointed thing. He can tell it to strike breast and brow, for he has lived. Death can rob him only of a long life not yet lived. Raymond writes school friendship, youth and the First World War with feeling, and the novel became a popular memorial to a generation cut short.
15109-a-woman-s-part-in-a-revolution:
Mrs. John Hays Hammond recalls the Jameson Raid and its aftermath in this 1897 memoir of South Africa. The story opens in quiet domestic calm, with children at play on a verandah, then breaks when a letter brings news of Jameson's cross-border move. From there, months of fear and strain follow.

Hammond writes as a wife and mother caught inside great events, not as a soldier or statesman. She describes arrests, trials, and the strain on families with a direct, personal voice. The memoir gives a rare woman's view of a famous imperial crisis, and it reads with the force of a tale told by one who lived it.
15131-with-rimington:
L. March Phillipps, late a captain in Rimington's Guides, recalls the Boer War in this 1902 memoir, dedicated to a friend killed at Lambrechtfontein in 1901. Letters from camp follow the march from the Orange River through Belmont, Graspan, and Modder River toward Pretoria and Basutoland. Battles, scouting, and camp life fill the pages.

Phillipps writes as a soldier who knew his men and his horses, with praise for brave comrades and plain talk about war's costs. The memoir's charm lies in its firsthand detail rather than grand strategy. For readers of war memoirs, it offers a clear, personal view of a hard South African campaign.
15207-the-new-physics-and-its-evolution:
Lucien Poincaré's New Physics and Its Evolution, translated for Appleton in 1909, explains the revolution that radium and new views of matter brought to science. Poincaré, an inspector-general of French public instruction, stood close to universities yet apart from fiercest disputes. His family gave France a finance minister and an academy president.

Chapters trace how old physics gave way to new ideas on atoms, energy, and radiation, in clear prose for educated readers. The book captures science at a turning point, before quantum theory settled. History of science readers will find it lucid, balanced, and full of period excitement.
15233-authentic-narrative-of-the-death-o:
William Beatty, surgeon of the Victory at Trafalgar, wrote this 1807 narrative of Nelson's death, with a professional report on his wound and anecdotes. Beatty felt called, from his post on October 21, 1805, to lay the account before the British nation. The book follows the Victory from September sailing to battle day.

Beatty describes Nelson's wound, his last hours, and the mode adopted for preserving his body, with incidents aboard ship. His tone is sober, medical, and patriotic. The narrative remains the classic firsthand source for Trafalgar's most famous death, essential for naval history.
15237-the-chemistry-of-food-and-nutritio:
A. W. Duncan, analytical chemist of Manchester, wrote this 1905 book on food chemistry for the Vegetarian Society. It explains how bodies take up food and build upon it, and why one diet suits one person and not another. A plain diet of fruit, Grape-Nuts, eggs, toast, and Postum coffee illustrates his advice.

Duncan's approach is practical: change food wholly when ailing, eat simply, and watch results. Advertisements for Grape-Nuts in the text show the era's blend of science and salesmanship. Nutrition historians will find the book a curious, earnest sample of early diet reform.
15248-success-second-edition:
Lord Beaverbrook's Success, in a second edition of 1921, collects weekly articles first printed in the Sunday Express. Readers asked for copies so often that the publisher gathered them into a volume, promising a tonic for will and a spring in the step. Chapters treat happiness, luck, moderation, money, and education.

Later chapters take up arrogance, courage, panic, depression, failure, consistency, prejudice, and calm. Beaverbrook writes in brisk, newspaper prose, urging effort, nerve, and steady purpose. The book offers early twentieth-century self-help in its purest form: short, confident, and aimed at men on the make.
15299-drake-nelson-and-napoleon:
Walter Runciman's 1919 studies of Drake, Nelson, and Napoleon pair three sea and war leaders across centuries. A dedicatory letter to Sir James Knott fronts the book, recalling their early friendship and Knott's work breaking weevilly traditions in steamship management. Runciman writes as a seaman admiring seamen.

Drake's daring, Nelson's genius, and Napoleon's fate each get a study, with sea detail and strong opinion. The book is popular history, not scholarship, and its judgments reflect a British sailor's pride. Readers who love naval heroes will find the studies vivid, brisk, and full of salt air.
15350-a-history-of-english-prose-fiction:
Bayard Tuckerman's 1894 history traces English prose fiction from early romance to the novel of his day, linking each work to the social character of its age. He describes rare early specimens in full, so readers can know their style and contents without hunting scarce books. Nineteenth-century novels get a different treatment.

For familiar later fiction, Tuckerman stresses the importance of the novel as a social force, rather than retelling plots. The book, dedicated to his father, serves students and general readers. It remains a clear, old-fashioned guide to how English fiction grew.
15378-atalanta-in-calydon:
Algernon Charles Swinburne's Atalanta in Calydon, a tragedy in a new edition of 1885, retells the Greek myth of Atalanta, Meleager, and the Calydonian boar hunt. A Greek motto from Euripides fronts the play, and Swinburne dedicates it to the memory of Walter Savage Landor, once inscribed while Landor lived. Chatto and Windus published it in London.

Choruses in Swinburne's musical verse carry fate, gods, and grief, while heroes and huntress drive toward doom. The play stands as a high Victorian attempt at Greek tragedy. Readers of poetry and drama will find it lyrical, intense, and beautifully wrought.
15443-heiress-of-haddon:
W. E. Doubleday published this historical romance in London, in an eighth edition, with Buxton and Bakewell imprints. Thirty-three chapters trace a heroine's path from first sight through jealousy, villainy, tournaments, and escapes to peace at last. Chapter titles name the turns: a jealous heart, Dame Durden's ordeal, a visit to Nottingham, and a tournament combat.

The villain De la Zouch schemes through the middle chapters, while plain John Manners at last wins his bride. A knight baffled by legal terms, names of Mary Burden and Nathan Grene, and Sir Ronald Bury show the plot's tangle of papers and claims. Doubleday writes in the old romantic manner, with abbeys, hermits, chambers of death, and tokens, for readers who liked history dressed as adventure.
15551-stories-from-le-morte-d-arthur-and:
Beatrice Clay retold these stories from Le Morte d'Arthur and the Mabinogion for the King's Treasuries of Literature. Sir Arthur Quiller-Couch edited the series. The volume first appeared in 1920, and was reprinted in 1922 and 1924. A frontispiece shows the Lady of the Lake telling Arthur of the sword Excalibur, and the volume is printed in Great Britain.

Book one tells the coming of Arthur: his birth, his kingship, the Round Table, the finding of Excalibur, Morgan le Fay's treachery, and Merlin. Later books follow Sir Launcelot, Sir Tristram and the fair Isolt, and Arthur's nephews, with the magic potion, the chapel perilous, and the falcon adventure. Clay retells Malory and Welsh romance in clear prose for young readers, keeping the wonder while trimming the tangle.
1557-men-of-iron:
Howard Pyle's Men of Iron opens in 1400, when Richard II has been dethroned and Henry IV declared king, and peace proves only seeming. The novel follows Myles Falworth, a young squire of humble birth, through training, tournaments, and service at court, as he seeks to restore his family's honour and win knighthood.

Pyle, who also illustrated the book, fills it with armour, heraldry, and the code of chivalry, told with boyish vigour. Myles's growth from page to knight drives the tale. Men of Iron is a classic American historical novel for young readers, and a founding text of the chivalry genre.
1558-the-profits-of-religion-an-essay-in:
Upton Sinclair turns his muckraking eye on organised religion in The Profits of Religion, arguing that churches have too often served wealth and power. The essay reads religion through economics, not theology. Sinclair wrote The Profits of Religion in 1918, after The Jungle had made him famous.

Sinclair cites preachers, sects, and institutions, charging that faith became a business. The book angered many readers when it appeared, and it remains a fierce example of Sinclair's socialist criticism. His economic reading of churches, as businesses selling hope, angered clergy of every faith.
15660-little-eve-edgarton:
Eleanor Hallowell Abbott, author of Molly Make Believe and The White Linen Nurse, published this novel in New York in 1914, with the Century Company, illustrated by R. M. Crosby. An illustration promises music, flowers, palms, and catering, and another shows Eve murmuring, I am riding, almost inaudibly. The book opens with two men arguing over boredom and living like a fool.

Later pictures catch Paul Reymouth Edgarton proposing a topic of conversation: his own consummate cheek. Barton stammers over a paper-doll book, Eve insists she must make four hundred muffins, and Edgarton's icy voice places himself in the middle of the floor. Abbott writes a light, witty comedy of manners, where a small, sharp heroine upends a household's plans with charm and sudden honesty.
15672-dictionary-of-the-chinook-jargon-o:
George Gibbs compiled this dictionary of the Chinook jargon, the trade language of Oregon, published in New York in 1863 by Cramoisy Press, as number twelve of Shea's Library of American Linguistics. The preface explains the need: an earlier Smithsonian vocabulary, drawn from a priest's notes at Chinook Point, was too short, kept words that did not belong, and gave no sources.

Gibbs builds on Horatio Hale's vocabulary from the United States Exploring Expedition, correcting Hale's errors on the Chihalis element of the jargon. The dictionary gives the trade tongue used between Native peoples, traders, and settlers along the Columbia and the Oregon coast. It records words, their sources, and their uses. The book remains a key source for Pacific Northwest contact language and frontier trade.
15695-doc-gordon:
A 1906 novel by Mary E. Wilkins-Freeman, a leading writer of New England village life. Doctor Gordon, a country physician, works through snow and hardship to serve a small town. Wilkins-Freeman builds her fiction on close watch of neighbours, speech, and domestic duty. The Authors and Newspapers Association issued the book in New York and London, with water-colour pictures by Frank T. Merrill.

Gordon arrives in storms, coat white with snow, to tend the sick and settle quarrels. Patients, kin, and rivals test his patience and his pride. Love and duty pull against each other as the doctor weighs his own happiness against his calling. The novel endures as a quiet study of service: a good man, a hard place, and the daily work that holds a town together.
1570-the-power-of-concentration:
Theron Q. Dumont writes a self-help manual on the power of concentration, promising that focused attention can improve memory, work, and will. Lessons and exercises lead the reader step by step. Dumont, a pen name for William Walker Atkinson, wrote many mind-power books.

Dumont, a popular writer on mental science, keeps his advice practical, urging daily practice and steady habits. The book belongs to the early twentieth-century mind-power movement, and it still draws readers seeking focus. His exercises, from staring at a point to holding a thought, aim at daily discipline.
15722-the-tysons-mr-and-mrs-nevill-tyson:
May Sinclair, author of The Divine Fire and The Helpmate, published this novel in 1906, in twenty-three chapters from Mr. Nevill Tyson to in memoriam. Chapter one opens in Drayton Parva, where few houses receive Mr. and Mrs. Nevill Tyson. A thrill of guilty expectation goes through a room when they are announced, and people watch them with fearful interest, as if in some enthralling but forbidden drama.

Mrs. Tyson has no peers in Drayton Parva; she is tried by an invisible jury of ideas in Miss Batchelor's head, for opinion sways all things there. Later chapters follow the Tysons at home, the first stone, the night watch, and a son and heir. Sir Peter's new clothes, an unnatural mother, and circumstantial evidence lead to a flat in town, the Criterion, and a conflagration. Sinclair writes a sharp study of marriage, reputation, and a village that judges without mercy.
15794-plum-pudding-of-divers-ingredients:
A miscellany by Christopher Morley, printed at Garden City by Doubleday, Page and Company in 1921. Walter Jack Duncan embellished the book with drawings. Morley, a beloved essayist and novelist, calls his mixture plum pudding, of divers ingredients discreetly blended and seasoned. Essays, sketches, and whimsies share the bowl.

Morley writes on books, travel, food, and the small pleasures of daily life, with humour and a bookman's warmth. Short pieces suit reading in odd moments, by fire or train. The tone stays genial, never bitter, and the learning wears lightly. The book charms as Morley at his most Morley: a friend talking books over pudding.
15826-uncle-noah-s-christmas-inspiration:
A Christmas story by Leona Dalrymple, author of Diane of the Green Van, issued by McBride, Nast and Company in New York in 1914. Charles L. Wrenn supplied pictures, Charles Guischard the decorations. The frontispiece shows a man catching sight of orchids and his wife's tear-stained face bending over them. Dalrymple writes Christmas tales with warmth and a touch of mystery.

Uncle Noah, a kindly old man, finds a Christmas inspiration that mends a home and softens hearts. Orchids, tears, and a holiday surprise carry the plot. The tale stays short, sweet, and suited to reading by the fire. It charms as a period Christmas keepsake: love renewed at the season when it counts most.
16158-the-facts-of-reconstruction:
John R. Lynch's 1913 book, published by Neale, tells Reconstruction from inside Mississippi politics. Chapters cover the state's early part, reorganization under Governor Alcorn, the Republican county convention of 1869, and important school and political measures of the new legislature. A contest for speaker, a fusion victory in 1873, and the sending of Blanche K. Bruce to the United States Senate follow.

Later chapters ask what Negro domination really meant, trace improved finances under Ames, and record the overthrow of the Republican state government and the rise of Democratic radicalism. Lynch writes as a participant and a defender of Black citizenship. The book remains a key first-hand source on Reconstruction's hopes and defeat.
16306-jacob-behmen-an-appreciation:
Alexander Whyte's appreciation of Jacob Behmen, delivered as a lecture opening his 1894-95 classes on mystics at St. George's Free Church, Edinburgh, was published by Oliphant, Anderson and Ferrier in 1895. Whyte calls Behmen the greatest of the mystics and the father of German philosophy, yet notes he was all his life nothing better than a working shoemaker. Born at Old Seidenberg near Goerlitz in Silesia in 1575, he died at Goerlitz in 1624.

Behmen has no biography, Whyte says, since his books are his best life story. The lecture guides readers through a visionary cobbler's thought with a preacher's warmth. Students of mysticism and German philosophy will find a short, reverent introduction to Boehme.
16345-ellen-walton:
Ellen Walton, an heiress jointly with her brother and reputed the wealthiest fair one in all the district, is beset with admirers in this old romance. Some love her, some love her wealth, and some love both, yet to all but one she turns a deaf ear. That one, the least presuming of the many and too diffident to press his claim, holds an unknown magnetic power over her heart.

Doubts and fears attend their sincere, devoted, unacknowledged love, until a mutual exchange of thoughts and plighting of faith dispels them. Vows made by the pure in heart, the narrator insists, are seldom broken except by some higher duty. Readers of early American romance will enjoy its earnest, sentimental tale of love and fortune.
1635-ion:
Plato's Ion, translated by Benjamin Jowett, is the shortest, or nearly the shortest, of his writings, and its genuineness rests on grace and beauty rather than early testimony. Socrates meets Ion, a rhapsode who recites Homer, and asks whether his skill comes from art and knowledge or from divine inspiration.

Ion, who can speak only of Homer, is led to admit that his power is a kind of madness passed like a magnet's force from Muse to poet to hearer. The dialogue is brief and witty. It is a delightful introduction to Plato's questions about poetry, knowledge, and inspiration.
16357-mary-a-fiction:
Mary Wollstonecraft's Mary, a Fiction, printed for J. Johnson in London in 1788, announces a heroine unlike the usual models. The advertisement insists this woman is neither a Clarissa, a Lady G, nor a Sophie, and warns that artists who copy great masters catch the gross parts while the subtle spirit evaporates. Affectation disgusts where grace was expected to charm, Wollstonecraft argues.

Only compositions that delight and carry readers willing captives, she adds, earn their power. The novel that follows tests sensibility, friendship, and marriage through a heroine of strong feeling and independent mind. Readers of early feminist fiction will find a short, bold experiment from the author of the Rights of Woman.
16359-sir-thomas-browne-and-his-religio-:
Alexander Whyte's appreciation of Sir Thomas Browne and his Religio Medici, published by Oliphant, Anderson and Ferrier in 1898, selects the physician's best passages with commentary. Dedicated to Sir Thomas Grainger Stewart, president of the British Medical Association, the book grew from Whyte's inaugural discourse at St. Giles's Cathedral on July 26, 1898, given at Stewart's request. An illustration from the 1642 Religio Medici fronts the volume.

Whyte calls the Religio Medici a universally recognized English classic, with Urn-Burial, Christian Morals, and Letter to a Friend worthy to stand beside it. Browne's meditations on faith, death, and learning unfold in rich, musical prose. Readers of seventeenth-century literature will find a warm, learned guide.
16432-esperanto-hearings-before-the-comm:
This volume prints hearings before the Committee on Education on Esperanto, the planned international language. The transcriber's note explains the language's alphabet: twenty-eight letters, with the English q, w, x, and y dropped and six accented letters added. Zamenhof's workaround for plain type, using h after certain letters, is also set out.

The hearings themselves record the case for and against teaching and using Esperanto in American public life. As a document, the book captures a hopeful moment when a world language seemed within reach. Readers of language history will find it a curious, earnest snapshot of that debate.
16447-the-clarion:
Samuel Hopkins Adams published this 1914 novel of newspapers and ideals, inscribed to his father, a soldier of ideals. The Clarion follows a paper's rise through chapters on an itinerant, a leading citizen, a shop, a partnership, and the power of print. Patriots, creeping flame, stern logic, and the good fight mark the later course, toward a tempered victory.

Adams writes as a muckraker turned novelist, keen on how presses shape towns and tempt owners. The tale mixes romance with reform, and its hero learns that a paper can serve truth or serve power. Readers of press fiction will find it earnest, lively, and still pointed.
16457-all-around-the-moon:
Edward Roth's translation of Jules Verne carries the Baltimore Gun Club's travelers around the moon and back toward Earth. The sequel to From the Earth to the Moon follows the shell's crew. They settle in, face the cold of space, study lunar mountains, and live through a night fifteen days long. Tycho, the southern hemisphere, and puzzling questions fill the middle chapters.

Verne mixes hard science talk with comic scenes, and the club men end by fishing and bidding farewell to their grand scheme. The book is pure adventure for young readers, full of wonder at a moon seen close up. It remains one of Verne's most beloved voyages.
16461-a-bird-s-eye-view-of-the-bible-sec:
Frank Nelson Palmer, a teacher of English Bible in Winona schools, sums up all sixty-six books of the Bible in this short 1914 guide. A chart opens the book, then chapters trace one story: the kingdom foreshadowed, forming, conquering, divided, captive, restored, and at last triumphant in its true king. Acts, epistles, and Revelation close the arc.

Palmer writes for students and Sunday school teachers who want the whole shape of the Bible in brief compass. The style is plain and the plan is easy to hold in mind. The book serves as a quick map for readers starting serious Bible study, or for teachers planning a course.
16470-the-profits-of-religion-fifth-edit:
Upton Sinclair studies supernatural belief as a source of income and a shield for privilege in this essay. First issued in 1917, it reached a fifth edition by 1926 with sales past sixty thousand. He says twenty-five years of thought and a year of digging went into it, and he published it himself to keep the price low.

Sinclair works through churches, creeds, and holy claims with a muckraker's eye for money and power. The tone is fierce and plain, meant to provoke rather than soothe. Readers who know Sinclair from The Jungle will find the same reforming fire turned here on religion as a business.
16486-celebrated-claimants-from-perkin-w:
This 1874 volume gathers the stories of famous pretenders, from Perkin Warbeck and Lambert Simnel to Don Sebastian, the sham Peter III, and Arthur Orton, the Tichborne claimant. Wandering heirs, lost kings, and bold rogues chase titles and estates, deceiving courts and crowds. Some claims sprang from true mystery, others from sheer fraud.

The preface notes that such excitements fade fast, leaving only scattered records. The book aims to fill that gap with full, readable cases. Readers who enjoy true tales of imposture will find a gallery of audacious figures, each tested against law, evidence, and public fancy.
16506-epistle-to-a-friend-concerning-poe:
Samuel Wesley's Epistle to a Friend Concerning Poetry (1700) and his Essay on Heroic Poetry (1697, second edition) get a scholarly reprint here, with an introduction by Edward N. Hooker. Issued by the Augustan Reprint Society in 1947, the booklet gives students direct access to two rare texts on how poetry should be made and judged.

Wesley writes as a working poet and critic of his age, defending heroic verse and weighing the poet's craft. The reprint serves scholars of Restoration and Augustan letters. Short as it is, the volume opens a window on poetry's rules before the age of Pope and Swift.
16508-american-men-of-action:
Burton E. Stevenson wrote this 1913 book for young readers who find biography dull. He opens by promising that lives can read like stories, then moves from beginners and Washington-to-Lincoln chapters to statesmen, pioneers, great soldiers, and great sailors. Washington, Columbus, Jefferson, Boone, Grant, Lee, and Dewey all appear in portraits.

Short summaries close each chapter, and the tone stays brisk and admiring. Stevenson aims to stir pride and ambition, not to weigh flaws. The book serves as a lively first gallery of American heroes for school readers of its day.
16520-the-girl-and-her-religion:
Margaret Slattery writes for girls, not about doctrine, in this 1913 Pilgrim Press book, fifth printing. Her note warns that the book is not technical, holds no philosophy, and solves no girl problems. It is simple and concrete, a record of what girls she knew made her think, with one request: that readers think of the girls, for action is born of thought.

Chapters sort girls by type, from the handicapped and privileged to the easily led, the drifting, and the girl with high ideals, then turn to religion itself. Slattery's tone is warm and practical. The book gives a kind, early twentieth-century guide to faith for young women.
16588-over-the-top-with-the-third-austra:
G. P. Cuttriss sketches life with the Third Australian Division in this brief volume, introduced by Major-General Sir John Monash. Contents run from there to here, Australians in various moods, and Sunday somewhere in France through soldiers' superstitions, the eve of battle, over the top, shells, Messines, and Bill the Bugler. A tragedy of the war and recreation behind the lines follow.

Cuttriss dedicates the book to the heroic dead and those who lost them, in unshakeable belief that right will win. The sketches are short and vivid, with pictures by Neil McBeath. Readers of Australian war writing will find a warm, soldierly record.
16597-square-deal-sanderson:
Charles Alden Seltzer's 1922 western follows Square Deal Sanderson from the north trail through curiosity, water and kisses, and a plot that worked. Dale moves, the voice of the coyote sounds, and a man is hanged before an ambush. Nyland meets a killer near the close, in a tale of brands, trail herds, and Devil's Hole.

Seltzer writes brisk western action with a hero whose square dealing earns his name. The frontispiece shows Streak running with long, smooth leaps out of the valley. Readers of ranch fiction will find a fast, colorful yarn of justice on the range.
16643-essays-by-ralph-waldo-emerson:
Edna H. L. Turpin selected and edited this 1907 school volume of Emerson's essays for Merrill's English Texts. The American Scholar, Compensation, Self-Reliance, Friendship, Heroism, Manners, Gifts, Nature, Shakespeare or the Poet, Prudence, and Circles fill the contents, with notes and a chronological list of Emerson's main works.

The series aimed to give schools complete masterpieces with sound scholarship and classroom sense. An introduction sketches Emerson's life and his place in his time's thought. Students meeting Emerson for the first time will find a well-chosen, well-guided door into his essays.
16734-retrospection-and-introspection:
Mary Baker Eddy wrote this life sketch, first under copyright in 1891 and 1892, as the approved text of the First Church of Christ, Scientist in Boston. It moves from her forebears and girlhood, through marriage, study, and illness, to her great find, her first book, and the rise of her church and college. Poems and short pieces break up the prose.

Eddy tells how she came to see mind-healing as a faith and a cure, and how she met doubt, theft of ideas, and church fights. The book is both memoir and defense of her work. It gives the clearest short account in her own words of how Christian Science grew from one woman's life into a church.
16757-life-of-john-milton:
Richard Garnett wrote this short life of John Milton for the Great Writers series, issued by Walter Scott in London in 1890. A note warns that many small lives of Milton exist, but Masson's large, authoritative life now sets the standard no memoir can ignore. Garnett adds that Mark Pattison's recent life slighted the religious and political fights that mattered most to Milton himself.

Garnett tracks Milton from youth through verse, prose, blindness, and the Commonwealth years, with religion and politics kept at the center. He writes in compact, scholarly prose for readers who want one small, sound life. The book serves as a clear first Milton biography, and as a guide to the larger lives behind it.
16776-poems-of-passion:
Ella Wheeler Wilcox wrote this illustrated 1883 book of poems on love and feeling, issued by W. B. Conkey in Chicago. It opens with a verse that likens songs to shells cast up by waves of thought, holding shape and color but not the deep seas beneath. Contents run from Love's Language and Impatience through The Common Lot to many more short lyrics.

Wilcox speaks in plain, musical lines about love, loss, longing, and the lot shared by all. Her verse is direct and bold for its day, with little veil over strong feeling. Readers who like short, heartfelt lyrics will find much to quote and to read aloud, piece by piece, in this early book of hers.
16786-the-world-s-best-poetry-volume-03-:
Bliss Carman led this third volume of The World's Best Poetry, issued by J. D. Morris in Philadelphia in 1904, with Lyman Abbott's lead essay as an interpreter of life. The ten-volume set splits verse by theme, and this volume takes sorrow and consolation. American poems in copyright appear by kind leave of their owners.

The book gathers lyrics of grief, comfort, and hope from many hands, meant to be read in hard hours. Its range runs from short laments to longer meditations on loss. Readers who want verse for mourning or for solace will find a broad, old-style anthology, useful for reading aloud and for finding a poem that fits a hard day.
16869-oonomoo-the-huron:
Edward S. Ellis wrote this 1911 frontier tale, issued by Hurst in New York. Chapters move from Hans Vanderbum and other characters into Oonomoo and the Shawnees. A young lieutenant and Cato, the home of the Huron, and adventures on the way follow. A plan for rescue and the exploit of Hans Vanderbum appear. A new danger and a conclusion close the book. Pictures show Mary Prescott, a young officer, and a grateful captive.

Ellis writes in the old dime-novel style, with Huron, Shawnee, and Miami folk, settlers, and soldiers in a rescue plot. The tale reflects its age's views of Native peoples, which modern readers will read with care. As period adventure, it offers brisk action, woodland scenes, and a hero whose skill saves friends from peril.
16889-the-enchanted-canyon:
Honore Willsie wrote this 1921 novel, issued by A. L. Burt in New York by arrangement with Morrow. It runs in four books: Bright Angel, The Secretary of the Interior, The Enchanted Canyon, and The Phantasm Destroyed. Chapters move from Minetta Lane and Bright Angel into twenty-two years later. Diana Allen, a photographer of Indians, and a newspaper reporter follow. The desert, the Colorado, and a cliff dwelling appear. An expedition, love in the desert, and revenge close the tale.

Willsie sets a boy who needs a mother at fourteen against canyon grandeur, desert love, and old wrongs. The tale mixes family, politics, and adventure in vivid western prose. Readers who like Willsie's desert novels will find a rich, long story of canyons, cliffs, and hearts tested by land and time.
1689-the-pivot-of-civilization:
Margaret Sanger argues in this book that birth control is the key issue for modern society. That is because poverty, child labor, and the strain on mothers all follow from families unable to limit their size. She writes from her work in clinics and her fights with the law, and she dedicates the book to Alice Drysdale Vickery, an early voice for women's freedom.

Sanger's case is blunt and of its time, and modern readers will meet views on population that now read as harsh. The book matters as a record of the birth-control movement at its most combative. Its argument is that women's health, not charity or punishment, should sit at the center of social reform.
16942-thoughts-on-religion:
George John Romanes wrote these thoughts on religion, edited after his death by Charles Gore, Bishop of Worcester, twelfth impression issued by Longmans in London in 1904. Part one weighs the influence of science on religion in two essays. Part two gives notes for a candid examination of religion, with sections on terms, causes, faith, and faith in Christianity. Gore adds a preface and a closing note.

Romanes, known for Darwin and After Darwin, turned late in life to metaphysics and theology with growing care. His notes ask how a man of science can still believe, in honest, searching prose. The book gives a thoughtful, unfinished attempt at faith after Darwin, valued for its candor and its calm, questioning tone.
16964-wage-earning-and-education:
R. R. Lutz wrote this 1916 Cleveland education survey volume on wage earning and education, issued by the Survey Committee of the Cleveland Foundation. Leonard P. Ayres directed the wider survey, and Allen T. Burns directed the committee's work. The first chapter sets out the industrial education survey, the jobs studied, and the staff and methods used.

Lutz links school to work in a growing industrial city, asking what training young wage earners need and what schools actually give. Tables and diagrams back the text. The book gives a detailed view of 1916 Cleveland work and schooling. It helps historians of education and labor, and readers who study how cities once tried to fit schools to jobs.
17043-the-sheriff-s-son:
William Macleod Raine's 1917 western opens with Dave Dingwell riding since daylight across New Mexico desert toward the range. A fine rain blots the peaks and softens the hills as he reaches the foothills, and the shower may spoil the errand he rides on. The frontispiece hints at the shock to come when Meldrum answers a summons.

Raine, known for Yukon and Wyoming tales, builds the plot around a sheriff's son, outlaws, and desert justice, with later chapters turning on a new leaf. The pace is brisk, the talk is terse, and the land itself shapes each move. Fans of classic westerns will find a straight, action-led tale with a hero caught between law and loyalty.
17103-the-double-life-of-mr-alfred-burto:
E. Phillips Oppenheim's Double Life of Mr. Alfred Burton opens with Burton, silk hat tipped back and a cigar in his mouth, standing at the door of fate. A client's gift cigar disagrees with him, yet he smokes it, and his deep-set blue eyes hint at the keen methods of the young man. Thirty chapters follow his transformation, his family, a shock to Mr. Waddington, and a legend of a perfect food.

Menatogen, the mind food, drives the second life, with a professor, a Mr. Bomford, riches, and repentance to follow. Oppenheim mixes fantasy with city comedy in his smooth popular style. Readers who like light tales of a changed man will enjoy Burton's double turn, and his return to his real self.
17109-through-palestine-with-the-twentie:
This squadron memoir follows the Twentieth Machine Gun Squadron through Palestine in the Great War, with biblical place names and old sites along the march. Transcriber notes flag uncertain scripture references and varied spellings of Arabic and Hebrew names, kept as in the original for honesty. The tale blends campaign detail with the holy land's long history at each stop.

Machine gunners, horses, guns, and desert roads share space with churches, wells, and battlefields of old. The voice is that of a unit history, plain and proud of its men. Readers of Palestine campaign history will find a close, ground-level record of a small unit in a storied land.
17113-indian-ghost-stories-second-editio:
S. Mukerji's Indian Ghost Stories, second edition from Allahabad in 1917, opens by asking whether ghost tales must end with a cat, a dog, or a boy behind the scare. Mukerji likes such jokes, yet he also tells of events that take the breath away, like a Texas tale of a jilted girl, a brother's shot, and a bullet in a tree. His own stories let readers draw their own conclusions.

Tales include a dead wife's photograph, a major's lease, an open door, a boy possessed, and a messenger of death, all set in Indian homes and offices. The tone is plain and curious, with physicists' explanations weighed beside the marvel. Ghost fans will find a charming Anglo-Indian set, half joke and half wonder.
17221-history-of-the-plague-in-london:
Daniel Defoe's History of the Plague in London, in this 1894 school edition, tells the great plague of 1665 as a vivid, journal-like narrative. Maps of wards, parishes, and suburbs open the book. Defoe, born in 1661 in St. Giles, Cripplegate, to a butcher father, was schooled for the dissenting ministry under Mr. Morton before turning to public affairs and adventure.

The narrative tracks bills of mortality, shut houses, nurses, watchmen, and the city's fear, with the energy of an eyewitness even where Defoe invents. Its plain, urgent prose made it a classic of plague writing. Readers of London history and epidemic tales will find a gripping, humane account of a city under a terrible visitation.
17247-a-selection-of-books-published-by-:
This September 1911 Methuen catalogue lists the London house's books by author, with series notes for buyers and booksellers. General literature runs from Ancient Cities and Arden Shakespeare to Handbooks of Theology, Little Guides, Oxford Biographies, and Westminster Commentaries. Fiction covers two-shilling novels, shilling novels, Dumas, and books for boys and girls.

Notes explain colonial editions for the colonies and India, and net prices that allow no discount. The catalogue suits book historians and collectors tracing Methuen's list at its Edwardian height. As a period document, it maps a publisher's world: art, church, school, travel, and story, all in one handy list.
17352-the-awakening-the-resurrection:
Leo Tolstoy's Resurrection, here called The Awakening in William E. Smith's translation, opens with scripture texts on forgiveness seventy times seven and the mote in a brother's eye. The novel follows a nobleman whose past sin returns in a courtroom, where a woman he wronged stands accused. From that meeting grows a long road of repentance, prison, Siberia, and spiritual rebirth.

Tolstoy writes with moral force and vast social sweep, judging courts, churches, and prisons alike. The book stands beside War and Peace and Anna Karenina as a late masterpiece of conscience. Readers who like great novels of guilt and grace will find a profound, demanding tale of a soul waking to its duty.
17358-the-romantic-settlement-of-lord-se:
George Bryce of Winnipeg, president of the Royal Society of Canada, wrote this history of Lord Selkirk's colonists, the pioneers of Manitoba. Chapters open with a patriarch's story, an extinct race, a gay Frenchman, the earlier peoples, Montreal merchants, dusky riders of the plain, and the stately Hudson's Bay Company. A Scottish duel, a stormy sea crossing, and a winter of discontent follow.

Bryce tells how Selkirk's settlers reached the Red River country and held on through hardship, rivalry, and cold. Readers get a romantic but factual account of a founding migration, written by a Canadian scholar close to the ground it describes. The book still serves as an introduction to Manitoba's pioneer past.
17437-health-and-education:
Charles Kingsley, canon of Westminster and fellow of the Linnean and Geological Societies, published this book on health and education in London in 1874 with W. Isbister and Company. His opening essay, The Science of Health, asks whether the British race is improving or degenerating. It asks what causes the evil if it seems to degenerate, and how those causes can be arrested if not destroyed.

Kingsley argues that such questions concern not statesmen and doctors only, but every father and mother in the islands. Readers get a Victorian clergyman's blend of science, morals, and public advice, urgent and plain-spoken. The book suits readers of public health history and of Kingsley's many-sided career.
17446-the-second-honeymoon:
Ruby M. Ayres, author of A Bachelor Husband and The Scar, published this romance in New York in 1921 with Grosset and Dunlap, copyright held by W. J. Watt and Company. The chapters promise a story in which the past intervenes, a jilting follows, and two women, Jimmy, and Sangster cross and recross each other's paths. Jimmy gets news, demands the truth, and faces love and poverty.

A second engagement, a motherless household, husband and wife, consultations with Sangster, and Christine hearing the truth carry the tale on through bitterness and riddles. Readers get a popular romance of love, secrets, and second chances, in Ayres's smooth, emotional style. It suits readers of interwar popular fiction.
17464-great-singers-first-series-faustin:
George T. Ferris compiled this first series of lives of great singers in 1879, published by D. Appleton and Company, running from Faustina Bordoni to Henrietta Sontag. Ferris is frank that his work is a compilation rather than fresh research. He drew freely on many sources and on the words of writers and critics who saw the singers in person. His aim was a digest that stayed compact, lively, and accurate.

Readers meet celebrated voices of the opera stage through anecdote, contemporary praise, and career highlights, with the freshness of first-hand report kept where possible. The book suits music lovers who want short, vivid portraits rather than a formal history. As a period collection it also shows which singers Victorian readers held up as models of art.
176-roderick-hudson:
Rowland Mallet, a wealthy young American, finds a sculptor of genius in a New England town. Henry James's Roderick Hudson follows Rowland as he funds Roderick's study in Rome. Talent, love, and pride pull the young artist in rival directions.

Roderick loves Mary Garland at home yet falls for Christina Light in Rome. Rowland watches, pays, and suffers in silence as his friend wastes his gift. Chapters move from Rome to Frascati and the Swiss Alps. The novel, James's first, already shows his eye for art and conscience. James revised the novel later, but its portrait of genius and patronage already feels mature.
17625-artificial-light-its-influence-upo:
M. Luckiesh, director of applied science at the Nela Research Laboratory of the National Lamp Works, wrote this study of artificial light for the Century Books of Useful Science. Chapters run from light and progress and the art of making fire. They move through primitive light sources and the ceremonial use of light, to oil lamps of the nineteenth century and early gas lighting.

Later chapters cover the science of light production, modern gas lighting, and the electric arcs, showing how each new light changed work, streets, and homes. Readers get a clear, popular science history of lighting, from flame to filament. The book suits readers of technology and of everyday life.
17652-the-history-of-sir-richard-whittin:
T. H. wrote this history of Sir Richard Whittington, edited with an introduction by Henry B. Wheatley for the Villon Society in London in 1885. The volume belongs to a series of chap-books and folk-lore tracts edited by G. L. Gomme and Wheatley. Its introduction explains that the popular story of Whittington and his cat grafts a wide-spread folk tale onto the life of a real man.

Readers get an early printed life of the lord mayor, with a scholar's guide to what is history and what is tale. The book suits readers of folklore, of London history, and of the Whittington legend. Wheatley's edition keeps the old text readable for modern readers.
17712-the-moon:
Thomas Gwyn Elger, who led the lunar work of the British Astronomical Association, wrote this 1895 guide to the Moon's face, with a full map of its chief marks. The London firm George Philip and Son put it out for sky watchers who owned a small glass and wanted to know what they were seeing.

The book first traces how men mapped the Moon, then lists its craters, seas, hills, and rays quadrant by quadrant, from west to east. Each entry notes place and shape, so a reader can match a mark in the eyepiece to a name on the map. It still serves as a clear, old-school field guide to lunar ground, written by a man who spent years at the task.
17720-history-of-ancient-civilization:
This survey of ancient civilization opens with prehistoric times, setting out prehistoric archaeology, remains, and science, and the four ages of stone, bronze, and iron. The rough stone age covers remains in gravels and cave men. The polished stone age covers lake villages and megalithic monuments. Bronze and iron ages follow, with weapons, objects, and epochs.

Later sections treat history and its documents, legends, and the great divisions of history, then races and peoples, Egyptians, and the Hellenes. Alexander, Macedon, and Philip carry the Greek story on. Readers get a compact school history of the ancient world, systematic and clear. The book suits newcomers to ancient history.
17748-the-extermination-of-the-american-:
William T. Hornaday wrote this study of the extermination of the American bison. He was superintendent of the National Zoological Park. The study came from the report of the National Museum for 1886 to 1887, pages 369 to 548, with twenty-two plates, printed in Washington in 1889. Part one gives the life history of the bison: discovery of the species, geographical distribution, abundance, and character.

Later parts trace the slaughter that brought the bison to the edge of extinction and the case for saving it. Readers get a landmark work of American conservation, written by the man who helped found the modern zoo movement. Hornaday's book remains essential for bison history and for the origins of wildlife protection.
17760-how-to-enjoy-paris-in-1842-intende:
F. Hervé wrote this guide in 1842 for English folk bound for Paris, printed in Paris by Amyot and in London by Briggs. Hervé had lived in Turkey and Greece, and he aimed to join useful facts with fun, so a stranger could enjoy the French capital without waste or snub.

Chapters give hints on manners, deals, and daily life, plus history, trade, theatre, and figures on the city. Hervé warns against pride and national scorn, and urges fair dealing with Parisians. The book still charms as a time capsule, showing what a well-off English tourist saw, spent, and feared in Paris near two centuries ago.
17771-winds-of-doctrine-studies-in-conte:
George Santayana, late professor of philosophy at Harvard University, published these studies in contemporary opinion in New York in 1913 with Charles Scribner's Sons, first printed that year. Chapters cover the intellectual temper of the age, modernism and Christianity, and the philosophy of Henri Bergson. A long chapter on Bertrand Russell follows, in four parts.

Russell's new scholasticism, study of essence, critique of pragmatism, and hypostatic ethics get separate treatment. Shelley on the poetic value of revolutionary principles and the genteel tradition in American philosophy close the set. Readers get Santayana at his most lucid, judging his age's ideas with poise.
17774-the-poetry-of-architecture-or-the-:
John Ruskin wrote The Poetry of Architecture as the first volume of his collected works, on how buildings suit the land and the folk who raise them. The book treats the homes of Europe, from lowland cottages to mountain villas, and asks what each form says about its place.

Parts cover the cottage in England, France, Italy, and Switzerland, with a chapter on chimneys, then turn to villas by Lake Como and in lowland England. Ruskin writes with a keen eye for stone, roof, and view. It is a young master's first book, and a fine start for readers who want to see buildings as poems in stone.
17823-the-hudson-three-centuries-of-hist:
Wallace Bruce wrote this history of the Hudson, three centuries of history, romance, and invention, in a centennial edition published in New York in 1907 by the Bryant Union Company. Its contents open with a centennial greeting, then a survey of history, romance, and invention. An open book, the Hudson and the Rhine, and the Half Moon follow.

The Half Moon's voyage and the river's discovery carry the early story on. Readers get a celebratory river history, patriotic and picturesque, written for the Hudson-Fulton centennial years. The book suits readers of the Hudson Valley and of American river lore.
17921-manual-of-surgery-volume-first-gen:
Alexis Thomson and Alexander Miles wrote this Manual of Surgery, volume one on general surgery, in a sixth revised edition with 169 pictures. Thomson taught surgery at Edinburgh University, and both men served as surgeons at the Edinburgh Royal Infirmary.

Chapters run from repair and inflammation to suppuration, ulcers, and gangrene, laying out how wounds heal and how healing goes wrong. The prose is plain and clinical, made for students and house surgeons. Though its methods are now old, the book shows how surgery was taught in the early 1900s, with care for fact and clear order.
18063-rabbi-saunderson:
Ian Maclaren wrote Rabbi Saunderson in 1898, printed in London by Hodder and Stoughton, with twelve pictures by A. S. Boyd. Maclaren, famed for his Scottish parish tales, dedicates the book to Mrs. Williamson of Glenogil, famed for witty speech.

Stories run from a supra-lapsarian and Kilbogie manse to the rabbi as confessor, the fear of God, the wounds of a friend, and light at eventide. Farmers cart the new minister's goods from the station, and a lost note tests a parish. Maclaren writes with humor and grace. It is a warm, Scottish book of kirk life, full of wit and kind hearts.
18145-lady-rosamond-s-secret-a-romance-o:
Re. Agatha Armour published this romance of Fredericton, New Brunswick, at St. John in 1878. Her introduction says she wove simple facts into a story shaped by the usages of society under Sir Howard Douglas, who governed from 1824 to 1830. She drew on local sources and on gentlemen of high social position who gave her facts.

The story opens on a September sunset at Fredericton in 1824, at Old Government House. From there it follows the manners, calls, and secrets of a small colonial capital. The style is plain, and the author calls herself an amateur. Readers get a local romance grounded in the Fredericton of the 1820s, rather than a tale of high adventure.
18146-the-children-s-portion:
Robert W. Shoppell selected and edited The Children's Portion in 1895, published by the Christian Herald in New York under Louis Klopsch. The book offers entertaining, instructive, and elevating stories for children, drawn from old and new sources.

Tales include The Golden Age, a retelling of The Merchant of Venice, Pious Constance and Patient Griselda from Chaucer, the woodcutter's child from Grimm, and the winter's tale. Each piece aims to teach a moral while it charms. It is a rich, old children's treasury, best for families who like classic tales with a gentle, Christian tone.
18191-essays-on-the-work-entitled-supern:
J. B. Lightfoot, late Bishop of Durham, gathered these essays on the work called Supernatural Religion into book form in 1889, with a second edition in 1893. The essays first appeared in The Contemporary Review. Lightfoot says the republication answers no present controversy; friends in England and America had urged him to collect pieces they thought of lasting value.

Written while Lightfoot was ill, the volume was seen through the press with help from his chaplain, Rev. J. R. Harmer, who checked references and added indices. The essays test the claims of Supernatural Religion with close scholarship and cool argument. Readers get a Victorian bishop answering a skeptical book on its own ground, with care for evidence, dates, and the early Christian writings.
18270-confession-and-absolution:
Right Rev. Monsignor Capel, domestic prelate of Pope Leo XIII and priest of the Archdiocese of Westminster, published this book at Philadelphia and New York in 1884. Capel first gave the material as one of twenty-four conferences in the Cathedral at Philadelphia during Lent, on God's conditions for pardoning sin. At the request of many hearers, he published it under the title Confession and Absolution, with changes for print.

Capel draws on Faith of Catholics, a three-volume collection of early Christian writers, for readers who lack a library of the Fathers or the classical languages. The book sets out Catholic teaching on confession: what sin requires, what the priest does, and what the penitent must bring. Readers get a pastoral manual, plain and doctrinal, from a noted preacher of his day.
18281-an-account-of-the-proceedings-on-t:
This 1874 Rochester volume prints the full proceedings of the trial of Susan B. Anthony for illegal voting in the presidential election of November 1872. It also prints the trials of Beverly Jones, Edwin Marsh, and William Hall, the inspectors who received her vote. The index lists the indictment, the speeches, and the rulings in order.

Readers get the whole courtroom record. It includes the opening speech for the prosecution and Judge Hunt's opinion. Hunt refused to submit the case to the jury and refused to let the jury be polled. The record then gives his sentence and Anthony's speech on receiving it. Her campaign speech is printed as well. The book stands as a primary record of the early fight for women's right to vote.
18347-carnegie-library-of-pittsburgh-deb:
The Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh published this debate index in a second edition in 1912. The index lists books on debate and on the leading controversies of the day, with call numbers for library use. It draws largely on material first prepared for students of argumentation at Harvard and the University of Pennsylvania.

Entries give Askew's Pros and Cons, a newspaper reader's and debater's guide to political, social, and religious questions, with briefs on more than twenty new subjects in its 1911 form. Brookings's briefs for debate on current political, economic, and social topics follow, with a bibliography of debating by A. B. Hart. Readers get a debater's tool: where to find both sides of a question, arranged for quick use in school, club, and library.
18451-ontario-normal-school-manuals-scie:
The Ontario Minister of Education authorized this manual for normal schools, published by the Ryerson Press in Toronto, with copyright in Canada in 1915 and printings in 1919 and 1923. It sets out the science of education for teachers in training, in two parts: principles and practice.

Part one covers the nature and purpose of education, forms of reaction, the process of education, and the growth of the child. Part two turns to method, discipline, and the teacher's work in the schoolroom, giving Ontario's student teachers a plain, systematic guide to how children learn and how teaching should be planned.
1849-the-yellow-crayon:
E. Phillips Oppenheim's Yellow Crayon opens in late summer, with flower perfume stealing through a half-opened window and sunlight forcing its way through a chink in the blind. Lucille, the heroine, learns that a prince is in love with her, and answers, looking lazily out of the window, that she wishes he were.

The novel follows Lucille through courts, conspiracies, and a yellow crayon mark that signals danger, with Oppenheim's usual mix of romance and intrigue. The prince's love, the heroine's coolness, and the political plot around them keep the story moving, and the book is a polished sample of the author's Edwardian world.
18492-star-surgeon:
Alan E. Nourse wrote this science fiction novel, published by David McKay in New York in 1959 and 1960, with a sixth printing in 1973. Part of the book first appeared in Amazing Science Fiction Stories. Star Surgeon follows a young alien doctor seeking a place in a galactic medical service that judges him by his species as much as by his skill.

The novel opens with Dal Timgar missing his shuttle from Philadelphia to Hospital Seattle, though he arrived thirty minutes early for boarding. A clerk tells him unsympathetically to wait for the next one. Chapters follow the intruder, Hospital Seattle, an inquisition, galactic pill peddlers, crisis on Morua VIII, plague, and a trial. Readers get a medical adventure in space: a healer fighting prejudice, disease, and the politics of who may practice.
18550-erechtheus-a-tragedy-new-edition:
Algernon Charles Swinburne wrote this verse tragedy, issued in a new London edition by Chatto and Windus in 1881. Its persons are Erechtheus, king of Athens, his wife Praxithea, their daughter Chthonia, a chorus of Athenian elders, heralds, and the goddess Athena. The play opens with Erechtheus calling on Earth, mother of all, as war from Thrace threatens his city.

Swinburne frames the action with Greek epigraphs from Pindar and Aeschylus and writes in rich, rolling blank verse. The tragedy weighs a king's duty to his city against the cost to his own house. Readers of Victorian classical drama will find it a bold, musical example of the form.
18582-gypsy-breynton:
Elizabeth Stuart Phelps wrote this Gypsy book, reissued at New York in 1894 by Dodd, Mead and Company, with the same 1895 preface as its sister volume. Gypsy is a lively tomboy in short dresses and long stockings who paddles rafts, climbs trees, skates, tramps, and coasts, usually muddy and a little torn. Phelps wrote the tales when hardly more than a girl herself and marvels that Gypsy is now thirty years old in print.

Chapters introduce Gypsy, a spasm of order, a dream, an apple tree climb, Peace Maythorne, camping out, and Gypsy's opinion of Boston. Fun, health, hope, truth, and kindness mark the heroine. The book remains a cheerful classic of girls' fiction from the 1800s.
18613-the-golden-scorpion:
Sax Rohmer published this mystery adventure in 1920. It opens in London, where Dr. Keppel Stuart wakes in fear, sure some evil presence has entered his house. A sealed envelope, a Chinese coin, and a cowled figure soon point to a hidden Eastern order called the Scorpion. The middle of the book gives detective Gaston Max's own statement of his Paris hunt.

Later parts move to the house of Ah-Fang-Fu, an opium den, and the lair of the order, with brain thieves, a red circle, and a green-eyed idol in the mix. Rohmer piles on exotic menace and narrow escapes. The novel is a brisk example of his popular thrillers of the period.
1862-tartarin-of-tarascon:
Tartarin of Tarascon has never left his town, but he talks, hunts, and boasts as if he had conquered Africa, and his townsmen love him for it. The narrator's first visit to Tartarin, ten or a dozen years before the telling, remains a never-to-be-forgotten date, and the garden round the giant trees sets the scene.

Tartarin's expedition to Algeria, his baobab villa, and his army of boot-boxes and smallswords who cannot hold a blade all feed the joke. Daudet writes with affection for his braggart, and the novel's comedy comes from the gap between Tartarin's stories and his deeds. A gap his townsmen love him for, and never close.
18629-nature-near-london:
Richard Jefferies published these nature essays at London in 1905 with Chatto and Windus, in a fine-paper edition. Chapters wander woodlands, footpaths, flocks of birds, Nightingale Road, a brook, a London trout, a barn, wheatfields, and the crows. Later essays cover heathlands, the river, nutty autumn, a London copse, magpie fields, herbs, and trees about town.

The book closes with a trip to Brighton, the Southdown shepherd, and the breeze on Beachy Head. Jefferies writes with close, loving eyes for plants, birds, and field work near a great city. The essays remain a classic of English nature writing.
18678-a-victorious-union:
Oliver Optic published this boys' naval novel at Boston in 1894, after a 1893 copyright, as the last of his Blue and Gray Afloat series. It follows the Bellevite crew on a mission to Mobile Point, a bivouac near Fort Morgan, and a cotton schooner voyage. Captain Sullendine of the West Wind, the Tallahatchie, and a lively chase to the southwest fill the middle chapters.

Later scenes bring a flank move, a lieutenant's daring exploit, a magnanimous foe, and Colonel Homer Passford of Glenfield. Optic dedicates the book to Frank L. Harris, a naval officer friend who aided his facts. The novel closes the series with brisk sea action for young readers.
18698-the-recitation:
George Herbert Betts, professor of psychology at Cornell College, Iowa, wrote this 1910 monograph for the Riverside Educational Monographs series. It treats the recitation, the daily meeting of teacher and class, as the heart of teaching, the point where a teacher succeeds or fails.

Betts separates organizing a school from teaching in it, arguing that good order exists only so that teaching may go on. His chapters cover the purposes of the recitation, its method, the art of questioning, the conditions of a good recitation, and the assignment of the lesson. The book speaks to teachers who want their questions and lessons to stir thought, not merely to hear answers repeated back.
18707-gilbert-keith-chesterton:
Maisie Ward published this life of Gilbert Keith Chesterton at New York in 1943 with Sheed and Ward. Ward worked six years in three countries, talking to friends from Chesterton's boyhood on, from E. C. Bentley and Hilaire Belloc to Bernard Shaw and H. G. Wells. Ten long letters from Annie Firmin anchor the childhood chapters.

Chapters run from background and school days through art school, marriage, Orthodoxy, the Marconi affair, war years, Rome by way of Jerusalem, distributism, and last days. Appendices add an early Chesterton, a school prize poem, and a bibliography. The book is a rich, first-hand life of a famous wit.
1881-the-call-of-the-canyon:
Zane Grey's Call of the Canyon follows Carley Burch, a New York society woman who receives a letter from the West and finds a subtle, strange message in it. The letter lays itself in her hands like a summons. Carley must decide whether to leave the soft, gold-green shadows of the Astor and the sumptuous air of the St. Regis for canyon country.

Grey writes the choice as a romance between two ways of life: the city, with its hotels and ease, and the desert, with its space and danger. The novel's pull is Carley's slow change of heart, and it remains one of Grey's most popular love stories, set against the Arizona landscape he knew best.
18816-stand-by-the-union:
Oliver Optic's Civil War sea story, copyrighted in 1891, is the fourth volume of his Blue and the Gray Afloat series. It follows Christy Passford aboard the Bronx, where a sick officer, an apparent double, and secret orders tangle the young lieutenant's duty.

Chapters move from a mysterious visitation and a conference in the captain's cabin to a fight on the quarter-deck, the disposal of prisoners, and an expedition to St. Andrew's Bay. A meeting with the Bellevite at night and a visit to a village on the Isle Grande Terre widen the cruise. The novel offers young readers brisk naval action with a hero who must keep his head when friend and foe look alike.
18834-prisoners-fast-bound-in-misery-and:
Mary Cholmondeley, author of Red Pottage, published this novel with Dodd, Mead in 1906 under the title Prisoners, Fast Bound in Misery and Iron. It opens at Frascati, where Fay, the young Duchess of Colle Alto, stands on her villa balcony looking toward Rome.

Fay is twenty-three, English by birth despite her Italian title, fair and childlike in face, and anxious in a way that sits strangely on her. Her eyes turn toward Rome because it holds the man of whom she is always thinking. Later illustrations name Andrea, Wentworth, and a delegato, hinting at chains worn for love and a trial to come. The novel's title frames its theme: bonds that hold fast through misery and iron.
18851-gibbon:
James Cotter Morison, of Lincoln College, Oxford, wrote this study of Edward Gibbon for the English Men of Letters series, published by Macmillan in London in 1878. The chapters follow Gibbon from his early life and his time at Oxford through Lausanne, the militia, and his Italian journey, then into his London years, Parliament, and the Board of Trade.

Morison gives most space to the making of The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, tracing its first three volumes and then its last three, written after Gibbon returned to Lausanne. The closing chapters cover his final years, illness, and death. Readers get a clear, compact life of a great historian, useful before reading Gibbon's own vast history.
18878-return-loads-bureaus-to-save-waste:
The Highways Transport Committee of the Council of National Defense issued this bulletin in Washington on April 2, 1918, as Bulletin No. 1. Its subject was return-load bureaus, set up to save waste in wartime transportation. The Council had approved the widest possible use of the motor truck, and asked state councils to remove rules that restricted trucking.

The bulletin explains how bureaus matched empty trucks returning from a delivery with loads needing carriage, relieving railroad delays and embargoes. State councils, chambers of commerce, and local war boards cooperated in the scheme. Readers get a short, practical document of wartime logistics, showing how a new technology, the truck, was organized to serve a nation at war.
18879-the-age-of-the-reformation:
Preserved Smith's history of the Reformation, published by Henry Holt in 1920 in the American Historical Series, sets out to put the movement in its proper relations. Its preface names the economic and intellectual revolutions of the sixteenth century as the frame the Reformation needs.

Smith gave most of his leisure for six years to the task, through sorrow and joy, and thanks readers including Harvard's Charles H. Haskins, who read the whole in manuscript and proof. Chapters were also revised by William Walker Rockwell and read by Peter Guilday and N. S. B. Gras. The book promises a Reformation seen whole, in its world rather than apart from it.
18901-woman-as-decoration:
Emily Burbank published this illustrated book in New York in 1917, with Dodd, Mead and Company. Its subject is dress as decoration: how women present themselves through clothes, color, and ornament, and what good taste means in practice. Burbank writes from the world of fashion and society, addressing readers who care about appearance and its social effects.

The book argues that dress is an art, not a vanity, and that a woman's choices in fabric, line, and detail shape how she is seen and judged. Illustrations support the advice. Readers get a period guide to style, revealing in its detail about the standards, costs, and pleasures of fashionable dress just before the First World War changed them.
18949-day-of-the-moron:
H. Beam Piper's science fiction novella Day of the Moron, first published in 1951, is set in 1968 around a nuclear power plant. Fear of atomic energy lingers there among older residents and security officials.
