William W. Mann, a member of the British Esperanto Association, wrote Esperanto Self-Taught with Phonetic Pronunciation, in Marlborough's Self-Taught Series, third edition, printed in London. Its object is twofold: full vocabularies for the tourist, traveller, visitor, resident, and business man, with conversational sentences classified by subject.

Every word carries its phonetic pronunciation under Marlborough's simple system. Mann promises that anyone may undertake a foreign trip knowing nothing of the local language, and, by writing beforehand to Esperantists in each place, find helpers everywhere. A grammar section gives the student full insight into the language, which opens not one country but the whole of Europe.
24014-in-blue-creek-can-on:
Anna Chapin Ray, author of Half a Dozen Boys and Half a Dozen Girls, published In Blue Creek Cañon with Thomas Y. Crowell in 1892. Its frontispiece shows a quartette of boys and girls darting about on skates, and its epigraph, from Oliver Wendell Holmes, urges sticking to each other through thick and thin.

Chapters open with a council on skates, a welcome for the coming guest, and the Everett household. On the cross-head, a meeting in the waters, and Marjorie's party lead to Janey's prophecy, darkness, and camping on the Beaverhead. Up the gulch, sweet charity's sake, and a home without a mother lead to the nine-hundred level, the beginning of an old story, and Mr. Atherden. A completed story, a tragedy of the unexpected, and orders round out a Western girls' book.
24076-vegetable-dyes-being-a-book-of-rec:
Ethel M. Mairet wrote this practical book of dye recipes, first published in 1916 by the Ditchling Press and later reprinted by Faber and Faber. It teaches dyers to color wool, silk, cotton, and linen with plants, lichens, and other natural materials. Mairet, herself a working dyer, wrote from the dye pot rather than from theory alone.

Chapters cover mordants, the chemicals that fix color in fiber, then British dye plants, lichen dyes, and separate recipes for blue, red, yellow, brown, black, and green. Later chapters treat cotton and silk on their own, since each fiber takes dye differently. A glossary, bibliography, and index close the book, making it a lasting handbook for hand dyers and craftspeople.
24140-the-northern-iron:
George A. Birmingham published this historical novel in Dublin in 1907, after a holiday in County Antrim. The author names real places from that trip, Dunseveric and Ballintoy, the Runkerry cliffs, the Skerries, Donegore, Antrim, and Templepatrick, and sets his tale among the unhappy far-off battles of 1798. His hero Neal, with Una, swims into the Rock Pigeons' Cave.

Most of the characters are invented, and of the men who truly lived and acted in 1798, only James Hope appears in a large role. Birmingham aimed to keep faith with history's facts and with the thoughts of those who took part. Readers get a story of old Ulster, rebellion, and boyhood places remembered with care.
24182-rollo-in-london:
Jacob Abbott wrote this boys' travel book, published in Boston in 1864 with copyright entered in 1854. Rollo, twelve years old, travels in Europe with his father and mother, Mr. and Mrs. Holiday, his younger brother Thanny, his cousin Jane, and his uncle Mr. George. The book is one of Rollo's Tour in Europe, beside volumes on Paris, Switzerland, the Rhine, Scotland, Geneva, Holland, Naples, and Rome.

Chapters cover the city and town, London Bridge, the river, the policeman, lodgings, breakfast, Westminster Abbey, Saint Paul's and its dome, the aristocracy, the docks, emigrants, and the tunnel and the Tower. Abbott mixes sights with lessons in conduct and arithmetic. Readers get a friendly young traveler's London.
24236-time-and-tide-a-romance-of-the-moo:
Sir Robert S. Ball, Royal Astronomer of Ireland, gave these two lectures in the theatre of the London Institution on the afternoons of November 19 and 26, 1888. Published under the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge, the little book treats the theory of tidal evolution, a subject Ball says blends science and poetry in a happy conjunction. Its frontispiece shows the moon two days after first quarter, from a photograph by Lewis M. Rutherford.

Ball added matter to the lectures as delivered, and thanked friends who read the proofs, signing his preface from the Observatory in County Dublin on April 26, 1889. Readers get a clear, graceful account of how the moon raises tides and how tides, in turn, shape the moon's long story.
24282-attrition:
Jim Wannamaker wrote this science fiction story, with pictures by Krenkel, on survival by faster adaptation. A faxgram orders the narrator to report at once, while a news obelisk outside Mega Angeles' Galactic Survey Building flashes that one of their star ships is missing. The narrator rides up to Interstel's level, recalling a trainer's scrawl that space treats kindly those who respect her, and a second hand adding that fear is the word.

At the end of a long corridor sits the Chief Special Agent, Gravis, a large, rumpled man showing every year of twenty spent in Interstel. The narrator has come by air-taxi from Xanadu, a resort two hundred miles off the California coast. Readers get a tense service tale of missing ships, strange worlds, and adaptation as a race.
24302-the-highest-treason:
Randall Garrett wrote this science fiction story for Analog in January 1961, with pictures by Gardner. Sebastian MacMaine, a prisoner of the Kerothi, lives in two plain rooms with metallic gray walls. They hold a bed, a desk, a couch, easy chairs, bookshelves, and a refrigerator. He dresses in the insignialess uniforms of a Kerothi officer. The rooms look comfortable, not like a cell, yet television pickups watch every movement.

Infrared lets his hosts watch him while he sleeps, and every sound is heard and recorded. None of it bothers MacMaine. He wants the Kerothi to know he means no escape and hatches no plot against them. Garrett's note adds that the true traitor here is not singular, but very plural. Readers get a prisoner tale of loyalty, watching, and treason.
24332-the-life-of-mrs-robert-louis-steve:
Nellie Van de Grift Sanchez wrote this life of Fanny Van de Grift Stevenson. Chatto and Windus published it in London in 1920, with copyright in the United States by Charles Scribner's Sons. It is dedicated to Isobel Field, in token of common love for her whose life story the pages tell. Pictures show Fanny in her English period, her father Jacob Van de Grift, and the house at Vailima with its additions.

Chapters run from ancestors and early days in Indiana through the Pacific slope. France and the meeting at Grez follow, then California with Robert Louis Stevenson. Later come Europe and the British Isles, sunnier lands, and the happy years in Samoa. The lonely days of widowhood, back to California, travels in Mexico and Europe, and last days at Santa Barbara close the book. Readers get the life of Stevenson's wife, in her own right.
24499-the-green-carnation:
Published anonymously at New York in 1894, this novel satirises London's aesthetic set of the 1890s. Its hero slips a green carnation into his evening coat, pins it in place, and studies himself in a long glass before going out into the bright summer evening. Piccadilly murmurs below like a tide on a smooth beach.

The story follows its witty, pose-loving characters through parties, talk, and affectation, and readers of the day recognised its portraits of fashionable London. The green carnation itself became a badge of the aesthetic movement. The novel remains a sparkling, if pointed, picture of a glittering and self-conscious world.
24550-the-rise-of-canada-from-barbarism-:
Charles Roger published the first volume of this history at Quebec in 1856, with Peter Sinclair as publisher. Its full title promises the rise of Canada from barbarism to wealth and civilisation, and its Latin motto pairs the pen with the sword. Roger tells the story of the colony from its early days.

Later chapters follow settlement, war, trade, and government, as French and then British Canada grew into a prosperous province. Roger's history is partisan and old-fashioned, but it preserves a mid-nineteenth-century Canadian view of the country's past. Readers of Canadian history will find it a lively early attempt at a national story.
24557-the-boat-club-or-the-bunkers-of-ri:
Oliver Optic wrote this boys' story of the Boat Club, or the Bunkers of Rippleton, in a new edition revised and enlarged at New York in 1896. In his original preface, Optic calls himself, in his own words, mostly a boy still, and says he had no trouble stepping back to meet the wants of Young America.

The story follows a club of boys and their boats, with Tim Bunker among its heroes, seizing an oar in a moment of action. Optic mixes boating, friendship, and fair play into a tale of youth on the water. Young readers get a classic of the boat-club genre, cheerful, energetic, and full of river adventure.
24621-the-american-family-robinson:
D. W. Belisle wrote this adventure of a family lost in the great desert of the West, published at Philadelphia by Porter and Coates with illustrations. Its preface praises the towering mountains, great forests, rivers, and valleys of the West, much of it still unexplored, as a field for naturalists and antiquarians.

The story groups startling incidents of prairie life, with relics of antiquity hinting at a high order of civilisation and science among earlier peoples. A picture shows the prairie on fire. Readers get a Robinson Crusoe tale transplanted to the American West, full of danger, discovery, and family courage.
24623-mother-goose-the-original-volland-:
Eulalie Osgood Grover arranged and edited this edition of Mother Goose, illustrated by Frederick Richardson and published by Derrydale Books at New York. The compiler and artist dedicated it to two girls, Virginia and Doris, and to their mother. Its foreword calls Mother Goose the one great nursery classic.

Grover asks what gives these simple rhymes so firm a hold in homes, schools, and libraries, beside Shakespeare for grown readers. The rhymes themselves need no praise: they have lived in children's mouths for centuries. This handsome edition gives families the classic rhymes in a form worthy of them.
24627-booker-t-washington-builder-of-a-c:
Emmett J. Scott and Lyman Beecher Stowe wrote this biography of Booker T. Washington, published at Garden City, New York, in 1918 with a preface by Theodore Roosevelt. Scott had been Washington's secretary, and Stowe was the grandson of Harriet Beecher Stowe. Their book follows Washington from slavery to Tuskegee.

Chapters cover his schooling, his building of Tuskegee Institute, and his work with the Negro businessman, among other themes. The biography is admiring, as befits friends writing soon after his death. Readers will find it a warm, detailed portrait of the most famous Black American of his age, and of the world he worked in.
24667-aether-and-gravitation:
William George Hooper published this scientific treatise at London in 1903 with Chapman and Hall. Its subject is the aether, the invisible medium Victorian physicists supposed to fill space, and its relation to gravitation. Hooper sets out his own theory in full, with chapters on atomicity, heaviness, and the nature of matter.

Hooper argues that the aether explains gravity and the forces of nature, a claim later physics abandoned in favour of relativity. His book remains a fascinating record of physics at a turning point. Readers of science history will find it a clear example of a once-serious theory, argued with confidence just before it fell.
24717-danger-a-true-history-of-a-great-c:
Howe and Hummel, the famous New York criminal lawyers, published this sensational book at Buffalo in 1886, subtitled a true history of a great city's wiles and temptations. Its preface admits the startling title, noting that logic has not yet framed a title page that clearly shows a book's nature.

The book lifts the veil on crime and its causes, and on criminals and their haunts, with facts and disclosures from the lawyers' own practice. Its chapters follow swindlers, gamblers, and vice through New York. Readers get a lurid, firsthand tour of the city's underworld, as its best-known defenders saw it.
24723-final-weapon:
Everett B. Cole wrote this short science-fiction story, illustrated by Leydenfrost. Its premise is that man has developed many deadly weapons, but today the surest way to ruin a man's hopes and safety is a file folder. District Leader Howard Morely knew and loved that weapon.

Morely leans back to glance down at a bay between two blunt points of land. He looks at a skeletonlike spire on green hills, which once held up one of the world's great bridges. It stands, a ruin, for a fallen age. Cole's story turns on bureaucracy as a weapon, and on something more potent still to come.
24727-spontaneous-activity-in-education:
Maria Montessori, author of The Montessori Method, wrote this book on spontaneous activity in education, translated from the Italian by Florence Simmonds and published at New York in 1917. It forms part of her Advanced Montessori Method, and its first chapter surveys the child's life.

Montessori parallels the laws of the child's psychical life with those of its physical life, and she answers objections to education based on liberty. Her method trusts the child's own activity, guided rather than forced. Teachers and parents will find here a classic statement of Montessori thought, still influential today.
24749-adaptation:
Mack Reynolds wrote this short science-fiction story, illustrated by Schoenherr. Its epigraph warns that a man with much knowledge may confuse knowledge with wisdom, and forget that wisdom's antonym is not ignorance but folly. Its forward tells how man, barely a century after exploring the Solar System, began to grope for the stars.

With religious zeal, mankind conceived a fantasy dream of populating the galaxy, though no one asked why. Reynolds's story follows that dream to its consequences, as men adapt, or fail to adapt, to new worlds. Readers get a sharp, thoughtful tale of space colonisation and its costs.
24756-the-story-of-general-gordon:
Jeanie Lang wrote this short life of Charles George Gordon for young readers in 1906, in a series on heroes for children. It opens with Gordon as a boy at Woolwich, born in 1833 to a family of soldiers, then follows him into army service. The chapters move from his first battles to his years in China and his fight against slave traders in the Sudan.

The closing chapters cover Khartoum, where Gordon held out while help failed to reach him. Lang keeps the tone plain and warm, stressing his courage, fair dealing, and care for the people under his charge. For a young reader, the book gives a clear first sketch of a Victorian soldier whose name became famous across Britain.
24795-an-entertaining-history-of-tom-thu:
William Raine of Baltimore printed this short verse history of Tom Thumb, with eight colored pictures. In King Arthur's reign, a farmer's wife longs for a son, and a fairy grants her wish: a boy so small he is named Tom Thumb. His size then drives every mishap, from slipping into pudding batter to being tied to a thistle stalk and swallowed by a cow.

Each short verse pairs with a picture, and the rhymes carry Tom through ravens, puddings, and narrow escapes. The chapbook keeps the plain, funny voice of early nursery tales. Young readers will enjoy a tiny hero whose bold shouts get him out of scrapes that would daunt a full-grown man.
24946-from-a-cornish-window-a-new-editio:
Arthur Thomas Quiller-Couch gathers essays written from a Cornish vantage point, looking out at literature, conduct, and the ideas of his day. He takes aim at the fashionable 'Superman' philosophy, treating it as cheap Darwinism stretched across the whole of life, and he defends plainer virtues against grand systems. His subjects range across reading, writing, and the habits of mind that make a person worth listening to.

The collection opens with a dedication to William Archer and moves easily between argument and anecdote. One essay praises honest laughter as a moral test, preferring cheer that costs nothing to wit sharpened at another's expense. Readers who enjoy criticism with a Cornish accent and a sharp tongue will find the pieces bracing rather than merely charming.
24976-roger-trewinion:
Joseph Hocking's 1905 romance, published by Ward, Lock and Company, illustrated by Gunning King, follows Roger Trewinion through prophetic warnings, a wreck on the 'Devil's Tooth,' and a witches' cave. The chapter titles promise a tale of omens and darkness: the witch's warning, the march of events, the shaping of events, link to link, and the beginning of the end. The frontispiece shows a woman lifting her skinny arm above her head, a fitting emblem of its eerie mood.

At the story's emotional center stands Ruth, whom Roger releases from her father's will rather than link her life to his. He tells her he loves her too well to ask obedience, and will seek only what makes her happy. Relief floods her face as a burden lifts, while Roger, in agony that her joy comes from his promised absence, stumbles blindly out. Romance and foreboding carry the tale together.
25027-peter-piper-s-practical-principles:
Peter Piper's Practical Principles of Plain and Perfect Pronunciation, published in Philadelphia by Willard Johnson in 1836, teaches pronunciation through alliterative tongue-twisters, letter by letter. The preface, itself a thicket of P's, explains that Peter puts pen to paper to produce puzzling pages to please pretty prattling playfellows. He prays parents to purchase the performance partly to pay him, partly to provide for printers, and above all to stop perverse pronunciation spreading.

Each letter brings its hero: Andrew Airpump asking his aunt her ailment, Billy Button buying a buttered biscuit, Captain Crackskull cracking a catchpoll's cockscomb, and Davy Dolldrum dreaming he drove a dragon. Every verse repeats its question in three forms, drilling the ear as well as the tongue. The book is a playful primer from the age of elocution.
2510-the-invention-of-a-new-religion:
B. H. Chamberlain's Invention of a New Religion argues that the imperial cult of modern Japan was deliberately constructed in the nineteenth century, not an ancient survival. The essay traces how Shinto was reshaped into a state religion around the emperor, with Chamberlain's scholarly skepticism and firsthand knowledge of Japan. His argument provoked debate in its time.

The work remains a landmark in the study of invented tradition, cited by historians of nationalism. Its brevity makes its case with force. Readers of Japanese history will find a provocative classic. Chamberlain lived in Japan for decades and taught at Tokyo University.
25172-moral-principles-in-education:
John Dewey's Moral Principles in Education, published by Houghton Mifflin in 1909, argues that morality belongs inside ordinary schoolwork, not in separate lessons. Dewey, professor of philosophy at Columbia, draws on his earlier essay on ethical principles underlying education.

He separates moral ideas, which improve conduct, from mere ideas about morality, which may leave conduct untouched. Schools fail, he says, when children do identical work for no social purpose and lose the natural wish to give, serve, and communicate. The short book remains a classic statement of Dewey's view of the school as a social place.
2536-amphitryon:
Moliere first staged this comedy in Paris on January 13, 1668, and this English version is by A. R. Waller. Jupiter drives the plot, borrowed from Plautus. The king of the gods takes the shape of Amphitryon, a Theban general away at war, in order to visit the general's wife Alcmena.

Mercury, also in disguise, guards the door, and the real Amphitryon returns to find his home, his wife, and even his servant Sosie doubled before his eyes. Mistaken identity piles on mistaken identity, with witty quarrels between masters and servants. The play stays a bright classic of comic confusion, and a test of how far a god's trick can strain a marriage.
25440-an-undivided-union:
Oliver Optic's last boys' story was finished by Edward Stratemeyer after Optic's death. The publishers' preface explains that the outline and incomplete material lay among the papers of William T. Adams. Stratemeyer closed the Blue and Gray on Land series from those notes, answering constant demand from young readers. Lee and Shepard published the volume in 1899.

The story follows Deck, Artie, Hope, Dorcas, and Levi through Civil War escapes and rescues. A bullet leaves Deck with only an ugly scratch, yet the sight of blood makes Hope faint in Artie's arms. Prisoners, a fort, and a daring overseer fill the closing chapters. The book ends a series that followed its heroes on land and afloat.
25467-a-big-temptation:
L. T. Meade's title story follows Netty, a ten-year-old girl nursing a sickly baby in a London court. Netty's face is white from air no fresher than a court's, though a year before the Holiday Fund sent her and her brother Ben to the country. There she spent a delicious fortnight among trees and wildflowers, sleeping in a tiny clean room and waking to doves and birdsong. Now, whenever she is not at school, she lugs the baby about or rocks him to sleep.

The volume adds other stories by M. B. Manwell and Maggie Browne, illustrated by Arthur A. Dixon. One follows Clary in the Swiss mountains, where boys beg for tales of snow-boots, moonlight tobogganing, and the funicular railway up the great mountain. Ernest Nister published the book in London, with E. P. Dutton in New York.
25499-the-great-white-queen-a-tale-of-tr:
William Le Queux sets a treasure quest in West Africa, where a young Englishman is drawn toward a hidden realm ruled by a queen known as the Great White Queen. Early chapters promise romance, a strange pledge, a giant's finger, royal fetishes, and the stronghold of Samory, a famed African ruler.

Later chapters raise the danger with torture, human sacrifice, a sacred grove, and a city in the clouds, as treason among the travellers threatens the whole venture. Le Queux, known for invasion and secret-service tales, keeps the pace brisk and the African setting strange and perilous.
25520-the-stock-feeder-s-manual-the-chem:
Charles A. Cameron, a Dublin physician and chemist, writes this manual on the chemistry of food for breeding and feeding livestock. A prize yearling short-horn bull, Victor Emmanuel, owned by Lord Talbot de Malahide, fronts the book as proof of good feeding.

Cameron explains what feeds contain, how animals use them, and how farmers can match rations to growth, milk, and work. The manual suits stock feeders who want reasons behind practice, not rules alone, and it draws on farm trials and show results of its day. Cameron, a licentiate of the King and Queen's College of Physicians in Ireland, writes with a chemist's eye for exact measures.
2556-mr-jack-hamlin-s-mediation:
Bret Harte gathers stories around Jack Hamlin, the handsome gambler who drifts through mining towns settling other people's troubles. The title tale opens on a rainy nightfall, with wind rising, and Hamlin stepping in where lovers, rivals, and old scores collide.

Other pieces follow a man at a semaphore station, an Esmeralda of Rocky Canyon, a family Christmas, and floods at Jules. Harte gives Hamlin cool courage and a gambler's code, and the West around him feels both comic and dangerous. The set shows Harte's late gift for turning a card sharp into an unlikely peacemaker.
25572-capt-n-davy-s-honeymoon:
Hall Caine writes this 1893 tale of a captain's honeymoon, published by Harper and Brothers. It opens in mid quarrel between newly married husband and wife, with the captain insisting his wife married his money, not him, and she coolly agreeing.

He vows to spend every penny in ten months, or ten weeks, pitching it into the sea and scattering it to smithereens, then to leave her doors for good. Caine, writing in Manx flavoured speech, turns a marriage of money and pride into comedy and feeling, as the pair test each other from the honeymoon onward.
25628-the-nothing-equation:
Tom Godwin writes this science fiction tale of a lone man in an observation bubble, a full ten thousand light-years past the galaxy's farthest sun. Space ships, miracles of power and precision, had been checked and double checked in every detail except one.

The cruiser vanishes back into hyperspace, leaving him alone above a gigantic sea of emptiness, wondering what danger terrified the men before him. The first bubble attendant killed himself, the second became a mindless maniac, and the hero feels sure nothing waits outside to kill him. Something inside the bubble must hold the answer.
25684-a-world-called-crimson:
Darius John Granger writes this science fiction tale of a boy and a girl on a strange new planet alive with hideous dangers. All young Robin wants to know is who stole her doll, while a cyclops regards her as a new toy.

The Annals of Space, volume twelve, frames the disaster: the starship Star of Fire struck a meteor swarm six parsecs north of the galactic hub in 2278, losing air within forty-five minutes. Four thousand one hundred and sixty-six aboard were thought lost, until a Purcell exploration twenty years later found otherwise. Survival on Crimson drives the story.
2573-the-caged-lion:
This historical novel turns on a strange friendship across enemy lines. Henry V of England holds James I of Scotland prisoner, yet the young Scot lives at the English court through his youth more as a friend than a captive. The preface owns that some dates are shifted for the story's sake, but the bond at its heart is history.

James grows from a caged prince into a king in waiting, sheltered by his captivity from the violence tearing Scotland apart. The tale follows his learning, his loves, and his slow road home to rule. Readers get a tale of loyalty across enemy lines, and of a young king formed in exile.
258-poems-by-adam-lindsay-gordon:
Adam Lindsay Gordon, steeplechase rider and poet, sang Australia's bush before his early death. Poems, in the 1893 edition, gathers Sea Spray and Smoke Drift, Bush Ballads and Galloping Rhymes, and miscellaneous verse. A dramatic lyric, Ashtaroth, closes the set.

An opening memorial mourns Gordon by the sea whose sounds mingle with his verse. His galloping rhythms suit horses, storms, and open country. Gordon's songs were among the first claimed as truly Australian poetry. The volume keeps his brief, bright career in print. Gordon's bush ballads still appear in Australian anthologies of classic verse.
25804-the-children-s-book-of-london:
Mitton writes The Children's Book of London, first published in 1903 in London, with eight full-page colour pictures including Tower Bridge. Mitton dedicates the book to Rena, Cu, and Elfie. The Tower Bridge picture fronts the book, giving child readers a famous London sight at the start.

Book one treats London as it is, from London children and the king's palaces through trains and horses, school, markets, hospitals, streets and shops, and dogs and cats. Book two tells historical stories, from Edward V and tournaments to Sir Thomas More, Lady Jane Grey, gunpowder plot, Charles I, and plague and fire. Book three tours the Tower and other sights. The author signs the book G. E. Mitton.
25835-the-branding-iron:
Katharine Newlin Burt sets a ranch novel of love, claim, and escape in the West, printed in 1919. Joan, a young wife, reads by firelight while her husband Pierre lays a hand on her heart and guards her as his own. A young parson, Holliwell, wakes her mind as Pierre once woke her heart, and the clash between the two claims drives her to run away from the Two-Bar brand.

The book runs in two parts, The Two-Bar Brand and The Estray, following Joan through delirium, dried rose leaves, a leopardess in training, and a wild cat of a second life. Morena's wife, Jane, Prosper, and Luck's play all shape her flight and her return to choice. Burt writes of marriage, duty, and a woman's right to her own soul with heat and plain force.
25857-patty-s-social-season:
Carolyn Wells follows Patty through a whirl of parties, dances, and house guests in New York and the country. The season opens with Patty near buried in flowers in her drawing room. It rolls on through happy Saturdays, Christmas Eve revels, a Lord of Misrule with trumpet and sceptre, and a ball at the country club. Guests come and go, secrets are shared, and old ties are tested.

Printed in 1913, the book gives Patty a proposal, a turn as bridesmaid, and a stormbound stay that forces the party indoors. Wells keeps the tone light and brisk, with songs, games of hide and seek, and a chase to close the fun. Through it all Patty stays warm, quick, and good humored, the still center of a very busy social round.
25977-my-recollections-of-lord-byron:
Countess Guiccioli, Byron's late love, recalls the poet in this book, translated by Hubert E. H. Jerningham and printed by Harper in 1869. An English publisher's note calls it the long promised work of the celebrated countess. Contents run from an introductory sketch and Byron's dealings with Lamartine to portraits of the poet, his religious views, childhood, friendships, and his goodness as father, brother, and son.

Guiccioli stresses Byron's heart, his benevolence, his constancy, and the strength of his instinctive affections. She notes his taste for women of intellect and learning, and his trust in reputation and looks when choosing a wife for life. The book is a lover's defense, written by an eye witness who knew Byron close at hand.
26005-armour-s-monthly-cook-book-volume-:
Armour's Monthly Cook Book for October 1913, volume two, number twelve, mixes household hints, menus, and reader stories. Contents list a necessity in the pantry, baked beans as a national dish, baking day, grape juice uses, Halloween hints, home dressmaking, informal porch suppers, and prize contest stories. Daily menus run across four pages, with fruit cocktail, ham mousse, tongue toast, and chicken in aspic.

Garden notes urge October planting of bulbs, roots, tubers, and shrubs, with diseased plants burned and beds manured and plowed for winter. Kitchen notes warn that cold potatoes keep a stale taste, and sautéing serves leftovers best. A quoted thought closes the number: seeing God in common things beats sighs for the unattainable. The issue is a homely snapshot of housekeeping in 1913.
26083-luke-walton:
Horatio Alger Jr.'s novel opens with Luke Walton as a Chicago newsboy, holding a letter from the dead that sets his course. He forms a resolution, survives an attack in the dark, and finds his way to Mr. Afton's office, where a strange encounter marks him for trouble.

Stephen Webb gathers information, a plot against Luke fails, and a house on Prairie Avenue becomes the center of the scheming. Thomas Browning, pressed about California, admits a brief trip to San Francisco, while Luke's father died there. Rescue, theft, and a prodigal's reception close a tale of pluck against men who trade on secrets.
26095-the-athenian-constitution:
Aristotle's Athenian Constitution, in Sir Frederic G. Kenyon's translation, traces Athens from early trials to the rule of the Thirty. An opening case tries the guilty of sacrilege before a court from the noble families, with Myron as accuser; bodies are cast from graves, the race banished, and Epimenides purifies the city.

Later parts show an oligarchy where the poor, called Pelatae and Hectemori, tilled rich men's land at a rent and fell into slavery for unpaid debts. Solon then appears as champion of the people. The narrative closes with the Thirty set up as governors under a peace term calling for the ancient constitution, while democrats, club men, and unclubbed citizens pull three ways.
26108-revolutionist-s-handbook-and-pocke:
George Bernard Shaw's handbook, written in the voice of John Tanner, Member of the Idle Rich Class, serves as the companion to his play on the revolutionist. Its essays argue that revolutions only shift tyranny to another shoulder, and that real change must come from people remaking themselves rather than from new institutions.

Topics run from good breeding and property and marriage to the perfectionist experiment at Oneida Creek, the political need for the superman, prudery, and the conceit of civilization. Shaw takes up the Fabians too, noting that polite circles praise them for drawing the teeth of insurgent poverty rather than for adopting their policy. The book is argument, aphorism, and provocation in one pocket volume.
26112-a-tar-heel-baron:
Mabell Shippie Clarke Pelton's 1903 novel, in its second edition, follows Friedrich von Rittenheim, a baron set down among the southern Appalachians. Chapters move from the snare of the fowler and a weak man's strength to coveting a neighbor's wife, a strong man's weakness, and Sydney's ride against time.

Local color fills the middle: a Fourth of July gander-pulling at Frady's field, advertised by placards in stores and post offices along the Haywood Road, draws country people from miles around. Mrs. Carroll explains her habit of attending such gatherings to the Baron. Illumination, reconciliation, business plans, and the Baron's rent collection close the tale.
26135-love-at-paddington: W. Pett Ridge's 1912 novel opens on a Sunday afternoon in Praed Street, near Paddington Station. Children have been sent to Sunday school, and the street stays lively with travellers racing for trains. Second-hand shops stand shuttered, folk hurry past with hand luggage, and every clock is watched with worry or hope. The opening sets a busy London neighbourhood scene, rooted in the daily life of the streets around the great station.
26163-creative-evolution:
Henri Bergson's Creative Evolution, in Arthur Mitchell's authorized translation of 1911, sets out the French philosopher's view of life's growth. Bergson revised the whole work himself, and Mitchell notes help from William James, who admired Bergson's thought. The book argues against treating life as a mere machine or as a fixed plan worked out in advance.

Its first chapter weighs mechanism against purpose, and it treats duration, the lived flow of time, as real rather than abstract. Later chapters follow how living things change, and how instinct and intellect split as life branches. The book made Bergson famous in English, and it still shapes debates about whether evolution is driven by a creative push within life itself.
26172-union-and-communion-or-thoughts-on:
J. Hudson Taylor's Union and Communion, here in its third edition, reads the Song of Solomon as a picture of the believer's walk with God. A foreword by Rev. J. Stuart Holden opens the volume, issued by Morgan and Scott for the China Inland Mission. Taylor sets God's purpose as that stated in Paul's letter: that God may be all in all.

Six sections trace a path from an unsatisfied life to its remedy, through communion broken and restored, to the joy of unbroken communion. Later parts treat the fruits of recognized union and unrestrained communion, with an appendix to close. The book suits readers who want a devotional guide to a book of the Bible many find hard, and it stays close to the text throughout.
26215-the-little-colonel-s-christmas-vac:
Annie Fellows Johnston's 1905 volume belongs to the Little Colonel series, whose earlier books cover a house party, holidays, a hero, and boarding school. This tale sends its heroine off for a Christmas vacation, with train travel, letters, and a worry over bad news from home. At first she fears a baby named Davy has met with an awful accident.

She soon steadies herself, plans a postal card at the next station, and turns daily letters into a game of riddles and tasks. The story mixes travel cheer with tender feeling for family left behind. Young readers get a gentle holiday tale, full of kindness, pluck, and the small adventures of the road.
26217-the-loyalist-a-story-of-the-americ:
James Francis Barrett's 1920 novel, published by P. J. Kenedy and Sons, tells a Philadelphia story from the American Revolution. It opens with two girls, Peggy and Marjorie, talking over a grand ball cut short by Washington's sudden attack. The ball was the Mischianza, a pageant staged to honour General Howe as he gave up command and sailed for England.

The Shippen family stands at the centre, with Edward Shippen, a Quaker gentleman of rank and fortune, counted a sympathizer with the crown. Marjorie Allison moves through a city split by war, where dances, rank, and duty pull young people both ways. The novel treats loyalist Philadelphia with sympathy, and it shows revolution as a family and social crisis, not only a battle.
26257-the-boy-scouts-on-the-yukon:
Ralph Victor's 1912 volume, sixth in his Boy Scouts series, sends the patrol north to Alaska and the Yukon. Contents list the Inside Passage, a guide called Swiftwater Jim, rough waters, Alaskan soil, and a new mode of travel. Later chapters promise the biggest bear in the world, Colonel Snow's ranch, an heirloom returned, and a camp built in the wilds.

The boys face the pest of the north, cheer Alaska's first airship, and travel down river to Nome. Mammoth tusks on the Seward Peninsula and a homeward-bound close round out the trip. The book mixes camp craft, travel notes, and boyish adventure, with officers met on the way praising the Scout movement.
26306-simon:
J. Storer Clouston's 1919 novel Simon is a Scottish mystery built around a taciturn lawyer. It opens on a long train ride through desolate brown hills and a winding northern river, where a solitary passenger keeps shifting compartments to stay alone. Contents list a procurator fiscal, an heir, a man from the west, a third visitor, and a letter that returns again and again.

Simon argues his case with a patience and fluency that surprise those who know his silence. Questions of motive, deduction, rumour, and a sum of twelve hundred pounds drive the plot, with an empty compartment and a walking stick among the clues. The novel moves from Stanesland to flight and return, and it closes with a yarn that ties the threads together.
26397-miracles-and-supernatural-religion:
James Morris Whiton, writing in 1903, tries to clear up what the word miracle can still mean in an age of growing natural knowledge. He argues that the miraculous element in the Bible has narrowed as discovery has explained more, and that no hard line divides the miraculous from the natural. Miracle, he says, is a provisional word, and its use shrinks as mastery of nature's secrets grows.

Whiton gives most space to the raisings of the dead, which he treats as the class of miracle open to the most doubt yet still capable of being weighed as possibly historical. He also weighs the demand that the virgin birth and bodily resurrection of Jesus be held essential to Christianity. In the Gospel accounts, he notes, the psychical side of the resurrection stories outweighs the physical.
26412-life-and-sport-in-china-second-edi:
Oliver G. Ready's second edition of 1904 sketches China as Europeans living there saw it, on its lighter side. Ready writes for British readers who lack the firsthand experience that only residence can give. He hopes his book will serve as a preface to the daily history of China in press and magazines. He describes European work, amusements, and daily interests rather than politics or war.

River life gets close attention, including the heavily built inland craft with watertight compartments, square bows, and covered sterns where the lowdah and his family live. Women and children peer from tiny windows at foreigners sailing past, and a mainmast some sixty feet tall towers over the scene. The tone stays that of a friendly guide to a foreign shore.
26430-essay-on-the-creative-imagination:
Théodule Ribot's Essay on the Creative Imagination, translated from the French by Albert H. N. Baron in 1906, treats imagination as a power to be studied, not a mystery to be worshipped. Ribot argues that psychology long kept imagination as a vague spook, an entity sui generis found only in wild-haired genius. His analysis replaces that fancy with growth, habit, and combination.

Imagination, he holds, needs a high power of abstraction, which matures slowly, so mathematicians prove precocious while other creators wait on wider knowledge. The creator begins by imitating, a paradox Ribot calls well known and nearly without exception. From imitation, memory, and feeling, new forms arise, and the book became a classic statement of its subject.
26440-fire-prevention-and-fire-extinctio:
James Braidwood, first superintendent of the London Fire Brigade, published this work in 1866, covering fireproof structures, safes, public brigades, private means of suppression, engines, annihilators, portable escapes, and water supply. A memoir opens the book, tracing Braidwood from the great fire of Edinburgh and his appointment there to the formation of the London brigade. He won the Society of Arts silver medal and the Telford Medal.

Braidwood praises weekly wages, strict discipline, and liberal treatment for drawing good men, and he records the ladders, hose reel, hand pump, and steam engines his brigades adopted. A standard hose coupling, inspection of dockyards, and the great Tooley Street fire mark his career. The book closes with his public funeral and the esteem in which firemen held him.
2645-the-second-funeral-of-napoleon:
William Makepeace Thackeray, writing as Michael Angelo Titmarsh, reports Napoleon's second funeral in three letters. The first covers the disinterment at St. Helena, the second the voyage to Paris, and the third the funeral ceremony itself.

Thackeray opens by doubting our power to tell the great from the mean, and his eye stays skeptical through pomp, crowds, and speeches. The letters mix travel writing, satire, and history, and they show a young Thackeray learning his trade. The book charms as a wry eyewitness account of France honoring its fallen emperor.
26478-the-wallypug-in-london:
G. E. Farrow's 1898 fantasy, illustrated by Alan Wright, brings the Wallypug, king of Why, to London with his suite. A chant royal addressed to Queen Victoria opens the book, marking the Jubilee of June 22, 1897, and sixty years of her reign. His Majesty arrives, gets lost, holds an at home, visits the Academy, and is interviewed, before going on to Windsor and the seaside.

The humor runs through a child's-eye history of London, where Romans in firemen's helmets and kilts build the Wall, make combs and glass tear-bottles, and then depart. Julius Caesar, stabbed by his friend Brutus, cries Et tu, Brute, which the narrator renders as Oh, you brute. The Wallypug's departure closes a gentle satire on London sights.
26541-the-vicar-of-bullhampton:
Anthony Trollope published this novel at London in 1870, with thirty illustrations by H. Woods. Its center is the Reverend Mr. Fenwick, vicar of Bullhampton, and the Brattle family at the mill, including Sam Brattle and his sister Carry. In his preface Trollope defends his portrait of Carry, a girl he calls a castaway, whom he brings back from degradation at least to decency.

Village life, the Marquis of Trowbridge, the police, and a murder charge tangle around the family, and Sam faces suspicion he denies. Flo's red ball, the miller's wife, and Miss Marrable's counsel fill the quieter chapters. Trollope asks whether good people can pity the fallen without sharing their fault, and he refuses his heroine either a rich marriage or a ruined end.
26557-if-you-don-t-write-fiction:
Charles Phelps Cushing published this short guide in New York in 1920 for writers who do not write fiction but hope to sell magazine articles. He dedicates it to Cousin Ann, who wants to market articles, and he draws on fifteen years in journalism. The book promises to save beginners some of the tribulations on the road to acceptances.

Chapters teach a nose for news, the sense of what counts as a story, and the craft of preparing a manuscript and taking photographs editors can use. Cushing covers finding a market, the beginner's first adventures, New York's Fleet Street, and what the editor wants. Timeliness, plain human interest, and knowing each magazine's character run through his advice.
26691-sanctification:
J. W. Byers published this doctrinal book with the Gospel Trumpet Company in 1902. Its epigraph comes from Hebrews: Jesus suffered without the gate to make his people holy with his own blood. Byers gives three scriptural senses for the key word: separation, dedication, and spirit-filling. He treats holiness, purity, and perfection as words for the same thing. The book is short and plain in aim, and it speaks to believers who seek a clean heart.

Old Testament holiness meant outward dedication, as with the tabernacle, altar, and Aaron and his sons. New Testament holiness, Byers argues, is an inwrought work. It permeates and purifies the affections by cleansing blood and heavenly fire. It fills the body, as a temple, with the Holy Ghost, as at Pentecost. Chapters cover consecration, the Holy Spirit of promise, faith, the subtraction process, Christian perfection, and personal experience. It ends with questions and answers.
26706-manual-of-military-training-second:
Colonel James A. Moss of the United States Army wrote this manual, second revised edition, copyrighted in 1917 and published by George Banta Publishing Company at Menasha, Wisconsin, priced at two dollars and twenty-five cents. It was officially adopted by one hundred and five military schools and colleges, and aimed to make efficient fighting companies in wartime.

Moss intended it first for cadets and company officers of the National Army, National Guard, and Officers' Reserve Corps, and secondly as a guide for Regular Army company officers. Its parts cover drills, exercises, ceremonies, and inspections, company command, rifle training, health, military courtesy, guard duty, organization, and map reading and sketching. A companion Questions pamphlet, fifty cents postpaid, drilled every point for recitations and examinations.
26743-the-putnam-tradition:
S. Dorman wrote this short story, illustrated by Schelling. Its tagline says the power has descended through generations, now weaker, now stronger. It asks which way the power ran in the four-year-old at play in the garden with a pie plate. The old Putnam house near the coast has passed down through generations to the women of the family.

A four-lane highway now runs two hundred yards from the lilacs, and power lines hum like cellos on cold nights. Grandmother Cecily, Simone, and four-year-old Nina continue the matriarchs, but Cecily fears the power weakened in Simone. Simone dries dishes by passing her hand above each plate, and sweeps dust by moving her hand across the floor. Engineer husband Sam fills the house with washer, dryer, toaster, and mixer. The question is whether Sam's strength or the old blood will shape Nina.
26841-successful-stock-speculation:
J. J. Butler wrote this guide for the National Bureau of Financial Information in April 1922, published that December and expressly left uncopyrighted, so anyone might reprint any part of it. Twenty-six chapters in five parts move from first principles to practice. They define speculation, explain the terms of the trade, and set a correct basis for speculating. Then they say what stocks to buy and avoid, and when to buy, not buy, and sell.

Later parts weigh the forces that move prices, from major movements and the money market to technical conditions and manipulations. They then turn to marginal trading, short selling, bucket shops, choosing a broker, puts and calls, and stop-loss orders. Butler calls the chapter on market information the most important in the book, warning that much prevailing market talk misleads, and that misleading talk alone accounts for many losses.
26881-the-gospel-of-luke-an-exposition:
Charles R. Erdman, Princeton professor of practical theology, published this exposition of Luke with Westminster Press, Philadelphia, in 1936. Its Bible text comes from the American Standard Revised Bible of 1901. The book is dedicated to the men who long to be like him. Erdman works through the gospel in order, from preface to ascension, treating Luke as a historian with tools, material, motives, and methods.

Luke's preface, Erdman writes, is a gem of Greek art, unsurpassed for brevity, modesty, and dignity, and its value lies in its testimony to the writer's veracity. Luke had many written accounts before him, weighed them against eyewitness testimony, and sifted his material to record only established facts, in order for his patron Theophilus. Later sections weigh Jesus' birth and childhood. They draw parallels between the gospel's demoniacs and persons tormented by envy, lust, anger, and greed.
26951-firebrand-trevison:
Charles Alden Seltzer's 1918 western introduces Trevison, a rider on a black horse who makes enemies fast and keeps them. The early chapters pit him against a rigged court, a judicial puppet, and the long arm of power in a town where land titles trace back to the Midland Company.

Trevison stands by neighbors like Lefingwell, whose land he never truly owned, and faces summonses from Judge Lindman's court with straight talk. Seltzer builds the feud toward open war between justice and law, in the vigorous pulp-western manner of his Range Boss tales.
27057-ireland-and-poland-a-comparison:
T. W. Rolleston's Ireland and Poland, A Comparison, published in 1917, answers a wartime charge against the Entente powers. Critics called Britain hypocritical for championing small nations while Ireland still lacked a local parliament, comparing Ireland's case to that of Prussian Poland.

Rolleston argues the two peoples do not suffer the same oppression, injustice, or denial of rights. Ireland, he notes, sits fully represented in a united Parliament of four distinct nationalities, while Poland's lot under Prussia differed in kind. The book is a wartime defense of the Irish Home Rule cause on its own terms.
27058-the-indian-question:
Francis A. Walker's The Indian Question, published in Boston in 1874, comes from a former United States Commissioner of Indian Affairs. Walker opens with Congress's act of March 3, 1871, declaring that no Indian nation or tribe would henceforth be recognized as an independent power for treaty-making.

He sets that act against William Penn treating with the Lenni Lenape under the elm at Kensington and Miles Standish marching against the heathen of Plymouth. Later sections take up Indian citizenship and give an account of the tribes, making the book a post-Civil War argument about law, land, and the nation's obligations.
27076-drug-supplies-in-the-american-revo:
George B. Griffenhagen's Drug Supplies in the American Revolution, Smithsonian paper 16 of 1961, traces how the colonies kept their armies dosed when England cut off their drug supply. A few drugs trickled from the West Indies, but by 1776 the shortage was acute.

Army hospitals lacked medicines even while druggists elsewhere advertised stocks for sale, for want of coordination and transport. Relief came from British prize ships taken by privateers, and the chaos eased only with the French alliance of early 1778. The paper ends at Valley Forge, with a summary of a supply war within the war.
27089-the-risk-profession:
Donald E. Westlake's The Risk Profession follows Ged, a roving claims investigator for the Tangiers Mutual Insurance Corporation, who handles policies for men who do dangerous work. Called in by his boss Henderson on his third day back in Tangiers, Ged takes a tricky case after good work on Luna saved the company money.

The new claim turns on McCann's death under suspicious circumstances, and the investigator soon finds himself a member of the very risk he was sent to price. Westlake mixes insurance procedure with suspense, in the dry, plain-living voice of a man who hates complications and keeps finding them.
27097-the-boy-ranchers-in-death-valley-o:
Willard F. Baker's 1928 volume The Boy Ranchers in Death Valley, or Diamond X and the Poison Mystery, takes Bud, Nort, and Dick to harsh country. The boys plan a round-up and a once-over of the whole ranch, with veteran Billee along for the ride.

Chapters bring frightened horses, Bud's disappearance, a search, and his strange tale, followed by avengers, gas masks, and glittering yellow. Testing a gold mine and a strange discovery close the book, in a desert mystery where poison, not rustlers, is the enemy. The boys also give the whole ranch the once-over, checking what cattle are left and the chances of getting more.
2718-the-chaperon:
Henry James wrote this tale of an old lady in a high drawing room, dressed in deep mourning, her chair moved close to the fire. She knits and warms her knees, her face holding a faded nobleness, while London fog oozes into a room full of dusky, valuable things.

A girl of twenty enters, and the old lady's meditation turns to chaperonage, reputation, and the claims of youth on age. James writes with exquisite tact about manners as morals. The tale charms as a miniature of society, where a chair by the fire can hold a whole lifetime of judgment.
27203-self-mastery-through-conscious-aut:
Émile Coué's Self Mastery Through Conscious Autosuggestion, published in New York in 1922, teaches a method that Coué calls both new and as old as the world. Autosuggestion, wrongly studied until now, is an instrument we possess at birth, holding marvelous power for best or worst according to circumstance.

The volume adds Coué's thoughts and precepts, observations on what autosuggestion can do, and a survey of his séances, with letters from patients treated by the method. Education as it ought to be closes the argument that the conscious and unconscious selves can be trained together.
27266-the-seventh-day-sabbath-a-perpetua:
Joseph Bates's The Seventh-Day Sabbath, A Perpetual Sign, second edition revised and enlarged, was printed at New Bedford in 1847. It argues the seventh-day Sabbath from the beginning to the entering into the gates of the holy city. Bates writes to the little flock that the commandment binds now as ever.

He holds that Imperial and Papal Rome changed the seventh-day Sabbath to the first day of the week, and that twenty days before Sinai, God already required Sabbath keeping in Exodus sixteen. The tract treats the Sabbath as one of all things to be restored before the second advent of Christ.
27355-shoe-bar-stratton:
Joseph B. Ames published this western novel in 1922, by arrangement with the Century Company, and A. L. Burt issued it in New York. The story opens with a solitary passenger watching a little three-car train cross the brown prairie toward distant mountains. He is a man back from the dead in the eyes of the country he returns to.

Chapters titled Crooked Work, The Branding-Iron, Rustlers, and The Hoodoo Outfit show the shape of the tale: cattle theft and a mysterious motor car. The Secret of North Pasture and The Fight on the Ledge add a trap and a sheriff's intervention, with Tex Lynch, Mary Thorne, and Buck among the chief figures. It is a fast-moving ranch mystery of the old West.
27362-the-chronicles-of-a-gay-gordon:
Brigadier-General J. M. Gordon tells his own life story in this 1921 memoir, published by Cassell in London with eleven half-tone illustrations. Gordon was of Scots-Spanish origin, and his career carried him from schooling and first war experience through soldiering in Ireland, a voyage to New Zealand, and long service in Australia.

Later chapters cover polo and hunting, the Soudan contingent, the South African War under Lord Roberts, command of a mounted column, and work organizing the Commonwealth of Australia. Merchant, actor, newspaper proprietor, and Adelaide policeman all figure along the way. The book reads as a restless soldier's tour of the late Victorian and Edwardian empire.
27375-if-winter-don-t-a-b-c-d-e-f-notsom:
Barry Pain published this cheerful parody in New York with Frederick A. Stokes in 1922, and it went through four printings before December of that year. Its target is A. S. M. Hutchinson's best seller If Winter Comes, and Pain's title twists the original into If Winter Don't, with a hero named A.B.C.D.E.F. Notsomuchinson.

Pain opens with a Stevenson motto in praise of kindly parody, and admits he found Hutchinson's novel sympathetic and interesting. He quarrels only with two points: the character Effie, whom he calls incredible novelist's machinery, and the easy use of the Great War for fiction. The result is a fond spoof, best enjoyed beside the book it teases.
27462-the-last-evolution:
John W. Campbell Jr. published this short science-fiction story in Amazing Stories in August 1932, and it is reprinted here as a classic of the magazine. Its narrator is the last of his type left in all the Solar System, once of the ruling type, now setting down his record on a mentatype before he passes forever.

The tale is set 2,538 years on from the Son of Man's year. Machines, developed over six centuries from ear apparatus to eye and then to brain, could think, act, and work with perfect independence by 2500. Most men, needing no productive work, sought games, contests, and adventure. Campbell imagines machines outlasting and succeeding their makers.
27478-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
This file holds the first slice of volume three of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica, running from Austria Lower to Bacon, part one of two of the volume. As with the other slices, volume and page numbers are worked into the text of each article, and special notation marks vowels and consonants for the reader.

The slice opens with a key to the initials that identify individual contributors in volume three, from Anna C. Paues on the English Bible to Algernon Charles Swinburne on Beaumont and Fletcher, and Albert Frederick Pollard on English history. The key alone shows the range of scholars behind the edition. The slice then proceeds through its alphabetical articles in order.
27488-lectures-on-the-french-revolution:
John Emerich Edward Dalberg-Acton, first Baron Acton and Regius Professor of Modern History at Cambridge, delivered these lectures in the academic years 1895 to 1899. Macmillan published them in London in 1910, edited by John Neville Figgis and Reginald Vere Laurence. The French Revolution of 1789 to 1795 was then a special subject for the Historical Tripos, which set the course's scope.

Acton's lectures trace the Revolution's course and ideas with his famous moral seriousness, and the editors add connected fragments on the literature of the Revolution as an appendix. They note that they themselves supplied the lecture titles. Students of the Revolution will find a thoughtful, principled guide here.
27525-bones-in-london:
Edgar Wallace published this comic novel with Ward, Lock in London and Melbourne in 1921. Its hero Bones moves through London business life. The chapters name his fields of action: big business, hidden treasure, wharfingers, a Plover light car, a cinema picture, a deal in jute, and detective work.

The book opens in a slump in the shipping market, when decent citizens longed for war's glory. Two bareheaded men walk dejectedly to the Commercial Trust Building, to offices inscribed Pole Brothers, Brokers. Wallace mixes city comedy with adventure. Bones hits back, judges poetry, and studies men along the way.
27569-gilbert-keith-chesterton:
Patrick Braybrooke, author of Oddments and Suggestive Fragments, wrote this study of Gilbert Keith Chesterton, with an introduction by Arthur F. Thorn. The Chelsea Publishing Company published it in London in 1922, with a photograph of Chesterton reproduced by permission.

Braybrooke's preface argues that most people find life exciting until middle age, often premature, steals the thrill. Routine and mechanical living destroy the divine sense of wonder, and existence goes on at a low ebb. From that numbed condition, he says, much blind anguish is born. The book examines Chesterton, the great defender of wonder, against that loss.
27588-the-jupiter-weapon:
Charles L. Fontenay published this science-fiction tale in Amazing Science Fiction Stories in March 1959. Its tagline poses the whole puzzle: a living weapon of destruction, immensely strong and wholly invulnerable. Only one question remains: is he human?

The story opens with Trella in trouble at the Golden Satellite, a shabby saloon in Jupiter's View's rougher quarter. That dome colony stands on Ganymede, and Trella's companion Motwick has dropped into a drunken stupor. Two evil-looking men watch her, and she hopes only for a telephone. Fontenay builds a tense tale from that saloon.
27642-lectures-in-navigation:
Lieutenant Ernest G. Draper, head of the department of navigation at the Officers' Material School of the Naval Auxiliary Reserve, prepared these lectures in navigation as a textbook for that school. He lists Bowditch's American Practical Navigator among the books consulted, with Muir, Poor, Henderson, Lecky, and Norie.

Week one treats piloting: the compass, the pelorus and parallel rulers, the lead and sounding machine, the chart, and the protractor and sextant, ending with fixes by bearings and sextant. Week two treats dead reckoning, beginning with latitude and longitude and useful tables. Draper's lectures give reserve officers the working knowledge of navigation their service required. The course is plain and step by step. Each week adds a new skill.
27682-the-panchronicon:
Harold Steele MacKaye's 1904 novel invents the Panchronicon, a machine for travel through time, and sends its characters from a New Hampshire village in May 1898 into the English past. Two sisters, Rebecca and Phoebe Wise, are at the center of the adventure.

Their journey brings meetings with Francis Bacon, Shakespeare, and Falstaff at the Boar's Head, mixing comedy, romance, and literary play. The book belongs to the early wave of time-travel fiction, using the past as a stage for witty encounters rather than for scientific speculation. The contents promise a nocturnal evasion, a shipwreck on the sands of time, and Shakespeare writing his plays.
27732-city-crimes-or-life-in-new-york-an:
First published in 1849, City Crimes, or Life in New York and Boston, promises to mirror fashionable life, picture poverty, and expose the secret crimes. Its hero is Frank Sydney, a wealthy young orphan in New York.

Frank resolves to use his fortune for the good of mankind, but fashionable life, flatterers, and midnight encounters pull him toward temptation. The book is a sensational urban novel of its era, mixing moral warning with lurid scenes of wealth, vice, and city nightlife. Frank, handsome and twenty-one, kept elegant rooms and a private table for friends and champagne suppers.
27741-colonel-carter-s-christmas-and-the:
F. Hopkinson Smith's Colonel Carter's Christmas, published by Scribner's in 1911, gathers two stories of an old-fashioned Virginia gentleman: the title Christmas tale and The Romance of an Old-Fashioned Gentleman. The colonel, once of Carter Hall near Cartersville, now lives in reduced circumstances in New York.

Smith's narrator recalls festivals omitted from earlier chronicles, including a Christmas in a little Bedford Place house reached through a narrow tunnel. Warm, nostalgic, and gently comic, the book celebrates Southern courtesy surviving poverty and change. The colonel's earlier fortune came from coal lands sold to an English syndicate, the money given by his aunt Miss Nancy Carter.
2776-the-four-million:
O. Henry gathers New York stories in this volume, whose title counts the city's four million souls. Tobin's Palm, The Gift of the Magi, A Cosmopolite in a Cafe, and Between Rounds open a parade of clerks, shopgirls, cops, and dreamers.

The Skylight Room, A Service of Love, and The Cop and the Anthem follow, each turning on a twist that reframes an ordinary life. O. Henry writes with wit, warmth, and a newspaperman's eye for the city's small dramas. The book remains the classic portrait of old New York in short story form.
27763-a-journal-of-a-young-man-of-massac:
Written by a young Massachusetts surgeon, this journal records his capture at sea by the British in May 1813 while serving on an American privateer during the War of 1812. The second edition, with additions, was printed in Boston in 1816.

He was confined first at Melville Island near Halifax, then at Chatham in England, and last at Dartmoor prison, where he witnessed the massacre of American prisoners. His observations and anecdotes compare the moral and political character of three nations at war. An engraving of Dartmoor prison, showing the massacre of American prisoners, was added to the volume.
27765-a-yeoman-s-letters-third-edition:
P. T. Ross, a corporal in the Yeomanry, collected these letters from the First World War front into a book praised by London papers for its breezy, vivid humor. The third edition gathers his prose, verse, and rough caricatures.

Ross writes about comrades, danger, and daily soldiering with a light touch, finding jokes even in grim circumstances. Reviewers called it the liveliest book about the war yet, and its deeper interest lies in the gravity a careful reader can sense beneath the jokes. The Daily Telegraph praised his Ballad of the Bayonet as particularly smart.
27790-a-practical-enquiry-into-the-philo:
James Gall, inventor of the triangular alphabet for the blind, published this practical enquiry into the philosophy of education in Edinburgh in 1840. Gall, a plain man writing a plain book, drew on more than thirty years of work in Sabbath schools and reflection on teaching the young.

He argues that his successful exercises rested on principles he only gradually understood. He uses nature as a popular name for the God of nature whose laws govern learning. The book is an early Scottish attempt to ground teaching in philosophy rather than routine, and it shows a teacher thinking through his craft.
27793-child-and-country-a-book-of-the-yo:
Will Levington Comfort published Child and Country in 1916 with George H. Doran Company of New York, subtitled a book of the younger generation. Dedicated to those who come after the wreckers, to the builders of the rising generation, it moves through essays on bees and blooms, imagination, workmanship, and compassion.

Comfort recalls moving to the country before his children came, feeling forgotten without the town's vibration, then learning order from the soil. Later chapters treat the new social order, the highest of the arts, and the choice of the many, making the book a hopeful meditation on raising children toward a better age.
27830-conversation:
Mary Greer Conklin published Conversation, subtitled What to Say and How to Say It, with Funk and Wagnalls in 1912. Dedicated to a friend whose delightful conversation stimulated her youth, the book teaches the art of talk through chapters on discussion, gossip, dinner talk, and leading a conversation.

Conklin also contrasts discussion with controversy, defends innocent gossip against slander, and draws on Johnson, Stevenson, Coleridge, and Gladstone as talkers. The book is a window into Edwardian social life, when good conversation was prized as both a pleasure and a social skill.
27917-the-strange-adventures-of-mr-middl:
Wardon Allan Curtis published The Strange Adventures of Mr. Middleton in Chicago with Herbert S. Stone and Company in 1903. The book follows Edward Middleton, a gallant youth of twenty-three, through a series of adventures set in motion by gifts from the Emir Achmed Ben Daoud.

Each gift brings a new episode: a virtuous spinster, William Hicks, Norah Sullivan and a student of heredity, Dr. McDill, and Miss Clarissa Dawson. The story opens on a rainy Chicago night on Clark Street, and it mixes fantasy, humor, and moral fable in an inventive Edwardian romance.
27924-mugby-junction:
Mugby Junction, the extra Christmas number of All the Year Round for 1866, gathers stories by Charles Dickens, Andrew Halliday, Charles Collins, Hesba Stretton, and Amelia B. Edwards. The 1898 Chapman and Hall edition reprints the set with a frontispiece.

Dickens contributes Barbox Brothers, Barbox Brothers and Company, The Boy at Mugby, and the famous ghost story The Signalman, while the other writers take branch lines on engines, drivers, and compensation houses. The volume is a classic of Victorian Christmas fiction, built around a railway junction. The opening finds a traveler stepping off at Mugby Junction at past three on a tempestuous morning, sacrificing his through ticket.
27953-the-new-nation:
Frederic L. Paxson, professor of history at the University of Wisconsin, published The New Nation with Houghton Mifflin in 1915, after a 1912 copyright and a frontispiece portrait of Woodrow Wilson. The book traces American history from the Civil War through the new nationalism.

Chapters also cover Reconstruction, the panic of 1873, Grover Cleveland, the farmers' cause, populism, free silver, the Spanish War, Theodore Roosevelt, big business, and the muck-rakers. Paxson also argues that the war's military success obscured readjustments in politics, finance, and business that shaped the nation for a generation.
27963-history-of-education:
Levi Seeley, professor of pedagogy at the New Jersey State Normal School, published History of Education with the American Book Company in a revised edition copyrighted in 1899 and 1904. Seeley added sketches of the Sophists, Plutarch, Marcus Aurelius, Rollin, and Jacotot, with an appendix on American movements.

Chapters survey China, India, Persia, the Jews, and the classical and modern systems, with criticism of each and attention to great educators. The book served generations of American teachers as a compact history of schooling, from ancient examinations to the Quincy and Herbartian movements.
27984-ralph-gurney-s-oil-speculation:
James Otis wrote Ralph Gurney's Oil Speculation, published in New York by A. L. Burt Company with copyright in 1883 by James Elverson and renewal granted to James Otis Kaler in 1911. The novel opens at Bradford, Pennsylvania, where a train brings two college mates together for a vacation.

George Harnett, a civil engineer working in the oil fields, promises his chum that the life is anything but monotonous, and the pair set out over bad roads toward the wells. Otis mixes boyish adventure with the excitement of the Pennsylvania oil boom, in the sturdy manner of his popular stories.
27995-the-history-of-london:
Walter Besant, author of London and Children of Gibeon, published The History of London with Longmans, Green in a second edition in 1894. The book is arranged as sixty-two lessons, from the foundation of London and Roman London through Saxon settlement, the wall, Norman London, and FitzStephen's account.

Later lessons cover London Bridge, the Tower, St. Paul's, Whittington, Westminster Abbey, Elizabethan London, trade, plays and pageants, plague, fire, and the government of the city. Besant writes for students and general readers, and the volume is a clear, orderly introduction to London's long story.
28031-resurrection:
Robert J. Shea wrote Resurrection, a short science-fiction story predicting a future where medicine grows new limbs for the dead and goes further, in experiments Baron von Frankenstein would have found interesting. The story follows a short, stocky man with Asiatic features and a long mustache, talking with a girl under two suns.

Revived in the twenty-second century on a world light years from his birthplace, the man struggled with robot waiters he took for demons, then learned all of history, including his own. Shea's tale mixes wonder, humor, and the strangeness of waking in a future that knows you better than you know it.
28036-public-school-education:
Michael Müller, priest of the Congregation of the Most Holy Redeemer, published Public School Education in Boston with Patrick Donahoe in 1872. Müller, who calls America his home and his country dearest after God and religion, argues that the public school system usurps individual rights and cannot truly educate.

Chapters charge evil consequences for boys and girls, call the state a robber violating constitution and common law, and conclude that only the denominational system can satisfy wants and save the republic. The book is a forceful Catholic critique of American public schooling in the age of common schools.
28040-robin-tremayne-a-story-of-the-mari:
Emily Sarah Holt's Robin Tremayne, set in the 1550s, follows an English Protestant family under Queen Mary. When Catholic worship returns as the law of the land, men and women who preach the reformed faith face prison and burning at the stake. Robin himself is jailed, and his account of prison cruelty forms the heart of the book.

Holt based much of the tale on well-studied fact, adding homely detail and footnotes that explain old words. The story ends as Elizabeth takes the throne and the faith of the land changes again. It offers a vivid, partisan view of the Marian persecution for young readers.
28073-a-yacht-voyage-to-norway-denmark-a:
W. A. Ross wrote A Yacht Voyage to Norway, Denmark, and Sweden, second edition, London, 1849, as a gentleman's sailing journal. Ross sails his yacht Iris from Greenwich through the North Sea to Christiansand, then on through fjords, towns, and inland rivers. He dedicates the volume to Robert, Lord Rodney.

Chapters report fog, fishing, bear hunting, rustic lodgings, and Norwegian hospitality, with notes on towns, trade, and local customs. Ross writes as a traveller of leisure, keen on sport and scenery. The book gives a lively view of Scandinavia before steam travel changed its coasts.
28089-tatterdemalion:
John Galsworthy published Tatterdemalion with Charles Scribner's Sons in New York in 1920, copyrighted 1914 through 1920 by Scribner, the Ridgway Company, the New Republic, and the Atlantic Monthly. The epigraph from Chaucer reads, Gentillesse cometh fro' God allone, and the book is dedicated to Elizabeth Lucas.

Part one, Of War-Time, holds fifteen stories from The Grey Angel and Defeat through The Muffled Ship and A Green Hill Far Away. Part two, Of Peace-Time, holds eight more, from Spindleberries to Buttercup-Night. Galsworthy's collection moves from wartime loss to peacetime reckoning, in the restrained, ironic manner of his best short fiction.
28103-the-doctrines-of-predestination-re:
Robert Wallace, pastor of Cathcart Road Evangelical Union Church in Glasgow, wrote this 1880 study of three linked doctrines. Predestination, reprobation, and election ask whether God chose some people for salvation before time began, and what that choice means for human freedom. Wallace treats the questions as part of a wider Evangelical Union series.

He opens with plain pictures, such as castaways judging the folk of a strange island, then argues from design in nature and from Scripture. The tone is earnest and careful, aiming to persuade rather than to scold. The book suits readers who want a clear nineteenth-century statement of these doctrines.
28178-sound-military-decision:
Sound Military Decision, issued by the United States Naval War College in 1942, reprints a 1936 textbook on how commanders should think. The book, published by the Naval Institute Press at Annapolis, teaches officers to weigh mission, enemy, and means, and to reach a clear, reasoned choice under pressure. An index closes the volume.

The 1941 foreword, dated at Newport, Rhode Island, frames the text for a navy now at war. Its method, drawn from staff study, stresses facts, estimates, and plain judgement over guesswork. The book serves historians of military thought and readers of Second World War staff training.
28244-the-gay-rebellion:
Robert W. Chambers wrote The Gay Rebellion in 1913 as a light novel of love and society, dedicated in verse to Suzanne Carroll. Chambers, who jokes in his dedication that he is no poet, tells a tale neither wholly new nor stale, with bright, winsome heroines and gay scoffers in Manhattan. Edmund Frederick drew the pictures.

The frontispiece shows a young woman looking almost insolently at a suitor, answering only, presently. That cool, teasing tone runs through the book, as lovers spar, part, and return. Chambers writes for readers who enjoy Edwardian romance with wit, fine clothes, and a light touch.
28256-thoughts-on-a-revelation:
S. J. Jerram, vicar of Chobham, Surrey, wrote Thoughts on a Revelation in London in 1862. Jerram asks how humans can know God, and argues that direct sight, natural reason, and implanted ideas all fall short, so knowledge of God must come by revelation. His abstract lists the conditions a true revelation must meet.

A revelation, he says, must have a distinctive character, be authenticated to its first hearers, and fit the knowledge of its time. Words and ideas, limited by experience, shape what it can convey. The book offers a careful Victorian argument for revealed religion, aimed at thoughtful readers.
28337-hushed-up-a-mystery-of-london:
William Le Queux wrote Hushed Up in 1911 as a mystery of London. The prologue asks whether a great man's death, certified as heart failure, was truly natural, or hushed up as a nation's loss. Phil Poland knows the truth, and a cigar on the floor hints at more. Eveleigh Nash published the novel in London.

Chapters follow Owen Biddulph through still waters, a dark house in Bayswater, a ghastly truth, forbidden love, and a man in gold pince-nez, to proof positive and a Frenchman's statement. Le Queux keeps the scandal brisk and the clues thick. Readers of Edwardian thrillers get a fast, lurid London mystery.
28357-by-conduct-and-courage-a-story-of-:
G. A. Henty wrote By Conduct and Courage as a boys' tale of the days of Nelson. The story follows a young hero through the naval wars of the French Revolution, with Lord Hood placing a squadron of frigates under Captain Nelson. A chapter titled With Nelson marks the hero's service beside the great admiral. Henty's long list of historical tales fronts the volume.

The hero learns seamanship, duty, and courage under fire, in the author's brisk, moral style. Battles, blockades, and shipboard life fill the pages. Readers of Henty's tales get a lively introduction to Nelson's navy, where conduct counts as much as daring.
28471-man-and-his-ancestor-a-study-in-ev:
Charles Morris's Man and His Ancestor, published in 1900, presents the case for human evolution against direct creation, chapter by chapter. Morris argues that creation rests on authority and cannot be argued, while evolution rests on evidence and can be tested.

Chapters examine vestiges of man's ancestry, relics of ancient man, the change from quadruped to biped, the freeing of the arms, and the growth of intelligence and language. Later chapters follow warfare, civilization, morality, and man's relation to the spiritual. Written a generation after Darwin, the book gives a clear popular statement of evolutionary thought for general readers.
28503-the-wit-of-women-fourth-edition:
Kate Sanborn's The Wit of Women, in its fourth edition of 1895, argues that women's wit has been ignored while men's wit has been discussed to threadbare. Sanborn, writing from Hanover, New Hampshire, in August 1885, presents a summer's gleaning of jokes, epigrams, and anecdotes with the pride of a discoverer.
