Chapters cover the melancholy tone of women's poetry, puns good and bad, epigrams, the cynicism of French women, the humour of literary Englishwomen, and writers from Anne Bradstreet to Mrs. Stowe. Later chapters offer samples, a brace of witty women, and ginger-snaps. The book is both an anthology and an early claim for women's humour.
28508-the-comical-creatures-from-wurtemb:
The second edition of The Comical Creatures from Wurtemberg, published by David Bogue of London in 1851, preserves a hit of the Great Exhibition. Herrmann Ploucquet of Stuttgart showed stuffed animals posed in comic scenes, and twenty illustrations here copy them by daguerreotype and wood engraving. Rabbits at lessons, a hare hunt, and kittens at tea lead the scenes.

The letterpress joins weasels, rabbits, and foxes in one tale, with the wonderful hare hunt in another. A tea party of kittens, the marten and Tabby, a duel of dormice, frogs, and Reynard the Fox follow in turn. Readers get a drawing-room souvenir that children could also thumb in the nursery.
28535-out-of-this-world-convention:
Forrest J. Ackerman's Out of This World Convention reports the 14th World Science Fiction Convention in New York as an eye-witness. Ackerman, who attended the first convention seventeen years earlier, calls himself a spy for the Fantasy Bureau of Investigation. The new gathering drew more than twelve hundred registered fans, authors, editors, artists, and publishers, against 125 at the first.

They came from 37 of the 48 states, plus Canada, Cuba, England, Germany, India, and Israel. Guest of Honor Arthur C. Clarke spoke for forty-five minutes to standing ovations, while Asimov, Sturgeon, Leiber, and many more filled the roster. A masquerade ball, filmed for television, crowned the Labor Day weekend.
28577-the-negrito-and-allied-types-in-th:
David P. Barrows's The Negrito and Allied Types in the Philippines, reprinted from the American Anthropologist of July to September 1910, rests on nine years of residence and travel. Barrows argues that the Negrito element has been slighted in Malaysian ethnology, with too much made of the Indonesian theory and pre-Spanish Chinese influence. Measurements taken between 1901 and 1909, by Topinard's methods, anchor the paper.

A community on Mount Mariveles in Bataan supplies the standard: nine men and ten women, nearly all of pure Negrito race. Their stature runs extremely low, with men's mean at 1440 millimeters, and arm reach exceeds stature in every case. Cephalic and nasal indices follow. Readers get early anthropology, frank in its categories and careful in its tables.
28728-bert-wilson-on-the-gridiron:
J. W. Duffield wrote this 1914 boys' sports novel about Bert Wilson and school football. The story opens with the despised scrubs holding the varsity at their ten-yard line, three plunges thrown back without a gain, until the ball goes over on downs. Later chapters bring a thrilling exploit, breaking the rules, tackling the Army, a lion's escape, a toboggan ride, a coach robbery, and a dash for the goal.

Duffield, who also wrote Bert Wilson at the Wheel and Bert Wilson, Wireless Operator, keeps the action fast and the talk full of school spirit. The book celebrates pluck, teamwork, and never saying die, in the style of the school sports stories of its day. Young readers who like football fiction get a lively period example, with a hero who earns his place by grit.
28769-ted-marsh-on-an-important-mission:
Elmer Sherwood wrote this boys' adventure about Ted Marsh, a Boy Scout who takes on a secret errand. Ted travels to Chicago, meets a man named Strong, and helps set a trap that uses a dictaphone to catch wrongdoers. The chase runs through Ottawa and back, ending with a reward and the Marsh family brought together again.

The story follows an earlier book, Ted Marsh, the Boy Scout, and it recaps Ted's time on a ranch in western Canada for new readers. Its pleasures are those of the scout adventure of its day: a brave boy, a clear mission, clever listening devices, and villains outwitted rather than fought. Young readers get a fast, straightforward tale of pluck and fair play.
28773-general-gordon:
Lieutenant-Colonel Seton Churchill wrote this 1907 life of Charles George Gordon, the British soldier remembered as a Christian hero. Born at Woolwich in 1833, Gordon served in the Crimean War, commanded forces against the Taiping Rebellion in China, and later governed the equatorial province and then the whole Sudan for Egypt. The book follows him to Khartoum, where he was besieged and killed in 1885.

Churchill dedicates the life to the young men of England, hoping Gordon's simple faith and sense of duty will shape future readers. Chapters treat his religion, his work against the slave trade, and his posts in Mauritius, the Cape, and Palestine. It is a hero-worshipping biography of its era, warm, earnest, and written to inspire as much as to inform.
28775-mendelism-third-edition:
R. C. Punnett, professor of biology at Cambridge, wrote this 1911 book explaining Mendel's laws of inheritance, in a third edition entirely rewritten and enlarged. It opens with the problem Mendel set himself, retells his experiments with peas, and then sets out the presence and absence theory, the interaction of factors, reversion, and dominance. Later chapters treat wild and domestic forms and the breeding of animals and plants.

Punnett writes for readers who know some biology but are not specialists, using clear diagrams and plain examples to show how traits pass from parent to child. The book helped carry Mendel's rediscovered work into English teaching and farming practice. It remains a landmark of early genetics, readable as both science and history.
2880-a-blot-in-the-scutcheon:
Robert Browning wrote A Blot in the 'Scutcheon as a verse tragedy of family honor, printed here with an introductory note contrasting his origins with aristocratic poets. Browning's father was a bank clerk and dissenter, and the poet attended neither a great public school nor Oxford or Cambridge. That outsider's eye shapes a play about rank, shame, and a father's power.

The action centers on Lord Tresham and his trusted old servant Gerard, who has eaten the family's bread for almost sixty years. Night after night, Gerard has watched something he must at last speak truthfully about. The play's verse drives toward a violent reckoning over a stain on the family name, and it remains Browning's most stageable drama.
28821-the-works-of-charles-dudley-warner:
David Widger edited this index to the Project Gutenberg editions of Charles Dudley Warner's works. Warner lived from 1829 to 1900 and wrote essays, travel books, and novels. The index gathers his essays and travel books: Backlog Studies, In a Garden, Being a Boy, Saunterings, and Our Italy. His novels Their Pilgrimage, A Little Journey in the World, and The Golden House appear with full chapter lists.

The volume is a finding aid, not a single work: it lets a reader move through Warner's long career title by title and chapter by chapter. It suits anyone exploring a once-famous American essayist whose garden writing and travel sketches were widely read in his day. Used beside the Gutenberg texts themselves, it turns a scattered set of files into a readable shelf.
28951-frontier-service-during-the-rebell:
George H. Pettis wrote this 1885 history of Company K, First Infantry, California Volunteers, during the Civil War. The Rhode Island Soldiers and Sailors Historical Society published it as number fourteen of its third series, in an edition limited to two hundred fifty copies. It tells of frontier service far from the great eastern battles. Pettis served as first lieutenant of Company K and later as adjutant of the First New Mexico Infantry.

The narrative opens after the first battle of Bull Run, when the North realized the rebellion would not be put down with seventy-five thousand men. Pettis records marches, posts, and desert duty with a soldier's plain detail. Readers get a rare account of the war's western edge, where California volunteers guarded a frontier while the nation's fate hung in the east.
28991-the-next-step-a-plan-for-economic-:
Scott Nearing wrote this 1922 book, The Next Step: A Plan for Economic World Federation, published at Ridgewood, New Jersey, by Nellie Seeds Nearing. Nearing, author of The American Empire and many books on wages, poverty, and social adjustment, dedicates the work to freeing the human race from economic servitude. His epigraphs quote Gantt on service first, and Macfarlane on coal and iron shaping Europe's peace.

The argument holds that men cannot exist in present numbers without world organization of economic life, and that common language and frontiers alone will not stabilize Europe. Nearing plans a federation built on production and distribution rather than armies. Readers get a bold interwar proposal from a famous American radical, clear in aim and earnest in its hope for peace through shared work.
28992-james-madison:
Sydney Howard Gay wrote this life of James Madison, in a series on the founding fathers called Giants of America. The chapters run from the Virginia Madisons and the young statesman through Congress, the state assembly, and the legislature, to the Constitutional Convention, the compromises, and adoption of the Constitution. Later chapters treat national finances, slavery, Federalists and Republicans, and French politics.

Madison's later years bring the resolutions of 1798 and 1799, service as secretary of state, the embargo, the presidency, and war with England. Gay writes a compact, readable life, with a frontispiece from Sully's portrait and a view of Montpelier. Readers get a solid nineteenth-century biography of the Father of the Constitution, clear on politics and character alike.
29001-five-mice-in-a-mouse-trap-by-the-m:
Laura E. Richards wrote this 1881 children's book, Five Mice in a Mouse-Trap, by the Man in the Moon, done in vernacular from the lunacular, with pictures by Kate Greenaway, Addie Ledyard, and others. The Man in the Moon introduces himself to earth children, denying nurses' nonsense about asking the way to Norwich, and promising a book about himself and about his readers.

The chapters follow the man in the moon, the mouse trap, and the mice. They pass through Jollykaloo, Tomty, a night journey, and a rainy day, to a picnic, a carriage cloud, and a birthday party. Richards writes playful nonsense verse and prose for young children. Readers get a charming Victorian fantasy, illustrated by Greenaway, in the spirit of Lear and Carroll.
2909-the-eldest-son:
John Galsworthy's The Eldest Son plays out over December seventh and eighth at the country house of Sir William Cheshire and Lady Cheshire. Their eldest son Bill, the second son Harold, and their daughters face a crisis when Bill's affair with Rose Taylor, a village girl, forces the family to choose between marriage and reputation. The Reverend John Latter, engaged to Joan, and the keepers Studdenham and Dunning fill the household.

Lady Cheshire warns Rose that marriage is for life and that self-respect must guide her, while Rose insists Bill ought to marry her. The play weighs class, duty, and love without letting any character off lightly. It remains one of Galsworthy's clearest country-house dramas, where a single engagement exposes a whole social order.
29131-out-of-the-depths-a-romance-of-rec:
Robert Ames Bennet published this novel in Chicago in 1913, with illustrations by George Brehm. Its subtitle names the theme: a romance of reclamation, the winning back of a life gone wrong. Chapters run from Deep Canon and a yearling sold, through downhill and up, into the depths, and toward a test of caliber.

Bennet, author of Out of the Primitive and The Shogun's Daughter, writes a western story of fall and recovery. A wild race, a chance of reclamation, and a hero tested by hardship carry the plot. Readers get an early twentieth-century western romance about a man climbing out of his own depths, told with the pace of the popular adventure novel.
29168-houlihan-s-equation:
Walt Sheldon wrote this short science fiction story about a tiny spaceship built for a journey to a star. Its small, mischievous pilots, however, have a rendezvous with destiny on Earth instead. The narrator first hears odd noises in a park near a nuclear propulsion center, a cool green spot that reminds him of a childhood sanctuary.

Sheldon, a former Air Force officer then living in postwar Japan, tells the tale lightly, letting the little crew's mischief carry the humor. The story turns on a simple joke of scale: a starship, a park, and pilots far smaller than anyone expects. Readers get a bright, brief fantasy, charming rather than grim, about a great voyage that lands very close to home.
29199-the-siege-of-boston:
Allen French published this history of the Siege of Boston with Macmillan in 1911. French begins well before the siege, with writs of assistance and the Stamp Act, then moves through Charles Townshend, Samuel Adams, the Boston Massacre, and the Tea Party and its consequences.

Later chapters cover the occupation of Boston, the powder alarm, the winter of 1774 to 1775, military preparations, and the nineteenth of April. French writes a full narrative of how a colonial port became a besieged city. Readers get a detailed, old-fashioned military and political history of the Revolution's opening siege, useful for its thorough march through causes and events.
29258-the-enclosures-in-england-an-econo:
Harriett Bradley, assistant professor of economics at Vassar College, published this study in 1918 in Columbia University's Studies in History, Economics and Public Law, volume 80, number 2. Bradley offers an economic reconstruction of the enclosures in England, when open fields were fenced and turned to private use. No attempt, she notes, had yet verified the rival explanations of the movement.

Chapters test the accepted theory that enclosure followed the price of wool, examine the fertility of common fields, and trace the disintegration of open fields. A final chapter covers enclosure for sheep pasture. Readers get a careful early economic history, using evidence to check theory, about a change that reshaped English farming and village life.
29274-people-of-position:
Stanley Portal Hyatt published this novel in New York in 1910, with a frontispiece by H. Richard Boehm. Hyatt, author of Little Brown Brother and End of the Road, opens with a prologue of war. Grierson refills his rifle magazine, taking no chances with South American patriots. Then he kneels beside a dead man whose kindly face seems to smile even in death.

Grierson smooths the dead man's hair, hides the bullet hole in his bronzed throat, and crosses his hands on his breast. The scene sets the novel's concern with position, loyalty, and the cost of conflict. Readers get an early twentieth-century novel of adventure and society, opening on a battlefield and moving among people whose standing shapes their fates.
29294-the-railroad-question-a-historical:
William Larrabee, late governor of Iowa, published this treatise on railroads and remedies for their abuses. It was copyrighted in 1893 and issued here in a ninth edition in 1898. Larrabee frames the main question directly. Shall railroads be owned as public or private property? Shall they be run for a few men's gain, or kept under strict government control for all users at fixed, equal, and reasonable rates?

Chapters trace transportation history, railroad monopoly, abuses, stock and bond inflation, combinations, and railroads in politics. Later chapters cover Iowa railroad legislation, the Interstate Commerce Act, and the rate question. Readers get a leading populist-era case for regulation, written by a governor who had fought the railroads from inside state government.
29339-the-practice-of-autosuggestion:
C. Harry Brooks wrote this revised edition on the practice of autosuggestion. It follows the method of Emile Coue, with a foreword by Coue himself. Dodd, Mead and Company published it in New York in 1922. The book went through fourteen printings between May 1922 and January 1923. Brooks dedicates it to all in conflict with their own imperfections.

Brooks explains Coue's discoveries as a help to happiness and efficiency, arguing that thought is a force. Chapters cover the nature of autosuggestion and a children's clinic, among other topics. The epigraph quotes Corinthians: what man knows the things of a man save the spirit of man within him? Readers get a popular self-help book from the Coue craze, earnest about the power of repeated suggestion.
29362-the-goat-gland-transplantation:
Sydney B. Flower's 1921 book tells the story of J. R. Brinkley of Milford, Kansas, and his much-touted goat-gland operations on men and women. Brinkley claimed more than 600 such operations, and Flower sets out his methods, his hopes, and his case reports in the booster prose of the New Thought press. A note added to the text recalls that Brinkley's Kansas license was later revoked in 1930.

Readers meet a striking case of early twentieth-century medical showmanship: bold claims, eager patients, and a blend of surgery with sales talk. The book is best read as a record of how such cures were sold, not as sound medicine. It gives students of quack cures and popular health fads a first-hand, if credulous, source.
29367-humpty-dumpty-s-little-son:
Helen R. Cross wrote this small children's picture book, number 37 in the Dumpy Books for Children, published in London in 1907 by Chatto and Windus. Edmund Evans engraved and printed the series. The Dumpy Books were cloth-bound, royal 32mo size, priced at one shilling net each, made for small hands.

The series around it shows its company: The Flamp, Mrs. Turner's Cautionary Stories, The Bad Family, The Story of Little Black Sambo, The Bountiful Lady, and A Flower Book. Humpty Dumpty's Little Son extends the nursery rhyme's world to a new small hero. Readers get a tiny Edwardian picture book, part of a beloved series, charming as an artifact of children's publishing even where its pages are few.
29404-the-very-small-person:
Annie Hamilton Donnell, author of Rebecca Mary, published this children's book in 1906 with Harper and Brothers, illustrated by Elizabeth Shippen Green. Its contents begin with Little Blue Overalls and The Boy. They continue through The Adopted and Bobby Unwelcome. They include The Little Girl Who Should Have Been a Boy. They close with The Lie, The Princess of Make-Believe, and The Recompense.

Chapter one opens with Miss Salome writing a gently frowning letter to John, wondering at one thing he did not think of, which she thinks of most of the time. Donnell writes of very small people with sympathy and humor, letting a child's view carry the story. Readers get an Edwardian children's book about little lives and big feelings, illustrated with Green's graceful art.
29422-the-meaning-of-evolution:
Samuel Christian Schmucker, professor of biological sciences at West Chester State Normal School, wrote this 1913 primer on evolution for general readers, printed by the Chautauqua Press. Chapters move from evolution before Darwin, through Darwin and Wallace, to the underlying idea itself. Later chapters treat adaptation for the individual and for the species, life in the past, the mammals, and the story of the horse.

Schmucker explains the theory in plain, schoolroom prose, with the horse as a favorite case of change over time. The book closes with evolution since Darwin, bringing the story up to its own day. Readers seeking a clear, early popular account of Darwin's idea, written before modern genetics, will find a friendly and readable guide.
29455-invasion:
Murray Leinster's short tale, first printed in Astounding Stories in March 1933, sets its action in a future year. It sets its action on August 19, 2037, when the United Nations is fifty years old and word of Martian ships reaches Earth. Thorn Hard, a high-level pilot with the Pacific Watch, sits atop Mount Wendel in the Rockies when the trap springs. The whole fighting fleet, the tale warns, has been caught in the snare of a foe named Kreynborg.

Leinster packs the future with gilt lipstick, flat color papers, and heat motors, then turns it all to war and flight. Hard must act fast against an enemy whose reach spans the sky. Fans of early pulp science tales will enjoy its brisk pace, its period charm, and its bold, wide-screen view of Earth under threat.
29478-a-letter-to-dion:
Bernard Mandeville's Letter to Dion, first printed in 1732, answers the critics of his famous Fable of the Bees and its bold claim that private vices can serve public good. The Augustan Reprint Society reissued it in 1953, with an introduction by Jacob Viner that sets Mandeville's thought in its own time. Mandeville writes as a defender, sharp and cool, against charges of vice and irreligion.

Viner's introduction notes the task Mandeville faced: to show his doctrine in accord with a great body of thought of his day. The letter itself argues, parries, and reframes, in the plain style of Augustan debate. Students of moral thought and early economics will find a key primary text on self-interest, virtue, and the public good.
29493-government-ownership-of-railroads-:
Otto H. Kahn gave this address before the National Industrial Conference Board in New York on October 10, 1918, on government ownership of railroads and war taxation. Kahn warns that paternalistic control usually harms even when meant kindly, and harms twice over when meant to punish. The history of American railroads in the prior ten years, he argues, proves the point.

Railroads in their early youth, Kahn says, were allowed to grow like spoiled, willful, untamed children, given nearly all they asked. War then forced the question of public control and taxation to the fore. Students of economic policy will find a banker's wartime case against state ownership, argued with force and clarity.
29508-the-ethics-of-coo-peration:
James H. Tufts gave these Barbara Weinstock Lectures on the Morals of Trade in 1918, printed under the Regents of the University of California. Tufts asks how ethics can guide business life when mastery over nature and cooperation among people pull in different directions. His answer makes justice and fair dealing the rules that order societies and the ties of friendship and peacemaking.

The lectures argue that trade needs more than profit rules: it needs habits of trust, shared purpose, and regard for the common good. Tufts writes for merchants, students, and citizens alike, in plain moral prose. Readers of business ethics will find an early, thoughtful case for cooperation as a working virtue, not a vague ideal.
29519-nelson-s-home-comforts-thirteenth-:
Mary Hooper, author of Little Dinners, Every-Day Meals, and Cookery for Invalids, wrote Nelson's Home Comforts, thirteenth edition revised and enlarged, printed in London in 1892 by G. Nelson, Dale and Company. Its pages list bottled jellies, soups, and stores, with beef and carrots, beef and celery, beef and onions, and mulligatawny sold in pint packets. Quart packets hold beef, peas, and vegetables, with beef and lentils beside them.

The book serves housekeepers who want ready, wholesome food without daily toil. Nelson's specialities, it notes, may be had from grocers, chemists, and Italian warehousemen throughout the world. Readers of cookery history will find a practical, commercial cookbook from the age of bottled and tinned convenience.
29614-the-game-of-rat-and-dragon:
Cordwainer Smith's tale, printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in October 1955, opens with a furious Underhill closing a door on a job he hates. Pinlighting, he fumes, is a miserable way to make a living, and wearing a uniform means little if people do not appreciate the work. He sits, lays his head back, and pulls a helmet down over his forehead as the pin-set warms up.

Smith's tag line promises that only partners could fight the deadliest of wars, and ending the partnership meant being personally dissolved. Rat and dragon, human and beast, fight together against the dark between stars. Fans of Smith will enjoy a strange, moving tale of partnership and sacrifice.
29620-sorry-wrong-dimension:
Ross Rocklynne's short tale opens with a mother who ran three steps to baby's crib. One step fell on Little Jack Horner, one on Bo Peep's sheep, and one on Old Mother Hubbard's cupboard. Baby stayed quiet all day, because a monster kept him company as a playmate, though only baby could see it. A couple of men drop out of thin air to check whether the monster is licensed.

Rocklynne's tag line asks what is strange about that: a baby with a pet monster, invisible to all but baby, and inspectors from another dimension. The mother, nerves at last under control, gets her ironing done and reads a serial. Fans of comic science fiction will enjoy a droll tale of nursery rhyme logic gone dimensional.
29630-the-curse-of-education:
Harold E. Gorst's book, printed in London by Grant Richards in 1901, argues that organized education has become a curse disguised as progress. Its opening chapter, Flourishing Mediocrity, claims humanity is less the outcome of natural growth and more the product of a planned schooling system. The average educated man, it says, possesses no real individuality, but bears the stamp of his maker like a manufactured article.

Year by year, the book argues, nearly every civilized country applied itself feverishly to a national plan of education, forcing the majority to swallow a uniform prescription. The author's contempt for time-serving politicians, Tory or Liberal, drew praise from contemporary reviewers. Students of education history will find a sharp, contrarian polemic from the age of mass schooling.
29632-competition:
James Causey's short tale opens with Greta's diary entry of January 18, Earth time, wishing Max would treat her like a woman. At dinner, John Armitage, head of WSC and a perfect example of the politician-scientist, toasts the colony and hopes its trouble is only transmittal trouble. Taylor Bishop, a gray little man and the best biochemist in the system, asks mildly if Farragut has hinted otherwise.

Causey's tag line promises the crew would discover the cause of the killing sickness, even if it cost them everything. Competition, cold war talk, and the sacred necessity of mission press on them. Fans of Causey will enjoy a tense, colony-bound tale of science, rivalry, and dread.
29680-decision:
Frank M. Robinson's short tale follows a captain who has learned to hate, as both profession and personal reason for going on. Even hatred, he knows, must be channeled for maximum use, and no truths exist forever. Fifty miles north, in the North Sea, the Josef Dzugashvili, a hundred-thousand-ton warship, holds maneuvers while the battle alarm catches him mid-dream.

The captain dreams of a white house in a small Ohio town, when he and Alice were young and their grown children were babies. He rolls out, dons life jacket and cap, and steps into the passageway. Fans of Cold War science fiction will enjoy a tense tale of duty, hate, and a decision that cannot wait.
29700-poetical-works-of-william-cullen-b:
Printed in New York in 1880 by D. Appleton and Company, with a London issue, this household edition gathers the poetical works of William Cullen Bryant. Copyrights from 1854, 1871, and 1878 mark its growth. Its opening memoir traces Bryant's ancestry and youth, noting that a later Bryant, born in 1767, followed his father in his profession, and that young Bryant loved Sarah Snell of Bridgewater.

Bryant's verse, from Thanatopsis onward, shaped American poetry with nature, death, and democratic hope. The household edition puts his poems in a form for family reading. Readers of American verse will find a complete, classic collection of a poet who was also a great editor and citizen.
29724-trees-of-the-northern-united-state:
Austin C. Apgar, professor of botany at the New Jersey State Normal School, wrote this guide for schools and private students. It was printed in 1892 by the American Book Company. Apgar's aim was plain: let teachers use real objects of nature in class, at all seasons and in all places, even without regular scientific training. Trees of forest, lawn, yard, orchard, street, and park give just such a subject.

Most botanies start with blossoms, which fail the winter student. Apgar starts with roots, stems, branches, and leaves, and adds a chapter on winter study of trees. Then he gives a plan for tree description, a key, and full accounts of the species. A student who learns to observe and describe a leaf, he says, gains a power of lifetime value.
29853-the-fathers-of-new-england-a-chron:
Charles M. Andrews wrote this chronicle of the Puritan commonwealths for the Chronicles of America Series, edited by Allen Johnson. Yale University Press printed it in 1919, in a textbook edition. Andrews opens with the coming of the Pilgrims, children of the same age as the pioneers of Virginia, Bermuda, and the Caribbean. The spacious times of great Elizabeth had passed, but a new national spirit stirred in England.

Eleven chapters follow the Bay Colony, the work of settlement, and early New England life. An attempt at colonial union, the winning of charters, and Massachusetts defiant lead to wars with the Indians and the Andros regime. A bibliographical note and an index close the book. It is a short, clear history for students and general readers alike.
29903-the-sexual-question:
August Forel, formerly professor of psychiatry at Zurich and director of its insane asylum, wrote The Sexual Question, a scientific, psychological, hygienic, and sociological study. C. F. Marshall made the English adaptation from the second German edition, revised and enlarged. The revised edition here was printed in Brooklyn in 1931 by the Physicians and Surgeons Book Company, under copyrights of 1906 and 1922, and it is illustrated.

The first chapter treats the reproduction of living beings, the history of the germ, cell division, parthenogenesis, conjugation, mneme, and the embryo. Later chapters, nineteen in all, carry the study through psychology, hygiene, and sociology. Forel writes as a clinician and scientist of his day, and the book should be read as a period work. It is a full, frank, and systematic study, influential in its time and dated in parts today.
2994-a-spirit-in-prison:
Robert Hichens wrote A Spirit in Prison from a 1908 Harper edition, setting its opening on a still sea holding a tiny islet in a warm embrace. Vere sits in the sun facing Nisida and the distant peak of Ischia, hearing a boy sing Napoli Bella from the water toward Naples. She shifts her position and turns toward the calm sea between her and the beautiful city.

The novel follows Vere, Hermione, and a man whose thoughts run to the calm of bodies and skies before a storm bursting from Ischia. That calm strikes him as unnatural, almost menacing, a combined lie straining to conceal passion. Hichens's Italian romance mixes beauty and moral danger, and it rewards readers who enjoy Edwardian novels of atmosphere and conscience.
29975-one-martian-afternoon:
Tom Leahy wrote One Martian Afternoon, with pictures by Brush. Its headnote calls its heroine sweet, gentle, and kind, a sort of Martian Old Mother Hubbard, but warns what happens when she goes to her cupboard. Marilou, a girl living on Mars, throws clods at a little Martian sand dog until it ducks into its burrow. She fills the hole with sand, then relents, fearing the creature might choke, and digs it out again.

The little fellow's yellow eyes peer out, and Marilou tells him magnanimously to go on and live. She brushes sand from her knees and dress and walks down the red road under a relentless noon sun. No rain cloud relieves her, and the fragile white puffs drift toward distant mountains. When she grows up, she vows, she will get to Earth and never come back to Mars. Leahy keeps the tale small, wry, and touching.
29994-irresistible-weapon:
H. B. Fyfe wrote Irresistible Weapon, with pictures by Ed Emsh. Its headnote warns that there is no such thing as a weapon too horrible to use: weapons will continue to become bigger and deadlier, like other things that cannot be stopped. The tale opens in the special observation dome of a colossal command ship just beyond Pluto, where every nervous clearing of a throat rasps through the silence.

Telescopes are available, but most scientists and high officials prefer the huge telescreen. It shows, from several million miles away, one small moon of the frigid planet, so insignificant it was not discovered until man pushed exploration past the asteroids. That satellite is about to matter enormously as the opening victim of humanity's latest superweapon. White-haired Co-ordinator Evora of Mars hopes success in the race against the former Centaurian colonies may prevent imminent conflict entirely.
30012-l-aiglon:
Edmond Rostand wrote L'Aiglon, a play in six acts, translated by Louis N. Parker and printed in New York by Harper and Brothers, with copyright in 1900 by Robert Howard Russell. The persons of the play are given as presented by Maude Adams at the Knickerbocker Theatre in New York in October 1900. Adams herself played the Duke of Reichstadt, son of Napoleon the First and the Archduchess Maria Louisa of Austria.

J. H. Gilmour played Flambeau, a veteran, and Edwin Arden played Prince Metternich, Chancellor of Austria. Percy Lyndall played Count Prokesch, Eugene Jepson played Baron Friedrich von Gentz, and William Lewers played the tailor, a conspirator. Edward Lester played Count Maurice Dietrichstein, R. Peyton Carter played Baron von Obenaus, and Jos. Francoeur played the Emperor Francis of Austria. J. H. Benrimo played Marshal Marmont, Duke of Ragusa, and William Crosby played Count Sedlinzky, prefect of the Austrian police.
30014-native-son:
T. D. Hamm wrote Native Son, a tale of a boy caught between two worlds. Tommy Benton, on his first visit to Earth, finds New York thrilling in the first week. By the second week it bores him and makes him unhappy. By the end of the third, he is definitely ready to go home. The racket of traffic tortures his abnormally acute ears, the heavier air troubles his chest and stomach, and Earth's gravity makes his quick, sure Martian movements clumsy.

Tommy is six inches taller than Terran boys his age. His Aunt Bee looks him up and down and tells his mother to take him to a good tailor and get those bones covered up. The headnote asks whether his mother might go home to Mars without him, and whether a robot might secretly take her place.
30017-my-father-s-dragon:
Ruth Stiles Gannett wrote My Father's Dragon, with pictures by Ruth Chrisman Gannett, printed in New York by Random House in 1948 and dedicated to her father. Ten chapters carry the story: my father meets the cat, runs away, finds the island, and finds the river. He meets some tigers, a rhinoceros, a lion, and a gorilla, then makes a bridge and finds the dragon. Chapter one opens on a cold rainy day when the father, as a little boy, meets an old alley cat on his street.

The cat is very drippy and uncomfortable, and the boy asks if she would like to come home with him. Once you start feeding stray alley cats, she warns, you may as well expect to feed every stray in town.
30029-lost-in-translation:
Larry M. Harris sets this short science fiction tale on Tr'en, a world whose people have reached the atomic age and stand close to travel among the stars. Their visitor from Earth, Korvin, sits alone in a bare cell after three days cut off from all talk. The Comity of Planets expects to invite the Tr'en to join it, yet it also expects refusal, and Korvin was sent to face that hard meeting of minds.

Guards teach Korvin the local tongue each night while he sleeps, so he wakes able to speak on topics from thought to plain trade craft. Talk still fails him, since a word-for-word rendering can miss the sense of what is meant. The tale turns that gap into its joke and its risk, as a man who can speak each word still must learn what his hosts truly mean.
30083-letters-of-madam-guyon:
P. L. Upham gathers selections from the religious letters of Madam Guyon, translated and rearranged from her private correspondence. Guyon's full correspondence ran to five printed volumes in a diffuse style, with frequent repeats as she advised many persons in turn. Upham therefore condenses and rewrites, aiming to give her true sentiments and a just account of her religious experience in a shorter, more useful form.

Henry Hoyt published the Boston volume, entered in 1858, and its preface quotes an older judgment that, next to the Holy Scriptures, no writings were thought more valuable than Guyon's. Readers will find counsel on dying to self, bearing fruit like a grain of wheat, and seeking God in quiet trust. The book serves as a devotional digest, not a full translation, and it says so plainly.
30126-the-church-the-schools-and-evoluti:
J. E. Conant, Bible teacher and evangelist, argues against evolution in a Chicago volume from the Bible Institute Colportage Association in 1922. Chapter 1 calls the theory unproven, weighing testimony for and against it in biology, from natural selection and acquired characters to the biogenetic law, and in geology. Conant then claims its logic harms inspiration, the fall of man, the nature of sin and of Christ, atonement, the new birth, and the holiness of God.

Chapter 2 offers his cure, insisting that truth must be classified scientifically by realms, so that Bible truth and science each keep their place. Conant, author of Why the Pastor Failed and Is Atonement by Substitution Reasonable, writes as a fundamentalist advocate, not a neutral judge. The book records the 1920s church-school fight in the voice of one side, plainly and without compromise.
30150-prize-orations-of-the-intercollegi:
Stephen F. Weston, executive secretary of the Intercollegiate Peace Association, edits a volume of prize orations by college students on war and peace. Charles F. Thwing, president of the association, writes the foreword, and Weston adds a history of the group itself. Paul Smith of DePauw speaks on the conflict of war and peace, while Glenn Porter takes up the United States and universal peace, and other student voices follow.

The World Peace Foundation published the Boston volume in 1914, dedicating it to Mary and Helen Seabury, whose help made the orations possible. Weston taught economics and sociology at Antioch College, and his introduction frames the student speeches as earnest civic argument. The book preserves a moment when young Americans argued, in public, that peace could be built by law and reason.
30183-a-manual-of-the-art-of-fiction:
Clayton Hamilton prepares a manual of the art of fiction for schools and colleges, published by Doubleday, Page in Garden City in 1919, under a 1918 copyright. Brander Matthews of Columbia supplies an introduction, and Hamilton, extension lecturer in English at Columbia, dedicates the book to Frederic Taber Cooper, critic and friend. A foreword and introduction lead to a first chapter on the purpose of fiction, treating fiction as a means of telling truth.

Fact and fiction, truth and fact, and the search for a story's core open the argument, which then builds a classroom theory of the novel and the short story. Hamilton, author of On the Trail of Stevenson and The Theory of the Theatre, writes for students who must learn both to read fiction well and to judge its craft. The manual remains a clear, early statement of fiction as an art with rules.
3024-the-last-stetson:
John Fox Junior wrote The Last Stetson as a mountain story of the Stetson-Lewallen feud's final generation. A midsummer freshet runs over old Gabe Bunch's water wheel into the Cumberland, while Steve Marcum lies in a dark mill corner with a slouched hat over his face. Old Gabe, a man of peace, once thought the feud done when Rome Stetson and Jasper Lewallen laid down guns and fought with bare fists on a ledge above the mill.

The beaten man was to leave the mountains and the winner to stay, yet the feud outlived that bargain. A boy named Isom, trembling and nearly convicted by a revival sermon, shows how the old violence weighs on the young. The novel pairs feud action with a conversion story, and it remains a strong example of Fox's mountain fiction.
30250-five-stages-of-greek-religion:
Gilbert Murray traces Greek religion in five stages, in a Boston volume from the Beacon Press. Saturnia Regna opens, followed by the Olympian conquest, the great schools, the failure of nerve, and the last protest. An appendix translates the treatise of Sallustius on gods and the world, and an index closes the book. Murray opens with a paradox: readers who grant Greek poetry, art, and philosophy their importance may still doubt that Greek religion mattered as much.

His answer follows stage by stage, as old earth powers give way to Olympian gods, schools of thought reshape faith, nerve fails, and a last protest sounds. The book suits general readers who want Greek religion as a living history, not a list of myths. Murray writes with the clarity that made him a famous popularizer of the ancient world.
30274-the-history-of-sandford-and-merton:
Thomas Day tells The History of Sandford and Merton, published in Philadelphia by J. B. Lippincott and Company in 1868, with six engravings. Harry Sandford and Tommy Merton open the tale, with an adventure with a snake, Harry in Mr. Merton's house, and Mr. Barlow undertaking Tommy's education. A day at Mr. Barlow's, stories of flies and ants, Harry rescuing a chicken from a kite, and a gentleman and a basket-maker follow, as Tommy learns to read.

Later chapters give Tommy and the ragged boy, Androcles and the lion, a conversation on slavery, and a conversation about an ass. The story of Cyrus, Squire Chase beating Harry, Harry saving the squire's life, making bread, and stories of two brothers and sailors on the island of Spitzbergen follow. Harry's chicken, Tommy trying kindness on a pig, accounts and stories of elephants, and boys building a house carry the lessons onward.
30390-dickens-london:
Francis Miltoun tells Dickens' London, published by L. C. Page and Company in Boston under a 1903 copyright, with a fourth impression in April 1908 and a fifth in April 1910. Miltoun, author of Dumas' Paris, Cathedrals of France, Rambles in Normandy, and Castles and Chateaux of Old Touraine, writes a uniform volume, illustrated. In library 12mo, cloth, gilt top, it costs two dollars, with a three-quarter levant morocco binding at five dollars.

James Bramston's Art of Politicks supplies the epigraph on time's devouring hand. All sublunary things of death partake, kings and comedians are mortal, and Caesar and Pinkethman lie underground. Crops of pease, cabbages, and turnips once covered the ground where Troy and the Strand's Maypole had stood. Now New Bond Street and a newer square stand there, with piles of buildings rising up and down, until London itself seems to be going out of town.
30444-the-turkish-bath-its-design-and-co:
Robert Owen Allsop, architect, writes The Turkish Bath, its design and construction, with chapters on adapting the bath to the private house, the institution, and the training stable. Published in London and New York in 1890 and illustrated with plans and sections from scale drawings by the author, the work grew from illustrated articles in Building News.

Allsop revised and enlarged those articles with much new matter, aiming both as a textbook for architects and as a treatise for the public. Readers could thus judge the relative merits of baths competing for patronage, using principles for good baths that he says are easy to grasp. The book blends practical building advice with public health sense.
30450-the-monk-of-hambleton:
Armstrong Livingston writes The Monk of Hambleton, a mystery published in New York in 1928 by Rae D. Henkle. Livingston, born in New York City and schooled at St. George's in Newport and in Europe, began writing in 1918 and lived in Algiers with his wife, with trips to Paris and London.

His earlier mystery books include The Mystery of the Twin Rubies, The Ju-Ju Man, Light-Fingered Ladies, and The Guilty Accuser. Contents here open with saying it with fruit, the head of the trail, a warning, and the legend of the monk, followed by Miss Lucy's man. Livingston builds a puzzle tale around a monk's legend, clues, and danger.
30541-a-treatise-on-anatomy-physiology-a:
Calvin Cutter writes A Treatise on Anatomy, Physiology, and Hygiene, designed for colleges, academies, and families. With one hundred fifty engravings, it appears in a revised stereotype edition published in 1858 and entered for copyright in 1852. Cutter opens with Agesilaus, king of Sparta, asked what boys should learn.

Agesilaus replies: those things which they will practise when they become men. Cutter applies that rule to health, teaching body structure, function, and care in a form schools and families can use. The treatise pairs clear text with many plates, making nineteenth-century medical knowledge accessible to students and general readers.
30565-the-art-of-lecturing-revised-editi:
Arthur M. Lewis writes The Art of Lecturing in a revised edition published in Chicago by Charles H. Kerr, after many requests to open a speakers' class or school of oratory. Twenty-two chapters move from an introduction and exordium to beginning well, speaking deliberately, and the peroration.

Later chapters cover reading widely and reading the best, subject, learning to stop, the chairman, mannerisms, and course lecturing with and without a chairman. Preparation, debating, tricks of debate, rhetoric, the audience, and street speaking follow, with notes on place, style, disturbers, and police interference. Lewis gives practical counsel for speakers who must hold a room.
30688-letters-of-a-radio-engineer-to-his:
John Mills writes Letters of a Radio-Engineer to His Son, published in New York in 1922 by Harcourt, Brace. An illustration shows lines of towers at Radio Central, courtesy of the Radio Corporation of America. Mills, of Western Electric's engineering department, also wrote Radio-Communication, The Realities of Modern Science, and Within the Atom.

Transcriber notes explain italics and subscripts in technical text, as in a capital E with a smaller C subscript. Mills writes to his son in plain, fatherly letters, explaining radio towers, signals, and the new wireless world. The book serves curious readers and young engineers who want radio explained by a working expert.
30693-renaissance-fancies-and-studies-be:
Vernon Lee published this 1895 sequel to Euphorion in London, dedicating it to her friends Maria and Pier Desiderio Pasolini at Easter 1895. Its five essays are The Love of the Saints, The Imaginative Art of the Renaissance, Tuscan Sculpture, a life of Domenico Neroni called A Seeker of Pagan Perfection, and a Valedictory. Lee writes as a critic of art and faith, not as a mere guide to old sites.

She opens on church hymns, including the Stabat Mater and Ave Verum, and says they strike her like old mosaics: stiff and childlike, yet solemn and full of feeling. From there she weighs saints, sculpture, and the pagan pull in Renaissance art, with close looks at Tuscan work. Readers who love art history with a personal voice will find Lee sharp, learned, and unafraid to disagree with her first impressions.
30701-a-critique-of-the-theory-of-evolut:
A Critique of the Theory of Evolution presents Princeton's Louis Clark Vanuxem Foundation lectures for 1915 to 1916. The series was established in 1912 by a twenty-five thousand dollar bequest under Vanuxem's will, class of 1879. Executors direct foundation income to annual public lectures at Princeton, at least half on current scientific interest, published for schools and libraries.

Earlier lectures in the series, from 1912 to 1913 onward, include work on the theory of evolution and related science. The full text carries this volume's own lectures. The book serves as a scholarly, early twentieth-century assessment of Darwinian theory, its evidence, and its limits, in lecture form for a general academic audience.
30724-absolution:
Clara Viebig writes Absolution, translated by H. Raahauge and published in London and New York in 1908 by John Lane, printed in Plymouth by William Brendon and Son. Chapter one opens with beautiful Mrs. Tiralla crying about rats in the cellar, where she and her maid went to fetch pickled cabbage from a tub.

Mrs. Tiralla drops her earthenware dish with a piercing shriek, lifting her skirts to show striped stockings and neat feet in shiny leather slippers. The maid, carrying the lamp, laughs, shows big white teeth, and says she sees no rats at all, giving her mistress a look both dull and sly. Viebig opens a novel of guilt, faith, and absolution with vivid domestic drama.
30737-my-schools-and-schoolmasters-or-th:
Hugh Miller, author of The Old Red Sandstone and Footprints of the Creator, wrote this story of his own education, published in Edinburgh in 1889. Miller, a Scotsman of Cromarty, tells how a boy with little formal schooling became a geologist and writer. His chapters move from a sailor's early career and a father's death to childhood visions, favorite books, and two maternal uncles who shaped him.

At Cromarty Grammar School, on the Sutors and in their caves, and on trips to the Highlands, Miller learns geology by walking, looking, and digging. Uncles Sandy and others guide his eye, while boyish games, a first friendship, and family losses fill the human side of the tale. It is a warm, detailed memoir of self-teaching, and a fine portrait of Scottish life and learning in the early nineteenth century.
30840-the-girls-of-central-high-on-lake-:
Gertrude W. Morrison wrote this girls' school story for Grosset and Dunlap in New York, subtitled The Crew That Won. Morrison had already written The Girls of Central High and The Girls of Central High at Basketball. The book opens on Lake Luna, where Dora Lockwood whispers that she sees a lone man on an island again, as drops patter from paddles.

Twenty-five chapters follow a missing short and long of it, Tony Allegretto, Aunt Dora, a new shell, hide and seek, a heroine, a boat found, a cave, and a strange man again. Practice, a stolen shell, Billy's great dive, and a big day lead to a canoe race that Central High wins. It is a wholesome, lively tale of schoolgirl crews, teamwork, and summer on the water.
30854-the-voice-its-production-care-and-:
Frank E. Miller, a doctor of medicine, wrote this guide to the voice, held here in a sixth edition published by G. Schirmer in New York in 1910, with a note by Gustav Kobbe. Miller was a leading New York throat, nose, and ear specialist, physician to the Manhattan Opera House, and a singer himself, once a tenor in a large New York church. He writes for singers and speakers who must keep a voice fit for work.

The book joins physiology with temperament, since Miller says he understands singers as people as well as patients. It covers how the voice is made, how to train and guard it, and how to save it from strain and harm. Music notation in this electronic text uses scientific pitch marks, with middle C shown as C4. Singers, teachers, and actors will find a practical, old-fashioned manual with lasting sense.
30971-industrial-revolution:
Winston P. Sanders wrote this science fiction story, printed in Analog in September 1963, about a machine with amnesia, and how deadly such a thing can be, and how easily it can be arranged. The tale opens in a club lounge, where Amspaugh, a teacher of interplanetary history, admits a war was unique in many ways, including its origin. Lindgren, a student of that history, argues with him over drinks.

A mine owner with a big voice asks what began the war. He asks when the asterites first saw themselves not as limbs of a dozen Terrestrial nations, but as a single nation in their own right. Missy Blades slips into the lounge, mixes gin and bitters, and stands framed by a view window against Orion. Sanders turns a bar-room debate into a story of revolution, memory, and machines that forget what they were made to do.
31057-the-wishing-moon:
Louise Dutton, author of The Goddess Girl, wrote this 1916 girls' book, published by Doubleday, Page and Company in Garden City, New York, with pictures by Everett Shinn. Its pictures follow Judith, from a frontispiece pleading, Oh, Judith, won't you speak to me, to scenes captioned Shut your eyes and Judith, you don't hate me, say it. The book opens on the worn old front doorsteps of the Randall house.

A little girl sits there very still and straight, her short white skirts gently fluffed daintily out on both sides. Her long, silk-stockinged legs are cuddled tight together. Bare-headed, her short, soft hair shows silvery blonde in the fading light. It is a gentle, old-fashioned story of a girl, her wishes, and the moon that gives the book its title.
31067-in-the-school-room-chapters-in-the:
John S. Hart, principal of the New Jersey State Normal School, wrote this 1868 book on the philosophy of education, published by Eldredge and Brother in Philadelphia. It is dedicated to the teachers of the United States, and to the alumni of the Philadelphia High School and of the New Jersey State Normal School. Hart's preface grounds the book in a teaching career.

His experience includes training more than five thousand young men and nearly one thousand young women. It was gained first in college, in boarding school in a state normal school. In all that varied experience, he says, he constantly put himself in the attitude of a learner. His aim is to place before younger members of the profession the views that experience taught him. It is a work of American teacher education.
31068-andrew-jackson:
William Garrott Brown's 1900 biography, first in the Riverside Biographical Series, follows Andrew Jackson in six chapters from the Waxhaws and the wilderness through Congress, the bench, and the militia. It continues through Tohopeka and Pensacola, the victory at New Orleans, the Seminole affairs and their political fallout, and finally the White House years.

Brown opens with the equestrian statue in Lafayette Square, a thin, long-headed old man with a firm chin and a hawk's glance. He writes with the admiration of his generation for Jackson's determination. Short and readable, the book serves as a compact introduction to the general and president who remade American politics.
31073-how-department-stores-are-carried-:
W. B. Phillips wrote this 1901 manual on how department stores are carried on, published by Dodd, Mead and Company in New York. Its contents run from general principles, management, and the system through advertising, the buying organization, receiving goods, taking care of stock, and serving customers. They end with exchanging goods, floor managers and ushers, and making out checks.

Later sections cover inspecting, checking, and parcelling goods, collecting goods for delivery, delivering goods, stables, the cash office, the check office or auditing department, and the cash-on-delivery business. The mail-order business takes up a large share, from catalogues and opening mail to assembling, packing, and sending goods by mail. It is a detailed guide to running a great store in 1901.
31104-the-place-of-anarchism-in-socialis:
Pierre Kropotkin's address, delivered in Paris and translated by Henry Glasse, asks why anarchism should stand as its own school beside the many socialist schools already in being. Opening from the close of the eighteenth century, he traces the ideals of liberty, equality, and fraternity through the Great Revolution. He also traces the slow nineteenth-century effort to put them into practice.

Across its two parts, the address argues that political change alone leaves older powers standing, and that a free society must rest on voluntary agreement rather than rule from above. Short, plain, and polemical, it gives readers Kropotkin's own summary of where anarchism fits inside the wider socialist movement.
31152-pleistocene-pocket-gophers-from-sa:
Robert J. Russell's 1960 paper studies Pleistocene pocket gophers from San Josecito Cave in Nuevo León, Mexico. The cave is limestone at about 7,400 feet on the east slope of the Sierra Madre Occidental, ringed by pine and live oak forest. Its animal remains rank among the most important Pleistocene finds in Mexico, holding the most extensive collection of fossil pocket gophers yet found there.

The remains are late Pleistocene in age, certainly post-Blancan, since genera such as Equus, Smilodon, and Aenocyon occur with them. Russell's study adds the gophers to a growing series of papers on the cave's mammals, helping reconstruct what lived in northeastern Mexico when ice-age climates ruled the high country.
31178-thoughts-on-african-colonization:
Published in Boston by Garrison and Knapp in 1832, Thoughts on African Colonization is a sustained attack on the American Colonization Society. The book attacks the society's plan to send free Black Americans to Africa. Part one argues, section by section, that the society is pledged not to oppose slavery, and it quotes the society's own documents, speeches, and reports against it.

The book's method is documentary: long extracts, answered point by point, showing colonization as a scheme to remove free Black people rather than to end bondage. As an abolitionist landmark, it helped turn antislavery opinion from gradual colonization toward immediate emancipation, and it remains a powerful example of argument by evidence.
3120-modern-fiction:
Warner argues that the worst fault of the fiction of his day is its boast of being true to nature. A photograph, a plaster cast, and a stage scene copied straight from life may be exact, he says, but exactness alone is not art. Art, in his view, selects and idealizes, shaping raw life so it can stir thought and feeling in the reader.

From that test he judges the modern novel harshly: praise for photographic fidelity is really a charge against it, since it denies the work the shaping mind that gives it value. Greek sculpture supplies his model, built by picking the best parts of many living forms. The essay defends craft, choice, and the ideal against a fashion for mere copying.
31202-the-strange-cases-of-dr-stanchon:
Josephine Daskam Bacon's 1913 collection, published by D. Appleton, gathers ten strange cases of Dr. Stanchon, a young doctor whose rounds lead into mystery. The stories are The Key, The Children, The Crystal, The Gospel, and The Gypsy. The Warning, The Legacy, The Miracle, The Unburied, and The Oracles follow, several first printed in magazines between 1908 and 1913.

The opening tale finds Stanchon calling at a flower-scented house where Mrs. Allen is at bridge, Alida is at her riding lesson, Suzanne is engaged somewhere, and Edmund lingers by the sideboard, while only Miss Mary matters to his visit. Psychological, eerie, and humane, the stories show a doctor confronting cases medicine alone cannot explain.
31255-the-educated-negro-and-his-mission:
W. S. Scarborough's 1903 paper, number eight in the American Negro Academy's Occasional Papers, takes up the educated Negro and his mission amid swinging opinions on education. Human thought, Scarborough says, sways like a pendulum from belief to belief and plan to plan, and nowhere has the swing mattered more than in Black education.

The age presses one question above all, how to learn a living, and the pendulum has swept beyond any earlier measure toward material ends. Meanwhile romance, sentiment, and idealism are swept aside by commercialism. Scarborough grants manual training's need and admits some of every race must be sons of toil, yet he defends a broader mission for the educated. The paper is a measured voice in the Washington-Du Bois era debate.
31317-the-campaign-of-the-jungle-or-unde:
Edward Stratemeyer's 1900 boys' book, published by Lee and Shepard in Boston and illustrated by A. B. Shute, follows the campaign of the jungle under Lawton through Luzon. Thirty chapters move from dismaying news and the situation at Malolos, through an adventure on the Pasig River, a gap in the firing line, and Luke Striker wounded.

Later chapters bring the advance into the jungle, the taking of Angat, a flag of truce fired upon, escape from a burning house, and a strange pitfall. The advance on Maasin, camping over a powder magazine, an ambush, a tornado in the cane-brake, and caves under the mountain follow. Boxer the scout, the departure of the Olympia, the advance on San Isidro, Larry sentenced to be shot, and a rescue under difficulties round out the tale. Stirring and episodic, the novel carries Stratemeyer's young heroes through the Philippine war.
31429-washo-religion:
James F. Downs's Washo Religion, published as University of California Publications in Anthropological Records, volume sixteen, number nine, pages 365 to 386, was submitted in September 1960 and issued in June 1961. Downs treats the religion of the Washo people, beginning with mythology. He notes that Washo mythology had been presented in interlinear texts by Dangberg in 1927 and in Lowie's Ethnographic Notes of 1939, and that two versions of the creation myth exist.

The study builds on those sources to give a fuller account of Washo belief, ritual, and cosmology. Downs writes as an anthropologist, with footnotes and careful attention to native categories. For readers of Native American religions, the paper is a compact scholarly source, valuable for its synthesis of earlier texts and its own field-based reading of Washo tradition.
31755-political-application:
John Victor Peterson's short story, first printed in Fantastic Universe in September 1956, mixes matter transference with politics for comic effect. Its narrator has long served as bodyguard to the physicist Allan Benson, and he tells how Benson slipped away from security at White Sands.

The joke is plain: if people from the past can appear anywhere, politicians face a problem no speech can solve. Readers get a light, fast science-fiction yarn in which a laboratory device upends campaigns, security men, and the sober claim that scientists should stay out of politics.
31784-the-frontiersman-a-tale-of-the-yuk:
H. A. Cody's 1910 Yukon novel, published at Toronto by William Briggs, follows Keith Steadman, a hardy northman and trailsman, down toward the mighty Yukon River. Its thirty chapters run from night in the wilderness and a grave in the snow to miners' meetings, a council, and the shining trail.

Along the way Steadman meets Constance, Yukon Jennie, Caribou Sol, and Old Pete, while chapter titles promise a shot in the night, a search, and a summons. Readers get a northern adventure of snow, rivers, and mining camps, with a missionary's interest in the people of the frontier.
31790-family-limitation:
Margaret H. Sanger's pamphlet Family Limitation, in its revised sixth edition of 1917, gives working men and women in America plain information on preventing pregnancy. Sanger says she translated the knowledge of the best French and Dutch physicians into the simplest English so that all may easily understand it.

She lists methods she knew from personal contact, warns that carelessness defeats any preventive, and argues that a woman should not bear children unless she desires to do so. Readers get a landmark birth-control pamphlet, blunt and practical, from the early years of a movement that faced legal and social attack.
31794-naturalism-and-religion:
Rudolf Otto's Naturalism and Religion, translated by J. Arthur Thomson and Margaret R. Thomson and edited with an introduction by W. D. Morrison, was published in London in 1907. Otto, professor of theology at Göttingen, asks how a religious view of the world stands beside a naturalistic one.

Early chapters compare the two outlooks, discuss Goethe's attitude to naturalism, and take up mystery, dependence, and purpose, before turning to Darwinism, descent, and teleology. Readers get a serious early twentieth-century work of theology and philosophy, arguing that scientific and purposive readings of nature are alike necessary.
31801-the-story-of-old-fort-loudon:
Charles Egbert Craddock's Story of Old Fort Loudon, copyrighted in 1898 and published by Macmillan in 1899 with illustrations by Ernest C. Peixotto, follows pioneers along buffalo paths from salt-lick to salt-lick through dense cane-brakes. No wheel had yet entered the deep forests of the western wilderness; frontiersman and packhorse were comrades.

The party faces a grim outlier of the Cumberland range, stretching northeast to southwest. Then a gap cut to the heart of the steeps opens their path like a splendid gateway to sheltered valleys and distant azure mountains. Readers get a Tennessee frontier novel, rich in landscape, that tells the story of a fort on the edge of wilderness.
3182-some-rambling-notes-of-an-idle-excu:
Mark Twain writes here about a trip taken for pure recreation, a novelty for him. All his earlier journeyings had been business, but pleasant May weather suggested a holiday with the bread-and-butter element left out. The Reverend agreed to come too, a good man, Twain adds, one of the best of men, although a clergyman. By eleven at night they were in New Haven, aboard the New York boat.

Tickets bought, the pair wandered the vessel and the town, taking the sights as idlers rather than reporters. The notes that follow keep that rambling pace, with jokes, scenery, and fellow passengers in loose order. The piece charms as a small holiday: Twain off duty, enjoying a trip that had no purpose beyond the going itself.
31864-henry-viii-and-his-court-6th-editi:
Herbert Beerbohm Tree's Henry VIII and His Court, in its sixth edition of 1911 from Cassell, was written as a holiday task at Marienbad in 1910. Tree says he does not intend an exhaustive record of Henry's reign. What he gives instead is a sketch of the leading figures in Shakespeare's play, meant to help playgoers grasp the forces shaping what they did.

Its pages discuss Shakespeare as stage manager and the pageantry of masques. They also discuss the fire that burned the Globe Theatre on June 29, 1613, when Burbage's company was acting Henry VIII and a cannon shot set the thatch alight. Readers get an actor-manager's guide to Shakespeare's Henry, rich in stage history.
31866-hansford-a-tale-of-bacon-s-rebelli:
St. George Tucker's Hansford, a tale of Bacon's Rebellion published at Richmond in 1857, aims to illustrate a period of colonial history. It presents this early fight for freedom as dawn heralding a light that has kept brightening ever since. Its preface says most of its characters have their existence in real history: Hansford lived, acted, and died in the manner narrated.

Thomas Hansford, though a son of Mars, sometimes worshipped at the shrine of Venus. Because he would not leave Virginia Temple for good, he was seized while lingering close to her Gloucester home. Readers get a historical romance woven from the meagre materials of Nathaniel Bacon's rebellion, with a lesson that vice may triumph for a season but not forever.
31875-an-introduction-to-the-study-of-co:
Frank Byron Jevons's Introduction to the Study of Comparative Religion, the Hartford-Lamson Lectures on the religions of the world, was published by Macmillan in 1920, with copyright in 1908. Jevons, principal of Bishop Hatfield's Hall, Durham, delivered the lectures at Hartford Theological Seminary under the Lamson Fund. The fund was founded to prepare students for the foreign missionary field.

He opens by noting that in the United States even the historic sciences are expected to justify themselves by practical application, and that the missionary needs an applied science of religion. Readers get a pioneering textbook that treats religions comparatively, asking what such study can do for those who must live and work among other faiths.
31980-rough-translation:
Jean M. Janis's short story Rough Translation, printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in December 1954, is a comedy of alien language. Its headnote warns not to be ashamed if you cannot blikkel any more, since it is because you could not help framishing.

The story opens with a tape recorder speaking nonsense words to Dr. Blair: shurgub, krandoor, vrillipax, framish, guttip, and bevvergrit, while Jonathan Blair hears his own tinny voice played back asking what framish means. Readers get a linguistic puzzle story, in which translation itself becomes the alien encounter.
31989-to-alaska-for-gold-or-the-fortune-:
Edward Stratemeyer's 1899 novel To Alaska for Gold, or The Fortune Hunters of the Yukon, is the third volume of the Bound to Succeed Series. It tells of two Maine boys who leave their lumbermen's home and travel to California to join their miner uncle and several other men. They set out for the Klondike via Dyea and Chilkoot Pass, then the lakes and streams at the Yukon's headwaters.

Its preface notes that the Alaska rush, after rich gold finds on Klondike Creek, resembled the earlier rush to California. Men young and old poured forth to endure hardship for the prize. After many perils they reach the gold district, spending a summer hunting the precious metal and a winter struggling to sustain life until spring. Readers get a Klondike adventure for boys.
31995-the-reluctant-weapon:
Howard L. Myers's story, printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in December 1952, turns on a weapon that will not do its job. Its tagline states the joke at the heart of the tale: a live weapon is a liability, because it is apt to get qualms of conscience. The story opens about a billion years in the past. The Zoz Horde then passes through a sector of the galaxy and leaves behind a sentient killer, numbered VT672, after an unexplained fault.

The action then shifts to the court of Tresqu the Wisest, ruler of Hova. His Lord of War, Wert, bursts in with urgent news while dancers scatter across a near-frictionless floor. The humour comes from the mismatch between rulers who expect a tool of war and a thinking weapon that hesitates. It is a satire on power and a weapon that judges its own orders.
32016-st-paul-s-epistle-to-the-ephesians:
Charles Gore's practical exposition of St. Paul's Epistle to the Ephesians, in its fifth impression and twelfth thousand, was published in London by John Murray in 1902. It belongs to Gore's series of simple expositions of portions of the New Testament. Gore, Lord Bishop of Worcester, dedicates the volume to James L. Houghteling of Chicago, founder of the Brotherhood of St. Andrew.

Its introduction covers the study of the New Testament, the gospel of the Catholic Church, the Roman Empire, and Ephesus. It then works through the letter section by section, from life in Christ and grace not merit to the unity of the Church and doctrine and conduct. Readers get a bishop's clear, pastoral commentary for general readers.
32033-vivisection:
Albert Leffingwell's Vivisection, published in New York by John W. Lovell Company, collects essays first printed in Scribner's Monthly in July 1880 and in Lippincott's Magazine in August 1884. Leffingwell thanks the Century Company and Lippincott's proprietors for permission to republish the papers in this form.

Its introduction recalls that the first essay immediately drew the attention of the medical press. Time after time, critics pressed the point that the article itself left the title's problem unsolved. Leffingwell notes that the question "Does Vivisection Pay. " was never raised by him; the single word Vivisection was his title, and the more taking headline was affixed by the magazine's editor. Readers get a nineteenth-century medical-ethics debate, argued from inside the profession.
32041-one-man-s-poison:
Robert Sheckley's short story, printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in December 1953, is a comic tale of two hungry spacemen. Hellman and Casker share a ship, and their supper is a single radish, plucked from a can with dividers and laid on a workbench beside a razor. Casker calls it a poor meal for two grown men. Hellman, examining the razor's edge, makes a practice incision in the radish while Casker watches with his mouth open.

The ship is approaching a red dwarf, the only sun nearby with planets, and the men want supper finished before they get much closer. The cover line jokes that hunger was fierce enough for a horse, though none appeared, since one might have eaten them first. Readers get Sheckley's dry humour at work on hunger, shipboard routine, and the question of what counts as food when the larder runs out.
32054-stamped-caution:
Raymond Z. Gallun's short story Stamped Caution was printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in August 1953 and illustrated by Kossin. It opens with a tagline: it is a funny thing, but most monsters seem to be of the opinion that it is men who are the monsters, and they have a point. Somebody phoned for the Army ten minutes after the crash, and that meant the narrator's unit.

The black smoke and oily residues proved a probable petroleum derivative, heavily tainted with radioactivity, most likely fuel from the odd, conchlike reaction-motors whose principles died with the crash. From the crumpled wreckage dug out of a Missouri hillside, the craft proved mainly aluminum, magnesium, and stainless steel. Readers get a first-contact story told by soldiers picking over an alien crash.
32066-the-fundamental-principles-of-old-:
Zelia Nuttall's study, issued as volume II of the Peabody Museum's papers at Harvard in March 1901, compares ancient Mexican civilizations with those of the Old World. Based on Mexican religious, social, and calendar systems, it looks for shared principles behind them rather than for borrowed customs. Nuttall states plainly that she does not wish to put forward a final theory, and she invites scholars of both regions to test her findings.

Her central thread traces the swastika in Mexico to an astronomical source. It links its use as a sacred sign in many lands to pole-star worship. It also links it to states planned as celestial kingdoms on a set numerical plan, ordered by circumpolar stars. Appendices add comparative lists of Quechua, Nahuatl, and Maya words and an account of a prayer meeting of star worshippers.
32074-book-repair-and-restoration-a-manu:
Mitchell S. Buck's manual, published in Philadelphia by Nicholas L. Brown in July 1918, offers practical suggestions for bibliophiles on repairing and restoring books. Only a thousand copies were printed, and the type was distributed after printing. Buck, author of Syrinx and Ephemera and translator of Lucian's Dialogues of the Hetaerai, also includes translated selections from A. Bonnardot's 1858 Paris essay on restoring prints and books.

Buck's foreword explains the book's place: many books about books already exist, but this one is designed for collectors who love tending their own volumes. Such a reader, Buck writes, finds an echo of reading pleasure in seeing books in good condition through his own efforts. In translating Bonnardot, he abridged or paraphrased freely. Readers get a hands-on guide for collectors who mend their own shelves.
32077-breeder-reaction:
Winston Marks's short story, printed in If Worlds of Science Fiction in April 1954, is told by a man in the advertising business. He warns that a campaign is not always won by bright slogans or clever wording. Sometimes the product itself does the work, and when that happens, people in the trade lose their heads trying to cash in on freak good fortune. Disaster, he says, can follow.

His example comes from his time on loan to Elaine Templeton, Incorporated, a large cosmetics firm. The firm planned a big build-up for Atummyc Afterbath Dusting Powder, which gave users the lovely, radiant, atomic look its advertisements promised. It also gave them a little something more. The story is a satire on advertising hype, consumer fashion, and a product that works far too well.
32088-instant-of-decision:
Randall Garrett's short story, printed in Space Science Fiction in May 1953, opens in the middle of a firefight and a philosophical puzzle. The cover line asks how anyone could spot the fraud if Earth life proved a vast trick, or just a lesson staged for history pupils. Karnes takes cover behind a neat stack of cement bags, fifteen feet from a sandpile that receives a pistol slug from a half-finished building.

Three hundred yards behind him, the burning ruin of the former Assembly Section of Carlson Spacecraft throws reddish, unevenly pulsing light over the ground. Blue-white flashes from flaring magnesium punctuate it. The action is sharp and concrete, while the question behind it is not. Readers get a story that pairs spacecraft warfare with doubt about reality itself, in a single instant of decision.
32293-for-every-man-a-reason:
Patrick Wilkins's science-fiction story, printed in If Worlds of Science Fiction in November 1954, strands Aron Myers and his wife alone on a wild planet after their rocket departs. The pair must face a harsh landscape with no other human help in sight, and the shock of being left behind strains their marriage. Aron is torn between loyalty to his wife, loyalty to his state, and the claims of his own survival.

The tension sharpens because an enemy force understands Aron's loyalties and can use that knowledge against him. Wilkins builds the story around a hard choice: what a person will protect first when wife, country, and self cannot all be saved at once. The planet's empty hills and silence press that choice home at every turn.
3231-the-rifle-and-the-hound-in-ceylon:
Samuel White Baker writes this sporting memoir of Ceylon, now Sri Lanka. Upwards of twenty years had passed since the book first appeared when he wrote a new preface, and readers had asked for it. The long interval had been spent more profitably than in simple sport, he says, yet nine years of African exploration had added much to his knowledge of wild animals.

Elephant, buffalo, and boar hunting fill the narrative, with hounds, rifles, and jungle craft described in detail. Baker writes as a Victorian sportsman, frank about danger and proud of skill. The book now reads as a record of a vanished Ceylon: its forests, its game, and the colonial world that hunted them, told by a man who knew both well.
32368-peerless-prestidigitation:
Herbert de Caston's manual of stage magic, copyrighted in 1910, gathers new tricks and effects for performers, with help from leading South African magicians. Its contents cover card forces, rising cards, phantom cards and coins, handkerchief combinations, and routines using eggs and flags. Each effect states what the audience should see, then explains the handling step by step.

An opening speech sets out de Caston's view of the craft: the performer aims to deceive, and the audience aims to catch the method. He rejects any claim to supernatural power, arguing that quick hands, misdirection, and careful practice do the work. The book suits readers who want workable stage routines rather than theory alone.
32398-brood-of-the-dark-moon-a-sequel-to:
Charles Willard Diffin's serial, printed in Astounding Stories from August to November 1931, continues the Dark Moon story with Chet, Walt, and Diane. Its opening sidenote reunites the three for another wild ride to the Dark Moon, this time as prisoners of their deadly enemy Schwartzmann. Chapter one, The Message, opens in a Vienna hospital room flooded with sunlight through crystal that lets ultraviolet rays pass.
