Walls shift colour from hot reds to cool yellows, greys, and greens at the directing surgeon's order, while charts record temperature, breathing, and every heartbeat. From that clinical calm, the story moves toward capture, flight, and a moon-bound struggle. Diffin writes fast, visual pulp science fiction, with heroes, a ruthless foe, and a hostile moon as the prize.
32449-japanese-girls-and-women-revised-a:
Alice M. Bacon's Japanese Girls and Women, in a revised and enlarged edition copyrighted in 1891 and 1902, describes girls' and women's lives in Japan for American readers. Dedicated to Stematz, the Marchioness Oyama, in the name of a girlhood friendship unchanged by changes and separations, the book draws on Bacon's long acquaintance with Japan. A holiday edition offered twelve full-page colour illustrations and forty-three outline drawings by Japanese artists.

Bacon treats home, school, marriage, work, and manners, showing how Japanese women lived, learned, and managed households in a period of rapid change. Her tone is sympathetic and observant, aimed at young readers and general audiences alike. The book remains a useful period source for Japanese social history, even where its views reflect its own time.
32483-sketches-of-church-history-from-a-:
J. C. Robertson's Sketches of Church History, from A.D. 33 to the Reformation, published in London in 1887 under the Tract Committee, gives short chapters on the early church for general readers. Robertson, late canon of Canterbury, opens with the age of the apostles, then treats Ignatius, Justin Martyr, Polycarp, the martyrs of Lyons and Vienne, and Tertullian with Perpetua and her companions. Origen, Cyprian, the last persecution, and Constantine follow.

Later sketches cover the Council of Nicaea, Athanasius, monks, Basil and Gregory of Nazianzum, Ambrose, the temple of Serapis, and church government. A map of church history during the first six centuries accompanies the text. The book suits readers who want a clear, brief survey of ancient and medieval Christianity before the Reformation.
32565-aletta-a-tale-of-the-boer-invasion:
Bertram Mitford's Aletta opens with a packed meeting of Boers addressed by Andries Erasmus Botma, a delegate from Pretoria. Old and young, hairy and shaven, moleskin-clad and neatly dressed, the men hang on the orator's words, while the local minister and Jan Marthinus Grobbelaar, called Swaart Jan, sit beside him.

The gathering, opened with long prayer and a speech of welcome, turns to insurrection, capitulation, and the politics of the Transvaal. Mitford's tale of the Boer invasion follows that community of farmers and patriots into conflict, where loyalty, faith, and the land itself are all at stake.
32567-forging-the-blades-a-tale-of-the-z:
Bertram Mitford's Forging the Blades opens on a river reach in sweltering heat, where two dark shapes lie motionless on the water. Behind each floats a crocodile, its underwater stroke holding it still against the current, while a man on the bank faces a large green mamba rising from the grass.

The man abandons his revolver and whistles, holding the snake spellbound tune after tune until fear gives way to a strange sympathy. That opening, a tale of the Zulu rebellion, sets danger, patience, and an uneasy truce with wild country against the wider forging of blades for war.
32680-the-worlds-of-joe-shannon:
Frank M. Robinson tells of Joe Shannon, a young genius at Stellar Electric in Fremont, through the eyes of his friend Harry. Joe loves his work and his wife Marge, yet one evening he declares the world unhappy, and blames people rather than the world itself.

Joe then builds machines that offer each user an ideal world of their own choosing, from palaces to log cabins. Harry fears the scheme. No one can now tell who is well-adjusted and who is not. He begs Joe to pull the booths down before the whole country takes them up.
32681-the-use-of-a-box-of-colours-in-a-p:
Harry Willson offers a practical treatise on composition, light and shade, and color, published in London in 1842. He wrote for students caught between costly, prolix works and books that teach nothing, and he sets out the principles behind his own teaching in plain order.

Chapters treat angular and circular composition, light and shade, and the three primitive colors, yellow, red, and blue, which yield orange, green, and purple. Later pages weigh harmony and contrast, effect and keeping, backgrounds, watercolor, and tints, with plain and colored plates to show each rule at work.
32723-the-minute-boys-of-boston:
James Otis tells of the Minute Boys of Boston, a company of Boston lads in the American Revolution, published by Dana Estes and Company in 1910 with illustrations by L. J. Bridgman. Archie Hemming sets down the tale from the Cambridge camp.

A baker's dozen of boys take the high-sounding name and earn praise from General Israel Putnam for their aid to the Cause. Eighteen chapters follow their enrollment, the raising of a company, a prisoner, Hog Island, Breed's Hill, a retreat, and a secret passage. The story mixes camp talk, captures, and important documents with boyish daring.
32756-some-essentials-of-religion:
This first volume of the Layman's Library of Practical Religion gathers seven essays by Canadian churchmen, published in Toronto in 1922. An editorial council of bishops, led by J. C. Roper of Ottawa, frames the book with a message from the premiers of Britain and the Dominions on the Fatherhood of God.

Essays treat God our Father, Jesus Christ, the Bible, faith, prayer, Holy Communion, and immortality. Writers argue that human goodwill depends on spiritual forces, and that Christ shows what God is. The volume aims at lay readers who want clear, practical faith rather than technical theology.
32771-here-and-there-in-london:
J. Ewing Ritchie, author of The Night Side of London, sketches the city here and there, published by William Tweedie in 1859. He opens at the House of Commons, a pile that draws reverence from bridge and steamer, and answers the cynic Henry Drummond, who calls the House utterly corrupt.

Ritchie judges the Commons a mixed assembly, right in the main, of well-informed business men with common sense and integrity. Later chapters visit a night with the Lords, the reporters' gallery, and the lobby. They visit a Sunday at the Obelisk, Exeter Hall, the Derby, and Vauxhall Gardens. The penny gaff, Rag Fair, the Stock Exchange, the London Hospital, Mark Lane, an omnibus yard, and Paternoster Row complete the tour.
32773-about-london:
J. Ewing Ritchie writes about London again, published by William Tinsley in 1860, pleading the success of his earlier books as apology for trespassing once more. He admits the book here and there shows signs of haste, but trusts it reliable and not unworthy of public favor.

Twenty chapters run from newspaper people and spiritualism through coal, Highgate, and Tom Tiddler's Ground. They pass Westminster Abbey and London charities to pedestrianism, the House of Commons, and town morals. Matrimonial London, breach of promise cases, commercial London, London gents, volunteers, cabs, and free drinking fountains follow. Brown with his morning paper, Guizot on charities, and juries weighing a deserted bride all illustrate Ritchie's London.
32774-the-night-side-of-london:
J. Ewing Ritchie tours London after dark in this second edition, revised. It was published by William Tweedie in 1858. Ritchie opens with census figures, counting more than two million three hundred thousand Londoners. Then he leads readers through streets most respectable citizens never see.

Chapters visit a public hanging, Catherine Street, and the bal masque. They visit the Haymarket, Canterbury Hall, and Ratcliffe Highway. Judge and jury clubs, the Cave of Harmony, and cyder cellars follow. Night-houses, Highbury Barn, boxing nights, Cremorne, and the police court complete a moral guide, curious and censorious by turns.
32844-the-religious-life-of-london:
J. Ewing Ritchie surveys the churches, missions, and sects of Victorian London in a volume from Tinsley Brothers dated 1870. The book is dedicated to Samuel Morley, whose activity and munificence, Ritchie writes, shaped much of the city's religious life. Its introduction argues that religion has been the great moving power of English history, for good or bad.

Ritchie weighs foreign critics first: Louis Blanc finds the English pulpit a piece of wood, and Döllinger calls the Church of England the church of only a fragment of the nation. Dissent, he insists, is as active as the State Church, and may claim the Free Church in the Free State. Later chapters cover city missions, Agricultural Hall services, and the Swedenborgians, whose hundred chapels in England and larger number in America surprise the scoffer. Emerson's praise of Swedenborg as a colossal soul closes one portrait.
32849-oscar-wilde-an-idler-s-impression:
Edgar Saltus offers an idler's impression of Oscar Wilde, published in Chicago by the Brothers of the Book in 1917 in four hundred and seventy-four copies, with the type distributed. Saltus opens in a Paris club, where one man tells another that England's only genius has been put in jail.

Saltus first met Wilde at Delmonico's, after Wilde told Customs he had nothing to declare but genius. Wilde spoke of Vera, a play for which a manager offered five thousand dollars, mere starvation wages, and refused to tamper with a masterpiece. Later, in London, Wilde seemed conventional, married, a father in Tite Street. Saltus judges him a third-rate poet who sometimes rose to the second class, yet lord of language in talk.
32855-natural-history-of-the-bell-vireo-:
Jon C. Barlow studies the Bell Vireo in a University of Kansas Museum of Natural History paper, volume twelve, number five, pages 241 to 296, dated March 7, 1962. Six figures illustrate the monograph. The bird summers in riparian and second-growth country in the central U.S., below North Dakota.

Barlow notes that the species has lately grown fairly common in western Indiana, shifting its breeding range eastward, and breeds commonly in northeastern Kansas. The study follows seasonal movement, song, territoriality, and courtship, in which males direct strong aggressive attacks toward females. It details nest building, egg laying, incubation shared by both sexes, and nestling care. Both parents clear fecal sacs from the nest, swallowing them during the first five days, and cowbird parasitism limits reproductive success.
32990-a-day-with-lord-byron:
M. C. Gillington's A Day with Lord Byron follows the poet through a single February afternoon in 1822, beginning about two o'clock at the Palazzo Lanfranchi in Pisa. Byron, the most notorious personality of his century, rises languidly with the help of his valet Fletcher. It wakes as usual in low spirits and despair, a mood Gillington traces partly to constitution and partly to reaction after feverish excitement. The day then unfolds in visits, talk, and writing.

The book belongs to a series that spent a day with famous writers, from Longfellow and Tennyson to Keats and Shelley. It uses the device to bring Byron close: his rooms, his habits, his friends, and his talk. A verse from She Walks in Beauty stands at its head. Readers get a vivid, intimate portrait, less a full biography than a guided visit to a poet at home in exile.
32993-a-daughter-of-the-union:
Lucy Foster Madison's Daughter of the Union, copyrighted in 1903, follows a young woman through the Civil War. The chapters run from what girls can do and a great awakening to starting for Dixie and life in Dixie land. Early chapters send her through shot and shell, to a meeting with the hero of New Orleans, and into suspicion, deceit, and arrest as a spy. They go on to an escape, a recapture, and Vicksburg. The plot keeps its heroine at the center of danger and decision.

Madison, author of A Colonial Maid, writes for young readers, giving them a heroine who acts with courage and judgment in wartime. The novel's Union viewpoint is plain, and its episodes, from General Butler's headquarters to the enemy's camp, teach history through adventure. It remains an engaging period story for readers who like a brave girl at the heart of a great war.
33011-thomas-jefferson:
Henry Childs Merwin's Thomas Jefferson, in the Riverside Biographical Series and copyrighted in 1901, tells the third president's life in short, clear chapters. It moves from youth and training on a frontier estate in Albemarle County, Virginia, where Jefferson was born on April 13, 1743. It goes through Virginia in his day, Monticello and its household, and his part in the Revolution, to reform work, the governorship, Paris, and the secretaryship of state.

Later chapters cover the rise of the two parties, Jefferson as president, his second term, and his life as a public man in private retirement. Merwin writes for general readers, balancing facts with character, and the book's compact size makes it a handy introduction. It presents Jefferson as a man of ideas and action, shaped by Virginia and shaping the republic in turn.
33050-drainage-modifications-and-glaciat:
Ruth Sawyer Harvey's Drainage Modifications and Glaciation in the Danbury Region, Connecticut, studies how ice and water reshaped a Connecticut landscape. It was published by the state in Hartford in 1920 as bulletin number thirty of the State Geological and Natural History Survey. The survey's earlier bulletins had covered protozoa, hymeniales, clays, smuts, and a manual of the state's geology, and Harvey's volume adds the Danbury region's drainage history to that series.

Harvey traces how glaciers blocked, diverted, and remade streams, leaving the modern pattern of valleys and ponds in the Danbury area. Her work is technical but grounded in field observation, mapping old channels and deposits to read a landscape's past. For geologists and local historians, the bulletin remains a solid record of Connecticut's glacial history, written when the survey was systematically mapping the state's natural ground.
33058-gabriel-tolliver-a-story-of-recons:
Joel Chandler Harris's Gabriel Tolliver, a story of Reconstruction published in New York in 1902 and dedicated to James Whitcomb Riley, follows a Georgia town after the Civil War. Its chapters run from a prelude and kettledrum and fife, through a town with a history and the return of two warriors, to the story of Margaret Gaither. The pases of Margaret, and Silas Tomlin going a-calling. Later chapters bring the political machine and the Union League organizing.

Harris, author of Uncle Remus, writes Reconstruction through local people, their loyalties, quarrels, and romances, in the manner of his day. The novel's viewpoint is that of a white Southerner looking back, and modern readers will read it with that history in mind. As a period novel, it remains a detailed picture of a town remaking itself after war, with all the tensions that remaking brought.
3312-the-native-son:
Inez Haynes Irwin dedicates this novel to proud native sons and to apologetic adopted sons, naming both companies in full. James W Coffroth, Meyer Cohn, Porter Garnett, and John Crowley lead the natives, with Willie Ritchie, J Cal Ewing, and James Wilson among them. Albert M Bender, Austin Lewis, and Sam Berger head the adopted list, with Gelett Burgess and Fremont Older.

The double dedication sets the novel's theme: belonging claimed by birth and belonging earned by choice, in a city that prized both. Irwin, a California writer, writes of local loyalties with wit and affection. A roll of names at the front already tells you whose town this is, and the novel keeps that local faith.
33175-the-voice-and-spiritual-education:
Hiram Corson's book argues that training the voice matters far beyond mere speech, touching literary taste and general culture as well. First set up in 1896 and reprinted through 1914, it urges readers and students to read aloud with care, so that sound, rhythm, and sense work together. Corson, a professor of English at Cornell, links vocal practice to a deeper grasp of poetry and prose.

The book is short and direct, written for teachers, students, and all who love good reading. It does not teach tricks of elocution so much as a habit: to hear words as well as see them, and to let voice shape meaning. Its plea still rings true for anyone who reads aloud, acts, teaches, or simply wants verse to come alive off the page.
33180-book-of-hymns-for-public-and-priva:
A Book of Hymns for Public and Private Devotion gathers hymns for worship and for home use. It is in a fifteenth edition from Ticknor and Fields in Boston in 1866 and first entered in 1848. Its preface notes that many hymns in the collection do not follow commonly recognized meters. Some hymns in the book already carry tunes of their own, while others fit easily onto simple chants a choir leader finds in sacred collections. An asterisk marks hymns changed by the compilers, and supplementary hymns are woven into the main table.

The index of first lines gives a sense of the book's range across devotion, praise, and penitence. As a hymnal, it served congregations and families for decades, and its many editions show its use. For historians of American worship and hymnody, it preserves the songs a nineteenth-century household might sing on Sunday and through the week.
33221-father-brighthopes-or-an-old-clerg:
J. T. Trowbridge's Father Brighthopes, or An Old Clergyman's Vacation, opens with a preface that compares its opening leaf to a garden gate. An aunt tells children to go through the gate if they wish to see the garden. Merry urchins scale the fence instead. One jumps into a blackberry bush full of prickles, another thrusts his curly head between rails and sticks fast, blaming the benevolent uncle who owns the grounds. The wise, Trowbridge suggests, go through the gate, though reckless youth rushes straight for fruits and flowers.

The novel gives an old clergyman a vacation, letting his kindness and faith meet the world outside the pulpit. The book remains a gentle, old-fashioned story of a good man's holiday, full of children, gardens, and the small adventures of a life well lived.
33278-the-black-watch-a-record-in-action:
Scout Joe Cassells's record tells of the Black Watch in the first months of the First World War, as part of the small British force sent to France. Published in 1918, it opens with Cassells trying to forget those months, when the regiment marched into the unknown against a fierce and well-armed foe. As one of the few survivors of that force, he writes from the ranks, not from headquarters.

The book's power lies in its plain soldier's view: marches, battles, fear, and comradeship, told without gloss. Cassells honors the men beside him and the cost they paid. For readers of war memoirs, it is a short, stark account of a famous regiment's trial by fire, and a tribute to the ordinary soldiers who bore it.
33290-the-door-of-heaven-a-manual-for-ho:
A. E. Burgett's manual, The Door of Heaven, prepares young people for Holy Communion, in a twenty-first thousand printing from 1922. Burgett, a venerable archdeacon, wrote it short and very simple, to help Confirmation candidates in everyday living and at the altar. Its frontispiece shows Holman Hunt's Light of the World, a fitting image for its theme.

The manual's value lies in its plain, devotional guidance, leading young communicants step by step toward the altar. Its language is gentle and direct, suited to first communion classes. For readers of Anglican devotion, it is a small classic, still useful for teaching the meaning of the sacrament to the young.
333-robert-louis-stevenson:
Walter Raleigh, Oxford professor of English literature, asks the fashionable question: will Stevenson live? His Robert Louis Stevenson, from a Royal Institution lecture of May 17, 1895, in the 1906 Arnold edition, refuses to promise immortality. Criticism cannot mortgage great-grandchildren's tastes.

Raleigh weighs Stevenson's style, romance, and essays against time's opium, which dulls all fame. The essay treats Treasure Island, Kidnapped, and the essays with clear-eyed praise. Raleigh's lecture remains a model of honest criticism. It suits readers asking why Stevenson still matters. Raleigh's essay remains a clear guide to Stevenson's lasting appeal.
33310-on-the-principles-of-political-eco:
David Ricardo's classic treatise sets out the principles of political economy and taxation that shaped a century of debate. Ricardo argues about rent, wages, profit, and the gains from trade, building a system that later economists both used and fought. His prose is dense and logical, aimed at readers who want reasons, not slogans, for how wealth is made and shared.

The book's fame rests on its clear, hard reasoning, especially its case for free trade and its theory of comparative advantage. It remains a founding text of economics, read in classrooms long after its age. For students of the subject, it is essential reading, best taken slowly, chapter by chapter, with a pencil in hand.
3332-the-variation-of-animals-and-plants:
Charles Darwin gathers his evidence on variation in this two-volume work, companion to the Origin of Species. A foreword, a preface to the second edition, and an introduction open it. Chapter one takes domestic dogs and cats: ancient varieties of the dog, and the resemblance of domestic dogs in various countries to native canine species.

Animals unacquainted with man at first show no fear, Darwin notes, and dogs resemble wolves and jackals in form. Barking is acquired and lost, feral dogs return to wild ways, and tan eye-spots recur across breeds. The book argues from the farmyard and the kennel to nature at large: if breeders can reshape life so fast, nature, given time, can reshape it farther.
33325-the-spoils-of-poynton:
Henry James's novel, copyrighted in 1896, centers on the spoils of Poynton, a house full of fine things whose fate drives its people to strife. The story opens with Mrs. Gereth, who had said she would go to church with the rest. She then suddenly changes her mind, a small turn that hints at the larger battle over taste, love, and possession to come. James writes with his usual fine attention to motive and talk.

The novel's power lies in how objects become moral tests: who should own beauty, and at what cost to love and honor. Its characters weigh, scheme, and suffer over chairs and cabinets as if they were souls. For readers of James, The Spoils of Poynton is a sharp, elegant study of desire, where the spoils themselves are both prize and trap.
33349-the-shepherd-psalm-a-meditation:
William Evans's Shepherd Psalm, a meditation on the Twenty-Third Psalm, offers a Bible teacher's slow reading of a beloved text. Evans, author of The Book of Books and How to Memorize, writes for readers who want to dwell on each line, from green pastures to the valley of shadow. His meditation is plain, devout, and practical, aimed at daily use.

The book's charm lies in its unhurried pace, as Evans turns each image over with care and applies it to common life. Its tone is pastoral, not academic, and its lessons suit private prayer and group study alike. For readers who cherish the Shepherd Psalm, it is a gentle, thoughtful companion, best read a little at a time.
33397-lrl-accelerators-the-184-inch-sync:
The Lawrence Radiation Laboratory's report on the 184-inch synchrocyclotron, published in June 1964, explains a giant machine for speeding atomic particles. Its contents move from the principle of a conventional cyclotron and phase stability to the design and construction of the 184-inch machine, with sections on magnet, vacuum, ion source, radiofrequency, and targets. The report is illustrated with a view of the synchrocyclotron building.

The volume suits readers of physics and engineering history, offering a technical yet clear account of a landmark accelerator at Berkeley. Its tone is systematic and factual, aimed at scientists and students. For those who study big science, it is a valuable record of how the atom's secrets were chased with ever larger machines.
33431-the-dangerous-classes-of-new-york-:
Charles Loring Brace's Dangerous Classes of New York, published in 1872, tells of twenty years' work among the city's poorest children and outcasts. Brace, author of Hungary in 1851 and Home Life in Germany, writes of lodging-houses for homeless boys as they were, and of the charities that sought to lift them. His motto, from Demetz, urges improving man by the soil and soil by man.

The book's power lies in its first-hand reformer's view, full of street scenes, shelters, and schemes for rescue. Its tone is earnest and Christian, aimed at readers who might give or work. For students of urban and charity history, it remains a classic account of New York's poor, and of one man's long effort to help them.
33476-the-auto-boys-vacation:
James A. Braden follows four friends through a summer holiday that turns into a hunt for answers. Billy Worth, Willie Creek, Paul Jones and their companions return to a garage on the South Fork road where a break-in and the killing of a dog remain unexplained. Their talks with the local chief, a detective, and a stranger keep pulling the mystery in new directions.

Road travel, a swift night ride, a tavern stop, and a kidnapping carry the boys eastward across sixteen chapters. The story mixes motoring adventure with detective work, as small kindnesses and sharp observations help the friends piece together who was behind the garage crime and why it happened.
33514-a-mechanico-physiological-theory-o:
Carl von Nägeli sets out a mechanical and physiological account of how living things evolved. The summary was translated for American students by V. A. Clark under the supervision of F. A. Waugh. Working backward from the main argument, Nägeli begins with unorganized matter. He tries to show how organized micellar substance arose within it, and how organisms with their varied properties developed from that substance.

The summary is the accessible core of a difficult larger work, chosen for publication because American students could otherwise hardly reach it. Its interest today is historical: it preserves a nineteenth-century attempt to explain evolution through the physics and chemistry of living matter, before genetics reshaped the field. Students of the history of biology will find it a revealing document.
33582-rhyme-and-reason:
Lewis Carroll gathers comic and nonsense verse in this 1883 volume, illustrated with sixty-five drawings by Arthur B. Frost and nine by Henry Holiday. The contents open with Phantasmagoria in seven cantos, a ghostly conversation in mock-medieval spelling. The contents continue through Echoes, A Sea Dirge, a carpet knight, Hiawatha's Photographing, Melancholetta, a valentine, and the Three Voices. Several pieces appear here for the first time.

The book is inscribed to a dear child in memory of golden summer hours and whispers of a summer sea, and its playful dedication poem sets the tone. Carroll's wordplay, parody, and logic games run through the collection, with illustrations to The Hunting of the Snark among its treasures. Readers of Alice will find the same wit turned to verse, riddles, and mock-heroic nonsense.
33613-stories-of-london:
E. L. Hoskyn, with a preface by Sophie Bryant, tells the story of London for young readers in this illustrated 1914 volume. Seven chapters move from very old stories of the city's beginnings through Westminster Abbey, the Charter House, two famous charities, Dick Whittington, the reign of Elizabeth, and the story of St. Paul's. Maps and illustrations, including a sketch map of Norman London, support the text.

Hoskyn mixes legend with history, letting readers see coronations in the Abbey, prisoners in the Tower, pensioners and schoolboys at the Charter House, and the Fire of London. The book is written as an introduction rather than a scholarly history, and it remains a pleasant first guide to the places and people that shaped the capital.
33648-the-mammals-of-warren-woods-berrie:
Lee Raymond Dice studies the mammals of Warren Woods, Berrien County, Michigan, in this 1920 occasional paper from the University of Michigan Museum of Zoology. Dice notes that few detailed studies of mammal associations in American forests existed, and argues that habitats and their limits must be described before native areas are altered by human activity. Warren Woods, a state preserve under the Edward K. Warren Foundation about three miles north of Three Oaks, offered a rare chance.

The preserve covers about two hundred acres, somewhat less than half in clearing and the rest mostly forest, much of it still nearly primitive. Ravines drain to the Galien River, flood-plains carry heavy forest and small buttonbush swamps, and higher ground holds beech-maple forest. Dice maps mammal habitats across this landscape, giving ecologists a baseline for a Michigan forest community.
33696-the-alternative-a-separate-nationa:
William H. Holcombe, a New Orleans physician, published this secessionist pamphlet in 1860, on the eve of the Civil War. Holcombe argues that a sectional party hostile to Southern institutions is about to take possession of the federal government, and that Lincoln's election would put Garrison in power. The Constitution, in his view, has become powerless for Southern protection, and the South faces a plain question: submission or secession.

The only alternative, as the title states it, is a separate nationality or what Holcombe calls the Africanization of the South. He insists the quarrel runs deeper than territories, court decisions, or the Constitution itself, and cannot be settled by new lines or compacts. The pamphlet is a primary document of secessionist argument, valuable for understanding how its advocates framed their case, and it should be read as such.
33765-the-church-of-england-cleared-from:
Thomas William Allies, rector of Launton, Oxfordshire, defends the Church of England against the charge of schism in this 1846 book. He argues from the witness of councils and fathers from the first six centuries. Allies insists the whole question between Rome, England, and the East turns on whether papal supremacy as presently claimed is of divine right. If it is, he writes, England must submit; if it is not, the Church of England's position is tenable and its internal evils may gradually be overcome.

The advertisement contrasts practical abuses in England with the Roman Church of the tenth century. Allies writes in the heat of the Oxford Movement's debates over authority and tradition. The book remains a primary source for Anglican apologetics and for Victorian arguments about church, papacy, and schism.
3377-criticism-and-fiction:
William Dean Howells argues for realism in this classic of American criticism. The question of a final criterion for appreciating art, he writes, perpetually recurs to those interested in any aesthetic endeavor. John Addington Symonds supplies his example. In a chapter of The Renaissance in Italy on the Bolognese school of painting, Symonds treats a school once vaunted as the supreme exemplar of the grand style. He now believes it fallen into lasting disrepute.

Taste changes, Howells argues, and criticism must change with it, toward truth rather than grandeur. The book became the manifesto of American realism: fiction judged by its fidelity to common life, not by its height. Readers interested in how the American novel found its theory will find it here, argued with Howells's usual clarity and calm.
33790-delayed-action:
Charles V. De Vet writes a science fiction novelette in this story from Galaxy Science Fiction, September 1953, about a perfect crime on an imperfectly remembered planet. A sidenote promises that this planet gave a man the perfect chance to commit the perfect crime, only he could not remember just what it was he had committed. Johnson, trusting hunches that have often paid off, waits five hours in wooden stands under rumpled canvas at Marlock, sweating under a yellow sun.

Marlock's one claim to fame is its Nature's Moebius Strip. Its one export is desert-ox fur, but for two months each fall and spring tourists pour in to gape at the Strip. Johnson watches them line up for a thrill journey while his man fails to appear. De Vet builds suspense from memory, identity, and a strange world, in the compact, idea-driven manner of 1950s magazine science fiction.
33844-the-cocoanut-with-reference-to-its:
William S. Lyon, in charge of the Division of Plant Industry in the Philippines, describes the cocoanut with reference to its products and cultivation. The text is his 1903 Manila bulletin, Farmers' Bulletin No. 8. Written chiefly for planters, in answer to numerous inquiries, it covers history, botany, and uses. It then covers copra (dried nut meat), cocoanut oil, coir (husk fiber), tuba (palm wine), and minor uses, followed by cultivation in full.

Cultivation chapters treat selection of location, soil, seed selection, planting, manuring (feeding the soil), irrigation (watering), harvest, enemies, remedies, and renovation of old groves. Lyon argues that the cocoanut palm is bound to assume great agricultural (farm) importance in the islands. The bulletin remains a practical, detailed guide to early twentieth-century Philippine coconut farming, from planting a seed to getting the crop ready for sale.
33854-ask-a-foolish-question:
Robert Sheckley writes a classic science-fiction short story in this 1953 tale from Science Fiction Stories. Answerer was made to endure as long as necessary, large to some and small to others, complex to some and simple to others, but above all The Answerer, who knows everything. The race that built him, a service to less sophisticated races, departed in a unique manner, and where they went only Answerer knows.

Upon his planet, circling his sun, Answerer sits through durations long or short by different reckonings, waiting for questions. Sheckley's point, developed with wit and irony, is that the way a question is put determines not only the answer received but the type of answer possible. Readers of golden-age science fiction will enjoy a compact fable about knowledge, limits, and the folly of asking without care.
33889-the-salvaging-of-civilization:
H. G. Wells set out this 1921 program for repair after the Great War. War had, in his view, broken the faith that human affairs must keep moving forward on their own. He answers with a plan for a world state, a wider patriotism, and a shared body of teaching to guide all peoples.

Chapters take up the future of mankind, schooling for the whole world, and the roles of college, press, and book. Wells argues that only common teaching and common rule can tame the forces that war had loosed. The book is a bold, plain-spoken plea for world order from a writer who had watched an old order fail.
33905-the-sages-and-heroes-of-the-americ:
L. Carroll Judson compiled this gallery of American founders, revised in 1854 after an 1851 entry. Two hundred and forty-three sages and heroes get full entries, with many more named along the way. The set includes the signers of the Declaration of Independence beside soldiers, statesmen, and other leaders of the Revolution.

Each life is told in brief, with the aim of holding up examples of public service for later readers. Judson, who had already written lives of the signers, arranges the material so a reader can dip into one figure at a time. The book works as a nineteenth-century hall of fame for the men of 1776 and their age.
33920-the-menace-of-prohibition:
Lulu Wightman, an advocate of civil and religious liberty, wrote this Los Angeles pamphlet against prohibition, dated 1916 in the evidence. Wightman argues that no American can rest easy while the energies of democracy are demanded to save American institutions, and she presents prohibition as a menace to liberty itself. Lectures on great questions of the hour back the pamphlet.

Wightman writes for citizens thinking and talking about public matters, political, religious, and economic. Her tone is urgent and plain. The pamphlet preserves one strong voice in the debate before national prohibition took hold.
33953-the-boke-of-noblesse-addressed-to-:
A medieval treatise on nobility, addressed to King Edward the Fourth on his invasion of France in 1475. It survives in this Roxburghe Club edition of 1860, with an introduction by John Gough Nichols. The Boke of Noblesse sets out what true nobility means, how it is won and lost, and what duties rank lays on a king and his men.

Its pages speak to a king about to wage war, urging honor, good rule, and care for the realm. Nichols's edition gives modern readers the text with scholarly care. The book remains a key source for chivalry, kingship, and the ideals of late medieval England.
340-the-soul-of-the-indian-an-interpreta:
Charles Eastman, a Sioux writer known as Ohiyesa, sets out Native faith as it stood before white contact in this short book. He writes for readers who knew Indians only through war tales, and he stresses a faith that was silent, solitary, and free of priests. Prayer, he says, rose in wordless awe before a Great Mystery.

Chapters treat the family altar, rites, moral codes, unwritten lore, and the border land of spirits. Eastman contrasts this inward faith with the creeds and schools pressed on his people. The book stands as a calm, proud account of a spiritual life that valued thanks, unity, and love of neighbor.
34077-on-germinal-selection-as-a-source-:
August Weismann wrote this essay on germinal selection as a source of definite variation, translated from the German by Thomas J. McCormack, in a second edition published in Chicago in 1902 by the Open Court Publishing Company, with copyright in 1896. London agents were Kegan Paul, Trench, Trubner and Company. A preface opens the short work.

Weismann argues that variation is not mere chance, but takes definite direction through selection among the living units of the germ. The essay belongs to the fierce debate over Darwin's theory in the 1890s. It offers a clear, short statement of Weismann's view of heredity.
34085-shelley-and-the-marriage-question:
John Todhunter wrote this study of Shelley and the marriage question, printed in London in 1889 for private circulation only, in twenty-five copies. Todhunter, author of Notes on The Triumph of Life and A Study of Shelley, opens by noting that marriage, like most time-honoured institutions, now stands accused at the bar of public opinion.

The marriage problem, he says, turns on hard questions: whether marriage is divine or human, for what ends it was instituted, and how far it attains those ends. Marriage, in his account, is a bond society lays on sexual relations, as a contract endorsed and enforced by society. The book offers a Victorian debate on Shelley and marriage.
34097-household-organization:
Mrs. Caddy's 1877 essay Household Organization argues that English homes had grown costly, wasteful, and hard to run. She blames late hours, showy habits, too many servants, and a fear of plain work, and urges simpler manners and steadier routines.

Chapters take up the servant problem, the value of doing work with one's own hands, thrift in spending, and training children to thoughtfulness. The book speaks to householders who want easier, happier homes, and it still reads as a blunt Victorian plea for plain living over display. Caddy wrote the essay after a bank holiday spent thinking on the waste of modern life.
34105-idonia-a-romance-of-old-london:
Arthur F. Wallis's romance of old London, issued at Boston in 1914, follows a young narrator. He learns he has an uncle and makes his way to the city. His path runs through Petty Wales, a tangle of old stone buildings near Thames Street, where traders, cheats, and men of law cross his road.

Idonia, the girl of the title, teaches the narrator and a guard captain to keep books, and a great ledger becomes a tool of rescue. Sieges, sea voyages, a Chinese jar, and a lost uncle's luck fill a tale that leans on real London lore while keeping its plot brisk and plain.
34164-a-blot-on-the-scutcheon:
May Wynne, author of Henry of Navarre and A Maid of Brittany, wrote A Blot on the Scutcheon for Mills and Boon in London. The book came out in January 1910 and reached a second edition within a month. Wynne dedicates the story to her mother, and a Gutenberg note warns that two pages are missing from the source copy.

Thirty-three chapters run from Sir Henry's Heir to The Cave of Lost Souls, moving through Brittany, a cousin's arrival, and Count Jehan's doubts. Chapter one finds Sir Henry Berrington in his wainscotted library, railing against his heir Michael, a lad he calls brainless and ill named. The name's shame ties to Michael's father, whom Sir Henry will not praise. Later chapters take the tale onto Breton soil.
3418-captain-brassbound-s-conversion:
George Bernard Shaw sets this play on the west coast of Morocco, where an elderly Scottish missionary tends his garden in the late afternoon. The missionary, a man of the Free Church and the North African Mission, cultivates a huge red geranium bush on a Moorish stool, calm in his faith though far from home. Into this quiet scene come travelers, a ship's captain, and questions of law and honor.

Captain Brassbound, a seafarer with a grievance against English justice, forces the party to judge him by a rougher code. Shaw turns the adventure into a debate about courts, revenge, and conscience, with wit running through the action. The play suits readers who like Shaw's blend of romance, argument, and sudden moral turns.
34216-notes-of-a-staff-officer-of-our-fi:
E. Burd Grubb's 1910 memoir gives a staff officer's notes on the Seven Days' Battle on the Peninsula in 1862. Grubb, a brevet brigadier general of volunteers, wrote at the request of Camille Baquet, historian of the First New Jersey Brigade.

The notes centre on Gaines' Mill, tracing the brigade from Mechanicsville, near the Chickahominy, to its ground for the fight. Grubb writes from memory, with the plain detail of a man who was there: roads, bridges, pickets, and the slow build to battle. Grubb's letter to Baquet opens the book, and the notes that follow keep its plain, first-hand tone.
34257-means-and-ends-of-education:
J L Spalding wrote Means and Ends of Education. A C McClurg and Company issued it at Chicago in 1895. Spalding served as Bishop of Peoria. Three of his books show at one dollar each. Seven chapters fill this volume. Truth and Love heads the first two.

The Making of One's Self comes third. Woman and Education takes the fourth chapter. Public-school scope fills the fifth. The religious element in schooling takes the sixth. The Higher Education closes the course. A Ruskin line opens chapter one in praise of thought. Fairy palaces of bright thought resist all care, it says. Milton's hopes for brave patriots join it. A bishop's counsel joins school craft to soul craft, urging teachers to build minds that wealth and loss cannot shake.
34262-octavia-the-octoroon:
Lee, a doctor, wrote a novel printed in New York, London, and Montreal in 1900. The tale opens just before the civil war between the states. A large plantation on the Alabama River holds several hundred enslaved people. It yields five hundred bales of cotton a year, plus corn, oats, wheat, and stock of all kinds.

On that farm Octavia is born, baptized, and raised. She nearly drowns, rides the underground railway, and studies with a governess. Later she goes to college, serves in the Red Cross, and travels in foreign lands. Love, error over who she is, and escape from a bear all mark her path in a tale shaped by slavery and its end.
34307-condensed-guide-for-the-stanford-r:
Lewis Terman of Stanford University wrote a Condensed Guide for the Stanford Revision of the Binet-Simon Intelligence Tests for Houghton Mifflin in 1920. Some test pages print upside down, so an examiner can read them while a child sits across the table. Terman thanks Bridges and Bingham for help drawn from army testing work.

A preface warns that beginners should keep using the complete Record Booklet, not this cheaper condensed blank. Full records, he argues, foster sound method, allow scoring errors to be fixed, and permit later comparisons of a child's answers. Only seasoned examiners, and perhaps only in special cases, should swap accuracy for low cost. Ten repeated cautions for testers follow in the general directions.
34379-the-theory-and-policy-of-labour-pr: A volume in the Social Science Series, issued by Swan Sonnenschein of London in scarlet cloth, treats the theory and policy of labour protection, as its title states. The front pages of the hosted copy are given to the series list and press notices rather than the author's own opening. Reviewers quoted there praise the series for low price, clear style, and fair treatment of all sides of social questions. The series aimed, one notice says, to redress errors and faults of society that its writers agreed in deploring.
34464-sinn-fein-an-illumination:
O'Hegarty wrote an illumination of the Sinn Fein movement, published at Dublin and London in 1919. Its contents are marked as passed by censor, and a note explains that the first seven chapters were written in October 1917. The last chapter is a rearrangement of what it was permissible to publish of the original ending.

The first chapter indicts the policy of peaceful penetration in Ireland, forced through with the Act of Union. Three dates, he says, are vital: 1691, when Ireland lay unarmed under the invader; 1800, when the penetration began; and 1893, when the Gaelic League turned Ireland back to her own culture. Chapters follow on the movement's genesis, its policy, Arthur Griffith, and the Irish Volunteers.
34506-german-fiction:
German Fiction, a Harvard Classics Shelf of Fiction volume from P F Collier and Son in 1917, was edited with notes and introductions by William Allan Neilson. Four authors carry the book. Goethe gives The Sorrows of Werther, with Carlyle's criticism in front of it. Gottfried Keller gives The Banner of the Upright Seven.

Theodor Storm gives The Rider on the White Horse, and Theodor Fontane gives Trials and Tribulations, twenty-six chapters strong. An opening essay, The Novel in Germany, traces how foreign models, Rousseau, Richardson, Scott, and Dickens among them, were turned to German account. A compact national survey results.
3451-marie-antoinette-and-her-son:
Louise Muhlbach tells the last years of Marie Antoinette in this historical novel, following the French queen from court splendor to prison and trial. Her young son, the dauphin, stands at the center of the later chapters, as revolutionaries, guards, and loyal friends struggle over his fate. The novel moves between Versailles, the Temple prison, and the streets of revolutionary Paris.

Muhlbach writes as a popular novelist of the nineteenth century, filling gaps in the record with invented scenes and dialogue. Readers should treat the book as romance built around real people, not as a scholarly life. Its value lies in its sympathy for the queen and in its vivid picture of how the Revolution felt inside a family.
34510-some-constituents-of-the-poison-iv:
William Anderson Syme wrote this study as his doctoral dissertation at the Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, printed there in 1906. The work asks a plain question with a painful edge: what are the chemical parts of the poison ivy plant, Rhus toxicodendron? Syme thanks his teachers by name, among them Remsen, Morse, and Jones.

The contents show a chemist's order. First comes the literature, with the work of Khittel, Maisch, and Pfaff, the men who had attacked the plant before him. Then comes his own bench work. He reports gallic acid, fisetin, and rhamnose among the plant's constituents, and a long section treats the poison itself. A last study tests potassium permanganate as a remedy for the poisoning. Parke, Davis and Company supplied the crude material. Chemists get a founding analysis of a plant every American schoolchild learns to fear.
34535-digby-heathcote-the-early-days-of-:
Digby Heathcote tells the early days of a country gentleman's son. Kingston wrote the tale for boys. Its first chapter introduces Bloxholme Hall and its people. The squire there heads one of the oldest families in the county. His son Digby is nine years old.

The book opens with a scolding in the store-room. The housekeeper, Mrs Carter, has caught Digby at her jam pots. He has eaten a whole pot of raspberry jam. Half a pot of greengage is gone too. Digby answers that he likes jam. He complains that his puddings hold too little. Digby is the long-wished heir of the house. Parents and sisters have spoiled him fondly. Only the housekeeper dares to thwart him.
34548-the-african-colony-studies-in-the-:
John Buchan studies how South Africa might be rebuilt after the Boer War in a book issued by William Blackwood and Sons in 1903. He dedicates it to Hugh Archibald Wyndham. The dedication recalls their African housekeeping together.

Three parts divide the work. The first treats the earlier masters: primitive South Africa, the gentlemen-adventurers, and the Great Trek. The Boer appears in sport and in all seriousness. Travel notes follow, with evenings on the high veld and the tracks of war. The last part faces the political problem. Chapters weigh the economic factor, the settlement of the land, and the subject races. Johannesburg and federation close the case. Buchan had served in the colonial administration. He wrote before his fame as a novelist, with a young official's zeal.
34582-mozart-the-story-of-a-little-boy-a:
Mozart, in the Child's Own Book of Great Musicians series, was written by Thomas Tapper and published by the Theodore Presser Company of Philadelphia in 1915. Its subtitle gives the story: a little boy and his sister who gave concerts. The book was sold with a cord and needle enclosed, and directions for binding it, and leaves blank lines for its young owner's name and for the composer's birth and death.

Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, the text begins, was called Wolferl when he was a little boy. His sister Maria Anna, called Nannerl, was five years older and took harpsichord lessons from their father. At three, Wolferl listened and watched; at four he began lessons himself, and practised so seriously that no one spoke to him while he played. A family trio picture shows the father on violin while Wolferl plays and Nannerl sings.
34656-evolution:
A churchman's library volume treats evolution and faith in this careful book. Burn edited the Churchman's Library series in which the volume stands on its title page. A transcriber's note adds that an October 1901 publisher's catalogue follows the final chapter inside.

Victorian clergy faced Darwin's theory with alarm, argument and, in time, acceptance attempts. Such a volume weighs descent, design and scripture for parish readers who wanted both honestly. Greek words appear in curly brackets through the text, the notes explain, in a work of the years when evolution was theology's hardest question.
34665-christmas-penny-readings-original-:
George Fenn wrote these Christmas penny readings, sketches for the season. Routledge issued the book in an edition dated 1867. Chapter one, Cutting Times, pairs a frost and a thaw. Hezekiah Thornypath had luck once, then luck kicked him out.

Hez took wife and children to London to make a fortune. He meant to make his crown a pound, the song says. Few hundred pounds melted, friends forsook, troubles came on fast. A doctor shook his head over their youngest child deathbed. Blinds drawn and hushed steps mark the sad house as the child lies dying there.
34697-the-lost-wagon:
The Lost Wagon is a western novel by Jim Kjelgaard. Dodd, Mead published it in New York in 1955. A jacket by Al Orbaan dresses the book. The contents promise a wagon journey in seventeen chapters. Their titles run from Pondering to Besieged.

The hero is Joe Tower, a farmer at his plough. A biting fly torments him as he works. He hates his two roan mules with a settled passion. The mules balk and tangle their harness. Tower knows their tricks too well to be hurt. The early chapters stage a family discussion. Destroyers and a mountain man follow. The party starts west and crosses a river. Winter, spring, and a farm fill the later chapters. A siege closes the tale.
34703-the-tower-of-oblivion:
The Tower of Oblivion is a novel by Oliver Onions, printed in 1921. Macmillan of New York brought the book out that November in print. Onions had writ A Case in Camera before this long strange tale. He gives the book to Nigel Playfair and the Beggar's Opera company. Ten titled parts divide the tale between England and France in turn.

The side-slip, the stern chase, and the straphanger open the England part. The double cross and the pivot close that first home section. France holds the long splice, the even keel, and the cut-out. The desert island and the home stretch end the whole design. Poe is quoted at the start on how unusual things should be told. Plain telling suits a thing unusual in its very nature, he says. The Lyonnesse Club meets in a basement suite off the Strand.
34738-the-ivory-gate-a-new-edition:
The Ivory Gate is a novel by Walter Besant, issued in a new edition by Chatto and Windus in London in 1893. A note explains that the tale first ran in Chambers's Journal. There it was found that Mortimer Collins had used the title in 1865; his representatives kindly made no objection. Lines from Virgil head the book, on the twin gates of sleep: horn for true shades, ivory for false dreams.

Besant dedicates the book to Doctor Sprigge. It was Sprigge, he writes, who first taught him of the brain disease that forms the motive of the story. He also furnished instances of its working. A hero whose brain disease splits his life between truth and false dreaming stands behind the motto. Besant, author of All Sorts and Conditions of Men, builds a London tale on a medical marvel.
34749-the-girls-of-central-high-on-track:
A girls' school novel by Gertrude W Morrison, copyrighted in 1914. Grosset and Dunlap held the copyright, and Saalfield published this edition. It belongs to the Girls of Central High series. Earlier volumes visited Lake Luna with the same friends. Track and field supplies this book's arena. Twenty-five chapters mix sport with a gypsy mystery.

Seven girls climb to an overhanging rock in spring. Bobby, black-eyed and be-curled, flits like a robin among them. Her friends ache just watching her energy. A gypsy camp and a gypsy queen draw the plot sideways. The races and the field day supply the athletic climax. Bobby wins one sprint by a clean two yards, the frontispiece boasts. Margit's mystery and debt close the human threads.
34839-the-short-constitution:
Judge Martin Wade and Dean William Russell wrote The Short Constitution, a study of the Constitution of the United States in the Elementary Americanism Series. Charles Meyerholz added the notes. The third revised edition was copyrighted in 1920 and 1921 at Iowa City.

The book stresses the guaranties of life, liberty, and property, sometimes called the Bill of Rights. Its front matter asks what America has done for me and for my children. The answer, the authors argue, comes only by teaching each citizen those guaranties. Wade was a federal judge; Russell dean of education at the University of Iowa. The book was built for home reading, study clubs, and schools.
34845-the-evolution-of-fashion:
The Evolution of Fashion is a history of costume by Florence Mary Gardiner, printed at London. The book is dedicated, by special permission, to Frances Evelyn, Countess of Warwick. It appeared in the year of Queen Victoria's Diamond Jubilee, 1897. Portions of it first ran in the Ludgate Illustrated Magazine.

Gardiner begins with the dress of our progenitors, chiefly remarkable for its extreme simplicity. No difference in design was made between the sexes, she writes. A few leaves entwined by their stalks, the feathers of birds, the bark of trees, or roughly dressed skins served the beaux and belles of the Adamite period. From those roots the book traces dress down the centuries. Gardiner thanks authors and firms for drawings and engravings she was allowed to reproduce. A frontispiece grouping shows great ladies of the day in ball dress. The work is a popular history of how fashion grew.
34846-robert-tournay-a-romance-of-the-fr:
William Sage wrote Robert Tournay, a tale of the great revolt in France put out in 1900. Eric Pape and Mary Ayer drew the plates for the book. Sage gives the tale to his mother, to whom he owes all, in fond words. A plate shows a cheer for the goddess of free rule.

Parts trace how Tournay came to Paris, and a small meal at the home of Saint Hilaire. A baker and his kin, a good patriot, and a broke door set the town in flame. A man and a marquis, a trip by Gaillard, and guests of a priest named Louchet fill the midst. A jail boat, a flight past the edge of the land, and a choice of flag raise the stakes.
34858-the-ordeal-of-richard-feverel-a-hi:
George Meredith's The Ordeal of Richard Feverel, a history of a father and son, appears here in the Modern Student's Library from Charles Scribner's Sons. Frank W Chandler, professor at the University of Cincinnati, edited the volume with an introduction. The Scribner copyrights run to 1896 and 1917. The series promises works essential to a liberal education.

The contents open with the inmates of Raynham Abbey, then show how the fates selected the fourteenth birthday to try the strength of the System. Later headings promise a magian conflict, arson, juvenile stratagems, and Daphne's bower, before Richard passes through his preliminary ordeal and is the occasion of an aphorism.
3490-the-admirable-crichton:
James Matthew Barrie writes a comedy about rank turned upside down when a lord's household is shipwrecked on a desert island. At Loam House in Mayfair, the Honourable Ernest Woolley drives up smiling and thinking, as usual, mainly of himself. Once the party is stranded, the butler Crichton, practical and calm, becomes the natural leader, while his masters prove helpless without servants.

Barrie uses the island to test English class habits. Crichton can build, hunt, and govern, yet back in London he returns to his place below stairs. The play mixes wit, romance, and social satire, and it remains one of Barrie's best known comedies. It suits readers who enjoy theater that asks who is really fit to lead.
34912-woman-in-science-with-an-introduct:
Mozans wrote Woman in Science, published by Appleton and Company in New York and London in 1913. He had earlier written travel books on the Orinoco, the Magdalena, the Andes, and the Amazon. An introductory chapter treats woman's long struggle for things of the mind, taking its motto from Dante.

The book then argues woman's capacity for scientific work, field by field. Chapters cover women in mathematics, astronomy, physics, and chemistry. Others treat the natural sciences, medicine and surgery, and archaeology. Women appear as inventors, and as inspirers and helpers of men of science. A final chapter looks to the future, backed by a bibliography and index. Mozans writes as an advocate, marshaling lives and records against the prejudice of his day.
3495-the-king-of-ireland-s-son:
Padraic Colum retells Irish folk tales as a single story about the king of Ireland's son in this book for young readers. The contents name its parts. They include The King of the Cats, The Sword of Light, The Town of the Red Castle, The King of the Land of Mist, and The House of Crom Duv. The hero, one of King Connal's three sons, sets out with a boat fastened for a year and a day.

Along the way he meets a spae woman named Fedelma, an enchanter's daughter, giants, and talking beasts. Colum writes in clear, musical prose that keeps the old tales' wonder without smoothing away their strangeness. The book suits families who want Irish legend in story form, and it remains a classic of children's fantasy.
34965-irish-history-and-the-irish-questi:
Irish History and the Irish Question is a short history by Goldwin Smith, published in New York in 1905. Smith had also written histories of the United Kingdom and the United States. His preface frames Ireland as a tragedy. Its theatre is a large island beside one nearly three times larger, which cuts it off from the continent of Europe. On the other side it fronts the wide ocean.

The contents run in fifteen chapters from early times to the present state of the question. They pass through the reigns of Edward the First, Henry the Eighth, Elizabeth, and James the First. The penal code, the revolution of 1782, and the rebellion of 1798 each get a chapter. The Union of 1801, Daniel O'Connell, and Gladstone carry the story to living memory. An appendix gives an account of the Irish land code by Hugh McCann of the Irish Bar.
34985-six-women-and-the-invasion:
Gabrielle and Marguerite Yerta wrote a war book published at London in 1917, with a preface by Mrs Humphry Ward. It tells what befell six women when the German invasion reached their village in 1914. The place is Morny, a village of the Laonnois. It lies in the Île de France, ten miles east of Laon.

The narrator speaks to her husband, gone to fight for his country, and owns the difference between them. He wished for the contest with the rage of youth; she met it with terror and remorse. The six women are her mother-in-law, her sisters-in-law, and herself. Fields, orchards, and the dark forest of St Gobain frame a peaceful scene about to be broken.
35140-the-blind-mother-and-the-last-conf:
The Blind Mother and The Last Confession are two tales by Hall Caine. Collier of New York issued them in a set of his best books. The same volume of that set also holds his novel The Bondman. The first tale opens in the Vale of Newlands on a summer morning.

It is Saint Peter's Day, and the children of the dale are rush-bearing. They walk in procession from the schoolhouse toward the church, singing as they go. The youngest, a boy of four in a braided pinafore, strides gallantly in front. Rushes, ferns, mosses, and flowers fill the little hands along the line. Sheep bleat and distant waterfalls rumble under the birdsong of the scene. Against that bright innocence the sorrows of the title figures unfold. Caine made his name with such tales of love, blindness, and confession.
35165-the-crooked-stick-or-pollie-s-prob:
Rolf Boldrewood, author of Robbery Under Arms, wrote The Crooked Stick, or Pollie's Probation, published at London in 1895. Chapter one sets the scene at the close of a lurid, sultry February day. A long dry summer has followed a rainless winter in the arid region of West Logan.

A blood-red sun sinks slowly and angrily into a crimson ocean. The scene is a limitless plain, its monotony broken by belts of timber and an infrequent pine ridge. The earth is parched, the sky a hopeless steel blue, the air stagnant. The Wannonbah mail-coach toils over a sandhill. Thank God, the sun is down at last. Readers get an Australian bush novel opening in drought and dread.
35204-sense-of-obligation:
Sense of Obligation is a science fiction novel by Harry Harrison, serialized in Analog across September, October, and November 1961. A verse by Stephen Crane stands at its head, about a man who told the universe he existed. The title comes from that poem's cold reply. A head note promises a very special type of man for an onerous, dangerous job.

The tale opens in an arena before thousands of spectators. Brion stands sweating in a loincloth, a light fencing foil heavy as lead in his tired hand. A cut on his chest still drips blood. Only the button-tipped steel hovering before him matters. He has trained his body for a month of continual exercise, and rest comes in measured minutes.
35215-the-french-revolution:
The French Revolution is a history by Hilaire Belloc, published in London by Williams and Norgate in January 1911. Belloc had written lives of Danton, Robespierre, and Marie Antoinette, and books on Paris and the old road. This short volume gathers his view of the whole event.

The contents show his design. First comes the political theory of the Revolution, then Rousseau. A set of characters follows: Louis the Sixteenth, the Queen, Mirabeau, Lafayette, Dumouriez, Danton, Carnot, Marat, and Robespierre. Then the phases of the Revolution are traced from May 1789 to July 1794. The military aspect takes a long section of its own. The book closes with the Revolution and the Catholic Church, a subject on which Belloc, a Catholic, had firm views. It is a brief, argued history, written against the grain of the liberal reading.
35259-menotah-a-tale-of-the-riel-rebelli:
Menotah, a tale of the Riel Rebellion by Ernest Henham, was printed in London in 1897. The novel is set in the Canadian North-West during the rising led by Louis Riel. Its three parts bear the names The Heart's Joy, The Heart's Grief, and The Heart's Peace.

In a note at the front, Henham says Riel himself stays off stage as an active figure. He calls Riel too plain and dull a man to carry a tale well. The plot turns instead on love and rivalry, and on the harsh use of native women by white men. Henham lays much blame at the door of the Hudson's Bay Company and its long rule in the region. Forest, fort, and fight scenes open the tale.
3527-the-blue-moon:
Laurence Housman writes a book of fairy tales and fanciful stories. They include The Wind, A Capful of Moonshine, The Moon Stroke, How Little Duke Jarl Saved the Castle, The White Doe, and The Blue Moon itself. The tales open on lovers named Nillywill and Hands-pansy, described as the most unimportant and happy pair the world has ever gained or lost.

Housman's stories favor moonlight, gardens, and gentle magic over battles or monsters. A peasant boy and a girl who wants to return to him anchor the longest tale, while shorter pieces play with wishes, moons, and enchanted beasts. The book suits readers who enjoy dreamy, old fashioned fairy tales written with a poet's care for language.
35288-two-years-in-oregon:
Wallis Nash, author of Oregon: There and Back in 1877, wrote an account of two years in Oregon, with a front view of the anchorage in Yaquina Bay. Nash was an English barrister who helped promote a colony of English settlers in the Yaquina country. His two books report the venture from inside. Verse lines on new pleasures caught by the eye head the title page.

English emigrants of means sought Oregon farms in the 1870s. Nash describes land, climate, salmon, and the hardships of settlement. His colony at Yaquina Bay rose and faded within years. The book is now a primary source on British settlement in the Pacific Northwest.
35295-the-maroon:
Mayne Reid wrote The Maroon, a novel of Jamaica issued in London in a form dated 1862. The tale opens on Mount Welcome, one of the finest sugar estates in the land of springs, ten miles from Montego Bay. Twin wooded ridges of pimento trees run for a mile and meet at a steep hill the estate calls the mountain.

The great house stands on a raised shelf at the foot of that hill. Its lower floor is strong stone, and its upper floor is a wood frame roofed with shingles. Broad stone steps with iron rails lead up to the living rooms, where shuttered walls keep the rooms cool. From that planter's house the tale of slavery, flight, and the maroons of the hills unfolds.
35322-the-thistle-and-the-cedar-of-leban:
Habeeb Risk Allah Effendi wrote The Thistle and the Cedar of Lebanon, in a second edition printed at London in eighteen fifty-four. The title takes its text from the second book of Kings, where a thistle asks a cedar for a marriage and is trodden down by a wild beast. The author was a surgeon and an associate of King's College. His tale is a memoir of Syria and its coast.

Early parts recall his childhood at Shuayfat, his schooling, and his move to Beyrout. A pirate attack and a flight to the mountains follow. Damascus gets a long portrait, its bazaars, houses, ladies, and games. Later parts travel to Cyprus, Cilicia, Aleppo, and Antioch, with notes on missions, consuls, and the cedars themselves.
3534-a-complete-account-of-the-settlemen:
Watkin Tench follows his first Botany Bay narrative with a fuller account of the settlement at Port Jackson, the site of modern Sydney. Tench notes that much had already been written about New South Wales, so he offers a reason for one more book. He sailed with the fleet, stayed through anxious years, and could correct and extend earlier reports. Fresh news from the colony arrived even as his book went to press.

The account covers farming, food shortages, relations with Aboriginal peoples, and the growth of a town from tents and huts. Tench writes as a soldier and observer, clear about hardship and hopeful about the colony's future. It suits readers who want a second, deeper eyewitness view of Australia's founding years.
35344-third-biennial-report-of-the-orego:
The Oregon State Highway Commission issued its third biennial report at Salem in 1919 through the State Printing Department. It covers December 1, 1916 to November 30, 1918 in full. Benson chaired the commission, with Thompson and Booth as commissioners and Herbert Nunn as state highway engineer. A letter of December 1, 1918 sends the report to Governor Withycombe.

A front picture shows the Pacific Highway in the Siskiyou Mountains of Jackson County, macadamized in 1917. Text and tables resume the biennium's work road by road and county by county. Costs, bids, and materials fill long statements meant for public audit. Readers get early state road building in hard figures, as Oregon paved its way out of mud.
35409-beauty-illustrated-chiefly-by-an-a:
Alexander Walker wrote Beauty, a study of beauty in woman by close study and sorting, in a New York printing of eighteen forty-five. An American doctor shaped this edition for the press. Walker gave the book to George Birkbeck, head of the London Mechanics' Institution. His letter of thanks praises Birkbeck for spreading science among the working classes.

Walker calls his field a new branch of science and vows to follow proof with care. He had written before on marriage, on woman, and on the nervous system. The study sorts the forms and features of women and seeks rules behind them. Its claims rest on the body and its workings, in the manner of his past works on the frame and face.
35571-felix-lanzberg-s-expiation:
Felix Lanzberg Expiation is a novel in English dress from a German original named Ehre. The hosted text carries close notes matching the English pages to the German edition. Linda, her mother, and an art critic named Papa Harfink stand in the tale.

The notes show a priest demanding a yes at a wedding, and a charge that Linda mother has deceived the hero. Linda herself, they stress, knows nothing. Papa Harfink, the art critic, closes a scene by calling French pictures regular daubs of color. He says the French are tricky and that people let themselves be cheated by them. Other notes render a supper scene, where a lady eats without pose or greed and sips her champagne. Old Manuela snores while some officers grow sad. Tale fans get a German honor drama with a learned apparatus.
35598-tales-from-tennyson:
Molly Bellew, editor of Tales from Longfellow and Dickens's Christmas Stories for Children, retold Tennyson's Idylls of the King in plain prose for young readers. The Caldwell company of New York and Boston published the volume, copyrighted in 1902. Eleven tales make the contents, illustrated by Campbell.

Bellew's note to her young readers calls Tennyson the typically English poet, whose Idylls hold the loftiest deeds of English history, and promises that the high spirit survives the retelling. The Coming of King Arthur opens in a divided land of warring little kingdoms, twenty years after old King Uther died without an heir. Merlin appears in the council hall with the young Arthur and declares him king. Gareth and Lynette, The Marriage of Geraint, Merlin and Vivien, Lancelot and Elaine, and The Holy Grail follow, down to The Passing of Arthur.
35608-masterman-and-son:
Masterman and Son is a novel by Dawson, put out by Revell in 1909. Fleming Revell printed it in New York, London, and Edinburgh that year. Dawson had written A Prophet in Babylon before this family tale. Three parts divide the book: the father, a middle flight, and reunion. Twenty-four chapters run from the master-builder to the new world at last.

Archibold Masterman stands tall, heavily built, and past fifty at the start. At twenty a day-labourer, at thirty a jobbing builder, he rose fast. At forty he stood a contractor in a large way of business. Broadcloth on week-days and Eagle House mark his climb in the world. Young love, an accusation, and a contest shake the first part's close. Part two flies to New York and a millionaire in the Kootenay. Fear, return, and verdict bind father and son in part three.
357-a-dream-of-john-ball-and-a-king-s-le:
William Morris frames this tale as a dream that drops a modern man into fourteenth-century Kent. There he meets John Ball, the priest whose preaching stirred the Peasants' Revolt, and watches rebels gather at a village cross. A short second piece, A King's Lesson, follows the dream tale.

The talk between dreamer and priest turns on fair work, just rule, and hope for a better world to come. Battle, supper, and hard talk with the dead fill the later chapters. Morris uses the past not as costume, but as a mirror for his own age and its own fight for change.
35724-13-days-the-chronicle-of-an-escape:
Thirteen Days is the chronicle of an escape from a German prison. Captain Caunter of the Gloucestershire Regiment wrote and drew the book. Bell of London issued the escape account in nineteen eighteen. Part one covers Crefeld, the move to Schwarmstedt, and camp life there.

Part two tells the escape from Schwarmstedt camp and the flight west. Crossing the first two rivers fills the next chapter of the run. The fugitive meets Fox and Blank, then crosses the Weser River. A picture shows him wading with his bundle safe on his head. British officer escapes were rare feats in the Great War years.
35735-the-gnostic-crucifixion:
Gnostic Crucifixion, by Mead, is volume seven of Echoes from the Gnosis. The Theosophical Publishing Society of London and Benares issued it in nineteen o seven. Mead also wrote Thrice Greatest Hermes and Fragments of a Faith Forgotten. Did Jesus Live One Hundred BC and Apollonius of Tyana stand in his list.

The Echoes series draws small volumes from mystic and gnostic writings of old. It aims to make initiatory lore plain to a widening circle of lovers. Many long for gnostic light but cannot study the ancients at first hand. These little books serve as a first step to the harder literature. The crucifixion is read here in a gnostic key of meaning.
35772-religion-and-science-from-galileo-:
Religion and Science from Galileo to Bergson is a study by John Charlton Hardwick. The Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge published it in London in 1920. Macmillan issued it in New York the same year. A Bradley passage on philosophy's hard road fronts the book. Hardwick dedicated the volume to his father. The first chapter defines religion and science for the argument. Accurate and systematic knowledge affects our attitude to life, it holds. Can systematised knowledge sanction a religious attitude, it asks.

That is named the religious problem of the book. The religious harmony of the Middle Ages is recalled there. A second chapter treats the dissolution of the old synthesis. Aquinas and scholasticism describe the old world scheme in it. Copernicus, Bruno, and Galileo break that scheme apart. The new astronomy and physics drive the chapter forward. Hardwick traces a long quarrel toward a possible peace.
36093-tennyson-s-life-and-poetry-and-mis:
Tennyson's Life and Poetry, and Mistakes Concerning Tennyson, by Eugene Parsons, copyright 1892, is a short handbook on the poet laureate. An opening note surveys the shelf of Tennyson books already in print, from lives and concordances to school editions in German, French, and Italian.

The main essay treats the life and the poems, and a second part corrects common errors about Tennyson. A final list tracks translations of his works abroad. Parsons wrote for the many new readers who met Tennyson in school and wanted one clear guide. The little book also shows how large the Tennyson industry had grown by the year of his death.
36101-on-guard-mark-mallory-s-celebratio:
On Guard, or Mark Mallory's Celebration is a West Point novel credited to Frederick Garrison. A transcriber's note unmasks the name: it is a pseudonym of Upton Sinclair. Street and Smith copyrighted the book in 1903; McKay of Philadelphia published it. Mark Mallory is a plebe at the Military Academy. A letter from a furlough man opens the plot. Mark's idea and a new ally follow in quick chapters.

Schemes and counterplots fill the middle of the tale. Texas, a comrade, runs amuck and raids West Point. Yearlings plot against the plebes, and the plebes plot back. Traps are set before the hop, the academy dance. Benny is exposed, and Mark lands in hospital. Six come to the rescue, as one chapter promises. Cadet honour and hazing supply the stakes.
36146-dr-john-mcloughlin-the-father-of-o:
Frederick Holman wrote this life of John McLoughlin, father of Oregon. Clark printed it at Cleveland in 1907 with portraits. Holman gives the book to Oregon pioneers of the forties years. A daguerreotype of 1856 shows McLoughlin a year before his death.

Contents treat early settlements, joint occupancy, and the Hudson Bay Company. Fort Vancouver, Indian punishment, and French Canadian settlers follow in turn. Missionaries, provisional government, and the great immigrations come next in line. McLoughlin kindness to pioneers stands as the book warm core. The immigrations of 1842 through 1846 take long sections of the contents list in turn.
36155-the-invasion:
The Invasion, by William Le Queux, published by George Newnes at London, opens with a preface. It quotes Earl Roberts in the House of Lords: he despairs, he said, of the country ever becoming alive to the danger of its unpreparedness until too late.

Le Queux backs the warning with Lord Milner and the Marquis of Lansdowne, and with the Elgin Commission's call for powers of expansion beyond the regular forces. An empire that cannot defend its own possessions, Roberts warned, must inevitably perish, and the novel imagines the raid on British shores that follows.
36189-in-search-of-a-son:
In Search of a Son, by Uncle Lawrence, was printed by Lippincott at Philadelphia in 1890. Lawrence also wrote Young Folks' Whys and Wherefores. The tale opens in the great silence of the fields at an old French chateau. A gentleman in slippers and dressing robe takes vermouth and seltzer at a stone table in the shade.

The contents blend story and science in a curious way. One thread follows a despatch, two friends, and Monsieur Roger and his story, through a fire at sea toward a mysterious resemblance. Between the chapters of the search come lessons in physical science: the air pump, why lead is heavier than cork, why the moon does not fall, and oxygen.
36192-the-balkan-wars-1912-1913-second-e:
