Jacob Gould Schurman wrote a short history of the Balkan Wars of 1912-1913, issued by Princeton University Press in 1914. A second edition came out in December of that same year. Schurman opens with a bold claim: the end of Turkish rule in Europe was long set, and only its date was in doubt.

He traces how a small clan took land in Asia Minor, took Brusa in 1326, and crossed into Europe. The great loss at Kossovo in 1389, the fall of Constantinople in 1453, and the march to Vienna in 1529 mark the climb. Maps show the lands as they stood before the wars.
362-miss-billy-s-decision:
Eleanor Porter continues the story of Billy Neilson in this sequel to Miss Billy, with thirty-three chapters of Boston social life. Billy, now caught between love and duty, must choose how far to shape her own life. Around her move Aunt Hannah, the artist Bertram, the sharp-tongued Mary Jane, and old friends from the first book.

Letters, studio talk, an operetta, and a string of small crises test Billy's nerve and pride. Porter keeps the tone light, yet the choices bite: who to trust, what to give up, and when to speak plain truth. The book closes a chapter of Billy's youth with warmth and a clear sense of growth.
36235-old-kensington:
Miss Thackeray wrote this novel of old Kensington life and friends. Smith, Elder printed the book in London in 1908. A Tennyson line on more life fronts the tale as motto. The author gives her story to some new friends met midway.

The story began ten years before, older than god daughter Margie. Margie plays queen games with sisters and cousins at Eton nurseries. Dolly and the little Dorotheas hold first right to a copy. Children songs tell of past and future bound by hope. Laura song at home is her own, a sweet home song, the dedication tells the friends.
36268-heresy-its-utility-and-morality-a-:
Charles Bradlaugh's Heresy, Its Utility and Morality, a plea and a justification, was published in London by Austin and Co. The first chapter asks what heresy is, that it should be so heavily punished, when society condones many offences and pardons many vicious practices yet shows scant mercy to the heretic.

Bradlaugh answers that heresy is neither atheism nor theism in itself. The heretic is one who has selected his own opinions by mental effort, while the orthodox often hold opinions bequeathed by an earlier generation and accepted without question. He notes that Voltaire and Paine were heretics but theists, and that Garibaldi and Mazzini are heretics and not atheists.
36274-the-age-of-tennyson:
The Age of Tennyson is a handbook of English literature by Hugh Walker, ninth edition, printed at London. Professor Hales edited the series, whose volumes run from the Age of Alfred to the Age of Wordsworth. Walker defines his age as 1830 to 1870. The starting date needs no explanation, he says.

Why should the age end more than twenty years before Tennyson died? That question, Walker grants, may fairly be asked. His answer shapes the book's plan. The age belongs to the years when Tennyson's voice set the tone for English letters. The handbook surveys the poets and prose writers who shared those forty years.
36306-trial-of-the-officers-and-crew-of-:
The trial of the officers and crew of the privateer Savannah, on the charge of piracy, was reported by Warburton and printed by Baker and Godwin in 1862. The case sat in the United States Circuit Court for the Southern District of New York, Judges Nelson and Shipman presiding. The record was corrected by the counsel on both sides.

The contents lay out five days of law. First the capture of the Savannah, the prisoners' removal to New York, the indictment, and the arraignment. Then the jury is impanelled, and the district attorney opens for the prosecution. Witnesses include the flag officer Stringham. Arguments on jurisdiction and points of law fill the middle days, Evarts and Brady among the counsel heard. The summings up to the jury close the record, a Confederate privateer's crew tried as pirates by the Union whose ships they had taken.
36314-the-radio-boys-rescue-the-lost-ala:
The Radio Boys Rescue the Lost Alaska Expedition, by Gerald Breckenridge, is a boys' tale of wireless adventure. Burt published it in New York in 1922. Four earlier Radio Boys books stand in the series list at the front.

A frontispiece catches the boys at their set: what does she say, Frank, any luck yet. The tale opens in a Seattle hotel, the party homeward bound from South America. Jack Hampton, Bob Temple, and Frank Merrick are talking of the lost expedition. Hampton's father enters with news hot from a conference. A man who knows all there is to know of the expedition has been telling him of it. The boys had found and lost an enchanted city of the Incas in the last book. Now a rescue calls them north to Alaska, by radio.
36410-the-story-of-bacon-s-rebellion:
Mary Newton Stanard tells the tale of the 1676 rising in Virginia in a Neale volume from New York and Washington dated 1907. She gives the book to her husband, William Glover Stanard, her guide in trips into the past of Virginia. Sixteen chapters run from Sir William Berkeley to Peace Restored, with an appendix at the back.

Stanard calls the rising the most tense and grand event in the colony's seventeenth century after its first hard years. New facts from English public records, she says, now let readers grasp its causes and results with care. Chapter heads trace grievances, terror, Bacon's entry, civil war, and the siege and burning of Jamestown. Her aim is a clear, plain telling for readers drawn to the old story.
36471-united-states-government-publicati:
A catalogue of official print fills this volume: United States Government Publications, a monthly catalogue edited by John Hickcox. Volume eight covers January to June 1892, numbers one to seven, printed at Washington. A notice at the front offers to supply any publication named, for a fair charge where no price is given.

The catalogue's own account of itself is broad. It lists the titles of all current official publications of the United States: reports and papers from departments, bureaus, and commissions, and every document printed by order of Congress. Public acts, treaties, and maps are included too. Titles stand in alphabetical order under authors' names for special works, and under topics for the documents of Congress.
3654-alfred-tennyson:
Andrew Lang writes a brief life and appreciation of Alfred Tennyson, published in 1901. Lang rests his account almost entirely on the biography by Lord Tennyson, the poet's son, with the son's kind permission, and on the text of the poems themselves. He sets aside current anecdotes not given in that biography, preferring a sober sketch to gossip.

The book follows Tennyson from youth to laureate, and judges his work poem by poem, from early lyrics to In Memoriam and the Idylls. Lang writes as an admiring critic who also notes faults. The volume suits readers who want a short, reliable introduction to Tennyson's life and art.
36574-baby-jane-s-mission:
Baby Jane's Mission is a children's story book by Parnell, one of the Larger Dumpy Books for Children. The frontispiece shows a chase in hot pursuit of Baby Jane. The chapter list is a small world of play and animals. A dancing class opens the tale. Nuts in May and Santa Claus follow. A football match, Old Janies against the Junior Oakdene Athletic, fills a chapter of its own. Two new friends and a great circus stand in the mid run.

Baby Jane's army and a stay in the enemy's camp raise the stakes. The rescue and the finish close the book. The plates show a bear that whistles at the sky, a lion with a rider on his head, and a lady crocodile on a suitor's arm. The book is a cheerful animal romp of the nursery shelf.
36610-the-influence-of-the-bible-on-civi:
The Influence of the Bible on Civilisation, by Ernst von Dobschutz, was printed by Scribner in New York in 1914. Dobschutz was professor of the New Testament at the University of Halle Wittenberg. Sixteen plates open the book, from a Harvard papyrus of Romans to the first printed German Bible.

Eight chapters trace one small book through the centuries. The Bible makes itself indispensable for the church by the year 325, then begins to rule the Christian empire. It teaches the German nations, becomes one basis of medieval civilisation, and stirs nonconformist movements. Printers and translators train under it, it rules daily life for three centuries, and at last it becomes once more a book of devotion.
36618-carry-on:
Carry On is a book of war poems by Virna Sheard, printed at Toronto by Warwick Brothers and Rutter in 1917. The volume appeared under the patronage of the Imperial Order Daughters of the Empire, in aid of the Red Cross. Its Canadian copyright dates to the third year of the Great War, when Sheard's readers had sons overseas.

The title poem orders its refrain against the night of death and tears: carry on for the brave who fought and died, since only once can each man die. The Young Knights follows, for the boys who gave their youth away and remain forever young in Flanders fields. Other pieces include The Shells, The Watcher, October Goes, Crosses, and a closing Requiem and Lament. The book is home-front verse, meant to stiffen and console.
36623-dorrien-of-cranston:
Bertram Mitford's novel, in an edition dated nineteen three from Hurst and Blackett of London, opens at Cranston Hall. A letter arrives that should please a father and does not. General Dorrien, a handsome, iron willed soldier, reads that his son Roland is returning to England after eight years in America. His frown only deepens.

Father and son parted in bitter anger. The one was wild and imprudent under harsh restraint, the other merciless and unbending. A few curt money letters are all that passed between them since. The General has also buried his favorite, a cavalry son lost with two guides in a crevasse on the Lauteraar glacier. Time has hardened rather than healed him. Mitford sets up a homecoming in which two strong wills must either bend or break. The first chapter does its work quietly, at a breakfast table.
36636-a-night-in-avignon:
Cale Young Rice wrote A Night in Avignon, a verse play published by Doubleday, Page and Company in New York in 1907. Rice also wrote Charles Di Tocca and David. The play is set in the chambers of Francesco Petrarca, the young poet Petrarch, at Avignon. His room overlooks the church of Santa Clara and a Carthusian cloister. Candles, a wine table, and garlands of myrtle and laurel fill the stage.

Petrarch walks the room in fever while his brother Gherardo, a monk, watches with severe looks. Gherardo urges him to quench the lights and set the wine aside. Two ladies of light life, Filippa and Sancia, belong to the night's company. Above all stands Madonna Laura, the woman Petrarch loves and cannot win. Rice builds a single Provençal night into a drama of desire against devotion, with the monk's counsel pressing on the poet's restless heart.
36650-the-mystery-of-francis-bacon:
The Mystery of Francis Bacon, by William T Smedley, was published by Robert Banks and Son at London in 1912. A bust at Gorhambury shows Bacon at nine years of age as frontispiece, and an epigram from John Owen's Epigrammatum of 1612 stands at the front.

Chapters trace Bacon's stock, Cambridge years, early compositions, and time in France. Smedley then asks whether Bacon probably left manuscripts hidden away, and how the Elizabethan literature was produced. The 1623 folio of Shakespeare's plays and the authorised version of the Bible of 1611 both come under his clue to the mystery.
36654-cruisings-in-the-cascades-a-narrat:
Shields, who signed as Coquina, wrote Cruisings in the Cascades for Rand and McNally in 1889. The book tells of travel, hunts, and fishing, with tales of amateur photography too. Some parts had run in Harper's Magazine, and some in Outing, by leave of those sheets. Shields gives special parts to the grizzly bear, the buffalo, elk, and antelope. The Rocky Mountain goat and deer get parts of their own.

Trout fishing in the Rockies and a Montana round-up add range to the book. Life among the cowboys is drawn from the camp and the trail. Front lines from Marlowe and Longfellow set a fond tone for wild hills. Shields writes as a man who lived the hunts he tells. Readers get sport, place, and camp lore from the high West in one full book.
3670-peg-woffington:
Charles Reade writes a dramatic story about Margaret Woffington, the famous eighteenth century actress. Reade inscribes the tale to her memory, saying she was falsely summed up until his day, and he draws on stage memoirs for his material. The story opens about the middle of the last century, at eight in the evening, in a large but poor apartment where a man slumbers on a rough couch.

Woffington, witty and generous, moves through London theater life, where acting, love, and reputation tangle. Reade defends her against gossip that painted her as merely a flirt. The novel suits readers interested in theater history and in a heroine who won fame by talent in an age that judged actresses harshly.
36735-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
Encyclopaedia Britannica, eleventh edition, is the famous 1910 scholarly reference work, and this file holds a stretch of the letter E. Articles treat Evelyn the diarist, evolution at great length, and Evora among many entries. Transcriber notes record corrected misprints and conventions for subscripts, Greek letters, and root signs in the text.

John Evelyn was admitted to the Middle Temple in February 1637 and became a fellow commoner of Balliol College, Oxford, the article begins. The evolution article traces the idea through early thinkers to 1858, when Darwin and Wallace published natural selection jointly. Sense perception and early plant philosophy open the long argument in detail. Reference readers get Victorian-to-Edwardian scholarship.
36746-the-mountains-of-oregon:
The Mountains of Oregon is a small book by W G Steel, published at Portland in 1890. Steel was a fellow of the American Geographical Society. A row of portraits stands at the front, Steel among them. In his preface he owns the book grew by chance. Letters on set peaks were to have been a pamphlet. The space proved too small, so the letters became a book. The arrangement still shows that birth, he warns.

The contents mix peak tales with club business. The illumination of Mount Hood leads the list. Crater Lake gets the longest tale. A night on the summit of Mount Rainier and the Josephine County caves stand in the run. The Oregon Alpine Club, its constitution, and its departments take the rest. An Oregon bibliography closes the book. It is a record of the first mountaineering age in the northwest.
36761-charles-edward-putney-an-appreciat:
The Charles Putney Memorial Association published this appreciation of a New Hampshire teacher after his death. Putney was born at Bow in 1840, one of fourteen children of a farmer. He taught district schools, aimed at Dartmouth College, and then saw the Civil War break out before he could enter.

He served over three years with the Thirteenth New Hampshire Volunteers, rising to sergeant and fighting at Fredericksburg and Cold Harbor. After the war he took his degree and gave his life to teaching the classics. A birthday poem pictures his classroom: a wrinkled Homer on the wall, girls and boys murmuring Greek, and the gentle king on his throne. Pupils of thirty-five years' standing wrote the tributes that fill the book.
36762-the-reform-of-education:
Giovanni Gentile lectures on The Reform of Education, in an authorized English text by Dino Bigongiari. Harcourt and Brace of New York print the book in 1922, with a first word by Benedetto Croce. Gentile taught philosophy at the University of Rome.

A note tells the lectures' birth. Trieste had just fallen into Italian hands, and a lecture line was set for the school teachers of the city. Their new duties as citizens of Italy made the talks a welcome rite. Gentile opened the line. Heads treat education and nationality, the self, and the deep clash at the heart of teaching. Culture, character, and the ideal of education close the course.
3677-on-our-selection:
Steele Rudd writes humorous stories of Australian bush life on a selection, a small farm taken up under colonial land law. The book opens twenty years after the family settled on the creek, arriving from Stanthorpe on Jerome's dray, eight people with beds, tubs, and all their goods. Rudd dedicates the stories to the pioneers who gave the country birth, whose names were never carved on tablet or tombstone.

The tales follow Dad, Dave, Joe, and the rest through drought, floods, hard work, and family quarrels, with the bush itself as a character. Rudd writes in Australian vernacular, warm and funny about hardship. The book became a classic of Australian humor and suits readers who enjoy frontier family life told from inside.
36774-the-teacher-essays-and-addresses-o:
The Teacher is a set of essays and addresses on education by George Herbert Palmer and Alice Freeman Palmer, issued in 1908. The first part treats problems of school and college. Its chapters open with the ideal teacher, then turn to ethical and moral instruction in the schools. Self cultivation in English and doubts about university extension follow.

A second part gathers Harvard papers, on the new education, the elective system, and college expenses. One chapter recalls a teacher of the olden time. The third part holds papers by Alice Freeman Palmer, whose name shares the title page. The long contents list shows two careers in teaching joined in one volume. Specialization and the glory of the imperfect close the first part's argument.
36857-the-prophet-ezekiel-an-analytical-:
The Prophet Ezekiel: An Analytical Exposition, by Arno Gaebelein, was copyrighted in New York in 1918. Gaebelein wrote expositions of Daniel, Joel, Zechariah, Matthew, Acts, and Revelation, and edited the journal Our Hope. A note of praise from James Gray of the Moody Bible Institute fronts the book. Maps show the temple ground plan and the division of the land.

Gaebelein notes that Ezekiel was son of Buzi the priest, of the honored Zadok family, and knew the nobles of Jerusalem well. Eleven years before the city and temple fell to Babylon, Ezekiel was carried off with ten thousand captives. The exposition splits the book at Jerusalem's fall, treating warnings before it and hopes after it, verse by verse.
36879-nicotiana-or-the-smoker-s-and-snuf:
Henry James Meller's Nicotiana, the Smoker's and Snuff-Taker's Companion, came out in London in eighteen thirty-two from Effingham Wilson at the Royal Exchange. Its title page promises the history of tobacco, its culture, its medical qualities, and the laws that govern its import and manufacture. An essay in its defence follows, the whole laced with original poetry and anecdotes for genuine lovers of the herb.

Meller quotes Captain Bobadil's praise of tobacco as the most sovereign and precious weed the earth tendered to man's use, and dedicates the book to the Duke of Sussex. His preface argues a legal case. Smoking and snuff-taking needed sound arguments, he holds, and he stands as counsel against the anti-smokers.
36885-rheims-and-the-battles-for-its-pos:
Rheims and the Battles for its Possession belongs to the Illustrated Michelin Guides to the Battle-Fields of 1914 to 1918, published by Michelin at Clermont-Ferrand with copyright of 1919. Pages of advertisements for Michelin maps, wheels and the Touring Club de France precede the guide proper.

A memorial page honours the Michelin employees and workmen who died for their country. Then comes the honour done the city itself: on July 6, 1919, the President of the French Republic fastened the Croix de la Légion d'Honneur on the arms of Rheims. The citation calls Rheims a martyred city, destroyed by an infuriated enemy powerless to hold it, and praises a population that stayed more than three years under constant menace of the guns.
36926-man-s-redemption-of-man-a-lay-serm:
William Osler gave a lay sermon called Man's Redemption of Man at McEwan Hall, Edinburgh, in July nineteen ten. The address was made for students of the University of Edinburgh, at a meeting on stopping consumption. Constable printed the text at London in nineteen thirteen.

Osler speaks of three gospels in human life, of the soul, of goods, and of the body. The last, he says, brings man into touch with nature and its conquest. That conquest, won by study and care, lets men save men from disease. He calls it a true glad tidings, beside which other triumphs sink.
36929-leighton:
Lys Baldry wrote Leighton, in a series of masterpieces in colour. Hare edited the series, printed by Jack at London in 1908. Stokes sold the book at New York in the same dress. Eight reproductions in colour illustrate the painter's life and work. Leighton's dates, 1830 to 1897, head the title matter.

The front plate shows the sea giving up the dead that were in it. That panel hangs at the Tate Gallery in London, the note says. It was meant for a scheme of decoration for a cathedral dome. Both its subject and treatment depart from Leighton's usual direction, it adds. Its largeness of style gives it an important place, the note holds. The Syracusan Bride and Gathering Citrons follow in the plates. Clytemnestra and the Bath of Psyche stand among the colour plates. Baldry traces the bond between the man and his art.
37035-journal-of-dr-elias-cornelius-a-re:
Elias Cornelius served as a surgeon's mate in the American Revolutionary army, and his journal tells what he suffered as a prisoner in Provost Jail, New York, in 1777 and 1778. Judge Tompkins and Chester Sherman published the journal at Washington in 1903, with a biographical sketch of the doctor. The price on the title page is fifty cents, postpaid.

The journal opens on August 22, 1777, with a march down to East Chester with the main body of troops. Cornelius names the brigades, the piquet guards, and the officers set over them. He tells of a surprise attack on an enemy piquet and of stores seized within the enemy lines. The daily entries give a close, ground level view of the war before his capture.
3707-the-trimmed-lamp-and-other-stories-:
O Henry gathers two dozen New York stories under the title of his most famous collection, since four million was then the city's population. Shop girls Lou and Nancy, clerks, cops, con men, and chorus girls crowd these pages, each chasing a small hope in a large town. The opening tale defends working girls against a lazy label. Later tales turn on a last leaf painted on a wall, a lost coin, and a wedding guest who counts too much.

The plots twist at the close, but the real pleasure lies in the talk, the slang, and the author's fondness for his people. New York itself acts as a character, with its flats, shops, and streetcars. Readers new to O Henry will find here the full range of his art, from jokes to pathos, in stories short enough for a single sitting.
37124-a-foreword-to-the-panama-pacific-i:
A Foreword to the Panama-Pacific International Exposition is a short book by Juliet James. It was printed in San Francisco in January 1915. The exposition it introduces celebrated the opening of the Panama Canal. James opens with a prose portrait of the host city. She calls San Francisco a pastel city by the sea. Hills crown it, and a near land locked bay washes its shore.

Three years before, she notes, that shore was marsh and lagoon. Then she pictures a phantom fleet sailing through the Golden Gate. Its ships carry figures named Energy, Enterprise, and Youth. The Spirit of the East and the Spirit of the West sail with them. Last comes the stalwart Mother of Tomorrow. These powers, she writes, dug the great canal gap with Hercules. They then sailed on to celebrate in the land of their desires.
37143-subconscious-religion:
Russell Conwell wrote the lectures gathered as Effective Prayer, copyrighted in 1921. This volume, number ten of a university extension set, carries the title Subconscious Religion. Its heads ask whether God answers Christians only, and treat conflicting prayers.

Conwell drew on years of prayer at the Baptist Temple and on a mass of letters. He holds that God is no respecter of persons, yet that a soul in tune with the Infinite hears more clearly. Testimonies fill the chapters: a hardened sinner in agony, a teacher of psychology who tested prayer on purpose. Great prayers and the use of the Bible in prayer follow.
37158-the-pros-and-cons-of-vivisection:
Doctor Charles Richet, who taught the study of the body at Paris, weighed the case for and against cutting living beasts, in a book printed at London in 1908. A London teacher of the same science wrote the first word. The front picture shows Death, cut in stone at a Paris grave yard.

Eight chapters frame the plea. The needful limits of the practice and the facts of pain and death come first. Sleep drugs in the lab and other ways of search take their turns. A chapter counts what such work has done for science and for man. Morals, laws, and the future of the craft close the book, with death rates for one sickness at the back.
37222-insanity-its-causes-and-prevention:
Henry Putnam Stearns writes on madness, its roots, and its bar in a Putnam volume from New York dated 1883. Stearns ran the Retreat for the Insane at Hartford and lectured on insanity at Yale. A Spenser line on the mind that makes good or ill heads the title page.

Stearns gives the book to John Sibbald, a lunacy commissioner for Scotland and a friend from student days. A preface tells how a paper on the insane diathesis, read two years before, drew calls for copies. That call led to a fuller book for general doctors, teachers, and keen lay readers, not for specialists alone. Odd snatches of time and many breaks mark its making, Stearns grants with regret in that preface.
37287-abraham-lincoln-s-religion:
A short study of Abraham Lincoln's religion by Madison C Peters. Richard G Badger published it at Boston in 1909. Peters also wrote Justice to the Jew. Three chapters divide the argument. The first presents Lincoln the man. The second asks whether Lincoln was a Christian. The third asks why he never joined a church.

Longfellow's poem to the Ship of State opens the book. Peters then praises the lowly-born Kentucky boy. No caliph or conqueror, he writes, matches Lincoln's fame. Humanity honours him among the noblest sons of men. The centenary of Lincoln's birth fell in 1909. Books like this one fought over his faith for a wide public. Peters writes as an admiring minister, not a neutral scholar.
3740-complete-project-gutenberg-collecti:
This large file binds three first hand accounts of Napoleon into a single reading text. Louis Antoine Fauvelet de Bourrienne, the emperor's private secretary, gives the long official view, from the early campaigns to the fall. Constant, the premier valet de chambre, adds the private life, with mornings, moods, and household detail that no state paper shows. Stewarton closes the set with secret letters from Paris to London on the court of Saint Cloud.

Together the three memoirs let readers watch Napoleon from the desk, the bedroom, and the salon at once. Generals like Murat and Rapp pass through with their own voices, and the great events gain a human scale. The file is long, but each memoir stands alone, so readers can dip into Bourrienne for politics, Constant for character, or Stewarton for court gossip.
37443-the-fascinating-boston:
Sheafe, a master of dancing, wrote The Fascinating Boston for the Boston Music Company in 1913. Its subtitle promises to teach the popular new social favourite, the Boston, and how to teach it.

The book starts with the five fundamental positions of the feet. Then come the positions of the partners, the step of the Boston, and its long, short, and open forms, with the Boston dip. Shorter chapters add the turkey trot, the aeroplane glide, and the tango. Sheafe meets the controversy head-on: educators and parents objected to how partners held each other in the round dances, and the profession answered with fixed, proper groupings. The manual belongs to the years when new dances swept the ballrooms and alarmed the guardians of manners.
37466-lost-in-the-can-on-the-story-of-sa:
Lost in the Cañon is the story of Sam Willett's adventures on the great Colorado of the West, by Alfred Calhoun. Burt published it in New York in 1888. A picture shows Sam guiding his raft to a ledge of sloping rocks. Chapters open at a remarkable camp, then look backward and forward before Sam's trials begin.

A perilous situation and a stop at Hurley's Gulch lead to the wonderful voyage. Sam endures a night of awful gloom, runs out of provisions, and shoots the rapids. His father learns the news as the voyage is resumed and order gives way to disorder. The tale belongs to the dime-novel West of rafts, canyons, and boy heroes.
37467-daisy-thornton:
Mary Holmes wrote Daisy Thornton, a novel printed at New York with rights from 1878. Holmes had won a wide public with Tempest and Sunshine and Lena Rivers. A motto heads the book: those whom God has joined together, let no man put asunder. Journals and letters carry much of the tale.

Frances Thornton writes first, at Elmwood, among roses and white lilies praised by all the town. Her heart is sore: her brother Guy, thirty, rich, bookish, and held first man in town, plans to wed a girl of sixteen known since Christmas. Heads promise the author story, a divorce, five years later, and Daisy letter. Saratoga, a sick room, and that other one fill a tense tale of love, law, and kin pride.
37528-quick-action:
Robert W Chambers wrote a novel copyrighted in 1914, first run in Harper's Bazaar and elsewhere in 1913, drawn by Edmund Frederick. A verse dedication to Penelope Sears, a debutante, opens the book. A front picture shows a woman named Athalie holding a figure called the Green God. She asks a man whether he is preaching.

Chambers was known for tales of art, love, and strange gods. The title promises speed and decision. The Green God figure hints at the exotic strain in his work. Readers of his earlier romances will find the same mix of society talk and odd belief. The novel belongs to his popular middle period of fiction.
37529-the-adventures-of-puss-in-boots-ma:
The Adventures of Puss in Boots, in the edition of Marks of Long Lane, London, retells the famous tale in verse for children. Each page pairs a picture with short rhymed stanzas. The story opens with a poor young man whose whole wealth is a cat he means to kill for food.

Puss begs for boots and a bag and promises to make his master fortune. He traps a rabbit and partridges and brings them to the king in the name of the Marquis Carabas. Gift after gift wins the king favor for the master who does not exist. The king sets out on a journey with his daughter, and Puss runs ahead to work his tricks. Small readers get the whole rise of the clever cat in quick, musical lines.
37572-the-way-of-decision:
M C Pease wrote the tale The Way of Decision. Greg Weeks and helpers prepared this text. A photo note shows Tom meeting a new group member. Clan colonies based on odd family ideas fill the blurb. Most such colonies failed in practice, it says. Ideal notions ignored real needs in them, it adds.

What of a group built to fit real conditions, it asks. A stranger member must be taken in there. Tom Vord sits on his clan house porch at start. His feet rest on the railing in ease. A commuter track roars far off toward New Haven. Private houses string along the belt below. Larger clan homes stand apart behind them. Spring green lies fresh over all in 2013. Tom takes his clan's problems with full weight. A suburban future of clan houses poses the tale's quiet test of new kinship.
37612-bill-s-school-and-mine-a-collectio:
Bill's School and Mine is a collection of essays on education by William Suddards Franklin, published at South Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, in 1913. Franklin was a physicist at Lehigh University, and the book is dedicated to a university supported and controlled by the people of Pennsylvania. A saying of Nietzsche's serves as motto.

The time will come, Nietzsche promised, when men will think of nothing but education. A note added after August 1914 observes the prophecy darkening into war. Franklin writes as a working teacher of science about schools and colleges he knew. The Bill of the title stands for the ordinary student and his ordinary school. Against them Franklin measures his own training and his hopes. The essays argue, with a physicist's impatience, for teaching that makes students do and think rather than recite.
37656-thomas-hart-benton:
Thomas Hart Benton, by Theodore Roosevelt, came out in a set of lives of American statesmen, and was copyright in 1886. This fifth edition came from Houghton, Mifflin in 1890. Fifteen chapters track the great senator from Missouri, from the young West to his last fight.

Roosevelt opens with the westward push that turned sea board states into a vast land nation. Backwoods men crossed the peaks into the great river basin, and new states rose fast. Benton enters the Senate in that surge. Chapters treat the rise of Jackson and the spoils game, the fight with men who would void laws, and war on the Bank. More treat the slave theme as it creeps into high talk. A last set treats slave soil in new lands and a losing fight. History fans get a brisk life by a future chief.
37761-a-damaged-reputation:
Harold Bindloss sets a frontier novel in British Columbia in a book issued in New York in 1908. Rancher Brooke sits alone in his shanty on a hot night, with a whisky bottle at hand and a crisis in his affairs drawing near. The valley around him is grand, with cedar, hemlock, and snow peaks, but Brooke feels he has drifted too far to turn back with ease.

Chapter titles trace offers, hard journeys, a flume builder, a claim jumped, and a bridge thrown across a canyon. Barbara tests Brooke more than once, and a late confession clears the way for pardon. Readers get a tale of debt, work, love, and a name restored in the Canadian woods.
37813-martyria-or-andersonville-prison:
Martyria; or, Andersonville Prison is an account of the great Confederate prison camp by Augustus Hamlin, late a medical inspector in the United States Army. Lee and Shepard published it in Boston in 1866, the year after the Civil War ended. Hamlin illustrated the book himself.

A frontispiece shows the view from the main gate, taken from rebel photographs of the prison when it contained thirty five thousand men. Hamlin inscribes the book to the memory of the men who steadily upheld the cause of civil liberty. They preferred lingering death, he writes, amid unparalleled privations and horrors, to dishonour and denial of their birthrights. In a note he disclaims any care for style or language. He offers simply the story of the wrong and the heroism, the cause and the effect, and he does not seek, he says, to rekindle the embers of hate.
37863-essex-terraplane-six-1933-owner-s-:
The Essex Terraplane Six nineteen hundred thirty three Owner’s Manual of Information served new owners of that car. The Hudson Motor Car Company of Detroit, Michigan printed the book in the United States. A warranty leads it. Faults found in ninety days or four thousand miles would be made good at the factory.

Breaking in a new engine gets the first care notes. Keep the radiator full and the oil tank full, it warns. Heat can rise fast in one part while the panel gauge looks calm. Oil notes cover the chassis, clutch, engine, and rear axle by part. Settings for brakes, spark plugs, and wheel bearings fill the back half. A wiring chart and full license data close the small guide.
37964-feminism-and-sex-extinction:
Arabella Kenealy wrote a blunt book gainst the women's cause of her day. Kenealy held a Dublin cure degree in her own name. Ads at its front hail Olive Schreiner's Woman and Labour. That book is called the cause's gospel in one press quote. Kenealy's own front verse warns of good trees and bad fruit.

Her case holds that the cause warps women's true bent. Sex loss in the race is her dire end claim for it. She writes as a cure voice with a firm, cold hand. Each part takes one plank of the cause and tests it hard. Foe and friend of that cause both read her with heat. The tone is stark.
3812-the-mirrors-of-washington:
This anonymous volume holds up mirrors to the men who ran Washington in the Harding years, with a biographical note for each subject. Warren Harding, the Ohio newspaper man turned president, and Woodrow Wilson, the Princeton president turned war president, open the gallery. Colonel House, Wilson's close adviser, receives a long and searching portrait, with his kindheartedness, credulity, and surrender to a stronger mind all weighed.

The book argues that House, talking to Wilson, was a weaker Wilson talking to the real one, and that Wilson reached the peace conference without a capable critical adviser. The portraits are frank, partisan, and gossipy by turns. Readers who like political character sketches will find a sharp contemporary view of power, written while its subjects were still in the news.
3814-robert-louis-stevenson:
E Blantyre Simpson wrote this short life of Robert Louis Stevenson for the Spirit of the Age series. That set of little books covers men and women whose work reflects the cultivated thought of the day. The chapters follow Stevenson's apprenticeship, his Edinburgh student days, his brief career as an advocate, and his life across the seas to Samoa. Illustrations show him as an advocate in 1875, an Edinburgh student, and a teller of tales.

Anecdotes give the flavor, as when Stevenson, lured to a dinner he claimed to hate, promised to appear with temples wreathed like a victim come smiling to the altar. Simpson aims at a living personality rather than a formal record. Readers who want a brief, humane introduction to Stevenson will find a pleasant volume, short enough for an evening.
38161-a-master-of-deception:
A Master of Deception, a novel by Richard Marsh, was printed by Cassell in London, New York, Toronto, and Melbourne in 1913, with a frontispiece by Dudley Tennant. Marsh also wrote Twin Sisters and The Lovely Blake. Chapter one, The Inclining of a Twig, shows where the deception starts: in childhood.

Rodney Elmore is eleven, forbidden by his mother to visit the coming circus. At tea in a neighbour's house he is sent to play in the garden, passes an open door, and spots two half crowns stacked on a mantelpiece. The desire for the circus gathers sudden force. He whips the coins into his knickerbockers pocket and spends the afternoon fearing discovery, not guilt. The contents follow him to an uncle and cousin, three girls and three telegrams, and a dead man's letter.
38179-household-education:
Household Education is Harriet Martineau's book on the raising and teaching of children, published in London by Edward Moxon in 1849. Part of it had already appeared in papers in the People's Journal before that journal changed hands. Martineau finished the design at the request of readers and signed her preface at Ambleside on the sixteenth of November 1848.

The chapters move from Old and Young in School and What the Schooling Is For to The New Comer and Care of the Frame. Later chapters treat the will, hope, fear, and patience. Martineau holds that the subject is too deep for anyone to lecture on it with full authority. Her counsel is to reflect, to say what one thinks, and to learn from one another.
38185-fruits-of-philosophy-a-treatise-on:
Fruits of Philosophy is a treatise on the population question by Charles Knowlton, a medical doctor. The hosted edition was edited by Charles Bradlaugh and Annie Besant. Its publishers' preface tells the pamphlet's long history in print. It had lately been prosecuted under an act of Lord Campbell, and is reissued to test the right of publication.

The preface traces the work back forty years in England, through radical publishers who sold it unchallenged. It was listed in a freethought directory of eighteen fifty three. Later freethought printers kept it in circulation. The preface argues from that long open sale that the work's standing was accepted. Knowlton's degree is cited as a claim to be heard on a medical question.
38206-a-boy-of-the-dominion-a-tale-of-ca:
A Boy of the Dominion is a tale of Canadian immigration by F S Brereton, published by Blackie and Son of London in 1913. William Rainey illustrated the book. The hero, Joe Bradley, leaves England to make his life in Canada, and the chapters follow the settler's road.

Finding a profession comes first, then the ocean voyage. Volunteers are called for, and Joe gathers credit. The backwoods test him: he is lost in the forest and fights hand to hand. Hard-earned dollars go into the farm. The Canadian winter, a co-operative proposition, and moose hunting fill the middle chapters. Hurley's conspiracy is unfolded, and the settlers stand on the defensive. A ride across the snows seeks safety. The story ends back at the farm. Brereton wrote many such tales to draw British boys toward the empire's open land.
38230-the-odes-of-anacreon:
The Odes of Anacreon appear here in Thomas Moore's translation, printed in London by John Camden Hotten with fifty-four designs by Girodet de Roussy, now first produced in England. A line of Horace stands at the head, promising that time has not destroyed what Anacreon once played. The introduction to the English edition explains why the pictures matter as much as the verse.

Among Anacreon's many translators, the editor argues, one Frenchman beat them all without words. Girodet, a painter of genius with a wholly Greek spirit, translated the odes better with his pencil than any poet could by language. His designs blend clean execution with rich character so closely that they seem drawn under the old singer's own eye.
3825-pygmalion:
Bernard Shaw wrote Pygmalion around Henry Higgins, a professor of phonetics who wagers he can pass a flower girl off as a duchess by teaching her to speak. The preface argues that England needs a phonetic reformer, since no Englishman can open his mouth without making another hate or despise him. Shaw recalls the phonetic pioneers Melville Bell and Alexander Ellis, with his velvet skull cap, as the real models behind Higgins.

The play itself follows Eliza Doolittle from Covent Garden to the embassy ball, with Colonel Pickering, Mrs Pearce, and her dustman father Alfred in support. A sequel in prose tells what happens after the curtain. Readers who know the musical version will enjoy meeting the sharper original, with Shaw's wit at full stretch.
38312-the-mansion:
The Mansion is a story by Henry Van Dyke, printed at New York in 1911 with illustrations by Elizabeth Shippen Green. It opens on the Weightman mansion, which has an air of calm and reserved opulence. The house speaks not of money squandered but of wealth prudently applied. It stands on a corner of the Avenue no longer fashionable for homes.

The house is not beautiful. Its straight front is chocolate-coloured stone, with heavy cornices, broad staring windows of plate glass, and carved mahogany doors. Yet it is respectable and, in its way, imposing. John Weightman, the owner, is like the house he built himself into thirty years ago. He is a self-made man who chose a highly esteemed pattern and worked by the approved rules. Nothing about him is irregular or questionable.
38329-the-romance-of-industry-and-invent:
The Romance of Industry and Invention is a popular book of industrial wonders, selected by Robert Cochrane. Cochrane also edited Great Thinkers and Workers and other gift books of the kind. A picture of the rush for the gold-fields fronts the volume. The book gathers tales of invention, manufacture, and adventure for general readers.

Books of this Victorian kind told how steam, steel, and telegraphs changed the world. They mixed short lives of inventors with accounts of mines, mills, and famous machines. The aim was to make industry read like romance, as the title promises. The volume stands as a sample of self-improvement reading for the age of machines.
38334-the-homilies-of-the-anglo-saxon-ch:
Benjamin Thorpe edited the homilies of Ælfric for the Ælfric Society in London in 1844. Volume one gives the Sermones Catholici in the original Anglo-Saxon, with an English version beside it. Thorpe prints the text with care for scribal abbreviations, marked by signs explained at the front.

Ælfric, a monk and teacher of the late tenth century, preached these sermons for feast days. His clear Old English prose taught scripture and doctrine to lay folk in their own tongue. Thorpe's edition, with page numbers keyed to the contents, helped Victorian scholars recover the voice of the Anglo-Saxon church.
38444-a-discourse-being-introductory-to-:
Thomas Sheridan wrote this discourse opening his lectures on elocution. The Clark Library reprinted the 1759 work at Los Angeles in 1969. Mohrmann wrote an introduction for the Augustan Reprint Society issue. It stands as publication number 136 in that reprint series.

Notes cite Bacon study of Sheridan elocutionary career in print. Watkins memoirs of his son, the playwright Sheridan, stand cited too. Sheridan lectures treated elocution and the English language together here. Editors at California universities oversaw the reprint series work jointly. The Clark Memorial Library at Los Angeles houses the reprint series in its home.
38468-the-nibelungenlied-revised-edition:
The Nibelungenlied, in English by William Lettsom, is here in a revised edition published in New York, copyrighted in 1901. A special opening essay is by William Carpenter, teacher of Germanic language study at Columbia University. Carpenter calls the poem the great national epic of Germany.

He ranks it among the most weighty works of mind that Germany has made in any age. More than that, he calls it one of the world great classics. Its story, he says, can be grasped by all, and its folk stir broad human sympathy. Like the Iliad, it is first a picture of national life and the national soul. Readers get the old German epic of heroes, in verse, with a guide to why it still matters.
38523-the-noank-s-log-a-privateer-of-the:
Stoddard wrote this sea tale of the American Revolution for Lothrop of Boston in 1900. Will Crawford drew the plates for The Noank's Log. The Noank sails as a privateer, a licensed raider on British trade.

Stoddard's preface fights a myth. The last half of 1776 and all of 1777 are called the dark hour of the war, he notes. On land, raw armies had lost hard fights; that much is true. But at sea, he says, the American tale was one of bright success. By early 1778 a London alderman told the Lords that American cruisers had taken seven hundred British ships and more. The log of one such ship gives the war from the deck.
38566-the-roman-poets-of-the-republic-3r:
The Roman Poets of the Republic is a history of early Latin poetry by Sellar, professor of humanity at the University of Edinburgh. This text is the re-issue of the third edition, printed at Oxford in 1905. Sellar kept his first five chapters much as they stood, the preface says. Two chapters on Roman comedy are wholly new.

He enlarged the account of Lucilius, the father of Roman satire. The book covers the poets from the first Latin verse through the age of Lucretius and Catullus. It treats epic, drama, and satire as they grew under the republic. For generations it was the standard English work on its subject, read by every student of Latin letters.
38608-the-girl-scouts-at-rocky-ledge-or-:
Lilian Garis wrote a Girl Scout novel copyrighted in 1922, subtitled Nora's real vacation. Garis had written the Girl Scout Pioneers and the girls at Bellaire, Sea Crest, and Camp Comalong. The book opens with a girl asking to call a smiling woman Jim. She has always wanted a man named Jim to protect her, she explains.

She also praises Aunt Elizabeths as lacy and cameo like. Chapters name an attic, a broken dream, and a transplanting. A prince in hiding and a waif of the wildwoods add mystery. Strange disclosures and a danger squad in action come late. Fulfillment closes the contents list. Rocky Ledge gives the troop a woodland setting.
38612-city-scenes-or-a-peep-into-london:
Verse captions walk a child through the sights of London in a small book issued there in 1828. An introduction in rhyme invites the reader to view the things of most renown while sitting in a chair at home. Great St Paul's, the tall Monument, and the giants in Guildhall head the promised wonders.

The first scene brings Farmer Clodpole by stage coach to his first view of the city, smoke and all. The Monument scene retells the great fire that began in Pudding Lane and burned thirteen thousand two hundred houses. Post-boys, wharves, boatmen, knife-grinders, and beggars fill the later plates. Young readers get the capital as a picture gallery, with each wonder explained in plain, cheerful terms.
38646-the-eldest-son:
The Eldest Son, a novel by Archibald Marshall, was copyright in 1911 and reissued at New York in 1919. Marshall was known for Exton Manor. Chapter one finds the Squire at tea after a day of hunting, telling his wife Nina that he is most worried.

Thirty chapters move through a country house world of hunts, balls, and shoots. Names in the contents point to a match for Dick, the son, and to a hard money question. Miss Bird goes, a governess is picked, and Aunt Laura steps in. A late chapter is called An Engagement. Readers get a calm, wry tale of a squire, his heir, and the price of keeping a great house.
38716-slavery-and-the-constitution:
William Bowditch's Slavery and the Constitution was printed at Boston in 1849 by Wallcut of Cornhill. Bowditch opens by quoting the other side: a college president and a New Orleans minister who call slavery God's own ordinance. Against them he sets a plain fact: nearly three millions of men, women, and children held in slavery in the Southern States.

The chapters walk the ground in order: the teaching of slaves, their moral state, their lack of legal marriage, the soul-driving trade, and the domestic slave trade. Runaway slaves follow, then the flat claim that slaveholding is always wrong. The last chapters test the Constitution four ways, by its plain terms, its framers' intent, the government's practice, and its final interpreter, and end with no union with slaveholders.
38731-railroad-accidents-their-cause-and:
Railroad Accidents: Their Cause and Prevention, by Richards, was published in 1906 by the Association of Railway Claim Agents. Richards writes from inside the claims business, where every wreck arrived as files, injuries, and bills. He opens with the rising toll of American railroad accidents and the public demand for answers.

His argument is practical. The nearer the railroads come to doing their full duty, the fewer losses and damage claims they will pay. Care, he insists, serves the companies, the workers, and the families spared suffering in equal measure. The book addresses managers, employees, and officials at once. It is a period document of the safety movement, when the railroads first faced their accident record in print.
38801-the-works-of-robert-g-ingersoll-vo:
Volume one of the Dresden edition of Robert Ingersoll's works gathers his lectures, printed in 1901. The volume is dedicated to his wife, Eva Ingersoll, praised as a woman without superstition, and opens with the motto that the destroyer of weeds is a benefactor.

The contents list The Gods, from 1872, ranging over the making of deities, the priesthood, miracles, slavery, and the cemetery of the gods. A lecture on Humboldt follows, then one on Thomas Paine, of whom Ingersoll says the history of liberty cannot be written with his name left out. Readers get the famous orator's case for reason, in his own platform voice.
38802-the-works-of-robert-g-ingersoll-vo:
Volume two of The Works of Robert Ingersoll appeared in the Dresden edition of 1900. The set runs to twelve volumes of lectures and writings. This volume is dedicated to Sue Farrell, the author's sister-in-law and friend. Its motto taunts the clergy with knowing that they do not know.

The chief piece is Some Mistakes of Moses, a lecture from 1879. Ingersoll argues that force over the mind makes tyrants and slaves. He defends free schools and attacks sectarian teaching. He holds that Moses did not write the Pentateuch. Egypt, he says, supplied much of its lore. The lecture then walks through the days of creation in order. Each day's account is tested against science and common sense. Babylon, Egypt, and India, he notes, tell much the same story.
38803-the-works-of-robert-g-ingersoll-vo:
Robert Ingersoll's works fill twelve books in the Dresden form of 1900. Volume three holds his lectures. Ingersoll was famed for bold speech on faith and free thought. A quote at the front praises the storm of thought over calm faith. He asks to eat of the tree of knowledge first.

The lead piece is a long talk on Shakespeare from 1891. Ingersoll praises his brain and heart and mocks the Bacon claim. He deals with the stage in Shakespeare's day and his use of old tales. Talks on more themes fill the rest. Fans get his rich voice at full length.
38804-the-works-of-robert-g-ingersoll-vo:
Volume four of the Dresden edition of the works of Robert G. Ingersoll appeared in nineteen hundred, gathering lectures and essays from the eighteen nineties. Ingersoll was a famed public speaker who defended free thought and doubted church doctrine. The lead piece, Why I Am an Agnostic, dates from eighteen ninety-six.

Readers find his case that faith is often shaped by birth and place, not by proof. He tests claims about God, sacred books, and design against science and the work of Darwin and others. Later pieces take up truth, honest thought, and how to reform mankind. One plan cuts waste on war and churches, treats prisons as schools, and urges homes for all.
38805-the-works-of-robert-g-ingersoll-vo:
The fifth volume of the Dresden Edition of Ingersoll's works, issued in 1900, is given to discussions. Its motto stands on the title leaf: there can be but little liberty on earth while men worship a tyrant in heaven. The whole volume is the Six Interviews on Talmage of 1882, Ingersoll's newspaper duel with the Brooklyn preacher. Talmage had attacked the infidel colonel; Ingersoll answered him in detail, with jokes.

The contents read like a bout card. Ingersoll denies that great men's names prove the Gospel, and asks whether unbelief fills the penitentiaries. He takes up the Deluge and the Ark, the stopping of the sun for Joshua, and the whale and Jonah. He answers charges about Garfield's assassin and about his father. Woman's condition under the Bible, and the church's debt for schools and hospitals, are fought over. It is journalism at full stretch, preserved as literature.
38806-the-works-of-robert-g-ingersoll-vo:
This file holds volume six of the works of Robert Ingersoll, the Dresden edition of 1900, in twelve volumes. Ingersoll was America's most famous lecturer against orthodox religion, and this volume is given to discussions: his printed debates on the Christian religion. A motto stands at the front. Arguments cannot be answered with insults; kindness is strength, and anger blows out the lamp of the mind.

The first discussion opens with Ingersoll's statement of the case. He gives reasons for thinking parts of the Old Testament the product of a barbarous people. Passages upholding slavery, polygamy, war, and persecution, he argues, are no evidences of inspiration. Judge Black's reply follows, and the exchange runs on through the New Testament, the atonement, and eternal punishment.
38807-the-works-of-robert-g-ingersoll-vo:
The hosted text is the seventh volume of the works of Robert Ingersoll, the great American lecturer against the creeds. It belongs to the Dresden edition of 1900, in twelve volumes. This volume is headed Discussions. A line at the front says that every brain is a field where nature sows the seeds of thought.

The chief piece is called My Reviewers Reviewed, from 1877. In it Ingersoll answers the clergymen who had attacked him, town by town. The contents run over the whole field of fight. Liberty of mind, the equality of woman, slavery, and witchcraft all come up. He asks whether the Bible teaches men to enslave their brothers. He takes up its geology and its astronomy, the death-beds of Voltaire and Paine, and the slaughter of the Canaanites. The volume is a storehouse of his platform wars.
38808-the-works-of-robert-g-ingersoll-vo:
The Works of Robert Ingersoll, in its eighth volume, gathers the interviews of the famous orator. This Dresden Edition of his works runs to twelve volumes. The volume itself appeared in 1900. A creed of the author stands as motto over the whole set of books.

Happiness is the only good, that motto declares in ringing terms. Reason is the only torch, justice the only worship, it continues. Humanity is the only religion, and love the only priest, it concludes. The interviews open with questions on the Bible and a future life. Ingersoll classes the Bible with most other ancient books in his answer. Some truth, much error, and considerable barbarism meet in it, he says. His own views rest on reason, observation, and the discoveries of science.
38809-the-works-of-robert-g-ingersoll-vo:
Volume 9 of The Works of Robert G. Ingersoll is the political volume of that twelve-volume set. It came out in New York from the Dresden Publishing Company, C. P. Farrell, as the Dresden Edition. A motto stands on the title page: he loves his country best who strives to make it best. The contents open with an address to the colored people, dated 1867.

The heads under that address trace its scope. Slavery and its defense by law and religion stand first, with its ruinous sway on nations. The start of the modern slave trade by the Portuguese, and its planting on American soil, stand in the heads. The abolitionists are named: Clarkson, Wilberforce, Garrison, Phillips, Sumner, and John Brown. The Fugitive Slave Law and the Emancipation Proclamation stand there too.
38810-the-works-of-robert-g-ingersoll-vo:
Robert Ingersoll fills volume ten of his Works, in the twelve-volume Dresden edition. This volume is the legal one of the set, the title page says. A motto runs: justice should remove the bandage from her eyes. She should distinguish between the vicious and the unfortunate, it adds. Contents open with his address to the jury in the Munn trial.

Demoralization by alcohol, testimony, and perjury fill that address. Suspicion is not evidence, one head in the contents insists. His closing address in the first Star Route trial follows at length. Duties of jurors and lawyers, overt acts, and false claim routes fill it. Evidence against the Dorseys and the law of conspiracy take long sections. Ingersoll the lawyer stands here beside Ingersoll the lecturer. The volume gives courtroom oratory from the great agnostic at his trade.
38811-the-works-of-robert-g-ingersoll-vo:
Volume eleven of the Works of Robert Ingersoll, in the twelve volume Dresden edition of 1900, is given over to miscellany. Ingersoll, the great American lecturer for free thought, here speaks on law, faith, and punishment. The volume opens with his address on the Civil Rights Act, arguing that the government of the United States is secular and that no god belongs in the Constitution.

A reply to Bishop Spalding presses the same case: the founders left religion out of the frame of government on purpose. Crimes Against Criminals then attacks cruel punishment, urging kindness, pay for convicts, and doubt where knowledge fails, and asking whether the nation should take life at all. A Wooden God contrasts Christian worship with Chinese rites and scores injustice done in God's name. The speeches show his platform manner at full stretch.
38812-the-works-of-robert-g-ingersoll-vo:
Robert G Ingersoll works fill twelve volumes in the Dresden edition of nineteen hundred, and the hosted text is volume twelve, Miscellany. Ingersoll creed heads the set, that happiness is the only good, the place to be happy is here, the time is now, and the way is to help make others so. David Widger prepared the text for Gutenberg. The volume gathers late pieces and reviews.

A first piece treats Professor Van Buren Denslow book, Modern Thinkers. Ingersoll praises workers who divide gold from dross in volume after volume with infinite patience. Such men are like bees who save us journeys, he says. Yet some readers may lose happiness to learn Swedenborg was really insane, he warns. Swedenborg changed realities into dreams, then built facts from the dreams, Ingersoll holds. Freethought readers get Ingersoll wit and candour on thinkers, faith, and books.
38818-miss-ellis-s-mission:
Mary Smith wrote Miss Ellis's Mission, published by the American Unitarian Association at Boston in 1886. The little book is a memorial. After Miss Ellis's death, a Chicago minister suggested gathering her story with extracts from her letters, written and received, as a guide for post-office mission workers. The dedication addresses those workers, west and east, and earnest people everywhere.

The post-office mission was a Unitarian scheme of the time. Workers mailed sermons, books, and friendly letters to people far from any church of their faith. Miss Ellis gave her life to that quiet correspondence. The preface borrows a passage from a sister book, Miss Toosey's Mission. Her offering, it says, was a barley loaf beside the fine wheaten cake of youth and riches. Yet she offered her best freely, and faith counts no such offering wasted. The book preserves a small, devoted life of religious work by post.
38855-the-iron-furnace-or-slavery-and-se:
John Aughey, a clergyman and a refugee from Mississippi, wrote his war record for Martien of Philadelphia in 1863. The title comes from Jeremiah, who spoke of a people brought out of Egypt, from the iron furnace. Aughey says the book was written while he suffered much from the rigours of that furnace of secession.

Its heat, he holds, is sevenfold for the loyal men of the South. Many such men hide their views to escape death, and are to be pitied, not blamed. Ministers of worth fought secession till their states passed the ordinance. Then they urged a rebuilding of the Union while it was safe, and then fell silent, waiting on God in prayer. Aughey asks that the book's faults be excused on that ground. His aim, he says, is to serve his country and his age, whatever becomes of his name.
38887-how-to-write-a-novel-a-practical-g: A hands-on guide to the craft of fiction forms one part of a how-to set of short books. Mate books in the set treat work with a banker and meals in Paris. One more mate book treats how to write for magazines. Plain use, not high theory, is the pitch of the set. Clear steps and sound rules of thumb are the tools it trusts.
38998-solomon:
Solomon is a novel by Constance Fenimore Woolson set in Ohio coal country. James Neish and Sons of Odessa, Ontario, issued the book. The tale opens midway in the eastern part of Ohio state. Round topped hills there rise from the level plain toward Pennsylvania.

Those hills hold coal, and the folk care for them as fuel stores. Roads run along slow streams, and farmers ride in broad wheeled wagons. Dark mine holes in the banks send out small carts to daylight. Men with lamps in their hat bands walk behind those carts. Canal boats and coal cars leave full, and mill money flows back.
39029-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
One slice of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica is gathered in this volume. It covers the alphabet from Horticulture to Hudson Bay. The eleventh edition, published in nineteen ten and nineteen eleven, was the last great general encyclopaedia of its kind. Named specialists wrote its articles, and it filled twenty nine volumes.

The slice opens with horticulture and runs through hundreds of entries. They include the Howards and the Howes, hospital and hospice, hosiery, and the prophet Hosea. The town of Howrah, the howitzer, and Hudson Bay itself close the run. Short notices stand beside long treatises. The transcribers' notes record the care taken over subscripts, Greek letters, and small corrections to the print. Read today, the slice shows both the reach of Edwardian knowledge and its limits.
39080-my-mother-s-gold-ring-founded-on-f:
My Mother's Gold Ring is a temperance tale issued at Boston by Ford and Damrell in 1833. It is billed as founded on fact, and this printing is the eighth edition. The book is Number One of a projected series of stories. Its motto of purpose stands in the preface: the writer begs the reader to pass the copy on when done.

The preface makes the tract's strategy plain. Read Number One, the writer urges: it can do you no harm, and there is nothing sectarian about it. Let it take the course of the flying seed, which God entrusts to the winds. The tale itself, The Gold Ring, is told by a carpenter's wife who calls her husband one of the kindest in the county. It is an early American temperance story, built to travel hand to hand.
39309-a-day-at-a-time-and-other-talks-on:
A Day at a Time and Other Talks on Life and Religion, by the Reverend Arch Alexander, reached a second edition with H R Allenson at London. The book was written in war-time to minister comfort and reinforce hope and faith, and is dedicated by permission to Sir John R Jellicoe, admiral of the Grand Fleet.

Thirty talks follow the title piece: God in the Wheels, Finical Farming, The Real Martha, and A Khaki Virtue among them. The Overcoming of Panic, The God of the Unlovable Man, and The Sacrament of Sunset close the list of subjects.
39511-the-psychological-origin-and-the-n:
Professor Leuba wrote this study of where religion comes from in the human mind and what its nature is. It belongs to the series Religions Ancient and Modern, a set of short books by named scholars. Other volumes in the list treat animism, pantheism, Islam, Hinduism, Judaism, and the faiths of ancient China, Greece, Egypt, and Rome.

A series built that way puts Leuba's question in a wide frame. Rather than telling the story of one faith, his title points to the shared roots of belief in human thought and feeling. Readers who work through the series get each religion in its own volume, and then a study that asks why people hold religious belief at all.
39525-aspects-of-modern-oxford-by-a-mere:
A D Godley, signing himself A Mere Don, wrote a light look at modern Oxford, printed in London in 1894. Drawings by four artists show Cornmarket Street, college rooms, cricket in the parks, and boats on the river. Eight chapters make up the book, each named for a side of town and gown life.

First come dons and colleges, then the young men who study under them, then sightseers who come to stare. Tests, college papers, and how the place looks from outside fill the middle chapters. A diary of a don and a closing piece on Oxford as a place of learned ease round out the survey.
39538-a-soldier-s-son:
Maude Butler's Soldier's Son was published by Davis and Bond at Boston in 1912. The dedication addresses the children in years and the children in science. A note from the author states a rule of the book: no case of Christian Science healing is cited without a parallel case known to her in real life. The war is over as chapter one opens, and Father and Uncle Howard are coming home.

Uncle Howard, the mother's twin brother, was seriously wounded saving the guns and carrying a wounded soldier out of the line. His motherless boy Carol waits at home. The contents promise a forbidden book, a welcome letter, and first work in the vineyard. A physician's verdict and a rector's refusal precede the chapter titled It Is a Miracle. Letters and telegrams reach Cousin Alicia; joyful news comes from Eloise.
39643-the-bungalow-boys-along-the-yukon:
The Bungalow Boys Along the Yukon, a boys adventure tale by Dexter J Forrester, was copyrighted in 1913 by Hurst and Company of New York. Four pictures by Charles L Wrenn go with the text. Forrester wrote a line of Bungalow Boys books, set in the tropics, on the Great Lakes, and in the great north west.

The tale opens at Seattle, where Tom Jessop, a young reporter for the Post-Intelligencer, spots a mysterious craft at the Spring Street dock. Northward ho follows, with a mid ocean hunting trip and a libation to a totem. Sandy finds a mascot and swims for his life. The great bears of Kadiak, a tidal bore, and life on an island fill the middle. A dead man's mine and a sentence to the mines close the Yukon run.
39673-a-year-in-a-lancashire-garden-seco:
Henry Bright keeps a garden diary in A Year in a Lancashire Garden, second edition, printed in London in 1879. Macmillan made the book. The notes first ran month by month in 1874, in the columns of the Gardeners' Chronicle, at the editor's request.

His preface is modest to a fault. The volume pretends to little technical knowledge, he says, and is of little worth to the skilled. It holds only a slight record of a year's work in a garden. It also holds those associations which a garden is so certain to call up, he adds. He first printed some fifty copies for friends. Four years on, calls for copies still came that he could not fill, so the book went to press.
39714-d-c-powered-timing-light-model-161:
Sears issued this owner's manual for its direct current powered timing light, model 161.2158, for use on 12 volt ignition systems. The tool helps set engine timing to the maker's stated values. The manual warns that dwell angle affects timing. So a dwell meter should be used first, before the light. It also tells the user to check the vehicle manual for exact figures.

Early pages give rules for safe work. Set the brake, work in fresh air, and keep clear of fan blades and hot parts. Do not look straight at the lens while the light runs. Later steps cover cleaning the timing marks, setting idle speed, and hooking up the light. It is a plain shop guide for home mechanics.
39734-the-life-of-philip-melanchthon:
The Life of Philip Melanchthon, by Charles Frederick Ledderhose, was published at Philadelphia by Lindsay and Blakiston in 1855, in Krotel's translation from the German. A printer's notice confesses that pages 56 to 60 were bound out of order in the whole edition. Ledderhose opens his preface by granting Luther the first place among the Reformers, unrivalled and apostolical.

Yet gratitude, he argues, must not let the prince hide the other men of God of that age. Among them Melanchthon stands highest, called in his own day the Teacher of the German people for his sway over the learning and Christian culture of Germany. The life follows that double work, in the schools and in the church. English readers got it from the Lutheran publishing trade of the 1850s.
39875-highways-and-byways-in-london:
Highways and Byways in London is a guide by Mrs Cook, issued by Macmillan. Hugh Thomson and Griggs drew its many pictures. The first edition came out in 1902. Reprints ran through 1920. Eighteen chapters roam the whole city. The river is treated first, then rambles in the City. Saint Paul's and the Tower follow in order.

Southwark, old and new, and the Inns of Court come next. Westminster, Kensington, and Bloomsbury fill the middle. Theatres, shops, and markets get their chapters. Galleries and museums are surveyed with care. Historic houses and their tenants add the human note. The stones of London close the tour. Cook writes as a lover of the town. Her book is a companion for long walks.
39897-discoveries-among-the-ruins-of-nin:
Austen Layard's Discoveries among the Ruins of Nineveh and Babylon appears here in an abridged edition. Putnam published it in New York in 1853, after Layard's first book, Nineveh and Its Remains. The work reports his second expedition, undertaken for the trustees of the British Museum, with travels in Armenia, Kurdistan and the desert.

The abridgment keeps Layard's own language for the most interesting parts. It drops most cuneiform tables and minute details of sculpture, and keeps everything bearing on the Bible and prophecy. Layard's preface credits Rawlinson and Hincks for progress in reading the inscriptions. A frontispiece restores the grand entrance of Sennacherib's palace at Kouyunjik.
39932-the-lure-of-old-london:
Sophie Cole's The Lure of Old London was published by Mills and Boon at London in 1921, with eight illustrations. Cole also wrote A London Posy and The Loitering Highway, and the dedication thanks the friend who wandered with her in the footsteps of George and Mrs Darling. The photographs show the wax effigies of Queen Elizabeth and Charles the Second, Great Saint Helen's, the Charterhouse, old Smithfield, Doctor Johnson's house in Gough Square, and Carlyle's house in Cheyne Row.

Chapter one introduces the Honourable George Tallenach, sixty-five, ploughed at Oxford and settled into poetic loafing. His sister the Countess of Corbridge sends his quarterly fifty pounds addressed to Carrington Mansions, Mayfair. George actually lives in Carrington Mews, in a workman's flat, tended by Mrs Darling below stairs. The book wanders London through his kindly, gossiping eyes.
39966-curiosities-of-christian-history-p:
Croake James wrote Curiosities of Christian History Prior to the Reformation, issued by Methuen and Company in London in eighteen ninety two. James had earlier written Curiosities of Law and Lawyers. A preface states the difficulty. History is often a dreary study except to a few experts, he says. Yet Christians of today wish to know more about their predecessors, he adds.

From the time of Christ to the Reformation there were no Dissenters, only heretics deemed unworthy to live, James notes. But the Christian temperament can be traced through all the centuries, he holds. Martyrs and hermits, monks and nuns, friars, pilgrims and crusaders share the pages. The same aspirations, misgivings, and trials existed then as now, he says. Church readers get lively sketches of the pre Reformation centuries.
39999-the-great-acceptance-the-life-stor:
Guy Thorne wrote the life tale of Charrington, a friend of the poor. The book was printed in 1913 in its sixth form. Thorne wrote When It Was Dark and The Drunkard. Thirteen plates aid the life. The book is given to the poor of the East End of London.

Charrington gave his years to work among those poor folk. A front plate shows him from a pencil sketch with his own hand's mark. Thorne calls the tale the great acceptance, a faith name. A Bible verse at the front praises the just man's bold stand. Faith readers get a warm life of work for the low.
4003-androcles-and-the-lion:
Bernard Shaw's play retells the old tale of Androcles, a runaway slave who pulls a thorn from a lion's paw and later meets the same lion in the arena. Shaw sets the story among early Christians facing the lions in Rome, with a captain, Lavinia, and other prisoners arguing about courage.

Lavinia insists that a woman must be braver than a soldier, and the captain answers that what she calls courage is pride. Shaw turns the fable into witty debate about faith, pride, and mercy, with the lion's gratitude upsetting the arena's grim plan. The play mixes comedy and argument, and it suits readers who enjoy Shaw's sharp talk on stage.
40046-the-dispatch-carrier-and-memoirs-o:
The Dispatch Carrier and Memoirs of Andersonville Prison, a war memoir by William N Tyler, was printed at Port Byron, Illinois, in 1892 and sold for twenty five cents. Tyler served in the Ninth Illinois Cavalry and the Ninety-Fifth Illinois Volunteer Infantry. His preface states plainly that he kept no diary, so some dates may err, but that all he tells is strictly true.

The narrative covers his service from 1861 to 1865. He describes work as a dispatch carrier, then capture, prison, escape, and recapture. A chase by bloodhounds stands among its episodes. Andersonville, the most feared of Southern prisons, gives the book its weight. Comrades names are left out, since they were scattered and could not grant leave.
40072-nooks-and-corners-of-old-london:
Charles and Marie Hemstreet wrote Nooks and Corners of Old London for James Pott of New York, copyrighted in 1910, with special illustrations by Roberts. The pair had already done the same service for old New York.

The opening walk stays within sound of Bow Bells: a Wren church in Walbrook hidden behind the Mansion House, the gilded grasshopper, eleven feet long, on the Royal Exchange. It ends at Poultry, named for the poulterers' market once held there. Later chapters visit Milton's birthplace and Lamb's workshop, the Tower and London Bridge, the Temple and Inns of Court, and the Strand with its coffee houses. A final walk runs from Regent Street into Soho. The book collects street names, signs, and survivals that a passer-by would miss.
40106-loimologia-or-an-historical-accoun:
Loimologia is a past count of the plague in London by Nathaniel Hodges. He dwelt in the city through all that sick time of sixteen sixty five. A Bell and Osborn print of seventeen twenty pairs his count with more. John Quincy adds a piece on what makes such ills catch and spread. That add piece treats the sick in France and means to bar its road here.

Hodges count is the best yet writ of that late visit, the front word holds. Its old tongued style may dim its sense for some who read it now. Weights of the cure shop stand in a key at the front of the text. Dram, ounce, and scrap counts fix the dose marks in its cure lists. Guard rules gainst the like curse fill the aim of the whole book.
40130-a-day-with-john-milton:
A Day with John Milton, by May Byron, belongs to the Hodder and Stoughton series that spends an imagined day with a great writer. Byron, Burns, Shelley, Scott, and Shakespeare stand among the other volumes. Colour plates go with the text, one showing the close of Paradise Lost, the pair leaving Eden hand in hand.

The day is set in September 1665. Milton wakes near four in his house by the Artillery Fields in London. He is stone blind in both eyes, and his hands are crippled with gout. His manservant Greene helps him dress in black. Led into his small study, hung with rusty green, he takes his seat in an old elbow chair for the morning's dictation. The book builds a life of the poet out of one such day.
40186-baraboo-dells-and-devil-s-lake-reg:
Cole of Baraboo, Wisconsin wrote a guide to the Baraboo, Dells, and Devil's Lake region, published by the Baraboo News Publishing Company in 1920. The book has maps and illustrations, and an index of short trips. It covers the scenic country of Sauk County, long a resort ground in the upper Midwest.

The first chapter tells how Baraboo got its name from Jean Baribault, a French trader, the spelling corrupted over time. It also marks where the Ringling brothers first pitched a circus tent. Chapters follow on Devil's Lake, the Wisconsin River Dells, a deserted village, and Mirror Lake. Indian earthworks, the stone pillar of Chief Yellow Thunder, and the boyhood homes of John Muir enter the tour. Spring Green and Taliesin close the list of trips.
40190-science-and-practice-in-farm-culti:
Science and Practice in Farm Cultivation is a farming manual by James Buckman. Buckman had taught earth science and farm economy at the Royal Agricultural College.
