Hardwicke published the book at London in 1865. He dedicates the work to the editor of the Agricultural Gazette, whose journal first carried many of its facts.

The contents fall into parts on root crops and grasses. Early chapters trace the origin of root sorts and warn how roots run wild and spoil. Two chapters expose the tricks of turnip seed cheating, a trade fraud of the day. Later parts turn to growing good grasses. Buckman writes as both a man of science and a working teacher of farmers. The book aims to join laboratory knowledge to field practice.
40274-maps-of-old-london:
Maps of Old London was published by Adam and Charles Black in 1908. The volume reproduces nine early maps and views of the city, each with a short account of its maker, its date, and where the original survives. The series begins with the panorama of Antony van den Wyngaerde, the earliest representation of London that has come down to modern times.

Strictly, the editors admit, Wyngaerde's work is a picture, not a map. Yet it is wonderfully accurate, and full of architectural detail no true map could give. The Fleming may have come to England in the train of Philip of Spain. His drawing, dated between 1543 and 1550, runs ten feet long in the original at the Bodleian Library. Later plates give the Agas map, Norden's London and Westminster, Faithorne, Ogilby, and Rocque. The book lets readers watch London grow across two centuries of cartography.
40290-the-testimony-of-tradition:
David MacRitchie argued a case from folklore in a book issued at London in 1890, with twenty illustrations. Much of it had run as articles in a review of archaeology across 1889 and 1890, here altered and much enlarged. A frontispiece shows the great mound of New Grange in County Meath, seen from the south.

MacRitchie grants that readers may differ over his deductions, and names a learned critic, Alfred Nutt, who had already dissented. His theory, he claims, has one rare advantage: a tangible test of its worth. Future digs, he wagers, will confirm tradition, and beliefs, not tradition, will then have to change. The testimony of old tales is his witness throughout.
40322-modern-illustration:
Joseph Pennell wrote Modern Illustration for the Ex-Libris Series, edited by Gleeson White. George Bell and Sons issued the book in London and New York in eighteen hundred ninety five. Pennell had written on pen drawing and its masters. A Fred Walker drawing faces the title page.

The first chapter surveys the art of the day as a whole. Next comes how new block and press ways grew up. French work gets a chapter of its own praise. German, Spanish, and other lands share the next part. English work then takes the stage at length. American work closes the survey of lands. Prints from the Daily Chronicle and Century Magazine show the new styles in black and white.
40334-birds-in-london:
W H Hudson wrote Birds in London, a study of wild birds that live in a great town. Longmans, Green, and Company issued the book in eighteen hundred ninety eight. Bryan Hook and A D McCormick drew pictures for it. R B Lodge took photos from life to add proof.

Hudson says he did not set out to write a full hand list. He notes how the town bird stock has changed over time. The house sparrow fills the first chapter, begging bread in Hyde Park. Crows, rooks, and jackdaws get long, fond study next. Keepers in the royal parks shoot crows, he notes with heat. Wood pigeons and moorhens close the roll of new town guests.
4043-the-dynasts-an-epic-drama-of-the-wa:
Thomas Hardy's vast drama in verse covers the Napoleonic wars, from palace gates to battlefields, with crowds of citizens and soldiers as its chorus. Spirits watch over the action: the Spirit of the Years sends the Spirit of Rumour down to join the crowd and speak what comes into its mouth.

The Spirit Sinister will not miss another Austerlitz, and a young foreigner in disguise carries rumor into the streets. Hardy mixes history, philosophy, and stage spectacle on a grand scale. Readers who like epic drama will find a huge, strange work, part play and part poem, about nations, fate, and the men who steer them.
40442-a-day-with-the-poet-tennyson:
A Day with the Poet Tennyson invites readers into the poet's home for one day. Hodder and Stoughton published it in London. The book belongs to a series of like volumes. Sister books treat Longfellow, Keats, and Browning. Burns, Scott, Byron, and Shelley appear in the series too.

The opening quotes The Brook in full voice. Paintings by Haslehust show the brook and the house. The text then describes Farringford on the Isle of Wight. Tennyson shunned London society, the writer says. Yet he welcomed kindred spirits with cordiality. The house stood secluded among trees above Freshwater. The poet's wife and the poet himself crown the picture. A set routine governed his working day.
40445-the-life-of-john-marshall-volume-3:
Albert Beveridge wrote The Life of John Marshall, volume three, Conflict and Construction, 1800 to 1815, printed at Boston in 1919 from a portrait by Chester Harding. Contents open on a national capital described as an unsightly village in the woods, with danger in its streets. Warring interests made Washington a miniature of the whole country.

The Republican victory of 1800 brought anger and despair to Federalists and a programme of demolition against the judiciary. Jefferson feared and hated the national courts, whose partisanship gave him his opening, Beveridge argues in detail. Sedition trials of Lyon, Cooper, Fries, and Callender made the judiciary unpopular with the people. Marshall begins to strengthen the Supreme Court.
40479-in-the-foreign-legion:
Erwin Rosen's In the Foreign Legion was published by Duckworth at London in 1910. The prologue tells his story in the third person before owning it. A German student found life too joyous for professors, shipped to America, and knocked about: farm hand in Texas, translator in Saint Louis, war correspondent in Cuba. Back in Germany he succeeded as journalist and novelist, then lost the woman he was to marry and his hold on respectable life.

In despair he remembered the blood of adventure in his veins and enlisted in the French Foreign Legion, burning his boats so that those who loved him should think him dead. Five years in the uniform seemed five hundred, he says, of marching, hardship, and shameful treatment. A letter one day brought the great change. The memoir is a German's inside account of the Legion in Algeria.
40498-curiosities-of-civilization:
Andrew Wynter gathered essays on the odd corners of modern life. Robert Hardwicke issued Curiosities of Civilization in London in a seventh form. The essays first ran in the Quarterly and Edinburgh Reviews. A note dated August 1860 at Coleherne Court fronts the set.

Old advertisements open the book as a thread through past ages, Wynter writes. Food frauds, rats, lunatic asylums, shipwrecks, and the electric telegraph follow. Police and thieves, fires and insurance, and deaths by trade fill the range. Readers gain a doctor's sharp, curious tour of Victorian life.
40535-they-who-knock-at-our-gates-a-comp:
They Who Knock at Our Gates: A Complete Gospel of Immigration, by Mary Antin, was published in Boston and New York in 1914, with illustrations by Joseph Stella. Antin other book listed is The Promised Land. A frontispiece is captioned the sinew and bone of all the nations.

Contents are short: an introduction, then the law of the fathers, judges in the gate, and the fiery furnace. Pictures show rough work and low wages for the immigrant, an East Side mother, and a fresh infusion of pioneer blood. Antin writes as an immigrant herself, and the title states her case plainly. America gates, in her gospel, should open to those who knock. Biblical language frames a political argument: law, judgment, and trial by fire. Readers get a famous 1914 plea for open immigration, in three parts.
40589-a-brief-history-of-wood-engraving-:
A Brief History of Wood Engraving from Its Invention, by Joseph Cundall, was printed in London by Sampson Low, Marston, and Company in 1895. Cundall wrote Holbein and His Works. A plate from Holinshed Chronicles of 1577 shows Henry the Eighth in council.

The first chapter treats pictures of saints. It names the print of the Virgin with the Holy Child in her lap, held at the royal library in Belgium. The print of St Christopher in the Spencer Library at Manchester stands with it. The Annunciation and the St Christopher prints open the craft tale. Later chapters treat block books, the Speculum Humanae Salvationis, and the Mentz Psalter of 1459. The Cologne Bible and the Nurnberg Chronicle close the early run. Art fans get the woodcut story from saints prints to fine books.
40591-alexander-hamilton:
Alexander Hamilton, by Charles A Conant, is number ten of the Riverside Biographical Series, published by Houghton, Mifflin and Company of Boston and New York in 1901. Conant, a financial writer, treats Hamilton as the Union's great organizer. The first chapter is headed Youth and Early Services.

Its opening sentence fixes the theme: the life of Alexander Hamilton is an essential chapter in the story of the formation of the American Union. Conant argues that Hamilton's work was constructive, laying the foundations of a new state, and that without a directing genius like his the Union's consolidation must have been delayed. He sets Hamilton against Caesar and Napoleon, the two greatest organizing minds of other countries, to mark the difference in Anglo-Saxon political ideals. The series volume is a businessman's tribute to the first Secretary of the Treasury.
40609-memoir-of-rev-joseph-badger-fourth:
Memoir of the Reverend Joseph Badger, by EG Holland, is the life of an American preacher of the early republic. This fourth edition was published in New York and Boston in 1854.

The chapters follow Badger from birth and ancestry through a long, wandering ministry. He visited the murderer D D How at Angelica and preached a sermon at the gallows. A journey to the South produced a published journal. Later chapters cover his ministry at Boston, months of labour in the counties of Onondaga and Cayuga in 1828 and 1829, and years as an editor. The book ends with his retired life, travels, and death in 1852, then outlines of his character. Addresses, sermons, and the views of his fellows close the volume.
40691-kidnapping-in-the-pacific-or-the-a:
Kidnapping in the Pacific, or the Adventures of Boas Ringdon, is a sea story by Kingston. It is framed as a yarn told by a young midshipman just returned from a four years' cruise in the Pacific.

The narrator's ship visited many islands settling disputes, punishing evildoers, supporting consuls and missionaries, and surveying unknown harbours, all to make the British flag respected. The adventure begins when he lands with a boat's crew for a promised cargo of cocoa-nuts and breadfruit, and two men straggle inland against orders. Chasing them, the party misses the recall signal; returning late, they find a strong breeze set in, and their boat is overturned by tremendous rollers on the beach.
40785-strictures-on-nullification:
An unnamed writer took South Carolina to task in this essay from the North American Review, printed at Boston in 1832. Anger over the tariff had pushed the state toward a bold claim: that a state may void a law of the United States. The essay calls that claim nullification and sets out to answer it.

The state meeting at Columbia had passed an ordinance to nullify the revenue laws. The essay copies that act and takes it apart point by point. It grants that the governor's call of an early session may itself rest on shaky ground. Readers get a northern case against state defiance at a tense hour.
40793-the-rubicon:
The Rubicon is a novel by Benson, the author of Dodo, published in New York by Appleton in 1894. A short frame stands before the tale. A man who calls himself the Professor of Ignorance sits long over blank paper one evening.

At last he writes a single sentence: that men should be judged by their best, not by their worst. Next morning he smiles, sure he has seen the line before. He takes a book from the shelf by his hand and checks it. He is now quite sure, he says, that what he wrote is true. The novel then opens in Hayes, a little red-roofed town in a furrow of the Wiltshire Downs. Two inns face each other across its street. One bears the name of the Grampounds, whose marble tombs fill the church. The other bears the name of the Astons, who have no such monuments.
40927-scouting-with-kit-carson:
Everett Tomlinson wrote Scouting with Kit Carson for Every Boy's Library, the Boy Scout edition, copyrighted in 1916 with illustrations by John Frost. Tomlinson also wrote Scouting with Daniel Boone. The frontispiece shows a boy hailing Kit and begging him not to shoot. Twenty-nine chapters open with The Camp on the Plains.

In pursuit of a herd, three Cheyennes, and Rat True follow. The fame of the trapper, alone, mountain trout, and an unexpected meeting build the trail. Wolf's clothing, an attack, capture, a mountain lion, and wild horses fill the middle. The captive leader and the great scout and the great explorer close it. Readers get a Boy Scout historical adventure on Carson's trail.
40937-a-new-sensation:
Albert Ross wrote A New Sensation, a novel printed at New York with rights held from 1898. Front ads hail Ross as a star whose books sold in the millions. They say his tales treat love and vice with skill and high heat, yet keep vice from charm.

Chapter heads sketch the plot in bold strokes. A lady typewriter is sought, a scheme is laid out, a night at a famed hall follows, and Miss Marjorie walks in. Travel brings a theft on board ship, a card game, surf bathing, and a night at Martinique, plus a struggle on a balcony. The heads promise fast turns, bold talk, and clash, in the frank, showy style that made Ross a mass seller.
40998-the-day-of-temptation:
The Day of Temptation is William Le Queux's novel of intrigue, in an edition by Ward, Lock and Company of London dated 1919. Maurice Grieffenhagen supplied the illustrations. The first chapter is headed Aliens, and it opens on a decision: Vittorina must not come to England.

Two men dine in a secluded house at Lyddington in Rutland. Arnoldo Romanelli is a handsome Tuscan of twenty-eight, with a waxed moustache and an old blue Etruscan scarab on his finger. He sees no danger: the girl knows nothing and has barely half a dozen words of English. His companion disagrees and scents peril. Doctor Filippo Malvano, ruddy, clean-shaven, and so British in look that no one would dub him a foreigner, is an alien all the same. Between them hangs the plan that Vittorina's coming threatens, and the temptation of the title gathers.
41084-the-metal-moon:
Smith and Starzl wrote a space tale about flight to a metal moon. The tale ran in Wonder Stories Quarterly in the winter of 1932. Smith won a prize for the plot in a tale contest. Starzl helped turn that plot into full prose. A drawn plate shows a ship near a bright dome town.

Earth men come to a town of glass set on a black base. The front note says far flight will soon send men to far worlds. It warns that men who settle far worlds may change in time. New races may not know kin when they meet. The tale plays out that bold thought.
41215-selected-poems-of-francis-thompson:
Selected poems of Francis Thompson, with a biographical note by Wilfrid Meynell, were printed at London and reached a twenty fifth thousand. Thompson in 1877 stands as frontispiece. Poems on children open the contents: Daisy, the Poppy, to Monica thought dying, and the Making of Viola. To my godchild and Ex Ore Infantium follow.

From Sister Songs come a child's kiss, poet and anchorite, the omen, and the mirage. Love in Dian's lap gathers before her portrait in youth, to a poet breaking silence, a carrier song, and her portrait. Miscellaneous poems hold a fallen yew and the Hound of Heaven, his most famous chase of God. A poet of high thinking, of celestial vision, and of imaginings that found literary images of answering splendour died in London in the winter of 1907, the note says. His life was always a fragile one.
41266-the-american-revolution:
The American Revolution, by John Fiske, is a history of the war that made the United States, drawn from his larger works on the period. The text was first published in 1891, and this copy joins two volumes in one.

Fiske dedicated the book to Mary Hemenway, who saved a noble Boston meeting house and made it a centre for teaching American history. The first chapter sets out the ties between the colonies and Britain in the early seventeen hundreds. Side notes at the head of each paragraph give an outline of the argument. Many pictures fill the printed book, though the plain text copy can only name them. Footnotes gather at the ends of chapters.
41308-the-soul-of-a-nation:
The Soul of a Nation, a short prose piece by Sir Phillip Gibbs, was reprinted by leave of the Toronto Globe. Gibbs also wrote Now It May Be Told. The piece records Armistice Day 1920 in London. On that day the body of an unknown warrior came down Whitehall on a gun carriage, to be buried among kings.

Gibbs stood in the crowd and watched. The dead man, he writes, did not seem unknown at all. To weeping women he was their own boy, missing and never found. To men in civil clothes with ribbons and badges, he was the comrade they liked best. A steel helmet on the flag showed him plain: not a mythic warrior, but one of the fellows in mud stained khaki who went into dirty ditches with faith and fear together.
41354-the-incredible-honeymoon:
Nesbit wrote a tale of a honeymoon too strange to be believed. The book came out in New York in October 1916. Nesbit wrote The Red House and The Enchanted Castle. A front plate shows the pair at a meal by tree roots. They eat and drink like children on a day off.

The tale's first page lists what the reader must grant. Love, youth, chance, and bright luck must all be taken as real. A true heart in woman and a false one in man both count. Yet the pair who ride the nine-seven train live plain lives. From that plain start, odd luck blooms fast. Light hearts get a warm, sly romp.
41362-the-gospel-of-st-john-a-series-of-:
Frederick Denison Maurice, professor of moral philosophy at Cambridge, preached this series of discourses on the Gospel of Saint John, issued in a new edition by Macmillan at London in 1882. A saying of Luther's heads the title page: John speaks poorly and simply, like a child, yet a majesty lies hidden under the words that no man can search out.

Maurice's preface to the second edition answers a friend's textual notes on two disputed passages without altering his text. The friend argues that the verse about the angel troubling the pool of Bethesda in chapter five is an interpolation. The best Greek manuscripts omit it, early versions lack it, and no Father before Ambrose knows it. A like question is raised over the verses at the end of chapter seven and the opening of chapter eight. Maurice prints the observations in full and leaves his discourses as they stood.
41365-the-colonial-cavalier-or-southern-:
The Colonial Cavalier, or Southern Life Before the Revolution, is a social history by Maud Wilder Goodwin, illustrated by Harry Edwards and published in New York in 1894. Its chapters build the cavalier whole: His Home, Sweethearts and Wives, His Dress, News, Trade and Travel, His Friends and Foes, and His Amusements. His servants, his church, his education, laws and punishments, and sickness and death complete the portrait.

The book opens in the wide hall of an old brick mansion on the James River, built a century and a half before by King Carter. Its doors frame the landscape like a picture, the drive running half a mile to the high-road. A passage preserved in the copy climbs the house's dark staircase. Its handrail, Goodwin writes, was hacked by the swords of soldiers in the Revolution.
41395-elementary-zoology-second-edition:
Vernon Kellogg, professor of entomology at Leland Stanford Junior University, wrote Elementary Zoology as a first course textbook, and Henry Holt issued this revised second edition in New York in nineteen two. The plan starts with study method. An opening part treats the study of animals and their life, the divisions of zoology, and what a first course should do.

Laboratory work drives the book. Pupils dissect the garden toad, outside and in, then study the animal body as a machine with its essential life processes. The crayfish follows, then the changes that fit organs to special lives, then single cells like the amoeba. Later chapters reach the many-celled body, the blood, the skin, the liver, and the muscles.
41420-in-the-days-of-washington-a-story-:
In the Days of Washington, a story of the American Revolution by William Murray Graydon, appeared in 1896. The Penn Publishing Company issued it at Philadelphia that year. A front plate shows Washington thanking a lad in a captioned scene. Noah Waxpenny introduces himself in chapter one of the contents.

A British officer loses a fine horse, and Nathan becomes a soldier, in the next heads. Nathan military career very nearly ends in chapter four of the tale. A memorable battle begins, an old enemy returns, and a button betrays its owner. Simon Glass makes a strange remark before the battle of Wyoming in the list. Nathan finds the papers, and Godfrey pleads for condemned prisoners near the close.
41454-the-lost-million:
The Lost Million, a novel by William Le Queux, was published in London by George Newnes in an edition dated 1915. Chapter one describes a man and his secret. In a small hotel bedroom a thin, white-faced, grey-bearded man rouses himself with difficulty in bed. With a skinny finger he points at his battered leather kit-bag in the corner.

The thing inside, he gasps, will make the whole world stand aghast. The keys hang on his chain. He is dying, he tells the young Kemball, and he heard the doctor whisper as much. Yet he will trust Kemball with a strange responsibility, because Kemball alone was kind to him on board while the rest shunned him. Le Queux opens a tale of a dying adventurer, a hidden fortune, and a secret passed hand to hand.
41496-addison:
Addison is a life of Joseph Addison by W J Courthope, in the English Men of Letters series. John Morley edited the series. The New York and London edition is dated nineteen oh two. A list at the front names the series' other lives, from Johnson and Gibbon to Scott and Shelley. Each was written by a named critic of the day.

Of the four English men of letters whose writings most fully embody the spirit of the eighteenth century, the book begins, Addison gives the biographer the scantiest materials. Swift left a journal and letters, Courthope notes by contrast. Addison's social verses and letters to friends are what we have, he says. The series list places this life among lives of Defoe, Burns, Milton, and Dickens. The volume takes its place in a standard shelf of short literary lives.
41572-the-golden-bough-a-study-in-magic-:
The Golden Bough, a study in magic and religion by James George Frazer of Trinity College, Cambridge, appeared in a greatly enlarged third edition from Macmillan. This fourth volume, part three of the work, titled The Dying God, was published in 1911. Chapters treat the mortality of the gods, the killing of the divine king, and the slaying of the king in legend.

Frazer asks why the King of the Wood at Nemi had to perish by his successor's hand. He asks further why peoples across the world put their man-gods to violent deaths when strength failed or a fixed term ran out. Annual, triennial, and octennial kingships are all mustered as evidence. The Dying God is among the most influential parts of a work that reshaped the study of myth and ritual.
41580-haunted-london:
Haunted London is a book about the capital and its ghostly lore, and it opens by letting famous voices praise the city first. Long extracts from Boswell's Life of Johnson give the doctor's opinions of London. No place, Johnson holds, cures a man's vanity like London, for there every man finds his equals and some his superiors.

Boswell's own opinion follows, turning on how different a place London is to different people. The choice of opening is a statement of method. Before the hauntings begin, the book grounds itself in the sheer weight of human life in the metropolis. A city of so many habitations, so much learning, and so much life crowded together is the natural home of ghosts. When a man is tired of London, Johnson's famed line runs, he is tired of life.
41629-harper-s-new-monthly-magazine-no-x:
Harper's New Monthly Magazine, number twenty-three, for April 1852, is one monthly number of the new Harper's magazine, volume four. Its lead fiction is Rodolphus, a Franconia story by Jacob Abbott. Chapter two, The Snow-Shoes, finds Ellen making preparations for the night in a house where her aunt lies ill. She places the furniture of the room in order.

She brings in wood from the back room and lays it gently by the fire, to have a sufficient supply of fuel at hand. She puts the water pail under the seat of the settle so that the water might not freeze. With a long-handled tin dipper she fills the tea kettle full, against any occasion requiring hot water. She warms a small blanket thoroughly at the fire and puts it gently under the counterpane, around her aunt's feet.
41662-the-spell-of-the-white-sturgeon:
Jim Kjelgaard's The Spell of the White Sturgeon was published in New York in 1953 by Dodd, Mead, under the author's copyright. Kjelgaard gives the book to David LeClair and Richard Smith. Twelve chapters make the story: Storm, Wreck, On the Beach, Trouble for the Spray, Rescue, New Venture, and Partners among the first.

Chapter one puts Ramsay Cartou on the rail of the side-wheeler Holter, watching stevedores load cattle hides by hand because the winch is broken. Ramsay has come north from Chicago toward Milwaukee, and not since leaving has the sun shone. From the river mouth he gets his first clear view of Lake Michigan, grey under a grey sky, and it excites him. Action, Pirates, The Great Fish, Fisherman's Luck, and The Pond close the contents.
41666-the-story-of-ancient-irish-civiliz:
Joyce wrote The Story of Ancient Irish Civilization to share early Irish life with a wide public. Longmans, Green, and Company issued the book in London in nineteen hundred seven. Joyce had worked on the old laws of Ireland for years. A plan of Tara opens the book.

The survey covers Ireland from about the fifth century to the twelfth. Native kings ruled the land through that whole span. Joyce shows ranks, trades, and laws at work in daily life. He argues the old Irish led Europe in learning at that time. Irish monks and scholars, he says, helped keep books and faith alive abroad. The book pushes back on claims that Ireland was wild before English rule.
41701-the-love-affairs-of-lord-byron:
The Love Affairs of Lord Byron is Francis Gribble's biography of the poet told through his attachments, published by Eveleigh Nash of London in 1910. Gribble had made a shelf of such books. George Sand and Her Lovers, Rousseau and the Women He Loved, and Chateaubriand and His Court of Women stand in the front list. A portrait of Byron illustrates this volume.

The chapters begin with ancestors, parents, and hereditary influences, then follow the boy through Aberdeen, Dulwich, and Harrow. A schoolboy's loves come next: Mary Duff, Margaret Parker, and Mary Chaworth. Cambridge flirtations at Southwell, revelry at Newstead, and the grand tour carry him to Florence Spencer Smith and the Maid of Athens. Gribble opens the ancestry with the Byrons who came over with the Conqueror and were granted lands in Lancashire.
41717-samplers-and-tapestry-embroideries:
Marcus B Huish wrote Samplers and Tapestry Embroideries, shown here in a second edition with twenty four plates in colour and seventy seven more pictures. A verse from The Needle's Excellency heads the book. It says the land is full of ladies skilled in the rare art, yet the book may teach them more. Plate One forms the front print.

That plate shows a tapestry piece with Henry the Eighth, Edward the Sixth, Mary, and Elizabeth. The Corporation of Maidstone holds the piece. Huish thinks it may date from the accession of Elizabeth. If so it is the earliest embroidery picture he has seen, he says. It seems the work of a joyful Protestant at the return of his faith, he holds. Sampler forms, stitches, and old pieces fill the book for collectors and workers.
41770-studies-in-moro-history-law-and-re:
Studies in Moro History, Law, and Religion is a scholarly volume by Najeeb M Saleeby, printed at Manila in 1905 by the Bureau of Public Printing. It forms part one of volume four of the Ethnological Survey publications. Saleeby offers original studies and translations from Moro texts on the Muslim peoples of the southern Philippines.

Contents begin with a history of Magindanao built from the Tarsila genealogies, tracing lines from Adam and Mohammed to Kabungsuwan, who brought Islam to Magindanao. A second part prints the Luwaran, the Magindanao code of laws, with its Arabic marginal quotations translated and its articles transliterated. The letter of transmittal, dated December 1904, commends the papers to the Secretary of the Interior as science in the service of governing a new possession.
41832-the-golden-bough-a-study-in-magic-:
Macmillan issued the third edition of The Golden Bough in many volumes, and this one, from 1911, is the second part of the third volume: Taboo and the Perils of the Soul. James George Frazer, of Trinity College, Cambridge, had by then rebuilt his study of magic and religion into a library of its own.

The contents proceed by his great method, example on example. The burden of royalty treats royal and priestly taboos. The perils of the soul follow: the soul as a mannikin, the soul as a shadow and a reflection, its absence and recall. Tabooed acts and tabooed persons fill the rest: mourners, warriors, manslayers, hunters. Frazer's thesis, that magic precedes religion and science succeeds both, organized a world's worth of custom into one argument. This volume is the engine room of the taboo chapters.
41857-the-broken-sword-or-a-pictorial-pa:
Worthington wrote this tale of the South after the Civil War and had it printed at Wilson, North Carolina, in 1901. Its full title is The Broken Sword, or A Pictorial Page in Reconstruction. James Dempsey Bullock drew the plates. Worthington gave the book to the Daughters of the Confederacy.

Alice Seymour fronts the book as its heroine. Chapter names trace the tale: Looking Backward, Our Scotch-Irish, and The Assassins of the Peace of the South. A Knight of the White Camelia, The Black Diplomat, and The Writ of Ejectment mark the plot turns. Memorial Day, a coroner's inquest, and an hour with Dickens vary the scenes. The book states a white South view of those years.
41923-the-golden-bough-a-study-in-magic-:
James George Frazer continued his study in magic and religion in the third edition of The Golden Bough, published at New York and London in 1911. This is the sixth of twelve volumes, the second half of the part on Adonis, Attis, and Osiris, and it is given wholly to Osiris. The contents open with his myth.

The official Egyptian calendar and the farmer's calendar follow, with the rise and fall of the Nile and the rites of irrigation, sowing, and harvest. The nature of Osiris is then argued four ways: a corn-god, a tree-spirit, a god of fertility, and a god of the dead. Isis, the sun and moon, the king as Osiris, and mother-kin close the treatise. Comparative religion at its most massive is the volume.
41996-frank-merriwell-s-athletes-or-the-:
Burt Standish wrote this Merriwell story, Frank Merriwell's Athletes, or The Boys Who Won, copyrighted by Street and Smith in 1903. Chapter one opens inside a Chinese theatre in San Francisco. Jack Diamond complains of the racket, and Frank Merriwell and his friends can hardly stand it, in a crowd where it is hard to move.

The contents take the boys far from the city. Frank buys a yacht, a storm strikes, and the scene changes westward. A Yale combine, a struggle for life, a sun dance, and a religious race follow. Ball game, wrestling match, and foot race test the athletes of the title, with cowboys, a ranch morning, shooting, and a last cast for life at the end.
42067-the-golden-bough-a-study-in-magic-:
James Frazer wrote The Golden Bough, a study in magic and religion. Volume seven is part five of the work. Spirits of the Corn and of the Wild names this part. It runs to two volumes, of which this is the first. Macmillan put out the third edition at New York in 1912.

Dionysus opens the contents. Demeter and Persephone follow as its second chapter. Games carry magic meaning in farming, chapter three holds. Woman's part in farming takes the next chapter. Corn-mother and corn-maiden stand in the list. A corn-mother in many lands follows across the contents. Rice-mothers and barley brides fill that survey. Lityerses and the killing of the corn-spirit take later chapters. The dying and reviving god stood examined in the part before. Frazer gives the harvest its spirits in learned array.
42086-the-boy-scouts-at-the-panama-pacif:
Howard Payson wrote a boys' tale of the Panama-Pacific fair, with rights held in 1915. Pictures by Charles Wrenn join the text. Rob and Andy of the Eagle Patrol ride their motorboat Tramp past Captain Jerry Martin's old Sea Gull, once famed for speed.

The scouts long for the great show in California, where their mate Tubby Hopkins has gone with his uncle, Mark Matthews, a famed world traveller. Chapter heads promise a rescue, a ride west across the land, rogues turned, and the gates of the fair. A thief under a bed, a mad dog scare, and a scout's triumph close the trip west and home.
42089-abolitionism-exposed-proving-the-t:
Abolitionism Exposed is a pro slavery pamphlet arguing that abolition harms the slaves themselves. Its title page calls abolition destructive to the nation as well. It claims to stand on the express commands of God in the matter. Strong evidence is promised against the champions of abolition.

The tract sets its claims in double columns for close comparison. A pointing hand mark in the original flags its key passages. Such pamphlets flooded the mails in the decades before the Civil War. Enslavers and their allies printed them to answer the abolition press. The book is evidence of the defence of slavery in its own words. Reading it shows how the pro slavery mind argued scripture, law, and profit together.
42187-catholic-colonization-in-minnesota:
Catholic Colonization in Minnesota is a settlement guide issued in a revised edition by the Catholic Colonization Bureau of Minnesota. It appeared under the auspices of Bishop John Ireland, as the title page states. Contents move from the religious view of immigration to the land, to state and crop statistics. Catholic colonies in the state are then named one by one.

Swift County, Graceville, Saint Adrian, and Avoca colonies each get a section. Chapters tell the best time to come and how to secure government land. Advertisements close a frankly practical book. Church and railroad interests joined to fill Minnesota farms with Catholic settlers, and this guide was their recruiting tool in print.
42197-with-the-king-at-oxford-a-tale-of-:
With the King at Oxford, a tale of the Great Rebellion by the Reverend Alfred Church, was issued at London in 1886. Sixteen pictures go with the story. Church was professor of Latin at University College, London, and the author of Stories from Homer. He dedicates the book to a physician and friend.

Church thanks a fellow of Lincoln College for college records lent to him. Those records gave him the domestic history of Oxford in the war. His tale puts a young hero in the king’s wartime capital. Charles held Oxford while Parliament held London, in the civil war. Boys read Church for history that walks and talks. Latin learning and a good story go hand in hand in his books.
42209-the-devil-in-iron:
The Devil in Iron is a tale of Conan by Robert Howard. It first ran in a weird tale magazine in August of nineteen thirty four. Its first scene is a lone fisher man on the isle of Xapur. A long knife at his belt can not slay the thing he fears there.

Old halls in ruin and walls lost in trees mark the isles dead past state. The man is of a shore folk who have fished those banks since old days. No man or beast is the threat, but a thing of dark old craft. From that still isle scene the tale strides to theft, fire, and sword play. Howard packs dread and brawn in his famed pulp mode.
42228-camp-fire-yarns-of-the-lost-legion:
Colonel G Hamilton-Browne, known as Maori Browne, wrote Camp Fire Yarns of the Lost Legion. T Werner Laurie issued the book in London. Browne had led men in colonial forces abroad. He gave the yarns to an old comrade from the wars of the late eighteen seventies.

Part one stays in New Zealand, where Browne knew Maori life well. Tales tell of scouts, bush rangers, and a swim in bad company. One yarn claims a scout won the New Zealand Cross. Part two moves to Natal in South Africa. A lost pay chest and a changed rogue fill late tales. Old soldiers swap such tales round a fire, and Browne writes them in that loose, fond voice.
42243-the-hour-of-the-dragon:
Robert E Howard wrote The Hour of the Dragon as a serial for Weird Tales, where it ran from December 1935 into April 1936. Four men stand at night around an ebony table and a green case carved like jade. Each holds a black candle with a greenish flame.

One man lays a blazing jewel, the Heart of Ahriman, on the breast of a dried mummy. The lid of the case bursts open as the dead thing stirs. An old spell, said to date from before Atlantis sank, drives the rite. Sword and sorcery, kings, and dark magic fill the tale that follows this grim opening scene.
42251-the-expositor-s-bible-the-book-of-:
The Expositors Bible is a run of verse by verse books on the whole of Scripture. A famed clerk of the church press shaped the set. This part takes the last book of the New Word. That is the book of the end of days. A new cheap form is told of at its front. It was struck from the first plates in full.

Its price per book is set there in plain terms. The mail cost is told as well. Lists at its front name each part of the Old Word in its run. The first book comes by a famed Scot. The flight from Egypt comes by a dean. The laws come by a doctor of the faith. Counts of the law and the first land won fill the row.
42314-mount-rainier-a-record-of-explorat:
Edmond S Meany edited Mount Rainier, a Record of Exploration, issued in New York by the Macmillan Company in nineteen sixteen. Meany taught history at the University of Washington and led the Mountaineers. He had earlier written Vancouver Discovery of Puget Sound and a History of the State of Washington. A front plate gives the first picture of Mount Rainier, drawn from a sketch of seventeen ninety two for Vancouver Journal.

Chapters gather the early sightings, Indian names, and first ascents of the great peak. Surveyors, scientists, and climbers tell their own tales in the record. The mountain glaciers, forests, and park making fill later pages. Meany aim was a full archive of exploration in one volume, from Vancouver day to the national park. Mountain lovers get the primary sources on Rainier, with maps and plates.
42336-the-golden-bough-a-study-in-magic-:
The Golden Bough, a study in magic and religion by James George Frazer, is one of the great works on myth and custom. The hosted copy is volume eight of twelve in the third edition, printed in 1912. Frazer was a fellow of Trinity College, Cambridge. This volume is the second half of part five, on spirits of the corn and of the wild.

Its chapters ask how ancient gods of vegetation took animal form: Dionysus as goat and bull, Demeter as pig and horse. Eating the god, in first fruits and in Aztec rites, comes next. Killing the divine animal treats the sacred buzzard, ram, serpent, turtles, and bear. Frazer suggests that peasants often picture the corn spirit as an animal, which may explain the beasts of the old gods.
42353-deaf-and-dumb-third-edition:
Deaf and Dumb is a tale for the young in its third edition. Darton, Harvey, and Darton printed it in London in the year 1818. Its author also wrote The Twin Sisters, the title page notes. A Cowper verse on speech and praise stands as its motto in front. A frontispiece invites the children in the tale to come for a ride.

The preface hopes the title will stir notice and pity in readers. The state of deaf and dumb children should demand compassion, it says. Some kind minds have already felt that call, the author grants. A story then shows such a child among friends and family at home. Moral tales of that age taught pity by close, domestic scenes.
42383-hugh-walpole-an-appreciation:
Hugh Walpole: An Appreciation is a study of the novelist by Joseph Hergesheimer, published in New York in 1919. Notes and comments on the novels go with the main essay. A list of Walpole's books stands at the front. The Wooden Horse, The Dark Forest, and The Secret City head the novels. Fortitude and The Duchess of Wrexe stand among the romances. Hergesheimer begins with rare pleasure, he says, in his task.

His path runs from tales of inner pressure to books of the seen world, and ends in Russia, where seen and unseen mingle. But his true concern, he owns, is the glow a reader takes from the pages. The feelings roused belong to the heart, not the head. They are the final mark of the true novelist. Their name, in one word, is magic. The piece is praise from one working novelist to an other.
42389-the-pirate-andrew-lang-edition:
The Pirate, by Sir Walter Scott, is a Waverley novel of the Shetland and Orkney islands, here in the Andrew Lang edition of 1893. The Bibliophile Edition was limited to one thousand numbered sets, with new openings, notes, and glossaries by Lang.

Lang's opening essay has a personal warmth. He recalls scribbling at the old desk at Chiefswood where Scott wrote the novel, and summer days under the great tree while Erskine read the fresh chapters aloud. That summer of 1821, he writes, can still be conjured back at the cottage under Eildon Hill. The picture list names scenes of the tale: Mordaunt in Yellowley's cottage, the sword dance, Minna on the cliff, and the pirate's council. The motto from The Tempest promises a sea change.
4239-an-essay-on-the-principle-of-popula:
Thomas Malthus published this essay in 1798. It grew from a conversation with a friend about William Godwin's ideas. Godwin had written on the future improvement of society, and Malthus answered him. His argument was stark: population tends to grow faster than the food supply.

Checks such as hardship, disease, and restraint must therefore limit growth, unless societies plan for it. Malthus wrote against hopeful thinkers such as Godwin and Condorcet. His preface admits the essay is less complete than he wished. Its single plain claim shaped debates about poverty, poor relief, and progress for a century.
42430-colonel-washington:
Archer Butler Hulbert wrote Colonel Washington, published at Western Reserve University in 1902. A university publication fund paid for the volume. Maps and illustrations accompany the text. Hulbert's note states his aim: a glimpse of the youth Washington when he first stepped into public view. The President and General are known to us, he says, but George Washington is an unknown man. Three chapters divide the little book.

The first is a prologue named The Governor's Envoy. It opens in 1753, with vague rumors coming over the Alleghenies to Governor Dinwiddie of Virginia. The second tells the story of the campaign that followed. The third treats Fort Necessity and its hero. The plates show the site of Fort Necessity, its embankment in the foreground, and the hill called Mount Washington. Maps by Lowdermilk, Sparks, and Lewis plot the little fort.
42514-lectures-on-bible-revision:
Lectures on Bible Revision, published at London in 1881, is Samuel Newth's case for the new revision of the English Bible. Newth was principal of New College, London, and a member of the New Testament company of revisers. He wrote for Sunday-school and Bible-class teachers who cannot consult many books. His lectures survey the argument in a compact form.

An appendix gathers the prefaces to the chief old editions of the English Bible. Newth calls those prefaces hard to reach and rich in reward. They put readers in touch with the men whose work gave England its Scriptures. For deeper study he points to Eadie's volumes and Westcott's history of the English Bible. The lectures end by urging that love of the Bible itself demands faithful change.
42557-letters-of-samuel-rutherford-third:
Letters of Samuel Rutherford gathers the famed letters of a Scots churchman in a third edition from the Religious Tract Society of London. Andrew Bonar edits the book. He adds a sketch of Rutherford's life and short lives of the men and women who got the letters.

The old preface, kept here, says the letters need no praise from any man. Their master has writ their praise on the hearts of all who love the things of God, it claims. Page notes from the maker of this text fix small faults and mark the care taken. Church readers get warm, grave letters of counsel and faith, framed by lives on all sides.
42558-the-art-of-illustration:
The Art of Illustration gathers five lectures by C H Spurgeon, the London preacher, delivered to students of the Pastors' College at the Metropolitan Tabernacle. Published in New York in 1894, it was the first of his unfinished books to appear after his death, under a title he chose himself.

Spurgeon taught young preachers how to use illustrations in sermons, speaking, as he put it, as if at home among family. Two lectures he revised fully, two partly, and one survives much as a reporter took it down. Readers get practical advice on making sermons vivid from one of the most heard preachers of his century.
42575-washer-the-raccoon:
George Ethelbert Walsh's Washer the Raccoon, issued by the John C Winston Company with a 1922 copyright, is the eleventh book of his Twilight Animal Series. The series is written for boys and girls from four to ten years of age, and Edwin John Prittie supplied the colored illustrations.

Walsh's own preface rounds up the animal cast of the earlier books. Bumper the white rabbit, Bobby Gray Squirrel, Buster the big brown bear, and White Tail the deer all appear there. Washer's frontispiece shows his board raised on the crest of a wave and tossed over the falls, a hint of the scrapes the little raccoon gets into.
42611-in-to-the-yukon:
William Seymour Edwards wrote letters from a two month trip into the Yukon, printed in Cincinnati in 1905. Maps and many photos fill the book. Edwards gave the book to the comrade, his wife, whose company made the outing a joy. A photo at the front shows the pair upon the trail.

The letters were not first meant for print, the preface says. They tell of steamers, the White Pass and Yukon Railway, mining camps, and cold northern rivers. Edwards thanks railway and steamship officials for their many courtesies on the way. Readers get a warm, plain record of gold country travel just after the rush, seen by a keen and grateful guest.
42661-the-golden-bough-a-study-in-magic-:
Golden Bough, a study in magic and religion, volume nine of twelve, is Part Six, The Scapegoat, by James George Frazer. Macmillan published the volume at New York and London in 1913 for the third edition. Frazer was fellow of Trinity College, Cambridge, and professor of social anthropology at Liverpool. Contents open with the transference of evil in its first chapter.

That chapter treats the transference of evil to inanimate objects, to stones and sticks, to animals, and to men. The transference of evil in Europe and the nailing of evils follow in its sections. Public scapegoats, the expulsion of embodied evils, are the heart of this part of the great work. Frazer scapegoat, the man or beast loaded with a people sins and driven out, became a household figure of modern thought from these pages.
42742-the-indian-chief-the-story-of-a-re:
Gustave Aimard wrote a tale of Mexico, issued in London in 1861 by Ward and Lock. The preface says the book ends a set that told the sad fate of the Count de Raousset-Boulbon, who fell by Mexican deceit. A next book would give the early lives of some of the same folk.

The first chapter looks back at Jesuit missions in Mexico, where priests drew Indians to farm and learn the faith. The mission of Nuestra Señora de los Ángeles stands by the Rio San Pedro, sixty leagues from Pitic, under huge rocks. Chapters promise a spy, a blast, a cock-fight, the taking of Hermosillo, and a sad close.
42764-the-ethics-of-medical-homicide-and:
The Ethics of Medical Homicide and Mutilation is a study of right and wrong in the heal craft by Austin OMalley. OMalley held three degrees in lore and law. The book bears the marks of the church censors of his faith, and its rights date is nineteen nineteen. This form is a late print of that work.

The first part lays down broad rules on self slay and on the slay of men, in law and in faith. The next part treats the cut of the frame, by the state and by the self. A long part asks when the life of man starts, with views old and new and the lore of the cell. A part on when life ends, and on the wake of the seem dead, comes next in the list.
42824-scenes-and-characters-of-the-middl:
Edward Cutts wrote Scenes and Characters of the Middle Ages, here in its third edition of 1911. The London De La More Press issued the book with 182 pictures. Cutts had served as honorary secretary of the Essex Archaeological Society. His subject is daily life in medieval England.

Cutts states his aim at the start. He offers sketches of medieval life and character, not a general history. Chapters treat monks, hermits, and anchoresses in turn. Pilgrims, parish priests, and other clergy follow. Minstrels and their guilds get a section of their own. Knights close the book, with chapters on Saxon and Norman arms and armour. The days of chivalry and the knights-errant end the survey.
4295-songs-of-action:
Arthur Conan Doyle gathered these poems of action in a volume published by John Murray in 1916, in its seventh impression. The contents range from the Song of the Bow and Cremona to the Storming Party, the Frontier Line, and Corporal Dick's Promotion. Later pieces turn to hunting, racing, and the sea.

Titles such as A Rover Chanty, A Ballad of the Ranks, and The Home-Coming of the Eurydice show Doyle's taste for stirring scenes. The poems suit readers who know Doyle for Sherlock Holmes and want his verse voice: direct, martial, and fond of soldiers, sailors, huntsmen, and the open air.
42951-a-new-century-of-inventions-being-:
James White's A New Century of Inventions was printed for the author at Manchester in 1822. It sets out designs and descriptions of one hundred machines relating to arts, manufactures, and domestic life. White, a civil engineer, says in his preface that a long and eventful passage through life drew his attention forcibly to a multitude of mechanical subjects.

He publishes, he says, not because the inventions form a system of mechanical truth, but because they are distinct objects of immediate application, with some wider ideas for artists yet unborn. The form and title, he confesses, have only one example before them, the work of the illustrious Marquis of Worcester.
42959-the-survey-of-london:
Stow's Survey of London appears here in Everyman's Library, edited by Ernest Rhys, with an opening essay by Henry Wheatley. Front pages list the library's thirteen classes of books, from travel and science to poetry and romance. John Stow, citizen of London, first published his survey in 1598, with a second edition in 1603, as the bibliography shows.

Stow's own works ran from Chaucer and chronicles of England to the Annales. Later hands enlarged the Survey across three centuries. Stow walks London ward by ward, recording churches, halls, streets, customs, and worthies from his own deep knowledge of the city he loved. The survey stays the base source for old London, part guide, part memorial, part civic history.
43049-the-golden-bough-a-study-in-magic-:
The Golden Bough, volume ten of twelve, is part seven of Frazer's study of magic and religion. It treats Balder the Beautiful, the fire festivals of Europe, and the outer soul. Macmillan published this third edition volume in nineteen nineteen at London and New York. Frazer held posts at Cambridge and Liverpool when the work appeared.

The preface ties Balder to the King of the Wood at Nemi in Italy. Both, Frazer argues, stood for the sacred oak of our forefathers' worship. Each kept his life hid in the mistletoe that rarely grows on an oak tree. Chapters first treat girls shut away at puberty across many lands. Then the myth of Balder is told, and Europe's fires are listed by season. Lenten, Easter, Beltane, midsummer, and need fires each get their section.
43088-the-chief-of-the-ranges-a-tale-of-:
Chief of the Ranges is a tale of the Yukon by H A Cody, author of The Frontiersman. The London edition is dated nineteen thirteen. The book is dedicated to the author's father and mother. Contents run to twenty eight chapters. The raiders open the list, then foiled and out of the storm. A warning and secret depths follow.

Tokens, the vanguard, and chivalry take their turns in the middle. A maiden's will, capture, and the spirit of Klota build toward the late tale. The fettered chief and regions beyond close the list in the part shown. Chapter one opens on a crooked river winding between gently shelving banks. Pebbles along the shore sparkle like mirrors under the sun. Dark forests of spruce and fir whisper in the breeze, the tale says.
4310-will-warburton:
George Gissing opened this novel with Will Warburton bounding out of a cab near Chelsea Bridge, fresh from Alpine snows and sea wind in his hair. He pays double fare, shoulders a heavy bag, and runs up four flights to his flat. His landlady, Mrs. Hopper, greets him with a thin, cautious face at the door.

Warburton returns to London life with energy, but Gissing soon tests that energy against work, money, and love. The novel follows a young man of spirit learning the limits of his own will. It is a story of homecoming that turns, as Gissing's stories often do, into a study of character under pressure.
4315-the-life-of-sir-richard-burton:
Thomas Wright, author of a life of Edward Fitzgerald, wrote this life of Sir Richard Burton, explorer, linguist, and writer, in two volumes bound as one. Wright began fifteen years after Burton's death, and twelve years after Lady Burton's biography of her husband, which she wrote while dying of an incurable disease.

Lady Burton had asked whether she would live to tell the world how great her husband was, and to refute his enemies' calumnies. Wright takes up that task with fuller evidence, following Burton from youth through Africa, Arabia, and South America. The book gives a full Victorian life, with its quarrels, books, and journeys, in one large volume.
43203-kensington-notting-hill-and-paddin:
Kensington, Notting Hill, and Paddington, by an Old Inhabitant, was printed at London about 1882 by Griffiths and Company, with the profits going to a chapel organ fund. The author writes for young friends who want to know their own streets as they were thirty eight years before.

He remembers oil lamps, night watchmen crying the hour, four horse coaches, and light struck from flint and tinder. Coronations and the great Reform Bill pass through his boyhood. Part one then digs into parish history back to the Domesday Book. Few London suburbs keep so warm a memory of their village days.
43234-bright-ideas-a-record-of-invention:
Bright Ideas, a record of invention and misinvention, is a book of comic tales by Herbert Strang, printed at London in 1920. C E Brock drew the illustrations. The frontispiece shows Noakes spluttering and shaking the soot from his clothes, crying that it is all Templeton's doing. The contents list six tales.

They are The Smoke Machine, Trespassers Will Be Prosecuted, A Gas Attack, The Clipper of the Road, The Cold Water Cure, and A Brush with the Enemy. The picture captions promise mishaps: riders flung into a hedge, men tripped over a wire, and the whole contents of an experimental tank poured down. The first tale opens with Bob Templeton on a bridge parapet. He watches the roach dart among the weeds, then straightens with a smile and a comical glance at his coins. Strang wrote many boys' adventure books under this pen name.
43235-first-on-the-moon:
First on the Moon is a science fiction novel by Jeff Sutton. Ace Books published it in New York under a 1958 copyright. Sutton dedicates it to Sandy. The cover copy calls the flight a suicide race to Luna. Four men, screened and trained for over a year, will crew the pioneer rocket. Whoever wins Luna, East or West, controls the Earth.

Commander Adam Crag carries the mission's secret burden. A saboteur hides among his three crewmates. Any one of them could be the hidden enemy. If Crag fails to unmask the agent, the Reds gain the Moon. The prologue shows four sister rockets on the Western Desert. One is silver, three ashen grey. Only the silver ship carries a crewed cabin. The drones haul scant payloads to the crater Arzachel. Their destination is a stark plain under tall cliffs.
43246-the-motor-routes-of-england-wester:
Gordon Home wrote this motor guide to the west of England for A and C Black of London. It is the Western Section of The Motor Routes of England, mate to a Southern Section south of the Thames. A view of Bettws-y-Coed in Wales stands near the front.

Praise from the Pall Mall Gazette for the mate volume sets the tone. The touring driver, it says, will find Home a bright mate for the day's run. He chats of the past, of building, and of old finds along the main roads. Facts come thick but never dull. Maps, plans, and plates in colour mark the Black house style for such guides.
4327-the-valley-of-decision:
Edith Wharton set this historical novel in eighteenth-century Italy, in four books: The Old Order, The New Light, The Choice, and The Reward. It opens in a small neglected chapel, where farm noises drift through closed doors and a February light falls on a foundling child in the kitchen. The scene is quiet, poor, and watchful.

Wharton dedicated the book to her friends Paul and Minnie Bourget, in memory of Italian days together. The story follows a young Italian through old loyalties and new ideas, toward a choice that gives the book its title. It is Wharton's early large novel, rich in Italian setting and moral argument.
43319-the-symbolism-of-churches-and-chur:
The Symbolism of Churches and Church Ornaments is a translation of Durandus. It renders the first book of his Rationale Divinorum Officiorum into English. William Durandus was sometime bishop of Mende in France. Neale and Webb of Trinity College, Cambridge, made the translation. Their introductory essay and notes accompany the medieval text. Scribner's Sons published this issue in New York in 1893. The translators dedicated it to the Cambridge Camden Society. Both men were founders of that church building society.

Their essay treats sacramentality as a principle of church design. Its analysis asks wherein old churches differ from new ones. Not in association, correctness, or the picturesque, the analysis argues. The difference lies in reality of meaning, it holds. Durandus read every part of a church as a symbol. The translation fed the Gothic revival's study of meaning.
43343-the-vegetable-lamb-of-tartary-a-cu:
The Vegetable Lamb of Tartary studies a curious fable of the cotton plant. Henry Lee wrote the book. Sampson Low published it in London in 1887. Lee had been naturalist of the Brighton Aquarium. He had earlier written on the octopus and on sea monsters.

The fable tells of a plant-animal called the Barometz. Travellers said a lamb grew on a stalk in Tartary. Lee traces the tale through old writers and pictures. The frontispiece shows the lamb after an old engraving. One chapter then interprets the fable. A second gives the history of cotton and its entry into Europe. A sketch of the cotton trade is added. The book mixes folklore with trade history.
43344-don-hale-with-the-flying-squadron:
Crispin Sheppard wrote Don Hale with the Flying Squadron, printed at Philadelphia in nineteen nineteen, with drawings by Bodine. Sheppard had written Don Hale in the War Zone and Don Hale Over There before this tale. A rickety cab with two boys and much luggage halts at a high iron gate in France. Over the gate stands the name of a military flying school at Beaumont.

The grey haired driver jokes that he hopes the Germans will not get the young monsieur, and asks for his life insurance. Don Hale starts his training as a pilot the next day, burning with zeal. Men inside note that one boy already wears the stars and wings of the air service as a corporal. Spies, training, the Lafayette, and a trial fill the chapter heads.
43350-the-anatomy-of-the-human-peritoneu:
George S Huntington wrote The Anatomy of the Human Peritoneum and Abdominal Cavity, issued in Philadelphia and New York in 1903. Huntington was Professor of Anatomy at the College of Physicians and Surgeons, Columbia University. The book holds 300 full-page plates with 582 figures, many in colours. Its standpoint is development and comparative anatomy.

The preface says Huntington aims to stress the value of embryology and comparative anatomy. Those aids, he argues, clear up hard problems in adult human anatomy. He hopes a broader reading of structure and function will add interest to the study. Spelling and hyphen forms vary in the text, as the transcriber notes. The book is a large teaching work for medical students and doctors.
43352-a-history-of-english-versification:
A scholarly history of English metre by Jakob Schipper. The Clarendon Press published it at Oxford in 1910. Schipper taught English philology at the University of Vienna. Honorary degrees from Oxford, Cambridge, Edinburgh, and Aberdeen crowd his title page. Book one treats the line itself. Its first part covers the native metre.

Definitions come first: rhythm, accent, rhyme, assonance, alliteration. Old English alliterative verse then fills chapter two. The four-beat and two-beat theories contend there. Hemistich types are analysed one by one with symbols. Schipper classifies verses the way botanists classify plants. His German school of metrics brought laboratory patience to English poetry. Students of Beowulf still meet his verse types.
43394-through-glacier-park-seeing-americ:
Mary Roberts Rinehart rides through Glacier Park with Howard Eaton's party in this 1916 Houghton Mifflin travel book. Her foreword argues that travel is a matter not only of seeing but of doing. New places are only new pictures to many, but regions are the setting for life, and the desert without its Arabs is the place that God forgot. To travel best is to be a sportsman of the road.

The book tells of a three-hundred-mile trip across the Rocky Mountains on horseback. It is about fishing, cool nights round a camp-fire, and long days on the trail, with a party of all sorts from everywhere. The contents run through the adventurers, the sporting chance, bears, and a run down the Flathead rapids. Photographs show the passes, lakes, and her buckskin horse, Gold Dollar.
43420-off-santiago-with-sampson:
Off Santiago with Sampson is a boys' war tale by James Otis, published by Dana Estes at Boston in 1899. It stands second in his Stories of American History line, after When Dewey Came to Manila. Both new volumes told of the recent Spanish-American War. Seventeen pictures by Bridgman illustrate the book, which sold for seventy-five cents in cloth.

The tale opens on a small but sturdy boy before a driveway, as great gates swing inward in a high board fence. Otis wrote history as adventure for boys, in the same line as his tales of the siege of Boston and the boys of 1745. The Santiago campaign, with Sampson's fleet off Cuba, gives this volume its ground.
43431-the-vertebrate-skeleton:
Sidney Reynolds's Vertebrate Skeleton was printed at the University Press, Cambridge, in 1897. It belongs to the Cambridge Biological Series, edited by Arthur Shipley of Christ's College. Reynolds lectured in geology and zoology at University College, Bristol. The preface fixes his terms: skeleton covers outer tegumentary structures as well as the inner frame. Some account of the lowest chordates is included though they are not strictly vertebrates.

For each group Reynolds gives the general skeletal characters first, then one or more type skeletons in detail. Last comes the skeleton treated organ by organ across the group. Beginners are told to start with the dogfish, pass to the newt and frog, then to the dog. Italics mark generic names and, in the type accounts, the membrane bones. Reynolds thanks Andrews, Harmer, Kerr, and Doctor Gadow among his proof readers.
43433-the-golden-bough-a-study-in-magic-:
James George Frazer of Trinity College, Cambridge, wrote this vast study of magic and religion. Macmillan printed the eleventh volume of the third edition in 1913. Its part is Balder the Beautiful, the second of two volumes on that theme.

Fire festivals of Europe fill most of the book. The fire-walk and its meaning come first. Then the burning of figures, and of men and beasts, in the fires. The magic flowers of Midsummer Eve and Balder and the mistletoe follow. The external soul, in things, plants, and beasts, takes a long chapter. A theory of totemism and the rite of death and rising stand in it. Farewell to Nemi closes all.
43503-the-origin-of-paul-s-religion:
J Gresham Machen, then an assistant professor at Princeton Theological Seminary, delivered lectures on the origin of Paul's religion at Union Theological Seminary in Virginia. They were published in 1921 as the ninth series of the James Sprunt Lectures. Machen dedicated the book to William Park Armstrong, his guide in New Testament study. The lecture fund began with a gift of thirty thousand dollars in 1911.

Machen frames his task as one view of the origin of Christianity, a problem both historical and practical. Chapters cover Paul's early years and the triumph of Gentile freedom. Paul and Jesus, the Jewish setting, and the religion of the Hellenistic age follow.
43525-medi-val-london:
William Benham, rector of St Edmund the King in Lombard Street, and Charles Welch, keeper of London's city library, wrote this book on medieval London. Seeley printed it in 1901. A front plate shows London Bridge and the Tower from an old poem book.

Plates from rich old copies crowd the list. A tournament from a romance, Richard the Second riding out to the Irish war, and that king given up to the citizens all show in colour. Froissart's Chronicles give two of the scenes. Two men who knew the city's stones and its books join forces here. The result is a walk through London's middle age with the men and rites that filled its streets.
43548-the-illustrated-key-to-the-tarot-t:
The Illustrated Key to the Tarot is a guide to divination by de Laurence. The de Laurence Company of Chicago brought the book out in 1918. Its subtitle calls the tarot the veil of divination throughout. The greater and lesser arcana both stand illustrated in the volume. Parts treat the veil and its symbols, then the art of reading.

Secret tradition under the veil of divination fills the second part. The outer method of the oracles and the tarot in history follow. Inner symbolism and the greater keys close the book's main parts. The four suits of tarot cards make up the lesser arcana. Divinatory meanings of both arcana stand listed for the reader's use. The recurrence of cards in dealing gets its own section here. An ancient Celtic method of divination ends the practical teaching. De Laurence had writ the Master Key and many occult works.
43557-a-handbook-of-illustration:
A Horsley Hinton wrote this handbook on book and magazine pictures, with prints from photos and sketches by himself and other artists. The book treats a craft then in fast change, as photo methods reshaped the drawn page. Hinton writes for art workers who must see their work through the press.

Early chapters weigh art, photos, maps, plans, and the bond between author and artist. Long parts teach the half-tone process and how to ready photos, wash drawings, and pencil work for it. Line process and pen-and-ink methods get the same close care. The book is a full shop guide to how pictures reached print.
43572-a-commentary-to-kant-s-critique-of:
A Commentary to Kant's Critique of Pure Reason is Norman Kemp Smith's guide to Kant's masterwork. Macmillan published it in London in 1918. Kemp Smith was McCosh Professor of Philosophy at Princeton. He dedicates the book to the memory of Robert Adamson. Three opening essays frame the commentary. One treats Kant's method of composing the Critique, as a textual question.

A historical essay sets Kant against Hume and Leibniz. General essays then define the a priori and the nature of consciousness. Phenomenalism, Kant's substitute for subjectivism, gets its own study. Self-consciousness and the threefold split of sensibility, understanding, and reason follow. The commentary proper tracks the Critique section by section. The introduction asks how synthetic a priori judgments are possible. The Transcendental Aesthetic receives over eighty pages. Kant's conflicting views of space and of time are faced squarely. The Analytic of Concepts opens the Transcendental Logic.
43598-the-fruits-of-victory-a-sequel-to-:
The Fruits of Victory is a sequel to The Great Illusion, Norman Angell's famous argument on war and wealth. The front matter gathers press comment on the controversy Angell's pamphlet raised. The New Statesman recalled in 1913 how Norman Angellism became a chief topic among politicians and journalists all over Europe.

At first men fastened on the most startling parts of the theory. The whole commercial basis of war was wrong, he said, and no modern war could profit the victors. Stranger still, a winning war might leave the conquerors worse off than the conquered. The winners took the indemnity, yet ended poorer than those who paid it. Folk raised on the idea that nations fight like two errand boys for an apple were amazed into curiosity. Admiral Mahan is quoted on the armaments of Europe, aimed at winning shares of unexploited regions.
43605-the-golden-bough-a-study-in-magic-:
Volume five of the third set of The Golden Bough treats three dying gods. James George Frazer wrote the vast study of magic and faith. The set ran to twelve volumes in its third form in print. This part came out in New York and London in nineteen fourteen.

Chapters trace the myth and rite of Adonis in Syria and Cyprus first. Sacred men and women, burnt gods, and priest kings fill the next long stretch. Tales of kings burnt on pyres lead to rites of cleansing by fire. The lore of Tarsus and its gods takes a large share of the book. Frazer stacks case on case from the near east to weigh one grand claim.
43785-ruth-erskine-s-son:
Ruth Erskine Son is a tale by Pansy, out from a Boston house in nineteen seven. Louise Clark drew the cuts for the book in its print form. Its true name should add Burnham, the front talk grants at once. Ruth name clings to her Chautauqua summer and her three girl mates there. Her boy Erskine is thus the son of Judge Burnham by full right.

A dull late fall day brings Ruth back to her old friends in the tale. Part names chart whims, a spoiled dam, and sense meets self give. Mamie Parker, fine state tests, and built on sand parts crowd mid ranks. A chief clerk post, a look back, and a loyal heart mark late parts. Give up and a strange change close the long scheme of parts.
43792-the-history-of-modern-painting-vol:
Richard Muther wrote The History of Modern Painting, here in volume one of four. Dent at London and Dutton at New York put out this revised edition in 1907. Muther was professor of art history at the University of Breslau. He continued the work himself to the end of the nineteenth century. A portrait by Anton Graff fronts the volume as its first plate.

Book one treats the legacy of the eighteenth century in art. Its first chapter opens modern art in England with Hogarth. Reynolds and Gainsborough stand compared in that chapter at length. Richard Wilson shows the end of classical landscape there, it says. Gainsborough begins the intimate landscape in the same account. English influence on the continent, Rousseau, and Goethe follow. Goya's pictures and etchings carry the Spanish section of the tale.
43794-my-religion:
My Religion, by Count Leo Tolstoi, was turned from the French and printed by Thomas Y Crowell and Company at New York, with a copyright of 1885. The translator's first words sketch the man's life for those who know no Russian. Born in 1828 on his father's land in Tula, he read tongues of the East at Kasan, then served as a gun officer. He held a post at Sebastopol in the Crimean War, and his war sketches made his name at once.

War and Peace, his vast tale of the French march of 1812, had by then sealed his fame. Yet this small book turns from fame to faith: what the great count held true, and how a man should live by it. Faith readers get the creed of a giant of letters in his own plain terms.
43812-through-the-south-seas-with-jack-l:
Martin Johnson tells his voyage through the South Seas with Jack London. Laurie printed the book in London with numerous illustrations. A front plate shows Johnson and a Pathe camera man hunting Solomons. Contents open on the trail of adventure and building the Snark.

On the high seas and a Pacific paradise follow the launch. Molokai leper island and the long traverse take chapters five, six. The Marquesas, Society Islands, and Samoan group fill the middle. Lost in Fiji, South Sea cannibals, and voyage end close it. Harrison wrote both an introduction and a postscript for the travel account here.
43894-the-history-of-modern-painting-vol:
The History of Modern Painting, volume two, by Richard Muther, came out in a revised edition in London in 1907. Muther taught art history at the University of Breslau. He carried the tale to the end of the nineteenth century. Book three is called The Triumph of the Moderns. Chapter sixteen treats the draughtsmen. Muther says painting had drifted away from life in the early eighteen hundreds. Caricaturists first brought modern life back into art.

Chapter seventeen covers English painting to 1850. Portrait men such as Romney, Lawrence, and Raeburn appear. Animal painting and genre scenes get their due. A chapter on the military picture follows. Names run from Gillray and Cruikshank to Daumier and Doré. The volume maps a shift toward the present day.
43911-a-dreadful-temptation:
Wedding guests at Trinity whisper over the match that opens the tale. Xenie Carroll, a young beauty with no dowry but her face, is marrying an aged millionaire. John St John is bent, white-haired, and dim-eyed, with one foot near the grave. Her rich aunt gave her two seasons in town and furnished the trousseau. The aunt engineered exactly the bargain the onlookers name: youth and loveliness for an old man's gold.

Munro copyrighted the novel in 1883, and the International Book Company of New York issued it. Its subtitle, A Young Wife's Ambition, fits an author who had already written Queenie's Terrible Secret and Jaquelina, and the marriage of winter and summer sets her stage.
43947-comparative-religion:
Comparative Religion is a short study of world faiths by J Carpenter. The author led a college at Oxford for free church men in his day. Verses from Wordsworth and a quote from a famed word man head the book. No year is shown in the front pages of the hosted text.

Parts scan the whole field of faiths, then faith in low and high lands. Ghosts and gods, rite acts, and rite goods earn their own heads in line. Faith and morals, then the riddles of life and fate, close the brief tour. A wall paint of the last doom in a small church opens the first talk. Plain speech aims the survey at keen lay minds, not just schools.
43968-the-book-of-coniston:
The Book of Coniston is a guide to the Coniston country in the English Lake District by Collingwood, here in a third edition, revised and enlarged, printed at Kendal in 1906. Press notices at the front call it a capital little guide book and the ideal of a guide book. Collingwood had written a life of John Ruskin, the great man of the place.

The book opens with a climb of the Coniston Old Man, the great hill above the village, by the most interesting path. Later chapters treat the lake, the moorlands and their old settlements, and the early history of the spot from Roman to Norman times. Industries get their due: copper, iron, slate, and wood.
43976-ancient-plants-being-a-simple-acco:
Ancient Plants gives a simple account of the past vegetation of the earth, by Marie Stopes, a lecturer in fossil botany at Manchester. Blackie of London issued the book in 1910. A stump of a Lepidodendron from the coal measures fronts the volume. The subtitle promises the new finds in this realm of nature study.

The first chapter is an introduction to fossil plants as a field. Kinds of fossil plants fill the second chapter of the book. Coal, the most important of plant remains, takes the third. Seven ages of plant life and stages in plant evolution follow. The minute structure of fossil plants is treated in its turn. Stopes writes for the general reader with a scientist’s hand. Her book brought the coal forests to life for lay readers.
44082-the-history-of-modern-painting-vol:
The History of Modern Painting, volume three of four, is a past of art by Richard Muther. Muther held a chair of art past at a school in the east of Germany. This fresh form was brought by the hand to the end of the past age but one. It came out at London and New York in nineteen seven.

This book runs on with a part on the true paint hands and the new dream hands. Parts treat the true school in England, with the band that sought to mend art past a famed wise man of the pen. The true school in the German lands takes the next part, past the shift of the year of war. The sway of the art of the far east isles and the band of the light mark school close the list shown.
44134-the-origin-of-the-werewolf-superst:
A learned paper asks where the werewolf belief came from. It opens with the claim that men turning into beasts is a near world wide belief. The wolf is the form most often taken. Such a changed man is the Germanic werewolf, a man in wolf's shape or wolf's dress.

Notes weigh the word itself, part man and part wolf, and old claims in Herodotus. One teacher blamed fur dress in winter for the tale of a whole people turning wolf. That, the writer says, will not fit the same belief in warm lands. Totem faith is put forward as one root. Heavy notes in German and English crowd the foot of each page with proof.
44189-florida-past-and-present-together-:
Samuel Upham wrote this book on Florida, past and present, printed at Jacksonville in 1883 with pictures. A second part gives notes from Sunland, on the Manatee River on the Gulf coast of south Florida.
