Its climate, soil, and products are the theme, in a land the title page sings of as the home of the orange and guava, the pine-apple, date, and cassava.

Upham's preface explains the book's birth. A few of his letters to friends in the North found their way into print. Letters then flooded in from all over the Union and from Canada. They asked about the Manatee region. Hundreds were answered, and many were not. This book was written to answer them all, and others like them.
44214-proceedings-third-national-confere:
Proceedings of the Third National Conference on Workmen's Compensation prints the talks at Chicago in June 1910. The conference had been founded at Atlantic City the summer before. A short report of the second meeting, at Washington in January 1910, stands in the appendix. Charles Neill, the federal labour commissioner, chaired the body.

Sessions run across two days, with a model compensation code set out for debate. State commissioners from Wisconsin, Minnesota, and other states led the work. The American Association for Labor Legislation stood behind the meetings. Copies sold at fifty cents from its New York office. The talks came as states weighed the first laws of their kind. This record shows reformers building the case for no fault payments to hurt workers.
44269-famous-houses-and-literary-shrines:
Famous Houses and Literary Shrines of London, by Adcock, was published in 1912. Dent issued it at London, with Dutton at New York, that year. Seventy four illustrations by Frederick Adcock and sixteen portraits fill the volume. A portrait of Samuel Johnson stands at the front of the book.

A prefatory note holds that a dead house of unknown former tenants stirs no one. Even a famed man house, now held by strangers, needs his story to live again. The writer tried to supply that word as complement to his brother drawings, he says. He cared less for his own opinions than for what the great men thought and said there. Johnson, Dickens, and Carlyle houses crowd these London walks in print.
44273-woman-in-prison:
Woman in Prison is a memoir by Caroline Woods, published by Hurd and Houghton in New York in 1869. A prefatory piece, Why Written, tells how Woods came to work among women prisoners. She was reading an evening paper when one advertisement held her eye.

The advertisement read: wanted, at the penitentiary, a matron; inquire at the institution. She read it over and over, turned to the news, and could not fix her thoughts. The thought came to her that answering it would place her on missionary ground. At the same time it would give her employment and a support while she taught the ignorant. The same appeal met her again in a morning paper at a friend's office. Woods took the post, and her book reports the world of the women's prison from inside, as a plea for its inmates.
44295-candy-medication:
Bernard Fantus, professor of pharmacology and therapeutics at the College of Medicine of the University of Illinois, wrote Candy Medication, issued at St Louis by C V Mosby Company in nineteen fifteen. A transcriber note warns not to attempt these formulas. A preface states the delight of the method. Candy medication has given such delightful results in practice among children that it should be more widely known, Fantus says.

A formulary is the common meeting ground needed for the prescribing physician and the dispensing pharmacist, he holds. Researches in the Pharmacologic Laboratory of the University of Illinois over five years ground the book, he adds. Sweet tablets should be freshly prepared on physician order, securing efficiency and palatability, he says. His fat covering process makes the tablets no harder to prepare than ordinary ones, he notes. Doctors and druggists get a formulary of medicated sweets.
44408-narrative-of-the-operations-of-a-d:
Major Johnston of the Third Ceylon Regiment wrote this narrative of a British detachment in Ceylon. A new edition from Dublin and London came out in 1854. Johnston had commanded the detachment as a captain. The expedition marched on Candy in 1804, and the title promises remarks on Candian warfare.

Johnston dedicates the book to the commander in chief of the army. He explains his purpose in the dedication letter. British troops had little practice in this kind of warfare. European tactics did not cover it. His account shows what pressed hardest on his men in the field. He hopes future detachments can remove or lessen those troubles. The narrative doubles as a lesson book drawn from hard experience.
44422-eccentricities-of-the-animal-creat:
John Timbs, author of Things Not Generally Known, published Eccentricities of the Animal Creation with Seeley, Jackson, and Halliday in 1869. Eight engravings illustrate it, king penguins among them. Timbs was the great Victorian retailer of curious knowledge.

The introduction surveys curiosities of zoology through history. Natural history appears in Scripture and in Egyptian records. Montezuma kept zoological gardens, and the Tower of London kept a menagerie. The Zoological Society of London and the Surrey gardens bring the story home. A chapter on the rhinoceros in England follows, one-horned and two-horned. Timbs writes the anecdotal natural history the newspapers loved: animal wonders, priced, dated, and attached to famous names, a museum in paragraphs.
44439-the-world-s-great-sermons-volume-0:
Kleiser put in one set some of the best-known sermons in English. Volume six came out in New York in 1908. It runs from Beecher to Punshon in A-to-Z name order. Kleiser had taught speech at Yale Divinity School. Great church men of the past age fill the list.

Beecher speaks on life that does not end. Chapin takes Nicodemus, and Stanley speaks in praise of Carlyle. Vaughan, Newman Hall, Robertson, and Kingsley fill the mid part. Caird deals with faith in daily life. Storrs closes on the drive for mission work. Church readers get strong prose to study and quote.
44508-the-myth-of-a-guilty-nation:
The Myth of a Guilty Nation is a political essay by Albert Jay Nock, who signed it with the pen name Historicus. It was printed at New York by Huebsch in 1922. The book argues against the charge, fixed on Germany after the Great War, that one nation alone bore the guilt of the war. Footnotes at the front point readers to works on secret diplomacy by Morel and others.

Nock opens with a claim about victory itself. Military victory, if it is to stand, must also be shown to be a victory for justice. There is no way of getting around this. He quotes Chesterton on the American South to back the point. It is a dissenting book, written against the settlement of 1919 while its ink was still fresh.
44547-polly-a-christmas-recollection:
Polly: A Christmas Recollection, by Thomas Nelson Page, was copyright 1894 and published in New York in 1897, illustrated by Castaigne. A uniform style list groups it with Page Marse Chan, Meh Lady, and other tales of old Virginia, each a small quarto at one price.

Pictures are listed from the text. A young man found it necessary to lean over and throw a steadying arm around her, reads the frontispiece caption. Drinkwater Torm fell sprawling on the floor, another promises. He made Torm, Charity, and a half dozen younger house servants dress him, says a third. The tale opens at Christmas Eve. It was Christmas Eve, the narrator says. I remember it just as if it was yesterday. The Colonel had been — and the recollection begins. Readers get his Christmas tale in that vein, all household, honour, and sentiment.
44665-things-a-boy-should-know-about-ele:
Things a Boy Should Know About Electricity is a primer by Thomas St John, here in a second edition dated 1900. St John wrote a line of Fun With books, on magnetism, electricity, puzzles, and soap bubbles, many sold with outfits of gear. A companion book told how two boys made their own electrical apparatus at home.

The publisher's note says the book explains, in simple and straightforward language, the things about electricity that the American boy is keenly interested in, wants to know, and should know. St John writes for the home experimenter, the boy who would rather handle a coil and battery himself than read of wonders at second hand. The book belongs to the first age of electric light and the telephone.
44683-south-london: Walter Besant wrote a set of books on London by district, and the pages at the front of this volume print reviews of the whole set. South London carries one hundred and twenty pictures. Reviewers praise Besant as an enthusiast and a close observer of life. They say he clothes plain streets with the romance that is their due. They call the book a worthy sequel to his London and Westminster volumes.
44701-british-regiments-at-the-front-the:
Reginald Hodder tells the stories behind regimental honours in British Regiments at the Front, a Daily Telegraph war book from Hodder and Stoughton in 1914. Hodder thanks Norvill for help and suggestions at the front. The volume lists companion war books on how the war began, the fleets, and the campaign of Sedan.

An opening chapter gathers regimental nicknames and how they were won, starting with the Rusty Buckles of the Queen's Bays. That regiment, we learn, took bay horses in 1767 when nearly all others rode black, the Scots Greys excepted. Chapters then treat the Dragoon Guards, Carabiniers, Scots Greys, Hussars, and Guards regiments one by one. Later chapters group famous fights, Fuentes d'Onoro and Albuera, then Balaclava and Inkerman.
44728-kinship-and-social-organisation:
Kinship and Social Organisation holds three lectures by Rivers, given in London and printed in 1914. Rivers was a fellow of St John's College, Cambridge. The lectures rest on his field work in Melanesia in 1908. They also draw on notes about the Pueblo peoples of North America. The catalog title drops the first word, but the title page gives the full name.

Rivers argues that words for kin are shaped by social rules, not by chance. He sets out the system in which one term can cover a whole class of kin. He links such terms to forms of marriage and group life. The book shows how kin terms can serve as a tool for the study of past social forms.
44729-the-passenger-pigeon:
The Passenger Pigeon is a book on the great American wild pigeon by Mershon, published in New York in 1907. Its contents open with the editor's boyhood among the pigeons. Later chapters reprint classic accounts of the bird by Alexander Wilson and by Audubon. A chapter shows the pigeon as James Fenimore Cooper saw it.

The bird once filled American skies in flocks beyond counting. By 1907 it was nearly gone, hunted and netted without pause, and this book gathers what witnesses had written of it. Pictures show the male and female of the species. The volume reads as both a natural history and an early plea to mark what was being lost.
44750-the-library-of-work-and-play-home-:
Charles Warner wrote a book on how to dress a home with taste. It sits in the Library of Work and Play set. Warner ran a hand-work school at Rindge for eight years. He then led a trade high school at Springfield for twelve. The set's kin works span craft, wires, yard, and sport.

A plate on how to hang a picture leads his book. The wall's space is part of the frame, that plate's key says. Rooms, hues, cloth, and wood each take their due in turn. Cheap grace is the aim: taste need not cost wealth. Plans and plates guide the hand at each new step. Home folk get a skilled man's plain talks.
44771-perpetual-motion:
Percy Verance gathered the long, vain hunt for perpetual motion in this book of 1916. Its full title calls it a history of the efforts to attain self-motive mechanism. A set, pictured collection of the devices stands at its heart.

Verance sorts the tries by kind. Wheels and weights come first, then rolling weights and sloped planes. Water devices fill the third part, and air and siphon tries the fourth. Magnetic devices and capillary pulls follow. His book reworks Henry Dircks's two old histories of the search, from the 1200s on. Each device is shown and its flaw named: a graveyard of hopes, set in order.
44772-the-golden-bough-a-study-in-magic-:
James George Frazer wrote The Golden Bough, a vast study of magic and faith in old and folk life. The third form of the work ran to twelve parts in all. The part held here is part twelve, printed in 1920. Frazer taught at Cambridge and at Liverpool.

Part twelve is not the main text but the list of sources and the full index. The list names books and journals in many tongues that Frazer used or knew by name. A star marks works he had not seen at first hand. The index lets a reader find a rite, a god, or a place in the whole set. Scholars use this part to trace his claims back to their roots.
448-the-psychology-of-revolution:
Gustave Le Bon studies why crowds and nations turn to revolt in this early work of crowd psychology. He sorts revolutions into scientific, political, and religious kinds, and weighs how governments fail, how peoples follow, and how old habits survive new regimes. The Reformation serves as his key case for how belief moves masses.

Later parts treat the mystic mind, the part of leaders, and the slow return to order after upheaval. Le Bon writes with cool, generalizing sweep, often harsh on crowds. The book remains a landmark for readers who want to grasp revolt as a mental event, not merely a clash of armies or laws.
44891-the-works-of-the-right-honourable-:
John, Earl of Rochester, left the poems gathered in this volume, printed in London in 1718 for one shilling. The title page lists the kinds of work inside: satires, songs, translations, and other occasional poems. A Satire against Mankind leads the contents, followed by Tunbridge-Wells, a satire. A Satire against Marriage and a poem Upon Nothing stand in the list as well.

Songs fill much of the book, to mistresses, to Corinna, and on leaving a mistress. One piece turns the ninth elegy of Ovid's Amours into English. The opening satire says that, free to choose his flesh, the speaker would be a dog, a monkey, or a bear. Any shape, he holds, beats vain man.
44897-grammar-of-the-new-zealand-languag:
Maunsell wrote a grammar of the tongue of New Zealand, the Maori tongue. A second form of the book is this text. Marks show long and short sounds in its word lists. Small print holds notes of less weight for new learners. Maunsell was an archdeacon and a doctor of laws.

Rules of sound, word kind, and phrase build fill the book. Maori words keep their own spell, with fixes listed at the back. Each rule comes with Maori lines to make it plain. Such books served church men and staff in that land. Tongue past fans get a full, grave work of its age. Care for both tongues marks each page.
45045-a-little-girl-in-old-washington:
A Little Girl in Old Washington, by Amanda Douglas, was printed by Dodd, Mead in New York in 1900. Douglas also wrote little girl volumes for old New York, Boston, and Philadelphia, and the Sherburne stories. This book is inscribed to a friend whose ancestors, she writes, made worthy efforts in the earlier history of the South.

Chapter one brings a new home. Jaqueline Mason, sixteen and in long gowns, informs a cousin who is coming to live with them that she will have to take sides. Their side, of course: the newcomer's mother was own cousin to the Masons' late mother. Patty protests her name, and a young fellow on the window seat teases Jaqueline for sighing after a court. Twenty one chapters follow, through a new president, the beginning of a love story, and the midst of war.
45049-my-first-mission:
George Cannon wrote My First Mission, the first book of the Faith-Promoting Series. The Juvenile Instructor Office at Salt Lake City put out this second edition in 1882. The work was first entered in 1879, and aims to teach and hearten young Latter-day Saints. Chapter one treats Cannon's shyness when he first spoke in public. He held on, trusting in God, and felt the Spirit near him as he spoke.

A voyage from San Francisco to Honolulu, with storm and sea-sickness, comes next. The elders split up to work the four chief islands of Hawaii. On Maui they meet the consul and governor, preach in public, and set out to learn the tongue. Cannon meets Napela at Wailuku in a striking way.
45067-new-house-that-jack-built-an-origi:
New House That Jack Built, an Original American Version, is a verse pamphlet by L. Whitehead, Senior, printed at New York in 1865. It recasts the old cumulative children's rhyme as a hymn to American freedom and free labour. Its Jack is the Laborer, who has worked with muscle, brain, and pen for ages to ransom the children of men.

Jack lays his foundation in human equality and builds a tenement house on a national plan. The foundation is deep and wide: it took half the continent for its location. Jack came to Plymouth Rock with the Pilgrims and worked till the top-stone was laid in the Temple of Freedom. The verses praise free speech, free worship for Gentile and Jew, and the plough-boy who may rise to the highest place. It weds an old rhyme to Civil War era politics.
451-the-shadow-line-a-confession:
Joseph Conrad tells of a young seaman who takes his first command in this short novel, subtitled a confession. Bored and restless, the narrator quits a good berth, then accepts a ship in the East whose captain has died at sea. Fever, calm winds, and a crew on edge test him as he crosses into adult command.

Conrad frames the tale as a shadow line between youth and age, crossed by all in early manhood. The prose is grave and inward, tracking doubt, duty, and the slow gain of nerve. The book endures as a compact study of how a man becomes responsible when no one else can steer.
45106-the-life-of-francis-thompson:
The Life of Francis Thompson, by Everard Meynell, came out in London in 1913. A photo of the poet in 1894 faces the title page. Meynell thanks the poet's sister, a nun at Manchester, and friends who gave letters and memories. Sixteen chapters track a strange, sad life.

Thompson was born on December 16, 1859, at Preston in Lancashire, in a box of a house on a narrow road. His father was a doctor who had served in a Manchester clinic. Chapters treat the child, the boy, and study of physic at Manchester. Dark chapters treat life on London streets, then a find and first books of verse. More treat cloister gates, the death of Patmore, and the last years. Verse fans get the full tale of a frail, famed Catholic poet.
4512-gardening-without-irrigation:
Steve Solomon wrote this practical gardening book from his own experience in the maritime Northwest, where summers turn predictably dry. After moving to Lorane, Oregon, in 1978, he found that his well, first rated at fifteen gallons a minute, soon fell to about three gallons a minute in August. That failure pushed him to learn how to grow food with little or no added water.

Chapters cover water-wise science, ways to help plants need less water, year-round planning, and an alphabetical guide to crops grown with less irrigation, closing with Solomon's own garden plan. The book suits gardeners in dry-summer regions, and anyone who wants a productive plot without depending on constant watering. It is hands-on, plainspoken, and built from trial in a real garden.
45199-the-war-poems-of-siegfried-sassoon:
The War Poems of Siegfried Sassoon gathers sixty-four poems by the author of The Old Huntsman and Counter-Attack. It was printed at London by William Heinemann in 1920. A note says twelve of the poems appear here for the first time. The rest are chosen from two earlier volumes.

The contents open with poems of the troops: Dreamers, Trench Duty, Wirers, Break of Day, and A Working Party. Others bear titles like Suicide in Trenches, Attack, Counter-Attack, and Died of Wounds. A second part turns home with poems such as Base Details, The General, Glory of Women, and Survivors. The book opens with lines from Henri Barbusse on men worn by fatigue, rain, and a night of thunder. Sassoon's verses show the trenches as the men in them lived them, in anger and in pity.
45247-india-for-indians-enlarged-edition:
Chitta Ranjan Das gave speeches for home rule in India, bound in one book. A large form came out at Madras in April 1921. Motilal Ghose wrote the front words for the book. First forms ran in 1917 and 1918, the title page says. A plate shows Das in calm, grave dress.

A joint Hindu and Muslim meet at Calcutta leads the set. Meets at Mymensingh, Decca, and Barisal fill the next parts. He speaks out gainst the jailing of men with no trial. Self rule, the great change, and the great denial mark his themes. A talk to students closes the book of his voice. Past fans get a chief's words as he spoke them.
45295-tom-the-piper-s-son:
Tom, the Piper's Son is an anonymous chapbook priced at one half-penny, sold at Webber Street in London. The little book tells the nursery tale in verse, with a picture for nearly every stanza. Tom, he was a piper's son, he learned to play when he was young. The only tune that he could play was Over the Hills and Far Away.

The verses run through the old story beats. Tom stole a pig and away he ran; the pig was eat, Tom was beat, and Tom ran roaring down the street. Then his pipe makes cattle prance, pigs dance, and a donkey shed its load. He plays a lass's cow into dancing and breaks Dame Trot's eggs. The mayor threatens jail, and the court itself falls to dancing. Cheap print for children carried the rhyme across generations.
45410-composition:
Arthur Wesley Dow, who taught fine arts at Teachers College in New York, wrote a set of drills in art structure, in a ninth printing revised and enlarged in 1914. It serves both students and teachers. Dow had taught at the Pratt Institute and wrote on the Ipswich prints. Colour plates stand among the pictures.

Three elements rule the book: line, notan, and colour. Line drawing begins with Japanese stuff and brush practice. Ways of making harmony lead into designs in squares, circles and oblongs. Landscape and picture making follow. Notan treats dark and light in two, three and more values. Colour schemes drawn from Japanese prints and woven cloth close the course.
45466-afternoon:
Émile Verhaeren wrote the poems gathered as Afternoon, brought into English by Charles Murphy and issued at New York by John Lane Company in 1917. Verhaeren had already published Poems and The Sunlit Hours in English dress. Thirty numbered pieces make up the book, and most of them turn on a shared home, a garden, and a love grown calm with years.

The first poem tells how slow maturity came as a surprise and laid its hands on love's brow. Roses of June, lamps lit at dusk, dead kisses of long dead years, and gold ships of summer all pass through the verses. The mood is late and still, a poet looking back on joy that time has both dulled and kept.
45497-nancy-brandon:
Lilian Garis wrote Nancy Brandon, copyrighted in 1924 and issued by Grosset and Dunlap. Thelma Gooch drew the pictures. The story bills its heroine as Nancy Brandon, enthusiast, and a plate shows the Whatnot Shop being readied.

Nancy and her small brother Ted have just moved into the old Townsend place at Long Leigh. Ted rides a clothes basket like a boat while Nancy preaches her principle: girls should do no more housework than boys. Chapters promise a special sale, a big day, a failure, and then resolve. A cave-in, a dog named Nero, and a midnight alarm close the list.
4552-the-border-legion:
Zane Grey sets this western on the wild southern border of Idaho, in a year when gold rushes, vigilantes, and lawless camps had unsettled the whole region. Joan Randle, twenty years old, tall and strong, rides out on a cedar ridge regretting a quarrel with Jim Cleve. She fears he has ridden straight for the border country, and her taunt may have pushed him toward danger.

Joan follows into a world of outlaws, prospectors, and hunters, where blood and gold mix in camp talk and in real violence. Grey writes the mountains, horses, and border towns with the speed of a campfire tale. Readers get a classic western adventure about pride, regret, and rescue, in which a young woman must face the harsh country her words helped to unleash.
45580-woman-church-state-the-original-ex:
Matilda Joslyn Gage wrote this book, Woman, Church and State, first published in 1893, and billed in this edition as the original expose of male collaboration against the female sex. A contents page sums each chapter in a long paragraph of claims, and the first three chapters stand at the front of the hosted text.

Chapter one treats the matriarchate, a time of mother-rule that, Gage argues, came before father-rule and gave women great freedom. She finds its traces among many nations, in the Six Nations of America among them. Chapter two turns to celibacy, charging the church with degrading marriage and women alike. Chapter three takes up canon law, and the church's grip on the marriage ceremony.
45585-the-seven-curses-of-london:
The Seven Curses of London is a study of the city's dark side by James Greenwood, who signed himself the Amateur Casual. The hosted text follows the London edition of 1869. Greenwood was known for dressing as a tramp and reporting the world of the poor from inside it.

The first curse is neglected children. A hundred thousand children, he says, run loose in the London streets. Baby-farming, the errand boy's hard life, and the child of the gutter fill the first chapters. The second curse is the professional thieves. Twenty thousand of them, he reckons, work the city. Their speech, their homes, and their haunts are described. In disguise he attends a thieves' raffle and hears their speeches and songs. The book counts the curses one by one, with facts meant to shock the comfortable.
45684-my-mamie-rose-the-story-of-my-rege:
Owen Kildare wrote My Mamie Rose, the story of his regeneration, an autobiography printed at New York in 1903. A map of the Bowery district fronts the book. Kildare was born on Catharine Street in that small slice of Manhattan and lived there till he was thirty, as the map note says.

At thirty he could not read or write the simplest sentence. Eight years later he earned his living by his pen, and he calls that change a miracle. Chapters trace a tenement kid, street nomad, and worker by muscle and then by wits, through Bowery politics and a saloon world. A kindergarten of one, a debut in society, and an inheritance close a stark, hopeful tale of self remade.
45752-london:
Walter Besant wrote a history of London printed at New York in 1892, with many illustrations. Besant had written All Sorts and Conditions of Men and Fifty Years Ago. After the Romans opens the tale, then Saxon and Norman times. Three long Plantagenet chapters follow, then two Tudor chapters, Charles the Second, and George the Second. An index of five hundred pages of text closes the book.

Stowe's monument, a Roman marble coffin in the Guildhall, and statues of Mercury, Apollo, and Jupiter found in the Thames head the pictures. A bronze bust of the emperor Hadrian from the river, a bit of Roman wall, lamps, keys, and hair pins fill the early plates. Besant packs street finds and church tombs into a people's history of the great city.
45914-on-foreign-service-or-the-santa-cr:
On Foreign Service, or The Santa Cruz Revolution is a naval adventure novel by Staff Surgeon Jeans of the Royal Navy, published by Blackie and Son in 1911. Jeans also wrote Mr Midshipman Glover. His preface says the story rests on his own experience in many parts of the world.

The tale follows a revolution in a South American republic and the part played by two armoured cruisers guarding British interests. The Hector and the Hercules wait out a gale at Gibraltar before sailing for Santa Cruz. Sub-Lieutenant William Wilson tells the story, fresh from midshipman days and not yet settled to bossing a gun-room. Chapters run through the rescue of a submarine, attacks on San Fernando, and fights with shore guns. Jeans notes that naval officers read his proofs, so the sea work may be trusted as exact.
45925-an-american-girl-in-london:
Sara Jeannette Duncan wrote An American Girl in London, published in New York in 1891 with illustrations by Townsend. Thirty chapters carry the tale, numbered in plain Roman figures with no titles. The narrator announces herself on the first page: I am an American girl.

That statement, she says, explains any question of her own conduct in England, where an unmarried person of her age is not expected to talk much, especially about herself. She has always talked a great deal and been encouraged to do it. Getting used to English reserve takes her time, and she has lately spoken with becoming care. The comedy of the book is set in that gap between two countries manners. Duncan, a Canadian writing for American readers, made her heroine a licensed observer of London society. Wit does the work of a plot.
45952-the-evolution-of-old-testament-rel:
William Orchard wrote The Evolution of Old Testament Religion, published by James Clarke in London in 1908. The book is cast as eleven lectures. Orchard begins with the Semitic races, reading the tenth chapter of Genesis as an ancient attempt at a scientific ethnology. He notes its principles of classification: geography first, and prejudice too, since the writer omits Moab and Ammon altogether.

The lectures then trace Israel's faith as it grows. Primitive Hebrew religion and Mosaism come first. The influence of Canaan and the rise of prophetism follow, from early stages to the literary prophets. The exile's effect, the work of the priests, and the religion of the psalmists and the wise fill the later lectures. Messianic expectations close the course. Orchard wrote as a liberal churchman, presenting the Old Testament as a developing faith rather than a finished system.
4599-the-small-house-at-allington:
Anthony Trollope's The Small House at Allington first ran in the Cornhill Magazine from September 1862 to April 1864. It appeared in book form in two volumes from Smith, Elder in 1864. Both serial and first edition carried eighteen full-page illustrations by John Everett Millais, with smaller vignettes at chapter heads in the serial. The contents open with the squire of Allington, the two pearls of Allington, and the widow Dale of Allington.

From the Allington household the story moves to Mrs. Roper's London boarding-house and to the wider world of suitors, cousins, and clerks. Lily Dale and her sister Bell, the two pearls, stand at the centre of a tale about love, jilting, and steady affection. Readers get a rich, humane Trollope novel, full of county life and London lodgings, and a fine entry point to his Barsetshire world.
46026-virginia-s-attitude-toward-slavery:
Munford's Virginia's Attitude Toward Slavery and Secession first appeared from Longmans, Green in 1909 and was reprinted in New York in 1969. Its argument stands in the part titles: Virginia did not secede in order to extend slavery into the territories, or to stop its threatened destruction at home.

Chapters work through the record in order: the colonial years, Virginia's statute abolishing the African slave trade, her part in the Ordinance of 1787, and her stand on the Federal Constitution. Later chapters print the legislature's debates of 1832, plans for colonization, the views of Jefferson, Clay, and Lincoln, and deeds and wills freeing slaves. Munford also counts the small share of slaveholders in the white population and weighs slavery's harm to the state's prosperity.
46090-lancashire-sketches-third-edition:
Lancashire Sketches is a book of local pieces by Edwin Waugh, here in its third edition of 1869. The volume came out in London and in Manchester. In his preface Waugh says the district is one he knows at close hand. He has gathered points of local interest from it.

Around those points he builds a picture of present life in South Lancashire. He joins traits of the people to accounts of the scenery. He adds gleanings from local history where they bore on his themes. Waugh is frank that richer matter exists than he could reach with the light he had. He leaves the verdict on his success to readers who know the country and the people. The sketches stand as a fond, first-hand record of a working county in his own day.
46094-the-romance-of-modern-mechanism-wi:
Archibald Williams wrote this popular science book, The Romance of Modern Mechanism, printed in London in 1910 with thirty illustrations. Williams wrote a whole shelf of such romances, of invention, mining, engineering, and exploration. His subtitle promises accounts in plain language of wonderful machinery, mechanical devices, and very delicate scientific tools.

A frontispiece shows the kind of wonder inside: a mechanical sculptor at work. The machine carves two blocks of stone at once, ranged on either side of a model, and can make four copies from one original at a time. A series page quotes the press on the set the book belongs to, praising its accuracy joined with charm for readers of all ages.
46143-experiments-and-observations-on-th:
Thomas Henry, an apothecary, published these experiments and observations in London in 1773. His preface argues that the right making-up of medicines matters so much to practice that any attempt to improve it deserves a fair hearing. He dedicates the treatise to Thomas Percival of Manchester, his friend and teacher in experiment.

Six subjects fill the book. Henry treats the preparation and medical uses of magnesia alba, the solvent powers of calcined magnesia, and the varied powers of quick-lime used in different amounts. He then turns to absorbents and how they speed or slow putrefaction, to the antiseptic powers of vegetable infusions made with lime, and to the sweetening properties of fixed air.
46146-the-riverpark-rebellion: The Riverpark Rebellion is a novel for young people by Homer Greene. Crowell of New York issued it in the Sunshine Library at fifty cents a volume. Its copyright dates are 1889 and 1892. The volume is inscribed to the memory of Colonel Otis Bisbee, principal of the Riverview Military Academy at Poughkeepsie, which points to a school story set in that academy world. A frontispiece shows a servant asking two young gentlemen if there is anything else he can get for them.
46149-medi-val-heresy-the-inquisition:
Mediaeval Heresy and the Inquisition is a history by Turberville, a lecturer in modern history at Bangor. It was published in London in 1920. Part one treats heresy itself, from its origins through the Waldenses and Cathari. Chapters follow the Everlasting Gospel, Averrhoist influences, and the reform movements of the fourteenth century.

Part two turns to the Inquisition. It tells the church's attitude before the tribunal arose, then the beginnings and spread of the Inquisition through Europe. Its composition and procedure are set out, and its penalties are weighed in a final chapter. A note on authorities guides further reading. The book is a sober academic survey of its dark subject.
46150-famous-days-in-the-century-of-inve:
Gertrude Stone and Grace Fickett, both teachers at state normal schools in Maine and Massachusetts, wrote Famous Days in the Century of Invention for young readers. The book came out at Boston in 1920. Its eight chapters tell the tales of the great new tools of the age just past. The sewing machine, long-distance speech by wire, new light, rubber, printing, the daguerreotype, the reaper, and electric cars each get a day of fame.

The first chapter opens in June 1845 with young Jonathan Wheeler, wild with joy at his first ride on a railway train to Boston. Each tale is told through the eyes of a boy or girl, so the facts come with the feel of daily life. The book shows how teachers of that day brought the tale of new machines home to school children.
46192-the-pan-german-programme-the-petit:
The Pan-German Programme prints two German documents in translation, with an introduction by Edwyn Bevan. George Allen and Unwin published the pamphlet at London in 1918. The introduction calls the two papers the fullest statement of the Pan-German party's aims. Both were drawn up in the first months of 1915. The expected advance on Paris had stalled, and Germans asked what the war was for. Rumors of a compromise peace alarmed the Pan-German circles in March.

Five great associations drew up a memorandum for the Chancellor, and a sixth joined them. The paper was laid before Bethmann Hollweg on May 20, 1915. Landowners and the great Rhenish ironmasters stood behind it, wanting the French iron districts of Briey and Longwy. The second document is the Manifesto of the Intellectuals, read to a great gathering on June 20, 1915.
46195-an-accidental-honeymoon:
An Accidental Honeymoon is a romance by David Potter. Lippincott published it in Philadelphia in 1911. Gage painted the colour illustrations. Holloway supplied the decorations. Potter had earlier written The Lady of the Spur. Advertising pages praise his fine character drawing.

The tale opens beside a stream. A man named Fessenden sets a girl gently on a flat rock. She had been splashing about in the water. She insists she screamed at an eel, not from fear. The illustrations preview a sailing romance. A golden afternoon of talk fills one plate. A cabin-door catch is broken in another. A toast in Jersey wine appears in a third. The girl is Madge Yarnell, to judge by the captions.
46199-sketch-of-the-history-of-the-knigh:
Sketch of the History of the Knights Templars is a history by James Burnes, printed at Edinburgh by Blackwood in 1840. It is the second edition, illustrated with plates. Burnes was a knight of the Royal Hanoverian Guelphic Order. He dedicated the book to Prince Augustus Frederick, Duke of Sussex, Grand Prior of England. The first edition had been exhausted by presentations to illustrious persons, leaving few copies even for the author's friends.

Five chapters carry the story. The Hospitallers come first, then the Templars themselves. The persecution of the Templars fills the third chapter. The continuation of the order and the Knights Templars of Scotland close the history. Burnes wrote as a brother of the revived order, arguing its survival through the centuries of suppression.
4621-the-two-wives-or-lost-and-won:
T. S. Arthur published The Two Wives, or Lost and Won, in 1851, as the third volume in Arthur's Library for the Household. His preface states its purpose plainly. Tender, earnest, self-forgetting love can win back a husband whose steps have strayed toward ruin. By contrast, the want of those virtues under like circumstances brings sad results. The story opens in the evening, with Mrs. Wilkinson at a small work-table under a shaded lamp.

Her husband John, who has been reading, stands ready to go out, while a smile on her lips hides a cloud on her heart. From that scene grows a tale of marriage tested by temptation, pride, and forgiveness. Readers get a short, moral domestic novel of its day, written to be read in families. It shows how patience and love, rather than scolding or pride, can reclaim a life heading the wrong way.
46216-carriages-coaches-their-history-th:
Ralph Straus traces the carriage from the primitive vehicle to the modern carriage in this illustrated history. Martin Secker published the book in London in 1912. Its pictures reproduce old prints, contemporary drawings, and photographs, with the State Coach of Great Britain as frontispiece.

Chapters move through the age of litters, the introduction of the coach, and an interlude of the sedan chair. Seventeenth-century innovations and early Georgian carriages follow, then a chapter called the war of the wheels. Inventions galore and the age of transition bring the story toward the present. Straus also wrote lives of Dodsley and Baskerville, listed among his earlier books. An index closes the volume at page 287.
46236-the-red-widow-or-the-death-dealers:
The Red Widow, or the death dealers of London, is a mystery novel by William Le Queux, issued in 1920. The contents promise a plot of locked rooms, nets, and traps from the first chapters on. It opens with a man in white and a question over a Mrs Braybourne. A locked room in Hammersmith and events in Bridge Place follow early.

Later chapters move to Loch Lomond, a gentleman named Greig, and news from Lancaster Gate. The middle of the book speaks of baiting a trap, a room of evil, and lost days. A cry in the night, a recluse, and an order to get rid of the girl raise the stakes. The closing heads run through darkness toward a conclusion in thirty one chapters.
4630-the-home-mission:
T. S. Arthur published The Home Mission at Boston and Philadelphia in 1853, gathering domestic sketches. Its contents include a vision of consolation, the step-mother, power of kindness, and bear and forbear. They go on to the social serpent, the young mother, a gentle warning, Kate's experiment, my fortune's made, and the good match. Later pieces cover a brother's temptation, the home of taste, two sisters, and an evening prayer.

Arthur's preface says good or evil impulses that become ruling affections can often be traced back to the home of childhood, where impressions last as long as existence itself. Home, he argues, is the nursery of all that is excellent in social or civil life, or of all that is deformed. Readers get a set of short, earnest tales about family influence, meant to show how early home life shapes a whole character.
46446-shifts-and-expedients-of-camp-life: Shifts and Expedients of Camp Life, Travel, and Exploration is a practical handbook for travelers in wild country. The text here survives with the transcriber's long note on its many illustrations, which the plain text version cannot show. Those pictures carry much of the teaching. Sketches show gear, shelters, and camp devices, often as numbered plates whose parts the text explains step by step. Sidenotes describe each paragraph's subject, so a reader in the field can find a needed hint fast.
46452-the-strand-magazine-vol-01-no-05-m:
Volume one, number five of the Strand Magazine came out in May 1891 as an illustrated monthly. Its lead piece is An Eighteenth Century Juliet, by James Mortimer. A picture shows Gabrielle joining her prayers to her lover's. Mortimer calls French judicial annals rich in strange and romantic episodes, and few match this one for pathos.

Gabrielle de Launay was the only child of an eminent judge of Toulouse, born about 1730. Captain Maurice de Serres, son of her father's late friend, was marked as her future husband. Birth and fortune matched well. Then an untoward tale reached the judge's house, and the young officer came early next morning to impart it in despair.
46480-magic-and-religion:
Andrew Lang wrote Magic and Religion, printed in London in 1901. Lang had written Myth, Ritual, and Religion and Custom and Myth before it. The contents open with science and superstition, then a theory of loan-gods, or borrowed religion. A chapter on magic and religion gives the book its title, and one treats the origin of the Christian faith.

The back half of the contents turns to Frazer's theory and its approaches. Heads cover the evolution of gods and the alleged mortality of gods. Religious regicide, yearly and in single acts, gets two chapters. The Saturnalia, the Greek Cronia, and the Sacaea close the list shown at the front. Corrections at the front mend dates and words page by page.
46544-the-theistic-conception-of-the-wor:
Cocker, professor of mental and moral philosophy in the University of Michigan, wrote an essay in opposition to certain tendencies of modern thought, published at New York in 1875. Its epigraph is from Martineau: science discloses the method of the world, but not its cause; religion, its cause, but not its method.

The preface, held back until the tendency ripened, traces a rapid slide: from criticism of the Christian religion to a direct assault on the personality and providence of God. The theistic postulate, he complains, has been degraded to a mere hypothesis, and a law-governed cosmos put in the place of a personal creator. Strauss is quoted owning that honest men must say they are no longer Christians.
46547-a-voyage-to-the-moon:
Cyrano de Bergerac, swordsman, poet, and thinker, wrote a fanciful voyage that Doubleday of New York reissued in 1899. A life of the author stands at the front.

The tale tells how the author set out, and how he reaches the moon at last. He talks with the viceroy of New France on the frame of the world. A small Spaniard joins him there with quaint wit. The chapters treat the tongues of the moon folk, their way of feeding, and their wars. Atoms and the working of the senses fill the deep talks. Books, burials, and the telling of time in the moon pass in review, before the return to earth.
46571-saunterings-in-and-about-london:
Saunterings in and about London is Max Schlesinger's sketchbook of the capital, Englished by Otto Wenckstern and published by Nathaniel Cooke of London in 1853. A German observer walks the city and reports what strikes a foreign eye. The first chapter introduces some of the author's friends and the Englishman's castle, his home.

Street life comes next: the masses, the fashionable quarters, advertising vans, and the puffing mania of trade. Later chapters take in the squares, Lincoln's Inn, a trip up the Thames to Vauxhall, and the periodical press with its morning papers and special trains. The book is a lively outsider's portrait of London at mid-century, curious about everything from crossing sweepers to newsboys.
46617-the-plan-of-salvation:
John Morgan wrote The Plan of Salvation, a Latter-day Saint tract. The Millennial Star Office printed it at Liverpool. Its house stood at 295 Edge Lane there. Morgan signs as an elder of his church. Conflicting theories fill the Christian world, he opens. Man's life here and hereafter draw those fights.

Where we came from asks for knowledge, he says. Why we are here asks the same. Where we go after this probation completes it. Such knowledge serves man's well-being, he holds. The tract sets out the Saints' belief in brief. Its quarrel is with the Bible's misreaders, he claims. The sects differ from scripture more than from him, he argues. Sincerity proves nothing by itself, he warns. Testimony of sound character alone proves a point. A mission tract from England's Mormon press states the faith's first principles for street and doorstep readers.
46618-the-story-of-london:
Henry Wheatley's Story of London belongs to the Mediaeval Town Series and was published in London by Dent, first in 1904. Wheatley dedicates the little book to the memory of Danby Palmer Fry, a lifelong friend who advised him on most of its subjects. A plate of London in 1588, from a manuscript in the British Museum, fronts the volume.

Chapters give the early history of London to the Norman Conquest, then the walled town and its streets. The reader walks the town with Chaucer and the poets of his time, and visits the river and the bridge and the king's palace at the Tower. Manners, and health, disease and sanitation, have chapters of their own.
46651-a-soldier-of-the-legion:
A Soldier of the Legion is Edward Morlae's memoir of service in the French Foreign Legion in the First World War. Houghton Mifflin published it at Boston in 1916. Pictures show Americans in the Legion with hand grenades and reading news from home. The first chapter opens in late August 1915.

Morlae's regiment, the Second Foreign Regiment, passed in review before President Poincaré and General Joffre. After twelve months of fighting, it received a battle flag from the president's hands. The honour admitted the Legion to equal footing with the regiments of the line. Two months later the regiment's remnants paraded through Paris. Morlae writes as one of the Americans who volunteered for France.
4672-the-galleries-of-the-exposition:
Eugen Neuhaus, assistant professor of decorative design at the University of California, wrote The Galleries of the Exposition. It is a critical review of paintings, statuary, and graphic arts in the Palace of Fine Arts at the Panama-Pacific International Exposition. He served on the international jury of awards for fine arts, and he dedicates the book to John E. D. Trask, director of fine arts for the exposition, an untiring worker and able executive.

Contents open with an historical review and the function of art, then retrospective art and foreign nations. France, Italy, Portugal, Argentina, Uruguay, Cuba, the Philippines, Japan, China, Sweden, Holland, and Germany each receive notice. American one-man rooms follow, with Whistler, Twachtman, Tarbell, Redfield, Duveneck, Chase, Hassam, Melchers, Sargent, and Keith. Graphic arts, a conclusion, a bibliography, and an index close a useful guide for art lovers.
46750-prison-journals-during-the-french-:
The Duchesse de Duras's Prison Journals during the French Revolution, in Mrs Carey's translation, was published by Dodd, Mead of New York in 1892. The duchess, born a Noailles, wrote the journal in 1801. Addenda, Madame Latour's memoir, and accounts of the events of July 1794 fill out the volume, with her letter to Grelet and an extract from the Memorial Europeen of 1809.

The journal opens with the arrests. On August 23, 1793, she was taken with her father and mother at their chateau of Mouchy-le-Chatel, in the Oise. The prisons followed in order: Saint-Francois at Beauvais, in the old convent, that October; Chantilly from October 20; then Paris, and the College du Plessis, in April 1794. She was freed on October 19 of that year. The time in the prisons of the Terror, she says, was too harassing for the thought of writing it out at the time.
46751-the-strength-of-the-mormon-positio:
Orson Whitney wrote a plea for the strength of the Mormon faith stand. Whitney sat in the Council of the Twelve of his church. He starts with the gold angel on the Salt Lake Temple. That form blows a horn for the Gospel made whole once more. A verse from Revelation backs that claim in his text.

First church years are told as a tale of loss from truth. Twelve men were sent to preach to all the world, he says. In fifty years their word lit most of the known earth, he holds. Then came a fall, and in due time a fresh call. Whitney's case rests on that arc of fall and rise. Saints get a firm brief in his hand.
46871-dixie-martin-the-girl-of-woodford-:
Dixie Martin, the Girl of Woodford's Cañon is a girls' novel by Grace May North, published at Boston in 1924. Elisabeth Warren drew the illustrations. The book is dedicated to a schoolmate of the author's who was like her heroine. Chapter one rouses Carolina Martin, called Dixie, on the morning a new teacher starts at the old log schoolhouse at Woodford's. Her mother has called her a score of times. The family must not be late and be thought shiftless.

The contents run through a school year of small events. A new teacher, gossip, a queer bank, and a charity barrel fill the early chapters. Ken's secret sorrow and Carol's choice and disgrace carry the heart of the tale. A little runaway, a blizzard, and a mystery solved stand near the end. It is a wholesome school and home tale of its day.
46951-the-adventures-of-bobby-coon:
Thornton Burgess wrote a tale for young readers dated 1918 about Bobby Coon, a fat raccoon in the Green Forest. Prints by Harrison Cady show the woods folk at home. Bobby sleeps in a big hollow chestnut tree through the worst of the cold, kept warm by his own fat.

Late winter brings short naps and a loud, empty stomach that will not let him rest. Bobby holds that bad dreams come from that hunger, not from fairies good or bad. Tales of his prowls, his hunts for food, and his woodland friends make a warm first book on wild life for the young.
46974-rays-of-living-light-on-the-one-wa:
Penrose wrote ray talks on the one way to be saved in his faith. He names his church, the Latter-day Saints, on the title. The talks date to 1904 in this copy of his work. So many faiths claim to be right, his first ray starts. A sane mind may grow sick at the clash of creeds, he holds.

All the sects can not be right, he says with plain force. Truth keeps faith with its own self at all times, he argues. Fault is what breeds the clash of creeds in men's minds. Both foes may err, but both can not stand true at once. Each ray strikes one beam of light on his one road. Church folk get his case.
47043-the-alien-invasion:
The Alien Invasion is a volume in the Social Questions of To-Day series, written by Wilkins. The series came out at two shillings and sixpence a volume, each by an authority on its subject. Wilkins served as secretary to a body formed to prevent the immigration of destitute aliens. The Bishop of Bedford wrote an introductory note.

Neighboring volumes treat trade unionism, poverty, and the co-operative movement. Wilkins states his object at the start. He gathers the main facts on destitute immigration in a popular and readable form. He sets out the evils he sees in the system of his day. The book shows how immigration politics argued its case in the 1890s.
47050-the-slavery-question:
The Slavery Question is a tract gainst bond hold by John Lawrence, out in eighteen fifty four. A Dayton press of the United Brethren church made this third print. Lawrence wrote plain thoughts on hid groups and brief tracts on the same theme. Bond hold is a great sin and a vast wild wrong, his front words open. Its depth of ill can scarce be sounded by man, he adds in that plea.

Three heaps of bound folk cry out while the land moral sense sleeps sound. State rule in all its arms has bent to a slave lord ring, he charges. Great churches shield the wrong in place of the wronged, he adds. Sumner tag at the front says the talk will flare where folk meet. Home fire, high road, hall, and church are its set grounds there.
47165-fighting-the-sea-or-winter-at-the-:
Edward Rand wrote a boys story of winter at a life saving station, printed at New York in 1887. Away went the shot, the frontispiece cries from page three hundred nineteen. Rand gives the book to the brave surfmen of the United States Life Saving Service and their superintendent Kimball. Visiting a station on the coast and passing a night there, he became deeply interested in the work of the hardy crew, he says.

He read the service reports with keen pleasure. The heroic runs through those plain government pages and makes them luminous. He's got a ladder, the old boat builder Zebulon Smith shouts to his grandson in the tale. Wrecks, patrols, and rescues in winter seas fill a story meant to stir young readers' pride.
47204-the-supernatural-in-modern-english:
Supernatural in Modern English Fiction is a critical study by Dorothy Scarborough, published in 1917. Putnam Sons issued the book at New York and London in that year. Scarborough was instructor in English in extension at Columbia University in her title. Contents list an introduction and eight chapters for the survey of the field.

The Gothic Romance, Later Influences, and Modern Ghosts open the study in order of the chapters. The Devil and His Allies and Supernatural Life fill the middle of the contents.  Chapter one calls the Gothic novel the real precursor of supernaturalism in modern English literature. That odd form, she writes, might be called a brief in behalf of banished romance in her figure. Scarborough study was the first scholarly map of the ghostly in fiction, and it is still cited wherever the tale of terror is studied.
47226-left-half-harmon:
Ralph Henry Barbour wrote Left Half Harmon, copyrighted in 1921 and illustrated by Leslie Crump. Barbour also wrote Left End Edwards, Quarter-Back Bates, and Full-Back Foster. A frontispiece urges a player to go out and play full-back as it should be played. Twenty-four chapters open with The Three Guardsmen.

Kidnapped, held by the enemy, and Harmon coming to terms follow. The wrong boy, first days at Alton, and the coach's room lead to the boy in the green sweater. McNatt on science, Alton squeezing through, a first defeat, and a forty-yard run build the season. Onions, revenge, black paint, and evidence carry it to Alton celebrating. Readers get a prep-school football novel from the master of the form.
47308-the-sanitary-evolution-of-london:
The Sanitary Evolution of London is a history of public health by Henry Jephson. Jephson was a member of the London County Council. He dedicated the book to that council. The Brooklyn edition is dated 1907. A quote from the Registrar-General heads the text. Laws of health found in one city, it says, profit all. The contents run in seven dated chapters.

The chapters move from 1855 to 1906 by decades. A sketch map of London's districts opens the book. Water supply, drainage, and cleanliness drive the story. So do food, housing, and the isolation of the sick. London held so large a share of the nation, Jephson notes. Its health shaped the health of the kingdom. The book records how a vast city learned to keep itself clean. It stands as a civic reformer's own account.
47315-private-spud-tamson:
Private Spud Tamson is a war story by Captain R W Campbell, published at Edinburgh and London in nineteen sixteen. The hosted copy is a twelfth impression, a mark of wartime demand. Campbell dedicates the book to his commanding officer, brother officers, and the men of his regiment. A note explains that its Glasgow militia regiment is no single real unit.

The story is a composite study of the types who fill the ranks of militia regiments, Campbell states. Spud Tamson stands for the cheerful Glasgow ranker at the front in the Great War. Dialect, humour, and trench hardship carry the tale. Campbell promises a later portrait of the Territorials in the same spirit.
47434-infatuation:
Lloyd Osbourne wrote a novel dated 1909 about Phyllis Ladd, who loses her mother at the age of twelve. Grief sets the girl apart from her school friends, though she still plays and talks with zest. The loss also brings her close to her father, a grave and rich man she had known in the main from afar.

Robert Ladd heads a railway firm in the old town of Carthage, where sons step into the firms of their fathers. Wealth, kin ties, and town pride shape the world Phyllis grows up in. The first pages stress how a keen heart can be both a gift and a cost in life.
47525-aunt-crete-s-emancipation:
Aunt Crete's Emancipation is a novel by Grace Livingston Hill, writing as Hill Lutz, issued at Boston in 1911. Pictures by Clara Atwood run through the book. The contents open with a telegram and a flight, then bring in a backwoods cousin. A wonderful day and Aunt Crete transformed follow in the early chapters.

A niece named Luella and her mother are mystified, then face an embarrassing meeting and a humiliation in turn. The last chapter head gives Aunt Crete a partnership of her own. Picture captions echo the arc: a dismayed face watched with alarm, a beaming woman on a train, and at last Aunt Crete emancipated. The story turns on a poor relation lifted out of her place as the household drudge.
47635-alice-s-blighted-profession:
A one-act sketch for girls by Helen C Clifford. The Fitzgerald Publishing Corporation copyrighted it in 1919. Dick and Fitzgerald's successors issued it at New York. The playing time is fifty minutes. Its scene is a modern business office in New York City. Alice Berning, a young lawyer, sits at a paper-covered desk.

Her friend Diana bursts in like a steam engine. She invites Alice touring in her machine next week. Alice refuses: correspondence buries her, and no stenographer fits. Twenty-five applicants clamoured at her door that morning. Not one proved qualified for the work. A nervous stenographer and a vivacious one join the cast list. A suffragette, a Salvation Army lassie, and society women complete it. Such sketches supplied school and club entertainments.
47640-the-woman-gives-a-story-of-regener:
Owen Johnson wrote a novel published in September 1916, with pictures by Howard Chandler Christy, subtitled a story of regeneration. Johnson had written the Lawrenceville stories and The Spirit of France. A front picture shows a man's face with torment and a flicker of terror. The tale opens at Teagan's Arcade in New York.

The arcade stood where Broadway and Columbus Avenue meet at Lincoln Square, above the subway and elevated lines. It covered a block in the form of a huge letter H, six stories high. Pictures show a figure called King O'Leary and a woman tearing a composition to pieces. A character called the Baron cries for his hat and cane.
47670-a-sketch-of-the-life-and-times-of-:
An unnamed writer sketched the life and times of Judge Thomas Chandler Haliburton, author of The Clockmaker. The sketch appeared around his centenary, when no proper biography existed. Haliburton was born at Windsor, Nova Scotia, on December 17, 1796. The sketch traces his family back to the Haliburtons of Mertoun and Newmains, a Border family linked by marriage to the Scotts.

His ancestors crossed the Atlantic by way of Jamaica and Massachusetts. His grandfather settled in Nova Scotia when Acadian lands were offered to settlers. His father became Chief Justice of the Court of Common Pleas in the province. The younger Haliburton made Sam Slick, the clockmaker, famous across the English-speaking world. This short account gives readers the family background, the Nova Scotia setting, and the career of the man whose humorous books made him the best known Canadian writer of his century.
4774-the-merry-devil-of-edmonton:
The Merry Devil of Edmonton is an English play, opening with a list of persons mixing knights, priests, tradesmen, and spirits. Sir Arthur Clare, Sir Richard Mounchensey, and Sir Ralph Jerningham stand beside Henry, Raymond, and Frank. Sir John, a priest, Banks, the miller of Waltham, and Smug, the smith of Edmonton, join Bilbo, Blague the host, Brian, and Friar Hildersham. Coreb, a spirit, and Fabel, the merry devil himself, complete the list.

The prologue asks friends for silence and attention, so free spirits may relish the life of the active scene, calmed by invoking spells. It introduces Peter Fabell, a renowned scholar whose fame later writers forgot. Born in Middlesex not seven miles from London, he was called the merry friend of Edmonton for fame in sleights and magic. Lady Clare, Millisent, an abbess, and nuns complete the cast. Readers get an Elizabethan comedy of magic, love, and mischief.
47785-the-rock-of-the-lion:
The Rock of the Lion, by Molly Seawell, was published in 1897. Harper issued the novel in New York and London. Keller drew the illustrations. A sonnet by Woodberry, At Gibraltar, fronts the tale. Baskerville watches the Seahorse in the front plate. Chapter one opens at sunset on the Mediterranean. The Rock of Gibraltar stands afar like a couchant lion. It keeps watch over sea and land, Seawell writes. One thing escapes dwarfing beside it: a ship of the line, the Thunderer. She sweeps along under a mountain of canvas. England's ensign flies at her peak, and a homeward bound pennant streams at the main.

A hundred and twenty guns arm her hull; a thousand men fight them. Plates show Archy and hands extended to Paul Jones. The tale is a naval romance of the old wars.
47796-bygone-london:
Frederick Ross's Bygone London was published by Hutchinson and Company at Paternoster Square in 1892, in an edition of five hundred copies, this being number 12. Ross, author of Legendary Yorkshire, opens with a preface arguing that the history of London still remains to be written.

By London he means the small fraction north and south of the Thames under the Lord Mayor, not the vast spread of buildings across four or five counties. The contents run through the walls and gates, episodes in the annals of Cheapside, Bishopsgate Street within and without, Aldersgate Street and St Martin's-le-Grand, and Old Broad Street. Later chapters treat Chaucer and the Tabard, the Priory of the Holy Trinity at Aldgate, and the Barons Fitzwalter of Baynard's Castle.
47817-the-brand-a-tale-of-the-flathead-r:
Therese Broderick, writing as Tin Schreiner, wrote this tale of the Flathead Reservation, printed by the Alice Harriman Company of Seattle in 1909. Front ads list the house's western books, from Marcus Whitman to Reminiscences of Seattle. Chapter titles name the HW Ranch, the motley spectators at Polson, and a line of plain speech: I would have done more for an Injun.

Bess learns the real cause of an accident in chapter eight. Helen appears at the St. Ignatius grounds in a later title, cut off in the contents shown. The tale is set on the reservation in Montana, among ranch folk, agents, and the Flathead people themselves, in the Seattle publisher's line of northwestern tales.
47910-the-wasted-generation:
Owen Johnson wrote The Wasted Generation, issued in Boston in September 1921 and given to Hugh Walpole. Johnson was known for the Lawrenceville Stories and Stover at Yale. The tale opens on August 29, 1916, the narrator's thirtieth birthday. Guns roar along the Somme front as another attack begins.

Brigadier David Littledale of the Legion Etrangere was wounded at Verdun on March 5, with shell wounds and gangrene. He now rests in a Savoyard courtyard, putting on flesh and calming his nerves. From his open window he watches old soldiers peel potatoes and play cards. He frankly writes that he has no wish, that day, to hasten his return to the front.
4795-the-circassian-slave-or-the-sultan-:
Lieutenant Murray wrote The Circassian Slave, or The Sultan's Favorite, A Story of Constantinople and the Caucasus, published at Boston in 1851. A publisher's note says the novelette first appeared in The Pictorial Drawing Room Companion, as a specimen of entertaining tales gracing that journal's columns. Its contents run through fifteen chapters, from The Slave Market and The Sultan's Harem to The Bedouin Arabs and Vales of Circassia.

The Slave Ship, A Singular Meeting, and The Sultan's Prisoner follow, with Punishment of the Sack, The Lover's Stratagem, and The Serenade. The Elopement, The Struggle for Life, and The Escape from the Harem lead to The Chase and a Happy Conclusion. Its preface says the story concerns that exceedingly interesting and romantic portion of the world bordering on the Black Sea, where Circassia meets the Ottoman capital. Readers get a mid-century Oriental romance of slavery, harem intrigue, and escape.
48020-aurora-floyd-vol-1-fifth-edition:
Volume one of Aurora Floyd, by M E Braddon, author of Lady Audley's Secret, in a fifth edition published at London in 1863. The contents open with how a rich banker married an actress.

Archibald Martin Floyd, of the Lombard Street banking house, owns the great red-brick Kentish mansion whose windows blaze in the August sunset. The chapters introduce Aurora, ask what became of the diamond bracelet, and follow the ball. John Mellish appears, is rejected and accepted, and returns poor and patient. Aurora's strange pensioner and Steeve Hargraves the softy darken the tale, and the volume ends at the spring meeting. Braddon opens her sensation novel in a blaze of landscape. Readers get the famous bigamy mystery begun.
48021-aurora-floyd-vol-2-fifth-edition:
M E Braddon wrote Aurora Floyd, in three volumes, of which this is the second. Tinsley Brothers issued this fifth edition at London in 1863. Braddon was the author of Lady Audley's Secret. The volume opens with a chapter headed by a line on love turning the glass of time. Mr Pastern's letter, Mr James Conyers, and the trainer's messenger follow. Out in the rain and money matters come next.

Captain Prodder enters, and carries bad news to his niece's house midway. The deed that had been done in the wood closes the contents. The first chapter brings Talbot Bulstrode to Mellish Park for two days. He hates himself for the concession: a visitor in his rival's house, watching Aurora's everyday happiness. Then he goes back to the Cornish miners and his bachelor's lodgings.
48022-aurora-floyd-vol-3-fifth-edition:
Aurora Floyd, volume three, was written by Braddon. Tinsley Brothers published this fifth edition in London in 1863. The full sensation novel runs to three volumes. Braddon had won her fame with Lady Audley's Secret. Fourteen chapters fill this last volume. The first is set at the Golden Lion. Constable William Dork reaches Doncaster in the small hours after a murder. The Reindeer hotel is shut, and his office must force a hearing. A young driver tells what he knows: he drove a seafaring gentleman straight to the station. The man caught the mail-train with three minutes to spare.

A half sovereign paid for the speed. Chapters promise Aurora's flight and a desolate home. The weapon that slew James Conyers is discovered. A brass button made by Crosby of Birmingham gives a clue.
48032-the-magic-ring-and-other-stories-f:
The Magic Ring and Other Stories, edited by Andrew Lang, gathers tales from the Yellow and Crimson Fairy Books in a Longmans impression of 1906. Henry Ford illustrated it, with a coloured frontispiece of Ilonka left with the swineherd. Thirteen stories stand in the contents. The Magic Ring, The White Duck, Lovely Ilonka, and Clever Maria lead them. The Language of Beasts, The Cat and the Mouse in Partnership, The Six Swans, and The Emperor's New Clothes stand among the rest.

The title tale opens with Martin, whose dying father leaves two hundred florins; his mother sends him to town with a hundred to lay in meal for a year. At the meat-market he finds butchers flogging a stag-hound tied to a post, and intervenes from pity. Lang's coloured fairy books mined the world's folk tales, and this selection mixes Grimm staples with Hungarian and other sources.
48083-history-of-the-war-in-afghanistan-:
John William Kaye writes History of the War in Afghanistan, volume 1 of 3, in a third edition printed in London in 1874. Allen, publishers to the India Office, made the book. Kaye gives the set to the officers of the Bengal Artillery.

A note to this edition tells its lineage. The text repeats the three volume edition of 1857, much revised at the time. Chief actors in the scenes helped Kaye mend the work, he says. Just one claimed error has reached him since, the note adds. His gift page names men famed in the Afghan War rolls, Pollock, Macgregor, and Lawrence among them. War history fans get a grave, sourced first volume.
48089-the-fall-of-a-nation-a-sequel-to-t:
The Fall of a Nation, by Thomas Dixon, is a novel offered as a sequel to The Birth of a Nation. Dixon had written The Clansman and The Southerner. Appleton published the book in New York and London in 1916, with pictures by Charles Wrenn.

A note to the reader states the aim. The tale is not, Dixon says, a mere rehash of a foreign conquest of America. It is a study of the origin, meaning, and destiny of American democracy, meant to revive the principles on which the republic was founded. The prologue opens in Scotland, where humble worshippers stand before the king's soldiers, guilty of worshipping God by their own conscience. Pictures show a hail of bullets from every window, an artillery battery clearing barricades, and a woman flyer circling to fire again.
48193-commentary-on-genesis-vol-1-luther:
Luther on the Creation, a critical and devotional commentary on Genesis, is the first Genesis volume of the Precious and Sacred Writings of Martin Luther. John Nicholas Lenker edited it in complete form, revising and enlarging Henry Cole's translation from the original Latin. Lutherans in All Lands published it at Minneapolis in 1904.

The series rests on the Kaiser chronological edition, with reference to the Erlangen and Walch editions. A second introduction reports the movement to translate and circulate Luther in English. The first volume, on the Psalms, sold quickly, the editor writes with gratitude. This Genesis volume follows because the books should appear first that are needed most. Lenker, a professor of Old Testament exegesis, argues the need twice over: Luther's place in the public library, and his rank among the Greek and Latin fathers.
48258-the-old-dominion:
Mary Johnston wrote a romance of old Virginia, issued in London in 1907 in its eleventh printing. First printings date from January 1899, and the book kept its crowd for years. Johnston gave the tale to her father.

A girl in a green gown with pink roses watches a sloop tack up a creek off Chesapeake Bay. Chapter heads name its cargo, a dinner party in the colony, a hut on the marsh, and a mender of nets. A man named Landless woos, plots, pays the piper, and fights at the end. A duel, a peace pipe, and a bridge of rock mark the path of the tale.
48323-the-roman-poets-of-the-republic-2n:
The Roman Poets of the Republic, by Sellar, professor of humanity at Edinburgh, appeared in a new edition, revised and enlarged, at Oxford in 1881. The Clarendon Press issued the work. Sellar had been a fellow of Oriel College, Oxford, before his chair. A corrigenda list at the front has been folded into the text.

His survey treats the Latin poets before the empire in their order. Ennius, Lucretius, and Catullus stand among the great names of that age. Plautus and Terence bring the comic stage into the account. Sellar weighs style, life, and the growth of Roman verse. His book long served as the standard English guide to the subject. Students of Latin met the republic through his chapters.
48328-coca-and-its-therapeutic-applicati:
Angelo Mariani's Coca and Its Therapeutic Application reached a third edition from Jaros at New York in 1896. A testimonial from Corning of New York fronts the book, praising the coca wine Vin Mariani for brain trouble and worry. The title page follows, with a branch of the coca plant pictured from Mariani's own hothouses. Mariani dedicates the pages to the medical profession. His laboratory at Neuilly, outside Paris, grows coca plants in all stages and species.

Physicians are cordially invited to visit and inspect the work. All illustrations were drawn from life under Mariani's direction. The introduction sets coca among the world's habits: the Indian munches betel, the Chinaman takes opium, the European smokes tobacco. The South American native, by happier instinct, chose coca. Without it he would fear vertigo on the Andean summits and weaken in the mines. The book is part botany, part medical brief, part advertisement.
48329-history-of-sanitation:
History of Sanitation is a book on the clean craft of towns by Cosgrove. His past books on the pipe craft, on the clean of waste wa ter, and on pipe plans are named past his name. A great house of the clean craft put the book out at a mill town. Its rights were held in nineteen hundred and nine. A set of words on its full page plates stands near the front.

Those plate words give the span of the book in brief. An old spring of Rome in a town of Greece heads them. Its pipes and stone work date from the days of the first faith, the word says. It stood there when a great teach man lived and taught in that town.
48356-elsie-at-ion:
Elsie at Ion, by Martha Finley, was printed in New York by Dodd, Mead and Company under an 1893 copyright. A list of the Elsie books stands at the front. The set runs from Elsie Dinsmore through Elsie Holidays at Roselands, Elsie Girlhood, and Elsie Womanhood, to Elsie and Her Loved Ones.

The list adds the Mildred Keith books, Casella, Signing the Contract and What It Cost, and the Tragedy of Wild River Valley. The tale opens in talk between Violet and Lulu. For some moments neither had spoken, then Violet broke the silence. She had been thinking of poor Mrs McAlpine and her daughter, whom Lulu met when her father took her and Max out to the far West. Girls of the day got one more volume of the long Elsie family story.
48439-a-book-of-the-west-volume-1-devon:
Baring-Gould wrote A Book of the West, volume one on Devon, printed in London in 1899 with thirty-five pictures. The volume serves as a doorway to Devon and Cornwall. A list at the front names his other works, among them a life of Napoleon, Songs of the West, and The Vicar of Morwenstow. He signs the book from Lew Trenchard House, Devon, in June 1899. Contents open with the western folk, then villages and churches.

Honiton, a landslip, and Exeter follow. Crediton, Tiverton, Barnstaple, and Bideford take their chapters. Dartmoor and its old remains fill one chapter, and its tenants another. Okehampton, Moreton Hampstead, Ashburton, and Tavistock come in turn. Torquay, Totnes, Dartmouth, Kingsbridge, and Plymouth close the volume. The picture list names Sweet Hay-Makers at the front, Clovelly fishermen, Sheepstor, and Honiton lace among its plates.
48491-views-of-st-paul-s-cathedral-londo:
Views of Saint Paul's Cathedral, London, pairs photographs of the cathedral with notes by Sparrow Simpson. Freeman Dovaston photographed and published the book from Ealing. The first view is the western facade, and the notes begin with dates: the first stone was laid by Christopher Wren and his master mason on June 21, 1675.

The last stone of the lantern above the dome was laid in 1710 by the architect's son, born a year before the first stone, in his father's presence. Dimensions follow from the official guide: exterior length 515 feet, width across the transepts 250 feet, and total height to the top of the cross 365 feet. The whole cost seems to have been about a million pounds. The dome, one quoted critic says, has been justly called the very crown of England's architectural glory.
48517-mother-stories-from-the-book-of-mo:
William A Morton retold tales from the Book of Mormon for young readers in Mother Stories from the Book of Mormon. Morton had also written a child life of the Savior and a gospel primer. He wrote from Salt Lake City, in Utah. The tales open as if a mother speaks to her child at night.

The first tale tells of Lehi, his wife Sariah, and their four sons. Nephi and Sam obey, while Laman and Lemuel do wrong and vex their kin. Later tales tell how Nephi got the good book and built a ship. Tales of Zeniff, the sons of Mosiah, and a visit by Christ fill the rest. The book ends with peace, then the last of the Nephites.
48563-interpretations-of-poetry-and-reli:
George Santayana wrote essays on poetry and religion, issued in New York in 1900. Charles Scribner's Sons brought out Interpretations of Poetry and Religion that year. Ten essays run from the Homeric Hymns to the parts and work of poetry. Emerson and a religion of disillusion stand near the close.

Santayana first weighs grasp, fancy, and mystic thought in the human mind. He grants that our hold on the world is slight and our systems shaky. The fall of pagan faith and the poetry of Christian dogma get cool, clear study. Readers gain bold thought on how verse and faith shape each other.
48588-english-industries-of-the-middle-a:
English Industries of the Middle Ages is an introduction to the working history of medieval England by Salzmann. It was published in London by Constable in 1913. The author had written Medieval Byways before it.

The chapters take the trades one by one. Mining comes first: coal, iron, lead and silver, and tin. Quarrying of stone, marble, alabaster, and chalk follows. Metal-working, pottery and brick, clothmaking, and leather work each get a chapter. Brewing of ale, beer, and cider stands near the end. A last chapter treats the control of industry by guild and town. The coal chapter opens with a surprise. The Romans burned coal all along their Wall in Britain. The use then died out for more than a thousand years.
48589-humanitarian-philosophy-4th-editio:
