Humanitarian Philosophy is a book of short sayings against killing, drawn from the letters of Emil Edward Kusel and printed at Los Angeles in 1912, in its fourth edition. Three texts stand at the head. One is the Bible's command, thou shalt not kill. One is a word from Mary Baker Eddy, that the God-made self does not eat flesh. One is Buddha's charge to kill not, but have regard for life.

In his note, Kusel says he meant no slight on readers who love the kind passages of the Testaments. He aimed to prove that the old law giving man leave to kill is no law of a kind and loving God. The flesh-eating religionist, he holds, shares in a crime most beastly in God's sight. Kind words from readers fill the front pages.
48673-elementary-composition:
Elementary Composition is a school book on the writ craft by Dorothea Canfield and George Carpenter. She had been the clerk of a set of schools named for a great man of the age. He held a chair of speech and of the writ craft at a great school of New York. The book was first put out in nineteen hundred and six. The host print is of nineteen eighteen.

The list of parts gives the path of the drill. A lead in heads the run. The line of words, the block of lines, and words them selves come next. Short form, long form, and the re word of a next man's work fill the next part. Whole works and their plans, and speech works, stand past them. Then come the kinds of writ in their turn.
48716-the-history-of-the-36th-ulster-div:
The History of the 36th (Ulster) Division is a record of that unit in the Great War. Lines from Virgil and from Chaucer stand at its front. The Virgil lines speak to comrades who have known past ills and worse, and hold that God will give an end to these as well. The Chaucer lines tell of a man who had been in chevauchées in Flanders, Artois, and Picardy, and bore himself well.

A note by the transcriber states the rules of the text. Italics are marked by underscores, and a raised figure by a caret sign. The form of times, with a hyphen, has been kept as printed. Clear slips of print and marks have been set right by check with the rest of the book and with outside sources. The work is the formal history of a division raised in Ulster.
48876-outlines-of-creation:
Outlines of Creation, by Elisha Noyce, was printed by Ward and Lock at London in 1858, with four hundred cuts by the Brothers Dalziel. Noyce also wrote The Boy's Book of Industrial Information. His plan sorts the world in groups, and the first is the sky: what stars are, the sun and its spots, the planets in their rounds, and comets. The moon's phases and Saturn's rings each get their due.

The air comes next: its weight, the glass that tells storms, dew, clouds, and lightning. Then the earth in depth: strata, faults, granite, and chalk. Trilobites, the great sea lizards, and the mammoth walk the old lists. Young science fans get the whole frame of the world in one clear, well cut book of the age.
49011-the-annals-of-the-barber-surgeons-:
Sidney Young compiled The Annals of the Barber-Surgeons of London from the guild’s own records. Blades, East and Blades issued the book in London in eighteen hundred ninety. Austin T Young drew its plates of kings and halls. Young sat on the Court of Assistants of the Barber’s Company.

Eight years of spare hours went to the work, Young tells us. Leave to search the records came from his own court first. Each line was copied by his own pen, he takes care to say. Thirteen charters and by law sets passed through his hands. Near one hundred books of record got a full reading too. The British Museum and the Record Office lent more stores. Old London’s guilds laid the base of its wealth, he holds. Style must yield to matter in such a store house book.
49206-rudiments-of-conchology-intended-a:
Rudiments of Conchology is a familiar introduction to the science of shells, with explanatory plates and references to the shell collection in the British Museum. Darton and Harvey printed this new and improved edition in London in 1837. Its anonymous compiler drew chiefly on Lamarck's Conchology and on Burrows's Elements of Conchology.

The teaching runs as family talk. Lucy shows her brother Charles a box of shells, a gift from their cousin Jane, and their father joins the lesson. Linnaeus, the father explains, divided shells into three great classes: multivalves, bivalves, and univalves. Charles asks to be shown bivalve shells and to learn their forms, and the dialogue carries the young student on from there.
49230-millbank-penitentiary-an-experimen:
Arthur Griffiths, late inspector of prisons in Great Britain, recounts Millbank Penitentiary as an experiment in reformation, in a Grolier Society volume limited to one thousand numbered sets. This copy is number 307.

The first chapter tells how Jeremy Bentham bought the Tothill Fields site and the great prison rose on marshy ground by the river, opening in 1816. Chapters follow the early management, a great epidemic, serious disturbances, and ingenious escapes. The women's wards, the Millbank calendar of punishments, and the prison's last days close the history. Illustrations show the penitentiary at Westminster and Dartmoor prisoners. Temple Bar, the old gateway by the Temple, serves as frontispiece.
49344-the-queen-s-favourite-a-story-of-t:
Eliza Pollard tells The Queen's Favourite, a story of the Restoration, for Blackie and Son in London, Glasgow, and Bombay in 1907. Frances Ewan drew the pictures, and Pollard had written The Doctor's Niece and The Lady Isobel. Twenty-three chapters run from the king's return to Home at Last, through plague and fire.

Chapter one sits in the Louvre, where widowed Henrietta Maria keeps her black mourning for her murdered husband Charles the First. Her daughter, sixteen and never having seen her father's face, leans on the chair as a messenger kneels with news from Holland. A deputation from England has invited Charles the Second to take the throne that cost his father his life. Contents promise Newgate, a great sea fight, the Great Plague, and London on fire.
49350-my-three-years-in-a-german-prison:
My Three Years in a German Prison is a war memoir by Henri Beland. Beland was a Canadian member of parliament and a doctor. William Briggs published the book at Toronto in 1919. Photographs secured in Belgium and Germany illustrate it. A portrait shows the author in a Berlin prison yard in 1917.

The contents trace his captivity in order. The war caught him in Belgium with his wife. He did hospital work as the Germans advanced. Antwerp fell and the exodus followed. Chapters then take him into Germany and the Stadtvogtei prison. He acted as jail physician there. Sensational escapes and talk of exchange fill the later pages. Liberty comes in the final chapters.
49447-history-of-the-war-in-afghanistan-:
History of the War in Afghanistan, volume two of three, is a war history by John William Kaye. The hosted copy is the third edition, published in London in eighteen seventy four for the India Office. Kaye's initials and fellowship mark his standing as a historian of British India. The other two volumes are held as companion ebooks, as a note states.

The war was Britain's disastrous Afghan campaign, and this middle volume carries its central course. Policy, marches, battles, and retreat are told from records and reports by a writer close to the India Office world. Kaye's history long stood as the standard English account. Volume two holds the heart of a cautionary imperial tale.
49467-radiation:
Radiation, by P Phillips, is a short textbook on radiant heat and light for students of physics. It was published in London in 1912.

The first chapter argues that heat and light share the same nature, both crossing empty space from the sun and bending and bouncing in the same ways. Chapters follow on drawing waves, the meaning of the spectrum, and the laws that govern radiation. Full radiation, the change of soaked-up radiation into other forms, and the pressure that radiation exerts each get a chapter. The last chapter links radiant heat to electric waves, the bridge on which the physics of the day was crossing toward the modern picture. An index closes the book.
49472-the-old-dominion:
James wrote The Old Dominion, a tale of Virginia, reissued in London in 1903 with an introduction by Laurie Magnus. The author, George Payne Rainsford James, had been Historiographer Royal to King William the Fourth. Magnus sketches a life of huge output and wide travel.

James wrote upwards of a hundred novels and edited nearly as many volumes of letters and lives. Scott encouraged him, Washington Irving admired him, and Thackeray twice burlesqued him. He ended his days as British consul at Venice after posts in America. Magnus argues that his work bears selection and revival despite his great output. The tale itself carries readers into old Virginia in the historical romance manner James helped to found.
49489-the-boy-s-book-of-industrial-infor:
Elisha Noyce published The Boy's Book of Industrial Information with Ward and Lock of Fleet Street in 1858. The Brothers Dalziel engraved its three hundred and sixty-five illustrations. A composite of industrial scenes makes the illustrated title page.

Noyce's preface states his object plainly. He supplies a clear and brief description of the materials, processes, and apparatus used in the industry and skill constantly before our eyes. The reader is to gain knowledge, and with it an interest in the workers whose hard work and patient ingenuity supply the world. Mere trades and handicrafts are avoided, as unprofitable to describe. Everything else (mills, mines, machines, manufactures) is fair game. The book is Victorian improvement at its best: industry explained to the boy who would soon be working in it, or buying from it.
49524-knowledge-for-the-time-a-manual-of:
John Timbs wrote Knowledge for the Time, a manual of reading, reference, and conversation on subjects of living interest, issued in London by Lockwood and Company in MDCCCLXIV. Timbs, a fellow of the Society of Antiquaries, had earlier written Curiosities of London and Things Not Generally Known. A plate shows Captain Coles new iron turret ship of war. Chapters range over historico political information, progress of civilization, dignities, laws, science, health, and religious thought.

The great value of contemporary history, written by actual witnesses, is now beginning to be appreciated, Timbs opens. Improved journalism is the best evidence of this advancement, he says. Truth is not of such easy acquisition as is generally supposed, he warns. Trustworthiness in written records grows with freedom of thought, he holds. General readers get a Victorian fact book for talk and reference.
49570-historical-record-of-the-first-or-:
Richard Cannon compiled the Historical Record of the First or Royal Regiment of Foot under a royal scheme for regimental histories. General orders from Horse Guards, dated January 1, 1836, set out the plan. William the Fourth ordered the work, and Queen Victoria later gave her patronage.

Each record must give a regiment's formation, its stations, and its battles and sieges. Names of officers and men killed or wounded belong in the account, with place and date. Gallant men who won titles or medals are named, as are badges and their causes. Cannon's series aimed to do full justice to regiments and to the men who served in them.
49648-red-rock-a-chronicle-of-reconstruc:
Thomas Nelson Page wrote this novel, Red Rock, a chronicle of Reconstruction, printed at New York in 1899 with pictures by Clinedinst. Page dedicates the book to an old-fashioned lady. A preface in the author's own voice sets the scene before the story starts, and argues the case of the people it portrays.

The region of the Grays and Carys lies too far from modern progress to be found on any map, Page says. It is the South, in one of the old states, in the land of memory. It was a goodly land of rolling country at the foot of blue mountain spurs, rich meadows, fat cattle, and bright streams. Its people were the product of a fallen system, and Page defends them warmly as rulers who bore defeat with splendid fortitude.
49663-adonijah-a-tale-of-the-jewish-disp:
Jane Margaret Strickland wrote Adonijah, a tale of the Jewish dispersion, published in London by Simpkin and Marshall. A Byron lament for those who wept by Babel's stream stands at the front. The frontispiece shows the hero's crisis: Adonijah no longer sees Lucia Claudia as the beloved of his heart, but as an idolatrous heathen priestess.

The preface fixes the ground. The reigns from Nero to Vespasian hold two great events, she writes: the first great persecution of the Christian church, and the fall of the Jewish state. Titus destroyed Jerusalem, and a whole nation scattered into long sorrow and oppression. Strickland sets her love story inside that ruin: a Hebrew hero, a Roman priestess, and the year the Temple fell. Readers of religious romance get the siege generation told as a tale of faith pulling two lovers apart.
4967-luck-or-cunning-as-the-main-means-o:
Samuel Butler's Luck or Cunning asks whether living things change mainly by luck or by intelligent design within nature itself. The second edition reprints the first of 1887, published in November 1886, with an enlarged index drawn from the author's own annotated copy, passed on by his literary executor.

Butler argues against a purely mechanical Darwinism, crediting organisms with memory, habit, and a kind of cunning in shaping their own evolution. The dedication honors the friend at whose instigation the book began. Readers get a Victorian argument about evolution that still provokes, written with Butler's combative wit and independence.
49681-the-constable-de-bourbon:
William Ainsworth opens his novel The Constable de Bourbon in the Forest of Fontainebleau in early June 1523. Three hundred gentlemen in black velvet with gold chains ride toward the palace. Their lord's badge, a sword in gold, marks his rank as Constable of France.

The leader is thirty-three, tall, dark-eyed, and stern, with a long black beard and a collar of the order of Saint Michael. Ainsworth paints him as a hardy warrior, not a court gallant of François I. He had shown skill in the field and could lead hosts to conquest. The first book is called The Affront, and pride and insult drive the tale from this proud entry.
49684-puck-on-pegasus-fourth-edition:
Puck on Pegasus, a book of comic and grave verse by Pennell, reached a fourth edition with Routledge in 1862. Leech, Phiz, Portch, and Tenniel drew the pictures, and George Cruikshank supplied the frontispiece. The preface thanks critics warmly and notes that slight pieces were dropped and graver ones put in their place.

The change came because two serious poems, The Night Mail North and Derby Day, won wide praise. The first poem stages Euston Square in 1840, with latecomers beating at the gate as the Glasgow mail pulls out. Pennell signs his preface from Weybridge on 20 May, 1862.
49701-the-mysteries-of-modern-london:
The Mysteries of Modern London, by George Sims, was printed in London in 1906 with a colour frontispiece. Sims had written How the Poor Live and other studies of the city's underside. His first chapter maps the ground the book will cover.

A mystery, Sims says, is what cannot be easily explained, and London's mysteries are as the sands of the shore. Some are blazoned in headlines, and some are guarded by men in high places. Mansions and garrets alike hide tales of criminal romance that pass as daily fare. The great river, he warns, hides more than the Seine ever gave up to the Paris morgue. Many end with a found drowned notice, an inquest, and a pauper's funeral. Sims sets out to tell the tales behind those flat endings.
49707-the-sure-to-rise-cookery-book-is-e:
The Sure to Rise Cookery Book was published by Edmonds, a baking powder maker of Christchurch. The Christchurch Press printed this third edition in 1914, post free to any address. That edition is marked at one hundred and fifty thousand copies. All recipes with baking powder were tested with Edmonds' Prize powder, the book warns. Other brands are not vouched for, since powders are not all made alike.

Contents open with scones of many kinds: ginger, cinnamon, girdle, tea, and Scotch. Caraway biscuits, brown scones, sultana scones, and plain scones follow in the list. A page praises custard with milk pudding for hot, sultry weather. Stewed peaches, pears, or apricots with custard tempt the appetite then, it says. Children may have all the custards they want, like Oliver Twist asking for more. The book gives everyday recipes and cooking hints for New Zealand homes.
49746-motor-matt-in-brazil-or-under-the-:
Street and Smith issued a weekly tale of motor adventure in New York on June 26, 1909, priced at five cents. Motor Matt, a lad at home with all kinds of motors, sails with Dick Ferral and Carl Pretzel. Ensign Glennie rides for the United States government on the ship Grampus.

The crew heads for Georgetown, then Para in Brazil, and the Amazon. Chapter heads promise a whale, a dive for safety, a fight hand to hand, and a boarding. Consul Brigham at Para helps the lads, while a foe named Tolo and the crew of a strange submarine drive the risk.
49747-the-evolution-of-modern-orchestrat:
Louis Adolphe Coerne traces The Evolution of Modern Orchestration for Macmillan in New York in 1908. Three parts divide the history: preliminaries, the classic era, and romanticism, with an appendix of musical illustrations and an index. An introductory note argues the age of specialisation needed such a history at last.

Treatises abound, the note grants, Berlioz's revised by Strauss, plus Gevaërt, Hofmann, and Prout, but they teach the creative musician rather than the historical inquirer. Coerne's chapters run from the cradle of instrumental music through Bach and Handel, Gluck, and Haydn, Mozart, and Beethoven. The romantic part then treats the new movement and national schools in France, Italy, Hungary, Bohemia, Scandinavia, Russia, England, and America.
49749-isla-heron:
Isla Heron is a prose idyl by Laura E Richards, printed at Boston by Estes and Lauriat and shown here in its fifth thousand. Frank T Merrill drew the plates. Richards had also written Captain January, Melody, Marie, and Nautilus.

The house list calls the book a charming idyl of quaint New England life, and Richards won her niche by her fine touch with village life in that region. Press notes praise her sweet, plain tales of rustic folk, full of clear character and true human feeling. Isla Heron stands in that line, a small tale of coast folk told with grace. Readers who like quiet New England tales of home and heart will find her manner at its best here.
49835-the-letters-of-gracchus-on-the-eas:
The Letters of Gracchus on the East India Question were printed at London in 1813 for Hatchard of Piccadilly, number 190. The letters had appeared in the Morning Post at the dates annexed to them. An advertisement tells the impartial reader what to expect. Gracchus upholds the public rights of the country in the India trade. He does not seek to lower the just and well-earned honours of the East India Company.

The first letter, dated Tuesday, January 12, 1813, gives a general view of the question. The crisis, Gracchus writes, involves the most important interests of the British empire. The term approaches that may conclude the Company's rights to the exclusive trade with India and China, and its powers of government. The public, suddenly appealed to, stands unprepared with knowledge of the true circumstances, and the letters mean to recover the time lost.
49895-manual-of-library-economy-third-an:
The Manual of Library Economy is the standard British handbook of librarianship by James Duff Brown. This third and memorial edition was revised and rewritten by W C Berwick Sayers after Brown's death. Brown had been chief librarian of the Islington public libraries. Sayers held the same post at Croydon and lectured in the University of London school of librarianship.

Brown's other works include Subject Classification and a biographical dictionary of musicians. Sayers wrote the Canons of Classification and books on children's libraries. Between them they cover the whole economy of a public library: buildings, staff, cataloguing, classification, and service. The manual trained generations of British librarians in their craft. A memorial edition, carried on by the author's leading disciple, is itself a piece of library history. Few professions possess so complete a founding handbook.
5-the-united-states-constitution:
The founding charter of the United States took shape in Philadelphia in 1787. Its preamble promises a more perfect union, justice, domestic peace, and the blessings of liberty. The articles that follow divide power among Congress, the president, and the courts.

Legislative powers come first, with a Senate and House set out in detail. Later articles cover the executive, the judiciary, relations among states, and amendment. This hosted edition presents the original articles without the later amendments. It remains the working frame of American government. Citizens still cite its articles in debates over power, rights, and the shape of government.
5002-the-rover-boys-in-business-or-the-s:
Arthur M. Winfield's Rover Boys in Business sends Sam, Tom, and Dick Rover from school themes and moonlight visits to Hope Seminary into the world of work. Sam worries over a theme due tomorrow, Tom proposes an auto trip to see the girls, and the brothers soon face a harder problem: the search for missing bonds.

Business, rather than boating, drives this volume, as the Rovers hunt for securities whose loss threatens their father's affairs. School loyalty and brotherly teasing carry them through. Readers get a boys' series novel where ledgers and offices replace rivers and camps, but the Rover spirit stays the same.
50029-the-story-of-the-book-of-mormon:
The Story of the Book of Mormon is a faith tale by Elder Reynolds, in its fourth form. He was the author of past works on the faith, on a found hand script tale, and on the Book of Abraham. A line from a Psalm heads the book: truth shall spring out of the earth.

Its print was held in law in the late eighteen eighties and set at Chicago. The front print shows the rise of Christ to the Nephites, from a paint in a temple of the faith. The text then sets out its case from the first years: America the first land peopled, the garden of Eden, the old world folk, and the first peoples of the new land.
5005-journal-of-an-overland-expedition-i:
Ludwig Leichhardt's journal of an overland expedition from Moreton Bay to Port Essington records a journey into Australia's wilderness in dated chapters. The party leaves the last station, crosses the Darling Downs and Waterloo Plains, endures heavy rains on the Condamine, and loses then finds Murphy and Caleb after a frightening separation.

Later chapters reduce the party, meet friendly Aboriginal people, pass native tombs, and follow the Dawson through ranges and creeks toward the north. Leichhardt notes fossils, coal, and country with a naturalist's care. Readers get a foundational Australian exploration journal, told day by day from inside a long and perilous trek.
50119-the-rocket-the-story-of-the-stephe:
Knight wrote a short life of the Stephensons, father and son, for boys, printed in 1897 with twenty-six prints. A first note warns boys that good work grows from good traits, yet traits alone can not save a soul. Life in the coal pits, clock mending, and the safety lamp fill the youth of George.

Puffing Billy, a prize for the best engine, and a bog that balked the road mark the rise of the railway. Robert comes home to build the prize engine, and the new road opens to great cheer. A late day of honor for the Stephensons closes a tale of grit, skill, and faith.
50123-the-river-motor-boat-boys-on-the-c:
River Motor Boat Boys on the Columbia, or the Confession of a Photograph, is a boys adventure tale by Harry Gordon. Burt published the book in New York in 1913, as its copyright page states. Gordon is named as author of sister volumes on the Saint Lawrence, the Colorado, the Mississippi, the Amazon, and the Ohio. A frontispiece shows the boat at full speed ahead.

Chapter titles promise mountains, trails, and a camera at the heart of the plot. Early chapters cross the mountains in a motor boat and give Captain Joe a trail to follow. Alex finds use for his Kodak, and the party mourns an empty Kodak. The tale opens with the motor boat Rambler at the very summit of the Rocky Mountains. She is not in a lake and not in motion there. That puzzle is what the first chapter sets out to explain.
50177-the-fourth-generation:
The Fourth Generation is a novel by Walter Besant, told in parts. The copy here is a fourth print, made in New York. The rights date from 1899 and 1900 in the front of the book. It opens on a bleak March day in the English countryside.

The first part is named for a far-off forebear of the clan. The tale then asks what the next in line wants of life. A lost son comes home in one of the mid parts. A girl named Mary Anne takes a part of her own in the tale. A book of clippings and a talk with a wise head move the plot. The last parts turn on a will and on signs of change. The name of the tale points to the fourth line of the house.
50192-the-boy-scouts-for-home-protection:
The Boy Scouts for Home Protection, by Scout Master Robert Shaler, was issued at New York by Hurst in 1915. A long list of his scout books stands at the front of the volume. Boy Scouts of the Signal Corps and of Pioneer Camp head that list. The Life Saving Crew, Picket Duty, and the Flying Squadron follow.

The Naval Reserve, the Great Flood, and the Field Hospital swell the run. Forest fire fighters and county fair guides stand among his titles. In this volume the scouts guard the home front, as its name declares. America was watching Europe’s war in 1915 and drilling its boys. Shaler turned every civic duty of the hour into a scout adventure. The series sold steadiness, skill, and patriotism to boys.
50260-the-motor-rangers-wireless-station:
The Motor Rangers' Wireless Station is a boys' adventure novel by Marvin West, published in New York by Hurst and Company in 1913. Charles Wrenn drew the illustrations. The frontispiece shows a flash of flame and the roar of an explosion. The contents open at The Wireless Island. A passenger for the shore, a storm, and a failed engine follow in quick steps. Nat to the rescue stands as chapter five. The heroes are three boys: Nat Trevor, Joe Hartley, and Ding-dong Bell.

Their camp sits on Goat Island, in a portable wood and canvas house. The drowsy calm of an afternoon breaks with the clang of the wireless alarm bell. Something is doing at last, Nat cries. The boys had feared a dull holiday of sea breeze and tan. West gives them peril by wire and by sea, in the brisk series way.
50318-after-the-pardon:
After the Pardon is a novel by Matilde Serao, issued by the Stuyvesant Press in 1909. A foreword praises how the romance pictures Latin love in its ravishing fierceness. Passion, it says, bends Latins beyond all laws, duties, and vows in the tale. Jealousy, base and physical, is confused with ardent love in her people.

Contents divide the novel into three parts with Latin titles for two of them. Solis Occasu opens, The Pardon makes the middle, and Usque Ad Mortem closes. The author gifts reach into souls and animal humanity alike, the foreword claims. Serao Neapolitan passion reaches English readers in this period translation.
50342-history-of-the-war-in-afghanistan-:
History of the War in Afghanistan, volume three, is the closing volume of John William Kaye's history of the First Afghan War. The third edition was published by Allen in London in 1874. This volume covers the disaster's end and the British recovery of 1841 and 1842. Its first chapter treats the efforts at retrieval and the close of Lord Auckland's administration, with the appointment of General Pollock.

The second chapter follows the halt at Peshawur, Brigadier Wild's difficulties, and the failure of his brigade. Pollock's arrival and the affairs at Jellalabad follow. Later contents treat the garrison there, letters from Shah Soojah, and the question of capitulation. An earthquake at Jellalabad and the renewal of its works appear, with succours expected. The final chapters describe the forcing of the Khybur Pass in April 1842 and the diplomacy at the court of Lahore.
50379-the-56th-division-1st-london-terri:
Dudley Ward wrote the war history of the 56th Division from London. The book came out in London in 1921. Ward held a major's rank and two awards for grit. Lord Horne wrote the front note for the book. A front photo shows the division's chief, Amyatt Hull.

The division was the first London Territorial force in the war. Its men were part-time troops turned to full war work. Ward traces their fights, marches, and losses year by year. Maps and plates in the full book aid his tale. He gives the book to the men who fell. Kin and vets get a proud, grave record.
50414-right-end-emerson:
Ralph Henry Barbour wrote Right End Emerson, of the Football Eleven Books, printed in New York, copyright 1922. Leslie Crump drew the pictures. A front plate shows a runner now blocked, now broken free again. A page at the front lists the eleven books by position. Contents run to twenty-four chapters.

A tip to the waiter opens the tale, then partners confer and a new year begins. Jimmy reads the paper, Russell explains, and Billy Crocker drops in. Jimmy goes shopping, the second team coach, and Jimmy conspires fill the next heads. Back in harness, the new assistant, and Jimmy's day follow. Alton squeezes through, Stick confides his troubles, and Stick sells out lead to a member of the team. The first chapter opens at the big hotel at Pine Harbor, where a gaudy red automobile whirls up the drive.
50434-the-story-of-wellington:
The Story of Wellington is a biography by Harold F B Wheeler, printed at London in 1912. Wheeler also wrote The Story of Napoleon and The Story of Nelson in the same uniform series, each with sixteen full-page illustrations. A frontispiece shows the Duke writing his Waterloo despatch. Tennyson's lines stand at the head: England's greatest son, who gained a hundred fights and never lost an English gun.

The contents begin with the fool of the family, covering the years 1769 to 1793. Wellington's baptism of fire follows, then the campaign of Seringapatam and war with the Marathas. His last years in India, service in England, Ireland, and Denmark, and the first battles of the Peninsular War come in turn. Victory abroad and displeasure at home mark the years 1808 and 1809. The book tells the great soldier's life for general readers, in the heroic key of its age.
50487-guidebook-of-palo-duro-canyon:
Guidebook of Palo Duro Canyon is a geology guide issued by the geological society of West Texas State University. Its opening pages describe the university's department of geosciences, home to geology, geography, and the study of man. Most of its students read for a science degree in geology, the guide says, aimed at work in the profession.

That degree calls for at least thirty nine hours of geology, with other sciences, mathematics, and writing or map making beside it. A master's degree in geology is also offered. Recent thesis topics named in the guide treat a cliff quadrangle in a Texas county and the rocks of a Big Bend formation. The canyon of the title, cut in the Texas panhandle, is the field classroom for that teaching.
50495-bohemian-paris-of-to-day-second-ed:
Bohemian Paris of To-Day is a memoir of Parisian art life by Morrow, built from notes by the artist Edouard Cucuel, who also illustrated it. The second edition was published in Philadelphia and London in 1900. Morrow and his friend Bishop, one bound to be an artist and the other a sculptor, arrive in Paris to begin years of hard work.

The opening follows their first weeks of sightseeing and their hunt for a studio. For eleven days they climb the waxed stairs of the Latin Quarter behind puffing concierges, past walls of placards offering artists' studios from two hundred to two thousand francs a year. At last they take a sixth-floor studio off the Rue Saint André des Arts, with overhead light, dirty walls covered in sketches, and a view over the rooftops of Paris. The book promises a working artist's view of the quarter from inside.
50523-the-boys-life-of-edison:
Boys' Life of Edison is a biography for the young by Meadowcroft. Meadowcroft worked at the Edison laboratory and wrote the ABC of Electricity. Harper and Brothers published the life in New York and London. Edison himself consented to the book, a note on its front says. Autobiographical notes by Edison enrich the boy's life throughout it.

Contents open with the early days of electricity and Edison's family. His early boyhood and the young newsboy fill the next two chapters. Stories of his newsboy days and the young telegraph operator follow. Adventures of a telegraph operator and work in Boston ensue there. From poverty to independence and a busy young inventor close it.
50568-the-art-of-the-bone-setter-a-testi:
George Matthews Bennett, a specialist for dislocated joints, fractures, and sprains, wrote this testimony and vindication of the bone-setter's art, published at London with portrait and diagrams. The Lancet's phrase, a neglected corner of the domain of surgery, stands as its motto.

Bennett, descendant of a long line of bone-setters whose name was a household word in Midland homes, dedicates the book to the hunting men of Warwickshire and the Quorn. His preface owns that he expects the sneers of the medical profession. The cures collected here, he argues, have pushed surgeons to adopt methods they once called charlatanry. Patients' testimony fills the record. Readers get the folk practitioner's case against the faculty, argued from results.
50659-vivian-s-lesson:
Vivian's Lesson is a children's novel by Elizabeth Grierson, issued in 1907. Chambers published it in London and Edinburgh. Hilda Cowham drew the ten illustrations. Grierson also wrote tales from Scottish ballads. The contents list runs to twenty-five chapters. A Christmas tree and a game of hide-and-seek come early. Burglars and a man in the summer-house stir the middle.

Later chapters bring a dark shadow and a dreary homecoming. Vivian conquers, then faces another mystery. A vain search and a runaway stretch the close. The journey west ends the tale on a fresh start. Such chapter lists map a full school-story arc. Lessons of conduct grow out of scrapes and scares. Grierson wrote for children in a clear, warm way. The book is a fair sample of Edwardian girls' fiction.
50696-railway-construction:
Mills, chief engineer of the Great Northern Railway of Ireland, wrote this text on how railways are built. Longmans placed it in their Civil Engineering Series, with 516 plates and plans. The series stood for sound, working guides for men in training and men on the job.

Railway Construction sits beside books on docks, water flow, mild steel, and harbour works in the same line. Its author brought a chief engineer's daily craft to the page. Students, draughtsmen, and working engineers form its stated audience across the series. Readers get a full, drawn guide to laying out and building a line, from a firm that shaped much of the trade's shelf of handbooks.
50713-one-against-the-moon:
One Against the Moon is a science fiction novel by Donald A Wollheim, in a first edition of nineteen fifty six. The Cleveland and New York publisher lists the author's other books at the front. Among them are The Secret of Saturn's Rings and The Secret of the Martian Moons. The dedication names a friend as a fixed star in a fickle sky.

Contents run to chapters called Dream of Stars, Up the Space Ladder, and Riding the Atoms. A hero named Robin Carew wakes, in the text shown, to his alarm clock as he has for two years. Later heads name a honeycomb place, incredible footprints, and a glass man. A long trek, a man from Lake Baikal, and a getaway bomb fill the later list.
50721-the-catholic-world-vol-17-april-18:
The Catholic World, volume seventeen, binds the monthly numbers from April to September 1873. The Catholic Publication House of New York issued the magazine of general literature and science. Its contents list reads as an index of the half year.

Public Charities opens the volume, and long serials run through it: Jerome Savonarola, Dubois' Madame Agnes, and the tales For Better For Worse and Grapes and Thorns. Essays take up Darwinism twice, the evolution of life, church and state in Germany, and the present greatness of the papacy. Brittany's people and poems, Fontainebleau, Chartres, and an art pilgrimage through Rome supply travel. Book talk weighs Fiske's Myths and Myth-Makers and compares Middlemarch with Fleurange. The volume shows an American Catholic monthly mixing doctrine, fiction, science, and letters.
50731-the-boys-nelson:
Harold F B Wheeler writes for boys in The Boys' Nelson, from Thomas Y Crowell Company of New York. A series list fronts the book: The Story of Napoleon, Famous Voyages of the Great Discoverers, and The Story of the Crusades stand uniform with it. A plate shows the Belleisle going into action at Trafalgar, Victory or Death chalked on her guns.

An admiral's verdict fronts the life: Nelson is the only man who has ever lived who, by universal consent, is without a peer. Wheeler's preface praises Nelson's letters as spontaneous and much to the point, and his care for his men's health, proved by a fleet surgeon's report of 1805.
50737-confederate-military-history-volum:
Volume five of Confederate Military History, published at Atlanta in 1899. The full set runs to twelve volumes. Distinguished men of the South wrote them. General Clement A Evans of Georgia edited the whole work. This volume covers South Carolina. It opens with the spirit of secession and the state militia. Charleston and its forts come next. The surrender of Fort Sumter closes the first chapter.

Later chapters follow South Carolinians through the war. They fight at Williamsburg, Seven Pines, and Malvern Hill. They march at Second Manassas, Sharpsburg, and Fredericksburg. Other chapters defend Charleston against naval attack. Participants wrote the volume a generation later. It preserves the Southern account in detail, state by state.
50774-contagion:
Katherine MacLean wrote a tale first printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in October 1950. The planet Minos looks like Earth in fall, with green, copper, and red leaves. A hunt party from the ship Explorer walks a trail in sealed suits, guns in hand.

June Walton, George Barton, his brother Hal, and Max hunt beasts to test them for germs. A world that feels like home can hide germs close to Earth's own, yet too strange to cure. Old tales of lost towns and dead ships warn the crew. The four doctors must learn if the sweet air of Minos is safe to breathe.
50908-a-relic-of-the-revolution:
Charles Herbert of Newburyport wrote a full account of American prisoners held at Plymouth in England. Charles H Peirce issued the book at Boston in 1847 for its owner. Herbert was taken in the brigantine Dolton in December 1776. He later served in the frigate Alliance in 1779 and 1780.

Herbert lists ships taken, crews, homes, deaths in prison, and escapes. Sickness, vermin, smallpox, and cold berths fill the grim chapters. The tale runs to the exchange of prisoners on March 15, 1779. An added part tells of cruises under Commodore John Paul Jones and prizes taken.
50910-the-story-of-napoleon:
The Story of Napoleon is a biography by Harold Wheeler. Harrap of London published it, with a frontispiece after David's painting of the emperor. A Carlyle quotation stands as motto: a soul to dare and do.

Early chapters treat Napoleon the boy, his schooldays, and Napoleon as officer and author. The Corsican volunteers and the eve of the Terror follow. His first fight with the English and his Italian campaign come next. The expedition to Egypt closes the portion of contents shown. The book belongs to a series of stories of lives and events. Companion volumes tell of Nelson, Wellington, the Crusades, and the French Revolution. Wheeler opens by noting that Napoleon's name usually means a hard-fought victory. He spent, the author grants, most of his life in the camp.
50955-the-cities-of-the-sun-stories-of-a:
The Cities of the Sun gathers stories of ancient America founded on incidents in the Book of Mormon, by Elizabeth Rachel Cannon. A second and enlarged edition came out at Salt Lake City in 1911. Paintings by Ottinger and photographs by the author go with the tales. A verse on Mexico and its ruined thrones heads the book.

The Martyr is the first story in the table of the volume. Its chapters run from a king’s council to an execution and a flight. The waters of Mormon name one scene of the tale. The Gadiantons, a band of robbers in the scripture, give the second story its title. Cannon writes fiction from the sacred history of her faith. The tales were made for readers of the Latter Day Saint world.
50970-an-account-of-the-escape-of-six-fe:
An Account of the Escape of Six Federal Soldiers from Prison at Danville, Virginia, by W H Newlin, was printed at Cincinnati in 1887, under rights entered in 1870. Newlin was a lieutenant in the Seventy Third Illinois Volunteers. The men traveled by night through enemy country to the Union pickets at Gauley Bridge, West Virginia, in the winter of 1863 and 1864.

In his preface Newlin says the account was first written in 1866. Print waited in hope of word of two comrades left behind. On the trip the men had neither pencil nor paper, so the tale rests on memory. Yet such scenes, he holds, stamp themselves on the mind, and each year makes the memory more vivid. War fans get a true prison break in the teller own words.
50985-a-treatise-on-acupuncturation:
James Morss Churchill, a member of the Royal College of Surgeons in London, wrote a Treatise on Acupuncturation, issued in London by Simpkin and Marshall. Churchill gave the treatise, by permission, to Astley Cooper. A plate shows acupuncturation needles. The operation was peculiar to the Japanese and Chinese, who named it Zin King, the title page says. Directions for its performance and cases of its success fill the book.

If the medical profession merits the reproach of being easily deluded by novelty, Churchill opens, he needs no apology for his pages. If a rational theory built on sound reasoning is the only evidence of value, he goes on in defence. Medical historians get the first English book bringing needle puncture into European practice.
51015-moral-poison-in-modern-fiction:
Moral Poison in Modern Fiction, by Brimley Johnson, was published in London. Philpot issued the book from Great Russell Street. Johnson had written on contemporary novelists. Eleven chapters state his charge. The first quotes a grim line on the young world: eye for eye, lust and loving alike. Johnson asks on what theories of private morals the young are now fed. Most thought, he says, reaches us through fiction. Most feeling comes through drama.

His claim is blunt: a great many new novels hold deadly poison. Yet he wants no return to Victorian silence on sex. Open talk is not his target. The war, he argues, threw back minds already unsettled by new ideas. Chapters weigh novels of gay life as strong moral intoxicants. Free love gets two pictures, both held up as warnings.
51043-the-good-gray-poet-a-vindication:
The Good Gray Poet, a defence printed at New York in eighteen sixty-six, answers an attack on the poet Walt Whitman. The writer dates his piece from Washington in September eighteen sixty-five. Nine weeks, he says, had passed since the outrage he brands.

He describes Whitman as thousands had seen him in New York, Brooklyn, Boston, and Washington. Tall, calm, and grandly built, the poet wore the rough dress of working folk. Strangers took him for a skilled workman or a seaman. Sunlight on his bare head showed a brow lined with noble wrinkles. The piece defends free letters as a sacred cause.
51065-german-and-austrian-prisons-prison:
German and Austrian Prisons is a crime history volume by Major Arthur Griffiths. The Grolier Society issued it in the History and Romance of Crime set. Griffiths was late inspector of prisons in Great Britain for many years. This deluxe set was limited to one thousand numbered copies in all.

Chapters treat the chief prisons of Prussia, Bavaria, Saxony, and Austria Hungary. Friedrich von der Trenck at Magdeburg fortress fills one long chapter here. Notorious poisoners, three famed cases, and clever impostors follow in order. Typical murderers, a vagrant story, and remarkable prisoners fill the middle. Silvio Pellico at Spielberg and brigandage in Austria Hungary close the book.
51082-coming-attraction:
Fritz Leiber wrote a tale of the future for Galaxy in November 1950. The scene is a New York street. A great coupe with fishhooks welded to its fender shoulders up over the curb toward a girl.

The teller, an Englishman, grabs the girl's elbow and yanks her back. The hooks tear a black rag from her skirt as the car shoots past. Police on rocket machines give chase, but the car throws out a cloud of black smoke. The girl wears a sleek black satin mask, as all women here do. She asks him to her place that night, south of a quarter called Inferno. She has something he can help her about.
51125-mars-is-my-destination:
Frank Belknap Long wrote this science fiction novel, first printed by Pyramid Books in June 1962. Mars is Earth's first colony in space, and men have killed for the ticket that lets them go there. Once there, the killing goes on, for the planet holds wealth beyond counting and danger to match.

Ralph Graham has wanted Mars since boyhood, and now he is bound there with authority that puts the whole planet in his pocket, if he lives long enough to use it. The tale opens at a spaceport bar in New Chicago, where the narrator has known for ten minutes that something terrible is about to happen. Long mixes frontier greed, murder, and wonder in a tense future key.
51134-a-book-of-dartmoor-second-edition:
S Baring-Gould wrote A Book of Dartmoor, with sixty illustrations. Methuen published the second edition at London in January 1907; the first came out in July 1900. Baring-Gould dedicated it to his uncle, Thomas George Bond, one of the pioneers of Dartmoor exploration. A long list of his other books stands at the front, from Songs of the West to A Book of Ghosts. The chapters open with the country itself: bogs, then tors.

The ancient inhabitants, the antiquities, and the freaks follow. Dead men's dust, the camps, and tin-streaming come next. The second half walks the moor place by place: Lydford, Belstone, and Chagford. Manaton, Holne, and Ivybridge follow. Yelverton, Post Bridge, and Princetown close the circuit. Yes Tor fronts the book as a plate, with Vixen Tor and Hey Tor behind.
51161-degeneration:
Max Nordau's attack on the art and thought of his day, in English from the second German edition, came out in a popular edition from William Heinemann in 1898. The book is dedicated to Caesar Lombroso of Turin, whose work on crime and madness Nordau credits as its root.

Nordau argues that many modern writers and painters show the marks of a worn-out nervous stock. In his letter to Lombroso he grants that such people are not all criminals or madmen, yet claims they share the traits of those who are. Whole schools of art are tried by that test and found sick. Few books of the 1890s stirred more talk, and the work still stands as the loudest case for the idea that new art meant decay.
51188-the-captain-s-story-or-the-disobed:
The Captain Story, or The Disobedient Son, was adapted from the German by William S Martin and printed in London by James Nisbet and Company in 1868. A plate shows the hero seated to rest. Chapter heads trace a full life of wandering and return.

The tale opens with a stranger, a castle, and the captain own thoughts, then a pastor invitation to tea. The captain tells how wilfulness took him to a university, where his bad acts led his father to refuse money. He ran away, was kidnapped at Amsterdam, robbed, and sent to sea. A tempest sank his ship, and he alone lived, clinging to a spar by a rock. Later news of his father death filled him with grief. He rose to captain and married. Church readers get a warning tale of a runaway made wise.
51229-the-reformation-and-the-renaissanc:
The Reformation and the Renaissance, 1485 to 1547, is a source book for English history, compiled by Bewsher of Saint Paul's School. Bell issued it at London in a second edition in 1916, in a series of English history source books. Its pages print the records themselves, year by year. The year 1485 opens with the device for the coronation of Henry the Seventh.

Then come the yeomen of the guard, the sweating sickness, and the insurrection of Lambert Simnel, all from the chronicles. Benevonces, the Cornish rebellion, and Perkin Warbeck follow. Later extracts give Skelton on Cardinal Wolsey, and Wolsey and the king's marriage from Burnet's records. Tyndale writes on translating the scriptures. Such books put schoolboys face to face with the words of the time. This one marches from Bosworth to the death of Henry the Eighth in documents, letting the age speak for itself.
51255-chain-reaction:
Boyd Ellanby printed Chain Reaction in Galaxy Science Fiction in September 1956. The story opens on a poker game played for the highest stakes imaginable. Would this be the last poker game, the blurb asks, with all life at stake and every card a mere deuce?

MacPherson shuffles the cards over and over. His hands are almost steady. Rothman, a mathematician grown thin in confinement, wears a gray hospital robe. He stands at a barred window, looking at the glittering Arizona desert. Today, he says, the sky's the limit. Three men who know too much are waiting out the end of something in an institution. Ellanby plays the scene quietly, which makes the arithmetic of the title colder.
51274-ambition:
William L Bade published his story Ambition in Galaxy Science Fiction in October 1951, with pictures by L Woromay. A headnote says the science goals of today will seem to future men as strange as the quest for the Holy Grail. Maitland wakes at three in the morning on a research reservation.

A thump and a movement in the dark strike him like a thousand volts. He wakes again to birdsong and a blue sky, then freezes at the ceiling. The room is not his room, and the lawn outside is no part of the reservation. Prairie grass and a river under huge old trees stand where labs and an oxygen plant should be. Displacement drives the tale.
51288-man-of-distinction:
Man of Distinction is a science fiction story by Michael Shaara. It ran in Galaxy Science Fiction in October 1956. Dick Francis drew its pictures. Its hero is Thatcher Blitt of the year 2180. Blitt is rich, yet that is not his distinction. He is small, gaunt, and wholly forgettable in face. Crowd scenes in films would suit him, the tale says. Yet he founded Genealogy, Incorporated, and grew rich on it.

Blitt's find was plain once seen, the narrator says. Every father had a father before him. Lines of descent run back without end. Counting those lines makes Blitt a freak of numbers. Shaara later won high honours for war fiction. This early tale plays with deep time.
51379-the-music-master-of-babylon:
Edgar Pangborn's The Music Master of Babylon ran in Galaxy Science Fiction in November 1954. Its headnote asks what more fitting place the last man on Earth could live in than a museum, if only he can avoid becoming an exhibit himself.

For twenty-five years, no one came. Brian Van Anda, in the seventy-sixth year of his life, keeps his facts straight. The present year is 2096; he was born in 2020, seven years after the close of the Civil War and fifty years before the Final War. His birthplace, New Boston, stood far inland from the ancient metropolis that the rising sea reclaimed after the earthquake of 1994. At evening he ties his canoe to the massive window that has long been a port and a doorway, and listens.
51388-redemption:
Redemption is a book of sermons on the way of salvation by Edward Hoare, vicar of Trinity, Tunbridge Wells, and honorary canon of Canterbury. Hatchards published it at London in 1878. The first discourse, Deliverance, opens on a text from the first letter to the Corinthians: Christ made unto us wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption.

Hoare opens by marking a happy sign of the age: men now study the religion of feeling far more than forty or fifty years before. He grants the worth of heart religion, while warning that feelings fail when not grounded in truth. Fourteen discourses follow, on Israel, the first-born, the bondsman, Ruth, atonement, forgiveness, purity, restoration, and heaven.
51392-hafiz-in-london:
Hafiz in London is a book of poems by Justin Huntly McCarthy, issued in London in 1886. McCarthy casts himself as a host to the Persian poet Hafiz. The dedication lays Persian roses at a lady's feet. It names Shiraz, Khayyam, and the Khalifate as its ground. The contents list runs to some thirty short poems. Titles include Memory, Eld, Kaif, and Consolation.

The title poem brings Hafiz to the Thames-side city. The singer roves there as he did by Persian streams. Later pieces praise wine and recall lost love. One poem stands at the grave of Omar Khayyam. Another lets Omar answer from beyond. McCarthy was known for verse in an Eastern dress. This book joins London moods to Persian forms.
51520-the-downfall-of-the-dervishes-or-t:
Ernest Bennett's The Downfall of the Dervishes, or The Avenging of Gordon, was published in London in 1899 by Methuen, with a portrait, map, and plans. Bennett, a fellow and lecturer of Hertford College, Oxford, went out as special correspondent for the Westminster Gazette. A photogravure of Lord Kitchener of Khartoum fronts the book.

The narrative is personal, of the final Soudan campaign of 1898. Chapter one, from Cairo to the Atbara, mixes the journey with the work. Correspondents' permits, fellow passengers to Alexandria, French animosity in Egypt, preparations, and a native medium fill it. The night journey runs south past Karnak and Wady Halfa. Chapter two rides on to Wad Hamed, past the pyramids of Meroe and Abu Klea, through a sandstorm, to a meeting with the Sirdar.
51561-puritanism-and-liberty-1603-1660-t:
Kenneth Bell, a fellow of All Souls College, Oxford, compiled this source book on Puritanism and liberty in the years 1603 to 1660. The hosted copy is the third edition. It belongs to Bell's English History Source Books, a series of cheap volumes, each covering one stretch of English history, from the welding of the race to the age of Gladstone.

Source books of this kind put the raw material of history into a student's hands. Rather than telling the story in the editor's own words, such a volume gathers the documents of the period itself. For these years that means the age of the early Stuart kings, civil war, and the republic, read through the writings of the time.
51581-the-way-of-the-air-a-description-o:
Edgar Middleton's The Way of the Air, a description of modern aviation, was published by Stokes in 1917. Middleton writes as an air pilot, late flight sub-lieutenant of the Royal Navy. The book is dedicated to friends who fell in the great fight, among them Liddell and Warneford, both holders of the Victoria Cross. They found glory, the page says, in the plain path of duty.

The author's note, from London in 1917, states the design. Part one is for the young man who wishes to take up flying as a profession. It describes the new race of men flying has bred, their conditions, difficulties, and dangers. Flying is a young man's trade, needing the vigour, recklessness, and iron nerve of youth. Part two is a set of incidents from the diary of an air pilot on active service in the north of France, given in their original form.
51605-jamieson:
Bill Doede wrote the tale Jamieson for Galaxy Magazine. The story ran in December 1960. A Konv cylinder was the key to space, the blurb says. One power existed that it could not match. Mrs Jamieson and her son live by the Wolf river. Their Wisconsin house began as a rich man's cottage.

The rich man died and his heirs sold it out. The widow insulates it well for hard winters. Row boats rent to fishermen in summer there. Overnight cabins by the road add their income. Neighbors know nothing of her brought money. She came from the East, she told them once. In truth she came from Bangkok, Siam, she hides. Agents killed her husband there in '07. He was bound for Alpha Centaurus that eve. A hidden spacer's widow in Wisconsin gives the space age a quiet, grieving secret keeper.
51610-solid-solution:
James Stamers wrote Solid Solution, a science fiction tale printed in Galaxy Magazine in April 1960. Its blurb jokes that David Adam Smith had the brains of fifty men, very literally. Morris, the narrator, is Smith's butt and strong man at the Desert Institute.

Three students are expelled for smuggling a bubble dancer into the school. Morris is sent with them on a last desert trip to gather samples. He warns them off the specimen plates, the dial, and the red and blue buttons. Smith, the great geologist who rules a whole desert, sneers at all of them. Something in the sand will change the count of brains.
51621-sinhalese-folklore-notes-ceylon:
Arthur A Perera, an advocate of Ceylon, wrote Sinhalese Folklore Notes, printed at the British India Press, Bombay, in nineteen seventeen. The pieces first ran in the Indian Antiquary as Glimpses of Sinhalese Social Life. They are now amplified and rearranged, Perera says. He follows the Folklore Society Hand Book scheme. An appendix gives a glossary from the Service Tenure Register of eighteen seventy two.

Eighteen chapters fill the notes. Belief and practice come first: the earth and the sky, the vegetable world, and the animal world. Human beings and things made by man follow. The soul and another life, superhuman beings, and omens and divination come next. The magic art and disease and leech craft close the belief part. Customs then treat social institutions, rites of individual life, occupations, festivals, and games. Stories, songs, and proverbs end the book. Folklore students get a Ceylon field collection.
51641-the-hermitage-home-of-general-andr:
The Hermitage, Home of General Andrew Jackson, is a guide booklet for the registered national historic landmark in Tennessee, revised in June 1963. Mary Dorris originally compiled it for the ladies association keeping the seventh president's home. Sections treat the historical page, the original log Hermitage, the museum, the mansion and grounds, and the tomb.

A portrait by Earl, presented in 1944, shows Jackson at the Hermitage at the front. His mother's advice is quoted in full: in 1781, aged fourteen, Jackson enlisted, was captured, caught smallpox, and she nursed him back to health. Her errand to nurse neighbours on a Charleston hospital ship cost her own life to fever. Historic house visitors get the guide.
51843-the-oregon-question:
Albert Gallatin wrote on the Oregon question at New York in 1846, while Britain and the United States disputed the north west coast. He owns he had been a pioneer in gathering the facts. His first case rested on printed voyages and on Humboldt's New Spain. Since then, journals kept in Madrid had come to light.

New facts were added, old ones better weighed, and some errors set right. Gallatin warns that state papers are not calm philosophy. Ministers write as advocates for their own claims, he says. Yet they are at heart ministers of peace, bound to find ways to settle clashing claims and keep friendly ties. War, he holds, is the thing to bar.
51905-the-invasion-of-1910-with-a-full-a:
The Invasion of 1910, with a full account of the siege of London, by William Le Queux, carries naval chapters by H W Wilson and an introductory letter by Field-Marshal Earl Roberts. The Macmillan Company of Canada issued the Toronto edition in 1906, with maps and plans of the German landings.

Book one brings the surprise, a fierce cruiser battle, and Germans landing at Hull and Goole. Book two gives the lines of London, the bombardment, and the fall of the city. Book three ends with a blow for freedom and a great British victory.
51914-when-men-grew-tall-or-the-story-of:
Alfred Henry Lewis's When Men Grew Tall, the story of Andrew Jackson, was published by Appleton and Company at New York in 1907 and dedicated to Theodore Roosevelt. The first chapter is Salisbury and the Law, in the year 1787. Salisbury, seat of justice for Rowan County in North Carolina, is drawn in loving detail: unpaved streets of red clay, plank sidewalks, and trees that arch overhead like a cathedral aisle.

In a one-room office on the lawn of Spruce McCay's white mansion sits the young Jackson, reading law. He is six feet and an inch, so slim he seems taller, straight as a lance, with a boy's horse face, hollow cheeks, and big blue eyes full of power. The shelves hold Blackstone's Commentaries, Coke on Littleton, and Hale's Pleas of the Crown, musty and dog-eared. Lewis builds his hero's life outward from this Carolina law office.
51939-from-now-on:
Frank Packard wrote a tale printed at Toronto in 1919. His Night Operator and his Jimmie Dale books are named as his earlier works. The first book of the tale is named The Chase. Its first chapter bears a sum of money for its title: one hundred thousand dollars.

A wild roar rolls round a race track. Outside the fence a squat, fat man sweats and tugs at his collar. Bookie Skarvan is wiped out, every last cent of years of gains gone. He clutches the arm of Dave Henderson in the car. Dave shifts a small black satchel with his boot toe and stays cool. He will not blame the bookie for trying to make a crook of him.
51950-the-prodigal-son:
Hall Caine wrote this novel of a prodigal son in Iceland. Morang printed it at Toronto, published November 1904. Omar lines on the moving finger front the tale as motto. Seven parts carry the story of worldly hope turned ashes.

Iceland in autumn moonlight opens the tale, calm and august. The little wooden capital stirs at morning by fiord and lake. The day was set for annual sheep gathering at Thingvellir, far off. No railways or coaches, few roads, hence the young men rode. Snow tipped mountains beyond the moorland frame the opening Iceland scene of the tale.
51954-a-man-his-mark-a-romance-second-ed:
A Man: His Mark is a romance by WC Morrow, here in its second edition, published at Philadelphia and London in 1899. Morrow had written Bohemian Paris of To-Day and The Ape, the Idiot, and Other People. A frontispiece by Elenore Plaisted Abbott ornaments the book.

The first chapter sets the scene on Mount Shasta in the winter of the great storms. Adrian Wilder, a tall, dark young man, watches the weather gather over his stone hut on a shoulder of the mountain. He built the hut with the help of Dr Malbone, stone by stone from the talus of a basalt cliff, and carried up boards, books, food, and fuel on his back. The oldest settlers, Morrow warns, did not foresee that this was the start of the most memorable winter of terrors in the white man's history of the region.
51955-the-man-of-last-resort-or-the-clie:
The Man of Last Resort is a set of tales by Melville Davisson Post. Putnam issued it in New York and London in 1897. Its subtitle names the clients of Randolph Mason. Mason is a lawyer of a strange kind. His clients come when law itself has failed them. The first tale is The Governor's Machine. A young governor of the far Southwest stands at his window.

Something is on the governor's mind, the tale begins. Such moods have always brought events in their train. Courts, lawmakers, and impeachment plots have all felt his hand. He looks out at brown tablelands and blue hills. Post writes of power with a cool, dry relish. His Mason stories made legal puzzles famous.
51956-the-strange-schemes-of-randolph-ma:
Melville Davisson Post wrote tales of Randolph Mason, a law man of dark schemes. The book came out in New York and London in 1896. Post wrote The Clients of Randolph Mason in the mate book. He gave this book to John Howard, a skilled law man in front. The teller of strange tales is a boon to men, his first page holds.

His cup of ease is dear to the strong in dull hours, it says. To the struck down it is a god sent balm in his bold claim. A sour judge bids tale men turn to wood and water work. No new thing can be made, that judge cries in his scorn. All builds are new joins of old bits, he grants in part. Law and crime mix.
51973-bill-nye-s-red-book-new-edition:
Edgar Wilson Nye wrote this Red Book, his fourth book of mirth, out at Chicago in eighteen ninety-one. Nye says the folk had called loud and long for a new book. He had long hoped to make one more large, more good, and more red than the first. In it he set his best thoughts, those thought when he felt well.

He left out each thought he held should stay unthought, which shrank the book much. His past books came in red, dark blue, and green, and were met with grace at home. Some were snatched up past the seas past the loose rights laws of the day, he jokes. The tone is droll from the first page, with tall claims for a book that will live for weeks.
52102-across-the-salt-seas-a-romance-of-:
John Bloundelle-Burton wrote Across the Salt Seas, a romance of the War of Succession, published in Chicago and New York in 1897. Burton had earlier written The Hispaniola Plate and A Gentleman Adventurer. A Shakespeare line on cutting foreign throats heads the first chapter.

The tale opens on the deck of La Mouche Noire, where the captain paces with the narrator, Crespin. Below, an old man shipped at Rotterdam lies dying and raving, and his cries make the captain shudder. The white-haired stranger had looked like a minister when he came aboard. What he has seen and known drives the mystery. Readers get a sea romance of the succession wars, told from the deck in the thick of the weather.
52179-the-geologic-story-of-palo-duro-ca:
Matthews wrote The Geologic Story of Palo Duro Canyon, a guidebook of 1969. The Bureau of Economic Geology at the University of Texas made it. It is guidebook eight in that bureau's series at Austin. A second printing came in August 1983, the title page notes. Contents open with park history and ancient man in the canyon.

Indians of the plains and the coming of the white man follow. The regional setting and the geologic story take the center. Formations exposed in the canyon are named one by one in order. Quartermaster, Tecovas, Trujillo, and Ogallala stand in that list. How the canyon was carved fills the next part of the guide. Running water did the main work, with weathering and gravity. A tour of sights closes it: the lighthouse, Capitol Peak, and the rest. Matthews gives the state park its rocks in plain order.
5218-the-satyricon-volume-01-introductio:
This first volume of W. C. Firebaugh's translation of Petronius's Satyricon opens with the translator's introduction, reflecting on the difficulties of rendering an author whose allusions were plain to his own public but obscure to later readers. Firebaugh defends a translation that honours both sense and tone, even where later hands have altered the text.

After the introduction, the volume begins the adventures of Encolpius and his companions, from the opening chapters onward. Readers starting the Satyricon here get both the translator's apology and the novel's first scenes, before the later volumes carry the story to Trimalchio's dinner and beyond.
52192-william-nelson:
Daniel Wilson, president of the University of Toronto, wrote this memoir of William Nelson for private circulation in 1889. Nelson and Sons of Edinburgh printed it. Wilson dedicates it to the widow, as the work of her husband's old friend and schoolmate.

The foreword calls Nelson a rare example of simplicity and thoroughness. He worked up to a high standard in all he undertook. He kept fidelity in his stewardship as a man of wealth and a captain of industry. Nelson built the Edinburgh publishing house that bore his family's name into an empire of cheap, good books. His friend keeps the volume modest on purpose. The friendship ran unbroken from early boyhood past threescore years and ten, and the memoir is a gravestone with a long inscription.
52212-my-winter-on-the-nile-eighteenth-e:
Charles Dudley Warner records an Egyptian journey in My Winter on the Nile, here in an eighteenth edition from Houghton, Mifflin and Company of Boston, 1876. Warner dedicates the record to A C Dunham and the voyagers on the dahabeëh Rip Van Winkle. An epigraph from Amrou, conqueror of Egypt, describes the country as black earth and green plants between mountain and sand.

Thirty-seven chapters run from Cairo and its bazaars, mosques and pyramids up the Nile past Thebes and Karnak to the cataracts, Wady Halfa and Philæ. A prefatory note explains the subscription origins of the book and its sequel, In the Levant.
52213-in-the-levant-twenty-fifth-impress:
Charles Dudley Warner wrote travel notes on Egypt and the Levant, issued at Boston in 1876. Warner made the tour in the winter and spring of 1875, and this book takes up the second half of the trip. A first book had told of his winter on the Nile.

The opening trip runs from Jaffa to Jerusalem, and Warner jokes that landing at Jaffa has been hard since the days of Jonah. Boats must anchor far off a shore with no harbor, and calm early hours give the best chance to get ashore. He wrote, he says, before new unrest in the East could color what he saw.
52242-the-life-of-tolstoy-first-fifty-ye:
Aylmer Maude wrote The Life of Tolstoy, First Fifty Years, here in a fifth edition of nineteen eleven. Maude opens with a note on the hard task of spelling Russian names in English letters. No settled method, he says, yet exists for the change.

Chapters run from Tolstoy's ancestry and youth to his time in the Caucasus and the Crimean War. Petersburg life, travel abroad, and work as a local arbiter follow. Maude then treats the school Tolstoy ran, his marriage, and the long approach to his crisis. A confession and a survey of works from eighteen fifty-two to eighteen seventy-eight close the volume. A portrait from eighteen seventy-three faces the title.
52273-evolution:
Edward Hoare, vicar of Tunbridge Wells and an honorary canon of Canterbury, wrote this twopenny pamphlet on evolution, reprinted from The Churchman by a London publisher around 1885. Hoare admits it may seem rash for a man who claims no science to give an opinion on the theories of scientific men.

His defence draws a line: the facts of science belong to the investigators, and outsiders should not question their information. But theories built on those facts are open to common sense, and any person of ordinary intelligence may judge the conclusions. Readers get a Victorian clergyman's careful terms of engagement with Darwin's century, conceding the facts while contesting the philosophy.
52274-sanctification:
Sanctification is a book of sermons by Edward Hoare, in a third enlarged edition printed at London in 1878. Hoare was vicar of Trinity, Tunbridge Wells, and a canon of Canterbury. Hatchards issued the volume. His preface says the pages hold the substance of sermons from his parish ministry, published at his congregation's request.

He claims nothing new for them. His aim is to set out the doctrine as Scripture gives it and the Church of England teaches it. The contents divide into separation unto God, legal cleansing, and personal holiness. Notes on Romans and on the word perfect close the book. The sermons are practical rather than controversial, he says, bringing out old truths.
52382-studies-of-birds-killed-in-nocturn:
Studies of Birds Killed in Nocturnal Migration is a paper by Tordoff and Mengel, printed at Lawrence, Kansas, in 1956. It stands as volume ten, number one, of the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History publications. Forty-four pages carry six figures and two tables. The study rests on a disaster of the autumn of 1954.

At Topeka, all the birds died against the new television tower of station WIBW-TV. The first casualties, a sora and a yellow-bellied flycatcher, were found on September 7. The great kills came on nights in late September and early October. The paper sorts the species killed, tests whether the sample is random, and reckons migrant numbers and survival.
5241-the-eye-of-zeitoon:
Talbot Mundy's Eye of Zeitoon is set among Armenians and Turks. Travellers join them in the years before the First World War, where, as one chapter says, the heart of Armenia is burning. Its chapters follow soldiers, robbers, and missionaries through mountain roads, with quotations from scripture marking a story of loyalty, faith, and rebellion.

Mundy writes of a people caught between empires, and of Westerners who must choose whether to help. The novel offers adventure with a serious edge. It gives readers a vivid, if dated, picture of Armenia on the edge of catastrophe, told by a writer who knew the region's tensions well.
52449-buell-hampton:
Buell Hampton is a novel by Willis George Emerson, published at Boston and Chicago in 1902. Forbes and Company issued the book in that year for its author. A long dedication poem, To My Old Sweetheart, stands at the front of the volume. The sweetheart of the poem, with rosy cheeks and raven hair, is at last named as the author mother.

 Once an American mother, with the wealth of a Croesus and a lovely daughter, longed for titled distinction. In her net she caught an adventurer, clothed in a frayed out remnant of rank, the note goes on. Emerson, a Chicago lawyer and founder of a California town that bears his family name, wrote romances of money and title. Buell Hampton, the Western hero of this one, must save the daughter from the bought title and the fortune hunter who wears it in the tale.
52456-harps-hung-up-in-babylon:
Harps Hung Up in Babylon is a book of poems by Arthur Colton. It came out in New York in the year 1907, given to his sire. The chief poem takes its name and its theme from a psalm of old. The harps of the exiles hang mute on the trees of the foe's land.

Their loose strings ring on in spite of the hush of grief. They sing that the home hills must not be lost to the heart. The town's two streams run swift, but its street stream runs more swift. Its towers smite the sky, but its sin smoke climbs more high to God. The harps wake at last when the feet of the folk turn home. In the halls of the home town the harps ring out once more. Tales in verse of far lands and kings fill the rest of the book.
52501-the-first-men-in-the-moon:
The First Men in the Moon is a romance by Wells, printed at London in 1901. Wells also wrote Tales of Space and Time and Anticipations. A line from Lucian's Icaromenippus stands at the front. Twenty-six chapters carry the tale from Lympne to the last message from the moon.

Bedford meets Cavor at Lympne, and Cavor makes cavorite, a stuff that cuts off gravity. The two build a sphere and fly to the moon. There they meet the Selenites in the mooncalf pastures. Bedford escapes alone, and Cavor's messages tell of the Grand Lunar. Wells makes his science a vehicle for wonder and satire alike.
5251-the-long-vacation:
Charlotte M. Yonge's Long Vacation returns to the Mohuns and Underwoods of her earlier novels, with a preface warning that its first chapters serve as a prologue for older readers. Chapters of retrospect and twaddle give way to Darby and Joan, slum, sea, or season, a happy sprite, St Andrew's Rock, and the hope of Vanderkist.

Yonge follows her characters into later life, where weary men and anxious women replace the smiling angel band of childhood. The novel offers a leisurely domestic sequel, full of moral reflection, for readers who have followed Yonge's families and want to see how their stories end.
52541-an-essay-on-the-effects-of-opium-c:
John Awsiter wrote An Essay on the Effects of Opium, Considered as a Poison, printed in London in 1763. Awsiter was apothecary to the Royal Hospital at Greenwich. The essay sold for one shilling and sixpence. He gives the book to the President and Fellows of the Royal College of Physicians, in a letter dated January 5, 1762.

Awsiter says the subject had been treated only triflingly and obscurely before. He promises a rational method of cure drawn from experience, plus means to use when medical help cannot be had. A preface attacks the common belief that a large dose brings an easy, quiet death. Instead, he says, convulsions and dreadful symptoms follow as the body fights the drug.
52571-evolution:
Watson wrote this small book on evolution for the Through the Eye line, printed by Jack of London. A tree at the front shows the likely course of animal ascent. The line's next book took up the civilization of the old Egyptians.

The proofs for evolution open the set. One-celled and many-celled beasts come next, then the worms and their kin. Early backboned beasts and the fishes mark the rise of the frame. The conquest of the land and the mammals and man close the climb. Plates lean on Günther and Haeckel, the great German hands at this theme. Plain words and strong pictures carry a hard new science to common readers.
52583-cupid-of-campion:
Cupid of Campion, a boys story by Francis J Finn, a Jesuit priest, was copyrighted in 1916 by Benziger Brothers. Finn also wrote Tom Playfair, Percy Wynn, and Harry Dee. His tales of Catholic school life were widely read. The hero here is Clarence Esmond, a boy who gives himself to the bright eyed goddess of adventure.

Chapter heads are written in a playful, old fashioned style. Clarence is passed from a butcher's boy to a steamer and a tramp, then taken captive by Ben the gypsy. He meets Dora, fights Ezra, and vanishes in a swim in the Mississippi. John Rieler of Campion College dares a lone swim and brings the strangest boy visitor ever seen to the college gates. The tale joins runaway adventure to school story.
52644-who-was-paul-grayson:
Who Was Paul Grayson is a boys novel by John Habberton, published by Harper in 1881. Habberton had won fame before this as the author of Helen Babies for readers. A frontispiece shows Paul as a chief son, hinting at the secret of his birth. The contents open with the new pupil, the fight, and music and manners.

Who will tell, those jail birds, and a beautiful theory ruined fill the middle heads. A benefit for Benny, a dare, and a party keep school and town life lively. The title question hangs over Paul through each scrape and kindness shown. Readers learn his hidden past as the boys around him piece it together.
52679-german-atrocities-an-official-inve:
German Atrocities, an Official Investigation, by J H Morgan, was held under a 1916 copyright and printed in New York by Dutton. Morgan was a law teacher at the University of London and a barrister of the Inner Temple. He had served as a Home Office man with the British force in France.

The first part sets out the British enquiry, picks apart the German White Book, and weighs German claims. The second part tells how the enquiry worked in France and what it found.
