Heads name harm to troops in the field, harm to townsfolk, harm to women, and loss of goods. Papers at the back hold proof on the town of Bailleul and on killings. The book is a wartime case, made to sway world thought.
5271-marjorie-s-vacation:
Carolyn Wells's Marjorie's Vacation follows Marjorie on a summer holiday that begins at home. It carries her to Haslemere, with chapters on the roof, a paper-doll house, interesting letters, a boat ride, a memory book, and the front stairs. Later chapters bring the Dunns, a bazaar, a birthday, Breezy Inn, a broken ladder, and firecrackers.

Wells, author of the Patty books, writes cheerful stories for girls, full of play, friendship, and small adventures. The book offers young readers a sunny vacation tale, where a long day and an old well find their place in Marjorie's summer. An eventful day joins them.
52730-portraits-in-plaster-from-the-coll:
A catalogue of plaster portraits collected by Laurence Hutton. Harper and Brothers published it at New York in 1894. The pieces are life masks, death masks, and busts. The illustration list reads like a hall of fame. Dante, Tasso, and Shakespeare open the roll. Actors follow, from Garrick and Kean to Edwin Booth. Beethoven, Schiller, Marat, Robespierre, and Newton appear as well.

Many casts came straight from life. Others took the face after death. Short notes explain each sitter and each mask's origin. Hutton's collection later won fame among students of portraiture. It preserved true features of writers, musicians, and statesmen. No photograph of the long dead could exist. These casts stand in its place.
52731-blessed-edmund-campion:
Blessed Edmund Campion, by Louise Imogen Guiney, belongs to the Saint Nicholas Series of saints' lives. Washbourne printed the book in London in 1914, with church approval dated 1908. A motto from Ben Jonson heads the life: who falls for love of God shall rise a star.

Guiney says her small book leans on Simpson's monograph on Campion, the Jesuit protomartyr of England. She also drew on the researches of Pollen, and on two witnesses of the time, Parsons and Allen. The chapters run from Campion's youth at London and Oxford in 1540 to 1566, through unrest at Oxford and Dublin. Douay follows, then the call to come up higher. A plate shows Campion reading an address of welcome to Queen Mary.
52734-the-scourge-of-god-a-romance-of-re:
John Bloundelle-Burton wrote a tale of faith and persecution, printed at New York in 1898 as number 251 of a town and country library. His other tales, named in the ads, deal with war and love in the days of Charles the First and with the campaigns of Turenne in Germany.

The contents open with a traveller awaited, a traveller from England, and a parting soul, then pass to scenes in France under Louis the Fourteenth. French heads and a quote from Saurin to the king mark the theme. The tale tells of harsh rule laid on French church folk who would not bend, and of love and flight.
52742-the-atonement-as-taught-by-the-chu:
Edward Hoare, of Christ Church, Ramsgate, preached this sermon at St Mary, Islington, on March 29, 1849. Jackson printed it that year for the Islington Protestant Institute. Its theme is the Church of England's own teaching on the Atonement.

A sermon on such a head, in such a year, was no mere talk. The church was split by tracts and fears of Rome. An institute for Protestant truth stood behind the print, with Wilson its head and a long roll of clergy on its board. Hoare sets out what the prayer book and articles say of Christ's death for sin. The print is short, but it is a shot in a real war of pulpits.
52748-england-s-stewardship-the-substanc:
England Stewardship is a fast day sermon by the Reverend Edward Hoare. Thomas Hatchard issued it at London in 1857 from Trinity Church, Tunbridge Wells. Its text is Luke chapter sixteen, verse two: give an account of thy stewardship. Hoare preached as news of revolt in India shook England at home.

He names Lucknow garrison, hemmed in by rebel thousands, short of food. Cawnpore massacre hangs over his plea for national humbling in prayer. Famine, pestilence, and war had already struck India in quick order, he says. Now outrage on women and children filled the land with wailing there. England must answer to God for her rule, the sermon argues.
52755-uncle-sam-s-boys-on-field-duty-or-:
Irving Hancock wrote Uncle Sam's Boys on Field Duty, or Winning Corporal's Chevrons, a boys army tale printed at Philadelphia in 1911. Hancock wrote many school and service series for boys of the day. The tale opens with a squad room row when Private Green cites a newspaper item to his mates at rest.

Young soldiers Hal and his friends march on a great summer hike and fall in with mock hostiles. Night attacks, traps, and a call to deadly work test the squad in the field over days. Captain Cortland speaks, missing men are rounded up, and promotion hangs in the air for weeks of drill. Two young corporals win their stripes by grit. Boys of the time got drill, camp life, and army values in story form.
52769-a-true-account-of-the-voyage-of-th:
A True Account of the Voyage of the Nottingham Galley of London was printed for Popping at Paternoster Row in 1711, priced six pence. Three crewmen attest the whole upon oath: Christopher Langman the mate, Nicholas Mellen the boatswain, and George White a sailor. Their pamphlet answers the captain's own published narrative point by point.

The title page charges Captain John Dean with obstinacy, attempted betrayal to the French, and wrecking the ship on Boon Island on December 11, 1710. The company endured twenty-four days on that desolate rock and were forced to eat a companion who died. A preface says Dean compelled sick men to sign his version in New England, and two of the three refused his attestation to his face in public company.
52801-the-factors-of-organic-evolution:
Herbert Spencer wrote an essay on the factors of organic evolution, first run in The Nineteenth Century in the spring of 1886 and reissued in New York in 1887. Passages cut for space in the journal were put back for the book form. Spencer says the direct theme is life science, but the reach of the plea runs to mind, morals, and society.

His core claim splits the field in two. Plain traits, he holds, can grow by the survival of the fittest changes. But the tangled traits of mind, he says, can only be read as the passing on of changes won by use and lost by disuse in each life. On that choice, he warns, hang our views of feeling, conscience, and right.
52979-the-sword-of-gideon:
The Sword of Gideon, a serial tale by John Bloundelle-Burton, bears a United States copyright of 1904. The tale ran in parts in The Quiver, and this hosted text comes from that magazine's annual volume for 1905. Cassell printed the volume in London, Paris, New York, and Melbourne.

The tale opens on the evening of May 15, 1702, with horsemen spurring fast to north, south, east, and west. As they ride through hamlets and villages, church bells begin to ring behind them. That rush of riders and bells sets the pace for a war-time story. The Quiver volume around it holds sermons, essays, and tales by many church names of the day. Burton's serial was one of its chief draws, spread across the year.
52992-food-and-morals-6th-edition:
Food and Morals, a sermon by the Reverend Clymer, was preached at Auburn, New York. This sixth edition, the 110th thousand, came out in New York in 1888. Fowler and Wells sold works on health, diet, and phrenology. A letter from Dr Deems of New York fronts the sermon. Deems read it in the Auburn Daily Advertiser of June 20, 1880. He urges its issue as a tract on hygiene.

Deems argues that body and soul stand linked. A blocked liver, he says, can dull a saint's joy. He tells of a girl in despair whom he treated first for her liver. Then she could hear words of faith. His rule runs: first the natural, then the spiritual. The sermon presses diet and care of the body as moral duties.
53026-smithson-s-theory-of-special-creat:
Smithson's Theory of Special Creation is a work by Noble Smithson, printed at Knoxville in 1911. Smithson states his belief plainly at the start: there is a personal God who made and rules all things. He holds that the first animal and the first plant were made at once by the Creator, not born from dead matter.

He asks how mind, memory, and will could be mere traits of matter, like length or weight. In his view they point to a soul. Smithson wrote to readers who would send him their views, and priced the book at one dollar by mail. His case stands against the rising tide of evolution teaching.
53062-at-the-sign-of-the-silver-flagon:
Farjeon published At the Sign of the Silver Flagon in a new edition with Tinsley Brothers in 1877. He had written Blade-o'-Grass, Joshua Marvel, and London's Heart. The novel opens at the other end of the world.

Part one is set in Silver Creek Township, in the gold country. A baby obtains her share in the Star Dramatic Company, and the company opens its theatre. Hart searches for a golden reef. Philip rides for flowers for Margaret. Romeo and Juliet is performed where the diggers can see it. Farjeon knew the Australian fields and wrote them warmly. His theatre in the bush, with its actors and its gold, mixes the two great excitements of the colonies: getting rich and being entertained.
53079-dinners-and-diners-where-and-how-t:
Dinners and Diners: Where and How to Dine in London is a guide by Lieutenant-Colonel Newnham-Davis. Grant Richards published it in London in 1899. The author thanks the managers and chefs who helped him make the book. 

Each chapter takes the reader to a table in turn. The Cheshire Cheese and the Holborn stand among the early stops. Romano's, Simpson's, and Verrey's follow in the West End round. The great hotels come in for their own chapters as the tour proceeds. The Savoy earns a chapter, with a second piece on its chef Joseph. The book's promise is plain in its title. It tells the diner where to go, and how to dine when there.
53115-the-history-of-tammany-hall-second:
The History of Tammany Hall is a study of a famed city ring by Gustavus Myers. This copy is a second print, revised and made wide in scope. Past books by his hand treat the sale of city rights in New York. The book came out in the year nineteen seventeen.

First parts trace the ring from a foe of rank rule to a tool of Burr. Rows with a great state chief and slow mend from loss fill the road. Full grip of the city, vote fights, and crowd pleas mark the rise. Bank wars and pres race splits test the ring in the mid heads. The book stands as a chief charge sheet gainst graft in the great town.
53138-the-jesuit-relations-and-allied-do:
Reuben Gold Thwaites shaped the seventh volume of The Jesuit Relations and Allied Documents, issued at Cleveland by the Burrows Brothers Company in 1897. The great series prints the travels and work of the Jesuit missionaries in New France from 1610 to 1791, with the French, Latin, and Italian texts beside English renderings and notes. Portraits, maps, and facsimiles aid the text. This volume covers Quebec, the Hurons, and Cape Breton in 1634 and 1635.

Its documents close Father Paul Le Jeune's Relation of 1634, printed at Paris by Cramoisy in 1635. They add his letter to the Cardinal of August 1, 1635, and the opening chapters of the Relation of 1635. John Covert and Mary Pepper turned the French, and William Giese the Latin. The volume is a brick in Thwaites' vast monument to the mission history of Canada.
53155-out-and-about-london:
Thomas Burke wrote this London book, Out and About London, printed at New York in 1919. Burke also wrote Limehouse Nights and Nights in London, and the front pages quote the press on the earlier book, one paper saying Burke writes of London as Kipling wrote of India. A set of verses by Burke on old age and youth stands before the contents.

Contents name the walks. Round the town in 1917 comes first, then back to dockland and Chinatown revisited. Soho carries on, out of town, in search of a show, vodka and vagabonds, crowded hours, and Saturday night follow. The first piece opens on a lucid, rain-washed morning. It is one of those rare mornings when London seems to laugh, disclosing her random beauties. The parks hang with young green, and the solemn bricks catch the colour of the day.
53165-a-day-with-robert-louis-stevenson:
Maurice Clare spends an imagined day with a famed author in A Day with Robert Louis Stevenson. Hodder and Stoughton of London printed the book in 1910. It stands in a line with like days spent with Dickens and Thackeray.

Clare sets the scene in April 1886 at Skerryvore, a house in Bournemouth. A guest might find the master shut upstairs, banned from speech for fear of a bleed. A guest with a cold would be turned away at the door. If fate is kind, the guest meets a lean man who paces as he talks. He burns with hectic energy, rich in mirth and life, though his frame is frail.
53177-travels-on-the-amazon:
Wallace went to the Amazon in 1848 to see the tropics for himself and to pay his way with natural history collections. This narrative, here in the Ward, Lock edition of 1911, tells his journeys from Para up the great river and its branches. He writes of the luxuriance of animal and vegetable life, of the strange and beautiful objects met with daily, and of the varied races of men he studied in their native wilds.

The book carries a famous wound: on the homeward voyage his ship burned, and with it went two years of notes, the greater part of his collections, and his sketches. Wallace rebuilt the middle of the narrative from what scraps he saved. The closing chapters treat the natural history of the country and the Indian tribes, the seed of his later fame.
53200-the-camp-fire-girls-by-the-blue-la:
Margaret Vandercook sends her Camp Fire Girls to New York and a house by a blue lagoon in a Winston tale held under rights from 1921. Front pages list fourteen books in the line, from Sunrise Hill to Merrie England. Vandercook also wrote the Ranch Girls and Red Cross Girls sets, the title page notes.

Chapter one, The City of Towers, finds two girls walking down Fifth Avenue as strangers in New York one October afternoon. Chapter heads then trace family roots, future plans, and a box party at the theatre. The House by the Blue Lagoon gives the set its place name at chapter nine. A disappearance, a return, and twisted coils add mystery before The Eternal Way closes the tale.
53304-the-gourmet-s-guide-to-london:
The Gourmet's Guide to London, by Newnham Davis, author of The Gourmet's Guide to Europe, was printed by Brentano's at New York in 1914. A Brillat Savarin line heads it: the pleasures of the table console us for the loss of all others. Sixty chapters walk the reader through the restaurants of London.

Chapter one defines old English fare as the best native material cooked in the plainest possible manner. Then come Simpson's in the Strand, a walk down Fleet Street, the Carlton, and two little Soho restaurants. Oyster houses, whitebait at Greenwich, chop houses, and grill rooms follow. The Savoy gets two chapters, one on the men who made it and one on the house today.
53311-the-life-of-sir-isaac-newton: A pocket life fills this item: The Life of Sir Isaac Newton, issued in a family library series of small volumes for adult readers. A line from Doctor Johnson heads the series notice. Books you may carry to the fireside, he says, and hold readily in your hand are the most useful after all. A man will look at them when a larger, graver book would frighten him off.
53316-statement-of-the-provision-for-the:
Statement of the Provision for the Poor, and of the Condition of the Labouring Classes, in a Considerable Portion of America and Europe. It is a report preface by Nassau Senior, published in London in 1835. It was written as the preface to the foreign communications in the appendix to the Poor-Law Report. Senior explains that its separate publication was not planned until the pages were nearly finished.

He admits the piece's glaring faults if judged as a free-standing work. The vast task of outlining poor relief and labourers' lives across Europe and America could not fit his spare professional time. Yet the value and bulk of the gathered facts overcame his objections. The only addition he could make was a translation of the French documents. He closes by praising the zeal and care of the king's diplomatic ministers and consuls.
53319-initiative-in-evolution:
Walter Kidd wrote Initiative in Evolution, a work on life science printed at London in 1920. Kidd had served long in the study of hair growth, touch in mammals and birds, and the passing on of traits gained in life. Plates and text notes face a key clash left cold while the Great War raged.

That clash pits Lamarck against Weismann, and Kidd speaks for the Lamarck side as a junior counsel with a brief. He holds that courts of science must stay open, since barred gates end growth as well as strife. Newton, Pasteur, and Darwin are held up as men who won without mere row. Readers get a clear plea for use and habit as live forces in how kinds change.
53548-jean-cabot-at-ashton:
Gertrude Fisher Scott wrote Jean Cabot at Ashton, published by Lothrop, Lee and Shepard in Boston in 1912. Her husband Arthur Scott drew the pictures; the frontispiece shows a freshman found asleep at the switch. The novel follows Jean Cabot through her first year at a college called Ashton.

Chapters cover the day before arrival, first impressions, the freshman reception, and initiation. The Harvard-Yale game, Thanksgiving holidays, and a chafing-dish party fill the middle of the year. A costume party, midyear exams, and a tennis tournament follow. The year closes with prize-speaking and Class Day, and a visit from Jean's father. Such college-girl novels formed a shelf of their own in the 1910s, mixing study, sport, and friendship.
53641-the-black-box-a-tale-of-monmouth-s:
The Black Box, a Tale of Monmouth Rebellion, by Bourne Cooke, was published in London, with pictures by John de Walton. A prologue warns readers to beware of slim legged, nimble footed men in sober grey who tell long tales, for they make mischief.

Chapter one treats a certain person, and chapter two the secret of the black box. Up a tree, three ships, and the man with the king evil follow. The plot moves through plotters, a fight for life, a solemn vow, and the landing of the Duke of Monmouth. Sedgemoor fight comes near the end, then service under King James left behind, prison, and the shadow of the gallows. Pictures show the hero before Judge Jeffreys. Readers get a stirring tale of rebellion and risk.
53719-the-nootka-sound-controversy-a-dis:
William Ray Manning's The Nootka Sound Controversy was printed at Washington in 1905 by the Government Printing Office. Manning, an instructor in history at Purdue, offered the work as his doctoral dissertation at the University of Chicago, and it won the Justin Winsor prize of the American Historical Association. Fourteen chapters and a bibliography make the study.

The chapters march the quarrel in order. English and Spanish plans for occupying Nootka Sound come first, then the conflicting claims before 1789, Martinez's operations, the quarrel itself and the seizure, and the English prisoners in Mexico. Europe prepares for war in chapter eight, and the Nootka Sound convention settles the matter, with final negotiations after. The preface notes that the French revolutionary period has crowded the incident out of most histories.
53836-intestinal-irrigation:
Intestinal Irrigation, or why, how, and when to flush the colon, is by Alcinous Jamison. Jamison was a physician and the author of Intestinal Ills. He published the book himself in New York, in a third edition of 1914. A motto from Thomson heads the book: even from the body's purity, the mind receives a secret sympathetic aid. Transcriber's notes warn that the figure numbering in the original is flawed.

The preface claims that three decades had greatly changed the diagnosis and treatment of bowel troubles. Better instruments, technique, and hygienic measures had, Jamison says, surprisingly limited the domain of surgery of the lower bowel. His book sets out the case for irrigation as remedy and habit. It belongs to the era's flood of colon literature, when flushing the bowel was sold as a key to general health.
53850-design-and-tradition:
Design and Tradition is a short account of architecture and the applied arts by Amor Fenn, of 1920. Chapman and Hall published the book in London in the Universal Art Series. Marriott edited that series, as its page states for the volumes. 

The full title promises the principles and historic development of architecture and the applied arts in the work. Wilde saying, that the elect are those to whom beautiful things mean only beauty, stands as its motto. The author preface allows that much modern art work fails to attain the level of the past in its judgment. Fenn argues the case of tradition against mere novelty in design. His book is a primer of the historic styles for the student, written when modernism was gathering and the old schools still held the academy.
54018-farmington:
Farmington is a semi-autobiographical book by Clarence S Darrow, published in Chicago in 1904. Darrow recalls a boyhood in a narrow Pennsylvania valley town. The town lay between two ranges of hills along a winding stream. He turns those memories into chapters on the people and places that formed him.

Contents move through his home, his father, the district school and its readers, the church, and the Sunday school. Later chapters take up the burying-ground, fishing, holidays, baseball, Aunt Mary, and Aunt Louisa, ending with how he failed. The famous trial lawyer writes without courtroom argument here. What he offers instead is a portrait of small-town American childhood in the years after the Civil War, drawn by a man who left it and looked back hard.
5407-the-recreations-of-a-country-parson:
A. K. H. Boyd's Recreations of a Country Parson, second series, published in Boston in 1862, gathers essays by a Scottish parish minister. Its chapters concern the parson's choice, disappointment and success, Scylla and Charybdis, churchyards, summer days, screws, solitary days, and Glasgow down the water.

Later chapters concern man and his dwelling-place, life at the water-cure, friends in council, and other parsonage topics, in the leisurely, reflective manner of Victorian essay writing. Readers get a gentle book of a clergyman's thoughts, on work, friendship, and the small pleasures of a country parish.
54099-shot-with-crimson:
Shot with Crimson is a mystery novel by George Barr McCutcheon, published in New York in 1918. Gruger drew its illustrations. The first chapter opens in a held breath: for thirty seconds no one in the room moves. A strange paralysis grips every mind and body. Then puzzled looks are exchanged.

A man by the fireplace glances at the ceiling beams and mutters of something smashing through the roof. A woman rules out thunder at this time of year and looks in fright at her husband. He sits up, asking if the others felt the house rock like an earthquake. The tale launches its mystery from that shudder in a country house.
54191-an-address-to-the-sisters-of-st-pe:
Edward Meyrick Goulburn gave an Address to the Sisters of St Peter's Home, Brompton, on June 30, 1864, the anniversary of its founding. The home took in women of good character who were mending from illness. They stayed till their health was whole. Goulburn was a prebendary of St Paul's and a chaplain to the Queen.

The address is given to Archibald Campbell, Bishop of London, visitor of the home. A first part praises new work by women in the English Church. Deaconesses, parish mission women, and sisterhoods are named as signs of life. Goulburn warns against a cold eye for new forms. A living church must shape its tools to the wants of the age, he holds. The speech then turns to the sisters and their charge.
5436-hyperion:
Henry Wadsworth Longfellow wrote Hyperion as a romance of travel, love, and learning in Germany. The contents run from The Hero and The Christ of Andernach through Heidelberg and the Baron, Lives of Scholars, and Literary Fame. A second book adds spring, colloquies, owl-towers, and partings. A young American travels among German towns, students, and legends.

Longfellow fills the journey with talk about books, art, and the German spirit, alongside a tender love story. The novel reads as both a travel sketch and a young writer's education. Readers get an early American romance, earnest and lyrical, by a poet better known for his verse.
54377-the-catholic-world-vol-21-april-18:
The Catholic World, volume twenty-one, is a bound half year of that month sheet of writ and lore. It runs from April to the fall month of eighteen seventy-five. A house of the church at New York put it out. Its list runs past scores of heads, from a tale in parts to lives of saints and talks on church rights.

A tale of a wife runs past six prints in the list. Heads take up a great church man of the age, a famed chief of Ireland, and a shrine town of France. Church work in two east states, the church in a far land, and the writ of a next land take heads. Verse, tales, and a Rhine tale fill the rows.
54414-courtship-of-miles-standish-minneh:
The Courtship of Miles Standish is a narrative poem by Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, given here in the Minnehaha Edition of 1905. Thompson and Thomas of Chicago published it. A portrait of the poet stands at the front. The poem opens in the old colony days at Plymouth. Miles Standish, the Puritan captain, strides his room in doublet and hose. His glittering arms hang on the wall: a sword of Damascus he fought with in Flanders, and a breastplate with the dint of a bullet.

Young John Alden, his scribe, sits at work in the same room. Standish breaks the silence with the pride of his heart. The tale that follows is known to all: the captain, shy in love, sends his friend to plead for Priscilla. The friend wins her for himself. Longfellow's hexameters carry the Plymouth tale in epic dress.
54444-the-real-captain-kidd-a-vindicatio:
Sir Cornelius Neale Dalton's The Real Captain Kidd argues that the famous pirate was more sinned against than sinning. William Heinemann published it in London in 1911. Dalton calls Kidd one of the unluckiest men that ever lived. He was hanged on Friday the 23d of May, 1701, after an unruly crew at sea and scheming politicians ashore.

Chapters follow the voyage of the Adventure Galley and Kidd's return home. They trace the growth of the arch-pirate myth and the trials at the Old Bailey. Appendices print the documents the case rests on: Kidd's own narrative, examinations of his men and the French passes he took. The report of Duncan Campbell to Lord Bellamont appears there too.
54621-rupert-s-ambition:
Horatio Alger wrote Rupert's Ambition, copyrighted in 1899 and issued in Philadelphia by the Winston Company. Alger's Ragged Dick series and his other boy heroes are named under his name. The frontispiece is called A Dangerous Lunatic, a flash of the danger inside.

Thirty chapters trace the climb. Rupert loses his place and stands out of work, in a tight place, with a false report against him. A scheme by Marlow's wife, a lucky meeting, and Rupert's own turn as a detective move him forward. He becomes a bell-boy and gathers a bell-boy's experiences, receives a commission, and sups in a scene at Delmonico's. Packard of Colorado enters with a gift, and the tale runs west to the Saint James Hotel in Denver. Leslie Waters rises as a dramatic star on a side line. Boys got the Alger gospel pure: work, pluck, and a patron at the end.
54713-a-treatise-on-the-diseases-produce:
L Deslandes, a Paris doctor, wrote this medical treatise, translated from the French with additions and issued at Boston in 1839 in a second edition. The preface defends printing on so delicate a subject.

The evil, it argues, is of great magnitude and often overlooked even by medical men, from false delicacy. A physician is quoted: many a young man came to him unconscious that his act was sapping his health. The preface cites the Massachusetts state asylum report blaming the cause for thirty-two cases of insanity in a year. The contents divide the subject into the effects of venereal excesses and the diseases that follow. Readers get a landmark of nineteenth-century medical moralizing.
54733-the-manatitlans-or-a-record-of-rec:
R Elton Smile set down a strange record of exploration in the Andean La Plata. The work was printed at Buenos Ayres in 1877, with United States rights held by Elton R Smile. Thirty-three chapters and a conclusion fill the hosted form. A front note frames the tale as told by a historiographer.

A German corps from Berlin hunts tiny parasites of tropical plants, the frame claims. Their finds grow stranger until the Manatitlans themselves dictate the tale. Thought dictation and dream-like claims tax belief, the writer owns at the start. Curious readers gain an odd, dated blend of travel, science, and vision.
54797-the-jesuit-relations-and-allied-do:
Reuben Gold Thwaites edited The Jesuit Relations and Allied Documents, a vast set of mission records from New France. Volume eight, published by the Burrows Brothers Company at Cleveland in 1897, covers Quebec, the Hurons, and Cape Breton from 1634 to 1636. The series prints the original French, Latin, and Italian texts with English translations and notes.

This volume completes the Relation of 1635 and opens that of 1636. Paul le Jeune wrote from Quebec in August of each year. Jean de Brébeuf reported from the Huron country, and Julien Perrault added his account. Bibliographical data and notes close the volume. The Relations remain a chief source for the French missions, the Huron people, and the early St. Lawrence settlements.
54808-the-presentation:
Stacpoole wrote The Presentation, a tale of the French court printed in nineteen fourteen, with a colour front plate by Earl Stetson Crawford. The scene is Versailles in seventeen seventy, on the night of the Duc de Choiseul's ball. The next day the Comtesse Dubarry is to be presented at court. France, the tale says, was ruled not by kings but by favourites and ministers.

Dubarry hates Choiseul, and the two play for the realm across the king, Louis, as if he were a table. Heads of parts promise arrest, flight, a duel of wits, and the catacombs of Paris. Rochefort rises through the plot, and poison touches a horse named Atalanta. The book mixes court show, spies, and love in a rich, swift tale.
54892-a-publisher-s-confession:
A Publisher Confession is a trade talk book from the Boston Transcript parts. A Doubleday house of New York brought the parts out in March of nineteen five. Part names ask why bad tales win and good ones flop in trade. Big fee pacts as a wreck plan head the part scheme at start. Are pens an irked tribe and has trade sold its soul are next asks.

Unknown pens odds and fee paid press men fill mid part names. Book ads as mere trials and the road of a book fill more parts. Trade room bounds and plain words to both sides close the scheme. One famed hand asks terms and draws a rich bid in part one. Five grand down and a fifth part fee burst out in that talk.
549-the-underdogs-a-novel-of-the-mexican:
Mariano Azuela tells of the Mexican Revolution through peasant fighters in this short, stark novel, written in El Paso in 1915. Demetrio Macias, a farmer turned rebel chief, leads his men through battles, loot, and doubt, while the cause they serve slips into self-seeking. Azuela, who served as a doctor with Pancho Villa's army, knew the war firsthand.

Azuela writes with bitter, spare prose, praising the underdogs yet mourning their betrayal. The novel, hailed in 1924 as the novel of the Revolution, endures as a classic of disillusion, where brave men fight for a better Mexico and watch it fade.
54957-the-new-german-constitution:
Rene Brunet wrote The New German Constitution, put out by Knopf at New York in 1922. Brunet was professor of constitutional law at the University of Caen. He had served as legal advisor to the French embassy at Berlin. Joseph Gollomb translated the book from the French for this edition. Contents open with the origins of the new order in Germany.

The old constitution of April 16, 1871, and the reforms of October 1918 come first. The fall of the old regime and the birth of the republic follow in the account. Later parts weigh the powers of the Reichstag, the chief holder of sovereignty. How laws are proposed, passed, and put in force gets close study there. Brunet gives English readers the Weimar frame of government in clear order.
54964-the-desert-mounted-corps-an-accoun:
Preston, a lieutenant-colonel who served in the campaign, wrote The Desert Mounted Corps, printed in 1921. General Chauvel, who led the corps, wrote the opening words. The book tells of cavalry work in Palestine and Syria in 1917 and 1918.

Preston calls the campaign the greatest ever fought by cavalry, in numbers and in results. The final drive advanced 450 miles and broke three Turkish armies. He is quick to credit the infantry, whose bayonets won the ground the horsemen then swept. Beersheba, Gaza, Jerusalem, Damascus, and Aleppo mark the road. Maps and photographs of the long desert marches fill out the record.
55017-the-diary-of-dr-john-william-polid:
The Diary of John William Polidori for the year 1816, relating to Byron and Shelley, was edited and elucidated by William Michael Rossetti and published by Elkin Mathews at London in 1911. Polidori had accompanied Byron abroad as his physician, and the diary records that famous summer at close quarters.

The volume opens, strikingly, not with the diary but with newspaper accounts of Polidori's own death in August 1821, at about twenty-six, in Great Pulteney Street, with a coroner's inquest to follow. Rossetti dedicated the edition to his two daughters, who kept the home of his closing years in good cheer. The diary itself, framed by such apparatus, preserves a young doctor's daily record of the Byron circle.
55039-the-man-who-found-himself-uncle-si:
The Man Who Found Himself, or Uncle Simon, is a novel by Margaret and H De Vere Stacpoole, published in New York in nineteen twenty. H De Vere Stacpoole's solo tales, including The Beach of Dreams and The Ghost Girl, are listed facing the title. Part one opens with Simon, then a man named Mudd, then a Doctor Oppenshaw who holds two chapters.

A chapter called I Will Not Be Him states the book's puzzle in five words. A wallet enters the plot, and part two is headed The Soul's Awakening. Identity lost and found, a Stacpoole habit from his companion tale of a man who lost himself, drives the story. Uncle Simon's second life is the prize.
55084-the-homing-pigeon:
The War Department issued a technical manual on the homing pigeon for the information and guidance of all concerned. The manual, dated January 1945, replaced an earlier edition from 1940. It teaches soldiers how the Army kept, trained, and used pigeons as messengers in the field.

Early sections treat the origin, nature, and use of the bird, then describe its body in detail, from plumage to digestion. Care sections cover the loft, feeding, watering, bathing, and handling. Later sections give loft routine, records, banding, and message holders. Training pages take up settling birds and training for messenger service, even delivery by parachute. Final sections treat mating, breeding, and disease. Keepers got a full working guide to a winged arm of the Signal Corps.
55109-blue-shirt-and-khaki-a-comparison:
James Archibald, a war correspondent, compares the British and American soldier in this book, published by Silver, Burdett and Company in 1901 with photographs he took himself. Blue shirt is the American, khaki the Briton. Chapters weigh the new soldier and his equipment, recruits in both armies, the common soldier in the field, the officers, and the tactics of the two services.

Feeding the armies, the railroad in modern war, and the transport of troops by sea get chapters of their own. The last part takes Archibald to South Africa in the Boer War: the last days of the Boer capital and the British in Pretoria. It is a working journalist's comparison, written when both armies were learning the lessons of modern war in Cuba, the Philippines, and Africa.
55153-memoirs-of-general-count-rapp-firs:
General Count Rapp, Napoleon's first aide de camp, wrote memoirs published by his family at London in 1823, with a portrait plate dated 1828. Contents open with the commencement of his military career and his promotion. A certificate from Desaix and good fortune in Egypt follow. His introduction to Napoleon and a sketch of Napoleon's character close the first chapter. The old nobility's servile conduct is noted.

Later chapters treat Napoleon's temper, his flatterers, and his clemency. His attachment to his family and Lucien's opposition appear. Rapp's intercession for Requier and Damas failed, the contents admit. Colburn published the translation on Conduit Street. Rapp's memoirs are a staff officer's inside view.
55172-evolution-and-creation:
Evolution and Creation is a book by Herbert Junius Hardwicke, a surgeon of Sheffield and Edinburgh. His title page lists fellowships in surgery, medicine, anthropology, and other societies in Britain and abroad. He was late editor of the Specialist and honorary physician to hospitals for skin diseases. Frontispieces of chimpanzees and gorillas face the title.

A motto from Huxley sums up the duty of man as learning what is true in order to do what is right. In his preface Hardwicke says the lectures and papers in the book are in part reprints from journals. Some he had printed himself in his leisure moments before this issue. He now offers them to the public in book form together as one volume. The title itself states the theme: the claims of evolution set beside the older doctrine of creation, handled by a medical man of his generation.
55220-five-acres-too-much-a-truthful-elu:
Five Acres Too Much is a comic account of amateur farming by Robert Barnwell Roosevelt. Judd published the new and enlarged edition in New York in 1885. Roosevelt had earlier written books on fishing and game birds. The title page promises a careful look at profit and loss.

A mock dedication addresses writers of farming books. It thanks them for advice he followed with strict obedience. The contents keep the joke running. The first chapter treats the purchase of a cow. Her arrival sparks a fray in the back yard. Immense profits are promised with a straight face. Later chapters treat house plans and builders. The author admires his own genius throughout. The book warns city buyers what country life really costs.
55235-lord-roberts-message-to-the-nation:
Lord Roberts' Message to the Nation, by Field-Marshal Earl Roberts, was published by John Murray in London in 1912. The book gathers his campaign for national service in four parts. Part one, Peace and War, holds his speech to the citizens of Manchester of October 25, 1912, and a letter to the Manchester Guardian.

Part two takes up the Territorial Force, with the Mansion House speech examining Haldane's scheme. Part three answers working men, meeting Blatchford's criticism of the Manchester speech and printing a letter to the Times on compulsory service and the social condition of the working classes. Part four addresses territorial officers on the present crisis. The Manchester speech opens by honouring the city's part in building the empire, from the elder Pitt's designs in India to the repeal of the Corn Laws under Bright and Cobden.
55314-the-english-housekeeper-or-manual-:
The English Housekeeper is a home rule book by Cobbett, in its sixth form, made rich with many new plans for the pot. It came out at London in the mid eighteen hundreds, at a set price in coin. A front print shows the meat room of a great house.

Its full title tells its span room by room. It gives word on the run of house affairs, and plain rules for the store room, the dry store, and the meat room. The cook room, the wine vault, and the milk room close the list. The whole is meant, it says, for young ladies who take the rule of their own house keep in hand. A wise line from the old book heads its first words.
55319-olympic-national-park-washington:
Olympic National Park, Washington is Natural History Handbook Number One of the National Park Service, written by Gunnar O Fagerlund. It was printed by the Government Printing Office in 1954 and revised in 1965, and sold for thirty cents. The handbook explains the natural history of a scenic and scientific area in the National Park System.

The administration note states that Olympic National Park was established on 29 June 1938 and contains about fourteen hundred square miles. A superintendent at Port Angeles is in immediate charge of the park. The National Park System, the note says, is dedicated to conserving the scenic, scientific, and historic heritage of the United States. It is held for the benefit and enjoyment of the people. The front matter also sets out the work of the Department of the Interior, created in 1849, as the nation's principal conservation agency.
55361-flemington:
Violet Jacob's novel, published by John Murray in London in 1911, is set among the grazing lands of Angus, north of the Sidlaws. Her author's note denies that it is an historical novel and that any principal person in it is historic. She grants one truth: the taking of the ship, and the manner of its taking, really happened.

The book opens with Duthie, a minister, walking up the hill to Ardguys, the house of Madam Flemington, set above the Kilpie burn where it runs toward the river Isla. The chapters promise a coach-and-five, treachery, the guns of Montrose, and a winter parting of the ways. Later titles include Inchbrayock, the Muir of Pert, and A Royal Duke, and an epilogue closes the tale.
55397-railroad-reorganization:
Railroad Reorganization, by Stuart Daggett, is a study in the Harvard Economic Studies. Houghton Mifflin issued volume four of the series in nineteen o eight. Daggett taught economics at Harvard University when the book appeared. The series was issued under the Harvard economics department direction.

Chapter one treats the Baltimore and Ohio railroad case at length first. The study examines how failed railroads are rebuilt under new plans. Sister volumes in the set treat lodging houses, tin miners, and wool tariffs. Public ownership of telephones and the British post office stand there too. Readers get a scholarly account of railroad finance in hard times.
555-the-unbearable-bassington:
H. H. Munro, writing as Saki, satirizes Edwardian society in this novel of a charming, idle young man. Comus Bassington, unbearable to his mother Francesca yet loved by many, drifts through London drawing rooms, debts, and schemes. His mother, once the beautiful Miss Greech, watches his follies with cool, witty despair.

Munro writes with sharp, epigrammatic prose, and his author's note warns the tale has no moral and no remedy. The novel endures as a Saki study in wit, where a young man's charm proves both his gift and his ruin.
55504-the-tower-of-london:
Arthur Poyser described and John Fulleylove painted the Tower of London in a volume published by A and C Black at London in 1908. A front view shows the White Tower, with the Lanthorn Tower in the foreground, from Tower Bridge. Poyser dedicates the book to his father, Thomas Cooper Poyser. Verse on the mighty pile with its iron grated gates heads the dedication.

Macmillan acted as agent in America, Canada, India, and Australasia. Black's colour books paired a painter's plates with a writer's history. The Tower's story runs from Norman keep to prison and jewel house. Fulleylove was famed for architectural watercolours. The volume served tourists and armchair travelers.
55513-sea-scouts-all-how-the-olivette-wa:
Percy Westerman wrote Sea Scouts All, how the Olivette was won, illustrated by Charles Pears. One plate shows her simply lying over and refusing to recover in a squall. Westerman's long list includes Sea Scouts Abroad, Sea Scouts Up-Channel, chums of the Golden Vanity, and many Golden Dawn adventures.

Contents open with the scoutmaster's plan, two offers, the Olivette herself, Peter to the rescue, and a downstream run. Thieves, stranding, a tow, being caught out, Woodleigh the pilot, the Rosalie, a squall, and a find on the Gunfleet follow. Bruin the dog earns vindication, then down Channel, on her beam ends, and weatherbound days fill the tale. Boys got sailing adventure.
55648-lord-palmerston:
Anthony Trollope writes a short life in Lord Palmerston, issued by Wm Isbister in London in 1882 for the English Political Leaders series. The chapters track the posts: junior lord of the Admiralty and secretary at war from 1807, then foreign secretary in long stretches. The story of Don Pacifico gets a chapter of its own.

Home secretary years, the Crimean War with Palmerston as prime minister in 1855, and the Indian Mutiny follow, down to his death in 1865. Trollope owns his debts to Evelyn Ashley's biography and to Kinglake on the war. A brisk political life results.
55676-told-by-uncle-remus-new-stories-of:
Told by Uncle Remus, new stories of the old plantation, by Joel Chandler Harris, was copyrighted in 1903, 1904, and 1905, and issued by Grosset and Dunlap of New York. Frost, Conde, and Uerbeck drew the pictures. Sixteen stories follow an opening chapter called The Reason Why.

Why Mr Cricket Has Elbows on His Legs opens the tales. How Wiley Wolf Rode in the Bag, Brother Rabbit's Laughing-Place, and Brother Rabbit and the Chickens follow. When Brother Rabbit Was King, Why the Turkey-Buzzard Is Bald-Headed, and Why Mr Dog Is Tame stand among them. The Reason Why explains the gap since the old books. The little boy who heard the tales grew too big to grow any bigger. His parents moved to Atlanta, and Uncle Remus went with them. But he tired of the dubious ways of city life, and asked leave to go back to the plantation.
55692-the-surgery-of-ritual-circumcision:
Jacob Snowman, a London doctor and medical officer of the Initiation Society, wrote The Surgery of Ritual Circumcision in 1904. The society's medical board backed the printing. Snowman wrote to teach the surgical side of the Jewish rite.

The preface notes that lay Mohelim, not doctors alone, perform the rite, so each needs sound knowledge of the task. The syllabus stresses asepsis above all. Chapters treat the causes and results of wound infection, the antiseptic method, surgical anatomy, and the technique of the operation. Dressing, odd cases, repair of the wound, and bleeding close the course.
55735-perfumes-and-their-preparation:
Perfumes and Their Preparation is a practical manual by George William Askinson, a manufacturer of perfumery. Furst translated the book from the third German edition for its English issue. Henley in New York and Spon in London published it in 1892, with corrections and additions by several experts. The book is illustrated with thirty two engravings for its processes.

Its subtitle promises complete directions for making handkerchief perfumes for the trade and the amateur. Smelling salts, sachets, and fumigating pastils stand in the same list of its contents. Preparations for the care of the skin, the mouth, and the hair follow in the promise. Cosmetics, hair dyes, and other toilet articles complete the shown scope of the manual. The book is the perfumer craft in one volume, from flower waters to pomades, written before synthetics remade the trade.
55738-the-genetic-effects-of-radiation:
The Genetic Effects of Radiation is a short science book by Isaac Asimov and Theodosius Dobzhansky. Its contents run from the machinery of inheritance to dose and consequence. Cells and chromosomes open the account, then enzymes and genes. Parents and offspring close the first part. A section on mutations treats sudden change and spontaneous mutation rates. The genetic load gets a section of its own.

Radiation itself is then explained: ionizing kinds, background levels, and man made sources. Radiation sickness and radiation's power to cause mutation follow. Dosage rates and effects on mammals end the argument. Asimov was a biochemist at Boston University and a prolific science writer. Dobzhansky, a Kiev graduate at Rockefeller University, was a leading geneticist. Suggested references close the forty odd pages.
55749-the-raven-and-the-philosophy-of-co:
Edgar Allan Poe pairs his famed poem with his essay on how it was built in a quarto photogravure edition held under rights from 1906. Galen J Perrett painted the plates and Will Jenkins drew the decorations. Paul Elder and Company of San Francisco and New York issued the large volume.

The essay opens with a note from Charles Dickens on Godwin, who wrote Caleb Williams backwards from its tangles. Poe grants the point in part and states his own rule at once. Each plot worth the name must be worked to its end before a word is set down, he holds. Tone and incident must all tend to one set aim, or the tale loses its air of cause and effect.
55793-tube-train-tram-and-car-or-up-to-d:
Arthur Beavan wrote Tube, Train, Tram and Car, a survey of up-to-date locomotion published in London by Routledge in 1903. Dutton issued it in New York the same year. Llewellyn Preece, an electrical engineer, wrote the introduction, and a Bible line serves as motto: the chariots run like the lightning.

Twenty-one chapters track the new electric age of travel. Early ones treat pioneer electric railways and the renewal of the Metropolitan Inner Circle. The Central London Railway and the tubular system get full chapters, with a tour of London's tangled tubes. Trams in London and the provinces follow. Then come horseless vehicles, electric and otherwise, and a forecast of electricity applied to ships. The book ends on the drawbacks of the new power and its place in national life. Readers get 1903 at full speed.
55832-richard-judkins-wooing-a-tale-of-v:
Richard Judkins' Wooing is a tale of Virginia in the Revolution. Jenkins Hains wrote it, having written Captain Gore before this tale. Neely published it in New York and London in the year 1898. Chapter one opens with the narrator at ease on a verandah in summer. His feet rest on the hand rail as he watches the turnpike.

Major Bullbeggor rides around the bend and comes into view at a trot. The narrator notes the mare's hind feet throwing little jets of dust. Those jets form a yellow cloud behind the riding pair on the road. The major's servant rides some fathoms behind on an old claybank horse. Sun, dust, and old Virginia ease set the wooing in motion.
55878-the-new-spirit-third-edition:
The New Spirit, a book of essays by Havelock Ellis, is shown here in its third edition, with a new preface. Ellis says he has made no changes to the text. Three of his subjects were alive when he wrote, he notes, but their work was mostly done. Nothing new from them, he holds, would change one's view of them as forces of their age.

An introduction sets out what the new spirit means. Then come studies of Diderot, Heine, and Whitman. Ibsen and Tolstoy follow, and a conclusion draws the threads together. Ellis treats each writer as an original personal force, a starter of the future. The book first spread his name as a critic of bold, free thought. This edition preserves his portraits of five restless minds who broke the moulds of their day in letters, drama, and verse.
5588-a-question:
Georg Ebers's A Question, translated from the German by Mary J. Safford, opens with a verse prelude set in the Art Palace on green Isar's strand. Before one picture, the speaker sits long, held spellbound by some magic band, unable to forget it even at home. A year passes, winter comes, and at last he plucks up courage, crying be it so, and wanders southward with those he calls his own.

The novel that follows grows from that picture's spell, carrying its characters south like birds of passage. Ebers writes art's power as a call to travel. Readers get a romantic novel about a painting, a journey, and a question that will not let go.
55919-william-caxton:
William Caxton, by E Gordon Duff, was published at Chicago in nineteen oh five by the Caxton Club. Duff was Sandars Reader in Bibliography at Cambridge. The edition was limited: two hundred fifty-two copies on American hand-made paper, plus three on Japanese vellum. One hundred forty-eight copies even carry a leaf from Caxton's first Chaucer.

The chapters follow Caxton's early life and his press at Bruges. The early Westminster press and the years to fourteen ninety-one come next. Plates reproduce leaves in Caxton's successive types, including the Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye. That was the first book printed in English. The Mirrour of the World plates show the first woodcuts used in England. Duff's short life remains a bibliographer's Caxton, measured in types and leaves.
55957-a-study-of-army-camp-life-during-a:
A Study of Army Camp Life during the American Revolution is a school thesis by Mary Hazel Snuff. She gave it to the school of Illinois in nineteen eighteen for a high arts rank. Parts treat house, food and garb, health, play, faith, and drill rule in camp. The work rests on books of the age and on a rich note list. Its first part opens with the raw host that met at Boston in seventeen seventy five.

That host was more mob than army in its first wild days, she writes. No chief hand set huts, gave out food, or held the stores in charge. Men came from New England in the main, some three thousand from the south. Each state held the claim on its own men in those days. The college chief house at Cambridge was seized for the chief in that press.
56039-lincoln-s-plan-of-reconstruction:
Charles McCarthy wrote Lincoln's Plan of Reconstruction, a work of history published in New York in 1901. McCarthy studies how President Abraham Lincoln tried to bring the seceded states back into the Union while the Civil War still raged. The book sorts the story state by state, then turns to the fight over slavery law in Congress.

Chapters on Tennessee follow military governor Andrew Johnson, the amnesty proclamation, and the steps toward a restored state government. Louisiana gets a long chapter, from the capture of New Orleans to Lincoln's letter on Black suffrage and the election of 1864. Arkansas and Virginia follow, with Virginia's chapter tracing the Wheeling convention and the making of a new state. A final part weighs compensated emancipation, fugitive slaves, and the military power over slavery. Readers get a close, document-based account of how reunion was first attempted.
56043-rock-climbing-in-the-english-lake-:
Owen Glynne Jones wrote Rock-Climbing in the English Lake District, first issued in 1897 and here in a third edition from G P Abraham at Keswick in 1911. Jones was a member of the Alpine Club. Thirty-one full-page plates and ten outline plates of chief routes support the text.

George and Ashley Abraham added two appendices to bring the climbs up to date. Jones had written of many new climbs before his death, and those pieces stand as he left them. W M Crook supplies a memoir of the author with a portrait. The publishers call the book unique and invaluable, and note that the first edition sold out fast. Routes, technique, and Lakeland crags fill the guide.
56081-a-traitor-in-london:
Fergus Hume wrote A Traitor in London, for Buckles at New York in 1900. Hume was the author of The Mystery of a Hansom Cab. Chapter one, Cupid in Leading Strings, opens with a quarrel over money. Harold Burton demands his money from his cousin Gilbert Malet. Malet answers that Harold's father's will gives him every right to hold it.

If Malet approves of the marriage, the money falls due on the wedding day. He does not approve: Brenda Scarse is not the wife for Harold, he says. Harold is young, fiery-tempered, and in love, the tale notes. Thwarted in love, he rages for five minutes at his cousin. Malet trembles for the furniture, yet keeps a dignified calm. Black oak and deep red, with stained glass, frame the tale. Hume opens a London mystery on a will and a wedding.
56104-walks-about-washington:
Walks About Washington, by Francis Leupp with drawings by Hornby, was published by Little, Brown of Boston in 1915, its frontispiece showing the house where Lincoln died. The preface disclaims ambition at once: not a history, not a guide book, not an encyclopedia, only a stroll about the city with the reader.

Leupp promises a general look at Washington and its century and a quarter of growth. Then come leisurely walks through its public places, peopled in imagination with the figures once there. His stories come from personal observation, dinner table gossip, old letters and diaries, and local tradition. Where versions multiply, he takes the most probable or the most picturesque. The dedication names Ada, Harold, Ethel, Constance, and Kathleen, and the memory of Graham.
56121-shout-treason:
Francis Beirne wrote an account of the treason trial of Aaron Burr, printed in New York in 1959. A portrait of Burr from a drawing from nature by Saint Memin fronts the book. Beirne notes that Burr's story has been treated in many ways by many writers. Yet no full account of the trial stood apart from the stenographic report and one small old volume.

Beirne leans on Albert Beveridge for the legal technicalities, he owns with thanks. A prologue and twenty one chapters trace Burr's plot, arrest, and trial. A bibliography and index close the book. Readers get courtroom drama, politics, and a famed fallen vice president fighting for his life and name.
5617-the-bobbsey-twins-in-washington:
Laura Lee Hope wrote The Bobbsey Twins in Washington as another adventure for the Bobbsey family. Earlier books took them to the country, the seashore, school, Snow Lodge, a houseboat, and Meadow Brook. This volume takes the twins to the nation's capital, with chapters promising a monkey trick, found money, river trips, an enemy raid, a colonel, a pursuit, and a race.

The twins form their patrol, organize, face a challenge and a defiance, while Pepper carries a message, goes missing, and becomes a quest of his own. Hope writes clean, cheerful adventure for young readers. Children get a Washington story full of twins, trouble, and teamwork.
56178-forward-from-babylon:
Louis Golding wrote Forward From Babylon, published in New York by Moffat, Yard and Company in nineteen twenty one. Golding dedicated the book to his father. Three books divide the novel. Their titles are Forward From Doomington Walls, Forward From Phylacteries, and Aphrodite. Sixteen chapters run across the three books.

Chapter one opens in Russia, which the narrator calls the first Babylon. Philip sits on a metal stool by an oven, his second hand velvet suit fraying against the heat. His big eyes are round with horror of the huge, strange place, the tale says. Talk in the kitchen turns to Cossacks, spikes before the governor's house, and blood in the streets. Philip's father, Reb Monash Massel, is among the men in the room. Novel readers get a Jewish childhood told from inside a house of dread.
56299-from-convent-to-conflict-or-a-nun-:
Sister Antonia of the Convent of the Daughters of Mary at Willebroeck, in the province of Antwerp, wrote an account of the invasion of Belgium, printed at Baltimore in 1916. Her superior's letter of September 29, 1914, stands at the front, approved by Cardinal Mercier. The sisters Mary Antonia and Mary Cecilia were sent to the United States to examine if a colony of the Daughters of Mary could be established there.

Sister Antonia was given power to act in her superior's name for that purpose. The parochial school, convent, and garden, and the cloister itself are described before the approaching storm chapter. The carnage of battle, the return of the army, and anxious days follow. A Belgian nun's plain witness to 1914 reached American readers while the war still raged. Such accounts shaped how the United States saw Belgium's suffering.
563-the-planet-mars-and-its-inhabitants-:
A writer calling himself Eros Urides, a Martian of the city of Urid, describes Mars in this psychic revelation. Canals, double and gridironed, carry water from polar caps to reservoirs; flying ships replace trade; and a commonwealth supplies all wants without barter. Property belongs to God alone, says the author.

Chapters treat climate, economy, and spirit visions seen by a shorthand recorder. The book presents itself as dictation from Mars, not as science. It serves as a curious relic of early canal-era Mars lore, where a better world was imagined in red sands and shared goods.
56411-st-andrews-ghost-stories-fourth-ed:
Linskill, dean of guild at St Andrews, gathered ghost stories of the old town in a book reaching its fourth edition in 1921. A verse on the title page warns that ghosts can creep, crawl, hover, howl, shriek, and wail. The contents list seventeen hauntings, from the beckoning monk to a very peculiar house.

Lausdree Castle, the prior of Pittenweem, a phantom coach, and the veiled nun of St Leonards follow. A screaming skull at Greyfriars and the white lady of the haunted tower are local fixtures. The first tale is framed in Edinburgh, about the time of the Tay Bridge gale, where an artist tells the author his queer story. Local lore, told as true, is the ware.
56424-shores-of-the-polar-sea-a-narrativ:
Shores of the Polar Sea, by Edward Moss, is a narrative of the Arctic expedition of 1875 and 1876. Moss served aboard the Alert. The book was published in London in 1878, illustrated by sixteen colour plates and many engravings, from drawings made on the spot by the author.

A front picture shows an Eskimo boy with a fish. In his preface Moss says he places these sketches in his publishers hands, believing careful colour copies of his drawings would serve readers. The expedition was a British attempt on the far north by ship, sledge, and winter quarters. Readers get an eyewitness Arctic narrative where the pictures matter as much as the prose. Ice, coast, men, and native life are drawn by a man who was there.
56455-rebellion:
Joseph Medill Patterson, author of A Little Brother of the Rich, wrote Rebellion, a novel issued at Chicago by the Reilly and Britton Company in 1911. Walter Dean Goldbeck made the pictures, and the frontispiece is called Peccavi. Patterson thanks Francis Hackett for reading the unrevised proofs. The thirty-four chapters open with Jim Connor and run through One Flesh, An Economic Unit, The Head of the House, and Triangulation.

Later chapters bear names like The Palace of the Unborn, Georgia Leaves Home, The Priest, Sacred Heart, Surrender, and Kansas City. The tale opens in a bar, where Jim Connor bargains for just one more roll of the dice though he promised to be home on time for supper. The novel treats marriage, money, and faith in the life of a working city man.
56685-mr-durant-of-salt-lake-city-that-m:
Ben Rich's Mr Durant of Salt Lake City, That Mormon, was printed by Cannon and Sons at Salt Lake City in 1893. Rich's preface says Mormonism has been handled by many authors, most of them actuated by hatred. He aims to present the faith of the Latter-day Saints in plain and simple words, to help young men of Mormondom without missionary experience explain their belief to the nations.

The story brings Charles Durant, a new arrival from the West, to the Southern town of Westminster and the Marshalls' hotel, Harmony Place. On the veranda, evenings of discussion follow: the Godhead, baptism by immersion, laying on of hands, and the conditions of salvation. A reverend argues and retires from the argument. The book is a dialogue-novel of conversion, produced here by the Mormon Texts Project.
56703-ketchup-methods-of-manufacture-mic:
Ketchup, a trade study in two parts, was printed at Lafayette, Indiana, in 1915 by the Murphey-Bivins Company Press. A W Bitting wrote the part on methods of manufacture. K G Bitting wrote the part on microscopic examination. The authors offer the book in thanks for favours shown them by manufacturers, and keep the text as free of technical terms as the subject allows.

Ketchup is defined as a spiced sauce used to give relish to other foods. It takes its name from its base: tomato, grape, currant, mushroom, or walnut. The book urges one doctrine through both parts: sound fruit, clean methods, and sterilization. The word itself is traced to a Chinese term for the brine of pickled fish.
56712-the-comic-poems-of-thomas-hood-a-n:
Comic Poems of Thomas Hood appears here in a new and complete edition. Thomas Hood the younger, the poet's son, wrote a preface. The London edition came from a Salisbury Square house. Two pictures at the front show scenes captioned Faults on Both Sides and a war dance. The preface weighs the man behind the comic verse.

If the public, knowing only the comic works, were surprised at his solemn themes, the preface begins, those who saw him in the flesh were equally astonished. The famous wit was grave and melancholy to all appearance, it says. Chronic ill health gave his face that cast. Yet it could not affect the tone of his mind, the son writes. Here lies one who spat more blood and made more puns than any man living, Hood jestingly proposed as his own epitaph.
56735-sewage-disposal-works-their-design:
W C Easdale wrote Sewage Disposal Works, their design and construction. E and F N Spon issued it at London in 1910. Spon and Chamberlain shared the New York issue. One hundred fifty-five pictures aid the text. Easdale had written on sewage works management. An intro opens at page one.

Screens of many kinds fill the first part. Simple, rotary, and deep-sewer screens stand there. Storm-water overflows follow with their weirs. Detritus tanks take the next part in turn. The Dortmund type stands among those tanks. Sludge removal gear gets full treatment there. Tanks of all types fill the long middle. Precipitation and hydrolytic tanks stand named. The Imhof tank earns its own study. A builder's manual for the new sewage age shows towns learning to clean their outflows by tank, screen, and sludge well.
56791-st-patrick-the-father-of-a-sacred-:
Reverend Loughlin's Saint Patrick, the Father of a Sacred Nation is a lecture printed at Philadelphia in 1889 for the benefit of the Church of Our Lady of the Rosary. Loughlin tells his hearers he can say nothing new on a theme that has engaged one of the most eloquent races for generations. The charm, he says, lies in the hallowed memories, like the old melodies of the fatherland. His text is the call of Abram in Genesis.

The lecture draws the parallel his predecessors drew: as Abraham was called to father a sacred nation amid universal gloom, so Patrick was called in the fifth century. Ireland becomes the dwelling-place of light and truth, to pass its blessings to all the kindred of the earth. The address is an Irish-American oration in full pulpit dress.
5681-the-laws-of-etiquette-or-short-rule:
An unnamed gentleman author wrote this short manual of polite conduct for nineteenth-century social life. It covers good breeding, dress, salutations, and the drawing room. It also covers letters, visits, dinners, balls, funerals, and servants. Its preface disclaims literary ambition: the book claims no merit beyond correctness and fitness of application, and it hopes for a kind reception on those grounds alone. Each chapter takes one social situation and states what is expected.

Readers today gain a clear window into the manners of an age when a call, a letter, or a dinner seating carried real social weight. The advice is direct, sometimes stern, and often amusing in its care over small points. It serves social historians, novelists, and curious readers alike, since it records not just rules but the values behind them: punctuality, restraint, and respect for company.
56811-adventures-in-american-bookshops-a:
Adventures in American Bookshops is a book by Guido Bruno, published in Detroit by the Douglas Book Shop in 1922. One thousand copies were printed and the type then distributed, a mark of the fine-book trade Bruno moved in. He had written on Greenwich Village life, and this volume turns the same eye on the trade in old books.

The romance of buying and selling old things opens the book. Auctions as amusement places follow. One chapter tells the strange discovery and disappearance of Stuart's portrait of Washington. Then come the New York book shops: a den of a pessimist, a Whitman enthusiast, an optimist, a gambler. Shops of enthusiasts and dealers in cobwebbed corners fill the later pages. Bruno writes as a collector among collectors, and the book is a tour of a vanished world of second-hand shelves.
5683-the-critique-of-practical-reason:
Immanuel Kant's Critique of Practical Reason, in the Abbott translation, examines how reason can guide action apart from desire and reward. Book one analyzes pure practical reason, its principles, its objects, and its motives, while book two turns to the dialectic that arises when reason overreaches itself. Kant defines practical principles as rules that determine the will, then separates maxims, which bind only one person, from practical laws, which bind every rational being.

The argument is dense, but its question is plain: can duty stand on reason alone, without appeal to happiness or fear? Kant answers that freedom, rightly understood, gives moral law its force, and that ideas of the soul and the world gain weight once freedom is established. Readers of ethics and philosophy will find here the core of Kant's moral system, stated with a rigor that still sets the terms of debate.
56903-introduction-to-the-scientific-stu:
Education is a textbook on the study of schooling by Charles Hubbard Judd. Judd was professor of education and head of the school of education at the University of Chicago. Ginn and Company published the book in 1918. The full title promises an opening to the scientific study of education.

The first chapter argues that pupils see only a narrow slice of their school. Judd calls for a broad, scientific study of school problems. He points to studies of pupils held back, of high school courses, and of schooling in social life. The second chapter compares schools of other lands and other times. It weighs the German model and its sway over American schools. Exercises and readings close each chapter for class use.
56933-the-village-champion:
The Village Champion, by Stoddard, was published at Philadelphia in September 1903. Stoddard had written Boys of Bunker Academy and other tales. Plates show Pat Murphy's trap and a fight with the Rodney boys. The hero is Barnaby, called Bar, whose tale starts in a hot city square. Chapter one is called Barnaby Learns His Name. Crowded tenements and beer shops fill the opening scene.

Contents promise a haunted house, a boxing match, and ghosts in the academy belfry. Zeb Fuller and Major Montague recur in the heads. A black valise, two key telegrams, and a dun heifer drive later turns. The close brings good news for Bar and a trip home. Village sport, school pranks, and mystery mix here.
56945-the-yellow-typhoon:
The Yellow Typhoon is a novel by Harold MacGrath. Harper and Brothers published the book at New York in October 1919, with pictures by Will Grefe. MacGrath's other novels named on the title page include The Girl in His House. The scene of the opening is Manila, in the Philippine Islands.

The first chapter follows a naval officer along the Escolta, the chief street of Manila. His stride and set lips show a cold anger carried for six bitter years. The narrator likens that anger to glacial ice, moving always yet never melting. This day it has cleared his mind to one fixed thought. He means to settle an old matter once and for all. A frontispiece caption hints at a girl seen in every port, in fire and in moon mist.
56979-the-man-from-mars-his-morals-polit:
The Man from Mars is a book of social criticism by William Simpson, subtitled His Morals, Politics and Religion. This third edition, revised and enlarged, was copyrighted in 1900 at San Francisco. A new preface and a chapter on woman suffrage were added. Simpson dedicates the book to the memory of James Lick, the California philanthropist.

The device of the book is a visitor from Mars judging earthly ways. Through his eyes Simpson weighs the morals, parties, and churches of his day. The preface speaks for a lifetime's reading and thought aimed at the bottom of things. The work joins the era's flood of utopian and reform writing.
56995-the-campaign-of-waterloo-a-militar:
The Campaign of Waterloo, by John Codman Ropes, stands here in its third edition. Scribner printed it at New York in 1893, after a copyright of 1892. A supplementary atlas of the campaign was sold apart. Ropes held seats in several historical societies at home and abroad. Chapter one weighs the plan of campaign. Napoleon chose to strike Wellington and Blucher, Ropes says. Their armies' places are set out in turn. Rival accounts of the plan, from memoir and narrative, are compared.

Notes after the chapter test other writers' views. Wellington and Clausewitz condemned one reading of the plan. Hooper and Quinet defended it. Ropes works through orders, marches, and fields in close detail. The book is a careful American study of the hundred days, made for readers of military history.
5701-the-tale-of-fatty-coon:
Arthur Scott Bailey's Tale of Fatty Coon, part of the Sleepy-Time Tales and published in 1915, follows a young raccoon through small woodland adventures. Its chapters send Fatty home, then into lessons about eggs, a turtle's secret, a mistake, fishing, and green corn. Harry Smith's illustrations accompany the text, and each chapter offers one clear incident for a young listener.

The stories teach gently, through Fatty's curiosity and its consequences, rather than through lectures. Children meet woodland neighbors, seasonal food, and the risks of taking what is not theirs, all in short, friendly scenes. Parents reading aloud will find a calm, old-fashioned animal book, and young readers will enjoy following a mischievous hero who learns, slowly, to think before he acts.
57031-cotton-weaving-and-designing-6th-e: A trade book on the weave of cotton and the plan of cloth fills this text, in its sixth shape. The men who made this text note that it rests on the shape of 1909. Worked sums are kept in it as they stood, save that a few wrong sums in the lists have been set right. The book is a desk guide for the mill: how yarn is put through the loom, and how the face of the cloth is planned thread by thread.
5719-janice-meredith-a-story-of-the-amer:
Paul Leicester Ford sets Janice Meredith in the American Revolution, weaving a romance through the war for independence. Ford was already known for historical fiction and studies of Washington and Franklin. He dedicates the book to George Vanderbilt. He opens with a reflection on how much of an author goes into every book. The story follows Janice among soldiers, spies, and households divided by loyalty.

Readers meet the Revolution as lived experience: roads, camps, letters, and drawing rooms where political choice becomes personal. Ford balances adventure with period detail, letting Janice's courage and judgment carry the plot. The novel suits readers of historical romance who want the founding era told through one young woman's changing fortunes.
57198-regeneration:
Thomas Hunt Morgan wrote Regeneration, a study of regrowth in animals. The Macmillan Company issued it at New York in 1901. Morgan taught biology at Bryn Mawr College then. The book stands seventh in Columbia's Biological Series. Henry Fairfield Osborn and Edmund B Wilson edited that line. Morgan gave the book to his mother.

Chapter One gives the history of the work. Trembley, Bonnet, and Spallanzani lead that tale. More examples of regeneration follow at page six. Terms get their definitions at page nineteen. External factors fill the second chapter in full. Temperature's effect leads those factors there. Food's effect on regrowth follows it next. Osborn's From the Greeks to Darwin heads the series list. Wilson's Cell in Development stands fourth there. Morgan's careful experiments on worms and crabs built the facts that later made him genetics' great name.
57237-david-cusick-s-sketches-of-ancient:
David Cusick wrote Sketches of Ancient History of the Six Nations, printed at Lockport, New York, in 1848. Parts treat a tale of the foundation of the Great Island, now North America, with two infants born and the creation of the universe. A real account of early settlers and their dissensions and the origin of the Five Nations' long house kingdom follow.

Cusick waited long hoping some English-educated person of his people would sketch the ancient history, he says in the preface. Finding none, he began himself, though the history is involved with fables and his English is that of a non-native speaker. Wars and fierce animals fill the legendary record of the Iroquois. Native history readers get a rare Tuscarora voice.
57259-a-colored-man-s-reminiscences-of-j:
A Colored Man Reminiscences of James Madison, by Paul Jennings, was published at Brooklyn in 1865. A preface introduces the author. Among the labourers at the Department of the Interior, it says, is an intelligent colored man, Paul Jennings.

He was born a slave on President Madison estate at Montpelier, Virginia, in 1799. His reputed father was an English trader there. His mother was a slave of Madison, and the granddaughter of an Indian. Paul was a body servant of Madison till his death. Afterwards he served Daniel Webster, having purchased his freedom from Mrs Madison. As a daily witness of great events, his recollections were worth writing down in almost his own words. Readers get the first memoir of the White House by an enslaved man freed, a landmark of American testimony.
57318-the-scriptures-able-to-make-us-wis:
The Scriptures Able to Make Us Wise Unto Salvation, or The Bible a Sufficient Creed, is a religious treatise by Berrick of Lowell, Massachusetts. Calhoun Brothers printed it at Hartford in 1853. No work of human making, it opens, holds such a variety of principles making so complete a system as the Bible. It is the great fund of knowledge.

There we learn the character of God, his justice and mercy, the book argues. There we learn the history of man, made in God's image, perfect and upright, a candidate for immortality. Restrained by one command, yet free, he broke the law and heard the sentence: dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return. Berrick holds that the Bible needs no creed of men to complete it. His treatise belongs to the era's many arguments for taking scripture alone as the rule of faith,.
5742-the-bird-woman-of-the-lewis-and-cla:
Katherine Chandler tells the story of the Bird Woman of the Lewis and Clark Expedition as a supplementary reader for first and second grades. The Bird Woman is Sacajawea, the young Shoshone woman who traveled with the expedition as guide and interpreter, carrying her infant son. Chandler, author of books on California plants and Pacific folk lore, writes for the youngest school readers.

The book gives children a simple, heroic account of a famous journey, stressing guidance, courage, and knowledge of the land. Its short sentences and clear scenes suit classroom reading aloud.
