Modern readers should note that later scholarship adds detail and corrects early accounts, but as a period school reader it shows how Sacajawea's story was first taught to American children.
57529-lexington-and-concord-a-camera-imp:
Samuel Chamberlain made Lexington and Concord, a book of photos put out in New York in 1939. Chamberlain set out to catch two famed towns through a lens, not long prose. Each photo comes with a short note on what it shows. The book was set by hand in Garamond type in New Jersey.

Photos show Buckman Tavern, the statue of Captain John Parker, and the Old Manse of 1769. One long note tells of Munroe Tavern, built in 1695. Earl Percy used that inn as his base and sick ward on April 19, 1775. Its bar room kept a shot hole and the old inn sign. The book lets readers walk the first ground of the war for free rule at a slow pace.
57608-church-needlework-a-manual-of-prac:
Church Needlework, a manual of practical direction by Hinda M Hands, came out in London in 1907. Hands gives the small book to the holy church, as the work of a true daughter. It grows from pieces she wrote for a church journal. She aims at workers keen to learn by doing.

Chapters treat stuffs, frames, and how to trace a design. Gold work and silk work come next, then outline work and laid cloth shapes. Figure work and the hues for church feasts follow. Parts treat copes, caps for bishops, and cloths for the altar. Linen work and altar linen close the book. Hands notes that English church work led all the Christian world for two ages. Guild workers get years of craft in short form.
57660-joseph-pennell-s-pictures-of-the-w:
Joseph Pennell made Joseph Pennell Pictures of the Wonder of Work, a book put out in 1916. The book came out in Philadelphia and in London at once. It holds copies of his drawn work, his etched work, and his stone prints. The works span the years 1881 to 1915, with notes by the artist.

Pennell gives the book in honor of Constantin Meunier, whom he calls a prophet of the wonder of work. Work is the great thing in the world of this day, Pennell holds. The artist who best keeps a record of work will be best kept in mind, he adds. He traces art of work from the Tower of Babel and the Temple to his own age. Mills, yards, and great builds fill the plates. The book is both a gallery and a plea for art of real toil.
57694-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
David Widger compiled this index of the Project Gutenberg works of Coningsby Dawson, gathering the war books and novels of the Canadian officer-writer into one finding volume. Fourteen works are listed, among them The Glory of the Trenches, Carry On, Out to Win, The Kingdom Round the Corner, and Murder Point.

For each work the index prints its table of contents, so a reader can see the shape of every volume before opening it. Carry On appears with an introduction and notes by the author's father and its fifty letters numbered in sequence. Out to Win, the story of America in France, shows chapters called A Preface for Fools Only and War as a Job. Murder Point, a tale of Keewatin dated 1910, lists twenty-three chapters running from John Granger of Murder Point to The Last Chance.
57706-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
The Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of Henry Lawson, compiled by David Widger, gathers the tables of contents of Lawson's volumes held by Project Gutenberg. Lawson, the Australian house-painter, author, and poet of 1867 to 1922, is represented by When the World Was Wide and Joe Wilson and His Mates. On the Track, Over the Sliprails, Children of the Bush, and While the Billy Boils follow. The Rising of the Court and Verses Popular and Humorous complete the list.

Contents run from Faces in the Street and The Drover's Sweetheart to Past Carin' and The Song of Old Joe Swallow.
57721-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
The Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of Booth Tarkington maps one author’s shelf. David Widger built the guide to Tarkington’s books in that free store. Each work in the set stands with its own table of contents. The Flirt leads a roll of near a score of tales and plays.

Penrod, the boy of the Pageant of the Table Round, stands second. A Boy and His Dog heads that loved book’s long chapter list. Tar, the smallpox medicine, and the birthday party crowd its fun. Alice Adams and The Turmoil show Tarkington’s grave town vein. Seventeen and Penrod and Sam keep the boy world in full swing. Monsieur Beaucaire lends the roll its bright French court gem. The Magnificent Ambersons crowns the set with its proud fall tale. Chapter lists let each reader chart a road through the works.
57722-the-sermon-on-the-mount-a-practica:
A practical exposition of the Sermon on the Mount works through the great teaching passage by passage. The book was reissued in a new form, the preface says, with a few words added on set pages where the author treats the question of divorce in the Christian scheme. An appendix returns to the same hard subject at length. Spelling in the old text had not yet settled, the copy notes warn, and odd forms stand as printed.

Beatitudes, salt and light, prayer, fasting, and trust are opened for daily use rather than for scholars alone. The aim is a guide a plain reader can follow verse by verse. Church readers of the age bought such helps by the shelf. The divorce passages show the author wrestling with his own church's rule in print.
57742-robert-fulton:
Robert Fulton is a life of the inventor by Alice Crary Sutcliffe, his great-granddaughter, printed at New York in 1925 in the True Stories of Great Americans line. The book was first copyrighted in 1915, and Sutcliffe had earlier written Robert Fulton and the Clermont. A portrait from a family miniature stands at the front.

The contents trace Fulton from an old time Fourth of July and his boyhood to portrait painting and study in England. Chapters then turn to invention: the first submarine, early steamboats, and the building of the Clermont. Her first voyage gets a chapter of its own. The book closes with Fulton's home and honours, told with a family's pride.
57785-new-york-its-upper-ten-and-lower-m:
New York: Its Upper Ten and Lower Million is a novel by George Lippard, author of The Quaker City, printed at Cincinnati in 1854. The contents open with a preliminary sketch and a prologue. Part first, Frank Van Huyden, is dated the evening of 23 December 1844. Its chapters treat Frank and her singular visitor, and the childhood of the Midnight Queen.

Maidenhood, on the rock, among the Palisades, and home, adieu, carry the heroine forward. A revelation, morphine, and the sale is complete darken the tale. Part second runs from nightfall until midnight of the same day, through the Canal Street shirt store and the seven vaults. The white slave and his sister and the house of the merchant prince appear. Part third goes through the silent city to the den of Madam Resimer.
57894-how-to-do-mechanical-tricks-contai:
A Anderson wrote How to Do Mechanical Tricks, a guide to more than sixty smart tricks. Frank Tousey issued the book in New York in nineteen hundred two. Drawings show each set-up step by step. The tricks rest on balance, force, and the laws of motion.

One trick stacks checkers in a pile that defies a blow. Others use coins, cards, string, and matches. A knife hangs in mid air by a fine trick of balance. Some items turn to real craft, such as cheap letter scales. A home photo camera and a small gas burner join the list. Light play and sight tricks close the set. Young tinkerers get both fun and a first taste of physics.
57904-the-doom-of-london:
Fred M White gathered six tales of disaster in The Doom of London, first printed in Pearson's Magazine in 1903 and 1904. Warwick Goble drew the pictures. The opening tale, The Four White Days, puts London in the grip of an Arctic winter.

An editor at the Daily Chat faces a thin paper as frost drives the glass toward zero. News from north of the Trent stops when wires fail in a huge blizzard. Famine, cold, and fire threaten the city, and a plate shows the Hotel Cecil in flames. Later tales treat a dust of death, an unseen force, and a river of death. White tests how fast a great city breaks when nature or science turns on it.
57907-seventeen-trips-through-soma-lilan:
Captain Swayne of the Royal Engineers recorded seventeen trips through Somaliland between 1885 and 1893, in a volume of exploration and big game shooting published at London in 1895. It narrates journeys in the hinterland of the Somali Coast Protectorate from the beginning of its administration by Great Britain, with notes on the wild fauna of the country.

Swayne dedicates the book to his brave and intelligent Somali followers, and thanks his brother for journals, sketches, and once saving his life. A frontispiece photograph, taken by a Somali at the noon bivouac on the Ambal river in March 1891, shows the author and his escort. Maps and photographs fill out a surveyor-sportsman's record of a protectorate's first decade.
57929-selections-from-saint-simon:
Arthur Tilley of King's College, Cambridge, edited these selections from the memoirs of Saint-Simon, published by Cambridge University Press in 1920. The contents begin with Louis the Fourteenth himself, then Madame de Maintenon, then the daily life of the king.

A set of portraits follows: Vauban, Fénelon, Vendôme, the Duc and Duchesse de Bourgogne, and the Duc d'Orléans among them. The introduction, glimpsed here, compares Saint-Simon's reform schemes with Fénelon's and finds a shared utopian streak, both men looking fondly backward. Appendices give the councils and secretaries of state, and extracts from Vauban's tax project. Students get the great court memoirist in a teachable compass, in French.
58001-spiritual-victories-through-the-li:
Spiritual Victories, Through the Light of Salvation is a sermon by J Church, a minister of the gospel. He preached it on Sunday, March 11, 1810, at the Obelisk Chapel, and it was printed that year in Southwark, London. Church published it only because friends who heard it pressed him hard. In his preface he admits he rebuilt the sermon from memory, leaving some ideas out and adding others.

His text is Judges chapter 7, verse 20, the night attack of Gideon, when three companies blew trumpets and broke pitchers. Church draws three lessons from Israel's history: proof of human sin, proof of God's patience, and proof of His anger at their conduct. He writes in a plain style, he says, to exalt Jesus and comfort believers. Readers get a full example of plain pulpit preaching from the early 1800s.
58032-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
David Widger compiled an index of the Project Gutenberg works of Gilbert Chesterton. The Innocence of Father Brown heads the contents, then The Wisdom of Father Brown and Heretics. The Man Who Was Thursday, The Club of Queer Trades, and What's Wrong with the World follow. Manalive, The Ballad of the White Horse, and The Man Who Knew Too Much stand in the long roll.

The Ball and the Cross, Tremendous Trifles, Alarms and Discursions, and All Things Considered come next. The Crimes of England, The Barbarism of Berlin, and The Appetite of Tyranny mark the war years. Orthodoxy, The Victorian Age in Literature, a life of Browning, a life of Shaw, and A Short History of England close the shelf. The index then prints each book's own contents in full.
58033-the-story-of-american-aviation:
Jim Ray tells and draws The Story of American Aviation, from the John C Winston Company, copyrighted in 1946. Ray illustrated the book himself, and the cover counts over 150 illustrations in color of America's most famous airplanes, old and new. The contents begin with the dreamers of flight in legend.

Chapters proceed through the first Army airplane, aviation in the Great War, the first transatlantic flight, and the first air mail. Pan American Clippers, superchargers, Thunderbolts, and the Superfortress carry the story to the Second World War, and a postwar chapter ends it. Boys get the whole sweep.
5815-the-great-impersonation:
Oppenheim opens The Great Impersonation in scrub country, where Everard Dominey fights toward thin, spiral wisps of smoke. He has pushed through brush for three quarters of an hour. He urges his pony to a last despairing effort. He crashes through a great oleander shrub and pitches forward on his head into a little clearing. From that fall, a tale of identity, impersonation, and hidden pasts unfolds.

This gives a classic thriller of doubles and secrets, set between English country life and wider intrigues. Oppenheim builds suspense through mistaken identity and the fear of exposure, letting Dominey's past shadow his present. Fans of early spy and mystery fiction will enjoy a brisk, atmospheric novel where no one is quite who they seem.
58182-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
David Widger compiled this index of the Project Gutenberg works of Thomas Dixon. The list names The Foolish Virgin, The One Woman, The Man in Gray, and The Clansman. It adds romances of Jefferson Davis and of Lincoln, plus The Leopard's Spots, The Traitor, and The Fall of a Nation. Full contents follow for the volumes in turn.

For The Foolish Virgin, chapter heads move from a friendly warning through temptation, a trial, and a wedding to a soul being born. The One Woman is billed as a story of modern utopia, drawn by B West Clinedinst. Its heads run from a stolen kiss to a scarlet flame in the sky. Readers can weigh each novel's shape before they choose one to read.
58271-the-tower-of-london:
The Tower of London, by William Benham, was published in 1906. Seeley issued it in London, with Dutton in New York. Benham was rector of a City church and a canon of Canterbury. He gives the book to the Major of the Tower, Sir George Bryan Milman. Milman had helped him in the labour of love, Benham writes. A front plate in colour shows the Tower from an old manuscript. Seven chapters make the account. Early history and a survey of the buildings come first.

The days of the later Plantagenets follow. Tudor kings and Tudor queens take two chapters. The Stuarts and the House of Hanover close the story. Colour plates from illuminated manuscripts in the British Museum enrich the volume. Benham writes a learned guide to the fortress and its memories.
58325-through-one-administration:
Frances Hodgson Burnett set this novel in Washington, and Scribner reprinted it in 1916 from the copyrights of 1881 and 1883. Eight years before the Administration of the story, a young officer came to Washington on a farewell visit. Philip Tredennis was a favorite of a distant relative, a well-known entomologist whom Burnett calls Professor Herrick. Tredennis was on the point of leaving the civilized world for a far-away Western military station.

At the Smithsonian, and in scientific society, the farewell round begins. The novel then jumps the eight years to the Administration that its events make important. Burnett had written That Lass o' Lowrie's and Haworth's by then, tales of Lancashire and America. Here her subject is the capital itself: its drawing rooms, its ambitions, and the price of place. The book was an early American political novel with a woman's eye for the social machinery of power.
5833-helping-himself-or-grant-thornton-s:
Horatio Alger follows Grant Thornton, a minister's son, in Helping Himself, opening with his mother lamenting their terrible poverty. Grant, fifteen, asks what is new, and his mother answers that nothing is new, only the old hardship grown heavier. Chapters follow Grant's business calls, a walk to Somerset, a timely rescue, his mother's pearls, unexpected trouble, and a day in Wall Street.

The book introduces a classic Alger hero whose ambition is honest work, not sudden luck. Grant takes decisive steps, makes friends, and learns business one call at a time, while family need keeps the stakes clear. The novel suits young readers who enjoy stories of effort rewarded, and it offers a clear example of Alger's hopeful, hardworking boyhood ideal.
58451-the-trials-of-a-country-parson:
Augustus Jessopp, a Norfolk clergyman and historian, wrote essays on the trials of a country parson, issued in London in 1890. In his preface he says a past book of his had been read quite against his intent. He had meant to show country folk as they were, faults and virtues both.

Jessopp had come back to village life after long years in a large town, and found much changed. Country folk, he says, had not shared in the gains of town life, yet kept their sturdy virtues and love of home. Their discontent, he argues, has real cause, and agitators feed on it. Sympathy with facts, not crude theory, is his plea.
58507-my-colored-battalion:
My Colored Battalion is a memoir by Major Warner Ross, published by the author in Chicago in 1920. Ross dedicated the book to the American Colored Soldier. The text is the speech of a white officer honouring the Black battalion he commanded in the First World War.

Ross tells his audience why they honour him: he commanded a wonderful fighting infantry battalion composed entirely, himself excepted, of American colored officers and colored men. For some time in the war, he recalls, they stood in the very front lines of the Allied wave in France. The battalion, he insists, had no doubt about its Americanism, no question of hyphens, and no love or hatred of another nation outweighing its love of its own. Their devotion, patriotism and loyalty, he says, did their duty by their country and did it well. The book is a rare white officer's public tribute.
58555-religion-morality-vindicated-again:
Religion and Morality Vindicated Against Hypocrisy and Pollution is an account of the life and character of John Church. The hosted copy is the second edition, printed at London in eighteen thirteen. Church is called the obelisk preacher in its subtitle. He was formerly a frequenter of Vere Street, it says. He had been charged with unnatural practices in various places, it adds. A copy of a letter by him is annexed.

A note to the public explains the editor's motives. The statements first appeared in a weekly dispatch, it says. Demand for those numbers was so great that many hundreds could not procure the papers. The editor therefore reprints them in defence of religion, the note claims. Church's trial was expected at the start of June, it adds.
58569-beyond-the-horizon:
Beyond the Horizon is a play by Eugene O'Neill, printed for the Dramatists Play Service. O'Neill's name stands on the service's advisory board alongside Sidney Howard, George Kaufman, and Elmer Rice. The service handled non-professional acting rights for its members' plays.

The front matter explains the service's work. It leased Broadway successes, standard plays, and unproduced new plays to college theatres, little theatres, and other amateur groups across the English-speaking world. O'Neill's tragedy of two brothers and the sea belongs to his first great period. An acting edition like this one carried modern drama far beyond Broadway. Rights notices for performance, radio, and reading fill the opening pages. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
58591-hygiene-a-manual-of-personal-and-p:
Hygiene, a manual of personal and public health by Arthur Newsholme, teaches the rules of healthy living for the body and for the town. Newsholme was medical officer of health for Brighton. This new edition, almost wholly rewritten, was published in London in 1902.

The preface notes that the book had sold steadily for nearly twenty years. New matter brings each subject up to the newest knowledge of the day. The manual now aims at medical students as well as the science students and general readers of the first editions. Pictures illustrate the text throughout. The catalog title is clipped, but the title page gives the book's full name.
58603-christ-the-true-melchisedec-being-:
Christ the True Melchisedec is the substance of a sermon preached on Sunday evening, July 24, 1813, at the Obelisk Chapel. Its preacher, Church, signs himself minister of the gospel, and Thomas printed the sermon in London in 1813. Three texts head it, among them the word from Hebrews: now consider how great this man was.

The sermon opens on the covenant of redemption. The sacred pages, Church preaches, exhibit the loving heart of a covenant God, Father, Son, and Spirit, from whom all blessings of eternal life flow to guilty man. Before the world began, he argues, the Son accepted the work of salvation: to assume the nature of his people, represent them, obey, suffer, and die for them. On the very day Adam sinned, the Redeemer hastened to make the covenant known, pronouncing the blessing before the curse.
58715-drawings-of-old-london:
Drawings of Old London is a museum catalogue of drawings by Philip Norman, issued in nineteen thirteen. The Victoria and Albert Museum published it at sixpence from the Stationery Office. Norman made nearly all the drawings from the buildings themselves, on the spot. Many of those buildings have since been pulled down or much altered.

The museum bought the set in January eighteen ninety six on expert advice. William Morris was one of those who urged the purchase for the nation. Entries give sizes in inches and a note on each old house shown. Southwark inns lead the list, the Queen's Head, White Hart, and Nag's Head. The Elephant and Castle tavern at Newington Butts opens the entries proper. Students may see the drawings in a named room of the museum.
5872-cashel-byron-s-profession:
Bernard Shaw's Cashel Byron's Profession opens at Wiltstoken Castle, a square building with circular bastions at its corners, each ending skyward in a Turkish minaret. The southwest front bears a Moorish arch fitted with glass doors, secured on occasion by gates of fantastically hammered iron, and enshrined by a Palladian portico. From that romantic castle, Shaw launches a novel about a prizefighter's profession.

Readers get Shaw's early blend of romance and social satire, as boxing, class, and love collide. Cashel's profession tests respectability, since a fighter's fame and a lady's world seldom meet. The novel suits readers of Shaw's fiction, Victorian romance with a twist, and stories where physical courage must answer to social judgment.
58722-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
The Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of Richard Burton is a guide list made by David Widger. It sets out the works of Burton held in that free book store, with the full lists of their parts. The first and great head is the vast set of tales of the east, in ten parts and in six more parts of a next set.

Next stand tales of ape lands and of falls of a great stream, a land of the mid east in two parts, and a chant poem of a false east sage. Works on the gold coast, on a prince and a blood drink beast of old tales, and on the love lore of the east take their rows. Trips to the holy towns and first steps in the east close the main list.
58764-cycle-rides-round-london:
Cycle Rides Round London was ridden, written, and drawn by Charles G Harper, and printed in London in 1902. Harper had made his name with books on the great roads of England, from the Brighton Road to the Holyhead Road. Here he turns to short rides out of the capital.

Routes lead to Chenies and the Milton country, from Surbiton to Leatherhead, and to Ightham Mote. Each ride mixes road notes with old inns, churches, and tales of the place. A plate shows the old lych gate at Penshurst. Harper writes for the new crowd of cyclists keen to flee town on free days. Readers get routes, lore, and views in one handy, well drawn guide.
58787-the-elements-of-child-protection:
Sigmund Engel wrote The Elements of Child-Protection, in Eden Paul's translation. Macmillan at New York put out the book in 1912. Engel was a doctor of laws and an official guardian in Budapest. Contents open with certain population problems for the general part. Child-protection and the population question stand first in his scheme.

The fertility of the lower classes and the tendency of evolution follow. Statistical problems of population take the second chapter's ground. Miscarriages, still-births, and mortality are weighed in its tables. The excess of women, marriage, and illegitimate relations stand there too. Child mortality takes the third chapter, with its causes sifted. Housing conditions in the towns bear much of the blame, he holds. Age, season of birth, and weather all enter his reckoning. Engel gives child welfare as a science of numbers and law.
58859-medical-inquiries-and-observations:
Benjamin Rush, a teacher of medicine at the University of Pennsylvania, wrote four volumes of medical notes. Volume one came out in a second edition at Philadelphia in 1805, revised and enlarged by the author. Rush taught both the rules and the bedside use of his art.

The preface lists fresh facts on strong drink and its harm to body and mind. Notes on tetanus, croup, and old age also grew in this edition. Rush reworked his account of fever and moved parts of his tale of the yellow fever of 1793 to a later volume. Dropsy, lung disease, and rabies fill much of volume two.
58860-medical-inquiries-and-observations:
Medical Inquiries and Observations, by Benjamin Rush, is a four volume work on the practice of medicine. Rush was professor of medicine and clinical practice at the University of Pennsylvania. This second volume is from the second edition, revised and enlarged by the author. It was published at Philadelphia in the early republic.

Rush writes on diseases, their causes, and their cures as he observed them in practice. The hosted text ranges beyond fevers into the mind, treating the moral faculty as a native power of telling good from evil. Paul and Cicero, he says, give the best accounts of it found in old or new writing. Rush was a signer of the Declaration of Independence and the leading American doctor of his age. His volumes show medicine when bleeding and purging still ruled, yet careful bedside watching was already reshaping the art.
58861-medical-inquiries-and-observations:
The third volume of Benjamin Rush's Medical Inquiries and Observations, in the second edition revised and enlarged by the author, came from Conrad at Philadelphia in 1805. Rush was professor of the institutes and practice of medicine at the University of Pennsylvania. Four pieces fill this volume. The Outlines of a Theory of Fever comes first, setting out the principles and language of the whole work. Rush declines to define fever, which appears in too many forms.

The rest of the volume is one disease in one city. Rush gives his account of the bilious yellow fever as it appeared in Philadelphia in 1793, at full length. Shorter accounts follow for 1794, and for the sporadic cases of 1795 and 1796. The 1793 epidemic made Rush famous and controversial in his lifetime. His theory of fever, and his practice against it, are argued here from his own case-books.
58862-medical-inquiries-and-observations:
Medical Inquiries and Observations, volume four, is the work of Benjamin Rush of Philadelphia. Rush was professor of medicine and clinical practice in the University of Pennsylvania. A second edition, revised and enlarged by the author, appeared in 1805. Four volumes make up the full set of his inquiries in print.

Volume four is ruled by accounts of yellow fever in Philadelphia year by year. The outbreaks of 1797, 1798, and 1799 each get a full account in the contents. Sporadic cases from 1800 to 1805 and the measles of 1801 fill in the record. Facts meant to prove yellow fever not contagious form a long later section. A defence of blood letting as a remedy in set diseases closes the medical argument. Rush stands here as a witness to epidemic years in his city.
58867-biology-and-its-makers-with-portra:
William Locy, professor at Northwestern University, wrote Biology and Its Makers, with portraits and other illustrations, published at New York in 1908. He dedicates the book to his graduate students, who worked by his side in the laboratory. Part one treats the sources of biological ideas apart from evolution.

Its first chapter outlines the rise of biology and the epochs in its history. Notable advances in natural science during the nineteenth century open the account. Biology, Locy argues, is the central subject in the history of opinion about life, and its progress, for all its detail, has been simple and orderly. Readers get a history of a science told through the men who made it.
58869-east-london:
Walter Besant's East London, published by the Century company at New York in 1901 with copyrights from 1899, surveys the great working-class half of the city. Twelve chapters map it: what East London is, the city of many crafts, and the Pool and the riverside. The wall, the factory girl, the key of the street, the alien, the houseless, and the submerged follow. Memories of the past, sports and pastimes, and the helping hand close the volume. Besant had already written London, South London, and Westminster in the same survey manner.

Illustrations by Phil May, Joseph Pennell, and Raven-Hill crowd the list: Limehouse streets, barge-builders, the West India dock gates, hooligans, Sunday gambling, Petticoat Lane, and a Salvation Army shelter. Besant writes of the East End as a city in itself, as populous and distinct as any capital, and largely unknown to the London of the West End.
58874-tarzan-and-the-golden-lion:
Tarzan and the Golden Lion, a novel by Edgar Rice Burroughs, was copyrighted in 1923 and issued by Grosset and Dunlap of New York. Pictures by J Allen St John go with the text. The book belongs to the Tarzan series, and its title beast is Jad-bal-ja, the golden lion.

The opening shows Sabor the lioness nursing a single cub after hunger thinned her milk. Early chapters tell how the golden lion was trained and how Tarzan met with mystery. Later ones bring golden ingots, a chamber of horrors, and a diamond hoard. A map of blood and a torture of fire raise the stakes. Escape and capture close the tale.
58886-the-crescent-moon:
Francis Brett Young wrote The Crescent Moon, a novel printed at New York with rights from 1918. Young had writ Marching on Tanga from the East Africa campaign. A narrator steps onto the platform at Nairobi with no idea what he is in for, on a hot November day with rains due.

His job is to load Indian sepoys, freed by the Belgian advance on Taborah, into ambulances for hospital. The platform swarms instead with mission folk come to greet missionaries held as German prisoners, now sent down by train. His wounded men must wait while the shabby, sad crowd pours out. Six thousand feet up, the air still sticks like an August school treat. War, faith, and pity meet in a tale of the African front.
58935-the-causes-of-prostitution:
The Causes of Prostitution is a sociological essay by James P Warbasse, reprinted from the Twentieth Century Magazine of July 1912. Warbasse begins with wonder that there is not greater public appreciation of the prostitute-making conditions which society harbors. Society foolishly thinks that it profits by them, he says. A prostitute, he defines, is a woman who offers her body for hire.

Prostitution means promiscuity for hire, and its study should be approached with sympathetic minds. The prostitute in America is likely to be a weak character who has fallen victim to the vicious conditions society maintains. The glamor spoken of as belonging to her traffic does not really exist for her. Once engaged in it, she finds escape difficult unless powerful social forces are brought to bear. The two fundamental causes, the essay holds, are sexual lust on the part of men and poverty on the part of women.
58991-inhibition:
Inhibition is a science fiction story by James Causey. It was printed in Worlds of If Science Fiction in February 1955. The hero, Saxon, is called a good agent. No culture and no person would sway his loyal judgment of a new world.

The story opens at planetfall. Saxon greets them with a bright, feverish smile. The engineers, he says, are behind schedule and will build their city the next day. He calls the world Eden and says the survey spent thirty years making it safe. In truth he knows that thirty percent of the newcomers will be dead within the week. Strange sounds come from the forest as he plays out the last minutes of the welcome. The tale turns on the gap between the fine report and the facts on the ground.
58994-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
The Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of Ralph Waldo Emerson is a guide to that author's works in the Gutenberg stock. It was put together by David Widger, who also produced the ebook. The contents list the books in order. The Essays, First Series, stand first, then the Essays, Second Series, and Representative Men.

The Correspondence of Carlyle and Emerson, in two volumes, stands in the list. May-Day and Other Pieces, the book called Essays, and Nature stand there too. The Conduct of Life and English Traits close the row. Tables of contents of the volumes follow in the index itself. The first such table, for the Essays, First Series, runs from History and Self-Reliance to Compensation, Spiritual Laws, Love, Friendship, Prudence, Heroism, and The Over-Soul.
58998-the-church-the-falling-away-and-th:
Shepherd's The Church, the Falling Away, and the Restoration was printed at Nashville, Tennessee, by the Gospel Advocate Company in 1961, under a copyright of 1929. Shepherd edited the Handbook on Baptism and Queries and Answers. Four parts divide the work, and the contents run to hundreds of short heads.

Part one asks what the church of the present should be: its worship, its fellowship, the breaking of bread, its elders, deacons, and evangelists, and the bar on infant baptism. Part two traces the falling away foretold, through the confessional and indulgences to John Tetzel. Part three follows the Reformation in Europe, through Wycliffe, Tyndale, and Luther at Worms. Part four brings the Restoration movement to America, with Barton Stone and the great meeting at Cane Ridge.
59019-the-road-away-from-revolution:
The Road Away from Revolution is an essay by Woodrow Wilson, printed by the Atlantic Monthly Press at Boston in 1923. The piece first ran in The Atlantic Monthly for August of that year. A portrait of Wilson, dated 1923, fronts the small book. The former president writes in a time of unrest across the world.

In these doubtful and anxious days, he begins, all the world is at unrest. He asks which way a nation should look for peace and order. His road leads away from revolution, toward calm reform and settled law. The essay is short, but it holds the creed of a statesman after war. Wilson speaks as a scholar of government as much as a past leader. Readers get his counsel in his own plain and formal style.
59122-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
David Widger compiled an index of the Project Gutenberg works of Lord Byron. George Gordon Noël Byron is the full name in its front line. Full contents for each Byron volume in the set then follow. Seven volumes of verse and prose lead the long roll.

Letters and journals of the poet take two volumes more. Fugitive Pieces and Childe Harold’s Pilgrimage stand on their own. Don Juan crowns the list of long works in the index. Hours of Idleness, his first book, fills a wide early part. Poems to Caroline, to Emma, and to Mary crowd those years. School themes, a Greek play in English dress, and epitaphs join them. A Day with Lord Byron caps the whole Byron shelf here. Readers can trace one poem to its book at a glance.
59132-what-have-the-greeks-done-for-mode:
John Pentland Mahaffy of Trinity College, Dublin, gave these talks as the Lowell Lectures of 1908-09, and Putnam printed them in 1909. He had spent more than half a century on old Greek life. Here he asks what the Greeks have done for the modern world, and answers field by field.

Greek poetry and prose come first, then Greek art in building, carving, painting, and music. Science follows, with grammar, logic, sums, and healing. Politics, law, and the life of towns take a full lecture. The last talk turns to higher thought, covering Greek ideas on the mind, on right and wrong, and on the gods.
59147-the-forest-monster-or-lamora-the-m:
The Forest Monster appears as number two hundred fourteen in Beadle's Dime Novels, a semi monthly series from Beadle and Company of New York. Then the title page names the tale in full: The Forest Monster, or Lamora, the Maid of the Canon. Chas E LaSalle wrote it, and the firm entered it for copyright in eighteen seventy.

His story is billed as a romance of the far West. Chapter one, The Mysterious Rescue, opens on a howling prairie wind. Feathery snow rides the air in spring, in a high part of the far West. The peaks of the Black Hills loom white in the distance. Night closes in and the peaks fade into thick gloom. Dime novel readers get a western romance that starts with storm, snow, and a rescue in the hills.
59163-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
An index of the Project Gutenberg works of Francis Bacon, compiled by David Widger, lists the writings of Bacon held in that library. The contents name the Essays first, then Wisdom of the Ancients. Novum Organum and The Advancement of Learning stand in the list. The New Atlantis and Valerius Terminus are there as well.

A piece called Bacon is Shakespeare shows the old quarrel in the set. The table of the Essays is given in full by title. Of Truth, Of Death, Of Revenge, and Of Adversity head that famous list. Of Parents and Children, Of Envy, and Of Love follow in order. The index is a finder for readers of the digital library. It maps a great prose writer in one spread of titles.
59174-task-mission:
Fox Holden wrote a short tale printed in Worlds of If in April 1955. Captain Nicholas Joel waits on the fore bridge of his ship, the White Whale. Through thick quartz panes he watches a jeep bound out of a planted forest. It races over yellow sand, kicking up clouds behind it.

Joel knows what the men will say before they speak. They have hit it again, they will cry. He works out how long the lift will take to bring them up to him. Then he opens his drink cabinet while he waits. Sam Carruthers, his surgeon and mind doctor of twenty two years, will speak first. The blurb hints the perfect world they found hides a twist.
59188-picturesque-london:
Picturesque London is a guide in words and pictures by Percy Fitzgerald, printed at London in 1890. Fitzgerald gave the book to David Plunket, the First Commissioner of Works. Seven artists drew for it, and a view of the Houses of Parliament, drawn by Hume Nisbet, stands at the front in photogravure.

In his preface Fitzgerald says he can only pick samples from so rich a field. His aim is to show that London holds as much of the picturesque as any foreign city, with romance in spots a plain guide book would miss. He writes as a living guide, the fruit of years spent walking far and little known quarters of the town.
59279-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
David Widger compiled this index of the Project Gutenberg works of Alfred, Lord Tennyson, the poet laureate. The file lists the volumes the project holds and prints the contents of each one. It is a finding aid for locating a poem or play quickly.

The contents open with Idylls of the King, its twelve books running from The Coming of Arthur through Gareth and Lynette, Merlin and Vivien, and The Passing of Arthur. Enoch Arden and its companion pieces follow, from Aylmer's Field to Tithonus and Boadicea. The Early Poems volume is laid out in scholarly parts, comparing the editions of 1830, 1832, and 1842, from The Lady of Shalott to Ulysses and Godiva. Queen Mary and Harold, Becket and other plays, Maud, and the suppressed poems complete the shelf. Readers get the whole shape of Tennyson's work at a glance.
59283-josiah-allen-on-the-woman-question:
Marietta Holley's 1914 satire hands the pen to Josiah Allen, husband of Samantha, who resolves at last to answer her writings against man's superiority to women. His chapters talk on women's duty to marry and man's protecting love.

Josiah argues in dialect that he kept silent for years lest argument ruffle a woman's mind and spoil her cooking, leaving his pie and cookie jar at risk. Chapters prove man's courtesy, condemn modern women, and warn of women's extravagance and exaggeration. The humor runs on his wounded feelings and mighty intellect, forever undercut by Samantha. Fleming Revell published the book in 1914 at New York, Chicago, and Toronto.
59295-the-isthmus-of-suez-question:
Isthmus of Suez Question is a pamphlet by Ferdinand de Lesseps, published in London in 1855. Longman and partners issued it in London, with Galignani in Paris, in that year. Lesseps is named as a minister plenipotentiary on the title page. A Latin motto bids to open the earth to the nations of the world.

Contents give the question submitted, and then an appendix of the papers of the scheme. Lesseps memorial to the Viceroy of Egypt and the firman of concession stand first in that appendix. His instructions to the engineers and a precursory scheme follow in the list of papers. The pamphlet is the birth certificate of the Suez Canal in print. Lesseps argues his concession, his levels, and his company before the public of two capitals, fourteen years before the canal opened.
59438-avoidance-situation:
James McConnell wrote the tale Avoidance Situation. Worlds of If ran it in February 1956. Captain Allen Hawkins commands the ship Sunward. He stands in the watch room, eyeing subspace. Gold crowds his sleeve and silver his hair. Years in the Space Navy taught him their link.

A ship's shrink, Doctor J L Broussard, speaks behind him. God forsaken fits the view better, Broussard says. Bridge noise hums behind the quiet room. Hawkins loves these lone looks beyond the shell. The blurb poses his hard choice in plain terms. One man must decide the fate of Earth. Slavery and death are the choices set before him. Cold-war space fiction at its starkest, the tale asks what one officer owes a whole world.
59461-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
The Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of Jack London, compiled by David Widger, lists London's volumes held by Project Gutenberg with their tables of contents. The Call of the Wild leads, its chapters running from Into the Primitive and The Law of Club and Fang to The Sounding of the Call.

Before Adam, John Barleycorn, Burning Daylight, The Iron Heel, South Sea Tales, and The Valley of the Moon follow. A second list names ebooks without tables of contents, among them Martin Eden, White Fang, The Sea Wolf, The People of the Abyss, and Jerry of the Islands.
59500-narrative-of-william-w-brown-a-fug:
William W Brown wrote the Narrative of William W Brown, a Fugitive Slave. The Anti-Slavery Office issued this enlarged second form at Boston in eighteen forty eight. Three thousand copies of the first form sold in six months. Brown took his very name from the Ohio man who fed him.

Wells Brown of Ohio took in the weary, nameless fugitive at his door. Thirteen years on, the freed man gives him this book in thanks. Slavery had denied him a name by which men might know him. Edmund Quincy of Dedham read the draft with deep feeling in eighteen forty seven. Douglass had shown one face; Brown shows the hell from new ground. Cowper’s curse on the man who grows rich on souls fronts it. Let the oppressed go free: that hope drives the whole small book.
59509-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
David Widger built an index to the Project Gutenberg works of Edward Gibbon. Gibbon's great work is the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire. His own life tale and his home letters stand in the list too. Each book's full part list is set out for the reader. File weights and plate notes aid the hunt in that store.

Volume one of the great work starts with the Antonine age. Its scope and war force are the first theme in the list. Home wealth and peace in that age come next in two parts. The index lets a reader jump to a theme at once. Widger's lists made the free shelf far more easy to use. Past fans gain a fast key.
5951-reno-a-book-of-short-stories-and-in:
The Van-Noy Interstate Company presents Reno as a book of short stories and information. It runs in seven parts. They cover social and industrial life, Reno tragedies, Reno romance, Reno comedies, Reno and its people, Nevada divorce laws, and sons of the sagebrush. The book opens by quoting the Bible on a man putting away a wife who finds no favor in his eyes, framing Reno's famous divorce trade in scripture's own terms.

Readers also get a portrait of Reno as an up-to-date city. Electrical stores show every new device there. Stationery, candy, music, hardware, drug, and department stores stand fine as those in cities twice its size. Shops employ hundreds, and buyers travel to New York for goods, the book boasts. It suits readers curious about early twentieth-century Reno, divorce history, and booster literature that mixes stories with civic pride.
59518-the-theory-of-stock-exchange-specu:
The Theory of Stock Exchange Speculation, by Arthur Crump, reached American readers in an edition published by H W Rosenbaum at New York in 1887, with Rosenbaum's preface and annotations. The English original had gone through several editions.

Rosenbaum, himself a broker, says a broker loses nothing by warning clients against danger and showing them the pitfalls. He sums up Crump's recipe for success in three attributes: first, a clear head; second, capital; and third, patience. He does not follow Crump so far as to call profit from speculation near impossible.
59556-communication:
Charles Fontenay's short story from Worlds of If in October nineteen fifty six begins with a famous problem: how do you talk to a Martian. Three expeditions were needed before men even found the few Martians left. When contact came, nobody had a working method ready. The landing party fell back on an old trick.

Von Frisch, the engineer, squats in the red sand and draws a right angled triangle. He marks three units on one side and four on the other. A tall, thin Martian with pipestem limbs folds itself down and draws five marks along the hypotenuse. It grasps the Pythagorean theorem. From that foothold the men try pictures of the sun and planets, while Captain Powers fires questions through the helmet radio. Fontenay keeps the scene short and dry: shared mathematics as the first shared language.
59560-animal-castration:
Animal Castration is a practical treatise on gelding farm animals, written by Liautard, a professor at the American Veterinary College. Jenkins published the book at New York in 1884. Forty four plates stand within the text. Liautard dedicates the work to his old teacher at Paris.

The author states plainly that he offers no new methods here. His aim is to gather the ways in use and let readers judge their worth. No English book, he believed, had yet done that for this branch of surgery. French and German works supplied much of the matter. Plates came from the fine wood cuts of Zundel and of Peuch and Toussaint. The book served country vets and stockmen who did their own work. It is a period manual of a rough necessity.
59641-figures-in-verse-and-simple-rhymes:
Young children learning their numbers are the readers of this small picture book, printed in New York by Kiggins and Kellogg. Its method is rhyme. Each pair of numbers gets a short chant that ties the count to a homely action. One and two fasten a shoe, three and four shut the door, and five and six pick up sticks.

The count runs to twenty in both Arabic and Roman figures. It ends with nineteen and twenty and an empty stomach. After the numbers come simple rhymes and old favorites: a paradox about children sliding on summer ice, and a washing day song that scolds Saturday washers. Several adventures of Simple Simon at the fair follow. Pictures throughout break up the text for small readers. Books of this kind taught counting, reading, and traditional verse all at once.
59669-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
David Widger compiled this index to the Project Gutenberg works of Frederic Remington, the artist and writer of the West. Remington illustrated his books, and the index gives the contents of nine of them. The Way of an Indian leads, then Crooked Trails, A Daughter of the Sioux, and An Apache Princess. Red Men and White, Pony Tracks, and John Ermine of the Yellowstone follow. The Way to the West and The Black Lion Inn close the list.

For each volume the index prints every chapter title and illustration caption. The Crooked Trails list alone runs to dozens of pictures, from Texas Rangers holding up bandits to the storming of Ticonderoga. Such an index is a reader's map of the Gutenberg shelf: it lets a searcher find Massai's crooked trail or the cracker cowboys of Florida without opening nine books. Widger made many such guides to the Gutenberg authors.
59716-the-night-of-temptation:
Night of Temptation is a novel by Victoria Cross, author of Life's Shop Window and Six Women. Copyrights of nineteen twelve and nineteen fourteen stand on its title page. A list of the author's many books fills a front page, one of them marked at half a million copies. Contents run to twelve chapters. Heads name home, the gift, and clear waters. Paradise or else and with the great river follow.

Lions of the desert and in the dark watches build the late tale. Dawn closes the list. Chapter one opens in a rectory garden. She lay in a quiet corner of it, looking up at white clouds, the tale begins. The clouds sailed like Viking ships under full sail, it says. A narrow stone church stood near, the text shown adds.
59775-alf-s-button:
Darlington tells a wartime comedy in Alf's Button, from Stokes in New York, first published in America in 1920 with copyright in 1919. Seventeen chapters run from Alf Higgins, Runner, to The Fate of the Button. Contents promise a miracle of the planes, a misguided Eustace fetching beer, and a police constable investigating.

Chapter one sits in a dugout where Captain Richards of the Middlesex Fusiliers plans taking over the front line from the 4th Battalion in two days. He wants one extra runner for company headquarters, and Sergeant-Major French offers only Higgins, dubiously. Alf is not bright, the sergeant admits, and will do no more than he is told, but no less either, and he is a good soldier. Richards laughs, then sends for the man whose button drives the plot.
5979-japan-an-attempt-at-interpretation:
Lafcadio Hearn attempts what he admits no single work can yet fully do: picture Japan within and without, historically and socially, psychologically and ethically. His chapters move from strangeness and charm through the ancient cult, the religion of the home, and the Japanese family.

Later sections treat Shinto, Buddhism, the social order, the rise of military power, the religion of loyalty, the Jesuit peril, and feudal integration, closing with modern restraints, official education, and industrial danger. Hearn writes as an interpreter between two worlds, careful and searching. An appendix closes a patient and wide-ranging survey.
5993-walter-sherwood-s-probation:
Horatio Alger Jr. opens with a letter for Doctor Ezekiel Mack, brought by his housekeeper Nancy Sprague, once a schoolmistress. Walter Sherwood writes often to his old guardian, and Nancy praises his heart while the doctor adds a wish about his head. The doctor, near sixty, adjusts his spectacles and reads with a contracting brow.

The letter disturbs him, and its contents set the probation of the title in motion. Alger follows a young man whose money, manners, and morals are tested away from home. The tale pairs a kindly guardian's worry with a boy's effort to prove himself worthy of trust.
59931-the-love-story-of-aliette-brunton:
Love Story of Aliette Brunton is a novel by Gilbert Frankau, published at Toronto in 1922. Goodchild issued the Canadian edition, the copyright resting with the Century Company. Frankau dedicates the book to his wife and loyal associate, Aimee de Burgh Frankau. He calls it, in that dedication, a story of a woman courage for his readers.

A verse motto on woman gamble stands at the front of the novel in six lines. There is only one such gamble, it says, and it takes some pluck to play the game.  Frankau, a poet of the Great War turned novelist, wrote of love as a risk taken blind by his heroine. The novel belongs to the shelf of postwar romances in which women who had nursed, worked, and waited claim their own stakes in the peace.
59969-a-selection-of-books-published-by-:
A Selection of Books Published by Methuen and Company is a publisher's catalogue from the London house of Methuen. It lists the firm's more weighty books, set out by author. Novels have their own named part in the list. A note at the front sets the terms of trade. Books marked net cannot be sold below the set price. Other books take the discount a shop allows. Colonial editions are made of the novels and of some works of general letters.

The entries give the form and price of each book in short lines. Lancelot Andrewes heads the run, with his private prayers in a new form. Aristotle stands near the top as well. The house offers to send sample copies on receipt of the price plus postage. A full catalogue could be had on request.
59980-comparison-of-methods-of-sewage-pu:
Comparison of Methods of Sewage Purification is a thesis by Theodore Clifford Phillips and Edward John Schneider, given at the University of Illinois in June 1900. It earned both men the degree of Bachelor of Science in Municipal and Sanitary Engineering. Their teacher, Arthur Talbot, head of the department, approved the work in May 1900.

The writers call sewage disposal one of the chief problems facing town engineers. They trace study of it to a London report of 1844 and to work in Massachusetts from 1872. Six methods are compared: dilution, irrigation, downward filtration, chemical treatment, the septic tank, and the contact bed, with a discussion and a verdict at the end.
60020-pretty-quadroon:
Charles Fontenay wrote a short science fiction story first printed in the magazine Worlds of If in June 1957. A short note at the start asks what would happen if a choice could be made again and a wrong path left behind. The action opens in Tennessee, near Tullahoma, where General Beauregard Courtney watches his troops move in dust and heat.

Courtney plans a frontal attack for the next day while armor moves in from the east and west. His aim is to surround a Union strong point and open the road north. A courier brings a message from Miss Piquette that pulls at the general on the night before the push.
60091-a-brief-history-of-the-worshipful-:
Noble wrote A Brief History of the Worshipful Company of Ironmongers, London, printed around 1889. Front matter lists the officers for March 1889: Henry Maudslay as master, wardens, clerk, chaplain, surveyor, and beadle. With forty-four others they form the livery and court of the ancient company.

Noble himself served as warden of the yeomanry, some 260 freemen strong in the company lists. His other works treat the Lord Mayor of London, Temple Bar, the Crystal Palace, and a Caxton memorial, all held in great libraries. Arms of the company head the illustrated history of charters, halls, and customs. Guild historians get a compact record.
60104-pilgrimages-to-the-spas-in-pursuit:
James Johnson, a doctor to the late king, wrote this tour of the German spas for Highley of London in 1841. Pilgrimages to the Spas tells of autumn trips made for health, rest, and facts. Baths and waters for the sick were then a great theme for English invalids.

Johnson weighs each water in turn: what ills it fits, and what ills it harms. His preface owns the book's mixed stuff and defends it. Why should a doctor be barred from broad thoughts, he asks, and held to his trade alone? His schooling, habits, and grasp of human nature fit him for more. Health, sights, and society mix in these pages.
60113-a-student-s-history-of-education:
Frank Pierrepont Graves, dean of the school of education at the University of Pennsylvania, wrote A Student's History of Education for Macmillan. Copyright dates to 1915, and this New York printing is dated 1922. Graves dedicates the book to William Oxley Thompson, president of Ohio State University.

Part one covers ancient times, from the earliest schooling in India and among the Jews to Greece, Rome, and the early Christians. Spartan and Athenian training, the Sophists, Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle all get sections. Part two moves into the Middle Ages, starting with monastic schools. Graves also wrote a three volume history of education and a study of Peter Ramus, listed at the front.
6019-the-earth-as-modified-by-human-acti:
George P. Marsh, revising his Man and Nature, argues that no winds, storms, earthquakes, seas, or seasons have changed the earth so much as man has since he received dominion over it. His object is to show the character and extent of changes made by human action in the globe's physical conditions.

Marsh warns of imprudence and urges caution in large operations that disturb organic and inorganic arrangements. He also holds out the restoration of disturbed harmonies and the improvement of waste and exhausted regions. The book stands as an early work of environmental thought, sober and far-seeing.
60236-george-washington:
Ferdinand Schmidt wrote this life of Washington for young German readers, and George Upton translated it for the Life Stories for Young People series. McClurg issued the volume in Chicago in 1911, with four illustrations. The chapters follow the boyhood, the surveyor, and three years in the wilderness. Then come the first battles, the quarrel with the mother country, and Washington's choice as commander-in-chief.

Upton's preface commends Schmidt's tight use of the most authoritative sources and his pertinent, never tedious moralizing. The book offers American youth the Father of his Country from a German point of view. The Delaware crossing and the foreign helpers Lafayette, Kosciuszko, and Steuben appear in the later chapters. The farewell to the army and the last days close the story.
60250-the-golden-bough-a-study-in-magic-:
Golden Bough, volume two, by James George Frazer, studies magic and religion. Macmillan of London issued the third edition, reprinted in nineteen seventeen. Frazer was a fellow of Trinity College, Cambridge, and taught at Liverpool. This volume holds part one, The Magic Art and the Evolution of Kings.

Chapter eight treats the King of the Wood at Nemi and nature kings. Rain kings in Africa and fire and water kings in Cambodia appear. Chapter nine turns to the worship of trees in great depth. Tree spirits, sacred groves, and rites at tree felling fill its sections. Frazer weighs how tree spirits grant good and grow into wood gods.
60313-agriculture-of-the-hidatsa-indians:
Gilbert Livingstone Wilson studies Hidatsa farming in Agriculture of the Hidatsa Indians, issued by the University of Minnesota in November 1917. It is number 9 in the Studies in the Social Sciences. The sub title, An Indian Interpretation, states the book's bent.

Most farm studies of the time speak for the Indian from the outside. Wilson's title promises the Hidatsa view from the inside: their own account of crops and work. The bulletin sells for seventy five cents and goes out for exchange with other schools and learned bodies. Readers of native life get a short, grave monograph on one tribe's farm craft.
60326-maradick-at-forty-a-transition:
Maradick at Forty, A Transition, is a novel by Hugh Walpole, published in New York by George H Doran. Walpole's other novels, including Fortitude and The Duchess of Wrexe, are listed in the front matter. A verse motto warns how fast angels can alter how sprucely we are dressed. The contents open in a part called The Room of the Minstrels.

There the hero and the place meet once again, as an early chapter head puts it. At forty, Maradick faces the turn from youth's plans to middle life's reckoning, the mark of a transition novel. Walpole builds the tale on place, memory, and a man taking stock. Early Walpole, before his great family sagas, is on show.
60349-an-account-of-the-late-intended-in:
An Account of the Late Intended Insurrection is an official report from Charleston. The city council of that town ordered the work to be made and printed. The hosted text is the third print of the report. It came out in Charleston in the year eighteen twenty two.

City heads said a full print was the just course, lest hush look like fear. The book gives the facts of a planned revolt by Black townsfolk. It adds a full report of the trials that came after the plot broke. Laws and court acts are set out to clear the name of the town. The text stands as the city side of a grim case in the south.
60380-the-history-of-sir-richard-whittin:
Henry B Wheatley edited The History of Sir Richard Whittington for the Villon Society in eighteen hundred eighty five. The book forms part five of a chapbook and folk tale set. G L Gomme shared the edit work on the series. Wheatley prints the oldest known life of Whittington.

That old text rests in the Pepysian Library and may date to about sixteen hundred seventy. Its writer signs as T H, perhaps Thomas Heywood. Three points rule the famed tale of the cat. A poor birth, bells at Highgate Hill, and wealth from a cat sale. Wheatley shows all three fail as true life facts. The real Whittington came of good stock, he proves. Folk tale and true life part ways in his notes.
60407-the-mystery-of-lost-river-canyon:
A bearded ranchman rides hard into a Santa Fe rail station and writes two telegrams in haste. Harry Castlemon opens his 1896 canyon tale at full pace. George and his Uncle Ruben stand at the heart of it, with Dick Langdon close by.

Contents promise a capsize, masked robbers, an angry miser, and a visit from the sheriff. The canyon keeps its secret through thirty chapters till the mystery is solved. Castlemon, a Civil War veteran, wrote shelf on shelf of boys' tales of the West and war. His Lost River mixes camp life, telegrams, and hidden wrongs in his plain, brisk way. A listener in a grove and a hurried flight raise the stakes late.
60444-from-billabong-to-london:
Mary Grant Bruce wrote a tale of a trip from an Australian station to London, printed at London, Melbourne and Toronto. Her Mates at Billabong and Glen Eyre are named as her earlier works. A front picture shows a cry: why, it is someone signalling. Twenty chapters carry the voyage.

Holidays at Billabong open the book, then upheavals and a chestnut baby. Good bye, settling down, and fishes and the sea follow. Norah spies something, a cabin stands empty, and Durban is reached. War breaks out in the middle of the trip home. Las Palmas and the end of the voyage lead to a last chapter on the thing that counts. Young readers in Australia loved the Billabong folk.
60462-conservation:
Charles L Fontenay published his short story Conservation in Worlds of If Science Fiction in April 1958. A starship comes home to Earth after two hundred and fifty-eight years of Earth time, though only ten years passed for the crew. Commander Tom Wallace finds a robot relay station in orbit but a deserted spaceport below.

Scout rockets report large cities with smoke, yet no one greets the ship. John Gray, the executive officer, calls the mix hard to square. Wallace orders an armed party out in a car across the yellow sands. The tale asks why a people with every means of power at hand used none of it.
60560-the-south-african-question:
Olive Schreiner published The South African Question in Chicago in eighteen ninety-nine under the byline of an English South African. She signs the copyright in her own name and names her earlier books, The Story of an African Farm and Dreams. Two mottoes frame the essay. Burns sings that man to man the world over shall brothers be, and a gospel line warns that those who hold the sword shall perish by it.

The essay surveys what newspapers had printed in the crisis weeks. Working men fresh from England opposed schemes aimed at war, which would strip their defence against employers. Some journalists hinted a war wave across rich mineral country might do good. Schreiner speaks for the African-born Englishman who loves both England and his birth-land.
60592-welsh-nationality-and-how-alone-it:
Davies preaches Welsh Nationality, and How Alone It Is To Be Saved, a sermon printed in London and Carmarthen in 1871. He spoke it in the chapel of Saint David's College, Lampeter, on Sunday, October 30, 1870. The print came out by request, the title page says.

Davies was chaplain of the Joint Counties Asylum at Abergavenny. His text is Luke, on the one thing needful that Mary chose. He speaks to the young men of the college, his own county folk. Born in the lower part of the county, he grew up among plain Welsh folk. He claims close knowledge of their views, ways, and habits, and builds his plea on that bond.
60597-the-postal-service-fifth-edition:
J J O'Reilly edited this fifth edition of a guide to the postal service, printed by the Chief Publishing Company of New York with a 1912 copyright. O'Reilly edited The Government Weekly, called The Chief. A portrait of Postmaster Edward M Morgan fronts the book. The publisher kept a staff of civil service experts to coach candidates for New York City and its area.

Inside sit the forms and questions of application: what post is sought, which service, and in what town. Citizenship must be sworn, with papers for the naturalized and sworn statements from two citizens. The book serves men and women hunting federal jobs, walking them through exams, forms, and the carrier stations of the city.
60693-growing-season:
Growing Season is a science fiction story by Wallace, taken from Worlds of If in July 1959. Its teaser asks why anyone would want to kill a tender of mechanized vegetation, and with a watch and a little red bird, of all things. The tale opens in a park of the future. Richel Alsint sits still, feeding a furry animal a kernel from his hand.

Outside the park, tiers of traffic run in every direction, but Alsint has the green space to himself. He watches a small blue bird balance on air currents without moving its wings. The quiet scene prepares a puzzle about the strange bird and what it portends. The story's copyright was never renewed.
60820-frances-mary-buss-and-her-work-for:
Annie Ridley writes a life in Frances Mary Buss and Her Work for Education, printed in London and New York in 1895. Longmans made the book, with portraits and other plates. The school motto stands at the front: we work in hope.

Three books shape the life. Early life treats childhood, girlhood, and the forces that formed her. Public work treats her school years, her fellow workers, and her home at Myra Lodge. Heads treat the Head Mistresses' Association and training colleges for teachers. One treats a university education for women, then a bold aim. Later years close with holidays, Rome, friendships, and rest.
60853-rachel-jackson:
Nellie Treanor Stokes wrote Rachel Jackson, a short biography issued with copyright in nineteen forty two. The cover picture copies a miniature that General Jackson wore daily, the book notes. The Board of Directors of the Ladies' Hermitage Association offers the book. Its foreword says historians have praised Andrew Jackson but only lightly touched his wife's sway over him.

Stokes grew up at Tulip Grove, a plantation next to the Hermitage. She visited the mansion often in her girlhood, the foreword says. She stayed close to the Jackson family in later years. She served as regent of the Ladies' Hermitage Association from nineteen twenty three to nineteen twenty seven. Her book joins first hand family tradition with careful research, the foreword holds. History readers get the wife of Andrew Jackson drawn by a neighbor of the Hermitage.
60948-the-last-secrets-the-final-mysteri:
John Buchan wrote The Last Secrets, the final riddles of travel and discovery, first printed in 1923. A front plate shows the summit of Mount Everest. Buchan gives the book to the memory of Cecil Rawling, who fell at the third battle of Ypres, a bold explorer and gallant soldier. Contents name nine pieces. Lhasa opens the set.

The gorges of the Brahmaputra and the North Pole follow. The Mountains of the Moon and the South Pole come next. Mount McKinley, the holy cities of Islam, and the probing of New Guinea fill the later heads. Mount Everest closes the book. The Lhasa piece opens on the city's mystery. Till the summer of 1904, Buchan writes, no spot on earth was so wrapped in riddle. No Englishman had cast an eye on it for a hundred years. The greatest wall of mountains shut it off from the south.
60985-misinforming-a-nation:
Misinforming a Nation is a blast at a great word book by Willard Huntington Wright, out in nineteen seventeen. Wright was known for books on paint, on a wise man of the east of Europe, and on the will to make. Parts treat the tale, the stage, verse, paint of two kinds, song, lore, and the church, each as that book shows them. A last part lists two hundred skips of that book.

The first part charges that England has long made a farm of the mind of the United States. Past her old rank in art and writ she mocks the work of that land and stamps her own false top place on it. The folk there, with no old safe base, took that view to seem in the know. Home snob pride fed the flame, Wright says, till a British scorn of home work grew in the land.
61070-poems-of-adoration:
Poems of Adoration is a book of devotional verse by Michael Field, issued by Sands and Company of London and Edinburgh. The contents list runs to more than seventy poems. Many titles are in Latin. Others name the sacraments, the Virgin, and scenes from the life of Christ.

The poems move through the church year and the life of prayer. Advent, the Annunciation, and the Ascension all appear. So do Purgatory, Extreme Unction, and the Viaticum. Several poems treat the Blessed Sacrament and Holy Communion. The opening poem, Desolation, pictures Christ coming in a blood-red garment like a treader of the winepress. The whole book speaks in a voice of worship and awe.
61116-pharos-and-pharillon:
Pharos and Pharillon, by Forster, came out in 1923 at the Hogarth Press, run by Leonard and Virginia Woolf. The book holds short pieces on Alexandria in Egypt, a city the author knew well. Some chapters had first appeared in The Nation and the Athenaeum.

The first half, Pharos, looks back to the old city, with pieces on Philo, Clement of Alexandria, and Saint Athanasius. One piece tells of the god who leaves Antony. The second half, Pharillon, turns to the Egypt of the author's own day, with cotton, streets, and daily life. It ends with the poems of Cavafy, given in translation. History and the living city stand side by side here.
61123-shafting-pulleys-belting-and-rope-:
Hubert Collins compiled Shafting, Pulleys, Belting and Rope Transmission, published in New York in 1908 as one of the Power Handbooks. The series sold at one dollar a volume, postpaid, as a library for the engineer and the man who hopes to be one. Its publisher issued journals such as Power and the American Machinist.

The chapters are workshop hints, gathered from practice. Early ones treat shafting and the truing up of line shafting, with apparatus for leveling and lining. Practical methods of loosening pulleys follow. Then come splicing leather belts, the care of belts, and belt creep, with a test of four belt dressings. Rope drives close the book, including how to order transmission rope. The handbook served the age when one engine drove a whole shop through belts.
61131-charles-dwight-or-the-missionary-s:
The Religious Tract Society of London issued 'Charles Dwight; or, The Missionary's Son' as a short life for young readers. Charles was born in Constantinople on February 16th, 1837, and lost his mother to the plague when he was only four months old. At about seven, the death of a child in a mission family and a sermon turned his thoughts to his sins, and he put his trust in the Saviour.

Companions loved his kindness, and the pious boys among them always prayed together before parting. On Saturday, February 5th, 1853, a headache seized him, and no skill could help him through the illness that followed. In his wandering he spoke of Christ in English, Greek, French, and Turkish. He told his father he did not yet want to die, because his heart was set on being a missionary.
61169-essays-on-the-microscope-containin:
George Adams, instrument maker to the king, wrote these essays on the microscope, and Frederick Kanmacher brought out a second edition in London in 1798. The book gives a practical description of the most improved microscopes of its day. Thirty-two folio plates show the tools and the tiny life they reveal.

Alongside the instruments sits a general history of insects, with their changes of form, habits, and way of life. Adams also describes the hydrae and vorticellae and gives an account of three hundred and eighty-three animalcula. A short catalogue of objects worth study closes the range, with notes on the build of timber and the shapes of salts seen under the glass.
61236-emily-of-new-moon:
Emily of New Moon, by Montgomery, came out in New York in 1923. Montgomery had written Anne of Green Gables, The Story Girl, and many more tales of the island. A colour frontispiece by Kirk shows Emily in the moment she calls the flash.

The book is given to George Boyd MacMillan of Alloa, Scotland, in thanks for a long friendship. The tale opens at the house in the hollow, a mile from anywhere near Maywood. The brown house sits in a grassy dale, ringed by young birches and reached by a green lane. Ellen Greene calls it the lonesomest place in the world. Chapters take Emily to New Moon farm, to school, and to Wyther Grange, through trials by fire and growing pains.
61242-the-winning-of-the-moon:
The Winning of the Moon is a science tale by Kris Neville, first set in a pulp sheet in the early nineteen sixties. A note at the front tells that a long hunt found no proof its rights were made new in law. A tag line at the head sets the trap of the tale.

The foe was fair and kind, that line warns. The snag was that their friendship was as full of risk as their hate. A general tells a major that a deep blast under the moon soil is set for the next day. The major weighs what steps to take with three fellow Americans. At dawn the four don space suits and sit by their dome to wait, as the sun climbs with a bright, still flash.
61353-saline-solution:
Saline Solution, a science fiction tale by Keith Laumer, ran in Worlds of If in March 1963. A blurb teases the hero: blast you, Retief, your violent ways are the disgrace of Earth's diplomatic corps, but your salty jokes are worse. The tale opens in a consulate, where Consul-General Magnan fingers a rubber-banded sheaf of dog-eared documents.

Magnan insists he has not rushed into precipitate action on a claim. The consulate, he says, has grave responsibilities in the Belt, and all aspects must be weighed. Retief answers that the claim looked fine to him: seventeen copies with attachments. Why not process it? It has sat on the desk a week, and every day of delay costs the miners money. Laumer's Retief tales pit one brisk man against the corps' happy faculty of delay.
61364-crystallizing-public-opinion:
Crystallizing Public Opinion is the first book of the new craft of the press agent of firms, by Bernays. Its rights were set in law in the early nineteen twenties at New York. Its gift word makes it out to his wife, of a famed meat house name.

Its first part sets the scope and tasks of the craft. The new post, its growth in weight, and its role as a hired plea hand are its themes. Its next part takes the group and the herd. What makes the mind of the mass, and is that mind stiff or soft to shape, are its asks. How that mind plays with the forces that make it fills the rest.
61380-the-five-hells-of-orion:
The Five Hells of Orion is a science fiction story by Frederik Pohl. It appeared in Worlds of If in January 1963. A headnote sets the scene in the Orion Nebula. Out in that great gas cloud McCray found an ally and a foe.

Herrell McCray is a ship's navigator. He serves aboard the starship Jodrell Bank. The ship is on the long jump from Earth to the Betelgeuse colonies. McCray makes his hourly check-sightings as always. While he looks at the beacon stars, something happens. He wakes in a dark room no bigger than a prison cell. Sharp and sticky objects crowd the floor. A voice hovers at the edge of hearing. A suit like medieval armour appears in a pink glow.
61426-joan-and-peter-the-story-of-an-edu:
Joan and Peter is a novel by Wells, printed by Macmillan at New York. Its subtitle calls it the story of an education. Wells also wrote Mr Britling Sees It Through. The book appeared in 1918, and this printing is of 1921. Its hero's birth opens the tale in darkness and fear.

The contents map two childhoods. Peter's parentage and first impressions of the universe lead to a christening and a fourth guardian. The School of Saint George and the Venerable Bede, then High Cross Preparatory School, test the boy. Oswald takes control, and a searching of schoolmasters follows. Adolescence, the world on the eve of war, and the graduation of Joan and Peter close the arc. Wells uses the pair to try every English theory of how a child should be raised.
61455-alone-in-london:
Alone in London is a tale of street children printed by the Religious Tract Society. Its author had written Jessica's First Prayer and Little Meg's Children. The frontispiece, called Playmates, shows the book's small world. The story opens on one of the hottest days of the dog-days.

Barefoot children feel the pavement burn in the slum alleys. Fish and vegetable refuse rots in the gutters, and thick vapours hang in the heat. The first chapter is called Not Alone, promising comfort inside the misery. Chapters follow Tony and old Oliver through forsaking, thieves and hospital. A little peacemaker, new boots and a fresh day dawning carry the waifs toward the golden city of the close.
6149-the-boy-aviators-treasure-quest-or-:
Captain Wilbur Lawton, pen name for John Henry Goldfrap, sends the Boy Aviators on a treasure quest for a golden galleon, the fourth of six cloth-bound titles at fifty cents. Earlier books took them to Nicaragua with insurgents, on secret service with wireless, and to Africa on an aerial ivory trail.

Contents promise the eagle and the buzzard, Billy's strange tale, a trial flight, Eben Joyce appearing, and a strange story. The golden galleon, a fire alarm by aeroplane, a race nearly lost, and fog follow. Lawton writes brisk air adventure, where young fliers chase treasure by engine and nerve.
61583-daybreak-in-turkey-second-edition:
Daybreak in Turkey, by James Barton, secretary of the American Board of missions, was published at Boston in a second edition in 1908. A view of Galata, Pera, and the bridge of boats at Constantinople fronts the book. Barton dedicates it to the memory of the men and women of all races and creeds who toiled and died that Turkey might be free.

The early chapters survey the country, its resources, and its history. Later chapters reach the work of missionaries, completed work, and changes in industry and religion.
