American rights, religious toleration, and the Macedonian question each get a chapter. The book closes with the general political situation and constitutional government. Barton wrote in the year of the Young Turk revolution. His title claims a dawn: schools, presses, and a new constitution rising over the old empire. It is a hopeful report from an American mission leader.
6162-herbert-carter-s-legacy-or-the-inve:
Horatio Alger Jr. tells Herbert Carter's Legacy, or The Inventor's Son, in the same spirit as his tales of street boys. Alger, son of a clergyman, Harvard graduate, and former Unitarian pastor at Brewster, settled in New York in 1866 and drew public attention to the needs of street boys.

He mingled with them, gained their confidence, showed personal concern, and stimulated honest, useful living. With his first story he won boys everywhere, and over seventy stories sold more than a million copies in his lifetime. Herbert Carter inherits an inventor father's name and must turn legacy into honest effort.
61674-war-lords-of-the-moon:
Linton Davies wrote this science fiction tale for Planet Stories in the winter of 1939. Bruce Ross, on the Earth-Moon run, asks how the stars are behaving in the opening blurb. Harrell Moore can only stare in horror in answer, for the stars have run amok as engines of destruction.

A faint quiver runs through the great rocket ship as the tale opens in space. Her motors die from a harsh drumming to a singing drone as she shakes off Earth-drag. Flight-Commander Ross watches the speed indicator climb past twelve hundred miles an hour, on the way to a pale Moon looming in his telescope.
61764-tennyson:
G K Chesterton and Richard Garnett wrote Tennyson, a short life of the poet with many pictures. The book shows Somersby Rectory, where Alfred Tennyson was born, and his later home at Freshwater. Views of his mother, his wife, and Arthur H Hallam fill the plates.

The authors hold that Tennyson was at heart a pure lover of beauty. Chance and the call of his age, they argue, made him a thinking poet as well. He loved beauty in a deeper sense than Keats or Robert Bridges. Scenes from The Lady of Shalott and In Memoriam are shown beside the life.
61774-beautiful-philippines-a-handbook-o:
The Philippine Commission of Independence prepares a handbook on the islands at the Bureau of Printing, Manila, in 1923. Its aim is plain general information for foreign readers.

Contents open with a historical background. Discovery, Spanish rule, and its wars and uprisings come first. Reforms of the nineteenth century follow. The Filipino-American War and civil government close the sketch. A second part lists what Spain found: literacy, laws, traders, and able farmers. The Code of Calantiao gets a page. The first Philippine Republic and the Malolos Constitution follow. Later parts count the people and map the land. Manila, Pagsanjan Falls, and the Los Baños springs draw the traveller's eye. The book argues the Filipino case in the language of facts.
61805-goddess-of-the-moon:
John Murray Reynolds wrote Goddess of the Moon, a planet novel from Planet Stories in Spring 1940. Death hides behind a smile in Gral-Thala, a white-and-gold city. Gibson, an Earth spy from a derelict ship, knows his fate as a captive. If he dies, the narrative warns, the good green planet falls to the Gray Death, and Diana dies with it.

The tale opens as a Tokyo-to-New York stratholiner lands on a winter evening. A strange plague, the Gray Death, rages from Alaska to Cape Horn unchecked. A fellow rider tells Larry Gibson that a thousand deaths a day strike New York City. Larry, a seasoned pilot, drinks to steady himself and hides his face. Reynolds sets a spy tale against a world-wide plague in the twenty-fourth century.
61844-the-stellar-legion:
Leigh Brackett's story The Stellar Legion ran in Planet Stories in the winter 1940 issue. No one, the blurb says, had ever escaped from Venus's dread Stellar Legion, and betrayal meant death. Thekla, a low Martian, learns that rule at first hand in the tale.

Barracks silence hangs over outlander soldiers sweating in Venusian swamp heat before the rains. Commandant Lehn calls for three volunteers to scout Nahali country, and Earthman Ian MacIan steps out first. Thekla and Bhak, a hulking strangler from Titan, follow him into the mission. Beyond a moat of charged water and four electro-cannons, the six foot scarlet eyed Nahali pray for rain, after which they plan to swarm the fort.
61872-treasure-of-triton:
Baker's Treasure of Triton ran in Planet Stories in the spring of 1941. Wolf Larsen, a black pirate of space, works alone under the Temple of Triton while the Space Patrol hunts him.

Triton, Neptune's moon, looks dead by day: snow glows green in the dying light, and the ground itself is gravel of ruby and sapphire with boulders of diamond. The temple is built of blocks of bort, black diamond, hewn by Tritonians whose lives run ten times a human span. Larsen blasts at the temple door, sleepless for sixty hours, racing the dawn that will wake the world's strange life. The prize inside is billed as the richest in creation.
61927-invaders-of-the-forbidden-moon:
Raymond Gallun wrote Invaders of the Forbidden Moon, a tale printed in Planet Stories in the summer of 1941. Evan Harwich of the Interplanetary Patrol shouts by radio at a ship flying straight for Io, the Forbidden Moon of Jupiter. No ship that came within five thousand miles of that grey, near airless world had ever got back whole, and the rule of space men was to give it a wide berth.

The ship ahead, marked X911 and sleek with a trial look, holds its course all the same. Harwich knows the odds are near suicide, yet he blasts out from Jupiter to solve the riddle of the death trap. Gallun sets a lone patrolman against a moon wide fear with pulp speed.
61943-the-victory-of-klon:
Wilbur S Peacock wrote a science fiction tale that ran in Planet Stories in the fall of 1941. Klon, a wriggling, slimy lord of cloud veiled Venus, brings his people light in a deadly triumph. Klon flees from fern to fern like a drifting shadow. He circles a new clearing torn in the steamy jungle by a gleaming monster from the fog.

Stagnant water covers nine tenths of his planet. Klon's lidless eye gleams in unchanging darkness, where shadows are only two shades of black. He covets a light shadow on the visitor's round hull. Holding it would make him mightier than Valok. His nation is about to declare a new leader, and his time runs short.
62048-london:
G K Chesterton wrote an essay on London, with ten photographs by Alvin Langdon Coburn. The book was printed in London in 1914 for Coburn, Edmund D Brooks, and their friends. Chesterton opens with a tale of a stout country lady on the Underground Railway. She rode in a circle, pitched back in at each stop by the guard.

Chesterton holds that station names are nobler than the places they mark. Blackfriars, the Temple, and Charing Cross each stir old, grand tales. The rustic who reads names sees more than the crowd that hurries past. Readers gain a witty, fond plea to see London with fresh eyes.
62064-rules-of-the-western-grammar-schoo:
Rules of the Western Grammar School, Brompton survives as a short pamphlet. A Tilling edition of about 1832 is its source. The front pages name the school's honor men. Sir Theophilus Lee of Crescent House serves as president. The Honorable Gerard Valerian Wellesley stands among vice-presidents. Clergy and local esquires fill that bench.

Three joint treasurers hold the school's funds. E Knowles serves as secretary at Brompton Crescent. A physician and two surgeons attend the school. W F Pocock is its architect. A committee of twelve named men guides the work. Two auditors check the books each year. Messrs Cockburn and Company bank for the school. A bare roll of officers still shows how a London suburb school was run by local gentlemen in the 1830s.
62102-education:
Ellen White wrote this book on education, entered for copyright in 1903 and issued by the Pacific Press Publishing Company. She dedicates it to parents, teachers, and students, all pupils, she says, in earth's preparatory school. Two Bible lines frame the title page, among them the saying that the knowledge of the Holy is understanding.

The contents set out her scheme in order. First principles treat the source and aim of true education, the Eden school, and the tie between education and redemption. Later parts take up nature teaching, the Bible as an educator, and physical culture, with temperance, diet, and manual training. Character-building closes the plan, down to methods of teaching and the relation of dress to education.
62142-the-history-of-whittington:
The History of Whittington is William Davies's account of the Shropshire village and its castle, printed and sold by E Edwards of Oswestry. Davies was head-master of Carnarvon School, and he inscribes the history to R Poole, master of Malden School in Essex. It is not the tale of Dick and his cat: it is a local antiquary's work.

Davies begins with the picturesque ruins of the castle, birthplace of a baron to whom England owes Magna Charta. Learned antiquarians, he says, identify the place with Drev-Wen, the White Town, of the Welsh poet Lowarch Hen, who lived in the year 590. There the prince Cynddylan fell fighting the invading Irish. In the time of Roderick the Great, Ynyr ap Cadfarch built the castle, and his son Tudor Trevor, lord of both Maelors, Whittington, Chirk, and Oswestry, made it his chief residence.
62153-a-letter-to-the-kensington-canal-c:
John Valance wrote A Letter to the Kensington Canal Company in eighteen thirty three. George Wightman printed the plea at London by the company’s order. Its plea: swap the common railway for the pneumatic plan. Air, not steam or horse, would drive the new line’s cars.

The company sought a link from its Kensington basin west and north. The Grand Junction Canal and the Birmingham Railway both drew its eye. High ground blocks a plain ditch cut, Valance grants at once. Canal gigs on the Paisley line run ten miles an hour, he notes. Nine hundred pounds might buy two such swift passenger boats. Passengers would ride faster and far cheaper than by omnibus. Mockers will call the scheme absurd and chimerical, his front quote warns. Commissioners with hardihood must brave such sneers, it urges them.
62242-doorway-to-destruction:
Doorway to Destruction is a science fiction story by Garold Hatfield, printed in Planet Stories for winter 1942, where it was billed as the doorway to Earth's destruction. Kelvin Martin, the one man who could lock it had lost the key.

The story opens with Martin bound and bruised in a windowless room. His assistant Vance couples batteries behind the glittering machine in the corner. Martin warns him the machine can bring nothing but trouble. He offers a deal: eight thousand dollars if Vance frees him and stops. Vance laughs: one gem from the other people's world would bring that much. Martin remembers the cruelty of the creatures beyond the doorway. With their weapons, he warns, they would conquer the world in days.
62270-dramatis-person:
Dramatis Personae is a set of sharp notes on writers and the stage by Arthur Symons. The front list runs past twenty heads, near all names of men and wives of the pen. Tales men, poets, a stage star, and the dance of a far land all stand in it. Two parts treat the craft of the note itself and the schools of verse.

The first note, on Conrad, paints him as a spider in a hid nook of wild lands. From there he casts out threads to snare dreams and lays them bare for sport. A core of bleak scorn sits at his heart, says Symons. His depth of lore should shake and scare those who read him for mere fun, the note warns.
62546-prey-of-the-space-falcon:
Prey of the Space Falcon is a science fiction story by Wilbur Peacock, printed in Planet Stories in the fall of 1943. Curt Varga, the Falcon, watches from a shadowed corner of a Martian night club. A radi-stylus moves in his hand, and an amplifier set in the bone of his temple links him to his brother Val across the room.

The Administrators of the Solar System rule by monopoly, and their Food Administration destroyed the brothers' father. Now the Falcon and his outlaw brood fight back with a strange weapon. The magazine blurb promises that their fate rests with a girl and her Judas kiss. Peacock delivers pulp rebellion at full tilt, complete with secret signals, hidden implants, and a tyranny to defy.
62572-milton:
Thomas Babington Macaulay wrote this famous essay on Milton, in an edition printed in New York in 1900. The essay opens with a find: late in 1823 a keeper of state papers named Lemon came on a large Latin manuscript among the presses of his office. With it lay corrected copies of foreign letters written by Milton in office, and papers on the Popish Plot trials.

The manuscript proved to be Milton's lost Essay on the Doctrines of Christianity, finished after the Restoration and left with his friend Cyriac Skinner. Macaulay judges the new editor's work as clear and faithful, with notes that truly help the text. He warns that the treatise itself will add little to Milton's fame. From that opening the essay builds its wide account of the poet's life, politics, and verse, in Macaulay's bold, ringing style.
62589-molly-the-drummer-boy-a-story-of-t:
Molly, the Drummer Boy, a story of the Revolution by Harriet Comstock, was copyrighted in 1900. Altemus of Philadelphia published the tale for young readers. Half tone pictures by Curtis Wager Smith illustrate the book. A verse by Holmes on a bold rebel heads the title page.

The verse tells of mist creeping over a meadow at dawn. A father rises while his children sleep, and shoulders his gun. Comstock turns the war for independence into a boy’s adventure. Her drummer boy beats the march for men like that rebel father. Drums, camps, and redcoats fill the pages of the story. Such tales taught the Revolution to children at the century’s turn. Molly stands in a long line of patriotic juveniles.
62633-the-catalpa-expedition:
Pease wrote the story of the Catalpa expedition, issued at New Bedford in 1897 with illustrations. The frontispiece shows Captain George Anthony, who commanded the ship. The first chapter opens on an April morning in 1875, with the whaleship Catalpa at anchor and ready for sea.

Behind the voyage lay Fenian history: Irish political prisoners held in Australia after court-martial and banishment. Chapters tell of earlier escapes, of appeals from Australia, and of the plot laid in America. The Catalpa sailed as a whaler, met her shore party, and took the prisoners off in an open boat. A race with the guard boat and a night of peril crown the rescue.
62678-some-common-birds-useful-to-the-fa:
A government bulletin fills this item: Some Common Birds Useful to the Farmer, Farmers' Bulletin number 630 of the Department of Agriculture, written by Beal of the Bureau of Biological Survey. It was first issued in February 1915 and revised in April 1926. Notes at the front credit parts on the crow and the blue jay, and on the nighthawk and bobwhite, to other hands.

An introduction argues the case in plain terms. Birds' beauty is real, it says, but their cash value is greater: as destroyers of insects they rank among the chief checks on crop pests. The pages then discuss the haunts, food habits, and farm value of more than fifty common species, from bluebirds and robins to meadowlarks, blackbirds, and the crow.
62696-some-common-birds-useful-to-the-fa:
Some Common Birds Useful to the Farmer is Farmers' Bulletin 630 of the United States Department of Agriculture. F E L Beal, assistant biologist, wrote it. The Bureau of Biological Survey issued it on February 13, 1915. Henry W Henshaw was the bureau's chief. The bulletin supersedes Farmers' Bulletin 54. It discusses the food habits of more than fifty birds.

Beal's introduction settles the method first. Whether a bird helps or harms depends almost entirely on what it eats. Field observation alone, he argues, is fragmentary and inconclusive. Only stomach examination solves the question satisfactorily. The survey had examined stomachs systematically for years. The contents proceed species by species. Bluebirds, robins, titmice, and wrens come first. Swallows, sparrows, orioles, and meadowlarks follow. The crow and blue jay get their hearings. Kingbirds, the nighthawk, woodpeckers, and cuckoos close the list. Birds, Beal notes, destroy an incalculable number of insects yearly.
62715-drug-plants-under-cultivation:
Drug Plants Under Cultivation is a farm guide from the state farm branch. It is guide six hundred and sixty-three in that long set. It first came out in June 1915 and was reworked in 1920. The guide tells how to grow, pick, and sell plants used as drugs.

Wild drug plants grow scarce as woods fall and fields spread, it warns. The trade in such plants is small and needs a sharp hand. A few pounds picked at a guess leave the grower out of pocket. The price at sale is not the point, the guide holds. The gap between cost and sale price is what counts for gain. Kind by kind notes give the yield and the care of each plant. Drying, packing, and the hunt for a buyer are all dealt with.
62724-americans-drawn-by-charles-dana-gi:
Americans, drawn by Charles Dana Gibson, was published by Russell in New York and Lane in London in 1900. A prefatory note calls it the fifth book in the regular series of Gibson's published drawings, after Drawings, Pictures of People, Sketches and Cartoons, and The Education of Pipp. Each book in the series holds eighty four of his best cartoons, uniform in size and binding.

The plates carry their captions in the text. One shows the American girl addressing all the world on the golf links. Another promises fortune telling by cards: if the jack of clubs falls between the four and ten of diamonds, the next offer of marriage should be accepted. Their First Quarrel jokes that the couple have been engaged about twenty minutes. Other plates treat wireless telegraphy, rival beauties, and picturesque America anywhere in the mountains.
62729-aeroplane-construction-and-operati:
John B Rathbun, an aeronautical engineer, teaches aeroplane building and flying in a manual issued at Chicago in 1919. Rathbun had taught aviation and machine design at the Chicago Technical College. A Curtiss JN4D biplane of the air mail service fronts the volume.

The manual serves constructors, aviators, mechanics, flight officers, and students, at school or at home. Chapters open with the principles of the aeroplane and types of military machines, then turn to elementary flight science and test laboratories. Lists of American and English flying journals help readers keep up with a fast-changing field. Readers get the state of the art just after the Great War, when the aeroplane passed from wonder to trade.
62738-london-as-seen-by-charles-dana-gib:
London as Seen by Charles Dana Gibson is a picture book by the American artist Gibson, published in New York by Scribner in 1897. Some of the drawings had appeared in Life and in the London Graphic. Gibson's pen made the Gibson Girl famous, and here it turns on the London street.

The text opens with the arrival. After a short ride through country divided by hedges into a green and gold checkerboard, the thatched roofs vanish. Chimney pots take their place until the Thames appears, with black barges waiting for the muddy tide. Then come the Gothic buildings of Parliament, Big Ben, and Charing Cross station. In another moment the traveller is in a cab, hat-box safe beside him, riding through the restlessness of the streets. Policemen guard the crossings and shop windows blaze. The book is an American's delighted stare at the world's greatest city.
62769-the-radio-boys-with-the-forest-ran:
The Radio Boys with the Forest Rangers, or The Great Fire on Spruce Mountain, is a boys' novel by Allen Chapman. Grosset and Dunlap published it in New York in 1923, with a foreword by Jack Binns. It belongs to the Radio Boys series, which began with The Radio Boys' First Wireless. A picture shows a blue streak crackling near a bear's nose.

The series followed a group of boys through the new wonders of wireless. Earlier books took them to ocean points and sending stations, and through a voice-trailing mystery. In this tale they join the forest rangers and face a great fire on Spruce Mountain. Chapman also wrote the Railroad series about Ralph of the roundhouse.
62782-sweet-clover-utilization:
Coe, an assistant agronomist in forage-crop work, wrote this farm bulletin, Sweet Clover: Utilization, Farmers' Bulletin number 820 of the Department of Agriculture, issued at Washington in May 1917. It comes from the Bureau of Plant Industry. Its opening pages state the crop's uses in plain terms.

Sweet clover, the bulletin says, serves for feeding as pasturage, hay, or silage. Alfalfa on rich soil excepted, it yields as much good grazing from early spring to late fall as any other legume. It seldom causes bloat. Stock may refuse it at first, but a few days on young plants cures the dislike, and cattle on it should have dry roughage besides. Hay directions follow: never let the plant show flower buds before cutting, and cut the second season's first crop high, leaving tall stubble so new growth can come.
62846-take-a-can-of-salmon:
Take a Can of Salmon is a recipe booklet built around canned salmon. Its opening pages praise the fish before printing a recipe. Salmon, it says, has nourished the human race since prehistoric times. Modern canning makes it a cosmopolitan food. The protein is complete, of the meat and poultry class. Most recipes use the whole can, liquid, bones, and skin included.

Those parts supply iodine, phosphorus, and vitamins A, D, and the B group. The booklet also sells salmon to the figure-conscious. Four ounces of salmon hold about 150 calories. Four ounces of lamb chops hold 450, with the same protein. The fish comes from Alaska, Puget Sound, or the Columbia River. Appetizers and dips open the recipe sections, keyed to page 16. A salmon mousse in aspic leads the party dishes. Salads and buffet presentations follow.
62860-hidden-foes-or-a-fatal-miscalculat:
Hidden Foes, or A Fatal Miscalculation, is a Nick Carter detective story in a cheap weekly library. The New Magnet Library issued the Carter line. Each number cost fifteen cents. The detective's name stood for a reliable story, the publisher boasts. One specialist author wrote the whole series. His mind concentrated on new plots alone.

The front matter prints the line's catalogue. Dozens of Carter titles are listed in number order. Wanted, A Clew begins the run. Tangled skeins, bullion mysteries, and gloved hands follow. Each hero's triumph lands the criminal behind bars. The advertisement promises no dull book in the list. It invites new readers to get acquainted at once. Ten cloth-bound novels, it claims, give no more interest than one Carter number.
62879-gems-in-the-smithsonian-institutio:
Paul Desautels, a curator of minerals, wrote a guide to the gems held by the Smithsonian Institution in Washington. The guide came out in 1965. A huge egg shaped rock crystal of seven thousand carats, cut in Brazil and set on a gold stand with Montana sapphires, fronts the book.

Chapters tell of the national gem collection, the study of gems, and how stones are shaped. Gem substitutes and gem lore follow. The main part names the chief gem kinds one by one and tells what each is. A last part picks out famed stones in the collection. Clear facts help a museum guest or a new collector know what they see.
62934-drawings-by-charles-dana-gibson:
Charles Gibson drawings fill this album of society scenes and jokes. Russell printed Drawings in New York, copyright 1894 and 1896. Captions open To a Little American Girl, then a dog case. The American Girl Abroad stands chaperoned by a real duchess there.

Trials of a Bud and running the gauntlet among rivals follow. Young girls who marry oldish millionaires wander plains with cowboys here. Fourth of July, Lenten confessions, and a bright outlook appear. A father grieves a penniless match till the girl answers brightly. No respecter of a widow grief and danger shore wrecks stand among the captioned plates within.
62988-the-complete-manual-of-catholic-pi:
William Gahan, an Augustinian priest, made this complete manual of Catholic piety, printed in Dublin in 1844. The title promises fervent prayers, pious reflections, and solid instruction fit for every state of life. A supplement adds approved devotions and the epistles and gospels for all Sundays and feasts of the year.

The contents open with a calendar of feasts and fasts, rules on marriage, and a guide to lay baptism. Morning and night prayers come next, with acts of faith, hope, and charity, litanies, and prayers before and at Mass. Long sections prepare the reader for confession, with an examination of conscience, and for communion, with prayers before and after. Daily and monthly reflections, prayers for the sick, and devotions to the Sacred Heart fill the later pages. The manual served as a full prayer book for home and church.
6301-the-eve-of-the-french-revolution:
Edward J. Lowell looks at the French Revolution in two ways, first at great events that astonished Europe and America, and second at the slower causes beneath them. The Bastille, the march on Versailles, the September massacres, and the Terror all draw the eye. Napoleon's restoration of order does too, yet Lowell warns that historians, scenting battle, have sometimes hurried over the ground before it.

The book opens with king and administration, as Louis XVI takes the throne in 1774 with power nearly absolute in theory. Provincial estates still meet but with narrow functions, and the Paris parliament, once a check on law, has been dissolved. Lowell writes a clear, sober history of old France on the eve of upheaval, asking what made a despotic seeming order crack.
63048-wanderers-of-the-wolf-moon:
Nelson Bond wrote this science fiction tale for Planet Stories in the spring of 1944. A crew was marooned on Titan, their ship wrecked and the radio smashed, the blurb says. They had to build a new life on a hostile world to survive there, it goes on at the front.

Command fell to Gregory Malcolm, a bespectacled secretary among the castaways of the tale. His only adventures had come through the pages of a book before the wreck, the blurb jokes. Sparks the radio man begs Greg not to tell the boss yet as the story opens, and the little man's fear starts the trouble.
63068-the-washington-peace-carillon:
Marion Shull's The Washington Peace Carillon is a brochure issued by lovers of the bells, done in the interest of a greater Washington. Shull's piece first appeared in the Boston Transcript of November 29, 1918, then in the Washington Star and the Literary Digest. A picture of Ghent stands near the front, whose carillon of fifty-two bells rang out in December 1814 at the signing of the treaty of peace.

The church towers of Flanders and Artois, Shull writes, stand silent, their bells robbed and recast for war. His proposal answers in kind. From the metal of captured enemy cannon, let the finest carillon the world's best makers can cast be struck, and duplicated. So the capital of each great allied nation may hold a set of peace bells. Towers worthy of them would rise, perhaps with a block from shattered Rheims built into the walls.
63088-the-castles-and-abbeys-of-england-:
William Beattie's Castles and Abbeys of England, volume one of two, was published at London by George Virtue. The work draws on the national records, early chronicles, and other standard authors. Upwards of two hundred engravings illustrate it. Beattie, a physician, had written Switzerland, Scotland, and The Waldenses before this survey. The volume opens at Arundel Castle, and the picture list lingers there for pages. Views show the castle from the town, the river Arun, the Swan Lake, and the meadows.

Archer and Allom drew most of the Arundel plates; Jackson, Evans, and Nicholles engraved them. Subjects include the Norman door in the keep, horned owls in the keep, and the inner gateway during the Parliamentary siege. Arms of the Montgomery and Fitzalan earls and the seal of William de Albini appear among the plates.
6310-the-pastor-s-son:
William W. Walter writes, in his preface, that his sole reason for this book is to point readers to another book, whose Christ truth will free them from trouble. If in sin, it shows the way out; if sick, it will heal; if grieving, it will mend a broken heart; if poor, it will give plenty. The novel that follows is built as a witness to that claim, plain and earnest.

On a beautiful Thanksgiving morning, the Reverend James A. Williams tells his son Walter that the sky is cloudless and the breeze almost June like, though it is November 30. He expects a large church crowd for an excellent sermon, yet his joy fades at his son's face, for Walter, nearly seventeen, has been sickly and feeble since birth. Physicians, climate changes, and every promised relief have failed, and father and son must talk faith through suffering.
63132-the-problem-of-the-rupee-its-origi:
Ambedkar, once a professor of political economy at Sydenham College in Bombay, wrote The Problem of the Rupee, printed at London in 1923. He gives the book to his father and mother, in thanks for the sacrifices they made for his schooling. Edwin Cannan writes a preface that owns plain disagreement with much of the case.

Cannan says Ambedkar hits some nails squarely. His practical close may be right, Cannan grants. A plain gold standard is harder for rulers to tamper with than a gold exchange system. It costs a bit more metal, but buys safety. Freshness and sting mark the argument even where the old teacher demurs. Close study of India currency history fills a book that made its young maker a name in economics.
63172-a-pacific-coast-vacation:
Morris tours the far west in A Pacific Coast Vacation, printed with copyright in 1901. The Abbey Press of New York, London, and Montreal made the book. Photographs taken en route by James Edwin Morris illustrate it. The writer gives the book to Alaska's beautiful daughter, Edna McFarland.

Twenty chapters run from farewell to farewell. Off for Alaska leads, with first views and further glimpses. Gold fields, the Muir Glacier, and Sitka fill the northern span. Farewell to Skagway turns the tour south through Washington and Oregon. San Francisco, California farms and vineyards, and Yosemite follow. Southern California and the Walla Walla valley vary the close. Historical references and Yellowstone Park end the long vacation.
63224-with-the-persian-expedition:
With the Persian Expedition is a war roam book by Major Donohoe. An Arnold house of London brought it out in nineteen nineteen, cut rich. He served late in the army spy corps in the great war years. He gives the book to his mates who fell in Persia in its last year. Part one starts the hush hush brigade with a Tower of London meet.

From Flanders mud to east dust, that part sings its move in heads. Egypt to the Persian Gulf, small pox, and a shark scare fill part two. Basra, the town of Sinbad, gets part three in the scheme ranks. A Persian feast, the Tigris run to Kut, and Bagdad fill mid parts. Dunster force past, a seven hundred mile raid lost, stands in part seven.
63280-four-lectures-on-the-english-revol:
Thomas Hill Green lectures on the English Revolution in four talks given at Edinburgh in January 1867. The lectures were printed after his death in the third volume of his works, issued in London in 1888. Green did not plan them for print, and editor R L Nettleship brought them out on the advice of sound judges.

Green opens by calling his period one of the most trodden grounds of history. He faults partisans for heat and dry historians for light that shows nothing of the actors' temper and purpose. Against Carlyle, he stresses the force of custom and institutions, which shape a hero's will and set its limits. Readers get a philosopher's steady view of the Puritan revolution and its place in English life.
63327-chatterton:
Chatterton, by Ernest Lacy, is a play about the boy poet Thomas Chatterton. The scene is a garret in Brooke Street, London, on the night of August 24, 1770. A rough bedstead, a table with manuscripts, and a candle set the stage.

The lodging keeper knocks in vain, then lets in Henry Burgum and his daughter Bertha. Burgum is a rich Bristol pewterer who styles himself de Burgum in hope of a grander title. He has come about a pedigree Chatterton was lucky enough to discover for the family. Birth, like murder, will out, Burgum declares with pomp. Bertha rebukes him: no title is more honourable than the one he has. Burgum surveys the bare room and calls it the rewards of poetry. His daughter answers that only poets know those rewards.
63346-on:
On, by Hilaire Belloc, was copyrighted in 1923 and published in New York. Belloc other books, listed at the front, include Paris, The Pyrenees, Marie Antoinette, and earlier On volumes: On Nothing, On Everything, and On Something. Each essay in the book takes the form its title promises: On, and then a subject.

On Achmet Boulee Bey opens the set, then On an Educational Reform, and On Kind Hearts Being More Than Coronets. On Mumbo-Jumbo, On Footnotes, and a few kind words to Mammon follow. On Treves, On the Cathedral of Seville, and On the Bucolics of Virgil treat place and poem. On titles, bad verse, convincing people, controversy, inaccuracy, technical words, accent, and truth fill the rest. Later pieces treat sailing the seas, a piece of rope, the word and, and hatred of numbers. Readers get Belloc essays at play.
63353-the-treasure-of-the-bucoleon:
Arthur Howden Smith wrote a treasure tale printed at New York in 1923. Smith had written The Doom Trail and Beyond the Sunset. The book is given to Jack Nash. The cable from Hugh's uncle opens the chapters, then the broken message and the papers in the charter chest. The gunroom at Castle Chesby and a fight in the gunroom follow.

The prior's vent, hide and seek, and stole away lead to the Balkan trail. The road to Stamboul and Watkins playing the goat fill the middle. I have a theory, explained my uncle Vernon King within. The upheavals of the war and the occupation of the city by Christian garrisons should give rich chances to bibliophiles like myself, he held. Constantinople's buried palace treasure pulls English hunters east.
63355-studies-on-fermentation:
Louis Pasteur's studies on the ills of beer came out in English at London in 1879, with his leave. Frank Faulkner and Constable Robb made the translation, with notes and an index. Pasteur gives the book to his father's memory. His father had served as a soldier under the first empire.

In his preface Pasteur says the woes of France woke the work. He began right after the war of 1870 and never let it drop. Germany, he grants, beat France in the brewing trade. His aim was a way of making beer that stood free of season and place. It should keep its goods sound for any length of time, without costly cooling.
63356-sir-charles-warren-and-spion-kop-a:
Sir Charles Warren and Spion Kop, a vindication, defends a British general blamed for a famous defeat in the Boer War. Its author signs himself only as Defender. Smith, Elder published it at London in 1902, with a life sketch, a portrait, and a map. The appendix restores passages cut from the published dispatches of 1900, marked here for the reader.

A sketch of Warren's life opens the book: son of a major general, grandson of a dean of Bangor. Chapter one begins the war, with Warren crossing the Tugela river. The position of affairs, the advance to Venter's Laager, and the attack on the hills follow. Spion Kop, a hilltop seized and lost with heavy slaughter in January 1900, fixed Warren's name in blame. This book argues his case from the papers. It stands as a period piece of military controversy, when generals fought their battles again in print.
63397-a-select-glossary-of-the-texas-rev:
A Select Glossary of the Texas Revolution was put together by Jean Carefoot, of the Archives Division of the Texas State Library, in 1986. The head opens with a short account of the revolt itself. In the summer of 1835, unrest grew as Texans learned that troops would be used to force them to obey rules from Mexico.

The account names Travis and an attack on the fort at Anahuac. It tells of fear for rights under the Mexican charter of 1824, as power grew more centred in Mexico. Then came the demand for a cannon at Gonzales, and the first battle. Goliad, Espada, and Concepcion follow. Readers get a word list backed by a clear, brief history of how the revolt began.
63429-joe-carson-s-weapon:
James Adams wrote Joe Carson's Weapon, a science fiction tale from Planet Stories in the spring of 1945. From Mars they had come, vanguards of a ruthless horde that would conquer Earth if they could steal Joe Carson's fertile mind's weapon. Joe grins broadly, rereading his letter to the editor of Galactic Adventures.

The magazine was Joe's favourite, and he spent happy hours roaming the cold of space through its pages in imagination. Its latest issue lies open at the readers' section, garish cover mercifully hidden from view on his desk. Vituperative gripes and gushy praise fill the letter columns he hopes to join in print. One letter from Henry Snade is a lulu he tries to match. Fan fiction readers get Adams.
63521-raiders-of-the-second-moon:
Gene Ellerman wrote Raiders of the Second Moon, a tale from Planet Stories in the summer of 1945. Beyond our moon hides a smaller second moon, Sekk, less than five hundred miles across. Sekk holds air, a star-shaped sunken lake, and eleven green jungle valleys between ragged cliffs.

A white savage called Noork, whose memory was wiped by a strange fate, watches a golden-skinned girl pass below his tree. A huge gleaming bird once carried him to this world in its talons, he recalls. The hairy Vasads and their leader Gurn taught him their tongues over time. Readers get wild pulp adventure on a hidden moon.
63540-evolution-and-adaptation:
Thomas Hunt Morgan wrote a book on evolution and adaptation published in 1903, when he taught at Bryn Mawr and Columbia. The question at its center is whether adaptive traits arise by selection or by other means. Morgan then doubted parts of Darwin's mechanism and pressed the claims of mutation. He weighs adaptation's appearance of design against natural processes. The book surveys variation, heredity, and the struggle for existence.

Morgan later founded the fruit fly laboratory that remade genetics. This early volume shows him mid argument, before the chromosome work settled his views. It belongs to the mutation theory debates of the decade. Scientists read it as a challenge to orthodox Darwinism from within biology.
63569-the-watsons-by-jane-austen-conclud:
The Watsons is Jane Austen's unfinished novel, here brought to an end by a writer named Oulton. The edition was published by D. Appleton and Company in 1923. Austen's fragment opens with the first winter assembly in a Surrey town. The Watsons, a poor family in a village three miles off, are invited by the wealthy Edwards family to dress, dine, and sleep at their house for the ball.

Miss Emma Watson, newly home from the aunt who raised her, is to make her first public appearance in the neighborhood. Her sickly father, a widower, must keep one daughter at home as companion. Oulton's ending carries Austen's cast of county families and officers through the story Austen left incomplete.
6358-the-history-of-england-a-study-in-p:
A. F. Pollard traces England as a study in political evolution, from foundations in 55 B.C. to a century of empire ending in 1911. An American visitor at Hastings, musing that a little island has often been conquered, sets the theme: how a conquered island became an empire that conquered others. Pollard warns that mere incidents will not satisfy readers who see history as interpretation of human development, not a simple story.

Nine chapters carry the argument, from submergence after 1066 and emergence of the English people to nationalism, struggle for self government, expansion, industrial revolution, and democracy. Edward's peerage policy, Richard II as a new monarch born before his time, and noble factions fighting for the crown illustrate the method. Pollard writes a compact, argument driven history, with chronology, bibliography, and index to support it.
63603-andre-e-and-his-balloon:
Henri Lachambre and Alexis Machuron wrote Andrée and His Balloon, issued at Westminster in 1898 with a coloured frontispiece and forty four full page pictures from photographs. The book is dedicated to Salomon August Andrée, a fervent believer in the aerial conquest of the North Pole. Its plates show the balloon in its shed, the valves, the car, and the departure of July 11, 1897.

Page by page the venture is laid out: the ship Virgo, Dane's Island, the first icebergs, and ships among the ice under the midnight sun. The balloon case in the ice and the landing of the car close the picture list. Written while the fate of the flight was still unknown, the book holds the hope and the gear of the attempt together.
63638-electron-eat-electron:
Noel Loomis imagines a future war fought by one boosted champion in a story from Planet Stories for spring 1946. The editor bills the tale as the magazine's scoop on how wars of the future will be waged. President Jeffrey Wadsworth lies under a cosmic-ray lamp while generals watch his treatment.

Wadsworth is sixteen, with a tested mind far above any other member of the Mutant College. The ray drives his reflex speed to three times normal, though his staff doubts a boy's loyalty and grit. He jokes that nine dishes of a new ice cream, not sabotage, slowed him earlier. Readers get a brisk pulp tale that asks whether one enhanced boy can stand in for seven hundred million people.
63689-on-the-eve-of-redemption:
S M Melamed gathered editorial pieces on Jewish nationalism and Zionism, copyrighted in 1918 in New York. The pieces first ran in the American Jewish Chronicle during 1916, 1917, and 1918. The first essay, Judea and Rome, opens with news reaching Rome in August of the year 70. Judea was conquered, the temple burned, and the Jewish people subjugated, the report ran.

Melamed remarks that even history has reasons that reason often fails to grasp. The book's title places its moment on the eve of redemption. Written as the First World War ended, the essays weigh the future of a Jewish national home. Editorial leaders give the collection its form.
63695-prodigal-weapon:
Vaseleos Garson's science fiction story Prodigal Weapon appeared in Planet Stories in the summer of 1945. Earth is held by the Kraks, hairless alien masters. They brand chosen humans with a burning light and ship them as slave cargo to the Krak home planet.

Sean McKenna takes the brand, a crooked X burned into his shoulder. He nearly breaks ranks when the girl he loves is left behind. The teaser frames the remnant of mankind in slave quarters on Karrar. They are dying under Krak rule and hunting for the weak point in their masters' armor. One man still fights, though he knows his weapon is a lance of straw.
63735-subscription-the-disgrace-of-the-e:
A church pamphlet by the Reverend C N Wodehouse, Canon of Norwich. Longman, Brown, Green, and Longmans published the second edition at London in 1843. Its full title is Subscription the Disgrace of the English Church. The subject is the clergy's required subscription to the Thirty-nine Articles. Wodehouse attacks that requirement head-on.

His opening pages work through a general warning. Minds fix on one lit point of a great question. Neglected parts grow quietly until they demand attention. Charles the First and Laud missed the opinions ripening around them. James the Second missed a revolution already accomplished in hearts. Canning missed the coming reform of Parliament. Wodehouse argues that subscription hides the same kind of blindness. Reformers in the Tractarian era made this pamphlet part of a live fight.
63738-subscription-the-disgrace-of-the-e:
Canon Wodehouse of Norwich attacked required subscription to church articles as the disgrace of the English Church, in a pamphlet printed in London and Norwich in 1843. He opens with a general truth. When a question grips the mind, half the subject hides from view. One point takes all the light while greater points grow unseen in the shade.

So it was, he argues, when Charles the First and Archbishop Laud nursed their plans for church and state. Deep rooted opposite opinions grew till they burst forth. Wodehouse warns Parliament men who resist the minutest change that delay can make reform too late. His plea is for honesty in clergy who must sign what they may not believe.
63739-english-cathedrals-illustrated-sec:
Francis Bond made a picture guide to English cathedrals, in a second and revised edition printed in London in 1900. One hundred eighty illustrations from photographs fill the book. Ely north aisle of the choir and the Southwell choir screen stand among the first plates. Bond aims to make the study of cathedrals more interesting, he says.

Every ancient building has a life history of its own and should be studied as a biography. Bond scorns the hop, skip, and jump method that leaps from a twelfth century choir to a sixteenth century chapel and maddens the reader. He sorts work by date and school so a visitor can read a cathedral stone by stone with pleasure.
63740-a-letter-on-the-late-post-office-a:
A Letter on the Late Post Office Agitation is a pamphlet by Charles Vaughan, head master of Harrow School, issued at London in 1849. It is written as a private letter that its author was driven to print. We have lately been invited, he begins, to sign a parish protest against planned changes in the business of the London post office. I, for one, declined the invitation, he says plainly.

He never thought of pressing his reasons on others, he adds. He is not the minister of the parish, and his views claim no special hearing from his neighbours. But a charge now compels him to explain himself. He and those who agreed with him cannot hear in silence the charge of being careless of the nation's day of rest. The changes at issue touched Sunday labour in the posts, a hot question of that sabbath keeping age.
63742-sixty-year-extension:
Sixty-Year Extension is a science fiction story by Alan Nourse. It appeared in Planet Stories in May 1954. Daniel Carter Griffin has volunteered to die, the blurb says. They told him only half the story when he agreed. Life reborn, youth regained, and love rewon were promised. Free agenting around the cosmos was dangled before him. The lurid second death was never mentioned. The tale opens with Griffin waiting in an office.

He cannot recall what day it is. The gap upsets him far beyond its size. His pocket calendar does not help him. He does not know the month or even the year. His right arm is sore, but he feels strong and elated. The thing he has done floods back into his mind. Nourse wrote tales of medicine and the mind. This one turns on a bargain half explained.
63753-a-second-letter-on-the-late-post-o:
Charles John Vaughan wrote A Second Letter on the Late Post Office Agitation, issued by John Murray in London in eighteen hundred fifty. Vaughan led Harrow School and had been a fellow at Cambridge. His first letter drew both praise and loud attack. This one answers a mild critic in the midst.

The row turns on Sunday work at the London Post Office. A new state order had changed the terms of that work. Clergy urged Vaughan to protest it as a sin. He holds the change helps more than it harms true worship. It eases the class it touches, he argues, and leaves faith whole. He will not sign a protest he does not hold true. The letter weighs duty, rest, and the reach of state rules.
63755-a-few-words-on-the-crystal-palace-:
Charles John Vaughan, head master of Harrow School, wrote this pamphlet on the Crystal Palace question, in the edition printed by John Murray in 1852. The question turns on Sunday observance, as Vaughan states at the start. He warns that a clergyman who writes on either side draws blame from both. One side charges him with bigotry, and the other marks him as too lax.

Vaughan holds that the truth must be spoken all the same. He finds deep unrest in the state of the Sunday question in England. Folk profess one rule and live by an altered practice, and teachers will not speak out. Consciences are left puzzled, with no clear answer on why the day is kept as it is.
63776-eight-dramas-of-calderon:
Edward Fitzgerald freely translated Eight Dramas of Calderon for this London edition of 1906. Calderon was Spain's great playwright of the 1600s, and Fitzgerald says up front that he chose lesser-known plays, not the famous ones. Only The Mayor of Zalamea, he notes, had won much praise before. His advertisement explains the free method without apology.

Fitzgerald argues that a word-for-word Calderon would fail in English, since Spanish stage passion can sound like bombast to English ears. So he cut, softened, and reshaped scenes, keeping what was fine while trimming conceits and repeats. The eight plays include The Painter of His Own Dishonour, Keep Your Own Secret, Beware of Smooth Water, The Mighty Magician, and Such Stuff as Dreams Are Made Of. Readers get Spanish drama recast in English verse by a translator who valued smooth effect over strict copying.
63799-tepondicon:
Carl Jacobi sends a lone agent into plague country in Tepondicon, from Planet Stories in the winter of 1946. The blurb weighs the hero: not the savior type, and no craver after martyrdom. Yet treasure beyond price waits in the darkened plague-cities of Ganymede, if a man can measure up to it.

At seven by Earth time the narrator sights Profaldo, the first plague city, its spires glowing through grey light. He hides his tracto-car and swallows three white pellets. Then he pockets a heat pistol and one of seven transmitting sets, and shows his papers from the High Ganymedian Council at the gate.
63815-frank-merriwell-on-the-road-or-the:
Frank Merriwell on the Road is a boys tale by Burt Standish in the Medal Library line. Its next name calls it the All Star Combination in full. The Medal line ran week by week with tales for boys by famed hands. Frank is its hero, a true type of the American lad by its own words. He holds a strong bent to do right at all costs in the tales.

Alger and Optic stand in the same line with their own boy sets. Lists in the front leaves name the week books of late months. Merriwell hard luck, chance, and chase books crowd those list ranks. Reid, Henty, and Marryat tales stand in the same boys line scheme. This book sends Frank on the road with his star team in sport.
63819-claude-s-confession:
Claude's Confession is an early novel of the French writer Zola. George Cox put the book in English for the trade of the day. The tale is drawn from Zola's own youth, by the front note. He is Claude, the hero, in all but name through the book.

Claude is a poor scholar in the Latin part of Paris town. His rooms, his friends, and his loves fill the dark tale told here. A girl of the streets and a pure girl stand at its heart. A painter friend and a gay small dame join the cast of the tale. Youth is spoilt and spent in its pages, the note warns the reader. The style is raw and true, of the school Zola went on to lead.
63827-asleep-in-armageddon:
Ray Bradbury wrote Asleep in Armageddon, a science fiction story printed in Planet Stories in the winter of 1948. A warning stands at its head: avoid Planetoid 787, lush and sunny with fine air, because sleep there is death. Leonard Sale, a spaceman, crashes on just that world.

Sale climbs from the wreck with two months of food and a working radio. Marsport answers at once: a rescue ship, the Logarithm, will reach him in six days. It sounds simple, and Sale dances for joy. But in the darkness after the crash, hidden voices had already asked his name and trade, and welcomed him. The planetoid keeps its dead in a strange way, and sleep is their door. Bradbury turns a routine rescue wait into a haunted siege.
63832-the-castles-and-abbeys-of-england-:
Castles and Abbeys of England, volume two, is an illustrated antiquarian survey by William Beattie. George Virtue of London and New York issued the second series of the work. Twenty seven engravings on steel and numerous woodcuts illustrate the volume. Chepstow Castle, from the iron bridge across the Wye, leads the plate list.

Beattie drew his matter from the national records, early chronicles, and standard authors. His earlier books on Switzerland, Scotland, and the Waldenses stand on the title page. Ruined abbeys and border castles carry the national story building by building. Victorian parlours learned English history from such steel plate tours of ruins.
63836-morley-s-weapon:
Morleys Weapon is a tale of a space boat by D Barefoot. It first ran in a planet tale magazine in March of nineteen fifty four. A stone swarm from deep space heads for death in the sun, its blurb says. One half pound chunk of that swarm has a date with a space boat.

Morley sweats at the board of his small ship as the tale opens. He must pick: wake a scorn prone chief or land the boat by his own hand. The moon Japetus lies less than five hundred miles past his hull. Self blame for his fix gnaws him as he weighs the two ills. Doubt and cold math drive the brief tale of the far lanes.
63854-the-death-from-orion:
Matthews's The Death From Orion is a space story from Planet Stories, Winter 1948. Its epigraph sets the stakes: tiny suns set in rare metals, crystals of fire that mocked Earth's diamonds. The ancient treasure left behind it a trail of sudden blood and stiffening corpses.

The scene is a cell at night. Gion, Marward of Jupiter, comes to the chained outlaw Kurland, who is to hang at dawn. The corridors glow dim with atomics; leg-irons tinkle as the prisoner swings a crossed leg and returns the stare with infuriating coolness. Gion has come far to see him hanged, he says, and rates him higher than Kurland thinks. Then the offer: suppose, come dawn, you did not hang. Kurland eases back against the cold stone, smiling thinly. He is not for sale, he answers, even at such a price. Nor are his comrades.
639-the-god-idea-of-the-ancients-or-sex-:
Eliza Burt Gamble traces how sex shaped early god ideas in this study, grown from her Evolution of Woman. She argues that gods reflect the inner life of peoples, and that sex is the root fact in nature and in worship alike. Tree, sun, and fire cults, dual gods, and the split of female and male elements fill the chapters.

Gamble writes with earnest, scholarly care, drawing on monuments, symbols, and sacred sites. Later chapters treat Israel, Phoenicia, and Christianity as continuations of older faiths. The book serves as a bold early feminist history of religion, where the divine bears the marks of human sex and society.
63987-wreck-off-triton:
Alfred Coppel wrote the science fiction story Wreck Off Triton, first printed in Planet Stories in November 1951. The blurb lays out the prize: Ron Carnavon, a ruthless convict, means to loot a wrecked spaceship of its sapphire treasure. Carnavon had been skipper of the Thunderbird, and every port in the Earth-Mars-Venus triangle knew he had scuttled her himself.

He left the treasure ship ruptured in orbit a million miles off Triton, her vault heavy with Plutonian sapphires, and kept the chart of her position. With a price on his head, he crossed Mars in disguise, his face changed by a renegade surgeon, and hired Pop Wills and the rusty Carefree at the spacemen's boneyard. Pop, broke and fond of gin, fits the plan perfectly, since nobody will miss him when something happens to his ship. Readers get a cold caper told from the wrecker who planned every step.
6402-the-romance-of-isabel-lady-burton:
Volume two of Isabel Lady Burton's romance, told in part by herself and in part by W. H. Wilkins, continues Book Two through Damascus and beyond. Chapters run from in and about Damascus and early days there, through the desert to Palmyra, Bludan in the Anti Lebanon, gathering clouds, and Jerusalem and the Holy Land. The recall follows, with true reasons for Burton's recall, the passing of a cloud, and early years at Trieste.

A journey to Bombay, India, Trieste again, and shadows lengthening lead to Gordon and the Burtons, a sword hanging and a sword falling. Book Three, widowed, opens with the truth about The Scented Garden, a return to England, and the tinkling of a camel's bell. At Safed, Jews flock to the travellers' tents with hospitality. Wilkins and Burton write a life of travel, faith, and loss, in her voice and his.
64022-the-virgin-of-valkarion:
Poul Anderson opens a sword tale of prophecy and a falling dynasty in a piece from Planet Stories for July 1951. A head note quotes the Temple Prophecy for that night in full. A sword-scarred outlander will ride in, a queen will play the tavern bawd, and the Thirty-ninth Dynasty will fall, it claims.

Alfric reins in his hengist at dusk and scans the land with care learned in long wandering. The old Imperial Way runs cracked and weed-grown down the slope to Valkarion below him. Peasant fires glow red and ruined temples loom against a greenish-blue sky as dark falls. A falkh hangs on still wings above, and a prickling at Alfric's spine warns him not to drop his guard.
64057-agnes-mary-clerke-and-ellen-mary-c:
Agnes Mary Clerke and Ellen Mary Clerke, An Appreciation, was written by Lady Huggins and printed for private circulation in 1907. Lady Huggins was an honorary member of the Royal Astronomical Society. Agnes Clerke wrote on the stars, and her sister Ellen wrote poems and tales.

A portrait of Agnes, from a photo, stands at the front, with a bust of their mother from Rome in 1868. The piece lists Agnes papers for the Edinburgh Review, then treats Ellen in a second part. Agnes was born on February 10, 1842, at Skibbereen in County Cork, to John William Clerke. Frail in health, she found her chief delight in study and music, and in talks with great star men. Readers get a fond life of a famed woman of science.
64071-open-invitation:
Open Invitation is a short story by H B Fyfe that appeared in Planet Stories in May nineteen fifty-one. The headnote states the problem simply. The scout Zoya Lar-Tul must keep the aggressive little Earthmen from discovering his home star.

The opening sits with Yaradirian officials in a mud-floored communications chamber on Yaradir, second planet of Zillor. These tentacled colonizers run a scouting sector from their tubs of water. A preliminary report on system LL-255-13 lists one intelligent species, on the third planet. Its star is Sol and its planet is Earth. Fyfe builds the comedy from alien bureaucracy: nepotism, dry footing, and snapping eyestalks. The menace of Earth is filtered through office politics light-years away.
64120-house-and-home-papers-seventh-edit:
Harriet Beecher Stowe wrote a set of home papers under the pen name Christopher Crowfield, in a seventh form printed at Boston in 1887. The papers first came under protection in 1864. A list of her works heads the book. Uncle Tom's Cabin leads it, in three forms and many tongues.

Contents open with the ravages of a carpet. Home keeping follows. Such papers treat the small wars of the house: dust, drafts, servants, and taste. Stowe's fame as a novelist lent weight to her house lore. The same press sold Little Foxes and The Chimney-Corner beside it, at a set price each. Plain, chatty counsel on running a Christian home is the set's whole aim.
64152-the-strange-visitation:
Marie Corelli wrote a tale that opens on a wild Christmas Eve of storm. Hodder and Stoughton issued the book from London, New York, and Toronto. Corelli had written Thelma, Holy Orders, and The Sorrows of Satan. Wind tears at doors and windows like an angry cat in her first lines.

Corelli sets the howling night against the peace the season should bring. She quotes Milton on the calm night when the Prince of Light began his reign. She then asks if the first age knew a true trade lord grown fat on sweat. Faith, wealth, and the soul stand at the heart of her tale.
64159-planet-of-creation:
Chester Geier's Planet of Creation ran in Planet Stories for spring 1947. The blurb promises the joker: to hardened spacemen the planet was heaven, with grass sprouting on bald rock, metal parts appearing as required, and new men relieving the weary at a thought. The story opens in the flagship's control room, where Commander Thettumir of the Urgollian fleet studies the scanner. His astronomer Vandumonn reports no other planet near the dying red sun, and the engines will not reach the next sun, ten light-years off.

The one planet is wrapped in dense gray clouds, which promise air but make landing dangerous for a fleet already battered. Thettumir orders deceleration and an orbit, with scout ships to descend and report. Geier builds the tale on the fleet's need for a repair base that answers wishes too well. The byline is Chester Geier, a pulp regular of the Planet Stories stable.
64229-a-century-of-parody-and-imitation:
A Century of Parody and Imitation, edited by Walter Jerrold and Leonard, was issued by the Oxford University Press in 1913. A motto from Gay heads the book: no author ever spared a brother. A plate shows James and Horace Smith, the fathers of the modern form. The object of the compilation is stated in its prefatory note.

That object is a corpus of representative parodies and imitations of a century. The span begins with Rejected Addresses of 1812, printed here in full. That work practically marked the birth of modern parody, the editors say. Prose parodies are excluded, except those in Rejected Addresses itself. Wordsworth, Shelley, Byron, and Scott all suffer loving imitation in such pages. The anthology is a museum of English comic verse.
64268-blood-transfusion:
Geoffrey Keynes wrote this medical handbook on blood transfusion practice. Frowde and Hodder and Stoughton printed it in London in 1922. Keynes served as second assistant in a surgery unit at Saint Bartholomew. Chapter one gives a historical sketch of the art from old times.

Indications follow, first for haemorrhage and shock in the wounded. Blood diseases and toxaemias take the next chapter in the book. Dangers of transfusion, blood group science, and donor choice come next. Methods of transfusion close the text before a full bibliography. An index of topics closes the handbook after its long list of source works cited.
64277-letters-from-an-old-time-salesman-:
Letters from an Old Time Salesman to His Son, by James, sales manager of Libby, McNeill and Libby, was published by the Dartnell Corporation in 1922. The contents follow one career in chapters: the boy starts out, green and gullible but full of pep; he arrives as a regular salesman. He is promoted to special salesman; he has his troubles as a branch manager.

Later letters counsel team work, warn why it pays to advertise, and tell the boy to throw away his knickers and put on long pants. Hal, the son, becomes district manager, with the problem of winning the respect of men. A closing note insists these are real letters, written by a real salesman to a real son, not for publication. The writer has been through the mill; the motive is a father's, which the note calls the refreshing difference from other books of the kind.
643-the-death-of-the-lion:
Henry James writes of fame and its costs in this short novel, first published in 1915 in Martin Secker's edition. A young journalist, taken on by a weekly paper, sets out to write on Neil Paraday, a writer once obscure and now celebrated. The narrator hopes the piece will lift his own career as much as his subject's.

James writes with dry, watchful irony, letting the press, friends, and admirers crowd a shy author till his work suffers. The tale turns on how praise can harm the praised. It endures as a sharp study of literary fame, where a lion dies not from neglect but from too much attention.
64302-mo-sanshon:
Bryce Walton wrote a science fiction tale that ran in Planet Stories in the summer of 1947. Doctor Jonathan Ward alone knows that beings called Mo Sanshon are on Earth. He can almost hear them rustling behind their humanoid faces. A world psychometric council delivers its verdict by telaudio in his bare room.

The council finds Ward a paranoiac with delusions of persecution and grandeur. His belief in a super insect menace is judged unsupported by evidence. He is sentenced to reconditioning clinics under solar statutes of 2166. Panic hits as he finds doors and windows that open only from outside. He sits two hundred floors up, awaiting guards. A helper named Red raises the question of trust.
64340-woman-in-political-evolution:
Joseph McCabe published Woman in Political Evolution in London in 1909, tracing women's standing from early societies to his own day. Chapters move through woman before civilisation, ancient Egypt and Assyria, Greece, and Rome, then a dark age, the Renaissance and revolution, and the struggle in the nineteenth century.

McCabe says earlier sketches lacked a connecting principle, and he seeks one law running through the whole sweep of history. His final chapter rests enfranchisement on a moral base. Readers get an Edwardian case for women's votes built as a single long argument from ancient evidence to present politics, written while the suffrage fight was still live.
64534-on-the-brink-of-a-chasm-a-record-o:
Meade's 1899 record of plot and passion opens at a crush in Mrs Evershed's beautiful Mayfair house, where the hostess smiles at her guests while standing on the verge of bankruptcy. Her creditors clamor behind the welcome.

Her only daughter Barbara, nineteen and a reigning beauty, hides in a curtained window recess watching for someone, unwilling to make the rich match that would save her mother. Chapter titles promise a man's revenge, a post obit, the wrong medicine, circumstantial evidence, and an ace of trumps. Buckles and Company published the novel at New York, with Chatto and Windus at London.
6456-public-opinion:
Walter Lippmann's Public Opinion, dated 1921 at Wading River, Long Island, opens with Plato's cave: beings chained in an underground den, seeing only shadows before them, firelight behind. Chapter one, The World Outside and the Pictures in Our Heads, tells of an island in 1914 where Englishmen, Frenchmen, and Germans lived without cable, mail steamer coming once in sixty days. In mid September they still talked of Madame Caillaux's trial, then learned they had been at war for six strange weeks.

For six weeks they acted as friends when in fact they were enemies, yet their plight, Lippmann argues, differs little from our own. A mid passage contrasts two business partners in war: one enlists for a dollar a day, sacrificing all, while the other takes a war contract for handsome profit over costs. Lippmann writes democracy's central problem: how opinion forms from pictures in heads, not the world outside.
64567-nordenholt-s-million:
Connington imagines a world blight in Nordenholt's Million, printed in London in 1923. The tale is told in the first person by a motor car man. He made the Flint car a hit by mass methods and was trained as an engineer.

His skill with large scale work brings him to the notice of Nordenholt. The heads map the crash to come: the coming of the Blight, panic, and strain. Then come the Clyde Valley, the nitrogen area, and a last stand named Asgard. A rich man's vast plan to save seed and stock drives this stark tale of hunger and rule.
64678-the-first-man-on-the-moon:
Alfred Coppel tells a bleak tale of the first moon flight in a story drawn from Planet Stories for spring 1950. John Thurmon swore he would be first on the moon, and the opening warns he became its first murderer instead. His ship lies wrecked on a white pumice plain, its nozzles fused and its hull crushed.

Inside, Thurmon knows there can be no return, yet counts the cost worth the fame. He recalls killing his friend Wayne, the one man who might have shared or stolen the glory. His radio still works, and he waits to send word to a watching world. Readers get a sharp, cold study of pride, guilt, and hunger for fame at any price.
64695-moon-of-treason:
Emmett McDowell wrote a science fiction tale printed in the Summer 1950 issue of a pulp magazine. Clyde Vickers, branded an outlaw and feared as a mutant, lands at Luna City after two years on Jupiter. Two years in hard gravity have built huge muscle on his frame, and his odd eyes mark him at a glance.

An officer at the gangplank reads his green book and calls him a parolee out loud. Vickers must report to the parole board in a day or be shipped back to the penal mines. Shame, rage, and a hunt for a foe drive the tale from its cold first pages.
64712-a-brief-guide-to-the-food-collecti:
A brief guide to the food collection at the Bethnal Green branch of the South Kensington Museum was printed in London in 1872, priced at one penny. It was the first issue of the guide. Opening sections trace how the branch museum grew out of the parent house at South Kensington.

That museum stood on twelve acres bought by the government at a cost of 60,000 pounds, from the surplus of the Exhibition of 1851. An iron building went up in 1855 under Sir William Cubitt, and opened on June 22, 1857. Loans from the Queen and others enriched the stores. The food collection was meant to teach working folk what they ate.
6473-practical-argumentation:
George K. Pattee, assistant professor of English and rhetoric at Pennsylvania State College, writes Practical Argumentation to be practical from the student's standpoint and the teacher's. Argumentation is often criticised as purely academic, or a mere stepping stone to law, but Pattee defines it as the art of presenting truth so others accept it and act on it. Debate is its special oral form, carried on by opposing sides.

By argumentation, he argues, men overthrow error and discover truth, threshing a problem until chaff blows away and kernels of truth remain. Courts, assemblies, and all discussing bodies recognise this, and men of affairs hear advocates of different systems before great enterprises. A mid passage turns to government and armies, where discipline and subordination entrusted to leaders outweigh private convenience in war. Pattee writes a working rhetoric for students.
64734-the-cause-and-cure-of-the-cattle-p:
James Galloway Cowan, perpetual curate of St John's at Hammersmith, preached this sermon on the cattle plague in 1866. William Skeffington printed it at London. His text is from Isaiah: I form the light and create darkness, I make peace and create evil.

Cowan warns that talk of 'nature' can hide God from men's minds. Laws of nature, he says, are only the rules by which God's power works. The plague killing the herds must be read in that light. His cure begins with seeing the hand behind the blow, not in fleeing to chance causes.
64801-the-warwickshire-avon:
Quiller Couch wrote notes for a river book on the Warwickshire Avon, with art by Alfred Parsons, issued in New York in 1892. Parsons gave his drawings to all the friends with whom he had spent happy hours on that river. The trip opens in Northamptonshire in late autumn, with a stray gun cracking at partridges in the stubble.

First stop is Naseby, a plain village of cottages under a high ridge. Here on a bright June day the armies of king and Parliament fought the battle that cost Charles the First his crown. The notes mix that grim past with black oxen, bullfinches, and dog rose berries along the road. The river road south is told as both tour and tale of old England.
64817-lunar-station:
Harl Vincent's Lunar Station ran in Comet in January 1941, a story of the other side of the Moon. Bill Bonwitt, young chief engineer at the mercury mines in the crater Tycho, feels the Moon move under his boots. Radio operator Val Crane first blames the departing transport, then feels the swing himself. From the crystal dome they watch Earth, which should hang fixed, swing across the sky and snap back. The ethertype brings word from Mount Palomar by way of New York.

Luna had shifted three and a half degrees eastward by an unaccountable rotation, then returned to her place. Bonwitt reckons sixty-six surface miles in as many seconds. Crashes and shouts rise from the machine shop below as the story opens its crisis. Vincent builds the tale on a mining station crew facing a Moon gone haywire.
64846-the-planet-of-illusion:
Millard Gordon printed The Planet of Illusion in Comet in March 1941, opening with a verse about a phantom land and a phantom folk sailing out of the deep unknown. Kendall at the electro-telescope sings out a planet sighted, five point on ten left from star, and Broster at the controls answers that he is daft and dreaming.

The space-chart shows nothing but a particularly empty species of nothingness where the planet ought to be. A world that one instrument sees and another denies is the story's riddle, and illusion is in the title for a reason. Comet ran only a handful of issues; short pulp tales like this one are nearly all that survives of it.
6485-hugh-wynne-free-quaker-sometime-bre:
S. Weir Mitchell's Hugh Wynne, Free Quaker, sometime brevet lieutenant colonel on General Washington's staff, first appeared in book form in 1896 and reached a nineteenth edition with corrections. Mitchell used the new edition to rectify mistakes in names, dates, and localities. Those errors passed unnoticed by ordinary readers, but troubled local archaeologists and readers who ask a novelist to combine scholarly accuracy with creative imagination. Howard Pyle's pictures include a frontispiece asking, is it yes or no, Darthea?

A mid passage shows a gay, winning creature telling her story freely, unlocking her heart for her listener, who laughs that she has a key called love. She kisses him and asks if he says such pretty things to other women. Mitchell writes Revolutionary Philadelphia through a Quaker turned soldier, where conscience, love, and war pull one man three ways.
6486-the-life-of-the-venerable-mother-ma:
A religious of the Ursuline community writes The Life of the Venerable Mother Mary of the Incarnation. Its materials come from her son's life of her, published in 1677, and the history of the Ursuline monastery at Quebec, published in 1863. Her infancy, childhood, and youth open it: early call to union with God, charity to the poor, purity of soul, and inclination for religious life. Married life follows, with rule of life, love of prayer, fulfilment of duty, and patience under trial.

Her husband's death brings a first year of widowhood, solitude in the world, and charity to the poor, then a call to divine union, austerities, and vows of poverty and obedience. A mid passage shows the obstacle removed by her husband's death, leaving her free when duty allows separation from her son, now twelve, who can dispense with care. She watches his infancy with tenderness before answering her call.
64890-essay-on-the-principles-of-transla:
Essay on the Principles of Translation is a classic treatise by Alexander Fraser Tytler, Lord Woodhouselee, here in a cheap library edition. The publishers' pages at the front lay out the whole library's plan in twelve heads. Travel, science, fiction, theology, history, and the classics lead the list. For young people, essays, oratory, poetry and drama, lives, and romance complete the dozen.

A Bacon motto adorns the volume: the most current writing comes home to men's business and bosoms. Tytler's essay, first issued in the eighteenth century, lays down the laws of good translation. A translation should give the ideas of the original wholly, in a style of the same character, with the ease of original writing. That threefold rule made the essay the seed of translation study in English. The library edition put it in every cheap bookcase.
64898-judgments-in-vacation:
Judgments in Vacation, by Judge Edward Abbott Parry, was printed at London in 1911 and dedicated to Lord Alverstone, Lord Chief Justice of England. Parry owns that a county court judge, used to judging all day, keeps the habit into his holidays. County court work leaves no leisure in term, so the judgments must be written in vacation or not at all.

The pieces range widely: The Box Office, Cookery Book Talk, A Day of my Life in the County Court, and The Folk-Lore of the County Court. Others treat debtors, daughters, young advocates, and the insolvent poor. Advice and laughter mix through the whole.
64930-the-goddess-a-demon:
The Goddess: A Demon, a mystery novel by Richard Marsh, was published in London in 1900. Marsh had already written The Beetle and other tales of mystery. His narrator lives at number 79, Imperial Mansions, next door to Edwin Lawrence at number 64, and the two men gamble after a night at the Empire music hall.

Drinking more than he is used to, the narrator loses nearly a thousand pounds to Lawrence, who has juggled with the pack. From there the chapters move through a woman who comes through a window, a doctor's charge, and a photograph known again. At last come the goddess herself and the legacy of the scarlet hands. The book is a late Victorian tale of fraud and dread, told in the first person.
64977-the-protocols-and-world-revolution:
Printed in Boston in 1920, this volume presents an English rendering of the 'Protocols of the Meetings of the Zionist Men of Wisdom' text, with notes and argument around it. Its opening pages frame the world after the Great War as a place in grave crisis. Bolshevism in Russia is treated as a rising force that threatens other lands.

The text draws on Serge Nilus and on scripture verses about a near end. Readers should approach it as a period polemic. Its claims about Jewish people and world revolt are presented as fact by its makers. The book shows how such charges were spread in print after the war.
64997-the-joss-a-reversion:
Joss, a Reversion, is a novel by Richard Marsh, issued at London in nineteen oh one. Contents split the tale into four books, each told by a different voice. Mary Blyth tells the first, named for her uncle Benjamin. Emily Purvis gives the facts of the case in the second. A lawyer tells the third, and a sea captain the fourth, named for the joss itself.

Chapter heads in the first book name a doll, a missionary's letter, and a sole residuary legatee. Entering into possession and a back door key follow. The narrator opens on an aggravating day when luck ran against her. She was fined for lateness at her shop, she says. She had forgotten her cuffs and was marked sixpence more.
65026-the-social-ladder-drawings-by-char:
Charles Dana Gibson drew The Social Ladder, a book of cartoons published in New York in 1902. It was the seventh book in the regular series of his published drawings. Each book in the series holds eighty-four of his best cartoons in matching size and binding.

Gibson girls and their beaux fill the pages, along with henpecked husbands and grand hostesses. One caption shows a young man listing all he has done for love, from debt to having his appendix removed. Another follows a husband whose room is taken over at his wife's housewarming. The drawings poke fun at money, fashion, and courtship among the rich of the day. Readers get sharp pen work and gentle mockery of high society.
