65058-old-greek-education:
Old Greek Education, by Mahaffy, surveys schooling in ancient Greece. Harper of New York issued the little book in eighteen eighty two. Mahaffy was a fellow and tutor of Trinity College, Dublin. He also wrote Social Life in Greece and a Greek literature history.

Mahaffy gives the book to the Greek nation, still a pioneer of schooling. Eastern Europe owed its lead in education to Greece, he holds. The gift marks the year eighteen eighty one in his memory there. A note gives plain English for Greek words where readers need help. His many debts to other authors go unnamed for want of space.
65117-the-dazzling-miss-davison:
The Dazzling Miss Davison is a society novel by Florence Warden, printed at New York in 1910. Warden also wrote The House on the Marsh. The tale opens in Bayswater, in a roomy, comfortable, old-fashioned house. High windows and little balconies hold a wealth of flowers in summer.

In October a row of asters backs the foliage plants and makes the house look bright. The young faces at the drawing-room windows make it prettier still. Aldington and his wife, who keep the house, think nothing in life pleasanter than the gayety of young people. Their own son and daughter are grown, so the house fills with guests. Among them is Gerard Buckland, a clever young barrister tired of hearing of the great things he will do some day. Warden spins her dazzle over this mild London circle.
65124-voyage-to-procyon:
Voyage to Procyon, a science fiction story by Robert Silverberg, ran in Imagination in June 1958. Peter Conroy was born in deep space aboard Starship One, a generation ship bound for the star Procyon. The ship left Earth more than fifty years ago, and a hundred years of flight remain. Its farms, factories, and living centres are the only world its people know.

Conroy hides in a cornfield on the lowest level while Bayliss Kent and his men hunt for him. Kent's party of malcontents wants to turn the ship back to Earth. Conroy, raised in the agronomy section, knows the ground better than his hunters. The chase turns on who owns the future of the voyage.
65200-perfect-companion:
Perfect Companion is a science fiction story by John McGreevey. It appeared in the magazine Imagination in June 1951. A motto at its head gives the tale its chill. If the devil had wanted a playmate, it says, this thing would serve.

The thing lies on an operating table as the story opens. It is about the size of a large dog, and made of metal. Yet it lives, because Craig Stevens has given it life. Across the table stands Sheila, his wife of three years, leaving him. She tells him she hates him, and that he taught her how. Craig answers with the cold calm of a laboratory worker. He picks up a small battery and will not lose his temper for her.
65241-rescue-mission:
Robert Silverberg wrote a space tale that ran in Imagination in December 1957. Snaring both Earthmen in a mind web was easy for the mutant telepath, the blurb says, but once you've caught your prey, how do you get rid of them. Rick Mason's ship was still high over Mordarga, coming in for a landing, when the cry for help sounded in his audio phones.

Rick frowned and reached to turn up the volume, then knew the voice had not come over the audio at all. It had spoken in his mind. Help, Rick, they've caught me, his partner cries. Klon Darra the Venusian, the other half of a mind linked Solar System intelligence team, had landed on schedule and fallen into the ruler's hands. Prison and torture wait. Mason goes down alone to break him out.
65312-the-divine-lady-a-romance-of-nelso:
E Barrington wrote a romance of Nelson and Emma Hamilton, issued in New York in 1924. Dodd, Mead and Company brought out The Divine Lady that June. Twelve printings ran from June 1924 to February 1925, a sign of wide demand. A front plate shows Lady Hamilton as Circe, from a painting by G Romney.

Twenty-seven chapters run from Greville's meeting with Emma to a sunset close. The bargain, Naples, the Nile, and triumph mark the great turns. Emma sings by a window at the start, her voice drawing children to listen. Readers gain a lush, fond tale of beauty, love, and fame.
65325-they-reached-for-the-moon:
William Oberfield wrote this tale of rockets that reached the moon. The story ran in Imagination magazine in November 1951. Men had beaten gravity and reached the moon, the head note says. Strangely, they never returned from any of those trips out.

A thousand days built the great gleaming monster rocket ship. Two hundred more groomed it for a trip around the moon. Three rockets went before it and not one came back. Robot rockets landed but could not plant the wished base there. A military base on the moon was the leaders aim behind the manned flights.
65350-john-holder-s-weapon:
John Holder's Weapon, by Robert Moore Williams, ran in October 1957. Imagination printed the novelette that month. A blurb gives the turn at once. Holder, a captive scientist, hates his Communist captors. He wishes them out of existence; impossible, of course, and yet they vanish. Holder has borne commissars breathing down his neck in every test. Cameras watch each laboratory in the Ural stronghold. His dreams run to hydrogen bombs and death rays. Then he shouts at Nocher, the commissar set over him. Nocher stands six foot two, with Cossack blood and open contempt for the prisoners.

His face turns blue, then a thin shade of white. Clothes and all, he vanishes like smoke. A ghost outline hangs a moment where he stood. Holder feels horror, and under it a thundering elation.
65399-plank-frame-barn-construction:
John Shawver wrote this practical guide to building barns with plank frames, published in New York in 1904 from articles in Carpentry and Building. The system had been used in central Ohio for twenty years and kept spreading, above all in the Central West.

The preface promises data on saving time, labor, and material. Shawver's own list claims a saving in timber of 40 to 60 per cent, plus the chance to use timber too poor for solid mortise and tenon frames. Sawing, cutting, and hauling costs fall by about half, he says, and framing costs by half or more. Farmers short of timber get a full working method.
65416-clubfoot-the-avenger-being-some-fu:
Valentine Williams wrote Clubfoot the Avenger, more adventures of Desmond Okewood of the Secret Service, printed at New York with rights from 1923 and 1924. Rain floods the first scene. In Pump Yard off Saint James, lamps blur on wet stone while a police man peers into a plum cabriolet as men crowd round in the downpour.

Chapter heads fan the plot wide. Miss Vere Slade comes in, then the man with the clubfoot, a strange tale from Miss Patricia Maxwell, and an ikon of Smolensk with a secret. A top flat, steps in the dark, and a Constantinople courier raise the stakes. A leather packet, a flight, and plain speech from Miss Mary Brewster close a fast spy tale of codes, icons, and old scores.
65483-the-sinister-invasion:
Alexander Blade wrote this science fiction tale for Imagination, where it ran in June 1957. Ross Birrel, an electrical engineer and a bachelor who is stone broke, comes home to his New York apartment and finds a stranger waiting inside. The gray man in the gray suit has no credentials, a gun in his pocket, and official business he will not explain.

Birrel is sure the man is crazy, and tries the trick of a sudden turn and a blow at the neck. The cover note gives the game away: Birrel, much against his will, is to become a cosmic counter-spy, the one Earthman fitted by a quirk of nature for the job. The tale is brisk pulp work, all threat and pace.
65490-magic-london:
Magic London is a children's history of London by Netta Syrett, published in London in 1922. Helen Jacobs illustrated the book, and a colour frontispiece shows the Great Fire of London. It belongs to the Royal Road Library series.

A godmother takes a girl named Betty through the city in story form. Five chapters move through the ages. Roman London comes first, then the Middle Ages of Dick Whittington, then Tudor days with Shakespeare and Queen Elizabeth. The Restoration chapter brings Charles the Second and Samuel Pepys. The eighteenth century closes the tour with the Georges and Doctor Johnson. The dedication hopes every young reader finds such a guide. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
65492-the-goose-step-a-study-of-american:
The Goose-Step, a study of American education by Upton Sinclair, was published by the author in 1923. Sinclair issued it from Pasadena, with a wholesale distributor in Chicago. The first edition ran to ten thousand copies in cloth in February of that year. His earlier books, The Jungle and The Brass Check, are named on the title page.

Sinclair turns the same muckraking eye on colleges that he turned on meat packing and the press. The goose step title mocks drill like obedience in the schools of the rich, by his framing. Boards, money, and control of teaching form the charges such a study lays out. Readers of his earlier exposes knew the method well by 1923. Education as a business run for the few is the claim the book sets out to prove.
65518-the-southern-case-for-school-segre:
James Jackson Kilpatrick wrote The Southern Case for School Segregation, first published by the Crowell-Collier Press in 1962 and dated from Richmond in May of that year. The book is arranged in three parts called The Evidence, The Law, and Prayer of the Petitioner, with an appendix.

Its first chapter recalls that when the Supreme Court decided Brown against the Board of Education in May 1954, seventeen southern and border states kept racially separate schools. Five soon abandoned segregation, the author notes, each in a different spirit. Readers get a leading segregationist editor's brief against school integration, a primary document of the massive resistance era, arguing the losing side in legal form.
65542-the-romance-of-the-moon:
Romance of the Moon is a whimsical tale by J A Mitchell, issued at New York in eighteen eighty six. A mock preface in verse or prose opens the book. Science is very good in its own way, it says. But a wide spread ignorance covers all that belongs to the romantic side of Earth's history, it laments. The facts that follow are made public to dispel that ignorance, it jokes.

Numbered scenes tell the story in short strokes. One summer's night, about a million years ago, the Moon was pensive, it begins. The Earth floated leisurely about in space, affecting not to see her. Old Saturn understood it all, for he had loved the Moon for ages. She had chilled him whenever he approached, the tale says. An ugly fight in the heavens followed his rage.
65630-zelda-dameron:
Zelda Dameron, a novel by Meredith Nicholson, author of The Main Chance, was copyrighted in Indianapolis in 1904, with drawings by John Cecil Clay. Nicholson dedicates the book to his father, a captain of volunteers in the Civil War. Thirty-six chapters follow Zelda from her return home to a crisis and a settling of accounts.

Kin say Zelda is like Margaret and really one of us, dark and self-possessed as Margaret was in girlhood. Contents name Ezra Dameron, the Merriams, and the Balcombs, with money pleas, overheard talk, and a rehearsal of a play. River roads, the Patoka Flats, and Seminary Square ground an Indiana tale of family duty, debt, and love.
65638-the-principles-of-the-art-of-conve:
The Principles of the Art of Conversation, a short treatise by J P Mahaffy, was published by Macmillan of London and New York in 1887. Mahaffy dedicates the book, with a smile, to my silent friends. An analysis at the front maps the whole argument in brief. Talk, he holds, is universal and necessary, and yet an art that must seem no art at all.

The manner of talk comes first: a sweet tone of voice, no local accent, no tricks or catchwords. Knowledge, quickness, modesty, simplicity, unselfishness, sympathy, and tact are the mental and moral conditions. The hearers matter too, in number, rank, age, sex, and degree of intimacy. The matter of talk, its topics, fills the second part. Mahaffy argues that the rules are obvious, yet only natural gifts can apply them with skill.
65705-forest-trees-of-illinois-third-edi:
Forest Trees of Illinois, third edition, by Robert Mohlenbrock of the botany department at Southern Illinois University, was issued by the Illinois Department of Conservation's Division of Forestry. Photography is by Richardson and Mohlenbrock, and illustrations by Meyer and Burton.

The book opens with an illustrated glossary of the leaf and twig characters by which one tree is known from another. Dichotomous keys follow, one for spring, summer, and fall and a separate one for winter, leading the user through paired choices to the specimen in hand. The trees of Illinois then fill nearly three hundred pages. Closers include special places to study trees, the white oak as state tree, big tree champions, and an index of common and scientific names.
65779-charles-darwin-and-the-theory-of-n:
Edward Poulton, professor of zoology at Oxford, wrote the life and work of Charles Darwin for the Century Science Series. Sir Henry Roscoe shaped the series, which also holds lives of Dalton, Lyell, Maxwell, Davy, and the Herschels. Poulton's book treats Darwin's thought of natural selection, the plan by which he held that new kinds of living things arise from old ones through the slow sifting of small changes.

The series aimed to tell the tale of modern science through the men who made it, one life at a time. Poulton was well placed for the task: he held the Oxford chair in zoology and worked on the very questions Darwin raised. The book gives a clear, short account of Darwin's life and of how his great claim grew, suited to a reader meeting the subject for the first time.
65806-christmas-at-monticello-with-thoma:
Christmas at Monticello with Thomas Jefferson is a tale by Helen Topping Miller, out in nineteen fifty-nine. Miller wrote a row of like feast tales past great homes of the past. The tale opens in the chief town in March of eighteen nine, at the ball of the new chiefs swear in. Jefferson climbs the long curve of stairs of the great house and knows he is now an old man.

He was past sixty-six, his red hair but paled, his knees sore from miles in the sad and from long hours at his desk. Past him the crowd still danced, led by the bright wife of the new chief in white cloth and a vast head wrap. He was glad to have seen his friend take the post, and more glad that his own years of work were done. No third term, he had told them.
65838-final-examination:
Final Examination is a science fiction story by Robert Sheckley, from Imagination of May 1952. A deck line asks what you would do if the stars were vanishing by millions. Five days to prepare for your judgment is the time the tale allows mankind. The narrator supposes it started long back, perhaps thousands of years before notice.

He first knew of it one March evening, opening his newspaper after supper at home. Jane was in the kitchen while he skimmed war talk, price controls, and murders. One small article in the back of the paper caught his eye that night. Sheckley dry wit turns the end of the world into a quiet joke.
66005-children-of-the-chronotron:
Children of the Chronotron is a science fiction story by Byrne, printed in a magazine of science and fantasy in December 1952. Its head note gives the premise in three lines. Facing ruin, Earth's last deathless men sent a messenger through time to change history. Thus he appeared in 1952, searching for the children of the title.

The opening, set in words apart, tells a far future tale. The Xlarnans, as their sun waned, first fled underground to hoard the heat their engines could supply. As their world grew colder over the centuries, they built a shield for the sky itself. A layer of glowing gases would warm them, give them lasting light, and soak up its own hard rays. So sealed off, they came up again into a warm paradise of their own making.
66036-the-etchings-of-charles-meryon:
Campbell Dodgson, keeper of prints and drawings at the British Museum, wrote this art book, The Etchings of Charles Meryon, edited by Holme and printed at London in 1921. Contents divide the work into short studies: an introduction, the early life, and the early etchings. The etchings of Paris follow, then other etchings of the fifties and the late etchings. A list of the etchings themselves closes the book.

A list of plates reproduced names the Paris of the prints. A portrait of Meryon by a fellow artist stands first. Then come the title plate of the Paris set, an old gate of a palace of justice, and the arms of the city of Paris. The gargoyle called the Stryge follows, with small and great bridges, a clock tower, streets and churches. Two states of one bridge plate are shown side by side for comparison.
66142-preferred-position:
Dave Dryfoos published 'Preferred Position' in Imagination in April 1953, and its blurb asks bored workers to meet a man from the future who would gladly trade places. The story opens as a talking bed wakes Les and Janet and lets their mattress drift to the floor. A marionette doll minces in with coffee at the mere mention of the word, and Janet is long past being amused by the dance.

Les is sixty and Janet fifty-five, and both are crushed by having nothing to do. Les faces sixty-five more years of doctor-guaranteed life without illness, want, or risk, and Janet seventy, with five years still to wait before her first child. She warns that sleeping on could get them accused of a hunger strike and enslaved, and Les answers that slavery would at least be a change.
66153-the-neptunian-or-water-theory-of-c:
The Reverend J M Woodman, professor of natural science at Chico Academy in California, set out The Neptunian or Water Theory of Creation at San Francisco in 1888. He had also written God in Nature and Revelation and The Song of Cosmology. His text at the head runs: if they speak not according to thy word, there is no truth in them. The first chapter reviews three theories of creation in the light of admitted facts.

Against the Plutonic or fire theory, Woodman argues that heat in mine shafts comes from chemical action, and that the layered nature of the oldest granite kills the fire account. His own theory holds that all matter was made at once in cold gas and that water raised the mountains. The book weds Genesis to geology on the side of water.
66228-unnoticed-london:
Unnoticed London, by Montizambert, was published at London in 1923 by Dent. Twenty four illustrations go with the walks in the first edition of 1922. A plate of Cheyne Row stands at the front of the little guide. Chelsea opens the contents at page one of the book.

The Chelsea of Sir Thomas More, Crosby Hall, and Cheyne Walk fill that chapter summary. Sandford Manor, Chelsea Hospital, and the Physic Garden follow in the same heads. Ranelagh closes the Chelsea list in the contents of chapter one. Knightsbridge to Soho and Trafalgar Square to Fleet Street carry the walks onward. Round about the Tower brings Roman baths and London stone in chapter four. Quiet corners of a loud city get a lover guide in these pages.
66358-rasputin-and-the-russian-revolutio:
Princess Catherine Radziwill wrote on Rasputin and the Russian revolution, published at New York and London in 1918 under the copyrights of 1917 and 1918. A photograph of Gregory Rasputin, captioned the Black Monk of Russia, fronts the volume. A publisher's foreword explains her pen name: her earlier court book had appeared as the posthumous memoirs of a Count Paul Vassili.

Living in Russia while the Romanoffs reigned, she could not own her work without risking Siberia, the foreword says. So the count was reported dead, while she went on collecting information and consigning it to a diary. A dedication letter thanks the Paris editor who first encouraged her to write. Court gossip hardened into revolution history is the ware.
66371-inside-the-russian-revolution:
Inside the Russian Revolution is a true tale of the great change in Russia by Dorr, a news hand who was there. Prints fill its form, put out at New York in the fall of the year of the change. Its rights were held that year by a news sheet and by its book house.

A front print shows the small grand mum of the change, a famed old ward of the Tsars jails come home. Its tale is of the months when the old realm fell: crowds in the streets, the new rule of the folk, and the women who marched for bread and peace. A womans eye at the heart of it is its stamp.
66441-reputation:
Tuttle wrote this Western story, Reputation, about a killer known only by the fear his name carries. The narrator lives at Santa Ynez, a small mission village near the Mexican border. Riders stopping at the little cantina tell, over tequila or warm beer, of new deviltry done by Jeff Tigard, called El Tigre, the Tiger.

Felipe, who draws the beer, trembles at the name, and the others laugh at him. Tales of the Tiger come closer to Santa Ynez all the time, Felipe warns, and some day he will come. Ramon jokes that the Tiger strings the ears of his victims on a gold thread. Mendez answers hotly that one man is mortal, and mortal man dies, when he is killed.
66453-corporal-jacques-of-the-foreign-le:
Corporal Jacques of the Foreign Legion is a tale of the French Foreign Legion by H de Vere Stacpoole. Stacpoole also wrote The Pearl Fishers. A marching song in verse stands at the front of the book.

The book opens with a letter from a real soldier of the Legion. He wrote to say that one man at least had escaped its ranks. His flight took two years across the Sahara with a band of Touaregs. That stark letter sets the tone for the tale. Desert marches, harsh sun and iron discipline shape the life it describes. Stacpoole knew the Legion's lore and used it with skill.
66455-the-lords-of-high-decision:
The Lords of High Decision, a novel by Meredith Nicholson, came out at New York in 1909, with pictures by Arthur I Keller. Nicholson had written The House of a Thousand Candles and The Port of Missing Men. A verse from the Book of Daniel, on a realm strong as iron yet part clay, heads the book.

Forty chapters follow Wayne Craighill, his sister, and Jean Morley in an iron city. Signs in the contents point to great mills, a club called the Allequippa, and rich men who rule work and town. Love, pride, and money pull the young pair apart and back. Readers get a big city tale of steel wealth, family power, and a hard choice of the heart.
66482-highways-and-highway-transportatio:
Highways and Highway Transportation, by George Chatburn, came out in 1923. Crowell published the textbook at New York. Chatburn taught applied mechanics at the University of Nebraska. He lectured there on highway engineering as well. A plate of the Storm King Highway fronts the book. That road runs along the Hudson between Cornwall and West Point. Chapter one calls transport a measure of civilization. Stages of society are traced from taking wild food to the railway age. Rome's roads and early American highways close the survey. Chapter two turns to the United States alone. Settlement hugged the waterways first, Chatburn writes.

Trails through the Alleghanies, Boone's Trace, and the western roads follow. The Cumberland Road shows the nation itself at work. Canals fill chapter three, ending with Panama and the French attempt there.
66498-the-boy-and-the-baron:
The Boy and the Baron, by Adeline Knapp, is a boys' tale in the Saint Nicholas Books set, copyrighted in 1901 and published in New York in October 1902. Fifteen chapters follow a lad named Wulf in a land of castles, armorers, and outlawed lords. Chapter heads are told in an old, storybook style.

Wulf starts at Karl the Armorer's hut, where a shining knight's treasure is found among the reeds. He climbs an ivy tower, frees a maiden ward named Elise from the Swartzburg, meets the emperor in a forest, and saves the day in a great battle. Baron Everhardt's fall and a lost baby add stakes. Knights dash at each other in the front plate, setting the brave mood.
66577-we-were-there-at-the-normandy-inva:
We Were There at the Normandy Invasion, written and drawn by Clayton Knight, was published in New York in 1956. A retired air force general served as history adviser. The story for young readers follows French boys and an American paratrooper in June 1944, in and near Sainte Mere Eglise.

Chapters move from house-to-house searches and a midnight landing to prisoners, tanks, and the fight for Saint Sauveur. Names in the contents include Andre, Victor, Father Duprey, Marie, and Slim of the 82nd Airborne. A secret tunnel, a lost pilot, and Bastille Day 1944 add pace. The book blends fact-based war action with a clear, brave view of the invasion for children.
66610-practical-agitation:
A book of political essays by John Jay Chapman. Charles Scribner's Sons published it at New York in 1900. Chapman dedicates it to the memory of Theodore Bacon. Seven chapters move from election time to conclusions. Between-elections work, the masses, literature, and principles fill the middle. The argument begins with the agitator's ambition.

That ambition, Chapman says, is moral. The agitator uses government's machinery to make men more unselfish. Success would build a living church inside the state. Campaign platforms, he argues, are merely creeds. Civil service reform meant, at bottom, I do not believe in theft. Thirty years of quiet revolution had raised public standards. Evils seemed worse only because standards rose faster. Chapman wrote as a patrician reformer of the mugwump stamp.
66617-lord-alistair-s-rebellion:
Allen Upward writes a political romance in Lord Alistair's Rebellion, printed in New York in 1910. Kennerley made the book. A motto at the front sorts one stuff by place: scum in the pot, foam in the sea, light in the sky.

Twenty three chapters run from Westminster Bridge to high treason. A family council, a cooperage, and the whole duty of woman stand in the early run. A legitimist demonstration and a pretender raise the royal theme. The powers that be, royal patronage, and virtue triumphant build the clash. The tale opens on the Thames at night, with tugs that drag barges through gold hoops of bridge light.
6663-country-life-in-canada-fifty-years-:
Canniff Haight, looking back as a man past sixty, recalls country life in Canada fifty years before his writing. Haight dedicates the book to the young men of Canada. Their honor and energy will shape their great heritage, he says. The book opens with a preface in which Haight steps to the footlights to state his aim. He writes as one who lived the days he paints.

Farm, town, and home life in old Ontario fill the pages, with the warmth of a man who would be a boy again. Haight quotes Childe Harold on happy years, and his tone stays fond throughout. Country Life in Canada Fifty Years Ago is a pleasant, personal memoir of a vanished rural world.
66667-penmanship-teaching-and-supervisio:
Penmanship, Teaching and Supervision, is a school method book by Leta Severance Hiles, copyrighted in 1924. Hiles was supervisor of penmanship at Long Beach, California, when she wrote it. Jesse Ray Miller of Los Angeles printed and published the course in April 1924. Contents open with the penmanship problem, its commercial and educational factors weighed.

Fundamentals follow: correct posture, correct movement, and visualization of letter forms in the mind. Practice and the application of correct habits to daily requirements fill the second chapter. The generally accepted solution, muscular movement, heads the third chapter of the course. Handwriting supervisors gained a full system in this normal school text.
66671-mr-clutterbuck-s-election:
Mr Clutterbuck's Election is a novel by H Belloc, as its title page names him. The hosted opening carries a publisher's list of new six shilling novels, with press praise for its companions. A Times quote calls one of them a document of the hour. Belloc's tale takes its own hour, an English election, for its ground.

A candidate named Clutterbuck, money, newspapers, and the machinery of a modern campaign drive the plot in Belloc's satirical manner. Belloc wrote history, verse, and fierce essays beside his novels, always with a polemical edge. Elections as bought theatre are his target here. The ads around the text show the Edwardian fiction market that carried such satire.
6668-annette-the-metis-spy-a-heroine-of-:
Edmund Collins tells of Annette, a Métis maiden who becomes a heroine of the North-West Rebellion. The chapters open as a chief falls in love with the half-breed maiden, then follow Annette's brave resolve, her lover in danger, and divers adventures on the prairie. A daring escape, a fight, a capture, and a guardian swan all lie ahead.

The tale opens at sunset, with two riders hurrying ponies along a blind trail toward purple hills. Collins writes in the bold, romantic style of his day, with the prairie itself as a stage. Annette, the Métis Spy, is a stirring, old-style adventure of love and courage in a troubled Canadian west.
66729-pneumonia-its-care-and-prevention:
Pneumonia: Its Care and Prevention is a health pamphlet issued in 1940 by the John Hancock Mutual Life Insurance Company of Boston. It came from the company's Life Conservation Service. An urgent message heads the pamphlet. If you suspect pneumonia in your family, it says, call your doctor without a moment's delay.

Hours count, because newly introduced drugs can cure pneumonia when treatment starts early. The pamphlet explains what the disease is, the medical treatment and nursing care it needs, and the ways to prevent it. Pneumonia is an inflammation of the lungs, and it stayed among the most common causes of death despite new progress. Such pamphlets were insurers' tools for keeping policyholders alive.
66744-the-life-of-the-scorpion:
Henri Fabre wrote a life of the scorpion, here in English in a New York edition of 1923. He opens by noting that the creature's build is well known from dissection, while its private habits are hardly known at all. Yet no segmented animal, he says, more deserves a full account of its life.

Fabre met the Languedoc scorpion fifty years before, under stones in the Villeneuve hills near Avignon. Chapters treat its dwelling, its food, and its poison, then its mating and its young. Later chapters turn to other small creatures, among them the masked bug and the terebinth louse. Patient watching, not the knife, is his method.
66745-belshazzar-a-tale-of-the-fall-of-b:
Belshazzar, a Tale of the Fall of Babylon, is a historical novel by William Stearns Davis. Doubleday, Page published it in New York in 1902. Zigler drew the illustrations. Twenty-seven chapters carry the story. The contents move from Babylon the Great to a closing cry. Bel is dead, the last chapter announces.

The tale weaves scripture into its plot. Ruth and Daniel both appear as characters. Cyrus enters late as father of the people. Temples of Nabu and Bel host the religious struggle. A wise man named Gudea prospers midway. The first chapter opens on the Euphrates in spring. A bireme speeds down the tawny current. Phoenician oarsmen bend to the double tier. A flute-player on the prow pipes them faster.
66756-dalrymple-s-equation:
Paul Fairman wrote Dalrymple's Equation, a science fiction mystery printed in Imagination in June 1956. The blurb promises screwy people in police work: a man pops up in a murder case and offers to solve it with an equation. The narrator is Kennedy, a homicide detective working with Donovan.

He opens by saying the not knowing is what gets you. Someday the case may be solved, and they will know whether they were suckered, or let the biggest thing since fingerprints slide by. The case began with a crazy murder in a bar on Tenth Avenue. A young man lay with his head on the bar, dead, as if sleeping off one drink too many. The barkeep swore he knew nothing. Fairman mixes the police procedural with a touch of the uncanny.
66806-the-young-continentals-at-trenton:
John McIntyre wrote a boys' tale of the war of freedom, printed at Philadelphia in 1911 with drawings by Ralph Boyer. Two earlier books sent the same lads to Lexington and Bunker Hill. Contents open with merchant Dana boarding the Nancy Breen. George Prentiss then meets a rough welcome in New York town.

A bully at an inn changes his mind, and General Putnam has his say. Peggy gives a warning, Washington comes to New York, and British ships enter the bay. The battle of Long Island is fought in the tale. Two patriots reach Trenton as Colonel Rahl plans a Christmas concert. The concert is broken in the last chapter, as heads promise.
66807-on-the-border-with-andrew-jackson:
John McIntyre wrote On the Border with Andrew Jackson, put out by Penn at Philadelphia in 1915. Anderson drew the plates for the book. It opens in the Creek country, in green woods of what is now Alabama. A young Cherokee brave, Running Elk, picks a camp by a stream. His white friends, Jack Davis and Frank Lawrence, agree to pitch there for the night. From the first, the tale moves among settlers, trappers, and Native foes.

Chapters bring Tecumseh, an attack by Indians, and the onslaught at Fort Mims. Old Hickory, Jackson himself, then takes the stage. Blows at Tallushatchee, capture by the Creeks, and the battle of the Horseshoe follow. A last chapter gives the life of Andrew Jackson in brief. Young readers get border war, scouts, and a famed chief in one brisk tale.
66812-the-lake-regions-of-central-africa:
The Lake Regions of Central Africa is a travel book by Richard Burton, of which this is the first part. It came out at London in eighteen sixty. Burton was a chief of the host in India and a star of the guild of earth lore. The book is writ with love to his sister.

Burton meant the tale to come out at once past his come back in May of the past year. Ill health, low heart, and the vex of state mails held it back, he owns. A guild print gave the bare earth facts first. In this book he blends those facts with the tale of deeds and the bright points of the road. His house had urged strong meat past his wish for a light work, so gay and grave stand side by side.
66813-the-lake-regions-of-central-africa:
The Lake Regions of Central Africa, volume two, is an exploration narrative by Richard Burton. Longman issued the London edition in 1860. Burton was a captain in the Indian army. He was also a fellow of the Royal Geographical Society. A plate of the navigation of Lake Tanganyika fronts the volume. The second volume begins at chapter twelve.

Its chapters cover Unyamwezi, its land and peoples. Then the party sights Lake Tanganyika at last. They explore the lake and trace its full circuit. The return march leads back to the coast. Village life in East Africa fills a chapter. A closing chapter treats character, religion, and slavery. Appendices give trade figures and official letters. Burton's journey with Speke opened the lake country. This volume holds the second half of that record.
66816-automatic-finger-control-seventh-e:
Automatic Finger Control is a mail-order music method issued by the United States School of Music of New York, in its seventh edition of 1921. The school calls it a scientific method that gets at the foundation of musical skill. It promises to disclose the secrets that let a pupil learn any instrument easily and quickly.

The method was taught only by the school and could be used with any other course of lessons. Its preface stresses one habit above all: regular practice at a set hour. Pupils are told to work through the exercises night and morning. What is done just before sleep, the school argues, is best remembered, and morning practice clinches the gain. The book is a sample of the correspondence-school boom in American music teaching.
66848-engravers-and-etchers-six-lectures:
Engravers and Etchers gathers six lectures by Fitzroy Carrington, given on the Scammon foundation at the Art Institute of Chicago in March 1916. Carrington was curator of prints at the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston. He also lectured on engraving at Harvard and edited a print collector's quarterly. The book carries one hundred and thirty three illustrations.

The lectures begin with German engraving from its start to Martin Schongauer. Italian engraving of the Florentines comes next. A third lecture joins the Master of the Amsterdam Cabinet with Albrecht Durer. Then the line runs from Mantegna to Marcantonio Raimondi. Later talks treat masters of portraiture and the etching of landscape. The Scammon lectures were endowed by Maria Sheldon Scammon for talks on the fine arts. Carrington's series gives a clear, learned tour of print making's great ages for collectors and students.
66895-our-show-a-humorous-account-of-the:
Our Show, a humorous account of the International Exposition at Philadelphia, came out for the centennial year of 1876 from Claxton, Remsen and Haffelfinger. The cover plays on the dates 1776 and 1876, one hundred years a republic. Mock press notices at the front set the comic tone, with fake praise and fake scorn side by side.

Two guides, Daisy Shortcut and Arry O'Pagus, lead the fun. The notices joke that the fun is harder to find than Livingstone was, and that no library is complete without the book in its waste basket. Pictures credited to Jacques Frost go with the text. The book rides the wave of print spun off by the great fair.
66915-the-spring-of-a-lion:
Rider Haggard issued this Allan Quatermain tale in a New York booklet series in June 1899. The frame is a Yorkshire evening after dinner, when Quatermain, the old hunter, grows talkative over his port. The narrator had been his guest, and Captain Good sat with them as the story came out.

Quatermain tells of his hunting years in South Africa, among hunters, transport riders, and hard drinkers whose ways taught him to hate drink itself. The tale looks back from his quiet English home to the wild life that made his name. It appeared just as Haggard sent his hero off in print toward a last, lost quest in the heart of Africa.
66987-life-of-frances-power-cobbe-as-tol:
Life of Frances Power Cobbe is the life of that writer as told by herself, with additions by the author. It came out in London in 1904 from Swan Sonnenschein and Company. A portrait of Cobbe from 1894 stands at its front. The opening essay states the shape of the book. The story of the fine life that ended on 5 April 1904 is told by Cobbe herself, it says, up to the close of 1898.

Nothing is left for another pen, the essay holds, but to sketch in the events of the few years that remained. It then gives the rise of the book. One spring day in 1891 or 1892, the writer recalls, Cobbe walked with her through the Hengwrt grounds on the way to the station. After hours of her bright tales, the writer asked if she would one day write the tale of her own life.
6699-inns-and-taverns-of-old-london:
Henry Shelley sets forth the historical and literary ties of old London's inns, taverns, coffee-houses, clubs, and pleasure gardens. His preface notes a puzzle: Teutonic folk are said to love home above all, yet Londoners of the sixteenth, seventeenth, and eighteenth centuries poured zeal into substitutes for home. Those substitutes fill these pages.

From ancient hostelries to famed coffee-houses where writers, wits, and plotters met, Shelley traces who drank, talked, and schemed where. The book, dated 1909, reads as a walking tour through literary London. Inns and Taverns of Old London is a rich, anecdotal guide for lovers of the city and its books.
67004-the-young-continentals-at-lexingto:
John McIntyre wrote a boys' war tale printed at Philadelphia in 1909, with drawings by Ralph Boyer. His With John Paul Jones is named as his on the title page. A broad shouldered youth of seventeen stands at the front. Twenty two chapters carry the book, told in the old shows how style.

Ben Cooper sees the war from far off to open. Nat Brewster walks to Cliveden in the dark and meets Grumpy Comegies. Startling news waits at Chew House. Nat meets Mister Washington and rides through the night with the Porcupine. Doctor Warren and Paul Revere hear him out. The close brings Nat taken by foes, Revere's midnight ride, and the march to Lexington.
67011-a-poem-on-the-earthquake-at-lisbon:
An unnamed poet set down A Poem on the Earthquake at Lisbon in verse, printed at London in 1755 for W Owen near Temple-Bar and sold at sixpence. The poem opens on a calm sky and a sun over the sea, with breezes in the orange groves and the silver Tagus smooth below the town. Gay crowds stray in the streets on the feast day. Mechanics earn their bread and misers count their store.

A youth sits by his bride-to-be while a train of girls makes ready the clothes for the wedding day. Then the matin bell rings, the pious matron kneels in the house of God, and fate comes like a thief in the night, with no warning voice. The poem treats the great quake that struck Lisbon that year, asking what such ruin means for man's pride and faith.
67018-in-the-rockies-with-kit-carson:
John McIntyre's boys' adventure, published by the Penn Publishing Company of Philadelphia in 1913, sends two lads into the Rockies at Kit Carson's side. Ralph Boyer and Edwin Kromer drew the pictures, one showing a trapper's cry of warning as frontispiece.

The chapters run from The Trapper of Taos and Santa Fé and Around the Camp-Fire to Indian signs, two nights of danger, and a desperate brush with grizzlies. The Village of the Blackfeet and The Last Battle close the tale, with a sketch of Carson's life at the end. The story opens at the Pueblo of Los Angeles, where two bronzed boys ride in on a tall Spanish mule, each with a long-barreled rifle. They tell the sentry they belong to the trading schooner Gadfly and hunt Lopez, a deserter who robbed them and swam ashore.
67021-the-sabbath-a-sermon:
William Wood, rector of Coulsdon and vicar of Fulham, printed a sermon on the Sabbath at London in 1831. It was meant for the afternoon of October 23 in his own church. Bad weather kept him from preaching it, so he put it in print for his flock. His text is the command to remember the Sabbath day and keep it holy.

In a plain note Wood owns the sermon makes no claim to merit. Thousands like it are preached each week, he says. He had seen slack worship in his quiet parish. It sprang not from unbelief or vice, as in great towns, but from plain lack of knowledge. The sermon was printed to teach his own people first.
67039-mind-and-hand-manual-training-the-:
Mind and Hand, by Charles Ham, argues for manual training. The American Book Company issued this third edition. Its first form appeared in 1886 under a longer title. Manual training, that title claimed, solves social and industrial problems. The preface answers thirteen years of reviews. Schools of the old kind met his chief claims with strong dissent. His reading of Greek history drew the sharpest fire. Ham replies with fresh notes and old authorities. Herodotus, Thucydides, and Plutarch are cited in his support. The Greeks were no ideal people, he insists. A passion for Greek models in schooling is, to him, a moral crime.

Footnotes carry the authorities this time. An appendix tables the facts of physical progress. Ham writes as a reformer sure of his ground.
67141-corea-the-hermit-nation:
William Elliot Griffis wrote Corea, the Hermit Nation, a full account of Korea in three parts. Charles Scribner’s Sons issued the ninth edition in New York in nineteen hundred eleven. Griffis had taught at the Imperial University in Tokio. The book had served as a handbook for near thirty years by then.

Ancient and medieval Corea fills the first of the three parts. Court, town, and home life fill the second at length. The third brings the tale to Griffis’s own day. Japan took Corea as a province in nineteen hundred ten. A last chapter, Cho-sen: A Province of Japan, weighs that change. Twelve million Koreans saw their crown fall in that span. Griffis aims to judge the acts fair, not to praise one side.
67153-the-fourth-dimension:
Fourth Dimension is a book by Hinton on higher space for general readers. Press notices quoted in front praise his aim to avoid mathematical subtleties in the argument. Readers not conversant with mathematics should be able to follow his reasoning, one says. A Notts Guardian notice calls the fourth dimension a subject of great fascination for teachers.

Much of the text discusses illustrations that are not included in this file, readers are warned. Hinton cubes, shadows, and analogies lead the mind from flatland toward fourfold space. His work fed both geometry talk and the mystic fourth dimension craze of the age. Curious readers gain the classic popular door into higher dimensions.
67168-the-chinese-dragon:
Newton Hayes wrote a study of the Chinese dragon, in a third edition published by the Commercial Press at Shanghai in 1923, with an introduction by a Chinese scholar. Its first chapter asserts the premise flatly: there are real dragons living in China to-day, friendly creatures highly revered, in the belief of at least seven out of every ten Chinese.

Nine chapters treat the dragon's place in Chinese life, the origin of the idea, its varieties, its true looks, and people who have seen dragons. Western mythology, quaint beliefs, and the dragon's hold on men's fortunes follow. The illustrations crowd thrones, screens, staircases, and robes of the Kang Hsi period. Sympathetic folklore from inside the belief is the aim.
67293-the-sixth-marine-division:
James R Stockman, a Marine captain, wrote the history of the Sixth Marine Division. The Historical Division at Headquarters, United States Marine Corps, made the work. Maps show the division's movements and its Okinawa ground. The division stood up on September 7, 1944, on Guadalcanal.

Major General Lemuel C Shepherd led the new division into the war. Its regiments, the Fourth and Twenty Second Marines, came from the Guam brigade. The maps mark the ground won on Okinawa from April 1 to June 21. Service readers gain the official tale of the last Marine division raised.
67308-the-river-of-london:
The River of London, by Hilaire Belloc, author of The Path to Rome, was published in London and Edinburgh in December 1912 by Foulis. Five chapters run from an introduction through the approach up river. They treat London as the first crossing of the Thames, and London as the port of the Thames. The lower Thames in warfare closes the set. Plates after paintings by John Muirhead show the river from Pangbourne to Erith.

Belloc opens on the intimate bond between city and river, felt by instinct. The Thames, he argues, is all that every other river is to every other capital, and more. Paris draws little sea traffic by the Seine; the Tiber could never be a street for Rome; Vienna neglects the Danube. London alone unites every function of a great stream in one city. The front plate shows Saint Paul's from Blackfriars.
67326-the-a-b-z-of-our-own-nutrition:
The A B-Z of Our Own Nutrition is a book on food and health by Horace Fletcher. It was put out at New York in nineteen hundred and three. Two men of the heal craft gave their aid in its tests. One is of a great town of Italy. One is of a great school town of England. The book went through print on print in its first two years.

The same hand's past books are list at the front. They treat true life, the new glut ton, and joy past fear thought. The list of parts of this book starts with first words and a late add. Then comes a first drill in the theme. A set of keen doubts and asks comes next.
6734-drusilla-with-a-million:
Elizabeth Cooper opens with a call down a sunny line of old ladies: Drusilla Doane, O Drusilla Doane. A little old woman, birdlike in glance, brings word that two men wait in the parlor to see Drusilla, and the darning of a tablecloth stops as all stare. Drusilla, white-haired and expectant, answers that she is here.

From that homely start grows a tale of a plain old woman who comes into a million, and of the kin, suitors, and schemers who follow the money. Cooper writes with humor and warmth, in a voice close to small-town talk. Drusilla with a Million is a gentle, funny novel of wealth, worth, and a late chance at life.
67429-the-thing-beyond-reason:
Elisabeth Sanxay Holding wrote this short novel of mystery, billed as the strange adventure that led Lexy Moran to a house of tragedy and mystery in the suburbs of New York. Holding was also the author of Angelica and other novels.

The story opens on a quiet night with Alexandra Moran bent over a crossword puzzle, chewing a damaged pencil and refusing to give up on a word. That stubborn, careful temper is the point of the scene: whatever she undertakes, she does thoroughly. Readers get a character study that turns into a mystery, led by a heroine whose persistence drives the plot.
67465-poultry-diseases-causes-symptoms-a:
Poultry Diseases, causes, symptoms and treatment, with notes on post mortem examinations, by E J Wortley, was printed in New York by the Orange Judd Company in 1915, with a London house. A plate is captioned Profit or Loss. The book is a working manual for the poultry keeper.

Chapter one treats general methods of controlling disease. It weighs the importance of control, the dangers of introducing disease, and control measures. Nursing sick birds, the use of drugs and medicines, and disinfection follow. Chapter two sums external symptoms and treatment, for diseases of the head and breath organs, of digestion and reproduction, and of legs and feet. The text opens by saying the ravages of disease add greatly to the difficulties of raising poultry in all parts of the world. Farm readers get a 1915 sick bird handbook.
67471-the-invention-of-typography-a-brie:
The Invention of Typography, by Frederick W Hamilton, is a short history of how printing began, written for apprentices in the printing trade. It came out in Chicago in 1918 as number fifty in the Typographic Technical Series for Apprentices.

Hamilton first paints the world of books in the middle of the fifteenth century, when copies were still made by hand as they had been for two thousand years. Chapters then follow the steps toward movable type and the rival claims to the honour of the invention. A further chapter describes the invention itself, and a last one the materials and methods of the first printers. Lists of further reading and review questions close the manual, since it was made for study in trade classes.
67518-the-art-of-home-furnishing-and-dec:
The Art of Home Furnishing and Decoration, by Frank Alvah Parsons, came out in a second edition in 1921. The Armstrong Cork Company issued it from Lancaster, Pennsylvania. Parsons led the New York School of Fine and Applied Art. A foreword by the firm calls him a top American voice on decoration. His rule stands at the head of his text: man is what he lives in. Surroundings, he argues, shape the person day by day.

Parsons treats taste, colour, and arrangement for the whole home. The firm's own later section takes up linoleum in that light. Pictures and plain talk aim at home makers, not experts. The book mixes high ideals of beauty with a maker's interest in floors that sell.
67621-hilda-s-home-a-story-of-woman-s-em:
Rosa Graul wrote Hilda's Home, a story of woman's emancipation printed at Chicago in 1899. A publisher's preface sets out the book's gospel. The ideal, it says, precedes the actual, and the ascent of life is the ascent of ideals. Graul preaches discontent: dissatisfaction with the old, desire for the new. Contentment means inaction, and all great achievements spring from life's unrest.

Freedom is the second gospel of the book. With Spencer, Graul holds that everyone may do as he pleases so long as he does not invade the equal right of others. The cure for the evils of liberty is more liberty. Much space goes to rebuilding industry. The central aim, the preface states, is the freeing of womanhood and motherhood from the rule of man. Self-ownership of woman is the thought that runs through all.
67655-jason-son-of-jason:
Giesy wrote a tale of a man who dies and lives again, told by the head of a home for the insane. Patient number 27 dies at midnight, just as he said he would. The teller had known him before in a past life as Jason Croft.

Croft had told of trips to Palos, a world that circles the Dog Star Sirius, first in spirit and then in flesh. In a new body he came back, took up his tale where he left off, and showed how he had turned the trick back. Death here is a husk cast off, and the son of Jason holds the key to two worlds.
67744-the-silver-stallion-a-comedy-of-re:
The Silver Stallion is a novel by James Branch Cabell, issued in 1926. McBride of New York published it. Its subtitle calls it a comedy of redemption. A list of Cabell's many books opens the volume. Jurgen, Domnei, and Figures of Earth stand there. The motto comes from Doctor Johnson's Rasselas. Kalki will come as a silver stallion, it says. At his coming all evils will perish.

True right will be restored to the world. Men's minds will be made clear as crystal. The dedication is to Carl Van Doren. Its verse asks why dreamers cannot rest. Cabell sets his tale in the dream land of Poictesme. Knights there seek a redeemer of their own making. The book ran through four printings in two months.
67745-yorktown-climax-of-the-revolution:
Charles Hatch and Thomas Pitkin edited Yorktown, Climax of the Revolution, a park source book. The Government Printing Office at Washington made it in 1941, and it was reprinted in 1956. It is number one in the National Park Service Source Book Series. The book tells of the Yorktown part of Colonial National Historical Park, in Virginia. That park joins Jamestown and Yorktown, and guards the scenic and historic heritage of the land.

Sixteen short parts trace the campaign from start to finish. Cornwallis comes to Yorktown, the French fleet shuts the Chesapeake, and the allies gather at Williamsburg. The siege, the parallels, the bombardment, and the storming of redoubts follow. Cornwallis tries to escape, then chooses to surrender, and Washington congratulates the army. A list of books closes the volume, sold at twenty cents a copy.
67872-peculiar-a-tale-of-the-great-trans:
Epes Sargent published the novel Peculiar in New York in 1864, while the Civil War was still being fought. The story is set in a nation split over slavery, and its forty-nine chapters move between New York rooms, Southern homes, and scenes shaped by the war. Chapter titles such as A Fugitive Chattel, The White Slave, and The Upper and the Lower Law show where the book's weight falls.

The opening chapter places a woman named Emily at a writing table in a small, faded room off Broadway, warned in the chapter motto not to wed for wealth without love. From there the contents promise heiresses, lawyers, a wedding in doubt, and a visit to the White House. Sargent builds a wide cast and a plot about money, rank, and bondage in a country on the edge of deep change.
67888-anticipation:
Anticipation is a political satire by Richard Tickell, reprinted at New York by King's Crown Press in 1942. The reprint follows the first edition of London, 1778. Butterfield supplies an introduction, notes, and a bibliography of Tickell's writings. A foreword by Randolph Adams of the Clements Library opens the volume.

The editor calls it the first reprint since 1822 of a politico-literary satire. It delighted a generation of readers during and after the American War of Independence. The text is followed literally from the first issue, except where later corrected editions mend it. Tickell wrote in the voice of a prophet of the opposition, foretelling the follies of the ministry as if they were already history. The 1942 reprint, made at minimum cost in wartime, rescued a minor classic of the pamphlet wars for scholars of the Revolution.
6806-the-hallam-succession:
Amelia Barr's Hallam Succession moves from Americans in Yorkshire and Martha Craven's trouble to Richard and Elizabeth, Wesley and Methodism, and Antony's plans. Christmas, renewal of a covenant, separation, and a return home follow, with Texas and liberty, a squire's death, Antony's sin, and Elizabeth's trial ahead. The tale ends in Texas, at the sunset of life.

Barr, author of Jan Vedder's Wife, writes a long family saga across England and the American southwest, with faith and love as its threads. Her tone is earnest and romantic. The Hallam Succession is a rich, old-style saga of two families, two lands, and a lasting covenant.
68062-the-play-that-won:
The Play That Won, a school story by Ralph Henry Barbour, was first issued in book form in 1919. Parts had run in magazines from 1916 on. Barbour wrote many sports tales for boys, in series set at Yardley Hall and Hilton. This book stands apart from those series. Its hero, Ted, plays at Warwick.

The tale opens on a Saturday night after a hard baseball game. Warwick beat Prospect Hill in the tenth inning. Ted rests at home with a magazine instead of going to a lecture. Chapter heads name Larry Logan, Terry, and Billy Mayes. One head is called The Quitter, another The Two Miler. Sport, school honor, and team play drive the plot.
68068-female-affection:
Basil Montagu published a short treatise on female affection at London in 1845, inscribed to his dear Edith from her affectionate grandfather. His preface lists the charges laid against the female mind: fondness for ornament, for gaiety, action from impulse rather than foresight, and variableness.

Women, he grants, are also fond of intellect, courage, and virtue, and capable of the most heroic acts. But on one property, he insists, no doubt can exist: it is the nature of woman to be affectionate. Bacon is quoted that for the pleasures of the affections we must resort to the poets. Montagu answers that facts around us tell it better, with female affection as the glaring instance.
68208-circle-of-confusion:
Wesley Long wrote a science fiction tale that ran in Astounding Science-Fiction in March 1944. Its Pluto is a world made fit for men by human work. Ships brought frozen gases from Umbriel to give the cold planet air to breathe. Towns then rose on ground that no life had marked before.

Uranium lies in the Styx Valley, across the Devil's Mountains from the River Styx. The ore must cross that range to reach the town of Mephisto. Long builds his setting from mining, haulage, and harsh cold. The tale shows how pulp writers of that era turned new finds in space into tales of work and risk.
68233-the-incredible-invasion:
George Smith wrote this tale of a United Nations weapon council in crisis. It ran in Astounding Science Fiction in March of 1948. Jim Franklen reads the door sign with a surface of pride. The sign names the United Nations Weapon Security Council in black.

Thomas Winter, its president, sits behind a desk of paper work. Trouble, Franklen, bad trouble, is his greeting at the door. The Central Power rattles the saber and makes demands still. Franklen notes they know they cannot win, yet grow bolder daily. Watchers crowd even the janitors coffee cups at dawn, Winter says, yet no dangerous motion shows.
68247-vocation:
George O Smith spins a tale of withheld knowledge in Vocation, printed in Astounding Science-Fiction in April 1945 with illustrations by Williams. Terran Andrew Tremaine visits Gerd Lel Rayne, a larger and better-proportioned man of a superior breed, and stifles his jealousy because he needs a favor. Gerd offers refreshment and asks whether the visit is business or personal.

Tremaine asks firsthand why Gerd's race denies Earth the secret of interstellar travel. Gerd answers that Terrans have not developed it yet and could not use it. He offers a case from a hundred years past, when solar phoenix power had only just freed Terra from wire and machinery.
68313-meddler-s-moon:
George Smith wrote a science fiction story that ran in Astounding in September 1947. Peter Hedgerly hears his door open and smiles at the mirror, sure his girl Joan Willson has come early. A deep, pleasant masculine rumble answers that it will sit down, but is not his honey.

The stranger is Peter's near double: a few pounds heavier, an inch taller, the same sandy blond looks, and a beatific smile. He knows Peter will not call the police, and says his presence will make no difference. Then Joan walks in on Peter in his shorts and brief shirt, and both men cry out. Comic confusion opens a tale of a meddling visitor.
68393-my-sweetheart-s-the-man-in-the-moo:
My Sweetheart's the Man in the Moon is a science fiction tale by Milton Lesser, printed in Infinity in December 1956. Pictures by Stallman go with it. The tale supposes the first flight to the moon, and watches it not from the ship but from a small house on Earth, through the eyes of the flyer's girl.

Jeanne turns off the radio and goes downstairs, where her mother, father, and Aunt Anna wait in strain. Tom has reached the moon, and the family hardly dared to listen. Talk turns on distance, pipes, and wasted oxygen, plain home talk against a vast deed. A note warns that profiteers like Lubrano saw the flight in colder terms.
6844-the-poetical-works-of-mrs-leprohon:
Mrs. Leprohon, born R. E. Mullins, sings in her poetical works as a brave pioneer of Canadian letters, giving her people her best in songs of duty, patriotism, and hope. Her introduction hopes that, when Canada's literature is written, room will be kept for pioneers who sang ere life in the young land ceased to be a struggle. Wealth and leisure, it says, will in time give writers an audience prepared by culture.

Leprohon's verse is earnest, patriotic, and domestic, with a love of home and country. The volume gathers her best lyrics in one place. The Poetical Works of Mrs. Leprohon is a warm, historic Canadian poetry book, worth a look for lovers of early Dominion verse.
68464-specifications-for-street-roadway-:
Specifications for Street Roadway Pavements, by Whinery, is an engineering rule book. McGraw Hill issued the second edition in nineteen thirteen, reset and enlarged. Whinery was a member of the American Society of Civil Engineers. The book pairs set contract terms with guidance for paving inspectors.

Part one lays out why broad specifications matter and how they should read. Fair terms for builders and towns, bid notices, and contract links are covered. The engineer is cast as arbiter when disputes arise on the work. Set sections then define the work, materials, and checks in full detail. Rules guard quality, safety, health, and public ease during street work.
68472-the-slave-auction:
The Slave-Auction is an anti-slavery pamphlet by Dr. John Theophilus Kramer, late of New Orleans, printed at Boston in 1859. Its preface calls the nineteenth century an enlightened age of great discoveries in science. Yet in one respect, Kramer says, civilization has stepped backward. The backward step is the institution of slavery, which he calls an institution of ancient barbarity.

Kramer asks how a white Christian can treat a Christian of colour like a beast. He asks how one man can have the right to sell his black or yellow brother or sister at public auction for money. His aim, he says, is not political. He tries to answer one question: can slavery and Christianity go together? The pamphlet argues from faith against the auction block. It speaks from a city, New Orleans, where such sales were a daily sight.
68492-the-story-of-iron:
Elizabeth Samuel wrote The Story of Iron for young readers, published in Philadelphia in 1920 with illustrations by Velma Simkins. Samuel had earlier written a companion story of gold and silver. The tale follows Billy Bradford through sixteen chapters that mix adventure with the working of iron.

Chapter titles move from Old Iron and A Mountain of Iron to The Foundry, Iron Horses, and The Giants. Scenes show men filling moulds with moist sand and polishing metal. Readers get a story that teaches how iron is dug, cast, and shaped by following one boy through mines, foundries, and rail yards of the period.
68520-the-van-roon:
J C Snaith published his novel The Van Roon with D Appleton and Company in 1922, in New York and London. Snaith also wrote The Sailor, The Undefeated, and The Council of Seven. The tale opens on a narrow street north of the Strand, east of the National Gallery.

Antique shops line the lane, where Swinburne once found a famous copy of The Faerie Queene. S Gedge keeps one shop, though Snaith jokes the sign should read Antique, not Antiques. Gedge himself looks like a true antique, seventy at least once dressed, with a yellow face full of cunning. Collectors, rare finds, and sly dealing set the scene for the plot to come.
68550-the-pearl-lagoon:
Charles Nordhoff wrote a South Seas tale for young readers, issued at Boston in 1924 and dated from Tahiti. He dedicates it to his parents, in hope their grandchildren will one day read it. The narrator, Charlie, grows up on the California coast, on a Spanish grant in the Santa Brigida Valley.

His adobe house, built before the Civil War, looks over salt marshes at the river's mouth. A schooner comes, and Charlie ships aboard the Tara for a pearl lagoon. Chapters bring the pearls of Iriatai, the end of a shark, and his own turn as a pearl diver. A cave of a shark god and an act of piracy raise the stakes.
68574-the-case-against-evolution:
George Barry O'Toole, a teacher of theology and of animal biology, set out the case against the theory of evolution in a book from Macmillan. New York printed it in 1925, with a fresh run in February 1926. A note added at the front shows the kind of proof he trusts. It cites fresh work on the sex chromosomes of mammals.

That work, O'Toole argues, bars the idea that new kinds arose by a doubling of the seed stock. He is hard, too, on the made up figures of early man built from scraps of bone. In his view such models dress guesswork in flesh and hair. The book joins church teaching to the science of its day. It asks readers to weigh how far the facts of life, as then known, can carry the claims made for change of kind over time.
68598-the-band-played-on:
C Shook wrote the tale The Band Played On. Astonishing Stories ran it in June 1942. A trombone man tells the story in first person. He plays in a five-piece combo at Benny's Bar. Benny's draws all the town's musicians, he says. Four of Bill Gundry's boys sit in that night.

Eddie Smith and Mart Allen join from The Pines band. Whiteman himself once dropped in, he recalls. The band plays its own charts early in the night. Past one, jamming takes over the room. Jazz Me Blues gets a fast Dixieland run. The player's horn trembles as he rides the beat. Stardust slows the set for his solo stand. Then the strange thing strikes mid-tune. A dance-band tale with a weird twist, the story swings from hot jazz into the uncanny.
68609-the-skylark-of-valeron:
Edward Smith wrote a space epic serialized in Astounding Stories from August 1934 to February 1935, illustrated by Elliot Dold. Its prologue is a frame: Richard Ballinger Seaton the fourteen hundred and seventy-first is a sturdy auburn-haired boy of twelve. He begs his mother to let him see the rest of the exploits of Seaton the First.

The boy recites the saga as a holiday showing tells it. Seaton One, a chemist of old Washington, discovered the metal Rovolon, which turned copper into energy. He built the first space ship with Martin Crane. The World Steel Corporation sent its chemist DuQuesne to steal the secret, and men died. Attractors, repellers, rays, and screens followed. A dynasty's founding legend opens the serial.
68610-love-s-labor-won:
Southworth's novel opens at the last reception in the old presidential mansion at Philadelphia, before General Washington retired from office. The beauty, talent, and fashion of the Republican Court are present, and all eyes turn to a lady at the harp. Marguerite De Lancie of Virginia is the improvisatrice, a dark and queenly beauty. The French ambassador and a young English lord, William, murmur their admiration.

Southworth, author of Ishmael and Self-Raised, was the most read American novelist of her day. Street and Smith reprinted the tale in their New Southworth Library for a new century of readers. The scene she chooses is deliberate: the young republic's court, with the heroes of the Revolution in the room, and a Virginia heroine at its center. Love's labor, the title promises, will be won in such company.
68630-the-lively-adventures-of-gavin-ham:
Molly Elliot Seawell wrote this tale for the young, printed by Harper and Brothers of New York and London with an 1899 copyright. H C Edwards drew the plates. Seawell had written The Rock of the Lion and A Virginia Cavalier. Her note vows that, as in all her tales for the young, few or no liberties have been taken with history and its order of events.

The front plate shows Gavin shouting that it is his turn now. Gavin throws away his trooper's sabre in another plate, and a king drags him from a hiding place in a third. The tale opens in a land wrecked by the armies of Maria Theresa and Frederick the Great in the autumn of 1757. There the houseless died by thousands of cold and hunger.
68640-the-chutney-lyrics-a-collection-of:
R C Caldwell wrote The Chutney Lyrics, comic verse on Indian themes. Higginbotham and Company issued this second edition at Madras in 1889. Caldwell was son of the missionary bishop of Tinnevelly. He trained for the ministry at Canterbury first. Field work in Trichinopoly and Tanjore followed. He left orders unclaimed and turned to journalism.

Caldwell wrote for the Daily News and the Athenaeum in England. Punch and the Illustrated London News took his work too. Some twelve lyrics first ran in a Madras paper. They brought him his first fame in India. He co-edited the Madras Times for a spell. A front plate shows a threat to smash a survey man's head. Anglo-Indian comic verse mocks the heat, the red tape, and the club talk of the Raj from inside.
68659-the-impossible-invention:
The Impossible Invention is a science fiction tale by Robert Moore Williams, printed in Astonishing Stories in June 1942. It opens at a stormy meeting of the Institute of Radio Engineers, where a small man named James Arthur Fradin faces a hall of angry scientists. Fradin carries a string of honorary degrees from half a dozen colleges, yet the hall gives him merry hell.

Voices shout that his claim is gross nonsense, absolutely impossible, and call him a faker. The narrator, a reporter sent down for a human interest yarn, sits back and grins at the prospect of a free fight. One tall, cadaverous man alone listens eagerly, without joining the name calling, and the narrator feels he ought to know that face.
68738-the-lanchester-tradition:
The Lanchester Tradition is a school novel by Bradby, first published in 1913 and reprinted by John Murray in 1919. The scene is Chiltern School, just outside the sleepy town of the same name. The school's motto is Providendo nec timendo, and its colors, cerise, orange, and green, are known across the Empire. The narrator insists the school is second to none in Chiltern opinion.

The fifteen chapters open with an election at the school. Flaggon pays a visit, Gussy departs, and a first skirmish follows. Later chapters bring the parents' committee, the Lanchester letters, an explosion, and a day of decision, with an aftermath to close.
68772-an-inaugural-dissertation-on-pulmo:
Edward Delafield wrote this inaugural dissertation on pulmonary consumption, printed in New York in 1816. Delafield dedicated the work to Samuel Borrowe, a surgeon of the New York Hospital, whose practical lessons he had received as a pupil. A medical dissertation of this kind marked the end of a young doctor's training. Its subject, consumption, was the great killer of the age.

Delafield begins by noting a revival of inquiry. The disease had long been thought beyond remedies and had nearly ceased to excite learned attention. New works and new remedies had lately changed that mood. Yet in New York the deaths from consumption were rising fast. The city's air had once been thought remarkably healthy, with few lung diseases. Delafield quotes older remarks on the climate to make the contrast. His dissertation surveys the disease's treatment at a hopeful moment.
68786-modern-bookbindings-their-design-a:
Modern Bookbindings, Their Design and Decoration, by Prideaux, surveys the craft of fine binding at its modern height. Dutton published it at New York in 1906. Three essays make the book: modern English binding, modern French binding, and edition binding. A front plate shows a book bound by Zaehnsdorf, the great London firm.

Dozens of plates follow, naming the binders one by one. Riviere, Morrell, de Coverly, Fazakerley, and Chivers show the English trade. The Guild of Handicraft and Douglas Cockerell speak for the arts and crafts side. French masters arrive with Marius Michel, Ruban, and Chambolle. Women binders hold their own plates: Miss Adams, Miss MacColl, Miss Pattinson, and others. Prideaux wrote as a historian of the craft. Her book is a gallery of leather, gold, and design from the years when binding was a living art.
6898-the-boys-of-columbia-high-on-the-gr:
Graham Forbes follows the Columbia High football boys in their struggle for the silver cup, opening with practice and a road to town. The chapters mix sport with school mystery, from the strange history of Ralph and treachery in camp to the abduction of Bones and a singing school night. Frank turns chauffeur, an unwilling pilot flies, and a great marsh hides dangers of its own.

Rivals from Clifford press hard, and the side faces a feared epidemic scare and a hard fought first half. The tale builds to a finish won by four inches, with a message from Tokio closing the book. Forbes writes for boys who love a game played hard and a team that holds together under strain.
69009-definition:
Damon Knight's Definition, printed in Startling Stories in February 1953, opens with a future dictionary entry: Man, noun, a pentagonal, dipolar, monoplane dominant, of intelligence 96, native of District 10039817, unabsorbed. Against that cold wording Knight sets Charles Samson, a trained troubleshooter patrolling a vast slice of the galaxy with his wife Midge. At the moment of the opening he is simply hungry, waiting on Midge's soufflé from the autochef.

Samson and Midge are one of a thousand two-person teams watching over Slice 103 for their headquarters. Two days before, they were sent off course toward Kenilworth IV, a lonely one-man post on the rim of the Slice. Knight builds the tale on the gap between the grand words used to define man and the small wants of one hungry man.
69027-mammonart-an-essay-in-economic-int:
Upton Sinclair wrote a long essay that reads art through wealth and class. The book came out from his own hand at Pasadena in 1925. Its name, Mammonart, joins the god of wealth with art. Short parts march from cave folk to the age of jazz. Sinclair asks one blunt ask through all of it: who owns the artists?

Cave man Ogi and his wife stand for the first art trade. Rich homes order jazz, pipes, and manners as class marks. Greece, Rome, and the church age get the same hard test. Sinclair holds that art bends to those who pay for it. Rad minds get a bold, plain brief.
69070-the-isle-of-retribution:
The Isle of Retribution is a novel by Edison Marshall. Little, Brown published it in Boston in 1923. Douglas Duer drew the frontispiece. The tale opens on a late August afternoon in Seattle. Its hero is Ned Cornet, a young man of idle habits.

Circumstance conspires against Cornet that day. He passes the time at the Totem Club on Fourth Street. His friend Rodney Coburn has just returned from a salmon stream in Canada. Coburn brought back dark bottles of fine liquor. The two celebrate with drink after drink. Cornet raises his usual limit of two cocktails to four whiskies. He drives into the rainy twilight too fast. The powers of circumstance are only beginning their work.
69102-the-moon:
Oliver Farrington, keeper of geology at the Field Museum in Chicago, wrote a short leaflet on the Moon dated 1925. A relief model of the seen face of the Moon, in a hall of the museum, fronts the piece. The Moon is our next world past stray comets and meteors, and it swings in an oval path round the Earth.

Its width is near a fourth of Earth width, and its bulk a small share of Earth bulk. One face is all we see, since spin and swing share the same span of days. Shifts in view, called librations, let us peek past each pole and edge in turn, the leaflet notes.
69112-the-quest-for-the-rose-of-sharon:
The Quest for the Rose of Sharon is a tale by Burton Stevenson. Butterick held the rights in 1906, then Page and Company in 1909. Page printed this Boston copy as the first impression of April 1909. Stevenson had writ The Marathon Mystery and The Halliday Case before. Fourteen chapters run from Grandaunt Nelson to the Rose of Sharon itself.

A messenger from Plumfield brings the problem that starts the search. A new home, an ally found, and kinds of the rose fill the road. The House Beautiful and a talk with the enemy crowd the mid tale. Retribution, a shadow in the orchard, and a lion bearded follow on. Surrender comes before the last chapter names the flower at last. Grandaunt was eccentric, the teller owns, in dark days of doubt. Pictures show diggers mocked for hunting treasure in the yard.
69121-an-outlaw-s-diary-revolution:
Cecile Tormay kept this diary through the Hungarian revolution, and it was first published at London in 1923, with a foreword by the Duke of Northumberland. The first entry is dated October 31, 1918, in a Budapest decked with white chrysanthemums for the Day of the Dead. That night Count Michael Károlyi's National Council took power, and Tormay, an outlaw in her own country, records what followed with anger and grief.

Photographs show the men of the revolution, Károlyi, Béla Kún, and the rest, beside the ruined homes and fleeing crowds. Tormay dedicates the book to her mother, a gentle victim of the revolution. It is a diary of the losing side: royalist, Catholic, and bitter, and all the more vivid for its partisanship.
69141-on-adipocire-and-its-formation:
On Adipocire, by Wetherill, comes from a learned society's transactions. The American Philosophical Society printed the paper. Wetherill held degrees in chemistry and medicine. Adipocire is the fatty matter found in corpses. Its making, he argues, bears on how fat forms in the body. Liebig's theory of fat stands behind the inquiry. Fourcroy first examined the stuff in 1785, Wetherill notes. A liver hung ten years in a Paris laboratory had turned fatty and smooth. Potash lye dissolved it into a soap. Graveyard fat gave Fourcroy his wide test in 1786. The Innocens cemetery in Paris was then being emptied. Thouret watched the workmen's health through the two year task.

In the paupers' ditches the substance lay in plenty. Chevreul corrected Fourcroy's grouping of the fats. Gall stone fat and spermaceti fat are their own kinds, he showed.
69233-examination-of-the-rev-mr-harris-s:
Ramsay's Examination of Harris's Scriptural Researches on the Licitness of the Slave-Trade was printed at London in 1788. James Ramsay, a clergyman, answers a work that defended the trade from scripture. An advertisement explains the Examination was drafted in the country for whoever might answer Harris.
