When Harris's reasoning began winning back waverers from the freedom cause, Ramsay published at once. The text proceeds datum by datum, in Harris's own mathematical manner.

The first data grant both Testaments equal authority as the unerring word of God. Ramsay accepts the grant and qualifies it: scripture passes many things without censure that Christians now know to be forbidden. Laws, he argues, adapt to the state of society and of the human mind. The eating of swine's flesh serves as his example, allowed, forbidden, then allowed again. The pamphlet belongs to the abolition debate of 1788.
69285-a-manual-of-face-brick-constructio:
The American Face Brick Association of Chicago issued this manual in 1920, under a slogan set in brickwork on the title page: Use Face Brick, it Pays. The book is at once a handbook of construction and an argument for the material.

It opens with the old Roman rule from Vitruvius, that all good building needs firmness, utility, and charm. Chapters then cover modern brickmaking, types of face brick wall, foundations, and solid, hollow tile, and veneer construction. Brick bonds, mortar joints, and fire protection follow, then a long section of face brick house designs, with tables, estimating problems, and a glossary of bricklaying terms. The aim stated in the text is to serve the master builder with plans and practical methods.
6929-poemata-latin-greek-and-italian-poe:
John Milton's Latin, Greek, and Italian poems appear here in William Cowper's translation, with spelling modernized and notes set after each poem. The contents open with complimentary pieces addressed to the author, then elegies, including verses to Charles Diodati, on the death of the Cambridge beadle, and on the Gunpowder Plot. Poems in various metres follow, on the Fifth of November, on bishops, and on nature's decay.

Other pieces sing of Leonora in Rome, tell the fable of the peasant and his landlord, and mark the approach of spring. The collection shows Milton as a young scholar poet writing across tongues before Paradise Lost. Cowper's English keeps the verse clear for readers who lack the Latin, Greek, and Italian.
69290-american-slavery-and-the-means-of-:
The Reverend Jonathan Ward wrote American Slavery and the Means of its Abolition, printed in Boston in 1840. The essay was first given as an address at Plymouth, New Hampshire, on May 5, 1840. Ward says he read Wilberforce on the slave trade more than forty years before. Those accounts of Africa, the middle passage, and the West Indies won his sympathy.

Ward says he never felt prejudice against colour and ate at one table with coloured neighbours and hired help. In 1824 he refused a Fourth of July invite, citing the clash of praising liberty while holding men in bondage. A sermon the next year called that conduct inconsistent, absurd, and criminal. Ward backs abolition, though he regrets harsh words by some of its friends.
69295-the-land-of-gold-reality-versus-fi:
The Land of Gold: Reality Versus Fiction, by Hinton Helper, was published at Baltimore in 1855, for the author. It is dedicated to John Morehead of North Carolina, the author sincere friend and admirer. A preface explains the book origin in private letters.

Before his departure for California, Helper says, near and dear friends extracted a promise. He would write by letter, on every convenient occasion, such intelligence as would give them a distinct idea of the truth. They wanted to know the truthfulness or falsehood of the many glowing descriptions, and the reputed vast wealth, of California. His own observation would picture its present and future. The letters were never meant for the public eye, he adds. Readers get a cold water account of gold rush California.
69388-the-official-chaperon:
Natalie Sumner Lincoln set this novel in Washington, where a young woman serves as the official chaperon of the title. The story opens with a night train pulling into the capital and a tall traveler handing his suit-case to a porter in the great station. Marjorie Langdon appears in the frontispiece, and the chapters promise missing persons, false witness, and a hearing ear before all is uncovered.

Appleton published the book at New York and London in 1915. Lincoln was already known for The Trevor Case and other tales of crime and society. A visit to Fort Myer, a diamond sunburst, and a tangle of questions and queries carry the plot. It is a society mystery in the Washington manner: drawing rooms on the surface, secrets underneath.
69430-madame-margot-a-grotesque-legend-o:
John Bennett wrote a strange legend of old Charleston, issued by The Century Company in 1921. Rights were held that same year, and the book was printed in the United States. A poem by John Drinkwater fronts the tale as a gift to friends. Bennett sets his scene in a rich, gay age of the town.

Gardens, rare fruit, and bright birds fill the lush first pages. Proud men and fair girls move through green shade in a world still young. Bennett hints that the age fell at last into a deep abyss. Readers get rich scene craft wrapped around the odd tale of Madame Margot.
6946-the-complete-works-of-artemus-ward-:
Charles Farrar Browne, known as Artemus Ward, speaks here in his complete works, opening with a biographical sketch by Melville Landon. Part one gathers essays, sketches, and letters, from his first business letter and a piece on forts to the Shakers, the Atlantic cable fete at Baldinsville, and a visit to Brigham Young. The showman, the lecturer, and the humorist all appear in these pages.

Part two turns to war, with the show confiscated, thrilling scenes in Dixie, and a Fourth of July oration. Later pieces include an interview with President Lincoln, a talk with Prince Napoleon, and notes on woman's rights and the press. The collection preserves a comic voice that charmed America and England alike.
69543-around-the-world-in-eighty-minutes:
Walsh made a photo tour of the world's great sights in one fat book. The book came out in Philadelphia in 1894. Photo plates show the grand works and fair scenes of Earth. The Statue of Liberty leads his list of sights in full. The Tower of London and Westminster Abbey come next in line.

Saint Paul's, the Houses of Parliament, and the Bank stand in town. Kenilworth, Warwick, and Windsor hold court in the list as well. Shakespeare's house and Osborne House share the home isle part. Blarney Castle and the Lakes of Killarney cross to Ireland. Each plate bears short words on what the eye takes in. Armchair guests got the world in a flash.
6960-a-narrative-of-the-life-of-mrs-mary:
Mary Jemison, taken by Indians in 1755 when only about twelve, lived among them to old age, and James Seaver took this narrative from her own words on November 29, 1823. It tells of the murder of her father and his family, her sufferings, her marriages to two Indians, and her troubles with her children. It also records Indian barbarities in the French and Revolutionary wars and the life of her last husband.

An appendix adds the tragedy at the Devil's Hole in 1783, Sullivan's expedition, and the traditions, manners, and customs of the Indians as Jemison knew them. Seaver presents many historical facts never before published, in her voice as he heard it. The book remains a rare first hand account of captivity turned into a life.
69609-martin-of-old-london:
Herbert Strang wrote Martin of Old London, a boys adventure printed at Oxford and reprinted in 1936. Strang's stories for boys list Dick Trevanion, Harry Rochester, Barclay of the Guides, Boys of the Light Brigade, Humphrey Bold, Rob the Ranger, and With Drake on the Spanish Main. Contents open with a waiting boat and Martin at home.

An assault, a lost job, a noise in the night, a mysterious passenger, a blow in the dark, and a face at the window follow in quick chapters. A brass-bound box, Blackbeard visiting a baker, the Santa Maria, coffee for two, and a Pudding Lane adventure fill the middle. Fire, prisoners, escape by swimming, pursuit, and rescue close the tale. Boys got seventeenth-century London adventure.
69827-a-manual-on-the-origin-and-develop:
A Manual on the Origin and Development of Washington is a state work by Caemmerer, a doctor of the study of the past. It came out from the state print house at Washington on the eve of the forties, as a paper of the Senate. Its front plate, from the air, shows the heart of the nations seat.

A quote at its head gives a famed French guests words on the city, as guest of the nation in the past age. He called it the central star of the star group that lights the whole world. The work traces how the seat of rule was planned, laid out, and built up age by age: its site, its plan, its great halls, and its growth as a city.
69835-the-negro-and-the-nation:
Hubert Harrison published The Negro and the Nation with the Cosmo-Advocate Publishing Company at New York. A note explains his path with care. Two opening articles first ran in the International Socialist Review in 1912, while he belonged to the Socialist Party. He later left, holding to the doctrine of Race First and his own line of work.

The first essay, The Black Man's Burden, answers Kipling head on. Harrison sorts his facts into four groups, political, economic, educational, and social. He argues that rights denied mean citizenship denied, whatever a republic calls itself. Southern disfranchisement anchors the case with hard counts. Readers get a Black radical's brief, plain spoken and built to indict.
69849-mr-arnold-a-romance-of-the-revolut:
Francis Lynde's romance of the Revolution, Mr Arnold, with a frontispiece by John Wolcott Adams, came out at Indianapolis in 1923 under the Bobbs-Merrill imprint. The narrator, Dick, tells the story in the first person. It opens on December 14, 1780, his twenty-second birthday, in a tavern at Nyack on the Hudson.

Dick has rowed down from Teller's Point, and Jack Pettus rides over from Washington's headquarters at Tappan to drink the birthday bottle with him. The talk is grim: the patriot army is ragged and starving, men are slipping home, and Benedict Arnold's treason has soured every camp. The chapters promise a drumhead court, a powder-room, a walk up Gallows Hill, and traitors all.
69851-the-medieval-inquisition-a-study-i:
The Medieval Inquisition: A Study in Religious Persecution, by Charles T Gorham, was published in London in 1918. The Nationalist Association issued the book. Gorham surveys the machinery of persecution built by the medieval church. He covers the sin of simony and the crusade preached against Christians. He then turns to the daily method of the inquisitor's court.

Later chapters take up the fall of the Templars. The trial of Joan of Arc gets a chapter of its own. So does the censorship of books. Each case shows how charges of heresy served power as much as faith. Gorham writes as a rationalist critic, and his history is also an argument. Free thought, he holds, survived centuries of organised suppression. The book appeared as the First World War ended, when questions of conscience and obedience carried fresh weight.
69866-dark-of-the-moon:
Sara Teasdale gathers her later lyrics in Dark of the Moon, published by Macmillan in New York in 1926. The poems, first printed in journals from 1921 on, are set in nine groups, from There Will Be Stars and Pictures of Autumn to Sand Drift and Portraits. Midsummer Nights, The Crystal Gazer, and Berkshire Notes follow, and the book closes with Arcturus in Autumn and The Flight.

Titles like On the Sussex Downs, At Tintagel, Low Tide, and Effigy of a Nun show her range: sea coasts, seasons, lovers, and quiet deaths. Readers who know Love Songs and Flame and Shadow will find the same clear voice here.
69876-the-ideal-cookery-book-a-reliable-:
Lilian Clarke's The Ideal Cookery Book, a reliable guide to home cooking containing 246 useful and dainty recipes, is kept here in its third edition. The publisher is Brumby and Clarke of Hull and London. Clarke's preface concedes that cookery books are endless, and blames their practical worthlessness for the lasting demand for a reliable one. Hers claims to be the best, cheapest, and most useful culinary handbook yet produced.

A large proportion of the recipes are her own compilation, she says, and all have been carefully revised and repeatedly tested, arranged for ease of preparation, daintiness, and economy. The contents begin with savouries, numbered like a ledger: forcemeat, mince meat, potato balls, a tasty dish of cold cooked beef, savoury puffs. Then veal mould, timbales of mutton, rolled steak with potatoes, salad dressing, cabbage balls, cheese croquettes, and rissoles a la Lilian.
69979-aunt-lydia-s-rug-yarn-collection:
Aunt Lydia Rug Yarn Collection is a crochet pattern booklet, Star Book number 225, priced at thirty five cents. American Thread issued the book for its Aunt Lydia heavy rug yarn in its pages. A Belle Shell, a crocheted top, is the first pattern shown in the book. Sizes are small, medium, and large for that garment in the pattern.

Materials required are eight to ten skeins of the rug yarn in chartreuse for the shell. An aluminium crochet hook, size K, or any size giving the stitch gauge, is specified in the directions. The gauge is three stitches to the inch for the work of the pattern. Rug yarn, made for floors, here makes a fashion top, in the postwar craft economy of the booklets. The Star Books taught a generation of crocheters from a rack at the five and dime, thirty five cents at a time.
70035-syria-the-land-of-lebanon:
Lewis Leary, formerly an instructor in the American College at Beirut, published Syria, the Land of Lebanon with McBride, Nast in 1913. He had written The Real Palestine of To-day and a book on Andorra. Evening in the harbor of Beirut illustrates the front. He dedicates the book to George Robinson, the preceptor who first turned his thoughts toward Syria.

The chapters are a resident's itinerary: the white mountain, the left-hand land, the city of Saturn, and the spirit of Olympia. Across the mountains, the land of Uz, and the earthly paradise follow. Syria in 1913 was Ottoman, and Lebanon's cedars shaded a country of silk, emigrants, and mission schools. Leary writes as a teacher who stayed, not a tourist who passed. His Syria is a country explained to Americans who were beginning to arrive in it in thousands.
70100-the-turner-s-companion:
Instructions for fine lathe work fill a turner's companion issued at Philadelphia in 1868. The book teaches concentric, elliptic, and eccentric turning, with plates of chucks, tools, and instruments. Patterns and directions for working them run through the whole volume.

A history of the lathe opens the teaching, followed by the choice and making of chucks in wood. Contents range over ivory work, dyeing and bleaching ivory, Chinese balls, chains, bottles, and boxes lined with orange peel or tortoise-shell. The eccentric cutter, drill, vertical cutter, and circular rest each get full directions. Turners get a complete bench book for the ornamental lathe work that filled Victorian parlors with carved ivory and wood.
70115-the-creator-and-what-we-may-know-o:
Creator and What We May Know of the Method of Creation is a lecture. Dallinger gave it as the Fernley Lecture of eighteen eighty seven. Woolmer of London issued the seventh thousand that same year in print. A long Wordsworth passage on nature fronts the discourse as its text.

Dallinger was a doctor of laws and a fellow of the Royal Society. The lecture is printed as spoken, with cut passages put back in. It asks what men may truly know of how creation was wrought. Nature shows a presence interfused in suns, ocean, air, and mind of man. He gives the volume to James Budgett in fond friendship memory.
70165-elizabeth-hooton:
Emily Manners wrote the life of Elizabeth Hooton, first Quaker woman preacher. Hooton lived from 1600 to 1672, the book's title says. Norman Penney added notes to Manners's work. The book came out in London in 1914. It is a back part to the Friends' own past journal.

Skegby village shows in the front plate of the book. Parts deal with her first work in England for the Friends. Two trips to New England brought her harsh tests there. Her last years close the main tale of her life. Notes on her husband and on Noah Bullock end the book. Faith past fans get a brave woman's full tale.
70176-the-history-of-steam-navigation:
The History of Steam Navigation, by John Kennedy, was published at Liverpool in 1903, with numerous illustrations and a view of Liverpool in 1837. Kennedy gathered much of his material from the press of the period, chiefly the Times, the Liverpool Mercury, and the Glasgow Herald. He thanked steamship officials and librarians for their help.

Part one starts with inventors and alleged inventors before 1807, from De Garay in 1543 to the Charlotte Dundas of 1803. Fulton's Clermont of 1807, the first passenger steamboat in the world, gets a chapter with her first voyage. Clyde steamers, Irish packets, and the Thames follow, and part two turns to historical steamship companies.
70234-hugh-worthington:
Mary Holmes wrote this novel, Hugh Worthington, printed at New York and London in 1875, though entered for copyright in 1868. A publisher's list at the front shows it as the tenth of her popular novels. Tempest and Sunshine, English Orphans, and Lena Rivers stand among the earlier nine. A notice praises her gift for winning her readers' sympathy.

Contents give some thirty chapters of names and places. Spring Bank opens the tale, and a chapter asks what Rover found. Hugh speaks a soliloquy, and Terrace Hill, Anna and John, and Alice Johnson follow. Matters in Kentucky, Sam and Adah, and how Hugh paid his debts fill the middle. A letter, Saratoga, a meeting of Alice and Hugh, a sale, a ride, and Adah's journey bring the story toward its result.
70304-the-inquisition:
The Inquisition, a political and military study of its establishment by Hoffman Nickerson, was published at London in 1923. Hilaire Belloc wrote a preface for the volume. Two maps in a pocket at the end show Languedoc in 1209 and the town and battle of Muret. Chapter one treats the medieval recovery of civilization as the ground.

Languedoc and the Albigenses come next, then the preliminaries of the crusade against them. The Albigensian Crusade fills two chapters, with Muret and its sequel at the core. Mendicant orders and the rise of the Inquisition form the sixth chapter of the study. An epilogue on Prohibition closes the book in a bold modern turn. Nickerson treats the Inquisition as a tool of state as much as of faith.
70320-the-navy-of-the-american-revolutio:
Charles Oscar Paullin traces how the young United States built, ran, and used a navy in the war for independence. He sent the study to the Graduate School at the University of Chicago as his thesis for a degree in history. The Chicago printing dates to 1906, with a full contents list that maps the work chapter by chapter.

Early chapters cover the Naval Committee of 1775 and the small fleets fitted out by Washington and by Arnold. Later parts take up the Marine Committee, navy boards at Philadelphia and Boston, and the men who served as agents. Paullin weighs orders, cash, ships, and prizes to show how sea power grew under weak central rule.
70329-arctic-exploration:
Douglas Hoare's Arctic Exploration was published in New York by Dutton in 1906. Eighteen illustrations and four maps accompany the narrative, and a frontispiece called Sailing the Arctic Seas opens the volume. The contents run in thirty-three chapters from the early voyages to the expeditions of the author's own day.

Early chapters move from Hudson to Phipps and Nelson, then weigh Ross's failures against Parry's successes. Franklin's overland journeys and his last voyage follow, and the search for him fills several chapters. Collinson, M'Clure, Belcher and M'Clintock in the Fox all appear there. Later chapters treat Kane and Hayes, Hall and the Polaris, and the Greely tragedy. The story of the Jeannette, Nordenskiöld's work and Nansen's voyage in the Fram close the survey, with Sverdrup and Peary last.
7037-beric-the-briton-a-story-of-the-rom:
G A Henty tells of Beric the Briton at the Roman invasion, opening with a preface to his dear lads. His series on England's wars would be incomplete, he says, without the age when Romans ruled the island. Native valor, acknowledged even by Roman historians, yielded only to superior discipline, not to want of bravery or physical strength.

Roman rule, for a time, greatly benefited a people who had wasted strength in perpetual tribal wars, since it brought Roman civilization. In the end it proved disastrous, since Britons defended by Roman soldiers lost their military virtues. When the legions left, they could not resist the Saxons. Beric's tale follows that rise and fall through a young Briton's eyes.
70371-colas-breugnon:
Romain Rolland wrote a gay French tale, turned into English by Katherine Miller and held under copyright in 1919. Rolland had won fame with Jean Christophe, a grave long novel. He tells readers this light book took him by surprise as much as it will surely take them.

Back in his home country of Burgundy for the first time since youth, Rolland felt the past wake in him. Old Colas Breugnons under his skin, he jokes, made him their clerk and would not let him speak till they had done. Saint Martin of Gaul, patron of Clamecy, gets the book, with an old verse on his drinking.
704-the-mansion:
Henry van Dyke wrote this short tale about John Weightman, a rich New York man whose grand house stands as a sign of his success. Weightman prides himself on wealth well used, yet he has shut his heart to need. A dream-like journey after death tests what his mansion, and his life, were truly worth.

Van Dyke sets earthly splendour against a heavenly standard, where love and mercy count more than stone and bronze. The tale is brief and pointed, written for readers who enjoy a moral fable with a twist. Its fame rests on that closing reversal, which asks whether a life built for show can stand when judged by grace.
70416-emmanuel-burden-merchant-of-thames:
Emmanuel Burden, by Hilaire Belloc, is a mock record of a London merchant. Methuen issued this third and cheaper edition in 1915; first came 1904. Thirty four illustrations by Chesterton picture Burden kin and circle in fun. Burden exported hardware from Thames Street in the City of London trade.

His lineage, speculations, last days, and death fill the solemn comic record. A sketch of Burden from memory fronts the book as its frontispiece. Nephew Hildebrand Worthing, wife, son Cosmo, and pastor Legros fill the plates. Belloc had written Paris, Marie Antoinette, and The Pyrenees before this jest. A dedication to Herbert Fisher carries a Coleridge tag: or words to that effect.
70434-americans-by-adoption:
Joseph Husband wrote short lives of great citizens born in foreign lands. The Atlantic Monthly Press issued the book in Boston in 1920. William Neilson, head of Smith College, adds a front essay. Portraits show each subject, with Agassiz at the front of the book.

Lives cover Stephen Girard, John Ericsson, and Louis Agassiz in turn. Carl Schurz, Andrew Carnegie, and James Hill follow in the set. Saint-Gaudens the sculptor and Jacob Riis the reformer close the nine. The book praises what newcomers gave to American public life and work.
70474-queenie-hetherton:
Holmes wrote Queenie Hetherton, a novel first published in the New York Weekly. The story is given in memory of a little girl who sleeps among the New England hills. Fifty-one chapters carry it, at a stately pace.

Merrivale's morning mail opens the tale: letters for Colonel Rossiter, for his son Philip home from Harvard, and for Arthur Beresford, the town's only lawyer. A girl called Reinette arrives by sea, and there turn out to be two Reinettes. Margery La Rue, old letters, and a Christine carry the middle secrets. Yellow fever, an explosion, and Phil's own story come before Queenie learns the truth.
70554-sir-richard-s-grandson:
Eleanora Stooke wrote this children's story, Sir Richard's Grandson, or A Soldier's Son, published at London by Gall and Inglis. The contents follow Dick from India to England, a grandfather, a secret passage, and a joyful home-coming.

Chapter one opens on a verandah as the Indian day's heat lifts. Captain Gidley and his wife watch their eight-year-old Dick, pale and delicate, and sigh: the climate is telling on him, and they cannot keep him in India much longer. Dick has never hidden a thought from his mother, his chief companion and playmate. Sir Richard tells him of the secret passage in England. A blunderbuss, a storm, and a spell adrift follow. Young readers get an Anglo-Indian parting story.
7061-a-march-on-london-being-a-story-of-:
G A Henty tells Wat Tyler's insurrection in A March on London, opening with an illustration of Edgar striking a foe a buffet that sends him reeling. His preface notes the later fourteenth and early fifteenth centuries are known better than ages before or after, thanks to Froissart, Monstrelet, and Holinshed, whose full detail leaves nothing to desire. The uprising of the Commons, chiefly folk still in serfdom under Richard the Second, was in itself justifiable.

English serfdom never reached continental harshness, yet serfs bore grievous disabilities, giving part of their time to a feudal lord's work. Henty follows Edgar from such a world to the march on London, where commons demand justice from a young king. The tale blends chronicle fact with a boy's adventure in revolt.
70648-the-course-of-creation:
John Anderson joins faith and stone study in The Course of Creation, printed at Cincinnati in 1851. Moore made the book, with a glossary of scientific terms at the back. A long quote at the front states his creed in full.

Nature, from the morning days of the world, stamped beauty and fitness on all she made, it says. Naught was left out to be supplied later, and naught was made faulty in a part. The first finds of geology speak of a plan of creation devised from the start. That plan is linked with the first intelligent cause, he holds. His preface owns he has oft asked if his love of geology fits his strict duties.
70714-demobilization:
Demobilization is an official account of America's return from war after the Armistice, 1918 to 1920. Benedict Crowell and Robert Forrest Wilson wrote it. Yale University Press published it at New Haven in 1921. Crowell had been Assistant Secretary of War and Director of Munitions from 1917 to 1920. The volume commemorates the eight thousand Yale men who served.

Photographs from the War and Navy Departments illustrate the volume, part of the series How America Went to War. The contents follow the army home. The A E F embarks, and the transatlantic ferry runs at ebb tide. Chapters cover the process of discharging soldiers and soldier welfare. War contracts and their settlement take two chapters. Ordnance, artillery, aircraft, and quartermaster supplies are demobilised in turn. Buildings and lands, the selling of the surplus, and foreign liquidation follow. A balance sheet closes the account of the giant hand at rest.
70776-the-curse-of-clifton:
The Curse of Clifton, or the widowed bride, is a novel by Mrs Southworth, the most popular American woman writer of her century by her publisher's boast. Her earlier works crowd the title page in a long roll: Self Raised, Ishmael, Fair Play, The Changed Brides, A Beautiful Fiend, and dozens more. The advertisement promises that this tale will be found equal, if not better, than any of her previous works.

Critics concede her, the puff goes on, to be the most read woman writer living. Her books are called among the greatest novels in the English language, and the most splendid besides. Behind such trumpeting stood a real fact: Southworth's serial tales of wronged brides, lost heirs, and haunted houses were devoured by millions. The curse of Clifton hangs, as the twin title tells, over a bride widowed at the altar's edge.
70894-the-life-of-adoniram-judson:
Edward Judson wrote the life of his father Adoniram Judson, printed in New York in 1883. The book is given with love to the children of missionaries. Edward calls them the heirs of both the pains and the rewards of their parents. He draws on his father's letters and journals in large extracts.

Those own words let the reader see the man's home life, friendships, and private traits, not just his public work. Edward says the tale of foreign mission work in his father's day needed to be told anew for his own time. The result is both a family record and a close look at a life spent far from home in hard service.
70906-sherwood-anderson:
Sherwood Anderson, a bibliography, is a reference book compiled by Eugene Sheehy and Kenneth Lohf, issued in California in 1960. A photograph of Anderson by Edward Steichen, dated 1926, fronts the volume. The contents divide the work in two great parts. The first gathers works by Sherwood Anderson himself. The second gathers writings about him by other hands.

Under the first head stand his single works, then essays and stories, introductions and forewords, letters, and stage versions. His pieces in magazines fill a long run of pages, and his own work for a county newspaper closes that half. The second part lists books and articles about him, poems and parodies, and reviews. A sentence of Gertrude Stein's stands in praise: Anderson had a genius for the sentence that carries feeling straight.
70919-miles-murchison:
Agnes Giberne, who wrote Sweetbriar and Ready, Aye, Ready, stands behind this tale of a boy's start in life. Nisbet printed Miles Murchison in London. A plate at the front shows Miles brought in with the words: this is the boy, Mr Laurence.

The tale is told in turns by three voices. Mrs Murchison tells the first stretch: a day's pleasuring, the way out, and how it all happened. Mrs Kingscote then gives the same days from her side. Miles takes up his own tale at chapter eight, with a talk with Mr Laurence. Trustworthiness, wise counsel, and a difficult moment fill his part. Small Miss Adela and a ride in the pony cart sweeten the later list.
70981-the-romance-of-excavation:
David Masters wrote a popular account of digging up the old world, first issued in London in 1923 with twenty nine art cuts. Its full scope covers finds in Egypt, Assyria, Troy, and Crete. The first part tells of the Rosetta Stone, found by the French, lost to Britain, and read at last by Young and Champollion.

Later parts show the grind of the work: seventy thousand tons of rubble shifted to find the tomb of Tutankhamen, and long dull years of digging in vain. Masters praises Flinders Petrie and his finds at Abydos, and shows how bits of pot can date a layer like a calendar. Grave goods, Nile floods, and bold tomb thieves all play a part.
71009-the-ainu-group-at-the-saint-louis-:
Frederick Starr recounts bringing a group of Ainu from northern Japan to the Saint Louis Exposition of 1904, where the anthropology department stressed living exhibits. Upwards of thirty tribes lived in their own houses and worked at their own arts.

Starr left Saint Louis in January 1904 with his photographer Manuel Gonzales, reaching Yokohama in February as Japan declared war on Russia. Despite the war, officials aided the mission with courtesy and prompt care. The book is dedicated to the men who made the trip possible and a success, and it follows the group to the fair. At the fair the Ainu lived in houses of their own building, cooked their own food, and practised their own arts.
71039-the-illustrated-story-of-evolution:
The Illustrated Story of Evolution, by Marshall Gauvin, president of the American Secular Union, was published in New York in 1921. Gauvin also asked, in print, whether there is a real God and a life after death. A portrait of Charles Darwin fronts the book, which Gauvin inscribes to his wife in a note from Pittsburgh dated August 30, 1921.

Figures show the great nebula in Orion, lunar craters, rock strata, Cambrian fossils, and the segmentation of the fertilized egg. Later plates trace early fishes, lung fishes, the frog, great reptiles, and the archaeopteryx. Gauvin tells evolution as a clear, pictured story for lay readers, in a freethought spirit that treats science as the foe of dogma.
71058-holidays-at-brighton:
Holidays at Brighton, or Sea-Side Amusements, came from Darton and Harvey at London in 1834. Chapter one opens early, with little Lewis Ashton wide awake and dressed. His brother Edward still sleeps, and Lewis calls him to open his eyes. They are not in London now, with its dull streets and black houses. Nor are they at school, where a great bell calls boys to lessons.

They are in Brighton at last, where the king and queen live, Edward cries. Grand things wait to be seen, but the deep wide sea draws him most. Last night it looked like a line of black clouds as they rode in the dark. This morning it lies bright and blue, its waves sparkling in the sun. Fishing boats dot the distance, small with range or truly small. The book gives boys seaside days of sight and lesson.
71087-home-education:
Home Education is the first book of a set on the school of the young by Charlotte Mason. This form is the fifth print, made large and fresh, from nineteen six. It treats the teach of young ones past the age of nine. A long verse in an old tongue, in both its own words and an English form, heads the text.

The verse tells of a smooth rush that sprang up fresh where it was torn from wet sand. Mason takes that plant as a sign for how a young one must be taught. The front talk of the set owns that the view of teach was then dim and low. Her books set out a bright path for the home school of the small child.
71090-the-prisoners-memoirs-or-dartmoor-:
An American prisoner compiled memoirs of Dartmoor Prison, giving a complete and impartial history of the Americans' captivity in England during the War of 1812. The account runs from the war's commencement until the Treaty of Ghent freed all prisoners. A particular detail covers the massacre at Dartmoor on the fatal evening of April 6, 1815. A Virgil motto heads the title: these sufferings I myself have seen.

The compiler was a captive during the whole war, the title says. Guards fired on prisoners in the yard that April evening, killing several. The memoirs answer British accounts of the event. Such narratives fixed Dartmoor in American memory as a byword for cruelty.
7116-vestiges-of-the-natural-history-of-:
Vestiges of the Natural History of Creation, published in London by John Churchill in 1844, traces the world from space to man in a single scheme. Contents run from the bodies of space, their arrangements and formation, through the constituent materials of earth and other bodies, to the earth formed in the era of primary rocks. Sea plants and corals mark the commencement of organic life.

Fishes abound in the old red sandstone, land plants begin with the carboniferous formation, and reptiles open terrestrial zoology in the new red sandstone. Mammals commence with the oolite, grow abundant in the tertiary, and present species begin with superficial formations. The book closes with general and particular thoughts on the origin of animated tribes, including man.
71171-the-negro-in-american-fiction:
Sterling Brown wrote The Negro in American Fiction, copyrighted in 1937 as a Bronze Booklet and reissued in 1968. An editorial foreword calls it the first full-length survey of the Negro in American fiction, both as character and as author. It differs from the usual academic survey, the foreword says, by analysing the social factors behind each school and period.

Brown was associate professor of English at Howard. He had graduated from Williams in 1922 with Phi Beta Kappa honours, taken a Harvard master's in 1923, and taught at Virginia, Lincoln, and Fisk before Howard. Readers get a landmark of Black literary criticism, tracing the stereotype and its answer across a century of novels.
71322-wilhelmina-in-london:
Barry Pain sends a daughter to town in Wilhelmina in London, printed in London in 1912 in a new edition. John Long made the book. Pain had writ Eliza and its sequels. Nine chapters carry the tale, from Stranded to A Loss and a Gain.

Chapter one opens with a confession. It is quite possible to love a person whom one does not respect, the narrator holds, of whom one even disapproves. I loved my father, but I certainly did not respect him. He did not even respect himself. He married her mother against his family's wishes, she recounts. Her grandfather bought him an annuity of two hundred a year and wished nothing more to do with him. In the frequent money crises her father caused, her parents sat staring at one another over the fire. Her father generally made a will on those gloomy occasions.
71398-the-excavations-at-babylon:
The Excavations at Babylon reports the German dig that uncovered the ancient city. Robert Koldewey directed the excavations and wrote the account. Agnes S Johns translated it into English. Macmillan published the book in London in 1914, with 255 illustrations and plans. A coloured enamelled vase fronts the volume.

The contents march through the ruins mound by mound. The outer city walls and the mound Babil come first. The Kasr, the ascent, and the Procession Street follow. Koldewey describes the Ishtar Gate and its wall decorations of bulls and dragons. The southern citadel and the palace of Nabopolassar fill long sections. One chapter asks whether a vaulted building held the hanging gardens of Semiramis. Etemenanki, the tower of Babel, and Esagila, the temple of Marduk, get full treatment. Graves and small finds at Merkes, and even a Greek theatre, close the survey.
71402-outline-history-of-greek-religion:
Lewis Richard Farnell, rector of Exeter College, Oxford, wrote an outline history of Greek religion, first issued in 1920 with a new edition in 1921. Farnell had written a multi volume study of Greek cults. Chapter one treats the sources and the evidence. Serious study of Greek religion, he says, distinct from mere mythology, is a recent achievement.

Only recent research, Farnell argues, shows the Hellenic spirit working worthily in religion as in art and science. The Greek world was never one state, so its religion varies by tribe and city. Chapters proceed by periods: prehistoric times, then 900 to 500, then 500 to 338. A final chapter covers the age after Alexander.
71485-the-married-woman-s-private-medica:
The Married Woman's Private Medical Companion was published in 1847. Mauriceau issued the guide at New York that year. He styles himself professor of diseases of women. His office stood at 129 Liberty Street. The title page lists the book's whole scope. Monthly turns, in stoppage, irregularity, or suppression, come first. Pregnancy, and how it may be known, follows. A discovery to prevent pregnancy is promised in capitals. Miscarriage, and when it may properly be effected, are treated next. Barrenness ends the list, with its causes and cure. The preface speaks to wives, mothers, and daughters.

A woman may judge her own maladies here, Mauriceau writes. She need not impart them to another. Causes, symptoms, and remedies are laid side by side. The matter is drawn, he owns, from celebrated medical authors.
71530-the-night-of-no-moon:
Fyfe wrote The Night of No Moon, a science fiction tale from Infinity in June 1957, illustrated by Orban. The planet Boyd the Third suffers from one satellite too many, a blurb warns readers. A third moon, large and close, confuses the tides and wrecks the weather of the rough world.

Surveyor Pete Guthrie lost his rocket to incredible tides on a rashly chosen shoreline landing place. Now he is stuck among natives whose harsh customs fit a world of coastal catastrophes and wild air. A local named Polf tells him the wind spirits want him to stay for good. Guthrie wishes he had stayed on the moon Jhux with an oxygen mask. Pulp readers get stranded-man adventure.
71551-the-french-revolution:
The French Revolution is a school book in a set of aid books for the spread of high learn to the towns. A sage of a Scots school shaped that set. Its plan word at the front tells its aim in full.

The set was made, it says, to aid that spread through two great lands. It meets a need felt far and wide by students: text books for study and for shelf use, tied to the true courses of talks in that plan. Books on the split fields of letters, science, thought, past, and art were set to pens of fame, to chairs of the great schools, and to talk men of those schools. These books are not for first school days. They serve those who have made some way in their theme.
71562-greece-and-babylon:
Greece and Babylon is a comparative sketch of Mesopotamian, Anatolian, and Hellenic religions by Lewis Farnell. Clark published the book at Edinburgh in 1911 from George Street. Farnell was fellow of Exeter College, Oxford, and author of Cults of the Greek States. The book is dedicated to Henry Wilde, founder of the Wilde lectureship in comparative religion at Oxford.

Farnell was the first Wilde lecturer, and these are the first fruits of that endowment, as the dedication states. The question is how far Greek religion drew on the older faiths of Babylon and Anatolia in their lands. The lectures came when new finds in the Near East were forcing scholars to rethink the Greek miracle. His answer, learned and cautious, still frames the terms in which that debt is argued by students of the ancient world.
71568-the-show-must-go-on:
Henry Slesar wrote The Show Must Go On, a tale printed in the July 1957 issue of Infinity, with pictures by Engle. Its head line offers work: actors wanted, no experience needed, pay excellent, life expectancy brief. The tale opens in darkness, with a man waking and trembling with the thought of escape. He crawls till his fingertips find a wall, then strikes a match.

By its flicker he faces a steel door with no latch or knob, and a sign that says PUSH. Outside lies a moonlit courtyard ringed by a wire fence four times his height, and a second sign reads YOU CAN DO IT. He climbs, drops to the ground, and a voice booms that they haven't got all night. Slesar builds a grim puzzle of signs, fences, and a show that waits for its man.
71577-a-patriot-lad-of-old-boston:
A Patriot Lad of Old Boston, a boys' historical novel by Russell Gordon Carter, was published at Philadelphia in 1923. Henry Pitz supplied the illustrations. Its hero Don lives in Boston as the quarrel with Britain heats up. The front plate shows untaxed tea with the caption that nobody need fear it, since no tax was paid on it.

Chapters run from Tea and Salt Water through a trip to Concord and the coming out of the regulars. Don sets traps, watches from a housetop, and stands by the Liberty Tree. He meets General Washington before the book ends. Carter wrote the Bob Hanson books for boys as well. This tale walks a young reader through the tea crisis and the first fights of the Revolution. It mixes schoolboy adventure with real events and places of old Boston.
71628-the-band-played-on:
Band Played On is a science fiction tale by Lester del Rey. Schoenherr drew the illustrations for its magazine appearance in print. The text comes from Infinity magazine of June 1957 here. The Heroes' March suits most spacemen, the blurb says at front. It did not apply to a space borne garbage man, though.

Del Rey says he likes tales laid near home in probable fact. Inside the rocket grounds the band plays the march for cadets. Captain Thomas Murdock stops at the gate by the visitors' section. He waits until the final blatant notes blare out over the field. Drill, pride, and one overlooked crewman drive del Rey's story.
7171-linda-condon:
Linda Condon first appears as a grave girl of about ten, slim and still, with a straight black bang across a clear pale brow. Her eyes stay longest in the mind: blue, velvet-rich, and sharp with a colour that startles the heart. Joseph Hergesheimer draws her with care, letting one face carry the whole opening scene.

Her mother supplies the gaiety for the whole family, bright where Linda is sober, and the contrast shapes their home from the first page. The novel follows Linda from this quiet childhood portrait onward, watching how a watchful, uncommon girl meets the world around her. Hergesheimer's prose stays slow and exact, lingering on looks and moods.
71722-the-evolution-of-religion:
Farnell gave talks on how faith grows, set as a study of man's kinds. His book came out in New York and London in 1905. Farnell taught old Greek lore at Exeter College, Oxford. He wrote Cults of the Greek States in his past work. Two first talks deal with how faiths are set side by side.

A fair, kind study of all faiths is the way, he holds. Faiths show man's heart at its best and worst, he says. Wash rites and the thought of purity take the next talk. Prayer then climbs from low forms to high in his scheme. A list and notes close the short set of talks. Thought fans get a calm guide.
71799-new-englands-plantation:
New England's Plantation is a facsimile volume of printed documents from about the year 1630, concerning the first English settlements in New England. The transcriber's note explains that the text keeps the originals' errors, wild spelling, and uneven punctuation, to preserve the documents as they were printed.

Such tracts were the prospectuses of colonisation. Settlers and promoters wrote home of the soil, the fish, the timber, and the natives, to draw money and men across the Atlantic. The facsimile keeps even the old long s of the first printings, rendered in modern type. Readers meet the voice of the plantation pamphlet as its first audience did: part report, part advertisement, and part prayer for a godly commonwealth in a new world. The volume serves historians who need the words as written, not smoothed.
71804-the-romance-of-isabel-lady-burton:
The Romance of Isabel Lady Burton, volume one, tells the life of Isabel Burton, in part by herself and in part by Wilkins. It came out at London in 1897, with portraits and pictures, and was given to her sister. A drawing of Isabel at the age of seventeen stands at the front.

The first book, Waiting, covers her birth, her first season, and her meeting with Richard Burton at Boulogne. Four years of hope deferred end in marriage. The second book follows the wedded pair to Fernando Po, Madeira, Brazil, and at last toward Damascus. Her own voice gives the tale its warmth and dash.
71813-the-long-question:
The Long Question is a short tale by David Mason from the November nineteen fifty seven Infinity. A quiz show named Win a Mint puts up its great prize of one hundred thousand dollars. Don Gerson, a young clerk of an insurance firm, won the right to play last week. Host Larry Lonigan calls him out to bright lights and loud claps. Don is tall, thin, and grave, with a shy grin for the host jests.

The show has told him near naught of what waits for his play. His firm lent him for two months to the show by kind leave. The host jokes that claim craft taught Don to guess what comes next. A wed lock quiz starts the patter as the crowd looks on. Time spent to win proves worth the cost, the tag line claims.
71847-the-garden-of-resurrection:
E Temple Thurston wrote The Garden of Resurrection, being the love story of an ugly man. Mitchell Kennerley in New York issued the book in nineteen eleven. Thurston gave the book to W R Dakin, a doctor and dear friend. He tells Dakin that after a talk with him one night he went home and wrote chapter one on a clean sheet. The debt, he says, makes the book doubly Dakin own.

Chapter one opens on the first, the very first, day of spring. A man walks past with a narcissus in his coat, humming a tune. By his tail coat, bowler hat, and small bag, the teller puts him down as an electrician. He had been at a job up West and heads back to Bond Street. Yet he walks through the Park when he ought to ride a bus. A tender tale of love, looks, and gardens follows.
71870-a-pound-of-prevention:
A Pound of Prevention, a science fiction tale by Edmondson, ran in Infinity in April 1958. Drawings came from Richard Kluga. Three young men face General Carnhouser across a table. They are set to ride a rocket shot at Mars. Past shots flew true, then failed at the slowing stage. If this one fails, funds may not come again for a hundred years.

Talk turns to food for the four month flight. The men joke about pickled fire bombs, prune soup, and codfish balls. Outside, trucks load bagged meat at the gantry. The meat is treated and sealed in clear wrap. Food, pride, and fear mix in this tale of a crewed flight that can not afford one more miss.
719-the-plays-of-w-e-henley-and-r-l-stev:
W. E. Henley and Robert Louis Stevenson wrote these plays together, blending Stevenson's romance with Henley's stagecraft. Deacon Brodie, the best known, turns on an Edinburgh tradesman who is respectable by day and a burglar by night. Beau Austin, Admiral Guinea, and Robert Macaire round out the set, with rogues, sailors, and gallants.

The plays are brisk melodramas, built for strong acting and sharp scenes rather than for the closet. They show Stevenson trying his hand at the theatre, with Henley's help, before his novels made him famous. The volume is a treat for those who like Victorian stage romance and the roots of the Deacon Brodie legend.
71906-the-adopted-son:
A L O E wrote The Adopted Son, a tale built on the Lord's Prayer, issued by Gall and Inglis. The author had earlier written Ned Franks and Pictures of Saint Paul. Each chapter takes one line of the prayer as its head.

The first chapter, Our Father Which Art in Heaven, opens in a baker's shop. Goldie the fruiterer holds that a man must mind his business and push his children on. Mrs Winter answers that the next life counts too, as she serves a small girl her biscuits. Her shop is spotless, with gilt letters over the door. Faith is taught through plain daily scenes.
71964-the-x-bar-x-boys-in-thunder-canyon:
The X Bar X Boys in Thunder Canyon, by James Cody Ferris, was published by Grosset and Dunlap at New York in 1926, illustrated by Walter S Rogers. The series list names The X Bar X Boys on the Ranch, on Whirlpool River, on Big Bison Trail, and at the Round-Up.

Chapter one, The Landslide, opens with Roy's horse Flash walking stiff-legged around a porcupine in the trail. The contents promise a missing brother, a message in the night, a jumping bucker, captives, and a woman with a long-barrelled rifle in the frontispiece. Rescue and retribution close the western tale.
71988-foods-nutrition-and-digestion:
Foods: Nutrition and Digestion is a diet handbook of the Know Thyself series, here in a second edition. Its author wrote from ten years of giving exercises and diets fitted to single patients. The aim is a clear book for the homemaker. She is to learn the uses of foods and build diets of her own.

Since the blood is made from food, the book holds, its states can be steered by knowing and ruling those foods. Help came from Winfield Hall of Northwestern Medical School, a lecturer on nutrition. Alida Pattee, late instructor in dietetics at Bellevue, also lent aid, as did the use of Hall's food tables. The work belongs to the first age of scientific diet advice, when the kitchen became a small laboratory of health.
72004-h-p-lovecraft-an-evaluation:
Joseph Payne Brennan's evaluation of Lovecraft was printed in 1955 by Macabre House of New Haven, Connecticut. Brennan had put out a bibliography of Lovecraft in 1952 and was pressed to give his view of the work. A full-time library job and his own tales and poems left him little room, he says, so the essay is brief.

Brennan grants that a final word is not yet possible: the poems and letters were still unpublished, and no full life of Lovecraft had been written. Still, the tales of note were all in print, so a judgment could stand. He takes up Edmund Wilson's flat claim, in the New Yorker, that Lovecraft was not a good writer.
72026-infiltration:
Infiltration, a story by Algis Budrys, ran in Infinity in October 1958. If werewolves exist, the blurb warns, they do not conform to all the superstitions. They may even know fear, it adds in a colder note. The tale opens at sunset with a man who knows they are coming for him tonight.

He wakes as the shadow of the next building falls over his windows. The red globe of the sun still hangs over the cliffs of New Jersey. He pushes a cigarette between numb lips and swings his feet from the bed. Fumbling with a match, he starts another hunted evening. Budrys writes the monster tale from inside the monster. Fear, not appetite, is the engine of this short piece.
72096-recent-discussions-on-the-abolitio:
Recent Discussions on the Abolition of Patents for Inventions gathers evidence, speeches, and papers against patent law, printed in London in 1869. The case spans the United Kingdom, France, Germany, and the Netherlands. Names on the title run from Sir William Armstrong to Count von Bismarck.

Other voices hold M Benard of the Siecle, M Chevalier of France, and Lord Stanley, who chaired the late royal commission on patent law. A French quote at the front calls a patent a privilege and a monopoly, which the law can own only if it rests on clear right or plain public good. The book adds plans for world deals on inventions and copyright. Law and trade readers get the anti patent case in its prime.
72222-jefferson-and-hamilton:
Claude G Bowers wrote a study of Jefferson and Hamilton subtitled the struggle for democracy in America, copyrighted in 1925 and in its tenth impression by 1927. Bowers had written on the party battles of the Jackson period. A preface in John Fiske's name states his purpose: to show the struggle as picturesque and dramatic, not a calm debate of principles.

Steel engravings, Bowers warns, hide the disheveled fighters their contemporaries saw. The field held marching mobs, duels, fist fights, and hangings in effigy. Theater crowds pelted aristocrats and forced orchestras to play the Marseillaise. Bowers calls the contest the most important waged in America, fought over elemental differences.
72292-joseph-hergesheimer-an-essay-in-in:
James Branch Cabell wrote an essay in interpretation on the novelist Joseph Hergesheimer, printed at Chicago in 1921 in a limited run for the Bookfellows. He dedicates it to Hergesheimer with friendship and large admiration. The tale he starts from is a striking one of rejection.

For fourteen years, the gossip of the literary world said, Hergesheimer could find no editor to take his stories. Story followed story, each met by bland refusal, while magazines printed far weaker work. Cabell holds that those fourteen years shaped and coloured every book his friend has since published. Readers of the novels get a key to their polish and patience.
72301-lead-poisoning-and-lead-absorption:
Thomas Legge, the government's medical inspector of factories, and Kenneth Goadby wrote this study of lead poisoning and lead absorption. Edward Arnold published it at London.

The book gives the signs of the disease, how it harms the body, and how to stop it, above all where the risk comes from men's work. It also lists the trades and processes where lead puts workers most at risk. The series it belongs to also treats digestion, syphilis, blood-vessel surgery, caisson sickness, diabetes, and shock. A free circular describing the series could be had from the publishers. Longmans, Green and Company handled the New York sale.
72318-the-cup-and-the-falcon:
The Cup and The Falcon are two plays by Alfred, Lord Tennyson, poet laureate, printed at London in 1884. The Cup, a tragedy, was produced at the Lyceum Theatre under Henry Irving on 3 January 1881. Irving played Synorix, an ex-tetrarch of Galatia, and Ellen Terry played Camma, wife of Sinnatus and later priestess in the temple of Artemis.

The scene opens among rocks above a city of Galatia, with priestesses singing in the temple. Roman soldiers lead a chained prisoner down the path. Synorix enters and sings the beauties of the city where Camma dwells. He recalls how she passed him three years before, when he was flying from his tetrarchy to Rome. He calls her his fate. The second play, The Falcon, gives its speaker a boast of service to Rome against the clans. Tennyson's volume preserves two late works for the stage.
72337-stay-off-the-moon:
Raymond Jones wrote Stay Off the Moon, a science fiction tale printed in Amazing Stories in December 1962. Its teaser asks how one fills a pipette from a quarter million miles away. The answer is the Prospector, a robot lab bound for the moon.

Chemist James Cochran drew up the plans for the analyzers that will test what the moon is made of. Signals from Earth will open valves, apply heat, and send results back by radio. Forty hours before countdown, crews swarm the hangar for final checks. Sam Jarvis, in charge of electronics, grins that the package is perfect.
7234-species-and-varieties-their-origin-:
Hugo De Vries delivered these lectures at the University of California on the origin of species and varieties by mutation, edited by Daniel Trembly MacDougal for the Carnegie Institution. De Vries sets his own claim beside Lamarck and Darwin in the opening pages. Where they saw origin as a natural fact or an object of inquiry, he makes it an object of experiment.

The lectures argue that new forms can arise by sudden mutation rather than by slow shading alone, and De Vries supports the claim with botanical work. His prose stays that of a lecturer, clear and stepwise, moving from old views to new tests. The book marks a bold early statement of mutation theory in the years after Darwin.
72441-redemption:
Redemption is a science fiction story by Robert Young, taken from Amazing Stories for July 1963. An epigraph in verse promises the search of Captain Nathaniel Drake for Saint Annabelle Leigh, and hints the story will be read many times as a classic. Drake is called the Jet-propelled Dutchman, though he is neither Dutch nor jet-propelled. He is a neo-Terran shipmaster whose vessel uses the Lamarre displacement-drive.

Legend says that whenever Drake put into port he searched for a certain woman, hoping to redeem himself through love. The narrator corrects the legend. Drake did search for a woman, but she was even more of a ghost than he was. And it was not love through which he hoped to redeem himself, but hate. A note preserved with the text places him carrying pastelsilk between two Sirian worlds.
72446-the-writing-of-fiction:
Edith Wharton wrote The Writing of Fiction, printed at New York in 1925, given to Gaillard Lapsley, with a Traherne motto on ordering the beauty even of beauty. Contents treat fiction in general, telling a short story, constructing a novel, character and situation in the novel, and Marcel Proust.

Modern fiction began when the action of the novel moved from the street to the soul, Wharton argues at the start. La Fayette's Princesse de Clèves, a tale of hopeless love and mute renunciation in the seventeenth century, first took that step. Prévost's Manon Lescaut advanced character beyond conventional puppets of hero, heroine, and villain. Writers get a master's craft lectures.
72479-hand-book-of-punctuation:
W J Cocker wrote a Hand-Book of Punctuation for A S Barnes at New York in 1878, with instructions for capitalization, letter-writing, and proof-reading. The preface argues that punctuation, like pronunciation, rests on the usage of the best writers. Three aims guide the book.

Cocker states general rules most good writers accept, illustrates them from English classics, and notes where even the best writers differ. He answers those who say taste alone should rule, by pointing to speech: speakers differ too, yet standards hold. Some rules never vary, others bend with a writer's mind, and a few rest on taste alone. Gestures and pauses guide speakers, he says, and marks on the page must do the same work for readers.
72490-points-of-friction:
Agnes Repplier gathered ten essays in Points of Friction, published by Houghton Mifflin in 1920. Six of them, among them Living in History, Dead Authors, Consolations of the Conservative, and Money, first appeared in The Atlantic Monthly. Others came from The Century Magazine, The Yale Review, and The Nation. The titles show her range: The Cheerful Clan, The Beloved Sinner, The Strayed Prohibitionist, Woman Enthroned, Cruelty and Humour.

The first essay takes up Bagehot's words about a fatigued way of looking at great subjects, and asks why people tire of living in stirring times. Repplier writes with a clear, combative grace, defending old books, old manners, and common sense against the fashions of 1920. Her essays were among the most quoted American prose of the period.
72507-the-maugham-obsession:
August Derleth's short science fiction tale first ran in Fantastic Universe in June-July 1953. A reporter named Harrigan tells the story of Quintus Maugham, a plodding inventor in Oak Park who became fixed on one idea. Maugham built machines, and his best known work was Herman, a neat, well-oiled robot man kept in a large private lab.

Harrigan recalls being sent to interview Maugham about a small gadget made for the army. The visit led down to the lab and to Herman. The tale turns on a grim hint given at the start: Maugham was a bit too successful for his own health, and success itself is the danger here.
726-a-psychological-counter-current-in-r:
William Dean Howells wrote this essay on a shift he saw in recent fiction: against a strong tide in one direction, a counter-current was already forming. He notes how reform breeds reaction and reaction breeds reform, and how a new turn in taste often starts as a faint drift before it becomes a flood.

Howells applies this law to the novels of his day, praising the inward, psychological turn he saw rising against coarser fashion. His prose is reflective and urbane, the work of a critic watching his own age. The essay offers a short, shrewd guide to how literary fashions change, and why no single school holds the field for long.
72636-social-organization:
Social Organization, subtitled A Study of the Larger Mind, is a work of sociology by Charles Horton Cooley, professor at the University of Michigan. Charles Scribner's Sons copyrighted it in 1909 and issued this New York edition in 1911. Cooley had already published Human Nature and the Social Order.

Part one treats the primary aspects of organization, starting from mind as an organic whole. Cooley's key term is the primary group: the family, the playground, and the neighbourhood, which he calls the nursery of human nature. From these groups spring the primary ideals of loyalty, truth, service, and kindness, and the sense of a moral we. Part two turns to communication, from the rise of speech and writing to printing and the modern world. Modern communication, he argues, enlarges feeling, feeds public opinion and democracy, and still fosters individuality rather than flattening it.
72740-miles-lawson:
Miles Lawson, or The Yews, came out from Ira Bradley and Company at 162 Washington Street, Boston, without a date on its title page. Its author had written How to See the English Lakes, and a Wordsworth motto promises a homely history told for natural hearts. Seven chapters run from The Homestead to Changing Seasons.

Chapter one describes an old farm house below crags in a deep Westmoreland valley, with low windows wrapped in jasmine, rose, and ivy. Two vast yew trees, stiff and furrowed with age, shade the flagged path to the porch and give the place its name. A stone slab above the porch bears the date 1559. Miles, the oldest son, built a seat round one yew for his sister Alice.
72775-clinton:
Clinton, or Boy-Life in the Country, by Walter Aimwell, was printed at Boston by Gould and Lincoln in 1855. It is the second of the Aimwell Stories, after Oscar, and its motto runs: take heed will surely speed. The preface states the aim in plain words. The tale shows why boys need early habits of heed and work, the risk of bad mates, and the strength to say no when urged to wrong.

It also hopes to wake a taste for the calm joys of home. The first head sets Clinton at Brookdale: his duck yard, his hens, and his small books of gains. He keeps accounts, builds a duck house, and learns at home with no school. Boys of the age got farm days with a firm, kind moral in each.
72789-r-l-stevenson:
Frank Swinnerton wrote a critical study of Robert Louis Stevenson, published in London in 1914. He says the book is critical first, so the life is sketched only in outline. Chapters treat the early work, travel books, essays, and poems in turn. Plays and short stories each get a chapter of their own.

A long chapter on the novels and romances closes the main survey. A bibliography follows the conclusion. Swinnerton notes that Stevenson worked in many forms and was never held to one of them. The study gives readers of his time a map of a varied career. It still serves as a period view of his standing.
72795-weapon:
Jesse Bone wrote Weapon, a science fiction story printed in Amazing Stories in June 1961. The blurb sets the stakes. The Dauntless is one of the most powerful ships in the Confederation space navy. Yet in the showdown with the Eglani, victory will not necessarily go to the mighty. Bernklau illustrated the story.

Bone opens far from any battle, in a clean, conditioned room full of bright chatter. Ellen Fiske listens to women talking of dresses, children, and grocery bills as though there were no war. She feels what is not being said: fear, longing, grief, and hope beneath the talk. Then a spaceship's jets shriek overhead and every eye turns to the ceiling. The scene grounds the coming fight in the lives of the women who wait at home. The story asks what weapon can matter when fleets are evenly matched and courage is spent on both sides.
72820-the-man-who-won:
The Man Who Won is a novel of love and strife by Baillie Reynolds. It came out in London in the year 1905 with a Browning line at its gate. The line bids a man fight to the last for the prize of his life. The book is given to a kind friend and keen judge of her work.

A girl named Millie and two men who vie for her start the tale. A ward ship of a girl named Carol Mayne turns the plot at home. A grave rite in the war land of the south breaks the home calm. A glove thrown down, a loft, and a save fill the next stretch. A tea bout, a break of bounds, and a storm at the vicar's house crowd on. New kin, a cheat, and slurs lead the tale to its last rounds.
72825-captain-shannon:
Coulson Kernahan wrote Captain Shannon, a detective novel published by Dodd, Mead in New York in 1896. Kernahan had already written A Dead Man's Diary and A Book of Strange Sins. His mystery opens with a question: who is Captain Shannon? A manifesto by the unknown man follows, and a newspaper, the Daily Record, comes to the rescue. A murder in Fleet Street sets the hunt moving.

The narrator resolves to find Shannon himself. His trail leads through a dynamite hulk, lodgings at Canvey, and a ship called the Cuban Queen, boarded twice. A man named James Mullen crosses the path again and again, under the alias Henry Jeanes. The narrator becomes a hairdresser's assistant and loses an inquiry agent his life. Kernahan sustains the chase for thirty-one chapters, ending with Shannon's arrest. The book is a brisk specimen of the eighteen-nineties sensation novel.
72848-masterpieces-of-the-masters-of-fic:
Masterpieces of the Masters of Fiction, by William Dudley Foulke, was published by the Cosmopolitan Press at New York in 1912. Foulke's other books include Slav or Saxon, a life of Oliver P Morton, and a translation of Paul the Deacon's History of the Langobards.

The survey opens with Stevenson and Treasure Island of 1883, then runs back through the centuries. Rabelais, Cervantes, Le Sage, Defoe, Swift, and Prévost take their chapters in turn. Fielding's Tom Jones, Johnson's Rasselas, Voltaire's Candide, Sterne, and Goldsmith follow in Foulke's catalogue of typical masterpieces.
72910-on-the-art-of-writing-fiction:
On the Art of Writing Fiction gathers eleven essays by working novelists, printed at London with a title page dated 1894. Each writer takes one part of the craft. The set was made for beginners in the trade.

Norris opens on style in fiction, doubting the dogma that the main thing is to have a story to tell. Parr answers that a story to tell comes first. Walford treats the novel of manners, and Baring-Gould colour in composition. Macquoid writes on vision, Maxwell Gray on the growth of character, and Molesworth on writing for children. Church takes the historical novel, Douglas the ethical novel, and Meade the editor's standpoint.
72918-the-flight-of-the-heron:
The Flight of the Heron is a novel by Broster, first printed in 1925 at London by Heinemann. Broster also wrote Mr Rowl, The Wounded Name, and The Yellow Poppy. A motto at the front likens the heron's flight to a heavenly messenger bearing grave tidings to a waiting people, and the book is given to Violet Jacob in homage.

The contents run from a prologue, A Promise of Fair Weather, through five parts to an epilogue, Harbour of Grace. One part is named for Ewen Cameron, whose debt closes the tale. The prologue opens on a fine July morning over Loch na h-Iolaire, the Loch of the Eagle, in the West of Scotland, where fine days are none too plentiful.
72948-annihilation:
Isabel Ostrander wrote Annihilation, a tale of crime in a mean river ward. Robert M McBride and Company issued the book in New York in nineteen hundred twenty four. Ex-roundsman Timothy McCarty stands at the heart of the hunt. His nose for a wrong gait serves him as in his force days.

Rain soaks McCarty’s new seven dollar fifty derby. He walks the wet streets at nine to clear his head of books. Tenements, shacks, and great warehouses loom by the dark river. A lone man lurches ahead with a shambling, halting stride. Old police instinct wakes and McCarty quickens his pace behind. Dennis Riordan’s nose, Ching Lee’s errand, and a blue balloon mark the clues. A closed house and the breath of death deepen the case. Checkmate, the black pyre, and the last fierce end await the reader.
72991-compulsory-manumission:
Compulsory Manumission is a pamphlet on the West India question by Alexander McDonnell. John Murray published it in London in 1827. Its full title promises an examination of the actual state of that question. An advertisement opens by conceding the odds against the writer. He writes as an upholder of a condition Englishmen find repugnant, namely slavery. He asks that prejudice not preclude inquiry by readers. He claims the real and permanent welfare of the enslaved holds a conspicuous place.

The pamphlet intervenes in the British debate over emancipation in the West Indies. Its title names the policy it examines, compulsory manumission. McDonnell hopes independent members of the legislature will weigh his case. He argues a measure shown to be positively bad should draw disapproval. The work is a period document of the pro-slavery side of that argument. It shows how defenders of the system framed their appeal.
73035-compensation:
Ralph Waldo Emerson wrote an essay on the law of balance in life, first set down when he was young in thought if not in years. The Roycrofters printed it as a fine book at East Aurora, New York, in 1904, with rights held from 1903. Emerson says life itself taught the theme before the church did.

He takes aim at a sermon that put all fair pay in the next life, with the good sad here and the bad glad. Emerson argues that justice works now, in debts and credits, in work, in homes, and in how folk treat each other. Tools, bread, and street deals all serve as his proof.
73074-immigration:
Henry Pratt Fairchild wrote a study of the movement of folk into new lands and what it means for America, printed at New York in 1913. He gives the book to Albert Galloway Keller, called an inspiring teacher and constant friend. Nineteen chapters and a list of sources fill the book, with an index at the back.

Fairchild opens by placing the study of such movement inside the wider spread of mankind over the earth. Chapters then run through the colonial age, the years to 1882, and the modern age of federal law. Causes, ship terms, checks at landing, work, wages, crime, and schooling all get chapters of their own.
73090-non-technical-chats-on-iron-and-st:
Non-Technical Chats on Iron and Steel and Their Application to Modern Industry is by La Verne Spring, chief chemist and metallurgist of the Crane company at Chicago. Stokes of New York copyrighted the book in 1917. Two hundred and ninety-four illustrations and diagrams go with the chats. Spring dedicates the book to his fellow workers in the vast iron and steel industry.

A long roll of firms and books is thanked for pictures and facts, from the United States Steel Corporation to the Tennessee Coal, Iron and Railroad Company. Trade journals, handbooks, and makers across the country all lend a hand. The talk is pitched for the lay reader throughout.
73092-the-jewish-religion:
The Jewish Religion, by Friedlander, is a handbook printed in London in a second edition, revised and enlarged, in 1900. Friedlander claims little originality in his preface. He aims to reproduce the religious principles sown into his heart by his parents and cultivated by the great teachers of Israel: the Prophets, the Soferim, and their successors.

The book serves as an interpreter for readers who need help with the Scriptures and post biblical Jewish literature. It was urged on by Jacob Franklin, whose trust fund for the advancement of Judaism paid for the printing. Friedlander bids his brethren turn the matter over and over, in the words of an ancient teacher of the Mishnah.
73182-the-quest-of-iranon:
The Quest of Iranon is a tale by Lovecraft, first run in a press sheet of weird tales in March of nineteen thirty-nine. Into the stone town of Teloth walks a youth with vine in his gold hair and a torn robe of deep hue. The men of that town are dark and stern, with square houses and no song. They ask his name and his wealth.

He calls himself Iranon, a singer from a far town he scarce recalls yet seeks to find once more. His wealth is in small dreams and hopes, sung in yards past moon rise. The stern men bid him sing in the square, though they scorn his robe and his youth. Most yawn or laugh at his songs of youth dreams, since he tells naught of use.
73188-possession:
Louis Bromfield wrote this novel, first printed by Stokes in 1925. Nine printings ran from September 1925 to May 1926 in New York. Bromfield gives the book to Mary with a long, grave note. It says life is hard for children with no frontier left.

They stand with backs to the rough middle west, faces east. They belong to neither world, lost between two lives, he writes. A second quote warns that trouble follows a cursed, gifted woman. Grandpa Tolliver reads Gibbon in October twilight as the tale opens. The ponderous Gibbon volume lay too heavy for his hands to hold up.
73211-the-technic-of-the-baton:
The Technic of the Baton, a handbook for students of conducting by Albert Stoessel, carries a preface by Walter Damrosch. Carl Fischer of New York copyrighted the book in 1920. The first chapter sketches how conducting grew, starting from a terse definition in Grove's Dictionary of music.

Stoessel holds that a performance rises only to the level of the conductor's grasp of the score. A good conductor, he says, draws good results from lesser players, while a poor one can throw the finest orchestra into confusion. The gap between grasp and hearing is what the art must cross. The handbook speaks to students of conducting throughout its pages.
73217-mission:
John Hollis Mason lands an alien scout on Earth in a tale from Science Fiction Quarterly, Spring 1942. The headnote gives the invader's thought away: it would be so easy to conquer these primitive creatures.

A gold-glowing cylinder stands on a grassy plain. Two still figures lie before it, one strange and one more human. Krai lands at the forest edge. His stalked eyes, set a foot long, turn in all directions. He is barely four feet high, with a tapering, triangular body. Earth gravity troubles him at first. He seeks a village of tree-dwellers he saw from the air. A portable pressure projector serves as his tool and weapon. The tale views mankind through cold alien eyes.
73231-the-great-implication:
Stanley Lee wrote this science fiction tale, The Great Implication, printed in the August 1961 number of Amazing Stories, with pictures by Finlay. A blurb at the head gives its hook: Pendelton outlined an experiment to test the existence of the God-idea, and the question then became whether the experiment was Pendelton's idea, or God's.

Pendelton opens by insulting his hosts. Blackburn and Shaheen are accomplished physicists with a time machine under construction, and he tells them, smiling, that they know nothing about time travel. They are babes in the temporal woods, he says, no better than the science fiction writers they scorn. They hear him out only because he carries a letter from a department head, and because throwing him out looks harder than listening.
73304-tongues-of-the-moon:
Tongues of the Moon is a science fiction story by Philip Jose Farmer, printed in Amazing Stories for September 1961. Its premise is stated up front: Earth was dying, and possibly the only human beings left in the universe were those on the Moon. On this last outpost the age-old controversy between ideologies continued.

Through the dome in the centre of the crater of Eratosthenes, men and women watch pin-points of light blossom on the shadowy face of Earth. The flares can be located as London, Paris, Brussels, Copenhagen, Leningrad, Rome, and Athens. Then a flare near Moscow spreads out and out. At a reception for South Atlantic Axis officers, Soviet North American officers move to defend themselves. The Axes pull small automatics and flat bombs from clips within their caps. Farmer carries the Cold War to the Moon and lets it end there in fire.
73316-the-justice-of-gideon:
Eleanor Gates, author of The Plow-Woman and The Biography of a Prairie Girl, collected these tales in a 1910 Macaulay volume from New York. The title story opens in the place of Justice at Manzanita, a little town in northern California. The courtroom is a low, square, cloth-and-papered room, bare but for the judge's pine desk, two chairs for constable and prisoner, and four benches. A squat stove stands in its sawdust box though it is midsummer.

One bright spot hangs behind the desk: the flag, draped in careful folds against the fly-specked wall. The judge sits with his coat off, legs stretched into the prisoner's dock, deep in a calf-bound law book while pipe smoke rolls across its pages. Twelve more tales follow, from Doc and The Boomerang to Yee Wing the powder-man and The Revenge of Manuelita.
73324-sun-and-moon:
Sun and Moon is a novel by Vincent H. Gowen, published in Boston in 1927 by Little, Brown and Company. It was issued as an Atlantic Monthly Press book. The dedication is to a mess group in China and to the memory of friends who can never gather again. The first chapter opens in a July garden.

Sunbeams fall through locust branches onto a courtyard pool in that opening scene. The setting is China, with flagged courtyards, trumpet flowers, and a walled garden after summer rain.
