The novel follows life in that world of expatriate messes and Chinese households. Gowen writes in a slow, rich descriptive style, as the first pages show.
73382-into-the-fourth-dimension:
Into the Fourth Dimension is a science fiction novel by Ray Cummings, reprinted from Science Fiction Quarterly for winter 1941 and 1942. A blurb asks if other worlds exist side by side with ours, yet unseen and unsuspected. Three people go through the wall that bars the way.

An editor note says the magazine reprints the famous novel at many requests. Chapter one is named the Ghosts of 46. The first of the ghosts made its appearance in February of 1946. It was seen just after nightfall near the bank of a little stream known as Otter Creek, a few miles from Rutland, Vermont. Heavy snow was on the ground, and willows line the creek bank. It seemed the figure of a man standing with folded arms. Space tale fans get a doorway into a shadow realm.
73383-the-great-illusion:
Manly Bannister wrote The Great Illusion, a science fiction tale from Super-Science Fiction in February 1957, illustrated by Kelly Freas. Something phony marks the whole set-up on the planet Hume: their culture is counterfeit. Cliff Rowley, a lean survey man sweating in a tent, glares at a communicator as orders arrive.

Commander Spliid, in the survey ship far above the atmosphere, gives Hume a final closed-world classification and a week to clear out. Only eleven men work the field, and Rowley is the odd ball, the survey's only psi-sensitive on the planet. Top rating trusts what he cannot do more than what he can, Spliid admits with calm. Rowley begs for months and gets seven days.
73389-miss-con:
Agnes Giberne wrote a tale for girls, drawn by her kin Edgar Giberne, which had reached its ninth thousand in London printings. The preface makes no excuse for one more tale of everyday girl life. Modern girlhood, she says, still hungers for such books. The tale also speaks to girls who write, or hope to write, for print.

Contents name Constance Conway, whose short name gives the book its title. Chapters treat sentiments, flashing gems, train fancies, and a mother's swans. Thyrsa's small room, Maggie's tries at writing, and a publisher all play their parts. Later heads promise glad news, a storm, strange holes, and plain advice not gladly taken.
73410-colour-vision:
Abney wrote this science book, Colour Vision, printed at New York with a coloured plate and many diagrams. Its title page states its origin: lectures given in 1894 at a London institution of science. Abney, a former officer of engineers, had worked for years on the subject with a general, and sat on a royal society committee on colour vision.

Contents run from the eye itself to the testing of the colour blind. Simple colours and their mixture come first, then the claim that three colour sensations may serve, and two rival theories of the seeing of colour, named for Young and for Hering. Chapters follow on the brightness of colours across the eye, on tobacco blindness, and on blindness from disease. A preface owns the limit of three one-hour lectures: the treatment keeps to what a physicist can best explain.
73411-doctor-dolittle-in-the-moon:
Hugh Lofting told and illustrated Doctor Dolittle in the Moon, first under copyright in 1928 and reissued in 1956. The book sends the doctor who talks to animals farther than any earlier volume: to the Moon itself. His party lands on a new world of colors and perfumes, and the young narrator Stubbins tells the tale.

Twenty-five chapters follow the landing. Chee-Chee the monkey turns hero in a thirst crisis, and Polynesia the parrot scouts from the air. The travelers cross a moon lake, find a giant's tracks, and study plant languages among singing trees. Later they meet a council and its president, and learn how Otho Bludge came to the Moon and made himself a king. The doctor even opens a surgery there before the party returns to Puddleby.
7344-archibald-malmaison:
Julian Hawthorne's Archibald Malmaison opens with a child's wish that fairy stories were true, set against an adult's preference for acknowledged fiction. Hawthorne calls the inconsistency more apparent than real. Experience teaches that the greater the fairy story, the less the truth, and the greater the truth, the less the fairy story, since romance's graces clash with fact's crude straightforwardness.

Childhood idealism, he writes, believes the most beautiful must on that account be most true, and the novel tests that belief in a strange tale. Hawthorne, author of Garth, Sebastian Strome, and Dust, writes in his father's shadow yet with his own eerie touch. The book invites readers to weigh wonder against truth.
7350-how-to-prepare-and-serve-a-meal-and:
Lillian B. Lansdown joins two household arts in one volume: how to prepare and serve a meal, and interior decoration. The meal chapters run from before the meal is served and the waitress's entrance through breakfast, luncheons, and informal home dinner. Formal dinner, afternoon teas, and suppers follow, with carving hints, menu planning, and menus for Thanksgiving, Christmas, and Lent, including a chapter outside the Eighteenth Amendment.

Decoration follows, on lines and curves, form, colour, and proportion, then on single rooms: living room, drawing room, library, bedroom, nursery, play room, and hints on period furniture. Lansdown writes for a hostess who must feed guests well and house them beautifully. The book makes domestic craft orderly and gracious.
73566-aeroplane-construction:
Sydney Camm wrote Aeroplane Construction, a handbook on the methods and details of building aeroplanes. Crosby Lockwood and Son published it at London in 1919. Camm was an associate fellow of the Royal Aeronautical Society. Fifteen chapters divide the work. Materials come first, then spars and struts. Plane construction and its details follow. Interplane strut connections and wing-trussing systems come next.

Fuselage construction and fittings fill the middle chapters. Undercarriage types and details, control systems, and wires follow. Engine mountings come late, and erection and alignment close the book. Camm's introduction sets the aim: construction, not design, though first principles enter where needed. The aeroplane looks flimsy, he owns, but it solves a hard problem. Maximum strength for minimum weight demands the best engineering procedure, he argues.
73647-the-psychology-of-speculation:
The Psychology of Speculation, the human element in stock market transactions, by Henry Howard Harper, was privately printed in Boston in 1926, with drawings by Haydon Jones. Harper lists a shelf of his own books, all out of print, from Booklovers to The Devils' Nest. A purpose note opens the study in plain terms.

Many men, Harper says, know much about the market yet cannot beat it, because they know too little about themselves. Others know their limits and leave the monster alone. As one should learn to swim before deep water, so one should learn the market's dangers first. His aim is not to bar anyone from trade, but to mark the stumbling blocks that trip speculators and even investors.
73652-the-whys-and-wherefores-of-navigat:
The Whys and Wherefores of Navigation is a textbook by Gershom Bradford 2d. D Van Nostrand published it in New York in 1918. Bradford served as navigating officer and senior instructor on the schoolship Newport. He had also been a nautical expert at the Hydrographic Office. He dedicates the book to the American sub-patrol, whose war-zone record he admired.

The opening chapter starts with the compass. A mariner must convert courses between points, degrees in quadrants, and the full circle. Dead reckoning follows, with its corrections for variation, deviation, current, and wind. Later chapters take up nautical astronomy and time. Latitude and longitude each get a chapter. The Sumner method, including the new navigation, fills a long one. The moon and charts close the course. Bradford insists that navigation is an art of estimating position, and that the gift for it is partly born in the man.
73760-laddie-and-miss-toosey-s-mission:
Laddie and Miss Toosey Mission was published at Philadelphia, copyright 1897. A frontispiece shows Miss Toosey herself. The first story, Laddie, opens at a railway station, in a rush of guard shouts. Third class forward, here you are, mum; plenty of room this way.

Doors bang, a whistle blows, and the train moves off. The guard has thrust into a third class carriage, already nearly full, a bandbox with a blue spotted handkerchief round it. A marketing basket, a bundle, a pale green umbrella, and pattens follow. Oh yes: an old woman belonged to the things. She was so small and frightened that she might easily have been overlooked altogether. Readers get a Victorian temperance era tale of a tiny traveller and her goods.
7377-five-lectures-on-reincarnation:
Swami Abhedananda, a disciple of Ramakrishna who taught Vedanta in the West, sets out the Hindu doctrine of rebirth in five plain lectures. He begins with the body itself: the gross physical body, he argues, expresses a subtle body, a minute germ of living substance carrying mind and vital force in potential form. Birth, growth, decay, and death follow the changes of that subtle body.

From that basis the lectures explain how the soul passes from life to life, carrying its tendencies forward like a seed carrying a plant. The talks draw on Vedanta philosophy while keeping the language direct, so readers new to the subject can follow the argument. The book serves as a clear, short introduction to reincarnation as taught in the Hindu tradition.
73811-american-painting-and-its-traditio:
John C Van Dyke traces the line of American painting through nine masters in a Scribner volume dated October 1919. Twenty-four plates back the talks, first given as university lectures in New York. Van Dyke had written Art for Art's Sake and The Meaning of Pictures before this survey.

Names on the title page run from Inness, Wyant, and Martin to Homer, La Farge, and Whistler. Chase, Alexander, and Sargent close the list of nine who carry the tradition in Van Dyke's view. Contents open with The Art Tradition in America at page one, in the part shown. Ads list his guides to old masters in twelve volumes and his nature books — The Desert, The Opal Sea, and The Mountain — in the same house style.
73834-a-first-book-in-organic-evolution:
First Book in Organic Evolution, by Kerfoot Shute, is a primer on evolution. Open Court of Chicago issued the book in eighteen ninety nine. Shute taught anatomy at Columbian University and served as an eye surgeon. He wrote the book chiefly for medical students at that university.

The preface calls the book an introduction only to the Development Theory. Shute hopes the subject is made clear and of interest to all readers. A front plate shows a wild rock pigeon bred into a large pouter. That change within known times shows how plastic a living form is. Evolution, he notes, has reshaped views of man origin and fate.
73923-my-larger-education:
Garden City publishers issued Booker Washington's 'My Larger Education' in 1911, being chapters from his experience, with a new portrait as frontispiece. Washington, author of 'Up From Slavery,' opens by saying he has been associated all his life with a hard, perplexing, but important problem. What once seemed a misfortune, being born poor, became the ground of his education.

Chapter titles name his teachers: learning from men and things, building a school around a problem, and some exceptional men. He writes of reporters and newspapers, of the intellectuals and the Boston mob, and of a commencement oration on cabbages. Colonel Roosevelt gets a chapter, Denmark another, and the book ends with the mistakes and the future of Negro education. Photographs show Hampton and Tuskegee at work.
73955-marigold-s-decision:
Agnes Giberne wrote Marigold's Decision, a tale put out by James Nisbet of London in 1896. Lance drew the plates for the book. It opens in a small, damp house where no nail will hold in the thin walls. Josiah Plunkett, a carpenter with long, strong arms, calls for his girl Marigold. He has done his best to mend the poor home from inside. Marigold comes late, eggs in hand.

Chapter names trace a path through service, a guest, and trouble for the mother of the house. A late-night scene and a bold step lead toward a close marked Not So Bad. Giberne wrote many tales for the young, such as Miss Con and Decima's Promise. This one turns on a girl's choice in a plain, hard-pressed home, and on love that holds such a home in one piece.
7404-john-james-audubon:
John Burroughs, himself a famous American naturalist, writes the life of the man who painted America's birds. The pioneer before Audubon was Alexander Wilson, a Scottish weaver turned poet. He emigrated in 1794 and described more than three hundred species before his death in 1813. Audubon did not simply continue Wilson's work; he began again, as a pioneer in his own right.

Burroughs stresses what the two men shared. Both were famous walkers, covering hundreds of miles on foot. Both loved nature at first hand rather than from books, and both kept journals of their wanderings. The book follows Audubon from his studies and drawings of birds to his place as chief of American ornithologists. It is a naturalist's tribute to a naturalist, warm and well informed.
74076-the-reign-of-king-oberon:
Reign of King Oberon is a gathering of fairy tales, edited by Walter Jerrold. Charles Robinson drew the pictures. The book belongs to a set called The True Annals of Fairyland. London, Toronto, and New York houses issued it together. A foreword by the editor opens the book, before a dedication to his children.

Some of these stories a reader may have met before, the editor owns. Most of our best writers have been made free of Fairyland, he says. Andersen and the Brothers Grimm are named among them. Tales by Ben Jonson, Perrault, and Hood stand in the company too. Old or new, the tales keep the endless youth of the fairies themselves, he writes. A poem of a fairy ring follows, where Titania's court held its revels. As long as we can truly enjoy them we shall not grow old, the editor says.
7412-coningsby-or-the-new-generation:
Benjamin Disraeli wrote Coningsby in 1844, between his early novels and his later career as prime minister, and it is his great political novel. Its hero, Harry Coningsby, grows up in early nineteenth-century England. Educated among the young men of his class, he must find his way in a political world of parties, patronage, and reform. The title names the theme: a new generation coming to power.

Disraeli, himself a young politician turned novelist, writes from inside the world he describes. The novel mixes drawing-room comedy with serious argument about what England should become after the Reform era. Readers meet ambitious young men, powerful patrons, and the clash of old Toryism with new ideas. It remains the classic novel of English politics in the 1830s.
74129-the-history-of-the-twentieth-light:
History of the Twentieth Light Division is a unit history by Captain V E Inglefield, first published in nineteen twenty one. An introduction by the Earl of Cavan stands at its front. A portrait of the division's general serves as the frontispiece. The contents map the division's war from its formation to the final advance.

Chapters cover training in England, then the Laventie sector and the Ypres salient. The Somme takes two chapters, with winter in that area and the German retreat after. Third Ypres and Cambrai follow, then the Menin Road sector. The German offensives of nineteen eighteen fill two long chapters. The book opens by noting the declaration of war in August nineteen fourteen.
74139-the-woman-obsession:
William Campbell Gault wrote this short science fiction tale, printed in Fantastic Universe in September 1954. In its future world, women are few and are kept for scientists. Love is unknown, and a device called the Massago-Lust serves in its place.

Johnny 'Horse' Collins, once a star football player, is now one of only three Level-One navigators in the galaxy. He flies the Mars-Jupiter run for Gideon Shipping, Inc. Yet he still dreams of women and of a fuller life. His pilot friend thinks him a fool, and their talks drive the tale. The story first ran as a magazine tale, short and sharp in the pulp style of its day.
74176-from-berlin-to-bagdad-and-babylon:
The Reverend J A Zahm, who also wrote as H J Mozans, published this travel book with Appleton in 1922. He dedicated it to Charles Schwab and his wife, in whose home his books of a quarter century were begun or finished. Verses from Saadi, paraphrased by Edwin Arnold, stand as motto.

The foreword sets the route: from one of Europe's greatest capitals to the crumbling remains of Asia's greatest ancient one. It is the road of the migrations and the armies, from Ashurbanipal, Darius, and Alexander to Harun-al-Rashid and von der Goltz. Zahm traveled not as a tourist but as a student of the peoples' present condition, social, economic, religious, and intellectual. His earlier journeys took him up the Orinoco and down the Amazon.
74215-fire-of-retribution:
Fire of Retribution, by Laurence Donovan, is a flying tale about a fire trapped logging crew. A front note sets the feat: for a man who never flew before to step from an airplane into space, thousands of feet above the earth, takes nerve. Yet old Beth knew that was the only slim chance for his men.

Slow timed fire bombs started the blaze, and the crew ran onto one that had not exploded. Whoever did it knew a cross fire would trap the men at camp. Old Beth reckons the boys could fly round the fire before it hits camp. He has never been up in a plane, but he has heard a man can be dropped with a parachute. Nick Mims, fire patrol pilot, demurs at first, because orders are orders. Readers get a pulp rescue tale of fire and air.
74250-yoga-as-philosophy-and-religion:
Surendranath Dasgupta, professor of philosophy at Presidency College, Calcutta, and author of A History of Indian Philosophy, wrote Yoga as Philosophy and Religion, published at London in 1924. He dedicates the book to the Maharaja Sir Manindrachandra Nundy, whose patronage fed his zeal for learning in a time of need.

Book one treats Yoga metaphysics: Prakriti, Purusha, the reality of the external world, and the process of evolution. The evolution of the categories, change of qualities, and evolution and God follow. Book two turns to Yoga ethics and practice, opening with mind and moral states and the theory of karma. Readers get the system expounded by a leading Indian scholar for Western readers.
74251-in-ship-and-prison:
In Ship and Prison, by William Pendleton Chipman, was printed in 1908. Saalfield issued the tale at New York, Akron, and Chicago. Arthur de Bebian drew the pictures. Its subtitle gives the frame: five years in the Continental Navy with Captain Samuel Tucker. A front picture shows a threat of forty blows for a missed shot. Twenty three chapters make the story. The narrator goes in search of Captain Tucker, then defies him. A first taste of a British prison comes early. Prizes, a captured frigate, and a distinguished passenger follow.

Halifax prison, Charleston taken, and an escape mark the later heads. The author's note pleads Tucker's case. Other heroes got monuments and biographies, Chipman writes. Tucker, who took more prizes than almost any naval hero of the age, lies in a neglected grave.
74310-lucia-in-london:
Benson wrote Lucia in London, a novel printed at Garden City in 1928, continuing the famed Queen Lucia and Miss Mapp books. Philip Lucas's aunt died early in April at eighty-three, after seven years bedridden in a private asylum. Friends reasonably hoped the Lucases would not treat the loss as an intolerable tragedy.

Mrs Quantock of Riseholme sends a neat note of condolence that hints at a happy release without the words. She instructs her parlour maid to wait for any reply, hoping for a vague hint about the inheritance expectations. All Riseholme is dying to know what the will may bring Lucia. Social comedy of the sharpest Benson kind follows.
74324-the-heart-of-london:
Morton wrote this love letter to London for Methuen, who first printed it on June 11, 1925. The Heart of London ran to a third edition by 1926. A line from Davidson heads it: an ever-muttering prisoned storm, the heart of London beating warm.

The New Romance opens the walks. Where the Eagles Sleep and Petticoat Lane, marked Oriental, follow. Ships Come Home walks the docks; Treasure Trove walks the Caledonian market. Cenotaph stands in lone state among the pieces. Faces in the Strand, women and tea, and an open door at St Martin's fill the middle. Morton walks by night and day, through fog, markets, and crowds, and finds a tale on each street.
74375-piebald-rats-and-selection:
Castle and John Phillips report a set of breeding tests with piebald rats, printed in Washington in 1914. The Carnegie Institution issued the work. It came from the genetics work at the Bussey Institution and the station at Cold Spring Harbor, New York. The test asks if picking parents can shift a trait, and if Mendel's purity idea holds.

Rats were bred in plus and minus lines by the amount of color in their coats. Other crosses used wild rats and black Irish rats. The book gives full tables, plates, and a summary of results. A long discussion weighs what the numbers mean for how traits pass from parent to young.
74378-remarks-on-a-passage-from-the-rive:
Remarks on a Passage from the River Balise is a travel account by Lieutenant Cook, printed at London in seventeen sixty nine. Cook made the trip by order of Admiral Sir William Burnaby of Jamaica. He carried dispatches to the governor of Yucatan. The trip ran from the Balise river in the Bay of Honduras to Merida, capital of that province.

The concern of the trip was the logwood cutters in the bay, in February and March seventeen sixty five. The first part of the route is by water, coast ways to the Rio Hondo. It then runs through an arm of that river to lagoons and a lake. Flat land, mangrove trees, and small islands mark the coast in his telling.
7441-the-writings-of-john-burroughs-volu:
John Burroughs named this volume for the stream of his boyhood. Pepacton is the Indian name of his native stream in the hills where he was born and where his kindred sleep. The name is said to mean marriage of the waters, and Burroughs likes the fit: the book is itself a union of many currents, essays gathered from years of walking and watching.

The chapters include footpaths, a bunch of herbs, and the ways of birds and beasts along the water. Burroughs writes as a neighbor of nature, not a distant scientist, finding lessons in common sights. Readers of his earlier volumes will recognize the voice at once: plain, observant, and rooted in one beloved countryside, the watershed that made him a naturalist.
7443-windy-mcpherson-s-son:
Sherwood Anderson dedicated this novel to the living men and women of his own Middle Western home town, and it begins there. Sam McPherson is thirteen, tall and big-boned, walking the board platform of Caxton, a little corn-shipping town in Iowa, on a long summer twilight evening. He walks with extreme deliberateness, lifting his bare feet with care, a boy already taking his own measure.

The novel follows Sam from that platform into manhood, as the son of Windy McPherson, the town talker, tries to make his own way in the world of business and ambition. Anderson writes about the price of success and the pull of home, in the plain Midwestern voice that would soon make Winesburg, Ohio famous. It is a novel of growing up in small-town America.
74435-the-champion:
Charles Egbert Craddock, the pen name of Mary Murfree, wrote this novel, published by Houghton Mifflin in 1902. It opens inside a southwestern city's daily newspaper, where the devil is looking out of the window.

The devil is a printer's devil, a small imp whose beguiling chirp of copy links the composing room to the editors. He shows his friend Peter Bateman the plant: the type-setting machine, still a novelty, and the rinktum where the writer sits alone, unable to work if anyone gabs at him. The illustration's caption cries: I can't hide it, I burnt the copy. Murfree, famous for her Tennessee mountain tales, turns to a newspaper office. Readers get a comedy of the press room floor.
74466-first-through-the-grand-canyon:
Major John Wesley Powell led the first boat expedition down the Colorado River through the Grand Canyon in 1869 and 1870, and this book is his record of that pioneer exploration. Horace Kephart edited the narrative for the Outing Publishing Company in 1915. The chapters run from Green River City through Flaming Gorge and the Canyon of Lodore. They pass Echo Park, reach the junction of the Grand and the Green, and then enter the Grand Canyon itself.

Powell begins with the whole river system, from the alpine lakes near Long's Peak to the Gulf of California, some two thousand miles of stream. The account mixes survey work with adventure: rapids, cliffs, and country no white man had passed through before. It remains the classic telling of the first run of the Colorado.
74484-the-octoroon:
The Octoroon is a novel by Braddon, the famed hand of tale of crime and love in the age past. It came out at Chicago from a house of cheap books. Its first part is named for a young slave girl at its heart.

Its first scene is a ball in a great square of London. The last notes of a loved waltz ring through the fine rooms of a rich house. Bright eyes and gems flash in the lamp light. The queens of rank and grace shine side by side in the crowd. Rich scent of far blooms floats on the air. Brave men and fair women have met for a parting ball, for a rich dame of America who sails for the south with her niece.
74638-tension:
Tension is a novel by Delafield, author of Zella Sees Herself. Macmillan published it in New York in October of the year 1920. Delafield also wrote The Pelicans and Consequences before this tale. A mock dedication to a maternal parent supplements an early unfinished effort. The tale opens with a cry: Auntie Iris has written a book.

Two auditors echo the news in keys of astonishment and of dismay. The book will be published, bound in blue, sold, and bring heaps of money. Lady Rossiter asks its title with a gloomy, apprehensive eye fixed near. It is called Why, Ben, a Story of the Sexes, the niece declares. Family pride, snobbery, and letters supply the tension of the title.
7472-the-duke-of-stockbridge-a-romance-o:
Edward Bellamy, later famous for Looking Backward, wrote this romance of Shays' Rebellion from his own Berkshire ground. It opens on August 17, 1777, as the first sunbeams glance down the long valley of Stockbridge, where the Housatonic creeps around the base of Fisher's Nest. The village, with its wide grassy streets, rail fences, and low houses, is drawn with loving local knowledge.

From the march of the minute men, the story moves through the Revolution toward the postwar years, when debt and taxes drove Massachusetts farmers to rebellion under Daniel Shays. Bellamy follows Stockbridge folk through those troubles, mixing romance with history. The novel gives a local, human view of a rising that shook the young republic and helped bring on the Constitution.
74827-the-yankee-mining-squadron:
Captain Reginald Belknap, who commanded the squadron, tells how American ships laid the North Sea mine barrage. The Naval Institute at Annapolis published The Yankee Mining Squadron in 1920, with copyrights in 1919 and 1920. Twenty-four chapters end with a summary of mines laid and a look at the force after the war.

Belknap opens at morning colours off Scotland, with green slopes, the Firth, and snow capped Ben Wyvis in view. Chapters cover bases in Scotland, the supply and handling of mines, and the first laying trip. Thirteen fields in all crossed the sea, the first thirteen minefields being American, as the front chart shows.
74871-on-the-phenomena-of-variation-and-:
On the Phenomena of Variation and Geographical Distribution is a paper by Alfred Wallace, read before the Linnean Society on March 17, 1864. It was printed in the society's Transactions, volume twenty five. Wallace studies the swallowtail butterflies of the Malayan region to test how species vary and spread. Eight plates of figures go with the text.

He begins by noting that all groups of animals offer endless matter for study. Yet groups differ greatly in value for tracing how kinds are spread across the earth. Some range too narrowly, others lack varied forms, and many lack full study over their whole ground. Groups loved by collectors give the best material, he argues. These butterflies add wings of endless pattern, colour, and texture, varying more than those of any other insects. The paper stands beside Wallace's famed work on natural selection.
74873-poems-of-reflection:
Ella Wheeler Wilcox published a book of poems of reflection at Chicago under a copyright of 1905. Some sixty pieces fill the contents, from Bohemia and Life to Whatever Is, Is Best. Her better-known books of passion and pleasure are listed on the title page as her credentials.

The opening poem praises Bohemia, whose unmapped borders many cross with half-reluctant feet, to find delights more wholesome than the elite's. No pretense or stilted pride thrives there, it says; all creeds have room, and all worship together at art's sacred shrine. Other pieces treat the king and the siren, a tribute to the sculptor Vinnie Ream, and the doomed city's prayer. Wilcox writes for the heart, plainly.
74928-cycling-art-energy-and-locomotion:
Robert P Scott wrote on the growth of bicycles, tricycles, and man-driven carriages. J B Lippincott Company issued the book at Philadelphia in 1889, with many pictures. Scott gave the work to the Baltimore Cycle Club and its members. Old patent plates, such as one from 1830, show early forms.

Scott grants that cycle books had sold poorly next to the size of the sport. He aims to spur close study of the art, even at the cost of dry parts. Force, build, and motion get full, careful treatment. Riders and makers of the boom years gain a deep look at how their machines grew.
74934-poems-of-evolution:
E Haldeman-Julius edited Poems of Evolution as Little Blue Book 71. His company issued it at Girard, Kansas in 1924. Langdon Smith leads the poets gathered. William Herbert Carruth's short verse fronts the set. A fire mist and a planet start his lines. A crystal and a cell come next.

Some call the long chain evolution, Carruth ends. Some call it God, his last line says. Smith's long poem Evolution follows in full. A tadpole and a fish open its tale of love. Two lovers sprawl in Paleozoic slime there. They die and wake as amphibians later. Drift and mold hold their forms between lives. Cheap pocket verse on Darwin's theme shows how deep the new science had sunk into common song by the 1920s.
75144-a-boys-life-of-booker-t-washington:
Boys' Life of Booker T. Washington is a biography for young readers. Jackson, a history professor at Greensboro, wrote the life in brief. Macmillan published it in New York in June of the year 1922. A symbolic group erected at Tuskegee Institute in 1922 fronts the book. Jackson thanks Doubleday for leave to quote Stowe's life of Washington.

He hopes some boy will rise in ambition from reading these pages. Chapters run from early childhood and boyhood days to planning an education. School days at Hampton and a return there as teacher follow in order. Building a great school forms the heart of the Washington story told. Boys got a model of self help and race uplift in plain terms.
75200-the-man-of-iron:
The Man of Iron, a novel by Richard Dehan, was copyrighted by Stokes in February 1915. Grosset and Dunlap of New York published this edition. Dehan had written Between Two Thieves and The Dop Doctor before it. The tale opens when Patrick Carolan Breagh attains the age of six years.

The boy is tall enough to see his scarlet curls in a big mirror. His stepmother’s toilet table holds that shining glass in the first scene. He needs no tin bonnet box to stand on, the narrator smiles. In one brief half hour hidden under a Pembroke table, his fate turns. There he gains more knowledge of life and death than childhood should hold. Dehan builds an Irish tale of a hard man from that small beginning.
7523-the-lady-of-the-decoration:
Frances Little tells this novel in letters, and the first is dated San Francisco, July 30, 1901. Its writer calls herself a soldier on the eve of battle, whistling in a stuffy hotel room to keep her courage up. In the morning she sails for the Flowery Kingdom, Japan, after years in which roses never strewed her path at home. A crowd of loving, tearful faces fades as her train pulls out.

Behind her lies a sudden release: death put an end to a bondage, and a kindergarten course, taken to please a friend and keep her mind off things, pointed a new way. The letters that follow trace a young American woman making a life abroad, among strangers, schools, and ceremonies. Little dedicates the book to all good sisters, and to hers in particular.
75233-dragon-moon:
Dragon Moon, a novelette by Henry Kuttner, ran in Weird Tales in January 1941. Kuttner bills it as a tale of lost Atlantis. Its hero is Elak of Atlantis, a lean, wolf faced adventurer. His companion Lycon is a fat little man with a heavy purse and a sour temper.

The scene opens in a wharf side tavern at Poseidonia, full of seamen, wine, and cooking smoke. Elak quarrels with a huge sea captain over a tavern wench. Behind the brawl looms Karkora, the Pallid One, a presence from outside the world that rots the souls of kings. The tale mixes swordplay with cosmic dread.
75262-calvin-morgan-mcclung-historical-c:
The Calvin Morgan McClung Historical Collection catalog, printed at Knoxville in 1921, lists a great private library given to the Lawson McGhee Library. McClung was born May 12, 1855, and died March 12, 1919. Collecting the history of his own state and city filled his later years. His widow presented the books, pamphlets, manuscripts, pictures and maps to the library.

Laura Luttrell and Mary Rothrock compiled the catalog, arranged by author or by title keyword. Sections cover books and pamphlets, Knoxville items apart, then manuscripts, pictures, maps and newspapers. The subjects are early western travel and the history and genealogy of Tennessee and other southern states. Entries give place, printer, year and page counts.
75309-paul-ralston:
Mary Holmes wrote Paul Ralston, a novel printed at New York in 1897. Holmes also wrote Lena Rivers, Gretchen, Marian Grey, Meadow Brook, and Tempest and Sunshine. Contents open with Miss Phebe Hansford, Paul Ralston, Paul's news, the Percys, Clarice, and Elithe's photograph, then move to Samona and a stranger at Deep Gulch.

Shadows fall and deepen, a tragedy strikes, and chapters run through a funeral, an arrest, prison, and two days of trial. Free, excitement, a second trial, and a last glimpse of Oak City close the long contents list. Phebe Hansford stands in her cottage doorway in May, watching the early boat come slowly up in chapter one. Sentimental fiction readers get Holmes.
75381-wreck-of-the-london:
Wreck of the London is a full account of a famed sea disaster, issued in London in a second, revised form. The publisher begs word from any who had kin or friends aboard, a sign of how fresh the loss still was. The year 1866 had opened with a grim run of storms and wrecks on all coasts.

The London was one of the finest ships of the Wigram line, with a rich cargo and, it was first said, more than three hundred souls aboard. She foundered in the Bay of Biscay, and first word said not one soul had lived. Parts treat her captain, a minister named Draper among the guests, three days and nights of danger, last words, and the few who got away.
7539-quotes-and-images-from-chesterfield:
Lord Chesterfield's letters to his son, written between 1766 and 1771, are the classic manual of eighteenth-century worldliness. This volume gathers their most quotable passages with images. The quotations run in alphabetical order, so a reader can browse advice the way one browses a dictionary of conduct. Each entry is short enough to carry away and use.

The advice is unmistakable Chesterfield. A little learning is a dangerous thing, and a joker is near akin to a buffoon. A favor may make an enemy while an injury may make a friend. Above all, keep absolute command of your temper, avoid speaking of yourself, and never be vehement about trifles. The collection distills a father's worldly wisdom into its sharpest sentences.
75471-rhoda-s-education:
Rhoda's Education, or Too Much of a Good Thing, is a girls' story by Lucy Ellen Guernsey. The American Sunday-School Union published it at Philadelphia in 1873. It belongs to the Boonville series. Nineteen chapters carry Rhoda from little brother to the end. Aunt Hannah, a growing cloud, and the change open the tale. A new life and a Miss Brown follow in order.

Affairs at Boonville and a new home fill the middle chapters. A chapter explains the origin of the harp. An old enemy and a new friend arrive in turn. What a bit of soap did gives one chapter its curious title. The preface insists the tale's most improbable incidents are literally true. Guernsey says the book fails if its moral is not plain. School and Doctor Douglass close the cast.
75589-the-dark-eyes-of-london:
The Dark Eyes of London is a crime novel by Edgar Wallace, issued by Doubleday, Doran for the Crime Club in 1929. Its jacket names the terror: a gang of blind giants in London's foulest corners. Inspector Larry Holt challenges them to a monstrous game in the dark.

Forty-five chapters open with Larry Holt in Paris and bring him to Sir John Hason. Titles promise a will, writing in braille, and a telegram from Calgary. Fanny Weldon, Flash Fred, and Diana Ward move through the chapters. One chapter announces that John Dearborn is not blind, and asks who runs Dearborn. The first scene seats Holt at the Café de la Paix, watching the boulevard crowds in sunshine.
75596-the-belle-of-a-season:
The Countess of Blessington wrote The Belle of a Season, a poem issued in London in 1840. Drawings are by A E Chalon, painter to the Queen, under Charles Heath. An introduction in verse tells readers what the poem will not hold. There is no wild romance, no terror, no scowling villain, and no poisoned cup.

Instead, the heroine Mary lives in scenes of real life, much like the readers themselves. Blessington says any reader may see her own portrait in Mary, save for hair or eye colour. The poem opens at noon in spring, with primrose, violet, and laburnum in bloom. An ancient hall looks out on the fresh green scene. The hope held out is that Mary, and her readers, may soon be blessed as wives.
75687-the-cycles-of-speculation:
Cycles of Speculation is a stock market study by Thomas Gibson of New York. The Moody Corporation published it at 35 Nassau Street in 1907. Contents divide the work into two parts on market cycles. Part one opens with an introduction, then the cycles of speculation. The gold supply, money, and political influences with crops follow.

Part two treats puts and calls and the question of dividends. Basing railroad values and effects of business depression stand there next. Undigested securities, rights values, and a barometer of averages ensue in print. Best method of trading and indication of crises close Gibson's heads. Wall Street readers of 1907 got a cycle theory of booms and breaks.
75711-the-meaning-of-a-liberal-education:
The Meaning of a Liberal Education, by Everett Dean Martin, came out in 1926 in a lectures in print line. Martin led the People's Institute in New York and taught at the New School. He gives the book to his mother, who gave him his first lessons and his love of study.

Martin mocks the hunt for short cuts, as if learning could be poured in while a man sleeps. Chapters set free learning against mere animal training, and against ads and cant. Later chapters praise doubt and the free spirit as marks of a taught mind. Great names close the book, from Plato and Aristotle to Erasmus, Montaigne, and Huxley. A last note treats adult schooling in America.
75754-some-honeymoon:
Charles Everett Hall wrote a comic novel with pictures by Robert Gaston Herbert, held under copyright in 1918. A front view calls itself the first quarter of the honeymoon, a joke the tale soon earns in full. Twenty five chapters run from a man of business to a close in which John Ryder forgives fate itself.

John Ryder boards a ship home from Europe a bachelor of thirty five summers who has never counted his winters. A man, he held, starts that count only once he is wed, and fate meets him on deck in the form of a lady. Suspicion, shock on shock, a house detective, and a bride who claims to be another woman follow.
75759-the-coasts-of-illusion:
Clark Firestone's The Coasts of Illusion, a study of travel tales, was published by Harper & Brothers in New York and London in 1924, with drawings by Ruth Hambidge. Sir John Millais's Boyhood of Raleigh fronts the book. Twenty-five chapters and a bibliography make the survey, and its titles draw the map of mankind's false geography.

The world that was and the earth itself come first, then the animal kingdom and its fabulous beasts, fable upon wings, and the dragon. Denizens of the deep lead to the peoples of prodigy: satyrs, pygmies, and the Amazons of legend and of history in turn. Horizon lands, islands of enchantment, the Sargasso Sea, and Atlantis follow, with the gilded man and the dream quests of Spain. The closing chapters weigh the fabric of illusion itself, and the gains of fable.
75887-jacques-louis-david-and-the-french:
Jacques Louis David and the French Revolution, by W R Valentiner, came out at New York in 1929. A portrait of a young woman by David fronts the book. Long lists of plates map his rise, from Minerva's Conquest of Mars in 1771 to Napoleon as First Consul.

Plates show the Oath of the Horatii of 1784 and the dead Marat of 1793. One shows a pen sketch of Marie Antoinette, drawn from a window as her cart paused on the way to the scaffold. Valentiner asks if great art can grow in a time of revolt and a tyrant's rule. He notes that famed golden ages, from Athens to Rembrandt's Holland, were years of strife, not calm. Art fans get David's life set in the storm that made him.
75958-the-decay-and-the-restoration-of-c:
Albert Schweitzer wrote The Decay and the Restoration of Civilization, Part One of The Philosophy of Civilization. The Dale Memorial Lectures of nineteen twenty two form the book. C T Campion rendered the work into English. A and C Black in London issued the book in nineteen twenty three. Schweitzer held degrees in theology, philosophy, and medicine from Strassburg. He gave the book to Annie Fischer in deepest gratitude.

Schweitzer says in his preface that he has worked on a full philosophy of civilization since nineteen hundred. Part two, Civilization and Ethics, was to follow at once. The clear lines of the work ripened, he says, in the stillness of the primeval forest of Equatorial Africa in nineteen fourteen to seventeen. Part one states the problem of civilization. Its real nature, he holds, is ultimately ethical. Readers get a grave, searching intro to a famed thinker system.
75982-recollections-of-a-chaperon:
Recollections of a Chaperon comes out in one volume as number 114 of the Standard Novels, from Bentley of London in 1849. The front pages praise fiction as the most loved kind of writing. A long notice warns lending libraries of fines for pirated foreign prints under the new Copyright Act.

A plate shows the heart of one scene. Isabella bends over a marble basin, fair to see, and twists dahlias in her hair with a laugh. The plate was printed in 1848, a year before this issue. The frame of a chaperon's memories suits tales of balls, visits, and young hearts. Readers of manners get a reprint once sold for the library trade.
76007-our-business-civilization:
James Truslow Adams examines American culture in Our Business Civilization, published by Albert and Charles Boni in New York with copyright in 1929. Adams dedicates the book, subtitled Some Aspects of American Culture, to Kay. Thirteen chapters run from A Business Man's Civilization to The Art of Living.

Chapter one warns against easy generalisations: age breaks stock types into many varying individuals, as a prism breaks white light into a rainbow. Yet group types still emerge, and Adams sets out to fix the genuine traits of a nation from weltering impressions. He denies that America shows only Babbitts to a sharp observer. Later chapters weigh the cost of prosperity, dissolving ethics, Jefferson and Hamilton today, and a lawless heritage under Hoover.
76016-the-pillow-book-of-sei-sho-nagon:
The Pillow-Book of Sei Shonagon is a classic of Japanese letters, rendered into English by Arthur Waley. It came out in London from George Allen and Unwin, first published in 1928. The book is given to Hazel Crompton. Notes at the front state the scope of the rendering and its sources.

Waley states that he has here rendered about a quarter of the Pillow-Book. Cuts have been made only where the first text was dull, past grasp, repetitious, or so packed with allusion that it called for too much note, he says. Short pieces of the book had come out in Aston's Japanese Literature of 1899 and in Florenz and Revon, he adds. Save for a line or two here and there, and two tales, the parts so rendered are not the same as his. The book is a court lady's notebook of lists and scenes.
76077-probation:
Jessie Fothergill's Lancashire novel, in a new edition from Richard Bentley and Son at London in 1887, opens inside a great cotton mill. Book One is called Pride and Plenty, and its first chapter treats an absentee employer. The weaving shed is drawn at length: long lines of looms, wheels, straps and beams, rows of standing workers, and a deafening roar that strangers find stunning.

Fothergill calls the shed the perfection of mechanism, human and metallic, and asks which is most alive, the girls at the looms or the flying shuttle itself. The head overlooker moves along the rows, stopping looms, fingering cloth, and warning a laughing girl, Sarah Alice, that her work will not do. Adrienne stands in the frontispiece.
76117-the-swimming-baths-of-london:
Dudgeon, a London doctor, wrote a sixpenny pamphlet on the swimming baths of London, issued in 1870. He holds that swimming is at once healthful, pleasant, and useful. Its full gains, he argues, come only in the open air, in clean water at its own heat.

Sea towns, he notes, have a fine bath given by nature, though drains too often foul it. Inland towns must build baths or go without, and too many neglect to build. He goes on to the gains of cold water and of the air bath before and after a swim. Town councils and bathers alike are his target readers.
76167-stanley-s-emin-pasha-expedition:
A J Wauters wrote Stanley’s Emin Pasha Expedition, a full account of the relief march. J B Lippincott issued the book at Philadelphia in eighteen hundred ninety. A map and thirty three portraits and views fill its pages. Wauters shaped the Brussels journal called the Mouvement Geographique.

Egypt’s fall in the Soudan and the Mahdi’s revolt open the tale. Gordon’s death at Khartoum and Wolseley’s late relief come next. Emin Bey, cut off at the equator lakes, waits for help in vain. Stanley lands on the Congo and fights his way up its dark streams. Tippu Tib, the Arab chief, lends and withholds his aid by turns. Yambuya camp starves while the rear guard rots in the forest. Barttelot falls by murder and his men by hunger and flight. At last Stanley and Emin meet on Lake Albert’s wide shore.
76265-the-musket-boys-of-old-boston:
The Musket Boys of Old Boston, or The First Blow for Liberty, by George Warren, was copyrighted in 1909 and published in New York. Warren had also written The Musket Boys Under Washington. Chapter one, A Puff of Powder, opens with two boys watching a fellow at work.

Phil Warrington whispers that the puff is gunpowder. He knows the boy by his long tailed muskrat cap. Chapter heads move through a fruitless chase, duty, a great name, and the road to Boston. The boys fall into enemy hands, find a nest of Tories, and board the Vixen. Paul Revere ride, the road to Lexington, the battle of Concord, and Bunker Hill all follow. Readers get a boys tale of the first days of the American Revolution.
76278-a-history-of-evolution:
A History of Evolution, by Carroll Lane Fenton, is Number 321 in the Ten Cent Pocket Series. Haldeman-Julius issued the booklet at Girard, Kansas, with a copyright of 1922. The editor's line heads the series, and a motto praises the search for nature's laws.

Fenton starts with the ancient world and calls Aristotle far ahead of any other early thinker on descent. Aristotle, he says, might have been the Greek prophet of Darwinism had he backed the survival idea. Epicurus, who lived from 341 to 270, opposed him and denied anything beyond nature. Epicurus barred purpose and plan from his scheme but never said what his natural causes were. Lucretius then carried the teaching to Rome in a long poem on the nature of things.
76305-the-catholic-church-and-conversion:
The Catholic Church and Conversion is a short book by Chesterton, published by Macmillan in 1926. It belongs to the Calvert Series, edited by Hilaire Belloc. Sister volumes treat the Church with history, philosophy, reason, and science. Belloc's editor's note opens this one with a confession of diffidence. A man born into the Faith, he writes, grasps conversion only from outside. The experience belongs to those who have lived it.

Chesterton himself was such a convert, which gives the book its angle. The note warns that cradle Catholics often pass through another kind of experience. They may know the Faith from childhood yet meet it fresh later. The imprimatur of Cardinal Hayes dates to September 1926. The book was reprinted twice within a year of issue. It stands as a convert's account of what conversion means.
76387-pig-iron:
Dudrea Parker, listed as Mrs. Sumner Parker, wrote three short tales issued at Baltimore in 1921 under the title Pig Iron. The first, An Ephemeral Love, opens with Betty's cool farewell to Walter, a man of thirty with a lumber trade in that city. He has paid his late father's bills and kept his mother since that death.

Walter fears that Betty's coldness comes from his lack of wealth, and he broods on a bold business plan that might make him rich. The White Petal and The Reporter make up the rest of the small book. Love, money, and pride drive each of its tales.
76411-the-last-dragon:
The Last Dragon is a children's fantasy by Dan Totheroh, illustrated by Eleanor Osborn Eadie. The Doran Company published it in New York in 1927. Totheroh dedicated the book to Kay, who first saw the last dragon.

The story begins at the edge of a farm: a meadow, and a shadowy woodlot with a thick thimbleberry thicket, the likeliest lurking place for a coily, fire-breathing beast. Peter enters the woodlot, and the dragon meets the children. Grandma meets the dragon too, and comes with the children to be measured for suits of mail. The chapters wander into fairy tale: enchanted silver toes, Allan the armorer, a princess with toes of silver, a fair, a magician named Mig, and a road toward Giggletown. The plates show Peter standing on the dragon's neck and Beppo balancing Peter's sword on his chin.
76460-the-art-of-fiction:
Art of Fiction, by Walter Besant, began as a lecture at the Royal Institution on 25 April 1884. A new edition came from Chatto and Windus in London in 1902. Besant sets out to treat fiction as one of the fine arts. He lays down three propositions at the start of his argument.

First, fiction is an art worthy to stand as sister and equal to painting, sculpture, music, and poetry. Its field is as boundless and its heights as worthy of praise as theirs. Second, it is an art ruled by general laws like the rest. Those laws can be stated and taught with the same care as the laws of harmony. The lecture helped spark a wide debate on the novel as a serious art in its day.
76550-the-censorship-of-the-church-of-ro:
The Censorship of the Church of Rome, in two volumes, traces how Rome watched, banned, and cut books from the early church to the year 1900. A full list of contents by chapter opens the work, and the title page names no author in this copy.

The first volume follows bans in the early church and the Middle Ages, then rules in England, France, Spain, and Germany before the official Indexes. It covers the Roman Inquisition, the first lists of banned books, and the Index of Pius the Fourth after the Council of Trent. One chapter notes the Index that records the condemning of Galileo. The second volume turns to the treatment of the Scriptures, the part played by the monastic orders, and later Indexes under Benedict the Fourteenth, Pius the Ninth, and Leo the Thirteenth.
76682-the-censorship-of-the-church-of-ro:
Censorship of the Church of Rome sets out, in two volumes, how Rome banned and cut books across five centuries. A full contents list maps the work from the early church to modern times. Heads treat bans in the middle ages, rules in England, France, Spain, and Germany before the first Indexes, and the Roman Inquisition.

Later heads list Indexes town by town and year by year, from Louvain and Venice to Rome in 1559 and the Index of Pius in 1564. Erasmus and Luther in the Index, the Jansenist clash, and the case of Galileo all get room. Volume two turns to the Bible under bans, trade from 1450 to 1800, the stage, and bans by states and by Protestant lands as a check on one sided blame.
76728-helen-vardon-s-confession:
R Austin Freeman writes a novel told as a woman's own account in a Hodder and Stoughton volume from London. Freeman had written The Eye of Osiris and The Red Thumb Mark before this tale. Three books divide the work: Tragedy, Romance, and Crime in set order.

A prologue opens with Helen Vardon at her dressing table, brushing out her black hair one quiet day. Among the tresses she spots a single white hair, the first she has seen in her life. That small sign of time starts her long backward look at her life, she tells the reader. Heads promise a covenant, a hidden hand, a crystal-gazer, a dreadful inheritance, an indictment, and a verdict in the books ahead.
76774-the-future-of-an-illusion:
The Future of an Illusion, by Sigmund Freud, was issued in 1928. Liveright published it with the Institute of Psycho-Analysis. The book stands as number 15 of the International Psycho-Analytical Library. Ernest Jones edited that series. Robson-Scott made the translation, thanking James Strachey for help. Chapter one turns from a culture's past to its future. What fate awaits it, Freud asks, and what changes lie ahead? He warns at once that such prophecy is weak ground. Few men can survey human life in all its branches.

The less a man knows of past and present, the worse his judgement of the future. Personal hope and fear bend the answer, he adds. Freud then narrows to his own small tract of territory: religion as an illusion.
76803-regeneration:
Regeneration is a reply to a famed charge on the age by Max Nordau. Nordau had called the art and thought of the age sick and spent. A Columbia man of thought writes the first words for the reply. The book came out in New York and London in 1896.

The reply asks first who the judge is who makes such a charge. It asks if the age stands at dusk or at dawn in its course. Faith, the claims of science, and the new schools of art are weighed. Ibsen and Wagner get long parts to test the charge on their work. A faith of the self and a call to firm words close the book. The last part takes the name of the book as its theme and aim.
76856-how-to-get-a-government-position:
How to Get a Government Position is number 31 of the Multum in Parvo Library, published monthly by Courtney at 45 Milk Street, Boston, in July 1896, price five cents. The pamphlet argues the Civil Service case to young men and women without private means: pleasant work, regular hours, punctual pay, and no ruinous overwork. The system, it says, is now the only avenue into thousands of lucrative positions, and the examinations are competitive.

An example works the arithmetic: of one hundred candidates in Boston, sixty-five pass, and the top forty take the forty vacancies in order. Application routes follow, to the Civil Service Commission at Washington for departmental service, and to the customs and postal boards elsewhere. Age limits run from sixteen to thirty-five for ordinary posts, with veterans of the late war exempted. The pamphlet gives hints for study rather than full courses.
76864-german-composition:
Hermann Lange, a teacher of French and German at Manchester, wrote a guide to turning English prose into German, in a third edition from Oxford in 1900. German spelling in the book meets the state rules of 1880. Pupils who have reached the fiftieth lesson of his German Manual may start it.

Lange says the book also stands alone for those who know German forms and have read some prose. It aims at the tests of London and Victoria, the civil and army posts, and the Oxford and Cambridge local tests. Picks come from the best new English and American writers, most of them whole pieces, with short lives of famed folk in German in the notes.
76871-the-magnificent-possession:
Isaac Asimov pits a poor chemist against luck in The Magnificent Possession. A plate cry sets the stakes: my God, watch out, it is nitroglycerine. The head text says Walter Sills worked for years as an unknown laboratory worker. At fifty he makes his great find.

Fame and riches are to be his fate, the blurb says. Then shaky folk step in, and nature herself steps in too. Sills sits in his dingy lab and grins at his hard, joyless life. Ore tests barely pay for the tools he must have. Eugene Taylor bursts in with a loud, gay hail. Sills tells him things are bad: the more he needs cash, the less he has.
77016-the-trail-of-deception:
Tuttle wrote this western tale of a young man who plays a bold game. Jim Bailey is reported dead, the head note says. That report gives him a clear field for a paying game, and the tale turns on the lie.

Jim sits on a park bench at dusk, sick at heart and out of luck. He is twenty-five, well dressed and good looking, a common young man bucking the world. Two days of job hunting have failed him. He has two dollars in his pocket and owes ten in room rent, due right now. A man in that fix, with death as his mask, can do things a live man would not dare.
77050-does-civilization-need-religion:
Niebuhr asks whether civilization needs religion in this study of faith. Its subtitle weighs social resources and limits of religion today. Macmillan published it in New York in December of 1927. Niebuhr dedicates it to the memory of his father, a pastor. That father taught him to unite a critical faculty with reverence.

His mother shared twelve years of a Christian pastorate with him. Contents open with the state of religion in modern society. Nature and civilization as foes of personality fill the second chapter. Social resources and social conservatism of religion stand opposed next. Conflict and compromise, and ethical impotence, follow in argument.
77059-illustrations-of-taxation:
Harriet Martineau wrote tales meant to show how taxes work, and this volume gathers five tales first issued on their own. Each tale keeps its own title page and page count in the set. The first tale, The Park and the Paddock, came out in London in 1834 from a house in Paternoster Row.

That tale opens in a town split on whether a new road near its market place is a gain or a loss. Old folk recall a time when the town held more weight, and carved gateways still feed local pride. Eight chapters move through pride in a family estate, church duty, and a vowed sisterhood.
77131-drug-themes-in-science-fiction:
Robert Silverberg, the famed science fiction writer, surveyed drug themes in his field for the National Institute on Drug Abuse. The study came out in November 1974 at Rockville, Maryland. It is number nine in the Research Issues line.

The line's other volumes treat drugs and jobs, sex, family, and death. Silverberg's task is the made-up side: how tales of far worlds treat drugs and those who take them. William Blake's Urizen, the Ancient of Days, fronts the cover. A fed'ral health body here turns to a master of the genre to map a theme that ran through much post-war science fiction.
77188-school-education:
Charlotte M Mason sets out the schooling of children over nine in volume three of her Home Education series. Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner and Company issued this second edition at London in 1907. She inscribes it to Henrietta Franklin.

The book opens with Dante. Virgil girds the poet with a smooth rush from a little island in the Purgatorio. The plant springs up again the moment it is plucked. Mason takes the rush as her emblem of humble, yielding growth. Her series runs to five volumes at three shillings and sixpence each. Home Education and Parents and Children precede this one. Ourselves, Our Souls and Bodies follows. Mason held that children are born persons, owed a wide feast of living books. Her schools and the Parents' Union spread that creed across the English-speaking world.
77204-east-of-the-sun-and-west-of-the-mo:
Theodore Roosevelt and Kermit Roosevelt wrote East of the Sun and West of the Moon. Charles Scribner's Sons issued it in 1926. Kermit took the photos that fill it. James Simpson made the trip possible, they say. Their one regret is his absence from it. Kashmir opens the contents at chapter one.

The father writes the odd chapters in turn. Kermit writes the even ones beside him. From Kashmir to Ladakh's barrens goes chapter two. Lofty Himalayan passes lead to Yarkand in three. Turkestan's deserts and oases fill the fourth. Beyond the last barrier waits the hunting ground. Ibex, sheep, and bear crowd chapter six. The Asiatic wapiti of the Tian Shan takes seven. Kashgar closes the road in chapter eight. The Pamirs end the contents shown here. A father and son's big game trek across High Asia mixes sport with a famous name's travel charm.
77209-larry-barlow-s-ambition:
Arthur M Winfield wrote a boys' tale of a young fireman and his ambition. The Saalfield Publishing Company issued Larry Barlow's Ambition at Akron, Ohio. Rights rest from 1902, with a New York form in 1907. Pictures by W H Fry show a fork held to a lion's throat.

Chapters run from the extension ladder to a daring leap for life. Larry joins the New York Fire Department and wins full standing at last. Mary Vern, strangers, and a trap like a rat's stir the plot. Boys of the day got a fast tale of nerve, rescue, and grit.
77237-the-electress-sophia-and-the-hanov:
The Electress Sophia and the Hanoverian Succession is a historical study by Adolphus William Ward, master of Peterhouse, first published in 1903 and here revised and enlarged for Longmans in 1909. Sophia, Electress of Hanover, was the granddaughter of James the First and the heir named in the Act of Settlement. Ward gives her claim the prominence of his design.

The opening essay sets out her double inheritance. A Stuart by descent and sentiment, she was also shaped by the ruined Palatine house of her youth, as daughter of the Winter Queen of Bohemia. Her title was parliamentary, Ward argues, but it rested on the great conflicts of the age: the struggle against France and the resistance to Rome. He praises her vivacity and candour as the marks of an intellectually liberal mind. The book is the standard scholarly life of the woman from whom the Hanoverian kings descended.
77318-reincarnation:
Reincarnation: A Study of Forgotten Truth, by E D Walker, was published by Houghton, Mifflin and Company at Boston and New York in 1888. Its motto is Ex oriente lux, light from the East. Verses from Quarles, Carlyle, Chapman, Whittier, and Waddington crowd the opening pages.

Walker dedicates the little volume to the Spirit of Truth and to that embodiment of truth named Ariel, hoping they are not dishonoured by their disciple. His guiding question comes in Waddington's sonnet: where wert thou, soul, before this body was born to be thy dwelling-place?
77361-adrift-on-the-amazon:
Leo Miller wrote a boys' tale of the Amazon that Scribner of New York published in 1923. Chapter one is named for its hero's nickname. To his friends, David is Fighting Jones, for his two good fists have often been used.

The name holds no disgrace. Each fight was for a just cause, in defence of some one too weak to stand up alone. Yet the final word has always gone against him, and the penalty always falls. The chapters carry David from home to the great river. He harpoons a river monster, works in the rubber forest, and fights a crocodile. An ant army and a charge of Indians fill the later pages.
77425-the-test-of-donald-norton:
Robert Pinkerton wrote The Test of Donald Norton, a northern novel printed at Toronto with copyright in 1924. Contents open with a mystery of birth, the portent of a dream, the making of a man, victory and promotion, and a pilgrimage for a friend. Donald meets a strange god, loses a friend, and sees red smear his dream.

Corrigal drives his men, revenge comes, Corrigal bares his soul, Donald builds a defense, tastes defeat, and fights to the finish. A bear came out of the brush behind the drying racks, attracted by curing fish odour, in chapter one. A baby in a back cradle waved both hands at the bear within six feet of her nose. North woods readers get Pinkerton.
77430-edward-burton:
Edward Burton is a novel by Henry Wood, issued in Boston in a ninth edition dated 1899. Lee and Shepard published the book, cloth at one dollar and a quarter and paper at fifty cents. Wood is named as author of studies in thought and of a work on natural law. A verse motto on the search for the hidden essence of things stands at the front.

Chapter titles trace the life of Burton from school to a wider world in the tale. They run through a dinner party, his school life, and his theological education in order. His illness and its results, a down east cruise, and a pleasant entertainment follow in the list. The novel belongs to the line of fiction in which Wood set out his views on mind and spirit.
77466-jesuit-education:
Jesuit Education is a study of the Jesuit school system by Robert Schwickerath of Woodstock College in Maryland. Herder of St Louis published it, and this hosted text is the second edition of 1904. The preface notes that English readers had little sound information on Jesuit schools, and much unreliable writing instead.

Schwickerath sets out the history of the order's teaching and the principles behind it. He then tests that system against the live questions of his day. Those questions include the elective system, the worth of the classics, and the place of the college between school and university. Moral and religious training close the list. The book is both a defence and a handbook from inside the system.
77582-the-scorpion:
The Scorpion, by Anna Elisabet Weirauch, is a German novel in Whittaker Chambers's translation. The Willey Book Company issued it in New York, from a copyright of 1932. The narrator opens by owning a frank motive.

She sought Myra's acquaintance, she says, because of the girl's evil reputation. The tale of Myra comes from Aunt Antonia, a pious lady of sharp eye and set views. As a child, Myra was given to lying and stealing, and was thought stupid and lazy at school. She ran with a sharper, a woman of masculine manner. Misled by that friend, she stole her father's silver service and pawned it. A fit of madness followed, and an attack on the aunt who raised her. Sent to Uncle George, she stole freely and fled with his money.
77596-maza-of-the-moon:
Otis Adelbert Kline wrote a scientific romance copyrighted in 1930. Ted Dustin, young head of his own company, opens the tale in trouble: the firm has spent every cent, and borrowed besides, preparing a projectile for launching. If they do not win the reward, creditors will be picking their bones in thirty days.

A radiovisiphone disc on his desk flashes his clerk's face at the spoken word yes, and twenty-seven reporters wait below. The contents promise startling results: moon people, an ultimatum from P'an-ku, death rays, flying reptiles, and torture chambers. An aerial battle and the fall of Peilong close the list. Pulps' space opera, bound in cloth, is the fare.
77600-the-maltese-falcon:
Maltese Falcon is a detective novel by Dashiell Hammett of America. Knopf published it in New York with rights held in 1930. Hammett dedicates the book simply to Jose on its front page. Chapter one, Spade and Archer, opens on Samuel Spade in his office. Spade's jaw is long and bony, his chin a jutting v shape.

His yellow grey eyes sit horizontal under thickish rising brows. His pale brown hair points down on a high flat forehead. Hammett says he looked pleasantly like a blond satan in that sketch. Effie Perine, a lanky sunburned girl, enters as his secretary in talk. A case of a missing sister and a fabulous falcon follows fast.
77682-lyrics-selected-from-the-works-of-:
Mary Robinson's lyrics are selected here in the Cameo Series, published by Stokes in New York in 1891. A picture from Botticelli's Spring ornaments the opening of the little volume. Surely the very Spring here half afraid is, runs a quoted lyric beneath that picture.

Music opens the contents at page three, and a pastoral of Parnassus follows. Going south, spring under cypresses, the sleeping beauty in French and dawn angels fill the list. Lyrics not published before are marked with a star in the contents, for Robinson, who wrote as a poet of Italy and Provence in two tongues.
77683-obstipation:
Thomas Charles Martin wrote a practical study of disorders of the rectal valve. The Philadelphia Medical Publishing Company issued Obstipation in 1899. Martin taught proctology at the Cleveland College of Physicians and Surgeons. The book is given to his generous colleagues at the front.

Martin sets obstipation apart from constipation by cause and seat. One springs from a block in the rectum; the other from delay higher up. Long review of past writing, anatomy, and treated cases fill the work. A stern quote from a doubter fronts the text as a foil. Doctors gain a dated but sharp brief for a contested organ.
77699-a-greater-than-napoleon:
A Greater Than Napoleon is a military biography of Scipio Africanus by Captain B H Liddell Hart, published by William Blackwood and Sons of Edinburgh and London. The edition at hand is the fourth impression, of 1930. A bust in the Capitoline Museum, supposed to be Scipio, serves as frontispiece, and maps accompany the text.

Liddell Hart states his excuse plainly in the preface. No recent biography of Scipio exists, and the last English one, from 1817, was written by a country clergyman. That writer omitted any study of Scipio as a soldier. Liddell Hart argues the Roman's military work outvalues every other great captain's for modern students. Scipio founded Rome's world dominion by beating Hannibal at his own art. The book helped make its author the century's most read writer on war, and Scipio a staff college name.
77756-the-magnificent-profession:
The Magnificent Profession is a science fiction story by Leonard Lockhard, printed with an editor's delighted introduction. Lockhard was an experienced patent attorney in life. The editor marvels at how he slips an inventor's nightmare onto his writing hand, chuckling until dawn. Readers, the editor promises, will chuckle too.

The hero, Saddle, works for Helix Spardleton, patent attorney extraordinary. A dreaded client, Marchare, is on the phone, and Saddle's palms go moist. Other lawyers serve normal scientists with new plastics and insecticides. Marchare invents stranger things, among them an underground diving suit with a very sharp point. Krome, Mr Patent Office in person, is a hard man to needle, the blurb warns. Lockhard turns the patent office into comic science fiction, where every invention threatens its examiner first.
7779-of-captain-mission:
Daniel Defoe's Of Captain Mission, drawn from The History of the Pyrates, volume two, presents a pirate captain of unusual principle. Modern scholarship, the introduction notes, has traced the great pirate history to Defoe since John Robert Moore's 1932 case, despite its old mask as Captain Charles Johnson.

Editors from Michigan, California, and other universities frame the text with notes on its making. Mission's story, part of a larger gallery of sea robbers, raises a sharp question: can a man who lives by plunder also live by a code? The volume offers Defoe's answer in brisk, vivid prose.
77793-conversation:
Conversation is a Texas tale by Frank Davis of a post office shooting. Of twenty odd legal grounds for homicide in Texas, one opens the story. The second most common is an epithet never spoken before ladies there. No ladies stood before the Somersworth post office that day, Davis notes.

Jim Begley capped a sharp horse trade quarrel by speaking that word to Newt Shaw. Newt drew a forty five, set it to Begley stomach, and fired three shots. A metal breastplate under Begley vest saved him, bruised and staggering still. Begley drew slower than expected, then killed Newt with one shot in turn. The coroner jury found self defence without any difficulty at all.
77957-the-dragon:
The Dragon is a novel of future war by Shiel, author of The Yellow Danger. It was printed at Edinburgh in 1913. The contents begin with Prince Edward and a coup d'état, then turn to Australian gold and thundery weather. A liner, the Mauretania, and a ship called the Asahel carry parts of the tale.

Later chapters speak of Germans in Pall Mall, a haunted submarine, and a redlike ray that is buried, radiates, and migrates. Six millions in gold are lost, found, and fought over. The book ends with a yellow deluge and a pass through a comet's tail. Shiel writes invasion fantasy in the fevered mood just before the First World War.
77963-what-they-said-about-the-fourth-ar:
What They Said About the Fourth Armored Division is a division tribute book of 1945. The public relations section at division headquarters compiled and published the volume. It was printed at Landshut, Germany, in September 1945, just after the war. Contents open with shiniest helmet in the ETO and Tiger Jack spearheads.

Bastogne, the rat chase to the Rhine, and the victory of the Rhine fill the chapters. Ohrdruf and death and apple blossoms mark the dark spring of 1945 in the list. A presidential citation to the division is printed from the March SHAEF message. Unit pride speaks through the words of generals, papers, and the BBC.
77986-the-tarpon:
The Tarpon is a game fish book by Gray Griswold, home printed in nineteen twenty two. The fish bears nine folk names, from Silver King to Grand Ecaille in French. It is the great one of the herring tribe in the book count. Warm seas of the Atlantic and the Gulf Stream are its home range. Brazil, the mid lands, and the West Isle coasts all hold its schools.

Some few fish reach New England seas in mid warm months of the year. One fine fish was net took in Narragansett Bay in nineteen nineteen. Schools come to the Florida Keys in small bands in February. Counts grow from that month till mid warm time each year. Rail cause ways built south broke their old fair ways through the Keys.
7800-outlines-of-english-and-american-li:
William J. Long's Outlines of English and American Literature introduces the chief writers of both nations, the books they wrote, and the times they lived in. Dedicated to his sister Millie, it opens with Chaucer's line on the way to good adventure, and a portrait of Shakespeare after the Chandos picture.

That portrait's history runs from player John Taylor through Davenant, Betterton, and the Duke of Chandos, a chain the notes trace with care. Through short lives, summaries, and context, the book gives students and general readers a clear, friendly map of two literatures side by side.
78009-a-guide-to-the-history-of-physical:
A Guide to the History of Physical Education, by Fred Eugene Leonard of Oberlin College, was published in Philadelphia and New York in 1923, with ninety-nine engravings. The book belongs to a physical education series edited by Tait McKenzie of the University of Pennsylvania. Leonard dedicates it to Edward Mussey Hartwell, who first blazed the trail in America.

Leonard says that thirty years before, when he took his chair, no full survey of his field existed in English. Hartwell's reports gave good summaries, but the best European work had to be hunted down. A summer in Germany in 1896 whetted his thirst, and a full year on the Continent in 1900 and 1901 let him use great collections at Stockholm and Berlin.
78017-the-swiss-family-robinson:
The Swiss Family Robinson is the classic tale of a family shipwrecked on a desert island, in an edition illustrated by T H Robinson. It was issued in New York by the Garden City Publishing Company, as the title page states. A frontispiece shows a morning that dawned without a prospect of hope. Contents open with a shipwreck and preparations for deliverance.

A landing, a voyage of discovery, and a return to the wreck follow in order. Animals in cork jackets, a bridge, a ladder, and a new home mark the family's building campaign. Chapter by chapter the Robinsons turn wreck goods and island nature into a working home. Resource and family order are the tale's lasting lessons.
78039-boston:
Upton Sinclair wrote this long novel, printed at Pasadena in 1928 in two volumes. The first chapter, titled The Runaway Grandmother, opens with a death: old Josiah Thornwell is found cold at his desk in the morning, still in his dinner coat. His widow Cornelia, freed at last from a husband who directed her whole life, feels fear and loneliness more than grief.

The contents map a wide Boston world: Plymouth Rock, deportation days, a detective machine, the legal system, and a graft ring. Later chapters move through trial by jury, the mills of the law, and days of grace, to a final chapter called The Triumph. Sinclair uses one old family's shock as the door into a city of mills, courts, and fear. The novel is his broad attack on wealth and law in Boston.
78065-the-anatomy-of-revolution:
Anatomy of Revolution is a comparative study of revolutions by Crane Brinton. Brinton, associate professor of history at Harvard, wrote the study. Norton published it in New York in 1938 in a first edition. He dedicates it to Alden and Helen Hoag, who listened to it all. Chapter one argues the necessity for a scientific approach to revolutions.

Bare elements of scientific method and their application fill that chapter. Limitations of the subject close the first part with due caution. Chapter two turns to the old regimes that revolutions overthrow in time. Diagnosis of preliminary signs and structural weaknesses fills its pages. Economic and political flaws, plus desertion of the intellectuals, mark decay.
78115-the-story-of-nelson:
