Edmund Sellar wrote this life of Nelson for the Children's Heroes series, with pictures by Orr. Jack of London and Edinburgh published the little book for young readers. Sellar dedicates it to Ruth Dent, telling her it holds the story of the greatest seaman ever known.

Enough is said to make her want to read more for herself one day, he hopes. Early boyhood and joining his ship open the contents at the front. First command, the West Indies, Vincent, the Nile and the Mediterranean fill the chapters, toward Copenhagen and Trafalgar in a hero life sized for a child's shelf.
78152-powder-river-invasion:
A S Mercer wrote Powder River Invasion, subtitled War on the Rustlers in 1892, rewritten by John Mercer Boots and copyrighted in 1923. Seventeen chapters and an appendix carry the account. An introduction surveys the vast region between the Missouri River and the Sierra Nevada.

That country, covering nearly two-fifths of the United States, was long reckoned an unproductive waste fit only for wild beasts, bison, and Indians. Wagon lines of 1849 crossed it without settling. The book then turns to Wyoming's Johnson County war, when cattlemen invaded against alleged rustlers. Readers get a participant-side history of the Powder River invasion, a famous episode of the range wars.
78157-strong-poison:
Strong Poison is Dorothy L Sayers's detective novel, copyrighted in 1930. An old ballad of Lord Rendal, poisoned at his sweetheart's table, stands at its head. The book opens in court, with crimson roses on the bench that look like splashes of blood.

An old judge, three days into a distressing trial, gathers his notes and turns to sum up for the jury. The prisoner watches him: a woman whose eyes, dark smudges under heavy brows, show equally no fear and no hope. He reminds the twelve of the great principle that the accused is innocent until the Crown proves guilt beyond reasonable doubt. Three tradesmen, a company director, a publican, two artisans, an artist with a red beard, and three women hold her life in their hands. The verdict is where the novel truly starts.
78228-two-happy-years-in-ceylon:
Two Happy Years in Ceylon is a travel book by Gordon Cumming on the island now called Sri Lanka. Press notices at the front praise the work in high terms. One calls it the classic work on Ceylon.

The writer had travelled over most of the Isle of Flowers, as she names it. She knew each kind of life there, plant and beast alike. The Daily Chronicle judged her account full, accurate and lively. No description since Emerson-Tennent's great work had matched it, that paper said. Readers get a rich tour of towns, hills and coasts from a keen eyed guest. Her two years on the island gave the book depth and ease.
78248-prolegomena-to-the-study-of-greek-:
Jane Ellen Harrison wrote this study of the old faith of Greece, printed at Cambridge in 1903. She was a fellow and teacher at Newnham College in that town. The first pages state the aim of the book in plain terms. The faith of Greece, as set out in handbooks and in works of more weight, is an affair for the most part of myth. And it is myth as seen through the lens of verse and prose tales.

Harrison holds that no grave try has yet been made in England to look at Greek rite. Yet the facts of rite are the base of her study. The book turns from the tales of the gods to the acts men did in cult. It asks what the old Greeks did with their hands and feet at altars and feasts.
7829-american-prisoners-of-the-revolutio:
Danske Dandridge's American Prisoners of the Revolution, dedicated to her grandfather Lieutenant Daniel Bedinger, gathers scattered accounts of patriot suffering in British hands. A boy in prison stands in the dedication for all that was bravest and most honorable in the patriots of 1776.

Dandridge admits little here is original. She reprints scarce, out-of-print narratives, above all Captain Dring's, in their own words, since retelling would weaken them. For students and general readers, the volume preserves firsthand testimony of prison ships, hunger, cold, and endurance under a foe. It keeps their voices alive.
78317-the-soil-solution:
The Soil Solution is a work on soil chemistry by Frank Cameron, subtitled The Nutrient Medium for Plant Growth. Cameron was in charge of physical and chemical investigations at the Bureau of Soils of the United States Department of Agriculture. The book was published at Easton, Pennsylvania, in 1911. Its preface begins by noting the two old ways of looking at soil chemistry.

Cameron argues that the water held in the soil, carrying dissolved minerals, is the true food supply of plants. The book sets out his measurements and his theory against the older view of soil as a store of plant food. It is a landmark in the science of soils, written for chemists and students of farming.
7833-samantha-on-the-woman-question:
Marietta Holley's Samantha on the Woman Question, by Josiah Allen's Wife, follows Samantha to a family reunion near Washington, birthplace of the first known Allen. Chapters promise a woman wanting her rights, tender eyes, striving with an emissary, moth-millers and minny fish, and a women's parade.

Pictures ask whether any woman can blame Serepta for wanting her rights, show a visit planned to the Capitol, and quote Josiah asking if a thing knows enough to vote. Through dialect humor and plain argument, Samantha presses votes for women, home rights, and fair dealing, with warmth and bite.
7839-a-foregone-conclusion:
William Dean Howells's A Foregone Conclusion opens in Venice. Don Ippolito walks a long narrow calle from Campo San Stefano toward the Grand Canal, peering back for followers. He passes palace walls, balconies, and a cat on a garden gate, while black boats pass noiselessly on the canal.

A parrot screams in a high window, a peasant cries pots of pinks and roses, and gondoliers jest across the water. Spring tenderness fills the air. Through Venetian lanes and society, Howells traces a priest's love, an American girl, and a conclusion the title says was settled from the start.
78410-the-man-from-oregon:
Mary Arbuckle wrote The Man from Oregon, illustrated by Frank Hoffman. A cover line quotes praise of its heroine: ploughing is nothing to her, and she can rope and tie a steer quick as any man. Far beyond the rim of cities these things happen, the epigraph says.

The Brownlie woman and her children sit at supper in their usual depressing silence. Kendall leaves the table and plunges into the sunset glamour outside. The yard gate, weighted with a wired stone, slams behind him. He looks out over the canyon, a spare, greying man with eyeglasses and a schoolmaster's worried, kindly face. He must get away from this place for a few days. Readers get a western novel of loneliness and a woman who can out-work the men.
78424-the-art-of-narration:
The Art of Narration is a school book on how tales are told well. Mary Ellen Chase and Frances Del Plaine wrote it for class use. It came out in New York in 1926, with a fresh print in 1928. The book is a mate to a like book on the art of description.

The plan sorts prose tales by kind and gives a model for each. One part takes plain tales that teach, with a tale of a salmon. Short scenes from lives come next, with Mark Twain among the names. Tales of past times form a third part of the book. Old tales and myths of the folk close the run of parts. Each part ends with a list of more books to read on its kind.
78446-the-irish-cause-and-the-irish-conv:
William O'Brien, a member of Parliament, gave this speech in the House of Commons on May 21, 1917, in the debate on Lloyd George's Irish proposals. Maunsel and Company of Dublin and London printed this third edition in 1917 at one penny. Letters between O'Brien and the Prime Minister are added at the back.

O'Brien splits the plan in two. One part is a bill cutting six Irish counties away from the body of Ireland, which he says Irishmen must refuse outright. Longford, he claims, has shot the fox and killed partition for the nationalists. The other part lets Irishmen draft their own constitution in convention, a plan he says came years too late. Ulster and partition remain, for him, the chief danger.
78519-the-art-of-scansion:
The Art of Scansion is a letter by Elizabeth Barrett Browning, privately printed at London in December 1916. Clement Shorter printed it, and Alice Meynell wrote the introduction. The letter itself was written at Hope End in April 1827, when its author was still Elizabeth Barrett. She addresses Uvedale Price on his essay about accents in verse.

She goes straight to her subject, asking his indulgence in advance. Scholars disagree over whether Greek verse should be read by Greek or Latin accent, she notes. At Charterhouse, she reports, the boys read Greek by the Greek accents. She then weighs the anapaest against the dactyl, quoting Marmontel on their different rush. The letter shows a young poet already sure of her ear.
78535-the-paper-dragon:
Johnny Gruelle writes and illustrates The Paper Dragon, a Raggedy Ann adventure copyrighted in 1926 by the P F Volland Company. Raggedy Ann and Raggedy Andy, rag dolls stuffed with clean white cotton, live in the nursery at Marcella's house and play with the other dolls when no people are watching. Each carries a magic gift sewn inside: Andy a wishing stick, Ann a magical wishing pebble.

Gruelle dedicates the book to Evelyn, David and Judy Chambers, dating his letter from Norwalk, Connecticut, September 2, 1925. In the first chapter the two dolls slip through the garden gate into the deep woods and hear a cry for help beyond a great stone.
78546-caruso-s-method-of-voice-productio:
P Mario Marafioti sets out a science of singing in Caruso's Method of Voice Production, subtitled The Scientific Culture of the Voice, from D Appleton in 1922. The book is dedicated to Enrico Caruso, whose singing was its inspiration. A letter from Caruso, dated May 25, 1921, accepts the dedication with pleasure and pride.

Caruso writes that Marafioti's research restores, in scientific form, the fundamental principles of natural singing. A second letter, from Victor Maurel in March 1922, praises the proofs from forty years of stage practice. Maurel says he had long urged the doctor to pursue his patient research into the natural functions of the vocal organs. Singers get a method blessed by its model.
78643-thornley-colton:
Clinton H Stagg wrote detective stories about a blind detective, published at New York in 1923 by G Howard Watt, author of High Speed. Contents arrange the cases as problems. The first problem is the keyboard of silence. The second runs unto the third generation. The third treats the money machines. Colton's blindness is the series' hook and method.

A blind sleuth must solve by ear, touch, and logic where others use their eyes. Stagg's problems appeared first in magazines. Watt published several mystery lines in the twenties. The problem format promises fair clues. Colton stands among the earliest blind detectives in American fiction, modeled on Ernest Bramah's Max Carrados.
78653-nerves-of-iron:
Nerves of Iron is a Western story by Tuttle, written in the tall-tale dialect voice of his range narrators. The tale follows two wandering prospectors, the narrator and his partner Magpie Simpkins, who take their bearings from a lead burro nicknamed Lodestone. When the burro leaves the beaten trail, they follow his hunch. This time the hunch leads them back toward a village, and toward gunfire.

Rounding a bend after the shooting stops, they meet a tiny man who stopped growing at ten, scared-eyed and carrying a full-size six-gun. He dives into the brush at their approach, then pops up behind them to apologise. He introduces himself as Stonewall Jackson. Magpie, never outdone, presents himself as Ulysses Grant and his partner as Robert Lee, with the burros as Lodestone and Caesar. The comedy of the meeting sets the story's tone of rough humour on the trail.
78811-war-medals-of-the-british-army-and:
A history of British army medals by Thomas Carter. W H Long revised and enlarged it. His edition brought the record to the present time. Norie and Wilson published it at London in 1893. The preface recalls a long neglect. Before Queen Victoria, almost no medals reached common soldiers. The men of Assaye, Salamanca, and Vittoria waited undecorated. So did the sailors of Saint Vincent, the Nile, and Trafalgar. Their reward came only in 1847.

The book describes each medal with care. Engravers worked from the medals themselves. Short campaign accounts explain how each clasp was won. Notes record regimental and individual acts of bravery. Collectors gain a reference work. Readers gain the deeds behind the ribbons.
78816-the-kilima-njaro-expedition:
Johnston led a trip to the Kilima-Njaro area and wrote the record, issued in London in 1886. The book gives a full account of the land, its plants and beasts, its tongues, and its trade. Johnston drew the maps and most of the more than eighty pictures himself. He gave the book to Sir John Kirk of Zanzibar, a friend and guide in British work there.

A poem at the front hails the snow-capped peak as a lone king of African hills. It sets the peak beside Mont Blanc, Orizaba, and Chimborazo. The text that follows mixes trip notes with close study of the district. Readers get both a travel tale and a field report from eastern Africa near the equator.
78850-possession:
Mazo de la Roche wrote Possession, a novel printed in London in 1923 and given to Christopher Morley. A young man walks a country road past the fishing village of Mistwell on a May evening at the start. The farm called Grimstone stands at the heart of the tale in two long parts.

Chapters move through May morning at Grimstone, a sale at Durras, cherries at dawn, and Christmas at the farm. Gretta Van Lowe, Solomon in his folly and glory, and Edmund thread through the family story of land and desire. A rill in the wood, sweet apples, and a struck tent mark turns of fortune. Readers get a rich Canadian farm novel.
78884-the-looker-on:
William Le Queux wrote The Looker-On, subtitled A Romance of Journalistic London, published in London in 1908. Le Queux was known for tales of secrets and crime, among them Sins of the City. Forty-one chapters carry this story, and the contents alone swing between newsroom life and dark affairs.

The tale opens with a special correspondent and a curious affair at Barnes, then steps behind the scenes of the Herald. Daisy Marvin enters early, and later chapters bring a house of shadows, a tape message, and a night at the Savage. A stranger, a mysterious Mr Stonor, and a M'sieur Smith deepen the plot. Grave charges and a chase close the run before the truth comes out.
78915-there-is-confusion:
Jessie Redmon Fauset's There Is Confusion (Boni and Liveright, New York, 1924) went through three printings by August. The novel opens on the close understanding between Joanna Marshall and her father, Joel. As a small girl left home from church with a slight complaint, she climbs on his knee and demands a story about somebody great, great like she is going to be.

Joel Marshall, born a slave in Richmond, Virginia, had asked his own mother the same question. He became a great caterer in New York, summoned once to fix a banquet for President Grant, and his mother counts that as greatness. But father and daughter, the narrator warns, mean different things by the word. Across thirty-six chapters, Fauset follows the Marshalls' ambitions and the confusions they breed. The title is Tennyson's: there is confusion worse than death.
78955-inside-information:
Tuttle's western tale, told by Ike Harper in broad dialect, turns on three men near Piperock who are all named Jones. The first, christened Alexander Claypool, renamed himself Mighty Jones after standing on his coat and declaring that he was small but mighty. The second, Arthur Chesterton, became Dirty Shirt Jones from wearing a buckskin shirt that no laundry could help.

The third, Amos Carter, came to be called Jewelry Jones after a pawnshop mix-up. He went into a jewelry store to pawn his gun, and the clerk, mistaking his errand, filled a sack with the store's plunder and handed it over. The clerk then joined the marshal to break up Amos's spree, and Amos rode broke into Piperock, leaving his pistol behind.
78989-the-facts-about-rejuvenation:
The Facts About Rejuvenation, by Morris Fishbein, a physician and medical editor, is Little Blue Book number 648, published at Girard, Kansas, in 1926 and edited by Haldeman-Julius. Fishbein opens with a short history of medicine itself. The old medicine, he says, was a medley of superstition, faith, theory, and tradition, lit by gleams of exact observation.

Modern medicine, by contrast, rests on the study of disease in the living and the dead. It has split the old family doctor's trade into a dozen professions, taking in prevention and public health. Against the gland-grafting and serum cures then in fashion, Fishbein sets this standard: claims for restoring youth must show evidence, not testimonials. The booklet is a skeptic's guide to a noisy trade.
79020-the-spoon:
The Spoon, by Habbakuk Westman of the Globe Tavern, formerly a public school teacher, carries upwards of one hundred illustrations: primitive, Egyptian, Roman, medieval, and modern. It was published in London, as part of the transactions of a society of literary and scientific rag pickers.

An advertisement explains the project. The Spoon is the first of a series of papers meant to elucidate the origin, history, and value of primitive devices. From their apparent insignificance, such devices have been overlooked by writers on the useful arts. Yet they have not been without influence on the progress of civilization. To treat every subject with the gravity of research would make a writer the personification of melancholy herself, the notice jokes. So the papers are embraced under a comic society name. Readers get a mock learned monograph on the spoon, half antiquarian, half jest.
79086-three-base-benson:
Three-Base Benson is a school baseball story by Ralph Henry Barbour. It came out in 1921. Barbour was a steady hand at tales of school sport for boys.

A new boy, Jerry, arrives in the first chapter and meets a hazing. The tryout and the batting net test his worth on the diamond. A deserted mine and a cabin in the woods add scrapes off the field. The ninth inning brings the big game to a head. Jerry gives a party before the close. The tale mixes sport, pluck and school loyalty in Barbour's brisk way. A great discovery late in the tale rewards Jerry's grit.
79092-the-lavender-dragon:
The Lavender Dragon is a fantasy novel by Eden Phillpotts, printed at London in 1923. It opens nigh about the middle of the Dark Ages. A knight and his squire ride toward their destination under the setting sun. The knight is Sir Jasper de Pomeroy, descended from a man who helped William the Conqueror and was paid in Devon hundreds.

Sir Jasper favours his English mother and shows little of the Norman. His hair flashes golden, his eyes are large and very blue, and the purest ideals mark his quality. His father told him bluntly that he had a heart of gold and a brain of clay. The chapter titles promise an appointment for Rainbarrow, a vigil, and a dragon who keeps his word. Later the dragon explains, and then explains some more. Another dragon gives a louder roar.
79215-separation:
Separation is a short story by Helen Hull of a girl and her mother. It ran in a magazine in March of the year nineteen twenty. Cynthia, the girl, begs leave to call on a new wife in town. Her mother holds the bond like a rope that tugs the child back.

Practice is done, she pleads, and the call is long past due in her mind. The mother calls the wife a stranger who plants wild thoughts in the girl. Sulk and hush at home are laid at that womans door in the talk. Leave is grudged at last, with a hope it ends there, as a part threat. One short scene holds a whole war of love and rule.
79253-napoleon:
Emil Ludwig wrote this life of Napoleon, rendered into English by Eden and Cedar Paul and printed in New York in 1926. A line from Goethe heads the book, on a man who sought virtue and got power. The book ran through thirteen printings in little more than a year. Portraits trace Napoleon from boyhood in 1783 to the crown.

Ludwig builds the life in five books, each named for water. The Island comes first, then The Torrent, The River, The Sea, and The Rock. A table of dates and a long picture list aid the reader. The shape suggests a rise from a small island start to a flood tide of power, and at last a bare rock.
7926-endymion:
Benjamin Disraeli, Earl of Beaconsfield, published Endymion in 1880, near the end of a career that had already made him a novelist and a prime minister. The novel follows the young Endymion Ferrars, who arrives in London society with little money and, through charm, friendship, and his sister Myra's ambition, climbs toward the centre of political life. Its opening night scenes in St James's set the tone of clubs, drawing rooms, and whispered intrigue.

Disraeli drew on a lifetime inside the world he describes, so the politics, parties, and social climbing feel observed rather than invented. The book is long and leisurely, full of conversation and character sketches. Readers interested in Victorian politics, or in how a politician imagined his own rise in fiction, will find it the most personal of his late novels.
79266-terror-station:
Terror Station is a science tale by Swain, of beasts that burst from no place at a hid base in the waste. A head note sells its stake in plain terms: its hero knew the thing was not mad thought. He fought a foul foe, and the stake was Earth.

Its first scene is a night drive in the waste. A woman comes first to his sight. Blind, she stumbles out of the moon less night a stretch in front, into the dim edge of the path his car lamps cut. She lurches and staggers through the loose stones of the road side. She gains the hard road and takes two short, unsure steps out on it. She sways as if the shift to smooth ground had near made her fall. He slams his brakes down.
79272-the-tank-in-action:
Browne writes the tank's first war in The Tank in Action, printed at Edinburgh and London in 1920. Blackwood made the book, with illustrations. Browne was a captain with the Military Cross. A frontispiece shows tanks crossing the Steenbeek for the attack beyond Saint Julien in August 1917. He gives the book to the officers and men of the 7th and 12th tank battalions.

Two phases divide the tale. The first phase, from the Somme to Ypres, opens with the genesis of the landship. The Mark One and Mark Four tanks and the first companies follow. The Somme battles, the battles in front of Arras, and a Palestine detachment fill the span. Messines and Ypres close it. The second phase takes Cambrai and after: the German offensive, the tank corps in retreat, and the great advance. Hamel, Moreuil, and the fighting for the Canal du Nord end the shown run.
79284-winds-of-rebellion:
Ernest Haycox wrote this tale of the American Revolution, set in the hard spring of 1777. Young Jeffry Peale sits in a leaking hut with a copy of Grotius, while Washington's army rests in the Morristown hills. Rain tattoos the window, cold currents pour through the chinks, and his fingers stiffen like marble as he reads.

Peale gives up his book and heads for the warmth of the Black Frigate Tavern, where his brother officers have long been gathered. The chapters that follow promise a captain of the king's own, a prison ship, an escape, and blade meeting blade. Haycox, a master of the western, turns the same clean craft on the war for independence.
79296-genius-and-degeneration:
Genius and Degeneration is a study of the mind by William Hirsch, a German doctor of nervous diseases. The hosted text is the English version from the second German edition, published in London by Heinemann in 1897. The book is dedicated to Mendel, professor at the Royal University of Berlin.

Hirsch's preface faces a problem of tongues. His cases are drawn from the heroes of German thought and art. Their traits can be read best by their own people. Yet he trusts the English reader to know them well enough. His aim is to test the claims of his day about genius. Was the great mind a sign of decay in the stock, or its crown? He analyses noted lives and works to reach a sound notion of both genius and degeneration.
79385-five-miles-to-perdition:
Henry Herbert Knibbs wrote Five Miles to Perdition, a western tale of his hero Young Pete. Pete and Dave Hamill ride through a dry land and pass a worn sign by a water hole. The sign says the town of Perdition lies five miles off. Pete jokes that there are many kinds of hell, and many names for it.

Perdition calls itself a tough town, though its mines have shut down. Cow hands and graft keep its dance hall and wheel alive. Town law makes each guest hang up his guns at the door, or pay a fine. Pete and Dave do not know that rule when they sit down for steak. Marshal Collins steps in from a side door, and the clash starts at once.
79416-boswell-s-life-of-johnson:
Charles Finger wrote a short life study of Boswell and his famed Life of Johnson. The book came out in Girard, Kansas, in 1923. It is number 394 in a ten cent pocket series. Haldeman-Julius ran that cheap book line. Finger grants that most folk credit Boswell for all we know of Johnson.

He calls that claim false, though Boswell's Life is the best of its kind. No life book beats it, he says, and few come close. He ranks Frank Harris on Wilde as next in line. Hunt's own life tale wins a nod as well. In brief, cheap form, Finger gives new readers a door into Johnson.
79448-woman-and-the-higher-education:
Woman and the Higher Education, edited by Anna Brackett for the Distaff Series, gathers seven essays on the schooling of women across the century. Harper and Brothers issued it at New York in 1893, and Brackett closes the volume with her own piece on the private school for girls.

Emma Willard opens with her 1819 plan for improving female education, and Emma Embury follows in 1831. Maria Mitchell of Vassar writes on the collegiate education of girls, Lucia Gilbert Runkle knocks at an old door, and Alice Freeman Palmer reviews the higher education of women in 1889. Lucy Salmon's piece on teaching history in academies and colleges dates from 1890. The set formed part of the New York women's exhibit of their own literature.
79505-the-ladies-of-lyndon:
Margaret Kennedy, author of The Constant Nymph, wrote The Ladies of Lyndon, published at Garden City by Doubleday, Page in 1925. Five long chapters make the book, and their titles name the acts: The Virtuous Stepmother, The Florentine, The Kind Companions, The Braxhall Frescoes, and The Fools' Progress.

The first chapter opens on a London phenomenon. The town held many distinguished gray-headed bachelors who owed their single state to one woman. Varden Cocks had refused most of them in her youth. Unable to choose again, they gloried in their shackles. At 47 she stood at the zenith of her attractions, handsome in the style of the First Empire, with a rich contralto wit. Her husband, a scholar of fatigued learning, was never heard to speak after the marriage. Kennedy builds her comedy on that marriage.
79550-kick-formation:
Kick Formation is a football story for boys by Ralph Henry Barbour. Appleton published it in New York. The front matter lists Barbour's many series: the Yardley Hall books, the Purple Pennant books, and others. A picture caption cries touchdown, implored by the North Bank rooters. Barbour wrote school sports fiction by the shelf.

His heroes play football, baseball, and crew races at boarding schools and colleges. Yardley Hall and Erskine College host most of the games. Kick Formation takes its title from the punt formation of the old game. The tales teach clean play, loyalty, and nerve under pressure, and they were staples of boys' reading for thirty years.
79561-some-ethical-gains-through-legisla:
Florence Kelley argues from experience in Some Ethical Gains Through Legislation, copyrighted in 1905 by the Macmillan Company and reprinted in 1910 in the Citizen's Library edited by Richard T Ely. Kelley writes as general secretary of the National Consumers League. Her preface traces the book to her work as a special agent investigating the needle-trades in Chicago tenements in 1892.

She served as chief inspector of factories for Illinois from 1893 to 1897, then ran the Chicago division of the federal slums investigation. Thirteen years of residence at Hull-House and the Nurses' Settlement underlie her account of statutes and court decisions.
79646-underestimation:
Underestimation is a science fiction story credited to Alger Rome, a pen name shared by Algis Budrys and Jerome Bixby. A teaser warns never to underestimate the power of a woman. The ship RAM-E/M 3 lifts from Flushing Spaceport, bound for Mars, built to run by robot at least ninety percent of the time.

When the jets cut out, a girl staggers into the control room, blood at her nose, grinning. Gerris, the pilot, tells the stowaway Marilyn that the ship has no airlock, no full manual controls, and no way to turn back. She is fleeing a house of correction and does not care, while his wife and two children wait in Marsdome.
79654-race-and-reason:
Carleton Putnam wrote this book on race and the school ruling of 1954. Public Affairs Press printed it at Washington in 1961. Senator Harry Byrd urges the book on readers in a foreword note. The North-South Council sent copies free with its own funds.

Contents frame the hidden issue, then treat the case point by point. Anthropology, intermarriage, democracy, Christian ethics, and sociology get sections here. Communism and the constitutional issue close the long third chapter. Putnam opens by recalling his own past indifference to the ruling. A summations and outlook section ends the long point by point part before the conclusion.
79669-alias-napoleon:
John Jakes spins a carnival tale around a wax works owner in the hosted story. Jack Morris bought his pitch from an aging carny who left for Arizona for his health. Morris lacks an inventive mind, the tale insists, and his good seasons end with a week in a Miami Beach hotel.

On a warm July night at Peelsville, Illinois, Morris walks back from supper with Major Mite, a small man with a Police Gazette in his pocket. The lot glows with chains of colored bulbs and smells of sawdust as crowds wait at the gates. Morris spots a falling star with a green tail and laughs it off. Readers get a tale that asks what changes when a plain man meets a thing he cannot explain.
79698-george-washington:
George Washington is a life of the first president by Woodrow Wilson, first held by copyright in 1896 and printed in a later edition by Harper. Howard Pyle drew many of its pictures from old prints and paintings. The Stuart portrait of Washington stands at the front, and Wilson gives the book to the wife whose counsel, he says, inspired his literary work.

The chapters run from Washington's day and his Virginian breeding to his years as colonel and general. Mount Vernon days, the heat of politics, and the stress of victory each get their place. Wilson closes with Washington first in peace and first president, writing history as literature for general readers.
79708-twenty-five-years-as-bishop-of-lon:
Charles Herbert wrote Twenty-Five Years as Bishop of London, issued at London by Wells Gardner, Darton and Company. The book marks the twenty-five years of Doctor Winnington Ingram in the see of London. A photograph of the bishop stands at the front. The publishers own the book is not official and not issued with his leave. It is a tribute from outside to a bishop and a man.

The chapters run from birth and parentage through school days at Marlborough and Keble College. Curacies at Shrewsbury and Lichfield, Oxford House, Bethnal Green, and the bishopric of Stepney follow, to the see of London and the bishop during the war. Arthur Foley Winnington Ingram was born on January 26, 1858, at Stanford Rectory in Worcestershire. The book gives a life of a churchman and a view of London's religious change.
79726-the-house-of-the-falcon:
The House of the Falcon is an adventure novel by Harold Lamb. Appleton published the book in New York in 1921, from magazine rights of the year before. Lamb had already won readers with Marching Sands. The tale opens at Kashgar, where the spurs of great ranges meet, in the land natives call the roof of the world.

The narrator tells how a white man was carried up out of the city before five thousand watching natives. Not one of them cared to follow him. The contents promise a seller of rugs, a garden, and a ride alone by the heroine Edith. Later chapters reach the country of the Falcon, a bronze bowl, and a stone chamber. A pledge is made and broken, and a caravan passes at the close. The story blends Central Asian travel with peril, secrets, and rescue.
79734-a-japanese-artist-in-london:
Japanese Artist in London was written and pictured by Yoshio Markino himself. George Jacobs of Philadelphia issued the American edition in nineteen ten. Chatto and Windus held the English copyright of the book that year. Colour plates show Fulham Road, Chelsea Embankment, and Hyde Park Corner.

Chapters trace his arrival in England and life in Greenwich and New Cross. Kensal Rise, a tombstone maker shop in Norwood, and Brixton follow in turn. One dark chapter tells how he resolved to kill himself, then loosened the rope. Japanese impressions of England and his Japanese friends fill later pages. The Color of London and hospital chapters close the artist memoir.
79744-the-impulsive-mr-morrison:
Fred MacIsaac wrote a novelette of intrigue in Central America. James Vincent Morrison looks from his room at the Hotel Trinidad over Rosa Blanca and curses it as a hot, festering tropic hole. His clothes are wringing wet at two in the afternoon while all others take siesta. A hundred yards across the plaza stands the president's palace.

Morrison has lingered a week in Rosa Blanca, White Rose, a lovely name for a pest hole. Ellen Goring is here, the consul's daughter, though she has told him plainly she will not marry him. Central Americans are temperamental and quick to act, the blurb says, but none as wildly impulsive as young Jim Morrison. Revolution, love, and heat drive the whirlwind plot.
8066-the-bible-king-james-version-book-6:
John received the Revelation of Jesus Christ, sent by an angel, and wrote it to the seven churches of Asia. The book opens with letters to those churches, praising and rebuking them, then unfolds in visions: seals opened, trumpets blown, a dragon and two beasts, Babylon fallen, and a final battle. It closes with a new heaven and a new earth, the river of life, and the promise that Christ comes quickly.

Revelation is the Bible's apocalypse, written in symbols for a church under Roman pressure. Its images have inspired art, music, and countless interpretations, some sober, some wild. In the King James Version, its language is unforgettable, and the book remains both the most mysterious and the most hopeful ending to the Christian Scriptures.
810-george-silverman-s-explanation:
Charles Dickens wrote this short tale in the voice of George Silverman, a clergyman who sets out to explain his life. He begins with the abrupt words that first came to his pen. He then looks back on a childhood of poverty, a youth of struggle, and a career shaped by conscience and by the help of others.

Silverman tells his story with humility, owning his faults and his debts. Dickens uses the first-person form to probe guilt, gratitude, and the accidents that make a life. The tale is brief and reflective, a late Dickens piece that rewards readers who like character studied from within.
813-reminiscences-of-tolstoy-by-his-son:
Count Ilya Tolstoy, son of Leo Tolstoy, wrote these reminiscences of his father, translated by George Calderon. He recalls the great novelist at home, describing his children in a letter to his great-aunt, and painting family life at Yasnaya Polyana with candour and affection. The father's genius and his moods both appear.

Ilya writes as a son, not a scholar, and his memories are intimate: games, quarrels, work, and talk. The book gives readers Tolstoy the man, seen by one who lived under his roof. It is a warm, frank memoir, valued by all who want to know the person behind War and Peace and Anna Karenina.
8201-mary-marston:
George MacDonald wrote Mary Marston, a novel whose contents move from the shop and its customers, through the arbour at Thornwick, Godfrey Wardour. Tom Helmer, and Durnmelling, to the oak, confusion, the heath and the hut, William Marston, Mary's dream, and a human sacrifice. Later chapters follow Mary in the shop, a wedding-dress, Mr and Mrs Redmain, a menial, and Mary's reception and position. The story centres on a young woman's work, love, and moral growth.

MacDonald, known for fantasy and sermons, here writes realistic fiction about a shop girl's integrity and independence. Mary's plain goodness, tested by suitors and employers, carries the novel. For readers of Victorian fiction, it is a warm, earnest story, and a good example of MacDonald's belief that ordinary life holds spiritual drama.
821-dombey-and-son:
Charles Dickens wrote this novel about Paul Dombey, a proud London merchant who values his firm above his family. He longs for a son to carry on Dombey and Son, and when little Paul is born, he dotes on the boy while coldly neglecting his daughter Florence. The boy's frail health casts a shadow over the house.

Paul's death breaks the firm and the father in different ways, and Florence must find her own path through pride, marriage, and ruin. Dickens fills the tale with clerks, captains, and rogues, and with the life of city trade. The novel stands as a powerful study of pride, love withheld, and a daughter's quiet strength.
8249-the-world-english-bible-web-song-of:
Song of Solomon is a sequence of love poems, unlike anything else in the Bible, linked by tradition to King Solomon. Two lovers speak in turn: a young woman and her beloved, praising each other's beauty in images drawn from gardens, vineyards, spices, and the hills of ancient Israel. They seek each other, lose each other, and find each other again, in verses full of longing and delight.

Jewish and Christian readers have long read the poems both as a celebration of human love and as a picture of God's love for his people. Either way, the poetry itself is the point: bold, tender, and physical. In this modern English version, the lovers' voices stay direct and warm, with the old images left intact.
8293-the-world-english-bible-web-revelat:
John, exiled on the island of Patmos, wrote Revelation as letters to seven churches in Asia Minor, wrapped in visions. Lambs and dragons, seals and trumpets, a beast from the sea and a whore on its back: the images are wild. Their message to readers under Rome was plain, that empires fall and God wins. The book ends with a new heaven, a new earth, and a city with gates that never shut.

Readers have argued over its symbols for two thousand years, matching beasts to emperors, popes, and dictators in turn. Read as its first readers likely read it, it is resistance writing in code, meant to comfort a hunted minority. In modern English, the visions keep their color and terror intact.
83-from-the-earth-to-the-moon-and-round-:
After the American Civil War, a club of artillery lovers plans a shot at the Moon. Jules Verne's From the Earth to the Moon follows the Baltimore Gun Club as President Barbicane proposes a giant cannon. Members debate powder, metal, and the best launch site.

Florida wins over Texas, and the Columbiad cannon rises at Stones Hill. A French adventurer joins the crew, and a second volume carries the travelers around the Moon. Verne mixes real ballistics with bold guessing about space flight. The novel helped invent science fiction's voyage tale.
8300-the-bible-douay-rheims-complete-the:
Here stands the whole Douay-Rheims Bible in Bishop Richard Challoner's revision, the English Catholic Bible translated from the Latin Vulgate. The Old Testament first appeared from the English College at Douay in 1609 and 1610. The New Testament came from Rheims in 1582, and Challoner reworked the whole text between 1749 and 1752, comparing it again with the Vulgate. English Catholics in exile and at home read Scripture in this form for centuries.

The complete volume runs from Genesis to the Apocalypse, with the longer Old Testament canon of the Catholic Church, including Tobias, Wisdom, and the Machabees. Its notes and older names, Isaias for Isaiah and Jeremias for Jeremiah, mark it out from modern translations. For readers and scholars, it is the classic English Catholic Bible in one place.
8302-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-02-exod:
Exodus tells how Israel left Egypt, and the Douay-Rheims text gives the story in Challoner's Vulgate-based English. Moses, drawn from the Nile, confronts Pharaoh, and ten plagues break Egypt's grip. The people cross the sea, grumble in the desert, receive the law at Sinai, and build the tabernacle, a portable sanctuary, while Moses pleads for a stiff-necked people.

The book's center is the covenant: ten commandments, laws for worship and daily life, and a God who dwells among the people he freed. Exodus has fed liberation movements ever since, from enslaved peoples to modern preachers. In Challoner's phrasing, the old story keeps a formal, almost liturgical tread.
8306-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-06-josu:
Josue is the Douay-Rheims name for Joshua, Moses's successor, and his book tells how Israel entered the promised land. The Jordan parts, Jericho's walls fall to trumpets and a shout, and the land is divided among the tribes by lot. Battles, treaties, and one long day when the sun is said to stand still fill the middle chapters, and the book closes with Joshua's farewell: choose whom you will serve.

Challoner's text from the Latin Vulgate keeps Josue for the hero modern Bibles call Joshua. The conquest story has troubled readers, ancient and modern, with its harshness toward Canaan's peoples. Read whole, it is a book about promise kept, land shared, and a people's choice to stay faithful after victory.
8307-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-07-judg:
Judges tells of Israel in the unsettled generations after Joshua, when no king ruled and each tribe fended for itself. In the Douay-Rheims telling, revised by Bishop Challoner from the Latin Vulgate, the pattern repeats. The people stray, an enemy oppresses them, they cry out, and God raises a judge to deliver them. The judges are rough heroes, not saints.

Readers meet Deborah, who leads an army from under a palm tree; Gideon, who tests God with a fleece; and Samson, whose strength and weakness drive the closing tales. The book ends in civil war and chaos, a dark warning about life without leadership. Its stories are violent, vivid, and frank about human failure.
8308-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-08-ruth:
Ruth is a quiet story set in the violent days of the judges, and its gentleness is the point. Naomi, widowed in Moab, returns to Bethlehem, and her Moabite daughter-in-law Ruth refuses to leave her, gleaning barley in the fields of Boaz, a kind relative. Boaz marries Ruth, and their child Obed becomes the grandfather of David.

The Douay-Rheims telling, revised by Challoner from the Vulgate, keeps the tale short, just four chapters, and lets loyalty do the work of theology. Ruth shows how outsiders enter Israel's story through faithfulness rather than birth. Readers love it for its harvest setting, its plain dialogue, and its ending, where a family line leads to a king.
8317-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-17-tobi:
Tobias is a short tale of family loyalty, told in the Douay-Rheims Bible under the name Tobias, where modern Bibles say Tobit. An old blind man in exile sends his son Tobias on a journey to collect a debt, and the young man travels with a hidden companion, the angel Raphael. Along the road he catches a fish whose parts heal blindness and drive off a demon.

The story ends with debts paid, a marriage blessed, sight restored, and a father's song of praise. It reads like a folk tale with a moral core: bury the dead, honor parents, give alms, and trust the guide beside you. Challoner's Vulgate-based text keeps the tale in its older Catholic dress, plain and warm.
8318-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-18-judi:
Judith is a heroine who saves her city with beauty and a sword. When the Assyrian general Holofernes besieges Bethulia, the widow Judith dresses in her finest. She enters his camp claiming she will betray her people, and beheads him in his tent after he drinks himself senseless. His army flees in panic, and Judith returns home singing praise.

The tale belongs to the Catholic canon, and its history is more legend than chronicle: the places and kings do not quite match known records. That never mattered to its readers, who loved Judith as a picture of courage and cunning. Challoner's Douay-Rheims text tells it plainly, with prayers and songs that frame the daring deed.
8319-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-19-esth:
Esther is a court tale with no mention of God, and all the more gripping for it. A Jewish orphan becomes queen of Persia, hides her origin, and then risks her life to expose Haman, the minister plotting to wipe out her people. The plot turns on banquets, sleepless nights, and a gallows built for the wrong man, and it ends with the Jews defending themselves and feasting.

The Douay-Rheims text, in Challoner's revision from the Vulgate, keeps the older names, Assuerus for the king and Mardochai for Mordecai, and adds the longer Catholic passages. Esther explains the feast of Purim, still kept by Jews each spring. It is the Bible's great story of courage timed to a single bold speech.
8320-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-20-job-:
Why do the good suffer? Job asks it louder than any other book in the Bible. A blameless man loses children, wealth, and health, and his friends arrive to explain it away: he must have sinned. Job refuses the easy answer and demands that God explain himself. Their debate, in long poetic speeches, fills most of the book.

God's answer comes as a storm of questions about creation, wild animals, and the sea, and Job falls silent. His fortunes return at the end, though the book never quite says why he suffered. The Douay-Rheims text, revised by Challoner from the Vulgate, gives the poetry in older, formal English. Readers in grief still find Job honest where comfort books are not.
8321-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-21-psal:
One hundred and fifty songs make up the Psalms, the prayer book of Israel and, for centuries, of the Christian church. Most are linked to David in the Douay-Rheims headings, though the book's own introduction admits others, like Asaph, also wrote. Lament, praise, thanks, and trust follow one another: cries from pits and sickbeds, royal hymns, and the long meditation on the law in Psalm 119.

Challoner's revision from the Latin Vulgate gives familiar lines in older Catholic wording, with the Hebrew title Tehillim, hymns of praise, noted at the head. Readers have prayed these poems in grief and joy alike, and monks once sang the whole book weekly. It remains the Bible's most used book, meant to be spoken aloud.
8325-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-25-wisd:
Wisdom speaks as a lady calling to the young in this book, which belongs to the Catholic Old Testament and not to the Hebrew canon. The book praises wisdom as God's companion at creation, warns rulers that power will be judged, and contrasts the fate of the just with the empty hopes of the wicked. Its final chapters retell the Exodus as a contest between God's care and Egypt's idols.

Tradition linked the book to Solomon, and its Greek style and philosophy show a Judaism speaking to the wider ancient world. Challoner's Douay-Rheims wording keeps its stately, churchly tone. Readers meet here the most philosophical book of the Catholic Bible, where faith argues in the language of reason.
8327-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-27-isai:
Isaias is the Douay-Rheims name for Isaiah, the great prophet of eighth-century Jerusalem. He preached through the reigns of four kings. He warned that empty ritual and unjust courts would bring Assyria down on Judah, and promised a child called Emmanuel and a servant who suffers for others. His oracles swing between judgment on nations and comfort for a bruised people.

The book's second half, written in exile, speaks to a people with nothing left, promising a highway in the desert and a new creation. Christians read the servant songs as pointing to Jesus, and Handel set the comfort passages to music. In Challoner's Vulgate English, Isaias keeps the older spelling and the full sweep of the longest prophetic book.
8330-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-30-baru:
Baruch speaks for exiles in Babylon, and his short book belongs to the Catholic Old Testament. It opens with a confession: the people sinned, Jerusalem fell, and only repentance opens the way home. A prayer for wisdom follows, praising the law as the wisdom other nations seek in vain, and the book closes with Jerusalem herself speaking comfort to her scattered children.

Tradition names Baruch, Jeremiah's scribe, as author, though the book likely took shape later, in Greek. Challoner's Douay-Rheims text gives it in Vulgate-based English, with the letter of Jeremias sometimes attached. Readers find here exile theology at its plainest: sin named, mercy sought, and a city told to rise and shine.
8332-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-32-dani:
Daniel serves kings in Babylon and Persia, and his book mixes court tales with apocalyptic visions. In the Douay-Rheims text, Daniel reads handwriting on a palace wall, survives a lions' den, and interprets dreams of beasts and empires rising and falling. The longer Catholic form adds the stories of Susanna, and of Bel and the Dragon, tales of a framed woman and of idols exposed.

The visions, beasts, horns, and a son of man coming on clouds, have fed readers under persecution ever since. Challoner's revision from the Vulgate keeps the older Catholic shape, with those added stories in place. Daniel suits readers who want faith tested in a foreign court, and hope pictured in wild, unforgettable images.
8333-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-33-osee:
Osee is the Douay-Rheims name for Hosea, the prophet whose marriage became his message. In the northern kingdom's last days, Hosea married a woman who left him, and he read Israel's worship of other gods through that betrayal. Judgment oracles, naming children with names like Not Pitied, alternate with sudden tenderness, as God speaks of teaching Israel to walk and calling a son out of Egypt.

Challoner's revision from the Latin Vulgate preserves the older spelling and the book's raw, domestic imagery. Short and fierce, Osee asks whether love can survive betrayal, and answers that it can, but not cheaply. Later writers, Jewish and Christian, have drawn on its picture of God as a wounded husband and father ever since.
8335-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-35-amos:
A herdsman from Tekoa walked into Israel's shrines and told the comfortable they were doomed, and that is the book of Amos. In the Douay-Rheims text, the prophet's oracles strike Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, and the rest. They then turn on Israel itself: the poor sold for shoes, courts rigged, and festivals that God says he hates. Visions follow, a plumb line, ripe fruit, and an altar shaken.

Challoner's revision keeps Amos short and blunt, closing with a promise that the fallen house of David will rise again. The book's cry for justice to roll down like waters has been quoted by preachers and civil rights leaders alike. It remains the Old Testament's sharpest protest against religion that ignores the poor.
8348-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-48-mark:
Mark's Gospel is the shortest and fastest of the four, and the Douay-Rheims text gives it in Challoner's older English. Jesus moves from baptism to desert to crowded healings with hardly a pause, and the word immediately drives the story on. Parables are few, miracles many, and the disciples misunderstand again and again, until the crucifixion leaves them scattered.

The book ends abruptly, with frightened women at an empty tomb, and later endings were added by copyists. Mark's Jesus is a man of action and secrecy, ordering demons and healed people to stay silent. Readers who want the Gospel story at its rawest and quickest start here, before the longer, more orderly accounts.
8349-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-49-luke:
Luke's Gospel, in Challoner's Douay-Rheims text, is the longest and most polished of the four. It alone tells of shepherds at the manger, the boy Jesus among the teachers, and the parables of the good Samaritan and the prodigal son. The poor, women, and outcasts stand near the center throughout, and shared meals recur as signs of welcome.

From the birth stories to the road to Emmaus, Luke stresses mercy, prayer, and joy, and its story continues in the Acts of the Apostles. The Vulgate-based wording gives familiar scenes in older Catholic English. Readers who want the most humane portrait of Jesus, told with a historian's care, usually turn to Luke first.
8350-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-50-john:
John's Gospel differs from the other three in tone, structure, and depth. Instead of parables, Jesus speaks in long discourses: I am the bread of life, the light of the world, the good shepherd, the resurrection. Seven signs, from water turned to wine to Lazarus raised, build the claim that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.

The Douay-Rheims text, revised by Challoner from the Vulgate, gives those great I am sayings in older Catholic English. John's farewell discourses at the Last Supper and the piercing scene at the cross have shaped Christian devotion more than any other Gospel passages. It is the most theological Gospel, and the most intimate.
8351-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-51-acts:
Acts picks up where Luke's Gospel leaves off, and the Douay-Rheims text tells it in Challoner's Vulgate English. The Spirit falls at Pentecost, Peter preaches to crowds, and the young church grows through arrests, miracles, and the death of Stephen. The gospel then crosses borders: to Samaritans, to an Ethiopian courtier, and to a Roman officer's household.

Paul dominates the second half, converted on the Damascus road, traveling the empire, shipwrecked, and finally preaching under guard in Rome. Acts is the church's first history, written with a traveler's eye for ports, prisons, and crowds. It shows how a small Jewish movement became a faith spanning the Roman world.
8352-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-52-roma:
Paul's letter to Rome is his fullest statement of faith, and the Douay-Rheims text gives it in Challoner's Vulgate-based English. He argues that all people, Jew and Gentile alike, stand guilty before God, and that trust in Christ opens mercy and new life. The letter moves from guilt to grace, wrestles with Israel's place in God's plan, and closes with plain rules for daily conduct.

Romans has shaped Christian thought more than any other letter, quoted by Augustine, Luther, and every reformer since. Its long sentences reward slow reading, and its chapters on love, rulers, and conscience remain preaching staples. In Challoner's wording, Paul's careful argument keeps a formal, almost legal tread.
8366-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-66-jame:
James is the New Testament's plainest moral letter, and the Douay-Rheims text gives it in Challoner's older English. Writing to scattered Jewish Christians, James urges patience under trials, warns the rich, and insists that faith without works is dead, a claim that troubled Luther, who called the letter straw. Its images are homely: tongues like rudders and fires, wealth rotting in storehouses.

Advice on prayer, on the sick, and on bringing back wanderers closes the short book. James has no grand theology, only conduct, and that is its power. For readers who want Scripture as a rule of life rather than a system, James remains the go-to letter, quoted in sermons on speech, money, and mercy.
8369-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-69-1-jo:
How can believers be sure they know God? This letter answers with tests repeated like a refrain: keep his commandments, love the brothers, and hold to the truth about Jesus. God is light, the writer says, and God is love, and claims to faith without love are empty. Warnings against false teachers and against loving the world run between the comforts.

The Douay-Rheims text, in Challoner's revision from the Vulgate, gives the letter's short sentences in older English. Readers find 1 John the easiest New Testament book to follow and one of the hardest to live up to. It ends with a final guard, brief and blunt: keep yourselves from idols.
8427-home-missions-in-action:
Edith H. Allen wrote Home Missions in Action as a textbook for 1915-16, under the general topic The Church at Its Task, chosen by the Committee of Twenty-eight. That committee joined four missionary organizations, the Home Missions Council among them, and Allen's book, dedicated to her father, a Christian patriot, explains what home missions did across America.

The volume covers churches planting, serving, and organizing in cities, frontiers, and immigrant communities, as a study text for missionary societies. Readers interested in American religious history get a clear, earnest account of how churches saw their domestic task a century ago. It is a period textbook, useful for its picture of mission work at home.
843-the-life-of-francis-marion:
W. Gilmore Simms wrote this life of Francis Marion, the Swamp Fox of the American Revolution in South Carolina. Marion led small bands of partisans against British troops, striking from swamps and woods and vanishing before a larger force could catch him. Bryant's lines, quoted at the head, say British soldiers trembled at his name.

Simms, himself a South Carolinian, tells Marion's campaigns with local pride and detail, from raids to retreats. The book praises Marion's cunning, patience, and care for his men. It remains a classic Southern account of the partisan war, valued for its vigour and for its portrait of a hero who won by eluding, not by meeting, the foe.
8457-frenzied-fiction:
Stephen Leacock, the Canadian humorist, gathers comic pieces in Frenzied Fiction. Contents ranging from My Revelations as a Spy and Father Knickerbocker to The Prophet in Our Midst, Personal Adventures in the Spirit World, and The Cave-Man as He Is. Ideal interviews follow, with a European prince, a great actor, a great scientist, and typical novelists.

Leacock's humor is gentle and absurd, poking at spies, spirits, prophets, and literary fashion with a professor's wit. Readers get the best-selling humorist of his day at his most playful. The book suits anyone who likes parody without malice, and a reminder that Leacock, an economist by trade, was also the age's favorite funny man.
846-the-life-of-general-francis-marion:
Mason Locke Weems, the parson-biographer famous for his Washington, tells the life of Francis Marion, the Swamp Fox of the Southern campaign in the Revolution. Marion's guerrilla raids harassed British troops in South Carolina. Weems, a travelling bookseller and parson, wrote lives that mixed fact with moral tale.

Weems writes with anecdote and moral purpose, shaping Marion into a patriot hero for young readers. The life is more legend than strict history, but it fixed Marion in American memory as a master of swamp warfare. Marion's swamp raids in 1780 and 1781 harassed Cornwallis and heartened Southern patriots.
8464-rest-harrow-a-comedy-of-resolution:
Maurice Hewlett's Rest Harrow, subtitled A Comedy of Resolution, follows its heroine through books that promise a bruised philosopher in retirement, Sanchia at home, and a story of resolve. With illustrations by Frank Craig, the novel takes its title from a British plant that grows in any soil, a quiet emblem for a heroine putting down roots after trouble.

Hewlett, known for historical romances, writes here a modern comedy of character, where resolution means choosing a life and standing by it. Readers get an Edwardian novel of manners and feeling, less famous than his earlier work but graceful. The book suits readers who like character over plot, and a heroine who thinks her way to happiness.
8469-the-harlequinade-an-excursion:
Dion Clayton Calthrop and Granville Barker published The Harlequinade in March 1918. Its opening note warns readers plainly: this isn't a play at all, and it isn't a novel, or a treatise, or an essay, or anything easy to name. The book is an excursion into the world of Harlequin, Columbine, and the pantomime, asking what Columbine should be like, rose in hand.

Calthrop, a writer on costume and theatre, and Barker, a leading stage director, mix fancy, history, and stage lore. Readers get a meditation on pantomime's stock figures and their hold on imagination, written when music hall and pantomime still ruled Christmas. It is a small, charming oddity, best enjoyed as a ramble rather than an argument.
8529-the-world-decision:
Robert Herrick wrote The World Decision as a study of the First World War's opening, in parts on Italy and France. Part one follows Italy hesitating, the politician, the poet, and the piazza speaking, Italy deciding, and the eve of war. Part two turns to the face of Paris, the wounds of France, the barbarian, the German lesson, the faith of the French, and the new France.

Herrick, an American novelist in Europe, writes as a witness to nations choosing war. Readers get wartime essays, literary and political, from an American abroad. The book interests students of the war's cultural history, and of how writers tried to make sense of 1914 while it was still unfolding.
8569-the-far-horizon:
Lucas Malet, the pen name of Mary St Leger Harrison, wrote The Far Horizon as a novel. It follows her earlier books The Wages of Sin, A Counsel of Perfection, and Colonel Enderby's Wife. Little Peter, The Carissima, The Gateless Barrier, and The History of Sir Richard Calmady came before it too. Malet, a leading woman novelist of the late Victorian and Edwardian years, wrote fiction of strong feeling and moral seriousness.

The far horizon of the title suggests a life looking outward, toward distance and change, and Malet's novels typically follow characters tested by passion, duty, and faith. Readers of Victorian and Edwardian women's fiction will find her characteristic voice here: earnest, psychological, and unafraid of large themes. The novel rewards readers who like character-driven stories of conscience.
8579-daughters-of-the-cross-or-woman-s-m:
Daniel C. Eddy gathers lives of distinguished female heroines in Daughters of the Cross, or Woman's Mission. The motto that there are deeds which should not pass away, and names that must not wither. His preface explains that the women toiled and suffered on heathen soil, as missionaries, and their names have been gathered from many sources.

Eddy, a nineteenth-century minister and writer, writes missionary biography as inspiration, for readers who admired women's work abroad. The volume's heroines faced disease, danger, and loneliness in foreign fields, and their stories show Victorian ideas of woman's mission. Readers get a period collection, earnest and admiring, and a window onto missionary history.
8601-the-early-poems-of-alfred-lord-tenn:
John Churton Collins edited this scholarly volume on the young Alfred Tennyson, pairing the poems with a long critical introduction, commentaries, and notes. It covers the work that led to the two 1842 volumes which made Tennyson, by general consent, the leading poet of his time. Variant readings show how lines changed between drafts, and a separate section prints poems Tennyson later suppressed.

A full bibliography closes the book, tracing where each poem first appeared. Readers can watch a major poet finding his voice: early experiments in metre, story, and mood, revised and sometimes withdrawn as his judgment hardened. The volume serves students of Tennyson first, but any poetry reader gains a clear view of how a reputation was built poem by poem.
861-the-dominion-of-the-air-the-story-of:
Rev. J. M. Bacon wrote this story of aerial navigation, from the dawn of aeronautics to the airships and aeroplanes of his day. He opens with the old counsel that he who would learn to fly must practise from youth, as a tame goose tries its wings, rising by degrees until it soars.

Bacon traces balloons, dirigible craft, and the first heavier-than-air trials, with the pioneers who risked their lives in the air. His prose is popular and enthusiastic, full of the wonder of flight. The book serves readers who want the long story of man's attempt to rule the air, told before flight became commonplace.
8646-an-essay-on-the-history-of-civil-so:
Adam Ferguson, the Scottish philosopher, asks in this essay how human societies grow from rude beginnings to polished, commercial states. He moves through human nature, self-preservation, union, war, intellect, and moral feeling, arguing that society is natural to humans rather than a trick invented by rulers. Later sections weigh commerce, luxury, and political corruption against liberty and public spirit.

This eighth edition reprints a landmark of the Scottish Enlightenment, first published when Britain was debating empire, wealth, and revolution. Ferguson warns that refined nations can lose courage and virtue even as they gain arts and riches. Students of political thought still read him beside Smith and Hume, and general readers will find a clear, forceful argument about what holds a free society together.
8653-east-o-the-sun-and-west-o-the-moon:
Gudrun Thorne-Thomsen retold this set of Norwegian folk tales for English-speaking children, with pictures by Frederick Richardson. The title story sends a girl east of the sun and west of the moon to rescue her prince, and the rest of the book ranges just as widely. Readers meet the Three Billy Goats Gruff, the lad who went to the North Wind, the giant with no heart in his body, and the pancake that runs away.

Other tales explain why the bear has a stumpy tail and why the sea is salt, while farm folk, parsons, and clever lads outwit trolls and giants. The retellings keep the tales short, plain, and easy to read aloud. Families gain a sturdy introduction to Norway's story stock, and the book preserves the humour and toughness that made these tales travel far beyond their valleys.
8770-milton:
Mark Pattison, rector of Lincoln College, Oxford, writes this life of John Milton in three periods, from 1608 to 1674. The first period covers family, school, and college, residence at Horton with L'Allegro, Il Penseroso, Arcades, Comus, and Lycidas, and the journey to Italy. The second, 1640 to 1660, follows Milton's educational theory and teaching, his marriage and divorce pamphlet, his political pamphlets, and his Latin secretaryship under the Commonwealth.

Blindness, the controversy with Morus, and the great defences occupy the middle years, before the third period traces the Restoration and the writing of Paradise Lost. Pattison's Milton is learned, proud, and uncompromising, a poet who sacrificed ease for principle. The biography remains a classic Victorian life, valued for its scholarship and its clear sense of Milton's mind, even where later research has softened its judgments.
8845-weymouth-new-testament-in-modern-sp:
Paul, prisoner for Christ Jesus, with Timothy his brother, writes to Philemon, dearly loved fellow labourer, and to Apphia, Archippus, and the church meeting in Philemon's house. Grace and peace are wished to them all. Paul gives continual thanks while mentioning Philemon in prayer, because he hears of his love and faith toward the Lord Jesus and toward all God's people. The letter prays that sharing in faith may deepen understanding.

What follows is Paul's famous, delicate plea for Onesimus, a runaway slave now become a brother. Whom Paul sends back asking Philemon to receive him as he would Paul himself. Weymouth's modern speech keeps the letter's tact and warmth clear in only twenty-five verses. Readers get the New Testament's shortest, most human letter, and a text long debated for what it does, and does not, say about slavery.
8854-weymouth-new-testament-in-modern-sp:
Weymouth's Revelation opens with the revelation given by Jesus Christ. Which God granted him to make known to his servants events which must shortly come to pass, sent by angel and communicated to his servant John. John, who taught truth concerning God's Word and Jesus Christ, gives a faithful account of what he saw. Blessed are those who read, hear, and lay to heart this prophecy. The time of fulfilment is close at hand, and John greets the seven churches in Asia.

Letters, seals, trumpets, beasts, and the New Jerusalem follow in John's apocalyptic vision, rendered by Weymouth in modern speech that keeps the strange imagery readable without flattening it. Revelation has puzzled and inspired readers for centuries, and this version helps a first reader follow its structure. It suits devotional reading and study alike, as the Bible's closing book of hope amid persecution.
8891-with-the-procession:
Henry B. Fuller opens With the Procession with old Mr Marshall taking to his bed, an action his household views with more surprise than sympathy, and more impatience than surprise. It seems like the breaking down of a machine whose trustworthiness had been infallible, forcing the family to admit he is a mere human being after all. They had known a certain intimacy with him, varying with their ages. Never fully avowed that his being rested on any tangible physical basis, treating him instead as a disembodied intelligence turning values and credits into comfort.

From that wry opening, Fuller follows a Chicago family through social ambition, marriage, and the procession of new wealth that gives the novel its title. The book is a classic of American realism, satirizing Gilded Age society with a cool, precise eye.
9190-the-greater-inclination:
Edith Wharton gathered eight stories in The Greater Inclination, opening with The Muse's Tragedy. Danyers fancies he recognized Mrs. Anerton at once, though he had seen no portrait of her, since she kept strict anonymity and refused even her photograph. From her friend Mrs. Memorall he drew one impression: she is like an old print where lines hold the value of color.

Other tales include A Journey, The Pelican, Souls Belated, and A Coward. Wharton's early stories probe art, society, and the costs of feeling. The collection remains a fine introduction to her fiction, sharp, ironic, and finely wrought.
925-united-states-presidents-inaugural-s:
This volume gathers the inaugural addresses of the presidents of the United States, from George Washington to George W. Bush, covering 1789 to 2005. Washington's first address, given in New York on Thursday, 30 April 1789, opens the set, and each later president's oath-day speech follows in order.

The speeches trace the nation's hopes and crises in its leaders' own words, from union and war to depression and cold war. Read together, they show how American rhetoric changed, and how each age framed its task. The book is a ready reference for students, citizens, and anyone who wants the presidency in its own voice.
928-alice-s-adventures-in-wonderland-htm:
Lewis Carroll wrote this tale of Alice, a girl who, tired of sitting by her sister on a bank with nothing to do, follows a white rabbit down a hole into Wonderland. She grows and shrinks, meets a caterpillar, a Cheshire Cat, and a Mad Hatter, and she faces the Queen of Hearts and her court of cards.

Carroll's logic, wordplay, and dream logic have charmed readers since 1865, and this Millennium Fulcrum edition presents the text in readable form. The tale is both a children's classic and a puzzle for adults, full of jokes that reward a second reading. Alice remains one of literature's great travellers, in a world that never quite makes sense.
9408-by-water-to-the-columbian-expositio:
Johanna S. Wisthaler wrote By Water to the Columbian Exposition in 1894, a travel tale of a trip to Chicago's great fair. She and her friends sailed from Schenectady, New York, by canal and lake, bound for the fair grounds. The book follows each leg of the water road: the Erie Canal, Buffalo, Niagara Falls, and the Great Lakes. It reads as a plain, glad account of American travel by boat.

Chapters stop at canal towns, mills, and lake ports, and pause for the falls and the cities of Detroit and Cleveland. Wisthaler notes fellow travellers, sights, and the small mishaps of a long voyage. A reader gets a cheerful window on 1893 travel, when a fair trip could still be a slow water journey, rich in towns and talk.
947-the-life-of-horatio-lord-nelson:
Robert Southey wrote this life of Horatio Lord Nelson, the admiral who won Britain's sea wars against France. Southey dedicated the book to John Wilson Croker of the Admiralty, a man placed to judge its historical accuracy and its literary merit alike. The life runs from Nelson's youth to Trafalgar.

Southey tells of the Nile, Copenhagen, and Trafalgar, with Nelson's daring, his wounds, and his care for his men. His prose is clear and stirring, without hero worship that hides faults. The book became the classic Nelson biography, read by sailors and schoolboys for generations, and it still serves as a vivid introduction to the admiral.
950-tom-swift-and-his-electric-runabout-:
Tom Swift hopes for a prize in this tale by Victor Appleton, and he builds an electric runabout to win it as the speediest car on the road. Mr. Damon's steering, a motor-cycle race, and a tale of a new bank lead to building the car, while a midnight encounter and a capture test Tom's nerve.

The runabout, silent and swift, races rivals and crooks alike, with Tom at the wheel and Ned Newton at his side. Appleton writes with the brisk optimism of early motoring, when electric cars seemed the future. The book is a lively Tom Swift adventure, full of speed, invention, and fair play.
9605-chico-the-story-of-a-homing-pigeon:
Lucy M. Blanchard wrote Chico, the Story of a Homing Pigeon, in 1922, a children's tale set in Venice. Dedicated to all who love Venice, the book aims to teach Italian scenes and words without a child's notice. Explanations of Italian phrases, pictures for visual learning, and short readings suit primary grades. The tale hopes to foster love of birds.

Chico's story turns on a boy who gives up his precious pigeon to his country in a time of peril. Maria's birthday and Venetian streets fill the scenes. A reader gets a gentle, instructive animal tale, rich in Venice color and in a lesson on sacrifice.
9630-proportional-representation-a-study:
John H. Humphreys, secretary of the Proportional Representation Society, wrote Proportional Representation in 1911, a study of election methods. Lord Courtney of Penwith, in his introduction, notes the system's swift spread across Northern Europe and its coming test in France. Humphreys dedicates the book to Catherine Helen Spence of Adelaide, a tireless worker for real representation. The book aims to show how votes can mirror voters.

Chapters weigh majority rule's direct and indirect results, the case for minorities, and the single transferable vote against list systems. Humphreys writes with reformer's clarity, not party heat. A reader gets a classic brief for fair voting, still apt whenever seats fail to match ballots.
9635-the-end-of-her-honeymoon:
Mrs. Belloc Lowndes wrote The End of Her Honeymoon in 1913, a suspense tale that starts on a bride's last honeymoon night. John Dampier and his bride Nancy, wed three weeks, ride through Paris by night in an open carriage. Dampier, who knows French, jests with the driver and vows Nancy shall see Paris from its best angle. Nancy, who knows little French, creeps close to her husband.

Something odd and disconcerting happens in the Gare station yard, and Nancy remembers it long after. Lowndes, famed for crime tales, builds dread from small, strange moments. A reader gets a tense Edwardian thriller, where a honeymoon turns on a single night's mystery.
9817-peter-ibbetson:
George du Maurier's novel is presented as the memoir of Peter Ibbetson, a man who looks back on a strange and happy life. As a boy he loved his cousin Madge Plunket, and as a grown man he finds that dreams can carry him back to her and to his childhood.

Peter tells his story simply, mixing memory, prison, and dream in a way that blurs waking life and sleep. The book's pull comes from its tender idea: that love and imagination can keep a person free even when his body is shut away. It remains du Maurier's most dreamlike romance.
9866-freeland-a-social-anticipation:
Theodor Hertzka, a Viennese economist, wrote Freeland, a Social Anticipation, here in Arthur Ransom's 1891 translation. Hertzka, of the Manchester school, edited economics for the Neue Freie Presse and founded the Society of Austrian National Economists. His German Freiland appeared in early 1890 and ran through three abridged editions. Ransom translated the unabridged text, with later emendations.

The book imagines a free land built on economic reform, where labor, land, and trade find a new order. Hertzka argues as a reformer, not a dreamer alone. A reader gets a classic utopian economics tale, and a window on 1890 hopes for a just society.
9914-the-babylonian-legends-of-the-creat:
Baked clay tablets dug up at Nineveh, in the palace library of King Ashur-bani-pal, carry the creation stories retold here. Explorers such as Layard, Rassam, and George Smith recovered the tablets between 1848 and 1876, and scholars pieced the broken pieces together.

The legends open when nothing exists but the waters Apsu and Tiamat, and they tell of gods, battles, and the fight between Bel and the dragon. Readers meet a creation story far older than Genesis, from the same ancient Near East. It is a clear doorway into Babylonian myth and early archaeology.
9940-life-in-london:
Edwin Hodder's 1890 book, subtitled The Pitfalls of a Great City, follows a young man from schoolboy days into London life. Chapters trace his start in the world, a meeting with a schoolfellow, a farce, a lecture, and his slow rise, with friendship tested along the way.

Later comes exile, discoveries, and a sick chamber, as the city shows both its chances and its traps. Hodder writes as a moral guide, warning young readers against the snares of the capital while keeping the story moving. It is a Victorian cautionary tale, full of London streets, lodgings, and temptations.
9981-the-spenders-a-tale-of-the-third-ge:
Harry Leon Wilson's 1902 novel, subtitled a tale of the third generation, follows the house of Milbrey after its second generation is removed. The fortune made by hard work passes to heirs, and Billy Brue finds his man as West meets East.

Chapters follow the young multi-millionaire's diversions, a journey east, house parties, and the dignity of Horace Milbrey upheld under strain. Wilson writes with humor about new money in old society. Readers get a lively cautionary tale about riches, and a portrait of an age that loved to spend.
9990-brave-and-bold-or-the-fortunes-of-r:
