Horatio Alger Jr.'s novel follows the fortunes of Robert Rushton, opening with young rivals at Millville Academy. The schoolroom, brilliantly lighted, holds boys and girls of ten to eighteen writing under Professor George W. Granville, a traveling teacher of plain and ornamental penmanship.

From that schoolroom start, Robert faces rivals, hardship, and chances to prove himself brave and bold, in Alger's familiar pattern of pluck rewarded. The novel preaches work, honesty, and self-help to young readers. Fans of Alger get his formula at its most direct: a good boy, a hard road, and success earned.
a-bird-s-eye-view-of-the-bible-second-ed: Frank Nelson Palmer gives a short survey of the whole Bible for pupils and teachers. Charts and devices trace the sixty six books from the kingdom foreshadowed through its forming, conquest, division, captivity, and restoration. The book then follows the story to the kingdom's true king in the New Testament. Its aim is to help readers see the shape of the Bible at a glance and to guide their own study.
a-blot-in-the-scutcheon:
Robert Browning's verse tragedy turns on the honor of the house of Tresham. The introductory note sets Browning apart from aristocratic poets: a bank clerk's son, a dissenter, educated by tutors and his widely read father. His play puts that outsider's intensity into an old family's pride. The scenes move between a lodge in Lord Tresham's park, the mansion's saloon, and his sister Mildred's chamber.

Lord Tresham discovers that a lover visits Mildred by night and reads disgrace into the visits. Truth comes too late to stop the sword. Browning builds the tragedy on silence: three people who love each other refuse the one plain talk that would save them. The verse is swift and stage-worthy, rare in his work.
a-book-of-exposition: Homer Heath Nugent gathers model expositions on mechanisms, machines, natural processes, and ideas. Its pieces explain the levers of the human body, the linotype machine, the pea weevil, and modern paper making. Later essays treat relaxation, science, and religion, with notes on each writer. The collection shows students how clear writing can unfold a subject step by step.
a-century-of-negro-migration: Carter Godwin Woodson traces a century of Black migration in America. His chapters follow the search for refuge, movement to the North, struggle on free soil, and colonization schemes. Later chapters treat the successful migrant, the exodus to the West, the talented tenth, and migration during the World War. Woodson grounds the story in maps, tables, and a full bibliography.
a-christmas-sermon: Robert Louis Stevenson preaches a Christmas sermon on how to live and die well. He opens with Charles the Second, wit and sceptic, who summed up his life in a famous dying jest. Stevenson then turns to the reader with counsel on kindness, courage, and the use of time. The short sermon is warm, plain, and seasonable in tone.
a-complete-account-of-the-settlement-at-:
Watkin Tench resumes his subject, as his preface says, having already published a narrative of the colony brought up to July 1788 that passed through three editions. He resided at Port Jackson nearly four years, from January 20, 1788, to December 18, 1791, and this fuller account covers the whole term. Gratitude, he writes, must be shown by fresh information, not by claims on indulgence.

Nineteen chapters follow the settlement's hunger, discipline, building, and exploring, and its dealings with the Aboriginal people of the harbor. Tench writes of friends and enemies among them by name. His two books together form the classic first history of Sydney, valued for fairness rare in first accounts of colonization.
a-dream-of-john-ball-and-a-king-s-lesson:
William Morris wrote these two short prose works of revolt and counsel in a medieval dress. The contents list twelve chapters for A Dream of John Ball. Its narrator dreams himself into Kent at the time of the rising of 1381. He hears John Ball preach. Ball is the hedge priest of the revolt. His theme is that fellowship is heaven, and the lack of it hell. The chapters move from a meeting at the cross to a township battle. They end with talk of the days to come.

A King's Lesson, printed after the dream tale, is a brief fable. In it a king learns what his rule rests on. Morris was a socialist as well as a poet and craftsman. He used the fourteenth century to argue with his own age. The dreamer keeps asking whether the old fight for fairness was lost. The book refuses a simple answer.
a-foregone-conclusion: William Dean Howells sets a foregone conclusion in Venice. A man hurries down a long narrow calle from the Campo San Stefano toward the Grand Canal, glancing back at palace walls and sky. The Venetian setting frames a story of love and social judgment. Howells writes with his usual care for manners, character, and place.
a-history-of-english-prose-fiction: Bayard Tuckerman follows English prose fiction from early romance to the modern novel. He links each period's fiction with the social character of its age. The nineteenth century chapter notes how numerous and familiar novels had become. Tuckerman's history helps readers grasp fiction's growth and significance. The book remains a useful guide to the rise of the novel in England.
a-march-on-london-being-a-story-of-wat-t:
G. A. Henty opens his preface with the chroniclers Froissart, Monstrelet, and Holinshed. They make the fourteenth century unusually well known. He grants at once that the uprising of the Commons was in itself justifiable. Serfs owed their lords labor and labored under grievous disabilities. His hero is young Edgar, drawn into the march on London in 1381.

Nineteen chapters follow Wat Tyler, the rescue of prisoners, death to the Flemings, a combat in the Tower, and Tyler's death before the boy-king Richard. The tale then carries Edgar to the wars in Flanders, a starving town, and civil war. Henty teaches solid medieval history inside a fast boys' adventure, as was his signature method.
a-narrative-of-the-life-of-mrs-mary-jemi:
James E. Seaver took this narrative carefully from Mary Jemison's own words on November 29, 1823, as the title page states. She was taken by the Indians in 1755, when only about twelve years of age, and remained among them for life. The title page also promises what the book holds: the murder of her father and family, her sufferings, and her marriages to two Indians.

Her account covers the French and Revolutionary wars on the frontier, the customs of the Seneca among whom she lived, and the loss of her sons. An appendix adds the tragedy at the Devil's Hole and Sullivan's expedition. Jemison's story, told in old age, is one of the most remarkable captivity narratives in American letters.
a-psychological-counter-current-in-recen:
William Dean Howells wrote this essay on a turn he saw coming in the fiction of his day. Fiction, he argues, moves in tides. Realism had swept romance aside. Then romance flooded back. The flood sank the novel's good name once more. Yet Howells spots a drift against the tide. He names it psychologism. It means close care for motive and inner life. He finds it at work in the newest books.

He tests the idea on recent novels. The first case is Gilbert Parker, a popular writer of romance. Parker's latest book, Howells says, is saved by its inner study of character. The essay is criticism with a program. Howells was the dean of American letters. He argues that the novel's future lies past the fight of romance and realism. It lies in the study of character from inside.
a-question:
A Question, by Georg Ebers and translated from the German by Mary J Safford, begins as a poem before it becomes a tale. Ebers tells how a picture in an art palace on the river Isar held him spellbound in his seat. A year later, wintering with his family on a palm shaded shore in the south, the image kept returning to his mind unbidden.

The prelude explains that the words for the story arrived one bright day without searching, as if the painting itself supplied them. Alma Tadema, the painter of classical scenes, is the friend whose picture Ebers credits. What follows the verses is a prose idyl, a short tale in an ancient setting, built scene by scene from that canvas. Readers meet the artwork first as the author did: as a question that would not let go.
a-selection-of-books-published-by-methue: Methuen and Company present this selection of their books, issued from Essex Street in London in September 1911. The catalogue orders its titles by author, marking books in the press with an asterisk. It ranges across general literature, ancient cities, antiquary's books, the Arden Shakespeare, little guides, and libraries of devotion and medicine. Fiction, boys' and girls' books, travellers' books, and books on Italy complete a publisher's shop window.
a-simpleton:
Charles Reade defends his method in a fighting preface before his novel begins. He borrows facts from every source, he says. But a man who takes only facts, not treatment, is no plagiarist. All fiction worth a button, he argues, is founded on facts. The novel then tests that method on a hero of unusual simplicity.

His simpleton is a good-hearted, trusting young man set among sharper people who live by their wits. Reade follows him through love, business, and betrayal, using documented fact to fill in the worlds he crosses. The book runs long, in nineteen chapters, with Reade's usual energy, research, and moral heat on every page.
a-spirit-in-prison:
A Spirit in Prison is a 1908 novel by Robert Hichens, an English writer whose career produced more than forty novels. Hichens, full name Robert Smythe Hichens, also worked as a journalist, dramatist, and music critic. He gained notoriety with The Green Carnation and his widest popularity with The Garden of Allah, and A Spirit in Prison was among the books that won him critical praise.

Written at the height of that reputation, the novel belongs to Hichens's serious fiction rather than his satires. Its title suggests a self trapped by circumstance, a theme his psychological novels pursued in polished, atmospheric prose. The book stands as a sample of the literary craftsmanship that set Hichens apart from ordinary popular novelists of his time.
a-victorious-union: Oliver Optic tells a victorious Union story in this volume of the Blue and the Gray series afloat, published by Lee and Shepard of Boston. The series runs from Taken by the Enemy and Within the Enemy's Lines through On the Blockade and Stand by the Union to Fighting for the Right. An illustration shows Christy leaping upon the rail. It is a boys' naval adventure of the Civil War, sold separately at a dollar and fifty cents.
a-voyage-in-the-sunbeam-our-home-on-the-: Annie Brassey sails the yacht Sunbeam, her home on the ocean for eleven months, in this illustrated volume published at Chicago in 1881. The dedication thanks friends in many climes and countries, of white and coloured races and every grade in society, who made a year of travel a year of happiness. Farewell to old England opens a voyage whose illustrations include Cape Brassey in Smyths Sound, marking a family's year at sea.
a-woman-s-part-in-a-revolution: Natalie Harris Hammond tells a woman's part in a revolution in this 1897 volume, under a Thackeray epigraph on telling the truth always. The opening picture is quiet and African. A terrier blinks in hot sun, and a house kitten sits in a cigar box labelled African Lion. A young son hunts big game among flower beds with a riding crop, while canvas awnings flap over a wide red-tiled verandah in the last restful moments before upheaval.
acts-peter-twelve-mattison:
Peter and the twelve sail, preach, and face marvels in a tale from the Nag Hammadi codices. The Acts of Peter and the Twelve Apostles, in Mark Mattison's public-domain rendering, gives that story in English. It is a work of adventure first and doctrine second.

A pearl merchant named Lithargoel draws the apostles to a strange city and a hard lesson. The tale praises care for the poor and turns the hunt for a pearl into a sign of the soul's quest. Its mix of travel yarn and teaching is rare among the codices. Mattison's version keeps the tale brisk and plain.
aesop-s-fables-a-new-translation: Aesop presents his classic animal fables in a fresh translation by V. S. Vernon Jones, with an introduction by G. K. Chesterton and pictures by Arthur Rackham. The short tales of fox, crow, wolf, and tortoise carry morals on prudence, honesty, and patience, stated without preaching. This edition pairs clear, modern English with Rackham's art, making an old book feel new for readers of every age.
air-service-boys-over-the-atlantic-or-th: Charles Amory Beach sends his Air Service Boys across the Atlantic on a record-breaking flight, after a rescue and a bold project set the venture in motion. The boys face storms, engine trouble, and the strain of long hours aloft, in the brisk style of early aviation adventure. Written when flight itself was still news, the book celebrates daring, teamwork, and the new machines of the air.
alfred-tennyson:
Andrew Lang writes a brief life of Alfred Tennyson from the 1901 Blackwood edition. He rests, as he says in his introduction, on two sources. The first is the official biography by the poet's son. The second is the text of the poems. He refuses the anecdotes and local researches Tennyson disliked. The contents run from boyhood and Cambridge through the poems of 1831 to 1833 and the long silence after.

Chapters treat The Princess, In Memoriam, the Idylls of the King, Enoch Arden, the dramas, and the last years. Lang, himself a poet, gives his own impressions of the poems rather than the commentators'. The book is a compact, admiring portrait of the laureate by a fellow craftsman.
alice-s-adventures-in-wonderland-html-ed:
Lewis Carroll sends young Alice down a rabbit hole after a White Rabbit with a watch, in this Millennium Fulcrum edition of his famous story. Alice had been sitting bored beside her sister, whose book had no pictures or talk in it. Underground, size, sense, and manners all stop behaving.

Twelve chapters bring the pool of tears, the caucus race, the Caterpillar, the Cheshire Cat, the Mad Tea-Party, and the Queen's croquet ground, where flamingos serve as mallets. Alice ends in a courtroom where the Knave stands trial for stolen tarts. The mix of logic games, songs, and nonsense has kept the story loved by children and adults alike.
all-around-the-moon: Jules Verne continues From the Earth to the Moon in All Around the Moon, as translated from the French by Edward Roth. The travellers circle the moon in their projectile, observing its surface and debating what they see, while the wonders and dangers of space fill every chapter. Verne's blend of science, humour, and suspense made this a landmark of early science fiction.
all-in-it-k-1-carries-on: Ian Hay dedicates All in It to all second lieutenants, and in particular to the memory of one, as K(1) carries on through the First World War. The book follows young officers through training, trenches, and the daily grind of service, with Hay's mix of humour and feeling. Pip, a romance of youth, forms part of the same wartime picture.
alone-in-london: Hesba Stretton tells of a child alone in London, opening with waifs and strays and a little peacemaker among the city's poor. Chapters on old Oliver's master, forsaken children, and the grasshopper a burden trace a story of loss, kindness, and rescue. Stretton's tale, written to stir compassion, remains a moving example of Victorian charity fiction.
american-men-of-action: Burton Egbert Stevenson profiles American men of action, companion to his guide to men of mind, in a book of short lives for general readers. The sketches celebrate soldiers, explorers, and builders whose deeds shaped the nation. Stevenson writes briskly and admiringly, making the volume a popular introduction to American biography.
american-prisoners-of-the-revolution: Danske Dandridge tells of Americans held as prisoners in the Revolution, and gives the book to her grandfather, a boy in prison, and to the patriots of 1776. She writes of jail, want, and grit among men held by the foe. The book keeps the memory of one hard, oft missed side of the war, as told in homes and towns.
amphitryon:
Molière's comedy was first played in Paris at the Palais-Royal on January 13, 1668, as A. R. Waller's translation notes, and it held the stage for months. The cast list gives the trick plainly: Jupiter, under the form of Amphitryon, visits Alcmène while her husband the general is at war. Mercury likewise doubles the valet Sosie.

The doubled masters and servants collide in scenes of perfect confusion, with Sosie beaten by himself and Amphitryon shut out of his own house. Beneath the farce sits an uneasy point about power: gods may do what would hang a mortal. Molière based his play on Plautus and sharpened it with courtly verse and nerve.
an-account-of-the-proceedings-on-the-tri: An anonymous account records the proceedings on the trial of Susan B. Anthony, charged with illegal voting at the presidential election in November 1872. It also covers the trial of Beverly Jones, Edwin Marsh, and William Hall, the inspectors who received her vote. The volume is a key source on the women's suffrage struggle and its day in court.
an-essay-on-the-history-of-civil-society: Adam Ferguson writes an essay on the history of civil society, in an eighth edition that traces human nature from the state of nature through self-preservation to union among mankind. The work asks how societies grow, corrupt, and endure. Ferguson's essay stands as a founding text of sociology and Scottish thought.
an-essay-on-the-principle-of-population:
Thomas Robert Malthus's Essay on the Principle of Population, in its first form of 1798, grew out of a conversation about Godwin's speculations on society's future. The title page promises remarks on Godwin, Condorcet, and other writers who dreamed of human perfectibility. Malthus's preface says he sat down only to state his thoughts to a friend more clearly. The thought was his principle: population, unchecked, grows geometrically, doubling by generations, while food grows only arithmetically.

From that disproportion the essay derives its machinery: misery and vice, the checks balancing mouths and meals. Perfect societies, Malthus argues, founders on arithmetic before they reach philosophy. Readers get the founding text of the dismal science here in its sharp, short first edition, before the data and the softened doctrine of later versions. Few pamphlets have argued with the future so successfully.
an-essence-of-the-dusk-5th-edition: Francis William Bain translates An Essence of the Dusk from an original manuscript, in a fifth edition dedicated to the other sex, with a preface from Poona. The tale offers an Indian romance in Bain's lush, dreamlike manner, where love and fate intertwine. Bain's invented oriental tales won a devoted following among readers of his day.
androcles-and-the-lion:
George Bernard Shaw's fable play Androcles and the Lion, written in 1912, retells the old story of the slave who pulled a thorn from a lion's paw. Shaw's prologue shows the lion limping and roaring in the Libyan forest while Androcles, a Greek tailor, hides with his shrewish wife Megaera. Kindness to the beast, done in terror, becomes the debt the arena will collect. Shaw frames the tale as a parable about religion.

Inside the play, Roman soldiers round up Christians for the Colosseum, and Androcles joins converts like the gentle Lavinia and the giant Ferrovius. Shaw gives each prisoner a different faith to argue: some love doctrine, some love courage, some simply love life. The Emperor demands sacrifice to his own godhead as the price of pardon. Readers get Shaw's wit turned on martyrdom itself, ending with the lion remembering its friend in the arena, and a tailor dancing free.
annette-the-metis-spy-a-heroine-of-the-n:
Edmund Collins sets his tale on the prairie at sunset, where two riders hurry their ponies along a blind trail toward purple hills along the Red River. His contents announce the shape at once: Le Chef falls in love with the half-breed maiden, Annette forms a heroic resolve, and her lover falls into danger. The setting is the North-West Rebellion in Canada.

Nine chapters give Annette escapes, a fight, a capture, and a guardian swan, as she carries word between camps at the risk of her life. Collins adds notes and a further tale, Nancy the Light-Keeper's Daughter. The novel is popular adventure fiction of its moment, written while the rebellion of the Métis under Riel was still fresh news.
apocalypse-adam-mattison:
Adam speaks to his son Seth at the end of his life in a revelation found at Nag Hammadi. The Apocalypse of Adam, in Mark Mattison's public-domain rendering, gives that Sethian text whole. The codex that holds it was buried in Egypt and found again in 1945.

Adam tells Seth of the flood to come, of fire and quake after it, and of a savior to rise at the end. He warns that the world's rulers will fight the truth in each age. The tale is dark, vast, and told in the voice of the first man. Mattison's version lets readers meet this rare apocalypse in full.
apollonius-argonautica-seaton:
Apollonius of Rhodes composed the Argonautica in the third century BCE. R. C. Seaton translated the Greek epic into English prose. Jason leads the Argonauts aboard the Argo toward distant Colchis.

Their goal is the Golden Fleece, guarded by King Aeetes. The sorceress Medea falls in love with Jason and makes success possible. Apollonius writes a polished, learned epic quite unlike Homer's rougher power. Scholars value his psychology, especially Medea's divided heart. Seaton's clear prose lets modern readers follow the voyage, the monsters, and the uneasy triumph at its end.
apuleius-golden-ass-adlington:
Apuleius, a Roman writer of the second century, composed the novel called Metamorphoses, or The Golden Ass. William Adlington Englished it in 1566, in lively Tudor prose. It is the only Latin novel to survive complete.

Young Lucius, dabbling in magic, turns himself into a donkey by mistake. As a beast he witnesses theft, cruelty, comedy, and human folly everywhere. The tale of Cupid and Psyche sits at the book's heart. After long suffering, the goddess Isis restores his human shape. Bawdy and strange, the novel still feels fresh. Adlington dedicated his translation to the Earl of Devonshire in print.
archibald-malmaison:
Julian Hawthorne called Archibald Malmaison a true story, and his long introductory essay argues with himself about whether truth or invention makes better fiction. The tale concerns Archibald, second son of Sir Clarence Butt Malmaison of Malmaison in Sussex, a family of Huguenot descent, and the strange mental affection that sets him apart from other men.

The narrative rests on the professional notebooks of Dr. Forbes Rollinson, the family physician, whose own father held the same trust before him. Family history, childhood signs, and later episodes are arranged as evidence in a case the reader must judge. Hawthorne leaves the doctor's material explanation and his own doubts standing side by side, which gives the novel its uneasy, casebook air.
around-the-world-in-eighty-days-junior-d:
Jules Verne's race around the world appears here in a Junior Deluxe Edition made for young readers. The contents open with Phileas Fogg hiring Passepartout, then the club conversation that leads to Fogg's famous wager: around the world in eighty days. A detective named Fix soon betrays a very natural impatience.

Chapter by chapter the pair cross the Red Sea and Indian Ocean, India, China, Japan, and America, by train, ship, elephant, and sled. Passepartout talks too much, loses his shoes, and saves the journey more than once, while Fix follows, sure Fogg robbed a bank. The final twist turns on a day gained by traveling east. This edition keeps the full, swift plot.
artificial-light-its-influence-upon-civi: Matthew Luckiesh traces light from fire and oil lamps through gas lighting to electric arcs and modern lamps. He shows how each step changed work, streets, homes, and worship, and he links progress in light to wider progress in science and daily life. Chapters on ceremony, gas, and electric science mix plain history with clear technical notes. The book is both a history of lamps and a case for research as a civilizing force.
aunt-jane-s-nieces-on-vacation:
Edith Van Dyne, L. Frank Baum's series pen name, published this volume in 1912. A hobo at Chazy Junction and a private car on the sidetrack open the tale: the nieces invade Millville and conceive a great enterprise. They will run the Millville Daily Tribune, dividing the responsibilities of a country newspaper among themselves.

Mr. Skeelty of the mill becomes their enemy, Thursday Smith joins the staff, and the Honourable Joy Boglin blusters from the sidelines. Bob West, justice of the peace, promises the girls his help at the first hint of trouble. Open warfare, the penalties of journalism, and the coming of Fogerty fill the summer before the journalists abdicate. Baum writes from newspaper experience, and the small daily's pride in serving Chazy County rings true.
authentic-narrative-of-the-death-of-lord:
William Beatty, surgeon of the Victory at Trafalgar, published this account at London in 1807. Beatty felt his post on the day called him to lay the facts before the British nation. His full title promises the circumstances before, during, and after the event, a professional report on the wound, and several anecdotes of Nelson's last hours.

Nelson lived about two hours and forty-five minutes after being hit. Within the first hour and a quarter, Captain Hardy brought him word of the decisive victory. A partial cannonade still ran on as enemy ships passed, and the last distant guns sounded minutes before his death. Beatty writes as witness and doctor at once, giving the cockpit scene, the wound's course, and the composure that made the story a national relic.
authorised-guide-to-the-tower-of-london:
W. J. Loftie wrote this official handbook, printed for His Majesty's Stationery Office and sold at the Tower for one penny. The revised edition of 1904, reprinted in 1907, carries twelve views and two plans. Viscount Dillon, curator of the Tower Armouries, describes the armoury. Loftie opens with a general sketch: the fortress founded in 1078 by William the Conqueror to protect and control London.

Visitors are led through courts, towers, and collections in order. Staff weapons fill the enclosures: boar spears, halberds, partizans, bills, glaives, and holy water sprinkles, down to the eighteen-foot pikes of the Civil War. A suit of bronze armour from Cumae, an old Greek settlement near Naples, shows the range. The guide mixes history with hard fact, built for a tourist's pocket and an afternoon's walk.
b09-melanchthon-augsburg-confession:
Philipp Melanchthon, Luther's close ally, wrote the Augsburg Confession and saw it presented to Emperor Charles V in 1530. Lutheran princes and cities had been called to state their faith before the empire. Melanchthon, a scholar of calm temper, drafted a text meant to show unity with the old church where unity held.

The confession sets out teaching on God, sin, faith, the church, and the sacraments in orderly articles. Its tone seeks peace, yet it concedes nothing on the core of the gospel. The text became the chief doctrinal standard of Lutheranism worldwide. The rendering here is by F Bente and W H T Dau.
bacon:
R. W. Church, Dean of St. Paul's, wrote this life of Francis Bacon for the English Men of Letters series edited by John Morley. Church's Bacon stands in the series list beside Stephen's Johnson and Huxley's Hume. The biography follows Bacon from courtier's son to Lord Chancellor, weighing the philosopher against the politician at every step.

Court intrigue fills the middle chapters. Edward Coke haggles over a marriage portion for a Villiers match, loses his chance, and finds Secretary Winwood reopening the matter, while Lady Hatton flatly refuses the terms for her daughter. Church writes with a churchman's fairness: Bacon's fall over bribes is neither hidden nor allowed to swallow the Novum Organum and the Essays. The volume remains a compact Victorian life of England's great, flawed man of science.
balder-the-beautiful-volume-i-a-study-in:
J. G. Frazer published this first volume of Balder the Beautiful in 1913, as part seven of the third edition of The Golden Bough. Frazer, of Trinity College, Cambridge, studies the fire-festivals of Europe and the doctrine of the external soul. His first chapter, Between Heaven and Earth, begins with the priest of Aricia and sacred kings forbidden to touch the ground with their feet.

Holiness, Frazer argues, was imagined as a charge that could run to waste or explode on contact with earth, so sacred persons and things were insulated. Midsummer bonfires fill later chapters: in Brittany a girl who danced round nine of them would marry within the year. Parents leapt the abated flames carrying children, for purification and luck. Frazer's method is comparison on a vast scale, custom beside custom.
bell-s-cathedrals-the-cathedral-church-o:
A. Clutton-Brock wrote this description of York Minster's fabric, with a brief history of the archi-episcopal see, for Bell's series in 1899. Forty-one illustrations accompany the text. Clutton-Brock, later a well-known critic, treats the largest Gothic cathedral in England as both document and work of art, guiding readers from the west front through nave, transepts, and choir.

Roofing earns a full technical passage. Fan-shaped brackets spring between the clerestory windows and spread to the vault's central ridge. A true vault, he notes, wastes the space between itself and the outer roof. The barrel roof avoids that loss by nearly matching the roof's own shape. Such reasoning, applied to glass, stone, and timber throughout, makes the volume a small treatise on Gothic construction disguised as a visitor's guide.
beric-the-briton:
G. A. Henty published this story of the Roman invasion in 1892, opening with his usual letter to his dear lads. England's wars, he says, demanded the Roman period: native valour acknowledged even by Roman historians, beaten only by superior discipline. The conquest brought civilisation and ended tribal wars, yet in the end it cost the islanders their military virtues.

Beric, a young Briton of Boadicea's people, is carried to Rome and returns to face Suetonius. In one dialogue the Roman Norbanus concedes that Christ was put to death most unjustly, no crime alleged but perverting the Jews' religion, which was no concern of Rome's. Beric objects that Suetonius attacked the sacred island and slew the priests on the altars. Henty gives both empires their arguments before the burning of the cities settles them.
beric-the-briton-a-story-of-the-roman-in:
G. A. Henty's Beric the Briton tells the Roman invasion of Britain for boys. Henty argues that his series on England's wars would be incomplete without the period when Romans mastered the country, and he praises the valour with which the natives defended themselves.

Only Roman discipline, Henty says, finally triumphed over British bravery and superior physical strength. The conquest brought Roman civilisation and ended perpetual tribal wars, yet it proved disastrous in the end, since Britons defended by Roman soldiers could not resist the Saxons when the legions left. Young readers will find Beric a vigorous introduction to Roman Britain.
black-beauty-young-folks-edition:
Anna Sewell's horse autobiography appears here in the Young Folks' Edition of 1902, shortened and simplified for child readers. Black Beauty tells his own life from the pleasant meadow of his early home, with its pond of clear water and six young colts. In the daytime he ran by his mother's side; at night he lay down close by her. The warm shed near the grove waits for cold weather.

Later masters pass in review through other horses' talk. A chestnut came to one good home snappish and suspicious, her master reports, for she had had bad treatment from a dealer. Three years of kindness never showed the smallest sign of temper again. The young folks' text keeps Sewell's argument whole: cruelty makes the vicious horse, and patience unmakes it, in chapters a child can finish at a sitting.
boy-scouts-on-motorcycles-or-with-the-fl:
G Harvey Ralphson wrote Boy Scouts on Motorcycles, a tale of New York scouts on secret work in China. Ralphson opens at Taku, on the Gulf of Pechili, where Jimmie McGraw stands guard and longs for Broadway. Ned Nestor leads the Wolf and Black Bear boys.

Spies are the quarry, and Taoist priests on the highway draw Ned's sharp eye. Captain Martin warns the boys that such priests beg from strangers when money shows. Masks drop as the flying squadron's motors carry the hunt between river towns. Ned files his report at Washington and banks a fat reward. Ralphson gives boy readers foreign intrigue, wireless-age speed, and patrol loyalty in one fast package.
brave-and-bold-or-the-fortunes-of-robert:
Horatio Alger Jr wrote Brave and Bold, a boys' novel of Millville school and mill life. Alger opens at a penmanship class, where Professor Granville drills a hundred pupils for a dollar a course. Young Robert Rushton, poor and proud, shines among his young rivals there.

A lost father leaves the plot's charge: money placed with mill superintendent Davis, who keeps silent for two years. Robert reads the secret in a letter and faces the man down. School prizes, work, and steady pluck turn the boy's fortune page by page. Alger's creed runs through it all, that honesty and grit beat birth and cash. The tale served the newsboy and errand-boy readers who made Alger a household name.
brave-tom-or-the-battle-that-won:
Edward Sylvester Ellis wrote Brave Tom, first of his Brave and Honest series, issued in 1894. Ellis sets the tale in Briggsville, Pennsylvania, where Tom Gordon lives with his widowed mother and Aunt Cynthia. Tom leads his school in study and sport alike.

A circus poster fires the village boys, and harder tests follow the fun. Jim, a second boy, ships on a coasting schooner down the Jersey shore at a wage that stuns him. Honest work and the Golden Rule form the spine of both boys' trials. Ellis ends with Tom sure that rule, kept through a stormy youth, won his battle. The series title says the moral outright: brave and honest, in that order, for boy readers.
brigands-of-the-moon:
Ray Cummings published Brigands of the Moon with Ace Books, from a 1931 copyright. Cummings sets his tale in 2070, aboard the space-flyer Planetara on mail and passenger runs to Venus and Mars. Gregg, the narrator, and Snap Dean, the radio man, open the case.

A code flash calls both men to Detective-Colonel Halsey on landing at Greater New York. Moon brigands are the charge: Johnny Grantline's camp holds a share of gold leaf worth guarding. Weighted shoes, air locks, and Earth time kept on chronometers give the lunar scenes their grit. Cummings packs the tale with tubes, rays, and daring raids. Early science fiction readers got a crime story moved whole to the Moon, police work and all.
britannica-1911-aaron:
Aaron receives a long, careful entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Aaron stands in tradition as founder and head of the Jewish priesthood, who with Moses led Israel out of Egypt. The entry warns early that late narratives carry later practice back to Exodus days.

Signs at Pharaoh's court give Aaron a second place beside Moses. Hur and Aaron hold charge while Moses takes the Law, and Aaron's hand makes the golden calf in the people's panic. That fault nearly costs his life. Later tales raise him to high priest and prove his rod by its budding. His death place wavers between Moserah and Mount Hor. A historical Aaron, the entry holds, hides hard behind grown tradition, clan names, and priestly claims.
britannica-1911-abaddon: Abaddon is the headword of a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry gives the Hebrew word's plain sense as destruction. In poetry the sense widens to the place of destruction, the underworld or Sheol, with lines from Job and Proverbs cited. In Revelation the name turns personal: Abaddon stands as prince of the underworld, glossed as Apollyon, the destroyer. A note from Baudissin adds that rabbinic writing uses Hades and Abaddon as personal names.
britannica-1911-abduction:
Abduction receives a law entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The term, from Latin abducere, to lead away, names the forcible or fraudulent removal of a person. Custom limits it to women as victims; kidnapping serves for men and children.

Old English law aimed chiefly at heiresses and their fortunes. The Offences against the Person Act of 1861 rebuilt the offences: taking a woman of property for marriage or carnal knowledge, for gain, counts felony. Girls under twenty-one drawn from parents or guardians fall under the same shield. The Criminal Law Amendment Act of 1885 tightened procuration and detention further. A girl's consent is no answer, nor belief about her age, the entry notes. Scotland handles the matter by practice, without statute.
britannica-1911-aberavon:
Aberavon receives a borough entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The Glamorgan town stands on the Avon near Swansea Bay, with 7,553 folk in 1901. Port Talbot's docks, once Aberavon Port, lie half a mile east across the river.

Metal work rules the short Avon valley: tinplate and engineering in the borough, copper at Cwmavon since 1838, iron and steel at both spots. Caradoc, son of the beaten Prince Lestyn, founded its castle to hold the river crossing after the Norman conquest. His De Avan heirs chartered the town under it. Charters slept for centuries till incorporation came in 1861. Swansea's district has returned its member with Aberavon since 1832, the entry notes.
britannica-1911-aberdare-henry-austin-br:
Henry Austin Bruce, first Baron Aberdare, receives a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Bruce, born at Duffryn in 1815, was called to the bar in 1837. Coal found under the family estates made him rich early, and Merthyr Tydvil sent him to Parliament in 1852.

Gladstone made him home secretary in 1869. His Licensing Act of 1872 put magistrates in charge of drink licences, raised penalties, and cut selling hours. Lord president of the council and a peerage followed in 1873. Later years went to learned societies, Royal Commissions, and West Africa, where he chaired the company that became the Royal Niger Company. A charter for the university of Wales at Cardiff crowns the record. He died in 1895.
britannica-1911-abernethy-john-surgeon:
John Abernethy the surgeon receives a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Abernethy, grandson of the Irish divine, was born in London in 1764 and apprenticed to Sir Charles Blicke of St Bartholomew's. Hunter and Pott lectured to him in his training years.

Assistant surgeon in 1787, he lectured so well that the hospital built him a theatre, founding the St Bartholomew's school. Principal surgeon came in 1815, after twenty-eight years. Aneurism work ties his name to the external iliac ligature. His Surgical Observations of 1809, called My Book by his own habit, taught that local disease springs from disordered digestion, cured by purge and diet. Brusque speech hid a just, kind nature, the entry insists. He died at Enfield in 1831.
britannica-1911-abich-otto-wilhelm-herma:
Otto Wilhelm Hermann von Abich receives a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, inside a shared chunk of text. Abich, a German mineralogist and geologist born at Berlin in 1806, began with spinels and other minerals. Volcanoes then drew him: fumaroles, vent deposits, and volcanic structure.

Dorpat made him professor of mineralogy in 1842, and Russian ground became his field. Years at Tiflis went to the geology of the Caucasus. His illustrated studies of Vesuvius and Etna in the 1830s open the book list, and three volumes on the Caucasus lands close it. The mineral abichite bears his name. Retirement at Vienna ended in death in July 1886, the entry records.
britannica-1911-abingdon:
Abingdon receives a town entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, inside a shared chunk of text. The Berkshire market town stands on the Thames where the Ock flows in, six miles south of Oxford. St Helen's church, five-aisled with a fine spire, rules the river views.

A Benedictine abbey of great wealth, founded about 675, made the town. Danes burned it, Edred restored it, and William the Conqueror kept Easter here in 1084, leaving young Henry to its schooling. Dissolution in 1538 sank the town till Mary's charter of 1555 raised it again. Wool and clothing trades flourished early and revived later. Radley College near by and Henley rowing close the modern sketch, with 6,480 folk in 1901.
britannica-1911-abinger-james-scarlett-1:
James Scarlett, first Baron Abinger, receives a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Abinger, born in Jamaica in 1769, read at Trinity College, Cambridge, and took to the bar in 1791 with no connexions. Steady work built the largest practice of his day.

Silk in 1816 crowned the rise, with fees reaching a high-water mark for the age. Parliament, the attorney-general's post under Canning, and a knighthood followed. Reform's fight moved him from Whigs to Tories. Lord chief baron of the exchequer from 1834, he gained a peerage in 1835 from his Surrey estate. Partial, dictatorial, and vain on the bench, the entry charges, yet acute and clear to the end. He died on circuit in 1844.
britannica-1911-abjuration: Abjuration is the headword of a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, read here inside a shared chunk of text. The entry gives the word, from Latin abjurare, to forswear, as a solemn giving up on oath. At common law it named the oath of a sanctuary man to leave the realm for ever, struck out under James the First. The Oath of Abjuration denied the Stuarts' crown right. Parliament, clergy, and laymen took it under William the Third and two Georges. Allegiance's oath has since replaced it.
britannica-1911-ablation: Ablation is the headword of a very short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, read here inside a shared chunk of text. The entry gives the word, from Latin ablatus, carried away, as the process of removing anything. Two trades take it as their own term. In geology it names the wearing away of a rock or a glacier. In surgery it names operative removal, the cutting away of a part. One spare notice fixes both technical senses for readers of the 1911 volumes.
britannica-1911-abomination: Abomination is the headword of a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, read here inside a shared chunk of text. The entry traces the word to Latin ab and ominare, to forebode: a thing against omen, held in aversion. Bible use turns it on evil doctrines and impure rites. A false derivation from ab homine, inhuman, shaped the old spelling abhominable, kept through the first Shakespeare folio, the entry notes. Common speech now spends the word loosely, for anything excessive in a disagreeable sense, the entry closes.
britannica-1911-abortion:
Abortion receives a medical entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The term, from Latin aboriri, to fail to be born, names the early separation and expulsion of the contents of the pregnant womb. Miscarriage marks the accidental kind, abortion the induced, whether by medical need or crime.

Causes sort into local and general: pelvic malformation, injury, uterine disease, and ovum or placenta faults on one side; system states on the other. Recurrence warns the practitioner. Bleeding leads the symptoms, and treatment aims to prevent where threat shows, or to complete removal where the event is sure. A long close weighs ancient practice and law, from Plato and Aristotle to Christian severity. Frequencies given by accoucheurs vary widely, the entry cautions.
britannica-1911-abrasion: Abrasion is the headword of a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry gives the word, from Latin ab and radere, to scrape, as the process of rubbing off or wearing down. Rock worn by moving ice and coins worn by handling show it in nature and use. The result takes the same name, as in an abrasion of the skin. Machinery fights abrasion with fit materials, good fitting, and lubrication. Craftsmen also harness it, shaping and polishing work with emery and carborundum, the entry closes.
britannica-1911-abrogation:
Abrogation receives a law entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The term, from Latin abrogare, names the annulling of a law by legislative action. Abrogation kills a law whole, where derogation cuts only part of it away.

Express abrogation speaks in the new law itself, generally against all contrary laws or by naming its victims. Implied abrogation hides in new provisions positively against the old, or in changed conditions that leave the old law nothing to govern. Killing a statute revives the common law it had displaced, the entry adds. Cross-references to Statute and Repeal close a notice prized for sorting two terms that loose speech confuses.
britannica-1911-absalon:
Absalon receives a long life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Absalon, a Danish archbishop and statesman born about 1128, grew up at Fjenneslev beside the future Valdemar the First. Paris schooling and the near-assassination at Roskilde's banquet of 1157 open the tale.

Bishop of Roskilde from 1158, he counseled Valdemar toward Baltic dominion. Wendish pirates had wasted a third of Denmark, and clearing them became his life's task. Arkona fell in 1168, its god Svantevit surrendering; Garz followed, its seven-headed idol burned and its folk baptized. Strela's sea victory of 1184 ended his campaigning. He then defied Barbarossa's homage demand, built churches and schools, and became archbishop of Lund. He died at Sorö in 1201.
britannica-1911-abscission: Abscission is the headword of a very short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry gives the word, from Latin abscindere, as a tearing away or cutting off. Three trades take it as their own term. In prosody it names the elision of a vowel before another. In surgery it names removal of the cornea, or of the eyeball part before the recti muscles' attachments. In botany it names the separation of spores by loss of their connexion. One spare notice fixes all three senses.
britannica-1911-absolution:
Absolution receives a law and church entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, signed with the initials of Winfrid Oldfield Burrows. The term, from Latin absolvo, to loosen or acquit, means in civil process the acquittal of an accused person where proof fails or falls. Scots law keeps it as assoilzie and absolvitor.

Church use differs root and branch: sin committed, not charge laid, is loosed, from guilt, from church penalty, or both. Public confession and completed penance came first; secret confession grew from the third century, and the Lateran council of 1215 made yearly confession binding. Trent fixed the Roman form in Ego te absolvo. Anglican and Lutheran forms, precative and declaratory, close the survey of a rite that changed slowly across fifteen centuries.
britannica-1911-abstraction:
Abstraction takes its name from Latin words for drawing away, and the 1911 Britannica entry follows that idea through several fields. In everyday use it can mean a summary that keeps the gist of a larger work, or the absent-minded state of a person drawn away from the matter in hand. Philosophy gives the word sharper, technical senses.

Logic uses abstract terms for qualities, as friendship names a quality while friend names a thing. Psychology and metaphysics ask how the mind moves from single things seen and heard to general ideas that group many things together. Readers also get the contrast with analysis, and the old dispute among nominalism, realism, and conceptualism over what such general ideas really are.
britannica-1911-acceleration:
Acceleration, from a Latin verb meaning to hasten, is treated in the 1911 Britannica as a term of mechanics, the science of motion. It denotes the rate at which the velocity, or speed in a given direction, of a moving body increases or decreases when that motion is not uniform. A body moving at a steady speed has no acceleration in this sense.

Readers are pointed onward to the articles on mechanics and on the hodograph, a diagram used to study changing velocity, for the working detail. The entry's job is the definition itself: acceleration measures change of velocity over time, whether a body is speeding up or slowing down.
britannica-1911-acceptilation:
Acceptilation, in Roman and Scots law, was a verbal release of a verbal obligation. The 1911 Britannica entry explains a formal way of wiping out a debt that had itself been created by spoken words. Its name comes from a book-keeping term, acceptilatio, meaning the entering of a receipt, or carrying a sum to credit.

Form mattered strictly. The words of the release had to correspond to, or strictly cover, the obligation as it had been expressed, or the release failed. The word also took a figurative life in theology, where acceptilation means the free remission, or forgiveness, of sins. Readers get both the legal mechanism and its borrowed religious sense in a few lines.
britannica-1911-accession:
Accession, in law, is a way of acquiring property taken from Roman law, summed up in the principle that the accessory follows the principal. Where two things are closely connected, ownership of the main thing draws ownership of the lesser after it. The 1911 Britannica entry sorts the cases into land added to land by accretion, moveables fixed to land, moveables joined to moveables, and moveables changed by human industry.

Industry raises the hard cases, as when wine is made from grapes or liquids are mixed together. Ownership then follows whichever substance matters more, with compensation generally payable to whoever lost property. The entry also notes accession to a throne, and the Scottish deed by which creditors accept a trust settlement.
britannica-1911-acclamation:
Acclamation, from a Latin word for shouting at, is a shout of approval. Assemblies use it to adopt resolutions without a formal ballot. The 1911 Britannica entry traces the practice to the Roman senate. There, votes were passed by acclamation in set forms. Praises of the emperor were also chanted in arranged sentences.

Church practice kept the custom alive. Councils commonly vote by acclamation. They put the question as placet or non placet. Cardinals have sometimes elected a pope this way. All of them acclaimed one of their number at the same moment. In modern parliaments, a motion is carried by acclamation when approval is simply shouted. Words such as Aye or Agreed do the work of a vote.
britannica-1911-accommodation:
Accommodation, from a Latin verb meaning to make fit, is the process of fitting, adapting, or supplying what is needed, as with housing. The 1911 Britannica entry spends most of its length on the theological sense. There the word describes using a phrase or idea in a context other than its original one, often to make a hard idea graspable for hearers who would otherwise miss it.

Three kinds are distinguished. Later Bible writers quote earlier passages as arguments, sometimes in ways that now look forced. Parable and metaphor count as divine condescension to human weakness. German rationalists of the eighteenth century claimed the Bible writers consciously trimmed dogma into moral commonplaces, a view others called economy or reserve.
britannica-1911-accordion:
Accordion is a small portable reed wind instrument with a keyboard, the smallest member of the organ family, invented by Damian in Vienna in 1829. Bellows of many folds carry a keyboard of five to fifty keys. Pressing a key while working the bellows opens valves that admit air to free reeds, narrow metal tongues whose length and thickness set the pitch.

Each key gives two notes, one as the bellows compress and another as they expand. The right hand plays the melody while the left works the bellows and a few bass keys that sound simple chords. The entry judges the tone coarse, links the instrument to the Chinese cheng, and credits its improvements with producing the concertina.
britannica-1911-accretion:
Accretion, from Latin words meaning to grow toward, is an addition to something that already exists, an increase made by particles added from outside. The 1911 Britannica entry gives the general sense first, then the legal one in which the word does most of its work. Nature adds such particles slowly, and law must decide who owns the result.

Property is where the term bites. In law, accretion names the increase of property caused by gradual natural additions, as when silt builds up a river bank or the sea leaves new ground along a shore. Because the growth is slow and imperceptible, the added land generally follows the land it joins.
britannica-1911-accrington:
Accrington is a market town and municipal borough in Lancashire, north-west of Manchester, set in a deep valley on the Hindburn. Its population passed forty-three thousand by 1901. Cotton spinning and printing works, cotton-mill machinery works, dye-works, chemical manufactures, and nearby collieries keep its industrial population employed. The church of St James dates from 1763, while other public buildings are modern.

Growth came late and fast. Granted in early centuries to the de Lacy family and then to the monks of Kirkstall as a grange, Accrington was still a straggling village of five thousand people in 1836. Its place as a railway junction pushed numbers upward, and a charter of incorporation followed in 1878.
britannica-1911-accumulation:
Accumulation, in law, means adding a fund's interest to its principal. The gain piles up for people who will benefit in the future. English law once allowed this freely. It stayed within the limits set against perpetuities. One will changed the rule. Peter Thellusson was a London merchant. His will directed his estate's income to pile up. It was to grow through the lives of his descendants. The fortune was estimated above fourteen million pounds.

Parliament answered with the Accumulations Act of 1800. People call it the Thellusson Act. It capped accumulation at the settlor's life. It also allowed twenty-one years after his death. The minority of certain living persons set another limit. Later acts extended the rule to Scotland.
britannica-1911-accusation:
Accusation is a legal term for charging another person with wrongdoing, criminal or otherwise. The 1911 Britannica entry is chiefly about protection and risk around such charges. An accusation made in a court of justice during legal proceedings is privileged, shielded from suit, though a person maliciously prosecuted can sue for that abuse.

Outside court the ground shifts. A false spoken accusation exposes the accuser to an action for defamation of character. A written accusation can bring indictment whether it is addressed to the accused or to a third person. Threatening or conspiring to accuse someone of a crime, or even of lesser misconduct, in order to extort money is itself an indictable offence.
britannica-1911-acheron:
Acheron, in Greek mythology, was the son of Gaea or of Demeter, earth in her two forms. Punishment made him a river: for supplying the Titans with water in their contest with Zeus, he was turned into a river of Hades, the underworld. Over that river the ferryman Charon carried departed souls, a scene fixed in Greek and later imagination.

Names widen as the entry closes. Acheron means, in effect, the river of woe, and the name eventually came to designate the whole lower world, not one stream within it. The entry cites Stobaeus as its authority for that wider use of the name.
britannica-1911-acron:
Acron was a Greek physician born at Agrigentum in Sicily. He lived in the fifth century before Christ. That made him a contemporary of Empedocles. One famous measure is credited to him. Great fires were lit during the Athenian plague. Perfumes purified the air around them. The plague of 430 B.C. then stopped, tradition says. The entry adds a caution at once. Chronology makes the story doubtful. Acron may not have been there at all.

Writings survive only as titles. Suidas lists several medical works by Acron. He wrote them in the Doric dialect. Nothing of their text is quoted here. Readers get a name, a city, and a legend. The entry leaves his real practice in shadow.
britannica-1911-act-on-petition: Act on petition was a term of English court procedure. It named part of the practice in the Probate, Divorce and Admiralty Division. This entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes that the procedure was already rare when it was written. Lawyers used it more freely in the old Admiralty and Divorce courts. That was before the Judicature Acts reshaped the court system. Readers meeting the phrase in older reports should treat it as a survival from that earlier practice.
britannica-1911-actaeon:
Actaeon was a Theban hero and hunter in Greek myth. Aristaeus was his father, Autonoe his mother. The centaur Cheiron trained him in hunting. Ovid tells the famous story of his end. Actaeon chanced on Artemis bathing on Mount Cithaeron. The goddess changed him into a stag at once. His own fifty hounds pursued and killed him. He could not speak to call them off.

Worship and art kept the tale alive. Statues of Actaeon stood on rocks and mountains. They were thought to protect against excessive heat. The entry suggests a nature meaning underneath. The myth may picture vegetation destroyed in the fifty dog-days. Aeschylus used the story on stage. A small marble group in the British Museum illustrates it.
britannica-1911-action:
Action, in law, carries three senses at once. Jurists use it for a right to sue. They use it for the proceeding itself. They use it for the proceeding's particular form. The term descends from the Roman actio. Roman actions passed through three historical stages. The legis actiones came first, under the Twelve Tables. Five rigid forms governed all claims. A praetor settled each dispute's formula later. That formulary system proved far more flexible. Finally the magistrate decided cases himself.

Classifications fill the long entry. Actions in rem claim a thing against all the world. Actions in personam claim against a specific person. English procedure runs from writ to execution. Summons, pleadings, trial, judgment, and enforcement follow in order. County courts begin by plaint instead.
britannica-1911-acton:
Acton is an urban district of Middlesex, England. It lies nine miles west of St Paul's Cathedral. London's suburbs have wholly absorbed its character. Fewer than four thousand people lived there in 1861. By 1901 the population passed thirty-seven thousand. The name may derive from Oak-town. Extensive forest once covered the whole locality. The land belonged to the see of London early. A grant of it is recorded in 1220.

Puritan and literary names mark its past. Henry III kept a residence at Acton. The Commonwealth era made it a Puritan centre. Richard Baxter lived among its residents. So did Chief Justice Hale and novelist Henry Fielding. Botanist John Lindley died there in 1865. Acton Wells, of saline waters, enjoyed eighteenth-century fame.
britannica-1911-acton-john-emerich-edwar:
John Emerich Edward Dalberg Acton (1834-1902) was an English historian. He was born at Naples, an only son. His grandfather was the Neapolitan admiral Sir John Acton. His mother was heiress of the duc de Dalberg. A Roman Catholic, Acton studied at Oscott and Edinburgh. Cambridge was closed to Catholics then. At Munich, Dollinger inspired his love of research. He dreamed of writing a great History of Liberty. That work was never realized, despite a magnificent library.

Politics and faith tested him alike. Acton sat in the Commons from 1859. He opposed papal infallibility at the Vatican council's era. Yet he refused to join the Old Catholic secession. His letters against Gladstone's pamphlet stirred English Catholicism. Editors later published his lectures on modern history.
britannica-1911-adalberon:
Adalberon, also called Ascelin, was a French bishop and poet. He studied at Reims and became bishop of Laon in 977. War swept him into prison in 988. Charles, duke of Lorraine, had taken Laon then. Adalberon escaped and sought Hugh Capet's protection. He won the confidence of both his captors. Charles and Archbishop Arnulf trusted him again. Restored to his see, he betrayed them. He handed Laon to Hugh Capet instead.

Poetry preserves his opinions for us. His satirical dialogue poem addresses King Robert. It attacks Abbot Odilo of Cluny sharply. It also objects to low-born men becoming bishops. Valois first published the poem in 1663. Adalberon died in July of 1030 or 1031. The entry warns against confusing a Reims namesake.
britannica-1911-adaptation:
Adaptation means the fit of a thing to new uses. The word comes from a Latin verb, to fit to. A novel made into a play shows it. A piece of music reset for more hands shows it too. The 1911 entry spends most of its space on life, though. In the life sciences, the term holds a large place. It is the way a plant or beast comes to suit the place where it lives.

Life, the entry says, is a steady act of such fit. What is in the beast must match what is round it. If the match is good, the beast thrives. If the match is poor, it fades and at last dies out. How far these fits are made fresh in each brood was an open point. So was how far they pass to the young.
britannica-1911-administration:
Administration, a word from a Latin term that means to serve, is covered in a law entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In broad use it means the running of affairs or of a state. In strict law use it means the handling of the estate of a dead person. Letters of administration are the court grant at the heart of the topic.

When a person dies with no will, or a will names no executor who can act, the court must name an administrator. That person does the work of an executor. Grants may be general or limited to a set case. For a general grant the court follows a set order. A spouse comes first, then close kin, then the Crown, then a creditor, then a stranger. A creditor who gains the grant must post a bond with two backers.
britannica-1911-admiralty-jurisdiction:
Admiralty Jurisdiction is set out in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica as the sea law reach of a set of courts. The first courts to hold that reach in civil cases are named at the start. In England the courts of the sea lords merged in time into one High Court of Admiralty. A like court for the Cinque Ports held the same reach in its bounds.

Some towns held small vice courts of the same kind. Scotland and Ireland each had a high sea court of their own. Of all these, the Cinque Ports court stands as the sole one left as it was. The Scottish court was shut down. Its civil work went to the Court of Session and to the courts of the sheriffs. That shift came by an act of eighteen thirty. The entry gives a clean map of who judged sea cases in the isles.
britannica-1911-adoption:
Adoption in law creates parent and child ties between people not so linked by birth. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica draws the word from the Latin adoptare, to choose for oneself. Greeks and Romans used the practice often and ruled it with care. Athens let sound minded citizens with no sons adopt by will or in life.

Roman use turned more on power and rights than on affection alone. A father had to be at least eighteen years older than the child. Two forms are set out, based on the status of the person taken in. Rights, duties, and loss of claims through the birth father are spelled out in detail.
britannica-1911-aegean-civilization:
Aegean Civilization is the broad name used in a long entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica for the old culture of the Greek lands before written history. It was once called Mycenaean, from Mycenae, where Heinrich Schliemann dug in 1876 and brought it to wide notice. Later finds showed Mycenae was not its chief centre in its early stages.

The first part traces how the remains came to light and where they are spread. At Mycenae and Tiryns, Greeks of the classic age had long seen huge walls, a gate with carved lions, and the great tomb called the Treasury of Atreus. Folk took them as signs of a rough heroic age. Schliemann's finds in the graves inside the gate changed that view at a stroke. The goods buried there showed a high level of art among folk who lived long before the Greece of Homer.
britannica-1911-affection:
Affection is sorted in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica from a Latin root for to do a thing to a man. In strict terms it is a state of mind that grows from a force past the self. In street use it names a bond of more than good will or mere friend ship between two folk.

Writers on the right life use the word in more than one way. Some use it for states of feel in the large, both long and short. Some set it off from passion as free of the flesh part. A more strict use holds it to feels that deal with a person. The Greek peer of the wide sense is named in the text. A famed French thinker and the first British writers on the right life use it in that wide way.
britannica-1911-agamemnon:
Agamemnon, one of the most famed of the Greek heroes, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of Atreus, king of Mycenae, and the brother of Menelaus. When Atreus was murdered, the killer seized the throne of Mycenae. The two brothers took refuge with the king of Sparta, whose daughters they married.

The article follows his rise to power. With his brother's help he drove out the usurpers and won back his father's kingdom. He spread his rule by conquest and became the strongest prince in Greece. When Paris of Troy carried off his brother's wife Helen, Agamemnon went round the princes of the land. He called them to join in a war of revenge, the call that set the Trojan War in motion.
britannica-1911-agglutination: Agglutination is a short language article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes from Latin roots meaning to fasten together with glue. In philology it names a way of building words from joined roots, each keeping its own sense. This joining of roots is the mark of languages such as Turkish and Japanese, which are therefore called agglutinative. They stand against the inflexional languages, where changed endings do the work. Wundt called the simplest form of combination by this name.
britannica-1911-ainsworth-william-harris:
Ainsworth, William Harrison, an English novelist of 1805 to 1882, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Manchester, the son of a solicitor, he was educated at Manchester Grammar School and trained in his father's firm. Legal study took him to London's Inner Temple in 1824. At twenty-one he married his publisher's daughter and tried publishing himself.

That business failed, and praise from Sir Walter Scott for an early novel pushed him toward fiction for good. Rookwood succeeded at once in 1834, and about forty historical novels followed. Jack Sheppard, The Tower of London, Guy Fawkes, and Old St Paul's are the best known. He edited Bentley's Miscellany, where Jack Sheppard appeared as a serial, and later owned magazines of his own. His later stories struck readers less than the early ones had.
britannica-1911-ajax-son-of-telamon:
Ajax, son of Telamon, towers in a myth entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Men call him the great Ajax to split him from a lesser namesake. In the Iliad he stands huge in frame and vast in strength. Achilles alone tops him in might and nerve among the Greeks. Homer names him the bulwark of the whole Achaean host.

Ajax fought Hector hand to hand in the war at Troy. With Athena's help he saved the corpse of Achilles from Troy. Then he and Odysseus vied for the dead hero's armour. The prize went to Odysseus, and rage broke the mind of Ajax. In madness he slew sheep, thinking them foes in the camp. Come to his senses, he fell on the sword Hector gave him.
britannica-1911-alabama-arbitration:
Alabama Arbitration, a landmark case between Britain and the United States, is treated at length in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Arbitration here means one state pressing money claims for its subjects against another before appointed judges. The entry calls the case important both historically and in law. It stands as a strong example of arbitration averting war.

During the American Civil War, Britain's neutrality proclamation recognised the Confederates as belligerents. Confederate cruisers built in Britain, the Alabama chief among them, savaged Union shipping, and the United States demanded payment. Under the treaty that followed, named arbitrators were to decide by majority, guided by three agreed rules and by principles of international law they judged to apply. The long article lays out the facts from Fort Sumter onward, then follows the settlement's terms article by article.
britannica-1911-albion:
Albion, the most ancient name of the British Islands, is examined in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Ptolemy and Pliny both use the name, though it is generally restricted to England. It may be of Celtic origin. The Romans, though, connected it with albus, white, pointing to the chalk cliffs of Dover as the reason for the name.

Holder's dictionary of old Celtic translates Albion without hesitation as Weissland, whiteland. A sixth-century writer whose voyage account survives through Avienus never uses Britannia. He speaks instead of the island of the Ierni and the Albiones. Pytheas of Massilia uses similar forms in the fourth century B.C. Some scholars, noting a tribe called the Albiones on Spain's north coast in Asturia, have placed Albion in that neighbourhood instead. Medieval writers took the name from Pliny and Ptolemy.
britannica-1911-alcester-frederick-beauc:
Alcester, Frederick Beauchamp Paget Seymour, Baron Alcester, a British admiral of 1821 to 1895, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in April 1821, he was the son of Colonel Sir Horace Beauchamp Seymour. He entered the navy in 1834 and served in the Mediterranean and the Pacific. For three years he was flag-lieutenant to his uncle Sir George Seymour.

Promotion followed steady service: commander in 1847, a volunteer in Burma in 1852, and captain in 1854. He took the ironclad battery Meteor to the Black Sea, commanded Pelorus on the Australian station, and led the naval brigade in New Zealand's Maori War, earning a C.B. Later he commanded the flying squadron, sat at the admiralty, and led the Channel fleet. As Mediterranean commander-in-chief he directed the 1880 demonstration off Albania and commanded at the bombardment of Alexandria in 1882, reaching full admiral that year.
britannica-1911-alciphron:
Alciphron wrote letters that nobody ever sent. The Greek rhetorician, who most likely lived in the second century A.D. as a man of Lucian's time, left a set of made-up letters: 124 in print, 118 whole and six in pieces. Each one is set at Athens and written in the purest Attic speech, so pure that the letters serve as models of style.

The fake writers come from the city's margins. Country folk, fishermen, hangers-on, and courtesans air their views and feelings on everyday matters in polished words. The courtesan letters win the highest praise. Their facts come mainly from the poets of the New Comedy, Menander above all, so the set keeps a view of Athenian life drawn from that lost stage world. Printings from 1499 onward and an English version of 1791 are listed.
britannica-1911-alcmaeon:
Alcmaeon of Argos, a figure of Greek legend, is treated in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of Amphiaraus and Eriphyle. Before joining the Seven against Thebes, an expedition he knew would kill him, Amphiaraus charged his sons to avenge him. They were to slay Eriphyle and lead a second expedition against Thebes in turn.

After Thebes fell to the Epigoni, the sons of the Seven, Alcmaeon obeyed and killed his mother. Madness and the Erinyes, the avenging spirits, hounded him from place to place for that deed. Purified at Psophis, he married King Phegeus's daughter Arsinoe and gave her Harmonia's fatal necklace. The land's barrenness drove him on until he found fresh silt land at the Achelous mouth, ground the sun had never shone on when he killed his mother. There he married Callirrhoe and forgot Arsinoe.
britannica-1911-alcott-amos-bronson:
Alcott, Amos Bronson, an American educationalist and writer of 1799 to 1888, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born on Spindle Hill at Wolcott, Connecticut, in November 1799, he was a farmer's son who changed the spelling of his family name in youth. Self-educated and early thrown on his own resources, he worked in a clock factory and peddled books and goods through the southern states.

Teaching began at Bristol in 1823, and schools followed in Connecticut, Boston, Germantown, and Philadelphia. His Boston school of 1834 became famous for original methods. Later he was known for his conversations, informal talks on spiritual, aesthetic, and practical topics held wherever hosts invited him. In them he stressed the Transcendentalist ideas of Emerson's school, above all the mind's direct communion with the Creative Spirit. Emerson himself remained his steady supporter and discreet admirer, the entry records.
britannica-1911-algae-plankton:
Plankton, a section of the Algae article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, treats the algae that drift rather than attach. Most aquatic algae are fixed plants, but some are wanderers. They swim actively with the aid of cilia, tiny beating hairs, or float inertly because their weight nearly matches the water's. The aggregate of such floating life, animal and vegetable together, is called plankton.

Recent investigation had pursued vegetable plankton with energy when the article was written. The German Plankton Expedition of 1889 greatly extended knowledge of the North Atlantic's floating plant life, and shore laboratories did the same for lakes. Counting this flora revealed its enormous total amount and its great importance in feeding ocean and lake animals. Most plankton organisms are single-celled, often gathered in colonies. Diatoms, Peridiniaceae, and Protococcaceae lead the sea plankton, with Volvocaceae important in fresh water.
britannica-1911-allston-washington:
Washington Allston (1779–1843), an American painter of historical scenes and a poet, was born at Waccamaw, South Carolina, on 5 November 1779, where his father was a planter. Harvard gave him his degree in 1800. Charleston then gave him brief art training, with miniature painter Edward Greene Malbone and with Charles Fraser.

London came next: sailing with Malbone in 1801, Allston entered the Royal Academy under Benjamin West and formed a friendship that lasted for life. A few months in Paris in 1804 gave way to Rome, which held most of the next four years and brought close ties with Coleridge and the sculptor Thorwaldsen. After two years back in America, he painted in England from 1811 to 1817, then visited Paris again.
britannica-1911-anglican-communion:
Only in the nineteenth century did churches linked with the Church of England gain a shared name: the Anglican Communion. The new phrase answered a double change — Anglicanism had grown hugely in modern times, and old ideas of its character and sphere had shifted with that growth.

For over two centuries past the Reformation, that story ran almost wholly inside the British Isles. Ireland kept an established church for more than three centuries, yet politics long threw its religious life into shadow; in Scotland the church soon yielded to Presbyterianism. All the while it claimed Catholic standing in creed and practice, even as its working life tied it to one state. Missionary societies and colonial churches then carried it outward, and a large bibliography of histories and record digests rounds out the account.
britannica-1911-annexation:
Annexation in world law is defined and shown with cases in a 1911 Britannica entry. The word means a state adds land to its own realm. A guard pact or a sphere of sway does not count as such an act. The old rule in the land must be fully pushed out. Such a gain may come by free grant, by war, or by bare hold on wild lands.

Cases in the text span Alsace Lorraine, Madagascar, and Bosnia. France held Madagascar as a guard pact, then made it French land in eighteen ninety six. Austria turned a bare hold on Bosnia into full rule in nineteen oh eight. The Boer lands lost in the South African War close the set of cases. Gains bring both rights and debts with the land.
britannica-1911-anselm-of-laon: Anselm of Laon, a French theologian who died in 1117, is covered in a brief life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born to humble parents at Laon, he taught at Paris with great success. Later his school at Laon became the most famed in Europe. His greatest work is a running gloss on the Scriptures, set between the lines of the text. It was a great tool of the middle ages.
britannica-1911-anson-george-anson-baron:
George Anson, Baron Anson, a British admiral, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in April sixteen ninety seven, he was the son of William Anson of Shugborough in Staffordshire. A family tie to Lord Chancellor Macclesfield proved very useful to him. He entered the navy as a boy in seventeen twelve.

His rise was rapid, the entry stresses. He became lieutenant in seventeen sixteen, commander six years later, and post captain two years after that. He served twice on the North American station in command of warships. In seventeen thirty seven he was appointed to the Centurion. The entry follows the voyages that made his name.
britannica-1911-ant-lion:
Ant lion, the name for a group of net winged insects, is explained in a nature entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Adult insects in the group fly most at night and are thought to eat flesh. They have short clubbed feelers and four large wings with a fine net of veins. The best known kind is found across much of Europe in late summer.

Strictly, the name fits the larva best, famed for its pit trap. The larva has a fat oval body and a large square head with strong toothed jaws. In dry sand it digs a round pit by crawling backward and flinging sand clear. It then hides at the base with only its jaws showing. Ants that slip on the loose sides fall in and are seized. Sand flung from below drags down prey that tries to climb out.
britannica-1911-antiphon:
Antiphon of Rhamnus, the earliest of the ten Attic orators, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in the year 480 BC. He took an active part in the public affairs of Athens. As a zealous backer of the oligarch party, he bore much of the blame for setting up the Four Hundred.

When democracy returned in 411, Antiphon was tried for treason and put to death. Thucydides speaks of him in terms of very high praise. The article calls him the founder of political oratory at Athens. Yet he never addressed the people himself, save at his own trial. His real trade was writing speeches for other men's cases.
