Litigants had to plead in person, so they bought his skill unseen. Fifteen of his speeches survive to this day. Twelve are school exercises on invented cases of killing. Three deal with real trials for homicide.
britannica-1911-antrustion:
Antrustion is an article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an old Frankish institution. The antrustions were the bodyguard and armed household of the Merovingian kings. Their name came from a word for trust and faithful service. A man joined by taking a special oath with his hands in the king's hands.

The entry explains the rights that came with that oath. An antrustion's life was valued at three times the price set for a common Frank. The article uses the Salic law and old formulas as its sources. It also clears up a common error: the antrustions were a military body, not the root of vassalage. The piece ends with a list of scholars who studied the subject.
britannica-1911-apellicon:
Apellicon is a 1911 Britannica article on a wealthy book collector of the ancient world. He was a native of Teos and afterwards an Athenian citizen. He spent large sums on the building of his library. He also stole original documents from the archives of Athens and other Greek cities.

Being detected, he fled to escape punishment. He returned when a tyrant hostile to Rome had seized Athens. That tyrant had the aid of Mithradates. He sent Apellicon with troops to Delos, to plunder the treasures of the temple. Apellicon showed little capacity for war. The Romans surprised him under their commander. He saved his life only by flight. He died a little later, most likely in the year 84 before Christ. The article notes that his chief pursuit was the collection of rare books. A thief of papers makes a dark footnote in the history of libraries.
britannica-1911-appenzell-canton:
Appenzell is the subject of a canton entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is one of the cantons of north east Switzerland, ringed by the canton of Saint Gall. Both grew out of the lands of the prince abbots of Saint Gall. The name itself is explained as meaning the abbot's cell.

The entry describes an alpine region, most of all in its south. There the Alpstein limestone range rises to the peak of Santis. Toward the north the land softens into green hills and hollows. Neat villages and small towns nestle in those hollows. Two streams that flow down from the Santis water the canton.
britannica-1911-apperception:
Apperception is a term of psychology for how the mind takes in a new object. It sets the object, on which attention is fixed, against all past awareness. The word joins Latin parts for to and for perceive in its root. Leibnitz first used it, in much the sense now given to attention. By it an object is grasped as not self, yet in relation to the self.

In Kant's terms the word splits into two kinds of use. One kind concerns awareness of the pure self as subject. The other concerns knowledge of the self in its concrete life. Herbart held that a mass of past impressions takes in new parts and becomes a system. From that view a rule for teaching follows at once. A teacher must learn what a pupil knows, so as to build on that store.
britannica-1911-apprehension:
Apprehension is the subject of a mind article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes from Latin words for seizing toward oneself. In the study of mind it names a state where the mind is merely aware of a thing. Nothing is affirmed or denied about that thing. Judgment, by contrast, is a different act of mind. Bare grasp of a thing, the text says, can be neither true nor false.

The article gives cases where grasp comes without judgment. We take in many familiar objects with no judgment at all. Two choices can be held in mind with no verdict on their worth. A reader can hold a vivid character in fiction with no belief in its real life. A hearer can follow an argument in full and yet judge nothing of its soundness. The line between grasp and judgment is a matter of degree.
britannica-1911-appropriation:
Appropriation, the act of setting a thing apart for one use, is treated in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica across three fields of law. In church law it means the binding of a living, for good, to the use of a body of clergy. In the middle ages the great houses kept most of the tithes of such livings for themselves.

The entry then turns to debts between man and man. A debtor with two debts may say which one a payment clears. If he does not say, the man who is owed may choose instead. If neither chooses, the law counts the first payment against the first debt. Last, in the law of the state, the word names the grant of public funds to a set end by act of parliament.
britannica-1911-aragon:
Aragon is the subject of a region article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Aragon is a district of Spain, once a kingdom of its own. It borders France across the Pyrenees to the north. Catalonia and Valencia bound it on the east and south. Castile and Navarre lie to the west. Its people numbered over nine hundred thousand at the census given. In 1833 it was split into three provinces.

The article describes a central plain ringed by mountain ranges. On the north the Pyrenees reach their greatest height, with peaks near eleven thousand feet. The river Ebro flows through the land toward the southeast. It splits Aragon into two near equal parts. Rivers from the north and south feed the Ebro along its course. A great canal, begun under an emperor in 1529, stayed unfinished for near two hundred years.
britannica-1911-arason-jon:
Jon Arason (1484–1551) was an Icelandic bishop and poet. He became a priest about 1504. Bishop Gottskalk of Holar noticed him early. Two missions to Norway followed. In 1522 he succeeded Gottskalk at Holar. The rival bishop, Ogmund of Skalholt, drove him out. His exile proved brief, though. Years later a religious dispute consumed him.

Christian III of Denmark pressed Lutheranism forward. Arason refused to further the reformed doctrines. By 1548 many islanders had accepted them. Arason and Ogmund then joined forces. They attacked the Lutherans together. Civil war broke out across Iceland. In 1551 Arason was captured with two sons. All three were executed that year. He was Iceland's last Catholic bishop. He also introduced printing to the island.
britannica-1911-arbitration:
Arbitration means submitting a dispute to a chosen judge. Parties agree to abide by that judgment. They avoid the established courts instead. The term derives from Roman law practice. This article covers municipal law only. International arbitration has its own article. Labour disputes have a separate article too. Avoiding litigation's delay and expense is natural everywhere. Traces appear in any state of society.

Roman law systematised the practice, though. The praetor arranged most private trials formally. He appointed judges for those cases. Such a judge was usually called judex. Sometimes the title was arbiter instead. European nations adopted the system from Rome. Even English common lawyers accepted it eventually. Their dislike of civil law was overcome. The long article surveys modern statutes country by country. American and foreign law bibliographies close it.
britannica-1911-arbitration-and-concilia:
Arbitration and conciliation settle disputes between employers and workpeople. An outside party intervenes in both methods. That party is not directly affected by the dispute. Advance agreement defines arbitration strictly. Parties promise to accept the third party's award. Conciliation lacks that binding promise. A mediator promotes agreement between parties instead. Joint boards may serve as the third party. Disinterested individuals may also serve.

British labour arbitration is rarely legal arbitration strictly. Trade unions lack full legal personality there. Employers' associations share that defect. Valid legal submission is therefore usually absent. The huge article surveys boards and statutes worldwide. British, colonial, and American practice receive detailed treatment. New Zealand's labour department reports are cited. The Labour Gazette supplies further data. Gilman's Methods of Industrial Peace anchors the bibliography. Pigou's Principles and Methods follows it.
britannica-1911-arcachon:
Arcachon is a coast town of south-western France. It lies in the Gironde department. Bordeaux is thirty-seven miles north-east. The Southern railway serves it. Population in 1906 was 9,006. The town borders the Arcachon lagoon's south. Dunes covered with pine-woods rise behind it. Two distinct parts compose the town. The summer town stretches along the shore.

That shore runs two and a half miles. A firm sandy beach fronts it. Bathers frequent that beach in season. The winter town lies farther inland. Villas scatter amongst the pines there. Its mild climate attracts consumptive patients. Those patients resort there for health. Oyster-breeding is the principal industry locally. It is conducted on a very large scale. Fishing follows in importance. The port trades with Spain and England.
britannica-1911-archenholz-johann-wilhel:
Johann Wilhelm von Archenholz (1743–1812) was a German historian. He was born at Langfuhr near Danzig. The Berlin Cadet school educated him. He entered the Prussian army at sixteen. The Seven Years' War's last campaigns employed him. Wounds forced his retirement as captain in 1763. Sixteen years of travel followed that retirement. He visited nearly all Europe's countries.

England hosted him for ten years. He returned to Germany in 1780. A Magdeburg canonry supported his literary career. His journal Litteratur- und Völkerkunde ran from 1782. England und Italien appeared in 1785. It appraised English institutions remarkably impartially. His British history annals filled twenty volumes. His Seven Years' War history is his best-known work. It is brilliantly written, the entry says. From 1792 he edited the journal Minerva. He died near Hamburg in 1812.
britannica-1911-archiac-etienne-jules-ad:
Étienne d'Archiac, who lived from 1802 to 1868, was a French student of rocks and fossils. He was born at Reims on 24 September 1802. The military school of St Cyr trained him. He served nine years as a cavalry officer and left the army in 1830. From then on, the study of the earth took all his time.

His first works of science date from 1835. They dealt with the Tertiary and Cretaceous beds of France, Belgium, and England. He traced how fossils are spread in space and in order of time. Later he worked on the Carboniferous, Devonian, and Silurian beds. His great book on the growth of geology ran to eight volumes. It came out in Paris from 1847 to 1860. In 1853 he won the Wollaston Medal. That same year, with Jules Haime, he wrote on the nummulite beds of India. In 1861 he became professor of fossils at the Paris museum.
britannica-1911-argenson:
Argenson is a family article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The name comes from an old hamlet in what is now Indre et Loire. The French family it names produced noted statesmen, soldiers, and men of letters. The entry opens at length with Rene de Voyer, a statesman who lived from 1596 to 1651.

Rene was a lawyer by training and rose through posts at the Paris parlement and in royal service. Richelieu trusted him with missions as an inspector of the forces. He held office over justice, police, and finance in Auvergne and then in Limousin. After the death of Louis the Thirteenth he kept his posts and served at Toulon and in Languedoc. He showed great skill in defending the crown against the rebels of the Fronde.
britannica-1911-arion:
Arion of Methymna, a half legendary poet and musician of Lesbos, is treated in a 1911 Britannica article. He was a friend of Periander, tyrant of Corinth, and worked near 625 before Christ. Some old writers credit him with the making of the dithyramb. His true gift was more likely to shape that wild song into set form.

None of his works survive, and little is known of his life. Herodotus tells the one famed tale. Rich from song tours in Sicily and Italy, Arion sailed home from Taras. The crew, keen for his wealth, swore to kill him. He asked to sing one last song, then cast himself into the sea.
britannica-1911-arlington:
Arlington, a township of Middlesex county in eastern Massachusetts, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Its people grew from 5629 in 1890 to 11187 in the census of 1910. Of those, 2387 were born abroad. The town covers about five and a half square miles and is served by the Boston and Maine railway.

Pleasant home villages, among them Arlington Heights, dot the town with fine views round them. The Robbins library serves as a strong public library. At the Heights stand several well known sanatoriums. Spy Pond, of about one hundred acres, ranks among the prettiest waters near Boston. Market gardening in hot houses is a key trade there. Mills and works along Mill Brook make chrome goods and cases for pianofortes.
britannica-1911-armstrong-william-george:
William George Armstrong, Baron Armstrong (1810-1900), was a British inventor and founder of the Elswick works, and this 1911 Britannica entry begins with his years in the law. He was born at Newcastle-on-Tyne and schooled at Bishop Auckland. He chose the law and practised as a solicitor in Newcastle from 1833 to 1847. All the while his heart lay with machines and science.

Several of his inventions date from before he gave up the law at last. In 1841 to 1843 he printed papers on the electricity of escaping steam. A colliery engine man had drawn his eye to the sharp shock got from a jet of steam. The inquiry ended in his hydro-electric machine, a strong generator that Faraday thought worthy of close study. Even earlier, the use of water power had held his attention, and the entry goes on to those works.
britannica-1911-arnim-boytzenburg-hans-g:
Hans Georg von Arnim-Boytzenburg lived from 1581 to 1641 and was a German general. The 1911 Britannica life adds that he served as a diplomatist too. He was born at Boytzenburg in Brandenburg in the year 1581. From 1613 to 1617 he served in the Swedish army of Gustavus Adolphus. He fought in the Russian war and then against the Turks for Poland.

In 1626, though a Protestant, he joined the new imperial army. Wallenstein himself had drawn him to that side in the wars. He rose fast to the rank of field marshal in that host. His men held him in high esteem, as did his commander in chief. He became the close friend and firm ally of Wallenstein for years.
britannica-1911-arnim-elisabeth-bettina-:
Elisabeth von Arnim, called Bettina, lived from 1785 to 1859. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica presents her as a German writer of famed letters. She was born at Frankfurt, sister of the poet Klemens Brentano. Her grandmother was the novelist Sophie Laroche. In 1807 she met Goethe at Weimar and fell hard for him. He wrote back kindly but did not return the flame.

Quarrels with Goethe's wife ended that friendship in 1811. That year she wed Ludwig Achim von Arnim and bore seven children. After his death in 1831 her old passion woke again. In 1835 she issued her book of letters with a child, meaning Goethe. Long held a fake, it proved to rest on real letters, worked over with a poet's free hand. One book of hers pleads for the Jews and against the death penalty.
britannica-1911-arnim-ludwig-achim-joach:
Ludwig Achim von Arnim, a German poet and novelist who lived from 1781 to 1831, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born at Berlin, he studied natural science at Halle and Gottingen and wrote a few science essays. Yet his bent was toward writing from the first. Goethe and Herder taught him to value German legends and folk songs.

The entry centres on the gathering he made of those songs. With Klemens Brentano he issued the result from 1806 to 1808 under a title meaning the boy's magic horn. From 1810 he lived with his wife Bettina, Brentano's sister, between Berlin and his estate in Brandenburg. The article praises his humour and refined imagination, while noting the song book lacks the strict faith to sources now expected.
britannica-1911-arson:
Arson, from a Latin word for to burn, is defined as a crime in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. One old account calls it the malign and wilful burning of the house of another. At common law in England it counts as a felony. In Roman civil law the same act drew a death sentence.

The crime shows up early in English law under an old term for burning. Cnut names it among the crimes that no payment could clear. Under Saxon law it drew death as its price. In the reign of Edward the First, fire setters were themselves burnt to death, the entry says. That grim match of crime and penalty held in Gothic codes as well. In time the gallows took the place of the stake for this felony.
britannica-1911-articles-of-association:
Articles of Association, in English company law, are the rules for the inner running of a joint stock company, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets them out in a law entry. In effect they are the terms of partnership that the shareholders agree among themselves. They cover the transfer and loss of shares, calls for cash, and the choice of directors.

They also govern what directors may do, how their meetings run, and how shareholder meetings and votes are held. Dividends, the keeping of accounts, and the audit of those accounts fall under them too. The law left each company free to frame its own terms. It gave a model set in a schedule to the act of 1862, but no firm had to take it. A firm that wrote its own had to number each rule, sign, print and stamp the set, and lodge it with the registrar.
britannica-1911-arundell-of-wardour-thom:
Arundell of Wardour, Thomas Arundell, first Baron, is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an English soldier and peer. He was born near 1562 and died in 1639. He was a son of Sir Mathew Arundell of Wardour Castle in Wiltshire. His mother was a daughter of Sir Henry Willoughby.

In 1579 Queen Elizabeth commended him in person to the emperor Rudolph the Second. He served with the imperial troops against the Turks in Hungary. At the siege of Gran in August 1595 he took the enemy's banner with his own hand. That December the emperor made him a count of the Holy Roman Empire. He came home in January 1596 after a shipwreck that near cost his life. His use of the foreign title roused envy among the English peers.
britannica-1911-ascalon:
Ascalon is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an old city of the Philistines. It stood on the Mediterranean coast, north of Gaza. It was one of the five chief Philistine towns. The place is named in the Tell el-Amarna letters. It rose against Egypt twice and was taken back both times. A carving at Thebes shows the storming of the town.

Ascalon was strongly walled and was a seat of fish goddess worship. The goddess named in the text is Derketo. Though the town lay in land claimed for Judah, Israel held it only briefly. The Bible links one tale to it, Samson's raid in Judges. Sennacherib took the town, and Alexander's conquest later made its culture Greek.
britannica-1911-ascension:
Ascension, an island in the Atlantic Ocean, is described in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. It lies about 800 miles north-west of St Helena, some seven and a half miles long and six broad. Its area is 38 square miles. The island sits in the path of the south-east trade wind, and its lee side feels heavy rollers.

Ascension is a volcanic mass raised on a platform under the sea, with many cones. Green Mountain, the chief height, is a huge oval crater rising 2,820 feet. Plains around it stand between 1,200 and 2,000 feet. Steep ravines cut those plains and open into small bays fenced with lava. The island was at first bare of growth save on Green Mountain, kept green by mist. The lower hills have since been planted with grasses and shrubs. The climate is remarkably healthy despite the heat.
britannica-1911-atchison:
Atchison is a city of Kansas described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the county seat of Atchison county and stands on the west bank of the Missouri river. Four rail lines serve it. Its people grew from 13,963 in 1890 to 16,429 in 1910, and the city holds a set of colleges and church schools.

Its place and its rail links make it a great supply centre. Its trade in grain and livestock is large, and it has great rail machine shops. Its chief goods are flour, furniture, lumber, hardware, and drugs. The worth of its factory goods near doubled from 1900 to 1905. Atchison was founded in 1854 by men of the pro-slavery party. It was named for their leader, Senator David Rice Atchison. Leavenworth soon passed it in trade, and its first city charter came in 1858.
britannica-1911-aubusson:
Aubusson is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a town of France. It is capital of a district in the department of Creuse. It sits in a fine spot on the river Creuse. Gueret lies to the north west by rail. A count from 1906 gives the town 6475 people. Its carpet works are famed far beyond the town. Those works employ about two thousand workmen in all.

A national school of decorative arts upholds their standard. That school was founded in the year 1869. No one knows for sure when the craft began there. It was in full swing by 1531 at the latest. From the tenth to the thirteenth century, Aubusson led a viscounty. Troubadours sang of one of its viscountesses in verse. The town later passed into the countship of La Marche. Louis the Fourteenth later revived its old title for a marshal.
britannica-1911-auscultation:
Auscultation is a medical article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes from a Latin term for listening. It names the method by which physicians judge the state of inner organs by the sense of hearing. Ancient physicians seem to have used a kind of listening of this sort. By it they could find air or fluid in the cavities of the chest and belly.

Yet no general use of the method came, the entry says, until anatomy grew exact. Only then could doctors know the place, build, and use of each organ, and how disease changes them. In 1761 a Viennese physician issued a work on percussion, the tapping of the body surface. By the sounds drawn out, a doctor could gauge how the parts beneath rang. That method drew little notice at first.
britannica-1911-automaton:
Automaton is a self-moving machine. Its principle of motion is contained within itself. The Greek roots mean self and to seize. Clocks and watches qualify under that definition. All similar machines qualify too. Usage generally narrows the term, though. Contrivances simulating animal life motions earn it. Human figure automata are called androides specially. Early notices of automata construction abound.

Vulcan's tripods are legendary examples. Daedalus's moving figures are another. Archytas of Tarentum made a wooden pigeon in 400 B.C. It could fly, reportedly. Regiomontanus made an iron fly in medieval times. It fluttered round rooms and returned to hand. His eagle flew before Emperor Maximilian too. Roger Bacon forged a speaking brazen head, reportedly. Albertus Magnus kept an androides doorkeeper. Aquinas broke that figure to pieces. Later exhibitors kept their secrets well.
britannica-1911-avallon:
Avallon covers a town of central France, capital of an arrondissement in the department of Yonne, set on a promontory above the Cousin river. Its population in 1906 was 5,197. Wide streets, walks, and parts of the old walls with seven towers give the town its pictured character in the entry.

Chief buildings include the church of St Lazare, dating from the 12th century, with carved Romanesque portals, and the 15th-century Tour de l'Horloge, which holds a museum. A statue honors Vauban, the military engineer. Local work covered biscuits, gingerbread, leather, and farm tools, with trade in wood, wine, and farm produce. In the middle ages Avallon was a viscounty under Burgundy, passing to the French crown after Charles the Bold died.
britannica-1911-avalon:
Avalon treats a place of legend, first in Welsh myth the kingdom of the dead, later an earthly paradise in the western seas. In Arthurian romance it became the home of heroes, where King Arthur was taken after his last battle. The Welsh name Ynys yr Afallon is usually read as Isle of Apples.

Other readings link the name to Avalloc, a Celtic king over the dead, and other forms mean Isle of Glass. Such glass-isle names match Glasberg, the Teutonic realm of the dead. Through confusion with Glastonbury in Somerset, Avalon was also placed on the low ridge ending at Glastonbury Tor. The entry notes further attempts to place Avalon elsewhere in England and Wales, and points readers to studies of Arthurian legend.
britannica-1911-avebury-john-lubbock-1st:
Avebury, John Lubbock, 1st Baron (1834- ), was an English banker, politician, and naturalist born in London, son of Sir John William Lubbock. Educated at Eton, he entered his father's bank at fourteen and became a partner at twenty-two, succeeding to the baronetcy in 1865.

Lubbock joined science with public life, leading the Entomological Society and the Anthropological Institute while writing Prehistoric Times and The Origin of Civilization. In parliament for Maidstone and later London University, he carried the Bank Holidays Act and measures on shop hours, libraries, open spaces, and ancient monuments. He led the Institute of Bankers, the British Association, and the Linnaean Society, joined the privy council, and was raised to the peerage as Baron Avebury in 1900.
britannica-1911-aveyron:
Aveyron is a department of southern France, matching nearly the old district of Rouergue, with 377,299 people in 1906 over 3,386 square miles. It lies on the southern edge of France's central plateau. Three rivers, the Lot, the Aveyron, and the Tarn, cross it from east to west toward the Garonne.

Between those rivers lie distinct zones: the pastoral Viadène under the Aubrac mountains, limestone causses cut by deep gorges, the Ségala plateau, and the great Larzac plateau in the south. Climate ranges from harsh mountain cold to mild sheltered valleys. Poor soil still yields wheat, rye, and oats as chief cereals, with potatoes, hemp, and flax among other crops. Megalithic monuments mark the early Celtic Rutheni who first peopled the region.
britannica-1911-avignon:
Avignon is a city of south-eastern France, capital of Vaucluse, on the left bank of the Rhone a few miles above its meeting with the Durance. Its 1906 population was 35,356. Gardens and parks fill much of its oval area, and the ruined Pont Saint-Bénézet still juts into the river.

Ramparts built by the popes in the 14th century still ring the city, with thirty-nine massive towers and battlements, among the finest medieval defenses surviving. On the Rocher des Doms stand the Romanesque cathedral of Notre-Dame des Doms. It holds the carved tomb of Pope John XXII. Beside it rises the vast Palace of the Popes. Begun in 1316, the palace covers over fourteen acres. Strength ruled its building, giving the palace a sombre, fortress-like air.
britannica-1911-avon:
Avon is the name of several rivers in England and elsewhere, and the word itself is Celtic for water or river, seen in Welsh afon, Manx aon, and Gaelic abhuinn. The entry traces the same root, kin to Sanskrit ap and Latin aqua, through river names across the old Celtic lands of Europe.

In England three Avons lead. The Hampshire Avon crosses Wiltshire past Salisbury, gathering the Bourne and Wylye, then passes the New Forest edge to Christchurch and the Channel, valued for salmon fisheries though not for navigation. The Bristol Avon curves through Gloucestershire and Wiltshire towns toward its gorge. Names like Evan, Aune, and Aven in France, Italy, Spain, and Portugal show how far the old water word travelled.
britannica-1911-baader-franz-xaver-von:
Baader, Franz Xaver von (1765-1841), was a German philosopher and theologian born at Munich, son of the Bavarian elector's court physician. He studied medicine and helped his father briefly, then turned to mining engineering, studying under Werner at Freiberg and living four years in England.

In England Baader met the writings of Jakob Boehme, whose mystic thought, with Eckhart and Saint Martin, suited him far better than Hume or Godwin. Back home he won a prize for using Glauber's salts in glass-making, rose to superintendent of mines, and was ennobled. Retired in 1820, he published Fermenta Cognitionis against modern philosophy, urging Boehme's study, and from 1826 taught philosophy and speculative theology at Munich's new university.
britannica-1911-babylon:
Babylon was a great old city on the Euphrates river, set out in a 1911 Britannica entry on its names and past. The Greek name comes from Babel, which means gate of the god in the local tongue. That god was most likely Marduk, the patron god of the city. The city also bore other old names, such as Din tir and the holy city.

One early name may at first have meant just the great temple and its grounds. Like other shrines in the land, that temple was founded before Semitic times. The entry works through what each name meant and how scribes wrote it. It gives readers a careful start on a city famed in both history and scripture.
britannica-1911-backgammon:
Backgammon is a board game for two players, played with men and dice, said to have been invented about the 10th century. Romans knew a like game, the twelve-line game, and Plato alludes to dice thrown with men placed after thought. The name is probably Saxon: baec, back, and gamen, game, a game where players can be sent back.

The board holds four tables of six points each, split by a raised bar, with fifteen white and fifteen black men. Dice decide the moves, men travelling point to point in opposite directions around the tables. The entry then gives the full rules of play, the old names for dice numbers, ace, deuce, trey, and notes the French name trictrac, echoing the dice's rattle.
britannica-1911-backwardation:
Backwardation, usually shortened to Back, is a London Stock Exchange term for the charge paid for carrying a stock sale over from one account day to the next. A seller on a bear account pays it to the buyer so delivery of the stock can wait.

The scene behind the term runs like this. The seller has sold stock he likely does not own, hoping to buy it cheaper before delivery day and pocket the difference. Settling day arrives, prices have not fallen as he hoped, and he pays the agreed interest instead. The payment buys time, either to get the stock or to wait for the price drop that would still let him profit. The entry sends readers to the Account and Stock Exchange articles for the machinery around it.
britannica-1911-bacon:
Bacon, the word, reached English through Old French. It came from a Low Latin form of a Teutonic term kin to back. Old High German pacho and Middle High German backe show that kinship. Backe means a buttock or flitch of bacon. The meat word and the body's back thus share one root.

As food, bacon is the flesh of the sides and back of the pig, cured for keeping and flavour. The curing, as the entry lists it, works by salting, drying, pickling, and smoking, methods often combined. Side, back, salt, smoke: those few facts, with the word's path from German speech through French into English, make the whole of this short entry.
britannica-1911-bagneres-de-luchon:
Bagnères-de-Luchon is a town of south-western France, in Haute-Garonne, south-west of Toulouse. It sits in a beautiful valley where the One and Pique rivers meet. The central Pyrenees rise at its back. Its 1906 population was 3,448. Hot springs and fashion made its name.

Forty-eight springs feed a bathing house counted among the most complete anywhere. They are chiefly charged with sulphate of sodium. They run from 62 to 150 degrees. The baths stand at the end of the lime-planted Allées d'Etigny. A large casino opened in 1877. Roman remains prove the baths' age: they match the Onesiorum Thermae Strabo named. Their modern revival dates from the late 1700s under the intendant d'Etigny, whose promenade still fronts the town.
britannica-1911-baird-spencer-fullerton:
Baird, Spencer Fullerton (1823-1887), was an American naturalist. He was born at Reading, Pennsylvania. He graduated at Dickinson College in 1840. One walking trip covered 400 miles in twenty-one days. Its last day alone ran sixty miles. He had met Audubon in 1838.

Audubon gave Baird part of his bird collection. Bird study ruled Baird's work from then on. In 1845 he became professor at Dickinson. He taught natural history and chemistry together. Physiology and mathematics fell to him too. From 1850 to 1878 he served the Smithsonian Institution. He was its assistant-secretary through those years. He succeeded Joseph Henry as secretary. From 1871 he also ran the national fish commission. His own writings ran past a thousand entries. Birds formed his most important volumes.
britannica-1911-balaton:
Balaton, called Plattensee in German, is the largest lake in middle Europe. It lies in south-west Hungary, between the counties of Veszprém, Zala, and Somogy. The 1911 Britannica entry gives its length as 48 miles and its area as 266 square miles, with a greatest depth of 149 feet.

Basalt hills of the Bakony range line its north shore, where vines grow in volcanic soil. The south shore is part marsh and part downs. The entry notes the Tihany peninsula, its old Benedictine church, and the tomb of King Andrew I there. About fifty streams feed the lake, which drains to the Danube.
britannica-1911-ballanche-pierre-simon:
Pierre Simon Ballanche (1776–1847) was a French philosopher of the theocratic school, born at Lyons. Delicate and highly strung, he was deeply marked by the horrors of the siege of Lyons and by a failed love affair. His thought turned to the nature of society, which brought him into the circle of Châteaubriand and Madame Récamier.

His great work, the Palingénésie, was planned in three parts. One covered the world before religion. One sought a universal law in history. One sketched the perfect state toward which mankind moves. Only the first was finished, though fragments of the rest survive. The 1911 Britannica entry also notes his Vision d'Hébal and his election to the French Academy in 1841.
britannica-1911-balloon:
Balloon, in its main sense, is a bag of varnished silk or other air-tight stuff filled with gas lighter than common air. Filled so, it can rise and float, and serves the art of flight. The word took this sense in 1783, with the invention of the brothers Montgolfier.

Older senses came first, and the 1911 Britannica entry lists them. One was a large ball or ball game, from the Italian ballone. Others were a crude bomb or firework, and a glass retort used in chemistry. A globe used as ornament in building also bore the name. New uses grew from the air balloon's shape, such as the balloon skirt in dress and balloon training for vines in gardening.
britannica-1911-ballyshannon:
Ballyshannon is a seaport and market town of County Donegal, Ireland, at the mouth of the river Erne. A bridge of twelve arches joins it to its suburb, The Port. Its population in 1901 was 2,359. Below the bridge the river drops in a wide cascade, 150 yards across with a fall of 16 feet at low water.

That fall is the salmon leap, where fish were trapped in large numbers and helped up by salmon ladders. The fisheries were of great value, and salmon went to England packed in ice. The 1911 Britannica entry notes a small harbour barred to all but small vessels, slight remains of an O'Donnell castle, and many old raths round about.
britannica-1911-balmerino-james-elphinst:
James Elphinstone, 1st Baron Balmerino (about 1553–1612), was a Scottish politician, third son of Robert, 3rd Lord Elphinstone. Rising under James VI, he became a judge and a royal secretary, went with the king to London in 1603, and took his title in 1604. In 1605 he headed the court of session.

His zeal for the Roman Catholic faith undid him. In 1599, for the king but without the king's knowledge, he had sent a warm letter to Pope Clement VIII and got the king's signature to it by stealth. When the letter came to light again in 1608, he confessed all. The 1911 Britannica entry tells of his trial and death sentence in 1609, then his release and death in 1612.
britannica-1911-baltimore-george-calvert:
George Calvert, 1st Baron Baltimore (about 1580–1632), was an English statesman, born at Kipling in Yorkshire and educated at Trinity College, Oxford. He rose as secretary to Robert Cecil, then held crown posts in Ireland and on the council, and sat in Parliament for Bossiney from 1609. Knighted in 1617, he became a secretary of state in 1619.

Calvert backed the Spanish marriage plan, and when it failed he declared himself a Roman Catholic and gave up office in February 1625. He was made Baron Baltimore and turned to planting colonies. His Newfoundland settlement of Avalon, chartered in 1623, proved too harsh, and he died in April 1632. The Maryland charter passed weeks later to his son Cecilius, who founded that colony.
britannica-1911-bandon:
Bandon, or Bandonbridge, is a market town of County Cork, Ireland, set in a broad open valley on both sides of the river Bandon. It lies twenty miles south-west of the city of Cork by rail, and its population in 1901 was 2,830. The setting is called picturesque.

The town is an important farming centre, with distilleries, breweries, and flour mills. Castle Bernard's open park lies on the riverside, and Innishannon, the head of navigation, sits two miles downstream. The 1911 Britannica entry gives its past: founded early in the 1600s by Richard Boyle, earl of Cork, and incorporated by James I. After its walls fell in 1689, Bandon long kept Catholic residents out.
britannica-1911-barbizon:
Barbizon is the subject of a place and art entry in the 1911 Britannica. Barbizon is a French village near the woods of Fontainebleau. It gave its name to a school of painters. Corot, Rousseau, Millet, and Daubigny led that school. They set aside set themes for their work. They went straight to fields and woods for their ideas. Their themes were views of land and the life of farm folk.

Rousseau and Millet show the mark of the school most clearly. Both men spent their youth in Paris. Both then made their home in the village. They were poor and little known for years. Rousseau died there in 1867 and Millet in 1875. Long quotes from their letters close the part shown here. In those quotes each man says art must draw life as it is felt in nature.
britannica-1911-barrett-wilson:
Wilson Barrett (1846–1904), an English actor, manager, and playwright born in Essex to a farmer, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He first acted at Halifax in 1864, toured the provinces with his wife Caroline Heath, and managed theatres at Leeds and London's Court theatre. There he introduced Madame Modjeska to London audiences in plays by Schiller and others, before wider fame arrived at the Princess's Theatre.

Melodrama made Barrett's name. The Lights o' London in 1881 and The Silver King in 1882, with Barrett as Wilfred Denver for three hundred nights in a row, fixed his place with the public. Later success came with the religious drama The Sign of the Cross in 1895, which drew many people who rarely went to plays. Tours of America and Australia, and his robust acting style, close the entry.
britannica-1911-barrot-camille-hyacinthe:
Camille Hyacinthe Odilon Barrot (1791–1873), a French politician born at Villefort in Lozère, is the subject of a long 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica biography. His father, a Toulouse advocate, had sat in the Convention and voted against the death of Louis XVI. Barrot studied law, was called to the Paris bar in 1811, and succeeded his mentor Jean Mailhe in posts before the council of state and the court of cassation.

Opposition politics shaped Barrot's career. He backed constitutional monarchy in the revolution of 1830, escorted Charles X out of France, and served as prefect of the Seine. Later he pressed Louis Philippe to widen the base of the monarchy, organized reform banquets, and tried in vain to save a regency in February 1848. He headed Louis Napoleon's first ministry, was briefly jailed after the 1851 coup, and ended as president of the council of state under Thiers.
britannica-1911-bartels-hans-von:
Hans von Bartels (1856– ), a German painter born in Hamburg, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of a Russian government official. His training took him to the marine painter Hardorff in Hamburg, then to teachers in Düsseldorf and Hamburg again, and finally to the Berlin School of Art. After wide travel, especially in Italy, he settled in Munich in 1885 and became a professor of painting in 1891.

Sea and fishing life define Bartels's art. The entry calls him a leading German watercolour painter, while also praising his power in oils. He painted marines and fishing scenes with rough vigour and strong technical skill, excelling in storms and in the sturdy fishing folk of the northern coasts. Named works include Sturmflut in Berlin, Lonely Beach, Potato Harvest—Rügen, Storm—Bornholm, and Moonlight on the Zuyder Zee. Art societies across Europe made him an honorary member.
britannica-1911-barth-kaspar-von:
Kaspar von Barth (1587–1658), a German philologist born at Küstrin in Brandenburg, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a strikingly precocious child, looked on as a marvel of learning. After study at Gotha, Eisenach, Wittenberg, and Jena, he travelled through most of the countries of Europe. Too independent to accept a regular post, he lived between Halle and his property at Sellerhausen near Leipzig, until fire destroyed his library there in 1636.

Writing filled Barth's life, though the entry judges it harshly. His works, drawn from wide reading and a strong memory, are called unmethodical and uncritical. They are marred by poor taste and unclear style, and Barth himself is painted as vain and hard to like. Still, his Adversaria of 1624, a storehouse of mixed learning on classical, medieval, and modern writers, is named as important, along with commentaries on Claudian and Statius.
britannica-1911-basel-canton:
Basel, in French Bâle, is one of the most northerly Swiss cantons, described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica as the only canton besides Schaffhausen holding land north of the Rhine. The Jura chain crosses it, and the Birs and Ergolz rivers water it, both flowing to the Rhine. Since 1833 the old canton has been split into two half cantons, each with its own constitution, a division the entry then explains in detail.

Basel Stadt, the city half, is tiny in land at 13.7 square miles, yet held 112,227 people in 1900, mainly German-speaking Protestants and Roman Catholics. Its executive and its 130-member legislature were elected by direct popular vote, and citizens could demand a referendum. Basel Landschaft, the country half, is larger at 165 square miles, with Liestal as capital, seventy-four communes, and 68,497 people in 1900, nearly all German-speaking.
britannica-1911-bastion:
Bastion, from a late Latin word for building through French, is a fortification term explained in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. A bastion is a work forming part of a line of fortifications. Its trace resembles an irregular pentagon: a triangle joined to a narrow rectangle, base to long side. The two sides of the triangle form the faces of the bastion, meeting at the salient angle, the outward point, while the rectangle's short sides form the flanks.

Arrangement mattered more than shape alone. Bastions were placed so flank fire from each protected the curtain wall's front and the next bastion's faces. No dead ground was left for attackers. Variants follow. A tower bastion is a roofed tower in bastion form. A demi-bastion is half a bastion, cut through its salient angle. A flat bastion sits on a curtain, with a very wide salient angle.
britannica-1911-baton:
Baton, from a French word for a stick or staff, is a word with four uses set out in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. First it is the truncheon, a short heavy stick carried as a sign of power. A field marshal bears one as the mark of his rank, and a police constable carries one. In music the same word names the thin stick with which the conductor of an orchestra beats time for the players.

Two more uses belong to heraldry, the science of coats of arms. There a baton is the fourth part of a bend, one of the broad bands that cross a shield. It is often cut short at the ends, so it looks like a plain rod on the shield. In English arms it appears only as a mark of illegitimacy, birth outside lawful marriage, in the form called the baton sinister.
britannica-1911-battalion:
Battalion is a unit of military organization explained in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is made up of four or more companies of infantry, foot soldiers, and the term is used in nearly every army in the world. The word comes through French from the Italian battaglione, tied to the Latin word for battle. In the 1500s and 1600s it meant a body of foot in the line of battle, at first a large one formed from several smaller bodies.

Present British use is spelled out in numbers. In the regular service the infantry battalion is led by a lieutenant-colonel, helped by an adjutant, the officer who handles its papers and orders. At war strength it holds about 1000 bayonets, armed foot soldiers, in eight companies. The entry adds that in some lands engineers, train troops, some kinds of artillery, and more rarely cavalry are also formed in battalions.
britannica-1911-baudrillart-henri-joseph:
Henri Joseph Léon Baudrillart (1821–1892), a French economist born in Paris, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica.  Henri was schooled at the Collège Bourbon with high marks. In 1852 he became assistant lecturer in political economy, the study of wealth and trade, at the Collège de France. In 1866 he took a new chair there, the chair of economic history.

Books and honours crowd the record. An Éloge de Turgot in 1846 first won him notice among economists. There followed a deep study of Jean Bodin and his times, a manual of political economy, works on morals and wealth, and on the freedom of work. His History of Luxury, from ancient times to his own day, ran to four volumes. He also wrote a four-volume study of the farming classes of France. He entered the Académie des Sciences Morales in 1863, and became inspector-general of public libraries in 1870.
britannica-1911-bauernfeld-eduard-von:
Eduard von Bauernfeld (1802–1890), an Austrian dramatist born in Vienna, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He studied law at the university of Vienna and entered the state service in legal posts. In 1843 he rose to a post of trust on the Lottery Commission. By then he was already in politics: a pamphlet of 1842 had sharply blamed the government, and a trip to England in 1845 sharpened his views. After the Revolution of 1848 he quit state work to give himself wholly to letters, and lived in Vienna till his death.

Comedy is his lasting claim. As a writer of comedies and farces Bauernfeld ranks high among the German playwrights of his century. His plots are clever, his scenes witty and natural, his speech elegant. Later he turned to Salonstücke, drawing-room pieces painting Vienna's social life in bright sallies. His full works filled twelve volumes.
britannica-1911-bedlington:
Bedlington is an urban district of Northumberland, England, described in this 1911 Britannica article. It lies on high ground above the river Blyth, south-east of Morpeth, and had 18,766 people in 1901. The church of St Cuthbert shows good details of the shift from Norman building, and its dedication recalls the flight of the monks of Durham with the saint's body.

The modern growth of the town came from the rich collieries nearby and from the making of nails and chains. It is one of the most populous mining centres in the county. The article then traces its past: the bishops of Durham bought the place early in the 900s, and it formed part of the county palatine of Durham for centuries. Only in 1866 did the lands pass to the church commissioners.
britannica-1911-beecher-charles-emerson:
Charles Emerson Beecher is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He was an American scholar of old life forms. He lived from 1856 to 1904 in the United States. He was born at Dunkirk, New York, in October 1856. He took his degree in Michigan in 1878. He then helped James Hall at the Albany museum. Ten years later he took charge of fossils at New Haven.

He worked under Marsh and then took his post in 1899. A study of old sponges won him a Yale degree in 1889. Good work on fossil corals followed that study. He rose to lead rank on shell beasts and kin groups. His work on how those groups grow drew wide note. Work on trilobites of two kinds shared that fame. In 1892 Yale made him a teacher of his science.
britannica-1911-belfort-division:
The Territory of Belfort is a small state division in the east of France. It was formed from the south part of a larger department, the rest of which was given to Germany by a peace pact after war. The 1911 Britannica entry sets its bounds by German land, Swiss land, and French districts on each side.

With a small area, it is near the smallest division in France. Hills from two ranges fill its north and south. Between them runs a broad low gap that links the basins of two great rivers, cut by a canal and by rail lines. That gap has been a road for peoples since the first ages, and still holds great worth for trade and for war.
britannica-1911-belhaven-and-stenton-joh:
John Hamilton, 2nd Baron Belhaven and Stenton (1656–1708), was a Scottish peer, eldest son of Robert Hamilton, Lord Presmennan. He took the title in 1679 through his wife Margaret, granddaughter of the 1st baron. In 1681 he was jailed for opposing the government and slighting James, duke of York, in parliament.

Belhaven stood at Killiecrankie, sat on the Scottish privy council, and directed the Scottish Trading Company behind the Darien scheme. He backed the Act of Security of 1705 and spoke famously against the union of the parliaments in November 1706. Held later over a planned French invasion, he died in London in June 1708, famed chiefly as an orator.
britannica-1911-bellerophon:
Bellerophon, or Bellerophontes, is a hero of Greek legend, grandson of Sisyphus and a local hero of Corinth. After killing a man by chance he fled to Tiryns, where King Proetus cleansed him of the guilt. The king’s wife Anteia desired him, and when he refused her she accused him falsely.

Proetus sent Bellerophon to Lycia with a sealed letter ordering his own death. King Iobates instead set him tasks meant to kill him: the fire-breathing Chimaera, slain from the back of Pegasus, then the Solymi tribe and the Amazons. He beat them all and cut down an ambush on the road home, a run of trials that makes his story a pattern for the wronged hero’s tale.
britannica-1911-benedek-ludwig-ritter-vo:
Ludwig Benedek, Ritter von (1804–1881), was an Austrian general born at Ödenburg in Hungary, son of a doctor. He took his commission as ensign in 1822 and served long on the general staff. His first laurels came in crushing the Galician rising of 1846, where bold leading and skill in organising won him a knighthood of the Leopold order.

Benedek’s bravery at Curtatone and his tactics at Mortara won praise from Radetzky in the Italian wars. He later fought at San Martino in 1859. His fame broke in 1866, when the army he led in Bohemia was beaten by Prussia at Königgrätz. The entry’s later pages weigh that defeat and the long argument over where the blame for it lies.
britannica-1911-benediction:
Benediction, from the Latin benedicere, to bless, is in plain terms the speaking of a blessing or a devout wish for someone’s good. In Catholic use it also holds a set place in the Church’s sacramental system. There blessings rank as sacramentals, acts set up by the Church rather than sacraments founded by Christ.

The power to bless in that churchly sense belongs to priests alone, by the powers given at ordination. One exception is named: the deacon blessing the paschal candle on Holy Saturday, using incense grains a priest has blessed. Later sections cover the Benediction of the Blessed Sacrament, and how reformed churches keep the word for the closing blessing of a service.
britannica-1911-bennett-james-gordon:
James Gordon Bennett (1794–1872) was an American journalist born at Newmills in Banffshire, Scotland, founder of the New York Herald. Trained for the Catholic priesthood at Aberdeen, he gave that up and sailed for America in 1819. Poor years in Halifax and Boston followed before printing work steadied him.

Bennett wrote for many papers, served as Washington correspondent, and ran the short-lived Globe before issuing the first Herald on 6 May 1835, a one-cent paper. He edited it for the rest of his life. His son of the same name took over the paper, sent Stanley to find Livingstone in Africa, and fitted out the Jeannette polar expedition.
britannica-1911-bennigsen-rudolf-von:
Rudolf von Bennigsen (1824–1902) was a German politician born at Lüneburg, of an old Hanoverian family. Göttingen trained him for the Hanoverian civil service, and in 1855 he entered the second chamber. When the government refused him leave to sit, he resigned his post and led the Liberal opposition.

Bennigsen’s weight across Germany came from the National Verein, the society he founded and presided over. Born of the excitement of the Franco-Austrian war, it united moderate Liberals behind one aim: a united Germany with constitutional freedom. William II later made him president of the province of Hanover. He held that post until 1897 and died in August 1902.
britannica-1911-bennington:
Bennington is a village and county-seat of Bennington county, Vermont, in the state’s south-west corner, about thirty miles from Troy, New York. It counted 3,971 people in 1890 and 6,211 by 1910. The Rutland railway serves it, and electric lines run to North Adams, Pittsfield and Hoosick Falls.

The village sits at the foot of the Green Mountains, with woollen and knitting mills, machine shops and small factories. Its great landmark is the Bennington Battle Monument, a shaft 301 feet high, said to be the tallest battle monument in the world. It marks the win of 16 August 1777, when Stark’s militia beat two detachments of Burgoyne’s army. Bennington also housed Vermont’s council of safety in its independent years.
britannica-1911-benson-frank-weston:
Frank Weston Benson (born 1862) was an American painter born at Salem, Massachusetts, on 24 March 1862. He trained in Paris under Boulanger and Lefebvre. American exhibitions showered him with distinctions, and the Paris Exhibition of 1900 gave him a silver medal.

Benson joined the group called the “Ten Americans” and the National Academy of Design in New York. Portraits made up much of his work, but he painted landscape and still life as well. He also helped decorate the Congressional library at Washington, one of the public commissions of his career. The entry is a brief record of training, honours and the range of his brush, no more.
britannica-1911-bering-sea-arbitration:
Bering Sea Arbitration names the settlement of the great seal-fishery dispute between Great Britain and the United States. The quarrel began with America’s purchase of Alaska from Russia in 1867. That deal put the Pribiloff Islands, the chief breeding grounds of the Bering seals, on the American side of the line.

Congress barred seal killing on the islands and in “the waters adjacent,” without saying how far those waters ran, and leased the island kill to the Alaska Commercial Company in 1870. Foreign sealers working the open sea were seized, and argument grew until both powers put set questions to arbitrators. The award of 15 August 1893 found for Britain on all points, and a later commission fixed the British sealers’ damages.
britannica-1911-bern-canton:
Bern, second largest of the Swiss cantons in area but the most populous after Zürich in political rank, stretches across Switzerland from the Jura to the snowy ranges above the Valais. The 1911 Britannica article gives an area of 2,641.9 square miles, much of it watered by the river Aar and its tributaries, and divides the canton into three regions.

Those regions are the Oberland, with the Finsteraarhorn and Jungfrau and resorts such as Grindelwald and Interlaken; the Mittelland around the city of Bern; and the Seeland and Jura near Bienne. The article closes with the canton's growth by conquest and purchase, and its losses in 1798.
britannica-1911-bernard-simon:
Simon Bernard (1779–1839) was a French general of engineers, born at Dôle. He trained at the École Polytechnique and entered the corps of engineers. He rose rapidly in rank. From 1805 to 1812 he served as aide-de-camp to Napoleon. He was wounded in the retreat after Leipzig. In 1813 he won praise for the gallant defence of Torgau.

After Napoleon's fall he emigrated to the United States. Made a brigadier-general of engineers, he built large military works for the government. Fortress Monroe in Virginia and the defences around New York were chief among them. He also did civil engineering on the Chesapeake and Ohio Canal and the Delaware Breakwater. Back in France after 1830, he became minister of war in 1836.
britannica-1911-bernstein-aaron:
Aaron Bernstein (1812–1884) was a Jewish scientist, author, and reformer in Germany. In the mid 19th century he took an active part in synagogue reform. This very short 1911 Britannica entry gives his work in three fields. He wrote fiction, he worked as a publicist, and he joined the reform movement in religion.

His two Ghetto stories are named with praise. They are Vögele der Maggid and Mendel Gibbor. The entry calls him one of the originators of that genre of modern fiction. His History of Revolution and Reaction in Germany ran to three volumes, dated 1883 to 1884. It gathered his key political essays. No birth or death place is given in the entry.
britannica-1911-berthon-edward-lyon:
Edward Lyon Berthon (1813–1899) was an English inventor, born in London of Huguenot descent. He studied medicine at Liverpool and Dublin, then gave it up on marriage in 1834. He travelled for some six years. From boyhood he loved mechanical science. His two-bladed screw propeller model met ridicule at the Admiralty. He never finished that patent, and Francis Smith won the field in 1838.

Berthon then read for the church at Cambridge. There he devised Berthon's log, a device to read a ship's speed. Ordained in 1845, he held livings at Fareham and Romsey. The 1911 Britannica entry ends with his collapsible boat. Perfected in 1873, it won Admiralty orders worth £15,000 in a year. Boats went to the Arctic, to Khartum, and to the Zambezi.
britannica-1911-besancon:
Besançon is a city of eastern France, capital of the department of Doubs. It lies 76 miles east of Dijon on the Paris-Lyon line. The 1911 Britannica entry gives 41,760 people in the town in 1906, and 56,168 in the commune. The Doubs river loops almost fully around the city proper. A citadel crowns the height at the loop's neck. Industrial suburbs spread across the right bank.

The cathedral of St Jean, founded in the 4th century, anchors the old town. It holds work from the 11th to 13th centuries and a Fra Bartolommeo Madonna. Saline springs at Miserey feed a bathing house in the Mouillère quarter. The article closes with a long history. Spain held the city until 1648, France took it for good in 1678, and Vauban then refortified it.
britannica-1911-bessel-function:
Bessel function is the name of a family of mathematical functions tied to one differential equation. The function of order m solves that equation for a variable written here as rho. It can also be written as an endless series of powers. Setting the order m to zero gives the zero-order function. The symbol used for the functions is J with the order attached. Schlömilch defined them through an exponential expansion instead.

The 1911 Britannica article names them for Friedrich Wilhelm Bessel. He brought them in during 1817, in work on Kepler's problem. He studied their properties and built tables for their values. Daniel Bernoulli had in fact found the zero-order case in 1732, for a hanging chain. Euler used zero and whole-number orders in 1764. Heine and Rayleigh later linked the functions to zonal harmonics.
britannica-1911-beust-friedrich-ferdinan:
Friedrich Ferdinand von Beust is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of an Austrian statesman. He lived from 1809 to 1886. He came of a noble family from the Mark of Brandenburg. One branch of it had settled in Saxony for 300 years. He was born at Dresden in January 1809. His father held office at the Saxon court there. He studied at Leipzig and at Gottingen universities.

In 1836 he became secretary of legation at Berlin. He afterwards held appointments at Paris, Munich, and London. In March 1848 he was summoned to Dresden as foreign minister. The outbreak of revolution stopped that appointment from taking effect. In May he was appointed Saxon envoy at Berlin. In February 1849 he was again summoned to Dresden. This time he was appointed minister of foreign affairs. He held that office until the year 1866.
britannica-1911-bevis-of-hampton:
Bevis of Hampton is the name of an English verse romance of old times. Its tale entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Bevis is the son of Guy, count of Hampton, and a Scots king daughter. His mother plots with a past suitor to have Guy slain in a forest.

The plot works, and she weds Doon, emperor of Almaine, in Guy place. When young Bevis vows revenge, she seeks to kill him as well. A true tutor saves him, and pirates sell him to heathen lands. At the court of King Hermin he wins fame and loves Josiane. The tale tracks his feats, his jail time, and his revenge at last.
britannica-1911-billiton:
Billiton, in Dutch Blitoeng, is an island of the Dutch East Indies. It lies between Banka and Borneo, split from them by the Caspar and Karimata straits. The island is roughly circular, 55 miles by 43 at its widest. Its area is 1,773 square miles. Coasts are sandy or marshy, and the interior rises to 1,670 feet. Heavy rain falls, 102 to 126 inches a year. The rock is Devonian and granite, with laterite soils.

Like Banka, Billiton is noted chiefly for tin, the 1911 Britannica entry says. Over eighty mines employ some 7,500 workmen there. Output has passed 6,500 tons of tin in a year. Iron is also worked on the island. Coastal rocks yield tortoises, trepang, and edible birds' nests for export. The sultan of Palembang ceded Billiton to Britain in 1812. Dutch title was only settled in 1824.
britannica-1911-bilston:
Bilston is a market town of Staffordshire, England, in the Black Country. It lies within the parliamentary borough of Wolverhampton. The 1911 Britannica entry gives 24,034 people in the urban district in 1901. The Great Western railway serves the town directly. Very productive coal and ironstone mines work in the vicinity. Fine casting sand and cutlers' grinding stones are also dug nearby. The town appears in Domesday, though no ancient relics remain.

Furnaces, forges, and rolling and slitting mills fill the town, the entry says. Factories make japanned and painted goods, brass-work, and heavy iron goods in wide variety. St Leonard's church stands mainly as rebuilt in 1827, on a 13th-century site. Bilston suffered badly in the cholera outbreak of 1832. The account is a standard industrial gazetteer entry, strong on trades and mines. It gives no notable people or events beyond the epidemic.
britannica-1911-binghamton:
Binghamton is a city in Broome County, New York, seat of the county. It stands on both banks of the Susquehanna's north branch, at the mouth of the Chenango River. The 1911 Britannica entry gives 39,647 people in 1900 and 48,443 in 1910. Three railways serve it, and electric lines link its suburbs. Ross Park and Ely Park cover 100 and 134 acres. A Carnegie library of 1904 stands among its chief buildings.

The city takes its name from William Bingham, a Philadelphia merchant and senator. His Bingham Patent covered land on both sides of the river. Settlers first called the spot Chenango Point, about 1787. A village was laid out under the name Binghamton in 1800. It became a village in law in 1834 and a city in 1867. Schools, orphan homes, and a state hospital fill out the entry's civic list.
britannica-1911-bison:
Bison is the name of the one living species of European wild ox, Bos bonasus, called zubr in Russian. Its near ally is the North American bison, known at home as the buffalo. Together they form a group set apart from other oxen. Their foreheads are broader and more curved, their limbs longer. Longer spine bones and strong muscles form the hump on their shoulders. They carry fourteen pairs of ribs, where the common ox has thirteen.

Long, shaggy dark brown hair covers the forehead and neck of both kinds. In winter the mane wraps neck, shoulders, and hump in a curly felt. The European mane falls away in summer; the American keeps much of its own. The 1911 Britannica article calls the bison the largest European quadruped of its day. The long piece goes on to range, habits, and hunting. It is a full natural history, not a short note.
britannica-1911-blaenavon:
Blaenavon is a small industrial town in Monmouthshire, in the far north of the county, 15 miles north by west of Newport. It stands high in the upper Afon Lwyd valley, over 1000 feet up, in wild hill country. Its population in 1901 was 10,869.

The town sits on the east edge of the great South Wales coal and iron field. Very large iron and steel works, with blast furnaces and rolling mills, employed most of its people, as the entry tells it. Three railway lines served the place. The short account gives little more than site, size, and the works that explain why a town grew in so high and remote a valley.
britannica-1911-blair-francis-preston:
Francis Preston Blair (1791–1876) was an American newspaper editor who stood close to power for decades. Born at Abingdon, Virginia, he moved to Kentucky, graduated from Transylvania University in 1811, and learned journalism on a Frankfort paper. In 1830 Andrew Jackson made him editor of the Washington Globe.

The Globe spoke for the Jackson party, and Blair sat in the president's Kitchen Cabinet of close advisers. Later he backed Van Buren's Free Soil run in 1848, helped found the Republican party, and aided Lincoln's nomination in 1860. In 1865, with Lincoln's leave, he went to Richmond and set up the Hampton Roads peace conference. The entry also follows his sons into Civil War service and politics.
britannica-1911-blaydon:
Blaydon is a town on the Tyne in County Durham, England, 4 miles west of Newcastle and served by the North-Eastern railway. It grew fast in the late 1800s, from 10,687 people in 1881 to 19,617 in 1901. Coal and factory work explain that growth.

Coal mining heads the list of trades, followed by iron founding and the making of pipes, fire-bricks, chemical manure, and bottles. Nearby stands Stella, a fine old mansion house. Below it lies Stellaheugh, the crossing place used by the Scots army in 1640 after the fight at Newburn. From there the Scots marched on and occupied Newcastle, a piece of local history the short entry is careful to keep.
britannica-1911-blazon:
Blazon is the heraldic word for a coat of arms, and for the exact verbal account of that coat under heraldry's rules. The entry starts from the shield itself. The Old French word blason seems at first to have meant a shield as a piece of defence, not the painted surface that showed a family's arms.

Where the word came from is left in doubt. A common guess links it to a German verb meaning to blow or proclaim, the same root as the English blaze in the sense of noising a thing abroad. The entry notes that in the 1500s the heraldic term and the proclaiming sense pushed each other back and forth. Readers who need the arms themselves are sent to the heraldry articles.
britannica-1911-boissier-marie-louis-ant:
Gaston Boissier (1823–1908) was a French scholar who brought Roman society back to life for common readers. Born at Nîmes, where Roman ruins stood all around, he turned early to ancient history and made inscriptions his special field. At twenty-three he was teaching rhetoric at Angoulême and stayed ten quiet years.

A visiting inspector heard him lecture and called him to Paris. Theses on the poet Attius (1857) and on Varro (1861) opened his writing career, and in 1861 he took the chair of Latin oratory at the Collège de France. Cicéron et ses amis (1865) won a rare success for a learned book. Later works, such as his study of Roman religion from Augustus to the Antonines, used the same vivid method.
britannica-1911-bolivar-simon:
Simon Bolivar (1783–1830) was the hero of South American independence from Spain. The entry is a full-length life. Born in Caracas, Venezuela, to noble parents, he was sent to Madrid to study. He lived there for years. He saw the last scenes of the French Revolution in Paris. He married in 1801, and lost his young wife to yellow fever soon after.

That loss sent him travelling again. A trip through the United States in 1809 showed him free institutions at work. Home again, he threw himself into the independence cause. The pages that follow trace his campaigns and the freeing of the northern colonies. They cover his rule and quarrels in the new republics. They end with his death in 1830 and a judgment on his place as liberator.
britannica-1911-bolton:
Bolton, or Bolton-le-Moors, is a great cotton borough in Lancashire, England, 196 miles north-west by north from London and 11 miles from Manchester. Its people rose from 146,487 in 1891 to 168,215 in 1901, over an area of 15,279 acres. The river Croal splits it into Great and Little Bolton, with high moorland all around.

Though old in origin, the town looks wholly modern, the entry says. Two houses of the 1500s in Little Bolton are the only old remains, one a fine piece of Tudor work. St Peter's church was rebuilt in 1870 on an ancient site. A town hall with a classical front and tower, market hall, museums, an exchange, and many charities are listed among its public buildings.
britannica-1911-book-scorpion:
The book-scorpion, or false scorpion, is a tiny spider-like creature that looks like a scorpion without a tail. It belongs to the order Pseudoscorpiones among the arachnids. Such creatures live in all temperate and tropical lands, mostly under stones, under tree bark, or in rotting plant matter.

A few kinds share our houses. The common British Chelifer cancroides and Chiridium museorum turn up in books, old chests, and furniture, which gives the group its name. Others live between tide marks or, blind, in dark caves. They eat minute insects and mites, and may ride under the wing cases of great beetles to feed on their parasites. For winter sleep and moulting they spin a small round cocoon, and the mother carries her eggs under her body.
britannica-1911-booth-barton:
Barton Booth (1681–1733) was an English actor of tragedy from a good Lancashire family. Schooled at Westminster, where a Latin school play lit his love of the stage, he was meant for the church. In 1698 he ran away from Trinity College, Cambridge, and joined a Dublin company, first appearing as Oroonoko.

After two Irish seasons he came to London, where Betterton now backed him fully. He acted at Lincoln's Inn Fields, then at the Haymarket, and for twenty years at Drury Lane, dying in 1733 and being buried in Westminster Abbey. The title part in Addison's Cato made his name as a tragedian. Hotspur and Brutus were among his best parts, his Lear was set beside Garrick's, and his ghost in Hamlet was said never to have been bettered.
britannica-1911-boucicault-dion:
Dion Boucicault (1822–1890) was an Irish actor and playwright whose melodramas filled theatres on two continents. Born in Dublin, the son of a French refugee and an Irish mother, he scored a hit before he was twenty with London Assurance at Covent Garden in March 1841. More successes followed fast, among them Old Heads and Young Hearts, Louis XI, and The Corsican Brothers.

He first acted in 1852, in his own melodrama The Vampire, then spent 1853 to 1869 in the United States as a popular favourite. Back in England his Colleen Bawn, adapted from Gerald Griffin's novel, played almost every city in Britain and America and made him a fortune. He lost the money running London theatres. The Octoroon (1861) is named among the hits that followed.
britannica-1911-bouillon:
Bouillon is a small town in the Belgian province of Luxemburg, once the seat of a dukedom in the Ardennes, with 2721 people in 1904. It sits 690 feet above the sea in a hollow on both banks of the Semois, crossed by two bridges. The river loops round the rocky ridge that carries the castle of Godfrey of Bouillon.

Views from the castle take in the winding valley and the wooded heights opposite, a scene the entry calls one of the most striking in Belgium. In the 700s and 800s Bouillon was a castle of the counts of Ardenne. Its lords rose to be dukes of Lower Lorraine, all named Godfrey, and the fifth was the great crusader. The entry corrects a common error: Godfrey was born in the castle here, not at the French port of Boulogne, despite his father's title.
britannica-1911-bridgeton:
Bridgeton is a city and port of entry in southern New Jersey, the county-seat of Cumberland county, set on Cohansey creek 38 miles south of Philadelphia. Counts put its people at 13,913 in 1900 and 14,209 in 1910. Railways, electric lines and Delaware river steamboats on the creek, navigable up to the city, link it to its region.

Glass leads its trades: bottle works alone turned out goods worth 1,252,795 dollars in 1905, over two-fifths of all factory output, ranking the city eighth in the United States for glass. Machines, clothing, canned fruit and vegetables, plus dyeing and finishing works, fill out the list. A park of 650 acres, a fine public library and schools such as West Jersey academy and Ivy Hall serve residents. Farm trade from a rich rural region keeps the market busy.
britannica-1911-bridlington:
Bridlington is a market town, borough and seaside resort in the East Riding of Yorkshire, England, 31 miles north-north-east of Hull. Its people grew from 8919 in 1891 to 12,482 in 1901. The place splits in two: the old market town about a mile inland, and Bridlington Quay, the watering-place, strung along the shore of Bridlington Bay.

In the old town, St Mary and St Nicholas church keeps the grand nave of an Augustinian priory church founded by Walter de Gaunt about 1114. Its gateway serves as town hall. The priory flourished until 1537, when its last prior was executed for joining the Pilgrimage of Grace. At the Quay, sea-bathing, a parade, gardens, a chalybeate spring and a harbour between two stone piers draw visitors, while northward the coast rises steep toward Flamborough Head.
britannica-1911-bright-sir-charles-tilst:
Sir Charles Tilston Bright (1832–1888) was an English telegraph engineer born at Wanstead, Essex, on 8 June 1832 into an old Yorkshire family. At fifteen he became a clerk under the Electric Telegraph Company, and his gift for electrical work showed fast. By 1852 he was engineer to the Magnetic Telegraph Company, laying lines across the British Isles.

In 1853 he supervised the first cable between Great Britain and Ireland, from Portpatrick to Donaghadee. Sure that a sea cable could join Ireland and America, he talked the plan over with Cyrus Field in 1855 and helped form the Atlantic Telegraph Company in 1856, serving as engineer-in-chief. After two failures, the 1858 attempt succeeded, and within days of landing the Irish end at Valentia he was knighted at Dublin. Later cable work under his charge fills the rest of the account.
britannica-1911-brinton-daniel-garrison:
Daniel Garrison Brinton (1837–1899) was an American archaeologist and ethnologist born at Thornbury, Pennsylvania, on 13 May 1837. He graduated at Yale in 1858, studied two years at Jefferson Medical College, then spent a year in Europe with further study at Paris and Heidelberg. Medicine came first in his working life.

During the American Civil War, from 1862 to 1865, he served as a Union army surgeon, running the general hospital at Quincy, Illinois, in 1864-1865. Afterward he practised at Westchester and edited the Medical and Surgical Reporter in Philadelphia from 1874 to 1887. Chairs followed: ethnology and archaeology at the Academy of Natural Sciences in 1884, and American linguistics and archaeology at the University of Pennsylvania from 1886 until his death on 31 July 1899. A score of books between 1859 and 1899 and presidencies of learned societies fill out the record.
britannica-1911-britton:
Britton is the title of the earliest summary of the law of England written in French, said to have been made by command of King Edward I. Who wrote it has been much disputed. One claim names John le Breton, bishop of Hereford, on the strength of a passage in some copies of Matthew of Westminster's history.

That claim runs into dates: the bishop died in 1275, yet Britton cites statutes passed later, above all Quia emptores terrarum of 1290. Selden held instead that the title grew from Henry de Bracton's name, spelt Bratton or Bretton in the fine rolls. That the book was a royal shortening of Bracton's great work with later statutes added. Yet the order of the two books differs, and only a small share of Bracton stands inside Britton. An early manuscript once Selden's, now at Cambridge, calls it a summary of the laws of England.
britannica-1911-brixton: Brixton is a district in the south of London, England, and the whole of the hosted entry is a single sentence placing it there. The sentence locates the district inside the metropolitan borough of Lambeth and points the reader onward to that borough's own entry for fuller treatment, marked with a cross-reference. Nothing further is given: no streets, buildings, history or population figures appear in the hosted text. The record amounts to a brief gazetteer pointer that fixes Brixton's position within Lambeth in south London and stops there.
britannica-1911-brockton:
Brockton is a city of Plymouth county, Massachusetts, about 20 miles south of Boston, covering 21 square miles of rolling ground. Growth was swift: 8007 people in 1870 became 27,294 in 1890, 40,063 in 1900 and 56,878 in 1910, served by the New York, New Haven and Hartford railway. A public library held 54,000 volumes in 1908, and voters banned the liquor traffic nearly every year from 1886.

Shoes made the city: in both 1900 and 1905 Brockton ranked first among United States cities in making boots and shoes. Total factory output rose from 24,855,362 dollars in 1900 to 37,790,982 dollars in 1905, a gain of 52 per cent, with boots and shoes alone at 30,073,014 dollars, 9.4 per cent of the whole national product. Cut stock and findings add millions more. Its death rate of 13.18 in 1907 is called very low for a factory city of its size.
britannica-1911-brompton:
Brompton is a western district of London, England, in the south-east of the metropolitan borough of Kensington.
