Brompton Road runs south-west from Knightsbridge and continues as Old Brompton Road and Richmond Road to Lillie Road, where the District and West London railway stations of West Brompton stand. The short entry maps the district by its roads and its great institutions.

Landmarks named are the Oratory of St Philip Neri, commonly called Brompton Oratory, close by the Victoria and Albert Museum, the Brompton consumption hospital and the West London or Brompton cemetery. Apart from those public anchors the district is mainly filled with residences of the better class. Readers are pointed to the Kensington article for the fuller treatment, so the notice serves as a compact pointer to the borough entry.
britannica-1911-brooke-fulke-greville-1s:
Fulke Greville, 1st Baron Brooke (1554–1628), was an English poet, only son of Sir Fulke Greville, born at Beauchamp Court in Warwickshire. He was sent in 1564, on the same day as his lifelong friend Philip Sidney, to Shrewsbury school, and matriculated at Jesus College, Cambridge, in 1568. Court service under Sir Henry Sidney began in 1576, but he resigned in 1577 to go to court with Sidney.

Greville became a great favourite with Queen Elizabeth. Who treated him with less than her usual caprice, though he was more than once disgraced for leaving the country against her wishes. With Sidney and Sir Edward Dyer he belonged to the Areopagus, the literary circle under Gabriel Harvey that pushed classical metres into English verse. Elizabeth flatly forbade Drake to carry Sidney and Greville to the Spanish West Indies in 1585 and refused Greville leave to join Leicester in the Netherlands. Sidney, who went, was killed on 17 October 1586.
britannica-1911-brougham-and-vaux-henry-:
Henry Peter Brougham, first Baron Brougham and Vaux, fills the start of a long life in the 1911 Britannica. Born at Edinburgh in seventeen seventy eight, he rose to head boy at its high school. At the city college he took to math and the lore of light. Papers on light and on curves won print from the Royal Society while he was still young. He won a seat in that body in eighteen oh three.

Law was his trade, though he held few briefs in Scots courts. He saw more scope in London and joined the English bar in eighteen oh eight. In the mean time he wrote to live. When the Edinburgh Review was born in eighteen oh two, he was its most quick and sharp pen, the text says.
britannica-1911-broughton-john-cam-hobho:
John Cam Hobhouse, Baron Broughton (1786–1869), was an English writer and politician. He was the eldest son of Sir Benjamin Hobhouse and was born at Bristol on 27 June 1786. He was schooled at Westminster and at Trinity College, Cambridge, where he took his degree in 1808. That year he won the Hulsean prize for an essay on the origin of sacrifices. At Cambridge he set up the Whig Club and grew close to Byron.

Hobhouse went with Byron on a tour of Spain, Greece, and Turkey in 1809. He was at the battle of Dresden in 1813 and went with the allied army into France. He saw Louis XVIII enter Paris in 1814. He was in Paris again after Napoleon came back from Elba. In 1816 he put out a pamphlet of letters from Paris in defence of his bent toward Bonaparte.
britannica-1911-brown-samuel-morison:
Samuel Morison Brown, who lived from 1817 to 1856, was a Scottish chemist, poet, and essayist. The 1911 Britannica entry gives his birth at Haddington to a famed library founder father. He entered Edinburgh university in 1832 and took a medical degree in 1839. Study in Berlin and Saint Petersburg filled part of those years of training.

Near 1840 he tried to prove that carbon could turn into silicon in some states. That failed claim hurt his bid for the Edinburgh chemistry chair in 1843. He held that all elements spring from one base atom in equal parts. Later he turned to verse, with a tragedy on Galileo in 1850.
britannica-1911-bruhl-heinrich-count-von:
Heinrich, Count von Bruhl (1700–1763), was a German statesman at the court of Saxony, born on 13 August 1700. His father, an Oberhofmarschall at the small court of Sachsen-Weissenfels, was ruined and forced to part with the family estate. The son began as page to the dowager duchess of Weissenfels, then entered the Saxon elector's court as Silberpage on 16 April 1719.

He rapidly won the favour of Elector Frederick Augustus the Strong, king of Poland from 1697. He made himself useful by procuring money for his profuse master and by muzzling the Saxon states, rising to chief receiver of taxes and minister for the interior in 1731. When the elector died at Warsaw in 1733, Bruhl seized the late ruler's papers and jewels. He brought them to the successor at Dresden. That speed secured his hold on the new reign's confidence. The entry follows the thirty years of power that opened.
britannica-1911-brydges-sir-samuel-egert:
Sir Samuel Egerton Brydges (1762–1837) was an English genealogist and writer. This 1911 Britannica entry gives his life and works. He was born on 30 November 1762. He studied at Queens' College, Cambridge. He entered the Middle Temple in 1782. He was called to the bar in 1787.

In 1789 Brydges took up a family claim. He held that the Brydges line were heirs to the barony of Chandos. The case was tried and lost. He never dropped the claim, though. He restated it in his edition of Collins's Peerage. He was made a baronet in 1814. He left England in 1818 and died at Geneva in 1837. His writings were very numerous. They include the Centura Literaria and The British Bibliographer. His Restituta described old and rare books. He also printed Elizabethan texts at a private press at Lee Priory, Kent.
britannica-1911-buch-christian-leopold-v:
Christian Leopold von Buch (1774–1853) was a German geologist and geographer. This 1911 Britannica entry follows his travels and his change of mind. He was born at Stolpe in Pomerania on 26 April 1774. He studied at the Freiberg mining school under Werner. Alexander von Humboldt was a fellow student there. He finished his studies at Halle and Göttingen.

Von Buch began as a keen Neptunian. He held that water had formed basalt and other rocks. Travel slowly changed his view. In Italy his faith in the theory was shaken. He visited Vesuvius in 1799 and again in 1805. He saw the extinct volcanoes of Auvergne in 1802. Their cones and lava strata broke his old doctrine. His travel volumes set out the new evidence. He also spent two years among the Scandinavian islands. There he studied plant geography and climate as well.
britannica-1911-bulow-bernhard-heinrich-:
Bernhard Heinrich Karl Martin, Prince von Bülow, German statesman, was born on 3 May 1849 at Klein-Flottbeck in Holstein and is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. His family spread wide across north Germany. Many of its men won note in Prussian, Danish, and Mecklenburg service. His great uncle Heinrich was Prussian ambassador in England from 1827 to 1840.

After service in the Franco-Prussian War, Bülow entered the Prussian civil service. He then moved to the foreign service. Paris took him as an attaché in 1876 and again as second secretary in 1880. He was first secretary at St Petersburg from 1884. Bucharest took him as envoy in 1888, and Rome as ambassador in 1893. In 1897 he became secretary of state for foreign affairs.
britannica-1911-bunsen-robert-wilhelm-vo:
Robert Wilhelm von Bunsen, who lived from 1811 to 1899, was a German chemist. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with his birth at Göttingen. His father was chief librarian and a language scholar there. Bunsen entered the university in 1828 and taught by 1834. Posts at Cassel and Marburg followed. In 1852 he took the chair at Heidelberg, and turned down a call to Berlin.

His first famed work dealt with the cacodyl compounds of arsenic. It cost him the sight of one eye in a blast. Arsenic poison in the work near killed him too. That study paved the way for work on metal bearing carbon compounds. His pupil Frankland led that field later. He also probed the gases of blast furnaces, and showed that German furnaces let near half their heat escape.
britannica-1911-burghley-william-cecil-b:
William Cecil, Baron Burghley, who lived from 1521 to 1598, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. By his own statement, he was born in September 1521 at Bourne, in Lincolnshire. Pedigrees drawn up by Cecil himself, with the help of Camden, traced his line to Wales. They linked him to the Cecils of Altyrennes in Herefordshire.

Those pedigrees reached back to an Owen of the time of King Harold. The article treats such deep claims with care. The tie to the Herefordshire family is called not impossible. But the earliest proven ancestor is his grandfather, David. Enemies said David kept the best inn in Stamford. David somehow won the favour of Henry the Seventh. The piece opens the life of a great statesman with a frank look at his roots. Family pride and hard fact are kept apart.
britannica-1911-burlingame-anson:
Anson Burlingame is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He was an American lawmaker and envoy from 1820 to 1870. He was born in New York state in November 1820. His parents took him to Ohio as a small boy. About ten years later the family moved to Michigan. He studied at a branch school there for three years. In 1846 he took a law degree at Harvard.

He practised law in Boston and won fame as a speaker. His speeches for the Free Soil party drew wide note. He sat in state bodies in the early 1850s. He then sat in the national House for six years. He helped form the new Republican party in his state. A fierce speech by him in 1856 drew a duel call. Posts as envoy to Austria and China follow in the tale.
britannica-1911-burr-aaron:
Burr, Aaron is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an American political leader. He was the son of a president of the College of New Jersey and grandson of Jonathan Edwards. He graduated from the college in 1772 and began law studies at Litchfield. On the outbreak of the War of Independence in 1775 he joined Washington's army at Cambridge.

The part shown here tells his war service. He marched with Arnold into Canada and carried word through the British lines to Montreal. He served on the staffs of Washington and Putnam and saved a brigade at Long Island. At Monmouth he commanded a brigade, and in 1779 he restored order in Westchester county. He left the army that year for ill health, returned to the law, and married Theodosia Prevost in 1782.
britannica-1911-button:
Button traces a small word from a French root meaning to push, in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. A button is a small piece of metal or other stuff pushed through a loop or hole to fasten parts of a garment. The name also fits knob-like things, from the guard on a fencing foil to the lump of metal from assaying.

Buttons served first as ornaments, noted on a gilt knife in Piers Plowman and on a velvet book cover in Froissart. They were used as fastenings by the 15th century, and the word soon stood for a thing of no worth. Clothing buttons fall into two great classes, those with a shank and those pierced with holes for thread. About 1807 a Dane named Sanders brought a better way of making them to Birmingham, locking two metal disks round a cloth filling.
britannica-1911-buxton:
Buxton, a market town and health resort in Derbyshire, England, is described in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. The town lies in the High Peak district, thirty six miles north west of Derby, served by two rail lines. Its urban district held 10,181 people in 1901. It stands high, between one thousand and eleven hundred fifty feet above the sea.

The entry sets the town in an open hollow ringed by hills, with the river Wye leaving to the south east. Old Buxton stands a little above the new town, with one wide street and a market place. The new town is the richer part. Its Crescent, built by the duke of Devonshire in the late seventeen hundreds, holds hotels, a ballroom, a bank, and a library.
britannica-1911-byron-george-gordon-byro:
George Gordon Byron, sixth Baron Byron, the English poet who lived from 1788 to 1824, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born in London in January 1788, he came of Norman stock. The article traces his line from Sir John Byron, who gained the lands of Newstead in 1540. The first Lord Byron was a Cavalier general raised to the peerage in 1643. The title then passed through the family.

Much of the opening treats the poet's father, Captain John Byron. The article calls him a libertine by choice. His first marriage ended in divorce, and one child, Augusta, survived. In 1785 he married Catherine Gordon of Gight in Aberdeenshire, the poet's mother. He is said to have squandered the fortunes of both wives. Gight itself was sold to pay his debts.
britannica-1911-cabrera-ramon:
Ramon Cabrera, the Tiger of the Maeztrazgo, stalks a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Tortosa in Spain in 1806, he was sent to train for the Church. An unruly pupil, he took minor orders and then was refused more. His bishop told him the sword, not the Church, was his call. On the death of Ferdinand he joined the Carlist plots at once.

Exiled, Cabrera fled to Morella and the camp of Don Carlos. Daring and fierce zeal raised him fast among Carlist chiefs. He led bands through Catalonia, Aragon, and Valencia in raid war. Queen Isabella's generals fell to him again and again in fights. Cruel acts stained his wins, the entry charges in plain terms. He shot men whose lives he had sworn to spare.
britannica-1911-caesarean-section:
Caesarean section is an operation in childbirth that is described in medical terms here. Its entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The method removes a child from the womb through a cut in the belly. A legend links its name to the birth of Julius Caesar in Rome.

Roman law required the method for women who died late in pregnancy. Venice in sixteen o eight set stiff fines for doctors who skipped it. Use on a living woman was first noted in about fifteen hundred. Death rates stayed high, with more than half of mothers lost early on. A new stitch method by Sanger in eighteen eighty two changed that record.
britannica-1911-caisson:
Caisson is a word for a chest or case that took on wide use in building works, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sorts its senses. The word comes from the French caisse, and a variant form came from the Italian casone. In military use a caisson is an ammunition wagon or chest. In building terms it names a sunk panel in a ceiling or arch.

The widest sense of all belongs to civil engineering, the entry says. There a caisson is a case or enclosure of wood or iron. It is used to keep water out while foundations are built. Such works go on in water bearing ground, beside or under rivers, and in the sea itself. The entry goes on to treat the chief forms of these water tight cases. It shows how one plain word grew into a key term of bridge and harbour work.
britannica-1911-caledon:
Caledon is the name of a South African town and a river. This 1911 Britannica entry treats both in turn. The town lies in the Cape Province. It stands 81 miles by rail east-south-east of Cape Town. Its population in 1904 was 3508. It sits on a spur of the Zwartberg, 800 feet high. The sea at Walker Bay lies 15 miles to its south.

Caledon has long been known for its mineral springs. The entry gives their yield as 150,000 gallons daily. Seven springs rise in the town. Six run hot, at a natural 120 degrees Fahrenheit. The seventh runs cold. Visitors valued the waters for their curative power. Blue gums and oaks line the town's streets. The district is rich in flowering heaths. The town took its name from the earl of Caledon. He governed the Cape from 1807 to 1811. The river Caledon, a tributary of the Orange, shares his name.
britannica-1911-cameron-simon:
Simon Cameron, American politician born in Lancaster county in Pennsylvania on 8 March 1799, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Left an orphan at age nine, he entered journalism early in life. Work in banking and railways built him a large fortune in time. He grew into a force in Pennsylvania politics as those ventures grew.

From 1845 to 1849 he served in the United States Senate. A mix of Democrat, Whig, and American votes put him there in place of James Buchanan. He failed to win a Senate pick from the Know-Nothing party in 1854. He then helped lead the new party first called the People Party in his state. In 1857 he won a Senate seat as a Republican, though Democrats held the state house. That win sparked loud charges of bribery at the time.
britannica-1911-canon:
Canon, a word of rule and list, is unfolded in an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The Greek word first meant a straight rod or pole in hand. From that it grew to mean a rule that keeps things straight. The New Testament uses it for a measure and for a district. Its uses fall in the main into two great groups.

One group keeps the sense of a rule for life or art. Church law as a whole is the chief case of that group. The other group holds the sense of a list or roll. Saints' rolls and the roll of true Scripture fit that group. In music a canon is a round where parts chase one tune. Each voice starts the same tune at a set gap after the last.
britannica-1911-canonization:
Canonization is the church act that grants a dead believer public honor. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces how the rite grew formal. In the early church no fixed process existed at all. Local martyrs gained honor by custom in their own towns.

At first a bishop gave the word when a case was pressed. Power then moved step by step toward the pope in Rome. John the Fifteenth made Ulric of Augsburg a saint in 993. That act is the first clear papal case on record. By 1170 popes barred bishops from starting new cults alone. Swift cases followed, some within months of a death. Proof was heard on the spot where the holy person lived.
britannica-1911-capel-arthur-capel-baron:
Arthur Capel, Baron Capel of Hadham, is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Capel was an English royalist of the civil war years. He sat in both the Short and Long Parliaments of 1640 for Hertfordshire. At first he opposed the king's arbitrary rule, but he soon joined the royal cause.

Charles raised him to the peerage in 1641. When war broke out, Capel led royal forces in Shropshire, Cheshire, and North Wales. He served as a councillor to the Prince of Wales and as a commissioner at the Uxbridge talks in 1645. He attended the queen in her flight to France in 1646. Then he withdrew to Jersey and later aided the king's escape to the Isle of Wight. The entry shows a man pulled from reform politics into war by loyalty.
britannica-1911-capillary-action:
The hosted text for this record opens in mid-article. It begins inside a discussion of surface tension and heat. The experiments of Brunner and Wolff are under review there. They measured how water rises in tubes at set temperatures. This part of the 1911 Britannica article treats the physics of liquid surfaces. It asks how surface tension can be known and compared.

One point is made with care in the text. The tension between two liquids that do not mix cannot be deduced. It cannot be got from the tensions of each liquid with air. Curved surfaces get a full treatment after that. Surface tension raises the pressure on the concave side. The rise depends on the surface's two radii of curvature. The text gives the formula for that excess pressure. It then turns to three fluids meeting at one surface. Their three surfaces of separation meet along a line.
britannica-1911-capitulation:
Capitulation is an agreement for surrender in war. It covers the giving up of troops, a town or a territory. This 1911 Britannica entry explains the term and its rules. The word comes from capitulum, a little head or division. Such agreements are an ordinary incident of war. No orders from home are needed before terms are settled. Usual terms protect religion and private property.

The side that gives up often promises a pause in arms. An officer may sometimes sign beyond his authority. That kind of pact is called a sponsion. It binds only when his superiors confirm it. The Hague Convention of 1899 speaks to the point. Its Article 35 says capitulations must fit the rules of military honour. Once settled, both parties must observe them in full. The entry also notes a second sense of the word. It names the treaties in the companion article on capitulations.
britannica-1911-caption:
Caption is a word that began in the law courts. It comes from the Latin captio, a taking or catching. This short 1911 Britannica entry traces its senses. In Scots law it still means arrest or apprehension. From a catching at any plea or objection comes “captious.” That adjective means fault-finding, or sophistical in argument. Lawyers also used caption for part of an indictment.

That part showed where and when the charge was taken. It named the authority by which it was executed. In short, it was the opening or heading of the document. From that legal heading comes the modern sense. A caption is now the heading of an article. Books and newspapers use the word in that way today. The whole notice is a few lines of word history. It moves from arrest, to objection, to the printed heading.
britannica-1911-carbon:
Carbon is a chemical element, with the symbol C. Its atomic weight is given as 12. This long 1911 Britannica article surveys the element. It is found native as diamond and as graphite. It forms part of all animal and vegetable tissues. It is a main constituent of coal and petroleum. As carbonates it enters many common minerals. Chalk, dolomite and calcite are named among them.

Carbon also floats in the air as carbon dioxide. The solid element occurs in several very different forms. Those forms differ greatly in their physical properties. Amorphous carbon comes from heating carbon compounds without air. Its kinds differ by their source and purity. Lampblack, gas carbon and wood charcoal are named. The article treats each form of the element in turn. It gives their making, their tests and their uses.
britannica-1911-cardoon:
The cardoon is a plant grown as a vegetable. Its Latin name is Cynara cardunculus. It is a near relation of the artichoke. This 1911 Britannica article gives its cultivation in detail. The plant is a perennial from southern Europe and Barbary. The edible part is called the chard. It consists of the blanched stalks of the inner leaves. Cardoons thrive on light, deep soils, the article says.

Seed is sown each year about the middle of May. It goes into shallow trenches, like celery trenches. The plants are thinned to 10 or 12 inches apart. In Scotland, seed is started under mild heat indoors. Water must be given freely in dry weather. In autumn the leaf-stalks are tied close together. Hay or straw bands wrap them for blanching. Earth is then drawn up around them, 15 inches high.
britannica-1911-carlingford-chichester-s:
Chichester Samuel Fortescue (1823–1898) was a British statesman. He became Baron Carlingford in the peerage. This 1911 Britannica entry traces his career. He was born in January 1823, of an old Irish family. His elder brother Thomas wrote the family's history. Thomas became Baron Clermont in 1852. The younger brother went to Christ Church, Oxford. He took a first in classics in 1844.

In 1847 Fortescue entered parliament for Louth as a Liberal. He became a junior lord of the treasury in 1854. Minor offices followed in Liberal governments of the day. In 1865 he became chief secretary for Ireland under Russell. He held that post again under Gladstone, from 1868 to 1870. He was president of the Board of Trade from 1871 to 1874. Later he served as lord privy seal and president of the council. He was raised to the peerage in 1874. He parted from Gladstone over Irish Home Rule.
britannica-1911-carlos-don-prince-of-bou:
Don Carlos (1848–1909) was a Spanish prince and claimant. He claimed the throne as Don Carlos VII. This 1911 Britannica entry tells his story. He was born at Laibach on 30 March 1848. He was the eldest surviving son of Don Juan of Bourbon. His mother was an archduchess, daughter of the duke of Modena. He was the grandson of the first Carlist pretender.

In February 1867 he married Princess Marguerite of Parma. She bore him a son, Don Jaime, and three daughters. Two years after the revolution of 1868 exiled Queen Isabella, he struck. He asserted his claim to the Spanish throne boldly. His manifesto found an echo among priests and peasants. The enlightened middle classes of the towns held back. The first rising began in Catalonia under his brother. Don Carlos himself entered Spain by Vera on 21 May 1872. The article follows the Carlist war that followed.
britannica-1911-carnarvon:
Carnarvon is a market town of north Wales. It is the county town of Carnarvonshire. It stands 68.5 miles west of Chester by rail. Its population in 1901 was 9760. This 1911 Britannica entry describes the town and its castle. The town stands near the site of Caer Seint. That was the capital of the Segontiaci in Roman times. A Roman fort, baths and villa have been dug up there.

Hugh Lupus fortified the place in 1098, after the Romans. The great castle was begun only in 1284, though. So Edward II cannot have been born in its Eagle Tower. He can only have been born outside its walls. The castle is an irregular oblong on the town's west. Thirteen polygonal towers rise from its surrounding walls. Much of the old town wall still stands extant. The town exports slates and copper ore through its harbour. A steam ferry links it with Anglesey across the strait.
britannica-1911-carnation:
Carnation is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on Dianthus caryophyllus, a garden flower native to southern Europe and now and then found seemingly wild in England. Growers prize it for the beauty and sweet scent of its blooms. The entry sorts its many varieties into three groups: bizarres, flakes, and picotees. Picotees, once raised from the carnation itself, differ enough in look that gardeners often treat them as a separate plant.

The entry explains each class by its petal markings. True carnations carry stripes or bars of colour on each petal, and bizarres show two stripe colours on a white ground. Flakes carry stripes of one colour only, while selfs show a single colour throughout. Picotees have laced petal edges instead, in heavy-edged and light-edged forms. The account gives the standards by which florists judged a fine bloom.
britannica-1911-carrick-on-shannon:
Carrick-on-Shannon is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a market town and the county town of County Leitrim, Ireland. It stands on the left bank of the upper Shannon, between Lough Allen and Lough Boderg, near where the Boyle river joins. Its population in 1901 was 1118. The town lies on the Sligo branch of the Midland Great Western railway, 90 miles west-north-west of Dublin, with its station across the river in County Roscommon.

Though small, Carrick-on-Shannon is the largest town in its county and the seat of the assizes. It has quays and some trade on the river. The entry closes by praising the country around it, where waterways, loughs, and woods give the district real beauty. In a few lines readers get the town's place, its court role, and the river setting that shapes its life.
britannica-1911-carrington-charles-rober:
Charles Robert Wynn-Carington, 1st Earl Carrington (1843–  ), is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an English statesman, the son of the 2nd Baron Carrington. He was educated at Eton and Trinity College, Cambridge, and sat in the Commons as a Liberal for High Wycombe from 1865. He succeeded to the barony in 1868, when his father died.

His later career ran through high office. He governed New South Wales from 1885 to 1890 and served as lord chamberlain from 1892 to 1895. In 1895 he was created Earl Carrington and Viscount Wendover, and in 1905 he became president of the board of agriculture, with a cabinet seat. The entry also traces the barony itself, granted in 1796 to Robert Smith, a banker and member of parliament for Nottingham, whose family later took the Carrington name.
britannica-1911-cartoon:
Cartoon is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a term from pictorial art, taken from the Italian cartone, pasteboard. In its first sense a cartoon is a full model for a large picture in fresco, oil, or tapestry, or for a statue. It once served glass and mosaic work as well. The entry explains how artists moved the design from paper to wall.

One method coated the back of the drawing with black lead, laid it against the wall, and traced the lines with a point. Another pricked the outlines with a needle and “pounced” colour through the holes from a bag. In fresco work the figure sections were cut out and fixed on the wet plaster in turn, so the lines stayed lightly cut in the surface. For tapestry, coloured cartoons were laid under the woof to guide the weaver. Great masters, the entry notes, produced cartoons of high standing.
britannica-1911-catherine-of-aragon:
Catherine of Aragon, queen of Henry the Eighth of England, born in fourteen eighty five, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. She was the daughter of Ferdinand and Isabella of Spain. She was born in mid December of that year. She left Spain in fifteen hundred and one to wed the prince of Wales. She came to land at Plymouth in October.

The rite was held in London in November. Soon past it she went with her young mate to Wales. There the prince died in his sixteenth year. In June of the next year she was sworn in wed lock to the king second son, the new prince of Wales. A grant from the pope was got to clear that match in church law. The rite did not take place in the life of the old king.
britannica-1911-caulon:
Caulon is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a town of the Bruttii district in Italy. It stood on the east coast. Its exact site is uncertain. The answer turns on identifying the river Sagras. Caulon was the southernmost of the Achaean colonies. Croton founded it, or Greece itself did. In the seventh century it stood allied with Croton and Sybaris. Its coins reach back to 550 B.C. They prove its early weight.

Caulon sided with Athens in the Peloponnesian War. Dionysius destroyed it in 388 B.C. It was soon restored. Campanian troops took it during the invasion of Pyrrhus. Strabo speaks of it as deserted in his time. The entry closes with finds near the coast. Work on the lighthouse at Capo Stilo uncovered a Greek wall and terra cottas. Other remains came from Fontanelle, including part of an archaic temple capital. Thomas Ashby signed the account.
britannica-1911-cavagnari-sir-pierre-lou:
Sir Pierre Louis Napoleon Cavagnari (1841–1879) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a British military administrator. He was born at Stenay in France, the son of a French general and an Irish mother. He took English naturalisation and entered the service of the East India Company. He served through the Oudh campaign against the mutineers in 1858 and 1859. In 1861 he became an assistant commissioner in the Punjab.

In 1877 Cavagnari became deputy commissioner of Peshawar. In 1878 he joined the British mission to Kabul, which the Afghans turned back. In May 1879 he negotiated the treaty of Gandamak with Yakub Khan. The treaty admitted a British resident at Kabul. Cavagnari took the post himself, with the Star of India. He settled there in July. On 3 September 1879 mutinous Afghan troops rose, and Cavagnari and the other Europeans of the mission were massacred.
britannica-1911-cavaillon:
Cavaillon is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a town of south eastern France, in the department of Vaucluse. It stands 20 miles south east of Avignon by rail. The town counted 5760 people in 1906. It lies at the southern base of Mont St Jacques, on the right bank of the Durance. A town hall of the eighteenth century and a church of the twelfth stand among its buildings. A broken Roman triumphal arch survives too.

Cavaillon is a major railway junction. It is also the trade centre of a rich, well watered plain. The plain yields melons and other fruits in profusion. It yields early vegetables as well, from artichokes to potatoes. Silk worms are reared, and silk is a leading article of trade. Local work includes preserving fruit, distilling, and making straw hats. The town stands near the site of ancient Cabellio and followed the fortunes of the Comtat Venaissin.
britannica-1911-ceylon:
Ceylon is a large island and British colony in the Indian Ocean, described at length in this 1911 Britannica article. It is split from India on the north-west by the Gulf of Manaar and Palk Strait. Its length from north to south is 271 and a half miles, its greatest width 137 and a half miles, and its area 25,481 square miles, about five-sixths that of Ireland.

In outline the island looks like a pear, with the point toward the north. The coast on the north-west is beset with sandbanks, rocks, and shoals, and may be said to be near joined to India. That link is by the island of Rameswaram and Adam's Bridge, a chain of bold rocks reaching across the gulf at its narrowest point. Two open channels of varied depth run between island and mainland, both beset by rocks and shoals.
britannica-1911-challenger-expedition:
“Challenger” Expedition is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a great voyage of oceanic exploration. Short expeditions between 1860 and 1870 had brought rich results. On that strength the Royal Society asked the British government for a ship for a long cruise. The government assigned H.M.S. Challenger, a wooden corvette of 2306 tons. Captain George Nares commanded her. Professor Wyville Thomson directed the scientific staff, which included John Murray and H. N. Moseley.

The Challenger sailed from Portsmouth in December 1872. For nearly a year her work lay in the Atlantic. She called at Teneriffe, the Bermudas, the Azores, and Bahia. In October 1873 she reached Cape Town. She then worked south and east to Kerguelen Island. She was the first steamship to cross the Antarctic circle. In March she left the polar seas for Melbourne. Long Pacific researches followed, by New Zealand, Fiji, and Torres Strait to Hong Kong and Yokohama.
britannica-1911-chameleon:
Chameleon is a beast entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It describes a group of lizards famed for shifts of hue and grip. Most kinds live in Africa and on one great isle off its coast. A few kinds range into Arabia and the south of Asia as well.

The entry gives the count of kinds as fifty to sixty in all. The largest kind grows to two feet in full length. Long thin limbs end in toes bound into two grasp groups. Such feet grip twigs with great force from both sides at once. The tail curls down and serves as a fifth hand for holds.
britannica-1911-champion:
A champion, in old law, was a man who fought in another's place. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica takes the word from the Latin for one who takes the field. In the trial fights of the middle ages, some parties could not bear arms. Youth, age, sickness, and sex all barred the way. Lombard law let such persons name champions to fight for them. Later codes kept the same rule.

Clergy, too, were fought for by champions. For bishops and abbots that duty fell to their advocate. Hired champions were held infamous persons in the records. A beaten hireling might lose a hand or foot. Some champions held the post as a service tied to land. England had a post all its own, the king's champion. At a crowning he rode forth to dare any man to dispute the king's right.
britannica-1911-chariton: Chariton of Aphrodisias in Caria was the author of a Greek romance. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives its title as The Loves of Chaereas and Callirrhoe. He likely wrote in the fourth century AD. The tale is set in the time of the Peloponnesian War and has some history in it. Views differ on the worth of the work, the entry notes. It copies the manner of Xenophon of Ephesus and Heliodorus. Editions and a study of the Greek novel are listed.
britannica-1911-charon:
Charon is a myth entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It tells of the boatman of the dead in Greek myth. He was said to be a son of darkness and of night. His task was to row the souls of the dead across a dark river.

The entry says he took a small coin from the mouth of each corpse as his fee. Only souls with due burial rites could make the crossing. He is shown as a grim old man in a dark sailor cloak. Other peoples gave him a darker role as a killer for the gods below. The entry ends with his form in Greek folk tales of later times.
britannica-1911-chatillon:
Châtillon is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a French noble family. Its history fills a large folio volume by A. du Chesne, published in 1621. The entry warns that the book, for all its merits, contains errors worth correcting. Du Chesne claimed that the family came from Châtillon sur Marne. In fact that castle belonged to the count of Champagne from the eleventh century. The head of the house was only its tenant there.

Gaucher of Châtillon did gain the lordship in 1290, by exchange. In 1303 a new agreement gave him the countship of Porcien instead. The entry then maps the great branches of the house. The St Pol line ran from 1205 to 1360. The Blois branch ended in 1397. The Porcien branch sold out in 1400. The Penthièvre branch died out in the male line in 1457. A family record and a warning about its source fill the account.
britannica-1911-chelmsford-frederic-thes:
Frederic Thesiger, 1st Baron Chelmsford (1794–1878), is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a lord chancellor of England, born in London. He was first destined for the navy. He served as a midshipman on the frigate Cambrian at the second bombardment of Copenhagen in 1807. His only surviving brother then died, and an expected West Indian estate turned his path to the law.

A volcano destroyed the family estate, so the law became his living. He entered Gray's Inn in 1813 and was called to the bar in 1818. On advice, he stayed in England rather than sailing for the West Indies. He joined the home circuit and built good practice at the Surrey sessions. In 1824 he distinguished himself in the defence of Joseph Hunt, tried with John Thurtell for the murder of William Weare. The entry follows his rise from that hard fought start.
britannica-1911-chemical-action:
Chemical Action is a long 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on any process in which a change of chemical composition occurs. Such processes can be started by applying energy, as heat, light, or electricity, or by mixing substances together. The entry sets out three things that can happen on mixing. The particles may simply intermingle. They may penetrate each other, as gases and solutions do. Or they may react chemically.

A simple case shows the test. Oxygen and hydrogen mix in all proportions at ordinary temperatures, and the mix keeps the properties of the two free gases. Pass an electric spark, and the two unite with great heat to form water, a substance wholly unlike either. Strong chemical forces give out much heat and yield products far removed from their parts. Weak forces give incomplete reactions. These end in a state of chemical equilibrium.
britannica-1911-cheribon:
Cheribon is a residency of Java in the Dutch East Indies, bounded by the Java Sea to the north and by Tegal and Banyumas to the east. Its people in 1897 numbered 1,577,521, including 867 Europeans and 21,108 Chinese. Middle Javanese live in the north and Sundanese in the south. The entry calls Cheribon a long standing centre of Islam in western Java.

The north of the residency is flat and marshy, while the south rises into hills below the volcano Cherimai. Rice fields ring the volcano, and its slopes hold coffee planting, forest, sulphur and salt springs. Sugar, coffee, rice, tea and pulse are the chief crops, mostly on European owned farms. The port and capital, also called Cheribon, trades in sugar and coffee despite an unhealthy climate.
britannica-1911-chersiphron:
Chersiphron was a Cretan architect, named as builder, with his son Metagenes, of the great Ionic temple of Artemis at Ephesus. The Greeks set up that temple in the 6th century, the entry says. Some remains of the temple were found by J. T. Wood and brought to the British Museum. Pillars with archaic reliefs form part of what survives from the building.

A broken inscription found with the pillars records that they were presented by King Croesus, and the entry notes that Herodotus says the same. That link ties the architect, his son and the temple to a named royal gift giver. The temple itself was burned on the day Alexander the Great was born. Chersiphron is thus recalled through one great work, its donors and its end by fire.
britannica-1911-chichester-of-belfast-ar:
Chichester of Belfast, Arthur Chichester, Baron (1563–1625) was lord-deputy of Ireland, born at Raleigh in Devonshire in May 1563 and educated at Exeter College, Oxford. He commanded a ship against the Spanish Armada in 1588 and later served abroad. Sent to Ireland late in 1598, he became governor of Carrickfergus under the earl of Essex. Mountjoy praised him to Cecil in 1601 as the fittest man to govern Ulster.

As lord-deputy from October 1604 he abolished the semi-feudal rights of the native Irish chiefs and set fixed dues in their place. Catholic measures forced on him by English ministers caused friction, though his own views were moderate and he eased the policy in 1607. The flight of the earls that year removed Tyrone and Tyrconnell, but the Ulster plantation that followed fell short of his fairer plan. Recalled in 1614, he died on 19 February 1625.
britannica-1911-chilon:
Chilon, of Sparta, son of Damagetus, was one of the Seven Sages of Greece, flourishing about the beginning of the 6th century B.C. In 560 or 556 he acted as ephor, an office he is even said to have founded. That office gives him his place in Spartan public life, and the entry dates him by it. A tradition about his death is also recorded, tied to his son's success in sport.

Chilon died of joy, the tradition says, on hearing that his son had gained a prize at the Olympic games. His teaching, as the entry sums it up, held prudence as the great virtue of man. Prudence here means well grounded judgment as to future events, a forward looking care in choice. Sayings attributed to him are gathered in Mullach's fragments, and Herodotus, Diogenes Laertius and Pausanias are named as sources for the reader.
britannica-1911-chipping-norton:
Chipping Norton, a market town in Oxfordshire, England, is the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies twenty six miles north west of Oxford, on a branch of the Great Western railway. The entry gives it 3,780 people in 1901. The town stands on the steep flank of a hill and is mostly one very wide street.

Its church of Saint Mary the Virgin stands low on the slope, in Decorated and Perpendicular styles. A six sided porch and the clerestory show the later style well. The town has woollen and glove factories, breweries, and a trade in farm goods. It was likely of some weight in Saxon times, and at the Domesday Survey it was held by Ernulf de Hesding. It sent members to Parliament in 1302, but was not counted a borough in 1316. Its only charter came from James the First in 1608.
britannica-1911-chirurgeon: Chirurgeon is an old word for a surgeon, one whose work is to cure disease by use of the hand, as the short 1911 Britannica entry explains. The word in its first form is now out of use. It came through French from a Greek term built on words for hand and work. The modern word surgeon grew from that early form. Chirurgeon itself was a sixteenth-century turn back toward the Greek shape of the word.
britannica-1911-chiton:
Chiton is the name for small shore beasts of the shell tribe that live by the sea edge. They bear a file tongue in the mouth, like their snail kin. Their chief mark is a frame that is the same on both sides. The back bears not one shell but eight lime plates in a row.

Those plates join at their rims so the beast can flex. A flat foot fills the low side, and a groove holds rows of gills. Old books classed them with the limpets. New work put them with two worm like kin that lack shells. The group was in time raised to a class of its own.
britannica-1911-choisy-francois-timoleon:
Francois Timoleon, abbe de Choisy, lived from 1644 to 1724 and was a French author born in Paris. The 1911 Britannica entry opens with one of the oddest childhoods in its pages. His mother, a friend of Anne of Austria, dressed the boy as a girl by whim. That dress stayed until he was eighteen, then returned by his own choice later.

Fine dress and intrigue filled his youth until a duke rebuke drove him to the provinces. Made an abbe as a child, he lived on his Burgundy benefice when funds ran low. There he found neighbours of kindred spirit in the quiet country retreat. The entry gives a life as strange as any novel of his age.
britannica-1911-cinnamon:
Cinnamon is the inner bark of a small evergreen tree of Ceylon. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica covers its history and tests. The tree belongs to the laurel family and bears greenish blooms. Peoples of old prized the spice as a gift fit for kings.

Scripture and Greek writers name cinnamon in early times. The tree now grows in India, Java, Brazil, and the West Indies. No crop matches the fine thin bark of Ceylon. Its sweet warm taste comes from a fragrant golden oil. Cooks use it in chocolate, drinks, and rich dishes. Drug sellers of the day praised it for colds. Cheap cassia bark is often mixed in, and an iodine test can spot the fraud.
britannica-1911-circumcision:
Circumcision is the cutting off of the foreskin. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes its use as a medical act and as a rite. Among Jews and Muslims it stands as a rite of entry. With Jews it stays a required step for converts, bar some reformed groups. Genesis places its origin in the age of Abraham. Flint knives used in the rite prove its great age.

The book of Joshua hints the custom lapsed in Egypt. At Gilgal the people were circumcised to roll away that reproach. Egyptians practised the rite in ancient times, Herodotus reports. Whether the Hebrews took it from Egypt is doubted in the entry. The rite shows up in too many lands for one source to explain it. All the folk of Palestine kept it, save the Philistines.
britannica-1911-cithaeron:
Cithaeron is a mountain article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a famed range in the south of Boeotia, in Greece. The range rises to 4,626 feet and parts Boeotia from Megaris and Attica. Its modern name, Elatea, comes from its pine forests. Greek myth made the mountain a stage for dark tales.

On Cithaeron, Actaeon was changed into a stag. There Pentheus was torn apart by the Bacchantes whose rites he had spied on. The infant Oedipus was left exposed on its slopes. The range also held the secret rites of Dionysus and a feast in honour of Hera. A road from Athens to Thebes crosses it by a pretty pass guarded in old times by a strong fort. Plataea lies on the north slope, and the passes shaped the great battle fought there in 479 before Christ.
britannica-1911-citron:
Citron is a species of Citrus, C medica, in the same genus that furnishes the orange, lime and shaddock. The plant is a small evergreen tree or shrub about ten feet high, with straggling spiny branches. Its large fruit runs five to six inches long, with a rough, furrowed rind whose inner part is thick, white and fleshy. The pulp is sub-acid and edible, while the seeds are bitter in taste.

Varieties range widely in size and weight, and the fingered citron of China splits its lobes into finger-like parts. Hooker placed its home in valleys at the foot of the Himalaya and nearby hills, while Bonavia argued for Cochin China or China. Theophrastus described it in Media three centuries before Christ, and Jews used citron branches at the feast of tabernacles. Candied rind is prized for dessert, and the rind yields two perfumes.
britannica-1911-civilization:
Civilization derives plainly from the Latin civis, a citizen, and civilis, pertaining to a citizen, the entry begins by noting. In practice the word is usually read in a narrower sense, covering only the recent brief period since the most developed races used systems of writing. That restricted use is called arbitrary here. Early societies long before the historical period had reached high stages of social and political development, recent study has shown.

The entry therefore takes civilization broadly, to include the long earlier periods called savagery and barbarism as well as the later higher stage. Palaeontology and prehistoric archaeology, from just after the middle of the 19th century, supplied proof of that long slow evolution. Successive stages of human progress are then outlined under the one comprehensive term. Citizens of early societies can thus be spoken of as attaining stages of civilization.
britannica-1911-cladel-leon:
Cladel, Léon (1835–1892) was a French novelist, born at Montauban on 13 March 1835, the son of an artisan who studied law at Toulouse. He became a solicitor's clerk in Paris, then made a reputation in a limited circle with Les Martyrs ridicules in 1862. Charles Baudelaire, whose literary disciple he was, wrote a preface for that first book. He then returned to his native Quercy district.

There he produced pictures of peasant life in Eral le dompteur, Le Nommé Qouael and other volumes, before returning to Paris. Le Bouscassié in 1869 and La Fête votive de Saint Bartholomée Porte-glaive in 1872 are generally acknowledged as his best work. Une Maudite in 1876 was judged dangerous to public morals and cost him a month's imprisonment. Short stories, later novels and a posthumous Juive errante in 1897 fill the list, and he died at Sèvres on 20 July 1892.
britannica-1911-clausewitz-karl-von:
Karl von Clausewitz, a Prussian general and writer on war who lived from 1780 to 1831, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Burg near Magdeburg, he joined the army in 1792 at age twelve. He first fought in the Rhine campaigns and won his commission at the siege of Mainz. Back in garrison he worked hard to make up for a thin schooling.

In 1801 Clausewitz entered the Berlin academy for young officers, then led by Scharnhorst. That teacher shaped his mind in depth and won him a post with Prince August. He was taken by the French at Prenzlau in 1806 and held for two years. On his return he served in the war ministry, taught in the military school, and trained the crown prince, all while Prussia rebuilt its army.
britannica-1911-clayton-john-middleton:
Clayton, John Middleton is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an American politician. Born in Dagsborough, Delaware, in 1796, he came of an old Quaker family. He graduated at Yale in 1815 and began to practise law at Dover in 1819, soon gaining a large practice. He entered the state House of Representatives in 1824 and served as Delaware's secretary of state from 1826 to 1828.

The article follows his national career. Elected to the Senate in 1829, he won a high place as a speaker against the administration. He later served as chief justice of Delaware and returned to the Senate in 1845. In 1849 he became secretary of state under President Taylor. He was in the Senate again from 1853 until his death in 1856.
britannica-1911-cleon:
Cleon (d. 422 B.C.) was an Athenian politician during the Peloponnesian War, son of Cleaenetus, from whom he inherited a lucrative tannery business. He was the first prominent representative of the commercial class in Athenian politics, the entry stresses. Notice came first as an opponent of Pericles, acting oddly in concert with aristocrats who also hated and feared him. In the dark days of 430, with plague devastating the city, Cleon headed the opposition.

Pericles was accused by Cleon of mishandling public money and was actually found guilty, though feeling soon reversed and restored him. Pericles' death in 429 left the field clear, and Cleon came forward as professed champion and leader of the democracy. Rough and unpolished, he had natural eloquence, a powerful voice and an exact sense of how to work on the people's feelings. Trebling jurymen's pay strengthened his hold on the poorer classes.
britannica-1911-clermont-ganneau-charles:
Clermont-Ganneau, Charles Simon (1846– ) was a French Orientalist, born in Paris on 19 February 1846, the son of a sculptor of some repute. Educated at the École des Langues Orientales, he entered the diplomatic service as dragoman at Jerusalem and then at Constantinople. His discovery in 1870 of the stele of Mesha, the Moabite Stone, laid the foundation of his reputation. That stone bears the oldest Semitic inscription known, the entry says.

In 1874 the British government employed him on an archaeological expedition to Palestine, and France sent him on like missions to Syria and the Red Sea. Vice-consul at Jaffa from 1880 to 1882, he later directed the École des Langues Orientales and held a Collège de France chair. He first exposed in England the Shapira forgeries of Hebrew texts in 1883. In 1903 he helped investigate the so-called tiara of Saïtapharnes, bought by the Louvre and judged modern work.
britannica-1911-clevedon:
Clevedon is a watering-place in the northern division of Somersetshire, England, on the Bristol Channel, 15 and a half miles west of Bristol. A branch of the Great Western railway serves it, and its urban district counted 5,900 people in 1901. The cruciform church of St Andrew has Norman and later portions in its fabric. It is the burial place of Henry Hallam the historian and of members of his family, including his sons Arthur and Henry.

Clevedon Court is a remarkable medieval mansion, dating originally from the early part of the 14th century, though much altered in Elizabethan and other periods. The house is considered the original of Castlewood in Thackeray's Esmond, the entry says. Thackeray knew the place through his friendship with the Reverend William Brookfield and his wife. She was the daughter of Sir Charles Elton of Clevedon Court, tying novel, house and family together.
britannica-1911-clifton:
Clifton is a suburb and residential district of Bristol, England, adjoining it on the west, 122 miles west of London by the Great Western railway. The river Avon runs in a gorge below it, followed by railways on either side and scarred by quarries. Brunel's famous suspension bridge bestrides that gorge at 245 feet above high water. Begun in 1832 and completed in 1864, it spans 702 feet and weighs 1,500 tons in all.

Hot springs at Hotwells, issuing at about 76 degrees, gave the town its rise, and a hydropathic establishment is attached to them. Clifton and Durdham Downs form Bristol's principal pleasure grounds, some 5,000 acres high above the river with wide prospects. Three ancient British earthworks witness early settlement on the spot. Clifton College, founded in 1862 in Gothic buildings, takes rank among the principal modern English public schools.
britannica-1911-clive-robert-clive-baron:
Robert Clive is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Clive was the statesman and general who founded the empire of British India. He lived from 1725 to 1774 and was born in Shropshire. His family was one of the oldest in the county. His father followed the law, since the family estate yielded little. Robert was their eldest son.

The article says young Clive was the despair of his teachers. He was sent from school to school and skipped his books for risky adventures. Yet he was less ignorant than writers claim, since he could read Horace in later life. At eighteen he was sent to Madras as a clerk in the East India Company. A long delay in Brazil taught him Portuguese, which he often found of use.
britannica-1911-clyde-colin-campbell-bar:
Clyde, Colin Campbell, Baron (1792–1863) was a British soldier, born at Glasgow on 20 October 1792 and educated at the Glasgow high school. At sixteen he obtained an ensigncy in the 9th foot through his uncle Colonel Campbell, and active service came early. He fought under Wellesley at Vimiera, shared Moore's retreat and Corunna, and served through the Peninsular campaigns. Severe wounds at San Sebastian, leading a storming party, and at the Bidassoa marked that service.

Gallantry brought promotion without purchase, and he commanded in the American expedition of 1814, then studied the theoretical branches of his profession in peace. He quelled the negro insurrection in Demerara in 1823 and took the 98th foot to distinguished service in the Chinese War of 1842. In the Sikh War of 1848 to 1849 under Gough he fought at Chillianwalla, where he was wounded, and at Gujrat. His steady coolness there largely served British success, the account breaks off in saying.
britannica-1911-co-optation:
Co-optation, from the Latin co-optare, less correctly spelled co-option, is the election to vacancies on a legislative, administrative or other body by the votes of its existing members. An outside constituency plays no part in that choice, which is the defining point of the term. The members already sitting fill the empty places themselves by their own votes. No election by the public or any district enters the process as described.

Bodies may be purely co-optative in this way, filling every vacancy from within their own number. The Royal Academy is given as an example of that pure type in the entry. Other bodies are elective in the ordinary way, yet hold a power to add to their numbers by co-optation. Municipal corporations in England are named as examples of that second, mixed kind.
britannica-1911-coen-jan-pieterszoon:
Jan Pieterszoon Coen (1587–1630) was the fourth governor-general of the Dutch East Indies. He was born at Hoorn and spent his youth at Rome. He lived there in the house of the Piscatori, famed merchants. In 1607 he sailed from Amsterdam to the Indies as second commercial agent. He stayed away four years.

His rise was swift on his return. In 1612 he led a trading voyage east. A year later he directed the East Indian trade as councillor. He then served as president at Bantam. On 31 October 1617 he became governor-general. He took and destroyed Jacatra. On its ruins he founded Batavia, capital of the Dutch East Indies. The entry credits his vigour for much of the Dutch empire's survival in the East.
britannica-1911-coercion:
Coercion, from a Latin word for restraint, means forcing a person to act or to hold back against his own will. Force may be moral or physical in kind. Where force is direct, the act forced is not in law a crime. A man driven to join a rebel army under threat of death gives the stock case.

Narrow limits bound that rule. A superior's order gives no cover to a soldier or servant. A parent's order gives none to a child. One old rule stands apart, though. A wife who broke the law in her husband's presence was held to act under his force. Grave crimes fell outside that shield. In politics, the word named the Crimes Act of 1887 in Ireland. Foes of the Unionist government used it as a charge.
britannica-1911-cognition:
Cognition, in psychology, covers all modes of being aware of an object. The object may be material or a matter of thought. At its core it is the showing of an object to the mind, through sense or in some other way. In full form it seems to hold a judgment as well. The mind picks the object out from others around it.

Theory here rests on one plain base. Mind that knows and thing known stand as two sides. The entry takes that split for granted. It sets aside the deep puzzle of how self and world can meet at all. Cognition thus stands apart from feeling and from will. It has no link with pleasure or pain as such. Nor does it tend by itself toward action. Two named books guide readers who want the tests behind the claim.
britannica-1911-colchester-charles-abbot:
Charles Abbot, first Baron Colchester (1757–1829), was born at Abingdon. His father was rector of All Saints, Colchester. By his mother's second marriage he became half-brother to Jeremy Bentham. He went from Westminster school to Christ Church, Oxford. There he won the chancellor's medal for Latin verse and the Vinerian scholarship.

He practised twelve years as a barrister. In 1795 he became clerk of the rules in the king's bench. That June he entered parliament for Helston. In 1796 he began his work as a reformer. He won the setting up of two committees. One dealt with laws about to lapse. The other dealt with better printing of new statutes. He rose in time to the peerage as Baron Colchester, with a pension. His speeches against Roman Catholic claims came out in 1828. He died on 8 May 1829.
britannica-1911-colepeper-john-colepeper:
John Colepeper, first Baron Colepeper, an English politician who died in 1660, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. He was the only son of Sir John Colepeper of Wigsell in Sussex. He began his career in military service abroad. At home he first drew notice for his knowledge of country affairs. The council board often called him to give evidence on such matters.

Colepeper was knighted and elected member for Kent in the Long Parliament. At first he took the popular side, speaking against monopolies in 1640. He helped impeach Sir Robert Berkeley and backed the attainder of Stafford. He split from the popular party over the Church question, on political rather than religious grounds. He defended the prayer-book and opposed the militia bill and the Grand Remonstrance. In January 1642 he joined the king's party as chancellor of the exchequer.
britannica-1911-coleridge-john-duke-cole:
John Duke Coleridge, first Baron Coleridge, who lived from 1820 to 1894, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica as lord chief justice of England. He was the eldest son of Sir John Taylor Coleridge. Born at Ottery Saint Mary, he studied at Eton and at Balliol College, Oxford. He was called to the bar in 1846.

Coleridge rose slowly on the western circuit through twenty years of hard work. In 1865 he entered parliament for Exeter as a Liberal. Party leaders soon meant to make him the lead voice in an attack on the government. A group of their own men blocked that plan as unwise. When the Liberals won power in 1868, he rose fast. He became solicitor general, then attorney general. At Oxford a fight over church tests on the university gave him a cause that fit his gifts as a speaker.
britannica-1911-collation:
Collation is a word article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The term comes from a Latin word meaning to bring together or compare. At its core, collation is the bringing of things together for comparison. From that root, several special uses grew in different fields.

The chief use concerns texts. Collation is the careful checking of documents or manuscripts against each other, and the record of what that checking finds. In printing and bookbinding, the word names the register of a book's gatherings and leaves. In Roman and Scots law it answers to the English term hotch-pot. The entry also traces a church use, from talks or readings in monasteries. One Latin sense, a conference or treatise, gave Cassian his Conferences of the Fathers. The piece untangles one word across books, law, and cloisters.
britannica-1911-collin-heinrich-joseph-v:
Heinrich Joseph von Collin (1771–1811) was an Austrian dramatist born in Vienna on 26 December 1771. He read law and entered the finance ministry of Austria. Promotion came fast there. In 1805 and again in 1809, with Austria under Napoleon's heel, he took on key political missions. He was ennobled in 1803 and made Hofrat in 1809.

His tragedy Regulus, from 1801, won warm praise in Vienna. Its strict classical form suited the taste of that city. Later plays tried to blend that form with Shakespeare and the German romantics. Coriolan, Polyxena and Balboa mark that shift. As a lyric poet he left stirring songs for men who fought for Austrian freedom. Good ballads stand beside them. His poems were gathered in 1812, after his death on 28 July 1811. His plays fill four volumes.
britannica-1911-collingwood-cuthbert-col:
Cuthbert Collingwood, Baron Collingwood (1750–1810), was a British naval commander born at Newcastle upon Tyne on 26 September 1750. At age eleven he went aboard the Shannon under a kinsman, Captain Brathwaite. That early care gave him much of his sea craft. He later served under Admiral Roddam. In 1774 he went to Boston with Admiral Graves.

He fought in the naval brigade at Bunker Hill in June 1775 and gained his lieutenancy there. Command of the Badger came in 1779, then the frigate Hinchinbroke. In 1780 that ship joined Nelson's venture toward the Spanish Main and the Pacific route by river and lake. The long entry follows his rise through war after war. Its middle turns to Trafalgar's great fleet action. There his line bore down beside Nelson's own line on the foe.
britannica-1911-collins-john-churton:
John Churton Collins (1848–1908) was an English literary critic born on 26 March 1848 at Bourton on the Water in Gloucestershire. He went from King Edward's school in Birmingham to Balliol College, Oxford. He took his degree in 1872 and turned at once to letters. Work as journalist, essayist and lecturer filled his days from that point.

His first book, a study of Sir Joshua Reynolds, came in 1874. He edited classic English writers and wrote on Bolingbroke, Swift and Voltaire in England. A study of English literature appeared in 1891, with essay volumes after it. His own essays cut sharp in tone but show deep knowledge. In 1904 he became professor of English literature at Birmingham. For years he lectured for university extension as well. He was found dead in a ditch near Lowestoft on 15 September 1908.
britannica-1911-collodion:
Collodion is a colourless, thick fluid made by dissolving gun-cotton and other forms of pyroxylin in alcohol and ether. Its name comes from the Greek word for glue. Louis Nicolas Ménard found it in Paris in 1846. Dr J. Parkers Maynard found it on his own in Boston in 1848. Mix and stock decide its quality in use.

Too much ether leaves a tough film as the fluid dries. Too much alcohol leaves a soft film that tears with ease. In hot lands extra alcohol helps, since it slows the ether's flight. Good collodion shows clear and without colour under the microscope. It should be kept cool and out of light. A strip of silver foil can clear iodized collodion stained by free iodine. The entry goes on to salts used in iodizing and to uses of the film.
britannica-1911-collusion:
Collusion is a secret pact made for an improper end. The word comes from a Latin verb that means, strictly, to play with. In court work the term has a sharp sense. It names a sly deal between two or more persons to bring a suit. A third party may join the deal as well.

The aim is to gain a judgment or remedy that fair play would not give. Parties may hide key facts to reach that end. The entry points to one field where the charge bites most. Matrimonial causes, the suits that end a marriage, draw the closest watch. The piece is short and tight in scope. It gives the root, the plain sense and the court sense. No cases are named and no law is cited by number.
britannica-1911-combination: Combination, a term for a union of people joined for a shared aim, is explained in a brief entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes from a Latin verb that means to combine. In history the term is bound most to pacts among workmen to raise their wages. Such pacts were banned by law for a long time. The entry gives no more detail in its own text. It points readers to the entries on trade unions, conspiracy, and strikes and lock outs for the full account.
britannica-1911-combustion:
Combustion is the burning of a substance, in science its joining with oxygen. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces how men explained fire. Flame and heat mark the common form of the process. The term stretches to slow rust like change in metals as well.

Heaps of oil soaked cotton waste can fire with no spark. Slow joining with air warms them until they burst alight. Thinkers of old knew some air was needed for burning. They also saw that burnt stuff weighs more than before. One French doctor showed that gain has a fixed limit. John Mayow in 1674 split air into a life giving part and a dead part. His early death left that insight lost for a century. Stahl theory of a fire stuff then ruled the field.
britannica-1911-commemoration: Commemoration is a broad term for marking a past event, says a short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. It is also the name of a yearly rite at Oxford. That rite, also called Encaenia, closes the academic year. It holds a Latin speech in honour of founders and donors. Prize works in prose and verse are read aloud. Honorary degrees are given to famed guests from home and abroad. The rite is held in the Sheldonian Theatre, most often in mid June.
britannica-1911-commendation:
Commendation comes from the Latin commendare, to place in the charge of a man, or to win a favour for him. In common use it means praise, above all praise passed to one man on behalf of a second. In church use it names a service that gives the souls of the dying and the dead to the mercy of God. The word has set senses in feudal law and in church law as well.

In feudal law, commendation was the act by which a free man placed himself under the shield of a lord. In church law, the term covers the grant of posts in commendam. A post was held in commendam when it was given for a time till a post fell free. It could also be given to a layman, or to a cleric to hold with the gains for life.
britannica-1911-commutation:
Commutation, from a Latin word for change, names the swapping of one thing for another, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica lists its chief uses. The term applies above all to payment. A money payment may replace payment in kind or by service. A lump sum may replace payments spread over time.

The word is used in law in a second sense as well. It names the swapping of a lesser sentence for a greater one, for a convicted criminal. In electrical work, it names the reversal of the course of a current. The device that does that work is called a commutator. In America, a commutation ticket lets a rider travel one route at a lower rate. The ticket holds good for a set time, the entry notes.
britannica-1911-companion:
Companion, a word for one who shares meals with another, is traced in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. It comes through Old French from a late Latin word built on cum, with, and panis, bread. A companion is a mess-mate or comrade, a word of like origin meaning one who shares a room.

The word is used above all of soldiers, as in companion in arms. It is also the title of the lowest rank in orders of knighthood. It names a person who lives with another, paid for the sake of company, and treated more as a friend than a servant. It can also mean one of a matching pair, as of pictures. A second shipboard sense names the framed windows over a hatchway. It also names the hooded stairs down to the captain's cabin.
britannica-1911-compensation:
Compensation is a law article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a word for making good a loss. The term comes from a Latin verb meaning to weigh one thing against another. English law uses the word for a range of forms of payment for loss.

The article lists the main fields where the word works. It covers loss from crime, harm done by rioters, and farm upgrades by tenants. It covers pay to workmen hurt in their jobs, and sums paid when drink licences are ended. Its chief sense, though, is pay to owners whose land is taken for public works. The piece sets the English rule beside the rule used in the United States. In England, fair money must be paid for what is taken.
britannica-1911-conant-thomas-jefferson:
Thomas Jefferson Conant, an American Bible scholar who lived from 1802 to 1891, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Brandon in Vermont, he graduated from Middlebury College in 1823. He taught Greek, Latin, and German at Waterville College for six years. Later chairs took him to New York and to Rochester.

From 1857 to 1875 Conant worked for the American Bible Union on a revised New Testament. His wife Hannah was a writer in her own right and a strong help in his Hebrew work. The entry calls him the top Hebrew scholar of his time in America. His study of the word baptizein sums the proof for Baptist teaching. He rendered and edited a Hebrew grammar and issued revised books of the Old Testament with notes. They run from Job and Genesis to Psalms and Isaiah.
britannica-1911-conation:
Conation is a term from the study of the mind, and an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out what the word means. Taken from a Latin verb meaning to try or strive, it was picked by Sir William Hamilton. It names a bent of mind that leans toward taking action.

The entry gives plain cases, such as moving a thing that causes pain or breaking off a bad train of thought. It then takes up the hard task of telling conation apart from feeling. It cites the German thinker Franz Brentano, who held that no real line could be drawn between them. The entry argues back that a smooth series can still have parts worth naming.
britannica-1911-conditional-limitation:
Conditional limitation is a law phrase used in two senses, both tied to land. In the first sense it names a term tied to the grant of an estate. That term ends the grant when a set event takes place. Such an estate can last only until that event comes. It is a present stake, lost when the set event fires.

An estate given to a man while he is parson of Dale shows the form. An estate given while he stays unmarried shows it as well. In the second sense the phrase names a future stake in land. That stake takes force when a set event comes. A grant that shifts land to a new holder when a named man returns from Rome gives the pattern. Such grants work by what law calls a springing or shifting use.
britannica-1911-confederation:
Confederation, at root, names any league or union of people or of bodies of people. The word runs back through French to a Latin term for a league. In modern political use it holds a tighter sense. It names a lasting union of sovereign states for set shared ends. The German Confederation of 1815 gives one case in point.

The Confederation of the Rhine, a league of German states under Napoleon's guard from 1806 to 1813, gives a second. Men at times called the post-1815 rule of Europe by the great powers a Confederation of Europe. The entry calls that phrase a pious hope more than a fact. A key split parts confederation from federation. The United States formed a confederation until 1789. Then the closer bond of federation took its place. That split in terms grew firm in the war years that came later.
britannica-1911-confession:
Confession means, in general, the open admission of a deed that might else stay hid. It bears most weight on the admission of guilt or wrong. The term holds a set place in two fields, religion and law. Among the Jews the high priest confessed the sins of the whole people on the Day of Atonement. That day is still kept with fasting and confession.

Jews were also bound to confess their own sins to God in private. In some cases they confessed to man as well. The Gospels say little of confession by name. They say much of forgiveness, though. The church holds power to give God's pardon, by texts from John and Matthew. The entry warns that binding and loosing first meant the laying down of rules. It did not first mean the pardon of breaches. The long entry then traces church practice age by age.
britannica-1911-confirmation:
Confirmation, in the Christian sense, is the rite of laying on of hands that rounds out baptism. It links most of all with the gift of the Holy Ghost to the person. The words confirm and confirmation do not show in the Bible in this set sense. That sense grew up since the 400s, in the Western churches and their offshoots. The rite itself runs from the church's first days.

Its history falls into three stages. In the first ages most new members came as grown converts. Confirmation then followed close on baptism, and the two often formed one service. Yet ranks parted the two acts in one way. Only the highest order of ministers could confirm. Priests, deacons and in dire need lay folk could baptize. A gap could thus stand between the two. Set ages for the rite close the tale.
britannica-1911-confiscation:
Confiscation, in Roman law, was the seizure of private goods for the fiscus, the imperial treasury. The word comes from a Latin verb for that act. From Rome the sense spread to all state seizure of private goods under legal form. In English law the term covers two kin acts. Forfeiture takes goods, and escheat takes lands. Crime or lack of heirs can ground the act.

Goods can also be seized for breach of set laws. Customs, excise and explosives laws all carry that threat. The entry then turns to the United States in war time. Acts of 1861 and 1862 seized goods used for revolt. The act of 1862 went wider and took the goods of rebels at large. Common speech gives the word a looser sense as well. It names any taking of goods under legal forms, or any seizure with poor pay in return.
britannica-1911-congleton:
Congleton is a market town and borough in Cheshire, England, set in a deep valley on the banks of the Dane. Hills rise past 1,000 feet to east and south, Cloud Hill and Mow Cop among them. Its people numbered 10,707 in 1901. The town holds few buildings of note for age or beauty. A few old timbered houses stand as the chief exceptions.

A grammar school stood there as early as 1553. Leather laces called Congleton points won high fame in the 1500s and 1600s. Silk making now heads the town's trades. A London man brought that craft in 1752. Coal and salt are raised nearby, and fustian works, foundries and corn mills add breadth. Biddulph, three miles south, holds more coal mines and iron works. Its Grange gardens draw praise in the entry.
britannica-1911-congleton-henry-brooke-p:
Henry Brooke Parnell, first Baron Congleton (1776–1842), was the second son of Sir John Parnell, chancellor of the Irish exchequer. He was schooled at Eton and Cambridge. In 1801 he came into the family estates in Queen's county. He wed a daughter of the earl of Portarlington. In 1802 he entered parliament for Portarlington, but soon gave up the seat.

From 1806 he sat for Queen's county until 1832. In 1833 Dundee chose him, and twice chose him again. In 1841 he rose to the peerage as Baron Congleton. Ill health and low spirits had worn him for some time. In 1842 he took his own life. He was a Liberal Whig and a keen party man. His motion on the civil list beat the duke of Wellington in 1830. A work on financial reform bears that same year.
britannica-1911-congregation:
Congregation names, at its core, a gathering of persons together. The word runs from Latin roots for with and for a flock. Its chief use points to worship.
