It may name the body met for worship at one time. It may also name the body that habitually attends one church. From that use grows the system called Congregationalism.

The word holds more fields than the church hall. In the English Bible it renders two Hebrew words for the whole people of Israel. The Revised Version parts those two with care. One keeps the name congregation and the other takes assembly. In the Roman Church the word names boards of cardinals. Those boards run the great departments of church rule. Orders of monks form congregations as well. The Trappists count as one such body within the Cistercians.
britannica-1911-conic-section:
Conic Section is a mathematics article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the curves formed when a plane cuts a cone. In ancient geometry the name covered three forms only: the ellipse, the parabola, and the hyperbola. Modern geometry adds the circle and a pair of lines under the same title, since all arise from cutting one cone.

One key test uses a fixed point, the focus, and a fixed line, the directrix. A conic is the path of a point whose distances from focus and line keep a fixed ratio, called the eccentricity. A ratio above one gives a hyperbola, a ratio of one a parabola, and a ratio below one an ellipse. The circle is the case of zero ratio. The article also views a conic as the projection of a circle and treats confocal conics, which share the same foci.
britannica-1911-conscription:
Conscription is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on forced service in the armed forces. The word comes from Latin roots for writing names together. The entry says the term first came into use in a French law of 1798. That law made men from age twenty to twenty-five liable to serve if called.

The text treats the French law as a turning point in modern history. It says the law let Napoleon raise the huge armies his wars of conquest needed. It also traces the older idea that each able man owed defence to the state. Readers get the social and money side of the draft, not just its army side.
britannica-1911-constellation:
A constellation is a named grouping of stars in the sky. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica takes the word from the Latin for studded with stars. The carving of the sky into such areas runs back to remote ages. Their figures and names are traced to the Euphrates valley. Sumerians, Accadians, and Babylonians are named as the source. Phoenicians carried the scheme west into Greece. Hittites bore it into Asia Minor.

Greek culture then spread it to Arabia, Persia, and India. Star groups and lone stars took names from weather and from myth. It was once thought those names and tales were Greek in birth. Cuneiform records have disproved that view. Greek star myths match older Euphratean tales point by point. The entry thus treats the study of star groups as a task for diggers and myth scholars.
britannica-1911-consumption:
Consumption, in its root sense, means the act of consuming or destroying, says a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. In common speech the word is applied to a wasting disease of the lungs. In economics the word holds a special technical sense. It has been defined as the destruction of utilities, set against production as their creation.

A utility here is anything that meets a desire or serves a purpose. Consumption may be productive or unproductive, the entry says. It is productive where it serves, direct or by a roundabout path, to meet an economic want. It is unproductive when it is spent on pleasures or luxuries. Its place in economics, and its close tie to production, are treated in every textbook. Two German works are named for special study.
britannica-1911-convention:
Convention is a word with several linked senses, and this 1911 Britannica entry traces them from the Latin for coming together. It can mean a meeting or gathering of people. It can mean a bargain struck between parties. It can also mean a shared habit on which a custom, a rule of conduct, or a rule of art rests, and from there a dead, stiff use of such rules.

The entry gives the political sense most weight. A convention is a gathering of the delegates of a nation, state, or party, set against the formal sittings of a lawmaking body. In English history the name fits parliaments that met without a royal summons while the crown was in doubt. The convention of 1660 restored Charles the Second. That of 1689 declared the throne empty of James the Second and settled the realm.
britannica-1911-convocation:
Convocation, from a Latin word for a calling together, is defined in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article as an assembly met in answer to a summons. The term is used in a narrower sense for assemblies of clergy or of university graduates. In the American Episcopal Church, a convocation is a voluntary meeting of clergy for discussion, with no power to make laws.

In England the name belongs to the assembly of the clergy of the realm. The archbishops of Canterbury and York summon it in their provinces by royal writ. It meets when Parliament meets and ends when Parliament ends. It has two houses, an upper and a lower. Bishops sit in the upper house. Deans, archdeacons, and elected proctors sit in the lower house, under a presiding officer called a prolocutor. The article then turns to the origin of this body.
britannica-1911-cooper-sir-astley-paston:
Sir Astley Paston Cooper (1768–1841) was an English surgeon born at Brooke in Norfolk on 23 August 1768. His father was a clergyman and his mother wrote novels. At sixteen he went to London to study under Henry Cline at Saint Thomas's hospital. Anatomy took his zeal from the first. He also heard the lectures of John Hunter.

In 1789 he became demonstrator of anatomy at Saint Thomas's. In 1791 he lectured there with Cline in anatomy and surgery. In 1800 he became surgeon to Guy's hospital on his uncle's death. The Copley medal came in 1802 for two papers on the ear drum. Fellowship of the Royal Society followed in 1805. That year he helped found the Medico-Chirurgical Society. His first paper there told of an attempt to tie a great artery. A statue by Baily stands in Saint Paul's.
britannica-1911-cooper-union:
Cooper Union is a school and charity in New York city, set up for the advancement of science and art. It stands in a brownstone building in Astor Place, north of the Bowery. Peter Cooper founded it in 1857 to 1859, and it gained its charter in 1859. His trust deed letter sets out his aims in his own words.

He wished the fund to serve science and art in their use for life, for ever. He called for a reading room and a school of art for women. He called for an office where employers could find young workers of known character. Pupils were to hold monthly meetings in due form. To run a meeting well, he held, forms part of a citizen's schooling. Talks and debates were to shun church and party strife. No religious test was to bar any pupil. The entry reports eager pupils and fine teaching.
britannica-1911-cordon:
Cordon is a French word from corde, a cord, used in a wide range of senses. The 1911 Britannica article gives pride of place to the sash of an order of knighthood. That sash runs from one shoulder to the hip on the far side. The sky-blue sash of the French order of the Holy Spirit was the mark of the highest prize a man could win. The blue ribbon of the English Garter serves the same use.

In heraldry, cordons are the cords hung with the hats of church chiefs above their shields. Rows of tassels end them, five rows for a cardinal and fewer for lesser ranks. In building, a cordon is a band of stone that juts from a wall face. In loose speech the word names any line of posts set to guard a space. A cordon of troops or of health guards are stock cases.
britannica-1911-cornelius-peter-von:
Peter von Cornelius is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of a German painter. He lived from 1784 to 1867. He was born in Dusseldorf in the year 1784. His father was inspector of the Dusseldorf gallery. That father died in the year 1799. The young Cornelius was stimulated to extraordinary exertions by that loss. He and an elder brother had to watch over a numerous family.

At that time some tried to persuade his mother to apprentice him. They urged the trade of a goldsmith over painting. Painting took long to qualify for, they argued. There were already so many painters in the field. His mother rejected all this advice outright. He felt himself impelled onward by an uncontrollable enthusiasm. His mother's confidence gave new strength to that drive. Continual work fed his zeal in those hard years. The entry opens with a widow's faith in her son's gift.
britannica-1911-coronation:
A coronation is the rite by which sovereigns are set in office. The Latin root of the word means a crown. In Europe before the Christian age, a king was raised on a shield at his choice. Chief men bore him on their shoulders round the crowd. That rite, the gyratio, was as a rule done three times. At its end a spear was placed in the king's hand.

A rich band of silk or linen, the diadem, was then bound round the king's brow as a mark of royal power. When Europe turned Christian, a rite of blessing was added to the old form, but the old form was not dropped. The Franks took the gyratio from the Teutons. Clovis, Sigebert, and Pippin were all raised to kingship in that way. From that blend the coronation rites of later ages grew.
britannica-1911-corporation:
Corporation is a law article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about how English law treats a group of persons as if it were itself a person. A corporation holds rights and duties of its own, apart from those of its members. It may own land its members have no claim to, and owe debts its members need not pay. Those rights pass to each new set of members, and this lasting succession marks the corporation off from other groups.

The idea was taken full grown from Roman law, where the matching term was collegium. A Roman collegium needed at least three persons, held goods in common, kept a shared chest, and could sue or be sued through an agent. It lived on though all its first members changed, and ruled itself by its own by-laws. Roman classes ranged from towns and priest bands to state clerks and trade groups.
britannica-1911-corydon:
Corydon is a town article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Corydon is a town in Indiana, the county seat of Harrison county. It stands on Indian Creek, west of Louisville, Kentucky. Its population was 1703 in the census of 1910.

Sulphur springs made the town a summer and health resort. Wyandotte Cave lay a few miles to the west. Farming filled the country around, and good quarries stood nearby. The town made wagons and cut building and lithographic stone. The entry gives most weight to Corydon's early honour. Settled about 1805, it became capital of Indiana Territory in 1813. It stayed the state capital until 1824, well after statehood. The meeting that framed Indiana's first constitution sat there in 1816. The plain old state house still stood when the article was written.
britannica-1911-coshocton:
Coshocton is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on a city in Ohio. It is the county seat of Coshocton county. Three rivers meet there, about seventy miles east of Columbus. The count grew from 3,672 in 1890 to 9,603 in 1910.

The city is built on four broad steps of land above the river. The top step stands 824 feet above the sea and gives fine views. Trade serves a wide farm district round the town. Mills make paper, glass, flour, china ware, and iron pipes there. The town stands on the site of an old Delaware village. White settlers first came in 1801, and the town took its name in 1811.
britannica-1911-covenant-religion:
Covenant, in the religious sense, is a mutual agreement of two or more parties. It can also be a pledge made by one party alone. The word comes through Old French from a Latin verb for agreeing. In the Bible the Hebrew word berith covers many kinds of deal. It can name a contract between two persons. It can name a treaty between two nations as well.

The covenant of Abimelech and Isaac gives that second case. Rites that mark such deals treat God as a party to them. One traces it to a root meaning to cut. That points to the old rite of cutting victims in parts. The parties to a deal then passed between the pieces. Genesis tells of such a sign in the covenant with Abraham. Later thought built a whole Covenant Theology on that base.
britannica-1911-cox-jacob-dolson:
Jacob Dolson Cox (1828–1900) was an American general, political leader and educationalist born in Montreal, Canada, on 27 October 1828. His father was a shipbuilder of German descent and his mother came of New York stock. The boy grew up in New York city. He read law in an office and worked in a broker's office in his teens. Church influence turned him toward the ministry for a time.

He graduated at Oberlin College in 1851, having dropped his theology in revolt at Finney's dogmatism. He ran schools at Warren in Ohio, then joined the Ohio bar in 1853 as an anti-slavery Whig. In 1859 he won a seat in the state senate. With Garfield and Monroe he formed a Radical Triumvirate there. In 1860 he became a brigadier of militia and threw himself into the study of war. In 1861 he helped raise Union troops and took a general's commission himself.
britannica-1911-cox-kenyon:
Kenyon Cox (born 1856) was an American painter born at Warren, Ohio, on 27 October 1856. He was the son of General Jacob Dolson Cox. From 1877 to 1882 he learned in Paris under Carolus-Duran and Gérôme. He then opened a studio in New York. Teaching at the Art Students' League brought him much success in time. His early work took the nude as its main theme.

That early work showed great academic correctness in rather set colour. He turned to mural decoration in its place, and rose to note in that field. A frieze for the Appellate Court in New York stands among his best known works. Wall work for Bowdoin College and for the Capitol at Saint Paul stand beside it. He wrote with authority on art as well. Old Masters and New appeared in 1905 and Painters and Sculptors in 1907. He became a National Academician in 1903.
britannica-1911-cox-samuel-hanson:
Samuel Hanson Cox (1793–1880) was an American Presbyterian divine born at Rahway, New Jersey, on 25 August 1793, of Quaker stock. He pastored a church at Mendham from 1817 to 1821. Two churches in New York then held him until 1834. He helped to found the University of the City of New York in those years. From 1834 to 1837 he taught pastoral theology at Auburn.

Seventeen years of active ministry at Brooklyn came next. A throat ailment forced him to Owego in 1854. He died at Bronxville, New York, on 2 October 1880. Fine oratory made his public name. A speech in Exeter Hall in 1833 laid the blame for American slavery on the British government. That speech made a great impression on its hearers. His son Arthur Cleveland Coxe changed the spelling of the family name. The son rose as a churchman in his turn, at Hartford and past it.
britannica-1911-cranston:
Cranston, a city in Providence county, Rhode Island, is described in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. It adjoins the city of Providence on the south. Its count rose fast, from eight thousand in eighteen ninety to over twenty one thousand in nineteen ten. Its area is thirty square miles.

The east part is level, while the west rolls a bit. Several villages lie within the city bounds. Farm folk in the country parts grow hay, corn, rye, oats, and garden produce. Village works make cotton and print goods, plus parts for electric machines. The state holds a large farm in the south of the city. On it stand the state prison, jail, workhouse, almshouse, and a hospital, all with one postal address.
britannica-1911-cranworth-robert-monsey-:
Robert Monsey Rolfe, Baron Cranworth (1790–1868), was lord chancellor of England. He was born at Cranworth in Norfolk on 18 December 1790, the elder son of a clergyman. He was schooled at Bury St Edmunds, Winchester, and Trinity College, Cambridge. He was called to the bar in 1816 and tied his work to the chancery courts. He sat in parliament for Penryn and Falmouth from 1832 till he rose to the bench in 1839.

In 1850 Cranworth was made a vice-chancellor and a baron. In 1852 he became lord chancellor in the ministry of Aberdeen. He held the post under Palmerston till that leader left office in 1857. He was not named again when Palmerston came back in 1859. On the fall of Lord Westbury in 1865, though, he took the great seal a second time.
britannica-1911-crayon:
A crayon is a coloured drawing material, used most often as a pencil and sometimes as a powder. It is made from earthy or stony matter, or from a base of pipe clay or china clay mixed with pigments. Prussian blue, orpiment, vermilion, and umber are among the colours named. Shades follow the amount of colour mixed into the base.

Artists use crayons to group colours and to gain landscape effects with ease and speed. Colour is softened and blended with a finger or a stump of leather or paper, and shading comes from cross-hatching and stippling. The entry traces crayon painting, or pastel, to Germany in the 1600s. It names Johann Alexander Thiele and Rosalba Carriera among early masters, and notes a later revival of the art.
britannica-1911-crediton:
Crediton is a market town in Devonshire, England, set in the narrow vale of the river Creedy near its meeting with the Exe. It lies eight miles north-west of Exeter and divides into an east or old town and a west or new town. Its population in 1901 was 3,974. The church of Holy Cross is a large Perpendicular building with a fine central tower. A grammar school founded under Edward VI holds exhibitions to Oxford and Cambridge.

Tradition makes Crediton the birthplace of Boniface in 680, and in 909 it became the seat of the first bishopric in Devon. In 1049 Bishop Leofric had the see moved to Exeter, citing pirate raids on the open town. Wool and serge trades once dominated, and a fair granted in 1231 is still held. Shoemaking, tanning, cider, and confectionery lead its later trades. In 1897 Crediton became the seat of a suffragan bishopric in the Exeter diocese.
britannica-1911-cremation:
Cremation, from a Latin word for to burn, is the burning of human corpses and is treated in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry calls it the common practice of the old world. Three great lands stand out as cases apart. Egypt embalmed its dead, Judaea buried them in tombs, and China buried them in the earth.

In Greece only set groups were denied burning, such as those who took their own lives. Rome barred both burial and burning of the dead inside the city by its Twelve Tables. From the late republic to the end of the fourth Christian century, burning on the pyre was the rule there. The entry weighs whether health or belief drove each choice, and finds the answer hard to fix.
britannica-1911-creston:
Creston is a city article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a town in Iowa in the United States. The town is the county seat of Union county. It stands about sixty miles south west of Des Moines, where a main rail line crosses two branch lines.

The article gives a run of town counts across four counts. The figure stood at 7,200 in 1890 and 7,752 in 1900. A state count in 1905 gave 8,382, but the 1910 count fell to 6,924. The town sits on the crest of the divide between two great river basins. That high seat, about 1,310 feet up, gave the place its name. Farm trade and stock shipping fill out the account.
britannica-1911-crew-nathaniel-crew-3rd-:
Nathaniel Crew, third Baron Crew, lived from 1633 to 1721 and was bishop of Durham. The 1911 Britannica life traces his line to a Speaker of the Commons. His grandfather Sir Thomas Crew held that post in his day. His father John was made Baron Crew of Stene in 1661. Nathaniel was born in January 1633 and schooled at Lincoln College, Oxford.

In 1668 he became rector of that same college at Oxford. The next year he was made dean of Chichester in the church. Soon after he served as clerk of the closet to Charles the Second. In 1671 he rose to bishop of Oxford, and in 1674 to Durham. His fast rise owed much to the favour of the duke of York.
britannica-1911-crimson:
Crimson is a strong, bright red colour tinged more or less with purple. It takes its name from a dye made from the dried bodies of the cochineal insect, Coccus cacti. Older spellings include cremesin, crymysyn, and cramoysin, the last also a name for red cloth. The word comes through medieval Latin cremesinus from the kermes insect, Coccus ilicis. Its Arabic form, quirmiz, links back to a Sanskrit word for worm.

From the shortened Latin carminus comes carmine, the related colour word the entry cross-refers. The whole entry turns on word history rather than on dyeing practice. It traces one colour name through cloth, insect dyes, and three old languages. That chain shows how a trade good carried its name across regions. Readers get the shade defined first, then the path its name travelled to reach English.
britannica-1911-croker-john-wilson:
John Wilson Croker (1780–1857) was a British statesman and author born at Galway on 20 December 1780. He graduated at Trinity College, Dublin, in 1800 and was called to the Irish bar in 1802. Verse satires on the Dublin stage and on Dublin society made his name in 1804 and 1805. A pamphlet on Ireland in 1807 backed Catholic emancipation. In 1808 he entered parliament as member for Downpatrick.

Croker's speech of 14 March 1809, defending the duke of York, won him the secretaryship of the Admiralty. He held that office for more than twenty years under changing governments. The entry praises his service and his reforms of the office, including the exposure of an official who had misappropriated 200,000 pounds of public funds. His friendship with Wellington lasted until the duke's death. His papers were published in 1884 as The Croker Papers, in three volumes.
britannica-1911-croker-thomas-crofton:
Thomas Crofton Croker (1798–1854), an Irish antiquary and humorist, was born in Cork on 15 January 1798. Apprenticed to a merchant, he became a clerk in the Admiralty in 1819 through John Wilson Croker, who was no relation. Thomas Moore owed him many curious fragments of old poetry used in the Irish Melodies. In 1827 he joined the Irish Academy.

Croker's most popular book was Fairy Legends and Traditions of the South of Ireland, published in 1825. Legends of the Lakes followed in 1829, and he later edited the Popular Songs of Ireland. He helped found the Camden and Percy Societies and, in 1843, the British Archaeological Association. For those societies he wrote on the Irish contests of 1641 and 1688 and on historical songs. He died in London on 8 August 1854.
britannica-1911-crompton:
Crompton is an urban district of Lancashire, England, within the parliamentary borough of Oldham and about two and a half miles north of that town. Its population in 1901 was 13,427. Shaw, a populous village inside the district, has a station on the Lancashire and Yorkshire railway. Cotton mills fill the district. The collieries of the neighbourhood share the work of employing its people.

Those two lines of fact, place and industry, make up the whole entry. It names no church, school, or public building. It gives no history of the district and no account of its government. The picture is of a dense mill population tied to cotton spinning and coal. A reader learns where Crompton sits, how many people lived there in 1901, and what work sustained them. Nothing in the entry reaches beyond those plain points.
britannica-1911-crookston:
Crookston is a city in Minnesota and the county-seat of Polk county, set on the Red Lake river in the Red River valley. It lies about 300 miles north-west of Minneapolis and 25 miles east of Grand Forks. Its population rose from 3,457 in 1890 to 7,559 in 1910, with many settlers from Norway, Canada, and Sweden. Two railways serve it, the Great Northern and the Northern Pacific. Dams on the river give it water-power.

The city holds a Carnegie library, two hospitals, a federal land office, and a state agricultural high school with an experimental farm. Its manufactures include lumber, leather, flour, farm implements, wagons, and bricks. Rich farmland around it makes Crookston a market for grain, potatoes, and lumber. Settled about 1872 and incorporated in 1879, the city took a fresh charter in 1906. It was named for William Crooks, an early settler.
britannica-1911-cross-and-crucifixion:
Cross and crucifixion are treated together in an entry that begins with the shape of the cross itself. A cross, in the usual sense, is a figure of two or more lines that meet or cross each other. The entry notes, after Lipsius and other writers, that a single upright stake could also bear the name. Such a stake was called a crux simplex, though the common idea of a cross is the compound figure.

Punishment by crucifixion, the entry goes on, was widely used in ancient times. It names Assyria, Egypt, and Persia among the peoples who used it, and adds the Greeks and the Carthaginians. The hosted text breaks off at that point, in the middle of its list of nations. Nothing of its later treatment of the rite survives in the hosted copy. The description above covers only what the hosted copy preserves.
britannica-1911-croydon:
Croydon is a borough of Surrey, England, ten miles south of London Bridge, in the suburbs of London. The 1911 Britannica article gives its count as 133,895 in 1901, up from 102,695 ten years before. Rail lines link it with all parts of the great city. The town stands near the source of the river Wandle, below Banstead Downs. Its old site is named in Domesday Book.

One odd feature is the Bourne, a spring that bursts out at gaps of one to ten years. It runs as a torrent for two or three months and then dries up. The flow comes from rain that sinks into the chalk hills. The manor went from William the Conqueror to Archbishop Lanfranc. His palace at Croydon housed later archbishops, and its chapel and hall still stand.
britannica-1911-crystallization:
Crystallization is the art of gaining a substance in the form of crystals. It matters in chemistry because it purifies a substance or parts the parts of a mixture. Most substances dissolve more freely in a hot solvent than in a cold one. So a boiling strong solution, left to cool, sheds its load as crystals. The slower the cooling, the larger and more perfect the crystals grow.

A stubborn solution can be started by seeding it with a minute crystal of the same substance. Shaking, or a drop of a second solvent, may also bring the change. Fractional crystallization repeats the process to part substances of unlike solubility. The study of the rare earths offers the entry's chief case of that method. For other conditions of crystal growth the entry sends readers to the article on crystallography. The whole note stays practical, a set of bench rules.
britannica-1911-csengery-anton:
Anton Csengery (1822–1880) was a Hungarian publicist and historical writer born at Nagyvárad on 2 June 1822. He took an early, active part in the movements that led to the Hungarian Revolution of 1848. With Baron Sigismund Kemény he is counted a founder of high-class Magyar journalism. After 1867 Francis Deák, the leading Hungarian statesman of the age, drew him into personal service. Many great state papers inspired by Deák were drafted by Csengery's hand.

Through those drafts his influence lives on in statutes that fix the relations of Austria and Hungary. As a historical writer he excelled in essays on the leading political figures of his time. Paul Nagy and Bertalan Szemere stand among his subjects. He also began a translation of Macaulay's History of England. The entry presents a journalist whose pen shaped both opinion and law. He died at Budapest on 13 July 1880.
britannica-1911-culmination:
Culmination, from the Latin culmen, a summit, means the reaching of the highest point. In astronomy it names the passage of a heavenly body over the meridian of a place. Two culminations take place in the course of the day. One passes above the pole, and the other below it. The first is called the upper culmination, and the second the lower.

Either passage, or both, may fall below the horizon and so pass unseen. That caution is the entry's last point. The whole note is a tight definition in two short parts, word first and sky second. It gives no method of observing a culmination and no worked case. A reader takes away the two names, upper and lower, and the fact that a culmination need not be visible to occur.
britannica-1911-curzon-of-kedleston-geor:
George Nathaniel Curzon, first Baron Curzon of Kedleston, born in eighteen fifty nine, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the eldest son of the fourth Baron Scarsdale. He was schooled at Eton and at Balliol College, Oxford.

At Oxford he led the Union and became a fellow of All Souls in eighteen eighty three. He entered Parliament in eighteen eighty six for a Lancashire seat. Posts on India and on foreign affairs soon followed. He had travelled widely in Asia and wrote books on its lands and its statecraft. In eighteen ninety nine he was made head of the government of India. There he set a strong foreign line and took up reform in each branch.
britannica-1911-cuvier-georges-leopold-c:
Georges Cuvier, baron and French naturalist born on 23 August 1769 at Montbéliard, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of a retired officer on half pay. His family was Protestant and had fled the Jura under pressure for its faith. He showed a bent for the study of nature from an early age.

Studious habits and a wondrous memory marked the boy at school. After four years at the Academy of Stuttgart, he took a post as tutor in a count family. Summers near Fécamp brought him into the circle of a famed farmer scholar there. That man wrote to friends in Paris in strong praise of his young charge. In 1795 Cuvier gained a post at the museum in Paris as assistant in the study of how animal bodies compare.
britannica-1911-dalmellington:
Dalmellington is a village in Ayrshire, Scotland, noted in a brief entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands fifteen miles south east of Ayr, at the end of a branch line of the Glasgow and South Western railway. The count in 1901 gave it 1,448 people.

The district around the village is rich in coal, ironstone, sandstone, and limestone. The place is of great age, and a Roman road runs near it. Few old remains of note survive there. The entry adds that the village was a centre of action in the Covenanting times, when Scots Presbyterians held to their covenants under pressure.
britannica-1911-dalton:
Dalton is a city in the state of Georgia, in the north west of the state. It is the seat of its county. The 1911 Britannica entry gives its span from Atlanta. It gives its counts at three census dates, which show steady growth. Three rail lines serve the city.

The entry sets Dalton in rich farm land. It ships cotton, grain, fruit, and ore. It makes goods that range from canned fruit and flour to iron castings and shop wares. A college for women sits in the city. The close turns to the Civil War. A beaten general fell back there after a loss. A new chief then took post in the town with a large host, set to face an invading army from the north.
britannica-1911-damon:
Damon of Syracuse was a Pythagorean famed for his selfless love of Phintias, a member of the same sect. The friend's name is Phintias, the entry stresses, not Pythias as commonly given. Phintias was condemned to death by Dionysius of Syracuse. He begged a short liberty to set his affairs in order before the sentence fell. Damon pledged his own life for his friend's return.

Phintias came back faithfully before the set day of execution. The tyrant, to show his wonder at such loyalty, freed both men. He also begged to be taken into their friendship. Diodorus and Cicero carry the tale in the sources cited. Hyginus tells a like story with the friends named Moerus and Selinuntius, and Schiller used that form in his ballad. Two friends, a pledge, and a tyrant softened make the whole entry.
britannica-1911-damophon:
Damophon was a Greek sculptor of Messene who made statues for Messene, Megalopolis, Aegium, and other cities of the Peloponnese. Large fragments of his work survive at Lycosura in Arcadia. They include three giant heads from a group of Demeter, Persephone, Artemis, and the giant Anytus. The group stood in the temple of the goddess called the Mistress. Parts of the finds rest in the museum at Athens, and parts stay on the spot.

Those fragments have set off a great quarrel over the sculptor's date. Scholars have placed Damophon anywhere from the 300s before Christ to the 100s after it. Frazer, in his Pausanias, argues wisely for an early date, the entry says. Cities able to found such temples were rare after Alexander's time. That argument from the cities' means, not from style alone, carries the entry's own judgment. The heads at Athens anchor the debate in stone.
britannica-1911-dancourt-florent-carton:
Florent Carton Dancourt (1661–1725) was a French dramatist and actor born at Fontainebleau on 1 November 1661. A Jesuit teacher tried to draw him into the order, but he chose law instead. Marriage to an actor's daughter turned him to the stage against his family's strong wishes. He appeared at the Théâtre Français in 1685 and won instant success. Louis XIV favoured him, and his Alceste in Molière's Misanthrope was a famous part.

Dancourt wrote some sixty plays, the first in the same year as his stage debut. Le Chevalier à la mode of 1687 is judged his best work, though his claim to its authorship has been disputed. His stock figure is the middle-class woman mad to be taken for an aristocrat. Palissot called him the Teniers of comedy for his sharp drawing of low life and peasants. His dialogue is sparkling and natural. He died on 7 December 1725.
britannica-1911-dandelion:
The dandelion, Taraxacum officinale, is a perennial herb of the order Compositae with a range across Europe, central Asia, North America, and the Arctic. Its name comes from the French dent-de-lion, lion's tooth, for the toothed lobes of its leaves. The leaves form a flat rosette on a very short stem. A long tap-root, black outside, makes the plant hard to root out. Hollow, leafless stalks carry the golden flower-heads from April to August.

Each fruit bears a beak topped with a plume of white hairs, so the wind scatters it far. The ripe heads form globes near two inches across. A milky juice runs through the whole plant, holding taraxacin and other bodies. Root extracts were long used in medicine for the liver. Varieties are told apart by the cut of the leaf and the set of the outer bracts.
britannica-1911-darcy-thomas-darcy-baron:
The text hosted here opens partway through the life, with Darcy surrendering a stronghold he might have held longer and standing with the insurgents at Doncaster as one of their leaders. Pardoned when the rising broke up, he pleaded illness rather than travel to London at the king's request. When a fresh rising under Sir Francis Bigod began early in 1537, the king believed him guilty of new treasons, and he was seized and hurried to London.

In prison Darcy aimed a famous warning at Thomas Cromwell, trusting that one head would remain to strike off Cromwell's own. Tried by his peers, he was found guilty of treason and beheaded on the 20th of June 1537. His barony was revived in 1548 for his son George but died out with George's descendant John in 1635.
britannica-1911-darlington:
Darlington is a market town and borough of Durham, 232 miles north by west of London on the North-Eastern railway. Its people numbered 44,511 in 1901, and the fine old church of St Cuthbert, mainly transitional Norman with a fourteenth-century spire, anchors an otherwise modern town. Worsteds, coal, ironstone, iron and steel, locomotives and shells lead its long list of industries. The town was incorporated in 1867 and covers 3956 acres.

The monks of Lindisfarne received the vill soon after settling at Durham in 995, and by 1083 Bishop William made its church collegiate. The Boldon Book of 1183 gives the first mention of Darlington as a borough. Its markets, long held by the bishops of Durham, passed to the local authority in 1854.
britannica-1911-declaration:
Declaration, in law, was the first step in an English pleading. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica explains the old form and its heirs. The word comes from a Latin term meaning to make fully clear. The suing side stated its whole matter in set counts.

Each count alleged one cause of action in broad terms. The same acts could appear in counts framed in different ways. A new system under an act of 1875 replaced the form. A statement of claim took its place in most courts. Old use clung on in a few London and local courts. American courts kept it too, under the name complaint. That paper opens a suit with court, place, parties, and claim. The word also serves in trusts, bankruptcy, and sworn statements.
britannica-1911-declination:
Declination, in the study of magnetism, is the angle between true north and the north a compass needle shows. The 1911 Britannica entry draws the term from a Latin verb that means to bend down or turn aside. It is, in short, the gap between the true line to the pole and the line the needle takes.

The entry gives a run of past counts at London across three hundred years. The needle swung from east of true north, through true north, far to the west, and then crept back by slow steps. It will in time hit true north once more, the entry says, then drift east as the north pole of the magnet wanders round the true pole. Small shifts each day, and wild jumps in storms, are also noted.
britannica-1911-defamation: Defamation is a very short law article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes from the Latin diffamare, to spread abroad an evil report. Defamation is the saying or writing of something about another person that is meant to injure his reputation, or to expose him to public hatred, contempt and ridicule. The article gives no more than the definition and the origin of the word, and sends readers to the articles on libel and slander for the law itself.
britannica-1911-dragoon:
A dragoon, from the French dragon, was originally a mounted soldier trained to fight on foot only. This mounted infantryman of the late sixteenth and seventeenth centuries took his name from his weapon, a short musket called the dragon. Dragoons were formed in companies like the foot, not squadrons, and their officers bore infantry titles. Always at a disadvantage against true cavalry, they steadily improved their riding and arms to the cavalry standard.

So dragoon came to mean medium cavalry, and kept that sense from Frederick the Great's wars onward. The words dragoon and dragonnade recall the older arm's police and guerrilla work, above all Louis XIV's Dragonnades against Protestants after the edict of Nantes was revoked. In British service the dragoons are heavy cavalry and the seven Dragoon Guards regiments medium.
britannica-1911-east-london:
East London is a town in Cape province, South Africa, at the Buffalo river mouth. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica places it on both banks of that river. Cliffs on the east side hold its rail end and business quarter. Sea bathing and river views make it a chief holiday resort there.

Trade for a rich farm hinterland passes through its port in bulk. Wool and mohair lead its exports, with cloth and food leading imports. Harbor works costing over two million pounds guard ships from all winds. The town began as a war port in 1847, first called Port Rex. German settlers who came in 1857 left many descendants there.
britannica-1911-electrum-electron: Electrum is the subject of a short metal article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Electrum is an alloy of gold and silver used among the ancients. Pliny describes it as holding one part of silver to four parts of gold. The word is the Greek word for amber. In the study of minerals the same term names native gold that holds silver. Such native metal holds from twenty to fifty percent silver. In both uses the name comes from the pale yellow colour, which resembles amber.
britannica-1911-ellenborough-edward-law-:
Ellenborough, Edward Law, 1st Baron (1750–1818), was an English judge born at Great Salkeld in Cumberland on 16 November 1750. His father, Edmund Law, was then rector there and later became bishop of Carlisle. Educated at the Charterhouse and at Peterhouse, Cambridge, he passed as third wrangler and won a fellowship at Trinity. Against his father's wish that he take orders, he chose the law.

Called to the bar in 1780, Law soon built a rich practice on the northern circuit. In 1787 he was made principal counsel for Warren Hastings in the impeachment trial before the House of Lords. A Whig who moved over to Pitt, he became attorney-general in 1801 and entered the Commons. In 1802 he succeeded Lord Kenyon as chief justice of the king's bench and took a peerage. His cabinet seat in 1806, held while he stayed chief justice, drew strong criticism. He resigned in November 1818 and died the next month.
britannica-1911-emanation:
Emanation, from the Latin emanatio, to flow out, is in philosophy and theology one of the three chief theories of how God relates to the world. Its central idea is that the world of separate things consists of forced “outpourings” of the final divine essence. That essence is all-inclusive and fully perfect. Things poured out from it grow worse as their distance from it grows.

The entry sets emanation against two rivals. Against the Jewish and Christian view, it denies a single free act of creation by a personal God. It also explains evil without charging it to God's own act. The whole process runs by fixed, almost mechanical laws. Against evolution, it runs the scale the other way. Evolution climbs from the loose lower to the firm higher, while emanation falls from the highest toward the endlessly lower.
britannica-1911-endymion:
Endymion, a figure of Greek myth, is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. He is named as a son of Aethlius and king of Elis. Selene, goddess of the moon, loved him, and by her he had fifty daughters. Those daughters are said to stand for the fifty moons of a festal cycle.

Other forms of the tale make him a fair youth, a shepherd or hunter, whom Selene visited each night. He lay asleep in a cave on Mount Latmus in Caria. Zeus let him choose any gift, one version says, and he chose a sleep that lasts forever, staying young for all time. Another version makes that sleep a punishment for daring to love Hera. The usual form, though, has Selene herself lay the sleep on him.
britannica-1911-epernon:
Épernon is a town of northern France, in the department of Eure-et-Loir, as this 1911 Britannica article describes it. It stands where the Drouette and the Guesle meet, seventeen miles north-east of Chartres by rail, and had 2,370 people in 1906. It first belonged to the counts of Montfort, who built a castle there in the 1000s, the ruins of which still stand.

In the 1200s the town became a lordship of its own, held for a time under the crown of Navarre. King Henry sold it to Jean Louis de Nogaret, for whom it was raised to a duchy in 1581. The new duke was a favourite of Henry III, loaded with high posts, and under Henry IV he made himself near independent in Provence. He helped give the regency to Marie de' Medici in 1610 and held great sway in the state, dying in 1642.
britannica-1911-epigonion:
Epigonion, from a Greek word for the instrument itself, was an ancient stringed instrument named in Athenaeus, probably a psaltery. It was brought into Greece, if not invented, by Epigonus, a Greek musician of Ambracia in Epirus. He was also the first, the entry says, to pluck the strings with his fingers instead of using the plectrum.

The instrument Epigonus named after himself had forty strings. So many strings, the entry reasons, must have been of differing lengths, since thickness and tension alone could hardly yield forty sounds. That points to a harp-like frame or to strings over harp-shaped bridges on a sound-board. Juba II of Mauretania said Epigonus brought the instrument from Alexandria. He played it with the fingers of both hands, sang to it, and brought in chromatic passages and a chorus of other stringed instruments.
britannica-1911-episcopius-simon:
Episcopius, Simon (1583–1643), the Latin form of Simon Bischop, was a Dutch theologian born at Amsterdam on 1 January 1583. He entered Leiden university in 1600 and studied theology under Jacobus Arminius, whose teaching he followed. In 1610, the year the Arminians presented their Remonstrance to the states of Holland, he became pastor at Bleyswick near Rotterdam. In 1612 he succeeded Gomarus as professor of theology at Leiden.

That appointment stirred the bitter enmity of the Calvinists and helped bring on the synod of Dort in 1618. Episcopius was chosen spokesman for the thirteen Remonstrant delegates, but he was refused a hearing, and the Remonstrant doctrines were condemned undefended. In 1619 he and the other twelve were stripped of their offices and driven from the country. He became preacher at the Remonstrant church in Rotterdam and then rector of the Remonstrant college in Amsterdam, where he died in 1643.
britannica-1911-erskine-thomas-erskine-1:
Thomas Erskine, later Baron Erskine, lived from 1750 to 1823. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica makes him a lord chancellor born in Edinburgh. He was the youngest son of the earl of Buchan. A poor purse kept his father from schooling him for a trade. At fourteen he went to sea as a midshipman. Slow rise then pushed him into the army.

There too he found promotion slow, and a wife as poor as himself. A chance visit to a court changed his course. Talk with Lord Mansfield fixed his resolve on the law. He entered Lincoln's Inn in 1775 and joined Trinity College, Cambridge. That step let him be called to the bar two years sooner. He studied under two strong lawyers of the day. His call came in July 1778, and his success was swift and bright.
britannica-1911-esar-haddon:
Esar Haddon, an Assyrian king and son of Sennacherib, is treated in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. His name in his own tongue means Assur has given a brother, the text notes. At the murder of his father in 681 BC he led the Assyrian army in war against Ararat. The men who held Nineveh for 42 days fled north and sought aid from that same foe.

At its close they hailed Esar Haddon as king, and he was crowned at Nineveh days later. The text calls him a good general and an able, mild ruler in his office. His first acts were to crush a revolt in the south of Babylonia and to rebuild Babylon. His father had destroyed that sacred city, so its walls and temple rose again, its gods came back, and Babylon became his second capital.
britannica-1911-eschenmayer-adam-karl-au:
Adam Karl August von Eschenmayer, a German thinker and physicist who lived from 1768 to 1852, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Neuenburg in Wurttemberg in July 1768. He was schooled at Stuttgart and then at Tubingen, where he took a degree in medicine. He worked as a doctor at Sulz and then at Kirchheim.

In 1811 he was made a professor of philosophy and medicine at Tubingen, and in 1818 full professor of practical philosophy. In 1836 he gave up his chair and went back to Kirchheim to give all his time to thought. His views stand close to those of Schelling, but he held that thought alone cannot reach the absolute. Faith, a kind of inner light, must round out what reason starts. That bent led him to a deep interest in animal magnetism and, in the end, to belief in spirits.
britannica-1911-eston:
Eston is a town article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a district in the North Riding of Yorkshire, England. It stands four miles south-east of Middlesbrough, on a branch rail line. The count of 1901 gave it 11,199 people. The article calls it one of the chief centres of a great iron field.

The ironstone beds of the Cleveland Hills are worked from Eston. The district holds large blast furnaces, iron foundries, and steam sawmills. Just west lies Ormesby, with near nine and a half thousand people, so the whole area is thickly settled. At Marton, west of Ormesby, Captain Cook was born in 1728. Old earthworks line the hills to the south. The entry is short, but it fixes Eston's place at the heart of the Cleveland iron trade.
britannica-1911-eton:
Eton is a Buckinghamshire town on the north bank of the Thames, opposite Windsor. Its urban district held 3,301 people in 1901. The town is famous for its college, the largest of the ancient English public schools. Henry VI founded the King's College of Our Lady of Eton in 1440–1441. He endowed it mainly from the revenues of the alien priories Henry V had suppressed. The plan followed William of Wykeham's Winchester and New College, Oxford.

The first foundation had a provost, priests, clerks, choristers and 25 poor scholars. In 1443 Henry raised the scholars to 70 and added commoners, the later oppidans. A link with King's College, Cambridge, dates from the same year. Edward IV cut its possessions, yet gifts and rising rents made it rich. Commissioners reshaped its government in 1870 and its foundation in 1872. Pupils now average over 1,000. The entry closes with the school's customs, including the Montem gathering on the Bath road.
britannica-1911-euphorion:
Euphorion was a Greek poet and grammarian born at a town in Euboea in the third century before Christ. He spent much of his life in Athens, where he grew rich. In time a great king of Syria called him to his court, where he helped build the royal store of books at Antioch.

He held the post of keeper of that store till his death, the 1911 Britannica entry says. He wrote epic tales of the myths, love verse in paired lines, short sharp poems, and a curse poem in the style of a famed peer. Prose works on old lore and past events are laid to his name as well. Like a peer of his school, he loved old and dead words, and his dense web of hints made his speech hard to read. Roman poets prized his love verse high.
britannica-1911-excommunication:
Excommunication is the judicial shutting-out of offenders from their religious community's rights and privileges. The article traces the practice in five stages: pagan likenesses, Hebrew custom, early Christian use, medieval and monastic usage, and modern survivals. Greek practice barred the blood-stained from holy water. Roman priests pronounced the exsecratio, a curse devoting enemies to destruction. Caesar reports that the Druids could exclude offenders from sacrifice.

In a theocracy the penalty is civil as well as religious. The Hebrew herem meant a thing set apart, whether for God or for destruction. Whole cities could fall under the ban, and Israelites as well as aliens. A milder form, niddah, was temporary separation for ceremonial uncleanness. By Ezra's time Jewish magistrates handled such discipline among their functions. The survey then follows the censure through church history to modern Free Church practice.
britannica-1911-excretion:
Excretion, in plant and animal physiology, names the separation of a substance from an organ. The word also covers the substance so separated. It comes from the Latin ex, out of, joined to cernere, to separate. The term usually points to waste or harmful products leaving the body. That use sets it apart from secretion. Secretion covers products that play a useful or needed part in the organism's work.

The entry is a bare definition, a few lines long, with no examples or history attached. It draws the one distinction the subject needs: out-thrown waste against retained, purposeful output. Nothing is said of glands, kidneys or particular organs. Readers wanting the machinery of either process must go to the physiology articles themselves. The brevity is the point here: a dictionary-style fixing of a term before it is used elsewhere in the volume.
britannica-1911-execution:
Execution, in law, is the process that makes court judgments and orders take effect. The article opens with Roman law. Rome's earliest mode seized the debtor himself as the creditor's slave. Imprisonment later replaced slavery. The actio judicati then let a creditor take payment or force security. Constantine abolished imprisonment for debt in A.D. 320, unless the debtor was stubborn. The time to pay a judgment debt grew from 30 days under the Twelve Tables to four months under Justinian.

Bankruptcy followed, by seizure of the estate or the debtor's own surrender. Under Antoninus Pius, debts were enforced by direct seizure and sale of property. Slaves, oxen and farm tools were privileged, and movables went before land. A money judgment is usually enforced by fieri facias, a writ ordering the sheriff to levy the sum from the debtor's goods.
britannica-1911-exhibition:
An exhibition is a public display, and the article traces the modern show from its beginnings. The first was held in London in 1756 by the Society of Arts. It offered prizes for better tapestry, carpets and porcelain, shown side by side. The same society showed agricultural machinery in 1761. France took up the idea at St Cloud in 1797. An official Paris show in the Champ de Mars followed in 1798, open to private exhibitors.

The Louvre show of 1801 set juries of practical men over the goods. Gold medallists dined with Napoleon, then First Consul. The 1802 show first printed an official catalogue, with 540 exhibitors including Montgolfier and Jacquard. Numbers climbed: 1,422 in 1806, 1,622 in 1819, 4,500 in 1849. Berlin drew 3,040 in 1844, and shows spread across Europe. The account runs on to Liège in 1905, Milan in 1906, Dublin in 1907 and the Franco-British show in London in 1908.
britannica-1911-exhumation:
Exhumation, from the medieval Latin exhumare, out of the ground, is the digging up and removing of an object from the ground. The word applies above all to taking a dead body from its burial place. For the offence of exhuming a body without legal authority, the entry points elsewhere. It sends readers to the articles on burial and the Burial Acts for the process of gaining that authority.

The notice is only a few lines long. It fixes the word's root, its general sense and its special sense. It offers no cases, dates or law of its own. Everything practical is deferred to the burial articles named. As a dictionary entry it does one job: it tells the reader exactly where the full treatment lives. Short as it is, the definition itself is complete and self-contained.
britannica-1911-expatriation:
Expatriation, from the late Latin expatriare, to exile, means in general the banishment of a person from his own country. In international law it means giving up or changing allegiance to one's native or adopted country. It can happen by a person's own voluntary act. It can also happen by operation of law. States handle it very differently, the entry notes.

France and England disclaim subjects who become naturalized in another country. Other states passively allow expatriation whether or not a new nationality has been gained. Germany, by contrast, ties it to continued absence from its territory. The entry gives no cases or dates of its own. It sends readers to the articles on Alien, Allegiance and Naturalization for the working detail. The whole notice is a short legal definition with national contrasts sketched in outline.
britannica-1911-expropriation: Expropriation is a short law word entry in the 1911 Britannica. It means the act of taking goods or land away from an owner. The word comes from late Latin roots that mean to take what is one own. The term is used most for one kind of taking. That is when the state takes land or goods for public use. A public body, not a private person, does the taking in that case.
britannica-1911-extortion:
Extortion in English law is set out in a short law entry in the 1911 Britannica. The word comes from a Latin verb for to twist out or take by force. In law it names the act of a public man who takes cash or goods not due. He may take too much, or take a fee too soon. A true slip in good faith is the sole guard the text grants. The wrong draws a fine or jail time.

Old laws add more teeth for set posts such as sheriffs, court clerks, and jailers. A jailer may not hold a dead man in jail as a pledge for debt. The term can also name cash forced by threats of harm or by threats to charge a crime. Those acts shade into theft by force and into blackmail.
britannica-1911-extradition:
Extradition, in the 1911 Britannica, is a law entry on handing a fugitive over for trial abroad. The word joins the Latin for out and for handing over. When a man who breaks the law in one land flees to another, what should the second land do? Try him at home, or send him back to face the law he broke? The entry says set law gives no sure answer.

Grotius held that a state is bound to give up such men, but most jurists rest the duty on goodwill, not right. In practice, lands hand men over only under a set treaty. Lands define crimes in unlike ways, and the tool could be used to seize men wanted for politics, not crime, so modern states keep political offences out of the system. The entry then lays out the British acts of 1870 to 1873.
britannica-1911-faringdon:
Great Faringdon is a market town in Berkshire, 17 miles west-south-west of Oxford by road. Its 1901 population was 2,900. The town slopes down from a low hill range above the Thames valley. A branch of the Great Western railway ends here, coming from Uffington. The church of All Saints is a large cross-shaped building with a low central tower. Its fabric is mainly Transitional Norman and Early English, with good details and many monuments and brasses.

Faringdon House, close by the church, was built by Henry James Pye, poet laureate from 1790 to 1813. Pye also planted the fir group on the eastern hill known as Faringdon Clump, or the Folly. The town's trade is agricultural. The entry is a short gazetteer notice, centred on the church and the laureate's house. No older history of the place is attempted beyond these landmarks.
britannica-1911-farnborough-thomas-erski:
Thomas Erskine May, Baron Farnborough (1815–1886), was an English constitutional historian born in London on 8 February 1815. Bedford grammar school educated him. In 1831 Speaker Manners Sutton made him assistant librarian to the House of Commons. Parliament thus claimed him in his youth. He was called to the bar at the Middle Temple in 1838. In 1844 he published the first edition of his Treatise on the law and usage of Parliament.

That book, through many editions, became the standing textbook of Commons procedure. Offices followed: examiner of petitions in 1846, taxing-master in 1847, clerk assistant in 1856. His Constitutional History of England, covering 1760 to 1860, appeared in 1861–1863. He became clerk of the House in 1871 and retired in April 1886. Raised to the peerage as Baron Farnborough, he died on 17 May 1886, days into the honour, and the title died with him.
britannica-1911-favart-charles-simon:
Charles Simon Favart (1710-1792), French dramatist, was born in Paris on 13 November 1710, son of a pastry-cook. Educated at Louis-le-Grand, he carried on his father's trade for a time after his death. A prize poem on Joan of Arc gave him his first literary success. His first vaudeville, Les Deux Jumelles, came in 1734, and soon he could leave business for the stage entirely.

Favart wrote many pieces for lesser theatres and directed the Opera Comique. With his wife, the dancer and singer Marie Justine Duronceray, he raised that house to a success that drew the jealousy of a rival and its suppression. He then ran a troupe following Maurice de Saxe's army in Flanders, writing verses on the campaign. Works such as Annette et Lubin, Les Trois Sultanes and L'Anglais a Bordeaux anchor the entry's account of his career and editions.
britannica-1911-fehling-hermann-von:
Hermann von Fehling (1812-1885), German chemist, was born at Lubeck on 9 June 1812. Planning a career in pharmacy, he entered Heidelberg University about 1835, then went to Giessen as assistant to Liebig. With Liebig he worked out the composition of paraldehyde and metaldehyde. On Liebig's recommendation he took the chemistry chair at the Stuttgart polytechnic in 1839 and held it until within three years of his death.

Fehling's early work covered succinic acid and the making of phenyl cyanide, the simplest aromatic nitrile. Later he gave most time to technology and public health rather than pure chemistry. His best-known method measures sugars with Fehling's solution, a mix of cupric sulphate with alkali and Rochelle salt. He contributed to the great chemical handbook of Liebig, Wohler and Poggendorff and served for years on the committee revising the German pharmacopoeia. He died at Stuttgart on 1 July 1885.
britannica-1911-ferdinand-i-of-aragon:
Ferdinand the First, king of Aragon from 1373 to 1416, was called Ferdinand of Antequera. The 1911 Britannica article says he was a son of John the First of Castile. His byname came from the town of Antequera, held then by the Moors. He was laying siege to that town when word came that Aragon had chosen him king. He came in place of his uncle Martin, the last male of the old line.

As a prince of Castile, Ferdinand had borne a fair name. When his brother Henry the Third died in 1406, nobles bid him take the crown over his baby nephew. He refused to rob the child of his right. As joint regent with the widowed queen he ruled well. The article notes how he curbed the wild acts of his sister-in-law in that shared rule.
britannica-1911-ferdinand-ii-of-leon:
Ferdinand the Second of Leon is the subject of a short life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a son of Alphonso the Seventh and of Berenguela, of the house of the counts of Barcelona. When his father's lands were split, he took Leon as his share. He died in 1188.

The article sums up a reign of thirty years of strife. He fought his own nobles and put some of them to death. While his nephew of Castile was a child, he tried to make himself regent there. On his west flank he warred with Portugal as it grew into a free kingdom. In 1180 he took the king of Portugal captive but made no use of the win. He pushed south into Estremadura at the cost of the Moors.
britannica-1911-ferdinand-v-of-castile-a:
Ferdinand the Fifth of Castile and Leon and the Second of Aragon was born at Sos in Aragon on 16 March 1452 and is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a son of John of Aragon by his second marriage. As husband of Isabella, queen of Castile, he bore the name the Catholic. He played a great part in the Europe of his day.

His share in firm royal rule across Spain fills other parts of the work. So do his expulsion of the Moors from Granada and his conquest of Navarre. His backing for the voyages of Columbus and his fight with France for sway in Italy rest there too. In person he lacked the warm traits of his wife, the entry says. He was, in the plain verdict given, purely a politician in his bent. Their 1469 marriage joined his claims with hers.
britannica-1911-fermentation:
Fermentation is the subject of a science article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The process, used in making wine, vinegar, beer, and bread, was known and practised in times before written history. The entry traces how loosely the word was once used. The alchemists spoke of fermentation, digestion, and putrefaction as if they were one thing.

Any change that showed chemical force at work counted for them as a fermentation. Even the fizz when an acid meets an alkaline fluid bore the name. Their dream of a stone that would set base metals fermenting and turn them to silver or gold muddied the idea still more. From that doctrine came a belief that the process cleansed and raised the stuff it worked on. The article quotes an old writer on yeast raising a change inside the wort of beer.
britannica-1911-feuilleton:
Feuilleton is a word study in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a French press term. The word is the small form of the French word for a leaf of a book. It first named a kind of extra part fixed to the news pages of French papers.

The article credits the elder Bertin, editor of a famed Paris paper, as its maker. The extra part was split from the news by a line and set in smaller type. Its stock was light news and gossip, notes on books and art, dress news, and jokes. The text calls its marks lightness, grace, and sparkle. English papers never took the form as such. In English the word came to name one part of a serial tale printed in a paper.
britannica-1911-food-preservation:
Food preservation is the art of keeping food sound and eatable beyond the short time it naturally lasts. From the earliest dawn of civilization, need drove men to store the plenty of one season or place against the want of another. The hunter dried, smoked and salted meat and fish. Pastoral man kept milk as cheese and butter, or fermented grape-juice into wine. Each old method fought the decay to which nearly all foods are liable.

Town life sharpened the problem. As manufacturing nations parted from food-growing ones, and civilized man spread from torrid to arctic zones, travellers and armies needed food that would keep. The article follows the answers: drying, salting, smoking, canning and cold storage. It ends with refrigeration, which ships frozen carcasses, butter, fruit and fish across the world and steadies prices, making the produce of distant ranches and orchards a daily thing in Britain.
britannica-1911-foucault-jean-bernard-le:
Jean Bernard Leon Foucault (1819-1868), French physicist, was the son of a Paris publisher and was born in Paris on 18 September 1819. Educated chiefly at home, he studied medicine, then quickly left it for physical science. His first work improved Daguerre's photographic processes. For three years he assisted Alfred Donne in lectures on microscopic anatomy, learning the craft of exact experiment that marked all his later work in optics and mechanics.

With Fizeau, Foucault studied the intensity of sunlight against carbon in the electric arc and lime in the oxyhydrogen flame. They worked on the interference of heat rays and of light rays, and on the chromatic polarization of light. The entry, published in 1911, goes on to the work that made Foucault famous: his measures of the speed of light and the pendulum that showed the earth turning. His name in the hosted text is spelled without its usual accent, as Foucault.
britannica-1911-foundation:
Foundation, from Latin fundatio, from fundare, to found, is the act of building, constituting or instituting on a permanent basis. It means above all the setting up of an institution by endowing it with funds for its continual upkeep. The word then serves for the institutions so set up, such as a college, monastery or hospital. Men on the foundation, or foundationers, are the fellows and scholars who enjoy the benefits of such an endowment in their college or society.

Formerly foundation also meant an institution's charter, and it is still used for the endowment funds themselves. The entry then explains old foundation and new foundation for English cathedral chapters. Those terms, it warns, say nothing about a cathedral's age. They belong to how its chapter was organized at the Reformation.
britannica-1911-fournier-pierre-simon:
The text hosted under this record is not an article on Pierre Simon Fournier. It is the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica biography of Joseph Jean Baptiste Xavier Fournet (1801–1869), a French geologist and metallurgist born at Strassburg on 15 May 1801. Educated at the École des Mines at Paris, he gained wide experience as a mining engineer, and in 1834 became professor of geology at Lyons.

The hosted article credits Fournet with memoirs on chemical and mineralogical subjects, eruptive rocks, the structure of the Jura, the metamorphism of the Western Alps, oolitic limestones, kaolinization and metalliferous veins. On metallurgy it names his observations on the order of sulphurability of metals, the loi de Fournet. He died at Lyons on 8 January 1869. His chief books were the Études sur les dépôts métallifères (1834), Histoire de la dolomie (1847), De l'extension des terrains houillers (1855) and Géologie lyonnaise (1861).
britannica-1911-franks-sir-augustus-woll:
Sir Augustus Wollaston Franks (1826-1897), English antiquary, was born on 20 March 1826 and educated at Eton and Trinity College, Cambridge. In 1851 he joined the British Museum as an assistant in the Antiquities Department. He became director of the Society of Antiquaries in 1858 and rose to be the leading English authority on medieval antiquities.

In 1866 the British and medieval antiquities and the ethnographical collections were made a separate department under his care. He also looked after the Christy collection before it joined the museum. Franks spent much of his fortune on ceramics and medieval art, and most of his collection passed to the nation by gift or bequest. He declined the chief librarianship in 1878, retired in 1896, and died the next year.
britannica-1911-fredericton:
Fredericton is a city and port of entry in New Brunswick, Canada, and the capital of the province. It stands on the St John river 84 miles from its mouth, on a plain between the broad river and a ring of hills. Long straight streets hold the parliament buildings, government house, the Anglican cathedral, and the provincial university.

The river carries large steamers up to the city, and two bridges join it to St Marye and Gibson across the water. Fredericton is the chief trade centre of the interior, with a large lumber trade and works for canning, tanning, and wooden ware. Sir Guy Carleton founded it in 1785 and made it capital for its strong position inland, against the wishes of St John. The population in 1901 was 7117.
britannica-1911-fribourg-canton:
Fribourg is one of the Swiss cantons, in the west of the country, named for the town around which its districts gathered. It covers 646 square miles, most of it farmed or wooded, with no glaciers. The land is hilly rather than mountainous, rising to the Vanil Noir at 7858 feet in the Gruyère district, and the Sarine river runs through it north to south.

This is the heart of pastoral Switzerland, famed for cheese and cattle and home of the Ranz des Vaches herdsman call. The people numbered 127,951 in 1900, most of them Roman Catholic, and the canton sits on the language frontier: 78,353 French speakers against 38,738 German speakers that year. Tobacco, cheese, and timber lead its products, with the great Cailler chocolate works at Broc. The constitution had changed little since 1857, and the canton sends two members to the Ständerath and six to the Nationalrath.
britannica-1911-friction:
Friction, from the Latin fricare, to rub, is the resistance one surface offers to another sliding over it. The entry traces it to roughness. Tiny points on each surface catch in tiny hollows on the other. Motion must wear them down or lift them out again and again. That resistance can always be felt and measured.

The article insists friction is better called a resistance than a force. It can pass on or change motion, but never start it. A worked case with a strap over a drum shows friction even causing motion in a second body. The laws of Coulomb, set out in 1781 and confirmed by Morin, give two rules. Friction grows with the pressure between the surfaces, not with their area. It also does not depend on sliding speed. Later tests by Galton and Fleeming Jenkin qualify the second law at very high and very low speeds.
britannica-1911-frommel-gaston:
Gaston Frommel (1862-1906), Swiss theologian, held the chair of theology at the university of Geneva from 1894 to 1906. An Alsatian by birth, he belonged mainly to French Switzerland. The entry places him as carrying on the spirit of Vinet under the changed conditions of the late 19th century. He drew his philosophy of religion from deep experience of the Gospel.

Like Vinet, Frommel tested every doctrine by direct spiritual experience and set moral personality as the crown of reality. He pressed further the analysis of conscience: liberty, he held, is not the first mark of conscience, since before being free it stands under obligation. That felt obligation points beyond the self to a real divine will. From this ground he argued against a merely psychological religion in the Paris School. His personal charm gave him great influence over students.
britannica-1911-fuchs-johann-nepomuk-von:
Johann Nepomuk von Fuchs (1774-1856), German chemist and mineralogist, was born at Mattenzell in the Bavarian Forest on 15 May 1774. In 1807 he became professor of chemistry and mineralogy at Landshut. In 1823 he took charge of the mineral collections at Munich. Three years later, when the university moved there, he became professor of mineralogy in that city.

He retired in 1852, was ennobled by the king of Bavaria in 1854, and died at Munich on 5 March 1856. His name is known chiefly for his mineralogical observations and for his work on soluble glass. His collected works were published at Munich in the year of his death. They include studies on the influence of chemistry and mineralogy, on the natural history of the mineral kingdom, and on theories of the earth.
britannica-1911-fuhrich-joseph-von:
Joseph von Führich (1800-1876), Austrian painter, was born at Kratzau in Bohemia on 9 February 1800. Rude pictures in wayside chapels fired him as a boy. He lived to see his own sacred subjects copied onto roadside churches across Austria. He has been fairly called a Nazarene, a romantic religious artist who revived the spirit of Dürer.

He composed with great skill, above all in outline, but he had little feeling for colour. His designs worked better as woodcuts than as monumental pictures. At Prague Academy from 1816, he took his bent from Dürer prints and Cornelius. In Rome in 1826 he added three frescoes to the Palazzo Massimi series, taking his subjects from Tasso. He became professor of composition at Vienna in 1841. His Prodigal Son and his pictures for the Psalms spread his name widely. He died in March 1876.
britannica-1911-fuller-melville-weston:
Fuller, Melville Weston (1833–1910) was chief justice of the Supreme Court of the United States. He was born at Augusta, Maine, on the 11th of February 1833, and he graduated at Bowdoin College in 1853. In 1856 he settled at Chicago, where he practised law for over thirty years. President Cleveland appointed him chief justice in 1888, in succession to Waite, when he was fifty-five years old.

In 1899 he served on the commission at Paris that arbitrated the boundary dispute between Venezuela and British Guiana. He held the chief justiceship until his death in 1910.
britannica-1911-fusion:
Fusion is the melting of a solid into a liquid, and its converse, freezing, follows the same laws. It sets crystalline fusion, shown by ice, against amorphous fusion, shown by glass, pitch and plastic sulphur. Ice melts at a definite freezing point, takes in a definite latent heat, and shrinks by some 9% as it melts. An amorphous solid softens gradually as it warms and hardens as it cools, with no fixed freezing point, no latent heat and no change of volume.

A solid may pass from one crystalline form to another at a fixed transition point, as rhombic sulphur changes at 95.6° C. into the monosymmetric form. Where solid and liquid differ in composition, as in alloys and solutions, the temperature moves during melting instead of staying fixed. The later sections treat freezing-point curves and the formation of mixed crystals, a field called most fruitful in recent years.
britannica-1911-gage-lyman-judson:
Gage, Lyman Judson (born 1836), an American financier, was born at De Ruyter in New York on the 28th of June 1836. A bank clerk at seventeen, he moved to Chicago in 1855 and rose to be president of the First National Bank of Chicago in 1891. In 1892 he chaired the board of the World's Columbian Exposition, whose financing owed more to him than to any other man. Though bred a Republican, he backed Cleveland in 1884 and declined the treasury post in 1892.

In the free-silver campaign of 1896 Gage worked for McKinley, and from March 1897 to January 1902 he was secretary of the treasury under McKinley and Roosevelt. His term, through a trying period, stood for a conservative policy: strengthening the gold standard, giving the currency more flexibility, and adjusting the relations between the government and the national banks. From 1902 to 1906 he presided over the United States Trust Company in New York.
britannica-1911-gagern-hans-christoph-er:
Gagern, Hans Christoph Ernst, Baron von (1766–1852), was a German statesman and political writer. He was born at Kleinniedesheim near Worms on the 25th of January 1766. After law at Leipzig and Göttingen he served the prince of Nassau-Weilburg. He represented the prince at the imperial diet in 1791 and was his envoy at Paris until 1811. Napoleon's decree then barred men born on the left bank of the Rhine from foreign service, and Gagern resigned.

When the prince of Orange became king of the Netherlands, Gagern was his prime minister, and at Vienna in 1815 he won the Netherlands a large gain of territory. Recalled from the German diet in 1818 at Metternich's instance, he retired in 1820 to Hornau. There he wrote a history of the German nation and his five-volume memoir, Mein Anteil an der Politik (1823–1845). His sons Friedrich, Heinrich and Maximilian each rose to eminence in arms, politics and office.
britannica-1911-galen-christoph-bernhard:
Galen, Christoph Bernhard, Freiherr von (1606–1678), was prince bishop of Münster, born on the 12th of October 1606 into a noble Westphalian family. Impoverished by the loss of his inheritance, he took holy orders yet fought for the emperor Ferdinand III in the closing stages of the Thirty Years' War. In 1650 he became bishop of Münster and crushed a rising of the citizens. With a strong army, the bishop grew a personage in Europe.

In 1664 Galen directed the imperial army against the Turk, and after the victory at St Gotthard he aided Charles II of England against the Dutch until 1666. Six years later he attacked Holland again, now allied with Louis XIV, but soon deserted France for the emperor. With Brandenburg and Denmark he then attacked Charles XI of Sweden and conquered the duchy of Bremen. He died at Ahaus on the 19th of September 1678.
britannica-1911-galion: Galion is a city of Crawford county, Ohio, about 75 miles south-west of Cleveland, with 7282 people in 1900 and 7214 in 1910. It stands some 1165 feet above the sea and is served by two railways and an interurban electric line. The Erie railway has extensive shops there, and the town makes brick and tile machinery, carriages and wagons, and grain and seed cleaners. The city owns its electric-lighting plant. Galion was laid out in 1831, became a borough in 1840 and a city in 1878.
britannica-1911-gallieni-joseph-simon:
Joseph Simon Gallieni (1849- ), a French soldier and colonial governor, was born at Saint-Beat on 24 April 1849.
