The 1911 Britannica entry follows him from the Saint-Cyr military academy in 1870 through service in the Franco-German War. Much of his early career went on extending French power in West Africa.

In the upper Niger basin he won a treaty from Ahmadu of Segu in March 1881. It gave France sole trading rights there. He later forced Samory to give up the Niger's left bank. He served in Martinique and Tongking, then governed Madagascar from 1896 to 1905, ending a wide revolt, exiling Queen Ranavalo III, and leaving the island at peace. The entry also lists his books on the Niger, the Sudan, Tonkin and Madagascar.
britannica-1911-galston:
Galston is a police burgh and manufacturing town in Ayrshire, Scotland, with 4,876 people in 1901. The 1911 Britannica entry sets it on the river Irvine, five miles east by south of Kilmarnock. It has a station on the Glasgow and South-Western railway.

Its manufactures are blankets, lace, muslin, hosiery and paper-millboard, and coal is worked nearby. About a mile north of the town, among woods and slopes the entry calls bonnie, stands Loudoun Castle, a seat of the earl of Loudoun. The entry is a short gazetteer notice, giving place, population, trade and the one notable house, with no history section.
britannica-1911-galvanized-iron:
Galvanized iron is sheet iron covered with a thin coating of zinc, as this 1911 Britannica article explains. Despite the name, electric action often plays no part in making it. The usual way is to dip the iron, first cleaned and pickled in acid, in a bath of molten zinc, with extra zinc cleared off by rollers.

The article sets out other ways of coating iron with zinc. In one, a thin coat of tin is laid on first by electric action in a bath. In cold galvanizing, zinc is laid on from a bath of zinc sulphate. A third way, called sherardizing, heats the goods packed in zinc dust in a closed vessel. That heat, kept well below the melting point of zinc, leaves a firm coat of the metal.
britannica-1911-gambetta-leon:
Leon Gambetta, a French statesman who lived from 1838 to 1882, has a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Cahors, he was the son of a Genoese grocer who had wed a French wife. At age sixteen he lost the sight of his left eye in an accident. He still shone at school in Cahors and went to Paris in 1857 to study law.

Gambetta was called to the bar in 1859 and was known as a fierce foe of the empire. His break came in November 1868, when he defended a journalist charged over a monument to a slain deputy. He used the plea to attack the coup of 1851 and the regime with a force that made him famed at once. In May 1869 he was elected to the assembly, and his rise as a leader of the left began from there.
britannica-1911-gambier-james-gambier-ba:
James Gambier, Baron Gambier, an English admiral who lived from 1756 to 1833, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in the Bahamas, where his father was lieutenant governor. He entered the navy in 1767 as a midshipman under his uncle. Family interest won him swift promotion, and by 1778 he was a post captain.

At the peace of 1783 Gambier went on half pay, but war with France brought him a ship again. He commanded the Defence under Lord Howe and won honour in the battle of the first of June 1794. A gold medal and a colonelcy of marines marked his service that day. The next year he became a rear admiral and a lord of the admiralty. He later governed Newfoundland and rose to full admiral in 1805.
britannica-1911-gaon:
Gaon is a title article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the heads of two Jewish academies in Babylonia. Gaon is Hebrew for Excellency, and the plural is Geonim. The two academies were Sura and Pumbeditha. The title is applied chiefly to rabbis who served from the close of the Talmud onward. They led the academies until the middle of the eleventh century.

They held wide authority and were appealed to from across the diaspora to settle social and religious questions. Their chief work took the form of answers to questions sent to them. The article names the most noted Geonim, from Ahai and Amram to Saadiah, Sherira and Hai. Hai Gaon died in 1038, closing a period of four and a half centuries.
britannica-1911-garrison:
The 1911 Britannica article on the word garrison traces a term that has narrowed over time. It once meant stores or supplies. It also meant a defence or protection. It now means only a body of troops. These troops are stationed in a town or fortress. Their task is defence.

The article follows the word's path through French. The old French form was garison. It comes from a verb meaning to furnish with stores, or to preserve. In later use it was confused with another French word for stationed troops. English used the form garnison until the sixteen hundreds. The article closes with British army usage. Garrison troops and garrison artillery do fortress work. They are distinct from troops in the field.
britannica-1911-garston: Garston, in the 1911 Britannica, is a brief port entry for a town in Lancashire, England. It stands on the Mersey, six miles south-east of Liverpool, in the Widnes division. Its count rose from 13,444 in 1891 to 17,289 in 1901. The docks, held by the London and North Western railway company, employ most of the working people. About a mile of quay is fitted with special gear for shipping coal, the chief export. The entry gives place, size, owner, and trade in four short lines.
britannica-1911-geraldton: Geraldton, a town in the district of Victoria in West Australia, is described in this short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. It stands on Champion Bay, 306 miles by rail north-west of Perth. Its people numbered 2,593 in 1901. It is the seat of a Roman Catholic bishop and an important seaport. It trades with the gold-fields and farms around it and centres a railway system. Its exports are gold, copper, lead, wool, and sandalwood.
britannica-1911-germiston:
Germiston, a gold town of the Transvaal, is placed in a town entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands nine miles east of Johannesburg in South Africa. In 1904 its town folk came to near thirty thousand in count. Just over nine thousand of those were white, the count says. The town lies at five thousand four hundred feet above the sea.

Gold rules that land, for Germiston sits in the Witwatersrand field. Its station is a great junction for the rail lines of the south. Lines from Cape and Natal ports meet lines to Pretoria there. Delagoa Bay sends its own line into that same busy yard. The station was once called Elandsfontein Junction in the old days. Though it rules itself, the town is in truth a suburb of Johannesburg.
britannica-1911-gerstenberg-heinrich-wil:
Heinrich Wilhelm von Gerstenberg is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Gerstenberg was a German poet and critic, born at Tondern in 1737. After studying law at Jena he entered Danish military service. He took part in the Russian campaign of 1762.

Twelve years in Copenhagen followed, in close company with the poet Klopstock. From 1775 he served Denmark as resident at Lubeck, and in 1786 he took a legal post at Altona. The article traces his writing through the phases of his nation's letters. He began with light Anacreontic verse, then wrote war songs as a Danish grenadier. A skald poem of 1766 placed him among Klopstock's bards. His Ariadne auf Naxos is called the best cantata of the eighteenth century. Readers meet a writer whose long life spanned his literature's growing years.
britannica-1911-geryon:
Geryon is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a figure of Greek myth. He was son of Chrysaor and Callirrhoe, daughter of Oceanus. He was king of the island of Erytheia. He is shown as a monster of three heads or three bodies. He owned herds of red cattle on that island. A giant shepherd named Eurytion tended those herds.

A two headed dog, Orthrus, guarded the cattle with him. To carry those cattle off to Greece was a set labour. It was one of twelve labours laid on Heracles by Eurystheus. Heracles crossed Europe and Libya to reach the island. He set up two pillars at the Straits of Gibraltar. He crossed the great river Oceanus to the island. There he slew the dog and the shepherd both. Geryon pursued him but fell to his arrows.
britannica-1911-gesner-konrad-von:
Konrad von Gesner is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He was a Swiss writer and naturalist from 1516 to 1565. He was born at Zurich in March 1516. His father was a poor furrier of that town. His father died in battle when Gesner was a youth. Good friends helped him keep up his studies in need. He studied at schools in two lands in his youth.

A kind patron in Paris helped his work in 1534. Faith strife drove him back to Zurich the next year. In 1537 he won a post to teach Greek at Lausanne. There he had free time for science, most of all plants. He took a doctor grade in medicine in 1541. He then settled to practise and teach at Zurich. He spent his life there on works of many kinds. He died of the plague in December 1565.
britannica-1911-gessner-solomon:
Solomon Gessner is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Gessner was a Swiss painter and poet who lived from 1730 to 1788. He was born at Zurich and spent nearly his whole life in his home town. There he carried on the trade of a bookseller. Some time in Berlin and Hamburg in his youth brought him under famed German writers.

The article lists the works that brought him wide fame. A song printed in 1751 first drew notice. Then came a pastoral tale, sets of idylls, and a prose work on the death of Abel. His writings are marked by sweetness and melody. Those traits won praise from Lessing, Herder, and Goethe. As a painter he worked in the set classical landscape style of his age. His works went through many editions and were translated into French and many other tongues.
britannica-1911-gibeon:
Gibeon, a town in Palestine of Bible fame, is the subject of a short place entry in the 1911 Britannica. Its folk won a truce from Joshua by a trick, the text notes first. Champs of David fought champs of Ish bosheth at its pool in old tales. Joab slew Amasa there, and Johanan chased Ishmael from its ground. A high shrine stood there where the tent of God lay for a time.

The town now bears the name El Jib in the text. It is a small village north west of Jerusalem on a lone hill. Flat corn land spreads at the foot of that hill. Springs made the place famed in old days and still flow there. Rock beds in neat layers make the hill look terraced from far off.
britannica-1911-gijon:
Gijon is a sea port in the north of Spain, in the tract of Oviedo, on the Bay of Biscay. Rail lines end there from three towns. Its count of folk in nineteen hundred was past forty-seven thousand. Old parts walled in part sit on a head land, while new parts spread past the shore both ways.

A church of the fifteen hundreds and a famed school are its chief sights. That school holds a fine store of drawn works and a good book room. The bay is the chief road for ships on that coast past two great ports. New rail links made it the port for coal lands.
britannica-1911-gindely-anton:
Anton Gindely, a historian who wrote in German, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Prague in 1829, the son of a German father and a Slav mother. He studied at Prague and at Olmütz. In 1862 he became a teacher of history at Prague and keeper of the records of Bohemia.

Most of the entry deals with his books on the Thirty Years' War. His great history of that war came out across the years 1869 to 1880. It was later put into English and printed at New York. Other works cover Rudolf the Second, Wallenstein, and the Bohemian Brethren. A book on the Counter-Reformation in Bohemia came out after his death.
britannica-1911-gladden-washington:
Washington Gladden (1836- ) was an American Congregational divine, born in Pottsgrove, Pennsylvania, on 11 February 1836. The 1911 Britannica entry has him graduating at Williams College in 1859, then preaching in Brooklyn, New York City, and Massachusetts towns. In 1882 he became pastor of the First Congregational Church of Columbus, Ohio.

Most of the entry is his books. Gladden urged personal, civil and above all social righteousness, in the pulpit and in print, and sat on Columbus city council in 1900-1902. His titles run from Plain Thoughts on the Art of Living of 1868 through Applied Christianity and Tools and the Man to Social Salvation and Christianity and Socialism. The William Belden Noble lectures at Harvard, on Dante, Michelangelo and others, are also listed. His Recollections appeared in 1909.
britannica-1911-glarus-canton:
Glarus is one of the Swiss cantons, taking its name from its chief town. The 1911 Britannica entry gives it 266.8 square miles, of which 173.1 count as productive and 13.9 are glaciers, ranking it fifth among Swiss cantons for ice. Its highest point is the Todi, at 11,887 feet.

The canton is the upper valley of the Linth, south of a line from the Lake of Zurich to the Walensee. The river rises in the Todi glaciers and has cut a deep bed with a fairly level floor, where a string of large villages sits. The entry distinguishes the main valley, the Grossthal, from its tributary, the Sernf or Kleinthal. Passes out are few: glacier routes to the Grisons, the rough Kisten footpath, and a new carriage road over the Klausen Pass into Uri. The long article covers the canton's land, people, industries and history.
britannica-1911-glutton:
Glutton, or wolverine, is a flesh eating mammal of the weasel family, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives it a nature entry. It is sole member of its genus. Its legs are short and stout, with large feet whose toes end in strong, sharp, curved claws, and it walks half on the sole of the foot.

In size and form the glutton is much like the badger, two to three feet long, not counting its thick bushy tail. Its head is broad, its eyes small and its back arched. The fur is a short woolly undercoat mixed with long straight hairs, which give the beast its shaggy look. The colour is blackish brown, with a broad chestnut band along each side. In winter, unlike most arctic beasts, its fur grows darker. It is a northern animal, found across the far north of both hemispheres, most thickly in the New World.
britannica-1911-glyptodon:
The 1911 Britannica article on the glyptodon describes a huge extinct animal of South America. Its name means fluted tooth. It was a giant kin of the armadillo. Its shell was one solid piece. The shell was formed from many bony plates joined together. It had no moving rings.

The article sets out the animal's build. Its face was very short. Its teeth were tall and grew all through life. Each tooth had deep grooves that split it into three lobes. The spine was almost one solid tube. The limbs were strong and the feet broad. The article names the family's kinds. The largest had a tail sheath like a huge club. Some kinds spread into North America. Fossils are rich in the silt of the Buenos Aires pampas.
britannica-1911-gneisenau-august-wilhelm:
Prussian field marshal August von Gneisenau, born in seventeen sixty, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of a Saxon officer named Neithardt. He grew up in great need at Schildau, then at Wurzburg and Erfurt.

He went to Erfurt as a student, then joined a force in Austria. He later served a German prince whose troops were in English pay in America. Back in seventeen eighty six, he sought Prussian service and got a post in the foot troops. He fought at Jena in eighteen oh six. The next year he held the small port of Colberg till peace was made.
britannica-1911-godfrey-of-bouillon:
Godfrey of Bouillon, a leader in the First Crusade who lived from about 1060 to 1100, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the second son of Eustace the Second, count of Boulogne. His uncle, Duke Godfrey of Lower Lorraine, named him as his successor. The emperor Henry the Fourth at first gave him only the mark of Antwerp.

Godfrey fought for Henry on the Elster and at the siege of Rome, and in 1082 he was invested with the duchy of Lower Lorraine. Godfrey was a man of notable piety. When the call to the crusade came, he all but sold all he had and followed. With his brothers Eustace and Baldwin he led a German host of some 40,000 men. They marched by the road of Charlemagne, through Hungary to Constantinople, in the autumn of 1096.
britannica-1911-goeben-august-karl-von:
August Karl von Goeben, a Prussian general who lived from 1816 to 1880, has a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Stade of old Hanover stock, he longed from youth for Prussian service, not that of his own land. At age seventeen he won a post in a Prussian foot regiment. Finding too little scope there, he left in 1836 to fight for Don Carlos in Spain.

Goeben fought five campaigns in Spain and met hard luck more than once. He was badly wounded and taken within two months of his start. He escaped after eight months, was taken again, and twice had to draw lots for his life. Freed at last, he served with honour until 1840. He then walked home to Prussia with no money and no clothes. Prussia took him back as a junior officer, and staff work soon showed his worth.
britannica-1911-gonfalon:
Gonfalon is a banner or standard of the middle ages, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica explains. The word comes through French and Italian from an old German word for a war flag. In its small form it was a pennon hung below the head of the lance of a knight. In church processions, or as the banner of a city, a state, or a military order, it took a grander form.

In that grander use it was a many streamered oblong ensign, often swinging from a cross bar fixed to a pole. The text calls that the most frequent use of the word. The bearer of a gonfalon held the title gonfalonier, a title both military and civil in that age. The counts of Vexin bore it as leaders of the men of Saint Denis.
britannica-1911-goodwin-william-watson:
William Watson Goodwin, an American scholar of Greek and Latin, was born in Concord, Massachusetts, in eighteen thirty one. He graduated at Harvard in eighteen fifty one and studied in Germany. He was tutor in Greek at Harvard, then held its chair of Greek for forty years. He resigned in nineteen o one and later served as an overseer. In eighteen eighty two he became first director of the American School at Athens.

Goodwin edited Greek works by Isocrates and by Demosthenes. He helped prepare a new edition of a Greek English lexicon. He also revised an English version of Plutarch's Morals in five volumes. His most prized work was a book on the moods and tenses of the Greek verb. It went through many revised editions.
britannica-1911-gordon:
Gordon is a family article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a great Scottish house whose historians trace 157 main branches. The line enters firm history with Sir Adam Gordon, who first took the English side in the Scottish struggle, then joined Robert Bruce after Bannockburn. Bruce granted him the lordship of Strathbogie in 1318, which he renamed Huntly from a village on the old Gordon lands.

His heiress Elizabeth wed Sir Alexander Seton, and their son Alexander became earl of Huntly about 1445. The line climbed to a dukedom in 1684, when George Gordon, fourth marquess of Huntly, was made duke of Gordon. A Catholic, he kept Edinburgh Castle for James the Second yet would not back the king's drive to impose his faith. When the forces of William besieged it, he gave the castle up with little fight.
britannica-1911-gordon-sir-john-watson:
Sir John Watson Gordon, a Scottish painter who lived from 1788 to 1864, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Edinburgh, the eldest son of a navy captain, he was educated with a view to joining the Royal Engineers. He entered a government school of design, and his gift soon showed.

His father let him take art as his profession, and the family circle helped. His uncle George Watson stood high as a portrait painter, second only to Raeburn. In 1808 Gordon sent a subject from the Lay of the Last Minstrel to an Edinburgh show. For some years he showed fancy subjects, sweetly painted but lacking force. His portraits were another matter. After Raeburn died in 1823, Gordon took much of his practice, and in 1826 he assumed the name Gordon. Sir Walter Scott was an early famed sitter.
britannica-1911-gottschall-rudolf-von:
Rudolf von Gottschall (1823-1909) was a German man of letters, born at Breslau, the son of a Prussian artillery officer. This 1911 Britannica article tells how he entered the university of Königsberg to study law in 1841, but was expelled for his outspoken liberal views. Other schools were no more open to him, and only at Berlin could he finish his studies.

In his restless early years he issued two books of poems shaped by his politics. He took a law degree, but when his views again blocked a teaching post he turned wholly to letters. He worked as a stage adviser, then as a newspaper editor at Posen and Leipzig. In 1877 the king of Prussia raised him to the hereditary nobility, and he edited Brockhaus journals until 1887.
britannica-1911-gould-augustus-addison:
Gould, Augustus Addison is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an American student of shells. He was born at New Ipswich in New Hampshire on the twenty-third of April 1805 and died in 1866. He graduated at Harvard in 1825 and took his medical degree in 1830. He had to win his schooling by his own hard work.

He set up as a doctor in Boston and rose to high rank in that calling. He became president of the Massachusetts Medical Society and edited the vital statistics of the state. As a shell scholar his fame is world-wide, the article says. He was one of the first men of that science in America. His writings fill many pages of learned journals. With Agassiz he brought out a book on the principles of zoology.
britannica-1911-gourgaud-gaspar-baron:
Gaspar Gourgaud (1783-1852) was a French artillery officer who rose close to Napoleon. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows his service from school skill in math to high rank. He fought at Austerlitz, in Spain, and in the Danube campaign of 1809. In Russia in 1812 he was among the first to enter the Kremlin.

Napoleon made him a baron and a chief ordnance officer. At Brienne in 1814 he saved the emperor from a Cossack band. After Waterloo he shared the exile to Saint Helena. Friction with others at Longwood and his sharp pride fill the last part of the account.
britannica-1911-gozlan-leon:
Leon Gozlan, a French novelist and playwright who lived from 1806 to 1866, has a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Marseilles on 1 September 1806, he was the son of a ship broker. His father had made a large fortune, then met a run of losses in trade. The boy had to go to sea to earn a living before his schooling was done.

By 1828 Gozlan was in Paris, set on the risks of a literary life. His townsman Joseph Mery brought him into newspaper work in that year. His bright pieces in the Figaro did much harm to the failing regime of Charles the Tenth. His first novel came out in 1828, and countless others followed it in swift order. His best known stage works came late, in the 1860s, near the end of his life.
britannica-1911-graduation:
Graduation is the art of dividing scales and arcs into equal parts. Its craft entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Straight scales, round arcs, and full circles all fall under the art. It is the most weighty and hard part of tool maker work.

Such marks are needed for sky, sea, survey, and physics tools alike. Clock makers first used the art to cut wheel teeth at set gaps. Fine work was not needed till astronomy grew in earnest study. Then exact place of stars and planets called for true measures. Named masters like Sharp, Bird, Ramsden, and Troughton honed the art greatly.
britannica-1911-grafe-albrecht-von:
Albrecht von Grafe (1828-1870) was a German oculist, son of the surgeon Karl Ferdinand von Grafe. The 1911 Britannica entry has him born at Berlin on 22 May 1828. Mathematics drew him first, then natural science, then medicine. He studied across Europe, in Vienna, Prague, Paris, London, Dublin and Edinburgh, with special attention to the eye.

In 1850 he began practice in Berlin and founded a private eye institution that became a model for many in Germany and Switzerland. He taught ophthalmology at Berlin university from 1853, rising to ordinary professor in 1866. In 1855 he founded the Archiv fur Ophthalmologie, with Arlt and Donders as collaborators. His two great contributions, the entry says, were a method of treating glaucoma and a new operation for cataract. He died at Berlin on 20 July 1870.
britannica-1911-grafe-karl-ferdinand-von:
Karl Ferdinand von Grafe (1787-1840) was a German surgeon, born at Warsaw on 8 March 1787. The 1911 Britannica entry has him studying medicine at Halle and Leipzig, then serving as private physician to Duke Alexius of Anhalt-Bernburg from 1807. In 1811 he became professor of surgery and director of the surgical clinic at Berlin.

During the war with Napoleon he superintended the military hospitals, and in peace he added the army's general staff and the Medico-Chirurgical Academy to his posts. The entry credits him with advancing German surgery, above all in the treatment of wounds. He improved the rhinoplastic process, and its revival was chiefly his work. His books include the Rhinoplastik of 1818 and yearly reports of his institute. Called to Hanover to operate on the crown prince's eyes, he died there suddenly on 4 July 1840.
britannica-1911-grand-canyon:
Grand Canyon is a deep gorge in the north west corner of Arizona. Its gorge entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The Colorado river carved the gorge in the high plateau region there. Captain Dutton called it by far the most grand of earthly sights.

The Colorado forms where the Green and Grand streams join as one. Snow and rain from the Rocky Mountains feed those two streams. The river runs about two thousand miles to the Gulf of California. It passes a mountain reach, a plateau reach, and a desert reach. The Grand Canyon lies in the plateau reach of that long course.
britannica-1911-grandson:
Grandson is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a town in Switzerland. In German the name is given as Grandsee. The town lies in the Swiss canton of Vaud. It stands near the south west end of Lake Neuchatel. Yverdon lies a few miles to the south. A count from 1900 gives the town 1771 people. Most spoke French and most were Protestant. Its ancient castle was home to a noted line of barons.

The very old church holds Roman columns from old sites. Its lords were vassals of the house of Savoy. In 1475 the Swiss took the castle by force. That taking opened their war with Charles the Bold. Charles retook it in 1476 and slew the garrison. The Swiss then beat him in a famous battle near by. They took much booty from his camp in victory.
britannica-1911-grantham-thomas-robinson:
Thomas Robinson, first Baron Grantham, was an English diplomat and man of state born about sixteen ninety five. He was a younger son of Sir William Robinson of Newby in Yorkshire. He studied at Trinity College, Cambridge, as a scholar and minor fellow. His first work abroad came in Paris, then at Vienna. He served as English ambassador at Vienna from seventeen thirty to seventeen forty eight.

In seventeen forty one Robinson sought to make peace between Maria Theresa and Frederick the Great. That effort failed, and in seventeen forty eight he spoke for England at Aix la Chapelle. Back home he sat in parliament for Christchurch for twelve years. In seventeen fifty four he became a secretary of state and leader of the Commons. Pitt mocked his choice for that post in harsh words. He resigned a year later and became a baron in seventeen sixty one.
britannica-1911-grantley-fletcher-norton:
Fletcher Norton, first Baron Grantley, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born at Grantley in Yorkshire in 1716, he was the eldest son of Thomas Norton. He became a barrister in 1739 and built a large, well paid practice. He later served as attorney general for the county palatine of Lancaster.

The entry tracks his seats in Parliament for Appleby, Wigan, and later Guildford. It notes his roles as solicitor general and then attorney general, and his part in the cases against John Wilkes and the fifth Lord Byron. Made a privy councillor in 1769, he was chosen Speaker of the House of Commons in 1770. The article also recalls his blunt words to George the Third in 1777.
britannica-1911-great-barrington:
Great Barrington is a township in Berkshire county, Massachusetts, on the Housatonic river. Its town entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies in the Berkshire hills, about twenty five miles south west of Pittsfield. The township holds three villages and covers about forty five square miles.

The entry gives counts of people for eighteen ninety, nineteen hundred, and nineteen ten. It notes rail links, two public libraries, and a church with a large organ. The main village is known as a summer resort in the hills. Farms shape the township most, though mills make cotton goods and paper. Marble and blue stone are also quarried there.
britannica-1911-great-rebellion:
Great Rebellion is a broad name for the civil wars of England and Scotland. The 1911 Britannica entry dates the wars from 1642 to 1652. They began when King Charles the First raised his standard at Nottingham. That act came on the twenty second of August in 1642. They ended when Dunottar Castle gave up to Parliament in May 1652.

Most accounts split the wars into two clear parts or phases. The First Civil War ran from 1642 to the year 1646. The Second Civil War ran from 1648 to the year 1652. All that while a third civil war raged in Ireland as well. Its course had scant link with the English fight in arms. Yet its end results swayed the struggle in England a great deal.
britannica-1911-greek-religion:
Greek Religion, in the 1911 Britannica, is a long scholarly article reshaped by the new sciences of its day. It opens by claiming that anthropology and the comparative study of religions can at last give ancient Greek religion its proper place among creeds. Local cults differed widely, the entry grants, yet a general account is possible.

That account defines the system as an anthropomorphic polytheism: gods in human form, keeping many traces of an earlier, pre-human stage. No exacting dogma and no revealed tradition checked it. So it bent pliantly to every change in Greek social and political life, and easily absorbed alien ideas and forms. Lasting in whole or part at least 2,000 years, it could progress as fixed dogmatic religions could not. The article then works through the gods, cults, festivals and beliefs of the Greek world in that frame.
britannica-1911-greene-george-washington:
George Washington Greene (1811-1883) was an American historian, born at East Greenwich, Rhode Island, on 8 April 1811. The 1911 Britannica entry makes him the grandson of Major-General Nathanael Greene. Ill-health cut short his Brown University course, and he spent most of the next twenty years in Europe.

He was United States consul at Rome from 1837 to 1845, taught modern languages at Brown from 1848 to 1852, and lectured on American history at Cornell in 1871-1875. His books include French and Italian text-books, Historical Studies of 1850, a Historical View of the American Revolution of 1865, and a three-volume Life of Nathanael Greene, published 1867-1871. A Short History of Rhode Island closed the list in 1877. He died at East Greenwich on 2 February 1883.
britannica-1911-grenville-william-wyndha:
William Wyndham Grenville, Baron Grenville (1759-1834), was an English statesman, youngest son of George Grenville, born on 25 October 1759. The 1911 Britannica entry has him educated at Eton and Christ Church, where he won the chancellor's prize for Latin verse in 1779. He entered parliament in 1782 for Buckingham.

His rise ran through family posts: secretary to his brother the lord lieutenant of Ireland, then paymaster-general under his cousin Pitt. A mission to the Hague and Versailles followed in 1787. In January 1789 he became Speaker of the Commons, leaving the chair the same year for the home secretaryship. Created Baron Grenville in November 1790, he directed government business in the Lords. In 1791 he moved to the foreign office. The long article follows his foreign secretaryship through the French wars and his later premiership of the Ministry of All the Talents.
britannica-1911-gresham-walter-quinton:
Walter Quinton Gresham (1832-1895) was an American statesman and jurist, born near Lanesville, Indiana, on 17 March 1832. The 1911 Britannica entry has him admitted to the bar in 1854 after a year at Indiana State University. A Republican campaign speaker from 1856, he entered the state legislature in 1860.

As chairman of military affairs he helped prepare Indiana's troops, then took the field himself. He commanded a brigade at Corinth and Vicksburg, and was made brigadier-general in August 1863. A wound before Atlanta on 20 July 1864 left him lame for life. Judge, postmaster-general, and briefly secretary of the treasury followed. His drift from his party ended with his backing Cleveland in 1892. As Cleveland's secretary of state he died at Washington on 28 May 1895.
britannica-1911-grey-de-wilton:
Grey de Wilton and Grey de Ruthyn are two English baronies treated together in the 1911 Britannica. The first Baron Grey de Wilton was Reginald de Grey, summoned to parliament in 1295, who died in 1308. His son John, the 2nd baron, was one of the lords ordainers of 1310, prominent under Edward II.

The later Wilton barons descend from John's eldest son Henry; the Ruthyn barons from a younger son, Roger. The entry follows the lines through the centuries. Its fullest figure is William, 13th Lord Grey de Wilton, who won fame soldiering in France in Henry VIII's last years. He led at Pinkie in 1547, served on the Scottish marches, and helped quiet the 1549 rebellions. Pardoned by Mary after backing Lady Jane Grey's claim, he defended Guines with great gallantry before its fall in January 1558. The article continues both families' history.
britannica-1911-grimthorpe-edmund-becket:
Edmund Beckett, 1st Baron Grimthorpe (1816-1905), was born on 12 May 1816, son of Sir Edmund Beckett Denison. The 1911 Britannica entry has him educated at Doncaster and Eton, then at Trinity College, Cambridge, graduating thirtieth wrangler in 1838. He was called to the bar at Lincoln's Inn in 1841.

A leader of the Parliamentary Bar and a Q.C. from 1854, he dropped the name Denison on succeeding to the baronetcy in 1874. But his fame lay outside the law, in astronomy, horology and Gothic architecture. By 1850 he was a recognized authority on turret clocks, having designed Dent's Great Exhibition clock. In 1851 he was called, with the astronomer royal and Dent, to design the clock for the new Houses of Parliament. The tower clock called Big Ben was built after his designs. He was raised to the peerage in 1886.
britannica-1911-grison:
The grison (Galictis vittata) is a carnivorous mammal of the weasel family, Mustelidae, common across Central and South America and Mexico. About the size of a marten, it has bluish-grey fur above and dark brown fur below. It feeds on small mammals and birds, and in settled districts it proves destructive to poultry.

Two relatives share its range and habits. Allamand's grison (G. allamandi) is somewhat larger, while the tayra (G. barbara) grows to about the size of an otter, ranges from Mexico to Argentina, and hunts in companies rather than alone. The entry is brief, fixing the animal's family, size, colouring, diet and place among its nearest kin.
britannica-1911-haddington:
Haddington is a royal burgh and county town of Haddingtonshire, Scotland. Its population in 1901 was 3,993. It stands on the Tyne, 18 miles east of Edinburgh. A branch railway from Longniddry ends there. Five bridges cross the river. On the right bank lies the old suburb of Nungate. John Knox was born at the Giffordgate in Nungate.

St Mary's church is the principal building. This cruciform church of red sandstone dates from about the 13th century. It runs 210 feet long with a 90-foot tower. The restored nave serves as parish church. The choir and transepts stand roofless. Lord Maitland of Thirlestane lies there in alabaster effigy. The duke of Lauderdale shares the vault. Carlyle raised a tombstone there for his wife Jane. The Knox Memorial Institute recalls the old grammar school.
britannica-1911-hahn-hahn-ida-countess-v:
Ida, Countess von Hahn-Hahn (1805-1880), was a German author, and her life and novels fill an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Tressow in Mecklenburg, daughter of a count who spent much of his fortune on the stage, she married a rich cousin in 1826. The marriage was deeply unhappy and ended in divorce in 1829.

The entry follows her travels and volumes of poetry, then her turn to novels in 1838 with Aus der Gesellschaft, a title kept as the name of her series. Her novels dealt almost wholly with aristocratic society and drew merciless parody for their lofty affectations. In 1850 she embraced the Roman Catholic faith, defending the step in print.
britannica-1911-halkett-hugh-freiherr-vo:
Halkett, Hugh, Freiherr von is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a British soldier who rose high in the Hanoverian service. Born in 1783, the second son of a major general, Halkett served in India from 1798 to 1801 with the Scotch Brigade his father had helped to raise. He served in the Peninsula and at Walcheren and led the second Light Infantry battalion at Albuera and Salamanca.

In 1813 Halkett left the Peninsula to help build the new Hanoverian army. At Gohrde and Schestedt he bore a marked part, taking a Danish standard with his own hand. In the Waterloo campaign he led two brigades of Hanoverian militia and captured General Cambronne in the fight with the Old Guard.
britannica-1911-haller-albrecht-von:
Albrecht von Haller (1708–1777) was a Swiss anatomist and physiologist. He was born at Bern on 16 October 1708. Ill health kept him from boyish sports. His mind developed precociously instead. At four he read and expounded the Bible to servants. Before ten he had sketched a Chaldee grammar. He also compiled two thousand biographies of famous people. At fifteen he wrote verse translations and an epic.

Medicine drew him while he lived with a Biel physician. He studied at Tübingen from 1723. Leiden followed in 1725, under Boerhaave and Albinus. He graduated there in May 1727. London, Oxford, Paris and Basel completed his training. John Bernoulli taught him higher mathematics at Basel. Botany seized his interest on an Alpine tour. A European reputation in anatomy and botany followed fast. His poems and journals round out the long account.
britannica-1911-hallucination:
Hallucination is a psychological term for false sense-perception. The word comes from a Latin verb meaning to wander in mind. Hallucinations form one of two great classes of false perception. Illusions form the other class. An illusion misreads a real sense-impression. A hallucination has the vividness of true perception. Yet no stimulus acts on the sense-organ at the time. The boundary between the two stays hard to draw.

Belief separates sane from insane experience here. A sane person often recognises the object as unreal at once. The insane, or people in abnormal states, may not. Hearing and sight produce the most reported cases. Other senses seem rarer, partly because their cases strike us less. The long article surveys causes, types and hypnotic cases. It ends with apparitions reported at moments of death. A psychical research committee found written proof scarce in those cases.
britannica-1911-hammer-purgstall-joseph-:
Joseph, Freiherr von Hammer-Purgstall (1774–1856), was an Austrian orientalist. He was born at Graz on 9 June 1774. Vienna gave him most of his early education. He entered the diplomatic service in 1796. Constantinople's Austrian embassy received him in 1799. He joined the British expedition against the French in Egypt. Home again in 1807, he became a privy councillor. Inheriting Styrian estates in 1835 brought him his title.

For fifty years he wrote incessantly on oriental subjects. He published Arabic, Persian and Turkish texts and translations. Specialists attacked his faults severely, Diez above all. Yet he did for Germany what Jones did for England. His chief work is a ten-volume history of the Ottoman empire. It appeared at Pesth from 1827 to 1835. His total output nears one hundred volumes. In 1847 he became president of Vienna's new academy.
britannica-1911-hampden-renn-dickson:
Renn Dickson Hampden (1793–1868) was an English divine. He was born in Barbados in 1793. His father was a colonel of militia there. Oriel College, Oxford, educated him. He took first-class honours in classics and mathematics in 1813. A fellowship at Oriel followed quickly. Keble, Newman and Arnold were his contemporaries. Curacies occupied him from 1816 onward.

His Bampton lectures of 1832 drew a charge of Arianism. The Tractarian party pressed that charge hard. Oxford still made him Regius professor of divinity in 1836. Violent controversy followed that appointment too. Lord John Russell nominated him bishop of Hereford in 1847. Organised opposition fought the nomination bitterly. His consecration went ahead in March 1848 anyway. As bishop he kept his studious, secluded habits. His diocese prospered quietly under him. He died in London in 1868.
britannica-1911-harizi-judah-ben-solomon:
Judah ben Solomon Harizi, a Spanish Hebrew poet and traveller of the 13th century, gets a brief entry in the 1911 Britannica. He turned works of Maimonides from Arabic into Hebrew, and did the same for the Arab poet Hariri. His own chief work was the Tahkemoni, made between 1218 and 1220. It is written in Hebrew rhymed prose.

The Tahkemoni is a chain of droll scenes, witty verses, and odd uses of Bible texts. A hero and a narrator, who is the author himself, bind the parts into one book. The entry credits Harizi with bringing the art of Hebrew secular satire to its peak. He was also a sharp critic of verse. His account of the Hebrew poets of Andalusia is called a rich source on them. A note points readers to a German study that renders much of the book.
britannica-1911-hatherley-william-page-w: William Page Wood, 1st Baron Hatherley, is the subject of this record, but the hosted text preserves only the closing passage of his entry, not the article itself. What survives says he was a particularly clear-headed lawyer whose judgments, always delivered extempore, commanded the greatest confidence with both the public and the legal profession. It also records that he left no issue, and that the title became extinct on his death.
britannica-1911-hatherton-edward-john-li:
Edward John Littleton, 1st Baron Hatherton (1791–1863), was an English politician. He was born on 18 March 1791. Rugby and Brasenose College, Oxford, educated him. Born a Walhouse, he took the name Littleton in 1812. A great-uncle's will required that change. He sat in Parliament for Staffordshire from 1812 to 1835. Roman Catholic emancipation was his prominent cause there.

In May 1833 he became chief secretary for Ireland. The post brought frequent conflict with O'Connell. Littleton boasted he could manage Dan, but proved unequal to him. A hasty compact over the Irish tithes question undid him. O'Connell charged him with deception in 1834. Grey, Althorp and Littleton all resigned that July. The barony of Hatherton came in 1835. He died at Teddesley Hall on 4 May 1863.
britannica-1911-haxo-francois-nicolas-be:
François Nicolas Benoît Haxo (1774–1838) was a French general and military engineer. He was born at Lunéville on 24 June 1774. He entered the Engineers in 1793. Years of obscure regimental duty followed. The second siege of Saragossa in 1809 gave him distinction. Napoleon made him a colonel for that work. Wagram and the Peninsula sieges employed him next. Suchet's siege operations in Catalonia were his charge.

In 1812 he was chief engineer of Davout's corps. The Moscow retreat made him general of division. His Hamburg works enabled Davout's famous defence in 1813. Kulm saw him captured by the enemy. After the Restoration he rebuilt France's old Vauban fortresses. His designs met the new requirements of the age. At Antwerp citadel in 1832 he completely outmatched the Dutch engineers. Louis Philippe made him a peer in 1832. He died at Paris in 1838.
britannica-1911-haxthausen-august-franz-:
August Franz Ludwig Maria von Haxthausen (1792–1866) was a German political economist. He was born near Paderborn on 3 February 1792. The Klausthal mining school and the Hanoverian army came first. Göttingen university received him in 1815. From 1818 he managed his estates and studied land laws. His book on Paderborn and Corvey land law appeared in 1829. It won him a Prussian commission.

Nine years of labour produced his treatise on Prussian rural law in 1839. In 1843 the emperor Nicholas commissioned a Russian study. His Studien on Russia's inner life appeared from 1847 to 1852. R. Farie translated it as The Russian Empire in 1856. Transcaucasia and The Tribes of the Caucasus reached English too. He sat in Berlin's combined diet in 1847 and 1848. The Prussian upper house took him later. He died at Hanover in 1866.
britannica-1911-hayton:
Hayton, or Hethum, was king of Little Armenia from 1224 to 1269. He was the son of Constantine Rupen. Marriage to Isabella, Leo II's only child, made him heir. Before his accession he was constable, head of the army. He was also bailiff of the realm. Forty-five years of reign ended in abdication. He became a monk and died in 1271. Mongol friendship was his reign's constant policy.

He sent his brother Sempad to Kuyuk Khan about 1248. Sempad returned in 1250 with the khan's letters. Mangu's accession brought a summons to Hayton himself. Disguised, he crossed hostile Turkish country to Kars. Batu welcomed him on the Volga. In May 1254 he set out for Karakorum. That journey made him a famous Asian traveller. His own account of the Mongol world survives in translation.
britannica-1911-heathfield-george-august:
George Augustus Eliott, Baron Heathfield (1717–1790), was a British general. He was a younger son of Sir Gilbert Eliott of Stobs. He was born on 25 December 1717. Education abroad prepared him for the military profession. He volunteered with the Prussian army in 1735 and 1736. Then he entered the Grenadier Guards. Dettingen wounded him in the Austrian Succession war. By 1754 he was lieutenant-colonel.

In 1759 he raised a new light horse regiment, later the 15th Hussars. Its efficiency made him well known in the campaigns. Gibraltar's governorship came to him in 1775. His magnificent defence in the great siege of 1779 made his fame. Reynolds' portrait of him hangs in the National Gallery. In 1787 he was created Baron Heathfield of Gibraltar. He died on 6 July 1790. His son died in 1813 and the peerage became extinct. Note: this record's hosted file is a shared page chunk; the Heathfield entry stands complete within it.
britannica-1911-hebron:
Hebron is a city of Palestine, some 20 miles south of Jerusalem. Its modern name, Khulīl er-Rahmān, means friend of the Merciful One. That title alludes to Abraham. The city lies 3,040 feet above the sea. Its antiquity is extreme, and it first bore the name Kirjath-Arba. Biblical tradition ties it closely to Abraham. It became a city of refuge in the tradition.

David ruled from Hebron in his early reign. Abner's murder happened there, and Absalom's rebellion centred there. Edomites held it for a time before Judas Maccabaeus recovered it. Vespasian's war destroyed it; Saladin took it in 1187. The modern town holds about 10,000 people, including some 500 Jews. Its great sight is the Haram over the cave of Machpelah. Glass bracelets, lamps and leather water-skins are made locally.
britannica-1911-heideloff-karl-alexander:
Karl Alexander von Heideloff (1788–1865) was a German architect. He was born at Stuttgart, a painter's son. The art academy of Stuttgart trained him. Coburg saw him practise architecture for a time. In 1818 Nuremberg appointed him its city architect. He became professor at the polytechnic school in 1822. He held that post until 1854. Conservator of art monuments was a later honour.

Gothic architecture claimed his chief attention. Buildings around Nuremberg attest his skill and pure taste. Reinhardsbrunn castle and Landsberg castle are his. The Rosenburg near Bonn and Rheinstein chapel show his range. Bamberg cathedral and Lichtenstein castle show his restoration powers. Watercolour painting brought him some success too. His writings include Nuremberg's medieval monuments in several volumes. Die Ornamentik des Mittelalters appeared from 1838 to 1842. He died at Hassfurt in 1865.
britannica-1911-heigel-karl-august-von:
Karl August von Heigel (1835–1905) was a German novelist. He was born at Munich on 25 March 1835. His father managed the court theatre's stage there. Munich gave him schooling and university philosophy from 1854. A Silesian prince made him his librarian afterward. Travels with the prince's nephew followed that post. Berlin took him in 1863 for journalism. He worked in newspapers there until 1875.

Munich then employed him in literary work for Ludwig II. The king conferred nobility on him in 1881. After Ludwig's death he removed to Riva on Lake Garda. He died there on 6 September 1905. His novels won him some popularity. Wohin? and Die Dame ohne Herz date from 1873. Das Geheimnis des Königs and Der Maharadschah came later. Plays on Josephine Bonaparte and the Czarina are also listed.
britannica-1911-henderson:
George Francis Robert Henderson (1854–1903) was a soldier and military writer. The hosted text preserves his article from mid-course. His first work, The Campaign of Fredericksburg, appeared anonymously. Sandhurst made him instructor in tactics that same year. From 1892 to 1899 he professed military art at the Staff College. Eight years produced his masterpiece in 1898. Stonewall Jackson and the American Civil War is that book.

In the South African War he directed intelligence for Lord Roberts. Overwork and malaria broke his health completely. The official war history was assigned to him. Failing health drove him to Egypt instead. He died at Assuan on 5 March 1903. His completed volume was suppressed by the War Office. Sir F. Maurice restarted the history from scratch. His lectures appeared in 1905 as The Science of War. Note: this record's hosted file is a shared page chunk; the surviving portion of the Henderson entry stands within it.
britannica-1911-hendon:
Hendon is an urban district in Middlesex, England. It lies in the Harrow parliamentary division. The river Brent runs through it. It stands 8 miles north-west of St Paul's Cathedral. The Midland railway serves the district. Its population grew fast between the censuses. It counted 15,843 people in 1891. By 1901 it counted 22,450. The township's nucleus sits on high ground.

That ground lies east of the Edgware road. The Welsh Harp reservoir lies across that road. It is a favourite fishing and skating resort. St Mary's church is mainly Perpendicular in style. More gazetteer detail follows on streets and buildings. The entry is a standard short town notice. Position, railway, population and church are its core facts. Note: this record's hosted file is a shared page chunk; the Hendon entry stands complete within it.
britannica-1911-herbert-of-cherbury-edwa:
Edward Herbert, Baron Herbert of Cherbury (1583–1648), was an English soldier, diplomatist, historian and religious philosopher. Born at Eyton-on-Severn on the 3rd of March 1583, he was the eldest son of Richard Herbert of Montgomery Castle. Taught at home, he entered University College, Oxford, in May 1596. He married his cousin Mary in 1599 and kept up his studies. James I made him a knight of the Bath in 1603.

In 1608 he went to Paris and was entertained by Henry IV. In 1610 he served as a volunteer in the Low Countries under the prince of Orange and won notice at the capture of Juliers. His offer to settle the war by single combat was declined. A later plan to lead 4,000 Huguenots into Piedmont for Savoy ended with his jailing at Lyons. Ambassador at Paris from 1619, he was recalled in 1621 after a quarrel with de Luynes, then sent back in February 1622.
britannica-1911-herbert-of-lea-sidney-he:
Sidney Herbert, 1st Baron Herbert of Lea (1810–1861), was an English statesman and the younger son of the 11th earl of Pembroke. Schooled at Harrow and Oriel College, Oxford, he made his name at the Oxford Union. He entered the House of Commons in 1832 as Conservative member for a division of Wiltshire. Under Peel he held minor offices, and in 1845 he joined the cabinet as secretary at war.

He held it again through the Crimean War, 1852 to 1855, and once more in 1859. It was Herbert who sent Florence Nightingale out to the Crimea. After the war he led the drive to reform the War Office, and the work broke his health. Made a baron in July 1861, he had to resign, and died on the 2nd of August 1861. His statue stands before the War Office in Pall Mall, and his eldest son later became 13th earl of Pembroke.
britannica-1911-herberton: Herberton is a mining town of Cardwell county, Queensland, Australia, 55 m. S.W. of Cairns, with 2,806 people in 1901. Tin was found in the district in 1879, and tin is the chief source of the town's prosperity, though copper, bismuth and some silver and gold also occur. Atherton, 12 m. away, is served by rail from Cairns, which acts as the port for the Herberton district. The entry is short and gives the town's place, size and minerals in a few lines.
britannica-1911-hercules-constellation:
Hercules is a constellation of the northern hemisphere, named by Eudoxus in the 4th century B.C. and by Aratus in the 3rd. Ptolemy catalogued it with 29 stars and Tycho Brahe with 28. It is drawn as a man kneeling, and was first known simply as the man on his knees. The Greeks later called the figure Cetheus, Theseus and Hercules.

Its noted objects include alpha Herculis, a fine coloured double star: an orange star of magnitude 2½ with a blue companion of magnitude 6. Zeta Herculis is a binary found by Sir William Herschel in 1782, a yellow star of the third magnitude with a bluish mate of magnitude 6. Gamma and mu Herculis vary in light in an irregular way. The cluster M. 13 Herculis is the finest globular cluster in the northern hemisphere, holding at least 5,000 stars. Of 1,000 of its stars whose light has been fixed, only 2 are variable.
britannica-1911-herschell-farrer-hersche:
Farrer Herschell is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Herschell was lord chancellor of England who lived from 1837 to 1899. He was born in November 1837. His father was a Polish born minister who had changed his faith from Jewish to Christian. His mother was a daughter of a merchant of Leith. He was schooled at a private school and at University College in London.

The article tells how he took his degree at the University of London in 1857. As a law student at Lincoln's Inn he kept a high standing. He read law with noted pleaders and was called to the bar in 1860. He joined the northern circuit, then at its height. For four or five years he gained little work.
britannica-1911-heyn-pieter-pieterzoon:
Pieter Pieterzoon Heyn (1578–1629), commonly Piet Heyn, was a Dutch admiral, born at Delfshaven, the son of a herring fisherman. He went early to sea, was taken by the Spaniards, and rowed in the galleys for four years. Freed by exchange of prisoners, he prospered as a merchant skipper. When the Dutch West India Company was formed he became a director on its Rotterdam board.

In 1624 he was second in command of the fleet that took San Salvador in Bahia, Brazil. In September 1628 he captured the fleet carrying bullion from the American mines home to Spain. Its richest part, four galleons and eleven trading ships with the king's treasure, was chased into Matanzas harbour in Cuba and taken. Spain's loss was put at four million ducats. Heyn came home and bought a house at Delft. In 1629 he was chosen lieutenant-admiral of Holland to clear the North Sea and Channel.
britannica-1911-hill-aaron:
Aaron Hill (1685–1750) was an English author, born in London on the 10th of February 1685. At fourteen he left Westminster School for Constantinople, where a kinsman, Lord Paget, was ambassador, and Paget sent him travelling in Palestine and Egypt. Home in 1709, he published a book on the Ottoman Empire, of which he was later ashamed.

Hill is said to have managed Drury Lane in 1709 and the Haymarket in 1710, and his first play, Elfrid, was staged in 1709. The rest of his life went on bright commercial schemes, all failures, and on writing. His companies aimed to draw oil from beechmast, plant Georgia, supply Scottish ship timber and make potash. Pope's place for him in The Dunciad rankled long.
britannica-1911-hippel-theodor-gottlieb-:
Theodor Gottlieb von Hippel was a German writer of wit and jest who lived from seventeen forty-one to seventeen ninety-six. He was born at Gerdauen in East Prussia, where his father ran a school. He first read church studies at the chief town school. A trip to the court at Saint Petersburg then changed his path.

He turned to law, rose fast, and in time ran his home town as its chief mayor. The entry paints a man of sharp contrasts, pious yet drawn to ease, plain yet fond of show. His best books mix life tales with sharp jests at pride and rank. One late book pleads for a fairer place for women.
britannica-1911-hirson: Hirson is a town in northern France, in the Aisne department, on the Oise river. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica places it near the Belgian frontier at a rail crossing of note. A fort and two batteries guard that key point. Local work covers glass bottles, tiles, iron and tin goods, wool spinning, and brewing. Its people numbered just over eight thousand in 1906.
britannica-1911-hochstetter-ferdinand-ch:
Ferdinand Christian von Hochstetter, an Austrian geologist, is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica biography. He was born at Esslingen in 1829. His father was a clergyman, professor, and botanist. The boy was schooled at a seminary at Maulbronn. He then studied at the university of Tubingen. There his early love of geology became fixed for life.

He won his doctor's degree and a travelling grant. In 1852 he joined the Imperial Geological Survey of Austria. He worked in Bohemia and the Karlsbad mountains until 1856. His fine reports made his name. He was then chosen as geologist for the Novara voyage round the world. In 1859 the New Zealand government hired him for a survey. He later taught at the Vienna polytechnic. He also ran the Imperial Natural History Museum. He died at Vienna in 1884.
britannica-1911-hodgkinson-eaton:
Eaton Hodgkinson (1789–1861) was an English engineer, born at Anderton near Northwich, Cheshire, in 1789. A farmer's son, he helped his widowed mother until, in 1811, he persuaded her to move to Manchester and start a pawnbroking business. There he met John Dalton and began his life's work: the strength of materials.

Hodgkinson tested cast iron with Sir William Fairbairn, and Stephenson sought his help on the tubes for the Britannia bridge. His paper on the strength of cast-iron pillars won a Royal medal in 1841 and a fellowship of the Royal Society. In 1847 he became professor of engineering principles at University College, London. He died near Manchester in 1861.
britannica-1911-hodgson-brian-houghton:
Brian Houghton Hodgson (1800–1894) was an English administrator, ethnologist and naturalist, born at Prestbury, Cheshire, in 1800. He went to India in 1818, and in 1820 was posted as assistant to the Resident at Katmandu, capital of Nepal. Ill health returned him to Nepal in 1824, and his life was given to that country from then on.

Hodgson collected Sanskrit manuscripts on Buddhism and studied Nepal's natural history, antiquities and aboriginal tribes. By 1839 he had sent eighty-nine papers to the Asiatic Society of Bengal. Resident from 1833, he won a treaty in 1839 after stormy years at a faithless court. His forward policy was upset by Lord Ellenborough, and after disobeying instructions he was recalled in 1843 and resigned.
britannica-1911-hogg-thomas-jefferson:
Thomas Jefferson Hogg (1792–1862) was an English man of letters, born at Norton, Durham, on the 24th of May 1792. He was educated at Durham grammar school and University College, Oxford. There he became the intimate friend of the poet Shelley. In 1811 both were expelled for refusing to disown a link with the pamphlet The Necessity of Atheism.

Hogg was sent to study law at York, then renewed the friendship with Shelley in London in 1813, after a breach over Harriet Shelley. He was called to the bar in 1817 and became a revising barrister. In 1844 he inherited £2,000 under Shelley's will. In 1855, at the wish of the poet's family, he began Shelley's biography. Two volumes appeared in 1858, but they were far more autobiography than biography. Shelley's people then refused him more material, and the life stopped. He died in August 1862.
britannica-1911-holden-hubert-ashton:
Hubert Ashton Holden (1822–1896) was an English classical scholar, of an old Staffordshire family. He was educated at King Edward's school, Birmingham, and Trinity College, Cambridge, where he was senior classic in 1845 and fellow in 1847. He was vice-principal of Cheltenham College from 1853 to 1858, then headmaster of Queen Elizabeth's school, Ipswich, until 1883. He died in London in December 1896.

Holden published school editions of parts of Cicero, Thucydides, Xenophon and Plutarch, and larger editions of Cicero's De officiis and the Octavius of Minucius Felix. His best-known works are classroom tools: the Foliorum silvula (1852), English extracts for translation into Greek and Latin verse; Folia silvulae, translations of the same; and Foliorum centuriae, prose extracts. Widely used in English schools, these books shaped how Latin and Greek composition was taught.
britannica-1911-holland-henry-fox-1st-ba:
Henry Fox, 1st Baron Holland (1705–1774), was an English statesman, second son of Sir Stephen Fox, born in 1705. He inherited much of his father's wealth, squandered it, and fled to the Continent from his creditors. A countrywoman of fortune kept him there, and he came home able to enter parliament in 1735, as member for Hindon. He became Walpole's favourite pupil, matching him in the worst political arts.

Fox could hold his own in debate against Pitt himself. He was surveyor-general of works, a lord of the treasury, and secretary at war in 1746. In 1755 he became leader of the House of Commons and secretary of state under Newcastle. Shut out of the cabinet in 1757, he took the paymastership and piled up a vast fortune in the war years. In 1762 he led the House under Bute and carried the treaty of Paris by cajolery and corruption.
britannica-1911-holland-henry-richard-va:
Henry Richard Vassall Fox, 3rd Baron Holland (1773–1840), was born at Winterslow House in Wiltshire in 1773. His father, Stephen Fox, died the next year, and his uncle was C. J. Fox, to whom he stayed loyal in politics all his life. He was educated at Eton and Christ Church, Oxford, where Canning and Hookham Frere were his friends. In 1791 he visited Paris and met Lafayette and Talleyrand.

At Florence Holland met Lady Webster, who left her husband for him; after her divorce they married in July 1797. He had taken his seat in the Lords in 1796, and for years he almost formed the Whig party in the upper house alone. His protests against Tory measures were later gathered as the Opinions of Lord Holland. In 1800 he was allowed to take the name Vassall, and after 1807 he signed himself Vassall Holland.
britannica-1911-honeymoon: The honeymoon is the first month after marriage. Two origins are offered for the word. Lord Avebury holds that the couple's seclusion in this period survives from marriage by capture. It matches the time a husband kept his wife hidden, so she could not appeal to her kin. Others point to the moon, which wanes as soon as it is full, just as the pair's fondness is said to do. On that reading the word need not mark any fixed span of time.
britannica-1911-hood-of-avalon-arthur-wi:
Arthur William Acland Hood, Baron Hood of Avalon (1824–1901), was an English admiral, born on the 14th of July 1824. He was the younger son of Sir Alexander Hood, second baronet, and grandson of Captain Alexander Hood, who fell in the Mars in 1798. At twelve Hood entered the navy, and while still a boy he saw active service off Spain and Syria.

After the gunnery course in the Excellent, he went to the Cape of Good Hope as gunnery mate of the President, and was made lieutenant in January 1846. He served in the Arethusa in the Mediterranean, and the Russian war lengthened that commission. In November 1854 he was made commander for his work with the naval brigade before Sebastopol. In 1856 he took the Acorn brig to China, shared in destroying the junks in Fatshan creek and in the capture of Canton, and won his post-captain's commission in February 1858.
britannica-1911-hopfen-hans-von:
Hans von Hopfen, who lived from 1835 to 1904, was a German poet and novelist born at Munich. The 1911 Britannica article says he was born on the third of January 1835. He read law at first. In 1858 his clear gift for verse won him a place in the circle of young poets around King Maximilian the Second. From then on he gave his life to letters. His first book came out in 1862.

After travel in Italy, France, and Austria, Hopfen took a post with a Schiller fund in 1865. He settled in Vienna, then moved to Berlin the next year. His lyric poems show real talent and a mind of his own. But his fame rests on his novels, five of which are named in the entry. His tales of the Tirol, printed in 1884 and 1885, are held the best of his short work.
britannica-1911-hopken-anders-johan-coun:
Anders Johan von Hopken is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Hopken was a Swedish statesman who lived from 1712 to 1789. His father was a founder of the Hat party in Swedish politics. When the Hats came to power in 1738, the younger Hopken gained a seat on the secret committee of the diet. He also served as an envoy in talks with Russia.

The article says his sway was greatest in the diet of 1746 and 1747. Through his efforts the estates issued a bold protest against Russian pressure on the crown prince. That stand restored the fading prestige of his party. In 1751 he became prime minister and ran Swedish foreign policy for nine years. He was made a count in 1762. His noble style as a writer earned him the name of the Swedish Tacitus.
britannica-1911-hopton-ralph-hopton-baro:
Royalist commander Ralph Hopton, born in fifteen ninety eight, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was son of Robert Hopton of Witham in Somerset. He seems to have been schooled at Lincoln College, Oxford. He served in German wars in his youth.

At his coronation, Charles the First made him a Knight of the Bath. In Parliament he sat for Bath, Somerset, and Wells in turn. At first he opposed royal policy, but he shifted to a staunch royal stance. When civil war began he was made a senior commander in the west. He rallied Cornwall to the royal cause, then carried the war into Devonshire. In sixteen forty three he won a brilliant victory at Stratton.
britannica-1911-horapollon:
Horapollon was a Greek grammarian from Egypt who flourished in the fourth century after Christ. The 1911 Britannica entry sums up what old sources say of his work. He came from Phaenebythis in the district of Panopolis and lived under Theodosius the First. Writers credit him with notes on Sophocles, Alcaeus, and Homer, and a work on sacred places.

Two books on hieroglyphics bear his name and claim to be turned from Egyptian into Greek. The poor Greek and late parts of the text make scholars doubt the claim in full. Still, some signs in the books match true values from old use. The entry lists the main printed editions and studies for readers who want more.
britannica-1911-horizon: Horizon is the circle where sky and earth seem to meet. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica takes the word from a Greek term for dividing. At sea the line is sharp and is called the sea horizon. In astronomy the horizon is a great circle set at right angles to the plumb line. The entry then defines the dip of the horizon at sea. That dip comes from the round shape of the earth and the height of the eye above water.
britannica-1911-hotham-william-hotham-1s:
William Hotham, 1st Baron Hotham (1736–1813), was a British admiral, descended from Sir John Hotham. He was schooled at Westminster and the Royal Naval Academy at Portsmouth, and entered the navy in 1751. Most of his midshipman's time was spent in American waters. In 1755 he became lieutenant in Sir Edward Hawke's flagship St George, and soon rose to small commands.

In the Syren he fought a sharp action with the French Télémaque, a stronger ship, and in the Fortune sloop he took a 26-gun privateer by boarding. From 1757 he commanded frigates. In 1759 his Melampe, with the Southampton, beat two hostile frigates and took one of them. The account follows his long service to flag rank. Its verdict is measured: he lacked the fire of a Nelson or a Jervis, but in subordinate posts he was brave and capable. He was made an Irish peer in 1797 and died in 1813.
britannica-1911-houghton-richard-monckto:
Richard Monckton Milnes, 1st Baron Houghton (1809–1885), was an English poet and man of letters, born in London on the 19th of June 1809. He was educated privately and entered Trinity College, Cambridge, in 1827. There he joined the famous Apostles club, whose members then included Tennyson, Hallam and Trench. After his degree he travelled, studied at Bonn, and went on to Italy and Greece.

In 1834 Milnes published Memorials of a Tour in some Parts of Greece. He returned to London in 1837 and entered parliament as member for Pontefract. His time in the Commons was marked by strenuous work on many causes. The long life follows his poems, his travels and his wide circle of friends, which made his house a meeting place for the writers of the age. His son's edition of his life and letters is named among the sources at the close.
britannica-1911-howard-of-effingham-will:
William Howard, 1st Baron Howard of Effingham (c. 1510–1573), was an English lord high admiral, son of the 2nd duke of Norfolk. He was a favourite of Henry VIII, served as deputy earl marshal at Anne Boleyn's coronation, and went on missions to Scotland and France. In 1541 he was charged with abetting his kinswoman Queen Catherine Howard, convicted of misprision of treason, and pardoned.

In 1552 Howard became governor of Calais, and in 1553 lord high admiral. Mary created him Baron Howard of Effingham in 1554 for his defence of London in Wyatt's rebellion. He had befriended the princess Elizabeth, yet his standing with the navy shielded him from Mary's anger. Under Elizabeth he held great influence and several high posts. His son, the second baron, became the famous sea commander later made earl of Nottingham. The short life sets the father in place before that greater fame.
britannica-1911-humboldt-karl-wilhelm-vo:
Karl Wilhelm von Humboldt lived from 1767 to 1835 and was a German philologist. The 1911 Britannica life adds that he was a man of letters too. He was the elder brother of the more famed Alexander von Humboldt. Born at Potsdam in June 1767, he was schooled at Berlin and Gottingen. At Jena he formed a close, lifelong bond with Schiller the poet.

He wed a lady of birth and wealth, Fraulein von Dacherode, in time. In 1802 Prussia sent him as its envoy to Rome in Italy. There he brought out a poem called Rom on that great city. His essay on Goethe's Hermann und Dorothea had come in 1800. That piece placed him in the first rank on the study of beauty.
britannica-1911-hungerford-walter-hunger:
Walter Hungerford is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Hungerford was an English soldier who died in 1449. He came from a Wiltshire family. His father had served as speaker of the House of Commons in 1377. Walter also served as speaker, but he won more fame as a warrior and envoy.

The article notes his service at Agincourt on the field of battle. It also notes his work at church and peace meetings abroad. He helped carry out the will of King Henry the Fifth. He sat on the council under Henry the Sixth. He became a baron in 1426 and lord treasurer soon after. Gifts from him still stood at Heytesbury, the family home. The text then follows his son and grandson in brief.
britannica-1911-hunter-sir-william-wilso:
William Wilson Hunter, who lived from 1840 to 1900, was a British writer on India. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica credits his vast survey work. He was born at Glasgow in July 1840. He studied there and in Paris and Bonn, and topped the India service exam in 1862.

Posted to a far Bengal district, Hunter gathered local lore and records. His Annals of Rural Bengal woke wide interest in Indian rule. In 1869 the viceroy asked him to plan a full survey of the empire. Local district books grew under his hand into 128 volumes. He squeezed that mass into the Imperial Gazetteer of India. It came out in nine volumes in 1881 and grew in later editions.
britannica-1911-hutten-philipp-von:
The 1911 Britannica article on Philipp von Hutten (about 1511-1546) gives the life of a German knight. He was a relative of Ulrich von Hutten. He spent some early years at the court of the emperor Charles the Fifth. Later he joined a band of adventurers bound for Venezuela. They sailed to exploit the land for the Welser family of Augsburg.

The party landed at Coro in February 1535. Hutten marched inland with its leader in search of treasure. After that leader died in 1540, Hutten became captain-general of Venezuela. He then vanished into the interior for five years. On his return a Spaniard held his post. Hutten was seized in April 1546 and put to death. His letters and a narrative of his adventures survive.
britannica-1911-hydra-constellation:
Hydra, a group of stars in the southern sky, is the subject of a short article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Old sky watchers named it early: Eudoxus spoke of it in the fourth century before Christ, and Aratus in the third. Ptolemy listed 27 of its stars, Tycho Brahe listed 19, and Hevelius listed 31.

The article picks out the sights worth a look. One is a cloud of gas whose light matches a star of the eighth size. Another is a triple star, with two yellow stars and a blue one. Two stars in the group change in brightness over time. One runs a long cycle of 425 days, swinging from the fourth size to near the tenth. The other changes with no fixed rhythm, within a smaller range.
britannica-1911-hyperion:
Hyperion is a Titan in Greek myth, set out in a short 1911 Britannica entry on names and tales. He was a son of Uranus and Gaea in the old theogony of Hesiod. By that line he was father of Helios, the sun god of Greece. Poets also use Hyperion as a name for Helios or Apollo themselves.

Shakespeare uses the name in Hamlet as a mark of radiant beauty in contrast. The entry weighs three views on what the name first meant in Greek. One takes it as he who moves above, though the vowel length speaks against it. Others read it as a family style name, like that of Cronus kin.
britannica-1911-imposition:
Imposition comes from the Latin imponere, to place or lay upon. In church use it is the laying on of hands by a bishop at confirmation and ordination. The act marks that a special gift is given, or that the person is set apart for a special service or work.

The word also covers the levying of a heavy or unfair tax or duty, and a penalty in general. From that sense it is used for a punishment task set for a schoolboy. From impose in the sense of passing something off on a person, it also means a trick or cheat. In printing, it is the placing of pages of type in the forme, a stage between setting the type and printing.
britannica-1911-incantation:
Incantation is the use of words, spoken, sung, or chanted, most often as a set formula, to win a result through their supposed magic power. The word comes from the Latin incantare, to chant a magic formula. Latin use is very old, and a line of the Twelve Tables quoted by Pliny already speaks of chanting a harmful spell.

From the Old French form come enchant and enchantment, words tied at root to magic. The early priests of Assyria and Babylonia were skilled in the art, and Akkadian spells have survived. Egypt and India used many formulas of sacred magic, and the Vedic mantras stand close to like forms in other lands. One common use was healing wounds, found in the Odyssey, in the Kalevala, and in folk tales across Europe. Songs were also sung to win back an unfaithful lover.
britannica-1911-injunction:
An injunction is, in English law, a court order that binds a party to hold back from a set act. The 1911 Britannica entry draws the word from a Latin verb that means to fasten on, or to lay a charge on a man. In plain terms it is a command from a judge.

The entry tells how the tool began in the court of chancery. That court did not block the work of rival courts head on. It sent its order to the man, and so gained the same end by a side path. In time the courts were reshaped, and the order came to be used in all parts of the high court alike. The piece notes that, though framed as a bar, such an order can act as a plain command to do a thing.
britannica-1911-ion:
Ion of Chios, a Greek poet who lived in the age of Pericles, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica article. At an early age he went to Athens, where he met Aeschylus. He was a great fan of Cimon and a foe of Pericles. He later met Sophocles on his home isle at the time of the Samian war.

Ion's first tragedy was staged between 452 and 449 before Christ. In 429 he placed third to Euripides and Iophon. In a later year he won both the tragic and song prizes at once. To mark the win he gave a jar of Chian wine to each Athens citizen. He wrote in many forms, from hymns to tales of the past.
britannica-1911-iophon: Iophon is a notice in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica on a Greek tragic poet, son of Sophocles. He took second prize to Euripides in 428 BC. In the Frogs, Aristophanes calls him the only good tragic poet left, yet hints his father helped him. He wrote fifty plays, of which only scraps survive. He is said to have accused his father of being unable to manage his affairs. Sophocles cleared himself by reading the famous chorus from the Oedipus at Colonus.
britannica-1911-ixion:
