Ixion, in Greek tale, was son of a king of a folk in Thessaly and spouse of Dia. By use he pledged a rich bride gift to his wifes father. When that man claimed the gift, Ixion slew him in a base plot. Mad grief seized him as his pay, till the chief god made him clean and took him as guest.

He then sought to wrong the chief gods wife, but a cloud took her place and bore him the horse men. The chief god bound him on a wheel of fire that rolls with no end. Some read him as the sun in its round path.
britannica-1911-james-i-of-aragon:
James the First of Aragon, called the Conqueror, is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. James was born at Montpellier in 1208, son of Peter the Second. His mother was Mary of Montpellier, of imperial descent. His father's troubled marriage hangs over the opening of the entry.

Peter tried to cast off his wife, and she fled to Rome, where she died in 1213. To calm the northern crusaders, Peter planned a marriage for his son. The boy was placed in the care of Simon de Montfort in 1211. But Peter was forced to fight the very crusaders he had courted. He fell at the battle of Muret in September 1213. Montfort, the entry notes, was glad to hold the young heir in his hands. Readers see a conqueror's reign begin in captivity and loss.
britannica-1911-james-of-hereford-henry-:
Henry James, 1st Baron James of Hereford (1828– ), was an English lawyer and statesman. He was born at Hereford on 30 October 1828, the son of a surgeon. He was schooled at Cheltenham College and won prizes at the Inner Temple. He was called to the bar in 1852 and joined the Oxford circuit, where he soon stood out. In 1867 he was made postman of the court of exchequer, and in 1869 he became a Queen's Counsel.

At the poll of 1868 James won a seat in parliament for Taunton as a Liberal. He kept that seat till 1885, when he was returned for Bury. His speeches in the talks on the Judicature Act in 1872 drew note. In 1873 he was made solicitor-general, and then attorney-general, and he was knighted.
britannica-1911-jargoon:
Jargoon, a gem form of the stone zircon, is the topic of a short earth entry in the 1911 Britannica. Stone men use the name for zircons fine for gems but not red in hue. Red stones of that kind bear the name hyacinth as a class. The word rests on an Arab word for zircon as its root. Fine stones may be green, brown, or yellow in tint.

Some stones hold no hue at all to the eye. Heat can bleach a hued stone clear and add to its shine. Pale stones from Ceylon were once sold as Matura diamonds in trade. Strong bend of light gives the stone a near diamond shine. Its weight for size sets it apart from tourmaline, a like gem.
britannica-1911-jeffreys-george-jeffreys:
George Jeffreys, 1st Baron Jeffreys (1648-1689), was lord chancellor of England, and his early rise is traced in an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Acton Park in Denbighshire, son of a Welsh country gentleman, he was schooled at Shrewsbury, Saint Paul's, and Westminster. He left Cambridge without a degree and entered the Inner Temple in 1663.

The entry warns that records of his life come almost wholly from hostile sources, so tales of his wild youth need care. He showed great talent from childhood, made friends among court attorneys in city taverns, and rose fast. Within three years of his call to the bar in 1668 he was elected common serjeant.
britannica-1911-john-i-of-aragon: John the First of Aragon is a brief royal entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. John, king of Aragon, lived from 1350 to 1395. He was the son of Peter the Fourth by his third wife, Eleanor of Sicily, and was born on the twenty-seventh of December 1350. He died by a fall from his horse, the same end met by his namesake and cousin of Castile. The entry calls him a man of small character whose one noted taste was for artificial verse.
britannica-1911-john-ii-of-aragon:
John the Second, king of Aragon, who lived from 1397 to 1479, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a son of Ferdinand the First and Eleanor of Albuquerque. The entry calls him one of the most stirring and least scrupulous kings of the fifteenth century. In youth he was one of the princes of Aragon who meddled in the feuds of Castile.

Till middle life John served as lieutenant general in Aragon for his brother, King Alphonso the Fifth. In old age he fought without pause against his Aragonese and Catalan subjects and against Louis the Eleventh of France. He also paved the way for the marriage of his son Ferdinand with Isabella of Castile. His troubles were bound up with strife in his own family, above all his jealousy of his son Charles, prince of Viana.
britannica-1911-johnston-joseph-egglesto:
Joseph Eggleston Johnston lived from 1807 to 1891 and was a Confederate general. The 1911 Britannica life opens near Farmville in Virginia, his birth place. His father Peter had fought in the War of Independence as a youth. That father later rose as a jurist of note in Virginia. His mother was a niece of the famed Patrick Henry of old.

Johnston graduated at West Point in the same class as Robert Lee. In 1829 he was made a brevet lieutenant of artillery there. He served in the Black Hawk and the Seminole wars in arms. In 1837 he left the army to work as a civil engineer. A year later he rejoined as a topographical engineer with rank.
britannica-1911-jomini-antoine-henri-bar:
Antoine Henri Jomini was a general in French and then in Russian service, and one of the most famed writers on the art of war. Born in a Swiss town where his father was a town officer, he longed for a war life from youth. The loss of the Swiss regiments of France in the revolt blocked that path.

For a time he was a clerk in a bank house in Paris, till revolt in his own land opened a door. At nineteen he won a post on the Swiss staff, and at near twenty one he led a battalion of troops. At peace he went back to trade in Paris, but his true work was a great book on the vast moves of war, put out in the next years. Brought to a famed marshal, he served in a great campaign as a free aide.
britannica-1911-josika-miklos-baron:
Baron Miklós Jósika (1794–1865) was a Hungarian novelist, born on the 28th of April 1794 at Torda in Transylvania. After legal studies at Kolozsvár he entered a cavalry regiment in 1811 and served in the Italian campaign. He was made lieutenant on the field of Mincio in February 1814, and marched into Paris with the allied troops.

He left the army in 1818 and turned to farming and writing on his estate at Szurdok. His novel Abafi, published in 1836, founded his fame with its vivid picture of Transylvania under Sigismund Bátori. He sat in the Transylvanian diet and joined the Hungarian Academy of Sciences and the Kisfaludy Society. He backed the union of Transylvania with Hungary. By the rising of 1848 he had produced about sixty volumes of novels and romances. He aided the rising in the diet and in print, and sat on the committee of national defence.
britannica-1911-josippon:
Josippon is a 1911 Britannica article on a popular chronicle of Jewish history. The chronicle runs from Adam to the age of Titus. It is ascribed to an author called Josippon, or Joseph ben Gorion. At one time that name was identified with Josephus, the historian.

The name is perhaps, the text says, a worn form of Hegesippus. From Hegesippus, one scholar held, the author drew much of his material. The chronicle was most likely compiled in Hebrew early in the tenth century. Its maker was a Jewish native of south Italy. The first edition was printed at Mantua in 1476. Josippon later appeared in many forms. One popular form was in Yiddish, with quaint pictures. The chronicle is more legendary than historical, the article warns. Yet it may still hold some good and even ancient sources within it.
britannica-1911-jouffroy-theodore-simon:
Théodore Simon Jouffroy, a French philosopher, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. He was born at Pontets, near Mouthe, in the department of Doubs. His father was a tax-gatherer. In his tenth year he was sent to an uncle at Pontarlier. There he began his classical studies.

At Dijon his written work caught the eye of an inspector. That man had him placed, in 1814, in the normal school at Paris. There he came under the sway of Victor Cousin. In 1817 he was made assistant professor of philosophy at the normal and Bourbon schools. Three years later he was thrown on his own resources. He began a course of lectures in his own house. He formed links with leading journals of the day. The article traces a scholar who made his way by teaching and the pen.
britannica-1911-kalckreuth-friedrich-ado:
Friedrich Adolf, Count von Kalckreuth (1737–1818), was a Prussian soldier. He entered the Gardes du Corps in 1752 and in 1758 became aide to Frederick the Great's brother, Prince Henry, serving with him through the later stages of the Seven Years' War. At the battle of Freiberg in September 1762 he won such credit that Frederick made him a major.

A breach with Prince Henry in 1766 left him for years in quiet retirement. He came back as a colonel in the War of the Bavarian Succession and rose again under Frederick William II. He shone in the invasion of Holland in 1787 and by 1792 was a count and a general. Under Brunswick he played a marked part at Valmy in 1792, at the siege and taking of Mainz in 1793, and at Kaiserslautern in 1794. In the campaigns against Napoleon in 1806 his role, at Auerstädt and after, was a marked one for good or ill.
britannica-1911-kalckreuth-leopold-count:
Leopold, Count von Kalckreuth (1855– ), was a German painter, a direct descendant of the field marshal Friedrich Adolf von Kalckreuth. He was born at Düsseldorf and had his first training at Weimar from his father, the landscape painter Count Stanislaus. He went on to study at the academies of Weimar and Munich.

He painted some portraits strong in expression. His chief work shows, with stern realism, the dull round of life among coast fishing folk and peasants in the fields. His colours are joyless, almost sad, and his handling bears the mark of the impressionists. He was one of the founders of the secession movement. From 1885 to 1890 he taught at the Weimar art school, then retired to his estate in Silesia to paint country life. In 1895 he became a professor at Karlsruhe.
britannica-1911-kemeny-zsigmond-baron:
Baron Zsigmond Kemény (1816–1875) was a Hungarian author, of a noble but fallen family. In 1837 he studied law at Marosvásárhely, but soon gave himself wholly to journalism and letters. His first work, an unfinished study of the causes of the disaster of Mohács, drew much notice in 1840.

In the same year he studied natural history and anatomy at Vienna. In 1841, with Lajos Kovács, he edited the Transylvanian newspaper Erdélyi Hiradó. He took an active part in provincial politics and backed the principles of Count Stephen Széchenyi. In 1846 he moved to Pest, where a pamphlet on partisanship and its cure had already made him famous. He mixed with the chief moderate reformers and worked for a time on the Pesti Hirlap. That year he brought out his first great novel, Pál Gyulay.
britannica-1911-kennington: Kennington is a district in the south of London, within the borough of Lambeth. A royal palace stood there until the reign of Henry VII. Kennington Common, now covered by Kennington Park, was the site of a gallows until the end of the 18th century. It was also the meeting place set for the great Chartist demonstration of the 10th of April 1848. Kennington Oval is the ground of the Surrey County Cricket Club.
britannica-1911-kensington:
Kensington is a western borough of London. Paddington and Westminster bound it on the northeast, Chelsea on the southeast, Fulham on the southwest, and Hammersmith on the northwest. Its people numbered 176,628 in 1901. It takes in Kensal Green in part, Notting Hill in the north centre, Earl's Court in the southwest, and Brompton in the southeast.

A broad but ill defined area next to Brompton is commonly called South Kensington, though West Kensington lies in Fulham. The name appears in early forms as Chenesitun and Kenesitune. Its origin is obscure. It has been tied to a Saxon royal seat, to a family named Chenesi, and to a word for wood. The forest that first covered the district could still be traced in Tudor times. The long entry walks the borough street by street through its squares, museums, and great houses.
britannica-1911-kenton:
Kenton is a city and the county seat of Hardin county, Ohio, on the Scioto river, 60 miles northwest of Columbus. Its people numbered 6852 in 1900 and 7185 in 1910. Three railways serve it. It is built on the watershed between Lake Erie and the Gulf of Mexico, here about 1000 feet above the sea.

The Ohio Central railway has shops in the city, and its factories make hardware. The town owns and runs its own waterworks. Kenton was named in honour of Simon Kenton, the famed scout and Indian fighter of the border wars in Kentucky and Ohio. It was laid out and made the county seat in 1833, and it was chartered as a city in 1885. The entry is a short town note: a river site, a railway junction, one industry, and a frontier name carried into a settled county town.
britannica-1911-kenyon-lloyd-kenyon-1st-:
Lloyd Kenyon, 1st Baron Kenyon (1732–1802), was lord chief justice of England. He came on his father's side from an old Lancashire family, and his mother was the daughter of a small landholder in Wales. He was born at Gredington in Flintshire on the 5th of October 1732 and schooled at Ruthin grammar school. At fifteen he was bound to an attorney at Nantwich in Cheshire.

In 1750 he entered Lincoln's Inn in London, and in 1756 he was called to the bar. For several years he was almost without work. He used the leisure to take notes of cases argued in the King's Bench, which he later published. By answering the cases of his friend John Dunning, the later Lord Ashburton, he slowly became known to the attorneys. His rise then was swift, and in 1780 he was made king's counsel.
britannica-1911-kervyn-de-lettenhove-con:
Constantine Bruno Kervyn de Lettenhove is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a Belgian historian who lived from 1817 to 1891. He was born at Saint Michel near Bruges. He belonged to the Catholic party and sat in the Chamber for Eecloo. In 1870 he joined the cabinet as minister of the interior.

The article says his time in office was short. A tainted appointment brought riots, and the cabinet was forced to resign. He then gave himself wholly to writing and history. He had won fame with a book on Froissart, crowned by the French Academy. He edited series of chronicles on Belgium under the dukes of Burgundy. He also wrote on ties between the Low Countries and England under Philip the Second. He died in his home village in 1891.
britannica-1911-keswick-convention:
The Keswick Convention is a yearly summer meet held in the town of that name in the lake country of England. Its chief aim is to spur plain holy living, by meets for prayer, talk, and face to face speech. The 1911 Britannica entry stresses that it shuts out no church group.

Most of its backers come from one wing of the Church of England. It began in a quiet way, led by the vicar of Keswick and a friend, and first met in the mid eighteen seventies. It grew fast in size and sway in a few years, despite jabs at the claim to pure lives by some of its chiefs and at its new ways. Its folk take a deep share in missions to far lands.
britannica-1911-king-of-ockham-peter-kin:
Peter King, 1st Baron King of Ockham (1669–1734), was lord chancellor of England. He was born at Exeter in 1669. In his youth he took a keen part in the study of the early church. In 1691 he put out, with no name, a book on the rule and worship of the first church. That work drew the eye of his cousin, the thinker John Locke. On Locke's advice, his father sent him to the university of Leiden for near three years.

King entered the Middle Temple in 1694 and was called to the bar in 1698. In 1700 he was returned to parliament for Beer Alston in Devonshire. He became recorder of Glastonbury in 1705 and recorder of London in 1708. From 1714 to 1725 he was chief justice of the common pleas.
britannica-1911-kingsdown-thomas-pembert:
Thomas Pemberton Leigh, Baron Kingsdown, was born in London on 11 February 1793 and is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the eldest son of Thomas Pemberton, a chancery barrister. Called to the bar at Lincoln Inn in 1816, he built a rich equity practice at once. He sat in parliament for Rye and later for Ripon.

Of a shy bent, he seldom spoke in debates in the House. Yet in 1838 he played a large part in the case of Stockdale against Hansard, upholding the rights of parliament. In 1841 he became attorney general for the duchy of Cornwall. A kin gift of Wigan estates worth some 15000 pounds a year led him to add the name Leigh. For near twenty years he gave his force to the judicial work of the privy council.
britannica-1911-kleist-ewald-christian-v:
Ewald Christian von Kleist (1715-1759) was a German poet who served as a Prussian officer, and this 1911 Britannica entry joins the two halves of his life. He was born at Zeblin in Pomerania and schooled by the Jesuits and at the gymnasium in Danzig. In 1731 he went to the university of Königsberg to study law and mathematics. On finishing, he entered the Danish army and became an officer in 1736.

Frederick the Second called him back to Prussia in 1740 and made him a lieutenant at Potsdam. He stood out at the battle of Mollwitz and the siege of Neisse, rose to captain in 1749 and major in 1756. At Kunersdorf in August 1759 he was mortally wounded leading an attack.
britannica-1911-knight-john-buxton:
John Buxton Knight (1843–1908) was an English landscape painter, born at Sevenoaks in Kent. He began work as a schoolmaster, with painting as a hobby. Later he gave himself to art full time. In 1861 his first picture was hung at the Academy. He was above all an open-air painter. He made constant sketching tours to the most scenic spots in England, and all his pictures were painted out of doors.

Knight died at Dover on the 2nd of January 1908. In the month after his death the Chantrey trustees bought his "December's Bareness Everywhere" for the nation. Most of his best work had passed into private hands. Mr Iceton of Putney held "White Walls of Old England" and "Hereford Cathedral." Mr Walter Briggs held "Pinner." Mr S. M. Phillips of Wrotham held two water-colours of Richmond Bridge.
britannica-1911-koksharov-nikolai-ivanov:
Nikolai Ivanovich von Koksharov (1818–1893) was a Russian mineralogist and a major-general in the Russian army, born at Ust-Kamenogork in Tomsk on the 5th of December 1818. He was trained at the military school of mines in St Petersburg. At the age of twenty-two he was chosen to go with Murchison and De Verneuil, and later with De Keyserling, on their geological survey of the Russian Empire.

Koksharov then gave his working life to mineralogy and mining. He became director of the Institute of Mines, and in 1865 director of the Imperial Mineralogical Society of St Petersburg. He wrote many papers on minerals such as euclase, zircon, epidote, orthite and monazite for the academies of St Petersburg and Vienna and for German journals. His separate works include the Materialen zur Mineralogie Russlands in 10 volumes (1853–1891) and lectures on mineralogy in 1865. He died in St Petersburg on the 3rd of January 1893.
britannica-1911-kolliker-rudolph-albert-:
Rudolph Albert von Kölliker (1817–1905) was a Swiss anatomist and physiologist, born at Zürich on the 6th of July 1817. He studied at Zürich, Bonn and Berlin, where Johannes Müller and Henle taught him. He took a degree in philosophy at Zürich in 1841 and in medicine at Heidelberg in 1842. In 1847 Würzburg called him as professor, and there he stayed for life, dying on the 2nd of November 1905.

Kölliker's name is bound up with the microscope. He began work just as the study of fine structure in living things was reviving, and he made the new tool serve anatomy and physiology alike. In embryology he was among the first to bring in the new methods of hardening, cutting thin sections and staining. The great strides of embryology in the later 19th century are tied to his name.
britannica-1911-kotzebue-otto-von:
Otto von Kotzebue (1787–1846) was a Russian navigator, born at Reval on the 30th of December 1787. Trained at the St Petersburg school of cadets, he sailed with Krusenstern on the voyage of 1803–1806. As a lieutenant he commanded the brig Rurick. With only twenty-seven men he set out on the 30th of July 1815 to seek an Arctic passage and explore little-known parts of Oceania.

Sailing by Cape Horn, Kotzebue found the Romanzov, Rurik and Krusenstern islands, then worked north along America's north-west coast. There he found and named Kotzebue Sound and Krusenstern Cape. Ill health forced him home, and he reached the Neva on the 3rd of August 1818 with many new plants and much new knowledge of native peoples. In 1823 he led a second voyage in two warships, carrying troops to Kamchatka, and came back to Kronstadt on the 10th of July 1826.
britannica-1911-kumaon:
Kumaon, or Kumaun, is a division of British India in the United Provinces, with its headquarters at Naini Tal. It is a great Himalayan tract, with two strips of low land at the foot of the hills, the Tarai and the Bhabhar. Its area is 13,725 square miles, and in 1901 it held 1,207,030 people. The low strips were dense forest until 1850; since then clearings have drawn many settlers from the hills. The rest is a maze of mountains, with over thirty peaks above 18,000 feet.

Its rivers, the Sarda, the Pindar and the Kailganga among them, cut valleys of great depth. The forests yield chir pine, cypress, fir, alder and sal, and the rocks hold mines of iron, copper, gypsum, lead and asbestos, none fully worked. Rain on the outer range is twice that of the inner hills, 80 inches against 40. Snow falls on the high ridges every winter.
britannica-1911-kyneton: Kyneton is a town of Dalhousie county, Victoria, Australia, on the river Campaspe, 56 miles by rail N.N.W. of Melbourne. In 1901 it held 3274 people. It is the centre of a rich farming and grazing district, with important stock sales and a yearly show of stock. Rich gold quartz reefs lie near the town. Kyneton stands 1687 feet above the sea, and its scenery, with fine waterfalls, draws visitors in summer.
britannica-1911-la-gueronniere-louis-eti:
Louis Étienne Arthur Dubreuil Hélion, vicomte de La Guéronnière (1816–1875), was a French politician of a noble Poitevin family. He drew close to Lamartine and wrote much for his paper Le Bien Public. He later wrote for La Presse and in 1850 edited Le Pays. A portrait sketch of Louis Napoleon in that journal split him from Lamartine, and he bound himself to the prince president's cause.

Under the Empire La Guéronnière sat on the council of state (1853) and in the senate (1861). He was ambassador at Brussels in 1868 and at Constantinople in 1870, and a grand officer of the legion of honour from 1866. He died at Paris on the 23rd of December 1875. His chief works treat the foreign policy of the Empire: La France, Rome et Italie (1851), L'Abandon de Rome (1862) and a study of French policy at home and abroad (1862).
britannica-1911-la-roche-sur-yon:
La Roche-sur-Yon is a town of western France, capital of the department of Vendée. It stands on a rise on the right bank of the Yon, 48 miles S. of Nantes on the railway to Bordeaux. In 1906 the town held 10,666 people and the commune 13,685. Its castle, which may date from before the crusades, was often attacked in the Hundred Years' War and the wars of religion. Louis XIII had it pulled down at last.

In 1804 Napoleon made this place, then of no account, the chief town of a department. The stones of the castle ruins went into the new offices, all built at once on one plan, with a dull sameness. An equestrian statue of Napoleon I stands in a vast square above the town. The town's name changed with the ruling house, Napoleon-Vendée or Bourbon-Vendée, until 1870 restored the old name.
britannica-1911-lacedaemon: Lacedaemon was in historical times an alternative name for Laconia. Homer uses only Lacedaemon, and in some passages seems to mean by it the Achaean citadel, the Therapnae of later times, as against the lower town of Sparta. The name carries the epithets "hollow" and "spacious," and it is probably tied to the Greek lakkos, the Latin lacus, any hollow place. Lacedaemon is now the name of a separate department. Its population in 1907 was 87,106.
britannica-1911-lacuzon:
Lacuzon, from the old French la cuzon, "disturbance," was the name taken by the Franc-Comtois leader Claude Prost (1607–1681). He was born at Longchaumois, in the department of Jura, on the 17th of June 1607. His first military experience came when the French invaded Burgundy in 1636, and he harried their troops from the castles of Montaigu and St Laurent-la-Roche. In 1640–1642 he wasted the frontier districts of Bresse and Bugey with fire and sword.

When Louis XIV invaded Franche-Comté in 1668, Lacuzon could make no effective resistance, but in the second invasion he played an important part. In 1673 he held Salins for some time. After the town capitulated he took refuge in Italy, and he died at Milan on the 21st of December 1681.
britannica-1911-laing-alexander-gordon:
Alexander Gordon Laing (1793–1826), Scottish explorer, the first European to reach Timbuktu, was born at Edinburgh on the 27th of December 1793. Educated by his father and at Edinburgh University, he went in 1811 to Barbados as clerk to his uncle Gabriel Gordon. Through the governor he gained an ensigncy in the York Light Infantry, and in 1822 took a company in the Royal African Corps.

At Sierra Leone the governor sent him into the Mandingo country to open commerce and fight the slave trade. He visited Falaba, capital of the Sulima country, and fixed the source of the Rokell; natives stopped him short of the Niger's source, though he fixed it approximately. After the Ashanti War of 1823–24 he carried the despatches announcing Sir Charles MacCarthy's death. The colonial secretary then sent him by Tripoli toward Timbuktu to clear up the Niger basin's hydrography; he left England in February 1825.
britannica-1911-lambermont-auguste-baron:
Auguste, baron Lambermont (1819–1905), Belgian statesman, was born at Dion-le-Val in Brabant on the 25th of March 1819. His family were small farmers who had held land for three centuries. Meant for the priesthood, he entered the seminary of Floreffe but left it for Louvain University, where he studied law and prepared for military examinations. When the first Carlist war broke out he hurried to Spain. His services were accepted in April 1838: he commanded two cannon, acted as aide-de-camp to Colonel Durando, and won the Cross of the Order of St Ferdinand for intrepidity.

Returning to Belgium, he entered the Ministry for Foreign Affairs in 1842 and served in it for sixty-three years. He was tied to the freeing of the Scheldt. Its Dutch tolls were strangling Belgian trade through Antwerp, the country's only port, and at his own request he was attached to the ministry's commercial branch.
britannica-1911-lamont-johann-von:
Johann von Lamont (1805-1879) was born at Braemar in Scotland. He spent his working life in Germany. His fields were astronomy and earth magnetism. Sent at twelve to a Scottish house of monks at Regensburg, he joined the Bogenhausen observatory near Munich in 1827. He became its director in 1835. A Munich chair followed in 1852.

His star work ran to eleven zone lists. Those lists held 34,674 stars. He measured nebulae and clusters in 1836-1837. He also fixed a mass for Uranus from its moons. A magnetic observatory rose at Bogenhausen in 1840 through his push. Wide magnetic surveys followed from 1849 to 1858. A ten-year magnetic period was announced in 1850. Earth currents were reported in 1862.
britannica-1911-lampoon:
Lampoon is a fierce piece of satire in prose or verse, defined in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. A sense of spite and foul play is part of the word itself. Though the word is in use almost only in English, its root seems French. One French guide traces it to a slang verb for drinking in great gulps.

A snatch of an old Paris street song with the cry of lampons is kept as proof. In English the word shows up by 1645 for the scurrilous sheets pasted up in public. Writers such as Tom Brown were masters of the form. His verses on Dryden are quoted as a sharp case. Most lampoons bore no name and no grace of verse. They lived on the sting of the attack.
britannica-1911-land-registration:
Land registration is a legal process tied to the transfer of land. It takes two forms: a register of deeds and a register of title. Both forms serve as tools to help a buyer or lender check a seller's title before a deal is closed. They also guard the buyer's place once the deal is done. The need for such checks is plain, the article says.

With goods, to hold a thing is as a rule proof that one owns it. With land, the man in plain view as holder is most often a mere tenant who pays rent to some other man. Even that man may be no full owner, but a life holder or a trustee with strict limits on his power to sell. Land has also been pledged for loans since old times, while goods seldom are. These facts make the search of title a grave task.
britannica-1911-lannion:
Lannion is a town of north-west France on the right bank of the Léguer, 45 miles west-north-west of St Brieuc by rail, with 5,336 people counted in 1906. The town stands five miles from the river mouth. Its small port ships farm produce out and brings in wine, salt, and timber, while fishing stays busy.

Old houses of the 1400s and 1500s crowd the streets, and the church of St Jean-du-Baly leads the older buildings. On a hill nearby stands the church of Brélevenez, first raised in the 1100s. Saw-milling, tanning, and farm tool making support the town, which also holds a court and a communal college. Some six miles south-east stand the ruins of Tonquédec castle, from about 1400.
britannica-1911-lasaulx-arnold-constanti:
Arnold von Lasaulx, a German student of minerals and rocks who lived from 1839 to 1886, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Castellaun, near Coblenz, in June 1839. He was educated at Berlin and took his doctorate there in 1868. In 1875 he became professor of mineralogy at Breslau.

Five years later Lasaulx moved to Bonn as professor of mineralogy and geology. He won note for his research on minerals and on crystal forms. He was also among the earlier workers in the study of rocks under the microscope. In 1878 he described the eruptive rocks of the Saar and Moselle district. He edited a great work on Mount Etna from the papers of a fellow scholar. His own books include an elements of rock study and a handbook on the same theme. He died at Bonn in January 1886.
britannica-1911-launceston:
Launceston, a market town in Cornwall in England, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands above the river Kensey, a stream of the Tamar, north-west of Plymouth. In 1901 it held a little over four thousand people. Its houses climb a steep south slope, with the keep of an old castle at the top.

The castle, in part Norman, was the seat of the earls of Cornwall. It was besieged more than once in the civil wars, and George Fox was jailed in one tower in 1656. Bits of the old town walls and a south gate still stand. The granite church of Saint Mary Magdalen is rich with carving. A Norman door from a lost priory serves as the entry to a hotel. Trade is chiefly in farm goods, with tanneries and iron works.
britannica-1911-lawson-cecil-gordon:
Cecil Gordon Lawson, an English landscape painter who lived from 1851 to 1882, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the youngest son of a portrait painter of Edinburgh. His mother was known for flower pieces, and two brothers also trained as artists. The family moved to London soon after his birth.

Lawsons first works were studies of fruit and flowers, then scenes by the river at Chelsea. His first Royal Academy piece came in 1870 and won praise from fellow artists. A turn to brighter colour came with work in Wales and Ireland. His large Hop Gardens of England was praised at the Academy in 1876. Real triumph came in 1878 with The Ministers Garden, now in Manchester. His health failed early, yet he worked on to the end. He died at Haslemere in June 1882.
britannica-1911-layamon:
Layamon, an early English poet, is the subject of a long entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He wrote the Brut, a chronicle of Britain based on the work of Wace, a clerk from Jersey. All that is known of Layamon comes from the two surviving copies of his poem, and the entry weighs them with care.

One copy sits close to the lost first text, while the later copy swaps old words for ones that were better known and drops some verse pairs. From the short prologue, readers learn that Layamon was a priest, the son of Leovenath, and that he lived at Areley Kings by the Severn. He loved books, and the entry names the three he prized most, works linked to Bede and to Wace. For students of early English verse, the piece is a guide to both the man and his texts.
britannica-1911-leamington:
Leamington is a borough and health resort in Warwickshire, England, on the Leam river. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica places it near the Avon junction, north west of London. Its people passed twenty six thousand in 1901. Three salt springs feed its pump rooms, baths, and gardens on the river bank.

A town hall, theatre, and assembly room anchor its public life. Churches there are mostly modern in build, the entry notes. Iron foundries and brickworks give the town its main trades. It stayed a small village until baths rose around 1786. Royal favor in 1838 gave it the name Royal Leamington Spa.
britannica-1911-legare-hugh-swinton:
Hugh Swinton Legaré, who lived from 1797 to 1843, was an American lawyer and statesman from Charleston, South Carolina. The 1911 Britannica article says he was born there on the second of January 1797. A childhood illness left his legs stunted, so he turned to books. He left the College of South Carolina in 1814 at the head of his class. He then read law and spent two years in Paris and Edinburgh.

Legaré sat in the state assembly and served as attorney-general of South Carolina. He helped found the Southern Review and wrote on law and letters. Though he backed states' rights, he fought the move to nullify federal law. His grasp of civil law won praise in the Supreme Court. He later served as envoy at Brussels and sat in the national House.
britannica-1911-legitimacy-and-legitimat:
Legitimacy is the status a child gains by being born in lawful wedlock. Legitimation is the means by which that same status is given to a child not so born. Under Roman civil law, a later marriage of the parents made such a child legitimate. Canon law took up that rule, as did most systems on the continent of Europe. Scotland and some American states follow it as well.

Early Germanic codes did not know this method of legitimation. Among the Anglo Saxons a natural child had no rights of inheritance. English clergy once urged the civil law rule, but the barons refused it. At the parliament of Merton in twelve thirty six they said they would not change the laws of England. English law asks only that marriage came before the birth.
britannica-1911-leif-ericsson:
Leif Ericsson, a Norse explorer of Icelandic stock, is the subject of a saga based entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a son of Eric the Red, who founded the Norse settlements in Greenland. In the year 999 Leif sailed from Greenland to the court of King Olaf in Norway. The king sent him back to preach the Christian faith in Greenland.

On the return voyage, storms drove Leif far off course to new lands in the west. There he found self sown wheat, vines, and maple wood, and took samples of each. He also saved men from a shipwreck on that voyage. From his finds and his rescue he gained the name Leif the Lucky. The entry weighs the Saga of Eric the Red against a later, less sound account in the Flatey Book.
britannica-1911-lejeune-louis-francois-b:
Louis Francois Lejeune, who lived from 1776 to 1848, was a French general, painter, and lithographer. The 1911 Britannica entry gives his birth at Versailles and his post as aide to Berthier. He fought through many Napoleonic campaigns and turned them into battle pictures of note. Truth and vigour mark the work, drawn from sketches made on the field itself.

Crowds in London pressed so hard to see his canvases that a rail was set up. Marengo, Lodi, the Pyramids, and Moskawa stand among his chief named works. A canvas of Charles the Tenth entering Paris hangs at Versailles today. A visit to Senefelder workshop in Munich links him to the birth of lithography.
britannica-1911-liliencron-detlev-von:
Detlev von Liliencron (1844-1909) was a German poet and tale writer. Kiel was his birthplace, on 3 June 1844. Army life came first. The campaigns of 1866 and 1870-1871 both left him wounded. He left the service as a captain. A spell in America followed, then Holstein, Munich, and at last Altona and Altrahlstedt near Hamburg.

Fame came with Adjutantenritte in 1883, a book of poems with a fresh note. Plays failed, but tale books came in a steady stream. Eine Sommerschlacht came in 1886 and a novel in 1887. Lyric sets of 1889, 1890, 1893, and 1903 kept his name up. A comic epic, Poggfred, came in 1896. His full works filled fourteen volumes in 1904-1905. He died in July 1909. Uneven gifts are charged against his prose.
britannica-1911-limon:
Limon, or Port Limon, is the chief Atlantic port of Costa Rica. San José lies 103 miles west by south. A bay of the Caribbean holds the town. The count of 1904 gave 3,171 people. Founding came in 1871. A rail line to Puntarenas on the far coast began that same year.

Swamps at the town's back have been filled in. The shallow coral lagoon in front met the same fate. A sea wall guards the port at low-water line. An iron pier takes large ships. A breakwater to Uvita island would make it first-class. Good water flows from the hills above. Near all Costa Rica coffee and bananas pass through Limon by rail. Europe and the United States take those crops. The wide Limon district takes in the whole Atlantic shore, rich banana lands, and San Juan valley woods.
britannica-1911-lingen-ralph-robert-whee:
Ralph Robert Wheeler Lingen, Baron Lingen (1819-1905), was an English civil servant, born at Birmingham, as this 1911 Britannica article recounts. He won scholarship after scholarship at Trinity College, Oxford, took a first in classics in 1840, and was called to the bar in 1847. Instead of practice, he took a post in the Education Office.

In 1849 Lingen succeeded Sir James Kay Shuttleworth as secretary of that office, holding the post until 1869. He was marked by bold judgment in spending and by strict saving, in charge of a chaotic system of state grants to local schools. With Robert Lowe he helped frame the Revised Code of 1862, which brought in payment by results. Shortly before the Education Act of 1870 he moved to become permanent secretary of the treasury.
britannica-1911-livermore-mary-ashton:
Mary Ashton Livermore (1821-1905) was an American reformer born in Boston on 19 December 1821. She studied at the female seminary at Charlestown and then taught French and Latin there. She taught in a plantation school in southern Virginia as well. For three years she ran a school of her own in Duxbury. On her return from Virginia she joined the foes of slavery.

Livermore took an active part in the cause of temperance. In 1845 she wed Daniel Parker Livermore, a Universalist clergyman. In 1857 they moved to Chicago, where she helped him edit a religious weekly. In the Civil War she worked with the United States Sanitary Commission. She set up many aid groups, helped make the North-western Sanitary Fair a success in 1863, and went to army posts and hospitals.
britannica-1911-loch-henry-brougham-loch:
Henry Brougham Loch, 1st Baron Loch (1827-1900), was a British colonial administrator, and his active career fills an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Midlothian, son of a member of Parliament, he left the navy after two years for the East India Company. In 1842 he gained a commission in the Bengal Light Cavalry.

The entry follows his service in the Sikh war, his command of irregular Bulgarian cavalry in the Crimean war, and his post with Lord Elgin's missions to the East. He was present at the taking of Canton and brought home the treaty of Yedo. In 1860 he went back to China and helped negotiate the surrender of the Taku forts.
britannica-1911-lockhart-john-gibson:
John Gibson Lockhart (1794-1854) was a Scottish writer and editor. Cambusnethan manse was his birthplace on 14 July 1794. His father held a church post there, then moved to Glasgow. Weak health cut his school years short. Glasgow University took him before he was twelve.

Greek strength won him a Snell place at Balliol, Oxford. He was not yet fourteen on entry. French, Italian, German, and Spanish all fed his wide store. A first in classics came in 1813. Law study at Edinburgh led to the bar in 1816. A Weimar call on Goethe came in 1817. That year he joined Blackwood's Magazine with John Wilson. Sharp, fierce review work marked the young Tory sheet. His share in that fire is left in no doubt here.
britannica-1911-lockwood-wilton: Wilton Lockwood (born 1861) was an American painter, born at Wilton, Connecticut, on 12 September 1861. He learned as pupil and aide to John La Farge. Paris study came as well. Portraits and flower pieces made his name. The Society of American Artists took him in 1898. The Copley Society of Boston counts him too, as does the National Academy of Design at New York, where he sits as an associate. The entry is a short note of posts and training.
britannica-1911-loudon-ernst-gideon-frei:
Ernst Gideon von Loudon is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was an Austrian soldier born in Livonia in seventeen seventeen. His family came from Scotland long before and his father had served in the Swedish army. The boy joined the Russian army as a cadet at age fifteen.

The entry tracks his move to Austrian service and his rise as a leader of light troops. He won fame in the Seven Years War and rose step by step in rank. The queen gave him a title, a high honour, and land in Bohemia. At one key battle he turned a loss into a clear win for his side.
britannica-1911-lovat-simon-fraser-12th-:
Lovat, Simon Fraser, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of a Scots chief. Born about 1667, he was second son of Thomas Fraser of the Lovat line. The barony dates from about 1460 in the person of Hugh Fraser. Young Simon was schooled at King's College in Aberdeen town.

His letters show good English, smooth French, and a sound grasp of Latin. The entry brands him a born traitor and deceiver in plain words. It doubts he ever felt true loyalty to the Stuart cause. One of his first acts was to raise three hundred clan men. They were to serve William and Mary under his command in arms. His aim was a trained force he could swing to King James.
britannica-1911-lull-raimon:
Lull, Raimon, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of a Catalan writer and mystic. Born at Palma in Majorca about 1235, he wed Bianca Picany young. By his own tale he led a wild life till 1266. Then, five times, he saw a vision of Christ on the cross.

From that change he vowed his life to work among the heathen. He spent nine years on the study of Arabic for that aim. In 1275 his kin had a state officer take charge of his estate. He withdrew to Randa and wrote his great Ars works there. He got the king to build a house at Miramar for tongues. There he taught Arabic and thought for ten years.
britannica-1911-lustration:
Lustration is a religion article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the ways of cleansing and atonement among the Greeks and Romans. Among the Greeks two ideas stand apart. Human nature must cleanse itself of guilt before it may meet God or mix with men, and guilt must be paid for by rites God has shown, lest punishment fall.

The rites of cleansing used water, fire, air, or earth, a branch of a sacred tree such as the laurel, and sacrifice. A worshipper dipped his hand in the holy water at the temple door, and sea water worked better than fresh; the Eleusinian initiates bathed in the sea. Torch, fire, and sulphur cleansed too, as did rubbing with sand and salt. The Greeks sacrificed a pig for cleansing; the Romans, a pig, a sheep, and a bull together.
britannica-1911-lycaon:
Lycaon, in Greek myth, was the son of Pelasgus, the fabled first king of Arcadia. He, or his fifty sons, set a dish of human flesh before Zeus as a guest. The god pushed the dish away in disgust. He then killed the king and his sons with lightning, or turned them into wolves. Some tales say Lycaon killed and served his own son Nyctimus.

The flood in the time of Deucalion was said to have been sent for the sons' sins. Pausanias tells that Lycaon gave a child to Zeus on Mount Lycaeus and was at once turned into a wolf. From this came the tale that a man turned wolf at each yearly rite there. He won back human form if he ate no human flesh for ten years. Arcadia's oldest city, oldest cult, and first culture are all traced to Lycaon.
britannica-1911-lycophron:
Lycophron was a Greek poet and grammarian of the Alexandrian age. The 1911 Britannica life places his birth at Chalcis in Euboea. He thrived at Alexandria under Ptolemy Philadelphus, who reigned from 285. By one account he was the son of Socles of that city. Lycus of Rhegium adopted him, and he bore that man's name in part.

Ptolemy set him to sort the comedies in the great library there. From that work came his treatise On Comedy for scholars of verse. His own works were chiefly tragedies, some twenty by title count. Few scraps of those plays survive to the present age at all. One poem, Alexandra or Cassandra, survives whole at 1,474 lines long.
britannica-1911-lyon-mary-mason:
Mary Mason Lyon, an American teacher who lived from 1797 to 1849, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. She was born on a farm in Franklin county in Massachusetts. At the age of seventeen she began to teach. In 1817 she paid for her own schooling with coin earned at the loom and the wheel.

She moved from school to school, at Ashfield, at Amherst, and at Byfield. At each she taught in the short terms to earn her keep for the next. From 1822 she served as aide at Sanderson Academy for two years. She then taught at a girls' school in New Hampshire led by Zilpah Grant. The school met in summer only, and she taught district schools in the winters. Her path led, step by step, toward the founding work of her later years.
britannica-1911-lyttelton:
Lyttelton is a borough of New Zealand described in a short note in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the port of Christchurch, on the east coast of South Island, on an inlet of Banks Peninsula. Its people numbered 3,941 in 1906.

Steep hills ring it, and a rail line runs through them to Christchurch by a tunnel more than a mile and a half long. Great walls guard the harbour, which has a graving dock for ships of six thousand tons. The rich farm land of Canterbury sends its goods out here, frozen or preserved. The town was the first settlement in the district, in 1850, and was once called Port Cooper and Port Victoria.
britannica-1911-lyttelton-george-lyttelt:
George Lyttelton, first Baron Lyttelton, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Hagley in seventeen hundred nine, he came from a noted family line. He was taught at Eton and Oxford. In seventeen twenty eight he set out on a grand tour of Europe.

The entry tracks his rise in public life after his return to England. He sat in Parliament for Okehampton and began work in the same years as Pitt. From seventeen forty four he served as a lord of the treasury. He later held the post of chancellor of the exchequer. In seventeen fifty six he left office and was raised to the peerage.
britannica-1911-m-lennan-john-ferguson:
John Ferguson McLennan, a Scots scholar of early peoples, gets a life in the 1911 Britannica. Born at Inverness in eighteen twenty seven, he took high marks at Aberdeen. He went on to Cambridge but left with no degree. The Scots bar took him in eighteen fifty seven. In eighteen seventy one he took the post of law drafter for Scotland.

His book Primitive Marriage came out in eighteen sixty five. In it he read mock capture rites at weddings as a key to kin growth. Greek kin lore and the lore of totem marks filled his next works. A fresh set of his essays came out in eighteen seventy six. More work on kin ties sat in piles at his death in eighteen eighty one, and kin hands brought it to print.
britannica-1911-macaulay-thomas-babingto:
Thomas Babington Macaulay, who lived from 1800 to 1859, was an English historian, essayist, and politician. The 1911 Britannica entry places his birth at Rothley Temple in Leicestershire. His father Zachary had governed Sierra Leone and fought the slave trade with zeal. The son showed a bent for letters at a strikingly early age at home.

Before age eight he had written a summary of world history from creation to 1800. A romance in Scott style and a long poem followed in boyhood years. That pile of early verse and prose marked a mind set for writing. The entry opens a life that joined parliament, India, and famed history.
britannica-1911-maldon:
Maldon, a market town and port in Essex, England, is described in a town entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on a slope above the south side of the Blackwater river, with rail links through Witham. The entry gives just over five thousand people in 1901 and lists its salt works, breweries and oyster beds.

Churches draw much of the space. All Saints has a rare three sided tower with a six sided spire, and Saint Mary shows Norman work built with Roman stone. The town hall, schools and the ruins of Beeleigh Abbey near by are also noted. The past runs deep here. Edward the Elder built a fort at Maldon, and Ealdorman Brihtnoth fell there to the Danes in 991. Charters from kings then fixed the rights of the town, a thread the entry follows down the years.
britannica-1911-marathon:
Marathon, a plain on the north-east coast of Attica, is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. The plain held four villages that once formed a league of their own. They kept old rites and legends tied to Heracles and Theseus. In the sixth century the plain served Peisistratus as a base. He held much land there and used it to gain the rest of Attica.

The plain is famed for the battle of 490, when Athens and Plataea beat the Persians. King Darius had sent the force to punish Athens and restore the tyrant Hippias. Some 50,000 Persians landed under Datis and Artaphernes. Athens sent out its full levy of 9,000 heavy infantry. A thousand Plataeans joined them on the march. The article tells how Miltiades urged the attack. The Athenians charged down from the Vrana valley onto the plain.
britannica-1911-marazion:
Marazion is a town article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a small seaport in Cornwall, England. It stands on the shore of Mount's Bay, two miles east of Penzance, on a main rail line. Its count in 1901 was 1,251.

The article notes a rough causeway of stones thrown up by the sea. At low tide that path joins the town to the island of Saint Michael's Mount. The church of Saint Hilary was burned in 1853 and rebuilt true to its old form. Its yard holds cut stones that date from the fourth century. One stone honours Constantine the Great. Market gardening and fishing form the chief work of the town. Much of the piece deals with old grants of its markets and fairs.
britannica-1911-marquand-henry-gurdon:
Henry Gurdon Marquand, an American philanthropist and collector who lived from 1819 to 1902, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born in New York City in April 1819, he became his brother Frederick's agent in 1839. His brother had retired from the jewelry trade and gave freely to Yale and to a theological seminary. Marquand later bought into the Iron Mountain railroad and became its president.

He was also a director of the Missouri-Pacific system. The article stresses his place in the art world above his business career. He was the first honorary member of the American Institute of Architects. From 1889 to 1902 he served as president of the Metropolitan Museum of Art. He gave that museum valuable works and loans from his own paintings. He also gave to Princeton and other schools. His art collection and rare books were sold in 1903.
britannica-1911-martens-georg-friedrich-:
Georg Friedrich von Martens, born at Hamburg in seventeen fifty six, was a German jurist and diplomat. He was schooled at Gottingen, Regensburg, and Vienna. In seventeen eighty three he became professor of law at Gottingen. Six years later he was raised to noble rank. The elector of Hanover made him a counsellor of state in eighteen o eight.

Martens later led the finance section of the Westphalian council of state. In eighteen fourteen the king of Hanover made him a privy cabinet counsellor. Two years later he went to the diet of the new German Confederation at Frankfort. He died there in eighteen twenty one. His great work was a vast store of treaties from seventeen sixty one onward. Its first volumes came out at Gottingen in the seventeen nineties.
britannica-1911-massenbach-christian-kar:
Christian Karl August Ludwig von Massenbach (1758-1827) was a Prussian soldier, and his career is set out in an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Schmalkalden, he was educated at Heilbronn and Stuttgart, devoting himself chiefly to mathematics. He became an officer in the Wuerttemberg army in 1778.

The entry says he moved in 1782 to the service of Frederick the Great, and, his pay being small, wrote maths school books in his spare time to make ends meet. Yet he never neglected the science of war, and made his name early as a theorist. He taught mathematics to Prince Louis, fought in Holland with credit, and later framed schemes to rebuild the neglected Prussian general staff.
britannica-1911-mattoon:
Mattoon, a city in Coles County, Illinois, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica place entry. It lies in the east mid part of the state, south east of Peoria. Two rail lines serve it and keep repair shops in town. Its folk count rose to eleven thousand four hundred fifty six in nineteen ten. A town book hall, a church run care house, and a home for old folk serve its folk.

Corn and broom corn from near farms ship out through the town in bulk. Fruit and stock move through it as well. Works make stoves, bricks, and shop goods of iron. Town growth dates from a first set down near eighteen fifty five. Its name honors William Mattoon, an early land owner there.
britannica-1911-melon:
Melon is a botany article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The plant named in Latin in the entry is given as a varied species of the gourd family, with many forms. It is a yearly trailing herb with lobed leaves shaped like a hand. By its tendrils it can be trained up over frames with ease.

The entry notes that male and female flowers grow on the same plant. Its flowers have a bell shaped crown of five deep lobes and three stamens. A pictured cross section shows the fruit's three parts, their walls, and the seeds fixed to them. The melon is native to south Asia, from the foot of the Himalayas southward, where it grows wild. Yet it is also widely grown by people, the article adds.
britannica-1911-memnon:
Memnon is the subject of a myth article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In Greek myth Memnon was a son of Tithonus and Eos, the Dawn. He was king of the Aethiopians. He is named in Hesiod and the Odyssey, but he is chiefly a hero of later tales. After Hector died he came to help his uncle Priam against the Greeks.

The article tells how he showed great valour at Troy. He killed Antilochus, the son of Nestor and friend of Achilles. Achilles then slew Memnon in return. His mother bore his body from the field, and Zeus is said to have granted him deathless life. Her tears each morning were said to be the early dew. His companions were changed into birds that came each year to lament at his grave. In Egypt his name was linked to two giant statues near Thebes.
britannica-1911-mensuration:
Mensuration deals with how we put numbers to size in geometry. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives the word from the Latin mensura, a measure. In broad terms it covers angles, lengths, areas, and volumes. In practice the term is kept more narrow for most use.

Angle work belongs to trigonometry, and straight lengths belong to geometry. Curved lengths need calculus in most cases beyond the simple ones. What remains is the finding of areas and volumes by formula. The entry stresses a key split in method. Lengths can be checked at once with a unit, while areas and volumes must be worked out from data.
britannica-1911-mercy-franz-freiherr-von:
Franz von Mercy was a German general in the Thirty Years War, born at Longwy in Lorraine. The 1911 Britannica entry says he served the empire from his youth and rose to high rank in about twenty years. He stood out in a famed early battle, then led a foot corps on the Rhine.

The entry praises his hold of a Rhine town against the Swedes, which he gave up only after a five month siege. He rose to lead horse troops, then guns, then the whole Bavarian host in the field. Made a field marshal, he won a great win over a French marshal, taking the man and thousands of his troops. By then he ranked among the top soldiers in Europe.
britannica-1911-merlon: Merlon is a term from building for the solid part of a battlement. It is the upright block that stands between two gaps along the top of a wall. This short 1911 Britannica entry defines it in a few lines. Some merlons, the entry notes, are pierced by loopholes for shooting through. The word is French, taken from an Italian form, with roots the entry traces to Latin words for a pitchfork or a wall.
britannica-1911-merriman-henry-seton:
Henry Seton Merriman is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an English novelist. That name was the pen name of Hugh Stowell Scott. He died in 1903, the heading notes. For some years he was an underwriter at Lloyd's. His literary career began in 1889 with The Phantom Future. He made his first decided hit with a Russian story.

That story was The Sowers, published in 1896. Many other well constructed novels followed from his pen. They are remarkable for excellence of plot and handling. The author was an enthusiastic traveller all his life. Many of his journeys were taken with Stanley Weyman, his friend. He was about forty when he died at Melton. That death fell in November 1903 near Ipswich. His best books include Roden's Corner and The Isle of Unrest.
britannica-1911-mesmer-friedrich-anton:
Friedrich Anton Mesmer, an Austrian doctor who lived from 1733 to 1815, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Weil near Lake Constance, he studied medicine at Vienna and took his degree there. His first book, in 1766, dealt with the pull of the planets on life on earth. He first linked that force to electric power, then to magnets.

Mesmer held that a hidden force ran through all things and bore most on the nerves of men. He thought stroking a sick body could cure it by that force. He moved to Paris in 1778 and caused a great stir with his cures. The Paris medical faculty called him a fraud, but he won many followers, and his name gave English the word mesmerism.
britannica-1911-metcalfe-charles-theophi:
Charles Theophilus Metcalfe, who lived from 1785 to 1846, ruled parts of India for Britain. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with his birth at Calcutta. His father was an officer who later directed the East India Company. Schooled at Eton, Charles sailed for India in 1800 as a clerk. He was the first student at the new Fort William college. At nineteen he aided General Lake in war.

In 1808 Lord Minto chose him as envoy to Ranjit Singh at Lahore. There he sealed a treaty in April 1809. It guarded the freedom of the Sikh states near the Sutlej. Posts at Delhi and at the nizam's court followed. In 1835 he stepped in as governor general for a year. His best known act freed the Indian press. That move pleased the public but strained his ties with the directors at home.
britannica-1911-methodist-new-connexion: The Methodist New Connexion was a Protestant Nonconformist church, covered in a short entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It was formed in 1797 by a break from the Wesleyan Methodists, led by Alexander Kilham, after a dispute over the rights of lay members. Kilham's party wanted more power for members and less for ministers. In its conferences, ministers and laymen sat in equal numbers. Teaching and order otherwise matched the Wesleyans. In 1907 it merged into the United Methodist Church, with some 250 ministers and 45,000 members.
britannica-1911-middleton:
Middleton, a market town in Lancashire, England, is described in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. It stands on the Irk river, near the Rochdale Canal, north east of Manchester. In nineteen oh one it had over twenty five thousand folk. Its rise dates from the coming of mills at the close of the seventeen hundreds.

The church of Saint Leonard is of mixed styles, with a low square tower. Its oldest part dates from the twelve hundreds, and most from the fourteen hundreds. Two chapels hold memorials of old local families. A grammar school was founded in fifteen seventy two. Cotton spinning and weaving form the staple trade. Silk weaving, bleaching, dyeing, iron founding, and soap making are also carried on. Coal pits lie nearby.
britannica-1911-midsomer-norton:
Midsomer Norton is an urban district in Somersetshire in the south of England. Its town entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies twelve and a half miles south south west of Bath city. Two rail lines, the Somerset and Dorset and the Great Western, serve it.

The town sits in a hilly district between two arms of the Somer. The church of Saint John the Baptist is mostly in Perpendicular style. Its tower holds three bells given by Charles the Second long ago. Coal trade drives both this town and near Radstock, its close neighbour. Mines in the area feed a coalfield that runs toward Bristol city. That field holds great weight for the factory trades of Bristol.
britannica-1911-migration:
Migration means the move of people who mean to change their home for good. A 1911 Britannica entry sets out its scope and key terms at the start. Moves may cross a border or stay inside one land in range. Cross border moves split into emigration out and immigration in by direction faced.

The same folk are both leavers and joiners, yet effects differ for each land. One land loses hands and mouths while the other gains both at once. So the entry treats the two flows apart in what follows the opening. Short trips for trade or pleasure count only where they blur into true settlement.
britannica-1911-miklosich-franz-von:
Austrian scholar Franz von Miklosich, born at Luttenberg in Styria in eighteen thirteen, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He took a degree in the study of mind at Gratz. For a time he taught that subject there. In eighteen thirty eight he went to Vienna and took a law degree.

He gave up law for the study of Slav tongues and took a post in the royal library. A review of a grammar book in eighteen forty four began a long run of learned works. Those works changed the study of Slav speech, the entry says. In eighteen forty nine he took a new chair in that field at Vienna. He held it till eighteen eighty six, and wrote also on Greek and other tongues.
britannica-1911-miles-nelson-appleton:
Nelson Appleton Miles, an American soldier born in Massachusetts in 1839, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was at work in trade in Boston when the Civil War broke out, and he joined the army as a lieutenant in 1861. He served with honour in the Peninsular fight and at Antietam and Fredericksburg.

Wounded at Chancellorsville, Miles came back to lead a brigade under Grant and won rank step by step, ending the war in charge of a corps for a time. In later years he was sent west and won fame in fights with the Cheyenne, the Sioux and the Nez Perces, and in the capture of Geronimo. He rose to lead the whole army in 1895, held top rank in the war with Spain, and left the service in 1903. His books of war memories close the account.
britannica-1911-misprision:
Misprision is a term of English law for a fault that the law once took with great weight. The 1911 Britannica entry calls the term near obsolete by its day. Its root is an old French word for to mistake or misjudge. Lawyers split the fault into two kinds, one called negative and one called positive.

Negative misprision meant to hide a known act of treason or felony. Each subject owed a duty to tell the king's judges of such crimes. Grand jurors bore that duty first in each county and town. Plain folk bore it too, at least in strict theory. To stay silent when one knew was itself a crime at common law.
britannica-1911-mohl-hugo-von:
Hugo von Mohl, who lived from 1805 to 1872, was a German botanist born at Stuttgart. The 1911 Britannica article says he came of a line of state officials. As a schoolboy he studied plants and rocks in his spare time. He entered the university at Tübingen in 1823 and took his degree in medicine with honours. At Munich he met a fine circle of botanists. In 1828 he began the studies of plant build that filled his life. He took the chair of botany at Tübingen in 1832 and never left it.

Unmarried, Mohl took his joy in his workroom and his books. He honed his skill with lenses and fine slices of plant tissue. The word protoplasm was his coinage. In 1844 he showed that protoplasm forms the living core of the plant cell. His works span forty-four years, on the build of the higher plants.
britannica-1911-mohl-julius-von:
Julius von Mohl, a German student of the East who lived from 1800 to 1876, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Stuttgart and read theology at Tübingen. He then gave up the plan of a pulpit and went to Paris in 1823. Paris was then the great school of Eastern letters in Europe.

The French state charged him with an edition of the Shah Nama, the Book of Kings. Its first volume came out in 1838, and its last was still undone at his death. He quit his chair at Tübingen and settled in Paris for good. From 1847 he taught Persian at the College de France. His yearly reports on Eastern studies, kept up for over twenty-five years, map the growth of that field.
britannica-1911-moncton:
Moncton is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a city in Canada. It is a city and port of entry in New Brunswick. It lies in Westmoreland county on the Petitcodiac river. The town stands at the head of navigation on that river. A count from 1901 gives it 9026 people. Saint John lies to the south west by rail. The town is a hub for rail work in the region.

The workshops of the Inter-Colonial railway sit in Moncton. Its general offices are based there as well. The town is the east terminus of the Grand Trunk Pacific line. Large stove factories stand among its works. Engine and boiler works add to its trade base. Fire swept the rail shops and much of the town in 1906. All was rebuilt on a larger and more modern scale. That rebuild marks the town as a rising rail centre.
britannica-1911-monition: Monition, in English church law, is an order that tells a person to do a named act or show cause against it, in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The order warns of pain of the law if it is ignored. It is the lightest form of church censure for clergy and lay folk alike. Once served in due form, refusal counts as contempt of court. Such orders can force a cleric to live on his benefice. They can also serve in suits to stop rites said to be unlawful.
britannica-1911-monkswell-robert-porrett:
Robert Porrett Collier, first Baron Monkswell (1817-1886), was an English judge from Plymouth. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces his path from Oxford to the bar in 1843. He won fame by freeing Brazilian pirates on a point of law. In 1852 he entered parliament in the Liberal interest for Plymouth.

He rose to solicitor general and then attorney general under Gladstone. In 1871 Gladstone placed him on the privy council court by a sharp maneuver. Public anger at that move hit the cabinet hard at the time. Collier still served with credit until his death. He was also a skilled painter who showed landscapes in public.
britannica-1911-monsoon:
Monsoon, from an Arabic word for season, is the subject of a science entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The name is given to winds that change with the season. They arise from gaps in air pressure between land and sea. Those gaps stem in turn from the way land and sea heat and cool at unlike rates.

In the warm season land grows hotter than the sea, so air flows from sea to land at low levels. In the cold season the flow turns the other way. The entry likens monsoons to land and sea breezes writ large across the year. It notes that lands near the equator lack the heat swings such winds need. Lands near the tropics, by contrast, suit them best.
britannica-1911-montbrison:
Montbrison, a town of east-central France, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the chief town of a district in the department of Loire. In 1906 it held a little over six thousand five hundred people. The town stands on a hill of volcanic rock above the river Vizezy.

The chief church was begun about 1220 and took two centuries to finish. A hall of the fourteenth century, the Salle de la Diana, stands near it and was restored by Viollet-le-Duc. Courts of law sit in the town, and a sub-prefect has his seat there. Local works distil liqueurs, grind flour, and weave silk ribbons. Grain trade is brisk in the town. In the middle ages it belonged to the counts of Forez. It was the capital of its department from 1801 till 1856.
britannica-1911-monteagle-thomas-spring-:
Monteagle, Thomas Spring-Rice, first Baron, is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an English statesman. He was born in 1790 and died in 1866, of a Limerick family. Spring-Rice entered parliament in 1820 as a Whig for Limerick, and from 1832 sat for Cambridge.

After minor posts he became secretary for war and the colonies in 1834. From 1835 to 1839 he served as chancellor of the exchequer. He had hoped for the speakership and missed it. In 1839 he was made Baron Monteagle of Brandon, a title once meant for his ancestor, and put in charge of the exchequer as controller. He clashed with the government over how far that control reached. He died on the seventh of February 1866. His grandson took the title after him.
britannica-1911-monteagle-william-parker:
William Parker, Lord Monteagle, is lit by one famed letter in a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was eldest son of the tenth Baron Morley, born in 1575. Wed young into a great Catholic kin, he felt for that cause. Queen Elizabeth's reign saw him in sympathy with Catholic hopes. Knighted in Ireland in 1599, he joined Essex's rising in 1601.

That rising cost Monteagle a gaol term and a vast fine. In 1602 he joined a plea for a Spanish landing in England. Yet he backed James at his coming and won the king's favour. On the twenty-sixth of October 1605 a strange letter reached him. It warned of the Gunpowder Plot set for parliament's opening day. He took that letter straight to Whitehall and the council.
britannica-1911-montgelas-maximilian-jos:
Maximilian Josef Garnerin von Montgelas is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a Bavarian statesman from a noble house of Savoy. Born in seventeen fifty nine, he was schooled in France and in Germany. French speech and thought shaped him for the rest of his life.

The entry tells how church foes drove him from post to post in his youth. He had ties to a secret group that pushed free thought and drew clerical hate. A duke took him in as a private aide and then as a minister. In that post he sat at a great peace congress for Germany. His later work reshaping Bavaria fills the rest of the long entry.
britannica-1911-montmorillon: Montmorillon is a town of western France in this short 1911 Britannica place note. It heads its district in the Vienne lands, on the Gartempe River east of Poitiers. Its folk count for nineteen oh six was three thousand nine hundred twenty four. A church school fills a house from the twelve hundreds, once a friar house. Its church is of the old round arch style. A queer two floor chapel of eight sides stands from the same age. The church of Notre Dame mixes round arch and Gothic work.
britannica-1911-motion:
Motion is a law article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a step taken in an English court case. A motion is a request made to a court while a case is under way. It can be made before or after judgment is given.

The article explains what sets a motion apart. Its aim is to win the court's help on a pressing point that needs a quick ruling. Unlike a petition, it is made by word of mouth in open court. It rests on a written statement all the same. Two kinds are named, motions of course and special motions. The first is a matter of right and needs no notice. The second is heard in court and needs sound proof. In one sided requests, the text warns, the fullest good faith is a must.
britannica-1911-mouflon: The mouflon, the wild sheep of Corsica and Sardinia, is described in a short 1911 Britannica note. It is now found in just a few spots on those isles. The ewes have no horns or quite small ones, while the rams carry good horns. In summer the rams show a light saddle mark on a dark coat. A kind from Armenia and Persia is larger and more red, with horns that curve the other way.
britannica-1911-mount-temple-william-fra:
William Francis Cowper-Temple, Baron Mount-Temple (1811-1888), was an English politician, and his career fills an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Brocket Hall, he was educated at Eton and served in the Royal Horse Guards. In 1835 he became secretary to his uncle, the prime minister Lord Melbourne, and entered Parliament for Hertford.

The entry is best known for his clause in the Education Bill of 1870, which barred set church teaching from the religious lessons in rate-aided schools. He also carried bills for the Thames Embankment and the new law courts. In 1880 he was raised to the peerage, and he died at Broadlands in 1888.
britannica-1911-mountstephen-george-step:
George Stephen, Baron Mountstephen, a Canadian financier born in 1829, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born at Dufftown in Scotland, he was educated at the parish school and worked for a time as a herd boy. In 1850 he went to Canada and soon became a leading business man in Montreal. In 1878 he joined his cousin in buying a railway.

That purchase led to his stake in the growth of western Canada, the entry says. From 1881 he was linked with his cousin in building the Canadian Pacific railway. For his services there he was made a baronet in 1886 and raised to the peerage in 1891. In 1888 he left Canada and lived in England and Scotland thereafter. He gave freely to charity and schooling, and helped build a Montreal hospital.
britannica-1911-mullion:
Mullion is a term in building for the upright pieces that divide the lights of a window, and this 1911 Britannica entry explains the word and the work. The word is a corruption of munnion, drawn from a French word for a stump. One scholar quoted calls the mullion the stump of the division before it breaks out into the tracery above. The pieces are of stone, sometimes like small columns and sometimes like slim piers.

In plainer work mullions are often left with a simple chamfer or a flat hollow on each side. As tracery grew richer, windows came to be divided by a larger order of mullions. Between these ran a lesser set, which flowed into each other in the tracery.
britannica-1911-musical-notation:
Musical notation is a way of setting sounds before the eye, treated at length in this 1911 Britannica article. The earliest attempts are thought to have been made by the Hindus and Chinese, with the practice passing from them to Greece. The Greek system used letters, though scholars dispute how many signs it held.

Boethius shows that the Latins did not take up the Greek method, though fifteen Roman letters were later applied to the sounds of two octaves. A second line of signs, called neumes, shows from early centuries: dashes, hooks, curves, and dots over the words. The gap between sign and text hinted at the rise and fall of the tune, which made the signs hard to read. A red line giving the singer one fixed note marks a clear advance in the 900s.
britannica-1911-muskegon:
Muskegon, a city in Michigan, is the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the seat of Muskegon county, on Muskegon lake, near the mouth of the Muskegon river. The census of 1910 gave it 24,062 people. Railways and steamboat lines link it with Chicago, Milwaukee, and other lake ports.

The entry dwells on the gifts of Charles Hackley, a rich lumberman of the city. His funds endowed the public schools, a manual training school, a public library, and a hospital. Statues of Lincoln, Farragut, and McKinley stand in its park and at its school. The city owns and runs its own water works. Muskegon lake is ice free all year, and its channel to Lake Michigan has been deepened by the federal government. Lumber is the chief good shipped out.
britannica-1911-myron:
Myron, a Greek maker of bronze figures, is the subject of an art entry in the 1911 Britannica. He worked in the mid fifth century before Christ. Born at Eleutherae on the edge of Attica, he cast near all his work in bronze. Gods and heroes came from his hands, but sports men made his fame. Bold poses and clean rhythm set his work apart, the text says.

Three works are named by Pliny as his best known. They are a cow, a runner named Ladas, and a discus thrower. Copies of the discus man still live, the best in a Rome palace. Critics in the text praise his gift for life and move in the body. They fault him for weak show of mind and mood in the face.
britannica-1911-neuchatel-canton:
Neuchatel, a canton of western Switzerland on the French border, is described in a 1911 Britannica article. It is the only Swiss canton set wholly in the Jura range. Its total area is given as near 312 square miles. Woods cover a large share, and vineyards a small one.

The land is made of long ridges and valleys, as is true of the Jura. Three zones are set out in the piece. The lake shore zone, called the Vignoble, sits the lowest.
