Two main valleys form the mid zone. The high zone holds the work towns of La Chaux de Fonds and Le Locle. Rail lines cross the canton and link it to Bern and to Paris.
britannica-1911-nicoll-sir-william-rober:
Sir William Robertson Nicoll, a Scottish Nonconformist divine and man of letters born in 1851, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Auchindoir in Aberdeenshire, the son of a Free Church minister, he took his degree at Aberdeen in 1870. He studied for the ministry and was ordained at Dufftown in 1874, then moved to Kelso three years later.

In 1884 Nicoll became editor of the Expositor, and in 1886 he founded the British Weekly, a Nonconformist paper that won great sway over opinion in the free churches. He secured many writers of rare talent for it, and he wrote much himself, under the pen name Claudius Clear among others. He also founded the Bookman in 1891 and served as chief literary adviser to the publishers Hodder and Stoughton. Other ventures included the Expositor's Bible and a Greek Testament. His knighthood came in the birthday honours of 1909.
britannica-1911-nordau-max-simon:
Max Simon Nordau, a German author and thinker born in eighteen forty nine, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born of Jewish parents at Budapest, he studied medicine and travelled wide through Europe. He settled as a doctor in his home town, then moved to Paris in eighteen eighty.

In Paris he kept his medical work and took up art, letters, and social themes. The entry praises his sharp care with facts and his bold lack of fear of set views. His best known work applied the thought of bodily decline to the mind of modern man. In it he argued that much new art and writing showed decay and strain. The entry gives a clear view of a harsh critic of his age.
britannica-1911-north-sea-fisheries-conv:
The North Sea Fisheries Convention, dated the 6th of May 1882, came from a conference on policing North Sea fishing. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out its terms and the cases that tested them. Great Britain, Germany, Denmark, Holland, Belgium, and France signed for five years, then ran on until a power gave notice.

The rules bite only beyond the three-mile limit, inside which each country's fishermen hold the sole right to fish. For bays the line is drawn across the mouth at the first point no wider than ten miles. A Scottish ban on beam trawling raised the case of Mortensen against Peters in 1906. The Edinburgh court held that limits in an act bound foreign crews too when the act made no split by nation. An act of 1895 owned that no such power could reach foreign boats outside home waters.
britannica-1911-northallerton:
Northallerton is a market town in the North Riding of Yorkshire, England, on a main rail line from York. The 1911 Britannica entry calls it a key rail junction and gives its town count at the turn of the age. It lies in a plain west of two hill ranges, on a small stream that feeds a larger river.

The entry notes the large cross shaped church, built in three old styles with a tall tower at its heart, and a grammar school. A sick house founded in the middle ages still serves as a town charity. No trace stands of the fort palace of the bishops, or of two friaries of old. Farm trade rules the town, with works for motor craft, and a famed strict priory stands near by.
britannica-1911-noumenon:
Noümenon is a term in philosophy tied to the teaching of Kant, and this 1911 Britannica entry explains it and the puzzle it raises. The Greek word means a thing known. In Kant's system, noümena are things-in-themselves, set against phenomena, things as they appear to us. Kant held that the human mind can never reach things-in-themselves by thinking alone. It can know only how things appear.

That leaves an odd result: the world of noümena is just the world thought can never enter. The entry notes the term belongs to an early stage of Kant's growth. In his mature view, moral action still gives some hold. Our life as free agents assures us of a deeper world, one where freedom, God, and the soul's long life have a real place.
britannica-1911-novation:
Novation is a law article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a term drawn from Roman law. In that law the word covered three swaps. A new debtor could take the place of an old one. A new creditor could take over a claim. Or a new contract could stand in place of an old one.

The article then sets the term beside English law, where it never quite took root. There the swap of a debtor or creditor is most often called an assignment. A swap of contracts is called a merger, though the fit is loose. The piece stresses that a valid new deal is a must. It also notes how the point comes up when firms change hands.
britannica-1911-o-hagan-thomas-o-hagan-1:
Irish judge Thomas O'Hagan, first Baron O'Hagan, born at Belfast in eighteen twelve, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was schooled at a Belfast institution and called to the Irish bar in eighteen thirty six. In eighteen forty he moved to Dublin.

There he acted for the repeal party in many political trials. His backing for the union with England cost him nationalist support. Yet he rose as solicitor general and then attorney general in the early eighteen sixties. He sat in Parliament for Tralee and became a judge in eighteen sixty five. In eighteen sixty eight he became lord chancellor of Ireland. He was the first Roman Catholic to hold that post since the reign of James the Second.
britannica-1911-okehampton:
Okehampton is a market town and borough in Devonshire in England. The 1911 Britannica entry sets it on the east and west Okement rivers. It lies 22 miles west of Exeter by the London and South Western line. Its count in 1901 was 2,569 souls in the town. The church of All Saints shows a fine late Gothic tower.

That tower stood unharmed when nave and chancel burned in 1842. Glass is made from stone found in the Meldon Valley near town. Both streams of the river teem with small trout for anglers. Okehampton Castle is one of the most scenic ruins in Devon. It most likely dates from the 1400s, with a Norman keep.
britannica-1911-oleron:
Oléron is an island off the west coast of France, across from the mouths of the Charente and the Seudre. It forms part of the department of Charente-Inférieure. Its people numbered 16,747 in 1906. In size, at 66 square miles, it stands next to Corsica among the islands of France. It runs about 18 miles from north-west to south-east, and seven miles at its most wide. The strait that parts it from the main land is less than a mile wide at one point.

The island is flat and low, with dunes on its coast. Most of it is very rich in crops, but broad salt marshes lie on it as well. Oyster culture and fishing are carried on there. Its chief yields are corn, wine, fruit, and garden crops. Most of the folk are Protestants, and they make fine sailors.
britannica-1911-opon:
Opon, a town in the province of Cebu in the Philippine Islands, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It sits on the small island of Mactan, split from Cebu island by a channel only about a mile wide. After Cordova and Santa Rosa were joined to it, its people in 1903 numbered a little over twenty thousand, in forty four villages.

The tongue of the town is Visayan. Opon acts as a shipping and trading suburb of Cebu city, whose harbour is sheltered by Mactan Island. Large groves of coconut trees stand there, and the chief work is the growing of Indian corn and maguey, and fishing. In the north east of the town stands a monument to Magellan. He reached the Philippines in March 1521 and was slain on Mactan late in the next month, a fact that still marks the place.
britannica-1911-ordinance-legislation:
Ordinance is a law article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a form of legislation in medieval England. An ordinance differed from a statute in that it needed no grant from parliament. The king issued it by his own prerogative, though under Edward the First he often took the assent of his council first. Stubbs, as quoted, calls the ordinance a rule made by the king, by himself or in council, and open to recall by the same power.

Jealousy grew when statutes were found bent or beaten by later ordinances. In 1389 the Commons asked Richard the Second that no ordinance be made against the common law or the statutes. The form fell out of use by the fifteenth century, and its modern match is the order in council.
britannica-1911-orelli-hans-konrad-von:
Hans Konrad von Orelli, born in 1846, was a Swiss theologian. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives his training and chief works. He was born at Zurich in January 1846. He studied at Lausanne, Zurich, and Erlangen, and also worked at other German schools.

Orelli became a preacher at an orphan house in Zurich in 1869. He then taught at the university there and moved to Basel as a professor. He rose to a full chair at Basel in 1881. His main work dealt with the Old Testament. He wrote notes on Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and the Twelve Prophets. He also wrote on prophecy and made a travel book on the Holy Land.
britannica-1911-organon:
Organon is the name for the books on logic left by the Greek thinker of old. The word means a tool, from the Greek term for work. Logic is so called since it is no science and no craft in the plain sense. It is a help and tool for all thought that seeks truth.

Bacon held that old logic did no good, so he gave his own book a name that means the new tool. He thought his path by close watch would lead to new facts of sure worth. Two more men gave like names to their books on thought. In old song the term named a sung line set past a chant.
britannica-1911-orientation:
Orientation, in architecture, is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. The word covers the placing of a building with regard to the points of the compass. More strictly, as its root suggests, it points to the east. Some temples in Egypt seem to have been set toward the sun or a chosen star.

The entry explains why that mattered. The star's place on a set day could tell a priest the exact time of year, a key point in a farming land with no calendar. Greek temples, it says, have let scholars work out the dates when early temples were founded. The chief front of a Greek temple always faced east. At sunrise, light through the great door lit the god's statue at the far end.
britannica-1911-orpington:
Orpington, a town in Kent, England, is described in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. It lies south east of London, on a rail line from the capital. In nineteen oh one it had just over four thousand folk. Its church holds carved wood work and old brasses, the entry notes.

An old mansion called the Priory dates in part from thirteen ninety three. Its oak lined hall and chief rooms are from the fourteen hundreds. In eighteen seventy three John Ruskin set up a private press for his works in the town. Fruit and hops are grown widely nearby. Set among hills and woods near the head of the Cray stream, the town has become a favoured home base for folk who work in London.
britannica-1911-osuna-pedro-tellez-giron:
Pedro Tellez Giron, third duke of Osuna, was a Spanish viceroy of Sicily and Naples. Born at Osuna, he was baptized in January fifteen seventy five. His father was the second duke, and his mother came from the house of Velasco. As a boy he went with his grandfather, the first duke, to Naples. At fourteen he saw service with troops sent to crush a revolt in Aragon.

Osuna wed young, to a granddaughter on her mother's side of Hernan Cortes. In fifteen ninety eight he took the dukedom. His wild early life raised scandals that led to jail at Arevalo in sixteen hundred. The lesson did him good, and that year he left for Flanders. He took troops raised at his own cost. There he served under others and shared work and fighting by land and sea.
britannica-1911-overstone-samuel-jones-l:
Samuel Jones Loyd, first Baron Overstone, an English banker who lived from 1796 to 1883, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. He was the only son of Lewis Loyd, a Welsh dissenting minister. He was born in September 1796. He was educated at Eton and at Trinity College, Cambridge.

His father had given up the ministry to join a Manchester bank. He later founded the London branch of that bank. Loyd joined his father in the banking business. He succeeded to it when his father retired in 1844. He ran the business with such success that he left a fortune at his death. That fortune in personal property came to more than two million pounds. He also sat in parliament, as the article goes on to tell. The piece joins a family bank, a great fortune, and a seat in public life.
britannica-1911-pack-otto-von:
Otto von Pack is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of a German conspirator. He lived from about 1480 to 1537. He studied at the university of Leipzig in his youth. He lost that post owing to his own dishonesty. In 1528 he revealed a dark scheme to Philip of Hesse. The scheme had been agreed at Breslau, he claimed.

The plot, he said, was led by Archduke Ferdinand. Other princes of weight stood in it with him. They meant to conquer Hungary for Ferdinand first. Pack was sent to Hungary to concert joint measures. He went to John Zapolya, Ferdinand's foe in that land. The elector of Saxony advised asking the princes to explain. Under that check, Pack's tale fell apart as false. The treaty copy he showed proved to be a forgery. He lived as a fugitive for some time after.
britannica-1911-page-thomas-nelson:
Thomas Nelson Page, an American author born in 1853, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Oakland Plantation in Hanover county in Virginia. He was the great-grandson of two governors of Virginia, one of whom signed the Declaration of Independence. He read law at the university of Virginia and took his degree in 1874.

He practised law, in chief at Richmond, until 1893. He then moved to Washington and gave himself to writing and to the lecture hall. In 1884 a tale of his, Marse Chan, came out in a magazine and won note at once. It told of life in Virginia in the Civil War. More tales of black life and character came with it in a book of 1887, In Ole Virginia, held his most telling work.
britannica-1911-paget-of-beaudesert-will:
William Paget, first Baron Paget of Beaudesert, an English statesman who lived from 1506 to 1563, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born in London, he was the son of a city officer. He was educated at a famed London school and at Cambridge, then at the university of Paris. Through the early friendship of Stephen Gardiner, he was used by Henry the Eighth on key missions abroad.

In 1532 he became clerk of the signet and soon clerk of the privy council. He served as secretary to a queen in 1539. In 1543 he joined the privy council and became secretary of state. Henry in his later years leaned much on his advice, the entry says. He named Paget to the council that would act during the young king's minority.
britannica-1911-paignton:
Paignton is a seaside town in Devon, England, and this 1911 Britannica entry gives a short portrait of the place as it stood then. It sits on Tor Bay, south-west of Torquay, on the Great Western railway line. The urban district held 8,385 people in the census of 1901. Its church of St John is mostly in the late Gothic style but keeps an older Norman doorway, a carved and painted pulpit, and family monuments in the Kirkham chapel.

The town also had a pier with a pavilion and concert rooms, a yacht club, and a science and art school. Little was left of an old palace of the bishops of Exeter apart from its Bible Tower, once home to Miles Coverdale. The entry says the town drew its crowds from its firm sands, good bathing, and mild weather.
britannica-1911-pakington:
Pakington is the name of a famed Worcestershire house in this 1911 Britannica kin entry. Sir John Pakington, a lawyer who died in fifteen sixty, won lands from King Henry the Eighth. His heir of the same name was a bright court man of Queen Elizabeth. Grand ways of life made that man famed at court in his day. A baronet line sprang from his son in sixteen twenty.

One of that line fought for the king and was caught at Worcester in sixteen fifty one. His wife was long thought to have wrote a famed book of duty. The line died out in eighteen thirty, then rose a new for a kin heir. That heir held war and sea posts in state rule. A new rank of Baron Hampton came to him in eighteen seventy four.
britannica-1911-pallas-peter-simon:
Peter Simon Pallas was a German naturalist and traveller of the eighteenth century. He lived from seventeen forty one to eighteen eleven. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Berlin, the son of a Prussian army surgeon, he studied medicine widely.

Pallas showed an early bent for natural history at Berlin, Halle, and Leiden. In seventeen sixty one he went to England to study collections and coasts. At age twenty three he was elected a foreign member of the Royal Society. In seventeen sixty eight Catherine the Second called him to Saint Petersburg academy. He then led a science trip through Russia and Siberia for years.
britannica-1911-palmerston:
Palmerston, the chief town of the Northern Territory of South Australia, is described in a short gazetteer entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The town stands in Palmerston county on the east shore of Port Darwin. It lies about sixty feet above the sea, which nearly surrounds it. A rail line links its jetty with Playford, some 146 miles away.

The entry notes a government house, a town hall, and a trial nursery garden in the town. It praises the harbour, which can take ocean going ships. Cool breezes blow for most of the year, and the mean yearly rainfall is given as just over sixty two inches. The 1901 count put the town at 1,973 people, most of them Chinese.
britannica-1911-pantheon:
Pantheon is the name of two famed buildings, one in Rome and one in Paris. An article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica also gives the word a wider sense. It can mean any hall where a land lays its great dead to rest, or raises stones in their honor. Westminster Abbey is at times called the British pantheon in this sense.

The Roman house was first built by Agrippa in 27 before Christ. Fire wrecked it, and the house that stands rose under Hadrian. Since the year 600 it has served as a Christian church. The Paris house was built as a church to Saint Genevieve. At the Revolution it was set apart for the great men of France. Its front bears words that thank them in the name of their country.
britannica-1911-panton: Pantón is a town of north western Spain, in the province of Lugo, and a brief note in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica records it. The town stands in a mountain district, watered by the rivers Miño and Cabe. Its count in 1900 came to 12,088 people. Livestock is reared on a large scale in the district. Wheat, wine, oats, and potatoes are grown in quantity. Distilling and linen making are its other industries.
britannica-1911-parallel-motion:
Parallel Motion is an engineering article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a linkage devised by James Watt. It is used in steam engines to join two parts that move on unlike paths. The head of the piston rod travels up and down in a straight line. The end of the beam swings in the arc of a circle.

The article gives the layout in a diagram. A link joins a point on the beam to a radius link that swings about a fixed centre. A chosen point on that link moves in a path that matches the straight line very closely. Other points can be made to copy the same motion by added links set parallel. As a rule a point of this kind is where the piston rod is fixed.
britannica-1911-pardon:
Pardon is a law article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the wiping away of the penalty for a crime. The word comes through French from a late Latin verb for letting a debt go. The power to pardon rests with the same power that carries out the laws.

The article weighs the worth of the power first. Used with care, it can soften harsh gaps in guilt or right a failed trial. By English law the pardon is the sole right of the king. In practice a home minister speaks for the Crown in its use. The text then lists firm bounds on that right. The king cannot pardon a wrong done to a private person in place of the state. Nor can a pardon block a charge brought by parliament.
britannica-1911-parent-simon-napoleon:
Simon Napoleon Parent was born in 1855 and is a Canadian politician. The 1911 Britannica life opens at Beauport in the province of Quebec. He was born there in September 1855, a merchant's son. He was schooled at Laval University and graduated in the year 1881. That same year he was called to the bar of Quebec.

In 1890 he won a seat on the town council of Quebec city. From 1894 to 1906 he served as mayor of that city. He also sat for Saint-Sauveur as a Liberal in the assembly. In 1897 he took the lands, forests, and fisheries portfolio. After Marchand died in 1900, Parent formed a cabinet as prime minister.
britannica-1911-partition:
Partition, in law, is the division of land or goods among joint owners, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out its forms. The goods or land in view belong to the parties as co proprietors. A maxim of Roman law lies behind the doctrine. It held that no one can be kept against his will in a joint holding.

Under Roman practice, partition was gained by a set action in the courts. In English law the term covers a narrower field. It applies to lands, tenements, and chattels real held in shared forms. Those forms are coparcenary, joint tenancy, and tenancy in common. Not all rights can be split in this way. There can be no partition of homage, of fealty, or of a peerage. Partition itself is either voluntary or forced by the court.
britannica-1911-passion:
Passion is a word with two main senses, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets them out in a short entry. The word comes from a late Latin term built on a verb meaning to suffer or endure. Its first sense is the suffering of pain, used chiefly of the sufferings of Christ from the agony in the garden to his death on the cross.

Early Christian writers used the term in that sense, and it was also applied to the sufferings and deeds of saints and martyrs. A book of such accounts was called a passional or passionary. The entry also names the order of Passionist Fathers, founded by Saint Paul of the Cross in 1720. The second sense, feeling or emotion, came from the use of the Latin word to render a Greek term of philosophy. Modern use narrows it to strong, uncontrolled emotion.
britannica-1911-paterson:
Paterson, the Scots projector behind the Darien scheme, ends this account in a state of ruin. The head opens with him weak and ill, still fighting the giving up of Darien. He was carried on board ship like a skeleton of a man. After a stormy voyage he and the remnant of his band reached home. They landed in December sixteen ninety nine, after great suffering.

In his native air Paterson soon got his strength back. His busy mind was at once at work on new schemes. He drew a full plan to grow Scots trade by a council of trade. He also urged King William to try a new Darien venture. In seventeen o one he moved to London and helped push the union. The United Parliament voted him a large sum in the end.
britannica-1911-patrick-simon:
Simon Patrick (1626-1707) was an English churchman, born at Gainsborough in Lincolnshire, as this 1911 Britannica article recounts. He entered Queen's College, Cambridge, in 1644 and took orders in 1651. He then served as chaplain to Sir Walter St John and as vicar of Battersea in Surrey.

In 1662 Patrick was made rector of St Paul's, Covent Garden, in London, where he kept at his work through the plague. He became dean of Peterborough in 1679 and bishop of Chichester in 1689. In that year he was sent, with other new bishops, to settle the affairs of the church in Ireland. In 1691 he moved to the see of Ely, which he held until his death in May 1707. His sermons and devotional writings are very many, and the article notes his commentary on the historical and poetical books of the Old Testament in ten volumes.
britannica-1911-pauncefote-julian-paunce:
Julian Pauncefote is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was an English envoy born in eighteen twenty eight. He trained as a lawyer and then served in Hong Kong as a law officer. He rose there to chief judge of the high court.

The entry tracks his rise through law posts in London to the top staff job in the foreign office. He was then sent to Washington as the British envoy. His skill in law helped ease hard talks on fish rights and a canal treaty. His post was raised to the rank of ambassador while he held it. He died in Washington in nineteen hundred and two.
britannica-1911-pavilion:
Pavilion is defined in an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In its proper sense the word means a tent. It comes, late, from the Latin word for a butterfly, by way of French. The term serves chiefly for a tent with a high pitched roof. It also names a small free-standing building used as a summer house.

The article gives the word a special place in sport and in building. Grounds for games have a pavilion for the use of players and members. In building, a pavilion is a part of a house that juts out from the sides or the centre, a mark of French building in the reborn classic style. Where a large hospital or school is split into detached blocks, each block may bear the name as well.
britannica-1911-peabody-andrew-preston:
Andrew Preston Peabody (1811-1893) was an American clergyman and author, and this 1911 Britannica entry notes his quick start in life. He was born in Beverly, Massachusetts, a descendant of an early settler of the colony. He learned to read before he was three, entered Harvard College at twelve, and graduated in 1826. With one exception, he was the youngest graduate Harvard had known.

In 1833 he became assistant pastor of a Unitarian parish in Portsmouth, New Hampshire. The senior pastor died within a month, and Peabody took charge of the church, which he held until 1860. From 1852 he also owned and edited the North American Review. In 1860 he moved to Harvard as its preacher and professor of Christian morals, a post he held until 1881. He died at Boston in 1893, and a bronze tablet in Appleton Chapel keeps his memory.
britannica-1911-peale-charles-willson:
Charles Willson Peale, painter of Washington, is set out in a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Maryland in 1741, he lost his schoolmaster father young. At Annapolis the boy was bound to a saddler at thirteen. About 1764 he took up art in a serious way at last. Help came from a Swedish painter and from Copley of Boston.

From 1767 Peale learned under Benjamin West in London town. Back home he set up a studio in Philadelphia in 1770. Success came at once to his brush in that busy city. In 1772 he painted Washington at Mount Vernon in full dress. That study is the first known portrait of Washington we have. More likenesses of the great man came from his hand.
britannica-1911-penrhyn-george-sholto-go:
George Sholto Gordon Douglas-Pennant, second Baron Penrhyn, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life story. He lived from 1836 to 1907 and was the son of the first baron. His father held large estates in Wales through his wife's line. George sat in parliament for Carnarvonshire in two spans and took the title in 1886.

Penrhyn is shown as a keen sportsman and a kind landlord, yet a proud and stern man. He won fame in a long strike at his Welsh slate quarries from 1897. He had first saved the quarry from ruin by tight new rule. He would not know the union, though he would hear each man's own plea. His stand held firm through the whole fight.
britannica-1911-pentstemon:
Pentstemon, a genus of plants in the foxglove order, is described in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Its kinds are chiefly natives of North America, with showy open-tubular flowers. The pentstemon of the florist has sprung from two named species, and possibly from others. The plants pass English winters unharmed in favoured spots. Gardeners multiply them freely by cuttings.

Cuttings are taken from young side shoots and planted early in September. They are kept in a close cold frame until rooted, then wintered under cover against frost. The plants also seed freely, and new kinds are raised that way. When set varieties are not needed, seed is the simplest route. It is sown in heat early in February. The seedlings are pricked out and hardened off for the open air by late May. Plants once classed as Chelone are now placed with the pentstemons.
britannica-1911-perpetual-motion:
Perpetual motion, or perpetuum mobile, is taken up in this 1911 Britannica article as an old and famed problem of science. In its usual sense it does not mean a machine that merely moves for ever. It means a machine that, once set going, does useful work with no outside source of energy, or gives out more energy in each cycle than it takes in.

Early seekers did not always grasp what they were after, and some aimed only at a clock that would rewind itself. Most, though, wanted real work done, such as raising water or grinding corn. The article likens the quest to squaring the circle and to alchemy. Out of the vain search, it says, grew the great law of the conservation of energy.
britannica-1911-personation:
Personation is a law article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a form of fraud in English law. It is the false claim, by words or by conduct, that one person is another, living or dead. At common law it was no offence on its own. It became one only when the claim was made on oath, as perjury, or when it amounted to a common law cheat.

Statute law later made it an offence in set cases. One covers false claims used to obtain property by fraud. Another covers posing as an heir, a widow, or a kin of a person to get land, money, or goods. A third covers the faking of votes at elections. The entry lists the acts by their regnal years and points to related heads, such as false pretences and corrupt practices.
britannica-1911-perspiration:
Perspiration is the giving off of sweat from the sweat glands of the skin. The word comes from Latin roots meaning to breathe through. Sweat is a clear, pale fluid that is neutral or a touch alkaline. It holds about two per cent of solid matter. The flow of sweat goes on at all times. Nerves from the central system keep the glands in check.

The one use of sweat, the article says, is to control the heat the body gives off. Too much sweat is one ill state, and foul sweat is another. Too much sweat can show up in ills such as consumption and rheumatic fever. It can also appear on its own, over the whole body or in one part only. Cold baths and tonics are named as ways to check it.
britannica-1911-petition:
Petition is a law and constitution article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In its general sense a petition is a prayerful request, from a Latin word for seeking. In its weightier sense it is a plea for redress by a wronged person. It goes to a power able to relieve him, such as the Crown, Parliament, or a court.

The entry traces the right to petition the Crown in English history. Magna Carta is said to touch it in a famed clause on justice not sold or delayed. Later records set set days in the week for petitions to the king. The case of the seven bishops in 1688 confirmed the right, the article says. The Bill of Rights of 1689 then declared plainly that subjects may petition the king, and that punishing such acts is illegal.
britannica-1911-pheidon:
Pheidon, a king of Argos in early Greek times, is the subject of an ancient history entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Tradition places him in the eighth or seventh century before Christ. He is often called a tyrant, though the entry says that label is wrong. He was a strong ruler who raised the power of Argos a great deal.

Pheidon drew the towns of the Argive league back under Argos. He tried to weaken Corinth by a plot against its picked young men, but the plan leaked out. He also helped drive out the men who ran the Olympic games and led the feast himself. The Eleans refused to count that year in their list. Later they beat him with Spartan help. The entry weighs hard clashes in the old dates for his reign.
britannica-1911-philemon:
Philemon (about 361 to 263 before Christ) was a Greek poet of the New Comedy, and a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry weighs his fame. He was born at Soli in Cilicia, or at Syracuse. He settled at Athens early in life, and his first play was staged in 330. He was a rival of Menander in the theatre contests of Athens.

Philemon often beat Menander in those contests, the entry records. Later ages reversed the verdict and gave the crown to Menander. They put Philemon’s wins down to unfair influence. He travelled to the east and lived for a time at the court of Ptolemy, king of Egypt. A tale told by Plutarch has a storm drive him to Cyrene. There he fell into the hands of King Magas, a man he had once mocked in verse.
britannica-1911-pigot-george-baron:
George Pigot, Baron Pigot, an English governor of Madras who lived from 1719 to 1777, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in 1719, he joined the East India Company in 1736 and rose to govern Madras in 1755. He held the place against the French and took Pondicherry for the company.

Pigot went home in 1763, was made a baronet, and took a seat in Parliament, and in 1766 he was made an Irish peer. He went back to Madras in 1775 and fell at once into a fierce fight with most of his council, over a plan to restore the rajah of Tanjore. His foes had him seized, and he died still a prisoner in May 1777. The directors first blamed him, then ordered him restored, then recalled him, all too late. Four men who had seized him were later tried and fined.
britannica-1911-pike-weapon:
Pike, in its sense as a pointed thing and a weapon, is the subject of a word study in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry links pike with its sister forms pick and peak. All share a basic sense of a thing that tapers to a point. The roots of these forms are said to be much disputed.

Inside, the text sorts through old forms in many tongues. Old English had two forms that gave pike and pick. French, Spanish, and Italian forms are set beside Welsh and Breton ones. Some scholars traced the word to Celtic roots, while others looked to Latin. The entry shows how hard the true source is to pin down.
britannica-1911-pillion: Pillion names a light pad seat tied to the back of a horse saddle. The 1911 Britannica note says a second rider, most often a woman, sat on it. Such pads held bags and goods as well as folk. They were in wide use from the fifteen hundreds to the seventeen hundreds. The word came from an Irish word for cushion, drawn from the Latin word for skin. A like word once named a tall cap worn by priests and doctors.
britannica-1911-pinzon:
Pinzon names a family of rich Spanish navigators of Palos in Andalusia, traced in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Three brothers of the house sailed with Columbus in the discovery of America. Martin Alonzo, Francisco, and Vicente Yanez were their names. Martin Alonzo gave key help to Columbus in carrying out his plan.

One writer puts it that if Columbus was the head, Pinzon was the right arm. In the voyage of 1492 Martin Alonzo led the Pinta, with Francisco as pilot. Vicente led the Nina on the same fleet. On 6 October Martin urged a change of course to the south west. A flight of birds backed his plea, and the fleet took that course the next day. Four days later it made landfall in the Bahamas.
britannica-1911-plankton:
Plankton is the name Professor Victor Hensen gave to the drifting population of the sea. A long entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica takes it as a heading for sea life at large. The entry also takes in the benthos, the crawling population of the sea bottom. Study of both, it says, dates from the reports of the Challenger expedition.

The entry calls that expedition still the most important of its kind, for the work done, the distance covered, and the means spent on publishing results. It laid the base for knowledge of ocean water, currents, the shape of the sea floor, and deep-sea life. Later work, it cautions, has widened but not overturned those findings.
britannica-1911-plinlimmon:
Plinlimmon is a mountain of Wales, 2,463 feet high. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives its Welsh name as Pumlumon, meaning five beacons. It stands midway between Machynlleth and Llanidloes. Though lower than Snowdon, it is called the most risky of the Welsh hills. The cause is its shaking bogs. The views are plain: sheep downs on one side, bare peat ground on the other.

Five streams rise on the mountain. Three are small: the Rheidol, the Llyfnant, and the Clywedog. Two are great and famed: the Wye and the Severn. The bogs saw hard fights in old Welsh wars. Owen Glendower raised his flag of Welsh freedom there in 1401. From that base he raided the land around, sacking towns and burning an abbey. Slate pits and lead and copper mines mark the slopes as well.
britannica-1911-ploennies-luise-von:
Luise von Ploennies, who lived from 1803 to 1872, was a German poet. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes her songs and her translations. She was born at Hanau in November 1803. Her father was a naturalist of some note in his day.

In 1824 she wed a physician and settled at Darmstadt. After his death in 1847 she lived some years in Belgium. She then moved twice more before dying at Darmstadt in 1872. Verse volumes flowed from her between 1844 and 1870. Love songs, patriotic poems, and scene pieces suited her best. Two Bible dramas on Mary Magdalene and David came late. As a translator she gathered English poems in two books. The second of those ran to a third edition by 1867.
britannica-1911-plunket-william-conyngha:
William Plunket, first Baron Plunket, lived from 1764 to 1854 and was an Irish lawyer and statesman. The 1911 Britannica entry follows him from schooling by his father, a Presbyterian minister. At Trinity College in Dublin he led the Historical Society debating club with flair. He joined the Irish bar in 1787 and built a strong practice in equity.

He was made king counsel in 1797 and entered the Irish parliament the next year. His views joined Burke style Whig thought with warm Irish patriot feeling. He praised the English constitution as settled in 1688. The entry presents a speaker of rare grace whose rise came by talent and steady work.
britannica-1911-poison:
Poison is a hard word to pin down in law or in fact, this 1911 Britannica entry warns at its start. No rule of law sets what counts as a poison in plain terms. In broad words it is a stuff whose own ill force can kill life. It may work from inside the frame or laid on the skin from outside. Powder glass kills by its edge, not by ill force, so it is no true poison.

The study of poisons is a chief branch of law linked cure lore. The law healer must know how each poison works and what signs it leaves. Cure paths for each case form part of that same lore. Poisons work near the spot they touch or far off in the frame. Rust like poisons eat the spot they touch in plain sight.
britannica-1911-polyperchon: Polyperchon gets only a brief notice in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was one of Alexander's generals and took over from Antipater as regent in Macedonia in 319 BC. His rule was short, for Cassander drove him out two years later. The notice sends readers on to the article on Phocion for the fuller story of those years.
britannica-1911-port-hudson:
Port Hudson is a place and battle article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a village in Louisiana, in the United States. It stands on the left bank of the Mississippi river, about 135 miles above New Orleans. The piece deals almost wholly with one siege of the Civil War.

The article sets the scene at a sharp bend of the river. In 1862 the Confederate side built strong guns on the high bluffs there. In March 1863 Admiral Farragut tried to run his ships past those guns. Only two of his seven ships got through. Land attacks in May and June failed at heavy cost. After a siege of forty five days the post gave up in July 1863. With Vicksburg gone too, the Union held the whole river.
britannica-1911-port-huron:
Port Huron, a city and county seat of Saint Clair county in Michigan, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands where the Saint Clair and Black rivers meet, at the lower end of Lake Huron. Detroit lies about sixty miles to the south south west. Its people numbered 18863 in the census of 1910.

Rail lines and steamboat lines to Chicago and other ports serve the city. A railway tunnel of 6025 feet runs under the Saint Clair river to Sarnia in Canada. That work cost about 2700000 dollars and was built from 1889 to 1891. Wide streets, fine parks, and mineral springs make the city a summer resort as well. Court house, city hall, and a temple of the Modern Maccabees lead its stock of buildings.
britannica-1911-porter-david-dixon:
David Dixon Porter, an American naval officer born in eighteen thirteen, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of Captain David Porter and was born in Chester, Pennsylvania. His first voyage was with his father in West Indian waters, and it ended with the Fajardo affair.

The entry traces a fast early rise at sea. Porter joined the Mexican navy as a boy, then became a midshipman in the United States navy in eighteen twenty nine. He worked in the coast survey, served at the naval post in Washington, and fought in the Mexican War. There he led the paddle vessel Spitfire and took part in the fire on Vera Cruz. The life shows how one officer grew with the navy.
britannica-1911-porter-endymion:
Porter, Endymion is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an English royalist courtier. He lived from 1587 to 1649 and came of a Gloucestershire family. He was raised in Spain, where he had kin, as a page in the household of Olivares. He then served Edward Villiers and, after him, Buckingham.

Through Buckingham's word he became groom of the bedchamber to Charles the First. In October 1622 he was sent to treat of the Palatinate and of a Spanish marriage for the prince. He went with Charles and Buckingham on their rash trip to Spain in 1623 and acted as translator. In 1628 he went as envoy to Spain to treat for peace. In 1634 he served on a mission to the Netherlands. In the Civil War he stayed a constant, loyal servant of the king.
britannica-1911-power-transmission:
Power Transmission is the subject of a technical entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry sorts the appliances used to turn natural sources of energy to work into three groups. The first group is the prime movers, by which natural energy is changed into mechanical energy, such as water turbines, steam engines and boilers, and gas and oil engines.

The second group is the machinery driven by that energy, from machine tools and textile machinery to pumps and cranes. The third group is the gear that carries the energy from the prime mover to the machine. Power itself is defined as the rate at which energy is transmitted. The unit in common use is the horse power, given as a set rate of foot pounds per second. In a locomotive, prime mover and machine are combined so closely that the transmitting gear cannot be told apart.
britannica-1911-prantl-karl-von:
Karl von Prantl, a German philosopher, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Landsberg on the Lech in eighteen twenty, he took his doctorate at Munich in eighteen forty three. He was made professor there in eighteen fifty nine. He was also a member of the academies of Berlin and Munich.

He stood strongly in the Hegelian tradition, which he defended and expanded. Two of his works on the task and methods of philosophy are named. In them he stressed that subject and object are one for consciousness. Grasping that unity, he held, is the special mark of human awareness. The entry is brief and focused on that stance.
britannica-1911-predestination:
Predestination is a term of theology used in three senses. The word comes from a Late Latin verb that means to fix a thing beforehand. In its first sense, it names God's fixed resolve from eternity of all that is to be. In its second sense, it names God's fixing of men for endless bliss or endless pain. In its third sense, it names God's choice of some for life, called election.

The choice of some for death bears the name reprobation, and the term foreordination is liked better for that act. In its first sense the thought is close to that of fate. Sophocles shows man's life as woven with a shuttle of adamant. The Stoics framed a teaching of providence or of necessity. Epicurus denies that the gods watch over the affairs of men at all.
britannica-1911-prel-karl-freiherr-von:
Karl, Freiherr von Prel (1839–1899), was a German thinker, born at Landshut on 3 April 1839. After study at the university of Munich, he served in the Bavarian army from 1859 to 1872. He left that service with the rank of captain. He then gave himself to work in thought, above all on the facts of hypnotism and the occult. He viewed those facts from the new view of the mind held in his day.

Prel sought to show that spirit has a life apart from the senses. Yet, he held, spirit at times comes into touch with the world the senses know. He made that case by a study of the tie between the self of thought and the age of felt life, as Kant had set it out. In 1868 Tübingen gave him a doctor's degree for a work on the mind in dreams.
britannica-1911-preston:
Preston is a borough and port town of Lancashire in England. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets it on the river Ribble, north west of London. Its people grew from about 17,000 in 1800 to near 113,000 in 1901. The old core sits on a ridge above the north bank. Flat land spreads out toward the river mouth. The church of St John, built in 1855, stands on a very old church site.

Civic buildings take up much of the entry. The town hall of 1867, by Sir Gilbert Scott, has a tall tower and spire. A free library and museum opened under a trust left by a rich citizen. A new home for them came in 1893. It holds a gift library of near 9,000 books from 1761. An institute funded by the same trust runs science and art classes. The grammar school dates back to a founding in 1550.
britannica-1911-pronunciation: Pronunciation, in the 1911 Britannica, is a very short word entry rather than a full article. It comes from the Latin pronuntiare, to proclaim or announce. The entry gives the act of pronouncing and the manner of uttering a clear vocal sound, and it sends readers to the Phonetics and Voice articles for more. The old Latin sense of a public statement lives on in the Spanish pronunciamiento. That word means a manifesto or call to arms put out by a party in revolt.
britannica-1911-protection:
Protection, a system of trade policy, opens a long study in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Its modern form grew out of the trade and mill growth of the nineteenth century. The plain sense of the term is the use of set duties on foreign goods. Those duties are meant to shelter home makers from rival goods shipped in.

The entry warns that the plain sense is now far too narrow. Grants, premiums, rebates, and drawbacks all count as part of the system. Its care has spread from mills to farms, woods, mines, fish, and ships. Backers claim the word should cover all state acts that build up the wealth of a land. On that view its defense rests on grounds of state, of wealth, and of the common good at once.
britannica-1911-quenstedt-friedrich-augu:
Friedrich August von Quenstedt, who lived from 1809 to 1889, was a German geologist and fossil scholar. The 1911 Britannica entry follows him from birth at Eisleben in Saxony to study at Berlin. After museum work he took the chair of mineral study at Tubingen in 1837. He held that post at the university until his death in 1889.

Early books on crystals and minerals won wide use as class texts in schools. His fame rests most on study of fossils from the Jurassic rocks. The museum at Tubingen owed its founding to his drive and labour. His large work on German fossils ran to seven volumes across four decades.
britannica-1911-raccoon:
The raccoon is the chief member of a group of American tree dwelling mammals. It belongs to the order of flesh eaters and to its own family group. The word is a worn form of a North American Indian name for it. French, German, and other names for it come from a curious habit. The raccoon dips or washes its food in water before it eats.

The common raccoon is a thickly built animal about the size of a badger. It has a coat of long, coarse hairs in greyish brown tones. Its ears are short, and its bushy tail is ringed in black and white. Its range covers the whole of the United States in its spread. It runs north to Alaska and south well into Central America. It eats almost anything, from mice and eggs to fish and maize.
britannica-1911-raton:
Raton is a city in Colfax County, New Mexico, below the Raton Mountains. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica puts it high above sea level, near sixty five hundred feet. Three rail lines served the town when the entry was made. A state miners hospital and a public park were among its features.

Coal made the town grow more than any other trade. The Raton field was the richest coal ground in New Mexico at the time. In 1907 most of the state coal output came from Colfax County. Gold, silver, and lead ores were also mined nearby. Rail shops added steady work, and the town was chartered in 1891.
britannica-1911-raynald-of-chatillon:
Raynald of Châtillon, a Crusader knight who died in 1187, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He served Constance, princess of Antioch, who chose him as her husband in 1153. His first acts set the tone of his career. He made a brutal attack on the patriarch of Antioch.

Two years later he raided Cyprus and ravaged the island without just cause. In 1159 he had to humble himself before the emperor Manuel. Soon after, raiders seized him near Marash and held him at Aleppo for seventeen years. Freed in 1176, he married an heiress of Krak and Mont Royal. Those castles ruled the trade roads between Egypt and Damascus. In 1177 he beat Saladin in the field at the head of the kingdom's army. Yet his greed for caravan plunder broke a truce in 1181 and lit a new war.
britannica-1911-reginon:
Reginon, or Regino of Prum, was a writer of annals in the mid age. He was born near Spires and schooled in the house at Prum. He became a monk there and was made abbot in eight ninety-two, just after Danes had sacked the house. Seven years on he lost that post.

He then moved to Trier and led a house there, which he set in good order. He died in nine fifteen. His chief work tells the tale of the world from the birth of Christ to nine six. The first part leans on old books, while the last part is his own and holds real worth.
britannica-1911-reichenbach-georg-von:
Georg von Reichenbach (1772-1826) was a German maker of instruments for star study, born at Durlach in Baden. This 1911 Britannica article notes that from 1796 he worked on a dividing engine. In 1804 he helped found an instrument works in Munich, and in 1809, with Joseph Fraunhofer and Joseph Utzschneider, he set up optical works that later moved to Munich.

He left both firms in time and took a post in engineering under the Bavarian state, dying at Munich in 1826. His chief merit, the article says, was bringing into use the meridian or transit circle, which joins the transit instrument and the mural circle in one tool. That form came into wide use on the continent of Europe at once, though England kept the older tools for many years.
britannica-1911-remainder-reversion:
Remainder and reversion are land rights that wait their turn in this law entry in the 1911 Britannica. Each is a right held now that turns to full hold when a first hold ends. The first hold and the wait right make up the whole right in the land. A wait right set on a full free hold is void in law. The two forms split on who takes the land when the wait ends.

A reversion falls back to the first giver or his heir at that end. A remainder falls to a third man named in the deed or will. Rent duty binds the first holder to a reversion lord but not to a remainder man. Each wait right may be sold or left by will in law. Forms of wait rights split into fixed and chance kinds by their terms.
britannica-1911-renton: Renton is a factory town in Dumbartonshire in Scotland, described in a brief place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the Leven river, north of Dumbarton. Just over five thousand people lived there in 1901. Its lead trade is Turkey red dyeing, with calico printing and bleaching as well. The town was founded in 1782 by Mrs Smollett of Bonhill. A column raised in 1774 marks her brother, the novelist Tobias Smollett, who was born there.
britannica-1911-retaliation: Retaliation is a term defined in a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It means the repayment of like with like, above all the return of hostile acts in kind. The old rule of punishment, an eye for an eye, rests upon it. The word comes from late Latin, built on a root meaning of the same kind. That root also gave the law its word talio for this punishment. A modern form is noted: unequal import duties on one country's goods.
britannica-1911-reynolds-john-fulton:
John Fulton Reynolds, an American soldier who lived from 1820 to 1863, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Lancaster in Pennsylvania, he finished at West Point in 1841. He became a lieutenant of artillery in 1846 and won brevet ranks for gallantry in the Mexican War. He also served on the Utah expedition.

In 1859 Reynolds was made commandant of cadets at West Point, where he stood when the Civil War broke out. He rose fast, to lieutenant colonel and then brigadier general of volunteers in 1861. In the Peninsular campaign he fought at Beaver Dam Creek and Gaines's Mill, then was taken prisoner at Glendale. Freed after six weeks, he led a division with skill and courage at the second Bull Run. He later guarded his home state, took command of the First Corps, and fought at Fredericksburg.
britannica-1911-rhododendron:
Rhododendron is a botany article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Old writers seem to have used this name for the oleander, the entry says. In modern use it names a large genus of shrubs and trees of the heath family. No clear line can be drawn between this genus and Azalea, it adds. Marks put forward for the split fail when tested more widely.

Rhododendrons are trees or shrubs, never herbs, with plain leaves that may stay green all year or fall. Their flowers grow in clusters at the branch ends. The cup of the flower is often small or missing, while the funnel or bell shaped crown is large and showy. That show is why many kinds are prized in gardens. The fruit ripens into a long, many celled pod.
britannica-1911-ricasoli-bettino-baron:
Bettino Ricasoli (1809–1880) was an Italian statesman, and the early trials of his life open a biography in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Broglio on the nineteenth of March 1809. He was left an orphan at eighteen, with an estate deep in debt. By a special decree of the grand duke of Tuscany, he was declared of age.

Ricasoli took charge of his younger brothers and broke off his studies. He withdrew to Broglio and cleared the family lands of debt by careful management. In 1847 he founded the journal La Patria at Florence. He also sent the grand duke a memorial with remedies for the troubles of the state. In 1848 he was elected Gonfaloniere of Florence. He resigned that post over the anti liberal course of the grand duke. As Tuscan minister in 1859 he worked to unite Tuscany with Italy.
britannica-1911-rich-richard-rich-1st-ba:
Richard Rich, 1st Baron Rich (about 1490-1567), was an English lord chancellor under Henry VIII, and his rise is traced in an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in London to a family of merchants, he trained in law at the Middle Temple. By 1533 he was a knight and solicitor-general, working under Thomas Cromwell.

The entry gives a harsh view of his part in the trials of Thomas More and Bishop Fisher, where his use of private talk as proof drew open scorn in court. It notes his role in closing the monasteries and his post as first chancellor of the court set up to handle their wealth.
britannica-1911-richardson-henry-hobson:
Henry Hobson Richardson (1838-1886) was an American architect born in Louisiana. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows his study at Harvard and then in Paris. The Civil War cut off his family wealth while he was abroad. He supported himself in Paris offices until late 1865 as a result.

Back home he set up in New York, then moved to Boston in 1878. Trinity Church in Boston became his best known early monument there. Town halls, libraries, and college halls across the east show his hand. He turned from French training toward a bold Romanesque manner of his own. His short career left a deep mark on builders after him.
britannica-1911-rigg-james-harrison:
James Harrison Rigg, who lived from 1821 to 1909, was an English Nonconformist divine born at Newcastle. The 1911 Britannica article says he was born on the sixteenth of January 1821. His father was a Wesleyan minister. Rigg was schooled at Old Kingswood in Bristol, where he later taught. In 1845 he entered the Wesleyan ministry. In the church strife of 1849 he wrote well in defence of Methodist rule.

His book of 1857 on modern Anglican thought cut sharp at great names, yet won praise. Kingsley, stung at first, became his warm friend. In 1868 Rigg became head of the Westminster training college for day-school teachers. He held that post with growing fame for thirty-five years. In 1870 he won a seat on the first School Board for London. There he shaped the place of faith teaching in the board schools.
britannica-1911-right-ascension: Right Ascension is defined in a 1911 Britannica article as a term of astronomy. It is one of the co-ordinates of a heavenly body. It is fixed by an angle. That is the angle which the meridian passing through the body makes with the prime meridian through the equinox point. The short entry gives the bare definition only. Readers who need the full working of the term are sent on to the main article on astronomy.
britannica-1911-riviere-briton:
Riviere, Briton, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of an English artist. Born in London on the 14th of August 1840, he was an art teacher's son. His father taught drawing at Cheltenham College and then at Oxford. The boy was schooled at Cheltenham and Oxford, taking his degree in 1867.

For his art training he owed near all to his father's hand. In 1857 he showed three works at the Royal Academy in London. From 1863 he sent works to the Academy shows each year. His early themes were tales, like the Eve of the Spanish Armada. In 1865 a Sleeping Deerhound began his long line of beast works. Beast themes then held his art almost to the end.
britannica-1911-rockefeller-john-davison:
John Davison Rockefeller was an American oil chief who was born in New York state in eighteen thirty-nine. His folk moved to Ohio, where he began as a book keeper in Cleveland. He then went into the trade in farm goods. In eighteen sixty-two his firm put funds into an oil works.

He soon bought a large share in a bigger works and took new men in as mates. In eighteen seventy they formed the Standard Oil firm with a vast fund. That firm won near full sway of oil work in America. He quit the trade in eighteen ninety-five, rich past all peers, and gave great sums to schools.
britannica-1911-rockhampton:
Rockhampton, a port of Queensland, is drawn in a town entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the Fitzroy River, forty-three miles from its mouth. Brisbane lies three hundred and thirty-five miles south-east of the town. Fine looks and a sound, warm air mark its site by the river. It serves as port for a wide farm district of the north.

Gold, copper, and silver come out of that wide back country. Side ports at the river mouth take the big sea steamers. Frozen meat makes a large share of the town's sea trade. Works for meat extract and meat keeping stand by the wharves. The town ends the Queensland Central rail line at its station. In 1901 the town folk came to over fifteen thousand.
britannica-1911-rodney-george-brydges-ro:
George Brydges Rodney is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He was an English admiral who lived from 1718 to 1792. He was born in February 1718, the son of an officer. His father had served in Spain and then in marines. George was sent to school at Harrow as a boy. In 1732 he joined a ship as a volunteer. He served in the Mediterranean in his early years.

He was made a lieutenant in the year 1739. In 1742 he rose to the rank of post captain. He then served in home waters for a spell. In a ship called the Eagle he fought off Ushant in 1747. That win over a French fleet won him first fame. In 1749 he was made governor of Newfoundland. Fishery gains were the chief ground for that choice.
britannica-1911-roe-edward-payson:
Edward Payson Roe is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He was an American writer of tales from 1838 to 1888. He was born in Orange county, New York, in March 1838. He studied at Williams College and at a school for clergy. In 1862 he became a chaplain with horse troops. He later served as chaplain at a war hospital.

From 1866 he was a pastor at Highland Falls for eight years. In 1874 he moved to Cornwall on the Hudson river. There he wrote tales and worked at growing fruit and plants. His first famed tale came out in 1872 as a serial. More tales followed year by year till his death. They sold widely in England and America in his day. Their firm moral tone helped make tale reading more welcome.
britannica-1911-romilly-john-romilly-1st:
John Romilly, first Baron Romilly and an English judge born in eighteen hundred and two, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the second son of Sir Samuel Romilly. Born in January of that year, he studied at Trinity College, Cambridge. He was called to the bar in eighteen twenty seven.

He first sat in Parliament in eighteen thirty two for Bridport. In time he rose to high law posts in the state. He served as a lead law aide and then as the chief law voice of the Crown. In eighteen fifty one he was made master of the rolls, a top judge post. He was the last man in that post to sit in Parliament at the same time. In eighteen sixty six he was raised to the peer rank. He did much to free old state rolls for men who search the past.
britannica-1911-rosmead-hercules-george-:
Hercules Robinson, first Baron Rosmead, lived from 1824 to 1897 and ran colonies for Britain. The 1911 Britannica entry traces his Irish roots and his army start at Sandhurst. He rose to captain in the 87th Foot, then left for public works in Ireland in 1846. Clear, strong reports and famine work in 1848 marked him as able.

At age thirty he became president of the island of Montserrat in the West Indies. Governorships of Saint Christopher, Hong Kong, and Ceylon followed in swift order. He was knighted for bringing coolie labour to Saint Christopher in his term. The Rosmead name came from his mother home in County Westmeath.
britannica-1911-rostov-on-the-don:
Rostov-on-the-Don, a Russian seaport in the land of the Don Cossacks, is described in an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The town stands on the high right bank of the Don river, thirteen miles from its mouth in the Sea of Azov. A small fort was first raised on an island in the river in 1731. Thirty years later the works were moved to the site the town now holds.

The article gives the width of the river, notes that shallow water hinders ships, and says ice closes it for more than one hundred days a year. It tracks fast growth, from 70,700 people in 1881 to well over 160,000 with the suburbs. Summer brings some 60,000 extra men to ship grain for export.
britannica-1911-rousseau-de-la-rottiere-:
Jean Simeon Rousseau de la Rottiere is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a French painter of room decor born in seventeen forty seven. His father held the post of sculptor to the king of France. The odd tail to his name was in use while he was still a boy.

The entry tells how he won a school prize for the best work of a term. He and his brother did decor work for the crown at Versailles from youth. Scholars still sort out which hands did which room of that vast work. Royal baths and halls bear work that is laid to the two of them. His best known task is one small rich room now kept in London.
britannica-1911-roussillon:
Roussillon was one of the old tracts of France, now the bulk of a coast shire by the high hills. High peaks bound it south, and the inland sea bounds it east. Its name comes from a small place near Perpignan, its chief town. Gallic chiefs met there to hear a famed foe ask for talks.

The tract was held by Rome, then by Goth kings, then by Saracen hosts for a time. Charlemagne gave land there to Goth folk who had fled Spain. Counts rose in each part, till the whole tract joined the crown of Aragon. Its port then grew as a hub of sea trade.
britannica-1911-rowton-montague-william-:
Montague William Lowry-Corry, Baron Rowton, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. He lived from 1838 to 1903. He was the second son of Henry Corry. His mother was a daughter of the sixth earl of Shaftesbury. He was born in London in October 1838.

He was educated at Harrow and at Trinity College, Cambridge. He was called to the bar in 1863. His father had deep roots in politics. He sat for County Tyrone in parliament for forty-seven years in a row. He served in a cabinet under Lord Derby. There he held posts first in the council, then at the Admiralty. The young Corry thus grew up close to Conservative party politics. Yet the text says something else marked him out. It was his winning manner and his social gifts, more than his politics, that won him his place.
britannica-1911-royston:
Royston is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on a market town in Hertfordshire. It lies near the Cambridge border, forty-eight miles north of London by rail. The town count for 1901 is 3,517 folk. Its church of St John the Baptist is in the main Early English in style.

A market house and a hall with a library and museum are named. Below a street lies a strange hermit's cave cut in the chalk. It holds rough carvings of the cross and other holy scenes. The cave was found by chance in the year 1742. The town stands on the Roman Ermine Street, and Roman finds are common near it. An Augustinian house was founded there late in the twelfth century.
britannica-1911-royton: Royton, in a short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry, is an urban district in Lancashire, England. It lies within the parliamentary borough of Oldham, two miles north of Oldham on the Lancashire and Yorkshire railway. The entry says the place is of early origin, yet as a town it is wholly of modern growth. Cotton making is its chief industry, and its population in 1901 was 14,881.
britannica-1911-ruabon:
Ruabon is a town in north Wales near the border with England, on a main rail line south west of Wrexham. The 1911 Britannica entry gives its town count at the turn of the age. It stands on a small stream that feeds the River Dee.

Its old Gothic church is said by some to have been founded by a brother of a Welsh prince. It holds stone tributes to a great local house and to a scholar who rendered a Welsh tale of the land into English. Round the town lie coal pits, works for machines, an iron foundry, and chemic works. A large trade in glazed and plain bricks thrives there. Near by stand an old ringed camp and a great house with a famed row of trees.
britannica-1911-rustication:
Rustication, in building, is a way of working stone. The centre of each block's face is left rough, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica explains the term in an entry on building craft. The word comes from the Latin for country. The same root gives the sense of a country holiday, and of a student sent down from a university as a punishment.

The entry finds the first case at Pasargadae in Persia, on a platform of Cyrus, where a smooth chiselled edge frames a rough centre. Like work stands in Palestine, and the finest cases are the walls of the temple at Jerusalem and at Hebron, with huge stones whose faces jut out by a foot. Crusader castles in Palestine used bold rustication too, their faces worked with slanting chisel lines. Later builders took up the rough face for its look, as on corner stones.
britannica-1911-rutherford-william-gunio:
William Gunion Rutherford, who lived from 1853 to 1907, was an English scholar of Greek. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with his birth in Peeblesshire. He was schooled at St Andrews and Oxford. At Oxford he read natural science with medicine in view. He dropped that plan for a school career instead. From 1883 to 1901 he was headmaster of Westminster school.

His death cost English classical study one of its brightest men. He gave special care to Attic idioms and the tongue of Aristophanes. His New Phrynichus of 1882 treats the Attic rules of an old grammarian. A work on Babrius followed as a sample of later Greek. His edition of the notes on Aristophanes, from a Ravenna copy, ran from 1896 to 1905. It met a cooler welcome than the rest. School books on Greek grammar round out his list.
britannica-1911-sabbation:
Sabbation, also called Sambatyon, is a river placed in legend more than on maps. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica links it in old Jewish sources to the exile of the Ten Tribes. Josephus tells the core tale in his history of the Jewish war. Titus saw the stream while marching through Syria, he says.

The stream ran strong for a time, then its springs failed for six days. On the seventh day it ran again as if nothing had changed. Pliny gives a flipped form, with rest on the seventh day. Later travelers claimed like streams elsewhere, but none matched the fixed pattern.
britannica-1911-sackville-mortimer-sackv:
Mortimer Sackville-West, first Baron Sackville, lived from 1820 to 1888. The 1911 Britannica life traces his line to Sir Richard Sackville of Kent. That Richard was a cousin of Ann Boleyn in Tudor days. He served in Parliament and at court under Henry the Eighth. In 1548 he took charge of the court of augmentations for the crown.

Richard amassed great wealth in those years of high royal favour. A wit of the age said his name should be Fill-sack instead. His son Thomas was made earl of Dorset in the year 1604. From Thomas sprang the earls and dukes of Dorset of that house. Mortimer was a younger son of the fifth Earl de la Warr.
britannica-1911-saint-andre-andre-jeanbo:
André Jeanbon Saint André, a French revolutionist who lived from 1749 to 1813, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Montauban, the son of a fuller, he was brought up by the Jesuits and took orders. He then turned Protestant himself and became a pastor, at Castres and at Montauban.

The grant of free worship made Saint André a backer of the Revolution, and his department sent him to the Convention. He sat on the Mountain, voted for the death of Louis the Sixteenth, and in July 1793 he was president of the Convention. That month he joined the Committee of Public Safety and was sent on mission to the armies. He won a vote of a hundred million francs to build ships, and he rebuilt the naval harbours of Brest and Cherbourg. In May 1794 he fought at sea beside Admiral Villaret de Joyeuse against the English.
britannica-1911-sarpedon:
Sarpedon, in Greek tale, is a Lycian prince and a hero of the Trojan war, and the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica tells his tale in brief. He was the son of Zeus and Laodameia. He fought on the side of Troy. He won fame for brave deeds in that war, then fell at the hand of Patroclus.

A fierce fight broke out for the hold of his corpse. Apollo saved the corpse from the Greeks at last. By the word of Zeus the god washed it and rubbed it with the food of the gods. He gave it to Sleep and Death, who bore it home to Lycia for burial. A shrine there bore his name. A later tale makes a second Sarpedon, a son of Europa and a brother of Minos, cast out of Crete in time.
britannica-1911-schack-adolf-friedrich-g:
Schack, Adolf Friedrich, Graf von, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of a German poet. Born at Brusewitz near Schwerin on the 2nd of August 1815, he read law at Bonn, Heidelberg, and Berlin. He then joined the Mecklenburg state service in Berlin. Tired of office work, he quit and toured Italy, Egypt, and Spain.

He later served the grand duke of Oldenburg and went with him to the East. In 1849 he was sent as envoy to Berlin. He quit that post in 1852 and spent time in Spain on Moorish past. In 1855 he settled at Munich and built a famed art hall. He died at Rome on the 14th of April 1894. His poems and verse tales are listed at the end.
britannica-1911-schwyz-canton:
Schwyz is the subject of a canton entry in the 1911 Britannica. Schwyz is one of the forest cantons of central Switzerland. Its full area is given as about three hundred and fifty square miles. Most of that land is counted as in use. Woods cover a fair share of the ground. Lakes take up much of the rest of its span. Its top peak rises to nine thousand two hundred feet.

Two famed peaks of the Rigi rise inside its bounds. The canton runs from one great lake to the next. Vales of two rivers cut through its core. It is a hilly land more than a high peak land. Farm work there is chiefly with herds and pasture. Few rail lines cross the canton at that time. One main line to the Saint Gotthard pass runs through it.
britannica-1911-scranton:
Scranton is a city and the county seat of Lackawanna county, Pennsylvania. It stands where the Lackawanna river meets Roaring Brook. It lies about 162 miles by rail north by west of Philadelphia and 146 miles from New York. Its people numbered 102,026 in 1900 and 129,867 in 1910. Of those in 1900, near 29,000 were born abroad, with the Irish, Germans, Welsh, and English the largest groups. Six railways serve the city, and it covers about 20 square miles.

Among the chief public buildings of Scranton are the United States Government building and the County Court House. The City Hall and the Albright Memorial building stand there as well. That last house holds the public library, with 55,800 books in 1908. The city has an armoury, a Board of Trade building, and fine churches and schools.
britannica-1911-sedition:
Sedition is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on a term of law. The Latin roots join words for apart and for going. In law it names a bid to disturb the calm of the state. In Roman law it was counted as a form of treason.

In English law the term is loose and hard to pin down. It spans wrongs from libel all the way up to treason. Most use is in forms like seditious libel or seditious meeting. One judge is quoted as doubting the crime exists as such. The chief acts on it came late in the reign of George the Third. They banned false oaths, armed drills, and closed groups of that age.
britannica-1911-session:
Session, from a Latin term for a sit, names the act of a sit or a state of be sat. In wide use it names the sit of a group, in law or state, to do its work. It also names the span that group sits till it breaks up. A term of the law house runs from its meet to its close.

The term is used most for the sits of law courts, chiefly those for crime. Peace chiefs hold sits of the peace for the work set by law. Small sits hear slight cases, while great sits meet four times a year. Scotlands top court bears the name Court of Session.
britannica-1911-shannon:
The Shannon is the chief river of Ireland. It flows in a bow-shaped course from north to south and south-west. It runs from the north-west of the island to its mouth in the Atlantic on the south-west coast. The river is about 240 miles long and drains 4,544 square miles. It rises in county Cavan, in pools at the foot of Cuilcagh Mountain. It then crosses county Leitrim through Lough Allen, the first of a chain of lakes.

In its mid course the Shannon parts county Roscommon from Leitrim, Longford, Westmeath, and King's County. There it forms Loughs Boderg, Forbes, and Ree, and takes in the Boyle and the Inny. The Royal Canal joins it in county Longford. Farther on it forms Lough Derg and takes in the Suck and the Brosna. It then reaches Limerick as a broad river and runs out to its mouth.
britannica-1911-sicard-roch-ambroise-cuc:
Sicard, Roch-Ambroise Cucurron is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a French abbe who taught deaf-mutes. Born at Le Fousseret in the Haute-Garonne on the twentieth of September 1742, he was trained as a priest. In 1786 he became head of a school for deaf-mutes at Bordeaux. On the death of the Abbe de l'Epee in 1789 he succeeded him at Paris.

The article follows his later years briefly. Sicard came through the troubles of 1792 unharmed and joined the Institute in 1795. Yet the value of his teaching work was hardly recognized until shortly before his death. The article is short and sends readers to the article on the deaf and dumb for the substance of his methods. He died at Paris on the tenth of May 1822.
britannica-1911-sickingen-franz-von:
Franz von Sickingen, a knight of feuds, strides a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Ebernburg in 1481, he fought Venice for the emperor. Rhine estates came to him, and feuds swelled his wealth and name. He set himself up as friend of the weak in those feuds. In 1513 he took up the cause of a cast-out man of Worms.

With seven thousand men Sickingen fell on that rich city. The ban of the empire did not check his wild course. He cut its trade and burned its lands till it paid him. Lorraine and Hesse felt his hand and paid him gold in turn. In 1518 he forced Metz to hand over a vast sum. The emperor freed him from the ban that same year.
britannica-1911-sicyon:
Sicyon is a history article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an ancient Greek city in the north of the Peloponnesus. The city stood on a low plateau about two miles from the Corinthian Gulf, where the Asopus and Helisson rivers meet. A rich plain of olive groves lay between it and its port. In the Iliad it appears as a realm under Agamemnon.

After the Dorian invasion the people were split into three Dorian tribes, one Ionian tribe, and a class of serfs. In the seventh century a line of tyrants, the Orthagoridae, ruled with a mild hand from about 665 to 565. The greatest of them, Cleisthenes, led the First Sacred War in 590 and fostered the crafts for which the city was famed: wood carving, bronze work, fine pottery, and painting. After the tyrants fell, Sicyon joined the Peloponnesian League.
