britannica-1911-sidney-algernon:
Algernon Sidney, an English statesman born in sixteen twenty two, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Penshurst in Kent, he was the second son of Robert, second earl of Leicester. His mother was Dorothy Percy of the Northumberland house. As a boy he showed much talent, and his father trained it with care.

At age ten he went with his father on a royal task to the king of Denmark. Four years later he went to Paris with him, then on to Rome. In sixteen forty one he was given a troop in his father regiment in Ireland. Two years later the brothers came back to England in the midst of civil war. The entry then sets up the clash that shaped the rest of his life. It is a strong start on a key voice for free rule.
britannica-1911-siemens-ernst-werner-von:
Ernst Werner von Siemens (1816–1892) was a German electrician, and a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows his path from the army to the telegraph. He was born on the thirteenth of December 1816 at Lenthe in Hanover. He attended the gymnasium at Lübeck. He then entered the Prussian army as a volunteer.

For three years Siemens studied at the Military Academy in Berlin. In 1838 he gained a commission as a lieutenant in the artillery. Six years later he took charge of the artillery workshops. In 1848 he had the task of guarding the port of Kiel against the Danish fleet. As commandant of Friedrichsort he built works for the defence of Eckernförde harbour. That same year he was charged with laying the first telegraph line in Germany, between Berlin and Frankfurt.
britannica-1911-sigwart-christoph-wilhel:
Sigwart, Christoph Wilhelm von is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a German philosopher. Born at Remmingsheim in Württemberg in 1789, Sigwart became professor of philosophy at Tübingen and died at Stuttgart in 1844. He wrote many books on the history of philosophy. His books include studies of Spinozism, a logic handbook and a history of philosophy.

Most of the article then turns to his son, Christoph von Sigwart, who taught at Blaubeuren and then at Tübingen from 1865. His chief work, the Logic of 1873, holds an important place among recent works on logical theory. Sigwart built his own system rather than judging his predecessors, drawing on English as well as German logicians.
britannica-1911-simmons-edward-emerson:
Edward Emerson Simmons, an American artist born at Concord in Massachusetts in 1852, is given a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He graduated from Harvard College in 1874 and studied in Paris under Lefebvre and Boulanger, where he took a gold medal. 

He won a prize for a mural scheme for the criminal courts building in New York. He went on to decorate the Waldorf Astoria hotel, the Library of Congress, and the Capitol at Saint Paul. He was one of the first members of the group known as the Ten American Painters.
britannica-1911-sion:
Sion, called Sitten in German, is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article on the capital of the Swiss canton of Valais. The town stands on the railway line that runs up the Rhone valley. It is built around two steep hillocks that rise from the level valley floor. That setting makes it one of the most scenic small cities in Switzerland.

The north hillock holds the castle of Tourbillon, built in 1294 and long the home of the bishops. The south hillock holds the castle of Valeria, with a museum and a church of the thirteenth century. Below stand a cathedral of the fifteenth century and another old castle. In 1900 the town held 6,048 people, most of them French speaking, at a height of 1,680 feet.
britannica-1911-skipton:
Skipton is a market town in the West Riding of Yorkshire, England, and this 1911 Britannica entry describes the place and its past. It sits in the hilly upper valley of the river Aire, north-west of Leeds, served by two railways and by the Leeds and Liverpool canal. Its urban district held 11,986 people in 1901. The town was the capital of the old district of Craven.

Its strong castle was built by Robert de Romille in the Conqueror's time. Part was pulled down in 1648, and the countess of Pembroke later restored it, as she did the church of the Holy Trinity. The town has large woollen and cotton factories and a big limestone quarry nearby. The entry traces the lordship from Earl Edwin through the Albemarle family to the Cliffords, who gained it in 1311.
britannica-1911-slatin-sir-rudolf-carl-v:
Anglo Austrian soldier Rudolf Carl von Slatin, born near Vienna in eighteen fifty seven, is given a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was an administrator in the Sudan. At age seventeen he made his first trip there, reaching Khartum by the Nile in eighteen seventy five.

He crossed Kordofan to explore hills in the Dar Nuba region. A revolt forced him back to Khartum, where he met Emin Pasha. He hoped to visit General Gordon, then governor of the equatorial provinces. He had to return to Austria first, but Gordon later called him to the Sudan. Slatin arrived in eighteen seventy nine and soon became governor of Dara in Darfur. He held that post till early eighteen eighty one, when he was promoted.
britannica-1911-smith-henry-boynton:
Henry Boynton Smith was an American church thinker who lived from eighteen fifteen to eighteen seventy-seven. He was born in Portland in Maine and trained at Bowdoin and then in Germany. Poor health and doubt of his new views at first shut him out of good posts. He served as a pastor and then taught at Amherst.

The bulk of the entry covers his long years at a New York school for church study. There he taught church past and then core faith. His key talk held that all faith thought must centre on Christ. Books made from his class notes came out after his death.
britannica-1911-smith-william-robertson:
Smith, William Robertson is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a Scottish scholar who edited the ninth edition of the Britannica itself. Born on the eighth of November 1846 at Keig in Aberdeenshire, he was the son of a Free Church minister. He took the highest honours at Aberdeen University, among them the Ferguson scholarship in mathematics. In 1866 he entered the Free Church College at Edinburgh to read theology, with summer study at Bonn and Gottingen.

In 1870 he took the chair of Oriental languages and Old Testament study at the Free Church College in Aberdeen. His articles on Bible subjects for the ninth Britannica alarmed the Free Church rulers, who put him on trial in 1876. He went on to lecture to great crowds and to take command of the Britannica after Baynes.
britannica-1911-smithsonian-institution:
Smithsonian Institution is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an American house of learning. It sits in Washington, the capital city. It was founded by the bequest of James Smithson. Smithson seems to have known of a plan for such a body. Washington had urged a national seat of learning in 1796. Smithson left his estate first to a nephew.

A condition in the will shaped the gift's path. If that nephew died without issue, all would pass across. The whole estate would go to the United States of America. It would found at Washington an establishment in Smithson's name. Its aim was the increase and diffusion of knowledge among men. The nephew died without issue in 1835. Much opposition rose in America to accepting the gift. The gift was accepted all the same in the end.
britannica-1911-smyth-sir-warington-wilk:
Sir Warington Wilkinson Smyth, a British rock scholar, fills a life in the 1911 Britannica. Born at Naples in eighteen seventeen, he was the son of a navy map maker. He learned at Westminster, Bedford, and Cambridge. A travel grant sent him for four years through Europe, Asia Minor, Syria, and Egypt. He used that time to study mines, coal fields, and salt works.

Back home he joined the state rock probe as a mine scholar. He taught at the School of Mines for thirty years. High posts on woods, forests, and mine safety came late in his life. He led a royal probe on mine blasts for seven years. His books treat Turks, coal, and the craft of mining. He died in London in eighteen ninety.
britannica-1911-soleure-canton:
Soleure, called Solothurn in German, is a canton of north west Switzerland, set out in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. Its total area is just over three hundred square miles. Most of that land is counted as productive, with a large share under forest. Vineyards cover a small part.

Save for two small districts in its south, the whole canton lies in the Jura range. It is said to be the most irregular in shape of all Swiss cantons. That shape came from lands won at sundry dates by the town that gives it its name. It holds most of a river valley between two towns outside its bounds. Three split off districts belong to it, one of them a famed pilgrim resort. Its highest point tops four thousand seven hundred feet.
britannica-1911-solon:
Solon, an Athenian statesman of the seventh and sixth centuries BC, is treated in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of Execestides, of the house of Codrus, and was born about 638 BC. Waste by his father forced young Solon to earn his bread by trade, much of it abroad. He won fame for love poems and later for verse on his city.

His first public act was the recovery of Salamis from the Megarians. A law banned all talk of the lost island, so Solon feigned madness and sang a fiery poem in the market place. He then led the force that won the island back for Athens. At home, debt and strife among rich and poor had reached a peak that the laws of Draco could not cure. All classes joined to call Solon in as archon with full powers.
britannica-1911-south-molton:
South Molton, a market town in Devonshire, England, appears in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. It stands on the river Mole, west of London on the Great Western line. In nineteen oh one it had two thousand eight hundred forty eight folk.

The parish church of Saint Mary Magdalene is a large stone church with an old carved pulpit. A guild hall and a market house stand in the town. Linen goods are made there, fairs are held twice a year, and mills on the river grind flour. The town is run by a mayor, four alder men, and twelve council men. Its past runs back to the Domesday survey and a grant of a market in twelve forty six.
britannica-1911-southampton:
Southampton is a seaport borough in Hampshire, England, and this 1911 Britannica entry describes its site, walls, and old buildings. It stands near the head of Southampton Water, on a point of land bounded on the east by the river Itchen. Its people numbered 104,824 in 1901. Large stretches of the old town walls survive, first raised in Norman times and strengthened in later years.

On the west side the wall runs arcaded on its outer face for nearly a hundred yards and is studded with towers. The castle site is built over, though a Saxon fortress stood there first. Near it stands a very old house known as King John's Palace, thought to be among the earliest of its kind in England. Of the town gates, the Bar Gate, South Gate, and West Gate still stand.
britannica-1911-southington:
Southington is the subject of a town entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It was a township of Hartford county, Connecticut, south west of the city of Hartford. Within it lay a borough of the same name, served by a rail line. Population and area figures for the township are both given.

The chief industry was the making of hardware goods, the entry says. Between eighteen hundred nine and eighteen seventy four, residents gained a large number of patents. The township was first part of Farmington and was settled about sixteen ninety seven. It became a separate parish under another name before it was incorporated as a township.
britannica-1911-speculation:
Speculation, a round card game for any fair number of players, is set out in a games entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Each player puts a stake in a pool, and the dealer stakes double. Three cards are dealt face down to each hand. The top card left in the pack is turned up for trumps.

Play goes round from the dealers left, one card turned up at a time. A card counts only if it is a trump higher than the trump card shown. Its holder may sell it to the top bidder or keep it. Play goes on until a still higher trump shows. The holder of the highest trump at the end takes the pool. If the ace of trumps is the turned card, the dealer wins at once. Side rules let players buy unseen cards or hands.
britannica-1911-spielhagen-friedrich-von:
Friedrich von Spielhagen, a German writer of tales born in eighteen twenty nine, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Magdeburg, he was raised at Stralsund, where his father held a state post. He went to the town school there. He then studied law, and in time letters, at three towns of high study.

On his school end he taught at a school in Leipzig. When his father died in eighteen fifty four, he gave himself in full to the pen. Two first tales came in the years that came next. Then a long tale won a sharp win. The text calls it one of the best tales of its time. A long row of tales came year by year past that crest.
britannica-1911-spontoon: Spontoon was a shafted weapon carried by infantry officers. A brief entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica places it in its weapon family. Officers bore it in the seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries. The word comes through French and Italian forms. Its root is a Latin term for a point or a prick. In kind it belongs with the partisan and the halberd. Those weapons join a spear head to a long shaft. The spontoon head had its own special form, the entry notes.
britannica-1911-spoon:
Spoon is a table implement with a bowl shaped end and a handle, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out. The word first meant a chip or splinter of wood in old English and in kin tongues. From that derivation the earliest northern European spoon would seem to have been a chip of wood. The Greek and Latin words point to the early use of shells for the same purpose.

Such shells are still used by primitive peoples in the present day. Examples are preserved of spoons used by the ancient Egyptians in ivory, flint, slate, and wood. Many of them are carved with the symbols of their religion in their make. The spoons of the Greeks and Romans were chiefly made of bronze and silver. Their handles usually take the form of a spike or pointed stem, and many examples in the British Museum show the types.
britannica-1911-spurgeon-charles-haddon:
Charles Haddon Spurgeon (1834-1892) was an English Nonconformist preacher, born at Kelvedon in Essex, as this 1911 Britannica article recounts. He was the grandson of an Essex pastor and the son of an Independent minister at Islington. He went to school at Colchester and Maidstone, and in 1849 became an usher at a school in Newmarket.

Spurgeon joined the Baptist communion in 1851, and at once his work showed his conversion. He handed out tracts, visited the poor, joined the lay preachers, and gave his first sermon at Teversham near Cambridge. In 1852 he became pastor of Waterbeach. Friends urged him to enter a college to train more fully for the ministry. A meeting with the tutor fell through by chance, and Spurgeon read that mishap as a divine warning against a college career.
britannica-1911-squadron:
Squadron, a military and naval term for a body of horse troops or a detachment of warships, is traced in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. The word comes from squadra, a square. A Florio definition gives it as a part of a company of twenty or twenty-five soldiers under a corporal. Such men no doubt formed in squares on parade or in battle. The root runs back to a Latin word for making four-cornered.

In army use, a squadron is a main unit of a cavalry regiment, matching the company in an infantry battalion. A regiment normally has four squadrons, numbering 120 to 200 men. In naval use, a squadron is a group of vessels, either one division of a fleet or a separate detachment under a flag officer. The shortened word squad names any small party of men on a set duty.
britannica-1911-st-gall-canton:
Saint Gall is one of the cantons of north east Switzerland, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out. It borders the Austrian province of Vorarlberg and the small state of Liechtenstein. It entirely surrounds the canton of Appenzell in its midst. Much of its land once belonged to the abbots of Saint Gall in former times.

Its area is 779.3 square miles, of which most is reckoned productive land. Forests cover 157.1 square miles of that area in the count. Its height above the sea runs from 1,306 feet at the lake of Constance to 10,667 feet at the Ringelspitz. The canton holds parts of the lake of Constance, of the Walensee, and of the lake of Zurich. It is hilly in the north, and the height grows steadily toward its south border.
britannica-1911-st-pol-de-leon:
St Pol-de-Leon is a town article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The town sits in the department of Finistere in north-west France. It stands about a mile from the shore of the English Channel. The entry gives the town's size and describes it as a quaint place with old houses.

Most of the article is given to its churches. The cathedral is largely Norman Gothic, with two tall towers and carved stalls inside. A wooden shrine there holds the bell of St Pol, said to cure headache and ear trouble. The church of Notre Dame de Kreizker is praised for its high spire. A short history closes the piece, from a Welsh monk made bishop in the sixth century to a failed rising in 1793.
britannica-1911-stanfield-william-clarks:
William Clarkson Stanfield was an English painter of the sea, born of Irish parents in a port town of the north. As a youth he was a sailor. On long trips he gained that close knowledge of the sea and of ships that showed so well in his later works.

In his spare hours he drew sea themes with a keen hand, the 1911 Britannica entry says. When a hurt barred him from sea service for good, he was hired to paint scenes for a sailors play house in London. With a famed peer he then worked at a south bank house, and rose to scene painter at a great royal house of plays. There his drop scenes and his work for the Christmas shows won him a high name. All the while he kept at small works on canvas of his own.
britannica-1911-starvation:
Starvation is the state of being kept from the needs of food, and the pain of the worst hunger and cold. The 1911 Britannica entry tells a tale of how the word was coined. A famed Scots lord is said to have first used it in a debate in the Commons, in a speech on American affairs.

The coinage stuck, and the lord bore the mock name of Starvation for the rest of his days. The piece then digs to the root of the older verb. To starve first meant to die in plain terms, as its kin words in Dutch and German still mean. In English it shrank in sense to death by hunger or by cold alone.
britannica-1911-steel-construction:
Steel construction for large buildings is the theme of a long piece in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The text ties its rise to the high price of land in the core of great cities. Each cubic foot built must earn its keep in rent or use, or it wastes the funds spent on it. That hard rule, the text says, long held street buildings to five or six floors.

Two new tools changed that limit in the late 1800s. The making of the wrought iron beam in 1855 let builders frame floors that resist fire at less cost. Passenger lifts came in about ten years later and made high floors easy to reach. Hotels, flats, offices, and factories could then rise to many more floors than stone walls alone had allowed. Looks, as in spires and domes, count for less in the account than cost and use.
britannica-1911-steer-paul-wilson:
Paul Wilson Steer (1860- ) was an English painter, and this short 1911 Britannica entry gives his training and his place in British art. He was born at Birkenhead. He was trained first at the Gloucester school of art and then in Paris, at the Académie Julian and at the École des Beaux Arts under Cabanel. He showed three pictures at the Royal Academy before 1886.

After that date nearly all his work was seen at the shows of the New English Art Club, where he was a leading member. The entry praises his figure subjects and his landscapes for great freshness and high technical skill. His portrait of himself had been taken into the collection of the Uffizi Gallery at Florence.
britannica-1911-steevens-george-warringt:
George Warrington Steevens, an English journalist who died in 1900, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was schooled at the City of London School and at Balliol College, Oxford, where he held a scholarship. He first wrote for college papers as an undergraduate. In 1893 he became a fellow of Pembroke College, Oxford, and edited a weekly paper at Cambridge.

Steevens then moved to London and joined the Pall Mall Gazette, while also writing for other reviews. In 1896 he joined the new Daily Mail and went on special trips for that paper. Those trips gave him books such as The Land of the Dollar, Egypt in 1898, and With Kitchener to Khartoum. In September 1899 he went to South Africa as a war reporter. He was besieged with the troops in Ladysmith, where his life came to its end.
britannica-1911-stein-charlotte-von:
Stein, Charlotte von is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the friend of Goethe whose bond with him shaped his Weimar years. Born at Weimar on the twenty-fifth of December 1742, she was the eldest daughter of the master of ceremonies von Schardt. At sixteen she became a lady in waiting to the duchess Anna Amalia. In 1764 she married Freiherr Friedrich von Stein, master of the horse to the duke, and bore seven children. Goethe reached Weimar in 1775 and was soon won by her charm, though she was seven years his elder.

For more than ten years Charlotte von Stein was the poet's constant companion. On his return from Italy in 1788 the close tie loosened, and his bond with Christiane Vulpius drove them further apart. Her jealousy at first knew no bounds, and only slowly did friendship grow back.
britannica-1911-steinmetz-karl-friedrich:
Karl Friedrich von Steinmetz, a Prussian general field marshal who lived from 1796 to 1877, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born at Eisenach, he was educated at the cadet school of Stolp in Pomerania from 1807 to 1811. Those were years of hardship and poverty under French occupation, the entry notes.

At the start of the War of Liberation, he and his elder brother slipped through the French posts to Breslau. Both were taken into the army at once, despite their poverty. The article tells how a general at first treated the new officers coldly, until the young Steinmetz spoke up boldly. The brothers then fought in the hardest battles of the 1813 campaign. The elder was killed at Leipzig, and the younger was wounded more than once.
britannica-1911-stephan-heinrich-von:
Heinrich von Stephan (1831-1897) was a German statesman who reshaped the postal service, and his rise is told in an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Stolp in Pomerania, he showed a gift for languages from his earliest years. At sixteen he entered the Prussian post office.

The entry follows his swift rise through posts in East Prussia and Cologne, where he saw at first hand the tangled charges that made foreign mail costly and unsure. Moved to Berlin in 1856, he was trusted with key duties, such as speaking for Prussia in postal treaties with Spain and Portugal. In 1864 he was set the task of rebuilding the postal service in Schleswig-Holstein.
britannica-1911-stephens-alexander-hamil:
Stephens, Alexander Hamilton, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of an American statesman. Born in Georgia on the 11th of February 1812, he was a weak, sickly child. His folk were poor, and he worked on a farm as a boy. At age fifteen he was left an orphan with no parents.

An uncle took him in, and a Sunday school head sent him to school. A state society then sent him to Franklin College in 1828. He took his degree there in 1832 and taught school for two years. He read law for less than four months and joined the bar in 1834. His rise at the bar was swift and marked. In 1836 he won a seat in the Georgia House.
britannica-1911-steuben-frederick-willia:
Steuben, Frederick William Augustus Henry Ferdinand, Baron von is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the German soldier who drilled the American army into shape. Born at Magdeburg in Prussia on the fifteenth of November 1730, the son of a soldier, Steuben served as a boy volunteer. He fought in the Seven Years' War and became an aide to Frederick the Great in 1762. In 1777 the French minister of war sent him to aid the American colonists.

Steuben reached Portsmouth, New Hampshire, in December 1777 and offered himself to Congress as a volunteer. At Valley Forge in March 1778 he began drilling the raw soldiers. By May he was inspector general with the rank of major general, having set up a sound system of discipline and economy. The fruit showed at Monmouth, where he rallied the broken troops of General Lee.
britannica-1911-stevinus-simon:
Stevinus, Simon is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a Dutch mathematician. He was born at Bruges in 1548 and died in 1620, at the Hague or at Leiden. Very little of his life is recorded. Even the day of his birth and the place of his death are unsure.

What is known comes in hints from his own works. He began life as a merchant's clerk in Antwerp. He travelled in Poland, Denmark, and other parts of northern Europe. He stood close to Prince Maurice of Orange, who asked his advice on many matters. The prince made him a public officer, first as head of the water works and later as quartermaster-general. The article notes, too, his habit of denying the worth of mere authority.
britannica-1911-stewarton:
Stewarton is the subject of a town entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It was a burgh in the Cunningham district of Ayrshire, Scotland, on the Annick Water. It lay south west of Glasgow on a rail line. The entry gives its population in nineteen hundred one as under three thousand.

The town lies in a fine farming district famed for its dairy produce, the entry says. Two cattle fairs and two horse fairs were held each year. At the October cattle fair came the largest show of Ayrshire dairy stock in Scotland. Nearby Dunlop gave its name to a cheese that once commanded a large market.
britannica-1911-stockton:
Stockton is a city in central California and the seat of San Joaquin county. The 1911 Britannica article places it at the head of the Stockton channel of the San Joaquin river. Its count rose from 17,506 in 1900 to 23,253 in 1910. Three rail lines serve the city, and boats trade with San Francisco by river. The site is flat, with broad streets laid out on a plain grid.

The city stands in a rich farm valley and ranks as a great market for grain, fruit, and greens in the West. Its mills turn out flour, lumber, and farm machines. The entry lists a public library, schools, homes for children and the old, and hospitals. Stockton grew fast in the gold rush days. A town was laid out in 1849 and named for Commander Robert Field Stockton.
britannica-1911-stonington:
Stonington is a township in New London county in Connecticut, covered in a 1911 Britannica entry. It sits in the south east corner of the state on Long Island Sound. The township held more than nine thousand people in 1910, counting its borough and villages. Rail lines, an electric line, and summer steamers link it to nearby towns.

Its harbour is fine, though foreign trade is small in the years described. Local work spans foundries, print presses, cloth mills, ship yards, and fishing. The entry traces settlement to 1649 by English planters from Plymouth Colony. It also notes the old burying ground and a monument raised there in 1889.
britannica-1911-stowell-william-scott-ba:
William Scott, Baron Stowell, who lived from 1745 to 1836, was an English judge born at Heworth near Newcastle. The 1911 Britannica article says his father was a coal trader. His younger brother John became the famed Lord Chancellor Eldon. Scott was schooled at Newcastle and at Corpus Christi College, Oxford. He won a scholarship in 1761 and rose as a tutor. As a reader in ancient history he matched the fame of Blackstone.

Scott came late to law, taking it up in earnest in 1776. His rise in the church courts was swift. In 1788 he was made judge of the consistory court and was knighted. In 1798 he became judge of the high court of admiralty. He sat in parliament for Oxford University from 1801. In 1821 he was raised to the peerage as Baron Stowell. He left the bench in full by 1827.
britannica-1911-strachwitz-moritz-karl-w:
Moritz von Strachwitz, a poet dead at twenty-five, is mourned in a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Silesia in 1822, he was a count of old stock. Breslau and Berlin gave him his years of study in youth. He then settled on his Moravian estate to write his verse. On a trip to Italy in 1847 he fell ill at Venice.

He died that December at Vienna, just twenty-five years of age. Yet his lyric gift had shown rare force and fresh fire. His first book, Songs of One Awakening, came out in 1842. New poems came out a year after his death in print. Ballads were his finest work in that short, bright span. Platen's sway and the stir of those years mark his songs.
britannica-1911-stratford-on-avon:
Stratford on Avon, a market town in Warwickshire, England, fills a place entry in the 1911 Britannica. The town lies on the west bank of the Avon River in a rich vale. A stone bridge of fourteen arches spans the river there. A canal links the town to Warwick and Birmingham. Its folk count for nineteen oh one was eight thousand three hundred ten.

The church of the Holy Trinity stands near the river on an old Saxon church site. Its choir, aisles, and tall spire span more than one age of church craft. A guild of the Holy Cross, open to men and women, left a hall and chapel in town. Trade notes name brew work, a corn mart, and schools and care homes.
britannica-1911-strathcona-and-mount-roy:
Donald Alexander Smith, Baron Strathcona and Mount Royal, was a Canadian statesman and man of finance born at Forres in Scotland on 6 August 1820 and profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the second son of Alexander Smith, a Highland merchant. His mother was a sister of John Stewart, a famed fur trader in the Canadian North West.

Through that uncle, Donald Smith gained a post as junior clerk in the Hudson Bay Company in 1838. That firm then ruled most of what is now the Dominion of Canada. He was sent to Labrador and posted at Hamilton Inlet. For thirteen years he roughed it there and mastered the fur trade. He showed that potatoes and other garden crops could grow on that bleak coast. Ten years on Hudson Bay followed as he rose in the firm.
britannica-1911-strathnairn-hugh-henry-r:
Hugh Henry Rose, first Baron Strathnairn, a British field marshal who lived from 1801 to 1885, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the third son of Sir George Henry Rose, a diplomat at the Prussian court. He was born at Berlin in April 1801 and schooled there, with his soldier's training at the cadet school.

He joined the 93rd Highlanders as an ensign in 1820 and soon moved to the 19th Foot in Ireland. There he helped keep order in the Ribbon troubles. His rise was fast: lieutenant in 1821, captain in 1824, and major by the end of 1826. In 1830 he became equerry to the duke of Cambridge. At Malta in 1836 he won praise for his zeal in care of sick soldiers in a cholera outbreak. In 1840 he was picked for special service in Syria.
britannica-1911-strongylion: Strongylion is named in a 1911 Britannica article as a Greek sculptor of old times. His famed work was a bronze horse set up on the Acropolis of Athens, late in the fifth century before Christ. The figure stood for the wooden horse of Troy. The Greek heroes were shown inside it, looking out. The carved base has been found. His other works named here are a figure of Artemis at Megara, a group of the Muses, and an Amazon that the emperor Nero greatly admired.
britannica-1911-sturgeon:
Sturgeon is the subject of a nature article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The name covers a small group of fishes, with some twenty known kinds, found in the rivers of Europe, Asia, and North America. The fish spend much of the year in the sea. At set times they swim up large rivers, some in spring to lay their spawn. A few kinds live in fresh water all the time.

The article says none are found in the tropics or in the southern half of the world. They are most thick in the rivers of southern Russia, where more than ten thousand may be caught at one station in a two week run. It also notes their great worth as a fishery in Russia and their place in the great lakes of North America.
britannica-1911-subinfeudation:
Subinfeudation, in English law, is a practice of land holding explained in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Tenants who held land under the king or a higher lord would carve out new tenures. They did so by subletting or by granting away part of their lands to others. Those tenants were called mesne lords toward the men who held from them.

The man who held at once from the crown was the tenant in chief. The lowest tenant of all was the freeholder at the base of the chain. In theory the crown owned all lands and stood as lord paramount over the whole. Great lords viewed the growth of such sub tenures with disfavour and alarm. In 1290 a statute called Quia Emptores put a stop to new ones. A tenant could grant land away at will, but the new holder must hold it from the same lord as before.
britannica-1911-suggestion:
Suggestion is a term that took on a special sense in the study of the mind, and this 1911 Britannica entry explains that shift. Older British writers on psychology used the words suggest and suggestion much as common speech does. One idea was said to suggest another when it called that other back to mind. Work on mental sickness and on hypnotism gave the words a sharper, technical use.

The hypnotists of the Nancy school spread the teaching that the heart of the hypnotic state is blind trust. The subject takes in each command or claim from the hypnotist and acts on it without question. Such commands or claims, even when hinted by a gesture or a glance, were called suggestions. A person who took them in this way was said to be suggestible. The entry credits French doctors with making the point plain.
britannica-1911-summary-jurisdiction:
Summary jurisdiction is a term of English law with more than one use. In its widest sense it covers the power of high courts to deal at once with contempt. No jury takes part in such cases. The power may first have been used only when the act was done in court. It has long been used for acts done outside court as well.

The term also covers powers given to the High Court and county courts by statute. Those powers let courts handle some cases by simpler and quicker means than a full action. In modern use the phrase points most often to justices of the peace. They deal with minor offences out of sessions and without a jury. Statutes were needed to allow this, since common law knew no trial without a jury.
britannica-1911-superannuation: Superannuation means release from office or service because of old age, unfitness, or passing the age limit set for a post, says a short entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word was built on annual and annuity, from a late Latin term for one who has lived beyond the year. By extension it also names the pension paid for past service at retirement. In schooling, the term is used for moving a backward pupil out of a class below the level his age calls for.
britannica-1911-supererogation:
Supererogation means doing more than duty asks, and a 1911 Britannica entry gives both the word roots and the church sense. The Latin parts point to payment beyond what is due or asked. In plain use it means work done past the call of duty. The term is best known from Roman Catholic teaching on merit.

In that teaching, works of supererogation are deeds done beyond what God requires of a person. Such extra merit forms a store that can be drawn on for others. Those whose own works fall short may gain help from that reserve. The entry states the doctrine in brief, clear terms for general readers.
britannica-1911-suppe-franz-von:
Franz von Suppé, an Austrian composer who lived from 1820 to 1895, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. His full name was Francesco Ezechiele Ermenegildo Suppé-Demelli. He was born at Spalato in Dalmatia and died at Vienna. He first studied philosophy at the university of Padua. After his father's death he turned to music and studied at the Vienna conservatoire.

Suppé began as a conductor in one of the smaller Viennese theatres. He worked his way up to become a popular composer of light opera. The article notes that his works won little success outside Vienna. Of his sixty comic operas, Fatinitza, staged in 1876, did best, while Boccaccio had only moderate favour. His overture to Dichter und Bauer is called his most successful orchestral work. He also wrote some church music.
britannica-1911-susarion:
Susarion, a Greek comic poet, is the subject of a short entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. He came from Tripodiscus in Megaris. About five hundred eighty years before Christ, he brought Megarian comedy to Icaria in Attica. That place was also an early home of Greek tragedy and of the worship of Dionysus.

The entry notes a contest said to have been held on that occasion. The prize was a basket of figs and a jar of wine. Susarion's changes were modest, with no lone actor and no fixed plot. He put the old rough jests of the chorus into verse made for recital. The Athenians did not take to the new shows.
britannica-1911-suttner-bertha-baroness-:
Bertha, Baroness von Suttner, an Austrian writer born in 1843, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. She was born at Prague, the daughter of an Austrian field marshal who died soon after her birth. After a careful schooling she travelled abroad and lived for long spells in Paris and Italy.

In 1876 Suttner wed a novelist and lived nine years with him at Tiflis in the Caucasus. Her many books include tales, romances, and works on social questions. Die Waffen nieder, from 1889, is the best known of them all. She once served as secretary to Alfred Nobel and held great sway over him. As a champion of peace among nations she wrote on war and on the Hague peace talks. In 1905 she won a Nobel prize for her work in the cause of peace. Her memoirs came out in 1908.
britannica-1911-swindon:
Swindon is the subject of a town entry in the 1911 Britannica. The town lies in Wiltshire in England on a rail line. Its count in 1901 was just over forty five thousand souls. It has two parts, called New and Old, in the entry. The new town grew round vast rail works there. Those works built engines and wagons for a great line. The new town is a key rail junction point. It rose fast on a strip of waste land.

Churches and chapels were built for its workmen in haste. Their count soon passed ten thousand men in all. Each man pays to a fund for sick and hurt care. That fund keeps hospitals, baths, and wash houses in town. The old town stands on a hill with wide views.
britannica-1911-swinton:
Swinton is a town district in the West Riding of Yorkshire, England, near Sheffield. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica places it where canal routes meet the river Don route. Its people passed twelve thousand in 1901 by the count given. Three rail lines served the town in that period.

Two Norman arches from an old church stand in the churchyard there. Coal pits, quarries, and brickfields lay in the area round the town. Glass bottle works, ironworks, and pottery shops gave other jobs. The town was once famed for its Rockingham ware goods. Henry II had granted it a free warren in old times.
britannica-1911-sybel-heinrich-von:
Heinrich von Sybel, a German historian who lived from 1817 to 1895, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. He came from a Protestant family long settled at Soest in Westphalia. Born at Dusseldorf, where his father held high posts under French and then Prussian rule, he grew up in a home alive with writing and art.

The entry traces his schooling in his home town and then at the university of Berlin. There he fell under the sway of Savigny and Ranke, whose most noted pupil he became. In 1841 he settled at Bonn as a lecturer in history. He was already known for close studies of the middle ages, chief among them a history of the First Crusade issued that same year.
britannica-1911-sydenham-charles-edward-:
Sydenham, Charles Edward Poulett-Thomson, first Baron, is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a British statesman. He was born on the thirteenth of September 1799 and died in 1841. His father was a London merchant, and the young man spent some years in the family business in Russia and London.

He entered parliament for Dover in 1826. In 1830 he joined Lord Grey's ministry at the board of trade. A free-trader and a skilled hand in finance, he was chosen for Manchester in 1832 and held that seat for years. He spent those years on talks about world trade. In 1839 he accepted the governor-generalship of Canada. There he set up the union of Upper and Lower Canada. A knighthood and a peerage marked that service in 1840.
britannica-1911-symonds-john-addington:
John Addington Symonds (1840-1893) was an English critic and poet, and his early career fills an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Bristol, the only son of a physician who wrote on beauty and on sleep and dreams, he was a delicate boy. At Harrow he took no part in games and showed no special promise.

The entry tells how Balliol College, Oxford, drew out his hidden gifts, and his time there was one long run of honors. He won the Newdigate prize in 1860 and a fellowship at Magdalen in 1862. The strain of study broke his health at once, and he had to seek rest in Switzerland, where he met the woman he married in 1864.
britannica-1911-talbot-of-hensol-charles:
Charles Talbot, first Baron Talbot of Hensol, was lord chancellor of England. He lived from sixteen eighty five to seventeen thirty seven. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the eldest son of William Talbot, bishop of Durham.

Talbot studied at Eton and at Oriel College, Oxford, in his youth. He joined the bar in seventeen eleven and rose in royal legal posts. In seventeen thirty three he was made lord chancellor and a peer. For three years he proved an equity judge of rare skill. Men praised his wit, and Butler gave his famed Analogy work to him.
britannica-1911-talfourd-sir-thomas-noon:
Sir Thomas Noon Talfourd, an English judge and author who lived from 1795 to 1854, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Reading, the son of a brewer, he was schooled at Hendon and at Reading grammar school. At eighteen he went to London to read law under Joseph Chitty, the famed special pleader.

Talfourd joined the Oxford circuit in 1821, the year he was called to the bar. He rose by hard, careful work in cases rather than by forensic brilliance, the entry says. In 1849 he became a judge of the court of common pleas. He also sat for Reading in the Commons for two spells. There he brought in a bill on copyright across borders, in a speech held the finest of that session. The bill passed in 1842 in a much cut form. Dickens dedicated the Pickwick Papers to him.
britannica-1911-tasman-abel-janszoon:
Abel Janszoon Tasman, born about sixteen o three, was the greatest of Dutch navigators in the entry's view. He found Tasmania, New Zealand, the Tonga islands, and the Fiji islands. He was also the first man to sail right round Australia. Born at Lutjegast in Groningen, he is first met in the East Indies in sixteen thirty four. He sailed from Batavia to Amboyna that year.

Tasman sailed home in sixteen thirty six and was back at Batavia by sixteen thirty eight. In June sixteen thirty nine he was sent out with a fellow captain. Their orders were to seek islands of gold and silver east of Japan. They went to the Philippines and added to Dutch knowledge of Luzon. They found and mapped islands to the north, most likely the Bonin group. The rich isles they sought were never found.
britannica-1911-taunton:
Taunton, a market town of Somersetshire in England, is surveyed in a place entry in the 1911 Britannica. It stands on the river Tone in the fair vale of Taunton Dene, 163 miles west of London by rail. Its count in 1901 was 21,087 people. Three broad main streets meet at the Parade, where a market cross stands, and most of the town lies south of the river.

The parish church of St Mary Magdalene ranks among the finest large Perpendicular churches in England, and its tower tops 150 feet. The castle, now a museum of old finds, keeps walls from the 12th century. A grammar school dates from 1522. Town trades ran to silk, linen, and gloves, iron and brass work, and brewing. The entry then traces Taunton from a Saxon strong place to fresh incorporation in 1877.
britannica-1911-taunton-henry-labouchere:
Henry Labouchere, Baron Taunton, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in seventeen ninety eight, he came from a French Huguenot family that had settled in Holland. His father was a partner in a rich Amsterdam banking firm. Henry was taught at Winchester and at Christ Church, Oxford.

The entry follows his long career in Parliament as a Whig. He first entered the Commons in eighteen twenty six. For most years from eighteen thirty he sat for Taunton in Somerset. He held the post of president of the Board of Trade twice. He also served as chief secretary for Ireland and later in other high posts.
britannica-1911-taxation:
Taxation is the subject of a state entry in the 1911 Britannica. The word comes from a Latin root for judging worth. Tax means the share of state funds got by forced dues. Those dues fall on the folk who live in the state. A state may also gain funds from its own lands. Crown lands in Britain are a trace of that old way. In past times such lands were a chief source of funds.

As a rule states now meet costs through tax dues. Some seeming bars to that rule are bars in name only. Land funds in India are held to act like a tax. A broad charge by a state works as a tax in effect. It takes in and spends part of folk income. The same broad effects flow from state held wealth. Kinds of tax and ways to levy them follow.
britannica-1911-tegetthoff-wilhelm-von:
Wilhelm von Tegetthoff (1827-1871), an Austrian admiral, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The son of an army colonel, he was born at Marburg in Styria in December 1827. He passed through the naval college at Venice and first served at sea in 1845. He was made an ensign in 1848 and was present at the blockade of Venice the next year.

The article follows his rise step by step. He became a lieutenant in 1852, and duty at the mouth of the Danube during the Crimean War brought him to the notice of Archduke Maximilian, the new head of the navy. A science voyage took him to Egypt, Arabia, and the Red Sea. By 1858 he commanded a corvette on the coast of Morocco, then in a state of unrest.
britannica-1911-tennent-sir-james-emerso:
Sir James Emerson Tennent, an English politician and traveller who lived from 1804 to 1869, has a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Belfast on 7 April 1804, he was the third son of William Emerson, a merchant of that city. He was educated at Trinity College, Dublin, in his youth. He took up the cause of Greek independence with zeal.

Tennent travelled in Greece and published a Picture of Greece in 1826, Letters from the Aegean in 1829, and a History of Modern Greece in 1830. He was called to the English bar at Lincoln Inn in 1831. In that year he married the daughter and co heiress of William Tennent, a wealthy merchant of Belfast. He entered parliament in 1832 as member for Belfast, and in 1845 he was knighted and appointed colonial secretary of Ceylon.
britannica-1911-thaton:
Thaton is a town and district in the Tenasserim division of Lower Burma. The 1911 Britannica entry sets the town below a range of hills. It lies ten miles from the sea on low ground there. In old days it was the capital of the Talaing kingdom. It served then as a seaport of that realm in trade.

The town held 14,342 souls by the count of 1901. The district spans 5,079 square miles with 343,510 folk in all. That count shows a rise of 29 in each hundred in ten years. The district was formed in 1895 from parts of two old ones. Rice is its staple crop, with much tobacco grown as well.
britannica-1911-thayer-abbott-handerson:
Abbott Handerson Thayer is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was an American painter born in Boston in eighteen forty nine. He learned his art in Paris at a famed school of fine arts. He joined the chief art groups of his land in due course.

The entry names his best known works, from enthroned virgin scenes to portraits. Wall work for a college hall is also noted in his list. He is famed as well for his study of how beasts hide in plain sight. His rule holds that dark backs and pale bellies cancel out in wild light. A book by his son sums up that life work on colour and concealment.
britannica-1911-ticino-canton:
Ticino is a canton of Switzerland on the south slope of the Alps. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica calls it the only canton set near wholly on that side. Most of its folk speak Italian. It takes its name from the Ticino river. The whole upper course of that river lies inside the canton. So does the head of Lago Maggiore. Three old districts, once part of the duchy of Milan, form the canton.

Swiss arms took the land, and in 1803 the parts were joined as one canton. Its area is 1,081 square miles. Woods cloak much of the ground. Vineyards cover near twenty square miles. Only four cantons are larger. One patch, Campione by Lugano, stays an Italian enclave. Lakes and glaciers eat up much of the rest.
britannica-1911-timoleon:
Timoleon is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a Corinthian statesman and general of ancient Greece. When his brother Timophanes seized the acropolis of Corinth, Timoleon protested, then stood aside while his friends put him to death. Public opinion called the act patriotic, but his mother's curses drove him into retirement for twenty years. In 344 envoys from Syracuse begged Corinth for relief from faction and from Carthage.

The article tells how Timoleon took the mission and freed Sicily. He landed at Tauromenium, beat Hicetas at Adranum, and took Syracuse after Dionysius gave up the island of Ortygia. He brought in new settlers, razed the citadel, set up a court of justice on its site and restored popular government. When Carthage sent a great army in 340, he won a decisive victory at the river Crimissus.
britannica-1911-tiverton:
Tiverton, a market town in Devonshire, England, is described in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It sits amid fair scenery where the Loman meets the Exe. Its count in nineteen hundred and one was ten thousand three hundred and eighty two. The upper town stands on high ground on the left bank of the Exe.

A bridge leads down to the lower town, called West Exe. The church of Saint Peter is a fine hall in the late style of its age. Its high tower has four tiers decked with odd carved forms. One side chapel was built in fifteen seventeen by a wool merchant of the town. Its stone work is cut very fine. Of the first church, one door is all that stands. The castle dates from about eleven hundred and five.
britannica-1911-toulon:
Toulon is a French seaport, fortress, and naval station on the Mediterranean Sea. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out its harbor and town. It lies east of Marseilles in the department of Var. Town counts given are about fifty-four thousand in 1886 and over one hundred thousand in 1901.

The bay splits into two roadsteads, the Grande Rade and the Petite Rade. Hills, capes, a breakwater, forts, and gun posts guard each approach. Old town streets are narrow, while a newer quarter grew to the north. Chief buildings named are the old cathedral, a naval hospital, schools, barracks, and a gallery and library block. Trade lists wine, grain, wood, coal, and fish among its goods.
britannica-1911-tournon:
Tournon is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a town of France. It lies in the south west in the department of Ardeche. It is capital of a district in that department. It stands on the right bank of the Rhone. Lyons lies far to the north by rail. Counts from 1906 give the town 3642 people. The wider commune held 5003 in that count. The town preserves a gateway of the fifteenth century.

An old castle serves as town hall, court, and prison. The church of Saint Julian dates chiefly from the 1300s. The lycee occupies an old college of the town. Cardinal Francois de Tournon founded that college in the 1500s. Two suspension bridges unite the town with Tain across the river. One was built in 1825 and is the oldest in France.
britannica-1911-traction:
Traction is the act of drawing or hauling, from a Latin word for to draw. As used in the article, it names the ways animal and machine power move people or goods from place to place in wheeled carts. The oldest form of such power is that of animals. Horses, mules, donkeys, and oxen are the beasts most used for draught work on plain roads.

On the continent of Europe dogs are often put to light carts or barrows. In England that use was barred by an act of 1854 on cruelty to animals. Camels and elephants serve as draught beasts only on rare occasions. The article notes a hard point in the study of such work. When men or beasts carry or draw loads, the work done is hard to gauge in set units. The push that has to be beaten cannot always be known.
britannica-1911-transcaspian-region:
Transcaspian Region, a Russian territory east of the Caspian Sea, is described at length in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is bound by Persia and Afghanistan to the south and by Khiva and Bokhara to the north east. Its area is over two hundred thousand square miles. For long its dry deserts were near unknown land.

Great puzzles of geography centre on this region. Old shifts in the courses of the Oxus and Jaxartes rivers are one case. The rise and fall of Lake Aral is another. A long mountain chain parts the deserts from the highlands of Khorasan. Its western peaks are granite, and its main ridge runs six hundred miles. A broad valley with two rivers that flow in opposed ways parts it from the plateau. Beyond that valley, higher border ranges fringe the plateau edge.
britannica-1911-treason:
Treason is a law article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica on the crime of striking at the safety of a state or its head. The piece gives the word's roots in French and Latin, then argues that laws against treason flow from the very idea of a state. Most lands, it notes, made rules to punish the crime early in their history.

The heart of the article is a plea for clear limits. What counted as a capital crime at Rome under Tiberius, it points out, may be no offence at all in England. The writer backs Montesquieu: if the crime is left vague, power can be strained in times of public heat, and rule can slide toward despotism. So the entry is both a survey of the law and a warning about how loosely drawn charges can be abused.
britannica-1911-treitschke-heinrich-von:
Heinrich von Treitschke lived from 1834 to 1896 and was a German historian. The 1911 Britannica life adds that he wrote much on politics as well. He was born at Dresden in September 1834, an army officer's son. His father rose to govern Konigstein and to rule Dresden in arms. Deafness barred the young man from state service as a career.

He studied at Leipzig and at Bonn under Dahlmann in his youth. He then set up as a lecturer on history and politics at Leipzig. Students flocked to his talks, but the Saxon state blocked his rise. His views made a chair there out of reach for him at first. At that time he was a strong Liberal who sought a united Germany.
britannica-1911-turner-sharon:
Sharon Turner, English historian, was born in Pentonville in London on 24 September 1768 and is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. His parents came from Yorkshire. He trained for the law in the Temple from 1783 and kept that work till poor health forced him to stop in 1829. He died in London in 1847.

A boyhood love for an old Norse death song drew him to early English history. He spent his spare hours on Anglo-Saxon and Icelandic sources in the British Museum. That rich store had been largely ignored before him. His history of England to the Norman Conquest came out from 1799 to 1805 in four volumes. Later works covered the middle ages and sacred history.
britannica-1911-turton:
Turton, a town district in Lancashire, England, is covered in a brief entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies north of Bolton, on the rail line that serves the county. Its count in nineteen hundred and one was twelve thousand three hundred and fifty five. That size is new, and the entry gives a plain cause for it.

Growth came from the rise of the cotton trade in all its branches. Large stone quarries near the town add a second base of work. One old house draws the eye of the past. Turton Tower stands in the town and dates in the main from the fifteen hundreds. It holds some fine wood work of its own age. Though the note is short, it ties mill growth, stone work, and one grand old house into a clear town sketch.
britannica-1911-typhon:
Typhon, also called Typhaon or Typhoeus, is a figure of Greek myth. He was the youngest son of Gaea and Tartarus. Tales show him as a grim monster with a hundred dragon heads. Zeus beat him and cast him into Tartarus. Other tales place him in the land of the Arimi in Cilicia, or under Etna, or in other lands of fire. There he is held to cause the bursts of volcanoes.

Typhon thus stands for the force of volcanoes in person. By Echidna he was the father of Cerberus, the Hydra of Lerna, and the Chimaera. He is also the father of harsh winds, the typhoons. Later writers linked him with the Egyptian god Seth. The article ends with a list of books on Typhon and on the giants and titans of Greek myth.
britannica-1911-typhoon: Typhoon is the name given to a heavy cyclonic storm in the seas off the east coast of Asia. The short 1911 Britannica note traces the word in part to an Arabic and Hindustani word for a tempest. Such storms strike the seas from Japan to the Philippine Islands. They come most often in a series during August, September, and October, when the belt of still air in the Pacific reaches its farthest point north.
britannica-1911-vaison:
Vaison is a town of southeastern France in Vaucluse. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica splits it by its Roman bridge. The river Ouveze divides the town into two quarters. Its count in 1906 was about twenty-one hundred.

The right bank holds the Roman and early medieval town. A church there, once the cathedral, has a choir of great age. A Romanesque cloister beside it keeps old carved stones. Ruins of a Roman amphitheatre stand in the old quarter. The left bank keeps the later town walls and a count keep. Wood shoes, bellows, and farm tools are made in town. Under Rome the place, then Vasio, held great weight. Rich finds from digging prove that old rank plainly. A famed athlete statue from there sits in the British Museum.
britannica-1911-valentine-and-orson:
Valentine and Orson is a romance tied to the cycle of Charlemagne, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica tells. It is the tale of twin brothers left in the woods as babes. Valentine is raised as a knight at the court of Pippin. Orson grows up in a bear's den as a wild man of the woods, till Valentine beats him and tames him.

Orson then serves Valentine as squire and comrade. In time the two free their mother Bellisant, sister of Pippin, from the hands of a giant. She had been cast off by her husband, the emperor of Greece, on a false charge. The tale rests on a lost French first form and lives in French, English, German, Icelandic, Dutch, and Italian. In the old forms Orson is the nameless one.
britannica-1911-venison:
Venison is a short word entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word first meant any beast killed in the chase, hunted game of any kind. In time its sense narrowed to one meat alone. By the age of the article it named only the flesh of the deer, prepared for eating.

The entry traces the word through Old French forms such as veneisun and venoison, down to the modern French venaison. In those older forms it covered the flesh of both deer and boar, the chief beasts of the chase. Behind the French stands the Latin venatio, meaning hunting. The note is brief, but it shows how a broad hunting term shrank to a single dish.
britannica-1911-vision:
Vision is a physiology article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Vision, or sight, is the work done by the organ called the eye. The entry explains how seeing happens, step by step. Light is the trigger: it acts on the retina at the back of the eye.

The retina is a special surface joined to the brain by the optic nerve. When light excites it, a change runs along the nerve fibres to the brain. The result is a perception of light or colour. The article then states a key condition for useful sight. Light spread evenly over the retina would give no picture of its source. An image must be formed on the retina, as a camera forms one. Bending structures in the eye do that work, focusing the world onto the sensitive surface.
britannica-1911-vollmar-georg-heinrich-v:
Georg Heinrich von Vollmar is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Vollmar was a German Socialist who was born at Munich in 1850. He was schooled at a monastery school at Augsburg. In 1865 he entered the Bavarian army as a young cavalry officer. In the war with France he worked in the army railway service.

The article tells how grave wounds at Blois left him crippled and pensioned. He turned to political and social study and embraced Social Democracy in 1872. He edited the party paper at Dresden and was jailed and expelled under the anti socialist law. He lived for a time at Zurich, then won a seat in the national parliament. He led the moderate wing of his party. He urged slow, lawful growth toward a socialist state and rejected sudden violent overthrow.
britannica-1911-wallenstein-albrecht-wen:
Albrecht von Wallenstein is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He was a German soldier and statesman from 1583 to 1634. He was born in Bohemia of a noble but poor house. His parents held the Lutheran faith in his youth. He was schooled by a church brotherhood at first. After their death an uncle sent him to a Jesuit school.

He studied at schools in Germany and Italy in turn. In Padua he gave much time to the stars. He held for life that stars could hint his fate. He served in Hungary under a skilled chief of war. Brave acts at a siege won him a company of troops. A rich widow he wed left him vast lands. With that wealth he raised horse troops for a duke. From then he held favour at court and fame in arms.
britannica-1911-walpole-of-wolterton-hor:
Horatio Walpole, first Baron Walpole of Wolterton, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in sixteen seventy eight, he was a son of Robert Walpole of Houghton in Norfolk. He was a younger brother of Sir Robert Walpole, the famed statesman. The family had held land in Norfolk for centuries.

The entry first traces the Walpole line back to its early members. A bishop of Norwich and Ely from that line is named. Later members who joined the Society of Jesus are also listed. Against that family backdrop the entry turns to Horatio's own career as an English diplomat.
britannica-1911-walras-marie-esprit-leon:
Marie Esprit Léon Walras, who lived from 1834 to 1910, was a French economist. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with his birth at Évreux. From 1866 to 1868 he edited a journal called Le Travail. Many sound papers on society ran in its pages. In 1870 he took the chair of political economy at Lausanne. He held that chair until his retirement in 1892. He died at the start of January 1910.

His fame rests on his handling of economics in maths. The entry praises his care in splitting theory from practice. His chief work, on pure political economy, came out in 1874 to 1877. A second book set out a maths theory of social wealth in 1883. Pareto, his successor at Lausanne, wrote the notice of his life. That notice in the Economic Journal is cited at the close.
britannica-1911-warrington:
Warrington, a market town in Lancashire, England, is described in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. It stands on the river Mersey, midway between Manchester and Liverpool. In nineteen oh one it had over sixty four thousand folk. Rail and tram links tie it to a wide district.

The church of Saint Elphin is a cross shaped building with a tall tower and spire. A crypt from a much older church sits below its chancel. The town hall is a grand house from the seventeen hundreds, bought by the town in eighteen seventy two. A museum, free library, and market hall are also named. Tanning is a chief trade, with iron, wire, soap, glass, and cotton works as well.
britannica-1911-weber-carl-maria-friedri:
Carl Maria von Weber, a German composer, was born at Eutin in seventeen eighty six. His family had long been devoted to art of many kinds. His father was a soldier and an excellent violinist in his craft. His mother had once sung upon the public stage in her youth. His cousins won high fame as singers, and Mozart wed one of them.

The entry spends much space on Weber's father and his wild ways. Wounded in war, the elder Weber left the army for court posts. He lost one post for neglect of duty after nine years. For years he lived idle, spending his wife's property at Hildesheim. He did little to support his children in that long spell. Later he led an opera house at Lubeck and became a court music chief.
britannica-1911-welles-gideon:
Gideon Welles (1802-1878) was an American political leader, and this 1911 Britannica entry lists the posts that led to his great office. He was born at Glastonbury, Connecticut, and studied for a time at Norwich University in Vermont without graduating. From 1826 to 1837 he edited the Hartford Times and made it the voice of the Jacksonian Democrats in southern New England.

From 1846 to 1849 he ran the bureau of provisions and clothing in the Navy Department at Washington. Leaving the Democrats over the Kansas-Nebraska question, he helped found the Republican party in Connecticut. When Lincoln took office in 1861, Welles became secretary of the navy. He held that post through the civil war years and on to the close of President Johnson's term in 1869.
britannica-1911-wellston:
Wellston is a city article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a city in Jackson county, Ohio, in the United States. It lies about thirty miles south east of Chillicothe. Four rail lines serve the town, with an electric line to the county seat near by.

The article gives a fast run of counts for the young city. The figure rose from 952 in 1880 to 8,045 in 1900. By the count of 1910 it had fallen back to 6,875. The town sits in a land of coal and iron mines. Iron and cement head its goods, and works output in 1905 topped one million dollars. The town runs its own water works and light plant. It was settled in 1871 and named for Harvey Wells, its founder.
britannica-1911-wensleydale-james-parke-:
James Parke, Baron Wensleydale, lived from 1782 to 1868 and was an English judge. The Britannica life from 1911 starts near Liverpool, where he was born. He shone at Trinity College in Cambridge and won top prizes there. Called to the bar, he built a strong practice in common law.

In 1828 he rose to the bench while still a junior lawyer. He later sat for some twenty years in the Court of Exchequer. New court rules in the mid 1850s proved too much for his old views, so he left. Plans to make him a life peer met blocks, and he took a plain peerage in 1856.
britannica-1911-westbury-richard-bethell:
Richard Bethell, first Baron Westbury, was lord chancellor of Great Britain in his time. He lived from eighteen hundred to eighteen seventy three. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Bradford in Wiltshire, the son of Doctor Richard Bethell, he shone at Oxford.

Westbury was called to the bar at the Middle Temple in eighteen twenty three. As queen counsel from eighteen forty he led at the Chancery bar. His chief public service was reform of legal study for young lawyers. He sat in the Commons from eighteen fifty one for Aylesbury and Wolverhampton. In eighteen sixty one he became lord chancellor as Baron Westbury.
britannica-1911-westhoughton:
Westhoughton is an urban district in Lancashire, England, and this short 1911 Britannica entry records its trade and its past. It lies west-south-west of Bolton on the Lancashire and Yorkshire railway and held 14,377 people in 1901. Coal mines work near the town, and the town itself has silk factories, print-works, and cotton mills.

Before the time of Richard the Second, the entry says, Westhoughton was a manor of the abbey of Cockersand. At the Reformation it was taken from the abbey and has since belonged to the crown. In the civil war years the army of Prince Rupert gathered on Westhoughton moor before its attack on Bolton.
britannica-1911-wharncliffe-james-archib:
James Stuart Wortley Mackenzie, Baron Wharncliffe, is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He was an English statesman who lived from 1776 to 1845. He was the son of a colonel of good birth. He joined the army and rose to colonel by 1797. He quit the army in 1801 for a life in politics.

He sat in parliament as a Tory for a Cornish seat. In 1818 he was returned for Yorkshire county. His views grew more liberal as years passed by. Backing Catholic relief cost him his seat in 1826. He was then raised to the peerage as a baron. At first he fought the Reform Bill in the house. He came to fear a clash with the crowd more. He split from the Tories and helped pass the bill. High seal and council posts came to him under Peel.
britannica-1911-wharton:
Wharton is the name of an old north of England house, and the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica traces its rise. The Whartons of Wharton held land in the north for ages. In fifteen forty three one of them was made a baron for his work in the wars of the border. Three barons came down from him in turn.

The fourth baron was the father of a son who rose far more high. That son was made an earl in seventeen hundred and six. Eight years later he was made a marquess. He was one of the chief Whig men of state past the great change of rule. In the world of letters he is famed for a sharp song of state. That song is said to have sung a king out of three realms. He held the top post in Ireland in the reign of Anne.
britannica-1911-whittington:
Whittington is an urban district in Derbyshire, England, north of Chesterfield town. Its town entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies on the Midland railway, south by east of Sheffield city. Counts from nineteen o one put its people at just over nine thousand.

The parish church of Saint Bartholomew was rebuilt after a fire in eighteen ninety five. Only its tower and spire lived through that fire of destruction. Stone bottles and coarse clay ware are made in the town shops. Large ironworks, coal pits, and brick works add to its trade base. A small stone cottage there is known as Revolution House today.
britannica-1911-wilton:
Wilton is a town article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a market town in Wiltshire, England. It stands eighty-six miles west of London, on two rail lines, with 2,203 people in 1901. It lies among pastures by the rivers Nadder and Wylye. Its church of Saint Mary and Saint Nicholas was built in 1844 in a round-arched style.

The church is rich with marbles and mosaics, and its belfry stands apart. Close by to the south stands Wilton House. The first earl of Pembroke built it on the grounds of a dissolved convent, lands granted him by Henry the Eighth. Tradition says Shakespeare and his company played there before James the First in 1603. The house also holds memories of Sir Philip Sidney, of the painters Holbein and Vandyck, and of Inigo Jones.
britannica-1911-wimbledon:
Wimbledon is a borough and suburb in the west of London, in the county of Surrey. A 1911 Britannica entry gives its growth in stark figures across two counts. It held under twenty six thousand people in 1891 and over forty one thousand in 1901. The common to the north west joins Putney Heath as a broad open ground.

That common hosted the Rifle Association from its founding in 1860 until 1888. The parish church of Saint Mary is thought to reach back to Saxon times. The entry notes rounds of repair and rebuilding that changed the church across the years. Readers get a brief portrait of a fast growing suburb with old roots.
britannica-1911-winkelried-arnold-von:
Arnold von Winkelried is the name at the heart of a famed Swiss tale told in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Next to the feat of William Tell, the act tied to this name is the best known tale of the early Swiss league. It is set at the great battle of Sempach.

The Swiss had failed to break the tight ranks of the Austrian knights. Then a man of Unterwalden came to the rescue. He left his wife and children to the care of his mates. He rushed at the foe and drew a bunch of spears to his own chest. He fell pierced through, but his fall tore a gap for his countrymen. The entry warns that the Tell and Winkelried tales stand in unlike light when tried by hard fact.
britannica-1911-winterfeldt-hans-karl-vo:
Winterfeldt, Hans Karl von, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of a Prussian general. Born at Vanselow in Pomerania on the 4th of April 1707, his schooling was poor. He always rued his weak grasp of French in later life. In 1720 he joined his uncle's cuirassier regiment as a trooper.

His height and soldierly bearing caught the eye of the king. Frederick William moved him to the famed giant grenadier regiment as a lieutenant. He soon became a close aide to the king in person. In 1732 he was sent to help set up the Russian army. At St Petersburg he wed his cousin Julie von Maltzahn. Back home he grew close to the crown prince, the later Frederick the Great.
britannica-1911-wolverhampton:
Wolverhampton is a town article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a borough in Staffordshire, England. It stands one hundred and twenty-five miles north-west of London, served by three rail lines. Its people rose from 82,622 in 1891 to 94,187 in 1901. It lies at the north-west edge of the great belt of factory towns that runs toward Birmingham.

To the west, though, lie pleasant suburbs in rich, well-wooded country, and the site is high and healthy. The church of Saint Peter is a fine cross-shaped building with a central tower. Parts of it date from the thirteenth century and more from the fifteenth, and its chancel was rebuilt in a restoration finished in 1865. The chief public buildings are the town hall of 1871, the exchange, and a free library.
britannica-1911-wolverton:
Wolverton is a town in Buckinghamshire, England, set out in a brief entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The town stands near the river Ouse, some fifty two and a half miles north west of London. The London and North Western railway serves it. Its count in 1901 came to 5,323 people.

The entry states plainly why the town grew. Its modern size and weight rest on the carriage works set up there by the railway company. Printing works add a second trade. A steam tramway links the town with Stony Stratford, an old market town on the Ouse two miles to the west.
britannica-1911-workington:
Workington is a port and market town in Cumberland, England. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets it on the south bank of the river Derwent. The river meets the Irish Sea at the town. Its people numbered 26,143 in 1901. The harbour is safe, guarded by a stone beach and a breakwater. The Lonsdale dock covers over four acres. In 1892 the port was placed under Maryport.

Coal and heavy works drive the town. Large pits nearby run in places beneath the sea. Blast furnaces, machine shops, and ship yards line the shore. Paper mills and cycle works add to the trade. The town is run by a mayor, aldermen, and councillors. Near the town stands Workington Hall, an old fort like house. One room in it is said to be where Mary, queen of Scots, slept. She fled there after her loss at Langside in May 1568.
britannica-1911-wrangel-friedrich-heinri:
Friedrich Heinrich Ernst, Count von Wrangel, a Prussian field marshal who lived from 1784 to 1877, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Stettin, he entered a dragoon regiment in 1796 as a boy. He fought Napoleon as a young officer and won a high order at Heilsberg in 1807.

In the War of Liberation in 1813 Wrangel won the Iron Cross near Leipzig and rose fast. He led cavalry brigades and divisions, then held commands at Konigsberg and Stettin. In 1848 he led a corps in the war over Schleswig Holstein. That autumn he was called to Berlin to crush riots there. He declared a state of siege and cast out the liberal leaders of the chamber. His stern hand worked twice in Prussias revival with no blood shed. In 1856, after sixty years of service, he became a field marshal.
britannica-1911-wrangel-karl-gustav-von:
Karl Gustav von Wrangel is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He was a Swedish soldier who lived from 1613 to 1676. His kin came from Esthonia and spread to three lands. His father was a field marshal in Swedish wars. Karl Gustav was born near Upsala in December 1613. At age twenty he shone as a horse troop captain. Three years later he held the rank of colonel.

In 1644 he led a fleet that beat the Danes at sea. In 1646 he took chief command of Swedish troops in Germany. He held that post through the last drives of a long war. With French allies he fought in Bavaria and Wurttemberg. He fought at Warsaw in a three day battle in 1656. He crossed ice to isles and took a strong fort in 1658. High posts at court came to him in later years.
britannica-1911-wrede-karl-philipp-princ:
Karl Philipp von Wrede, who lived from 1767 to 1838, was a Bavarian field marshal born at Heidelberg. The 1911 Britannica article says he was born on the twenty-ninth of April 1767. He was raised for civil office under the Palatinate. When war came in 1799, he raised a corps of volunteers and took command as colonel. The drilled Austrians laughed at his raw men at first.
