Bound for a doctorate at Pont-a-Mousson, he fled plague to Sainte-Menehould and died of it there.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edward-sheldo:
Edward Sheldon was an English translator of French devotional books, born at Beoley in 1599 and dead in London in 1687. Third son of Edward Sheldon of Beoley, he studied at Oxford and Gray's Inn and finished his schooling with a tour abroad. He married Mary Wake, with whom he had nine sons and four daughters, and lived quietly on his estate at Stratton in Gloucestershire.

In 1641, harassed for his religion, he moved to London and lived in retirement until his death. His four translations from French were The Holy Life of M. de Renty in 1658, The Rule of Catholic Faith by Dr. Veron in 1660, The Counsels of Wisdom by Fouquet in 1680, and Christian Thoughts for Every Day of the Month, also in 1680. The entry sketches a private man whose reading served English Catholics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-election:
Election in canon law is the subject of this long, orderly entry. It is laid out under six heads. They cover the juridical concept, the electors, the persons eligible, the act of electing, what follows election, and the elections now in use. In its strict sense election means the choice, by lawful electors, of a fit person for a church office. That choice gives the person a real right to the post, even before later confirmation.

The entry carefully sets election apart from look-alike modes. Postulation names a person who is legally barred, and asks a superior to dispense him, so it confers no right. Presentation is the act of a patron, who may be a layman, while true electors must be clerics. Nomination, recommendation, request, and free collation each get the same close treatment, making the piece a handy reference for church lawyers and historians.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-elizabeth-bar:
Elizabeth Barton, called the Nun of Kent, was a visionary put to death at Tyburn in 1534, probably born in 1506. At nineteen, a servant at Aldington in Kent, she fell ill, fell into trances, and spoke of things done elsewhere that she could not have known. Her parish priest reported her to the Archbishop of Canterbury, and a commission of Benedictines, Franciscans, and clergy examined her and judged in her favour.

Cured, so the tale ran, at a chapel of the Virgin before a crowd, she became a Benedictine nun near Canterbury and won wide fame for holiness. She protested against Henry VIII's divorce in God's name, wrote to the pope, and met Fisher, Wolsey, and the king. Cromwell moved against her in 1533, she confessed deception after examination, and a bill of attainder in January 1534 sealed her fate. The entry leaves open whether she was gifted or an impostor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ellakim-parke:
Ellakim Parker Scammon was an American soldier and educator, born at Whitefield, Maine, in 1816 and dead at New York in 1894. Appointed to West Point, he graduated in 1837 fifth in a class of fifty-two. He stayed on to teach mathematics. Future generals Grant, Rosecrans, and Newton were among his pupils. He served in the Seminole War and as an aide to General Scott in Mexico, winning promotion for bravery at Vera Cruz.

Just before sailing for Mexico in 1846 he became a Catholic convert. From 1847 to 1854 he surveyed the Upper Lakes with the topographical corps, and in 1856 he left the army. He taught mathematics at Saint Mary's College and at Cincinnati's Polytechnic College. He served as a volunteer brigadier-general in the Civil War from October 1862. He was consul at Prince Edward Island from 1866 to 1871. He taught at Seton Hall from 1875 to 1882.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-emancipation:
Emancipation in Roman law was the act by which a slave freed from his master, or a son freed from his father's power, was declared legally independent. The entry first notes the Church's early use of the process in freeing slaves. Unable to end slavery at once, the Church softened it toward serfdom. It replaced the elaborate Roman forms with manumission in church. There a master's plain statement before bishop and congregation sufficed.

Freedom was often a first step to orders, since a slave needed manumission before ordination. In canon law a son who takes solemn vows in a religious order is likewise freed from his father's legal power. No positive law states it. Modern civil law does not recognise it. The entry also covers the release of a cathedral school pupil from his master, and of a cleric from his diocese on election as bishop.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-encolpion:
An encolpion was a small reliquary worn on the breast, and this entry traces its forms and uses. The Greek name means that which is worn on the breast. Early Christians carried in such cases relics: cloth stained with a martyr's blood, parchments with Scripture texts, and fragments of the True Cross. The custom grew from the pagan habit of wearing bullae, or amulet cases, round the neck against enchantment.

The Church sought to cleanse the habit of superstition by swapping Christian objects for pagan charms. Jerome scolded women who treated little Gospel books and cross wood as magic. Encolpia came in oval, round, and four-cornered shapes, in materials from gold to glass. Two square gold examples were found in 1571 in tombs of the old Vatican cemetery. They were engraved with Christ's monogram between Alpha and Omega on one side and a dove on the other.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-england-befor:
England before the Reformation is a vast survey that limits England to the largest part of Great Britain south of the Solway, the Cheviots, and the Tweed, including Wales. Its area was 57,668 square miles, and its resident population in 1901 was over twenty-three million, nearly four-fifths of the United Kingdom. For history up to the Norman Conquest it points readers to the Anglo-Saxon Church article.

The account itself starts with William the Conqueror. It warns that pictures of a degraded English Church in the early eleventh century are much exaggerated. Edward the Confessor could not repair damage from Danish anarchy and long disorders at the centre of Christendom. Simony, neglect of clerical celibacy, and subjection of churchmen to secular power were real and widespread. Yet reform was already stirring, above all the monastic renewal begun at Cluny and taken up in Normandy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-england-since:
England since the Reformation takes the Protestant Reformation as the great dividing line in English history, as in Europe's. It quotes Macaulay's judgment that the Anglican Reformation sprang from no religious motive. Of its makers, Ridley alone did not treat it as a mere political job, though he played no very prominent part. The entry then traces the history of the change and marks its results.

Under Henry VIII the English schism was consummated in 1535 by the Act making the king Supreme Head of the Church of England, with power to reform errors, heresies, and abuses. That statute cut England from the unity of Christendom and handed the pope's jurisdiction to the Imperial Crown. The entry calls this the Anglican Reformation's unique mark: the bold taking of all papal authority by the sovereign, including the power to rule the Church and to define doctrine.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-enthronizatio:
Enthronization, from the Greek word for placing on a throne, has borne several meanings, and this entry sorts them out. In early use it meant placing relics on the altar of a church about to be consecrated. Such a church was called enthroned. In the Middle Ages the enthronization of marriage meant the blessing in the nuptial Mass. In the East the word was seldom used for induction to a parish benefice.

After consecration the new bishop was led to the episcopal throne and took possession of it. He received the kiss of peace, heard a passage of Scripture read, and gave an address. Letters announcing his communion in faith went to fellow bishops. Gifts went to those who had consecrated him. Today the rite keeps its form but has lost juridical weight. The pope's enthronization in the Chair of Saint Peter was once a ceremony of importance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-episcopal-int:
Episcopal intercession was the bishops' right to plead for criminals, granted by the secular power to the bishops of the early Church. It sprang less from any fixed law than from the great respect paid to the episcopal office in the early centuries. The seventh canon of Sardica, about 344, mentions it, as do Augustine, Jerome, and the historian Socrates.

Augustine pleaded repeatedly with Macedonius, governor of Africa, for condemned men. Martin of Tours pleaded with Emperor Maximus for the imprisoned Priscillianists in 384 and 385, and Flavian of Antioch pleaded with Theodosius I in 387 for citizens who had smashed imperial statues. Ambrose moved Theodosius to delay executions and confiscations for thirty days after sentence, to leave room for mercy and to shield the innocent. Bishops had free access to prisons and were urged to visit inmates twice a week and report cruel keepers to the emperor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ethelred-taun:
Ethelred Taunton was a writer, born at Rugeley, Staffordshire, England, on 17 October 1857, and dead in London on 9 May 1907. Educated at Downside, he desired to enter the Benedictine Order, but weak health prevented him. He entered the Institute of Saint Andrew at Barnet, founded by the convert George Bampfield, but health again prevented him from remaining. Finally he joined Manning's Oblates at Bayswater and was ordained priest in 1883.

Three years later he left the Oblates for the mission at Stoke Newington in North London. Here he built a new church, opened in 1888, but a fall of scaffolding injured him seriously, bringing partial paralysis and ending his active work. He continued, however, to be busy with his pen. He was widely read and wrote on many subjects. For a while he lived at Bruges, where he founded and edited Saint Luke's Magazine, which had only a brief existence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-etienne-miche:
Etienne-Michel Faillon, a historian, was born at Tarascon in France on 3 January 1800 and died at Paris on 25 October 1870. Avignon and Aix gave him his studies. He joined the Sulpicians in 1821 and was ordained priest in 1824. As director of La Solitude he wrote ascetic and biographical works and gathered material for later publications.

Montreal, during an official visitation in 1848, gave him the idea for his Histoire de la Colonie française au Canada. Twelve volumes were intended, covering the whole French domination from 1534 to 1759, but only three appeared, with the narrative ending in 1675. Two later voyages to Canada let him write biographies of Sister Marguerite Bourgeoys, Jeanne Mance, Mother d'Youville, and Jeanne Le Ber. Monuments inédits sur l'apostolat de Sainte Marie-Madeleine en Provence stands beside his life of Monsieur Olier among his chief works on Old France.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-euchologion:
The Euchologion is one of the Service-books of the Byzantine Church, corresponding more or less to our Missal and Ritual. It contains directions for the deacon at Vespers, Lauds, and Liturgy. The priest's prayers and deacon's litanies for those hours follow. Then come the Liturgies, with rubrics for the holy Liturgy in general and a note on arranging the breads at the Proskomide.

The Liturgy of Saint John Chrysostom is the frame into which the others are fitted. It gives the priest's and deacon's parts at full length, first for Chrysostom's liturgy, then for the differing parts of Saint Basil's, then for the Presanctified Liturgy. After the Liturgies come sacraments and sacramentals with rules, canons, and blessings. Comes the rite of churching the mother after child-birth, then canons about baptism, prayers over catechumens, the rite of baptism, and the washing of the child seven days later.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-evolution:
Evolution is the subject of a vast article. It sets out the scientific theory that today's species grew by descent from earlier forms, against the older theory of special creation of each species. It draws a sharp line between the bare fact of evolution and special systems that explain it, such as natural selection, the influence of surroundings, or Lamarck's use and disuse. The article is planned in seven parts, covering history, the meaning of species, variation and experiment, and the proofs from fossils, form, embryos, and geography.

Its history runs in three periods. Linnaeus built his system on the constancy of species, Buffon broke with him, and Lamarck founded the modern theory in his Philosophie zoologique of 1809. Darwin's Origin of Species of 1859 opened the second age, carrying natural selection into every branch of biology.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-examination:
Examination is a process for testing fitness, an inquiry or investigation, used in schools, seminaries, and universities as a test of learning. Examinations also serve as tests for offices and posts and as means of reaching truth, and it is under these aspects that the question chiefly arises here. The bulk of the article is canon law, section by section.

Trent ordered a competitive examination, or concursus, for parochial benefices, so that parishes go to men of virtue and learning and the best candidate wins. Bishops may promote no one to orders until prudent and learned priests pass on his birth, baptism, morals, faith, and knowledge. Like rules govern bishops-elect, confessors, preachers, couples before marriage, and witnesses under oath in church courts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-excommunicati:
Excommunication is the Church's chief and severest censure. From Latin words for out of communion, it is a healing penalty, not a vindictive one. It strips a guilty Christian of all share in the common blessings of church society. It presumes grave guilt, and it aims to correct the offender and bring him back.

The excommunicated person stays a Christian, since baptism cannot be erased. Yet he stands as an exile, barred from public worship and from the sacraments. This vast article treats the subject under seven heads, from its history and kinds to absolution and current cases. It grounds the right in the Church as a society, citing Matthew 18 and Saint Paul's exclusion of offenders.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-exemption:
Exemption is the freeing of a church person, body, or house, wholly or partly, from the superior next above it. The body thus freed passes under a higher authority, or the pope himself. At first all in a diocese stood under the bishop. But bishops at times oppressed monasteries, which sought the shield of synods, princes, and popes.

That shield often grew into exemption, first given by Honorius I in 628 to Bobbio. From the eleventh century, papal reform work spread exemptions, until by the twelfth century they were the rule. Trent tried to curb abuses by restoring bishops' sway in many matters, but monasteries resisted. Exemption may come by grant, by immemorial use, or by origin, and it ends by withdrawal, contrary custom, or extinction.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-extension:
Extension is the property by which the parts of material substance lie in order, one beyond another. That matter is not quite continuous to our senses, science shows. The microscope finds pores in the densest stuff, and gases seep through solids. Descartes held extension to be matter's very essence. Kant made it a subjective form stamped on sense by the mind.

Leibniz dissolved matter into unextended points, or monads, and Boscovich into simple forces, while atomists split bodies into minute particles. Catholic teaching, as summed here, calls extension successive, like a stream, or permanent. Permanent extension may be continuous, contiguous as a brick wall, or interrupted as a string of beads. Its marks are divisibility, measurability, and impenetrability. It is objective, not a mental mold, and distinct from substance, as the Eucharist shows, where bread's dimensions remain after its substance changes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-extreme-uncti:
Extreme Unction is a sacrament of the New Law for Christians who are gravely ill. It gives spiritual aid, comfort, and health, with remission of sins if need be, and bodily health on condition. A priest anoints the sick person, using set words. The article runs in ten sections, from the present rite and the name to effects, necessity, and repetition.

In the Western rite the priest anoints the organs of the five senses, eyes, ears, nostrils, lips, and hands, plus the feet, and for men the loins where custom allows. Each anointing says, through this holy unction and his tender mercy may the Lord pardon whatever sins thou hast committed by that sense. In urgent need one anointing on the forehead suffices. The East uses several priests, who bless the oil each time. Trent teaches Christ instituted it, hinted in Mark and proclaimed by James.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-family-of-lam:
The Lamoignon were a French robe family of judges and officials. Guillaume de Lamoignon took office as first president of the Parlement in 1658. He worked on codifying French law and defended Gallican liberties in 1663. His career ran through the Fronde and the rule of Louis XIV.

Earlier members included Chretien, a statesman, and Marie des Landes, called mother of the poor. Madeleine de Lamoignon aided foundlings and the Hotel-Dieu of Paris. Later came Nicolas, intendant of Languedoc during the Camisard rising. Malesherbes, the family's famous son, defended Louis XVI at his trial.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fanon:
A fanon is a shoulder-cape the pope alone wears at solemn Mass. It has two pieces of white silk striped in red and gold. A small gold cross marks it, and a round opening fits the head. The pope wears it over the alb at pontifical Mass only.

The oldest Roman Ordinal, from the eighth century, calls it an anabolagium. Clergy in general wore it under the alb until the twelfth century. Innocent III then confirmed it as reserved to the pope alone. Square until the fifteenth century, it later took a collar form.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-feast-of-the-:
The Ascension is kept forty days after Easter, always falling on a Thursday. It recalls Christ rising into heaven from the Mount of Olives near Bethany. Eastern Christians called it the taking up and the salvation. By ascending, Christ completed the great work of human redemption.

Augustine held the feast apostolic in origin and universal long before his day. Its vigil and octave prepared the Church for the novena before Pentecost. Old customs included blessing beans, grapes, candles, and first fruits. Processions with torches and banners marked Christ's triumphant entry into heaven.

The Circumcision falls on 1 January, eight days after Christmas. Christ, though not bound by law, submitted to it as a true descendant of Abraham. At the rite he received the name Jesus, meaning Saviour. The ceremony took place in a private house of hospitality, not the Temple.

Early Christians struggled to keep the day amid the wild Saturnalia revels. Augustine urged fasting and prayer against pagan feasting and excess. The feast appears in the Gallican rite by the Council of Tours in 567. Later prayers also honour Mary, whose own feasts shape the day's office.

The Feast of the Dedication recalls the cleansing of the Jerusalem Temple. Judas Machabeus set it in 164 BC after Antiochus had polluted the shrine. Kept on 25 Kislew for eight days, it is also called the Feast of Lights. Unlike the great annual feasts, it could be kept in any synagogue.

Worshippers carried branches and palms and sang the joyful Hallel psalms daily. Mourning and fasting were barred during the joyful eight days. Lights burned in homes, recalling the temple lamps relit at the cleansing. Modern Jews keep the feast, now called Hanukkah, in December.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-flagellation:
Flagellation covers the whip, rod, and stick as punishment and as voluntary penance. Scripture mentions whips from Exodus onward, and Roman citizens were exempt from scourging. Christ scourged the money-changers, and Paul counted five scourgings of forty stripes save one. Pilate's scourging of Christ was a Roman punishment, meant as a substitute for crucifixion.

Monks adopted scourging as discipline from the fifth century, under rules like those of Columban. In Sparta youths prided themselves on enduring the lash, and in Russia the knout ruled longest. English soldiers were whipped within living memory, and Delaware still kept whipping for criminals. The article weighs whether Paul's chastising his body means scourging or mortification in general.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-forty-hours-d:
The Forty Hours' Devotion, also called Quarant'Ore, is continuous prayer for forty hours before the Blessed Sacrament, the consecrated bread, set out for adoration. It commonly moves from church to church in succession. It opens with a solemn Mass of Exposition and closes two days later with a Mass of Deposition, each with a procession and litanies of the saints.

Its origin is obscure. A Milan chronicler describes the church-to-church round as a novelty beginning at Milan in May 1537. Pope Paul III soon granted indulgences, saying the prayers were meant to turn away God's anger and check the advancing Turks. St. Philip Neri and St. Ignatius Loyola helped spread the practice, which also took hold during carnival as an act of reparation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-foundation:
An ecclesiastical foundation is the gift of temporal goods, land, money, or income, to a church body or cleric, by lifetime gift or by will. It is given on condition that some spiritual work be done in perpetuity or for a long time.

After Constantine gave the Church political standing and the right to accept legacies, bishops set such gifts aside for hospitals, orphan asylums, and homes for the aged. By the twelfth and thirteenth centuries pious generosity founded guilds and charities across Europe. Foundations are contracts: founder and administrator must agree, the bishop must consent, and the promised work, often Masses, must actually be performed, or the gift fails its purpose.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-mayro:
Francis Mayron, also called de Mayronis, born about 1280, probably at Mayronnes in the Basses-Alpes, and dead at Piacenza probably on 26 July 1327. He was a Franciscan theologian surnamed Doctor acutus, the sharp doctor, and Doctor illuminatus. He entered the Franciscan order at Digne or Sisteron and taught theology at Paris for a long time as bachelor. John XXII, at King Robert of Naples' request, ordered him made master of theology on 24 May 1323.

Mayron was a noted pupil of Duns Scotus, whose teaching he mostly followed. He is generally credited with introducing the Actus Sorbonicus at Paris. It was a disputation lasting from five in the morning to seven at night, in which one man defended his theses against all comers without help, food, or drink. His commentary on the Sentences appeared at Venice repeatedly from 1507, with treatises on formalities and first principles.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-nicho:
Francis Nicholson, born at Manchester in 1650 and dead at Lisbon on 13 August 1731, was a controversial writer whose life crossed the religious divides of Stuart England. Son of a Manchester citizen, he entered University College, Oxford, as a servitor at sixteen. He took his bachelor's degree in 1669 and master's in 1673, and was ordained an Anglican clergyman. He served near Oxford and Canterbury with success in bringing Nonconformists back to the Church of England.

 Under James II he was a professed Catholic, writing on the Real Presence for Woodhead's discourse on the Eucharist. After the Revolution he joined the Carthusians at Nieuport, but his health failed. In 1699 he returned to England, entered the service of Queen Dowager Catherine of Braganza, and followed her to Portugal, where he lived at court and retired.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-thomp:
Francis Thompson, born at Preston in Lancashire on 18 December 1859 and dead in London on 13 November 1907. He was an English Catholic poet best known for The Hound of Heaven. His father was a provincial doctor, his mother died in his boyhood, and he was educated at Ushaw College. There he loved literature and neglected games, though he followed cricket with affection.

There he endured three years of destitution, working briefly as a bookselling agent and at a shoemaker's. He sold matches and called cabs in the streets, often hungry and cold, once turned away from a public library for his rags. Rescued from that life, he wrote poems and essays of mystical power that critics ranked among the great odes of the language. Meredith called him a true poet of a small band.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-doll:
Francois Dollier de Casson, born near Nantes in 1636 and dead in 1701, was the fourth superior of Saint-Sulpice at Montreal in Canada. First a soldier and captain under Marshal Turenne, whose esteem his bravery won, he entered the Seminary of Saint-Sulpice at Paris in 1657 and joined the company. He went to Canada in 1666.

In 1671 he succeeded Father de Queylus as superior of the Sulpicians. In that office he shaped the growth of Villemarie, Montreal, planning its streets, beginning the canal since known as Lachine, and stirring colonists' energy under trying and hazardous conditions. He wrote a History of Montreal, published in 1869 in the memoirs of the Montreal historical society. He also wrote an account of Courcelles's voyage to Lake Ontario, preserved in the National Library at Paris.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-fene:
Francois Fenelon, born at the Chateau de Fenelon in Perigord on 6 August 1651 and dead at Cambrai on 7 January 1715, was a celebrated French bishop and author. He came of noble birth but small means.

At Bossuet's suggestion he was sent with companions to Saintonge to labour for the conversion of Protestants, always with gentleness. Louis XIV secured him as tutor to the Duke of Burgundy, the future king, a post of immense importance and difficulty. His later years were darkened by the Quietism controversy, over the mystical teaching of Madame Guyon, which set him against Bossuet and Rome. Yet his writings on education, spirituality, and government kept his name among the great French authors.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-gira:
Francois Girardon, born at Troyes in 1630 and dead at Paris in 1715, was a noted sculptor of Louis XIV's reign. Son of a bronze founder, he first studied under Francois Anguier and afterwards at Rome, and returning to France he entered the king's service under Lebrun, whose favourite he became. After Lebrun's death in 1690 he wielded great influence as professor of the academy of sculpture and painting, later its chancellor, following Bernini's lead while keeping traces of the old Fontainebleau school.

The Louvre holds the model of his lively equestrian statue of the king, erected in the Place Vendome and destroyed in the Revolution. Among his finest works is the Richelieu monument in the Sorbonne church, where the dying cardinal rests on a richly draped sarcophagus held up by Religion, while Science mourns at his feet. Other monuments honour his wife, the Princesse de Conti, and minister Louvois.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-vero:
Francois Veron, born at Paris about 1575 and dead at Charenton in 1625, was a French controversialist, a public debater for Catholicism against Protestant ministers. After brilliant studies under the Jesuits he joined the Society and taught in several colleges, then left it to preach and dispute more freely. He challenged every minister he met, even the most learned, Moulin, Blondel, Daille, and Bochard, publishing his conferences and controversial writings afterwards.

With letters patent from Louis XIII allowing him to preach in public and debate ministers anywhere he pleased, he worked Paris and Charenton, where he was cure for ten years. He also worked Saintonge, Bearn, Brie, Champagne, Lorraine, and Normandy. His Rule of Catholic Faith, approved by the French clergy and praised by Leibniz, remains his chief book.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fraternal-cor:
Fraternal correction means a private person admonishing a neighbour in order to reform him or, if possible, prevent his sinful indulgence. It differs clearly from official discipline, whose mouthpiece is a judge or other superior and whose object is punishing the guilty. Its motive is less the offender's own advantage than the common good.

The obligation binds under pain of mortal sin only when several conditions meet. They are that the fault is grievous, the sinner will not adequately provide for himself, there is well-founded hope the admonition will be heeded. No one else equally fitted is likely to undertake it, and no graver harm follows.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fray-domingo-:
Born Juan de Ecija at Fuenteovejuna in 1510, Domingo de la Anunciación became one of the most active Dominican teachers of Mexico's native peoples. Refused by the Franciscans at thirteen, he sailed to New Spain with his elder brother. He entered the Dominican order around 1531, taking the name by which he is known. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry, it follows him from village teaching to high offices in his order.

During the epidemic of 1545 he walked from village to village as far south as Oaxaca. He gave the sacraments to the sick without regard for himself. In 1559 he joined a luckless expedition to Florida, survived shipwreck and hunger, and returned to teach again in Mexico. He served twice as prior at Santo Domingo in the capital. Blind from 1585, he died in 1591, leaving a rare 1565 dialogue on Christian doctrine in Spanish and Nahuatl.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fray-juan-de-:
Juan de la Anunciación, a Granada-born Augustinian, reached Mexico in the mid-sixteenth century and gave his working life to teaching Nahuatl speakers. He joined the Augustinians in 1554. He served several terms as prior at Mexico and Puebla, acted twice as definitor, and led the college of San Pablo. He died in 1594 at about eighty.

His three printed books, all from Mexico, were tools for instructing native Christians. The first, from 1575, was a Christian doctrine in Nahuatl and Spanish. That same year he published a set of sermons in both tongues. A 1577 sermon book followed, with a catechism and calendar in both languages. Few copies survive today, but the entry values them for early language study and mission teaching.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-french-revolu:
The French Revolution article stresses one thread above all: the Revolution's relations with the Church. It opens by reviewing recent historians, from Taine on the classic spirit to Cochin on the clubs where doctrine hardened, Sorel on diplomacy, and Aulard and Mathiez in their quarrel over Robespierre. The piece then turns to events themselves.

Its starting point is the States General called by Louis XVI, where the clergy numbered over three hundred, including forty-four prelates and two hundred eight parish priests. Parish clergy voted in force, and the clergy pressed nearly as hard as the Third Estate for constitutional rule. Later sections follow the clash between revolutionary France and a Church loyal to Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-frequent-comm:
Frequent Communion traces how often the faithful have received the Eucharist, from the early Church to the rule of Pius X. Christ gave no fixed number, the article notes, but bread and wine as daily food, manna in the desert, and the prayer for daily bread all pointed toward frequent reception. Its first part is history, its second the present practice.

At Jerusalem the faithful received daily, and later writers record reception on the Lord's day and, in time, on other days as well. Hermits and distant dwellers even carried the sacrament home. Yet practice often fell short of precept, and saints rebuked the faithful for receiving too seldom. Augustine's summary closes the survey: daily in some places, Sundays only in others.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gaboon:
Gaboon, a vicariate apostolic in French Congo, takes its name from the estuary where Libreville stands. Once called the Two Guineas, it covers the Ogowai River basin south of the Equator, between the Atlantic and twelve degrees east of Paris. The land runs broken and low, wrapped in dense tropical forest, with rivers barred by rapids and roads that are mere foot tracks.

Rain falls from September to May, yet the climate stays steady and, for temperate lives, fairly healthy. Peoples crowd the coast as the end point of inland trade, shifting villages every few years as fields wear out. Old slave-trading peoples like the Mpongwe hold the estuary, while fishing tribes work the creeks. The entry maps a land where a fresh ethnographic chart is needed every four or five years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gabriel-gerbe:
Gabriel Gerberon, a Maurist Benedictine born in 1628, became one of the most prolific writers of Jansenism in France. Schooled by the Oratorians at Vendôme, he joined Saint-Mélaine at Rennes in 1649. He taught philosophy and theology until his drift from scholastic method and toward Jansenism cost him his chair in 1663.

Gerberon openly fought Louis XIV's meddling in church affairs, and his book against commendatory abbots forced him to flee to Brussels and Holland under a false name. Back at Brussels, he wrote pamphlets with Quesnel, was seized in 1703, and spent years jailed at Amiens and Vincennes. After retracting his errors he died repentant in 1711, leaving a general history of Jansenism among his many works.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-galveston:
Galveston, a Texas diocese erected in 1847, covers 43,000 square miles between the Sabine and Colorado rivers and the Gulf. French Recollects with La Salle tried Texas missions in 1685, Spanish Franciscans followed in 1689, and early eighteenth-century friars rebuilt the missions until Spain suppressed them in 1812. Independence in 1836 then stalled the work for years.

Two Lazarists, Timon and Odin, revived Texas Catholic life, and Odin, made vicar apostolic in 1842, found only four priests in the state. As bishop of Galveston from 1847 he won back old churches, opened schools, and brought the Ursulines, the first sisterhood in Texas. By 1861, when he moved to New Orleans, he left forty-two priests, fifty churches, a college, and nine academies and schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-garzon:
Garzón, a suffragan diocese of Popayán in Colombia, covers the provinces of Neiva and Sur east of Popayán. Some 140 miles long and 40 to 100 wide, it runs from the first to the fourth degree north, between the seventy-fifth and seventy-seventh meridians west. Its see stands at Neiva, a town of 11,000 souls 150 miles from Bogotá, on the navigable Magdalena.

The diocese was cut from Tolima by Leo XIII in June 1900, since that vast mountain territory defied visitation. The northern half became Ibagué, the southern half Garzón. Esteban Rojas, bishop of Tolima since 1895, moved to Neiva as its first bishop. The cathedral honors the Immaculate Conception, and a people almost wholly Catholic long left schooling to the clergy alone.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-general-resur:
The General Resurrection is the rising of all the dead with their own bodies, elect and reprobate alike, as Lateran IV defined it. Creeds call it resurrection of the flesh, since the soul cannot die and cannot return to life. The article sets out the dogma, then the marks of the risen body, leaving Christ's own rising to its own entry.

Augustine warned that no doctrine meets fiercer denial, and the foes line up early. Epicureans mocked Paul at Athens, Platonists saw the body as a prison, and Gnostics and Manicheans called matter evil. Then came Cathari, Albigenses, and modern rationalists. Against them the article marshals creeds from Nicaea to Pius IV, the Old Testament hope of Martha and the Maccabees, and the New Testament witness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-generation:
Generation, in the Bible, renders two Hebrew words of shifting sense: dor and toledoth. The second, in its plural form, belongs to the genealogy article, while this entry follows dor through its chief uses. At its root lies a notion of circuit or period, the span of a human life and the company that shares it.

In patriarchal times a generation counts as a hundred years, later only thirty to forty. The word also marks vague time past and future, as in remember the days of old, and the concrete company of contemporaries, as in Noah, just in his generations. Apart from time, it names a race stamped by one quality, a just generation or a perverse one, and once, in Isaiah, even a dwelling, the round nomad tent.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-deshon:
George Deshon, a Paulist priest born in Connecticut in 1823, built the new order's house and church with a soldier-engineer's hand. A West Point graduate of 1843, classmate and roommate of Grant, he taught mathematics and ethics there, rose to captain, then resigned, entered the Church in 1851, and joined the Redemptorists. Ordained in 1855, he worked missions with Hecker, Walworth, Hewit, and Baker.

In 1858 the five won release from Redemptorist vows and founded the Paulist Institute, whose first New York house and church rose in 1859. Deshon ran its temporal affairs and superintended the great church of Saint Paul the Apostle, where his engineering training served well. His Guide for Catholic Young Women, issued in 1860, stayed popular. Elected superior general in 1897, he founded Chicago's Paulist house in 1903, his last act.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-georgius-gemi:
Georgius Gemistus Plethon, a Byzantine philosopher born at Constantinople about 1355, revived Platonism and paganism in the West. Renaming himself Plethon out of love for Plato, he mixed later Platonist thought with Eastern mystic lore he called Zoroastrianism. He openly left the faith to put paganism in its place as a rule of life. Settled at Mistra in the Peloponnesus, he spent most of his life there.

At eighty-three Plethon accompanied the emperor to Italy in 1438 as a champion of the Orthodox side at Florence. He skipped the council to talk Platonism instead, prompting Cosimo de' Medici to found Florence's Platonic Academy. His Laws, imitating Plato's, was condemned by Patriarch Gennadios, while his Differences between Plato and Aristotle attacked Aristotle's school. He died at Mistra in 1450, his remains moved to Rimini in 1465. Bessarion was his disciple.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-geraldton:
Geraldton, a diocese in Australia established in 1898, stretches from Kimberley's southern edge along the thirtieth parallel to the 120th degree of longitude, then the twenty-ninth parallel to South Australia's border. Suffragan of Adelaide, it counts twenty-eight churches served by ten secular and four regular priests, with five boarding and twelve primary schools holding 747 pupils under fifty-one sisters.

Presentation nuns, founded from Ireland in 1890, keep twenty-eight sisters in six communities, while Dominicans from Dunedin, New Zealand, came in 1899 with four communities and twenty-four sisters. The first bishop, William Bernard Kelly, was consecrated on August 14, 1898. The Bishop of Geraldton also holds jurisdiction over the Kimberley vicariate, a vast northern charge beyond his own diocese.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gideon:
Gideon, also called Jerobaal, was one of the Greater Judges of Israel, from the tribe of Manasseh and the family of Abiezer. His father Joas lived at Ephra. A Catholic Encyclopedia article retells his judgeship from Judges chapters six to eight, where Israel, humbled for seven years by Midianite raids, receives him as deliverer.

Called while threshing wheat, Gideon tore down his village altar to Baal and raised one to Yahweh. His father's taunt, Let Baal revenge himself, earned him the name Jerobaal. Comforted by the signs of the fleece, he saw his army cut from 32,000 to 300, then routed the enemy at night with trumpets, torches, and jars. He refused a hereditary crown, judged Israel peacefully for forty years, and died in old age at Ephra.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-godfrey-of-bo:
Godfrey of Bouillon was Duke of Lower Lorraine and first ruler of Jerusalem, son of Eustache II, Count of Boulogne, and Ida, daughter of Godfrey the Bearded. Born probably at Boulogne-sur-Mer in 1060, he died at Jerusalem on 18 July 1100. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a crusader whose early years legend has distorted.

Chosen to succeed his murdered uncle as duke, he first lost Lorraine to Henry IV, then regained the dukedom about 1089. Among the first to take the cross in 1096, he sold or pledged his estates. He marched with ten thousand knights and thirty thousand foot. On 15 July 1099 he and his brother Eustache first entered Jerusalem by movable tower, and he took the title Advocate of the Holy Sepulchre.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guillaume-and:
Rouen theologian Guillaume-André-René Baston, born in 1741, spent the Revolution in print opposing the Civil Constitution of the Clergy, then in exile for refusing its oath. After teaching theology at Rouen he fled in 1792 to London, Holland, and Kosfeld in Westphalia, returning in 1803 as vicar-general and dean under Archbishop Cambacérès.

A Gallican favoured by Napoleon, he was named Bishop of Séez in 1813. Pius VII withheld approval and the chapter revoked the choice in 1814, sending him into retirement at Saint-Laurent. His books range from a ten-volume theology course with Abbé Tuvache and a Catholic doctrine of marriage to memoirs begun in exile and late replies to de Maistre and Lamennais.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heber-macmaho:
Irish bishop Heber MacMahon of Clogher, born at Farney in 1600, was priest, patriot, and general in Ireland's struggle, executed at Enniskillen in 1650. Schooled by Donegal Franciscans and at Douai and Louvain, ordained in 1625, he laboured among a flock stripped of lands and churches and forced to worship in the mountains. He became vicar-general and then bishop in 1643.

A steadfast backer of Owen Roe O'Neill and the papal envoys against Ormonde's peace party, he condemned the Inchiquin truce and was proclaimed a traitor with O'Neill. After O'Neill's death he took command of the Ulster forces in March 1650. Defeated at Scariffhollis that June, he was captured near Omagh and put to death despite a promise of quarter, his head spiked at Enniskillen Castle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hebron:
Hebron, one of history's oldest towns, was founded, by the Bible's count, seven years before Zoan in Egypt, and first bore the name Kiriath-Arba after Arba, greatest of the Anakim. Abraham came to its vale of Mamre, bought the cave of Machpelah from Ephron for Sarah's burial, and was himself buried there with Isaac and Jacob, making Hebron the patriarchs' second homeland.

Spies brought grapes from nearby Eshcol, Joshua took the city, Caleb received it. David ruled there seven and a half years as king of Judah before Absalom made it his rebel headquarters. The Christian half weighs Hebron's claim as the city of Judah where John the Baptist was born against Ain-Karim. It follows the town through Roman retaking, Crusader rule, and later centuries as a titular see.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henoticon:
Emperor Zeno's Henoticon of 482 was a compromise law meant to end the Monophysite quarrel and instead opened the first great break between Rome and Constantinople. Egypt and Syria largely rejected Chalcedon, three patriarchates stood in schism. Zeno, champion of the Catholics against his rival Basiliscus yet friend to Monophysites, sought a formula all could sign.

Skilfully it affirmed Nicaea, Constantinople, and Ephesus, condemned Nestorius and Eutyches, called Christ one without saying one nature or one person, and slighted Chalcedon by vague allusion. Peter Mongus of Alexandria and Peter Fullo of Antioch accepted it, strict Monophysites broke away as the headless Acephali, Pope Felix excommunicated Patriarch Acacius in 484. The Acacian schism ran thirty-five years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henri-alexand:
French historian Henri-Alexandre Wallon, born at Valenciennes in 1812, earned the jesting title Father of the Republic by the amendment that carried France's constitutional laws. A history fellow and Sorbonne professor, his 1847 book on slavery in the colonies drew him into politics as Guadeloupe's deputy, and he resigned in 1850 over the suffrage restriction.

Deputy for the Nord in 1871, he voted against Thiers. After monarchist restoration failed he joined the Left Centre to pass the constitution, served as public instruction minister in 1875 to 1876, and sat as senator for life defending Catholic interests. His histories of Joan of Arc, St. Louis, the Terror, and revolutionary justice, with a critical life of Jesus against Renan, fill a long scholarly career.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henri-didon:
Dominican preacher Henri Didon, born at Touvet in 1840, moved France with a majestic pulpit presence and then reshaped Catholic schooling. Entering the Dominicans at eighteen and studying at Rome's Minerva, he began preaching at Paris in 1868. His carriage, voice, and gesture dominated hearers, and he gave the funeral oration for Archbishop Darboy, shot by Communards in 1871.

Attacked over marriage indissolubility in 1879 and over Church and modern society in 1880, he was sent to Corbara in Corsica. There seven years produced his Life of Christ of 1890, a remarkable seller in many tongues. Returning to preach for the Republic at Bordeaux in 1892, he spent his last years at Dominican colleges near Paris, teaching discipline as the road to liberty and self-reliance under authority.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henri-francoi:
Marseilles bishop Henri-François-Xavier de Belsunce de Castelmoron, born in 1671, won the name Good Bishop by staying with his city through the plague of 1720 and 1721. A Paris student turned Jesuit, then vicar-general of Agen, he became bishop in 1709. When plague struck, princesses, notables, and fleets fled while he remained with a few heroic friends to battle the disease.

More than 250 priests and religious died in that charity, and the king offered him Laon with its peerage and then Bordeaux, both refused for the pallium Clement XII sent. He fought Jansenism as a second plague, condemned Soanen at Embrun in 1727, ordered absolution refused to Unigenitus appellants, and wrote pastorals, translations of Augustine and Bellarmine, and antiquities of Marseilles church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-de-brac:
Henry de Bracton, also called Henry of Bratton, was a thirteenth-century English judge whose treatise De Legibus et Consuetudinibus Angliae remains the fullest statement of medieval English law. Probably born in Devon in King John's reign, he served Henry III as a professional judge from 1245 until 1267. He rode as justice in eyre in Devon and neighbouring counties and heard pleas before the king himself, though he never sat on the bench at Westminster.

Bracton's treatise, written before 1259, draws on Roman jurisprudence while grounding itself in some 450 decided cases, a body of case law unmatched in the legal literature of the Middle Ages. Like most judges of his time he was also a churchman, holding the archdeaconry of Barnstaple and then the chancellorship of Exeter Cathedral until his death in 1268. First printed in 1569, his work was translated in full by Sir Travers Twiss between 1878 and 1883.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-fitzsim:
Henry Fitzsimon, a Jesuit born in Dublin in 1566, was educated as a Protestant at Oxford and Paris. He meant to die for Protestantism until controversy with the Jesuit Thomas Darbishire overcame him, as he put it, to his happiness. Joining the Jesuits in 1592, he returned to Ireland in 1595 with Father Archer to refound a mission lacking Jesuit labourers for ten years. He reconciled Protestants around Dublin and Drogheda and challenged Anglican divines to disputation, even shouting challenges from his prison window after his capture in 1600.

Banished in 1604, Fitzsimon travelled through Spain, Rome, and Flanders. He served as chaplain to Irish soldiers in the imperial army as the Thirty Years War broke out, and published a lively diary of the Bohemian campaign of 1620. Returning to Ireland in 1630, he worked until the Civil War of 1640, escaped a death sentence to the Wicklow Mountains in 1641, and probably died at Kilkenny in 1643.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-james-a:
Henry James Anderson, a scientist and educator born in New York in 1799, graduated from Columbia College in 1818 and studied medicine. At twenty-six he became professor of mathematics and astronomy at Columbia, holding the chair for twenty-five years. In 1848 he served as geologist on Captain Lynch's United States Dead Sea exploration expedition, publishing two government geological reports on the Holy Land. Abroad the next year he became a Catholic, remaining ever after a zealous adherent.

Anderson led the St. Vincent de Paul Society in New York, presiding over its Particular Council from 1856 and its Supreme Council from 1860, and inspired the founding of the New York Catholic Protectory. Pius IX received him several times in Rome and made him a Knight Commander of St. Gregory. In 1875 he went as pilgrim to Lourdes and Rome, then to Australia for the transit of Venus, dying at Lahore on his way home.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-knighto:
Henry Knighton, a fourteenth-century chronicler, is known only as a canon of St. Mary's, Leicester, who was there for Edward III's visit to Leicester Abbey in 1363. The chronicle, first published by Twysden in 1652 and critically edited by Lumby in the Rolls Series, runs in five books from Edgar's accession in 959 to 1366. There it breaks off abruptly, suggesting he died about then. 

The first three books, transcripts of Higden with unacknowledged extracts from Walter of Hemingburgh, have little value, though Knighton preserved his name by making chapter initials spell Henricus Cnitthon. The fourth book, written from his own knowledge, is the important part: rich in economic detail on wages and prices of grain, wine, and cattle. It throws light on the Black Death's effect on the labour market, on the loosening of serfdom, and on a dearth of priests filled by ill-prepared ordinations.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-moore-j:
Henry Moore Jackson, a colonial governor born in Grenada in 1849, was the Anglican Bishop of the Leeward Islands' son, educated at Marlborough, Clifton, and the Royal Military Academy. He joined the Royal Artillery in 1870 and retired as captain in 1885. He then entered the colonial service, commanding the Sierra Leone police and serving as Colonial Secretary of the Bahamas and of Gibraltar. His scientific training let him correct harbour plans and save useless expenditure.

Knighted in 1899, he governed the Leeward Islands, then Fiji and the Western Pacific, whose exhaustive report the Colonial Office accepted. He finally governed Trinidad from 1904, calming a colony shaken by riots within three years. He became a Catholic in 1880 and never willingly missed daily Mass. The Church made him a member of the Order of St. Gregory in 1904, and he received the Grand Cross of St. Michael and St. George shortly before his death in 1908.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-of-hunt:
Henry of Huntingdon, a historian born probably near Ramsey between 1080 and 1085, was educated in the household of Robert Bloet, Bishop of Lincoln. He became archdeacon of Huntingdon in 1109 or 1110. A visit to Bec in 1139 introduced him through Robert de Torigny to Geoffrey of Monmouth. Bishop Alexander of Lincoln soon asked him to write a history on Bede's groundwork. He carried it down to Stephen's death in 1154, original and eyewitness from 1127, though his details are sometimes invented and his chronology unreliable.

To later copies Henry added De Miraculis, on miracles of Anglo-Saxon saints, and De Summitatibus, containing his epilogue and three letters, including the Epistola de Contemptu Mundi. Two books of epigrams survive, while books on love, herbs, aromatics, gems, and divine law are lost. He probably died in 1155, when a new archdeacon appears, and his tomb is in Lincoln Cathedral. Arnold's 1879 edition remains the critical text.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-pendlet:
Henry Pendleton, a controversialist born at Manchester, was educated at Brasenose College, Oxford. There he took his doctorate in divinity in 1552. Though he had preached against Lutheranism under Henry VIII, he conformed under Edward VI and served as an itinerant Protestant preacher appointed by Lord Derby, receiving the living of Blymhill in 1552. Described as able, handsome, and athletic, with a fine clear voice, he preached with force in either cause he served.

On Mary's accession he returned to the Catholic Church and received much preferment in 1554, becoming canon of St. Paul's and Lichfield and Bishop Bonner's chaplain, who wrote two homilies for him on the Church and its authority. His declaration of faith, written in sickness in 1557, answered slanderous reports against him. Foxe claims he repented of his conversion on his deathbed. The entry warns that Foxe cannot be accepted without confirming evidence, lacking here as so often.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hermon:
Mount Hermon is a mountain group at the southern end of Anti-Lebanon, marking the northern boundary of ancient Israel east of the Jordan. Its Hebrew name means sacred mountain, and old names for its peaks, such as Siryon and Sanir, point to a shining coat of armour, perhaps from snow glittering in sunlight. The range has three conspicuous peaks, and later writers called it the mountain of snow.

Today it is known as Jebel-esh-Sheikh, mountain of the chief, because in the tenth century it became a centre of the Druse religion. Its limestone ridges offer striking scenery, the River Jordan rises at its foot, and the view from the summit takes in Lebanon and the plain of Damascus. A smaller Hermon near the plain of Esdrelon takes its name from a misreading of a psalm.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hesebon:
Hesebon, called Heshbon in the Authorized Version, was an ancient city beyond the Jordan and a titular see of Arabia. It was the capital of Sehon, king of the Amorites, taken by the Israelites on their entry into the Promised Land and assigned first to Reuben and then to Gad. The Song of Songs praises its fish-pools, and the prophets name it in their denunciations of Moab.

Alexander Jannaeus took the town in the second century before Christ and made it Jewish, and Herod later built a fort there. Under Byzantine rule it grew into a town of note, and milestones on the Roman road to Jericho were numbered from it. Christianity took root there early, and the entry lists its bishops from the lists of Lequien onward.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hexaemeron:
Hexaemeron means a term of six days, and in technical use it means the history of the six days' work of creation in the first chapter of Genesis. The article treats the subject under three heads: text, source, and meaning. It first sets out the biblical text itself, from the first creation through the six days of the second creation to the seventh day of rest.

After laying out the text, the entry turns to its sources and to what the account means, weighing how the days of division and of adornment fit together. Readers find a full treatment of a passage central to Jewish and Christian thought on creation. It serves as a reference point for anyone studying Genesis or the theology of creation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hincmar-bisho:
Hincmar, bishop of Laon, was the nephew of the famous Hincmar of Reims, who raised him to the see of Laon early in 858 and added an abbey and a court office. His ambitious, overbearing, and violent temper soon set him against king, uncle, and metropolitan alike. To escape his uncle's authority he invoked the decretals of Pseudo-Isidore, and Charles the Bald stripped him of abbey and office.

After a reconciliation at Pistres in 869, fresh quarrels at Verberie led to his imprisonment, and he laid his diocese under interdict until his uncle set it aside. He appealed to Pope Adrian II with grave charges against metropolitan and king, but the appeal flagged. The two Hincmars grew wholly estranged, and the younger was deposed at the Synod of Douci in 871 for his conduct toward the king.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-history-of-to:
This article traces the church's historical attitude toward religious toleration. Two facts must be kept in mind throughout, it argues. First, church law against heresy assumed heretics were wilful rebels against lawful authority, apostates who had broken baptismal pledges. In the Middle Ages, when the church stood like a city on a hill, that assumption seemed far from unreasonable.

Cathari, Waldenses, Albigenses, Lollards, Hussites, and early followers of Luther, Calvin, and Knox all fit that picture at first. Only slowly did generations arise who had never known the old unity and could be seen differently. The entry follows that slow change in outlook across centuries of conflict and law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-holy-communio:
Holy Communion means actually taking the sacrament of the Eucharist. Ascetic writers distinguish three kinds of taking: purely outward, spiritual by desire and charity, and both together, by those in grace with the right spirit. This article treats the last kind, the full taking the church has in view.

Real taking requires the sacred species to be taken into the stomach, the eating Christ speaks of in John's gospel. The entry then treats the moral side, need, subject, and readiness, and the liturgical side, minister and method of giving. It teaches that communion is morally necessary for salvation, since without its graces resisting grave temptation would prove very hard.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-holy-simeon:
Holy Simeon was the just and devout man of Jerusalem who greeted the infant Saviour at his presentation in the Temple, as Luke tells it. One of the pious Jews awaiting the consolation of Israel, Simeon had received a promise from the Holy Ghost. He would not die before seeing the expected Messiah. Guided by the Spirit to the Temple that day, he took the child in his arms.

There he sang the canticle Nunc Dimittis and blessed the Holy Family. He prophesied that the child was set for the fall and rising of many in Israel, and that a sword would pierce his mother's soul. Later legends made Simeon a rabbi, son of Hillel and father of Gamaliel. But the entry warns those ties clash with Luke's simple portrait of a man in Jerusalem, and treats them with reserve.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-homoousion:
Homoousion, from Greek words for same and essence, is the word the Council of Nicaea in 325 used to express Christ's divinity. Arius had taught that the Son, as mediator between God and the world, was not eternal and not of divine substance, but a creature brought forth by God's free will. Homoousion answered that the Son shares one and the same substance with the Father.

Both parts of the word caused trouble. Homos could mean same or similar, and ousia was often taken as hypostasis, or person, which risked a Sabellian reading that denied distinct persons. Only after years of controversy did the words settle: orthodox faith speaks of one ousia and three hypostases. Tertullian had already used the Latin equivalent before Nicaea.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-huajuapam-de-:
Huajuapam de León is a diocese in the Mexican state of Oaxaca, erected by Leo XIII's bull Sedes Apostolica of 25 April 1902. It was formed from parts of the archdiocese of Oaxaca and the diocese, now archdiocese, of Puebla de los Angeles. The bull reached Mexico in March 1903, and the archbishop of Mexico, as executor, named the bishop of Cuernavaca as subdelegate.

Canonical erection followed on 12 May 1903, with Rafael Amador named bishop in March. Born at Chila in 1856, Amador studied at Puebla and at the South American College in Rome, taking a doctorate in theology. He served in Puebla's seminary, became pastor and dean, and was consecrated bishop in Oaxaca cathedral in June 1903. At first the diocese answered directly to the Holy See under the title Mixtecas.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hypostatic-un:
The hypostatic union is a theological term for the Incarnation, expressing revealed truth: one person in Christ subsists in two natures, divine and human. Hypostasis literally means what lies beneath as basis or foundation. Greek philosophers used it for reality as opposed to appearances, and Paul uses it in his letters, though not in the sense of person.

Before Nicaea in 325, hypostasis meant the same as ousia, essence, and even Augustine saw no difference between them. The distinction grew gradually through Christological controversies and was fixed by Chalcedon in 451: in Christ the two natures, each keeping its own properties, unite in one subsistence and one person. They are neither joined morally, as Nestorius held, nor mingled, as Eutyches held, yet they are substantially one.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-imagination:
Imagination is the power of picturing things to oneself without any sense impression of them. Scholastic writers count it one of four inner senses, distinct from memory, the sensus intimus, and the sensus aestimativus, and distinct from the intellect. That last distinction matters, given the likeness between imagination's acts and certain acts of intellect.

We know our faculties only from studying their operations, and the image's nature is endlessly disputed. Is it psychologically identical with perception, differentiated only by lesser intensity? Or has it a specific nature of its own? The problem resists easy solution, perhaps any solution. Still, the analogy and points of contact between image and perceptive representation are evident, but they hardly justify identifying the image with complete perception.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-immaculate-co:
Pius IX defined the Immaculate Conception on 8 December 1854 in Ineffabilis Deus. The teaching says Mary, at the very first moment of her conception, was kept free from every mark of original sin. God gave this singular privilege and grace because of the merits of Jesus Christ, Saviour of mankind.

What is protected here is Mary's person at the instant her soul was created and joined to her body. Conception in this sense is not her parents' generative act. Her body took shape in her mother's womb, with her father playing the usual part in forming it. Nor does the teaching touch how holy the parents' generative act was, or the passive conception that comes before the rational soul arrives.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-impanation:
Impanation is a heretical teaching about the Eucharist. It says Christ is present there because his human body is joined in substance to bread and wine, so that he is truly present as God turned bread: Deus panis factus. The word itself copies incarnation.

Just as the Incarnation lets us speak of the Divine Word with the man Christ's properties, so it lets us speak of the man Christ with the Word's. Impanation likewise lets predicates pass between the Son of God and bread's substance. That passing happens only by way of Christ's body. The teaching matches Luther's consubstantiation on two counts: both reject Transubstantiation, and both still affirm Christ's Real Presence. They part company because Luther said Christ's Body pierced the bread's unchanged substance while denying any hypostatic union.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-incardination:
Canon law terms for moving a cleric from one bishop's care to another's form the subject here. Excardination frees a person from the first bishop's rule, while incardination enrolls him for good in the new diocese. The entry roots both words in the Latin for a hinge, since the change turns a man from one fixed post to another.

A person could belong to a bishop by birth, by a church office, by home, or by service. The entry works through how those ties shaped a transfer. It stresses that excardination could not be forced on an unwilling man. It cites early uses of the terms from Gregory the Great and the old Roman chancery book called the Liber Diurnus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-induction:
Reasoning from single cases to general truths is the process this logic entry unpacks. Sense gives us single judgments, such as “this is so” or “some are so,” while a general truth claims “all are so” or “as such, it is so.” Induction is the conscious move from the first kind of claim to the second. The entry contrasts it with deduction, which starts from a general rule and applies it downward.

Four sections carry the argument: induction set against deduction, induction in science, the rational grounds for trusting it, and its use in history. The entry asks how scattered sense data can yield knowledge claimed as certain and universal, and it weighs the grounds and limits of that leap. Readers get both the textbook account and the doubts that still cling to it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-industrial-co:
Settling workplace disputes by talk between employers and workers is the practice defined here, set beside its close kin. Conciliation means the two sides thrash out their differences themselves or through their spokesmen. Arbitration hands the decision to a neutral third party; mediation has a neutral go-between who coaxes the sides toward mutual concessions. Boards of conciliation could be joint committees, state-appointed bodies, or private groups.

France led the way, the entry notes. Its conseils de prudhommes were expert panels of equal numbers of employers and workers. At work since 1806, they read labor contracts and settled small grievances. Within that narrow field they did well, and five-sixths of the strikes they handled reached settlement. The entry thus offers both a glossary of methods and an early case study in making them work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-inquisition:
Church courts set up to fight heresy, with special judges given lasting power over matters of faith by the highest church authority, form the subject of this long historical entry. Its mark was not a single trial or a ruler's whim. It was a standing office, universal in scope. Its purpose was to guard what the Church saw as a revealed deposit of faith entrusted to her keeping.

Modern readers struggle with the institution, the entry argues, because they no longer share two older views: that belief is an objective gift from God rather than private judgment. That the Church is a perfect, sovereign society whose first duty is to keep that deposit unstained. Before the sixteenth-century religious break, those views were common to all Christians, and the entry traces the courts from that shared ground.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-installation:
Putting a canon into his choir stall gives this short canon law entry its name. The name comes from a Latin verb meaning to place in a stall. Installation is the symbolic act by which a canon takes up the duties of his chapter seat and the chapter formally admits him. Local custom shapes the rite, which often means handing him a staff in the choir and a place in the chapter meeting hall.

At the same moment the dean clothes the new canon in chapter insignia and sets the biretta on his head. He then takes the canon's profession of faith and oath to keep the chapter statutes. The same word also covers putting any churchman into possession of a benefice, and a parish priest's solemn entry into his own parish. Readers get a compact account of a rite that turns appointment into visible office.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-institute-of-:
Franziska Lechner founded this congregation at Vienna on 21 November 1868. It followed the Rule of St Augustine. Its aim was to shelter girls without positions and help them find work. The Holy See approved the congregation in 1884 and confirmed it definitively on 22 July 1891. Its purpose was free of charge: board, care, and a way to earn a place for girls with none, plus care for servants too worn out to work.

Beyond that shelter work the sisters ran schools, orphan asylums, and kindergartens from their Vienna motherhouse and novitiate. By the time of the entry the congregation counted 36 branch houses, 766 sisters, and 59 postulants. Readers get a short, factual portrait of a practical charity: its founder, its rule, its approval dates, and the scale it had reached.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-intention:
Moral theology calls intention an act of the will that aims at an end. It reaches for the means to that end. The word comes from a Latin verb meaning to stretch toward. That drive to a goal sets intention apart from mere wishing. It also sets it apart from weak, half-formed desire. Intention carries a concentration of will those states lack. The entry then sorts the kinds of intention that can prompt an action.

Actual intention works with the mind's attention fixed on the end. Virtual intention borrows its force from an earlier act of will. That earlier will still works on through its effects, even though no fresh act of will is present. The distinction matters for judging an act's worth, since the same outward deed can spring from different inner aims. Readers get a compact toolkit for reading human action from the inside.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-intercession:
Going between two parties to plead for one before the other is the plain sense of intercession, and this entry applies it to prayer. In church use, mediation names Christ's standing between God and men. Intercession names the pleading of Mary, the angels, and the saints on men's behalf. The entry keeps that distinction firm, reserving mediation for Christ alone.

Christ's mediation is treated first, separating his position as God-man from his office as go-between, and the longer second part takes up the saints' intercession. Scriptural roots include the Greek verb behind Hebrews 7:25 and Paul's word for mediator in 1 Timothy 2:5. Readers get both the biblical grounding and the Catholic shape of a practice central to daily devotion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-intrusion:
Taking a church office without lawful appointment is the offense this canon law entry defines. Intrusion means seizing an ecclesiastical benefice while ignoring canonical institution. That institution is the formal grant of the office by the person canon law empowers to bestow it. Scripture is cited for the need of a lawful mission, in John's image of entering by the door and in Hebrews on the call to priesthood.

Trent reaffirmed the rule, and the Corpus Juris Canonici states it flatly: no benefice may be taken up without canonical institution. Force is not required for the offense; a person with no true title at the moment of taking possession already counts as an intruder. Readers get a short, strict account of how church law guarded offices against self-appointed holders.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-intuition:
This entry calls intuition a direct grasp of a fact, a being, or a link between two terms. It works without reasoning step by step. The word comes from a Latin verb meaning to look into. Systems that treat such direct grasp as the base of knowledge earn the names intuitionism or intuitionalism, with the Scottish school as a leading case. In ethics, intuitive morality grounds right and wrong in direct apprehension of moral principles.

Shaftesbury, Hutcheson, Reid, and Dugald Stewart stand among its champions in that field, while in teaching intuition means learning through concrete, hands-on, or intellectual grasp rather than rote. Sense perception of material things counts as sensuous or empirical intuition. The entry maps one word across psychology, philosophy, morals, and schooling, showing how much work a single term was asked to do.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-issac-austin-:
Brooklyn-born Issac Austin Henderson, born in 1850 and dead at Rome in March 1909, moved from newspapers to novels and from Protestantism to Catholic letters. Of Scots and Irish stock long settled in America, he was schooled privately and by tutors, then took bachelor's, master's, and doctor of civil law degrees at Williams College. In 1872 he joined the New York Evening Post, owned in part by his father with William Cullen Bryant and John Bigelow.

Assistant publisher by 1875 and publisher, stockholder, and trustee from 1877, he also belonged to New York's Union League, University, and Mendelssohn Glee clubs. Selling his Post interest in 1881, he lived in London and Rome. He published The Prelate in 1886 while still Protestant. Agatha Page followed two years later. It was soon dramatized as The Silent Battle. The entry traces a publisher turned Catholic novelist.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-davy-:
Theologian and diplomat Jacques Davy du Perron was born at St-Lô, Normandy, on 25 November 1556. He died at Batignolles near Paris on 5 September 1618. His parents were Calvinists who fled to Switzerland after his birth amid persecution. He gained a thorough literary, scientific, and philosophical education. He then studied the Fathers and church writers, above all Augustine and Aquinas. In 1577 or 1578 he converted to Catholicism.

He won favor with Henry III, to whom he was presented in 1576, and later with Henry IV. Henry IV's conversion owed much to Duperron's teaching and influence. Duperron and Cardinal d'Ossat won Henry's absolution from heresy at Rome in 1595. While there, Duperron was consecrated bishop of Evreux, a see Henry had already given him. The entry presents a convert who guided a king back to Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-anderto:
James Anderton, an English Catholic, lived from 1557 to about 1618. He came from the well-known Catholic family at Lostock Hall in Lancashire, and large estates there passed to him from his parents, Christopher and Dorothy Anderton. In 1582 he wed Margaret, daughter of Edward Tyldesley. Taking up his father's work in law, he took his father's place in 1592 as prothonotary of the Duchy Court of Lancaster.

At home, faith stayed strong on two sides: his mother and wife both kept loyal to the Church. James himself seems to have copied his father's course and compromised, signing in 1618 an address urging recusants be disarmed and doing other public duties a true Catholic would find repugnant. Father John Clark's eulogy of Henry Holland wrongly credits Anderton, under the name John Brereley, with a valuable work; this account corrects that error while sketching a conforming Catholic gentleman.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-atkinso:
Catholic confessor James Atkinson was tortured to death in Bridewell prison in 1595. His pathetic and romantic story tells nothing of his early life. He appears in Bridewell, one of London's worst prisons, handed to Topcliffe, the notorious priest-hunter. Topcliffe sought by torture to wring evidence against Atkinson's master, Robert Barnes of Mapledurham House. Barnes was accused of harboring priests, notably the future martyr John Jones.

Under torment Atkinson accused his master, then soon repented and fell into despair. He feared Topcliffe would torture him again, perhaps to death. He also feared no priest could reach him for confession before his end. Unknown to him, a Jesuit father was in the same prison. That was Father William Baldwin, who could hear his confession. The entry tells a prison story of betrayal, remorse, and hidden mercy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-burton-:
James Burton Robertson, a historian, was born in London on 15 November 1800 and died in Dublin on 14 February 1877. His boyhood passed in Grenada in the West Indies, where his father Thomas held land. In 1809 his mother took him to England, and in 1810 she put him into St Edmund's College at Old Hall, where he remained nine years. Law studies started in 1819 led to his being called to the bar in 1825, though he never practised.

Next came philosophy and theology in France, taught by Lamennais and Gerbet. In 1835 he brought out his translation of Schlegel's Philosophy of History, a book that went through many editions. From 1837 to 1854 he made his home in Germany and Belgium, rendering Möhler into English in work that swayed some Oxford Tractarians. In 1855 Newman named him professor of geography and modern history at Ireland's Catholic University, where he issued two series of lectures.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-clayton:
Priest and confessor of the faith James Clayton was born at Sheffield, England, on an unknown date. He died a prisoner in Derby gaol on 22 July 1588. He was a shoemaker's son, apprenticed to a blacksmith for seven years. He spent leisure hours educating himself, with special attention to Latin. His studies led him to embrace Catholicism. He was sent to the English College at Reims in 1582. He was ordained priest there in 1585.

He at once returned to England to labor in his native county. Four years later, while visiting Catholic prisoners in Derby gaol, he was arrested. He was condemned to death for exercising his priestly office. His brothers pleaded for pardon, and execution was delayed, though he stayed a prisoner. Prison life brought sickness, of which he died. The entry presents a blacksmith's apprentice turned priest-martyr in all but execution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-fitton:
James Fitton, a missionary, was born at Boston, Massachusetts, on 10 April 1805 and died in that city on 15 September 1881. His father Abraham had come to Boston from Preston in England, and his mother, Welsh by birth, was a convert to the faith. After primary schooling in Boston schools, he took a classical course at Claremont, New Hampshire, in an academy run by Virgil Horace Barber, an early New England convert. Bishop Fenwick taught him theology and ordained him priest on 23 December 1827.

For close to a quarter century, the whole of New England formed the field of his keen labors. With a valise holding vestments, chalice, and Mass necessaries, and his breviary tucked under his arm, he often went on foot. His rounds ran from Eastport and the New Brunswick line in the northeast to Burlington and Lake Champlain in the northwest.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-harriso:
James Harrison, priest and martyr, was born in the Lichfield diocese in England on an unknown date and died at York on 22 March 1602. He trained at the English College at Reims, taking orders there in September 1583. The next year he left for the English mission, working quietly and out of sight. Early in 1602 he served Yorkshire Catholics from the house of Anthony Battie, also called Bates, a local gentleman.

Pursuivants seized Harrison and Battie together. Both were tried at York and condemned to death for high treason. Harrison's sole charge was acting as a priest; Battie's, housing Harrison. The judge left York without fixing an execution date. Yet on the evening of 21 March Harrison learned he would die next morning, and with Battie he was hanged, drawn, and quartered.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jason:
Jason is a Greek name adopted by many Jews whose Hebrew name was Joshua, or Jesus. In the Old Testament it applies to three or four persons linked to the Maccabean period. Jason, son of Eleazar, was sent to Rome by Judas Maccabeus in 161 before Christ to secure an offensive and defensive alliance. Jason, father of Antipater, appears as father of an ambassador sent by Jonathan in 144 before Christ to renew that Roman treaty.
