Wellington is a New Zealand diocese originally part of the Vicariate of Western Oceania erected in 1835. In 1836 Gregory XVI entrusted New Zealand and the western Pacific islands to the newly founded Society of Mary, and. Owing to communication difficulties across the vicariate's many islands, New Zealand was made a separate vicariate in 1842 under Mgr Pompallier, titular Bishop of Amasia.

British colonists soon arrived in great numbers: the first body landed on 22 January 1840 and founded Wellington town, Queen Victoria's sovereignty was proclaimed days later. The Treaty of Waitangi ceded sovereignty to the queen while securing chiefs' territorial rights. New Zealand, first a dependency of New South Wales, became a separate colony in May 1841. In 1843 the colony was divided into two vicariates, Auckland province forming one and the remainder, including Wellington, the other, whose history the entry follows.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-allis: William Allison was one of the English priests who fell victim to the plots of 1679 and 1680, and he died a prisoner in York Castle about that time. John Joseph A'Becket's Catholic Encyclopedia entry preserves his name among those sufferers, a priest whose imprisonment ended in death in custody. No birthplace, ordination or trial is given for him there; his story stands as a brief witness to persecution ending in a York prison cell.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-cally:
William Callyhan Robinson was an American jurist and teacher who built Catholic legal education in Washington. Born at Norwich, Connecticut, in 1834, he died at Washington in 1911. He graduated from Dartmouth in 1854, trained for the Episcopal ministry, served parishes in Pennsylvania, entered the Catholic Church in 1863, and joined the bar in 1864. Yale kept him as law lecturer and teacher from 1869 to 1895, with spells as a New Haven judge.

Robinson also sat in the state legislature in 1874. In 1895 the Catholic University of America called him to teach, where he set up the School of Social Sciences and served as law dean until his death. His books range from Notes of Elementary Law and Elementary Law through a three-volume Law of Patents to Forensic Oratory and Elements of American Jurisprudence. Colleagues prized his thorough grasp of law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-caxto:
William Caxton was the first English printer and the man who brought printing into England. Born in the Weald of Kent about 1422, he died at Westminster in 1491. Little is known of his early life beyond his own prefaces. Apprenticed to the London mercer Robert Large in 1438, he became a merchant at Bruges about 1446, prospered, and in 1465 governed the Merchant Adventurers there, handling delicate trade talks with skill.

About 1470 he left trade for the service of Margaret, Duchess of Burgundy, and finished his translation of the Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye in 1471. Copying could not meet demand for it, so he learned printing, likely at Cologne, and printed the Recuyell at Bruges in 1474. Returning in 1476, he set up his Westminster press, issuing ninety-six books, including Chaucer, Gower, and Malory's Morte d'Arthur.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-errin:
William Errington was an English priest who founded Sedgley Park School after three failed starts. Born in 1716, he died on 28 September 1768. Son of Mark Errington of Wiltshire, he went to Douai in 1737, swore the mission oath in 1741, and took orders in December 1747. He reached London in March 1748 and lodged with Bishop Challoner, then coadjutor to Bishop Petre, who prized him as a zealous missioner and a shrewd man of business.

Challoner urged him to build a good middle-class school, and Errington tried Buckinghamshire, Wales, and Betley near Newcastle-under-Lyne without success. On Lady Day 1763 he opened Sedgley Park near Wolverhampton with twelve boys in Park Hall, once Lord Ward's home. Parliament attacked the venture, but Lord Dudley defended it, and the school served the Church for over a century, living on today as Saint Wilfrid's College, Oakmoor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-gasto:
William Gaston was a North Carolina jurist who won Catholics the vote in his state. Born at Newbern in 1778, he died at Raleigh in 1844. His father, a Presbyterian Irish surgeon in the British navy, was killed by British troops during the Revolution, leaving his Catholic English mother Margaret Sharpe to school him. He entered Georgetown College in 1791, graduated first in his class at Princeton in 1796, and joined the bar in 1798.

In August 1800 Gaston won a state senate seat despite a constitution barring Catholics from office. He served in Congress in 1813 and 1815 as a Federalist leader, then returned to law and joined the North Carolina supreme court bench in 1833 for life. At the 1835 convention he drove repeal of the clause that kept Catholics from office, and his gifts always served his faith and his fellow Catholics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-habin:
William Habington was a Worcestershire poet and historian of the Caroline age, praised for pure and seemly verse. Born at Hindlip in 1605, he died in 1654. Son of the antiquarian Thomas Habington, he studied at Saint Omer and Paris. A tale that he fled England to dodge Jesuit pressure to join their order rests only on a vague claim by the ex-Jesuit Wadsworth.

Habington married Lucy Herbert, daughter of Baron Powis, and in 1634 issued Castara, love poems chiefly to his wife, enlarged in 1635 and 1640 with sonnets and prose characters. His verse is skilful, tuneful, and touched by the metaphysical fashion of his day, yet marked by strict decency of thought and tongue. In 1640 he also staged the romantic tragedy Queen of Arragon and published a History of Edward IV, followed in 1641 by reflective Observations upon History.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-harri:
William Harrison was the third and last archpriest of England, who worked to heal the breach between secular priests and Jesuits. Born in Derbyshire in 1553, he died on 11 May 1621. He studied at Douai from 1575 to 1577, went to Rome as a deacon, took orders, and swore the mission oath at the new English College in April 1579. He laboured in England from 1581 to 1587, then read civil and canon law at Paris.

Harrison ran Father Persons's small school at Eu in Normandy from 1591 until war broke it up in 1593. He served as procurator at Reims, and taught theology at Douai after his 1597 doctorate. Five years in Rome gave him wide church experience. Back in England in 1609, he succeeded Archpriest Birkhead in 1615, backed Kellison against Jesuit sway at Douai, and pushed for restored bishops, dying just as Rome's envoy set out.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-henry:
William Henry Anderdon was an English Jesuit writer whose Catholic tales and sharp controversial pamphlets sold in thousands. Born in London in 1816, he died in 1890. After King's College, London, and Balliol, Oxford, he took his degree in 1840, served as an Anglican vicar at Withyam and Leicester, and entered the Catholic Church at Paris in 1850. Ordained at Oscott in 1853, he taught at Ushaw, preached in Dublin, and served Cardinal Manning as secretary until joining the Jesuits in 1872.

From 1875 to 1889 he lived at Manchester as preacher, guide, and writer. His tales, Bonneval, Owen Evans the Catholic Crusoe, Afternoons with the Saints, and In the Snow, ran to nine or ten editions each and spread into German and French. His controversial best sellers probed Luther, ritualism, and what Catholics truly believe, aiming to understand opponents rather than caricature them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-hough:
William Houghton was a Dominican scholar-statesman who became Archbishop of Dublin and brokered peace between France and England. His birth date and place are unknown; he died at Dijon in 1298. He took the Dominican habit in England, studied and lectured at Saint James in Paris, and was chosen provincial of England at the Vienna chapter of 1282. He governed five years with a charm that won love and respect.

Recalled to Paris lectures, favoured by Philip IV, then provincial again for seven years, Houghton became a favourite of Edward I. The king sent him to Rome in 1289 to seek aid for Holy Land Christians. Edward pressed Boniface VIII to name him to Dublin, and he was consecrated at Ghent in 1297. His mediation sealed a two-year Anglo-French peace, and he died at Dijon while carrying news of it to the pope, his body brought to London for burial.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-seton:
William Seton was a New York author and soldier, grandson of Saint Elizabeth Ann Seton. Born in New York in 1835, he died there in 1905. His father, a navy captain, was Elizabeth Ann's son, and his mother was Emily Prime. Burke's Peerage of 1900 named him head of the Parbroath Setons, cadets of the Earls of Winton. He studied at Fordham, Mount Saint Mary's, and Bonn, travelled widely, and joined a New York law office.

Answering Lincoln's first call in 1861, Seton fought as captain of the Forty-first New York at Antietam, where two wounds disabled him for a time. He then returned as captain of the Sixteenth Artillery in Grant's Richmond campaign. After the war he turned to letters: novels Romance of the Charter Oak and Pride of Lexington, the poem The Pioneer, Rachel's Fate, and science writing for the Catholic World. He also worked finding jobs for the poor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-the-w:
William the Walloon was an eleventh-century abbot caught between pope, archbishop, and emperor. His birth date is unknown; he died probably on 22 December 1089. He became Abbot of Saint Arnoul at Metz in 1050, kept his predecessor Warin's good rule, and spent leisure on Jerome and Augustine. In June 1073 Gregory VII scolded Archbishop Manasses of Reims for abusing Saint-Remi monks and ordered a fit abbot chosen; William won election but found the post untenable.

Manasses kept persecuting him despite papal letters, so late in 1073 William went to Rome seeking leave to resign Saint-Remi. The pope prized him and wished him to keep both abbeys, but Manasses seized his crosier and installed Henry of Hoimblière without consulting him. Back at Metz, William weakly let Henry IV intrude him into the Metz bishopric in 1085 after driving out Bishop Herimann, then publicly resigned at Gorze in 1086 and regained Saint Arnoul.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-westo:
William Weston was an English Jesuit missioner whose exorcisms and Wisbech prison quarrels divided Elizabethan Catholics. Born at Maidstone in 1550, he died at Valladolid in 1615. Schooled at Oxford, Paris, and Douai, he walked to Rome and joined the Jesuits in November 1575, giving all he owned to Douai College. After novitiate and work in Spain, he reached England in September 1584, when no Jesuit stood free, and received Philip Howard, Earl of Arundel, into the Church.

Weston's exorcisms, aided by other priests, impressed many for a year, though modern reading sees hysteria, then called mother, rather than possession. Persecution ended the movement, and Weston was seized in August 1586 and held at Wisbech from 1588. He was drawn into the 1595 split over common rules, twenty of thirty-three priests backing his call for order against Bagshaw's minority. Arbitrators settled a compromise rule in November 1595, and Weston later wrote his mission autobiography.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-wilmington:
Wilmington is the Delaware diocese erected on 3 March 1868 across the Delmarva Peninsula. It covers Delaware, nine Maryland counties, and two Virginia counties east of Chesapeake Bay. Jesuits founded the peninsula's first Catholic mission at Bohemia Manor, Maryland, in 1704 and remained its only priests until Patrick Kenny settled at Coffee Run, Delaware, in 1808. That year Wilmington's first church, Saint Peter's, now the cathedral, opened.

First bishop Thomas Becker, a Richmond priest, found only eight priests and fourteen churches, most little more than sheds, a Catholic flock under five thousand, and schools in Sisters of Charity hands. By tireless work amid poverty he raised churches to twenty-six and clergy to twenty-one, and brought Benedictines, Franciscans, and Visitation sisters. He founded a boys' orphan asylum, and grew the flock to about eighteen thousand before his 1886 transfer to Savannah. His successor Alfred Curtis then cleared debts and added thirteen churches.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-yukon:
Yukon is the Canadian prefecture covering the far northwest, from 54 degrees north to the Arctic Ocean and the Rockies' crest to 141 degrees west, about 312,000 square miles. It joins Yukon Territory with northern British Columbia, once split between Mackenzie River vicariate and New Westminster diocese. The prefecture arose on 9 March 1908 under Oblate Fathers of Mary Immaculate, with Father Bunoz as first prefect that April. Nine Oblate missionaries served it over five churches, twenty-two chapels, and six mission stations.

Twelve Sisters of Saint Ann run its school and hospital for some five thousand Catholics. Dawson gained its first church and hospital as log buildings in 1907 and 1908 from Jesuit Father Judge, who died there in 1899. A 1902 Yukon law guaranteed separate schools under the British North America Act. Prince Rupert, founded June 1909, holds the prefect's headquarters, and Stuart's Lake serves two thousand Indian missions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-zabulon:
Zabulon was one of Jacob's twelve sons and father of the Israelite tribe bearing his name. Scripture knows nothing of the man beyond his sons Sered, Elon, and Jahleel, heads of three tribal families. The name is of doubtful sense, with a wordplay on zebed, gift: Leah says God gifted her, and this time her husband will honour her, for she bore six sons.

At Sinai's census Zabulon counted 57,400 fighting men under Eliab, camping east of the tabernacle with Judah and Issachar. At Shittim a second census gave 60,500. Elisaphan son of Parnach shared the land division for them. Under the judges they shone: Deborah's song praises Zabulon for risking life at Merom, and they joined Gideon against Midian. They gave judge Elon for ten years, and sent fifty thousand warriors to crown David at Hebron.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-zambesi-missi:
Zambesi Mission is the Jesuit prefecture covering Rhodesia north and south of the Zambesi and northern Bechuanaland. British rule governs the whole field. Founded in 1877 under the English Jesuit province, its bounds were fixed by Propaganda in 1879, when Father Henry Depelchin's first party left Grahamstown for a thousand-mile trek to Bulawayo.

No railways eased that road, prices ran enormous, and fever and want killed many. The Matabele, under King Lobengula, were unready for Christianity, and Depelchin's push north past the Zambesi failed, as did Law's eastward venture to the Portuguese border. After the Company broke Lobengula in 1893, stations multiplied, Dominican sisters took hospitals and settler schools, and railways cut the old obstacle. Progress stayed slow, since adult pagan customs, above all polygamy, blocked converts, so hopes rest on schooling children. The mission now counts thirty-two Jesuits, twenty-two lay brothers, and Mariannhill priests and brothers.
celebrated-claimants-from-perkin-warbeck:
An unnamed compiler gathered famous pretenders and disputed heirs into one volume, issued in a second edition by Chatto and Windus in 1874. The preface argues that claimants fill an empty page in literature. Wandering heirs reappear after years. Rogues claim titles and estates that were never theirs. Yet the records sit buried in law books.

Cases run from Jack Cade and Lambert Simnel through Perkin Warbeck, the lost King Sebastian of Portugal, and Pugachev posing as Peter III. Later chapters reach the Tichborne claimant, Arthur Orton, whose name closes the title. Each story weighs evidence, backers, and trials. Some pretenders fooled nations; the book asks why people wanted to believe them.
chico-the-story-of-a-homing-pigeon:
Lucy M. Blanchard wrote a school reader for the Riverside Literature Series, published in 1922 and dedicated to all who love Venice. Her preface promises accurate Italian atmosphere for primary grades. Andrea Minetti, nearly eight, lives by a side canal. His father works in a Murano glass factory, and his mother makes lace.

Old Paolo, caretaker of St. Mark's, minds Andrea and his sister Maria each day. Andrea's wish brings Chico, a pigeon of the square, into the family. Training, a mean cat, and a blue rosette at a show fill the middle chapters. War then calls, and the boy gives his precious homing pigeon to Italy. The sacrifice is the story's stated lesson, and its hero is a bird.
christopher-carson-familiarly-known-as-k:
John S. C. Abbott wrote a life of Kit Carson for Dodd and Mead's Pioneers and Patriots series, published at New York in 1874, illustrated by Eleanor Greatorex. Chapter headings summarise a frontier childhood first. Birth, wilderness perils, a cabin and a fort, and an apprenticeship open the story. An alarm and a destroyed trading band follow quickly.

Trapping years fill the middle: the Colorado, the Sacramento, desert crossings, and the missions of San Gabriel and San Fernando. Carson's self-possession in a trappers' council is singled out for praise. Winter battles end with enemies retiring across Yellowstone ice to a fortified island. Abbott wrote popular biography for young readers, and his Carson is scout, linguist, and hero in one buckskin figure.
complete-project-gutenberg-collection-of:
Three memoir collections by various insiders of Napoleon's court fill this large Project Gutenberg gathering. Louis Antoine Fauvelet de Bourrienne, Napoleon's private secretary and school friend from Brienne, anchors the volume. His memoirs, edited by R. W. Phipps, show the emperor at work and at home. Bourrienne claims impartial aim, praising and blaming his old master in turn.

Constant, the emperor's premier valet de chambre, adds Recollections of the Private Life of Napoleon in Walter Clark's translation. Stewarton's Memoirs of the Court of St. Cloud close the set as secret letters from Paris to London. Together the three give campaigns, councils, dress, temper, and table talk from men who stood in the room. Editors extended Bourrienne past the Elba abdication through Waterloo to the death at St. Helena. Napoleon readers who want the private man behind the battles, in slippers as much as in uniform, start with these witnesses.
concept-great-power-mattison:
Ages of the world roll past in a short apocalypse from the Nag Hammadi codices. The Concept of Our Great Power, in Mark Mattison's public-domain rendering, gives that vision in English. The power of the title is the high God, whose plan the seer lays bare.

The text moves from creation through the flood and the age of flesh to fire and final rest. It tells how the savior comes, how the rulers fail, and how the saved are known. The sweep is vast for so brief a book. Mattison's free rendering lets readers trace that sweep in one sitting.
confession-and-absolution:
Confession and Absolution, by T. J. Capel, priest of the archdiocese of Westminster, was published at Philadelphia by Cunningham & Son in 1884. It grew out of a Lenten course. One of twenty-four conferences delivered in the cathedral at Philadelphia took up God's conditions for pardoning sin. At the request of many hearers, that conference is here expanded for print. A second edition the same year adds answers to questions sent to the author.

Capel's text is 2 Corinthians: God hath reconciled us to himself by Christ, and placed in us the ministry of reconciliation. His extracts from the Fathers come from the collection called Faith of Catholics, offered to readers without a patristic library. The argument meets the new Anglican controversy over confession, which the Convocation of 1873 had been forced to consider.
coningsby-or-the-new-generation:
Coningsby; Or, The New Generation, by Benjamin Disraeli, was published in 1844 and runs to nine books. The author's preface states its purpose plainly: to vindicate the just claims of the Tory party to be the popular political confederation of the country. England's youth, he writes, had sobered after the Conservative triumph of 1841 and begun to ask what, after all, they had conquered to preserve.

A publishers' note places Disraeli among the novelists of his century, from Vivian Grey in 1826 to Sybil in 1845. The fiction moves through drawing rooms and great houses. Sidonia, the wealthy, unattached friend of the elder Coningsby, pays court to Lucretia, Madame Colonna's daughter; being no marrying man, his homage only brings Coningsby and Lucretia more together.
consanguineous-marriages-in-the-american:
Consanguineous Marriages in the American Population, by George B. Louis Arner, is a study in numbers dated March 1908. Its preface thanks the many friends who sent in detailed cases of cousin marriage. Dr. Alexander Graham Bell gave data. Professors Giddings and Moore read the draft and advised on it.

Four chapters lay out the work. The first tells how the facts were gathered: from family records, from direct inquiry, and from isolated communities. The second asks how common such marriages are, using Darwin's method on American figures. The third takes up the sex ratio of the children. The fourth asks what cousin parentage does to childbearing. Tables close the case: the rates of grave defect run far higher, in his figures, for children of kin.
country-life-in-canada-fifty-years-ago-p:
Canniff Haight's Country Life in Canada Fifty Years Ago gathers the personal recollections of a sexagenarian looking back on pioneer Ontario. Haight dedicates the book to the young men of Canada, on whose integrity and energy, he writes, the future of their great heritage rests.

The recollections cover clearing land, building homes, travelling rough roads, worship, school and neighbourly life in a colony still close to the forest. Haight writes as a man who lived the changes he describes, contrasting the hardships of early settlement with the settled country of his old age. Readers interested in Canadian social history will find here a first-hand, unpretentious account of how ordinary settlers actually lived.
criticism-and-fiction:
William Dean Howells argued the case for literary realism in Criticism and Fiction, a collection of his critical essays. Howells asks whether any lasting standard of taste exists. Quoting John Addington Symonds, he answers that fashion changes but truth endures. What is simple, natural, and honest in art, he argues, stays beautiful. Fantastic and artificial work pleases briefly, then fades.

Essays take up fiction's aims, the role of the editor, and the faults of romantic storytelling. Howells praises novels that study ordinary life honestly. He attacks false sentiment and stagey plots. His manner is conversational, full of asides about dress, furniture, and painting. Readers get the clearest statement of the realist creed that shaped Howells's own novels and his editing of a generation of American writers.
daughters-of-the-cross-or-woman-s-missio:
Brief lives of women missionaries fill Daughters of the Cross, or Woman's Mission, by Daniel C. Eddy. In his preface Eddy says he has brought together heroines from many sects and churches. He calls their names a galaxy as dear to Christians as any on record.

Each sketch tells of toil and suffering on heathen soil, in the book's own phrase. Hymns sung on a last Sabbath, with a husband at her side, close one such life. Eddy hopes the tales will teach the cause of missions and stir zeal in the reader. He rates these women above the fallen warrior and the titled senator. The book is a wreath of praise, woven for the churches that sent them.
dave-darrin-s-fourth-year-at-annapolis-h:
Graduation year at Annapolis fills this fourth Dave Darrin book by H. Irving Hancock. First Classman Dave Darrin and Dan Dalzell share quarters as the year opens. Twenty-four chapters bring them to graduation day at last.

West Point stands across the tale, in football and in talk. Dave defends a cadet named Prescott, held in Coventry at the Military Academy, as a sad mistake. A search at the bottom of the bay and a prize trip on the Dodger add peril. Bad money, stale work, and Morton's treachery test the pair. The book closes the Academy years of Hancock's best-known heroes.
day-of-the-moron:
A tale of a nuclear plant in crisis fills H. Beam Piper's short story, made here from Astounding Science Fiction for September 1951. The scene is set in 1968, when a few folk still fear atomic plants. Scott Melroy, an engineer, is among the few who hold that a blowup is not impossible.

A foreword warns of the emotional moron, who is on no one's side, not even his own. At noon one day the whole gang hands in wrist Geigers and dosimeters and clears out. Two men, Burris and Koffler, claim they are persecuted, and the crew will not come back without them. Melroy must hold the plant and the men at once. The tale is a cold war study of fear at work.
de-carmine-pastorali-prefixed-to-thomas-:
An essay on pastoral poetry by René Rapin fills this reprint, taken from the front of Thomas Creech's 1684 translation of Theocritus. The Augustan Reprint Society issued it in July 1947 at seventy-five cents. J. E. Congleton wrote the introduction and a note on the books behind it.

The introduction says Rapin found the pastoral spoiled by wit, excess, and false art. He sought to strip those growths away and restore the kind to its first purity, by the ancients, Virgil above all. Rapin's own text holds that the country demands plainness and simple thought. Comparisons, he says, should be obvious and common. The piece is a rule book for a kind of verse the Augustans prized.
dictionary-of-the-chinook-jargon-or-trad:
Words of the trade tongue of the Pacific Northwest fill George Gibbs's dictionary of 1863. The Cramoisy Press of New York printed it as number twelve of Shea's Library of American Linguistics. Two parts give Chinook into English, then English into Chinook.

Gibbs tells in his preface how the Smithsonian had printed a small word list years before, from a navy doctor and a priest at Chinook Point. That list, he says, missed words in use and gave wrong roots. His own entries give each word's source tongue. Pahtl, or full, yields words for drunk, wet, and dirty, and mamook pahtl means to fill. The book is a field record of a working jargon of trade.
doc-gordon:
A country doctor with a buried past fills Mary E. Wilkins Freeman's novel of 1906. The Authors and Newspapers Association of New York and London issued it, with water-colour pictures by Frank T. Merrill. A snow-whitened doctor, coat still on, stands in the front picture.

Young James Elliot walks twenty-five miles at dawn to Alton, to serve as assistant to the town's one physician, Doctor Thomas Gordon, called Doc. Elliot is fresh from his studies and in his twenties. Gordon, in the sampled middle, argues with himself over the right and wrong of a thing in his mind. Twenty years, the text says, had evolved him into another man. Freeman builds the tale on that hidden change.
doe-osti-17033601-improving-neutron-scat:
Karl Daningburg authored this long Los Alamos report, issued July 14, 2026, on using modern machine learning to improve neutron physics models. Two problems anchor the work. One is fission, where models must predict how many neutrons and gamma rays each split atom releases. The other is neutron scattering, described by a tool called the optical model.

For fission, the author builds fast emulators that mimic a detailed emission model, including one that handles noisy output. For scattering, a neural optical model is trained with differentiable programming, which lets gradients flow through the physics code during fitting. Background chapters explain neutrons, fission, and automatic differentiation for readers new to any of those topics.
doe-osti-17038091-predictive-ultrafast-l:
Pierson Guthrey led this tri lab project report, issued by Lawrence Livermore in September 2026, on speeding plasma simulation with tensor networks. Plasma models must track particles across space, velocity, time, and uncertain inputs, so plain grids grow too large to store or solve. Tensor networks replace one huge array with linked smaller factors when the data has compact structure.

Livermore built a portable tensor library named BoBa and linked it to Sandia finite element software. The team showed compressed solvers for stiff collision problems that still preserved key physical quantities. Other work covered filling gaps in partial count data and measuring uncertainty without ever building the full array. Sandia partners added high order methods and realistic test problems.
doe-osti-17047522-final-scientific-techn:
Final report dated January 4, 2026, from Robert Anex at the University of Wisconsin Madison closes award DE-AR0001636, with Penn State and the University of Illinois Chicago as key partners. The goal was concrete building parts that store more carbon than their making emits. A direct air capture process based on carbon mineralization supplies the key ingredient.

The process pulls carbon dioxide from air in a water based cycle and treats industrial mineral wastes at the same time. Treatment raises the wastes power to help cement harden, and the captured carbon stays locked as solid carbonate. Treated material partly or fully replaces portland cement in ready mix concrete. Bench runs included eight hours of steady air contactor operation.
doe-osti-17049043-demonstration-of-spnds:
Milestone report INL/RPT-26-96046 from Idaho National Laboratory, dated September 2026, demonstrates self powered neutron detectors for live monitoring of a reactor neutron spectrum. Kevin Tsai and Johnathan Grissom built and tested a device holding several such detectors, each a small sensor that makes its own signal from radiation without outside power.

Computer models in MCNP mapped how candidate emitter materials respond at each neutron energy. A routine called GRAVEL then unfolded, or worked backward from, detector signals to rebuild the spectrum. The sensor package was irradiated in two exposure rooms at the AFRRI TRIGA reactor. Signal versus reactor power plots and delayed signal corrections from the metal sheath are reported.
doe-osti-17056539-predicting-neutron-cap:
Jutta Escher, Jeffrey Berryman, Oliver Gorton, and colleagues at Lawrence Livermore built tools to predict neutron capture rates on unstable nuclei, reported in September 2026. Capture reactions help forge elements in supernovae and neutron star mergers, yet many rates involve short lived nuclei that cannot be measured directly. Project 24-ERD-023 aimed to fill that gap with stated uncertainty.

Machine learning produced an uncertainty bearing nuclear interaction for large shell model calculations of level densities and gamma strength. A tailored global optical model, named POTLUQ, joined it in statistical reaction calculations. The new rates fed simulations of weak r-process element making and lab applications, and the method flags which rates matter most.
doe-osti-17076283-ornl-natural-resources:
Report ORNL/LTR-2026/4945 documents an Oak Ridge project to rescue decades of natural resources field data, by Rima Asmar Awad, Nick Oldham, James Nutaro, and Jamie Herold in September 2026. The archive holds wildlife surveys, mapping files, environmental assessments, photos, and sound recordings. It sat on a shared drive that was hard to search, slow from afar, and at risk of loss.

Phase one moved 1,452,590 files, about four terabytes, to secure cloud storage with a web search front end. Staff can now search by keyword, file type, date, or place on an interactive map from any browser. Original creation dates were recovered for 99.6 percent of files. A second phase adds AI powered library features.
doe-osti-17076701-report-summarizing-the:
Stephen Taller, Valentin Pauly, and Caleb Massey of Oak Ridge ask how neutron spectrum shapes damage in HT-9 steel, in report ORNL/SPR-2026/4778 dated September 2026. HT-9 is the reference cladding steel for sodium fast reactors, prized for resisting swelling. Few such reactors exist, so most damage data come from test reactors with differing spectra.

The team gathered published microstructure data from campaigns at the Fast Flux Test Facility and other sites. They then added fresh studies of HT-9 irradiated in the High Flux Isotope Reactor and in the Russian BOR-60 reactor. Comparing dislocation structures and precipitate types across spectra, at matched conditions where possible, builds a fuller picture of how the steel ages.
doe-osti-17120799-ier-622-paradigm-activ:
Ryan Charrette, Robert Weldon, Peter Brain, and Los Alamos colleagues report foil dosimetry from the PARADIGM experiment, document IER-622 issued 1 October 2026. Thin metal foils placed in a neutron field become radioactive at rates that reveal the field's strength and energy spread. Activation foils and fission foils together cover different energy bands.

Chapters describe where the foils were deployed, how their activity was counted, and how reactor dosimetry quantities are defined, with uncertainty treatment. Results compare measured reaction rates against simulation, including reaction rate ratios in an appendix. An appendix also gives the effective multiplication factor for the assembly. The paired data set lets modelers check their neutron transport predictions against bench truth.
doe-osti-17133598-effects-of-short-term-:
Yiren Chen, Zuotao Zeng, Srinivas Mantri, and Argonne colleagues exposed two reactor steels to flowing liquid sodium and measured the damage, in a September 2026 report. Sodium cooled fast reactors bathe their parts in hot liquid metal, which can leach elements and soften steel. Alloy 709 and laser printed 316H are both candidates for those parts.

Tensile samples rode in a forced convection sodium loop, with a sample chamber allowing swaps mid run. Companion samples were heat aged in furnaces to separate heat effects from sodium effects. Sodium chemistry is tracked in its own chapter. After exposure, the team weighed corrosion and mechanical property changes, including carbon movement in the steel, to judge how each alloy holds up in short term service.
doe-osti-17138816-high-altitude-infrared:
Xintong Deng and Taewoo Nam of Toyota Research Institute of North America report a field campaign for an airborne sensing platform, in ARM report DOE/SC-ARM-26-034 dated October 2026. The campaign ran 12 to 15 August 2025 at the Bankhead National Forest site in Alabama. The platform is an advanced tethered kite built for long duration environmental observation.

Crews collected a full set of infrared images paired with synchronized attitude measurements. The data improve and validate a vision based method for estimating the kite's orientation. That vision method is meant as a backup if the inertial measurement unit degrades or fails in flight. Results, publications, and lessons learned fill the short report, which guides the next round of flights.
doe-osti-17143209-quantitative-measureme:
Thomas Voisin of Lawrence Livermore tackles a missing measurement in metals science, in an October 2026 study report. Computer models predict how metals bend and stretch. The motion runs through line defects in the crystal called dislocations. But no method could check the predicted dislocation counts against real tests, so the models stayed unproven.

High energy x ray beams can gather the needed statistics from a sample. Reading those patterns in hard numbers was the gap. A new computer model of the diffraction process was built and used to simulate dislocation effects. Virtual patterns matched real ones well. The match shows dislocation counts and types can be measured at last. Next steps train a learning model on hundreds of simulated cases, then mine past data on stockpile metals.
doe-osti-17171716-lmx-file-format-specif:
Jason Kern of Los Alamos specifies the LMX file format, document version 1.0 issued 16 September 2026. A file format spec fixes how a program's data is laid out so other tools can read it years later. Early pages state the file extension, the file type, and the design goals and non goals that bound the format.

Encoding rules follow for header data and binary data, with special masks for channels and a scheme for timestamps. A file layout section then maps the byte order of every block. Later parts cover reading and writing expectations in enough detail for an independent implementation. The goal is that two programmers, working apart, produce files the other's code can open.
doe-osti-2482539-near-infrared-noise-in-:
Fermilab note FERMILAB-FN-1248-AD, by Sergei Kladov of the University of Chicago with Sergei Nagaitsev, Young-Kee Kim, and seven colleagues from Brookhaven, Fermilab, and SLAC, measures density noise in intense electron bunches. The noise sits in the one to ten micrometer wavelength range. It matters for coherent electron cooling, a method planned to keep hadron beams bright in storage rings such as the Electron-Ion Collider.

The team compared a shot-noise model against signals from near-infrared optical transition radiation picked up by photodiodes. Test bunches ran at a relativistic factor near 50, close to the cooler design values. For those design parameters, no major density fluctuations appeared, and no real drop in cooling rate showed up. A chicane-compressed bunch did show space-charge-driven microbunching, with coherent radiation up to one hundred times stronger, which helped calibrate the method.
doe-osti-2510496-coupling-relap5-3d-to-b:
Idaho National Laboratory report INL/RPT-24-82490, by Jason D. Hales, Jan I. C. Vermaak, and Mauricio E. Tano Retamales in December 2025, links two reactor simulation codes. RELAP5-3D models coolant flow and heat transfer across a plant. BISON models what happens inside the fuel itself. Joining them is a step toward coupled analysis of a loss-of-coolant accident, where coolant behavior and fuel behavior drive each other.

Two coupling routes are built and compared, one driven through RELAP5-3D's Python interface and one sharing memory through the MOOSE framework. A demonstration pressurized water reactor model couples the codes at the core's hot channel. Steady and transient runs at fuel rod powers of 4 and 24 kilowatts check the link against RELAP5-3D alone. The LOFT L2-5 experiment then serves as the validation case for the coupled system.
doe-osti-2583496-teamer-technical-suppor:
CRADA final report NREL/TP-5700-94429, dated April 7, 2025, reports TEAMER support for the University of Washington's wave energy work. Rebecca Fao was NREL's contact; Brian Polagye led the university side. The device is an oscillating surge wave energy converter, a flap hinged at the seabed that rocks in passing waves. In the Sea Wave Environmental Lab's tank, the team ran forced oscillation and excitation tests to extract the flap's hydrodynamic coefficients.

The second goal changed mid-stream. A data-driven predictive controller was planned, but early tests exposed artifacts, flap buoyancy and driveline stiction, friction that sticks then slips, distorting the dynamics. The team pivoted to characterizing those artifacts and how to compensate for them. Rounded versus square flap edges were also compared. The payoff is practical: guidance for telling real ocean physics apart from laboratory quirks, so tank results are not misread when the design scales up.
doe-osti-2584249-photovoltaic-mini-modul:
Swift Coat's anti-soiling glass coating went head to head with bare glass and a market rival at two NREL test stations. Report NREL/TP-5K00-95789, dated June 27, 2025, closes CRADA CRD-22-23086, with Michael Deceglie as contact. Dust is a silent tax on solar: soiling cuts the light reaching the cells, and the loss varies by place and season. Each station held three mini-modules, one bare, one with a commercial antireflective coating, and one with Swift Coat's PHOTOCLEAN coating.

The stations track short-circuit current from cells behind each glass type. A pair of reference cells, one brushed clean automatically every day, yields the daily soiling ratio and its rate of change. That design isolates the coating's effect from weather noise. Swift Coat's question was whether its coating keeps panels cleaner longer in real outdoor conditions, and the stations were built to answer it with numbers rather than photographs.
doe-osti-2584665-competition-for-managem:
Project report LA-UR-25-28634, by Imanol Benitez Hernandez and Daniel Arthur Humphrey in August 2025, simulates relativistic magnetic reconnection. In this process, tangled magnetic fields snap into new shapes. They dump their energy into particles as they do. It matters from solar flares to cosmic rays. Three-dimensional reconnection is known to produce power-law spectra of highly relativistic particles, a signature astronomers observe across the universe.

The team ran large fully kinetic simulations with the VPIC particle-in-cell code on the Perlmutter supercomputer. The flagship run spanned 2048 by 1024 by 1024 cells. Their focus was mechanism. How do Speiser orbits, the special paths particles ride near the layer, feed acceleration? And how do self-made turbulence and plasmoids reshape it? The report walks through the layer's stages, from inflow through outflow to the plasmoid-filled late state. It compares particle behavior in turbulent regions against existing theory.
doe-osti-2586387-development-of-an-inter:
Alison Holm and Karlynn Cory of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory wrote this final report, NREL/TP-7A40-95284, in August 2025 for CRADA number CRD-18-00762. Marshall Vogts shares credit for the work. The client was the Oklahoma Office of the Secretary of Energy and Environment, which wanted help judging the value of distributed energy resources such as rooftop solar in Oklahoma.

The agreement had two tasks. The first was a requirements document for an interactive model that would express distributed resource value from user inputs, covering data needs, gaps, methods, and limits on fidelity. NREL drafted that document with the office and a stakeholder group, the Oklahoma Distributed Generation Thought Group. The second task was a consumer protection assessment. Follow-on work continued under a separate agreement, CRD-19-00788.
doe-osti-2586390-comstock-measure-scenar:
Janghyun Kim and Chris CaraDonna of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory wrote this documentation report, NREL/TP-5500-95003, in August 2025. It belongs to the ComStock project, which models energy use across the United States commercial building stock. The measure documented here is chiller replacement: swapping old chillers for new ones and counting the energy effect building by building.

The report lays out the baseline approach and then the modeling steps in detail. Chiller performance data were gathered from public sources, cleaned, and reshaped into data files that EnergyPlus and OpenStudio can use. Related upgrades in the wider chilled water system are covered too, along with utility bill handling and carbon emissions accounting. An output variable list defines what the runs report, from average chiller coefficient of performance to counts of chillers by capacity in tons.
doe-osti-2586467-reservoir-dynamics-in-p:
Mina Khalaf leads a seven-author National Energy Technology Laboratory team in this field case study, DOE/NETL-2025/4941, dated August 1, 2025. Guoxiang Liu, Robert Dilmore, Gregory Lackey, Mohamed Mehana, Luciane Cunha, and Brian Strazisar join as co-authors. The question is practical: what happens underground when a carbon dioxide enhanced oil recovery field is converted into a dedicated carbon storage site?

The team built a generalized reservoir model informed by real field data from the SACROC field in Texas. Scenario simulations vary how much the reservoir was depleted, the boundary conditions, fluid properties, and model size. Cases cover business-as-usual flooding, dedicated injection into the hydrocarbon reservoir, injection into a saline reservoir, and starting pressures above and below the minimum miscibility pressure. The results track pressure buildup, plume movement, and long-term containment, informing how oil fields can be repurposed for storage.
doe-osti-2587211-comstock-measure-scenar:
Janghyun Kim and Chris CaraDonna of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory wrote this documentation report, NREL/TP-5500-95006, in August 2025. It belongs to ComStock, the laboratory's model of energy use across the United States commercial building stock. The measure documented here pairs two upgrades: a standard performance heat pump rooftop unit and new windows.

The report first describes the existing rooftop units and windows in the building stock, then gives the modeling approach for each upgrade and where it applies. Heat pump rooftop units replace conventional packaged systems in the model, and window replacement swaps in better glazing. Utility bills are computed with rates from the Utility Rate Database, adjusted to 2022 dollars, including time-of-use pricing and demand charges. Output definitions and limitations follow the same pattern as the wider ComStock measure library, so results can be compared across measures.
doe-osti-2587567-finite-geometry-correct:
Daniel Rhodes and six colleagues from Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory and Duke University's Triangle Universities Nuclear Laboratory wrote this report, LLNL-TR-2010950, in September 2025. Richard Hughes and Ching-Yen Wu are among the Livermore authors. The topic is a quiet correction that neutron scattering measurements cannot skip: the scattering sample has real size, and neutrons interact on their way in and out.

The corrections serve a completed campaign on uranium-238 at the Triangle lab, which used steady neutron beams of 2, 3, 4, and 5 megaelectronvolts. The team built a new Geant4-based framework to compute the corrections and checked it against a well-measured test case. One benchmark run recorded the histories of 16 million elastically scattered neutrons. The framework also gives the outgoing neutron energy dependence of each correction factor, which matters when the final states in the scatterer cannot be resolved one by one.
doe-osti-2587887-opcw-twining-project-vi:
Carolyn Koester of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory wrote this trip report, LLNL-TR-2010969, in September 2025. It records a visit from August 11 to 15, 2025, by staff of Morocco's National Laboratory of Scientific and Technical Police. The visit ran through the twinning program of the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons. Livermore's Forensic Science Center mentors the Moroccan laboratory toward OPCW Designated Laboratory status.

Livermore built a three-sample environmental test as the week's teaching tool. It was deliberately harder than the standard test samples the visitors had handled before. One spiked chemical appears in no OPCW database, forcing the visitors to solve a structure from scratch. Exercises taught them to fuse data from gas chromatography with element-specific detectors and from mass spectrometry. The five-day agenda mixed introductions, a laboratory tour, and hands-on analysis of the test samples.
doe-osti-2587981-evaluating-high-halide-:
Jincheng Bai, Harmony Werth, Brian Riley, and Miroslava Peterson of Pacific Northwest National Laboratory wrote this evaluation in September 2025. Salt-based nuclear waste from pyroprocessing is rich in halides such as chloride, and few waste forms will take it. The report reviews the glass systems that might, working from the published literature before any new experiments.

Tellurite glasses get the deepest treatment, in oxyhalide, lead, bismuth, and other variants. Zinc bismuth glasses and phosphate glasses, including an iron phosphate family, follow. Each system is weighed for how much chloride salt it can absorb and how durable the product stays. The recommendations name candidates for laboratory trials. One silver-tungsten-tellurite glass, at 30 percent silver oxide, 35 percent tungsten oxide, and 35 percent tellurium oxide, is flagged for tests on chloride incorporation and chemical durability.
doe-osti-2588044-evaluating-sup-240-sup-:
Denise Neudecker, Keegan Kelly, Amy Lovell, Robert Little, and Matthew Devlin of Los Alamos National Laboratory wrote this evaluation report, LA-UR-25-29062, dated August 16, 2025. It produces a new evaluation of the prompt fission neutron spectrum of plutonium-240: the energy spread of neutrons born in fission. The work was a fiscal 2025 milestone for the Nuclear Criticality Safety Program.

What makes the evaluation new is data. For the first time, measured spectra cover a broad range at once. Incident neutron energies run from 1 to 20 megaelectronvolts. Outgoing energies run from 800 kiloelectronvolts to 10 megaelectronvolts. The LANL-LLNL Chi-Nu team took the data with a full uncertainty assessment. Modeling used an extended Los Alamos model in the CoH3 code, plus an exciton model for pre-equilibrium emission. Results match the Chi-Nu data across most energies. They agree with the older library evaluation up to 4 megaelectronvolts, then differ distinctly above it.
doe-osti-2588283-sierra-solidmechanics-5:
The SIERRA Solid Mechanics Team at Sandia National Laboratories issued this verification tests manual, SAND2025-11140, printed September 5, 2025. It documents the test suite for Sierra/SolidMechanics version 5.26, the laboratory's flagship solid mechanics simulation code. Frank Beckwith, Gabriel de Frias, and Scott Gampert are among the credited contributors.

Verification asks whether the code solves its equations correctly, and the manual is the evidence file. It explains convergence testing and the types of verification problems used. It also shows how observed convergence rates are computed, including tests built on surrogate solutions and asymptotic analysis. Hundreds of test entries follow, each with expected behavior and measured results. One table tracks convergence rates for a time integration formulation across refined meshes. Codes that predict hardware behavior must pass exactly this kind of scrutiny before their results are trusted.
doe-osti-2588458-performance-and-durabil:
Andrew Park of the Chemours Company led this final report for award DE-EE0008836, covering March 2020 through December 2023. Los Alamos, Lawrence Berkeley, and the National Renewable Energy Laboratory partnered through the HydroGEN consortium. The target is cheaper green hydrogen from proton exchange membrane water electrolyzers. It serves the Department of Energy's one-dollar-per-kilogram hydrogen goal.

Proven membranes for these electrolyzers were thick, up to 250 micrometers. That thickness wastes energy as proton resistance. Thin membranes fix the efficiency but let hydrogen cross into the oxygen stream, an unsafe mix. Chemours' answer pairs thin, reinforced membranes with gas recombination catalysts inside them. Crossed-over hydrogen recombines with oxygen to form water within the membrane. The report tracks performance and durability. It also flags a subtle risk: recombination water hydrates the membrane unevenly. The effect showed near the active area's edge under hydrogen and oxygen, but not in nitrogen controls.
doe-osti-2588515-argonne-national-labora:
Argonne National Laboratory issued its Site Environmental Report for calendar year 2024, prepared by M. Mesarch, C. Klimek, P. Lynch, and colleagues. Argonne sits outside Chicago at Lemont, Illinois. The annual report is the laboratory's public record of environmental performance: what it emitted, what it monitored, and how it complied with the rules.

Early chapters describe the site itself, its population setting, climatology, geology, seismicity, groundwater, land and water use, vegetation, and fauna. A compliance summary then walks the major environmental laws, starting with the Clean Air Act. The monitoring program is analytical chemistry at scale. Hydrogen-3 in water is counted by liquid scintillation on small distilled samples. Transuranium radionuclides need ten-liter samples, chemical separation, and alpha spectrometry, with plutonium-236 as a yield tracer. Results across media fill the year's record.
doe-osti-2588551-comstock-measure-scenar:
Amy Allen of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory wrote this scenario documentation, NREL/TP-5500-95002, dated September 2025. It defines a behavioral ComStock measure: reduced thermostat setbacks for heat pumps. Homes and businesses often let temperatures drift down overnight to save energy, but deep setbacks can backfire on heat pumps, which recover slowly and may call on wasteful backup heat.

The scenario softens the setback instead, and the documentation treats the trade honestly. Cutting one pattern of consumption can raise another, the text warns, and many factors decide whether the strategy pays in a given case. Single-building tests apply the measure to two models in different climate zones before the stock-wide run. As with the rest of the ComStock family, the result is a published dataset of energy, bill, and emissions effects against the 2018 baseline stock, ready for custom aggregation by analysts.
doe-osti-2588877-qc4-10-connector-cracki:
Steven DiGregorio, Carmen Sowers, Laurie Burnham, and Bruce King of Sandia National Laboratories presented this investigation, SAND2025-11471R, dated September 11, 2025. QC4.10 connectors, the quick-connect fittings that wire solar panels together, are cracking within months of installation. The problem affects at least three sites across two developers, and the root cause is unknown.

The team ran a forensic comparison. Pristine and cracked connectors were tested side by side, and the QC4.10 was benchmarked against rival models from Staubli and Amphenol that do not crack. Infrared spectroscopy identified the base polymer and its cross-linking and oxidation state. Thermal analyses quantified plasticizer content and glass transition temperature. Mechanical tests measured stress-strain behavior and hardness. Suspects include polymer embrittlement, plasticizer loss, contamination, and swelling O-rings. One early result: thermogravimetric curves overlap, so aged samples have not lost a significant share of additives during aging.
doe-osti-2588996-comstock-measure-scenar:
Chris CaraDonna of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory wrote this scenario documentation, NREL/TP-5500-95119, dated September 2025. It defines a ComStock measure for commercial buildings: standard performance heat pump rooftop units, modeled not from catalog curves alone but from laboratory-tested data on how real units behave.

Rooftop units heat and cool a large share of American commercial space, and their rated efficiency hides field behavior. The lab-informed modeling captures details such as crankcase heaters, the elements that strap around a compressor to keep refrigerant from migrating into it while off. That matters below about 40 degrees Fahrenheit, when liquid refrigerant pooled in a compressor can damage it at startup. The document sets the measure's assumptions in a summary table, applies the scenario across ComStock's 2018 baseline stock, and publishes the resulting dataset of energy, bill, and emissions effects for public use.
doe-osti-2589343-on-possibilities-of-usi:
Brookhaven National Laboratory technical note BNL-228914-2025-TECH, by O. Chubar, examines a little-used kind of light given off at the edges of bending magnets. In the NSLS-II storage ring, fast electrons emit this edge radiation where a magnet's field starts and stops. Its properties differ from ordinary synchrotron radiation and resemble light emitted when electrons cross a foil.

The note describes the radiation's spectrum both with formulas and with computer models, focusing on long wavelengths below the bending magnet critical energy. Possible uses include aligning beamline optics and checking X-ray and electron beams without disturbing them. Edge radiation has served infrared beamlines and beam size checks at other facilities, but NSLS-II had not used it in practice. The calculations show what signals its beamlines could expect.
doe-osti-2997303-theorems-in-service-of-:
John Bender, Justin Kelm, and Zach Sullivan prove theorems that let engineers compose system models safely, in Sandia report SAND2025-11910R dated September 2025. The work formalizes labeled transition systems, the state-and-step descriptions used to model software and hardware behavior. Its core device is an abstraction relation: a declared link between a detailed machine and a simpler one.

A relation counts as lawful when it supports backward simulation and always lets the simple machine start in a matching state. Under a stated translation guarantee, time-based properties proven about the simple machine carry back to the detailed one, with the report giving a worked deduction theorem. Expression languages with implication, equality, and negation support partial variable values across time. Tool builders get proven rules for swapping model parts without re-proving everything.
doe-osti-2997307-materials-degradation-i:
Watching cracks grow inside molten salt closes out a laboratory project by Rebecca Schaller, Ryan Katona, Kenneth Armijo, and co-authors, in Sandia report SAND2025-12036R. Molten salt reactors run hot, corrosive coolant that also carries current, which blinds most crack gauges. No public in-situ crack growth measurement existed for those conditions before this work.

The team adapted a direct current potential drop method, which infers crack length from voltage changes, onto a horizontal load frame with high-temperature fittings and new sample shapes. Ten current reversals were averaged for each reading, and crack speed came from length-versus-time traces following the ASTM E647 method. One confirmed growth window ran about 1.5 hours of active cracking. Reactor designers gain a way to measure stress corrosion cracking where it actually happens.
doe-osti-2997321-simultaneous-celestial-:
Finding your position from the stars closes a laboratory project by Jose Rodriguez, Daniel Bender, Matt Stefanick, and co-authors, in Sandia report SAND2025-12178R. GPS signals can be jammed or denied, a real risk for high-consequence systems. The method here uses no radio signals at all: a camera reads star positions, an inclinometer reads tilt, and a clock supplies time.

An earlier version ran on a smartphone and placed itself within about 15 kilometers of the true spot. The best run on that hardware landed within 3 kilometers, with an uncertainty bound near 8 kilometers. Tilt precision dominates the error, so the team built a custom mount around a high-accuracy Wyler inclinometer. The next goal is 100 meters, a thirty-fold improvement. Because the method is all-optical, it works wherever the sky is visible and signals are not.
doe-osti-2998190-gyrokinetic-simulation-:
A final technical report on project DE-FG02-08ER54954, prepared 9 October 2025, closes Scott Parker's long-running grant on gyrokinetic simulation of tokamak plasmas. Gyrokinetic models follow charged particles spiraling along magnetic field lines, the right level of detail for plasma turbulence. Two goals led the work: how electron-scale turbulence settles into saturation, and how impurities move through the edge pedestal, the steep rim of a high-performance plasma.

The team ran the GENE code with a single unstable electron temperature gradient mode as a core test case. Collaborative papers cover zonal flows, the self-generated streams that tame turbulence, excited by mid-scale electron turbulence, presented at fusion theory meetings in 2020 and 2021. Journal work includes nonlinear particle-in-cell studies with Yang Chen. The report is the grant's closing account, listing people, runs, and publications.
doe-osti-2999072-testing-calibration-and:
Nicholas Wright and Sean Fournier of Sandia report in SAND2025-12871R, dated October 2025, on testing a small commercial radiation detector for robot use. The Kromek GR1 Plus uses a cadmium zinc telluride crystal to read gamma-ray energies and name radioactive sources. Sending machines instead of people toward strong sources keeps doses low, a core safety rule.

Bench testing and energy calibration came first. Then the sensor was fitted to uncrewed systems: robot dogs, multirotor aircraft and ground vehicles. Those machines drive or fly themselves, or take remote control. The report works through a common roadblock, since many commercial sensors keep their data protocols closed. Steps run from first remote operation to full runs on moving platforms. End uses span disaster response, site cleanup and routine checks of places too hot for hands-on surveys.
doe-osti-2999884-sf6-acetone-separation-:
Jihyeon Kim and Kwan-Soo Lee report in LA-UR-25-30348, issued 20 October 2025, on cleaning a potent greenhouse gas stream. Sulphur hexafluoride, used in electrical and industrial gear, often leaves mixed with acetone vapour, and the two must be separated before the gas can be purified or reused. The Los Alamos team tested activated carbon adsorption, trapping acetone on carbon while the rest passes, as a first cleaning stage.

Their bench testbed, named VAST, ran at one ten-thousandth of full scale. Feed held about 8 percent acetone vapour at 1 to 2.5 litres per minute, passing a 20-gram column of Carboxen 563 carbon. Breakthrough, the point where acetone slips through, came at 15 to 35 minutes while holding 95 percent removal. Working capacity measured 332 to 356 milligrams per gram of carbon. Scaling the numbers up suggests over 260 kilograms of carbon at 25,000 litres per minute.
doe-osti-3000254-plug-in-electric-vehicl:
Rex Green and Jason Harper of Argonne test how real electric cars obey charging commands, in this grid integration study. Smart charge management promises to shift car charging into cheap, green hours, but only if vehicles do what the charger asks. A charging station speaks to the car through a pilot signal, a pulse-width tone that sets the allowed current. The team borrowed production vehicles from a research fleet and from laboratory employees, testing them as delivered.

Two behaviours were measured. In response tests, cars were scored on how accurately and quickly they followed changes in the pilot signal's current limit. In wake tests, the team checked whether a sleeping car wakes and charges when the signal calls. Results show how much an aggregator can truly steer a session, and where cars lag or ignore the script. The authors caution that findings describe the tested vehicles, not whole brands.
doe-osti-3000802-spin-polarized-electron:
Harish Bhandari of Radiation Monitoring Devices, in Watertown, Massachusetts, proposes a new material for spin-polarized electron sources in this project narrative for award DE-SC0025504. Accelerators from CEBAF to the future Electron-Ion Collider need photocathodes that emit electrons whose spins point one way. Today's emitters are almost all gallium arsenide stacks, grown by costly methods, with gallium supply itself becoming a risk.

The plan swaps the material family entirely. Cadmium telluride, a group II-VI compound, would be grown by atomic layer deposition, a technique that lays down one atomic layer per pass for exact control of thickness, strain and make-up. That control could yield high-quality emitters and ultrathin surface stacks with simpler, more uniform manufacturing. The narrative sets out the case, the growth approach and the milestones. It is a funding-stage document, arguing why the alternative deserves its shot.
doe-osti-3001262-dipole-bend-magnets-des:
Kip Bishofberger of Los Alamos walks through a complete dipole magnet design in LA-UR-25-30614, issued 27 October 2025, written as a worked example others can reuse. The occasion is LAMP, a planned Los Alamos upgrade that must merge hydrogen ion beams of opposite charge; one bending dipole is the simplest merger. The design target: 3 kilogauss across a 6.35-centimetre gap, over pole pieces 25 by 15 centimetres, enough to deflect 3.0 MeV protons by about 17 degrees and 2.1 MeV protons by 21 degrees.

Every choice is costed in the open. Two coils of 100 turns each, 6-millimetre square wire with a water cooling channel, run at 75 amps and dissipate 350 watts; inductance lands near 0.4 to 0.75 henries, and cooling water pressure drop at 42 psi. Bishofberger stresses the aim: a self-consistent, reasonable point design, scalable elsewhere, rather than a correction-factor-precise final engineering package.
doe-osti-3001266-testing-horizontal-mome:
Alaina Hogan of Los Alamos verifies a modelling detail with wide consequences in LA-UR-25-30752, issued 29 October 2025. Ocean models must decide what water does at a coastline: stick, as if glued, or slide freely along it. MPAS-Ocean, the ocean engine inside the E3SM climate model, long offered only the no-slip option. Its successor system, OMEGA, needs both, so Hogan implemented and tested the free-slip boundary condition alongside the old one.

Two standard test cases do the checking. A barotropic gyre, a wind-driven swirling basin, and a barotropic channel each exercise the boundary mathematics on the model's hexagonal ocean mesh. Both boundary conditions behaved as the physics requires, which clears them for joint use in OMEGA. The short report explains how boundary conditions are coded in MPAS-Ocean and records the test evidence, the kind of quiet verification that keeps climate projections honest at every shoreline.
doe-osti-3001942-uncertainty-in-syntheti:
Sha Feng, Effy Baby John, Karthik Balaguru, Larry Berg and PNNL colleagues audit storm models in an October 2025 report. Insurers, planners and governments price hurricane risk using synthetic tropical cyclones, catalogues larger than the historical record. Five systems, RAFT, CHAZ, the MIT model, STORM and CLIMADA, each generate an artificial history of landfalls and losses. The report asks how much the machine choice changes the answer.

All were run against the same anchors, the IBTrACS archive and ERA5 reanalysis fields. Differences in how each model seeds storms, steers them, grows their intensity and converts wind to damage propagate into hazard and risk estimates. Those estimates diverge by region. The analysis names where the models agree, where they split, and which assumptions drive the splits. For anyone quoting a one in ten thousand year storm loss, the message is humility: the catalogue is a model, not a measurement.
doe-osti-3002124-disassembly-and-initial:
Peter Doyle, Zane Wallen, Jason Harp, Caleb Massey, and colleagues report the first look inside a new fuel test in Oak Ridge report ORNL/SPR-2025/4207, dated September 2025. The test is Mini99, the first MiniFuel experiment in the High Flux Isotope Reactor to use liquid metal inside its small capsules for tighter temperature control. Mini99 studies molybdenum-99 related fuel behavior.

After irradiation, the team opened the capsules and checked the fuel. Silicon carbide thermometers showed test temperatures close to the design values. Fission gas release stayed small, near 3 percent for most samples, with one near 8 percent. Four fuel samples had broken into small pieces and granules during the test. More examination is planned to explain the damage and finish the picture.
doe-osti-3002206-assessment-of-microstru:
Gerry Knapp, John Coleman, Matt Rolchigo, Benjamin Stump, Selda Nayir, and Alex Plotkowski grade computer models in Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2025/4111, dated August 2025. The models predict the grain structure that forms when stainless steel 316 is printed by powder bed fusion. Grain structure governs strength, so a model that gets it right saves costly test builds.

The team printed steel at three energy levels and imaged the grains with electron diffraction and etched optical views. Melt pool size was measured to tune the AdditiveFOAM heat model. The ExaCA grain model was then calibrated against the etched builds. Dendrite growth rates were computed as a function of undercooling. The assessment shows where predictions match the printed metal and where they drift, giving modelers a firm base for the next round.
doe-osti-3002215-measure-effects-of-molt:
R. Pillai, S. Cambier, T. Lowe, and A. Willoughby run a materials test program reported in Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2025/4105, dated August 2025. The program measures how molten halide salt changes the creep rupture life of three heat-resistant alloys: 316H, Alloy 709, and Alloy 617. Creep rupture is the slow stretching and eventual failure of metal held under load at high heat.

Molten salt reactor firms need these numbers, because legacy data on salt exposure are thin. Samples age in hot salt, then are pulled under load until they fail, giving lifetimes that designers can use. The alloys named are leading candidates for salt reactor parts. Results feed the case for licensing materials that must survive years of contact with hot halide salts.
doe-osti-3003118-radar-studies-of-convec:
P. Kollias of Stony Brook and Brookhaven, with S. Giangrande, E. Luke, M. Oue, S. Freeman, and P. Gatlin, report a radar field campaign in DOE report DOE/SC-ARM-25-022. Its title page is dated October 2026, though the catalog lists it under 2025. The CONVECT campaign studied convective storm dynamics with advanced radars at the S30 site. A phased array radar took part, guided by an adaptive sampling system.

Observations combined the phased array radar with the operational KHTX weather radar. Range-height scans crossed storm cells at four-degree azimuth steps. Products shown include reflectivity, radial Doppler velocity, and spectrum width, a proxy for turbulence strength. The team credits site support crews for keeping power, internet, and security running. Campaign reports like this one fix the record of what was deployed and measured, for later data users.
doe-osti-3003850-comparison-of-nuclear-t:
G. J. Youinou of Idaho National Laboratory compares rocket reactor designs in report INL/JOU-25-88349, dated October 2025. Nuclear thermal propulsion heats hydrogen in a reactor and expels it for thrust. All designs here are 300-megawatt cores with 211 fuel assemblies. The variables are fuel form, neutron spectrum, and enrichment: highly enriched uranium at 93 percent versus high-assay low-enriched uranium at 19.75 percent.

Fuel forms range from carbide blocks and graphite composites to tungsten and molybdenum cermets, plus uranium carbide and metal pins. Lower enrichment needs in-core moderator; beryllium is the reference choice. For highly enriched cores, the graphite composite needed the least uranium-235, at 62.3 kilograms, while metal pins needed the most, at 292 kilograms. High-assay cores weigh roughly twice as much overall.
doe-osti-3004328-analog-systems-for-edge:
Ben Feinberg, Sapan Agarwal, Chris Bennett, and ten colleagues explore a computing throwback in Sandia report SAND2025-14280R, printed September 2025. Analog computing, using continuous voltages instead of digital bits, is returning as an accelerator for optimization and linear algebra at the edge. The report studies analog matrix-vector multiplication hardware and how to simulate hybrid analog-digital systems honestly.

Precision is the hard part, and a full chapter quantifies it. Signal power and noise power are derived separately, with clipping and quantization errors treated as distinct noise sources. The result is a signal-to-quantization-noise framework for predicting accuracy before hardware is built. Power efficiency estimates follow from the same math. The audience is designers weighing analog accelerators against digital ones for field-deployed optimization.
doe-osti-3005856-analysis-of-the-automat:
Clara Saia, an Italian summer student at Fermilab, analyzes neutrino event reconstruction in manuscript FERMILAB-TM-2898-STUDENT. Her supervisor was Bruce Horward. The detector is ICARUS, the far detector of the Short Baseline Neutrino program, hunting for a possible fourth, sterile neutrino. ICARUS images particle tracks in liquid argon.

Saia worked with simulated charged-current quasi-elastic events. The task was separating proton tracks from showers in the automatic reconstruction, using a boosted decision tree's scores as the test bed. Getting that distinction right decides whether an event counts as a clean signal candidate. Three detectors sit at 110, 470, and 600 meters from the beam target in the program. Student manuscripts like this one document analysis training while adding a checked piece to the experiment's reconstruction effort.
doe-osti-3007297-streamline-collaboratio:
Final report by Christian Drischler of Ohio University, dated December 11, 2025, covers his university's share of the STREAMLINE collaboration, a DOE project applying machine learning to the nuclear many-body problem. The work targeted honest uncertainty estimates for nuclear theory predictions. Early-career researchers carried much of the work under Drischler's direction.

One thread combined rival nuclear models in a Bayesian framework to pin down the nuclear saturation point, the density at which nuclear matter settles. That point benchmarks the nuclear forces built from chiral effective field theory, the standard route to deriving them. Another thread built active-learning emulators, fast stand-in models for costly scattering calculations, choosing training points greedily to cut computing time. Publications and talks from the Ohio group are listed at the end.
doe-osti-3007646-integration-and-quantit:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report by Kendalynn Morris and Nathan Wiens, dated September 2025, checks whether soil data from the Molecular Observation Network, MONet, line up with two established soil databases. The comparison partners are the Soil Respiration Database and SoilGrids, a global mapped soil product.

To compare fairly, the authors converted each source onto common terms. MONet respiration combined 24-hour and 96-hour readings with weights of one third and two thirds, favouring the longer run. Database values were converted to mass-based fluxes using a bulk density of 1.33 grams per cubic centimetre and a soil depth of 10 centimetres. The methods, written in R Markdown, show exactly how each conversion was done.
doe-osti-3007983-streamline-collaboratio:
Final report by Richard Furnstahl of Ohio State University, dated December 2025, covers his university's share of the STREAMLINE collaboration under DOE award DE-SC0024509. STREAMLINE applies machine learning to the nuclear many-body problem, and the Ohio State work was carried largely by one supported graduate student, Simon Sundberg.

Sundberg built tools for a criticality analysis of neural networks that predict nuclear masses, treating the networks through effective field theory and renormalization group ideas. Critically tuned networks beat their non-critical equivalents on the AME2020 mass dataset. A second thread, shared with Ohio University and Michigan State colleagues, built active learning emulators for nuclear scattering calculations.
doe-osti-3009249-hanover-led-streetlight:
Final technical report for DOE award DE-EE0010144, from the Town of Hanover, New Hampshire, under public works director Peter Kulbacki, covers conversion of the town's streetlights to LED. The project ran from April 2023 to September 2025.

Hanover voted in 2017 to reach 100 percent renewable electricity by 2030, and by 2024 on-site generation already offset over 90 percent of the municipal load. Utility-owned streetlights burned 165 megawatt-hours a year, 7 percent of that load, from old sodium and mercury vapour lamps with no dimming. The project replaced them with compliant LED fixtures, though a search for compliant ornamental fixtures failed and no waiver was granted.
doe-osti-3010874-use-case-specification:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory's Use Case Specification, by Michael Brown, Jay Barlow, and Isabel Van Dyke, dated September 2025, defines test cases for the E-COMP grid co-design testbed. Each use case states a grid problem, the hardware and simulators involved, and what a successful run must show.

One flagship case gives offshore wind farms a black start job: after a total outage, inverter-based resources must reboot the grid themselves. The modeled system links an offshore wind farm to a multi-terminal high-voltage direct-current grid with storage and both grid-forming and grid-following inverters. Several simulators ran linked in real time, a combination the team flags as likely a first.
doe-osti-3010883-controlling-host-respon:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report Controlling Host Responses to Infection, dated September 2025, studies how human cells answer coronavirus infection at the molecular level. Hugh Mitchell, Sankarganesh Krishnamoorthy, Christopher Anderton, and a large team wrote it. The model virus is HCoV-229E, a common-cold coronavirus safe enough for detailed work.

Human liver HuH7 cells, 15,000 per well, were infected at two viral particles per cell and held at 34 degrees Celsius for 24 hours. Capture plates froze the cells' metabolite output for later analysis. The program reads chromatin accessibility and histone marks alongside metabolites, hunting the host switches, enzymes such as EZH2 among them, that an infection flips.
doe-osti-3010888-shear-assisted-processi:
Magnesium alloy machining chips are turned straight into wrought stock through ShAPE, short for Shear Assisted Processing and Extrusion. Scott Whalen and co-authors describe the work in a brief Pacific Northwest lab summary dated September 2025. Chips from dry machining were pressed cold into briquettes first. The briquettes then fed the ShAPE step.

Two round rod sizes came out of the work, 0.25 inch and 0.50 inch across. The hosted text is brief and mostly boilerplate beyond its abstract. It gives no test results for strength and no processing temperatures. The record closes with the two rod sizes rather than a full results set.
doe-osti-3011003-sulfate-conversion-of-r:
Used Reillex HPQ anion exchange resin is converted from nitrate form to sulfate form for disposal in an interim report by Mills, Denisenko, Morgan, and Mills of Savannah River National Laboratory. The nitrate form is an oxidiser and fails the Waste Isolation Pilot Plant acceptance criteria. The study gathers data to support the Savannah River Plutonium Processing Facility flowsheet for that conversion.

Resin arrived in chloride form and was first converted to nitrate form at lab scale. Passing about ten bed volumes of 1 M sodium sulfate still left nitrate detectable in the effluent. Only the 2 M sulfuric acid test reached a nondetectable nitrate level, below 0.002 M.
doe-osti-3011892-high-fidelity-analysis-:
Electric vehicle charging loads on real Colorado utility feeders are simulated at high fidelity by Shibani Ghosh, Derek Jackson, Mithat Kisacikoglu, and colleagues at the National Renewable Energy Laboratory. Adoption forecasts and synthetic travel itineraries generate the charging demand placed on feeder models. Managed charging strategies are then tested against transformer capacity limits.

Under first come first served charging, late connecting owners risk missing their energy needs. Equal share distribution spreads capacity but can leave vehicles short when capacity is tight.
