An energy satisfaction index counts sessions that fully meet vehicle needs. Long residential dwell times let grid aware charging meet most demand in the cases studied.
doe-osti-3012215-finite-element-analysis:
Finite element analysis of the TRUST nonlinear dynamics testbed is reported by Samuel Hinerman of Los Alamos National Laboratory in LA-UR-25-31593. The testbed stacks metal and foam in a cylinder: two pieces of SX358 cellular silicone foam act as nonlinear springs for a central aluminium block carrying six accelerometers. Foam thickness, density, and preload set the dynamic response under study.

Earlier models used a Lanczos eigensolver that only extracts natural frequencies linearly. The study instead applies the Abaqus 2024 explicit dynamics solver, whose central difference method captures nonlinear material response. Foam behaviour came from quasistatic load cycling tests, and an undamped single degree of freedom model cross checked the frequencies.
doe-osti-3012643-bioinorganic-chemistry-:
Kyle Matthew Lancaster of Cornell University wrote this final technical report, dated January 12, 2026, for award DE-SC0021003, covering September 2020 to September 2025. The project studied ammonia monooxygenase, a copper-bearing membrane protein that starts nitrification, the oxidation of ammonia to nitrite that many microbes live on. The protein had never been purified in an active form, which blocked close study.

Nearly all the effort went into building an expression system to produce the protein in lab bacteria. The expressed subunits reached the cell membrane and appeared folded, and parts of the related protein complex were isolated by high-speed centrifugation and washing. Understanding this chemistry bears on ammonia's possible use as a fuel and on how nitrogen moves through soil and water.
doe-osti-3013035-one-earth-energy-seismi:
Kendall Taft of the University of Illinois wrote this technical report, DOE-UIUC-0031892-07, issued January 13, 2026, for the Illinois Storage Corridor CarbonSAFE Phase III project. It interprets seismic surveys at the One Earth Energy site near Gibson City, Illinois, one of two planned carbon storage hubs. The surveys test whether the deep Mt. Simon sandstone can hold injected carbon dioxide under the Eau Claire confining layer.

The two- and three-dimensional seismic data confirm that both the storage interval and the confining unit run continuously across the project area. Faults do cut the Mt. Simon reservoir inside the modeled carbon dioxide plume. Reassuringly, none of those faults cross the Eau Claire confining unit, and the reservoir faults die out below it. The interpretation supports the site's Class VI permit applications.
doe-osti-3013244-standard-library-grid-f:
Technical report UNIFI-2025-1-28, dated November 2025, specifies REGFM_C1, the standard library model of a grid-forming hybrid control inverter-based resource. Wei Du of Pacific Northwest National Laboratory led the 24-author team drawn from Tesla Energy, EPRI, Siemens, GE Vernova, and other firms. Grid-forming inverters set their own voltage and frequency, unlike grid-following units that merely track the grid, and hybrid units blend both behaviors.

The specification defines two branches inside the model. The grid-forming branch runs as a virtual synchronous machine with voltage control and droop settings, while the grid-following branch takes current references. Current limiting algorithms cap the combined output at the inverter maximum without shifting its phase angle. A parameter table lists every symbol, unit, and example value needed to implement the model.
doe-osti-3013550-planar-systems-for-quan:
Cornell University's final technical report for award DE-SC0019481 is dated January 15, 2026. It covers the Planar Systems for Quantum Information project. Jie Shan led the team, with five co-principal investigators at Columbia, the University of Texas at Austin, and SLAC. The period ran September 2021 to September 2025. A one-year no-cost extension is included. The team developed two-dimensional moire materials as quantum simulators. These tabletop systems mimic hard many-body Hamiltonians.

Layered crystals stacked with a slight twist form a moire pattern. The pattern is about ten nanometers wide and traps electrons in a regular array. The platform lets researchers tune density, energy scales, and even lattice symmetry. The report collects several results. Among them is evidence of the fractional quantum spin Hall effect in moire MoTe2, published in Nature in 2024.
doe-osti-3014572-autonomous-hydrogen-fue:
Plug Power's Patrick Adam led this final technical report for award DE-EE0008421. The project ran October 2018 to September 2025. The National Laboratory of the Rockies partnered on it. The aim was fueling hydrogen vehicles without a human at the nozzle. Forklifts were the first target. A robotic arm would find the receptacle and couple on its own.

Baseline tests measured how accurately human operators park a lift truck at a dispenser. That set the motion range the robot must cover. The final design is a SCARA-type arm. It has two horizontal links and a ball screw for vertical travel. Fiducial markers guide it. Lidar gave better depth accuracy than stereo cameras in their trials. Sunlight, though, can overpower the marker system. A second phase laid the groundwork for autonomous liquid hydrogen transfer that minimizes boil-off losses.
doe-osti-3014657-enhanced-hlw-glass-prop:
Vitreous State Laboratory report VSL-15R3400-1 is the Phase 2 final report on enhanced property-composition models for high-level waste glass at Hanford. Wing Kot, Konstantin Gilbo, Hao Gan, Innocent Joseph, and Ian Pegg wrote it. The report is dated December 2015. The Waste Treatment Plant must turn tank waste into glass that passes durability and processing limits. Predictive models tell formulators which recipes will behave before they melt them.

Phase 2 expanded the glass dataset with new test matrices. They include high-aluminum and ultra-high-aluminum designs labeled HLW14 and HLW14UH. Target compositions are tabulated with grouped component variables. Inner and outer layer constraints from the matrix design are given too. The enlarged dataset strengthens the statistical models. Those models link glass composition to properties such as viscosity and durability. The plant's formulation algorithm depends on them.
doe-osti-3014922-techno-economic-analysi:
CRADA final report CRD-19-16288, dated January 2026, gives a techno-economic analysis of turning forest biomass residues into renewable natural gas and co-product chemicals. The National Laboratory of the Rockies ran it with West Biofuels and university partners. The plan scales a lab catalytic reactor into an integrated pilot process. A commercial gasifier sits at its core. Gary Grim was the lab technical contact.

The design adds a catalyst chosen to tolerate gas contaminants. It adds a hydrate-based separation step that simplifies downstream cleanup. Test data track carbon flows through the mass analyzer system. Output splits among methane, ethylene, ethane, propylene, and propane. A run of alcohols, from methanol to hexanol, takes the rest. The end product is pipeline-grade renewable gas. The chemical co-products add value to a residue stream drawn from forest thinning.
doe-osti-3015269-national-nuclear-securi:
The NNSA Graduate Fellowship Program annual report for the Class of 2024-2025 chronicles one fellowship year. Pacific Northwest National Laboratory produced it. The program hires, trains, and places graduate fellows across the Nuclear Security Enterprise. It approaches its 30th anniversary with the next class.

Growth frames the story. The program began with three fellows. It now fields more than 60 each year. That forms a standing talent pipeline for national security work. Cohort pages sketch individual placements and projects. One fellow analyzed interagency agreements in the partnership and acquisition office. Another checked whether the FS-65 container can serve as a transport option. A third helped coordinate a cross-laboratory operational workshop. A cover roster names the full class of sixty-plus fellows pictured at the front.
doe-osti-3015370-exploring-electrocataly:
A Georgetown University final report under award DE-SC0021218, dated January 29, 2026, targets turning methane straight into methanol at low temperature. YuYe Tong wrote it. The project tested a bifunctional mechanism on three alloy surfaces. They were platinum-ruthenium, palladium-gold, and nickel-copper. On them, one metal site splits methane and a neighboring site splits water. The fragments then combine into methanol.

In situ spectroscopy followed the surface chemistry during operation. Cyclic voltammetry runs showed a telling detail. The first sweep carried noticeably higher current on the peak's left ramp. Its carbon dioxide signal was higher too. Later sweeps overlapped each other. The extra first-sweep charge came from adsorbed species, such as adsorbed carbon monoxide. They built up during the roughly 30 minute methane purge before measurement. That is evidence of slow methane dissociation on the surface.
doe-osti-3015698-comstock-measure-scenar:
National Laboratory of the Rockies report NLR/TP-5500-96598, written by Marlena Praprost and dated January 2026, documents one modeling measure in the lab's ComStock tool. ComStock models the energy use of the whole United States commercial building stock. The measure covered here upgrades building envelopes, meaning walls, roofs, and windows, so they meet the energy code each state now enforces for new buildings.

Inside, the report sets out how code templates are assigned to buildings in each state. It also gives turnover rules for when old systems get replaced, plus baseline values for wall and roof insulation and window types. States covering more than 78 percent of United States commercial floor area now enforce 90.1-2013 or a stronger code. Modelers can use the measure to test how much energy a full code upgrade would save.
doe-osti-3015854-laser-powder-directed-e:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report M3MT-25PN0902031, by Subhashish Meher, Asif Mahmud, and Isabella J van Rooyen, dates to August 2025. It covers laser powder directed energy deposition, a metal printing method that melts powder with a laser as parts are built layer by layer. The team applied the method to two steels meant for nuclear service, A709 and the grade called G-92.

For each steel the report tracks structure under the microscope, hardness, tensile strength, and fracture surfaces, in as-deposited form and after heat treatments such as normalizing and tempering. Tensile results stayed consistent within each build direction, which points to even material quality. A separate section covers ion irradiation, used to mimic radiation damage. The data help engineers judge whether printed steel parts can be trusted in reactors.
doe-osti-3015894-bio-based-acetonitrile-:
David Brandner was the National Laboratory of the Rockies technical contact for this January 2026 cooperative research final report, NLR/TP-2800-97858, under agreement CRD-23-23758, and Eric Karp is also named on the record. The project made acetonitrile, a common industrial solvent, from plant-based starting material instead of fossil sources. The target was at least 100 grams at 99.8 weight percent purity.

The route used a nitrilation reaction, adding nitrogen to biologically derived acetic acid bought on the open market. Testing found a best point near 0.9 per hour space velocity with a five-to-one ammonia to acetic acid feed ratio, and the catalyst needed regeneration before the production run. Output was scaled up to 100 grams, and partner staff were trained in the process. A side task studied pulling the thickener pullulan out of fermentation broth.
doe-osti-3015964-improving-and-measuring:
San Diego State University's final technical report for award DE-SC0018310, dated February 9, 2026. It covers a water oxidation catalyst project led first by Douglas Grotjahn. After his death in 2023, Jing Gu took over, with Diane Smith also a principal investigator. Water oxidation is the half of water splitting that frees oxygen and electrons, the step that limits making hydrogen fuel from water.

The team worked to make catalysts last longer, to build better ways of measuring that lifetime, and to keep catalysts working in acid. Ruthenium catalysts with bipyridine dicarboxylate ligands were a main test case, and computer work favored a water attack path for forming the oxygen bond. Four papers came out in 2024 and 2025. Doctoral student Colton J Breyer finished his 2024 thesis on instruments for testing catalyst stability, work this report draws on.
doe-osti-3016090-engineering-b-ketoadipi:
Robert Baldwin and Gregg Beckham were the National Laboratory of the Rockies technical contacts for this January 2026 cooperative research final report, NLR/TP-2A00-98487, and Carol Gomez is also named on the record. The project engineered the bacterium Pseudomonas putida KT2440 to produce beta-ketoadipic acid, a chemical building block. The acid is a candidate for making performance-advantaged nylons from plant sugars.

Guided by techno-economic analysis, the two-year goals were steep. They were 40 grams per liter titer, 0.5 grams per liter per hour productivity, and 40 percent molar yield from hydrolysate sugars, at one kilogram scale. Work included hunting for non-obvious gene targets that raise production. One route combined fitness-based enrichment of a transposon library with a glowing biosensor readout to pick better strains. The filing records the plan, the targets, and the strain work behind them.
doe-osti-3016981-precision-time-protocol:
Mingyan Li of Oak Ridge National Laboratory wrote this technical bulletin, number 011 in its series, on Precision Time Protocol synchronization under network impairments. Precision Time Protocol, or PTP, keeps clocks on a network in step by exchanging timed messages between a master and a slave clock. The method assumes both directions of travel take equal time.

Unequal delays break that assumption and distort the offset the slave computes. The bulletin explains time interval error, a measure of long-term clock wander, and how packet delays or losses bend it. Tests ran on an in-house testbed with two ADVA OSA 5422 clocks linked through a Netropy network emulator. Injected jitter of 200 to 800 microseconds, followed by a 2,000 microsecond static delay, left clear steps in the error traces. Grid and telecom operators get evidence on which faults actually break timing.
doe-osti-3017120-integrative-computation:
Seogjoo Julian Jang of Queens College, City University of New York, wrote this final technical report for award DE-SC0021413, dated February 8, 2026. The project ran from September 2021 to May 2025. It built theory and computer methods for molecular excitons, the packets of electronic excitation that move through materials after light is absorbed. The setting was complex environments, not idealized crystals.

The project produced eleven completed works, with more under revision or in development. One generalized the energy gap law, a long-standing rule for how excited states decay without emitting light. Other works tackled strong control fields and the limits of common approximations in quantum dynamics. The stated aim is practical: help experimentalists use molecular quantum behavior for energy harvesting and quantum information work. Chemists modeling light-driven materials get methods tested across many real cases.
doe-osti-3017991-leadership-at-interface:
Nicholas Thornburg, a senior reaction engineer at the National Renewable Energy Laboratory, gave this seminar deck on March 3, 2025, at the Colorado School of Mines Leadership by Design seminar. The talk is a career reflection: how a chemical engineer ends up leading at the interfaces between science, technology, and education, and why the gaps between fields are where the value sits.

Thornburg tours the laboratory he works in, then his own research map. His projects span catalyst discovery for ammonia reforming, electrochemical reactor scale-up for carbon oxide reduction, photoreaction engineering for hydrogen carriers, and soot studies for aviation turbines. His stated common theme: every project involves a chemical reactor and a chemical reaction, and he stays agnostic to application. Slides on reactor taxonomy, from vessel geometry to scale-up strategy, ground the talk in his craft. Students hearing it get one engineer's honest account of building a career on boundaries.
doe-osti-3018733-sierra-solidmechanics-5:
Sandia's SIERRA Solid Mechanics Team issued this verification manual, SAND2026-16513, printed January 26, 2026. It documents the test suite for Sierra/SolidMechanics version 5.28. Verification asks whether the code solves its equations correctly. The manual opens with method: convergence, observed convergence rates, and tests that use surrogate solutions or asymptotic analysis. Then come the test families, starting with contact verification. Each test states its problem, its expected behavior, and the measured error. Element formulations were compared head to head on problems.

The numbers show a healthy code. All element formulations held displacement error under about half a percent, even on the coarsest mesh. Stress errors ranged from under ten percent on coarse meshes to under one percent as meshes refined. Analysts choosing an element type can see its measured accuracy, not a sales claim. The 5.28 edition freezes that evidence for one release, so results computed with it can be audited.
doe-osti-3020015-demonstration-of-electr:
Constellation Energy Generation's final report for DOE award DE-EE0008849 describes a working hydrogen plant built at the Nine Mile Point Nuclear Plant in Oswego, New York. The project ran from October 2019 to September 2024 with Idaho, National Renewable Energy, and Argonne national laboratories and Nel Hydrogen as partners. Its goal was grid-scale carbon-free hydrogen made with nuclear electricity, stored and used on site.

Hydrogen production began on March 7, 2023. The proton exchange membrane electrolyzer draws 1.25 megawatts of nuclear power and makes 560 kilograms of clean hydrogen per day, more than the plant needs for its own operations. The team also tested dynamic control, raising and lowering output to follow electricity market conditions. The report closes with the economics of that flexible operation and plans for much larger deployments.
doe-osti-3020129-strategic-energy-plan-p:
NLR report NLR/TP-7A40-96824, by Alexa Carrera, Melanie S. Ramos Beltrán, Daniel Bernal, and Angela Ortega Pastor, is a strategic energy plan for Playa de Ponce, a coastal community in Ponce, Puerto Rico. The plan grew out of community workshops held in March 2025. It sets an energy vision, reviews local strengths and challenges, and builds a baseline picture of energy costs, household income, and solar potential.

Residents ranked their preferred projects across the community's subareas. Solar lighting came first, followed by a resilience center and then a microgrid. The plan also tests, with the REopt tool, whether one existing building could serve as a resilience hub during outages. The result is a sequenced set of strategies matched to what residents said they value most.
doe-osti-3020204-townsend-s-ground-squir:
Hanford Site report HNF-72933, by B. A. Elias, M. F. Paulsen, and C. T. Lindsey of Hanford Mission Integration Solutions, documents calendar year 2025 conservation work for Townsend's ground squirrels on the Hanford Site in Washington. The squirrels are a species of concern on the shrub-steppe lands around the former nuclear production site. Crews monitored colonies through the active season with burrow surveys, trail cameras, and tagged animals.

The report follows individual squirrels by their implanted tags, including two males that returned to the Holocek colony in 2025 after dispersing the year before. It records when burrows first showed activity in March and how colonies fared through the season. Yearly reports like this one track whether the population holds steady, and they guide habitat protection on land the Department of Energy still manages.
doe-osti-3020521-hydrogen-production-cos:
Strategic Analysis, Inc. report for DOE award DE-EE0009629, led by Brian D. James with seven co-authors, prices hydrogen made by proton-conducting solid oxide electrolysis. This newer electrolyzer type conducts protons through a ceramic at high heat. Stakeholders reviewed the team's assumptions before the numbers were computed, and partners at two national labs checked the designs.

At an electricity price of $0.03 per kilowatt-hour and a 97 percent capacity factor, the projected levelized cost of hydrogen runs from $1.81 to $2.47 per kilogram in 2020 dollars. The range spans current and future tech cases at different plant scales, all assuming mature supply chains and nth-of-a-kind construction. The team expects first-of-a-kind plants using current tech around 2030 to 2035. The analysis separates the tech's cost promise from deployment timelines.
doe-osti-3020908-analysis-of-warped-apri:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory report ORNL/LTR-2025/4139, by Youngrock Yoon and Gavin Jager, tests what happens when an AprilTag marker is bent. AprilTags are printed square markers that cameras use to find an object's position and orientation, common in robotics and augmented reality. Mounting one on a curved surface warps its geometry. The study compared a warped tag against a flat control tag in video recorded at many viewing angles.

For detection, warping hurt: the bent tag failed consistently beyond 40 degrees and completely beyond 60 degrees, while the flat tag was detected at every angle. For pose estimation, the picture differed. Pose jitter, the wobble in measured rotation and position, was nearly the same for both tags, and the difference was not statistically significant. The practical lesson: a warped tag is harder to spot, but once spotted, its reported pose stays trustworthy.
doe-osti-3021593-enhanced-hlw-glass-prop:
Vitreous State Laboratory final report VSL-17R4220-1, by Wing K. Kot, Konstantin Gilbo, Hao Gan, and Ian L. Pegg of The Catholic University of America, is the third phase of work tying Hanford high-level waste glass properties to glass composition. Published in October 2024 and released under HFO-73182, the models let engineers predict how a proposed glass recipe will behave. That foresight matters before committing a melter campaign at the Tank Waste Treatment and Immobilization Plant.

The dataset covers glasses with measurements for product consistency testing, spinel crystallization, viscosity, electrical conductivity, cadmium leach release, and nepheline formation. Property-composition models fit those measurements so that waste loading can be pushed higher while staying inside every processing and durability limit. Phase 3 extends the earlier model set with additional glass data, tightening the predictions the plant's feed qualification relies on.
doe-osti-3021618-heat-batteries-for-deep:
Phase 1 performance report for DOE Office of Clean Energy Demonstrations award DE-CD0000102, from Diageo Americas Supply, Inc., tracks a project putting industrial heat batteries into beverage making. Rondo's heat battery stores energy as heat for plant processes, and Diageo is preparing installations at its Shelbyville and Plainfield sites to cut the carbon cost of making drinks. The document is a progress report, heavy on schedules, budgets, and task status tables.

The summary reports strong movement toward the go/no-go review for Budget Period 2 in July. The pre-FEED design deliverable for Shelbyville is complete, design and engineering are advancing at both sites, and techno-economic and total project cost reports continue. A siting Environmental Information Volume was drafted to about 80 percent, with permitting and NEPA paperwork in progress.
doe-osti-3022059-harvesting-energy-from-:
Worcester Polytechnic Institute's final research report to the Department of Energy, led by principal investigator Michael Timko under award DE-EE0009507, covers a project to turn sewage sludge into renewable natural gas. The Supercritical Sludge-to-Gas platform chains three steps: autothermal hydrothermal liquefaction, supercritical salt precipitation, and hydrothermal gasification. The aim is to let wastewater treatment plants become net energy producers instead of energy consumers.

Adding peroxide at an oxygen-to-carbon ratio of 0.05, at 300 degrees Celsius for 10 minutes, gave a 57 percent biocrude yield and 85 percent fluid carbon yield, with char near 7 percent. Corrosion tests at 350 degrees Celsius for 240 hours measured 0.21 mils per year for 304L stainless steel and 0.26 for 316L, values Pacific Northwest National Laboratory used in pilot design. Machine-learning models of gasification yields round out the results.
doe-osti-3022539-multiplexed-toxin-activ:
A PNNL report by Becky Hess and five colleagues, dated February 2026, builds a multiplexed assay that detects not just the presence of a toxin but its activity. Most field tests name a toxin without saying whether it is still functional. That distinction drives decisions about countermeasures, protective equipment, and whether an area is safe.

The approach is biomimetic. Membranes harvested from human HEK-293 cells expressing a toxin target, typically an ion channel, are laid onto electronic chips as supported lipid bilayers. Impedance spectroscopy reads the membrane's electrical response. Test agents bracket the likely signals: alpha-hemolysin at 5 and 25 micromolar forms pores and should drop membrane resistance, while verapamil at 30 micromolar blocks calcium channels and should raise it. Earlier work validated the platform against omega-conotoxin GVIA.
doe-osti-3022605-lac-attachments-moderni: LLNL memo LLNL-TR-2009951 by Ilya Golosker is a short plan, not a research report. It proposes modernizing the cutting attachments of the Liquid Abrasive Cutter. Its custom nozzles are near end of service life and costly to replace. It rides on a power unit upgrade from diesel drive to a variable-frequency electric drive. The plan swaps custom attachments for commercial parts: a fixed angle cut, hole punch, barrel crawler, nozzles, and hoses. The work runs one year at a total cost of $660k including labor.
doe-osti-3022764-singlet-fission:
A University of Colorado final report for DOE award DE-SC0007004 compiles the published record of a singlet fission research program. The program ran from August 2011 to March 2024 under Josef Michl. Michl died in May 2024, shortly after the award ended. Singlet fission is the splitting of one excited singlet state into two triplet states. It could raise solar cell efficiency past conventional limits. The Colorado group was central to mapping when and how it happens.

Because the lead investigator did not live to write a narrative summary, the report is assembled from the abstracts of journal papers the award supported. Entries range from intramolecular fission at the root of dual fluorescence in a nitrostyryl benzene to a correction of the record. In the correction, careful multireference calculations show that earlier claims for a BODIPY dimer as a fission candidate rested on an imbalanced active space and do not hold.
doe-osti-3022905-coastal-urban-boundary-:
A University of Oklahoma final report for DOE Atmospheric System Research award DE-SC0021194 closes the CUBIC project on coastal urban boundary layers. It was led by Petra Klein, with co-investigators from NOAA's National Severe Storms Laboratory and the University of Wisconsin. During the TRACER field campaign's intensive period in Houston, from June through September 2021, CUBIC deployed three boundary layer profiling systems. They watched how sea and bay breezes interact with the city's heat and surface.

Model evaluation against those profiles found real weaknesses. Ensembles captured the sea breeze's timing and intensity in a subset of members, but none reproduced the preceding bay breeze accurately. Radiation scheme choice shifted sea breeze onset, and planetary boundary layer schemes controlled its depth. Nonlocal mixing schemes developed the coastal circulations better, while overestimating boundary layer temperature and depth.
doe-osti-3023101-meadowview-neighborhood:
Sacramento Municipal Utility District reports the finished Meadowview Neighborhood Electrification Project in this final technical report, filed under award DE-SE0000737. Griffin Parikka is the named author, and Tara Porter directed the project. Funded by a 2023 Congressionally Directed Spend, the work brought energy efficiency, weatherization, and electrification upgrades to an under-resourced Sacramento neighborhood.

Crews first aimed to upgrade 300 homes and ended up retrofitting 374 as the team got faster. Homes received items such as new HVAC systems, fridges, stoves, and thermostats, often at little or no cost to residents. Customers praised courteous, on-time work and lower bills, though some reported delayed or incomplete jobs and asked for better follow-up and clearer updates.
doe-osti-3023853-development-and-full-lo:
Hendrik F Laubscher of Sandia National Laboratories and Eckhard Lüpfert of DLR, the German aerospace center. They report the build and full load demonstration of a 900 degree solid particle receiver for concentrating solar power, SAND2026-18414. The project name is noLimits, tied to the CentRec receiver line. Falling hot particles absorb focused sunlight and carry the heat to storage, letting solar plants run after sunset.

Sections cover project objectives, design, and commissioning, with partner Heliogen supplying rotating equipment. Structural engineers designed for gravity, wind, and seismic loads under the ASCE 7 standard for buildings and other structures. Dynamic loads from the rotating gear were still to be added to the structural model for future uses, based on assumptions about eccentric rotation that the partner provided.
doe-osti-3028496-processing-municipal-so:
Bo Li of GTI Energy led this final report, dated January 26, 2026, for a project turning municipal solid waste into jet fuel under contract DE-EE0009265, running October 2020 through September 2025. Key staff included Martin Linck of GTI, Jordan Klinger of Idaho National Laboratory, Sheng Dai of Georgia Tech, Robert Hallenbeck of Waste Management, and Nalin Kumar of NanoRanch. Trash is a stubborn feedstock: mixed, wet, and nothing like a refinery stream.

Processing chapters measure the machinery honestly. Cycle times for one unit were taken from video recordings that missed the first five cycles, and a four-second manual loading step by operators was excluded from the timing. Longer cycles are blamed on a flap valve that failed to reseat, triggering an automatic retry. Tables of cycle times by batch carry the throughput evidence the conversion design rests on.
doe-osti-3029248-self-diagnostic-capabil:
Megan Booher of Los Alamos National Laboratory leads this fiscal year 2026 mid-year report, LA-UR-26-23046, on self-diagnostic features for neutron instruments. The work sits under a nondestructive assay technology task, with Nina Rodriguez and Ramkumar Venkataraman named on the report. Its focus is INCC6, software used to read neutron counting instruments. In fiscal 2025 the team finished three automated self-diagnostic features and reached a stable version 6.0.

The first half of fiscal 2026 went to delivery. Working with the lab Feynman Center and its export control office, the team won an export license so the International Atomic Energy Agency could receive INCC6. Agency contacts now hold permission to take the software. A version 6 user manual is in its final stage, after which INCC6 goes to the agency for testing.
doe-osti-3030324-effect-of-surrogate-fis:
Ryan Chesser, Molly Ross, Peggy Milota, and colleagues at Oak Ridge and Idaho national laboratories measure molten salt traits in report ORNL/TM-2026/4487, dated April 2026. Their salt, a sodium chloride and uranium trichloride mix, is a candidate fuel salt for molten salt reactors. As fuel burns, fission products build up and can shift how the salt carries heat and flows. Designers need those numbers to model reactor behavior safely.

The team dosed the salt with stand-in fission products and measured heat conduction and thickness, or viscosity. A variable gap device drove a known heat flow across a thin salt layer and read the temperature drop. Comparing gaps cancels out errors from the rig itself. The work backs the Energy Department molten salt reactor campaign under its Advanced Reactor Technology program.
doe-osti-3030336-micro-hydropower-and-aq:
Evin Carter, Michael J. LaVoie, and Caleb R. Hickman of Oak Ridge National Laboratory study small water power on tribal land in report ORNL/TM-2026/4470, dated March 2026. The Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians holds ancestral land in Southern Appalachia, where steep, forested ground and thin infrastructure make energy access hard. The project pairs micro-hydropower, small turbines on local streams, with repair of the streams and fish habitat themselves.

Brook trout set the frame, since they need the cold headwater streams where small barriers matter most. The team ranked stream reaches by both power promise and habitat value, guided by tribal staff and tribal priorities. Jenkins Creek and Soco Creek, tied to the Tribal Reserve, rose to the top, along with the fish hatchery reach on Raven Fork.
doe-osti-3097333-richard-p-feynman-cente:
Lindsay Creighton Augustyn of Los Alamos National Laboratory compiled the 2025 annual report of the Richard P. Feynman Center for Innovation, LA-UR-26-23408, issued April 28, 2026. The center is the lab front door for business: it links firms to lab technology, expertise, and licenses, and it guards inventions along the way. Fiscal 2025 numbers headline the issue: 530 active agreements, 224 of them income-bearing, 55 patent applications, and 34 patents issued.

Story pages tour the year wins. A fusion firm, Pacific Fusion, licensed OpenSesame, a lab code for material behavior under extreme heat and pressure, and won a transfer excellence honor. Other features cover a New Mexico startup called VastVision, a partnership with Japan Nuclear Fuels Limited, an eco fitness venture, and plasma liner work.
doe-osti-3362487-scaling-up-demonstratin:
Carmen Cejudo of Pacific Northwest National Laboratory reports final results for CRADA 625 in December 2025, with Helen Townsend on the record. The project, called Scaling Up, tested commercial heat pump water heaters for big buildings such as hotels and apartments. Such systems can heat service water far more efficiently than boilers or resistance tanks. The catch is buyer risk: first costs and unproven field performance slow adoption, so the project chased both risk and cost down.

Deliverables included a measurement and verification plan. It fixed how system efficiency would be computed and which data points and meters were required. A test plan was written for Site 1, Casa Panorama. The load shift part stalled when control signals failed to reach the system. Funds ran out before it was run to ground.
doe-osti-3362564-arm-radiosondes-for-snp:
Lori Borg of the University of Wisconsin-Madison, Anthony Reale and Bomin Sun of NOAA, and E. Keeler of Argonne report on a weather balloon campaign, DOE/SC-ARM-26-008, dated May 2026. Satellites in the Joint Polar Satellite System sound the air from orbit, but their temperature and water vapor readings need ground truth. Radiosondes, balloon-borne instruments, supply it. This campaign extension covers two years ending October 17, 2024, inside a validation effort running since July 2012.

Launches are timed to satellite overpasses: one sonde 15 minutes ahead, or twins at 45 and 5 minutes ahead. Early work checked the Suomi NPP bridge satellite, then shifted to NOAA-20 in February 2018. NOAA-21 launches began in June 2023. The checks feed accuracy grades for the satellite soundings and tune the forecast products built on them.
doe-osti-3362947-sim2real-autonomous-rob: Catalina Herrera Cancelado of Idaho National Laboratory presents this August 2025 poster on training a walking robot inside a computer before trusting it in a real room. The robot is Spot, a four-legged Boston Dynamics machine, and the method is called sim2real. A reinforcement learning policy, trained in IsaacLab with many virtual robots at once, learned the joint targets for walking. A spinning 2D LiDAR was added in simulation so the robot could map a copied lab, plot its path, and steer around obstacles.
doe-osti-3363590-an-overview-of-potentia:
Kristi Moriarty, Justin Bracci, Nimal Naser, and Gary Grim of the National Laboratory of the Rockies survey the energy carriers that might power future flight (NLR/TP-5400-100028, May 2026). Global jet fuel demand is projected to reach 165 billion gallons by 2050, and the industry wants to know what alternatives can actually deliver.

Sustainable aviation fuel is the incumbent challenger: a drop-in blend, commercially available since 2016, though still only about 1 percent of jet fuel use despite U.S. consumption climbing from 26 million gallons in 2023 to 281 million in 2025. The review also treats hydrogen, where boil-off in storage drives work on glass bubble and aerogel insulation and on active recondensing systems like NASA's.
doe-osti-3364222-demo-ftes-development-m:
A February 2026 CRADA final report closes DEMO-FTES, a joint project on fracture thermal energy storage in crystalline rock. Pacific Northwest National Laboratory led with Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Sandia, and the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Lausanne; Jeffrey Burghardt was the responsible technical contact. The idea stores heat underground in fractured rock, then recovers it later, like a battery made of stone.

Partners designed and ran a meso-scale laboratory test of the concept and published the design at rock mechanics conferences. Work covered development, monitoring, and control of the storage fractures. Total contributions came to about 1.25 million dollars across the parties. As a CRADA closeout, much of the document is administrative: funding tables, partner contacts, and the publication list the project produced.
doe-osti-3364388-plan-energ-tico-estrat-:
Written in Spanish, National Laboratory of the Rockies report NLR/TP-7A40-99982 is a strategic energy plan for Playa de Ponce, a coastal community in Ponce, Puerto Rico. Authors Alexa Carrera, Melanie S. Ramos Beltrán, Daniel Bernal, and Angela Ortega Pastor published it in May 2026. The plan grew out of two rounds of in-person community workshops held in March, site visits, and a baseline energy assessment.

Strategies fall into three focus areas: energy reliability, safety and protection, and stakeholder engagement with education and capacity building. Proposed moves include public-private partnerships to reuse sites and geospatial analysis that folds in community input. The plan aligns each strategy with the vision residents set in the workshops. It gives the community and its partners a shared, written starting point for energy projects.
doe-osti-3364473-policy-and-cost-allocat:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report PNNL-38455, by Erik Anderson, Prathit Dave, Adrienne Rackley, and Devyn Powell, dates to September 2025. It surveys how states are deciding who pays when a very large electric load, such as a data center, connects to the grid. Data center load alone has tripled in a decade, and new substations and lines built for one customer can strand costs on everyone else if the project shrinks or leaves.

States are answering with special rate classes and tariff terms that make large loads cover their own costs. Maryland and Virginia directed utilities to build such schedules, while other 2025 bills stalled or remain pending. Regulators are also acting through utility commissions directly. The report maps the emerging policy menu for legislators weighing growth against ratepayer protection.
doe-osti-3364485-development-of-a-bench-:
A Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report dated August 2025, by AJ Goulet, Conner Holbrook, Nathan Bessen, Brad Jeffries, Rick Shimskey, and Gabriel Hall, develops a bench-scale dissolver for extracting nuclear fuel directly. Dissolving spent or fresh fuel material is the first step of many recycling and analysis processes. The concept had to satisfy hard constraints at small scale before anyone builds bigger.

Design requirements covered scalability, serviceability, mixing, phase separation, residence time, off-gas capture, temperature control, and geometry that stays safe from accidental criticality. The team down-selected among simple batch reactors and three mixing methods: mechanical agitation, air sparging, and pulse jet mixing. Rotating designs emerged among the promising options. The report gives the next builders a reasoned shortlist instead of a blank page.
doe-osti-3365793-drevl-radiometer-calibr:
Sandia National Laboratories report SAND2026-21410, by Christian A. Pattyn, Grace P. Dean, Jeremy B. Wright, and Park E. Hays, documents calibration of the DrEVL radiometer, an instrument that measures light spectra. The process converts raw detector counts into trustworthy physical values. The report derives the governing equation, then measures two response functions that define the instrument: its spectral response and its radiometric response.

Ground truth sources anchor both functions. A chapter covers changes that extend the method into the ultraviolet, and a validation section checks the result against independent measurements. The final chapter applies it to arbitrary spectra, including a flat white test case. Long appendices tabulate response values wavelength by wavelength, the working data future users will interpolate.
doe-osti-3365871-theoretical-understandi:
Boston University's final report for DOE award DE-SC0023402, led by Sahar Sharifzadeh and dated May 30, 2026, studies excitons in low-dimensional materials by first-principles computation. An exciton is a bound pair of an excited electron and the hole it left behind; excitons carry the light energy in solar cells and light emitters. The project, costing 475,868 dollars, sought rules for controlling exciton energy and motion by chemistry and structure.

Calculations separated the tangled roles of electrons, vibrations, spin, and defects. Work on magnetic layered materials showed how atomic vibration reshapes excitons there. Chromium-doped gallium nitride was tested as a quantum defect host, showing in-gap states that localize excitons and red-shift absorption. Exciton localization in doped carbon nanotubes was also mapped against measurements. The results feed design of optoelectronic materials and quantum devices.
doe-osti-3366677-gainesville-regional-an:
A January 2026 feasibility study examines building a regional anaerobic digestion facility for Gainesville, Florida. Digestion turns sewage sludge and food waste into biogas and fertilizer instead of landfill burden. The study, prepared with a strategic partnership involving the University of Florida, inventories what the region actually produces before sizing anything.

Data chapters tally sludge from three water reclamation facilities: Kanapaha, Main Street, and the University of Florida plant. They map food waste through the EPA's excess food database for the city, county, and university. Fats, oils, and grease streams are tallied too. A mass balance combines the streams. Two site options near the Deerhaven renewable plant are laid out. Leaders get feedstock-grounded sizing rather than a vendor's guess at what a regional digester could handle.
doe-osti-3367032-summary-of-the-initial-:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory letter report ORNL/LTR-2026/4441, by Valentin Pauly, Amy Godfrey, Stephen Taller, and Caleb Massey, summarizes first post-irradiation results on HT-9 steel, a ferritic-martensitic alloy candidates for fast reactor cladding. Two heats differing almost only in nitrogen, 0.001 versus 0.044 weight percent, were irradiated in the High Flux Isotope Reactor so the nitrogen effect can be isolated.

Silicon carbide thermometry fixed the irradiation temperatures, and damage levels are tabulated per sample and capsule position. The May 2026 summary is explicitly initial: characterization is underway, and fuller results follow in later campaign reports. Even so, the paired-heat design makes the dataset valuable, since nitrogen is cheap to vary in production heats and its influence on radiation swelling and embrittlement decides specification limits.
doe-osti-3367273-observation-based-const:
Final technical report for DOE grant DE-SC0021985, by Timothy Bertram's team, closes the AGENA project: Aerosol Growth in the Eastern North Atlantic. The question is what vapor lets tiny Aitken-mode particles grow into cloud condensation nuclei over the remote ocean, since those nuclei seed marine clouds and their climate effects. The team instrumented the ARM site on Graciosa Island in the Azores during summer 2022, at peak ocean biological activity.

Two high-resolution mass spectrometers measured gases and particle composition alongside particle sizing instruments. Marine air monoterpenes averaged 14 parts per trillion, dominated unusually by beta-pinene at about 46 percent, and outweighed isoprene by a factor of 3.9 on average, contrary to prior expectations. The dataset links precursor gases to growing particles directly.
doe-osti-3367557-transformative-efficien:
GTI Energy Building America report for DOE award DE-EE0009069, the TEAMH project, by Kaushik Biswas, Jason LaFleur, Kenneth Hultquist, and colleagues, studies modular homes built in factories with automation. Factory construction promises speed and quality control; the June 2026 project measured whether it also delivers energy performance, testing envelope designs across twelve climate zones.

Weighted average heating and cooling load savings were computed for each envelope scenario and home design, combining climate-zone results by housing starts. The disclaimers are explicit: the test homes are not certified rating facilities, and results estimate performance under measured conditions rather than rated values. For an industry trying to industrialize housing, the dataset ties factory methods to modeled energy outcomes.
doe-osti-3371558-the-development-of-kine:
A paper in Fusion Science and Technology, published online in April 2026, reports modeling work backed by the Department of Energy's INFUSE program. The ten named authors, led by Michael J. Lavell, come from a team-up between HB11 Energy and the TriForce Institute for Multiphysics Modeling at the University of Rochester. Their subject is thermonuclear burn in proton-boron fuel, held at uniform density, a fuel mix that gives off very few neutrons.

The team built methods for collisions and radiation into TriForce, a particle-in-cell code with Monte Carlo collisions. With those tools they show burn spreading through preassembled proton-boron fuel samples. Learning what burn spread requires should help set the laser and target needs for a future inertial fusion power plant.
doe-osti-3374194-geophysical-measurement:
INL/RPT-25-87102, an Idaho National Laboratory report, dated August 2025, records what the ground did when a large building came down. Its authors are David Shai Applbaum, Blaine M. Bockholt, Ken Eugene Hallett, and John Milton Sandru IV. On May 31, 2025, at about 14:40 UTC, crews used targeted explosives to demolish the former Submarine First Westinghouse structure. That crane housing stood at the Naval Reactors Facility inside the Idaho lab site. The lab's seismic monitoring program treated the blast as a known signal source.

The report explains how the raw seismic traces were cleaned: offsets removed, instrument response stripped out, and counts converted to ground velocity, then integrated into displacement. From those records the team assessed ground motion around the site. A controlled demolition gives seismologists a rare event with a known time, place, and size, handy for checking instruments and models.
doe-osti-3375170-driving-plasmas-to-extr:
A final technical report for Department of Energy award DE-SC0022250 covers a UC San Diego project led by Mathieu Bailly-Grandvaux with Farhat Beg. The project ran from August 2021 to July 2024. Its goal was a test platform for magnetized plasma compression on the OMEGA-60 laser. Strong magnetic fields may help fusion ignition, but field behavior during a crush is hard to study. A cylinder makes a simpler test shape than a sphere.

Runs used the MHD code GORGON to plan the shots. A seed field of thirty tesla was set to squeeze toward thirty kilotesla at peak crush. In the event, spectra pointed to a field near ten kilotesla. Dopant spectroscopy, a light-based probe, tracked core heat and density. Its readings matched the code well. The team reads that match as proof the probe can tease out high magnetization effects.
doe-osti-3375248-off-axis-rf-fields-extr:
Brookhaven National Laboratory technical note BNL-229841-2026-TECH, dated June 2026, by Stephen Brooks, works out how radio-frequency fields away from a cavity axis can be built from values on the axis. Cavity fields steer and bunch particle beams. Designers often know the field along the center line best. The beam, though, samples the field across the whole bore. A sound way to grow the off-axis field from on-axis data saves full field maps.

The note is a derivation from start to finish. Brooks expands the field in a series and links each term to its neighbors. Recurrence formulas tie higher terms to lower ones through second derivatives. One case needs care: when the index meets the wave number, the link to two field parts breaks down. The note flags that case and treats it on its own terms.
doe-osti-3375765-bryan-mound-groundwater:
Sandia National Laboratories report SAND2026-22454R, by Santiago L. Flores and dated June 10, 2026, evaluates groundwater at Bryan Mound. The mound is a Gulf Coast salt dome site in Texas, part of the federal oil reserve grounds. Any salt or brine work there must mind the fresh water above the dome. The study maps which aquifers sit at the site and how clean their water runs. It also traces how groundwater flows across the wider region.

Only one aquifer, the Chicot, is present at the site itself. Readings come chiefly from monitor well BM-MOW-1. Flores turns wireline logs into water quality numbers by depth. Tables give resistivity and total dissolved solids at set depths, under several conversion factors. Values are checked against water quality guide lines. The picture that emerges is a layered one, with saltier water as depth grows.
doe-osti-3375995-activation-of-thermal-i:
Idaho National Laboratory engineering analysis INL/RPT-25-88909, dated January 2026, by Mason Scott Walls and Kristy Diane Yancey Spencer, weighs a quiet hazard in a salt reactor test. The job is coded ECAR-8593. It supports the Molten Chloride Reactor Experiment at building MFC-776. Thermal insulation wraps the hot core gear. Neutrons will strike that wrap for the life of the test. It asks how hot the wrap itself gets, in dose terms, and how much dust it may shed.

Tables tally the dose from each isotope the neutrons wake. Iron-59 is one of the named lines. Totals come in under a thousandth of a unit for the mean case. The bounding case sums higher. A second half tracks contamination. Dust shed in handling will settle on test bed faces before the run. How much of it stays, and how much the vents strip out, sets the final spread.
doe-osti-3376732-stochastic-modeling-of-:
Los Alamos National Laboratory slide set LA-UR-26-25508, issued July 6, 2026, presents stochastic modeling work by Anil K. Prinja of the University of New Mexico and Patrick F. O'Rourke of Los Alamos. When a nucleus fissions, the number of neutrons freed and the energy dumped by the fragments vary together in a linked spread. Codes that track reactor power need that joint spread, not two lone curves. The slides build it from a point-kinetic model.

The path runs through a forward master equation for the joint counts. Generating functions turn the spread into a form that yields its moments by simple derivatives. Values at zero give the chance of each neutron count. First derivatives give the mean fragment energy for that count. Second derivatives give its square, and so on. The deck works the algebra in full, step by step, in dense equation slides.
doe-osti-3377006-study-of-sidis-unpolari:
Jefferson Lab paper JLAB-EXP-25-****, dated December 22, 2025, projects what the planned SoLID detector could learn from semi-inclusive deep inelastic scattering off a helium-3 target. Eleven authors sign it, Matteo Cerutti first. In such collisions an electron knocks a quark out of a nucleus, and the debris hadron carries clues about the quark's sideways motion. The team studies unpolarized cross sections at large Bjorken x, moderate Q-squared, and small hadron transverse momentum.

That corner of the map is barely charted. It is where transverse momentum dependent parton distributions and fragmentation functions shape the rates most. The study folds the planned 11 GeV measurements into current global fits, named MAPTMD24 in the plots. It then shows how much the errors would shrink with SoLID data added. Bins split by momentum fraction and energy share make the gains concrete. The point is to guide the experiment's design and its case for approval.
doe-osti-3377439-generator-chelator-and-:
Final technical report for grant DE-SC0023638, from the University of Wisconsin-Madison, covers the GeCKO project led by Jonathan W. Engle with Eszter Boros. The award ran from January 2023 to December 2025. GeCKO stands for Generator, Chelator, and Kit Optimization. Its aim is to bring titanium-44 and scandium-43 and -44 into radiopharmacy use. These isotopes suit PET scans, but supply chains and chemistry lag behind demand.

Work split into tasks on each side. One side probed titanium's chemistry to build solid-phase separation media from deferiprone ligands. The other side used scandium coordination chemistry to widen its use. A high point is a first full run of a solid-phase capture and light-release scheme. It produced a targeted scandium-44 drug aimed at PSMA, with a PET image to prove it. Trainees in both labs gained hands-on time with accelerator-made isotopes and mass spectrometry.
doe-osti-3380405-redesign-of-nuclear-mat:
An American Nuclear Society conference summary, Los Alamos report LA-UR-26-25797 issued July 14, 2026, redesigns the container used for medium to long term storage of small amounts of nuclear material. Six University of Texas at Austin students did the work: Jackson Edgar, Jacob Kessler, Jack Moyer, Josh Pahgn, Ryder Phillips, and Isiah Serenil. They worked with Andrew Hanneman of Los Alamos and Sheldon Landsberger of the university. Additive manufacturing is the redesign tool.

The current container is a stainless steel flat tube sealed with a copper crush gasket and ten bolts. The gasket must be replaced after every use, and storage can run up to 15 years. Steel shields gamma rays but does nothing for neutron dose. The redesign aims to cut worker dose and improve criticality safety. It also adds an ergonomic lid, so workers spend less time near the source, following the ALARA standard.
doe-osti-3382438-cooperative-education:
Los Alamos National Laboratory report LA-UR-26-26144, issued July 21, 2026, is the co-op education statement of work for Jillian Rose Grubenhoff. She is a Texas State University Ingram School of Engineering student. She was placed as a research and development intern for summer 2026. Austin Taylor Sutton is the laboratory contact named on the form. The document is an internship plan, written before the work it describes.

The project assigned is the design and testing of high-performance absorbing structures. The work runs through computer design, simulation, and engineering analysis. Such structures serve where damage control, structural protection, and material efficiency all matter at once. The plan uses 3D CAD software and finite element analysis to generate structural concepts. It tests their behavior under load. The aim is to soak up as much energy as possible while keeping weight and material use low.
doe-osti-3382450-innovative-biomonitorin:
Florida A&M University's final report for grant DE-FE0032198, submitted to the National Energy Technology Laboratory in July 2026, covers biomonitoring and remediation of heavy metals with phytotechnologies at the Savannah River Site. Principal investigator Ashvini Chauhan, a professor in the School of the Environment, led the project from January 2023 to January 2026. Co-investigators Xiaoyu Xu of the Savannah River Ecology Laboratory and Ashish Pathak worked with her.

The site holds legacy coal combustion product impoundments, ponds of coal ash residue. They carry elevated heavy metals and radionuclides that threaten soil over the long term. Phytotechnology uses living plants to monitor and pull contaminants from such ground. The report, marked as the final report for the period ending July 31, 2026, closes the grant's work on those impoundment sites.
doe-osti-3394811-agr-5-6-7-irradiation-e:
Idaho National Laboratory report INL/RPT-26-94325, dated July 2026, works out a fission product mass balance for the AGR-5/6/7 irradiation experiment. John D. Stempien and Lu Cai are the authors, under milestone M2FT-26IN080402015 in the Advanced Fuels Campaign. The AGR experiments irradiate TRISO coated particle fuel, the fuel form designed to lock fission products inside microscopic ceramic shells.

A mass balance accounts for every measured fission product atom: what stayed in the fuel, what lodged in the capsule hardware, and what escaped. The methods chapters describe the metallic hardware, the graphite holders, and the Grafoil disks and spacers that line the capsules. Capsule-by-capsule balance results follow. For a fuel whose whole safety case is retention, closing the books on where the fission products went is the central evidence.
doe-osti-3399445-comparative-assessment-:
Argonne National Laboratory report ANL/ESIA-26/3, dated June 2026, compares the frameworks used to calculate a battery's carbon footprint. Jingyi Zhang, Jarod Kelly, and Michael Wang of the Energy Systems and Infrastructure Assessment Division are the authors. The report's purpose is practical support for United States battery manufacturing, which must soon state footprints in forms foreign regulators accept.

The review moves region by region. European Union battery carbon footprint guidelines, regulations, and plans come first, the likely template for trade requirements. Asian and North American frameworks follow, then the global battery alliances that try to harmonize them. A footprint number depends on system boundaries and data rules, so two compliant calculations can disagree; the comparison shows manufacturers where the frameworks match and where they part.
doe-osti-3403180-trace-input-modernizati:
Dated June 2026, report ORNL/TM-2026/4667 from Oak Ridge National Laboratory updates how users write inputs for the TRACE reactor safety code. Robert A. Lefebvre, Shane C. Henderson, and Matthew Bernard wrote the guide. Old input decks are long lists of numbers that are hard to read and easy to break.

New filler rules let users build number arrays with compact commands. A repeat rule can expand one short line into a long list. A straight-line rule can fill values that rise step by step. Worked examples show each rule in use. The aim is shorter, clearer decks that staff can check with fewer errors.
doe-osti-3409078-adiabatic-longitudinal-:
Brookhaven note BNL-230063-2026-TECH, by H. Lovelace III and C. Y. Chen and dated August 2026, studies island formation in a beam's length-wise motion. Phase modulation of the radio-frequency system drives the effect. Simulations used the BLonD code named in the text.

Code layouts in the pages define result types for each run type. Outputs track bunch center, spread in time, and spread in energy. Islands in phase space can trap parts of a bunch and change beam behavior. Accelerator staff can use the modeled cases to plan settings that form or avoid such islands on purpose.
doe-osti-3409809-front-side-copper-metal:
Bert Thin Films Inc. closes award DE-EE0009638 with a final report on copper metallization for the front side of solar cells. Ruvini Dharmadasa served as principal investigator, with Thad Druffel as business contact. The project ran from January 1, 2022 to March 31, 2026.

Copper pastes printed through screens with 65 and 40 micrometer openings were aged at 200 degrees Celsius. Tests tracked the pseudo fill factor of 16 square centimeter PERC cells over time. Later tasks measured cell efficiency with a set assessment tool. Cheaper copper in place of silver could cut cell costs if aging losses stay low.
doe-osti-3413768-intensified-flexible-an:
Oak Ridge report dated September 2025 demonstrates a compact carbon capture system with a printed multi-use device inside. Costas Tsouris leads an eight-author Oak Ridge team. The device boosts contact between gas and solvent while cooling the column.

Cooling through the device cut average column temperature by amounts that varied with flow mix. Higher liquid-to-gas ratios gave smaller temperature cuts in the tests. Heat tests with feed water at 60 degrees Celsius or more exposed column faults. Those faults were fixed before flue gas and solvent runs. Compact gear could bring capture to smaller sites.
doe-osti-3419561-idaho-national-laborato:
Idaho report INL/RPT-26-93660, dated June 2026, computes public dose from radionuclides the lab might release to air during calendar year 2025. Kira Overin and A. Jeffrey Sondrup wrote the analysis. Federal rules under Title 40 of the Code of Federal Regulations set the method.

Dose was figured at public spots around the site boundary and at in-town facilities. The CAP88 code family handled the air pathway math. File scripts in the pages show how run files were prepared for each site. The yearly account shows whether lab air releases stayed within health-based limits.
doe-osti-3422015-ni-mediated-carboxylati:
NLR/TP-2800-100872 is a August 2026 report from the National Laboratory of the Rockies that covers turning polyethylene plastic into fatty acids with nickel-based chemistry. Katrina Knauer was the lab contact. The work ran under CRADA number CRD-22-22451.

Oxidation broke the plastic down into dicarboxylic acids, called DCAs in the text. Yields could be tuned toward short chains fit for surfactants. Mixtures were split by target chain length with low-energy liquid extraction. Cost and life cycle models were also built. A waste plastic stream could thus become feedstock for soaps and other useful household goods.
doe-osti-3424764-effectively-considering:
Berkeley Lab report, dated August 2026, guides utilities on counting the distribution system inside integrated resource plans. Grace Relf, Paul DeMartini, Jasmine McAdams, Lisa C. Schwartz, and Vinita Srinivasan wrote the guide. Resource plans often focus on big plants and wires, not local networks.

Good plans test several contrasting scenarios, the authors argue. Planners first name the biggest unknowns about future conditions. Each scenario then probes a distinct question under its own assumptions. Rooftop solar, electric cars, and heat pumps all land on distribution wires first. The guide helps planners size local upgrades before backlogs form.
doe-osti-3427064-a-compact-endf-ace-form:
Los Alamos document LA-UR-26-27391, by Jeremy Lloyd Conlin, Wim Haeck, and Paul Romano and issued August 14, 2026, specifies a compact form of the ACE nuclear data format. ACE files carry the cross-section data that transport codes read. A compact spec helps new code writers match the format exactly.

Tables map each data block's place in the file array. One table covers energy distributions for delayed neutron groups. Location formulas point readers to each law's array in turn. Software teams building fresh readers or writers get a tight reference instead of scattered legacy notes.
doe-osti-3428335-examples-of-state-and-u:
Pacific Northwest report, dated August 2026, collects examples of states and utilities planning grid upgrades before demand forces them. Jessica Shipley, Thomas S. Benson, and Juliet Homer wrote the survey. Proactive planning builds capacity ahead of need instead of after delays pile up.

One commission framework, set in September 2025, lists five reasons for early upgrades. They include faster customer connections and lower life-cycle costs. Xcel's 2023 distribution plan is quoted on strategy for such work. Regulators in other states can mine these cases for rules that fit their own grids. The cases span both state commission actions and utility-led planning programs.
doe-osti-3452364-complete-the-initial-te:
Dated August 2025, report ORNL/SPR-2025/4101 from Oak Ridge National Laboratory reports first tests of a friction stir welding machine that gave uneven weld quality. Jian Chen, Roger Miller, and Zhili Feng ran the tests. The machine works inside a hot cell, where remote handling limits repairs.

The same settings on a machine outside the hot cell gave no such defects. That contrast points to the hot cell hardware, not the settings. Surface cracks and craters marked the bad welds in photos. Later checks probed the cell setup part by part. Fixing the hardware should restore weld quality for remote nuclear work.
doe-osti-3520355-measure-impact-of-molte:
Report ORNL/TM-2026/4724 from Oak Ridge National Laboratory, dated July 2026, measures how molten halide salt affects creep and fatigue in alloys 625 and 316H steel. R. Pillai leads a six-author team. Reactor parts may sit in hot salt under load for years.

At 650 degrees Celsius and 130 megapascals, salt cut 316H rupture life sharply. Expected life without salt was 3000 hours in the case shown. One salt run failed near 91 hours, another near 116. Fluoride salt gave a longer 471 hours in the same chart. Such gaps decide which alloys can serve in molten salt reactors. Alloy 709 results are compared alongside in the same salt exposure charts.
doe-osti-3547199-allan-variance-is-boots:
Sandia report SAND2026-25291, by Michael R. Walker II and printed August 2026, shows that Allan variance acts as bootstrap aggregation for spectral estimation. Allan variance is a classic tool for clock and sensor noise. The paper reframes it in modern statistical terms.

Noise colors map to power laws, from white noise to random walk and drift. Tables align the many names used for the same noise terms. Clock error models extend to inertial sensors in the middle chapters. Sensor engineers gain a firmer reason to trust Allan plots, plus cleaner labels for each noise type they report.
doe-osti-3599476-analytical-dynamic-aper:
Brookhaven technical note BNL-230130-2026-TECH, dated August 2026, is a solo note by H. Lovelace III. It deals with dynamic aperture in the Hadron Storage Ring of the Electron-Ion Collider. Dynamic aperture is the region where a circulating particle stays stable over many turns. Finding it by tracking particles for millions of turns can take hours, days, or even weeks of computing.

Lovelace applies J. Gao's analytical theory as a faster route to the same boundary. The note compares the math results with tracking simulations for set sextupole and octupole magnet layouts. It also tests the use of Python tools and Bmad libraries to tune colour-related beam spread up to third order. The claim is modest: the analytical method may give quick, useful estimates of improved aperture. That would help designers screen magnet settings before paying for long tracking runs.
doe-osti-3625645-machine-learning-based-:
Fermilab report FERMILAB-TM-2934-STUDENT comes from a Visiting Faculty Program project on detector data quality. Juan A. Colón Santana of Aurora University led it, with Minerba Betancourt and Michael Carrigan of Fermilab. Neutrino detectors in the Short-Baseline program rely on photomultiplier tubes, which sense light. Staff now check those tubes by fixed thresholds and by eye, a slow process that can miss slow drifts. The hosted text is spaced-letter OCR, but stays legible.

A Python workflow pulled signal size data for each tube from detector files and built a feature set per channel. An Isolation Forest model learned normal behaviour, then flagged channels that stood out in fresh runs. Plots of scores, size patterns, and component views help experts judge each flag. The team calls the method workable as a proof of concept. With tuning, it could extend to ProtoDUNE and other liquid argon detectors.
doe-osti-3637871-ipo-tech-transfer-annua:
Lawrence Livermore's FY25 Technology Transfer Report, numbered LLNL-TR-2023526 and dated September 2026, was coordinated by Melissa Lewelling. FY25 means Fiscal Year 2025. The Innovation and Partnerships Office, or IPO, is the lab's point of contact for industry. It guards lab inventions and moves them to firms through licences and joint work. A letter from the IPO director opens the report and stresses teamwork across groups.

Inside, short stories show the year's deals and joint projects. One covers critical mineral recovery with Alta Resource Technologies, and one a knowledge tool called Sophia. Others pair the lab with BridgeBio Oncology on cancer treatment and with Biovind on diagnostics. A sodium battery project with Darmoktech and a neural interface with Canaery also appear. New office members are listed by role, and award winners get their own section. Contact pages close the report for firms that want to partner.
doe-osti-3824199-agentic-orchestration-o:
Lawrence Livermore report LLNL-TR-2013651, dated September 2026, hands a full computing study to a team of software agents. Vanessa Sochat and Daniel Milroy are the printed authors. Language model agents were asked to run the whole life of a computing job in the cloud. The job spans building a container, placing it on a Kubernetes cluster, tuning it, and running a scaling study. Five test applications served as the workload, across twenty-one cloud machine types.

A manager agent takes a plan written as a step list and farms each step to a worker agent. Builder, deployer, tuner, debugger, and parser agents each own one craft. The parser writes its own pattern to pull the score from each run log. A human checks that parse once; the checked pattern is then reused. The authors report a working agent-run scaling study, plus design habits that cut time to finish.
doe-osti-3914965-advancing-university-le:
Mohamad Metghalchi of Solar Dynamics reports on a teaching program that brought heliostat design and operation into Northeastern University courses from summer 2024 through spring 2026. The work ran under the Heliostat Consortium with help from the National Laboratory of the Rockies, and it appears as subcontract report NLR/SR-5700-101643 in September 2026.

Rather than add one elective class, the program wove solar tower content into nine courses, from first-year design up to graduate system study, plus a senior capstone track. Students designed real hardware: one team sized a mirror of one square meter on a welded frame, moved by lead screws to track the sun. The goal was that every mechanical engineering student meets the topic more than once.
doe-osti-3991145-quic-smoke-input-files-:
Matthew Kyle Huckins and Sara Brambilla of Los Alamos National Laboratory define every input file for QUIC-SMOKE in report LA-UR-26-28468, issued September 22, 2026. QUIC-SMOKE is a lab tool that models how smoke from fires drifts and settles. Users drive it through plain text files, and this guide is their dictionary.

Three main files get full treatment. One sets the run parameters, one holds the weather inputs, and one lists the materials that burn. Long tables give each field's name, type, units, and allowed range, down to the corner points of the grid boxes that gather results. A user who follows the tables can build a run file that the model reads without error. The guide pairs with a matching volume on the output files the model writes.
doe-osti-3991148-quic-smoke-output-files:
Los Alamos National Laboratory staff Matthew K. Huckins and Sara Brambilla explain the files that the QUIC-SMOKE smoke model writes, in report LA-UR-26-28471, issued September 22, 2026. The model tracks smoke plumes from fires, and its output files are what analysts open to judge where smoke lands.

Naming rules come first, so users can tell one run's files from the next. The main products are three-dimensional snapshots of smoke concentration, both for all particles at once and split by particle size. Ground-level maps split the dust into size bands, from fine grains up to grains ten micrometers wide, and the text notes that the largest grains settle fastest. A plotting script reads only these files when size bands are on. The guide completes the input volume issued beside it.
dombey-and-son:
Charles Dickens builds Dombey and Son around a shipping merchant whose firm name states his whole ambition: a son to inherit both. Paul Dombey arrives, frail and strange, while his sister Florence is dismissed as merely a girl. The contents trace Paul's christening, schooling, and decline, and the wooden midshipman at Sol Gills's shop.

Paul dies, the firm falters, and Dombey's proud second marriage to Edith collapses into recrimination, as the middle chapters' confrontation between Edith and her mother shows. Florence's steadfast love finally redeems her broken father. Dickens planned this novel more tightly than its predecessors, and its railway scenes, sea imagery, and study of pride made it a turning point in his art.
drake-nelson-and-napoleon:
Sir Walter Runciman, a shipping magnate turned writer, studies three sea heroes in a 1919 volume from T. Fisher Unwin of London. A long opening letter to Sir James Knott recalls their yachting cruises on the Clyde and strolls by the North Sea, and praises Knott's work in reforming steamship management. Runciman writes as a sailor about sailors.

Drake stands for the Elizabethan sea dogs, Nelson for the great age of sail, and Napoleon as the foe who tested British fleets. Pages on Nelson weigh whether his ships should have put back to Toulon to refit spars and sails, and doubt the French would ever catch the British showing the white feather. The style is fond and argumentative, full of deck-level detail. Ship owners and naval readers get hero history from a man who ran ships himself.
drusilla-with-a-million:
Elizabeth Cooper's Drusilla With a Million opens in an old ladies' home, where little Drusilla Doane sits darning a tablecloth in the sun. Two men arrive in the parlour asking for her by name, news so wonderful that every other woman stops her work to stare.

From that comic, touching opening Cooper builds a story about an elderly woman whose life is changed by sudden fortune. It asks what money can and cannot do for a person long used to plain living. Drusilla's birdlike neighbours, her modest habits and her good sense carry the tale. Readers who enjoy stories of late-life surprises, told with warmth and humour, will take to Drusilla at once.
east-o-the-sun-and-west-o-the-moon:
Gudrun Thorne-Thomsen retells Norwegian folk tales for English-speaking children in East o' the Sun and West o' the Moon, with pictures by Frederick Richardson. The title tale opens on a poor woodcutter with too many children and a lovely youngest daughter. On a stormy Thursday evening, three taps sound at the window, and a great white bear stands outside with a polite good evening.

Twenty-two more tales follow. The Three Billy Goats Gruff, Boots and His Brothers, The Giant Who Had No Heart in His Body, and Why the Sea is Salt are among them. In The Squire's Bride, a clattering entrance in wooden shoes sets a whole room laughing at the wrong bride. Thorne-Thomsen keeps the tales plain and brisk, in the Asbjørnsen and Moe line. Young readers get Norway's whole storehouse in one volume.
eight-years-wanderings-in-ceylon:
Samuel White Baker's Eight Years' Wanderings in Ceylon records his life as a planter and elephant hunter in the island's highlands from 1847. His contents begin with Colombo's dullness, cinnamon gardens, jungle fever, and the hill station Newera Ellia that Governor Barnes's energy created. Baker bought land at Nuwara Eliya and imported English stock, dogs, and settlers.

Chapters mix settlement disasters, eccentric grooms, insubordinate servants, and the sagacity of elephants with hunting of elk, hog, and leopard. His hounds, once in jungle, become their own masters, he warns, and training them is a study in itself. Baker later became famous as an African explorer; this first book shows the sportsman-planter learning his trade.
ellen-walton:
Alvin Addison, author of The Rival Hunters, sells a border sensation in Ellen Walton, or The Villain and His Victims, from Rulison's Queen City Publishing House at Cincinnati in 1855. Chapter one opens in 1785 at Fleming's Hotel in Pittsburgh, then the largest town west of the mountains. The house draws Indians on trading trips, and the landlord's two handsome daughters grow up amid bad company.

The Misses Fleming, Eliza and Sarah, lose early the fine line between propriety and politeness, the narrator warns. Ellen Walton herself leaves her childhood home as the promised bride of Walter Hamilton, a young man of talent and clean character. Chapter seven is headed simply The Lovers, and the text asks outright whether the villain will succeed in his satanic designs. Kidnapping, pursuit, and border peril drive the tale in the full dime-novel manner.
endymion:
Benjamin Disraeli, Earl of Beaconsfield, published his last novel, Endymion, in 1880, and it opens on a warm August night in St. James's Street. A cloaked gentleman leaves his club and confides a sacred secret about Chiswick and the road to Downing Street. The scene sets the novel's world: clubs, cabinets, and whispers that move governments.

Endymion rises through that world, guided by friends like Sidney Wilton and shadowed by men like Nigel, who distrusts political moderation. Disraeli, twice prime minister, wrote from inside the trade he describes. The talk runs to church, party, and ambition. Names and clubs are thin disguises for the real court of power in his day. The novel stands as his farewell portrait of Victorian politics.
england-s-antiphon:
George MacDonald traces England's sacred song from the thirteenth century to his own day in England's Antiphon, first published in 1868. Twenty-three chapters move from early lyrics and miracle plays through Spenser, Bacon, and Donne. Herbert gets a chapter to himself, and Milton follows.

MacDonald, novelist and minister, treats worship as the highest human condition and poetry as its first art. He prints the poems he praises, from divine epigrams to Vaughan's mount of vision. Herrick, Quarles, Crashaw, and Marvell all pass in review. The last chapters turn to questioning fervour and the plain beyond the hills. The book doubles as an anthology and a history, arguing that England's faith sang before it argued.
english-prose-a-series-of-related-essays:
